"It was pretty emotional for me just because it had taken a while to win anything of that caliber," he added. But the road to that championship was anything but smooth. The long road back from Daytona In March 2025, Kitchen suffered a violent crash during the Daytona Supercross that left him with a broken collarbone and fractures in his upper back. The injuries sidelined him for the remainder of the Supercross season. And while he eventually healed enough to return to racing, Kitchen said the mental recovery was a different battle entirely. "Oh yeah, big time," he said when asked whether it was difficult to regain his confidence after the crash. "If I look back at that season, even when I came back on the bike, in 2025, I was maybe a top-five guy outdoors. And then at least was able to compete for the championship this year." Watch Levi Kitchen's entire interview with OutKick OutDoors here: That progression didn't happen overnight. "Slowly but surely, I've made really good progress, and I have all my confidence back," Kitchen said. "It just goes to show, I think fans, or just anybody, don't realize how much injuries can really affect everything." "It can be a real pain in the butt to build yourself back up." For fans watching from the sidelines, a rider's return to competition might signal that the recovery process is complete. But as Kitchen explained, getting back on the bike doesn't necessarily mean getting back to the same level of confidence and performance. It took time, patience and a different approach to racing. Learning when to back off Looking back on everything he's experienced, Kitchen believes one of his biggest improvements has come from learning to trust his abilities while also recognizing his limits. "The biggest thing I would say is just finally the belief," he said. "The belief side of it is super important. And I think on any given day, if I show up with the belief that I can get something done, normally I can get it done." SUPERMOTOCROSS CHAMPION LEVI KITCHEN WANTS TO TRY TOURNAMENT BASS FISHING WHEN HE HANGS UP HIS HELMET But confidence alone wasn't enough. Kitchen also had to develop a little more restraint — something that doesn't always come naturally in a sport where riders are constantly pushing the limits of speed and control. "Just maturity of racing," he explained. "Now, if I don't really have it on a day, I try to be as smart as I can. Where before, I would probably still try and then end up on the ground or something." It's a lesson learned the hard way, but one Kitchen believes will serve him well beyond a single championship season. "I want to race for a lot more years to come and can't be too stupid," he said. That shift in mentality paid off in September when Kitchen secured the 250SMX World Championship at Thunder Ridge Nature Arena in Ridgedale, Mo. And the victory meant something special beyond his own accomplishments. Kitchen's title ended a seven-year championship drought for Monster Energy Pro Circuit Kawasaki, one of the most decorated organizations in 250-class racing. "Mitch has done so much for me," Kitchen said, referring to team owner Mitch Payton. "Me and Mitch have gotten close over the years, and he's been a great boss and friend of mine now. So it was super special." One championship down, but plenty more to chase Despite finally capturing that elusive first title, Kitchen insists he isn't suddenly feeling satisfied. In fact, winning the championship has only strengthened his belief in what he's capable of accomplishing. "It didn't really take any pressure off," he said. "The only thing it did was help me with the belief side of things. Just being able to execute." Kitchen has his sights set on both a Supercross and a Pro Motocross championship in 2027, and he plans to remain in the 250 class for at least another season. "The Supercross Championship has been a major goal of mine, so that's my first goal," he said. "But overall, just maybe be a little better than I was this year." And while the first championship was certainly worth celebrating, Kitchen knows there's no guarantee the next one will come any easier. "I don't think you'll ever be satisfied, really, which is a tough thing," he said. For now, though, Kitchen can take some satisfaction in knowing how far he's come. A year ago, he was still working to rebuild his confidence after a frightening crash. Now, he's a world champion. title: DOJ moves to boot two federal judges from immigration cases over remarks to media: 'Extraordinarily imprudent'
description: Two Minnesota federal judges who criticized Trump's Operation Metro Surge in a report published by the New York Times now face DOJ recusal motions tied to their immigration cases.
content: Two Minnesota federal judges who took the unusual step of publicly criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown to the New York Times are now fighting the administration’s efforts to disqualify them from cases involving immigration enforcement. One of those judges, Patrick Schiltz, is overseeing the Justice Department’s effort to strip U. S. citizenship from Salah Osman Ahmed, a Somali-born man who pleaded guilty in 2009 to providing material support to terrorists after joining al- Shabaab. The other, John Tunheim, is presiding over the prosecution of a South African national accused of falsely claiming U. S. citizenship and illegally voting in the 2024 election. The Justice Department filed separate motions asking Schiltz and Tunheim to recuse themselves, arguing that their participation in the New York Times report criticizing President Donald Trump's Operation Metro Surge has raised questions about whether they can fairly preside over the cases. "Impartiality is imperative to ensuring public trust in our Nation’s judiciary," the Justice Department said in a statement posted to X this week. "Judge Schiltz’s and Judge Tunheim’s on-the-record participation in a recent highly partisan New York Times Article, along with Judge Schiltz’s subsequent public comments, unquestionably calls into doubt whether they can be impartial in these cases." OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE AT CENTER OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND CASE HIT WITH MISCONDUCT CLAIM The Justice Department's formal recusal demand follows reporting by Fox News Digital last month detailing unusual behind-the-scenes coordination among Minnesota's federal bench as judges confronted a massive influx of immigration cases stemming from the administration's enforcement operation. The report came after Schiltz and Tunheim were among seven Minnesota federal judges who spoke with the Times in September about Operation Metro Surge. Schiltz sat for a roughly 90- minute interview during which he described the administration's handling of the operation as having created a "grave threat to the rule of law," while Tunheim suggested to the Times that agents carrying out the administration's immigration crackdown were not primarily apprehending dangerous criminals. DOJ had already raised the prospect that judges who publicly discussed the administration's immigration cases might need to step aside when the Times report was released in September. Last month, DOJ filed a judicial misconduct complaint against Schiltz, Tunheim and other Minnesota judges who participated in the Times report, accusing them of violating judicial ethics rules and asking the Eighth Circuit to investigate. Attorney General Todd Blanche said their conduct had "undermined public confidence in an impartial judiciary in Minnesota." "It is remarkable that sitting federal judges are giving on-the-record interviews attacking this Administration's policies rather than ruling from the bench," a Justice Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital in September. "Judges who have made public comments on pending or related matters should consider whether recusal is warranted going forward." 'WORST OF THE WORST' JUDGES ARE SABOTAGING TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION AGENDA, TOP DHS OFFICIAL SAYS The Times report in question revealed that Schiltz, Tunheim and the other Minnesota judges handling the flood of Operation Metro Surge cases regularly met, communicated through running email threads and used an informal spreadsheet created by court clerks to identify judges to consult about recurring legal questions. Chief Judge Eric Tostrud previously told Fox News Digital that the judges nevertheless independently decided every case assigned to them. "The bottom line is that each of us made an independent decision with respect to the merits of each and every petition we were assigned," Tostrud said at the time. The Justice Department, however, has accused Schiltz and the other judges of "publicly" taking sides in the ongoing battle over Trump's deportation agenda. "A judge who has publicly taken sides on the political issue of immigration enforcement cannot then preside over a case concerning one of the Justice Department’s key immigration initiatives: pursuing the largest denaturalization effort in Department history to restore trust and integrity in U.S. citizenship," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote. Schiltz declined to comment on the Justice Department's new effort to disqualify him when reached by Fox News Digital this week. But when Fox News Digital asked him about the possibility of recusal in September, Schiltz argued there was no basis for him to step aside — and pointed to the fact that DOJ had not asked him to do so. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY "I have seen suggestions from the Administration that I might have to recuse in immigration cases, but no one has yet identified any basis for my recusal, which is presumably why the Justice Department has not asked me to recuse," Schiltz said at the time. "Neither in the New York Times article nor anywhere else have I commented on the merits of a particular case," he continued. "Instead, I have spoken in defense of the rule of law, a component of which is compliance with court orders. That is not a cause for recusal." Tunheim did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Charles "Cully" Stimson, a senior legal fellow at the Heritage Foundation who previously served as a federal prosecutor and military judge, told Fox News Digital that judges ordinarily avoid publicly commenting on matters that could intersect with cases before them. "These judges did something extraordinarily imprudent, and that is to talk to any newspaper, much less the New York Times," Stimson said. "That was a big no-no." STATE'S LARGEST MOSQUE LEADER’S DEPORTATION FIGHT TAKES DRAMATIC TURN AS TRUMP ADMIN SCORES MAJOR WIN Asked what he would do if the New York Times interviews were the only facts at issue, Stimson said he would step aside. "If we were to just go off of the New York Times interview ... I would recuse myself," Stimson said, noting the recusal would only be from the particular case at issue as opposed to all future cases adjudicating the same principles. Stimson cautioned, however, that recusal motions put judges in the unusual position of effectively judging their own impartiality and said it would be inappropriate to predict how either motion should ultimately be resolved without the complete record. title: Chiefs place Josh Simmons on IR, raising questions about his entire future in the NFL
description: Josh Simmons' injured reserve placement raises deeper questions as conflicting timelines and pre-draft character concerns cloud the Chiefs' plans.
content: The Kansas City Chiefs are placing left tackle Josh Simmons on injured reserve, the team announced. But the story runs deeper than a Super Bowl contender losing its starting left tackle for, most likely, the remainder of the season. On Thursday, Chiefs Vice President of Sports Medicine and Performance Rich Burkholder told reporters that Simmons reported a leg issue on August 17, which the team determined was related to a bulging disc in his back. Burkholder said Simmons saw a specialist who recommended therapy instead of surgery. Simmons has not played a down this season. He practiced in a limited capacity last week for the first time since reporting the injury to Burkholder. On Wednesday, the team listed him as a non-participant in practice for "back/non-injury personal reasons." Burkholder said Simmons used the day to speak with his family before deciding it would be best to go on injured reserve. The designation requires Simmons to miss at least four games. Put bluntly, skepticism about the Chiefs' version of events is warranted. In August, reporters close to the team repeatedly reported that the injury was minor and that Simmons would return by Week 1. He didn't. The next explanation was that the Chiefs had not placed him on injured reserve because they expected him to play within the first four weeks. He never did. So what changed? Burkholder says Simmons "plateaued" in his recovery. If so, head coach Andy Reid was unaware. On Monday, Reid said Simmons would continue to "ramp up" this week. title: Supreme Court Justice Kagan warns some conservative rulings have been 'destructive of our democracy'
description: Justice Elena Kagan warned that Supreme Court rulings on gerrymandering and campaign finance have created a democracy that "doesn't work" for everyone.
content: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan suggested Tuesday that some recent decisions by her conservative colleagues have undermined democracy, while admitting at times they had also pushed back against the Trump administration. Kagan took part in a discussion on recent U.S. Supreme Court decisions while speaking at Catholic University's Columbus School of Law. She specifically took issue with cases like Louisiana v. Callais, which ruled in a 6-3 decision that race-based gerrymandering of congressional districts was unconstitutional. In her dissent, Kagan called the decision the "latest chapter in the majority's now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act" and she continued to criticize election and campaign finance decisions made by the court. KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS "Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said, according to NBC News. She went on to warn that decisions that undermined voters' ability to choose their candidates were "very destructive of our democracy." "I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn't work as well as it should," Kagan said. SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES She also criticized the conservative view of originalism in the Supreme Court, calling it "misconceived" and "not a very good match with the Constitution we have." Kagan claimed that these and other decisions have contributed to the country becoming more "polarized," particularly around campaign finance. "I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they're right," she said. CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION However, Kagan stopped short of accusing the court of being beholden to President Donald Trump, pointing out several cases where even conservative justices "definitely pushed back" on his agenda. Trump nominated three of the current justices on the court in Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett. In a comment to Fox News Digital, Heritage Foundation Senior Legal Fellow of Courts and the Constitution Zack Smith denounced Kagan and what he characterized as far-left politicians' efforts to delegitimize SCOTUS decisions. "The job of the Court is not to play politics with its decisions. Instead, its job is to faithfully apply the Constitution and other laws as they are written. Justice Kagan has disagreed with the majority of her colleagues in some of those decisions, but that doesn't mean they are illegitimate or even wrongly decided," Smith said. title: RILEY GAINES: Call Her Daddy's advice is a dangerous recipe for lifelong regret
description: Alex Cooper and Sophia Bush's viral marriage advice sparks a deeper debate about feminism, sacrifice, and what empowerment truly means for women.
content: In a viral exchange this week, Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper and actress Sophia Bush offered young women a familiar piece of relationship advice: If you're questioning whether to leave your marriage because you fear you won't find someone better, the answer is always yes. Bush went further, suggesting that the fear of being too old or unreasonable for wanting more is a product of the patriarchy. Cooper built her brand largely by celebrating sexual experimentation, including encouraging young women to engage in highly explicit sexual experimentation early in dating. This is the same podcast Kamala Harris joined prior to the 2024 election, but I digress. RILEY GAINES FIRES BACK AT ALEX COOPER’S GRAPHIC DATING ADVICE: ‘IT IS NOT EMPOWERMENT. IT IS POISON’ Bush is now on her third marriage, with the first one lasting 5 months, the second lasting about a year, and the third to a woman. These are the voices our culture elevates as influential guides for young women. But enough about the who. Let's examine the what. The exchange reveals a worldview in which something better is always waiting. That personal and fleeting dissatisfaction is sufficient reason to abandon a commitment, and that the pursuit of more is interchangeable with empowerment. More what, exactly? More excitement? More affirmation? More freedom? Another relationship that will inevitably encounter the same imperfections as the last? At what point do we consider whether the relentless pursuit of more is precisely what leaves us feeling we have less? AMERICAN WOMEN HAVE BEEN LIED TO ABOUT MOTHERHOOD AND IT’S TIME TO FIX IT For decades, women have been sold a particular vision of liberation. Prioritize your career. Maximize your independence. Explore your sexuality without consequence. Reject marriage, delay motherhood, and never compromise your ambitions for someone else's needs. Above all, put yourself first. We were assured that freedom from traditional obligations would produce unprecedented happiness. TRADITIONAL TWO-PARENT FAMILIES VANISH FROM BIG AMERICAN CITIES AS 'MARRIAGE DESERTS' EXPAND If that were true, we would certainly see it in society. But instead, what was promised as empowerment has delivered emptiness. Despite constant technological connectivity, loneliness and social isolation remain pervasive. Anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation are serious concerns, particularly among younger generations. These problems have many causes, and attributing them all to feminism would be intellectually dishonest. But ignoring the possibility that our prevailing philosophy has failed to deliver its promised fulfillment would be equally foolish. We’ve spent decades dismantling the institutions that tether individuals to one another, only to discover that autonomy is a poor substitute for belonging. Perhaps most tragically, we’ve taught women to regard sacrifice as oppression rather than an indispensable part of love. Consider the contradiction. A woman who sacrifices her time, energy, and health to climb the corporate ladder is celebrated as ambitious. A woman making comparable sacrifices for her husband and children is too often regarded as having surrendered her potential to the patriarchy. Why? ONE GROUP OF MARRIED AMERICANS IS HAVING MORE SEX — AND HAPPIER MARRIAGES I am profoundly grateful for the opportunities women have today. I’ve competed as a collegiate athlete, traveled the country, built a career, and achieved things my younger self could never have imagined. But no professional accolade, public recognition, or personal achievement has given me the satisfaction and purpose I’ve found in marriage and motherhood. They require more of me than anything I've ever done (even a 200-yard butterfly). It's hard. But "hard" and "bad" are not synonymous. Motherhood fundamentally changed my understanding of success. There's something remarkably clarifying about being needed by someone who has nothing to offer you in return except themselves. I don't view it as a limitation on my freedom, but instead a revelation of what my freedom is for. Which brings me back to Cooper, who just welcomed her first child with her husband. I genuinely congratulate her. But there's irony in continuing to promote perpetual self-prioritization through meaningless hookups and "girl-bossing" while building a life rooted in the very institutions modern feminism so often characterizes as oppressive. Perhaps motherhood will offer her the same perspective it offered me: that the deepest fulfillment isn't found in putting yourself first, but in loving someone enough to put them first. Of course, marriage and motherhood aren't the only paths to meaning. Women who are single, childless, or unable to have children are no less valuable. Purpose takes countless forms, but lasting meaning generally requires looking beyond ourselves. This is hardly a novel insight. Christianity has taught for centuries that a life centered exclusively on the self is ultimately impoverished. Love is not merely a feeling to be pursued while convenient. It is a commitment expressed through action, fidelity, humility, and sacrifice. Our culture treats these virtues as antiquated burdens, then wonders why so many feel unmoored. Cooper and Bush's advice is troubling because it reduces marriage to personal optimization. Marriage becomes less a covenant to honor than an arrangement to continually reassess against hypothetical alternatives. There are legitimate reasons marriages end, including abuse and betrayal. But reflexively encouraging people to search for something better without acknowledging the responsibilities of commitment isn't teaching empowerment like the self-proclaimed feminists like to claim. It teaches disposability. A generation encouraged to keep every option open may eventually discover that life's most meaningful commitments require closing certain doors. Choosing a spouse. Raising children. Building a family. Practicing faith. Serving a community. Creating something that will endure long after your own ambitions have faded. Like everything associated with risk, these commitments impose limits, but I’ve found they also give life its depth. Women deserve more than the hollow assurance that happiness is perpetually waiting in the next relationship, promotion, or reinvention of themselves. They deserve to know that fulfillment isn't always found in acquiring more and finding someone that validates your every desire. Often, it's found in giving more. The great lie of modern empowerment isn't that women are capable of extraordinary things. It's that a life devoted primarily to ourselves is the most extraordinary thing we can aspire to. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We should stop telling women that the ultimate goal is to have everything and start reminding them of the beauty of having something worth giving everything for. And perhaps the grass isn't always greener on the other side. It’s greener where you water it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM RILEY GAINES

title: Supreme Court justice turns on her own court with dire warning about American democracy
description: Elena Kagan argued the Supreme Court's gerrymandering and campaign finance rulings are destabilizing democracy and driving political polarization.
content: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan made the case that recent rulings from the conservative-majority high court are destabilizing democracy, suggesting that it isn't working "as well as it should." The remarks from the liberal justice came during a closed discussion before faculty and students at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C. The discussion between Kagan and law professor Joel Alicea Alicia, who previously clerked for Justice Samuel Alito, comes just weeks after the Supreme Court began its new term, during which it's expected to rule in major cases that will determine the scope of gun rights and state election integrity laws, among other issues. The conversation also comes less than two weeks before the midterm elections as President Donald Trump and Republican state lawmakers have pushed for new congressional maps drawn to favor Republicans and bolster their chances of maintaining control of the House. Democratic-led states have responded by redrawing their own maps, fueling ongoing lawsuits and court battles. SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE Kagan pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2019 ruling in Rucho v. Common Cause, in which she dissented, as the beginning of a "race to the bottom." She argued that the decision, which barred federal courts from invalidating maps solely because they unfairly favor one political party, deprived "masses of citizens" of their "rights to voting equality." Kagan suggested that the influx of gerrymandered maps is "driving people away from the center toward the wings, toward the extremes. "Making what I think is, unfortunately, a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said. Kagan also criticized rulings from the previous term, including the court’s decision limiting campaign finance restrictions and its ruling that made it more difficult to draw majority-minority congressional districts under the Voting Rights Act. "Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said. "I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should." DESANTIS SIGNS FLORIDA REDISTRICTING MAP TO POTENTIALLY FLIP 4 HOUSE SEATS RED Last term, the Supreme Court struck down federal limits on how much state and national political parties could spend in coordination with their candidates. Meanwhile, Kagan argued in dissent that the limits were necessary to prevent wealthy donors from working around direct contribution caps and that striking them down effectively allowed a political party to become an "alternative checking account" for a candidate. "The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare," Kagan said. "And they’re right." Kagan, who was appointed to the court by President Barack Obama in 2010, argued that it was in a much better position when there was greater ideological balance. "There was a period of time where the court was in a better place, and the country was in a better place because the court was more balanced, and it was unclear whether the court could push through anybody’s program." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Nobody in America thought that the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party," she said. "And the court had a kind of legitimacy. When the court has a legitimacy of that kind, it helps to create a stable country." However, Kagan pushed back against the characterization that the conservative-leaning court simply rubber-stamped Trump's entire agenda. She pointed to previous rulings by the high court rejecting birthright citizenship restrictions, tariffs and Trump's restrictions on mail-in voting. title: Ilhan Omar says she lives 'paycheck to paycheck' as DOJ probes financial disclosures
description: Ilhan Omar claims she lives "paycheck to paycheck," despite earning $174,000 and facing scrutiny over financial disclosures tied to Tim Mynett.
content: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., described herself as a member of the "working class" who lives "paycheck to paycheck" during an interview with MS NOW host Chris Hayes on Wednesday night. "I mean, it’s, you know, working — working class, I guess, like paycheck to paycheck still," Omar said. "We’ve got four kids, and we live, I think, like a basic life. I have a Toyota Camry that’s from 2016." Omar's characterization of her finances comes despite her $174,000 annual congressional salary and scrutiny over financial disclosures that once listed assets tied to her husband as being worth as much as $30 million. The comments came during Omar’s first public appearance since Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched her Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12 as part of an investigation into possible immigration-related offenses. ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING Since the raid, the representative has used the investigation twice as a reason to publicly fundraise. "That goes a long way as we fight Trump and his administration for trying to intimidate me and so many people right before the midterm elections," Omar said in a video she uploaded to social media on Wednesday. "We know that they’re running scared. We’re not going to be intimidated. We’re not going to be silenced." The Democratic National Committee has also sent out its own fundraising email based on Omar’s campaign request for money. "It’s Ilhan Omar — Trump’s DHS agents just carried out a raid and search of my home," the email says. "This is a drastic escalation of the ludicrous, partisan investigation that they launched into my immigration status." ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME Omar also acknowledged during the MS NOW interview that the federal agents who searched her home were "polite" and left the property in good condition, even folding some of her clothes. "When they left, what did you do?" Hayes asked Omar. "I just went back around the house just trying to make sure everything was put back," Omar replied. "And they did a really good job in putting everything back in its place. They actually even folded some of my clothing that [was] not folded. So it was … a very bizarre [situation]." The Minnesota Democrat added that she thought the HSI agents who raided her home were "intrusive, but polite." "And yeah, they, they left the house, I think, you know, in good shape," she told MS NOW. Omar claimed during the interview that the federal agents were searching her house for four to five hours. She added that they left the raid with more than a dozen items, including notebooks and a children’s Somali-language phrasebook. "[That] was why I was surprised when they handed me the receipt for the items that they take in, to do that long of a search and to walk away with 17 items, of like 10 that were just notebooks and, like, old phones. Was such a bizarre, bizarre thing," Omar said. A separate Justice Department investigation is examining Omar’s financial disclosures, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said during an appearance on Fox News’ "America Reports." The disclosures previously showed that the reported value of two businesses tied to Omar’s husband, Tim Mynett, rose from as much as $51,000 in 2023 to as much as $30 million in 2024, according to House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky. Omar later amended the filing, saying the original figures were the result of an accounting error. The amended disclosure listed the couple’s assets at between $18,004 and $95,000. Omar has denied wrongdoing, and no criminal charges have been filed against her in connection with the disclosures. Mynett’s businesses include eStCru, a winery, and Rose Lake Capital, an investment firm. The winery has reportedly shut down. ILHAN OMAR RAID SPARKS OMINOUS PREDICTION FROM WATCHDOG: 'THEY PROBABLY GOT THE GOODS' On Fox News’ "Sunday Night in America," Comer told host Trey Gowdy that his committee’s initial review of Omar’s disclosures identified multiple issues that could justify further investigative steps. "First of all, not only was there a huge discrepancy in the financial disclosure form, there was the winery that was the big base of her $25 million listing on her financial disclosure form," Comer said. "That winery has, according to the press, been shut down because of fraud." In a February letter to Mynett, Comer noted that Omar’s 2023 disclosure listed her stake in eStCru as being worth between $15,001 and $50,000. "The following year, her financial disclosure form listed a stake in eStCru ‘worth between $1,000,001 and $5,000,000,’" Comer wrote. "There are serious public concerns about how your businesses increased so dramatically in value only a year after reporting very limited assets." title: Jack Osbourne says doctors warned Ozzy not to perform final concert just 17 days before his death
description: Jack Osbourne reveals doctors warned Ozzy Osbourne about his heart and artery issues before the Birmingham farewell concert, but he refused to stop.
content: Jack Osbourne is reflecting on the weeks leading up to his father Ozzy Osbourne's death, revealing the stark warning doctors gave the rock legend before his final performance. During an appearance on "Great Company with Jamie Laing," Jack recalled how doctors urged the Black Sabbath frontman not to take the stage at his farewell concert due to serious health concerns. "They basically were just saying like you've got so many things going on," Jack explained. "We recommend you don't do this because the energy expenditure." .OZZY OSBOURNE KNEW THE END WAS NEAR DURING FINAL PERFORMANCE, FRIEND SAYS Jack revealed that his father had been dealing with multiple medical complications leading up to the show. "There was like something with his heart and he had some like artery stuff going on," he said, adding that Ozzy had experienced "a ton of medical kind of mishaps leading up to the show." Despite the warnings, the Prince of Darkness was determined to give fans one final performance. OZZY OSBOURNE'S SON JACK SHARES PRIVATE FAMILY MOMENTS IN EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO LATE FATHER "They were just like energetically, this is going to ... this is not good. This is not good. Like you don't have it in you," Jack recalled of the doctors' concerns. His father's response was simple: "I'm doing it." Just 17 days later, Ozzy died at the age of 76. KELLY OSBOURNE SAYS SHE 'WASN'T WELL' WHILE FACING HARSH SCRUTINY, BODY-SHAMING AFTER DAD OZZY'S DEATH Although Jack admitted he was heartbroken over his father's death, he said he wasn't angry about the rock legend's decision to perform despite the medical warnings. "But he wanted his journey. And so I can't ... I'm not angry at that," Jack explained. "I think everyone wants to at least have some say in how they go," he continued. "Obviously, deeply heartbroken that he's gone but also he went the way he wanted to." Ozzy performed his final show with his Black Sabbath bandmates Geezer Butler, Tony Iommi and Bill Ward at his "Back to the Beginning" farewell concert in Birmingham, England, on July 5, 2025. KELLY OSBOURNE BLASTS DEE SNIDER AS 'SPECTACULARLY CLASSLESS' FOR CLAIMING OZZY DIDN’T WRITE HIS OWN SONGS The 10-hour show, hosted by Jason Momoa, featured performances from Metallica, Guns N' Roses, Jack Black, Steven Tyler and more. For the closing set, according to a photo posted on X and various videos, the legendary rocker was lifted onto the stage while seated on a black throne adorned with skulls and topped with a black bat. He performed hits including "Crazy Train" and "Mama I'm Coming Home" while remaining seated throughout the set. ROD STEWART TURNS TO OXYGEN TANK MID-CONCERT AFTER NEARLY COLLAPSING ONSTAGE "It's so good to be on this stage... You have no idea how I feel," Ozzy told the crowd, according to Planet Rock Radio. "Thank you from the bottom of my heart." The Black Sabbath frontman died on July 22, 2025. He was 76. OZZY AND SHARON OSBOURNE'S LONGTIME LOS ANGELES HOME HITS THE MARKET FOR $17M AFTER HIS DEATH AT 76 "It is with more sadness than mere words can convey that we have to report that our beloved Ozzy Osbourne has passed away this morning," his family said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital at the time. "He was with his family and surrounded by love. We ask everyone to respect our family privacy at this time." Ozzy's death certificate listed cardiac arrest, acute myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease and Parkinson's disease. Jack's emotional reflections come as his mother, Sharon Osbourne, has also opened up about the final moments she shared with her husband of 43 years. During an appearance on "Piers Morgan Uncensored," Sharon, 73, broke down in tears as she recalled her last conversation with the rock legend. Sharon explained that Ozzy had been "up and down" throughout the night before waking her around 4:30 a.m. "He said, 'Wake up' and [I said] 'I'm already bloody awake, you've woken me up,'" Sharon remembered. "And he said, 'Kiss me.' And then he said, 'Hug me tight.'" Sharon emotionally confirmed that those were the last words her husband said to her before he died later that morning. The former "The Talk" host explained that Ozzy would often wake up early to exercise and had followed his usual routine on the day of his death. "He went downstairs and worked out for 20 minutes and passed away," she said. Sharon recalled hearing "screaming" inside their home before rushing downstairs and discovering that attempts were being made to revive her husband. "They were trying to resuscitate him and I'm like 'Don't. Leave him. Leave him. You can't. He's gone.' I knew instantly he's gone," she recalled. "And they tried and tried and then they took him by helicopter to the hospital and they tried and it's like, 'He's gone. Just leave him.'" Sharon admitted that her grief following Ozzy's death was so overwhelming that she "couldn't function." She also struggled with regrets about their final exchange. title: Australia pastor case 'canary in the coal mine' for American Christian freedoms: TPUSA leader
description: Lucas Miles of Turning Point USA says he contacted the White House Faith Office urging Trump to pressure Australia over a church investigation.
content: A Turning Point USA faith leader is calling on President Donald Trump to intervene after Australian lawmakers grilled a Christian church leader about his religious beliefs, including whether he influences members' marriages, hairstyles and even pet ownership. Lucas Miles, vice president of faith at Turning Point USA, told Fox News Digital he contacted the White House Faith Office and several administration officials over what he described as a politically motivated investigation into the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church. "We've reached out to the faith office, we've reached out to several members of the administration to make sure that they're aware of this," Miles said. "We're hoping to see some response and action soon." UK LAWMAKER WARNS IT’S ‘OPEN SEASON’ ON CHRISTIANS AS HE SOUNDS ALARM OVER ‘TWO-TIER JUSTICE’ The controversy intensified during an Oct. 16 parliamentary hearing examining allegations of coordinated political activity by church members during Australia's 2025 federal election. Independent MP Monique Ryan questioned the church's global leader, Bruce Hales, about whether members considered him an "elect vessel" or a direct messenger from God. She also asked whether members sought his guidance on marriage, housing, pets, clothing and facial hair. Liberal MP Ben Small objected to the questioning, calling it "patently ridiculous" and "so far off the terms of reference for this inquiry." Another lawmaker interjected that hairstyles had no bearing on electoral matters, while the committee chair allowed the questioning to continue. "When an Australian parliamentary committee tasked with investigating election matters begins interrogating a Christian leader about his theological convictions, serious questions must be asked about the purpose of the inquiry," Miles said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "Bruce Hales was summoned to answer questions about electoral conduct, not to defend the doctrines of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church before the government," he added. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE WAR ON CHRISTIANS IS REAL AND THE WORLD CAN NO LONGER STAY SILENT Miles argued that the line of questioning may illustrate a broader threat to religious freedom. "The troubling shift from election oversight to religious scrutiny gives every appearance of a politically motivated witch hunt," he said. Hales denied directing, funding or coordinating political campaigning during the 2025 election, maintaining that church members acted independently. "I had no involvement whatsoever in relation to any members who volunteered or took part in any aspect of the 2025 federal election," Hales told the committee. Lawmakers questioned whether a sermon in which Hales said Australia needed to be "happy again, smiling again" influenced members' political activities, citing subsequent campaign messaging that echoed his words. His son, Gareth, acknowledged encouraging people already involved in campaigning but denied directing an organized church campaign. CHRISTIAN WOMAN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO NEW 'ORWELLIAN' CHARGES FOR STANDING AND SILENT PRAYER The committee is also examining allegations of intimidation and coordinated campaigning during the election. Church leaders have denied organizing or condoning improper conduct. Hales said he did not support harassment or intimidation and maintained that individual members should be accountable for their own actions. "In a free society, government has every right to investigate violations of election law, but it has no business putting Christian doctrine on trial," Miles said. The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, which traces its roots back roughly 200 years, says its roughly 55,000 members worldwide follow a "Doctrine of Separation," distancing themselves from certain secular activities and practices they believe conflict with biblical teachings. The church rejects descriptions of the denomination as a cult, maintaining that its members freely practice their faith and contribute to their communities through businesses and charitable initiatives. The hearing also turned to the United States when Sen. Steph Hodgins-May questioned Hales about Turning Point USA's support for the church and whether church leaders had met with the Trump administration. Hales said he had never met Trump but understood that some church members in New York had briefly met the president. Miles, who is not a member of the denomination, said he wants Trump to apply diplomatic pressure on Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and urge an end to the inquiry. "What I would like to see, first of all, is some pressure applied, whether that be through diplomatic channels or through the president himself," Miles told Fox News Digital. Miles said he remains hopeful the administration will take action and warned that the controversy could establish a troubling precedent for American churches, pointing to past disputes involving religious organizations and government restrictions in the United States. "They're making this about trying to really smear the church because of specific doctrines that they might hold to, and I think this is a canary in the coal mine for religious liberty across the globe that when we see a Western nation like Australia," Miles said. "The government [is] against the church and against the Christian church in particular, I think this is reason for the rest of the world to wake up." "If this can happen in Australia, if it can happen places like England and Canada, it certainly can happen America if we don't stay alert," he said. Miles emphasized that Christians should be free to participate in politics without their churches automatically being held responsible for their individual choices. "Just because individual private citizens who happen to go to a church have a similar opinion about politics, that does not constitute a grand conspiracy," he said. He urged Trump to pursue what he called "faith-based diplomacy" to defend religious liberty abroad. The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Dementia risk may be linked to seemingly harmless daily habit, new research suggests
description: Even naps under 30 minutes raised dementia risk 40% in a Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health study of nearly 1,000 older adults.
content: Frequent daytime napping among older adults has been linked to a higher risk of developing dementia, according to a study published in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences. Researchers from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health tracked nearly 1,000 adults age 65 and older who showed no signs of memory or thinking problems when the study began in 2013. A decade later, the researchers found that daily rest habits — like how often people nap, how long they sleep and whether they fall asleep by accident — are linked to long-term brain health. ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES The study found that participants who napped frequently, defined as most days or every day, had a 48% higher risk of developing dementia compared to those who rarely or never napped. Whether the naps were intentional also appeared to play a role. Seniors who fell asleep unintentionally had a 39% higher risk, while shorter naps were also linked to poorer outcomes. Napping for 30 minutes or less was linked to a 40% increased risk of dementia, even after researchers adjusted for other health factors. For naps longer than 30 minutes, the association was less pronounced after researchers accounted for nighttime sleep patterns. The research team stressed that looking at daytime napping habits gives a much clearer picture of overall health than looking at nighttime sleep alone. THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS "Our study highlights the importance of looking beyond just how long people nap and considering other napping characteristics, such as how frequently they nap and whether their naps are intentional," study authors Adam Spira, Ph.D., a professor at the Bloomberg School, and postdoctoral fellow Kening Jiang, Ph.D., told Fox News Digital. "This study provides important longitudinal evidence that frequent and unintentional daytime napping were associated with a higher risk of developing dementia among older adults." The findings held true even after accounting for nighttime sleep length, daytime drowsiness and indicators of sleep apnea. "Nighttime sleep and daytime napping are closely related," Spira and Jiang went on. "Daytime napping may compensate for poor nighttime sleep, but it may also reduce the drive to sleep at night, potentially contributing to nighttime sleep disturbances, another important potential risk factor for dementia." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Researchers pointed out that daytime resting does not necessarily cause brain changes. Rather, changing nap habits could be an early warning sign of underlying changes in the brain. Brain regions that help regulate wakefulness can start to break down in the early stages of dementia, leading to more frequent daytime fatigue, they noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES To double-check this, the team re-analyzed the data after removing anyone who developed dementia during the first five years. The link between frequent, accidental naps and dementia remained just as strong, suggesting that changes in napping habits can show up years before a formal diagnosis. The researchers emphasized that this was an observational study with limitations. "We did not directly intervene on participants’ napping behaviors to examine whether changing these behaviors would affect their dementia risk," Spira and Jiang told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Although we don’t know whether napping causes dementia, our study findings suggest that daytime napping patterns may be useful indicators of future dementia risk," they added. title: Federal authorities charge 15 in massive $1.8B Southern California medical fraud sweep
description: Federal raids across Southern California targeted 15 suspects, including a cardiothoracic surgeon, in nearly $2 billion in healthcare fraud schemes.
content: Federal authorities conducted predawn raids across Southern California on Thursday, busting suspected fraudsters, including a cardiothoracic surgeon, accused of stealing nearly $2 billion through sham substance abuse programs, unnecessary surgeries and phony hospice care. In total, 15 people, including six medical professionals, were charged over $1. 8 billion in fraudulent claims submitted to government and private health insurance programs, the Justice Department said. "These charges include the largest sober home fraud scheme the Department has ever prosecuted and a scheme involving unnecessary invasive procedures that was detected through data analytics," said Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. Among the defendants are Dr. Harold Tabaie, 78, of Anaheim, a cardiothoracic surgeon, and his business partner, Hany Malek, 61, a Tarzana chiropractor. Both are charged in an alleged $135 million scheme to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary atherectomies, invasive arterial procedures using a bladed catheter to clear plaque. Prosecutors allege Malek posed as a medical doctor to diagnose patients with arterial disease and recommend atherectomies, even though the patients did not have the condition. CALIFORNIA DOCTOR CONVICTED OF $45M MEDICARE FRAUD SCHEME THAT FUNDED LUXURY VACATIONS AND A $12K CROSSBOW Tabaie then performed the procedures, sometimes repeatedly on patients for whom previous operations had already failed, according to officials. Authorities noted that several patients suffered extreme pain and discomfort as a result. Malek also faces charges for allegedly submitting fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan applications in 2021. He allegedly fabricated a 25% revenue loss for his business to secure loan funds, which he then spent on personal expenses, family credit cards, other ventures and rare coins. TOP FEDERAL PROSECUTOR CALLS CALIFORNIA A 'FRAUDSTER'S PARADISE,' WARNS STATE OFFICIALS COULD FACE CHARGES In a separate case, Nathan Young, 39, and his father, David Young, 71, were charged with operating a $1.6 billion substance abuse scam. Authorities allege the father-son duo trafficked drug addicts from across the nation to dozens of Los Angeles rehab centers. Federal prosecutors said the vulnerable patients were recruited by "body brokers" Honey Phipps, 42, and Cody Phipps, 36, both of Greenville, Texas. Body brokerage is the illegal practice of receiving kickbacks to refer insured individuals to specific rehab facilities. Once patients arrived, no actual treatment was provided. Instead, the Youngs allegedly recycled patients through their facilities to continuously bill insurance companies, even ordering staff to drug patients with sedatives to "knock them out" if they attempted to leave. VANCE ANTI-FRAUD TASK FORCE SUSPENDS 447 HOSPICES IN LOS ANGELES OVER MORE THAN $600M IN SUSPECTED FRAUD The duo also allegedly offered drugs to patients, cut them off from communication with family members, prevented them from accessing their belongings and physically blocked them from leaving the facilities to continue billing their insurance policies. When Nathen Young was informed that a patient wanted to leave detox so he could smoke marijuana, Young instructed that the patient should be given what he wanted, off-site from the detox, to keep him there, prosecutors said. "It is especially egregious when doctors and other health care professionals, who pledged to do no harm, resort to petty greed and criminality," said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. "Every dollar drained out of our private and public health insurance systems is one less dollar available to those who truly need it." The sweep also targeted several other major healthcare fraud schemes across the region. In one instance, defendants were charged with stealing more than $140 million by falsely certifying non-terminally ill patients for hospice care. In a separate prescription fraud scheme, Christina Mareik, 61, of Whittier, was charged for her role in allegedly submitting thousands of bogus prescriptions for high-reimbursement generic drugs to Medi-Cal, California's Medicaid program. title: DOJ has verified 20,000 noncitizens on California voter rolls, federal prosecutor says
description: Bill Essayli says federal investigators confirmed all 20,000 flagged California voter rolls entries are noncitizens who received mail ballots.
content: A top federal prosecutor in California said federal investigators have determined that all 20,000 people they flagged on the state's voter rolls as "likely noncitizens" are not U.S. citizens. Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for California's Central District, told Fox News Digital that federal investigators have evidence that these 20,000 individuals received mail ballots this month. His office sued California last week seeking a court order to prevent any ballots they return from being counted. "We're not asking California to take any drastic steps other than to sequester the ballots from the suspected noncitizens," Essayli said in an interview on Wednesday. "We believe it's at a minimum of 20,000. That's the floor." The potential ceiling, he said, is much larger. Essayli referenced a letter Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent to California in July that flagged nearly 200,000 voters as possible noncitizens. DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS Since then, federal investigators have been sifting through those records to identify people they believe they can verify as noncitizens. He said 20,000 is only the current tally and expects thousands more names to be added in the coming days. Earlier this week, Essayli got into a social media spat with Gov. Gavin Newsom over the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting. Essayli argued that California is allowing people without citizenship onto the voter rolls through its supposedly lax verification processes, while Newsom said the state follows all relevant federal law governing the integrity of elections. In court filings, California election officials have pushed back against the Justice Department's demands, arguing that county election offices lack both the authority and access to federal records needed to verify voters' citizenship status. They have also said that sequestering ballots from people on the DOJ list is impossible in cases where the ballots have already been processed. Once a ballot's signature is verified, it is removed from its identifying envelope and processed alongside other ballots, meaning it can no longer be traced back to an individual voter. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS "That is true. That's why we're getting an emergency court order requiring them to put those ballots aside," Essayli said. "Ballots have already gone out, people are filling them out and they're being returned in process as we speak. So, the crime is occurring in real time." The DOJ escalated its push for immediate court intervention Wednesday, asking the judge to rule on its emergency request by noon Thursday. In Los Angeles County alone, officials have already processed 331,000 ballots, according to court records. Essayli's office filed suit on Oct. 15, roughly two weeks after California sent out mail ballots, including to the possible noncitizens on the DOJ list, according to the federal government. When asked why the Justice Department didn't act sooner, Essayli explained that investigators did not know exactly which voters would receive ballots until they were sent. ELECTION CRIME ARRESTS KEEP PILING UP AS DEMS INSIST IT 'JUST DOESN'T HAPPEN' He said California should cooperate with the federal government to expedite the process of verifying voters' citizenship. That would involve providing additional identifying information, including driver's license numbers and Social Security numbers when available, that federal investigators could cross-check against government databases. California and dozens of other states treat this information as confidential and have refused to turn it over to the federal government, prompting the DOJ to take several of them to court. In a separate lawsuit from Sept. 2025, the DOJ tried to compel California to provide its complete, unredacted voter-registration database, including names, Social Security numbers, home addresses and voting histories. In January, a district court sided with California and dismissed the case, calling the government's request "unprecedented and illegal." The DOJ appealed the ruling and litigation is ongoing. MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY "If California will make available or submit its records, we can quickly put them through our established systems to determine who's a citizen and who's not," Essayli told Fox News Digital. "They're forcing us to do it the hard way, which we're willing to do because this is very important." He said every person on the current 20,000-name list was individually reviewed by a federal employee at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and Homeland Security Investigations. California officials, however, have questioned the reliability of the DOJ list. Monica Flores, an assistant registrar-recorder in Los Angeles County, said in a court declaration that her office conducted a preliminary review of a sample of 200 records from the list that were associated with LA County addresses. Of those, 112 corresponded to canceled or inactive voter registrations, meaning no ballot was mailed to those individuals for the November election, Flores said. TRUMP ADMIN WANTS TO REQUIRE TAX FILERS TO DISCLOSE CITIZENSHIP STATUS TO IRS "I don't believe that, actually," Essayli said. "The information we have is that they likely received ballots. So we are asking for the names of people they claim whose registration has been canceled." Essayli added LA County did not say when these registrations were canceled. He raised the possibility at least some were canceled after federal officials provided the state with their list. "If they're canceling now based on the records we provided, that's great news," Essayli said. "But that's all to be determined." In the 200-person sample reviewed by LA County, Flores said that among records where birthplace was "meaningfully reported," 38.9% indicated the person was born in the United States, which she called "strong evidence of citizenship." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Essayli similarly disputed this conclusion, arguing that the birthplace information — much like the citizenship information itself — was provided by the registered voters themselves. "They're not independently checking any of this information," Essayli said. "They're going off the information that was provided to them by the person who registered to vote." The California Secretary of State's office and the LA County Registrar-Recorder's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. Essayli said that his office is determined to follow through with its investigation because "one noncitizen voting is too many." "One illegal vote cancels out the vote of an American citizen. There are a lot of local elections that are decided on very few votes," he said. "Noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections, and we intend to enforce that law."

THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY – AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES "Look, what I want is to get this kind of money out of politics," Warren said. "We need to push back because, this campaign, this 2026 midterm, really is about the money or the people. Because the Democrats have got the people on their side. The Republicans have got the money, and they think if they can spend it, they can maintain control of this country, and I sure hope they're wrong," Warren said, arguing for a "very different" system. CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS "This is the part where we also have to continue putting pressure on the social media companies to make their algorithms safer for kids," she said. "They created an addictive product, they know it, and we need to keep the pressure on." In the documentary, Michaels examines the risks she says children face in the modern age, including excessive screen time, mental health issues and over-medicalization. "The truth is, a lot of parents probably don't realize the scale of what kids are dealing with today," she said. "From day one, the fragile little bodies and brains of the tiniest and most vulnerable among us are being targeted, treated and toxified from all angles." NATION'S SECOND-LARGEST SCHOOL DISTRICT MOVES TO LIMIT KIDS' SCREEN TIME Michaels is joined by several experts in "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink," including psychology researcher Jean Twenge, who argues that individuals who begin using smartphones at an early age are more likely to experience mental health issues later in life. "In some of the best design studies, the heaviest users of social media are about twice as likely to be depressed as lighter non-users," Twenge said. "Even in other studies, you see at least often a 40% or a 50% increase in depression from not using social media to being a heavy user of social media." "Gen Z and Gen Alpha know how bad these technologies can be for them," Twenge added. "They're the ones who came up with phrases like 'chronically online,' which make it sound like a disease, 'brain rot,' that it's bad for your attention span and your focus." FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15 Social media companies have faced increasing pressure to be regulated and be held accountable for the potential effects of their platforms. In August, Meta agreed to pay as much as $17.1 billion and implement restrictions on teen accounts to settle claims that it designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children and misled the public about the platforms' safety. Meta denied the allegations. title: France's Macron blames protests on 'ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic'
description: French President Emmanuel Macron blamed "ultra-left groups" for riots and looting as Paris businesses board up windows ahead of Saturday protests.
content: French President Emmanuel Macron vowed Thursday to ban protests by "individuals or groups with no legitimate authority" as he blamed "ultra-left groups" for riots and looting that spread across his country. Macron made the remarks as thousands of protesters took to the streets of Paris on Thursday, according to The Associated Press, ahead of larger demonstrations set for this weekend. "Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron was quoted by Reuters as saying following a meeting with intelligence officials. The news agency reported that businesses in central Paris have started boarding up their windows over concerns of violence on Saturday. Local authorities also told Reuters that protests planned for Saturday in Lyon have been banned. FRANCE COULD FACE EVEN WORSE DESTRUCTION WITH SECOND WEEKEND OF PLANNED RIOTS, STATE DEPT WARNS Macron said the strategy adopted for the coming days is to ban protests requested by "individuals or groups with no legitimate authority." "Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed" to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings, Macron said. "The rules are simple, and I think they're just common sense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days," he said. "For those who still want to protest, if they are trade unions, prefects will propose alternative routes." Organizers of the Paris protest on Thursday said an administrative court in the city overturned a ban issued by police after they challenged it. The Paris police prefecture previously said the ban was necessary, given the risk of street violence after groups of masked youth clashed with police forces, looted shops and torched cars over the weekend. AMERICANS WARNED ABOUT PARIS TRAVEL AFTER VIOLENCE, LOOTING AND TEAR GAS-FILLED STREETS The protests began in France in September with calls for education reform, before expanding into larger anti-government demonstrations that French officials say are being fueled by far-left groups. Protesters gathered peacefully and chanted in the southeastern part of Paris on Thursday while they were watched by a heavy police presence, the AP reported. title: Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner confirms he supports owners' salary cap proposals ahead of likely MLB lockout
description: Hal Steinbrenner confirmed he supports the owners' proposals that include an MLB salary cap, setting the stage for a heated labor showdown.
content: Hal Steinbrenner was not fond of answering questions about Major League Baseball's labor negotiations with the players' association, but he came as close as possible to answering a very important one. When asked at the New York Yankees' postmortem presser if he was in favor of a salary cap, the team's owner said he "support[s]" the owners' proposals - all of which include a cap. "I've said before - let me put it this way as a member of the labor policy committee - I helped craft, one of many, the proposals that we have given at the bargaining table. And I support those proposals in their entirety. That's absolutely the case, so that should answer your question," Steinbrenner told reporters. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "What I will say is as a member of the labor policy committee is that we are working hard on our end. We are completely focused on the task ahead of us, on the negotiating. And I'm optimistic we're gonna get a deal done, and we''e gonna get a deal done that's favorable for both sides." Players have adamantly opposed a salary cap and said it is non-negotiable. The owners are expected to lock out the players on Dec. 1, when the current collective bargaining agreement expires. The Yankees' $336 million payroll was the third-largest in baseball during the 2026 season, behind the Los Angeles Dodgers ($422 million) and New York Mets ($338 million). Arguments skew both ways, but a constant has remained in that the highest payrolls continue to go up, while the lowest payrolls remain at a stall. The Marlins' payroll is actually roughly half of what it used to be in 2017, despite a sale of the team and everyone in the league making more money than ever. Meanwhile, the Dodgers have already committed more money in 2030 than 12 teams have this season. HAL STEINBRENNER MAKES CLEAR WHO HE BLAMES FOR YANKEES' TROUBLES AS BRIAN CASHMAN MAKES ANNOUNCEMENT MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has said that owners are simply "listening to our fans" regarding a salary cap and said it "defies human experience... to think that the bottom end of that [payroll] gap has the same opportunity to win the top end." It should be noted, though, that the National League-winning Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers with the 11th-smallest payroll, and they will be facing the Tampa Bay Rays, who have the league's third-smallest payroll. They defeated the Cleveland Guardians, who rank 29th in payroll, in the American League Division Series. Major League Baseball has never had a salary cap. "Salary cap is the ultimate excuse not to compete. It's the ultimate excuse for an owner to say, ‘Gee, I would like to make the team better, but you know I can’t,'" interim MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer said during the All-Star break. "Salary caps are bad for fans. Salary caps prevent teams from doing the things that they believe are in their interest to make the team better." title: I'm independent Brian Bengs; this is why I want South Dakota's vote for Senate

content: I’m a retired military prosecutor, U.S. Air Force Academy instructor and former Wind Cave National Park Ranger. Self-dealing is screwing hard-working, honorable South Dakotans out of their chance to live the American dream. TRUMP VANISHES FROM GOP SENATOR'S CAMPAIGN WEBSITE AS POLL NUMBERS PLUNGE WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION I’m convinced that term limits are the best way to do it. Here’s a good example of why I believe that. There ought to be a law prohibiting that sort of thing. That is why, when I’m elected, the first bill I’ll introduce is to make ALL lobbying by congressional staff illegal. I’ve had enough. My second bill would be term limits. Washington’s culture is so corrupt and out of touch that the people who live there too long don’t even realize it anymore. I believe Mike Rounds is a good man. I agreed with President Donald Trump when he ran on "no new wars." As a patriot who’s proud to have served in both the Navy and the Air Force, I believe commanders in chief have a duty to only send our fighting men and women into harm’s way when it’s absolutely necessary. title: Slotkin's viral 'threat' to conservatives takes new twist as student moves to hold her accountable: 'Shocking'
description: Michael Bicksel, the University of Chicago student who broke the story, filed the ethics complaint arguing Elissa Slotkin's remarks targeted students.
content: FIRST ON FOX: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) is facing an ethics complaint filed to the United States Senate over comments she made earlier this month that many characterized as a "threat" to conservatives who are thinking about working for the Trump administration. During an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event, Slotkin drew criticism after a clip went viral showing her saying she wants to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" President Donald Trump and push a "deterrence message" for young people. "I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.' I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want, and so let me avoid participating in that,'" she said. "I want that deterrence message sent," Slotkin said. Slotkin is now facing an ethics complaint filed Thursday by Michael Bicksel, a University of Chicago student who first reported her remarks. The complaint was submitted to the Senate Select Committee on Ethics and argues that Slotkin proposed using congressional investigations and potential prosecutions to frighten young people away from serving in a Republican administration. FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS "Recently at an event at my college, the University of Chicago, Senator Slotkin laid out a legislative-oversight agenda that involved using the legal process to terrorize members of the Trump administration in order to ‘deter’ young people from going to work for it," Bicksel wrote. The complaint asks the committee to determine whether Slotkin's comments amounted to "improper conduct which may reflect upon the Senate," a standard described in the Senate Ethics Manual as applying to conduct that may be unethical even if it does not violate a specific law or Senate rule. "As a college student and a conservative, this was a shocking thing to hear," Bicksel's complaint reads. "A prominent U.S. Senator came to my college and laid out a goal that I and my peers should be afraid to serve our country in the executive branch. This is well below the standard of conduct expected of a U.S. Senator and deserves investigation by the Senate Select Committee on Ethics and appropriate subsequent disciplinary action." ELISSA SLOTKIN TELLS STUDENTS LIKE ME NOT TO WORK IN GOVERNMENT. DON'T LISTEN TO HER Bicksel argued that Slotkin's comments were directed at students considering government service, rather than exclusively at people who commit crimes or engage in unethical conduct. "The substance of the ‘deterrence message’ is clear as day," Bicksel wrote. "Her target was ‘young people coming out of school’ (like me and my classmates) who are debating whether they should ‘go work for the Trump administration.’" "We are obviously not debating — as she subsequently tried to clarify — whether to go commit crimes or behave unethically," he continued. "Those who commit crimes should be punished for doing so. No one disagrees with that. All we are debating is public service, pure and simple, and Senator Slotkin says we should think twice about doing so because it might provoke the full power of the United States Senate." Slotkin, when pressed on the response to her comment on CNN, referred to the controversy as "manufactured outrage." title: Washington foster parents score legal victory after state demanded they use children's preferred pronouns
description: Shane and Jennifer DeGross fought Washington state's foster care gender identity policies after the requirements clashed with their Christian faith.
content: A Christian couple who spent more than a decade caring for foster children is celebrating a major legal victory after Washington state agreed to change its licensing rules following a dispute over requirements that foster parents use children's preferred pronouns and comply with gender identity policies, even when those requirements conflicted with their religious beliefs. Shane and Jennifer DeGross told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that the dispute began in 2022, when they attempted to renew their foster care license and discovered the state had changed its requirements concerning gender identity. The couple said they were willing to love and care for any child placed in their home but could not agree to certain state-imposed requirements they believed violated their Christian faith. "We were made aware that the state had updated and changed some of their requirements," Jennifer DeGross told Fox News Digital. "While we agreed that we would love and care for any child in our home, they had specific things that we could not agree to as Christians." DOJ BACKS NUNS CARING FOR DYING CANCER PATIENTS IN FIGHT AGAINST NEW YORK TRANS IDEOLOGY MANDATE Shane DeGross said the state required them to affirm the state's views on gender identity and human sexuality. "Those views directly conflict with the biblical worldview of human sexuality," Shane DeGross said. "So, as Christians, we just couldn't accept that. Our allegiance is to God and the truth of Scripture. And we just couldn't abide by what they were requiring us to affirm." Washington's licensing policies required foster parents to affirm and support LGBTQ children, including expectations concerning gender identity and the use of preferred names and pronouns. The DeGross family challenged the requirements on religious freedom grounds. Jennifer said the state eventually partially reinstated their license but restricted the ages of children they could foster. AUTISM PROVIDERS WARN FOSTER KIDS AT RISK FROM UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES OF TRUMP'S MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN "We felt like even when they reinstated a partial license to us that they were still discriminating against us," she said. "When a child reached 5, they had to be removed from our home," Jennifer said. "So not only was that upsetting to us, but that's not good for kids, right?" Jennifer argued that such a restriction could disrupt a child's placement even if the child had already spent years living with a foster family. PATRIOTS RB TREVEYON HENDERSON SLAMS STATE OVERREACH AFTER CATHOLIC FAMILY LOSES CUSTODY IN GENDER CASE "If we had had a child for a couple of years, and then they have to be removed just because they turned or reached a certain age, it's definitely not in the interest of children," she said. The legal battle resulted in a settlement under which Washington agreed to revise its foster care licensing rules, addressing the conflict between the state's gender identity requirements and foster parents' religious freedom claims. Johannes Widmalm-Delphonse, senior counsel at Alliance Defending Freedom, told Fox News Digital that the DeGross' case should serve as a lesson for the rest of the country. "These foster care agencies, they have to respect the First Amendment rights of foster parents, as well as the children in the system and everyone that they work with," Widmalm-Delphonse said. "So, states should be on notice from this settlement, as well as some of the other cases that we've seen like the Bates v. Pakseresht decision, that they have to respect First Amendment rights, they have to respect free speech rights, and the way you do that is you invite as many foster parents into the system as possible on the front end, and then you match at the back end according to children's individual needs or family's abilities, comfort level, things like that, which is what they've been doing for decades, and this settlement shows that they can continue doing that now," Widmalm-Delphonse added. WASHINGTON FATHER SUES SCHOOL DISTRICT FOR DENYING RELIGIOUS OPT-OUT FOR 5TH GRADER FROM LGBTQ INSTRUCTION Widmalm-Delphonse said that since the settlement, Washington State has a new proposed regulation, WSR 26-20-103, currently undergoing the public notice and comment process which would in part give foster parents like Shane and Jennifer DeGross a religious exemption. "This new rule, in part, would give foster parents like the DeGross's a religious exemption from any rule requiring them to violate their religious beliefs on gender or sexuality," Widmalm-Delphonse said. Shane DeGross told Fox News Digital, "It's a great victory in the sense that more Christians can be available to love and care for foster kids without fear of being excluded because of their religious beliefs." "It's a huge victory for kids that need a loving home," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are proud of the diversity of our foster parent and kinship caregiver community who have different cultures, religious beliefs, and lived experience," the Washington State Department of Children, Youth, and Families said in a news release on the settlement. "We are grateful that they all open their doors and provide a loving home to children and youth in foster care." "This settlement agreement respects the religious beliefs of foster parents, while ensuring LGBTQIA+ youth are placed in an environment that is safe and supports their well-being," DCYF Secretary Tana Senn said. Fox News Digital reached out to the Washington DCYF for further comment.
