title: Anthropic AI sends fake murder tip to Philadelphia police
description: Anthropic's Claude AI submitted a fabricated eyewitness tip about an unsolved murder to a Philadelphia police website during automated testing.
content: Artificial intelligence can write your emails, research complicated questions and even handle tasks while you're away. But what happens when an AI system takes an action nobody intended? Philadelphia police recently got an unexpected answer. An AI model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated eyewitness tip about an unsolved murder through a Philadelphia police website. The submission happened during automated testing, and the model apparently believed it was generating an example interaction. Fortunately, the tip was flagged as spam before reaching investigators. However, the incident raises an uncomfortable question about what happens when AI agents interact with websites and public services without adequate safeguards. AG BLANCHE REJECTS CALLS FOR NEW AI LAWS AFTER ROGUE AGENTS TARGET US GOVERNMENT WEBSITES Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You'll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. How Anthropic's AI submitted a false murder tip The incident involved PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a website where people can submit information about unsolved homicide cases in Philadelphia. On July 18, 2026, an AI model submitted a tip claiming to have information about a killing. According to Anthropic's October 9 report, the model was Claude Haiku 4.5. It had been assigned to generate and perform example tasks on randomly selected webpages. During one test, Claude encountered a page about an unsolved homicide that included a police department tip form. Rather than simply demonstrating how someone might use the form, Claude filled it out with invented information and submitted it. Here's what the model wrote: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." There's a particularly troubling detail here. The website contained no description of the perpetrator. Claude invented that reference while presenting itself as someone who might have witnessed something relevant to the investigation. The model also left the name and contact fields blank, which the website permitted. It then submitted the tip. Fortunately, the police department's spam filtering caught the submission before it could reach detectives. Why Claude submitted a real police tip during testing Anthropic's explanation reveals how a relatively simple oversight can lead to an unintended action. Claude had been instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal information, make purchases or submit anything destructive. However, those restrictions did not explicitly prohibit submitting online forms. As a result, the model completed the tip form as part of its assigned task. Anthropic says the available transcript suggests Claude was generating example content rather than intentionally trying to mislead law enforcement. However, the company acknowledges that determining a model's intentions requires further analysis. That qualification is important. The evidence does not establish that Claude deliberately set out to deceive investigators. Instead, the incident shows how an AI system can carry out an action that its developers never intended, even while apparently attempting to complete its assigned task. Because Claude had access to the live internet during testing, it was able to submit the fabricated tip directly to a police website. Philadelphia police caught the fake tip before investigators saw it According to the Philadelphia Police Department's October 9 statement, the submission was flagged as spam and never forwarded to its Real-Time Crime Center for investigative review or distribution. After Anthropic briefed police on October 8, department personnel located the submission in the website's tip records and confirmed that the corresponding email remained in spam. Police also reported no evidence of unauthorized access to department systems or compromised police data. The department emphasized that all crime tips undergo human review before investigators act on them. Even when a tip appears credible, detectives must assess the information and look for supporting evidence. That process provides another layer of protection against fabricated submissions. While that is reassuring, the timeline raises additional concerns. The submission occurred on July 18, 2026, at 11:27 p.m. According to Philadelphia police, Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28 and notified the department on October 7. Police met with company representatives the following day. That means more than two months passed before Anthropic discovered the false submission. The department called the two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city "unacceptable" and urged technology companies to strengthen their safeguards. AI AGENT HACKS GYM SYSTEM TO MOVE UP WAITLIST Why the false murder tip raises serious concerns Think about what could have happened if the fabricated tip had reached detectives. Investigators might have spent time chasing information that had no legitimate source. An innocent person could potentially have faced unnecessary scrutiny. Neither outcome occurred here. However, the incident raises serious concerns for law enforcement agencies that depend on public tips. Police departments regularly receive information from witnesses, neighbors and people who believe they may know something about a crime. Those submissions can help investigators uncover new evidence, especially in cases that have remained unsolved for years. Now consider how easily an AI system can generate convincing text and submit it through a public website. Without adequate safeguards, automated submissions could overwhelm investigators or make legitimate leads harder to identify. There's also a legal question. Pennsylvania law generally prohibits knowingly providing false information to law enforcement. However, the law's application to AI-generated submissions and the people or companies responsible for them would require separate legal analysis. The available evidence does not establish that Anthropic or its employees committed a crime. Meanwhile, Philadelphia officials are also considering a broader response. The department said Mayor Cherelle L. Parker's administration will explore regulatory protections with state and federal partners to address incidents involving AI systems. Police are coordinating with the city's Law Department and technology officials as they continue reviewing what happened. Anthropic discovered other AI agents taking unintended actions The Philadelphia incident was one of several cases described in Anthropic's October 9 report, titled "Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use." The company identified four categories of unexpected behavior involving Claude models interacting with outside websites and systems. In one case, Claude exploited a software flaw on a university server to run commands after a scientific analysis tool stopped working. The model examined the website, found a vulnerable script and used it to complete the calculation. Another model found ways to access publicly available information that normally required a fee or an access token. Anthropic also observed models using URL-shortening services to work around limits designed to restrict certain web requests. And the Philadelphia case was not the only example involving an online form. Anthropic reported that some models submitted real forms when they were supposed to use practice versions or stop before final submission. These incidents occurred during evaluations and internal use. Anthropic said the incidents had minimal impact and, to its knowledge, did not involve customer data or its own internal systems. What Anthropic is doing to prevent more AI mistakes Following its investigation, Anthropic announced additional safeguards designed to prevent AI models from interacting with outside systems in unintended ways. The company said it has stopped running certain evaluations, moved others into offline environments and rebuilt some tests to avoid contacting live websites. It also expanded restrictions on live internet access to all internal evaluations until it can confirm that its security and monitoring systems reliably detect this behavior. Additionally, Anthropic strengthened restrictions on tools that allow Claude to retrieve information from websites. The company developed automated systems to identify and block unexpected actions. According to Anthropic, those systems blocked every incident described in its report when the company tested them against the previously identified cases. However, that result does not guarantee the safeguards will catch every future problem. Anthropic acknowledged that further work is needed to improve how its models handle ambiguous instructions and unexpected obstacles. GRANDMOTHER SUES AFTER ALLEGED AI FACIAL RECOGNITION ERROR LED TO MONTHS IN JAIL, EXPERTS SOUND ALARM What this means for people using AI agents You might be wondering what an incident involving a police website has to do with your own use of artificial intelligence. The connection is that AI agents are increasingly capable of performing actions instead of simply providing answers. Depending on the tools and permissions available, they can browse websites, complete forms and interact with connected services. That's incredibly useful when everything works as intended. However, an agent can misunderstand instructions or continue pursuing a task when it should stop. For example, you might ask an AI assistant to research travel arrangements. If that assistant has permission to complete bookings, a misunderstanding could potentially result in an unwanted reservation. The Philadelphia case shows why AI agents need clear instructions and firm limits, especially when they can submit information to police departments, government agencies or other organizations. We reached out to Anthropic for additional comment, but the company did not respond before our deadline. How to use AI agents more safely You don't need to abandon AI agents because of this incident. However, I recommend keeping control over actions that could affect your accounts or other people. These precautions cannot eliminate every risk. However, they can help reduce the consequences of an unexpected action. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me most about this incident is where the AI decided to act. We're talking about an unsolved murder involving real victims and families still waiting for answers. A model generated a fabricated eyewitness account and submitted it through a police website. Fortunately, the department's safeguards prevented that information from reaching investigators. But I find it troubling that Anthropic didn't discover the incident until more than two months later. title: Amelia Earhart search suffers crushing setback after researchers make disappointing find
description: Purdue University revealed the Nikumaroro lagoon anomaly suspected to be Amelia Earhart's missing plane was actually tree debris with a carbonate coating.
content: Researchers who embarked on a grueling journey to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane have suffered a devastating setback. Purdue University announced that the team had "found no conclusive evidence" to confirm the Taraia Object hypothesis — which suggested that wreckage from Earhart's aircraft lay in a lagoon on the remote Pacific island of Nikumaroro. The theory centered on the Taraia Object, a visual anomaly first spotted in satellite imagery in 2020 that researchers suspected could be wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER UNEXPECTED TWIST IN SHIPWRECK MYSTERY AFTER CLUES DON'T ADD UP But the university said the object was "likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit." The university added, "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment — a fraction of the anomaly’s original size observed in imagery when the Taraia Object hypothesis was developed." The remaining fragment's reflective surface was caused by a "carbonate veneer," which researchers said had made the debris appear metallic. "Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand," the university added. HAUNTING CLUES EMERGE IN 7-YEAR FISHING BOAT MYSTERY AFTER WRECKAGE FOUND OFF ISLAND Despite the setback, Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and leader of the expedition, said the team "remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished." "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we’re deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible," he said in a statement. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Officials added that the expedition uncovered several artifacts, including a 30-inch steel tube, that could offer clues about how debris travels through the island's lagoon and accumulates along the Taraia Peninsula. The discoveries will undergo further study, though officials did not report finding any artifacts conclusively linked to Earhart's missing aircraft. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Despite the disappointing development, researchers aren't giving up on the theory that Earhart ended up on Nikumaroro. "While the expedition did not uncover the 'smoking gun' connecting Earhart to Nikumaroro, the team reiterated its collective belief in the broader castaway hypothesis," Purdue University added. title: Photos show aftermath of riots as masked groups clash with police across France
description: Paris streets littered with burned cars and shattered storefronts as police report 1,800 arrests nationwide following violent clashes over living costs.
content: Protests over rising living costs and declining public services turned violent across France over the weekend, as more than 500,000 people took to the streets. Violent clashes broke out Saturday during nationwide demonstrations over rising living costs and poor school conditions. Hundreds of thousands marched across the country, while masked groups fought with police, looted businesses and set fires in several cities. Police reported 1,800 arrests nationwide, including 855 in the Paris region. VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED The destruction was not limited to Paris. In Limoges, about three hours south of the capital, fire tore through the city’s historic town hall, built in 1883 and designated a historic landmark in 1975. The local prefect, Maurice Barate, told AFP that the roof had collapsed onto the lower floors and about two-thirds of the building’s exterior had disappeared. He called it "a catastrophe for heritage." LIMOGES TOWN HALL ‘LARGELY LOST’ AFTER FAR-LEFT RIOTERS SET HISTORIC BUILDING ON FIRE French President Emmanuel Macron had called for "calm and respect" ahead of Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the right to protest must be exercised with respect for people and property. But as violence escalated, the French president and his wife, Brigitte, were spotted at a Celine Dion concert in Nanterre, west of Paris, according to French media reports. The couple reportedly arrived and left discreetly and joined roughly 35,000 spectators at the Plenitude Arena. Macron had spent Thursday and Friday in Brussels for a European Council meeting. WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED Macron addressed the nation in a televised speech Sunday, saying those who looted would have to pay for the damage and those who sought to "bring down the Republic" would be held accountable. He blamed the "unrestrained violence" on "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals." Prosecutors said he used the drug GHB to render the women unconscious before sexually assaulting them. Luster fled to Mexico in January 2003 while free on $1 million bail during his trial. He was convicted in his absence and later captured by celebrity bounty hunter Duane "Dog" Chapman in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. The Max Factor heir was originally sentenced to 124 years in prison, but a California judge set aside the sentence in March 2013 after finding that the trial court failed to adequately explain its reasons for imposing consecutive sentences, as Fox News Digital previously reported. title: DOJ official defends Trump's noncitizen voter probe on '60 Minutes,' accuses show of editing out her answers
description: Harmeet Dhillon pushed back on claims the Trump administration is sowing election distrust, saying thousands of noncitizen voting cases are under review.
content: Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon defended the Trump administration's investigation into noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections during CBS' "60 Minutes" on Sunday. "There are people who feel that the point is to sow distrust about the whole election system. There are very few people who are noncitizens who end up voting — very, very few. And so, therefore, what's the purpose?" Lesley Stahl, host of "60 Minutes," asked Dhillon. ELECTION CRIME ARRESTS KEEP PILING UP AS DEMS INSIST IT 'JUST DOESN'T HAPPEN' Dhillon responded, "The point is actually the opposite of what you were saying. It's not to sow distrust. The distrust is there. And so, all of these kinds of crimes are being prosecuted now for the first time really, in volume. And look, even the Biden administration prosecuted 13 people for noncitizen voting." Stahl interrupted and said the numbers were "tiny." "So Lesley, we've been in office for less than two years. We've had investigations ongoing for over a year, and it takes time. There are literally thousands of them out there that we are looking at," Dhillon responded. DEMOCRATIC NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED Dhillon pledged in July that the Trump administration will pursue every provable case of illegal voting under what she described as a "broken windows" enforcement strategy, marking a sharp shift from prior administrations as the DOJ intensifies scrutiny of voter rolls following revelations that noncitizens were registered to vote in New Jersey. Dhillon told Fox News Digital at the time the department's approach is to investigate every credible lead and prosecute every case supported by the evidence, rejecting what she described as the prior view that only widespread fraud or election-altering misconduct warranted federal action. Her statement came after Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill revealed that thousands of noncitizens ended up on the state's voter rolls through the motor-voter system. The "60 Minutes" host asked if there were plans to send Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to polling locations. Dhillon said there were "no plans" to do so. Dhillon dismissed concerns that President Donald Trump would challenge the results of the midterms as "paranoia," Stahl said during a voice-over moment in the segment. The "60 Minutes" host asked Dhillon, "So would you consider a noncitizen voting an irregularity that would lead to a challenge of the vote?" CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I think that would lead to the person's vote being challenged, but not the entire election," Dhillon said. Stahl went on to ask if Dhillon could rule out a challenge to a state vote. "Well, I don't know what is going to happen, but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states," Dhillon responded. "Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "In 2020, Iowa's 2nd Congressional District race was decided by six votes. The Department is now bringing more than double that amount of election fraud cases every week. Every federal race also shares the ballot with state and local contests, which are often decided by even narrower margins. Voting by noncitizens and other ineligible voters is a federal crime, and the Department will enforce the law whether a case involves one illegal ballot or hundreds. These prosecutions protect the integrity of our elections and deter others from breaking the law. title: Alberta holds non-binding separation vote as independence fight grips Canada
description: About 3 million Albertans are eligible to vote in the non-binding separation referendum, but polls show deep divisions within the UCP over it.
content: OTTAWA: Residents of Alberta began voting Monday in a non-binding referendum that will determine whether the western-Canadian province should pursue separation from Canada. The vote comes at a time when the province is mourning the deaths of four soldiers, while dozens of others were injured from a fast-moving fire that burned through a military base in Alberta. While the results of a poll involving 1,021 respondents released by Abacus Data on Saturday showed that 74% of decided voters favor Alberta remaining within the Canadian Confederation, the independence issue won’t disappear for the nearly 30% who want Alberta’s government to begin the process to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether Alberta should separate from Canada, according to veteran separatist organizer Cory Morgan, who leads a group called Pathway to Independence. "It will say that about one in three Albertans have had it," Morgan told Fox News Digital. "There is a big rift within Alberta and if things don’t change, it will be a growing faction in this province — so this vote is an important one." EXCLUSIVE: ‘BROKEN COUNTRY’ FILMMAKER WARNS CANADA’S SLOW DECLINE OFFERS CAUTIONARY TALE FOR AMERICANS About 3 million Albertans are eligible to vote in the referendum. Another recent Abacus poll found that 61% of the 1,021 eligible voters surveyed expect Albertans will vote again on separation, even if most choose to remain in Canada. On Friday, the Angus Reid Institute released the results of its poll that found 62% of 1,010 Albertans surveyed believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement" in the province. Morgan, who led the short-lived Alberta Independence Party from 2000 to 2001, said that while "a vocal minority" within the separatist movement favor Alberta becoming the 51st state, most pro-independence Albertans "don’t want to become a small fish in an even bigger pond." He added that "Albertans in general are not too thrilled with President Trump right now and that makes them less inclined to leave the federation." At a "Forever Canadian" rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he was raised, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a crowd of over 5,000 people that "this referendum comes at the worst possible time." He said that "the world is becoming more dangerous and divided [and] some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," making an indirect reference to Trump’s trade war against and annexation talk about Canada. Alberta-born and raised, 55-year-old Morgan said that his home province is "politically and culturally different" than eastern Canada. "There’s a lot more focus on individual freedoms and property rights," he noted, acknowledging that those values are traditionally viewed as American. "Most Albertans are going to feel much more comfortable sitting down for a beer with people from Great Falls, Montana, than they would in Ottawa," said Morgan. He explained that when Alberta became a Canadian province in 1905, its population grew largely from a migration of Montanans, and when oil was discovered in the 1940s, U.S. companies Chevron and Mobil helped develop what became Alberta’s biggest industry. Also, earlier this year during an appearance on Real America’s Voice at Davos, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described Alberta as "a natural partner for the U.S." and described Albertans as "very independent people." In response, Carney said that he "expect[ed] the U.S. administration to respect Canadian sovereignty." Earlier this month, The Globe and Mail reported that Alberta separatist leaders met with Republican strategists in Calgary in January to look at software designed to identify and mobilize supporters. Separatist leaders also reportedly suggested exchanging water and oil for U.S. support when they met with State Department officials in Washington last year. CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told CBC News that if most Albertans support staying in Canada, she would not hold another referendum on the matter as long as she heads the provincial government. However, on Oct. 18, 2027, residents of the province will vote again in a general election, and Smith could be out of her job by then, warned Morgan, a founding member of the former conservative Wildrose Party, for which Smith served as leader. That party merged with the then-Progressive Conservative Party of Alberta in 2020 to form the United Conservative Party (UCP) that Smith heads. But Morgan explained that more than half of the UCP’s nearly 55,000 members support Alberta’s independence. The premier has said that she will vote to keep the province in Canada. Angus Reid, founder and chairman of the Angus Reid Institute, told Fox News Digital that in his firm’s recent polling, 67% of the 293 UCP voters who support a future binding referendum on separation said that they would either "definitely support" or "consider" supporting the creation of a separatist provincial political party – not unlike the Parti Québécois, which won the recent election in Quebec. The emergence of an independence party in Alberta "would probably spell the death of the UCP since it is so badly divided between separatists and non-separatists, and it would likely end the career of Danielle Smith because of the amount of breakage in her party," said Reid, whose firm’s survey found that 60% of the respondents who support a future binding referendum are "more likely sending a message to Ottawa" about the Canadian government’s often fractious relationship with Alberta. "Separatist types are looking at how much leverage Quebec has been able to achieve in Canada as a result of its threats of exiting, and saying ‘Hold it, we can play that game too,’" explained Reid. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As of Saturday, more than 1.2 million Albertans had cast a ballot on the referendum, which, in addition to the question on separation, has nine others, five focusing on immigration, such as one asking voters whether their province should take more control "for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities."

title: Top tourist destination in the world shuts down amid violent protests
description: Protesters in Paris barricaded the Louvre's iconic glass pyramid and entrances, forcing the world's most visited museum to shut down amid turmoil across the city.
content: The Louvre, the globe's most visited and prominent museum, has closed its doors as turmoil sweeps across Paris. The institution, which houses renowned masterpieces like the "Mona Lisa," announced on Monday that it has shut down due to protesters barricading the entrances, pushing the disruption past a weekend of nationwide riots and demonstrations, according to local newspaper Le Monde. FURIOUS CROWDS PROTEST SKY-HIGH HOUSING COSTS AND MASS TOURISM IN MAJOR CITY No reopening time was provided at the time of publication. Visitors arriving for a Monday morning visit found the iconic glass pyramid, as well as the Carrousel du Louvre and Passage Richelieu entrances, barricaded by protesters from the École du Louvre, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP). The blockade — organized in solidarity with nationwide protests over the rising cost of living and recent police actions — forced management to turn away crowds at a site that normally draws up to 20,000 visitors on its busiest days, French media reported. title: Chris Janson has a message for hunting critics as country stars face social media backlash
description: Chris Janson reveals how he avoids hunting backlash on social media and why his conservation work with Bass Pro Shops goes far beyond the hunt.
content: Chris Janson isn't losing any sleep over people who get upset when he posts photos from his hunting trips. And if you've spent any time on social media lately, you know those people aren't particularly hard to find. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Anti-hunters always seem to find their way into the comments section when someone posts a photo of a successful hunt. But the trolls really come out of the woodwork when that hunter happens to be a country music star. Just ask Cody Johnson, who faced backlash over a grizzly bear hunt in Alaska earlier this year. Johnson defended the hunt as a conservation effort, explaining the role of predator management in protecting other wildlife, including moose and caribou. Then there was Jordan Davis, who caught heat for harvesting an axis deer in Hawaii. Never mind that axis deer are an invasive species that can wreak havoc on the islands' native ecosystems. And most recently, old hunting photos of Ella Langley resurfaced online, prompting some critics to call for the "Choosin' Texas" singer to be canceled. So, what does Janson think about all of this? Well, not much, actually. Because unlike the rest of us, the "Buy Me a Boat" singer has figured out the secret to a happier existence: Stay off social media and don't read the comments. "I don't watch much internet. I don't watch much TV," Janson told OutKick OutDoors. "I hunt and fish and raise kids and love my wife." Amen to that. Watch Chris Janson's entire interview with OutKick OutDoors here: Janson said he hadn't seen the controversy involving Langley, but he's certainly familiar with the criticism that comes with being a hunter in the public eye. "If you're in the public spotlight, no matter if it's me, Jordan, Cody, it doesn't matter who it is, you better be ready for arrows to come against you and just build your shield up," he said. "I don't really care what people think. I want them to like me. I think everybody wants someone to like them, but if they don't, that's okay too." Janson said his wife, Kelly, and his team handle much of his social media, allowing him to steer clear of the negativity. And frankly, he figures people will find something to complain about no matter what he does. Post a photo of a Ford truck, and the Chevy fans are upset. Drive a Chevy, and the Dodge guys have something to say. You get the idea. Hunting for more than a trophy photo While Janson isn't particularly concerned about what strangers on the internet think of his hunting habits, he does wish more people understood everything that goes into responsible hunting. "Who doesn't love a big rack on a great big elk or a big whitetail? And who doesn't love holding up a big fish in a picture?" he said. "But I'm also a conservation guy." For starters, Janson hunts for food, and much of that food actually ends up on someone else's dinner table. "Every animal that I've harvested, at least this year, at least 50% of it has gone to someone else to help somebody," he said. "And that's a big part of why I hunt." Regulated hunting also plays an important role in wildlife management across the United States. Hunting license fees and federal excise taxes on firearms, ammunition and archery equipment help fund habitat restoration, wildlife research and conservation programs. And in some areas, hunting is an important tool for managing animal populations and reducing damage to native ecosystems. In other words, there's often a whole lot more to that grip-and-grin photo than meets the eye. Giving back beyond the hunt Janson's commitment to conservation extends beyond his own time in the woods. Since 2019, he's partnered with Bass Pro Shops founder Johnny Morris on a signature conservation hat, with proceeds benefiting three nonprofit organizations: Tennessee Hunters for the Hungry, Tennessee Riverkeeper and the Harpeth Conservancy. Through the Tennessee Wildlife Federation's Hunters for the Hungry program, hunters can donate harvested deer to participating processors, who prepare the venison for distribution to food banks and other organizations serving people in need. The other two organizations focus on protecting waterways and aquatic ecosystems, including the Harpeth River, where Janson lives. "I have a very close connection with it," Janson said of the Harpeth. "Lots of Native American history there, and just the best hunting grounds you could ever imagine." EVA SHOCKEY SAYS SHE RECEIVED 'THOUSANDS AND THOUSANDS' OF DEATH THREATS FROM ANTI-HUNTING ACTIVISTS And he's taken that same give-back approach into other business partnerships. Through Crav'n Flavor, Janson helps recognize peer-nominated hometown heroes with grocery assistance and gift cards. He's also teamed up with agricultural seed company Pioneer on its "Hats Off to Farmers" initiative, which raises money for Rural Minds, a nonprofit providing mental health resources to farmers and rural communities. The partnerships may support different causes, but Janson sees them as part of the same commitment to giving back. For him, hunting and conservation aren't just about what happens in the woods. They're about taking care of the land, the wildlife and the people who depend on both. As for the critics, Janson isn't interested in arguing with them. "For any haters out there on social media, I would just encourage them to try it," he said. "If you haven't, you can't knock it." "The hunting thing may not be your thing, and I understand that. But the fishing thing, you can throw a fish back, and there's nothing like catching a great big fish or even a small fish. It's fun." title: LEE CARTER: 2026 election could all come down to just one type of voter
description: Trump won voters who skipped 2020 and 2022 by 14 points, suggesting voter turnout could matter far more than party persuasion in the 2026 midterms.
content: For decades, political consultants have been hunting the elusive swing voter. You know her. She's sitting in a Pennsylvania diner, staring into her coffee, agonizing over whether to vote Republican or Democrat. Pollsters call her. Reporters interview her. Campaigns spend millions trying to win her over. But maybe we've been looking for the wrong person. LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN What if the most important swing voter in America isn't deciding between Republicans and Democrats? What if they're deciding between voting and staying home? As a pollster, I've spent my career studying why Americans change their minds. But the numbers suggest we should be paying a lot more attention to Americans changing their habits. EVERYONE IS WATCHING TEXAS AND MICHIGAN. AS A POLLSTER, I KNOW WHERE THE REAL STORY IS Consider 2024. According to Pew Research, 12% of voters had skipped both the 2020 presidential election and the 2022 midterms, despite being eligible to vote. THE HISPANIC VOTE IS UP FOR GRABS IN 2026. CANDIDATES WHO IGNORE IT WILL LOSE President Donald Trump won that group by 14 points. Meanwhile, the people who voted in all three elections split almost evenly: Trump 50%, Harris 48%. And of all Americans eligible to vote in those three elections, just 41% actually voted in all three. We're spending fortunes trying to convince people to switch parties while millions can't be counted on to show up in the first place. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE CONTROL COULD HINGE ON WHETHER THE OLD POLITICAL RULES STILL APPLY In 2022, Republicans won the House popular vote. But among people who voted in both 2020 and 2022, just 6% switched parties or voted for a third-party candidate in either election. As a pollster, I've spent my career studying why Americans change their minds. But the numbers suggest we should be paying a lot more attention to Americans changing their habits. What changed? Turnout. MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE Seventy-one percent of Trump's 2020 voters returned in 2022. Only 67% of President Joe Biden's did. Republicans didn't need millions of Democrats to change their minds. They benefited because more of their own voters showed up. Now consider the strange arithmetic of 2026. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Republicans have made enormous gains in voter registration since 2018. Their registration margin relative to Democrats has improved by eight percentage points in North Carolina, seven in Pennsylvania, five in Nevada and four in Arizona. These aren't polls. They're actual voter-registration records. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT But Democrats have something Republicans currently lack: greater reported enthusiasm. A new Pew survey finds 63% of Democratic House candidate supporters say they're extremely motivated to vote. Among Republican supporters, just 46% say the same. So, Republicans have strengthened their registration position. Democrats sound much more eager to vote. And neither party should be celebrating just yet. In 2022, America had its highest midterm voter-registration rate in decades. Yet fewer eligible Americans actually voted than in 2018. Apparently, filling out the paperwork is easier than finding your way to the polling place. Which is why, with less than three weeks until Election Day, I'd be paying less attention to another two-point movement in the polls and more attention to who's actually voting. Are the people who skipped the last midterms coming back? Are the voters Trump brought out in 2024 showing up without his name on the ballot? Will Democrats' enthusiasm translate into votes? And are those newly registered Republicans actually voting? Republicans have made enormous gains in voter registration since 2018. Their registration margin relative to Democrats has improved by eight percentage points in North Carolina, seven in Pennsylvania, five in Nevada and four in Arizona. These are questions neither party can afford to ignore. Of course, persuasion still matters. People change their minds. I've made a career studying how and why. But we've spent decades treating elections like a tug-of-war, with Republicans and Democrats fighting over a handful of voters standing in the middle. Sometimes the outcome changes because people switch sides. Sometimes it changes because one side shows up and the other doesn't. The swing voter hasn't disappeared. We've just been defining the swing too narrowly. The old swing voter was deciding who deserved their vote. The new swing voter doesn't necessarily switch sides. Sometimes, they switch off. title: NASCAR's most hated driver attacked again, attacker's wife gives the double-bird & why did the sport die?
description: Tyler Reddick snapped a months-long winless streak at Phoenix, but the NASCAR Cup Series title race still favors five other drivers heading to Talladega.
content: Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists. And then, there were three. That's right. Three races left in this 2026 NASCAR season. I'd give you the usual, "Doesn't it feel like we were just at the Daytona 500?" line, but ... it doesn't. This is the longest season in all of sports. It's a grind. Name another sport that starts its season in February, and ends it after Halloween. You can't. It doesn't exist. CHASE ELLIOTT SAYS NASCAR'S GRUELING 10-MONTH SEASON CAN 'EAT YOU UP' WITHOUT AN ESCAPE So yes, it's a grind. These guys are GRINDING right now. They have been for eight months now, and we only have three races left to crown a champion. After Phoenix, I'd say five guys have a legit shot at a title: Kyle Larson, Christopher Bell, Chase Briscoe, Denny Hamlin and Ryan Blaney. None of those guys won yesterday, by the way. Nope. Tyler Reddick won yesterday at Phoenix for the first time since Kansas ... back in APRIL. As I was saying (see, there's a point to all of it!), the NASCAR Cup Series season is the longest in all of sports. I bet you forgot Tyler Reddick started the season with three straight wins, didn't you? Sunday's return to Victory Lane was probably too little, too late in terms of a title, but it does give him a puncher's chance. We'll see. Speaking of punching ... wait till you see what Zane Smith did to Carson Hocevar after the race. Do these two HATE each other, or what? Also, I've seen a lot of folks comparing modern day college football to peak NASCAR in terms of recent decision-making about playoff expansion. Some people believe college football is following the same ill-fated path NASCAR took way back in the day. THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF IS SACRIFICING ITS SOUL TO BE AN ATM FOR CONFERENCES WITH EXPANSION TO 24 TEAMS Honestly, it's not the worst comparison I've seen. We'll dive in here in a bit. Four tires, enough fuel to get us through three more races, and maybe a neck brace for Carson Hocevar ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'Wreckers After Checkers' edition — is LIVE! Zane Smith says hello to Carson! Let's spin the wheel and get this class started with ... BEEF! We love beef around here. It's what keeps me in a job, and what keeps this column an award-winner (allegedly). All the beef this season has revolved around Carson Hocevar. Pretty much all of it. If there's been an issue, Carson's somehow been involved. ROSS CHASTAIN CALLS RYAN BLANEY'S FIGHT WITH CARSON HOCEVAR AT BRISTOL MOTOR SPEEDWAY 'NASCAR 101' Whether it was Ryan Blaney attacking him last month at Bristol, or Brad Keselowski vowing to wreck him after Darlington, it's been the Garage vs. Carson in 2026. Hell, I'm not sure he even has one single ally in the entire garage. Not one. Least of all, by the way, is Zane Smith. Nobody — and I mean nobody — hates Carson more than Zane Smith: This rivalry goes back a while Lordy. You don't see that often, do you? Zane hits the gas and absolutely plows into Carson's backside (hey now!) ... and it was all for literally no reason at all. Carson, as you can see in the first video, did nothing wrong. Nada. Zero. Zilch. Ross Chastain got into Hocevar, which sent Hocevar up the track into Zane Smith. Clear as day. "I don't give a f–k," Smith said when he was told that info after the post-race fender-bender. Alllllll righty then! Clearly, this had nothing to do with the contact in the race, and everything to do with Zane Smith simply just looking for a reason to start a fight with a driver he admittedly despises. And I mean DESPISES. Take a look at this little clip from last summer: "I just don't like him as a human," is such a simple insult. Simple, and hilarious. You have to respect that, despite who you root for on the track. Calling him a "goon" was also funny. I may not agree with what Zane did yesterday, but I do think he's funny. I also very much appreciate his wife, OutKick OG, McCall Gaulding. She also hates Carson Hocevar, and has been incredibly open about it. I don't want to get into specifics, but if you're interested, I sort of talked about it last month after the Bristol stuff. More importantly — at least to me — McCall's also really good at pumping out Instagram content ... like this post from last week where the second slide features McCall wearing what appears to be only a T-shirt featuring her and Zane giving the double-bird. Patriot: Is college football making a NASCAR-sized mistake? Amazing. McCall has been an OutKick legend for years now — way before she became this Instagram superstar. We know how to spot talent around here, and we identified McCall early. Clearly, she's still got the fastball here in 2026. Head on a swivel, Carson! OK, let's put the pedal to the floor and rapid-fire this third-Monday-of-October in a big Talladega week. First up? Yes, Tyler Reddick won yesterday for the first time in months. Yes, it was a season-saving win given it keeps him in the championship discussion. No, it probably won't be enough ... But never say never: There you have it. The standings with three races to go, including this weekend's Big One in Talladega. Anything can — and will — happen at 'Dega. What happens if Larson and Bell, Briscoe and Hamlin are all caught up in a wreck early in the race? It sort of blows the door wide open for anyone behind them, right? Again, it's unlikely, but not completely out of the question. This is always my favorite race of the season. I expect this weekend to be no different. Next? On the way out, I'd like to give everyone in class some homework for the week, and it revolves around this now-viral X post in the wake of college football's decision to move to a 24-team playoff: NASCAR went from the second most watched sport to nothing by implementing postseason gimmicks and chasing a mainstream audience. They tried to undo it but they had their lowest ratings ever for the 2025 title race. I never thought we’d see another sport be so shortsighted. Thoughts? First impressions? I don't think NASCAR's massive ratings decline is because of the implementation of a playoff (The Chase) back in 2004. I don't. Ratings were just fine in '04, '05, '06 and '07. I think NASCAR had a lot working against them — a lot of it self-inflicted, and some of it not. Those are just a couple things that come to mind, by the way. I'm sure y'all have more. As always, let me know! Zach.Dean@OutKick.com. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP See ya at 'Dega.

title: Ancient DNA challenges theories about when humans first reached North America
description: University of Kansas researchers reviewed ancient DNA and 23,000-year-old White Sands footprints to trace early human migration into North America.
content: Researchers examining ancient DNA have narrowed down the timeline of early human migration into North America — shedding light on a question that's puzzled scientists for decades. The study, published online ahead of its appearance in the December 2026 issue of the journal Current Opinion in Genetics & Development, looked at previously published genetic and archaeological evidence to better understand when humans first arrived in the Americas. Genetic evidence most strongly supports humans reaching the Americas between 14,000 and 20,000 years ago, the study suggests — with an arrival before 15,000 years ago considered likely. CAVE DISCOVERY PUSHES BACK EVIDENCE OF HUMAN ANCESTORS USING FIRE TO 1.79M YEARS AGO Previously, scientists thought the first humans arrived in North America roughly 13,500 years ago, a theory known as "Clovis First." Later archaeological discoveries have challenged that timeline, suggesting humans may have reached North America thousands of years earlier. The researchers, led by Bethany Potter and Savannah Hay of the University of Kansas, reviewed existing ancient DNA and archaeological evidence, including 23,000-year-old human footprints found at White Sands National Park in New Mexico. The footprints suggest humans may have inhabited North America earlier than the timeline supported by currently available genetic evidence. DNA FROM THOMAS JEFFERSON'S HAIR DELIVERS COMPELLING NEW EVIDENCE IN CENTURIES-OLD PATERNITY MYSTERY Such early populations could have belonged to genetic lineages that have not yet been sampled or that left no surviving descendants, the researchers said. By comparing previously published genetic data from ancient human remains in Asia and the Americas, researchers examined shared ancestry to trace how early Indigenous populations split into distinct groups. Some ancestral lineages diverged roughly 21,000 years ago, according to the review. The researchers also highlighted evidence that ancestral Native American populations split into northern and southern groups roughly 15,500 years ago, likely south of the massive ice sheets that once covered much of North America. "Genomic data show us that the dynamics of the peopling of the Americas were quite different — at one point, a small group of people must have entered the American continents completely devoid of other humans," the researchers wrote. "The timing and geographic location of key divergence events mentioned above remain uncertain," the authors wrote. title: Adult children cutting off parents as some blame therapy for family estrangements
description: Richard Blake says therapy culture has raised the bar on parenting and may fuel parent-child estrangement through an overcorrection in cutoff culture.
content: Amid a reported surge in parent-child estrangements, some have questioned whether therapy could play a role in the family fracture trend. Nearly four in 10 Americans are currently estranged from at least one close family member, according to a 2025 YouGov poll of 4,395 U.S. adults, including 24% from a sibling, 16% from a parent and 10% from a child. While therapy can be helpful in facilitating communication and mending relationships, some believe it could contribute to "cutoff culture." 5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST In two recent large-scale surveys of over 5,200 U.S. parents who were estranged from adult children, 1,014 parents reported that their children began therapy within the year before the estrangement. Meanwhile, 515 parents reported that their adult children had indicated therapy influenced their decision about the relationship, and 1,254 said their child had received a mental health diagnosis. (The surveys were not peer-reviewed or nationally representative and relied on parents' accounts of their adult children’s experiences, limiting what can be concluded about therapy’s role in estrangement.) The therapy debate Richard Blake, Ph.D., a Texas-based psychology researcher with a focus on anxiety and family estrangement, refers to the trend as an "overcorrection" happening in today’s society. "There is a lot of debate online about whether it's happening or not," Blake, who was a researcher in the surveys referenced above and has written a book about how therapy could be fueling family estrangement, told Fox News Digital. "I hear it from both sides. I hear from parents who say, ‘My child said my therapist should cut you off,’ and people who've told me, ‘My therapist told me I should cut my parents off.’ How much it's happening and when it's appropriate and inappropriate is where the nuance comes in." Laura Wellington, a Connecticut mother who has been estranged from her adult daughter since 2024, also weighed in on the potential role therapists play in the growing divide. "Therapy has sort of raised the bar of what is good enough parenting." "Do therapists, in my opinion, play a role in the estrangement epidemic? 100%," she told Fox News Digital. "But that doesn't mean there aren't some really good therapists out there." Wellington, known on social media as "Doormat Mom," said she believes some therapists have contributed to family fractures by focusing too narrowly on one person's experience, when it’s actually a "multi-pronged situation." CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT She said some therapists have even contacted her to reconsider their approach to estrangement cases. "I've had them come to me and ask me, ‘What did we miss?’" she said. Wellington added that she has seen parents encouraged to apologize to their adult children — something she supports when the parent has done something wrong — but believes therapists should consider the broader circumstances surrounding the estrangement. What's driving the divide Differences in values can contribute to family fractures, even in the absence of severe behavior such as violence or abuse, according to Blake. "People are cutting people off because of divergence in values," he said. As one example, Blake pointed to a recent online comment in which someone wrote, "I cut my parents off because they didn't condemn ICE enough." At the same time, he emphasized that there are legitimate circumstances in which ending contact with a parent may be warranted, including physical or sexual abuse. "Then you get into the sort of very murky area of emotional abuse, and this is where therapy culture comes in," Blake added. WHEN IS A MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS TOO SEVERE FOR TELEHEALTH? WARNING SIGNS FAMILIES SHOULDN'T IGNORE The researcher said he believes the term "emotional abuse" is sometimes applied more broadly in therapy and online spaces, particularly in conflicts over politics, religion and language. "Emotional abuse can be [about] differing political values, a little difference in religious beliefs," he said. "It can be about the words people use." "If you don't listen to your child, then don't be surprised if you have conflict with them." What a parent views as legitimate criticism can sometimes be interpreted as emotional abuse by an adult child, according to Blake. "Therapy has sort of raised the bar of what is good enough parenting," he added. "There's just a massive sort of overselling in therapy of how much your parents affected you." In some cases, Blake said, he will hear from parents that their children never told them the issue that led to them being cut off. "They’ll say, ‘We were best friends. And then I got a letter saying, ‘never contact me ever again.’" Blake emphasized, however, that it’s important for parents to listen if the adult child makes an attempt to communicate. 1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC "A frequent complaint that most adult children make is, ‘My parents just don't listen. I cannot get through to them. It's like talking to a brick wall,’" he said. "And that is a genuine frustration." "If you don't listen to your child, then don't be surprised if you have conflict with them." Blake recommended active listening techniques, such as allowing the other person to speak without interruption, repeating their concerns back to show understanding, and asking whether they have more to share before offering a response. Blake emphasized that his concerns do not apply to all therapists, saying only a "small subset" may view cutting off family members as an appropriate response to conflict. In situations involving ordinary family conflict rather than abuse, he cautioned that ending contact can have longer-term repercussions even if it initially brings relief. ‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT "It makes you feel good, but there are consequences afterwards — very serious consequences," Blake said. He also challenged the idea that the sole act of cutting off a parent will necessarily resolve underlying mental health struggles. "This is the sort of myth that pervades in cutoff cultures, like, ‘I needed to cut my parents off to protect my mental health,’" he said. The assumption, he added, is: "My parents were the cause of my mental health issues, therefore cutting them out resolves that issue." Other experts have emphasized that people's experiences with therapy during family estrangement can vary. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Lucy Blake, Ph.D., a developmental psychologist in the U.K. who studies family estrangement, told the American Psychological Association that therapy can be "very helpful" in some cases. "I think people can find therapy very helpful if their therapist has an understanding of estrangement, so some appreciation that it’s rarely one relationship that’s affected when there’s an estrangement," she said. "This is the sort of myth that pervades in cutoff cultures." Therapy can also be beneficial when therapists understand underlying factors that can contribute to family estrangement, such as abuse or mental health challenges, the psychologist noted. Blake has also heard from people who found therapy "very unhelpful," particularly when they felt their therapist lacked warmth and validation or did not understand the "enormous impact" of estrangement and the grief and loss that can accompany it. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Overall, Blake said therapy can be a "really helpful avenue of support" for some, while noting that researchers are "still really learning" what is helpful or unhelpful for people experiencing estrangement. Finding a path forward For families experiencing conflict, bringing in a neutral third party may be a better option when both sides are willing to participate, experts agree. "Communication with a mediator, whether it’s a therapist or a professional mediator, can be really productive," said Richard Blake. Once a family member has already ended communication and asked not to be contacted, however, getting both sides into therapy may no longer be an option. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I certainly think it’s worth a try," he said of mediation. "I know a lot of very good mediators out there who can help people." Wellington agreed that bringing parents and adult children into therapy together could be helpful, although both sides need to be willing to repair the relationship. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ She also added that differing beliefs do not necessarily have to end a relationship. "You can have a different opinion," she said. "You can also have a relationship with your parent who has the other opinion, and that's OK."

title: 'You Can See Everything' Review: The buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary is worth the hype
description: Fox News Digital reviews A24's new documentary "You Can See Everything" featuring disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes. Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.
content: The best documentaries don't feel like documentaries. They have a connotation of being educational, but even career documentarians will tell you that all they're doing is telling a story just like any other film. Well, A24's "You Can See Everything" is not like any other film, nor is it like any other documentary. Comedian Nathan Fielder shocked the internet during the festival circuit earlier this year when he unveiled a documentary he spent three years developing featuring Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced Theranos founder who granted him unfettered access in the 34 days leading up to her 11-year prison sentence in 2023. ‘WHALEFALL’ REVIEW: AUSTIN ABRAMS IS SWALLOWED BY A SPERM WHALE IN IMMERSIVE SURVIVAL DRAMA You likely know the story already: Holmes became a media darling in the mid-2010s as her company had allegedly developed a medical device that can detect virtually all diseases from a single drop of blood. However, investigative reporting by The Wall Street Journal led to her downfall and she was ultimately found guilty of defrauding investors in 2022. Having lived in obscurity since the collapse of Theranos, Holmes providing unprecedented access to Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim certainly turned heads. Fielder serves as our on-camera shepherd, spending intimate moments with her, her husband Billy Evans and their two infant children. He isn't shy about expressing his skepticism towards Holmes and Evans as she maintains her innocence while the two of them are in the early stages of scheming a major comeback for what can be dubbed "Theranos 2.0." Both Fielder and the audience alike stare into Holmes' big blue eyes above her porcelain red cheeks, hoping to read between the lines of whether she's being as authentic as she claims to be or if she's the cunning manipulator the world believes she is. ‘THE SOCIAL RECKONING’ REVIEW: ZUCKERBERG, FACEBOOK ARE THE ENEMY IN PREACHY SLOP DISGUISED AS JOURNO DRAMA What's remarkable about "You Can See Everything" is how it becomes increasingly indiscernible on who we can really trust as the documentary progresses. Her husband is a peculiar character in his own right, and we begin to suspect his motives. We even start to question the filmmakers behind the documentary at one point, thanks in part to Fielder and Oppenheim pulling back the curtain. A fun psychological thriller develops in the process. While not notorious like Holmes, Fielder made a name for himself as the host of Comedy Central's "Nathan For You" and HBO's "The Rehearsal," both of which are part comedies, part docuseries. For comedic effect, Fielder often blurs the lines of what documentaries are supposed to do. So the strange twist and turns "You Can See Everything" takes in the second act may not exactly shock those who are familiar with his work, but the direction it goes is spellbinding nonetheless. Fielder is as awkward as he is hilarious, and the way he often uses bluntness to seek the truth is amusing. Despite the nearly three-hour runtime, it doesn't drag thanks to editor Adam Locke-Norton. The cinematography by David Bolen and the score from composer Ari Balouzian (both of whom also worked on Oppenheim's "Primetime") add to the documentary's high production value. And the internet rumors about Charlie Kirk being invoked in this documentary are true. I'll leave it to you as to how he comes up. DIGGER REVIEW: TOM CRUISE DESTROYS THE PLANET IN ALEJANDRO IÑÁRRITU'S GRANDIOSE, MESSY POLITICAL SATIRE CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS The Verdict: Films are a dime a dozen, but a cinematic experience is rare. "You Can See Everything" is not just a fascinating, thought-provoking documentary starring one of the 21st century's most vilified figures, it challenges the entire medium. And it's even more fun when you're able to discuss it with others after, so it's best not to go stag. Don't miss one of the biggest and best surprises of 2026 at the movies. ★★★★ — SEE IT NOW "You Can See Everything" is rated R for language and some graphic nudity. Running time: 2 hours, 54 minutes. In theaters now. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

title: SCOTT WALKER: Just three votes on one ballot helped decide Wisconsin’s future
description: Tyler August won his Wisconsin State Assembly primary by just three votes in a recount, launching one of the state's most consequential careers.
content: Three votes. That is the margin that helped launch one of the most consequential political careers in modern Wisconsin state government. In September 2010, Tyler August was a 27-year-old candidate running in a six-way Republican primary for an open seat in the Wisconsin State Assembly. When election night ended, it appeared he had lost. Adam Gibbs was reported ahead by four votes. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY Then came the recount. When it was finished, August had won 1,760 votes to Gibbs’ 1,757. Three votes. Out of more than 7,300 cast. Fewer people than fit around most kitchen tables separated winning from losing. GEORGIA VOTERS SET EARLY-VOTING RECORD AS MIDTERM ELECTIONS HEAT UP August went on to win the general election that November. Sixteen years later, he serves as majority leader of the Wisconsin State Assembly, one of the most powerful positions in state government. Think about everything that had to pass through that three-vote doorway first. Every vote he has cast in the legislature. Every bill he has introduced. Every budget he has helped shape. Every negotiation, committee assignment and leadership decision that came afterward. Every Wisconsin family, worker or business affected by legislation enacted during his time in office. None of it happens the same way if that primary ends differently. That is the part we tend to forget when we say our vote "doesn’t matter." August went on to win the general election that November. Sixteen years later, he serves as majority leader of the Wisconsin State Assembly, one of the most powerful positions in state government. We imagine elections as enormous things. Millions of people. Billions of dollars. Television ads, polling averages, consultants, candidates and endless political noise. Against all of that, one person standing in a voting booth can feel almost comically insignificant. But elections are not actually decided by "the electorate." They are decided by individual people, one ballot at a time. And my home state of Wisconsin offers a remarkable example of just how thin the distance between two outcomes can be. FOX NEWS POLL: COST-OF-LIVING CONCERNS WEIGH ON GOP IN MIDTERMS In the 2020 presidential election, more than 3.2 million Wisconsinites cast ballots. The final margin was 20,682 votes. Only Georgia and Arizona had narrower margins by percentage, with their presidential contests decided by just 11,779 and 10,457 votes, respectively. Four years later, more than 3.4 million Wisconsinites voted, and the presidential margin was 29,397, making Wisconsin the closest state in the country by percentage of votes cast. Those numbers sound large until you compare them with the millions of ballots cast. Then there is Tyler August. Three. Wisconsin's experience offers a lesson for voters across America: No election should be treated as a foregone conclusion. And the consequences stretch far beyond which name appears on an office door. GINGRICH: NOBODY SHOULD ASSUME THIS ELECTION IS OVER State and local governments across the country make decisions every year about taxes, regulations, housing, licensing, education, infrastructure, employment rules and the cost of doing business. Those decisions determine how easy it is to open a storefront, hire another employee, build a home, expand a farm or invest in a community. In the 2020 presidential election, more than 3.2 million Wisconsinites cast ballots. The final margin was 20,682 votes. Only Georgia and Arizona had narrower margins by percentage, with their presidential contests decided by just 11,779 and 10,457 votes, respectively. Free enterprise does not exist separately from government policy. The rules government writes shape the environment in which people take risks, build businesses and create opportunity. Which means the people who write those rules matter. And the people who choose them matter too. Voting is sometimes talked about as an expression of personal identity. Increasingly, politics itself feels that way. Pick a team, wear the jersey, argue about it online. But a ballot is much more practical than that. It is one of the few moments when every citizen gets the exact same unit of political power. One person. One vote. The business owner with 40 employees gets one. The college student voting for the first time gets one. The retiree who has voted in every election for 50 years gets one. So does the person who nearly stays home because the weather is lousy, the line might be long, they have errands to run, or they assume everyone else will decide the outcome anyway. The margin between having political power and never getting the opportunity to exercise it can be three people. And somewhere in southeastern Wisconsin are voters who helped create that margin. They probably went home that night without feeling particularly powerful. Free enterprise does not exist separately from government policy. The rules government writes shape the environment in which people take risks, build businesses and create opportunity. They were. On Nov. 3, Americans across the country will make thousands of similarly unremarkable choices. Get up early or hit snooze. Stop at the polling place or drive past it. Return the absentee ballot or leave it sitting on the kitchen counter. Most of us will never know precisely what depended on our decision. That is the point. Democracy asks us to participate before we know whether our vote will be one of the millions or one of the three. Whether you live in Wisconsin or somewhere else in America, the first step is knowing when, where and how to vote. Check your registration status, find your polling place and make a plan for Nov. 3. Election information and registration requirements are available through your state or local election office. So, vote for the candidates you believe will make your community, your state and your country stronger. Vote for the policies and principles you want represented in your state capital and Washington. But vote. Because somewhere in Wisconsin history are voters who helped create a three-vote margin, proving that the difference between "my vote probably won’t matter" and changing the direction of government can be almost impossibly small. title: NFL Week 6 Sunday takeaways: Giants have a new QB1, Bills keep rolling and Shane Steichen is on the hot seat
description: J.J. McCarthy sparked a Giants quarterback controversy with a furious NFL Week 6 comeback, while the Browns climbed into first in the AFC North.
content: Six weeks into the NFL season, the Giants and Browns are in first place, the Eagles should probably start thinking about next year, and I'm still not buying the Jaguars hype. Just a perfectly normal Sunday. We also got a reminder that a big fourth-quarter lead is only comfortable until your team decides to stop playing football. The Bears nearly turned a blowout into a disaster, and the Giants somehow went from getting embarrassed to creating a quarterback controversy. If you figured either game was over early and changed the channel, I can't blame you. But you missed a few things. Here's my biggest takeaway from each game on the Week 6 Sunday slate. Texans 34, Jaguars 31 Takeaway: I tried to warn y'all about jumping on the Jaguars bandwagon. Look, this isn't to say Jacksonville isn't a solid team. But the media was very quick to anoint them as a major contender in the AFC. I've said many times that this team isn't nearly as good as everyone thinks, and that showed against the 1-4 Texans. Jacksonville even had the advantage of already being in London, while Houston had to travel across the pond this week. FORMER NFL QB SEAN SALISBURY WANTS OFFICIALS TO FACE POSTGAME QUESTIONS LIKE PLAYERS AND COACHES The Jaguars allowed C.J. Stroud to throw for 312 yards and three touchdowns. Trevor Lawrence is definitely playing some of the best football of his career and the Jags are the best team in the AFC South. But they're not a true AFC Championship contender right now. Browns 13, Ravens 10 Takeaway: Don't look now, but the Browns are in first place. Well, kinda. With the upset win over the Ravens, Cleveland moves to 4-2 and into a tie with Baltimore and Pittsburgh. Yes, the Ravens were missing Lamar Jackson, but this was a huge win for the Browns. I don't think many people, myself included, would have predicted that Deshaun Watson and the Cleveland Browns would be 4-2 and tied for the AFC North lead after six games. Watson only threw for 164 yards and he still doesn't look that good, but, as the great philosopher Bill Parcells once said, "You are what your record says you are." Right now, it says the Browns are 4-2. Saints 34, Giants 27 Takeaway: There's a new QB1 in New York. Jameis Winston showed some of that Jameis magic in Week 5 when he led the team from two touchdowns down in the second half to force overtime and eventually a tie against the Commanders. But the magic wasn't there in Week 6. Winston threw two interceptions before New York turned to the recently acquired J.J. McCarthy … who promptly threw an interception of his own. But even after the rough start, McCarthy rebounded to lead three consecutive scoring drives, cutting the 34-10 deficit to 34-27. He finished with 243 passing yards and a touchdown pass in just over 11 minutes. He even moved the team to the Saints' 14-yard line in the final seconds, but couldn't quite make the game-tying play. Still, it's pretty clear that this team (which is in first place, by the way) has to give the reins to McCarthy moving forward. Titans 26, Colts 20 Takeaway: Shane Steichen's seat should be red hot. Losing to the previously winless Tennessee Titans at home is nearly a fireable offense on its own, especially when your team had a 13-0 lead at halftime. Last season, Steichen could point to Daniel Jones' season-ending Achilles tear in Week 14 last year as the Colts' season unraveled. This year, Jones is healthy and playing as badly as he did at times with the Giants. Jones threw two picks and was sacked six times. The offensive line struggled, but Jones holding the ball too long didn't help. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Panthers 25, Eagles 14 Takeaway: I want to feel bad for Nick Sirianni, but I don't. The Eagles placed Jalen Hurts on injured reserve Saturday because of a superficial blood clot in his calf, sidelining him for at least four games. His health is obviously the priority, and his absence isn't Sirianni's fault. And yes, playing with a backup QB is always tough. But scoring just 14 points against a Carolina defense that allowed 59 points earlier this season is not good enough. This is a Philadelphia team that should already be looking ahead to 2027, but whether Sirianni is still the head coach next year remains to be seen. My money is on no. Patriots 26, Jets 19 Takeaway: The Patriots still don't look like the defending AFC champions. Yes, the Patriots won. But it wasn't particularly pretty. They let the Jets hang around for most of the game, thanks in large part to two costly fumbles. Drake Maye is looking more comfortable as the season goes along, but a team like the Patriots shouldn't have this tough a time with the Jets at home. The defense clamped down in the red zone and on two crucial fourth-down plays, but still allowed New York to gain 324 yards. Bears 31, Falcons 23 Takeaway: The Bears have to finish better than that if they want to be true NFC contenders. The NFC is starting to look wide open beyond the unbeaten 49ers, and the Bears have a chance to make a run. But head coach Ben Johnson isn't going to be happy that his team nearly blew a 24-point lead with just over 12 minutes to go. Not only did the defense allow two quick touchdowns (and two two-point conversions), including one on a 91-yard drive that took just 2:38, but the offense went three-and-out, fumble, three-and-out on three consecutive fourth-quarter possessions. Atlanta had the ball with a chance to tie, and the defense redeemed itself with a strip-sack, but it got a little too close for comfort. Johnson had pulled most of his starting defense with Thursday night's game against the Patriots in mind, but this should serve as a reminder to the second-year head coach that the game isn't over until it's over. Steelers 26, Buccaneers 19 (OT) Takeaway: Teams should stop electing to kick off in overtime. I understand the strategy of wanting to know what the other team does before you get the ball. Here's the problem: regular-season overtime is only 10 minutes. The Bucs became the latest team to kick off and then watch their opponent run nearly seven minutes off the clock before scoring a touchdown. The Steelers got to run their normal offense, while Tampa Bay was forced into a must-throw hurry-up offense. Plus, if overtime becomes a three-possession period, the receiving team has the advantage. Adding it all up, it should be clear that receiving the ball in OT is the correct decision. Cardinals 18, Rams 16 Takeaway: So much for the superteam. Look, I still think the Los Angeles Rams are a good football team. But, as I wrote earlier, "you are what your record says you are." Right now, their 2-4 record doesn't say anything good about the preseason Super Bowl favorites. The Rams are too talented to struggle all season, but they should have serious concerns about the offensive line. Matthew Stafford was under duress all game, and he struggled badly when pressured, as he has all year. The upcoming schedule isn't overly difficult, so they can turn it around, but they did just lose to the Cardinals, so the opponents might not matter as much as the Rams would like. Yes, another questionable call helped cost the Rams a win. But it's their own fault for being in that position against a team that entered with one win. RAMS HAVE LEGITIMATE GRIPE WITH NFL OFFICIALS, BUT 2-4 RECORD IS A BIGGER PROBLEM Bills 33, Raiders 30 Takeaway: Josh Allen is a magician. If you didn't see Allen's ridiculous touchdown pass to Keon Coleman, I suggest you go take a look. The 2024 NFL MVP is in MVP form again this season, and the Bills are 5-1 and leading the AFC East. This is a good win for a Buffalo team that is wrapping up a two-game trip out West, beating the preseason Super Bowl favorite Rams and the better-than-expected Raiders. But, as we know, Allen's career isn't defined by his regular-season success. Buffalo is well on its way to another playoff berth, and Allen needs to finally break through and lead his team to the Super Bowl. Chiefs 22, Chargers 6 Takeaway: Do Chargers fans miss Brandon Staley yet? I kid. Sort of. But Staley was hated and run out of Los Angeles after posting a 24-24 regular-season record and zero playoff wins in nearly three seasons. Jim Harbaugh was hired to much fanfare, but he's now 22-18 in the regular season with zero playoff wins as the Chargers head coach. And it doesn't look like he's going to win a playoff game this year, since Los Angeles is basically out of it in Week 6. Say what you want about Staley, but none of his three Chargers teams started 0-6. Packers 23, Cowboys 13 Takeaway: The Cowboys are all hype, no bite... again. Feels like every year we hear, "This is going to be the Cowboys' year!" And, every year, it isn't. Dallas had a ton of hype surrounding it in the preseason, per usual, but this season actually felt a little different. Dallas used two first-round picks on safety Caleb Downs and edge rusher Malachi Lawrence to try to fix a defense that was basically a sieve in 2025.
