title: Our kids aren’t broken; we need to stop treating every struggle like a disorder
description: A neuropsychologist explains why a student scoring 34 on the ACT still felt like a failure and sought test accommodations for a perfect score.
content: My patient, Zach, was an objectively awesome tenth grader. He was academically talented and motivated, with a mix of A's and A-minuses in accelerated classes. He was a starter on the varsity basketball team. He did Math Olympiad. He even played the French horn in the school band, though he admitted that was mostly for his college application and to get out of an art history requirement that had a reputation for being pretty onerous. He started preparing for the ACT in April of his sophomore year, hoping to get it over with the following fall. His tutor charged $800 an hour, with a minimum of two-hour sessions, twice a week. Within weeks, he was in my office complaining that there was no way he was going to do well. STUDENTS DIVIDED OVER UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN HIDING FIRST-SEMESTER GRADES FOR 2027 FRESHMEN He couldn't get the pacing right and never finished all the questions in the allowed time. Mind you, he was consistently getting 34s on his practice tests. A perfect score on the ACT is 36. It's an exceptionally rare score. And Zach was very close to it. But Zach wanted to go to the University of Pennsylvania, and he said a 34 still wasn't good enough. Zach was already in the top percentile of test takers nationally, and he still felt like a failure. I am a clinical neuropsychologist. I offer psychotherapy and cognitive remediation to children with learning disorders and related developmental disorders. Zach came to see me because he wanted me to write him a letter saying he needed testing accommodations. Maybe with time-and-a-half he’d get the perfect score he really needed. When nothing is enough, when excellence is the minimum acceptable, we fall short. And when we fall short, we reach for labels and accommodations and services to close the gap. Of course, sometimes children have real disorders and disabilities, and labels and supports are crucial. But in other cases, the struggles are healthy, normal parts of development, and medicalizing them backfires. The supposed quick fixes may seem helpful in the moment, but more often than not, they make kids even more miserable. How we learn to live by the numbers Zach isn't alone in his anxiety about scores and percentiles. We're all socialized to care about measurements, and we think about how our data compare to everyone else's. From day one, pediatricians measure our kids' height, weight and even head circumference and tell us where those numbers fall relative to same-age peers. I remember my son's first checkup. I was so excited to hear that my chunky little guy was in the 95th percentile for both height and weight. When nothing is enough, when excellence is the minimum acceptable, we fall short. And when we fall short, we reach for labels and accommodations and services to close the gap. It’s only a matter of time before our obsession with toddler head circumference turns into an obsession with teenage ACT scores. We get emotionally attached to these numbers. We give them more importance than they deserve, and we read them more negatively than we should. I talk to parents all the time who are worried about a score in the 37th percentile. In reality, the 37th percentile is solidly average. More isn't better What I usually explain to parents is that, in most domains, more isn't better. The average range is wide, and it's the middle that’s often optimal. Take attention. With too little, we have trouble in school. With too much, we become hypervigilant about tiny, insignificant details and lose the forest for the trees. Anxiety works the same way. Too much and you can't leave the house; too little and you're reckless, walking into oncoming traffic. We want to land somewhere near the healthy middle. UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN PLANS TO SHIELD 2027 FRESHMAN LETTER GRADES FROM TRANSCRIPTS IN NEW MENTAL HEALTH PLAN Most scores are also imperfect descriptors of what we can do. We try hard to measure and quantify our traits and abilities, but those measurements are snapshots in time. How we do in a given domain today isn’t necessarily a good predictor of how we'll do tomorrow, since we’re constantly learning, developing, and growing. Also, there's always measurement error. Scores are estimates, not absolutes. And, finally, the best predictors of success are things like perseverance, creativity and people skills, which usually can't be measured at all. The squeeze from both ends But we're human, and we feel the squeeze from both ends. If our kids are struggling, we see a disorder, and, like Zach, we look for a diagnosis and accommodations. If our kids excel, we worry they're perfectionistic, people-pleasing or anxious. We can't win. The messy middle, where most healthy development actually happens, seems to have disappeared. And this tendency to pathologize everything is making our kids miserable. GAVIN NEWSOM AVOIDS QUESTION ON BRINGING BACK SAT SCORES AFTER UC OPEN LETTER, ASKS 'SHOW ME THE DATA' Nothing is free We bring in interventions and services to fix the problem, thinking, "What's the harm? It can't hurt." But there's an opportunity cost to everything. Every minute and every dollar spent on some kind of therapy is a minute and a dollar not spent on soccer practice, day camp, playdates or regular old homework. The choice isn't between an intervention and doing nothing. It's between an intervention and doing something else with that time and money, something that might bring our kid joy and enrichment (and might even build the perseverance, creativity, and people skills I mentioned earlier). Working against their mental health We mobilize all these supports to protect our kids' mental health, but we might actually be working against it. Start with depression. Depression is characterized by helplessness and an external locus of control, the feeling that we aren't in charge of our own destinies. Diagnostic labels locate problems in the brain, outside of kids' control. And when outcomes seem to hinge on rankings and status and paid accommodations, effort stops feeling like it matters. We need to reframe ‘average’ as good and talk about rankings differently. We need to broaden what counts as success. Anxiety is similar. Anxiety is maintained by avoidance, and the best treatment involves exposure to the feared thing. When we provide an accommodation that lets our kid avoid whatever seems hard, it brings short-term relief. But we deprive them of the opportunity to learn how to cope. They don’t internalize the message that they can do hard things, and the anxiety grows. We accommodate to relieve the pressure, but the accommodation actually keeps the stress going. I WORRY LESS ABOUT SCREENS THAN ABOUT THE CHALLENGES TODAY’S TEENS NEVER FACE We get swept up, too Of course, we want the best for our kids. I'm not saying we're hurting them on purpose. We get swept up in the same pressure they do. And how could we not? There's so much mom guilt. We're constantly told that every little decision we make on our kids' behalf matters, and we're trying to navigate an impossible landscape, bombarded with conflicting information. It's hard to separate what's valuable from what isn't, especially with a robust influencer economy that literally profits from our feelings of inadequacy. In that context, a diagnosis makes sense. It partly absolves us, and it offers a clear fix. So what do we do instead? If the diagnosis isn't the solution, what is? CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION We need to reframe "average" as good and talk about rankings differently. We need to broaden what counts as success. We can actively work against helplessness by giving kids real control and crediting their effort and hard work. We can reduce their anxiety by supporting them through hard things instead of constantly removing obstacles. And we have to be honest with ourselves about the difference between support and enabling. Most important, we should trust our instincts. When there's a real problem, it's usually obvious. In that case, seek help. When there isn't, take a deep breath. Support your kid informally. The struggle will pass, and, most likely, it will be a blip on the radar, eventually not mattering nearly as much as we think. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Zach will probably get into a really good college whether he gets a 34 or a 33 or a 35. And he'll probably be a happy, successful human regardless of where he goes to college. Development is resilient. Let's be resilient, too. title: Ilhan Omar should be jailed, deported if citizenship fraud is proven, Top House Republican says
description: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer says Ilhan Omar should serve jail time and be deported if the federal investigation proves she lied on paperwork.
content: EXCLUSIVE: The highest-ranking House lawmaker from Rep. Ilhan Omar's home state is calling for the embattled progressive to be jailed and deported if it is found that she or her father lied on federal paperwork to get her U.S. citizenship. Omar, D-Minn., is under federal investigation over allegations she or her father lied about her birth year on immigration paperwork to obtain her citizenship when her family fled Somalia in the late 1990s. She and other Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., have denounced the probe as political persecution of one of President Donald Trump's detractors weeks before a critical election. But Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., the No. 3 leader in the House of Representatives, told Fox News Digital "there have been rumors for years" about Omar and, if proven true, she should face consequences. "I would say, first, she should probably serve time in the gray bar motel and then get the hell out of here. She should go back to where she came from" if the allegations are proven to be true, Emmer said. "If it's determined that she lied to gain citizenship, then, absolutely, she should go back to the front of the line." REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES Omar is a member of the House "Squad," a far-left clique that includes Reps. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION Federal agents raided Omar's Washington, D.C., home earlier this week and took her cellphone and other possessions. The allegations stem from her father becoming a U.S. citizen in 2000. Omar was believed to be 17 at the time, and, as a minor, automatically qualified for citizenship under U.S. law along with him. HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’ But, recently, it’s been alleged she was actually 18 and would have needed to go through the process herself at that point. "I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," Omar posted on X after the raid. "I will not be silenced." DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ Omar’s allies and other critics of the probe have called it an unprecedented action with less than three weeks before Election Day Nov. 3. Jeffries and his top deputies said in a joint statement that the raid was "deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries." Emmer argued it was not political. He said the existence of a judicially authorized search warrant, which the Department of Justice (DOJ) said was being acted on, meant there was a reasonable basis to believe the allegations could be true. "That judge had to determine that there was probable cause that a federal crime has been committed. And I'll tell you what, as long as it was Ilhan Omar, it was going to be scrutinized to the very detail," Emmer said. "So, the fact that they issued the warrant in the first place and then executed it, I mean, maybe after all these years, someone is finally going to hold Ilhan Omar accountable." Fox News Digital reached out to Omar’s congressional office for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.

title: Leonardo DiCaprio's 'dad bod' puts spotlight on dangerous belly fat — and how to lose it
description: Leonardo DiCaprio's beach photos sparked a "dad bod" debate, and a trainer warns that excess belly fat and visceral fat carry serious health risks.
content: Recent beach photos of actor Leonardo DiCaprio have reignited the "dad bod" debate and raised questions about whether carrying a little extra weight around the middle can pose hidden health risks. The popular term generally describes a softer physique with extra weight around the midsection. While appearance alone isn’t an indicator of health, excess abdominal fat — particularly visceral fat surrounding the organs — has been linked to an increased risk of heart disease, diabetes and other medical conditions, according to the Cleveland Clinic. YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it. Suazo, who has not trained DiCaprio, defines a dad bod as a "loss of structure," an increase in waist circumference and a loss of muscle mass. "Maybe you're losing structure in your day-to-day eating … moving a lot less, taking fewer steps per day," he said of potential causes. "And, typically, you're eating and drinking more than you're moving. And the body just starts showcasing that stuff." BEST FOODS FOR REDUCING DANGEROUS BELLY FAT AND PROTECTING HEART HEALTH An expanding waistline can be an important indicator of health risk. According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, men with a waist circumference greater than 40 inches have a higher risk of developing health problems, including Type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Visceral fat, which lies deep within the abdomen and surrounds internal organs, has also been linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, the Cleveland Clinic states. "We want to try to mitigate these things as best as possible before they become an issue," Suazo said. Getting rid of a dad bod Reversing a dad bod starts with getting nutrition in check, according to Suazo. That includes understanding daily calorie intake and getting an appropriate balance of protein, carbohydrates and fats. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES He recommends pairing that strategy with full-body strength training two to three times per week, focusing on compound movements such as squats, stiff-leg deadlifts, back rows, push-ups and chest presses. Also among his favorite exercises are pull-ups. "It’s a tremendous exercise that targets the stomach, the biceps and the back," he said, noting that working larger muscle groups can help build overall strength. Suazo also recommends incorporating cardio into a well-rounded routine that includes nutrition, strength training and cardiovascular exercise. Federal physical activity guidelines recommend that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week, along with muscle-strengthening exercise on at least two days. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The trainer noted, however, that exercising the abdominal muscles alone won't eliminate belly fat. "When it comes to belly fat and any fat on the body, we can target our exercises through isolated movements, but we can only reveal it through a loss of body fat throughout the whole body," he said. Suazo said people who improve their nutrition may begin noticing changes within several weeks, although results can vary based on factors, including diet, activity level and starting body composition. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Upon four weeks of dialing in your nutrition, you will see a tremendous change in the body," he said. Nutritional improvements can also boost energy and confidence, the trainer noted, which may help people become more consistent in the gym. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Better nutrition can also support sleep and exercise recovery, he said. Combining those dietary changes with a smart exercise routine and cardio can create a "recipe for success," according to Suazo.

title: Ivy League football team gets ruthlessly mocked after losing game in dumbest way possible
description: The University of Pennsylvania's botched clock management against Columbia left a 52-yard field goal woefully short, ending an Ivy League thriller in chaos.
content: We had an Ivy League thriller during Friday night's three-pack college football weekend appetizer, with the University of Pennsylvania and Columbia going down to the wire in Philadelphia. That's right. Penn and Columbia. While the rest of the country flipped between Memphis, App State and Purdue, I was locked in the Ivy League battle of the year. It's called GRINDING, folks. Look it up. HERE'S WHY, EVEN WITH ALL ITS PROBLEMS, COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS STILL BETTER THAN THE NFL Anyway, I'm glad I was, because this one had it all. Big moments. Big comebacks. Big plays. And, of course, a finish that left me utterly speechless on multiple different levels. Before we dive into the Xs and Os, take a look: Feel like an Ivy League school should've thought this through Amazing. You just don't expect that sort of foolishness out of an Ivy League roster, right? Sure, there are other programs where you wouldn't be surprised to see this level of idiocy (I won't name names), but not Penn. Not the IVY LEAGUE. These are supposed to be the smartest dudes on the planet, and they can't run a simple fire drill with the clock ticking down? Get on the ball and SPIKE it! Why are they rushing their field goal kicker out there? There was plenty of time. He caught it was 10 seconds to go. The clock stops on a first down in college football when its under two minutes to go in a half. HARVARD FOOTBALL OUTSMARTS COLGATE ON HAIL MARY ATTEMPT TO WIN GAME IN FINAL SECONDS So the clock was stopped. There was plenty of time of left. And they instead opted to sprint the field goal unit onto the field, and have the kicker quickly try a 52-yard field goal? Clearly, the kicker had no idea what was happening, by the way. None. That's why he was the last one onto the field. He came sprinting into the camera with four seconds left, barely lined up (he looked too close), and then came up woefully short with the kick. Game over. Columbia wins. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Amazing. We've seen a lot of dumb football over the past week, mostly out of the NFL. You had Nick Sirianni doing dumb things across the pond with the ill-fated kickoff, and then Jayden Daniels and the Commanders running what just may be the dumbest play of all time in overtime against the Giants. title: Sophie Cunningham commends Washington state girls who walked off cross country race over male teammate
description: Sophie Cunningham praised Camas High School girls who walked out of a cross-country race to protest a transgender teammate's switch to girls' competition.
content: WNBA star Sophie Cunningham praised the Washington state high school girls who walked out of a cross-country race in protest of a transgender teammate. "Good work girls," Cunningham wrote in a comment on an XX-XY Athletics Instagram post about the protest. The three-word message echoed her earlier defense of teenage fans caught in a confrontation at a Seattle Storm game after showing support for her stance on women’s sports. RALLY PLANNED TO SUPPORT WASHINGTON GIRLS WHO REFUSED TO RACE AGAINST TRANSGENDER TEAMMATE IN CROSS COUNTRY About a dozen Camas High School runners walked off the course Oct. 13 during a meet against Battle Ground. Their teammate had begun the season competing in boys’ races before switching to girls’ competition. The dispute has drawn national attention and prompted plans for an Oct. 21 rally supporting the runners. Cunningham has previously argued that girls’ and women’s sports should be separated by sex. In a July ESPN profile, she described her position as protecting opportunities for girls while rejecting accusations that she hated transgender people. Later that month, two teenage supporters attended a Fever-Storm game at Seattle’s Climate Pledge Arena wearing XX-XY Athletics shirts and carrying a sign thanking Cunningham for speaking up for girls. The teenagers alleged that Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton confronted them and used profanity. The WNBA subsequently fined Keaton an undisclosed amount and suspended her from attending Seattle’s next five home games. Cunningham then reposted OutKick’s reporting of the Seattle controversy in July, writing "Bravo to those girls for standing up for what they believe," on X. STORM CO-OWNER SUSPENDED AFTER INCIDENT WITH SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS AS STAR BREAKS SILENCE ON CONTROVERSY Cunningham also emphasized that she welcomed people regardless of gender identity and believed disagreement should not prevent kindness. But she sharply criticized the conduct attributed to Keaton. "Truly embarrassing of the co-owner. Unfortunately shows the type of leader she is," Cunningham wrote. Storm majority owner Ginny Gilder apologized for the co-owner’s comments. "Everyone who attends a Storm game deserves to feel welcome," Gilder said in a statement that also reaffirmed the team’s commitment to treating fans respectfully. The Fever said at the time that neither the organization nor Cunningham had advance knowledge of the demonstration held outside the Seattle arena or contact with its organizers. The Camas dispute now brings Cunningham’s support back to Washington as voters prepare to consider Initiative 638 on Nov. 3. The measure would prohibit biologically male students from competing in certain female-only school sports and require health care provider verification of biological sex. Backers say the proposal would protect fair competition. Opponents say it would exclude transgender girls and create new medical and privacy burdens. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA) has said its gender-identity eligibility policy follows state law and that it cannot implement proposed restrictions that would violate that law. Amy Sousa, who helped organize demonstrations supporting Cunningham during the WNBA season, is organizing the "Camas Courage" rally for Oct. 21. title: DEPROGRAMMED: She was all in for socialism until the 'red flags' became impossible to ignore
description: Germania Rodriguez Poleo warns young Americans that socialism and capitalism are mutually exclusive, drawing on Venezuela's collapse as proof.
content: Germania Rodriguez Poleo, a Venezuelan American journalist who immigrated to the United States when she was 11 years old, grew up to vote for Bernie Sanders in support of some of the socialist policies her family fought to escape before she recognized what she described as the "red flags" of what she once supported. "Once I looked at the details, it looked more like Chavismo than Scandinavia[n socialism]," Poleo told Fox News Digital. "Ever since, I've been trying to share that message with fellow young people who truly just fall for the misinformation," she continued. SOCIALISM WILL 'CONTROL PEOPLE' AND 'TAKE EVERYTHING AWAY' FROM AMERICA, ACCORDING TO THESE EXPATS "[Venezuela has] done the suffering for you. We destroyed our country. Venezuela is an example for the entire world of how a democratic country can vote itself into total collapse. … One vote was enough to lose our country, and who knows if we'll ever get it back?" Poleo said. She went on to detail "the war over what the definition of socialism is," arguing that adding "democratic" before "socialism" creates a misleading distinction between socialist policies and the realities of life in Venezuela, Cuba and other countries. "Socialism and capitalism are mutually exclusive, and that's where [socialists are] lying to people," she continued. JONATHAN TURLEY: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS WANT TO REMAKE AMERICA IN THEIR IMAGE. THAT’S TERRIFYING "If you really talk to these DSA types, they'll admit it. They think capitalism has failed ,and they want to try a different system. … That's [where] they're lying. Social democracy is under capitalism. Socialism wants to end capitalism and that is a very, very important distinction," Poleo revealed. "When did I open my eyes? When the red flags became too many." She explained how she came to support candidates like Sanders, touching on the "immigrant experience" and pressure to "assimilate" to the new Western culture that surrounded her. OPINION: SOCIALISM LOOKS APPEALING WHEN SCHOOLS REFUSE TO TEACH ITS HORRIFIC, REAL-WORLD COST "By the time I got to NYU, I had fancy professors telling me that the problem wasn't socialism, but capitalism, unchecked capitalism, repeating the horrors of trickle-down economics. [I was] going to classes like ‘the politics of inequality,’ ‘Latina feminism.' This is what was building my world view, all taught by White American professors, of course," Poleo recalled. "I ended up believing their lie that what they're talking about is social democracy, like in Scandinavian countries and not what happened in Venezuela, Cuba and Nicaragua." Poleo, the narrator of "Escaping Venezuela," a documentary by Reason, said the lives, experiences and memories that encompass the stories of immigrants are "not convenient" for the people who support socialism. TODAY’S LEFTISTS ARE DANGEROUSLY WRONG ABOUT COMMUNISM. JUST LISTEN TO THE SURVIVORS "Our story and our tragedy is not convenient for people who say they care about victims of dictatorships or migrant. … They don't like our story because it shows what happens in the real world when an anti-Western, anti-U.S., supposedly anti-imperialist government gets to power and establishes socialist policies," Poleo noted. "They want to say that's not real socialism, and they don't want to listen to us. title: Your bumper sticker could help Flock cameras track where you go; new bill aims to stop it
description: Rep. Pat Harrigan's bill would require warrants for ALPR searches, delete records within 24 hours and ban tracking political or religious stickers.
content: FIRST ON FOX: Americans are sounding the alarm over privacy concerns over Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that can snap photos of cars and track locations, and one GOP lawmaker is moving to close the gaps. Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., introduced a bill Thursday that would ban ALPR searches targeting political or religious messages on vehicles, require warrants for most searches, mandate that records be deleted within 24 hours and prohibit vendors from selling or sharing location data. "When you consider that these systems track everything that you do, where you work, where your kids go to school, where you even go to church, I think it's pretty easy to understand why people are concerned," Harrigan told Fox News Digital. "So, that's an extraordinary amount of information about somebody that the government has that has never committed a crime." POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN' Flock cameras and other ALPRs have drawn widespread debate. Law enforcement uses them in criminal investigations to collect searchable license plate, location and other vehicle data that allow officers to search by location and identify vehicles matching a suspect’s vehicle description. Critics believe they raise constitutional concerns by tracking drivers without consent, while supporters say they are needed for crime prevention. President Donald Trump has voiced support for Flock cameras, telling reporters on Sept. 13 that he "sort of" likes them because of their use by law enforcement despite some people calling them "an infringement." Harrigan's bill would impose restrictions on all ALPR systems, including prohibiting government agencies from categorizing vehicles by "expressive attributes" like political or religious bumper stickers, flags or decals. HAWLEY RIPS FLOCK’S SPRAWLING SURVEILLANCE WEB AS TEXAS CITIES CUT CAMERAS OVER PRIVACY AND DATA FEARS "At the end of the day, they have nothing to do with whether you committed a crime or not," Harrigan said. "As all of this data comes in and is vacuumed in by the government, it becomes searchable, particularly with the new technologies that we have surrounding artificial intelligence." That means messages ranging from "Back the Blue" to "Jesus Saves" or "Black Lives Matter" could not be turned into searchable data. The bill would also block ALPR searches targeting political or religious activity, civil immigration violations, parking or non-moving traffic violations, debts and other civil penalties. As ALPR technology expands, Flock Safety says its systems can detect bumper stickers but cannot identify their type, "like a political party or a house of worship." However, its AI-powered FreeForm search allows users to search vehicle characteristics "in plain terms," raising questions about how bumper stickers and other markings could be used to identify vehicles. The company said safeguards are designed to block searches for vehicles based on political or religious bumper stickers and symbols. The bill would require law enforcement to have a probable cause warrant in most searches, with exceptions for immediate threats to someone’s life or safety. Records would have to be deleted within 24 hours, with exceptions for warrants, emergencies and court orders. It would also require agencies to log ALPR searches, publish annual reports and undergo audits. States without qualifying protections could lose 10% of certain federal criminal justice funding. Additionally, vendors would be prohibited from selling ALPR data or using it to train artificial intelligence (AI) models. And for Americans worried about their Fourth Amendment rights, the bill would offer legal protections, allowing people to sue over illegal searches for at least $1,000 per violation and keep illegally obtained evidence out of court. TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT MOVES TO CUT STATE FUNDING FOR AI-POWERED FLOCK CAMERAS AMID PRIVACY CONCERNS In August, The Washington Post found that at least 50 officers had been accused or charged with misusing license plate readers. Some reportedly used them to spy on romantic partners, exes or other women, with Flock’s system used in 46 cases. Harrigan said the bill would not stop the technology from being used as an investigative tool and would instead place limits on how far law enforcement can go. "Simultaneously, when we have technology that can benefit humanity and our experience here as Americans and make America safer, we should leverage that. But we have to strike the right balance," he said. He said he believes lawmakers can get behind the bill "regardless of your political philosophy." "Protecting Americans from criminals and protecting their constitutional rights, to me, those are two core responsibilities of government," he said. "And I think that that's something that members on both sides of the aisle can get behind." title: BROADCAST BIAS: Feminist freakout over Shane Gillis comment is the real joke
description: NBC's "Saturday Night Live" faced a media firestorm after Shane Gillis joked about women's gym clothes, drawing accusations of misogyny and even rape culture.
content: In recent years, NBC’s "Saturday Night Live" has followed the late-night trend of waging a self-righteous "humor" war on President Donald Trump. Almost every show begins with a Trump-mocking skit, and the "Weekend Update" fake newscast is heavily laden with snide comments about Trump and his conservative coterie. What caused thumping outrage this week was comedian Shane Gillis, who was announced as an incoming "SNL" cast member in 2019 before getting canceled almost immediately for some anti-Asian jokes. His opening monologue this week was denounced after he joked, "I haven’t been to the gym in so long. I didn’t know women just dress like whores now. Look, I'm sorry, there's no other way to describe. ACTOR DAN LEVY BLASTS SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE, CLAIMS MEN'S 'COMPLACENCY' FUELS SEXUAL ASSAULT "Have you seen it? I've seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts? Those neon, they’re, like, artificial vape-colored. The wrinkles go, like, around the cheeks and combine at the butthole." What drew less attention was the second half of it, Gillis mocking himself or men in general. "And don’t look," Gillis added. "You’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look, because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now." The first broadcast network to pounce on Gillis was actually NBC, on NBCNews.com. Reporter Rebecca Cohen lamented, "Gillis, who is known for his raunchy style of comedy, has a history of placing women — and other marginalized groups — at the butt of jokes. "Many people called it tone-deaf of Gillis to make such comments following the reports around a former Cornell University student who alleged she was gang-raped at an on-campus fraternity house in 2024." "Many people" were represented by feminist author Jessica Valenti. "This is his contribution to that conversation," she said. "This is him telling us what he thinks of the discourse on sexual assault. ... That is rape culture." SALLY YATES' CORNELL REVIEW OF ALLEGED GANG RAPE COULD SCRUTINIZE CRUCIAL POLICE INTERVIEW, ATTORNEY SAYS NBC’s "Today" picked it up on air on Tuesday in the fourth hour. "I wouldn’t want my kids to listen to that," co-host Jenna Bush Hager said. " It feels mean," co-host Sheinelle Jones agreed. "And that is the energy that I think made people upset." "Today" also put the controversy on TV when fake "Weekend Update" anchor Michael Che appeared to promote his new Netflix special. "How are you thinking about what happened this week with Shane’s opening monologue?" substitute host Laura Jarrett asked. "You’ve seen the pushback." SWIFTIES CLAIM TRAVIS KELCE DID THE UNSPEAKABLE BY LIKING SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE & THEY'RE NOT HAPPY "That’s comedy," Che replied. "It’s like, you think it’s funny, and then some people don’t." Jarrett asked Che if he laughed in real time. He denied seeing it in real time as he prepared for his skit. Che also did an interview on NPR’s "Morning Edition," but Gillis was never brought up. NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben posted an angry thread on Bluesky, saying, "I know this is nothing you haven’t heard before but like In the year of our Lord 2026 a dude went on the big comedy sketch institution program and said 'lol women dress like whores' and … it’s all fine and good? It’s not all over my feeds? Is it bc no one watches SNL or like I dunno normal misogyny?" Profanity followed. CORNELL PROTESTERS SWARM CAMPUS TO SUPPORT JANE DOE, CALL FOR UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT'S RESIGNATION On ABC’s "The View," co-host Sara Haines picked up the "rape culture" spin. "When the language like ‘whore’ is passed along, I might have not noticed it before in the past because it was under the guise of a joke. And as we’re talking about this Cornell 7, I'm not saying a joke makes an assault, but it makes it much easier to look at it as another human as an object." It wasn’t misogyny, apparently, on ABC’s "Jimmy Kimmel Live," when the host displayed a picture of then-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia in skin-tight gym clothes to make fun of how unqualified she was: "Katie met a number of qualifications for the job. "She has blonde hair. She can do a thumbs up and end of list. Really, what else do you need? Where do they all get that same face? Is that makeup or do they have a machine that stamps it on?" Che replied, "That’s comedy. It’s like, you think it’s funny, and then some people don’t." SETH MEYERS, JOHN OLIVER TELL JIMMY KIMMEL HE'S THEIR 'BULLETPROOF VEST' WHEN IT COMES TO TRUMP By the time the Gillis controversy was picked up on "CBS Mornings" on Oct. 14, there was at least a debate of sorts. Co-host Nate Burleson set it up, saying, "The question is: Is he being targeted unfairly by cancel culture, or does he deserve all of this criticism he’s getting?" After running through outraged clips, co-host Adriana Diaz admitted Gillis "recently broke a Guinness World Record for the largest attendance ever at a comedy show with nearly 74,000 audience members." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But they kept up the anti-women angle: "Sophie Carpenter is a fitness coach and content creator. She worries jokes like the one Gillis made Saturday could discourage some women from working out altogether." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP All this fuss might cause the sneaking suspicion that NBC wanted its comedy "institution" to make news, which would explain why it was the first to denounce it. It’s likely this will only help Gillis, just as he built his career on getting canceled by NBC in the first place.

title: Kelly Clarkson risks looking like 'rich and famous prima donna' in $15K bird fight, expert says
description: Crisis PR experts weigh in on whether Kelly Clarkson's dispute with Brooklyn boutique Art of Play over a $15,000 mechanical bird hurts her image.
content: Kelly Clarkson’s public dispute with a Brooklyn small business over a $15,000 mechanical bird could damage the relatable image she has built over the past two decades, a crisis PR expert warned. "There will certainly be some naysayers who think Clarkson was acting like a rich and famous prima donna and using her platform vindictively," Steve Honig, founder of The Honig Company, told Fox News Digital. "But most people will likely think that, for the most part, she acted accordingly and in many ways was a role model for standing up for oneself." The controversy began after Clarkson claimed she was treated like Julia Roberts’ character in "Pretty Woman" while shopping at Art of Play in Brooklyn. KELLY CLARKSON'S STORE CALLOUT SHOWS THE 'POWER' OF CELEBRITY STATEMENTS: EXPERT Clarkson said an employee appeared to judge her based on her appearance and suggested she look at "something comparable" instead of the $15,000 mechanical bird she wanted to purchase. She also called the employee an "idiot" and said the store lost a major sale. Art of Play, which sells puzzles, games, toys, books and other specialty items, responded to Clarkson's original social media post, saying the business had been bombarded with hateful messages from "8 million people" after the singer's accusations. "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It’s been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity," the store wrote on its Instagram page Sunday afternoon. "Thanks to all our friends for their support and welcome to all the curious folks who discovered us amidst the drama. We’re going to keep our heads down and hopefully, we can clear things up with Kelly someday. As a talented popular singer once said ‘what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.'" GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE After Art of Play's Instagram post, Clarkson responded Sunday afternoon on X and Instagram stories to the store's assertion that the mechanical bird wasn't for sale. "Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn't for sale. That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," Clarkson wrote, adding a thumbs-up emoji. "So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn't happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone "yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can." That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it. "And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things. I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t." Clarkson’s post also prompted criticism online, with some users accusing her of using her platform to target a small business. The store reportedly received a wave of negative Google reviews after the singer’s comments went viral. SELMA BLAIR SAYS 'NO ONE RETURNED MY CALLS' AFTER ANTI-ISLAM COMMENT LED TO HOLLYWOOD FALLOUT Art of Play shared another post on Instagram Sunday to "clarify one additional detail" about Clarkson's visit. "During the 5 minutes she spent in the store, she inquired about our mechanical bird puppet named Molly. We explained that while Molly is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a de facto mascot for our shop, a nearly identical automaton is owned by the creator of the machines, a brilliant artist named Bliss Kolb who lives in Seattle. He told us he would be willing to part with Molly’s twin for $15,000. We explained all of this to Kelly Clarkson. "We also offered to show her a different singing bird automaton, made by a traditional clockmaking shop in Germany, that she could have taken home with her that day. It costs about $2,000. She did not stick around long enough to see it. "We’ve reached out to Kelly directly to try and clear the air," the shop concluded. "We really do wish her the best and hope that someday we can all laugh about this misunderstanding." Adam Rubin, co-owner of Art of Play and a children’s author, spoke with Fox News Digital inside the Brooklyn store Tuesday morning, claiming the singer has put his business in danger after their viral dispute. Rubin claimed the backlash has extended beyond angry comments online, with people associated with the business allegedly facing threats and having their personal information exposed. "We've got incredible support from our neighbors and fans over the past few days, and all of them have been attacked, threatened, doxed," he said. Evan Nierman, CEO of crisis PR firm Red Banyan, said Clarkson’s long-established reputation will likely protect her from any lasting damage but warned that continuing to discuss the dispute could change how some people view her. "Arguing with a boutique toy store over a $15,000 mechanical bird is not going to make or break the long-term reputation of a literal ‘American Idol,’" Nierman said. "Right or wrong, she initiated this conflict by telling her 9 million followers that the owners of the store are idiots who lost a huge sale and mistreated her. TAYLOR HICKS CREDITS FAITH AND BLUE-COLLAR BIRMINGHAM ROOTS FOR KEEPING HIM GROUNDED AFTER 'AMERICAN IDOL' WIN "Prior to this incident, she was perceived as a down-to-earth and relatable celebrity, but this acrimonious back and forth over social media is sullying everyone involved." Honig argued that the dispute could ultimately strengthen Clarkson’s image because she presented herself as someone standing up to unfair treatment. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? "This was not really about a $15,000 item, but about how she says she was treated when she tried to buy it. "Just as in ‘Pretty Woman,’ someone appeared to be judging a book by its cover." Still, Honig acknowledged that the situation could become more damaging if the dispute continues. "The only risk is if the dispute drags on and starts to look like a celebrity using her platform against a small business," he said. Nierman also urged Clarkson to let the controversy fade rather than risk having the dispute overshadow her career. "Clarkson has built up over two decades of goodwill since winning ‘American Idol.’ She has built a deep reservoir of trust, and her fans will give her the benefit of the doubt every time in a fight like this," he said. "Every new round of arguing over Molly the Bird makes it more likely that the general American public will start to make conclusions about Clarkson and her character based on this dispute, which does not serve her. "Clarkson should do what she can to move past this, since she wants the first thing people think about her to be her musical accomplishments and not a petty and protracted fight over a singing birdie." Honig said Clarkson should eventually "declare victory and move on," while Nierman suggested she ask her supporters to stop harassing the store. "Kelly’s silence has been helpful and the right move," Nierman said. "But if she really wanted to win the day and come out permanently ahead, she could call on her fans to stand down and leave the store and its employees alone." title: Detective suspected in girl’s murder may have killed others, former investigator fears
description: A fingerprint on an 8-year-old's communion purse finally identified Chicago cop Thomas McInerney as Gloria Kowalewicz's killer after 65 years, police say.
content: More than 65 years of searching for a killer has ended, and Chicago police say they now know who shot an 8-year-old girl walking to mass. He was part of the force. Chicago cop Thomas F. McInerney Jr. has been identified as the man who abducted, shot and killed Gloria Kowalewicz Nov. 12, 1960. At the time, McInerney was a recent addition to the agency, a violent crimes detective with the Chicago Police Department. He died in 2006. But evidence pointing to him as the killer lived on. And recent improvements in technology finally brought answers. DNA TECHNOLOGY LEADS TO ARREST IN 1988 KILLING OF ORLANDO WOMAN AFTER NEARLY FOUR DECADES Just before 8 a.m. on the morning of her death, Kowalewicz began walking a few blocks from her home to St. Mary of Mt. title: Americans are secretly cooking during virtual meetings, and one age group is leading the way
description: A new survey reveals that 17% of remote workers have cooked during video meetings with their cameras off. A leadership expert weighs in.
content: Your colleagues might be chopping, stirring and whipping up a meal on the other side of your video call, a new survey found. A national survey of more than 2,000 U.S. adults found that 17% of respondents have cooked during a work meeting while their cameras were off. Among Gen Z, the figure rose to 26%. The poll, conducted by Savanta for AI meeting assistant company Bluedot, also found that 23% have used the restroom during a meeting with their cameras off, 14% have shopped online and 13% have exercised. BRINGING THIS POPULAR DRINK TO A JOB INTERVIEW COULD HURT YOUR CHANCES, EXPERTS WARN Twelve percent, meanwhile, have fallen asleep while their cameras were off, and that figure rose to 30% among Gen Z. John Coleman, co-CEO of Atlanta-based Sovereign's Capital, told Fox News Digital he has occasionally resorted to eating lunch during back-to-back meetings and taken conference calls while exercising with his camera off, but he draws the line at cooking while participating in a call. "I'd hate for someone to have a cooking accident while they're on Zoom and not be a full participant in the meeting," Coleman said. Some of the other behaviors are even riskier, he noted. "I had a colleague forget that his video was on and take his laptop into the restroom with him actually\, which gave a great view of the restroom to everybody on the call, much to his chagrin," Coleman recalled. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ His tip is to treat video calls — on camera or not — as if you were face-to-face. "You want to be engaged with the person across from you," he said. For those who need to step away and complete a task, he recommends sending a quick message to let the other people on the call know. Kristen Hadeed, a Texas-based leadership expert and author of the book "Human Leadership," said her company treats making lunch as "human time," an everyday need employees should be able to handle. "These moments are part of life, and I want my team to feel empowered to take the time they need while maintaining open communication with the team. Colleagues might be chopping, stirring and whipping up a meal on the other side of your video call. "When a person's time away from work will affect their availability, responsiveness or the team's ability to get work done, I expect that it is communicated so that we are all on the same page." For Catherine Fisher, LinkedIn's vice president of communications and a California-based career expert, the key question is whether multitasking affects someone’s ability to take part. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "The question isn't necessarily, 'Are you doing anything else?' It's, 'Can you still contribute when you’re needed?'" Fisher told Fox News Digital. "If you can't follow the discussion, answer a question or contribute meaningfully, that's when multitasking can start getting in the way of your participation." Coleman said part of the problem is how some meetings are organized. "A lot of this responsibility, I think, rests on organizations," he said. "We overcrowd meetings. We make them too long." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS When employees feel they're not needed in a discussion or that a meeting could have been handled by email, they may start multitasking, he said, and that erodes cognitive ability. Coleman recommends keeping virtual calls brief, limiting attendance to those who need to participate and asking whether a video call is even necessary in the first place. Fisher said the higher share of Gen Z respondents who said they've cooked during meetings may reflect how the pandemic shaped their expectations around work and home life. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I wouldn't look at this data and conclude that Gen Z cares less about work," she said. "Many started their careers during the pandemic, at a time when the boundaries between work and home had already been rewritten."

title: Bears star Caleb Williams could reinjure hamstring by returning too soon, surgeon says
description: Chicago Bears star Caleb Williams called his hamstring injury "pretty serious" after feeling a pop, and a surgeon warns rushing back could put him at even greater risk.
content: Caleb Williams is listed as questionable for the Chicago Bears' game on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons as he looks to return from his hamstring injury. Should he play, though? Former college football quarterback-turned-foot-and-ankle surgeon Dr. Drew Burdi isn’t sure if the juice is worth the squeeze. Burdi dealt with a hamstring injury during his playing days at Western Michigan and knows how tough they are to manage. "I think he could reinjure it," Burdi told OutKick in a recent interview. "I had, when I was playing, I had a hamstring, I pulled my hamstring. It felt the same way. I remember looking around, I was running and I felt like somebody came up and hit me in the back of my leg, and then I realized there was no one around me, and I knew exactly what happened." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Burdi said that when the hamstring is injured, it's actually partially torn. If it's not given time to heal properly, it becomes more susceptible to tearing again. "Then that just puts stress on other parts of the body, you could be running differently. It can put him in a compromising positions that he just normally wouldn't be in when he's 100%," Burdi said. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Williams refused to disclose the medical grade of his hamstring injury but called it "pretty serious." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "I felt a pop," Williams said. "That's why I looked back. I looked back just like everybody else does when you feel a pop. Think somebody grabbed you and nobody grabbed me." The Bears' star quarterback also said he wasn't sure whether he would play against the Falcons. Burdi said that if Williams has any trepidation, he should sit out another week. "'Cause they really look good (without him), except for the Packers (game). But I mean, without that game, I don't know. I'd probably say take more time because I think that they could. It depends on their schedule too. If their schedule is good enough where they can get out of it at .500 and have him come back healthy, I think it's better than trying to push himself, win a game, maybe this week, but then he injures it further, and then he might be out longer. It's one of those injuries where you can try to push it, but you really have to know yourself. If it feels like you're still not 100%, it's probably worth just holding off on it," Burdi said. They beat the Philadelphia Eagles with Case Keenum, beat the New York Jets with Tyson Bagent, and then lost to the Green Bay Packers. If the Bears heed Burdi's advice and sit Williams for one more week if he doesn't feel 100% and lose to the Falcons on Sunday, they will still have managed to go .500 without their star quarterback for a month. title: The Cignetti effect is real: Indiana football sparks an unbelievable 'revival' in Bloomington
description: From Upstairs Pub to Memorial Stadium, Bloomington is electric as Curt Cignetti's Indiana football hosts a historic top-five Ohio State showdown.
content: The crowd inside the "Upstairs Pub" started to grow as the clock turned toward Friday night on the campus of Indiana, with students getting out of class and heading towards to local drinking establishments for what was going to be a wild 24 hours. Obviously, the mood has shifted around this college town thanks to the Hoosiers winning last year's CFP title, along with having a head coach in Curt Cignetti who has turned this program into a football juggernaut in just two years. COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF IS SACRIFICING ITS SOULD TO BE BECOME AN ATM FOR CONFERENCES WITH 24-TEAM EXPANSION Whether it was the apparel stores that had fans waiting in lines for their chance to purchase Indiana gear, or the restaurants that were already filling up early Friday afternoon, it's obvious that the attitude has changed around this college town that once glossed over the football season in anticipation for basketball. Later today, it will be No. 4 Ohio State visiting No. 5 Indiana in what will be the most electric atmosphere Bloomington has seen in decades. You can call it a "revival," or the Cignetti effect, but it's not hard to notice the culture change in Bloomington. "We're a football school now, and I hate to say that about the basketball program," Edward, from just outside Indianapolis noted. "We spent years praying for some type of revival of college football within this fan base, and we finally have it during one of the craziest times in sports. "A lot of schools are trying to pull off the Indiana magic of rebuilding a program in such a short time period. And those expectations are truly centered around what transpired here in Bloomington. That part is wild to me. We expect to win football games now, which is a wonderful feeling to have. So, about Indiana beating Ohio State at home The last time a Hoosiers' football team defeated the Buckeyes in Bloomington was in 1988. It took thirty years for Indiana to snap a losing streak to Ohio State, which finally came to an end last season inside Lucas Oil Stadium in the Big Ten championship game. Also, this will be the first time a top-five college football matchup has taken place inside Memorial Stadium since 1960, as Indiana rises a 22-game winning streak into their showdown with the Buckeyes on Saturday. Essentially, there are a lot of firsts that could end up coming to fruition for an Indiana team that has defied the odds over the past two seasons, against plenty of odds and fans who might still be under the impression this was all just a fluke. I'm here to tell you that nothing Curt Cignetti is doing on this campus, and opposing ones, is centered around some magical voodoo that the Hoosiers head coach has placed on the Big Ten. CURT CIGNETTI WAS SO FOCUSED THIS OFFSEASON, HE TURNED DOWN ALL EXTERNAL REQUESTS: 'I'M 95% FOOTBALL' Whether or not folks outside Bloomington believe Indiana can do it again this season is not the point. The supporters who are lining Kirkwood avenue, or the thousands who made their way into town on Friday evening, are the true barometer of where this program has been taken in such a short time period that has other college athletic directors trying to replicate the Cignetti magic. "I don't think folks truly understood what we were going through as a fan base," Thomas, longtime season ticket holder told OutKick. "I've been coming to games for thirty years, and I've never seen this type of excitement, and it's hard to correlate it with basketball. Sure, we're not oblivious to the narrative that followed our football program like a black cloud. "But, why do you think we're not taking these moments for granted? We've earned this sh-t, and I promise you this fan base isn’t cocky. We just expect to win now, which clearly wasn’t the case just a few years ago. So yea, I expect us to beat Ohio State." If Indiana can do it, so can others around college football I've been around plenty of college campuses during my career, and the resurgent joy that you see in Bloomington is contagious. This is no longer a loyal group of fans waiting for November to roll around so they can walk into Assembly Hall to watch the basketball program, which has also had its problems over the years. But what Indiana football did for the school is provide hope that everything that has transpired over the last two years in one sport, can be done again across multiple venues across campus. Curt Cignetti has not just provided a championship mindset for the passionate fans that were sitting through days of blowouts and small glimmers of hope in past years. The man who told you all to 'google' him has reignited an athletic department and fan base that will make Saturday's atmosphere on Indiana's campus feel more like a cinematic backdrop that will host college football's premier matchup of the day. title: Pope Leo XIV discharged from hospital, will return to Vatican after surgery to remove lung cancer
description: Pope Leo XIV received blood tests and a chest X-ray at Gemelli Hospital, confirming he is well enough to return to the Vatican after surgery.
content: Thousands of supporters gathered outside Gemelli Hospital in Rome Saturday yelling "Papa!" after Pope Leo XIV was released after surgery to remove a cancerous node in his lung. The Holy See announced early Saturday he would be leaving to return to the Vatican. "Following the doctors’ assessment this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Hospital, where he was hospitalized for surgery on his right lung," a statement from the Holy See read. "He will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow, he will lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment." The pope received blood tests and a chest X-ray Saturday, both of which confirmed he is well enough to return to the Vatican, according to Vatican News. Before he departed, Pope Leo reportedly visited the children's oncology ward. While in the hospital, the Pope received letters from some of the children in the ward. "Pope Leo, our prayers are for you," a girl named Eleonora, who had been receiving treatment in the oncology ward, wrote to him, according to letters released by Vatican News. "May God, the Most Holy Virgin, and the guardian angels always protect you," she added. Eleanora's mother told the Pope that she was now healthy, according to the Vatican. "Faith moves mountains," Eleanora wrote to Pope Leo. "God has heard our prayers." DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH Pope Leo underwent thoracic surgery to remove a cancerous node in his lung Tuesday. After the successful surgery, doctors diagnosed him with lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer. "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," a statement from the Holy See press office read. title: Hasan Piker's influence tests breaking point of Democratic Party
description: Hasan Piker's Twitch influence is reshaping Democratic Party politics as DSA-aligned candidates gain momentum ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
content: Ahead of the midterm elections, one name has repeatedly surfaced in conversations about the future of the Democratic Party: Hasan Piker. The political commentator streams for hours each day on Twitch, promoting socialism, criticizing Israel and the U.S. and discussing the news of the day from his far-left perspective. But as Piker has gone from a niche online commentator to a real-life player in Democratic politics, his growing involvement has raised questions about what his influence could mean for the future of the party. While Piker's Twitch streams are viewed by tens of thousands daily, his online reach is not what has drawn the questions about the future of the party; rather, it is how engaged his followers are. "It's very clear to me that the people who do love and support him really love and support him. So, the followers that he has are super loyal, and I think they're really active, and they're very engaged," Isaac Saul, founder of the non-partisan politics newsletter Tangle, told Fox News Digital. OCASIO-CORTEZ CALLS FOCUS ON HASAN PIKER 'ABSOLUTELY LUDICROUS' AS SOME DEMOCRATS DEMAND DISTANCE Piker's followers are mostly young people, a demographic Saul called a "prized possession for the Democratic Party." He explained that Democrats were eager to hold onto young voters "because if they can turn out younger voters, that's going to increase their odds of winning in all manner of elections that happen in American politics." Mark Penn, a longtime Democratic pollster who served as an advisor to former President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, similarly pointed to Piker's appeal to young voters, describing him as almost a "Pied Piper." However, Penn questioned how closely those voters actually align with the streamer's views. "Nobody could possibly agree with the garbage that Hasan Piker says. It's anti-American. It's antisemitic. It's anti-virtually anything. It's anti-having any decorum, sensibility or intellectual component beyond kind of throwing everything and everyone overboard. So, the whole thing is nihilistic," Penn told Fox News Digital. STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’ Saul recently outlined his positions on Piker in a piece titled, "My honest thoughts on Hasan Piker." He told Fox News Digital that readers asked him repeatedly, "What's your beef with Hasan Piker?" It prompted him to explain his position fully. Saul started his piece by stating that he believes "Piker is a bad guy" and said he doesn't "trust" the Twitch streamer. Saul sees Piker as a "big pariah" within the Democratic establishment, even as he gains prominence. The Tangle founder believes, however, that the 2026 midterm elections could shift the party's perspective on Piker and the influence of the far left. HASAN PIKER VOWS HE WILL PRESSURE JAMES TALARICO TO GOVERN AS A LEFTIST, NOT A MODERATE "I still view him as kind of an outsider-y person trying to throw his weight around. I think the 2026 midterm has the potential to change that because Piker has endorsed some of the more progressive kind of DSA-type candidates. And if we see them win in House or Senate races, he said, 'We're gonna hold them accountable,'" Saul told Fox News Digital. Penn also sees the midterms as a potential test of Piker's influence, specifically in the Michigan U.S. Senate race where he was involved with Abdul El-Sayed's campaign. Beyond Piker, Penn sees the midterms as an evaluation of the effectiveness of socialist movements. "Obviously, I think the Michigan race is a big test case on all of this. I think that if El-Sayed wins in Michigan, then that will be a huge boost to these movements, to people like Piker and all of the outlandishness that they stand for because it wins elections," Penn told Fox News Digital. "If there's a setback here and a setback on the headline elections in Maine, Michigan and Texas, then maybe the Democrat Party is going to come much more to its senses and say these 'movements really didn't work.'" KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY While Saul and Penn see the midterms as a test of whether Piker can leverage his online popularity into real-world results, others argue that the shift is already happening, pointing to the growing number of candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Julian Epstein, a former chief counsel for Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee, told Fox News Digital he believes mainstream Democrats are underestimating the influence of Piker and the left-leaning movement behind him. "I think that the lie a lot of moderate Democrats are telling themselves is that you're only going to see 10, 12 members of Congress that fall under the DSA banner, and I think that's delusion," Epstein told Fox News Digital. "I think what you're increasingly seeing is that the socialist movement and the far-left movement is becoming the beating heart of the Democratic Party. Why? Because that's where all the activist energy is, and we saw that with the primaries." Mainstream and moderate Democrats, according to Epstein, are "scared of this movement" and that they are not willing to fight against it. "Democrats are increasingly scared to take this movement on because they fear the flying monkeys of the online left," he said. Epstein also argues that establishment Democrats have lost control of the party. He said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and other establishment Democrats have ceased being leaders and are increasingly turning into "marionettes of the far-left." While Epstein believes Piker appeals to "very frustrated" voters who "want to burn down the system," Saul sees some of the streamer's more mainstream views as part of the key to his popularity. INSIDE HASAN PIKER’S RADICAL VIEWS ON AMERICA, ISRAEL AND SOCIALISM "Hasan Piker supports Medicare-for-all. He wants to abolish cash bail. He thinks big agriculture needs to be broken up. He wants to renegotiate our relationship with Saudi Arabia. I mean, I think those ideas are not just broadly popular with progressives, but popular probably with some people in the populist MAGA right," Saul told Fox News Digital. "I think he could become an influential figure if there was more momentum in Congress to make some of those policy prescriptions law." As some Democrats attempt to reach Piker's young audience, they could risk losing voters who already feel that the party has gone too far to the left. JAMES CARVILLE VOWS TO ABANDON DEMOCRATIC PARTY IF FAR-LEFT HASAN PIKER BECOMES LEADING VOICE Penn noted that political parties could have much more to gain by saying no to extreme movements than going along with them. "So much time is spent on turnout and base and not enough realization that if I said no to the extremes, I could get a lot of those voters in the middle to switch. And those are twice as powerful as getting those extreme movements," Penn said. Tanya Tsikanovsky, a former Democrat who worked to elect Hillary Clinton in 2016 before leaving the party, told Fox News Digital she believes the Democratic Party's shift to the left is leaving voters like her politically "homeless." "I think that we need to stop focusing on how bad or how maybe salvageable the Democratic Party is and not think about them at all, and instead focus on the independents or on the moderate Democrats, like I once was, that feel completely homeless," Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital. "Because there are a ton of [Sen. John] Fettermans and Bill Mahers that are gonna really not have anywhere to go soon. Their party is going to be completely eaten up by the DSA." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Tsikanovsky agreed with Epstein's assessment that moderates in the Democratic Party have been left without power amid the rise of DSA candidates across the country. "The DSA candidates and people like Hasan Piker are the ones that are being platformed by that party and the moderate ones don't really have power anymore at all," Tsikanovsky said. The debate over Piker's role in the Democratic Party is at the heart of a larger question about how far left the party is willing to shift to gain voters and how much that change could cost or benefit them. title: Serial killer's ex-wife slept beside murderer for 8 years, never suspected his deadly double life
description: Bonnie Lou Gower reveals the haunting warning signs she missed while sharing a bed with serial killer Richard Evonitz for over eight years.
content: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255). For years, Bonnie Lou Gower shared a bed with a man she thought she knew better than anyone. She had no idea the man sleeping beside her was capable of murder. Her husband, Richard "Marc" Evonitz, was leading a double life, one that would ultimately expose him as a serial killer who preyed on young girls. His victims included a 16-year-old who lost her life while Evonitz was still married to Gower. SERIAL KILLER SURVIVOR WHO ESCAPED 18-HOUR CAPTIVITY REVEALS INSTINCT SHE WISHES SHE NEVER IGNORED Decades after Evonitz’s crimes came to light, Gower is revisiting the warning signs she didn't recognize with the help of a young woman who survived him. For Gower, one question has followed her since learning the truth about the man she married. "When I initially learned about [his crimes] and I told people, honestly their first response is, ‘Well, obviously you knew. How could you not have known?’" Gower told Fox News Digital. "That was my very first question to the FBI. ‘How could I not know this? How could I not know I was sleeping next to somebody for 8½ years that was doing this?’ And, of course, they assured me that there’s no way I could have known." Looking back, Gower admitted there were things she didn’t question at the time. Whenever she left town to visit family, Evonitz insisted on staying behind, claiming he had to work. Only later did Gower discover that he had actually taken time off while she was away. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "One of the reasons he never came with me was because he said he was working," said Gower. "And then, I come to find out, he had actually taken off work on the days that I was out of town. But, at the time, I wasn’t at all concerned about leaving him behind. I was just going and visiting my family. It definitely makes you look at everybody and everything now, whether you can trust someone’s words or actions." Gower met Evonitz, who was eight years her senior, in South Carolina. He was the older brother of one of her friends and would come home whenever he was on leave from the U.S. Navy. She quickly developed a crush on him as she got to know him and, at age 16, Evonitz asked her out on a date. They married in August 1988 when she was 17 and he was 25. "You think you know who you are when you’re 17, but I really don’t think I did," said Gower. "I don’t think I had a handle on that. And I was relatively sheltered. I was very naïve, very trusting, taking everything at face value. I think he knew that." During the marriage, there were moments when Gower suspected Evonitz was being unfaithful. Whenever she questioned him, Evonitz told her it was all in her head. She believed him. But as the relationship progressed, Evonitz began isolating her from friends and family as they moved around the country, from Maine to San Diego to Virginia. SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER "No one ever thinks that their significant other is going to be a serial killer," Chamberlain told Fox News Digital. "I think worst case, and this is something that she expressed to me, he was having an affair. No one ever thinks your spouse is out murdering someone. "He kept that part of himself very tightly controlled and didn’t show it to the people he was closest to." The marriage began to unravel after Evonitz left the Navy. Gower said financial pressures fueled growing tensions between the couple, while Evonitz became prone to mood swings and what she described as "rages." He also frequently criticized her weight. Behind closed doors, Gower was also uncomfortable with his interest in bondage, according to the docuseries. Even as the marriage reached its breaking point, Gower said she still didn’t see Evonitz as someone capable of hurting her. Walking away, she said, was a decision that came after years of mounting unhappiness. When Gower made the decision to leave the marriage, Gower said her fear was for him, not herself. "I was concerned for his safety when he said he was going to take the gun and kill himself," Gower recalled. "I never feared for my own life." SEND US A TIP Even after she finally walked away, Gower said Evonitz had left her questioning whether she had any justification for doing so. "When I left, I felt like I was leaving for no real good reason," she said. "[But] I wasn’t happy." According to Gower's TikTok, she and Evonitz were married from August 1988 until January 1997. Multiple reports indicate that their divorce was finalized in 1998. Years later, Gower would learn just how much she hadn’t known about the man she left behind. On June 24, 2002, 15-year-old Chamberlain was at a friend’s home in South Carolina when Evonitz pulled into the driveway. The stranger approached her with pamphlets and asked if her parents were home. Then, he held a gun to her neck and threatened to shoot her if she screamed. He forced Chamberlain into a dark storage container in his car. At Evonitz’s apartment, Chamberlain was repeatedly sexually assaulted. He restrained her to a bed. After hours of torture, Chamberlain managed to free one of her hands from a pair of handcuffs with her teeth, unclip a leather leg restraint and quietly bolt out the door as Evonitz slept. As she took off, Chamberlain encountered two men who took her to a police station. Chamberlain led officers back to her captor’s apartment. But when investigators arrived, Evonitz had escaped. Police tracked Evonitz to Sarasota, Florida, but as they closed in on him, Evonitz died by suicide. He was 38. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Once investigators began digging into Evonitz’s past, Chamberlain’s abduction proved to be only part of the story. Evidence recovered from Evonitz’s South Carolina apartment, former Virginia residence and vehicle linked him to three unsolved murders. On Sept. 9, 1996, Evonitz abducted 16-year-old Sofia Silva from the front steps of her home in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, where he and Gower had been living. Her body was discovered about five weeks later in neighboring King George County. Then, on May 1, 1997, sisters Kristin "Kristi" Lisk, 15, and Kathryn "Kati" Lisk, 12, vanished after returning home from school. Both girls had been sexually assaulted and strangled. Their bodies were discovered five days later in the South Anna River. Notes discovered by investigators indicated that Evonitz already had his eye on other potential victims, Fox News Digital previously reported. It would be months after Chamberlain’s abduction that Gower learned of her ex-husband’s other victims. "It felt like it wasn’t real at all," Gower admitted. "It felt like this was something that happens in the movies. This wasn’t real life. It was very hard to believe that he could hurt anybody. He had never hit me or physically abused me." GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB Now, Gower and Chamberlain are looking to Evonitz’s past for answers about whether there could be other victims. Gower has helped piece together a timeline of Evonitz’s movements during their marriage, providing investigators with dates, locations and old calendars as potential cold cases are examined. "Of course, he wasn’t always where I thought he was," said Gower. Chamberlain, meanwhile, has been investigating whether Evonitz could be responsible for other unsolved crimes, examining cases dating back to the 1980s and tracing his movements during his years in the Navy and in the decades before her own abduction. "I genuinely think that there is a level of escalation that we see between an indecent exposure [incident] and then three homicides in approximately nine months and then a break before me that is unexplainable to me," she said. "Everything’s possible and nothing has been confirmed," Chamberlain stressed. "It’s a frustrating place to be, but I will not stop searching." LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST One potential key to finding answers is DNA. While investigating cases for the docuseries, Chamberlain said she learned that Evonitz’s DNA profile was not in CODIS, the FBI’s national DNA database. However, she said authorities in Spotsylvania County still have a blood sample that can be provided to law enforcement agencies seeking to compare his DNA with evidence from other cases. Chamberlain said she hopes Evonitz’s DNA can ultimately be entered into CODIS, allowing for broader comparisons with evidence from unsolved crimes. "I genuinely believe that there’s no way he only murdered three girls and kidnapped me," she said. "I don’t think that there’s a world in which that’s true." While making the docuseries, Gower learned that Evonitz had kept a photograph of her when she was just 11 years old — years before they began dating — hidden behind another framed picture of her.
