title: California diners are cutting back as costs soar — but restaurant owner reveals one trend that's booming
description: Happy hour business jumped from roughly 8% to nearly 30% of sales at a San Diego restaurant group as California diners hunt for cheaper meals.
content: Happy hour is becoming the main event for some California diners as the state's high cost of living pushes more customers to seek out discounted meals instead of paying full price for a night out. Chef Alex Carballo of Grand Restaurant Group told Fox News Digital that happy hour once accounted for an estimated 5% to 8% of his business. Now, that figure has climbed to nearly 30%, even as customers cut back on dining out. "My happy hour has increased a lot, so I think people are looking for deals and looking for options," Carballo said. The shift reflects a broader affordability squeeze across California where residents told Fox News Digital that rising costs for housing, groceries and gasoline are forcing them to rethink everyday spending. California has the highest overall price levels in the nation, according to 2024 data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, with prices running roughly 11% above the national average. But affordability pressures extend far beyond the Golden State, as Americans nationwide grapple with elevated costs for housing, groceries and other everyday necessities. NEWSOM UNDER FIRE AS CALIFORNIA GAS TAX HIKE SENDS PUMP PRICES EVEN HIGHER Carballo said customers are visiting his restaurants less frequently, with some scaling back how often they eat out. "They're going out three times a week, where they were coming out to see me four or five [times]. And the people that used to see three times a week, they're only coming out once," he said. What was once a stop for drinks or appetizers before dinner is increasingly becoming the dinner itself, Carballo said. "Now it's like, that's where they're going and they're hitting those scenes," he said. Customers can still enjoy the same food, service and atmosphere at lower prices, Carballo said, making happy-hour deals particularly appealing. But those discounts also create challenges for restaurant operators who are already grappling with rising expenses. "I'm still paying the same amount for food. I'm still paying the employees. My rent didn't change. Nothing changed. Only thing I'm doing is trying to discount my product to gain people to come here," Carballo said. AMERICANS SAY TIPPING PRACTICES 'HAVE BECOME RIDICULOUS' AS DIGITAL PROMPTS PUSH HIGHER GRATUITIES Fox News Digital also spoke with residents in Southern California who described making financial trade-offs that extend well beyond restaurants. Jonas, a Santa Monica resident who is planning a wedding with his fiancée, said he and his fiancée are reevaluating their budget as everyday expenses continue to add up. "Certainly gas is expensive, rent is high, and then grocery prices are pretty high as well," Jonas said. He estimated that he spends approximately $100 a week on groceries and said rising costs are influencing their decisions about dining out and transportation. The couple is "eating out a little bit less," Jonas said, adding that he has also started walking to work to "save money on gas as well." "I think that people are just seeing prices go up everywhere, and feeling like they're getting less than what they had four years ago maybe," he said. "I think everybody's really feeling that." BELOVED RESTAURANT CHAIN DWINDLES FROM 850 LOCATIONS TO 87, BUT EXPERT SEES 'A LOT OF LIFE LEFT' For some Californians, the financial strain has gone beyond cutting back on restaurants. Justin, a California native from Glendora who moved to Las Vegas seven years ago, told Fox News Digital that the state's high cost of living was one of the reasons he left. "Affordability is crazy," Justin said while visiting Los Angeles for a Rams game. "I left seven years ago and I thought gas and you know rent was high then," he said. "Here I am seven years later and it's ... one of the reasons why I'm in Vegas now. It's just unaffordable." Justin said many of his friends who remain in California are still struggling with housing costs. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE LA'S HOMELESS HELLSCAPE — UNLIKELY CRITICS BLAST DEMS AS GOP HOPEFUL TOURS SKID ROW "90% of my friends are living with a roommate. It is really hard to live alone here," he said. Housing remains another major affordability challenge in the Golden State. Just 19% of California households could afford the state's median-priced home of $916,750 in the second quarter of 2026, according to the California Association of Realtors. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In Venice, resident Tatiana described rising expenses across everything from gasoline to groceries and neighborhood restaurants. "Everything is more expensive, gas is more expensive, food," she told Fox News Digital. "There's really very few affordable restaurants left on Abbot Kinney. Even our local co-op prices have gone up at least 15%. Everything costs more." "We're not getting any breaks in California," she said.

title: Ilhan Omar's turbulent week explained: The dueling probes that threw the Somali-born progressive into chaos
description: Federal agents raided Ilhan Omar's D.C. home, seizing her phone, computers and passport as part of a criminal probe into immigration fraud.
content: It was a week of legal turmoil for one of America's most recognizable members of Congress. Early Monday morning, federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. The raid was part of an ongoing criminal probe into Omar's immigration status, with sources telling Fox News Digital that authorities are scrutinizing whether she or her father committed fraud when filling out paperwork for her to become a U.S. citizen. A day later, Jeanine Pirro, U.S. attorney for the District of Washington, D.C., announced her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures, which had previously been subject to public scrutiny and congressional oversight, but never by authorities. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION Fox News Digital breaks down what we know so far about each investigation. Financial disclosure investigation In May 2025, Omar filed financial disclosure forms for the year 2024, a requirement for every member of Congress to complete every year. It showed that she had between $6 million and $30 million in assets connected to two businesses run by her husband, Tim Mynett. One was a venture capital firm, and the other was a California winery. Her financial disclosures from the previous year, covering 2023, said those assets were only valued at between $15,000 and $51,000 total. The now-defunct winery, eStCru LLC, saw its reported valuation jump from between $15,000 and $50,000 in 2023 to between $1 million and $5 million in 2024. Rose Lake Capital LLC showed an even sharper increase, rising from a reported value of between $1 and $1,000 in 2023 to between $5 million and $25 million the following year. The massive reported spike in net worth over the one-year span raised eyebrows, leading a watchdog group called the National Legal and Policy Center to file a complaint with the Office of Congressional Conduct in February of this year. 'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP Less than a month after the complaint was filed, Omar amended her 2025 disclosure form. The new filing reduced the couple's combined reported assets to between $18,004 and $95,000 and said the businesses had zero value after accounting for liabilities. ILHAN OMAR'S OFFICE SAYS SHE'S ‘NOT A MILLIONAIRE’ AFTER $30M FILING REVISED DOWN TO UNDER $100K: REPORT Omar blamed an accounting error and has since repeatedly insisted that she is not a millionaire. In September, the Office of Congressional Conduct voted 5-1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss misconduct allegations stemming from the financial disclosures. But the hubbub caught the eye of Pirro, who confirmed on Fox News' "America Reports" Tuesday that her office is investigating the discrepancies. Further details about the investigation have not yet been released. Criminal immigration probe Monday's judicially authorized raid of Omar's Washington, D.C., home sent shock waves through the political world, with many critics calling it politically motivated because it occurred three weeks before November's general elections. The Trump administration has denied those accusations. DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ HSI agents spent several hours at Omar's home, and The Wall Street Journal reported that the lawmaker's personal cellphone, computers and passport were seized during the search. She has not been seen publicly since before the raid. Sources told Fox News Digital that investigators are scrutinizing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork when Omar became a U.S. citizen decades ago. The Journal also reported that the goal of the probe is to strip Omar of her citizenship. A dozen people, including family members, were subpoenaed as part of the investigation. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE "Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully," President Donald Trump said Monday of the raid. "I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me. "I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is ... a non-country, and then she comes over here, and she complains about our Constitution," he continued. "I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it." On Tuesday, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital after rallying for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Tyler, Texas, Vice President JD Vance echoed a similar sentiment. "We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that, where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," Vance said. "We really want to let the law, the facts drive this. And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to." ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION Vance made it clear that taking that unprecedented step of denaturalizing a sitting member of Congress is possible, but only if the law requires it based on the facts of the case. "And to the question of it being unprecedented, I mean, what I'd say is that Ilhan Omar herself is a very unprecedented person," Vance said. "We have very rarely had a person in Congress who seems to have such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life," Vance said. "Now, that's not a crime. "But we're going to see whether she did commit a crime. And if she did, we're obviously going to follow the law." A spokesperson for Omar did not return multiple requests for comment throughout the week. However, Omar has responded on social media. "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar's office said in a statement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back. Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

title: Income inequality at Obama Foundation, as brass thrives and rank and file seeks union
description: Half of the Obama Foundation's reported workforce topped $100,000 in pay, outpacing five other presidential nonprofits examined in recent tax filings.
content: FIRST ON FOX: The beleaguered Obama Foundation has an income inequality problem. While half of its employees earn six-figure salaries, led by CEO Valerie Jarrett at $771,000, dozens at the other end of the scale are fighting for union representation. The workplace disparity comes to light just as Fox News Digital reported that the long-delayed Obama Presidential Center's price tag hit $1 billion, nearly triple the original estimate for the Chicago facility. The Obama Foundation, former President Barack Obama's private nonprofit, reported 172 employees receiving more than $100,000 in salary in its 2025 tax filing, roughly half its 342 reported employees. Jarrett, one of former President Barack Obama's closest advisors and a former senior White House official, has led the Obama Foundation since 2021, overseeing the final years of construction of the Presidential Center on Chicago's South Side. OBAMA'S BILLION-DOLLAR BABY: CHICAGO CENTER'S PRICE TAG HITS MONUMENTAL MILESTONE, TRIPLING ORIGINAL ESTIMATE Her total pay rose by around $15,500 from 2024, and she is one of at least four of the nonprofit's 10 highest-paid executives with previous ties to the Obama White House or campaign. "The foundation pays our employees rates that are competitive with the market," Emily Bittner, the Obama Foundation's vice president of communications, told Fox News Digital. "We have more than 500 employees worldwide, roughly 300 of whom are based at the center." The current workforce of more than 500 is substantially larger than the 342 employees reported in the Obama Foundation's 2025 tax filing, which covers the year ending nearly six months before the Presidential Center opened in June. The nonprofit did not provide an updated payroll breakdown. The Obama Foundation saw its annual payroll and benefits bill come in at $50.4 million in 2025, soaring from $18.5 million in 2018. The nonprofit brought in approximately $159 million in revenue last year, of which nearly $151 million consisted of contributions and grants. The spending surge came as the Obama Foundation expanded its leadership and civic programs at home and abroad while racing to finish the beleaguered Presidential Center. The sprawling 19.3-acre campus sits on publicly-owned parkland in Chicago's Jackson Park. WATCH: Professor breaks down Obama Foundation's finances amid $1B Presidential Center costs Expert view Brian Mittendorf, an accounting professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit finances, said the proportion of Obama Foundation employees earning more than $100,000 stood out compared with a typical nonprofit but noted that the organization relies heavily on specialized staff. "That's clearly a higher percentage than your average nonprofit," Mittendorf told Fox News Digital. "But here we're dealing with a nonprofit that's probably very expertise heavy. It's very heavy on, like, the think tank side. And as you look at a think tank, it would look very differently than, say, a local food bank." Mittendorf said the Obama Foundation's employees likely possess specialized skills that could command substantial pay elsewhere. "So, it does reflect that a lot of their employees are ones that they would consider having an outside opportunity that would justify them getting paid at that level," he said. "Like I said, it is atypical for a standard nonprofit, but probably not that unusual for a nonprofit of its type." The Obama Foundation also reported a higher proportion of employees receiving more than $100,000 than five other presidential nonprofits examined by Fox News Digital. Roughly half its reported workforce exceeded that threshold in 2025, compared with 37% at the George W. Bush Presidential Center, 29% at the Carter Center, 23% at the Clinton Foundation, 13% at the Reagan Foundation and 10% at the George & Barbara Bush Foundation, according to their respective 2024 tax filings, the most recent available for the review. OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER'S $470M SAFETY NET UNDER SCRUTINY AS SUBCONTRACTORS SAY THEY'RE OWED MILLIONS Executive pay Jarrett's salary rose from approximately $581,000 when she took over as CEO in 2021 to $740,000 in 2022, remaining at that level through 2024 before climbing to nearly $755,000 in 2025. For comparison, Fox News Digital reviewed the latest available tax filings from five other major presidential foundations, all of which reported lower CEO salaries than Jarrett's $771,000 in 2025. The Reagan Foundation paid its CEO approximately $735,000, and the Carter Center $531,000 for fiscal years ending in 2025, while the George W. Bush Presidential Center paid its top officer $661,000, the George & Barbara Bush Foundation paid $426,600 and the Clinton Foundation paid $425,000 for 2024. Beyond Jarrett, several former Obama administration officials continued to collect hefty six-figure paychecks at the Obama Foundation. Christina Tchen, former chief of staff to first lady Michelle Obama, received approximately $431,000 in salary in 2025, while Michael Strautmanis, a former Obama campaign and White House aide, collected approximately $404,000. Laura Lucas Magnuson, a former White House communications official, received approximately $396,000. Other top earners included Robbin Cohen, who received approximately $666,000. Cohen previously led Pritzker Realty Group, founded by billionaire Democratic donor and former Obama commerce secretary Penny Pritzker, a cousin of Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Former Cook County Chief Financial Officer Ammar Rizki received approximately $400,000. The Obama Foundation defended its executive salary practices. "The Board of Directors uses comparability data and a compensation consultant to review and approve the compensation of the CEO, officers and key employees on an annual basis," Bittner told Fox News Digital. OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25 The nonprofit also pointed to higher pay for top executives at other major charitable institutions, including approximately $2 million for the Getty Trust's president and CEO, $1.7 million for the Rockefeller Foundation's president and $1.5 million for the Mellon Foundation's president, citing figures from their recent tax filings. The Getty Trust, however, operates on a vastly different financial scale, with a multibillion-dollar endowment compared with the Obama Foundation's approximately $14.2 million in reported endowment funds at the end of 2025. Asked whether Jarrett's pay was excessive, Mittendorf said the answer was subjective, particularly given the Obama Foundation's size and financial resources. "This is not an unusual amount … to see for a highest paid employee for a director or a CEO," he said, noting the nonprofit's net assets exceeded $1 billion. Mittendorf acknowledged, however, that substantial executive pay at charitable organizations can attract criticism. "So, I think you see criticism from time to time of executive directors that get paid at this level, not that they could not get paid similar amounts in the private sector, but that there is a belief that, in the nonprofit sector, the pay should not just reflect what you would get in the public sector, but something more modest," he said. "It's quite common, though, for an organization of this size." Illinois Republican Party Chairman Bob Grogan, a longtime critic of the Obama Foundation's use of public parkland for the private organization, accused the nonprofit of enriching Obama's inner circle at taxpayers' expense. "The Obama Center is another far-left political operation that acts as a non-profit while using taxpayer dollars to make Barack Obama's inner circle rich," Grogan told Fox News Digital. The Obama Foundation maintains that construction of the Presidential Center was privately funded and that its operating costs are covered by revenues and private donations. Public funds have also supported infrastructure improvements surrounding the campus. Workers push to unionize The hefty executive paychecks come as rank-and-file Obama Foundation employees push to unionize, alleging rolled-back benefits and mounting workloads. Workers also claim deteriorating conditions have driven experienced colleagues to leave, taking valuable institutional knowledge with them and piling more work onto those who remain. The employees, organized under Obama Workers United with AFSCME Council 31, include visitor services and cleaning staff, museum and technology workers and employees involved in the nonprofit's educational and global programs. "Amidst increasing workloads we have seen our benefits rolled back and support from leadership to be minimal," the workers wrote in a public letter. SUBCONTRACTORS SAY THEY’RE OWED MILLIONS, FACE FINANCIAL RUIN, AFTER HELPING BUILD OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The workers also urged Obama Foundation leadership to respect their right to organize and refrain from spending money on anti-union lawyers, messaging or meetings. The Obama Foundation said it supports employees' right to organize. "We are deeply committed to the fundamental right of workers to organize and make their voices heard," the nonprofit said in a statement to Fox News Digital. " As members of our staff explore union representation, we approach this process with immense gratitude for their contributions, deep respect for unions, and a sincere commitment to working collaboratively with our partners in labor."

title: 'No Kings' foot soldiers ignore organizers' warning, go all in for Democrats

Main Street, and their "Sign Ideas" include: "Vote Blue Nov. 3," "Vote Early, Vote Blue" and "Time for a Blue Tsunami." Their announcement reads, "💙 Wear blue to signify the blue tsunami we are hoping we will see in Nov!" Some 3,000 miles away, in Roseburg, Oregon, Indivisible Douglas County activists are advertising their own "No Kings" rally with suggested signs reading, "DOUGLAS COUNTY VOTES BLUE!," "REPUBLICANS HAD THEIR CHANCE!" and "VOTE EARLY. VOTE THEM OUT!" "Be bold. Be direct. Don't hold back," the Oregon organizers told participants. Those are precisely the kinds of partisan political messages the national "No Kings" coalition has explicitly prohibited. After deadline as the protests were beginning Saturday morning, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz, national spokesperson for No Kings, called Fox News Digital and challenged the idea that the protests are partisan, saying, "No Kings is a nonpartisan, peaceful movement that has brought millions of Americans together to stand up for democracy, defend our freedoms, and reject authoritarianism." She asserted that the protests are drawing even Republicans, stating, "Today, No Kings is organizing the largest early voting activation in our nation's history, bringing together Democrats, Independents and Republicans who share a fundamental belief: voters should decide who leads our country, and every eligible voter deserves to have their voice heard." She added, "We are aware of partisan events circulating online that are not affiliated with or officially organized by No Kings. Many people utilize the No Kings name as a rally cry. But the coalition's focus remains clear: helping Americans understand where, when, and how to vote, encouraging people to cast their ballots as early as possible, and ensuring every voter has the information they need to make their voice heard." On a webinar Thursday night promoting the protests, a member of Indivisible Colorado Springs told Indivisible co-founders Leah Greenberg and Ezra Levin that the group's event is struggling to attract media attention without focusing on President Donald Trump. Levin replied, "By all means, make it about Trump. Y'all make it about Trump. Create some conflict. Use some strong language. There's nothing about No Kings that says you can't focus on the fascists in the White House." SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES Democratic Party recruits at 'No Kings' Under "Event Prohibitions," a "Host Toolkit" warns, "Events must not be partisan in nature or make references to preferred election outcomes." It bars "candidate campaign activity," "any political party or political committee attending or helping coordinate the event." The "Event Prohibitions" list bars events from being held at "overtly partisan organizations, or held at campaign offices, political party headquarters, or other locations principally associated with candidate or party political activity." The prohibitions explicitly state: "Events should not be jointly branded with partisan organizations,' and provides as "Examples: Democratic clubs, 'the Lincoln County Democratic Party.'" Yet, in Roseville, California, the Placer County Democratic Party is explicit in its connection to the "No Kings" voter drive, advertising a canvassing operation specifically tied to Saturday's "No Kings" rally at the Roseville Galleria. The party's website invites activists to attend a morning canvassing session at Harry Crabb Park, saying voters will be gathered at the rally at the Galleria and promising materials to help participants "support our endorsed candidates." On their Democratic Party website, the local party activists describe the "No Kings" rally as "a day of nonpartisan voter participation." ACTBLUE SCRUTINY FUELS NEW GOP BILLS TO TIGHTEN ELECTION DONATION RULES The advertisement raises questions about the relationship between the Democratic Party's candidate support operation and an event whose national organizers expressly prohibit political parties, political committees and candidate campaigns from coordinating activities. In Springfield, Pennsylvania, an event listed on the Women's March organizing platform advertises a one-hour "No Kings FOUR" demonstration at 1200 Baltimore Pike. The event calls for voter participation and, in another direct conflict with the national coalition's ban on "vote Blue" appeals, also declares, "Vote Blue. Vote. Make Your Voice Count." FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS Rules they wrote themselves The coalition's own documents leave little ambiguity about its official standards. In a five-page "Talking Points + Messaging" guide, organizers instruct participants not to use partisan political language, including telling participants to "vote for Democrats up and down the ballot" or saying, "We can get a Democratic Congress elected in 2026 to resist Trump." It bars any "speaker expressing bias for or against any candidate for office." It prohibits candidate campaign activities, including campaign literature, fundraising and coordination with campaign staff. Political parties and political committees are also barred from helping coordinate events. The instructions go beyond conventional warnings against endorsements. Organizers specifically prohibit references to "MAGA politicians" and calls to elect a Democratic Congress. Even urging participants to register as Democrats ahead of the midterms is explicitly forbidden. Another document, "Event Prohibitions + Things to Note," specifically prohibits "vote them out" and "vote Blue" messaging, campaign fundraising and political party coordination. Still, in Kingstowne, Va., Indivisible of Franconia is promoting its Oct. 17 rally at South Van Dorn Street and Kingstowne Village Parkway with the statement, "We vote for leaders to represent our interests — and if they don’t, we need to vote them out." The coalition also prohibits events hosted or co-sponsored by overtly partisan organizations, including Democratic clubs. Its "Election Law FAQs" and "Resources" go further, warning that merely describing an event as "nonpartisan" doesn't establish that it meets the standard. "Saying this doesn’t automatically make it so," the document states. Democratic infrastructure behind ‘No Kings’ The contradictions come as "No Kings" draws on a sprawling coalition of advocacy organizations, labor unions and political activists. In March, Fox News Digital identified about 500 organizations associated with the movement, representing an estimated $3 billion in combined annual revenues. The coalition partner list for today's protests is smaller but continues to include major labor organizations such as the American Federation of Teachers; the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees; the National Education Association; and the Service Employees International Union. It also includes organizations that align with the Democratic Party, including, Indivisible, MoveOn, Planned Parenthood Action Fund, End Citizens United, NextGen America, Our Revolution, Voto Latino and the Democratic Socialists of America. Most of these organizations or their affiliated political committees have histories of substantial spending to support Democratic candidates and causes. Their involvement places organizations with extensive electoral experience inside a coalition now publicly promising to avoid partisan campaign activity. The coalition's breadth also raises questions about how organizers distinguish between participating in a nonpartisan event and advancing the electoral objectives of affiliated political organizations. From a $250,000 protest to the ballot box The political infrastructure was visible during the March 28 flagship "No Kings" rally in St. Paul, Minnesota. Fox News Digital documented an estimated $250,000 production operation involving nine vendors, approximately 30 semitrucks, a massive stage, eight video screens and other concert-scale equipment. Roger Fisk, a former Obama and Biden administration political strategist, described himself as a senior advisor to the flagship event and credited its sophisticated media operation with generating hundreds of millions of digital impressions. The event featured Democratic political figures and celebrities, including rock star Bruce Springsteen and actress Jane Fonda, illustrating the extensive organizational and political relationships behind the movement. Former Gov. Tim Walz, Rep. Ilhan Omar and Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison — all Democrats — were among the event's political speakers alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. The involvement of Democratic officials in earlier anti-Trump demonstrations illustrates the movement's close relationship with Democratic political figures. Now the coalition is moving from street demonstrations to voter mobilization. In its October "Host Toolkit," "No Kings" describes Saturday's events as an opportunity to turn protest participation into electoral engagement. "Pivoting our strategy from marching to voting is our movement using the tool available to us when it matters most," the coalition tells organizers. The "Host Toolkit" insists, "Vote Early events are nonpartisan and are designed to increase participation from all eligible voters. The event should not reference, endorse, or oppose any candidate or political party. The event should not coordinate with any campaign or permit campaign materials. The event should comply with all applicable federal, state and local election laws." The campaign calls for voter education, early voting assistance, volunteer recruitment and election-protection training, with additional organizing sessions scheduled after Oct. 17. The coalition maintains that the effort is intended for all eligible voters, regardless of party preference. Legal dividing line The distinction between partisan advocacy and nonpartisan voter education matters, particularly for tax-exempt organizations. Under federal law, 501(c)(3) charities are prohibited from supporting or opposing political candidates. Other organizations, including 501(c)(4) advocacy groups and political action committees, operate under different legal restrictions. Indivisible, the coalition's leading organizer, operates through several affiliated entities with different legal structures, including a 501(c)(4) advocacy organization, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit and a political action committee. The coalition has scheduled an Oct. 21 training session on what happens after the demonstrations, followed by an Oct. 22 session on sustained mobilization and protecting election results. Just two days before the nationwide "No Kings" demonstrations, Indivisible co-founders Levin and Greenberg discussed the November midterms in openly partisan terms, celebrating Democratic candidates, criticizing Republicans and outlining their hopes for Democratic control of Congress. "Our candidates are quite good all around the country. Their candidates are quite trash all over the country," Levin said, referring to Democratic and Republican candidates, respectively. During the program, Levin, identifying himself as "a Texas Democrat," summarized the organization's immediate priorities, saying, "Right now, we're just full on let's win the election, but after that, we're going to shift." Levin said "you got to let people connect the dots" on the "nonpartisan" messaging. "No Kings" spokesperson Epstein-Ortiz asked that Fox News Digital include another part of Levin's comments, in which he stated, "You can't say, and that's why we've endorsed this Democratic candidate, go out and vote." The spokesperson also asked that comments by Levin and Greenberg be noted, asserting their support of candidates "regardless of party." "They're going to go out and they're going to exercise the right to vote," Levin said in the webinar. "That's your victory. That is your victory is getting as many people out to vote and as many people signed up for election defense as possible. We have a faith that if you do that, then pro-democracy candidates all over the country will win, and we'll have a pro-democracy Congress." Greenberg responded: "Regardless of party." Levin added: "Regardless of party. And in fact, Indivisible itself, we are backing several independent candidates in the election all over the country, where they are pro-democracy candidates." In a webinar last week, however, Levin was clear about the effort's political and electoral goals to win a "Democratic trifecta" in the White House, the House of Representatives and the Senate, saying: "It ain't over in November. It ain't over in 2027. It ain't over in 2028. We are building towards a national Democratic trifecta in 2029 that ushers in an age of accountability and reform." title: Trump says US 'may have to' strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site in future

title: ChinaAid raises alarm over imprisoned Chinese pastor's health as family seeks answers
description: ChinaAid founder Bob Fu says reports of Pastor Wang Yi's advanced liver cancer in a Chinese prison are credible but cannot be independently verified.
content: The founder of Christian human rights organization ChinaAid is raising concerns over the health of an imprisoned Chinese pastor who may be suffering from advanced liver cancer, and his family continues to face restrictions on visitation and access to medical information. Rev. Dr. Bob Fu, founder and president of ChinaAid, told Fox News in an interview that reports concerning Pastor Wang Yi's health are "very worrying," citing information received from multiple sources inside China. Wang, the founding pastor of Early Rain Covenant Church in Chengdu, has been imprisoned since December 2018 and is serving a nine-year sentence on charges of inciting subversion of state power and illegal business operations. Although Fu believes that reports of advanced liver cancer are credible, he acknowledged that his organization has not been able to independently confirm the diagnosis. REPORT DETAILS RISING PRESSURE ON UNDERGROUND CATHOLICS AS CHINA DENIES CRACKDOWN Fu said ChinaAid was "not able to really independently verify" the reports, citing restrictions on access to Wang and the absence of an independent medical examination. The organization first publicly raised concerns about Wang's condition on Sept. 28, calling on Chinese authorities to provide his family with access to him and disclose information about his medical treatment. During the interview, Fu revealed that authorities reportedly provided information by telephone about medical examination they claimed had been conducted on Oct. 1. According to Fu, prison officials cited medical information indicating Wang was in good health. However, his family has not been permitted a new in-person visit to independently assess his condition. Fu said that, despite repeated letters from Wang's wife and relatives requesting access, "no meeting had been granted at all" since the latest health concerns emerged. The pastor's church has also expressed uncertainty about his condition. TRUMP SHOULD PRESS XI ON CHINA’S PERSECUTION OF BELIEVERS AT HOME AND ABROAD In an Oct. 3 open letter, Early Rain Covenant Church acknowledged the reports but said it could not determine whether Wang had fallen ill. The church called on prison authorities to permit regular family visits, correspondence and telephone calls, as well as provide information about any necessary medical care. According to the church, Wang's family has been permitted fewer than five visits during nearly eight years of imprisonment. Fu likewise described severely restricted visitation, saying meetings have been brief and closely monitored by authorities. He alleged that discussions concerning Wang's health or religious beliefs have resulted in visits being abruptly terminated. "Two years, not a single letter for his wife," Fu said, describing the restrictions on communication. "That's not acceptable. That's even a violation of its own law." Wang was arrested Dec. 9, 2018, during a crackdown on Early Rain Covenant Church, an independent Protestant congregation operating outside China's state-regulated religious systems. In December 2019, a Chinese court sentenced him to nine years in prison. The U.S. State Department condemned the conviction at the time, describing the prosecution as connected to Wang's peaceful advocacy for religious freedom and calling for his release. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom lists Wang as a religious prisoner of conscience and has documented reports of medical neglect. Fu also raised concerns about the treatment of Wang's wife, Jiang Rong, who was detained during the initial crackdown. He said Jiang had previously been subjected to residential surveillance at a police-arranged location rather than being allowed to remain in her own home and described the lasting emotional consequences of her treatment. Fu said he believes the severity of the reports warrants immediate action, particularly given the limited access to Wang. He called on the Chinese authorities to permit Wang's wife, son and elderly parents to meet with him privately, allow an independent medical examination in the presence of legal counsel and release his medical records, including information concerning medications administered during his imprisonment. Fu also expressed concern about reports of mistreatment of other prisoners of conscience, including allegations of forced medication and serious physical and psychological harm. Those allegations were discussed as part of his broader concerns about the treatment of detainees in China, rather than as established evidence of what has happened to Wang. PENCE COMMENDS TRUMP FOR WINNING FREEDOM OF BEIJING'S ZION CHURCH PASTOR EZRA JIN FROM CHINESE DETENTION The ChinaAid president urged the Trump administration to raise Wang's case directly with Chinese officials during upcoming diplomatic engagements. "I really want to see the Trump administration to continue to speak up forcefully," Fu told Fox News, calling for the names of individual prisoners of conscience to be included in high-level discussions. He pointed to the July release of Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, who was reunited with his family after President Donald Trump raised his case with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a May visit to Beijing. Fu believes that example demonstrates the potential importance of direct diplomatic intervention, although the circumstances of Jin's release do not establish that such pressure would produce the same result in Wang's case. Trump and Xi are expected to attend upcoming international summits, including the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leader's meeting in Shenzhen, China, in November and the G20 summit in Miami in December. Fu urged U.S. leaders not to allow trade and security negotiations to overshadow concerns about religious freedom, human rights and the treatment of prisoners. "I think it's time to hold them accountable," Fu said. In a statement to Fox News, Chinese Embassy spokesperson Liu Chang said the embassy had no information to provide regarding Wang's specific case. The spokesperson defended China's religious policies, saying the government protects freedom of religious belief under Chinese law and does not interfere in religious groups' internal affairs. Liu added that China prohibits illegal activities carried out under the guise of religion and opposes foreign interference in its domestic affairs. The U.S. State Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment by publication time.

title: From ‘Third Reich’ to ‘not that informed’: Senate debates deliver fireworks before midterms
description: Candidates in Michigan, Georgia, South Carolina and Maine delivered personal accusations and unexpected admissions during debates that have led up to their elections.
content: With control of the U.S. Senate hanging in the balance this November, candidates across the country have been trading blows on debate stages, delivering everything from explosive personal accusations to embarrassing gaffes and unexpected admissions. The heated exchanges have unfolded in closely watched general election contests and contentious primaries alike, offering voters a glimpse of the personalities and policy differences shaping the battle for Washington. Some confrontations have drawn national headlines, while others produced memorable moments that quickly spread across social media. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK Here are five standout moments from Senate debates leading up to the 2026 midterm elections: 1. Michigan Senate candidates keep arguing through commercial break The first head-to-head debate between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed took an unusually combative turn Oct. 8, with the candidates repeatedly interrupting each other and trading personal attacks. The confrontation became so heated the arguing reportedly continued even after the televised debate went to a commercial break. "In 30 years of doing debates, I've never seen it continue during the commercial. But it did," moderator Rick Albin remarked when the broadcast resumed. The arguing got so bad that Albin had to get stern with the candidates. "Look, here's the situation. We've got dozens of questions we want to get to. You can't litigate all of these with 14 different rebuttals," he told them at one point. EL-SAYED REFUSES TO ANSWER WHETHER IRAN OR ISRAEL IS MORE DANGEROUS Throughout the hourlong showdown, Rogers questioned El-Sayed's medical credentials, accused him of misleading voters and repeatedly attacked his political ideology. The candidates also sparred over their respective property holdings, including Rogers' Florida home and El-Sayed's overseas investments. El-Sayed accused Rogers of enriching himself through corporate relationships after leaving Congress and criticized his support for President Donald Trump. Rogers described his Democratic opponent as a "con man" during Thursday night's debate, while El-Sayed accused the Republican of being "weak" and "cowardly." "I'd like to be part of the debate, too," Albin interjected during one particularly contentious exchange. 2. Democrat Senator accuses Republican rival of hiring 'half the Third Reich' Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., unleashed a series of accusations against his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., during their first head-to-head debate Oct. 8, accusing the congressman of associating with White nationalists and employing individuals with extremist ties. "Mike Collins has brought dishonor to our state through his personal bigotry and his widely documented ties to White nationalists," Ossoff declared in his opening statement. The Democrat later escalated his attacks while questioning Collins about his support for tax incentives benefiting data center developers. "It's not just that you've hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office, and you have promoted neo-Nazi content online," Ossoff charged. The accusations followed reporting about Collins' former congressional staffers and son-in-law, whose social media activity and alleged associations with White nationalists have drawn scrutiny. Collins rejected the characterization, insisting he has consistently condemned extremist rhetoric. TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY "I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is. And I tell him that too" Collins said. "It's wrong. We have no place in this world for that." Ossoff also invoked the late civil rights leader John Lewis, declaring that if Lewis were marching from Selma to Montgomery today, Collins "would be grabbing a billy club." Collins countered by portraying Ossoff as a radical liberal who was out of touch with Georgia voters, accusing him of supporting extremist policies and criticizing his connections to progressive political figures. 3. Republican Senate candidate admits she's 'not that informed' on national security A South Carolina Republican Senate primary debate produced an unexpected admission when Sen. Darline Graham acknowledged she wasn't very familiar with foreign policy. Graham, who was appointed to the Senate after the death of her brother, longtime Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, faced Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., during an Aug. 18 debate ahead of the state's Republican primary runoff. Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea represented national security concerns for the United States, Graham struggled to provide a substantive answer. "I'm just going to be honest here," Graham said. "I'm not that informed on national security." Graham went on to emphasize her support for the military, pointing to her late brother Lindsey Graham's 33 years of service in the Air Force and her father's service in the Army, while acknowledging that she was "not a polished politician." DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY'RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military," she said. The admission prompted audible reactions from the audience and a subsequent frenzy on social media. Among Graham's critics was former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who endorsed Graham's Republican primary opponent, Norman. In a post on X after the debate, Haley argued that national security expertise was not something Graham could inherit from her late brother, emphasizing its importance for serving in the U.S. Senate. 4. Collins demands apology after Democratic rival accuses her of profiting from Iran war Republican Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, demanded an apology from Democratic challenger Troy Jackson during an Oct. 8 debate after he accused her and her husband of financially benefiting from the ongoing war in Iran. Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, argued that Collins had failed to use her influence in Washington to stop the conflict because of her family's financial interests. "Sen. Collins and her husband are making money off this war," Jackson charged, suggesting that financial interests were helping prolong the fighting. Collins immediately rejected the accusation and called the allegations against her "absolutely false." DEM SENATE NOMINEE APOLOGIZES TO JEWISH VOTERS AFTER 'GENOCIDE' REMARK SPARKED BACKLASH "That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology," the Republican senator shot back at Jackson. But Jackson refused to back down, responding, "You owe me an apology." Collins' husband, Thomas Daffron, owns stock in two U.S. defense contractors, Boeing and RTX. According to the couple’s 2025 financial disclosure, filed in May 2026, Daffron held between $15,001 and $50,000 in stock in each company. A Collins spokesperson previously told The Maine Independent the investments were managed by a third party and that no individual stocks had been bought or sold from his account in more than three years. 5. Maine Senate hopeful goes viral after citing songwriting as qualification for office A Maine Democratic Senate candidate sparked widespread mockery on social media after citing songwriting and writing books among her qualifications for serving in Congress during a July 16 primary debate. Ashley Webb, one of eight Democrats competing to replace former nominee Graham Platner, who dropped out amid a flurry of accusations targeting his character, was asked directly what qualified her to serve in the U.S. Senate. "I ran for office several times, didn't win, but I did run and then, I'm a songwriter, and then I write my own books," Webb responded. Webb went on to emphasize her transparency and honesty, arguing that Americans were being deceived by politicians, particularly over the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies. The exchange quickly circulated on social media, drawing reactions from conservative commentators and political observers. title: Alex Murdaugh's defense makes 'high-risk' move to show DNA proves he didn't kill family, prosecutor says
description: Alex Murdaugh's defense team is betting on a Y-STR DNA test by Othram that prosecutors call "high risk" ahead of his April 2027 murder retrial.
content: LEXINGTON, S.C. — Alex Murdaugh’s defense team is gambling on a "high-risk" DNA test in its bid to point to another killer, a prosecutor said, citing the defense’s own expert. Judge Debra McCaslin sided with the defense over prosecutors’ objections Friday, allowing new testing on swabs from Maggie Murdaugh’s cellphone and clippings from under her fingernails, even though the process will likely use up the last of the testable samples. McCaslin said due process requires that a defendant be given "a meaningful opportunity to present a full and complete defense." Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County. The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury. His retrial is scheduled for April 5, 2027. Murdaugh has maintained his innocence in the killings. MURDAUGH WANTS IDAHO MURDERS DNA DREAM TEAM BEHIND KOHBERGER CASE TO HELP REWRITE SECOND MURDER TRIAL The defense team plans to employ Othram to conduct a Y-STR test, a method that isolates DNA from the Y chromosome to generate a profile of a male contributor in samples where female DNA is predominant. Murdaugh's attorneys contend that all three samples contain unidentified male DNA and are seeking to determine whether a single man was the source. Defense attorney Phil Barber said the findings could rule out certain individuals as contributors and may provide ancestry information, although the test cannot differentiate between men who share the same paternal ancestors. MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS NEWLY DISCLOSED RESERVE DNA SAMPLES SHOULD GO TO OTHRAM BEFORE STATE ANALYSIS The defense said the process will require approximately 90 days. Creighton Waters, the lead prosecutor, said in court that the testing would be "high risk" and unlikely to generate significant evidence. ALEX MURDAUGH'S 'WILD GOOSE CHASE' FOR MISSING MURDER GUNS TARGETS POLICE CHIEF: EXPERT "When we talked to their expert, he said, 'Yeah, that’s pretty much a sole source sample. This would be high risk and unlikely to generate anything, and [it] appears that that’s the case, because when we got back the quantification from [Othram], it’s goose eggs on the Y chromosome," Waters said. Barber laid out his reasoning for the new test, acknowledging the unknown male DNA could have an innocent explanation but saying the pattern is hard to ignore. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "Maybe it’s different male DNA. Maybe it’s the same. Maybe it’s red herrings. ... But as we keep progressing from one hand to two hands and now the phone, you know. It’s starting to look less and less like a red herring," Barber said. "If you have an unknown person under both her fingernails and throwing the phone out the side of the road after she’s murdered, it’s not him, I mean, that’s extremely important to the defense." ALEX MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS MURDER WEAPON MAY BE TIED TO SEPARATE KILLING AS JUDGE SEEKS ANSWERS Former prosecutor Joshua Ritter told Fox News Digital the strategy could backfire, saying the defense may have been better off leaving the DNA untested and using the unknown male profile to raise reasonable doubt at trial. There's somebody else out there who could potentially be linked to this crime,'" Ritter said. "Now, unless it comes back that it's a person who does have some reason to be suspicious, they've got a problem because if it comes back to a person with a rock solid alibi or a person with an innocent explanation as to why their DNA would end up underneath her fingernails, they've foreclosed any argument that they could have made. title: ICE arrests more than 100 alleged gang members in single week, including violent MS-13, TdA suspects: DHS
description: A suspected MS-13 member wanted for homicide and a teenage Tren de Aragua associate facing murder charges were among 131 ICE gang arrests.
content: In the last week, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested more than 100 suspected gang members in the country illegally, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) exclusively told Fox News Digital. Agents arrested 131 people allegedly affiliated with gangs between Oct. 4 and 10, including 22 affiliated with MS-13 and 13 with Tren de Aragua (TdA). ICE has made 12,018 gang-related arrests since President Donald Trump took office again in 2025, DHS said. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SAYS FEDERAL AUTHORITIES HAVE ARRESTED MORE THAN 10,000 SUSPECTED GANG MEMBERS "In less than a week, the brave patriots of ICE have arrested more than 100 gang members across the country, including members of MS-13 and Tren de Aragua," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. "The best that America has to offer are on the frontlines every day to ensure that the worst of humanity cannot threaten or harm innocent Americans." Mullin praised Trump’s leadership for helping ICE to smash the "gangs and cartels, making it impossible for them to do business in America and removing their members from our country. title: Biden-appointed judge deals Trump another sanctuary city defeat in major immigration fight
description: A federal judge ruled Trump's lawsuit against New York City's sanctuary policies fails, citing the 10th Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine.
content: A Biden-appointed judge dealt the Trump administration another legal blow Thursday, tossing its lawsuit seeking to upend New York City’s sanctuary policies after ruling that the Justice Department’s arguments amounted to a "backdoor around the Tenth Amendment." The Trump administration sued New York City in July 2025, alleging that its sanctuary laws unlawfully hinder federal immigration enforcement by restricting local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal authorities. The New York City case is one of more than two dozen lawsuits the Trump administration has filed against state and local jurisdictions over sanctuary and related policies restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities. But U.S. District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr. ruled the federal government lacked standing to challenge New York City’s restrictions on honoring ICE detainers and rejected the Justice Department’s claims that the city’s sanctuary policies are preempted by federal law. MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated the ruling in a post Friday on X, accusing the administration of attempting to turn city employees into immigration enforcement agents. "The federal government tried to turn our public servants into deportation agents and force New York City to carry out ICE’s cruel agenda," Mamdani wrote. "Today, a federal court rejected that effort and upheld our laws. Every New Yorker deserves to seek help from their city without fear of being targeted for deportation. We will stand by our immigrant neighbors, defend our laws and protect the promise that this city belongs to all of us." Reyes found the administration lacked standing because striking down the city’s restrictions would not remedy its alleged harm because separate state laws restricting cooperation would remain in place. But Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and partner at Holtzman Vogel, disputed that reasoning, arguing that the city's laws independently harm the federal government's authority regardless of whether similar state restrictions exist. "The sovereign harm is done just by the fact that New York City has the law (on) the books, no matter what other factors prevent practical application of the United States's position," Kambli told Fox News Digital. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS Reyes also rejected the Justice Department's argument that New York City's sanctuary policies are overridden by federal immigration law. "Even if the United States has standing — and it does not — its preemption claims fail," Reyes wrote. "All of the United States’ preemption claims — express, conflict and field — fail because the relevant federal statutes do not regulate private actors." The judge pointed to the 10th Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine, which prevents the federal government from forcing state and local governments from using their own officials and resources to administer federal programs. "If states cannot remain free to control their agencies and employees to resist federal immigration enforcement, which is within states’ constitutional prerogatives, the Tenth Amendment anticommandeering doctrine means nothing," Reyes wrote. Kambli, however, argued that Reyes misinterpreted the distinction between forcing local governments to assist federal immigration enforcement and preventing them from actively obstructing it. "Really what the 10th Amendment anti-commandeering means is you can't force states to go from doing nothing to affirmatively assisting. What these statutes are doing is basically preventing states from actively obstructing federal immigration enforcement," Kambli said. He argued that the Justice Department was not seeking to force New York City officials to carry out federal immigration enforcement, but instead to prevent local laws from interfering with federal authorities' ability to enforce immigration law. "That's different from the federal government saying a state or a city is required to actively assist ICE in operations," Kambli said. HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW The Justice Department also argued that New York City's sanctuary policies went beyond simply refusing to assist federal authorities by restricting information sharing with ICE that is protected under federal law. The administration additionally claimed that the city unfairly singled out federal immigration officials for restrictions that did not apply to other law enforcement agencies. Reyes, however, found that federal information-sharing protections apply specifically to information about an individual's citizenship or immigration status and do not require local governments to provide ICE with broader details, such as a person's release date or whereabouts. "The United States’ assertion that information regarding release dates and custody status is information regarding immigration or citizenship status is contrary to law," Reyes wrote. Kambli, however, argued that the distinction over what information is being withheld misses the greater issue at hand. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "The issue is mainly whether any state or locality that prohibits cooperation is preempted by federal law, regardless of what the information is," Kambli said. title: Dem congressional candidate's police employment record reveals suspensions over stolen gun, insubordination
description: Johnny Garcia faced two unpaid suspensions from the Bexar County Sheriff's Office for insubordination and negligence as he runs for Texas' 35th District.
content: Johnny Garcia, a candidate for Congress in Texas’ newly redrawn 35th District, faced a pair of suspensions for "job performance," "insubordination" and "conduct or action that would seriously impair job effectiveness" during his time with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office, records show. In the first suspension in 2009, Garcia brought a cellular device into a secure area against repeated instruction. The second, in 2020, arose when Garcia left a gun in an unsecured location, where it was later stolen. In both cases, Garcia was suspended without pay. The suspensions, discovered through a public records request, put new scrutiny on a law enforcement career that Garcia has made a central part of his campaign as he wages a race against Republican candidate Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran. The race to fill the seat being vacated by Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, is expected to be significantly more competitive in the upcoming midterms than in years past. FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON The first suspension came in 2009 when Garcia carried his cellphone into a secured jail area, something he had been told repeatedly not to do. "You have been instructed multiple times not to bring cellular phones or electronic equipment into the secured area and that doing so is a violation of policy. You stated you had been informed several times during Roll Call that cellular phones are not permitted in the secured area," a notice of suspension reads. "You are hereby notified that the Bexar County Sheriff’s Department is suspending you without pay for a total of three days … for insubordination [and] conduct or action that would seriously impair job effectiveness." The second suspension, according to the disciplinary record, came in 2020, when Garcia left his Glock firearm, four magazines and his badge — items that were later stolen — in his car. "Your equipment was not properly secured and was kept temporarily in your vehicle against Bexar County Sheriff’s policy. This negligent behavior has seriously impaired your job effectiveness and is a clear violation of the policies and procedures of the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office," a report read. Garcia received a five-day suspension without pay for "job performance," according to the county's records. The firearm was eventually recovered after Garcia reported it was missing. The sheriff’s office did not address questions about additional context on the suspensions, how frequently such suspensions are imposed and what other kinds of discipline the office would consider ahead of a suspension. Instead, it confirmed that Garcia had not faced any other forms of discipline as a result of the two incidents. TRUMP-BACKED AIR FORCE VETERAN WINS GOP RUNOFF IN NEWLY-REDISTRICTED HOUSE DISTRICT "The Bexar County Sheriff’s Office handles all policy violations in strict accordance with Civil Service Commission guidelines. Deputy Johnny Garcia served a 3-day unpaid suspension for bringing an electronic device into a secure facility and a 5-day unpaid suspension for failing to properly secure county issued equipment. The disciplinary actions were the agency's final decision of the incidents," Deputy Noel Diaz said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "All deputies are required to maintain complete knowledge of the Civil Service Commission policies. Disciplinary actions are handled independently on single incidents." Garcia, who has not held elected office before, faces considerably steeper election odds than other Democrats who have run in Texas’ 35th District. Casar, a progressive, last won re-election in the old district with a 67.4% to 32.6% victory in 2024. But Republicans targeted that electoral advantage through redistricting changes passed last year, prompting Casar to seek re-election in the state’s neighboring 37th district. "Trump and Abbott just rammed through maps designed to kick people like me out of office. They don’t want me in Congress because they don’t want us to be heard. But we’re not going anywhere," Casar said in a post explaining his move. To overcome that shift in political advantage, Garcia has brought a centrist message to voters, highlighting his service with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office, a post he joined at the age of 21. He would go on to work with the county jail and then as a hostage negotiator. On his website, Garcia lists border security as a top priority in addition to issues like affordability and protecting government programs like Social Security. He said he had faced border weakness firsthand, stating that he had seen "how Biden failed us on the border." "An old school Democrat … he believes true public safety means more than tough talk," his website states. SUPREME COURT HANDS GOP A REDISTRICTING WIN BY STRIKING DOWN LOWER COURT BLOCK ON TEXAS MAP CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked about the two suspensions, Garcia’s campaign pointed back at his record of safety as a law enforcement officer. "As a sheriff's deputy, I've spent nearly two decades putting my own safety on the line to protect my community to keep violent criminals off our streets. These politicized claims are Republicans' desperate attempts to distract from the fact that tariffs and his war in Iran have made everything more expensive for working families," Garcia said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Having cleared his party's primary in May, Garcia heads to the state's general election on Nov. 3.

title: Ilhan Omar raid sparks ominous prediction from watchdog: 'They probably got the goods'
description: Oversight Project's Mike Howell warns Ilhan Omar's HSI raid signals deeper congressional accountability failures and predicts more revelations ahead.
content: The federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., home prompted warnings Wednesday from a conservative watchdog leader that more revelations could be coming, as the Minnesota Democrat faces separate investigations involving her immigration records and financial disclosures. Oversight Project President Mike Howell, whose group pushed to strip a $1.031 million earmark backed by Omar, says the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) search raises broader questions about congressional accountability and what investigators may uncover next. His warning comes as U.S. Attorney Jeanine F. Pirro confirmed on "America Reports" that her office is investigating the Minnesota Democrat's financial disclosures, while separate reporting revealed that federal investigators had subpoenaed Omar's relatives as part of an immigration-related probe. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION "I think there's other shoes that are going to drop here," Howell told Fox News Digital. "That's why I think the Democrats really just couldn't resist the temptation to jump out of this before they saw any evidence and just circle the wagons [around Omar]," he said. DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ "I will say it appears they're walking that back a little bit. It has shifted from just a wholesale defense of Omar to a non-substantive defense, talking about, ‘well, this stuff was old,’ or ‘this is political since she's Ilhan Omar.'" Howell suggested that Omar’s defenders’ arguments indicate that it’s "not all peaches and cream underneath the hood." WATCH: ILHAN OMAR DENIES FEDS HAVE CONTACTED HER AFTER BORDER CZAR HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION Howell's warning extends beyond Omar to what he describes as a broader failure of accountability in Washington, where lawmakers can champion taxpayer-funded projects that later face questions about their legitimacy. Fox News has learned that federal investigators are examining whether Omar's age was accurately reported when she arrived in the United States in 1995 and when she acquired U.S. citizenship in 2000, including whether any inaccurate information could have affected her eligibility for citizenship through her father under the law in effect at the time. ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION The inquiry also encompasses paperwork completed by her late father and whether he provided inaccurate information. Sources told Fox News that investigators are examining potential immigration fraud spanning multiple years. Federal investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas as part of the immigration inquiry, including subpoenas to members of Omar's family. The immigration inquiry is separate from the financial-disclosure investigation being handled by Pirro, sources told Fox News. "We're in the speculation zone, of course," Howell told Fox News Digital, acknowledging uncertainty about the full scope of the federal investigations. DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS Still, Howell argued that obtaining a search warrant for a sitting member of Congress in Washington suggested investigators had developed substantial evidence, though the warrant establishes only that a judge found probable cause to believe the search would uncover evidence or other items subject to seizure, not that Omar committed a crime. Howell pointed to what he viewed as a unique combination of circumstances — an HSI investigation under the Trump administration, a warrant authorized by a federal judge in heavily Democratic Washington, D.C., and the proximity of the election — as reasons he believes investigators may have substantial evidence. "They probably got the goods on her," Howell said. "You don't get a federal judge to sign off on something like this in Washington, D.C., of all places, unless there is something that is rather convincing." Jonathan Fahey, a former acting ICE director and federal prosecutor in the neighboring Eastern District of Virginia, said the timing of the HSI search raises questions about whether investigators are examining more recent documents tied to longstanding immigration allegations. "I surmise that what they may be looking for is newer things that were used with what they believe is false information," Fahey told Fox News Digital, referring to the immigration investigation. Fahey suggested that knowingly repeating materially false information in more recent federal filings could create separate legal exposure, depending on the documents, circumstances and applicable statutes, even if criminal charges based solely on older paperwork would be barred by the statute of limitations. Former FBI agent Nicole Parker cautioned that Omar might not face criminal liability if her father completed allegedly false paperwork while she was a minor. "If her father lied and filled out the [citizenship/naturalization] forms, then in my opinion, she will not be criminally held responsible," Parker said. However, Parker said Omar could face a separate legal question if authorities establish she obtained citizenship through materially false information. "It could potentially cause her to be denaturalized and lose her citizenship if her citizenship was gained on false pretenses and false information," she said. In January, the Oversight Project challenged a proposed $1.031 million earmark for Generation Hope MN's Justice Empowerment Initiative in Minneapolis, a project backed by Omar and Minnesota's Democratic senators. The group raised concerns about the nonprofit's finances, operations and eligibility for taxpayer funding, including questions about its addiction recovery services at a location shared with a Minneapolis restaurant, whose owner previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that Generation Hope operated in upstairs office space. "We said, let's go check out those earmarks," Howell recalled. Conservative Republicans subsequently objected to the funding, with Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, among those pushing for its removal. The earmark was stripped, and Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, and Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, later requested Justice Department scrutiny of the nonprofit. The funding dispute raised questions about congressional vetting of proposed recipients, but its removal did not establish fraud by Omar or the organization. No connection between the earmark controversy and either federal investigation has been publicly confirmed. As part of his broader "institutional rot" argument, Howell argued that Omar’s earmark controversy is not unique, criticizing what he sees as lawmakers placing loyalties outside the United States ahead of their constitutional responsibilities. "This isn't normal. And it only seems normal because it's been happening so much. And I think it's about time we take the oath to the Constitution that members swear seriously," he said. Her office called the search an abuse of power and previously pointed to congressional ethics findings recommending dismissal of allegations concerning her financial disclosures, but did not respond to a request for comment on this story. title: Army expo attendees skeptical of Trump's Iran peace deal hopes: 'Beat 'em into submission'
description: AUSA Exposition attendees question Trump's optimism about an Iran deal, arguing military and economic sanctions must intensify before Tehran talks.
content: Attendees at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Exposition were skeptical of President Donald Trump’s signal that a deal with Iran to end the war may be near, arguing the United States needs to continue its military and economic pressure on Tehran to bring the conflict to a close. "Look at history, and that area only respects strength, right?" a member of AUSA’s Marne chapter in Georgia told Fox News Digital about Iran. "We're not going to get a deal with them. We're going to have to, unfortunately, beat them into submission. "There is no such thing as negotiation. So, I think we're probably looking at at least another year, if not two." TRUMP AGAIN SAYS DEAL IS CLOSE, THEN CONFIRMS A LAST-MINUTE AGREEMENT WITH IRAN, BUT DETAILS STILL SECRET The war began in February with joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. The conflict has continued despite an April ceasefire and a June agreement intended to pave the way for a broader settlement, which later collapsed amid renewed fighting. Trump still signals optimism about ending the conflict, saying earlier this month that Iran was "ready to fold up" and suggesting the war could end before the November midterm elections. "It looks like you guys are holding off because of the midterms," Lincoln from Australia said. "But it also appears that the Gulf allies need to step up and start doing something for themselves, for their own defense," Lincoln said. "Saudi Arabia doesn't seem to be doing enough. "It shouldn't just be the United States providing security for the entire world." TRUMP’S IRAN DEAL REACHES MAKE-OR-BREAK DEADLINE AS 60-DAY NEGOTIATING CLOCK EXPIRES Trump said Thursday he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran after reports started circulating that the Department of War was developing new strike plans that could include using a bomb known as the "Mother of All Bombs" against Iranian nuclear sites and energy infrastructure. "I know they tried diplomatic channels and … that's a good idea," Joe from Florida said. "It looks like we have to move beyond that. It looks like force is needed. They keep trying force on us. Let's talk their language." An Army veteran had more optimism toward the prospects of a deal, arguing that continued economic pressure on Iran could help to end the conflict. "Physically, they're having a hard time because there's a lot of pressure on them," Carl from Maryland said. "They're running low on resources, cash. US ECONOMIC CHOKEHOLD ON IRAN REACHES PEAK LEVERAGE AS COLLAPSE RISKS EMERGE "I think that more of … this continued pressure on them — economically, the sanctions — not allowing them to export the oil that they've done in the past to their other partners will continue to put pressure on them to cease hostilities." But even among those who expressed support for Trump's handling of the conflict, questions remained about whether the Trump administration could end the conflict through negotiations.
