"I think he'll do what he can, it's best for our country, but I'm very skeptical that there's any type of brokered peace between us and Iran."

title: Hero dad who took down Oregon school shooter identified along with teacher, student both killed in attack
description: The teacher killed in a shooting at a Bend, Oregon, school was identified by police Friday as 25-year-old Meghan Lambert. The hero who took down the shooter was Kaylub Giamanco.
content: The good Samaritan who police in Bend, Oregon, said "neutralized" the 16-year-old shooter who killed three children and a teacher Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School has been identified as 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, a law enforcement source confirmed to Fox News Digital. During a news conference Friday, police identified the teacher who was killed in the shooting as 25-year-old Meghan Lambert, and also announced that among the youngest of the victims was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. Police also revealed a school staff member threw a cellphone and tackled the attacker during the harrowing incident. "Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. Her friends became her family," Lambert's family said in a statement read at the news conference. ARMED BYSTANDER FATALLY SHOOTS SUSPECTED TEEN GUNMAN AFTER 3 CHILDREN, 1 ADULT KILLED AT OREGON SCHOOL: FEDS "Yesterday was a terrible day for our community," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said during the news conference. "Five people succumbed to their injuries at the scene, including the suspect. "The deceased at the school scene included three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and one 25-year-old teacher. One 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were transported by Bend Fire to Saint Charles Bend with critical injuries." The 7-year-old is in serious but stable condition, and the 54-year-old teacher suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Krantz said that, at 12:58 p.m., a witness who was driving by the school saw the suspect throw his gun over a fence and then climb the fence onto school property. He said the witness confronted the suspect, who then fired at his truck, hitting it at least three times. The driver, who was not injured by the gunfire, went down the street and made the initial 911 call at 12:59 p.m., he said. Giamanco, who Krantz only identified as a "36-year-old man" during the briefing, drove into the school parking lot after seeing the suspect shoot at the truck, Krantz said, and saw the suspect shoot the glass panes on two double doors to get inside. POLICE DISPTACH AUDIO RELEASED AFTER OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL SHOOTING Once he was inside, the shooter went straight into the classroom that was to the left and fired as many as 15 rounds. Krantz said the shooter used three types of ammunition and that all the victims were shot in the classroom. Giamanco grabbed a .40-caliber pistol he legally kept in his car and went into the school through the same doors. After hearing the sounds of a shooting, he went into the classroom, where he saw the suspect struggling with a teacher, who had thrown her cellphone at and tackled the shooter. Giamanco shot him multiple times. "In addition to the 36-year-old man who bravely stepped in to stop the suspect, I want to highlight another person whose heroic action we need to recognize," Krantz said. "A teacher in the classroom threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him. "She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed." DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED Police arrived at the school within minutes of the 911 call at 1:02 p.m. having been told that the "suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him, shooting him several times," Krantz said. Earlier Friday, Kenda Freeman said in a statement that her son, Giamanco, intervened in the attack and shot the gunman who killed three students and a teacher, The Associated Press reported. Giamanco, a local carpenter and dad, has two daughters who attend Silver Rail, his brother, Kyle Gianmaco, told NBC News. Kyle shared that Kaylub is shaken by the event and doesn't want to speak to the public. "We want the bystander who intervened to know we know he is going through a rough time, but we are grateful, and we think he is a hero," Lambert's family added in the statement. "You selflessly put yourself at risk for others. We would like the other families to know they are in our thoughts and prayers. Meghan loved those children, and so we will show you love for her." The shooter forced his way into the school by firing a shotgun at locked doors, Krantz said, citing the initial investigation. He said the shooter fired as many as 15 times and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On Thursday, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised school staff, parents and first responders, along with the community member "who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Silver Rail Elementary School is a public school in the Bend-La Pine Schools District with roughly 400 students, kindergarten through fifth grade, and approximately 40 staff members. Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price, and Fox News' David Spunt and Bill Melugin contributed to this story.

title: NCAA moves to block Ohio Governor Mike DeWine's executive order expanding college athletes' eligibility
description: The NCAA filed a federal lawsuit against Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, claiming his executive order gives Ohio schools an unfair competitive advantage.
content: The NCAA filed a lawsuit against Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine on Friday, escalating a dispute that began three days earlier when he signed an executive order giving state universities the option to allow athletes who graduated from high school in 2022 to compete for a fifth college season. The order challenges a new NCAA eligibility rule that excludes those athletes. The suit was filed in federal court in Ohio. NCAA President Charlie Baker described taking the legal action as an "extraordinary step" intended to prevent DeWine from making it "impossible for all schools to compete on a level playing field." In the lawsuit, the NCAA accused DeWine, a two-term Republican governor, of trying to give Ohio athletes "a hall pass" from following NCAA rules. NCAA WINS TENTH CIRCUIT 'STAY', BUT FACES MORE ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS FROM 2022 CLASS ATHLETES IN CHAOTIC TIME DeWine’s executive order and the NCAA’s lawsuit in response mark the latest escalation in a wave of legal maneuvering that is reshaping college sports rules on a state-by-state basis. The latest clash quickly prompted reactions from across the college athletics landscape. "This whole thing has become comical," University of Tennessee athletic director Danny White said on social media in reaction to the NCAA announcement. Ohio’s eight Division I programs have yet to publicly weigh in on DeWine’s order. The measure has received support from Lt. Gov. Jim Tressel, a championship-winning former coach at Ohio State and Youngstown State. The state’s Division I ranks include No. 4 Ohio State of the Big Ten, Cincinnati of the Big 12 and six members of the Mid-American Conference. Under DeWine's order, public and private universities in Ohio would be able to allow the Class of ’22 athletes to play, even though the NCAA’s new guidance excludes those who have already played four seasons. The rule, passed in June, is the subject of multiple court fights. DeWine’s office declined to comment on the lawsuit. Although it is unusual for the NCAA to sue a governor, the organization has done so before. In the early 1990s, the NCAA prevailed in a case against then-Nevada Gov. Bob Miller over a state law that would have required the association to provide greater due-process protections during enforcement proceedings. COURT RULING OPENS DOOR FOR MICHIGAN TO ADD FORMER MIAMI, BOISE STATE PLAYER TO ROSTER MID-SEASON IN WILD MOVE In its court filing, the NCAA said it was trying "to halt a misguided attempt to give Ohio colleges and universities an unfair, unprecedented and unwarranted competitive advantage in stadiums and arenas throughout the country." "College sports, like all sports, depend on participants following the rules. (DeWine) is attempting to give Ohio institutions a hall pass to break the rules," the lawsuit says. The Ohio Supreme Court has already said it will determine the legality of the executive order. As part of that, it paused an appeals court ruling in a case there that had declared the ’22 athletes ineligible; the court asked both sides to file briefs in the case, in which basketball player Filip Borovićanin is the lead plaintiff, by next Monday. Baker said the NCAA did not believe the Supreme Court's order did, in fact, declare those players immediately eligible to compete. That case, like others around the country, is becoming more urgent by the day, as it involves football players, along with a handful of basketball players whose status for the upcoming season is in jeopardy. Among them: Gonzaga transfer Javon Bennett, Cincinnati's MJ Collins and Borovićanin himself, who played in an exhibition against Tennessee on Thursday night after DeWine's order put him back on the eligible list. The Senate has sent the Protect College Sports Act, aims to provide that protection, to the House, but its fate remains uncertain in an election year. title: College Football Playoff expanding again, but the money behind it is not what some would call a 'win'
description: College football playoff expansion to 24 teams moves closer as ESPN and the CFP informally agree to a $345 million figure for additional games
content: Expansion of the College Football Playoff only needs a few approval signatures and final votes before we can officially start discussing what the sport will look like moving forward now that monetary figures are being finalized. Over the past month, college football commissioners have been dissecting what the financial terms would look like once ESPN presented its final offer for the next iteration of the postseason tournament to crown a national champion. According to sources familiar with the ongoing negotiations, ESPN and the CFP have informally agreed to a contract that would see the network pay an additional $345 million annually for the rights to eleven more football games that would take place with the 24-team playoff. COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANSION IS NOTHING MORE THAN A DESPERATE FINANCIAL BAILOUT DISGUISED AS PROGRESS ESPN was first to report the financial details of its offer to the CFP, which would eliminate conference championship games after this season. Over the next five years, with the loss of conference championship games, the network would pay for those leagues to get out of marketing agreements, along with the revenue generated from those same conference title weekends. ESPN will have to pay FOX upwards of $60 million annually for the Big Ten to exit its agreement with the network, sources added. THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF IS SACRIFICING ITS SOUL TO BE AN ATM FOR CONFERENCES WITH EXPANSION TO 24 TEAMS A lot can change in just three years for college football Just three years ago, CFP committee members agreed to increase the amount of teams from four to twelve, in what many around the sport thought was a pretty decent tradeoff if the postseason was going to expand. At that time, the thought of a 24-team playoff would have been laughed at, and was behind closed doors across college campuses. But, thanks to the increased spending across college sports related to revenue-sharing and NIL budgets, along with a plethora of power-four schools operating at a deficit, there was chatter that sometime in the near future that number would only rise again. Look no further than the NCAA Tournament, which recently expanded from 68 to 76 teams, as an example of college athletics looking to add more schools to an already crowded field. Now, after over a year of back-and-forth negotiating by conferences on what the right amount of teams should be if the CFP were to have expanded, that number increases by twelve. If you remember back to last year's conversation, the thought was that if college football was going to add more teams, that number could have just reached sixteen, thanks to a hard push by the SEC. GREG SANKEY MAKES IT CLEAR THAT SEC DIDN’T START THE 16-TEAM CFP FORMAT DISCUSSION, THAT'S ON THE BIG TEN At the same time, it was the Big Ten conference that held steady in its convictions that having a 24-team field would be the right move, giving more schools an opportunity to fight for the championship. More teams will make the college football postseason better, right? In reality, the additional twelve teams added a a justification mechanism to the postseason, given how many schools are spending over $30 million per year just to piece together a roster good enough to contend for a playoff spot. So, with a push from Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti, other conferences, including the ACC and Big 12, embraced the idea that a 24-team postseason would give their teams more opportunities to play meaningful football in December while creating a simpler path to the playoff. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On Friday, that thought process took another gigantic step, as those in charge of putting a product on television have all but signed the official paperwork to once again expand the college football playoff.

title: Bedbugs found in plane's economy seats force major airline to cancel flight
description: A Qantas passenger described bedbugs crawling on her belongings and blankets on the Boeing 787 Dreamliner that flew from Perth to Rome. A subsequent flight was canceled.
content: An international flight scheduled to travel from Italy to Australia was abruptly canceled last week when a bedbug infestation was discovered in the cabin during an earlier flight, and the airline issued an apology for the incident. The grounding came after passengers on the nearly 17-hour Qantas journey from Perth to Rome reported being bitten by the insects Oct. 9, The Sydney Morning Herald reported. "We sincerely apologize to customers for the cancellation of Saturday’s Rome-to-Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue [was] identified on a small number of economy seats," Qantas Airways Limited told Fox News Digital. MAJOR AIRLINE ABANDONS 3 KEY CITIES AS PASSENGERS FACE SHRINKING FLIGHT CHOICES Passenger Hailey Bagnall told the TV news program "9News Sydney" that bedbugs were "crawling over our belongings, our clothing, our Qantas blankets, and they were even crawling along the window." The aircraft involved in the incident was a Boeing 787 Dreamliner. Other travelers also recounted their experiences to "9News," with one passenger claiming to be "woken by screaming," while another noted that "the bugs just kept coming." As they collected their bags, the passengers discovered the pests were inside their shoes and crawling on their clothing. Bedbugs were "crawling over our belongings, our clothing, our Qantas blankets, and they were even crawling along the window." Travelers first alerted the flight crew about the bedbugs during the initial Sydney-to-Perth leg of the journey, according to "9News." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The airline said that, before departing on the subsequent long-haul leg to Rome, staff took several preventative measures, including deep cleaning the cabin, removing seat coverings and soft furnishings, and cordoning off the impacted seats. Qantas also noted that its aircraft are regularly cleaned to a high standard and undergo a precautionary disinfectant treatment every 50 days. To alleviate the itchy bites, travelers on the flight were provided with antihistamines, though the crew eventually ran out of the medication, The Sydney Morning Herald reported. Measuring between 1 and 5 millimeters, the insects feed on human blood. Health officials note, however, that while their bites cause itching and swelling, bedbugs are not known to spread disease and are not considered a public health hazard. Hottel noted that travelers can unknowingly carry bedbugs onto planes, into hotels and eventually back home. title: Eagles appear set to add QB from Cowboys' practice squad as Jalen Hurts deals with blood clot
description: The Philadelphia Eagles signed Joe Milton off the Dallas Cowboys' practice squad with Jalen Hurts sidelined indefinitely due to a blood clot.
content: In the NFL, availability is often described as a player’s best ability. Since taking over as the Philadelphia Eagles’ starting quarterback, Jalen Hurts has largely embodied that idea. The Super Bowl LIX MVP started all 17 games in 2023, missed two games with a concussion in 2024 and sat out Philadelphia’s regular-season finale that year as the Eagles rested most of their starters ahead of the playoffs. Backup quarterback Tanner McKee filled in for Hurts in Week 18 to close the 2025 season and will be called upon again this Sunday. Hurts has been ruled out by what the team has described as a superficial blood clot in his calf. FORMER NFL TEAM DOCTOR ADDRESSES JALEN HURTS' BLOOD CLOT AS QB'S SEASON HINGES ON ONE KEY WORD Hurts was considered a full participant in Friday’s practice leading into this past Sunday's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, despite dealing with a calf injury. He was not on the injury report for last week's game in London. While McKee will be QB1 this weekend, the Eagles appear to be turning to a division rival to bolster their quarterback room and potentially push rookie Cole Payton out of the backup role in Week 6. According to multiple reports, Philadelphia is set to sign Joe Milton off the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad. Under NFL rules, any player signed from another team’s practice squad must be placed on the new team’s 53-man roster. Milton will therefore be on the active roster when the Eagles host the Carolina Panthers and look to snap their three-game losing streak. The timeline for Hurts’ return remains unclear. The Eagles did, however, release a statement detailing how the blood clot was discovered. "On Thursday, October 8th, Jalen visited the training room after practice requesting treatment for his calf," the team said. "He informed the medical staff he had been cleated during the Rams game on October 4th. This was his first treatment session for the calf injury following the game, after having practiced in full both Wednesday and Thursday. On Friday, Jalen received treatment, practiced in full, and was added to the practice report." LEGENDARY AGENT WARNS NFL TEAMS ABOUT MAKING KEY QUARTERBACK MISTAKE THAT COULD DERAIL SEASON The statement also said team doctors recommended a follow-up scan after the game. "Out of an abundance of caution, an ultrasound was performed on Saturday following the team's flight to London and walkthrough. The ultrasound revealed a superficial blood clot. Our medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the results and concluded that activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play. Doctors recommended a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the return flight to Philadelphia." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Payton, a fifth-round pick in April’s draft, has appeared in just one game this season. He has yet to attempt a pass in a regular-season game. Milton has slightly more NFL experience, though he has never started a game. In limited action, he has flashed both mobility and the arm strength that made him an intriguing prospect. Sam Howell won the Cowboys' backup job during the offseason, prompting Milton’s departure from Dallas. Milton said he was surprised by the decision at the time. "It was shocking. But it's life. You got to be able to live with it and deliver blows back when it's time," he said. Milton was later added to Dallas’ practice squad, where he spent the past five weeks before the Eagles came calling Friday. It remains unclear what the Eagles’ decision to add a quarterback signals about Hurts’ status or whether they expect him to miss an extended period. title: Florida Panthers GM Bill Zito has unusual tie to Milwaukee Brewers' last World Series run

title: White House reporters react to Katie Zacharia's 'brutal' exit as Trump's press secretary
description: Fox News Digital spoke with several White House correspondents about Katie Zacharia's dramatic exit as President Donald Trump's press secretary.
content: White House reporters were stunned by the brief tenure of President Donald Trump's press secretary Katie Zacharia after just five days on the job. "Brutal," one White House correspondent reacted to Fox News Digital. Zacharia, who first took to the podium Tuesday after the August departure of her predecessor Karoline Leavitt, did not receive the warmest reception among critics who pointed to her nervous demeanor and how she only called on three reporters during her debut. "I knew she was out two minutes into her prepared remarks on Tuesday," a second White House reporter told Fox News Digital. "It was just too drastically different from Karoline. We were all shocked after. TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY OUT OF THE JOB JUST DAYS AFTER ROCKY DEBUT "Karoline was beautiful and hardcore MAGA ... and dignified and professional and substantive. She set a new standard for press secretaries. You can't just be hot and good on TV." A third White House correspondent expressed surprise Trump offered her the job in the first place, saying, "Usually, he’s spot on about who has 'it' and who doesn’t. "There is no excuse for Katie’s first briefing performance," the reporter said. "In that role, you have to be the best communicator because your job is speaking to the American people on the president’s behalf. No one expected her to have all the answers or even most of them. But I expected basic communication skills that were simply not there." "She probably could have been better than Karine Jean-Pierre if she had more time to prepare. But it was a brutal start," a fourth White House reporter told Fox News Digital. KATIE ZACHARIA ADDRESSES BREVITY OF FIRST PRESS BRIEFING, DEFENDS LEGAL CREDENTIALS AFTER CRITICISM While Zacharia's shaky performance in the briefing room drew a lot of attention, it was her repeated claims of having been a lawyer that may have been more lethal to her future in the Trump administration. The fourth White House reporter suggested that was a "bigger threat" than her first and only day at the podium. A fifth White House correspondent who spoke with Fox News Digital was of two minds. On one hand, the reporter said Zacharia deserves no sympathy since she accepted the job she was "manifestly unqualified for," noting her embellished resumé she knew would eventually be exposed. "On the other hand, shame on the president," the correspondent said. "He was clearly getting antsy and impulsive. He wanted his new press secretary now, and he wasn't going to let mean old Susie Wiles tell him to wait while she convinced someone more competent and more prepared for one of the hardest jobs in government to actually take that job." The correspondent pointed to current staffers in the White House communications shop like Anna Kelly and Lauren Bis as individuals who can handle the job but aren't "central casting" in Trump's eyes. "He took someone who seemed like a nice young woman who was defending him on TV, doing an OK job of that, and subjected her to a massive amount of humiliation and made her a national laughingstock because he didn't want to be told no," the reporter said of Zacharia. "I don't want to say he ruined her life, but she's gonna be a punchline for a very long time. And that's not fair." JEN PSAKI MOCKS TRUMP’S NEW PRESS SECRETARY, QUESTIONS IF SHE’S A 'POTENTIALLY FAKE LAWYER' As the search continues for Zacharia's replacement, a sixth White House correspondent insisted it "doesn't matter" who serves as press secretary during the current administration. "Trump lies every day about everything and frequently changes his mind completely, leaving his staff looking foolish," the reporter told Fox News Digital. NBC News White House correspondent Garrett Haake said the drama surrounding Zacharia reflects a "bigger problem" for Trump and his staff. "The ouster of now-former Press Sec Katie Zacharia highlights a bigger problem for the Trump White House two weeks til the midterms: They're struggling to drive any message. Meandering rallies, staff stories taking up oxygen, long hard-to-hear gaggles, no briefings," Haake wrote on X. "There is nothing more cringe than a bunch of reporters cackling amongst themselves because they’ll never have the talent to take on a job as important as press secretary," White House communications director Steven Cheung told Fox News Digital. "It’s easy to sling arrows at others, but when they are on the receiving end, they’ll complain like it’s the end of the world. Reporters have the thinnest skin." Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy reported Friday that Zacharia will be "transitioning out" of the job after Trump appeared unsure about her as his press secretary when speaking with reporters. "I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this really for you?'" Trump said. "I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it. "Maybe it's not for her," he later added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump's search for a new White House press secretary continues after the departure of Karoline Leavitt in August. title: Cookies, liquor and mocking Nazis fuel final stretch in fiery Texas House race
description: Katy Padilla Stout's Texas Democratic campaign reported over $4,300 in cookies, beer and wine and Mexican restaurant spending, according to FEC records.
content: A Texas Democratic congressional candidate's campaign reported more than $4,300 in spending on cookies, Mexican restaurant purchases and beer and wine earlier this year, according to federal election records, drawing renewed attention after a heated debate in which she apologized for a remark about her Republican opponent "making fun of Nazis." Katy Padilla Stout, the Democrat nominee for Texas' 23rd Congressional District, reported expenditures totaling $4,338.14 in five transactions in March and April, according to spending details cited in an August report by RedState and records attributed to the Federal Election Commission (FEC). The reported purchases included $675 for cookies for a campaign event, $1,289.22 at Total Wine and $2,373.92 at Las Guitarras Cocina Mexicana. SENATE REPUBLICAN SETTLES SIX-YEAR-OLD CAMPAIGN BILL AFTER BEING CALLED OUT ON SOCIAL MEDIA The expenditures have also become a line of attack for Republican Brandon Herrera, whose campaign website showcases the cookie purchase and accuses Stout of using donor funds to pay for the treats. According to the spending details, the campaign reported a $675 payment dated March 30 with the stated purpose "COOKIES FOR EVENT." Herrera's website identifies the payee as Denise Gamboa Zelle and categorizes the expense as a campaign event expenditure. Additional transactions included $1,089.08 at Total Wine on April 21 and $200.14 the following day, both described as "BEER AND WINE." The campaign also reported payments of $2,027.52 and $346.40 to Las Guitarras Cocina Mexicana on April 27 and April 28, respectively, according to the transaction details. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Stout said the disbursements "were for campaign and fundraising events which were attended by our supporters." "Sugar cookies, particularly Texas-shaped ones, hold a special place in Texan culture," she said. "We bought ours at a local bakery because we believe in supporting small businesses." SENATE HOPEFUL'S 'TREADING WATER' NARRATIVE CRUMBLES UNDER $500K CAMPAIGN PAYOUTS TO FAMILY The filings establish that the campaign reported the expenditures but do not establish whether the purchases were improper, whether any were for personal use or how many people attended the associated events. The spending has attracted criticism from Herrera's campaign, which maintains an opposition website, The Real Katy Stout. Under a section labeled "Cookie gate," the site highlights the $675 expenditure and displays the reported purpose, "COOKIES FOR EVENT." The website also criticizes Stout's positions on immigration, taxes and other issues. DEM SENATE NOMINEE APOLOGIZES TO JEWISH VOTERS AFTER 'GENOCIDE' REMARK SPARKED BACKLASH The spending questions come as the two candidates compete for a congressional seat representing one of the country's largest districts along the southern border. During Tuesday's televised debate in San Antonio, Stout also drew attention for an unusual exchange involving Herrera's online videos. "He made millions of dollars after making jokes online, making fun of Nazis, making fun of all of these things that we know he does not need to be doing," Stout said in a heated moment during the debate. Herrera responded, "And here I thought making fun of Nazis was a good thing." Stout later apologized and clarified her criticism after closing remarks. "I apologize, I did misspeak," she said. "He chooses to goose-step on YouTube for clickbait and money so that he can promote that type of ideology. He chooses to shame women." The exchange was part of a debate hosted by WOAI/KABB, during which the congressional candidates also sparred over gun rights, immigration and the cost of living. Stout told Fox News Digital "mocking Nazis is fine, and that is not what I objected to, nor is that what my opponent does." "I object to content that trivializes veteran suicide, rape, child murder, women’s bodies and the Holocaust, the type of content he churns out," she added. "You can hear his disgusting commentary straight from his own mouth at HeReallySaidThat.com. "Do I think he promotes Nazi imagery? Yes. In a video posted 5/24/22, he goose-steps to 'Erika,' and touts an MP-40 machine gun. In another video posted 6/23/20, he said 'for the fatherland' before firing a Nazi-made STG 44, calling it 'like a religious experience.' "Calling it a joke doesn’t change what it is: giving a platform to Nazi symbols and weaponry for clicks and money. In my view, the 'I’m only joking' defense is a familiar tactic among neo-Nazi and antisemitic content creators. His content has attracted bipartisan condemnation, including the Republican Jewish Coalition, which called my opponent 'a goose-stepping extremist who pals around with online Nazis.'" Stout, a former teacher and child welfare attorney, has emphasized affordability and corruption as central themes of her campaign. Herrera, a firearms manufacturer and online personality who has adopted "Let's Go Brandon" as his campaign slogan, has campaigned on border law enforcement, tax reductions and Second Amendment protections. The two are vying to replace former Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales, who resigned earlier this year after acknowledging an affair with a staffer. Texas' 23rd Congressional District stretches from the San Antonio area toward El Paso and includes hundreds of miles of the U.S.-Mexico border. Early voting begins Oct. 19, with Election Day scheduled for Nov. 3. title: WA schools chief dismisses girls' sports fairness concerns, says athletes' brains aren't fully developed
description: Washington Superintendent Chris Reykdal dismissed fairness concerns after Camas High girls cross country athletes protested a biological male competitor.
content: With every word, these leaders shed another shred of dignity. The latest to shrink was Washington state Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal. Appearing on the Seattle-based radio show "Jake and Spike," the head of Washington's public school system made some remarks about the boys-in-girls-sports debate that seemed outlandish by even a politician's standards. The issue at hand was Initiative 638, a Nov. 3 ballot measure in Washington that, if passed, would keep biological males out of K-12 sports. Host Jake Skorheim brought up the situation in southern Washington, where members of the Camas High girls cross country team walked off the start line Tuesday in protest of having to run in the same event as a boy. A CROSS COUNTRY RUNNER SWITCHED TO THE GIRLS TEAM MIDSEASON, PARENTS VOICE THEIR DISAPPROVAL AT MEET Answered Reykdal: "Let's face it, this is happening across the country, where we've empowered young people to make important decisions. And 99% of the time, they're good friends and colleagues, and they respect their transgender colleagues. But some don't agree with it, and that's their right to express that." This doesn't sound too objectionable on its face, but there did seem to be a subtle dig at the protesters. Reykdal said that 99% of young athletes are "good friends and colleagues" and that they "respect their transgender colleagues." It's almost as though he's implying the 1% are disrespectful. No. Surely there are some girls out there who are OK with competing against biological boys. The fact that protesters have received backlash from various teammates proves as much. But just because other athletes aren't going public with their disapproval doesn't mean they like it. They just don't want the smoke that comes with being outspoken. WASHINGTON HS GIRLS BLAST MALE ATHLETE PARTICIPATING IN TRACK MEET: 'DON'T THINK THAT THAT'S RIGHT OR FAIR' Second — choosing not to compete against a trans athlete does not make one disrespectful toward the trans community. It is simply acknowledging an unmistakable biological advantage and highlighting the unfairness. Reykdal continued: "The much larger issue here is: Can we accommodate 10, 12, 15 kids a year and make them feel included? Or do we have to go through an initiative process where every single girl has to prove, through one of three methods, that she's a girl in order to participate?" The term "inclusivity" has been co-opted to vilify anyone who opposes males in female sports. The truth is that sports at most levels are designed to be exclusive. Only a certain number of athletes make the team, or get to start, or reach the final heat, or get a scholarship. And those "10, 12 or 15 kids" often have great success. Last year, high school trans athletes won girls' state track-and-field championships in Washington, Oregon and California. And at Camas, a biological male went from 76th in a boys JV race to first in a varsity girls meet. Hence Skorheim's next question. "I hear what you're saying, but specifically, I want to ask about this case in Camas. They're racing against somebody who, earlier in the year, was 76th running for the boys cross-country team, who placed second here. Now, those girls had to forfeit because they had no chance of winning." Answered Reykdal: "Well, I raised two kids, and one of them was a daughter in sports. And my take is, you have a choice to make. You're going to compete and do the best you can and embrace your colleagues, or you're going to walk off and make a statement. And that's okay, too." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER I don't want to put words in Reykdal's mouth, but it almost sounds like he's telling these girls to simply compete, do their best and accept the circumstances — regardless of whether those circumstances are fair. But would he say something similar about athletes competing against people on steroids? That they should just embrace their "colleagues." Probably not. Again, this isn't about discrimination or hate — it's about fairness. But Reykdal's answer to the following question is much more egregious. "If your daughter was running against a boy—an athlete who raced as a boy and was 76th, and then had to race against that same athlete on your team—does that seem like a fair situation to you?" asked Skorheim. Answered Reykdal: "I don't see it that way, Jake. I just don't. These are young, developing people whose brains aren't going to fully develop until they're 25." Excuse me? Sorry, kids, we don't owe you fairness because your brains aren't fully developed. And while we're at it, we can shortchange college athletes because, unless they're at BYU, they're all under 25 as well. I've seen people try to dismiss this issue with an arsenal of arguments — that I-638 proponents are bigoted, that trans athletes are rare or that proving one's gender will require "invasive genital inspections" (untrue). But their brains aren't fully developed is a new one. Again, you won't see politicians bluntly say that it's OK to have boys compete against girls. That's a losing argument. So instead, you get mental gymnastics worthy of the all-around gold. title: Recovering from lung surgery, Pope Leo urges Putin to agree to ceasefire in Russian-held Ukraine city

title: Seth Meyers admits shock over second Trump victory prompted sit-down with late-night team to adjust tone
description: Seth Meyers revealed he held a tonal meeting with his team after President Donald Trump's second election victory, saying he didn't want to go through the motions again.
content: Late-night host Seth Meyers admitted to shifting his tone after President Donald Trump was elected a second time during an interview on Tuesday and held a meeting about it with his team. Nayeema Raza, host of the "Smart Girl Dumb Questions" podcast, asked Meyers if political comedy makes people feel too comfortable. Meyers said it was a concern but that he didn't know how else to approach it. He also said he didn't want to sound the alarm about the Trump administration every night on his show. "We did have this like tonal conversation at our show, because again, we did not, I mean, twice now, we have been shocked that he has been elected, right? First time more than second, but the second time we sat down with everybody," he said. "I'm like, 'Look, I don't think we can tonally be the same that we were for the first four years, right? I think it's going to be different, and it's going to feel different, and it will also — it will feel like, I don't know, just a little like neutered if we're like going through the motions again,'" Meyers continued. TRUMP IS 'UNFETTERED' AND MORE COMFORTABLE WITH POWER IN HIS SECOND TERM, JOURNALISTS SAY "And so what we do and like what I go out and tell the audience before the show every night is like, 'Look, this show is joyful to do. This is joyful to have you here. And like there's a real strength and joy.' Like, so what we're talking about isn't joyous, but like we — I don't want to perform with like the weight of it all on top of me," he said. "I want to be like honest about it," Meyers added. "We want to get our facts right. But we think there's a strength in, like, sort of being joyful about the fact that we're all together agreeing how f---ing crazy this is." The late-night host also addressed Jimmy Kimmel's suspension during the interview. Kimmel, host of ABC's "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" was suspended in 2025 after comments he made about the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. "With that said, like if, like, they turn the lights off fast, when they turn it off, right? Like when Kimmel went off the air, like I don't think he knew that morning that he would be off the air that night. And that was certainly the scariest time of all of this," he said. "The scariest thing about the second term is, like, I feel like there's a lot more going back to the drawing board when you don't get it your first try," Meyers said. Meyers credited NBC News for never telling him what he should "say," and called it a "special thing." BOB IGER BREAKS SILENCE ON DISNEY'S SUSPENSION OF JIMMY KIMMEL OVER CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION COMMENTS "These elitist hosts have spent a lifetime scaring audiences with every move from this administration, so they can insist they're going to lean into joy, but they cannot and will not help themselves," Curtis Houck, managing editor of Newsbusters, told Fox News Digital. "They have this belief that they're like Thomas Paine writing about how 'These are the times that try men's souls,' and any sort of happiness must be seen as a triumph. Cry me a river. Late-night hosts like Meyers have gained increased prominence on the left because of their rabid emphasis on everything Trump and a hyperbolic outlook," he added. Meyers, along with fellow late-night comedian John Oliver, recently joined Kimmel on his show, where the pair described Kimmel as a "bulletproof vest" when it came to Trump. DISNEY CHIEF DANA WALDEN DODGES WHEN ASKED ABOUT JIMMY KIMMEL'S FUTURE AS ABC'S LATE-NIGHT HOST Oliver said that Kimmel comes up a lot during the question-and-answer sessions at stand-up shows he performs with Meyers. "You draw all the ire," Meyers said. "We are fully supportive," Oliver told Kimmel. "We are fully behind you the way that we’re fully behind a bulletproof vest." title: International Olympic Committee scraps gender equality, diversity and inclusion panel in major reshuffle
description: The International Olympic Committee is eliminating its Gender Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Commission months after adopting new sex eligibility rules.
content: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) is eliminating its Gender Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Commission, as the organization undergoes cultural changes under its new president Kirsty Coventry. Under Coventry, the most notable change came earlier this year, when the IOC explicitly banned biological males from women's sports. This week's cuts come as part of a restructuring that will replace 12 permanent advisory bodies with smaller working groups assembled to address specific issues. Friday’s announcement comes months after the IOC adopted new eligibility rules reserving women’s Olympic events for biological females beginning with the 2028 Los Angeles Games, a policy addressing a central issue in the debate over fairness and safety in women’s sports. KAILLIE HUMPHRIES: IDENTITY IS NOT THE SAME AS BIOLOGY. THE SUPREME COURT AGREES The IOC’s Advisory Committee on Human Rights is also being discontinued, alongside commissions covering sustainability, technology, education and commercial partnerships. The organization said the changes followed more than a year of consultation and review. According to The Associated Press, the overhaul is a streamlining and cost-cutting measure that leaves 19 committees in place. The outgoing groups typically included between 10 and 30 members who gathered annually in Lausanne, Switzerland. The IOC said in an official announcement that the new arrangement would enable "more targeted engagement on key strategic priorities and policy development." Its Athletes’ Commission, Ethics Commission, Audit Committee and other institutional bodies will continue operating. Under President Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has already used a smaller expert group to examine eligibility for women’s competition. According to AP, the panel’s membership was kept confidential, and the review proceeded outside the gender equality and inclusion commission now being eliminated. The resulting policy, announced March 26, requires a one-time screening for the SRY gene, which is typically associated with male sex development. It excludes transgender women from female Olympic events and also affects some athletes with differences in sex development, with limited exceptions. The rules do not apply retroactively or to recreational sports. Coventry defended the policy as necessary to protect competition. "It would not be fair for biological males to compete in the female category," she said when the rules were announced. She also emphasized athletes’ dignity, access to counseling and medical guidance. SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS The policy aligns with President Donald Trump’s push for sex-based eligibility in women’s sports. His February 2025 executive order directed the secretary of state to press the IOC to adopt standards based on sex rather than gender identity or testosterone reduction. The IOC’s approach has drawn sharply different responses. Reem Alsalem, the United Nations special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, welcomed the eligibility policy as protecting female athletes’ fairness and safety. Human Rights Watch opposed mandatory genetic screening, arguing it threatens privacy and can expose women with variations in sex characteristics to discrimination. The IOC said it will now bring together experts through working groups with clearly defined assignments to guide future decisions.

title: Brain-infecting fungus that can kill 7 in 10 patients is on the rise across America
description: Cladophialophora bantiana, a neurotropic black mold with a 60%-70% fatality rate, surged nearly fourfold in U.S. detections between 2023 and 2025.
content: A rare fungal infection that can strike healthy people is rising across the U.S., prompting calls from public health officials for heightened awareness and national tracking. Cladophialophora bantiana (C. bantiana) is a black yeast-like mold that can infect the brain and contains a dark pigment called melanin, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Data from a microbiology laboratory at the University of Washington shows that detection of the fungus nearly quadrupled between 2023 and 2025. LOUISIANA GIRL, 8, DIES AFTER CONTRACTING SUSPECTED BRAIN-EATING AMOEBA LINKED TO LAKE SWIM Between January 2009 and July 2026, researchers identified 48 confirmed cases and one probable case of C. bantiana in tissue samples from 21 states and the District of Columbia. The median patient age was 68 years old. Unlike many fungal infections that mainly affect people with weakened immune systems, about half of C. bantiana infections occur in otherwise healthy people. Researchers believe the mold enters the body when it is inhaled or through a skin wound, then travels through the bloodstream to the brain. The CDC report states that 88% of cases were detected in brain tissue samples and 12% were identified in lung tissue, supporting the theory that respiratory inhalation is one of the main transmission mechanisms. DEADLY ‘FOX TAPEWORM’ LINKED TO LETHAL DISEASE DETECTED IN WEST COAST WILDLIFE The fungus causes a severe infection associated with a 60% to 70% fatality rate, even with aggressive medical intervention, according to a systematic review published in Medical Mycology. The pathogen has historically been rare, with the University of Washington laboratory identifying only one to five cases per year between 2009 and 2023. However, the CDC says annual cases surged to eight in 2024 and reached 14 in 2025. To make sure the increase wasn’t simply due to more testing, researchers compared the number of infections with the total number of brain tissue samples tested for fungi. title: ESPN allowing Troy Aikman to walk away from Joe Buck booth would make no sense | Bobby Burack
description: Troy Aikman says ESPN has not engaged in contract negotiations with him, suggesting his departure from Monday Night Football appears most likely.
content: When Joe Buck signed a $100 million extension with ESPN, the natural assumption around the industry was that Troy Aikman would soon follow. Buck and Aikman have worked together for 25 years, first at Fox and at ESPN since 2022. They are often regarded as the best broadcast booth in sports. Yet, within hours of the report about Buck's deal, industry chatter suggested that ESPN and Aikman were not close to an agreement. This week, Aikman addressed the situation — along with a reported confrontation between him and Buck during Monday Night Football — and said ESPN has not engaged in any contract negotiations with him. His deal expires in May 2027, after the Super Bowl in February that he will call. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Aikman suggested that leaving ESPN now appears to be the most likely outcome. "It just seems to be where they’re going," he said on KTCK The Ticket in Dallas. As of publication, there is still plenty of mystery surrounding why ESPN wouldn't want to keep Aikman. Yes, he's expensive. His current deal pays him around $18 million per year. ESPN, however, is paying others more, including Buck, Stephen A. Smith and Pat McAfee. As the lead NFL analyst for Monday Night Football and ESPN's first Super Bowl this February, there is an argument that Aikman is the most valuable member of that group. One industry-wide theory is that Buck wants a new partner. At the very least, Buck signing an extension before Aikman proves he is willing to work with someone else. He also apparently wasn't interested in using his leverage to ensure that he and Aikman remained together. Sources close to Buck have denied this. Another theory is that ESPN wants Peyton and Eli Manning in the booth and views this as its opportunity. However, unless the Mannings have privately agreed to such a move, which seems unlikely, pairing them with Buck sounds more like wishful thinking than an actual plan. Then there are the Kelce brothers. ESPN moved Jason Kelce into the color analyst role alongside Dave Pasch and Kurt Warner for its international games on NFL Network this season. Kelce has been polarizing, but impressive in the role. ESPN could envision eventually pairing him with his brother Travis, who is expected to retire from the NFL after this season, alongside Buck. On paper, that sounds intriguing. The problem is that there is no indication Travis is interested in becoming a full-time game analyst, much less that the Kelce brothers would be ready to anchor ESPN's most important NFL property. WITH TONY ROMO OUT AT CBS, TROY AIKMAN AND GREG OLSEN SUDDENLY BECOME LOGICAL REPLACEMENTS Greg Olsen is another possibility. He is an impending media free agent and is viewed as a potential No. 1 game analyst, a role he previously held at Fox before Tom Brady arrived. Olsen is good. Still, it's difficult to see why ESPN would prefer him to Aikman, who brings more gravitas, popularity and, most importantly, 25 years of chemistry with Buck. Sure, Olsen is 18 years younger than Aikman and would presumably cost less. If ESPN's goal were to get younger and cheaper, though, re-signing Buck — who is only two years younger than Aikman — to a nine-figure extension doesn't exactly fit that philosophy. From the outside, each alternative looks like a gamble, and probably one that wouldn't leave ESPN with a better booth than the one it already has. That's what makes the situation so puzzling. ESPN spent five years trying to find a suitable Monday Night Football booth. After Mike Tirico left in 2016 and Jon Gruden returned to coaching after the 2017 season, the network cycled through various combinations involving Steve Levy, Sean McDonough, Joe Tessitore, Booger McFarland, Brian Griese and Louis Riddick. For one reason or another, none of them clicked. And most of them are good to great broadcasters. There was even industry chatter at the time that the instability and poor reception surrounding ESPN's broadcasts affected the quality of games the NFL scheduled for Monday Night Football. For what it's worth, ESPN has enjoyed a noticeably stronger slate of games since Buck and Aikman arrived in 2022. Other factors — including ESPN's improved relationship with the NFL — undoubtedly played a role as well. Either way, ESPN finally found a booth worthy of the NFL's premier games, if not the standard for NFL broadcasting altogether, and now appears prepared to break it up. Unless there is more to the story than anyone outside the company knows, it's difficult to understand the logic. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Of course, skeptics have dismissed the entire saga as a negotiating tactic by ESPN. That doesn't appear to be the case. Usually, such tactics begin with, well, actual negotiations. According to Aikman, there haven't been any. The fact that ESPN locked up his partner before having a substantive conversation with Aikman suggests one of two things: The company has decided it doesn't want to keep him, or it hasn't decided that it does. Maybe ESPN is taking the old Bill Belichick approach with the New England Patriots: better to move on from a talent a year too early than a year too late. Maybe executives see a decline coming that viewers don't. We are skeptical.

title: Forgotten American 'cure-all' from 1903 makes comeback with one key ingredient missing
description: A papaya-based aperitif born from a forgotten homeopathic remedy was revived after a chance discovery at a state park. Its founders tell Fox News Digital how the drink found new life.
content: A forgotten American elixir once marketed as a "cure-all" more than a century ago has gotten a second life — all due to a chance discovery in Florida. Munyon's Paw-Paw, an alcoholic beverage dating to the early 1900s, has been resurrected by two longtime spirits industry veterans who stumbled upon its unusual history during a family outing. Jupiter, Florida, resident Joe Colucci was visiting John D. MacArthur Beach State Park in Palm Beach County when he spotted an antique bottle from 1903 in a display about Dr. James Munyon, a businessman who once owned a nearby island. GEORGE WASHINGTON'S 1757 BEER RECIPE BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE Intrigued, Colucci called his longtime colleague, Paul Massey, and the two began digging into the forgotten drink's past. title: Democrats' latest gun-control push runs into inconvenient fact about how school killer was stopped
description: An armed bystander helped end the deadly Oregon school shooting, but the gun control debate now centers on whether gun-free zones made it worse.
content: Democrats renewed calls for tougher gun laws after three children and a teacher were killed in an Oregon school shooting, but gun-rights advocates say the circumstances of the attack bolster their case against new restrictions. The teenage shooter reportedly opened fire with a shotgun purchased by his mother before an armed father-of-two-students, Kaylub Giamanco, pursued him into Silver Rail Elementary School and fatally shot him. Second Amendment advocates argue additional gun restrictions would not have stopped the killer and could make it harder for armed civilians like Giamanco to intervene. "Democrats are shamefully weaponizing this tragedy in Oregon to advance their political agenda on gun control," Aidan Johnston, director of federal affairs for Gun Owners of America, told Fox News Digital. "But more gun control isn’t the solution. The school was a gun-free zone, and the killer didn’t use a so-called ‘assault weapon.’ What did stop the mass murderer and save lives was an armed bystander with good aim." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS Gun-rights researcher John Lott, president of the Crime Prevention Research Center (CPRC), separately argued that restrictions on carrying guns can leave potential victims defenseless. "These gun-free zones actually serve as a magnet for these attacks rather than stopping them from occurring," Lott told Fox News Digital. Lott pointed to CPRC research examining active shootings from 2014 through 2024, which he said found that legally armed civilians stopped more attacks than police did. The National Rifle Association similarly questioned whether new restrictions would have changed the outcome. "Oregon already has nearly every gun-control measure on the anti-gun wish list — including an A- rating from groups that push them — yet that did not prevent this attack," the NRA said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The armed bystander who pursued the shooter inside and ended the threat is the clearest reminder that, when seconds count, a prepared law-abiding citizen can stop a killer." Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., was among the lawmakers calling for action after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where Bend-LaPine school policy bans firearms, including concealed guns. "The best way to honor these victims is to at long last pass commonsense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools," Wyden said in a statement. JONATHAN TURLEY: JAMES TALARICO'S DEFENSE OF GUN CONTROL LEAVES OUT A KEY WORD Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., whose district includes Bend, also called for action while acknowledging the armed bystander's intervention. "When are we going to practice that same bravery that that bystander had?" Bynum asked during a vigil, after urging action to keep guns away from people who should not have them. Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Jack Reed, D-R.I., also cited the shooting in calling for additional gun laws and urging the Supreme Court to change course. "It is far past time for the Roberts Court to make it clear their decision on guns does not endorse unfettered and unregulated access to weapons," Reed said. "In the absence of the Supreme Court ceasing its pro-gun rulings, Republicans need to join Democrats in enacting commonsense policies that could prevent these kinds of tragedies." The Roberts court has issued consequential gun-rights rulings, including District of Columbia v. Heller, which struck down the District of Columbia's handgun ban in 2008, and New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn. v. Bruen, which struck down New York's requirement that applicants show a special need to obtain a license to carry a handgun in public. LA GUN OWNERS STUCK WAITING YEARS FOR CONCEALED CARRY PERMITS SCORE MAJOR DOJ VICTORY The political fighting is unfolding as investigators examine how the teenage gunman gained access to his mother's shotgun, a key question in determining whether existing or proposed gun laws could have made a difference. Asked specifically about universal background checks and red-flag laws, the NRA argued that neither would likely have prevented the shooting, citing initial reports that the teenager obtained a family member's firearm. The organization noted that background checks generally apply to firearm transfers, not unauthorized access to a firearm already owned by someone else. It also argued that a red-flag order would likely have been ineffective, although the circumstances surrounding the teenager's access to the shotgun remain unclear. Lott also pointed to a 2021 change in Oregon law that allowed individual school districts to prohibit concealed carry permit holders from bringing guns onto school property, arguing that such restrictions can leave schools more vulnerable. Before that change, Lott said, Oregon teachers with concealed carry permits generally could carry guns at schools, although some districts imposed employment-related restrictions. He estimated that roughly 25 of the state's 197 school districts have adopted prohibitions since then. Lott said his organization is updating the research through 2025. He also argued that uniformed school resource officers face tactical disadvantages because attackers can identify them, avoid them or target them first. "Having somebody in uniform is like having a neon sign above them that says, shoot me first," Lott said. Lott also questioned whether penalties for violating gun-free zone restrictions would deter someone already facing multiple life sentences for murder. Does taking five years away from their seventh or eighth life [sentence] going to matter? Is that a penalty for them? And the answer is no," he said. The NRA also cited research finding that 94% of mass shootings since 1950 occurred in gun-free zones, echoing Lott's argument. "Law-abiding Americans have the right to defend themselves and their communities rather than rely solely on a sign or sticker. The tragedy in Bend is a clear example of how an armed citizen who is prepared and willing to act can stop an attacker and save lives. Policies that keep responsible people disarmed near schools leave those locations more vulnerable, not safer," an NRA spokesperson said. Lott maintained that gun-free zone restrictions can therefore disadvantage lawful gun owners without meaningfully deterring someone planning a mass shooting. title: Mamdani accused of betraying NYC workers as union boss blasts 'anti-labor' horse carriage ban
description: Zohran Mamdani and the City Council aim to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park by 2028, but union leaders say the move betrays workers.
content: New York City lawmakers are set to vote on a bill that would effectively ban all horse-drawn carriages from Central Park — a move that means the tradition dating back to the late 1800s would be taken out to pasture. The City Council is anticipated to approve a bill next week that would abolish the rides — which have been a staple in the Big Apple for more than 150 years — by June 1, 2028. The bill follows an agreement between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin and could mark the first successful effort to ban the rides after previous mayors unsuccessfully pushed to end the industry. "We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," a spokesperson for Mamdani’s office said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Tuesday. MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS Menin, who was the first sitting City Council speaker to support the legislation, also celebrated the decision. "Speaker Menin was clear that the transition away from horse carriages in Central Park must include meaningful protections for the workers," a spokesperson for Speaker Menin said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Through thoughtful conversations with labor and other stakeholders, the Council developed a framework to ensure better economic opportunities for these New Yorkers. As the Administration implements the plan, Speaker Menin’s office will remain engaged in the transition process, including through a new joint working group that she has invited TWU and the Administration to join," Menin's spokesperson added. A spokesperson from City Hall also echoed that officials anticipate a plan to be rolled out that would provide resources for the carriage drivers. "Our Administration has been working on a detailed plan for the transition of the workforce and industry, and we have begun discussion of compensation for medallion owners," a City Hall spokesperson said. For years, animal rights advocates have called for an end to Central Park’s horse-drawn carriages, pointing to high-profile incidents involving allegations of animal abuse and the deaths of carriage horses. "New Yorkers are sick and tired of seeing exhausted, sick, lame, elderly horses struggling to pull carriages through Midtown Manhattan, collapsing in the streets," PETA Director of Outreach Communications Ashley Byrne told Fox News Digital. "They've wanted this gone for a long time." Activists have largely denounced the industry as cruel and inhumane, pointing to incidents in which horses have been startled by Manhattan traffic and bolted into oncoming vehicles or onto crowded sidewalks. However, the push to ban the tourist attraction intensified in June. FIREWORKS REPORTEDLY TRIGGER MASS HORSE STAMPEDE THROUGH ROME STREETS, INJURING SEVERAL SOLDIERS On June 17, 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who was traveling from India with his family to celebrate his recent graduation, died after being thrown from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park. His death prompted renewed calls for legislation banning horse-drawn carriages. Lawmakers renamed the proposed "Ryder's Law" — named after an elderly horse who collapsed on a Manhattan street in 2022 and later died — "Romanch's Law." "It is tragic and absolutely unforgivable that this industry insisted on dragging this out until countless horses and a teenage human being with his whole life ahead of him died of accidents that never should have happened," Byrne said. The Central Park Conservancy previously reported that the June 17 crash marked the eighth horse-related incident in or around the park in approximately 13 months. Eight days earlier, on June 9, a carriage horse named Deniz collapsed and died while pulling tourists. Fox News Digital reached out to the Mahajan family attorney for comment but did not immediately receive a response. The bill’s new namesake — and the support it has attracted — drew the ire of Alexander Kemp, administrative vice president of the Transit Workers Union (TWU) Local 100, which represents approximately 160 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. LONG ISLAND RAIL ROAD WORKERS GO ON STRIKE, LEAVING 330,000 COMMUTERS WITHOUT SERVICE ON BUSIEST US RAIL LINE "Unfortunately, you had a fatality, a tragedy, with an 18-year-old young man, Romanch," Kemp told Fox News Digital. "And they used it to modify their position. It no longer became about animal welfare, and now this is about an 18-year-old tourist who lost his life tragically in an accident, in a horrific accident." Kemp argued that the City Council used Mahajan’s death to reshape the bill and win over lawmakers after years of unsuccessful attempts to pass a ban. "And they crafted legislation around that, because there was no appetite or evidence to prove that the animals were mistreated and that it was an animal welfare issue. Now they made it a human rights issue. Now they make it a safety issue," Kemp said. Byrne, however, said the issue is rooted in safety concerns, pointing to increased foot traffic and the growing number of wheeled vehicles moving through the park. "Central Park is filled with pedestrians, runners, cyclists, e-bikes and pedicabs," Byrne said. "It is no place for prey animals like horses who can spook at something as slight as a plastic bag blowing through the air or the sound of a car honking." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Kemp said many carriage drivers are immigrants nearing retirement age, making it difficult for them to find new jobs if the industry shuts down. "This is what they've done [in their home countries]," Kemp said. "And finding their way in America, this was their golden ticket. This was their street paved with gold. This was an opportunity for them to do something that they've done in their country to find a way to feed their family here." Under the legislation, city agencies would have until April 1, 2027, to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers and other industry workers. The plan would also require officials to consider compensation for carriage owners. Additionally, carriage owners would not be permitted to sell their horses for slaughter or for use in other horse-drawn carriage businesses. The animals would have to be rehomed or otherwise placed in a "humane manner." "I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani said at a press conference on Wednesday. Despite the bill’s promises, Kemp argued that Mamdani's administration, which campaigned on a pro-worker platform, is failing to protect the carriage drivers' livelihoods. "If you're going to say to my face that you got labor's back, and then in the middle of the night you take a vote to eliminate a whole industry, well, then that is anti-labor. That is not pro-worker," Kemp said. "So, I don't know how you can satisfy both, just by saying, ‘By the way, that we believe, in our heart, that this industry has come to pasture — no pun intended. And now guys, please, can we hug after we get rid of this industry? Because we have other things we can talk about.’" Kemp also criticized the mayor's administration for promoting pro-immigrant policies while supporting legislation that could eliminate roughly 160 jobs, many held by immigrant workers. "If that is in how you conduct business, and you look at the least of us as the most vulnerable and expendable, then what it tells me is that you are not rooted in the politics of people," Kemp said. "You're rooted in the politics of politics." "And please spare us with all the crocodile tears on how you care about workers and protecting workers and immigrants," he continued. "And just say you're more interested in satisfying the people who give you the most money." The City Council is set to vote on the bill Oct. 22, with supporters expecting it to pass. title: New Jaguars long snapper cuts camping trip short, scrambles for passport before Sunday's London game
description: Jacob Bobenmoyer was camping and changing diapers in Colorado when the Jacksonville Jaguars called him to fly to London as their emergency long snapper.
content: Last weekend's game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and Philadelphia Eagles at London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium was a wild one, and one thing that was a headache for the Jags was the long-snapping situation. Long snapper Ross Matiscik hurt his shoulder, and that meant defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton had to take over. title: 'The View' co-hosts cast doubt on Kamala Harris viability as 2028 candidate
description: "The View" co-hosts debated former Vice President Kamala Harris' 2028 prospects, with Sara Haines pointing to the public's desire for fresher Democratic candidates
content: Several co-hosts of "The View" expressed doubts Friday about former Vice President Kamala Harris running for president in 2028. Harris was asked during a Tuesday interview with podcaster Keke Palmer whether she was considering running for president in 2028. Harris laughed and said she hadn't decided yet. However, some of "The View" co-hosts urged the Democratic Party to seek another contender. "Let’s be real," co-host Ana Navarro said, noting that she spoke with Harris about how many women remain "scarred" by the fact both she and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton lost to President Donald Trump. When asked if a Black woman could be elected president, guest host Raven-Symone replied, "Not in America. In the days after Joe Biden dropped out in 2024, online platforms saw racist content directed at Kamala go up 525% and misogynistic content went up 2,328%." DEMOCRATS DEBATE KAMALA HARRIS 2028 RUN AS SURROGATE SAYS PARTY WANTS TO 'MOVE ON' FROM 2024 LOSS "We are not as progressive as we think we are, United States," Raven-Symone added. "There are other countries doing it much better when it comes to women in office. You need to catch the blank up, period." "If the Democrats want to win, but I don’t think she is the right candidate," Sara Haines said. "Because the Democrats have been screaming for new energy, that they would need something new to combat this. This would be her third time on this ballot from the first time when she didn’t — she was out really early when she ran, and then the time with Biden, this would be the third time." "People are clamoring for fresh energy and there is a lot of candidates – Pete Buttigieg, Mark Kelly, [Josh] Shapiro, Wes Moore. They’re moderate, moderate Democrats and I think they could sweep," Haines said, later noting that Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., would be viable down the road as well. JOY BEHAR DOUBLES DOWN ON ARGUMENT US WILL NOT ELECT A WOMAN PRESIDENT Democratic strategist and co-host of "The Huddle" podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, "I think America is ready for a female president. The two women who have lost were politically flawed, and it was known from the beginning." "For Harris in 2028, the challenge is that candidates that have successfully run three times — Reagan, Trump — were ideologically consistent, and the country came to them. Harris has been inconsistent, creating an authenticity problem," he continued. "You then have to look at the present dynamic of the Democratic Party — angry and demanding fight. Harris has been MIA the last two years, which is consistent with her history of caution and indecision," Turrentine said. "Lastly, if Harris runs, she will have to fight an establishment and media that are very skeptical and will likely look to pounce," he added. "There are a lot of reasons to question her chances. But, if she runs, she will be a serious candidate in the primary, and if she were to win the primary, in this bitterly divided country, would start the general with a decent chance."
