title: Houthis emerge as global threat beyond Iran control amid Saudi strikes, former envoy warns
description: Tim Lenderking warns Houthi rebels are building homegrown weapons capabilities independent of Iran, turning Yemen's conflict into a global threat.
content: The Houthis are increasingly operating independently of Tehran, posing a "clear and very present danger" on the international stage as the terror group rearms and sharpens its strike capabilities, a former U.S. envoy warned Thursday. The warning came amid deadly missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days and growing threats to global shipping routes and critical Middle East infrastructure in the run-up. Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, also confirmed Thursday that Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had killed 17 and injured 333 others from Oct. 7-11. Speaking at a news conference in Riyadh, al-Maliki said the Oct. 10 attack involved 10 drones, missiles and other projectiles. "King Khalid International Airport has been subjected to 20 attacks since (Oct. 1)," he noted. Tim Lenderking, who served as U.S. special envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2025 and was posted to Saudi Arabia from 2013 to 2016, said Saudi officials had warned more than a decade ago that the Houthis would become a major threat, a prediction he says has now materialized. SAUDI FOREIGN MINISTER WARNS HOUTHI THREAT GOES GLOBAL AS TRUMP HOLDS FIRE "The Saudis were very clear to our leaders that they viewed the Houthis as a major threat," Lenderking said of his time in the kingdom a decade ago. At the time, he said, the group was "quietly building up their capability, burnishing their narrative of why they sought to lead Yemen as a messianic group, as a group from northern Yemen, with an agenda, with a mission." The Houthis had emerged as a religious and political movement in Yemen in the 1990s, but their ties to Iran developed into a military partnership after 2014, when Tehran expanded its assistance and training during Yemen's civil war. "The Houthis don't really need the Iranians anymore," Lenderking, a former acting assistant secretary for Near Eastern affairs at the U.S. State Department, continued, adding it was still "a very important relationship that "enabled the Houthis to become the powerful force that they are." Lenderking, now a distinguished diplomatic fellow at the Middle East Institute (MEI), said, over time, the Houthis had developed their own "homegrown indigenous capability" as they capitalized on any disunity across the Gulf region. Saturday's missile and drone attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh raised concerns that President Donald Trump could be drawn into a broader regional conflict as Saudi Arabia seeks U.S. assistance. Asked whether the U.S. would defend Saudi Arabia against further attacks, Trump said, "You'll find out soon." NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT Speaking at an MEI briefing, Lenderking said the Houthis' sophisticated weapons and targeting capabilities have transformed the group from a regional insurgency into an international security threat. "They have the capability to hit around the region, including up into the northern reaches of the Red Sea. So, this is a regional problem, and given the fact that the Houthis control the west coast of Yemen," Lenderking said. "It's an international problem now." Lenderking cited the precision of the Riyadh airport attack as evidence of the Houthis' growing capabilities compared with earlier strikes during the Gaza conflict. "They can hit things better. Now, they are hitting Terminal Four of Riyadh Airport, very specifically. It's a clear and very present danger," he said. The Houthis reportedly launched multiple drones followed by cruise and ballistic missiles that traveled more than 620 miles to Riyadh, prompting an investigation into possible Saudi air defense failures, according to The Associated Press, citing regional officials. Saudi forces intercepted two more ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh on Monday. On Tuesday, a Houthi strike caused damage to Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, sparking a fire that spread across several floors, Reuters reported. Lenderking said the Houthis have built extensive weapons supply chains, smuggling networks and domestic financing operations that allow them to sustain attacks without relying solely on Tehran. HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS "They get a lot of supplies off the open market through the internet, through commercial exchanges. They have a very well entrenched smuggling network, from big boats onto small boats, onto tiny boats, on the pack animals, on people's backs. "They are able to move things undetected through government terrain, even through various borders and with a lot of wide open space there. They are constantly moving, building, resupplying, restocking, innovating." The group's self-sufficiency also extends to financing. Lenderking said the Houthis generate revenue through black-market oil sales, taxation and extortion while also forcing families to provide recruits, allowing the group to continue fighting even if Iranian assistance is cut off. "They have had support from Iran over the years, so they have money in the bank from that," Lenderking said. "They relied on sales of black market oil in the past. They extort Yemeni transport companies, businesses. They tax people in areas that they control. They force many families to offer up a son to fight on the front lines." The Houthis' expanding arsenal has raised concerns about potential Chinese involvement in their weapons supply networks. OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES Yemen's government has accused the rebels of seeking Chinese components for medium-range ballistic missiles, raising concerns about the group's access to advanced military technology. "There is a Chinese connection here that's very detrimental," Lenderking warned, adding that front companies have helped the group obtain weapons through commercial channels. Lenderking warned that the Houthis could also target Saudi energy facilities, pipelines and desalination plants, infrastructure critical to the kingdom's economy and water supply. "The Houthis have hit pipelines," he said. "They have diesel plants and other energy infrastructure in their sights." Attacks on such facilities could disrupt global energy markets, maritime commerce and regional stability. The Houthis also control Yemen's western coastline along the Red Sea, a vital shipping corridor connecting Europe and Asia. With the rebels now capable of striking targets hundreds of miles away, Lenderking warned that the threat extends far beyond Yemen's borders. "One blast at Riyadh Airport is a huge statement," the expert said. title: Ex-OpenAI engineer charged with planting recording device had one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia, DOJ says
description: Abdulrahman Alfozan had a one-way flight to his native Saudi Arabia booked days before federal custody, according to the Department of Justice.
content: The former OpenAI engineer charged with planting a recording device inside a conference room at the AI giant's San Francisco office had a one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia days before he was taken into federal custody, the Justice Department said. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, had a flight booked for Oct. 12 — days after his arrest — for himself, his wife, and another relative, according to court documents. Federal prosecutors cited his travel plans when asking a federal judge to seal the criminal complaint and arrest warrant against him, arguing that public knowledge of the case would prompt him to possibly flee the country. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS "Disclosure of the specified documents might jeopardize the defendant's arrest," court documents state. In an Arabic podcast last month, Alfozan recalled meeting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his 2016 visit to Silicon Valley. Alfozan said he had been contemplating whether to return to his native country. In response, the prince advised young Saudis living and working in Silicon Valley to refine their skills at premier tech companies before bringing their expertise home, the New York Post reported. "You learn from the source and then, God willing, bring that experience and knowledge back to the homeland," Alfozan reportedly said on the podcast. Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to the Department of Justice. OpenAI discovered the encrypted device Sept. 30, plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in a conference room used for "highly confidential" discussions involving proprietary research, product plans and business opportunities, federal prosecutors said. The device, concealed in toilet paper, had allegedly been installed two days earlier. OpenAI traced the device to Alfozan, and security footage showed him near the conference room multiple times, authorities said. In addition, a chatbot associated with his wife was allegedly used to field prompts about ways to install and hide audio recording devices. title: FBI probes suspicious white powder letters sent to Schumer, Dem senators as threat spreads nationwide

content: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and two other Senate Democrats were the intended recipients of mail that federal investigators say contained "suspicious substances," Fox News Digital has learned. title: Hasan Piker rips New York Jewish voters' shift away from Democrats, blames Israel
description: Hasan Piker faced antisemitism accusations after claiming Jewish voters are leaving the Democratic Party solely over Israel foreign policy.
content: Jewish voters in New York appear to be moving away from the Democratic Party, and controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker blamed the shift on their support for Israel. On Wednesday, Piker responded to a CNN clip in which the network's chief data analyst, Harry Enten, and anchor John Berman discussed the drop in support for Democrats among Jewish voters, expressing dismay that they were shifting away from the party. "It’s wild that this many jewish voters are leaving the democratic party over israel. It’s not like the republican alternatives are presenting a more appealing policy agenda, it’s just israel! It’s literally over the continuation of israel’s belligerence. A real shame," Piker wrote on X. CARVILLE WARNS DEMOCRATS ANTI-ISRAEL ‘LOUDMOUTHS’ COULD COST ELECTIONS In the segment, Enten explained that Jewish support for New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, dropped since her last election in 2022, according to recent Siena Polling. Enten then revealed that Democrats' advantage over Republicans among Jewish voters in New York had narrowed by 36 points since 2022, according to Siena Polling averages. "State of New York U.S. House polling among Jewish voters. Look at this. In 2018, Democrats were ahead by 40 points," Enten said. "In 2022, 49 points. Look at this, the average of polls this year. Its just 13 points. It's just 13 points. That is a shift of, what, 36 points, 36 points away from the Democrats. Their lead has absolutely tumbled into the Hudson River among Jewish voters. "Yes, they are still ahead. But we are talking about historically strong numbers for Republicans among Jewish voters," the analyst added. "It definitely seems to me that the developments over the past few years, at least in New York, at least in this polling, (have) had a huge impact on how Jewish voters say they are going to vote, not just for governor, but for Congress as well." HOCHUL DEFLECTS WHEN PRESSED ON TIES TO 'ANTI- CHRISTIAN' MAMDANI IN FIERY DEBATE MOMENT: 'SHAME ON YOU' Piker faced backlash over his assertion that the shift was solely about Israel, with Republican Jewish Coalition communications director Sam Markstein telling Fox News Digital that the streamer's accusation was rooted in an antisemitic trope. "Hasan Piker’s statement that American Jews’ voting preferences are all about Middle East policy plays directly into the oldest antisemitic trope of dual loyalty. He is flat out wrong and is trivializing the very real spike in Jew hatred which directly threatens our community’s safety," Markstein said. "Let’s be clear: American Jews are fleeing the Democratic Party because its leadership continues to elevate, embrace and appease the most radicalized elements of their anti-America extremist party base. The sad irony is that antisemitic bigot Hasan Piker, who said 'America deserved 9/11,' and who has been elevated by national Democrats, including campaigning with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, is Exhibit A," he added. Shai Davidai, a former Columbia University professor and author of "American Intellectual Antisemitism," also responded to Piker on X, saying, "It's not 'over Israel.' It's over people like you." EX-HILLARY CLINTON STAFFER WARNS DEMOCRATS THAT COURTING FAR-LEFT COULD COST THEM JEWISH VOTERS New York Post columnist Karol Markowicz argued in her response to Piker that Jewish voters have reasons to shift away from Democrats that go beyond Israel. "Even setting aside support for Israel, which Jews should absolutely not, Jews are regularly assaulted in NY and no Democrats care. They aren't allowed to defend themselves and the mayor regularly riles up the attackers. Easy call to vote Republican," Markowicz wrote on X. Piker, who has long been a vocal critic of Israel, has criticized Jewish Americans' support for the Jewish state. In August, the streamer was panned by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle after he said, "People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews." Critics accused Piker of blaming Jews for antisemitic attacks against them. Democratic Sens. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev., condemned Piker's remarks. "This shouldn’t be hard: no community should face the threat [of] violence for their political views. Period," Slotkin wrote in a statement posted to social media. "That goes if you’re pro-Israel, pro-Palestine, pro-choice, pro-life or any other cause you care about. And blaming the victims of violence for bringing it on themselves only further endangers people." Rosen said the remarks were "a new low" for the controversial Twitch streamer. "Blaming Jewish Americans for the violence and hate they’re facing is not just wrong, it provides an excuse to those perpetuating these anti-Jewish hate crimes," Rosen said in a statement. "Let me be absolutely clear: crimes against Jews for being Jews is antisemitism plain and simple. There’s no excuse for it." DEMOCRATS CONDEMNING HASAN PIKER AS BACKLASH SPREADS THROUGH PARTY Other Democrats joined in condemning Piker, including Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.; and Hillary Scholten, D-Mich. Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who was criticized for campaigning with Piker, distanced himself from the streamer after the controversial remarks. "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote on X. "My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk." title: Jerry Seinfeld turns tables on radical anti-Israel agitators after chaotic Chicago stunt backfires

I’m into it." He also joked that he would find out how much the protesters paid for their tickets and send the money directly to Israel. As security personnel escorted the demonstrators out of the auditorium, one audience member shouted, "Rough her up!" The Anti-War Committee Chicago and the Chicago branch of the US Palestinian Community Network have taken credit for organizing the disruption, writing on Instagram, "Friday’s disruption sent a clear message: Those who defend Israel’s genocide and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza and throughout Palestine will be met with protest and are not welcome on Chicago’s stages without opposition." COMEDIAN DECLARES JERRY SEINFELD 'UNCANCELLABLE' DESPITE 'WOKE' ANTI-ISRAEL FESTIVAL BOYCOTT Fox News Digital reached out to Seinfeld’s team for comment but did not hear back. Young compared the disruptions at Seinfeld's shows to protests at political rallies, arguing that some activists are willing to pay steep ticket prices to confront the comedian. title: Guardians shut down Rays behind pitching staff, epic Petey Halpin bat-flip for Game 3 win to take series lead
description: Petey Halpin's towering 385-foot two-run homer powered the Cleveland Guardians past the Tampa Bay Rays after weather moved the Game 3 start to 1 p.m. ET.
content: Game 3 was moved up from 6 p.m. ET to 1 p.m. ET due to weather, but the Tampa Bay Rays' offense did not get the memo. In the team's 3-2 loss to the Cleveland Guardians on Thursday at Progressive Field, the offense was dormant. The Rays scored just two runs on three hits, as the Guardians' pitching staff shut them down. In seven of the nine innings, the Rays went down in order. The 1 p.m. start was the earliest for an LCS game in the Eastern time zone since 1988, when the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets played Game 5 of the NLCS at 12:20 p.m. ET. Adell was able to score from first after the ball got away from right fielder Victor Mesa Jr., while Lowe advanced to second base. Jax was able to strand Lowe by recording the next three outs. Gavin Williams was lights out to begin the game, retiring the Rays in order the first time through the lineup. However, Rays first baseman Yandy Díaz broke through, ripping a leadoff double into the left-center gap for the team’s first baserunner of the game. Surprisingly, Guardians manager Stephen Vogt pulled Gavin Williams from the game after just 70 pitches in five innings, bringing in Daniel Espino. title: Warriors rookie's reaction to learning he'd guard Lakers superstar Luka Dončić goes viral: 'What the f---?'
description: Yaxel Lendeborg revealed his stunned reaction when Frank Vogel told him he'd guard Luka Dončić in the Golden State Warriors' preseason game.
content: A "Welcome to the NBA" moment almost occurred for Golden State Warriors top draft pick Yaxel Lendeborg on Tuesday night in a preseason bout against the Los Angeles Lakers. He was supposed to guard Luka Dončić — an assignment many veteran defenders don’t wish to have, let alone a rookie. Lendeborg, the No. 11 overall pick coming out of the national-champion Michigan Wolverines program, told reporters that he was just on his phone before the game when assistant Warriors coach Frank Vogel came up to him and said something that left him baffled. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "’Hey, you’re guarding Luka tonight,’" Lendeborg said. "I said, ‘What the f---? You’re just gonna throw me in the fire?’" To be honest, not an over-exaggerative answer at all for a rookie trying to get acclimated to the league. Lendeborg’s reaction was genuine because he didn’t think his assignment would be the Lakers’ star player and one of the most prolific offensive weapons in the league when he’s on the court. Ultimately, Lakers head coach JJ Redick decided to rest Dončić, leading to Lendeborg matching up with center Walker Kessler, who debuted this preseason for Los Angeles. The Warriors ended up winning the game, 101-89. LUKA DONČIĆ SAYS HE 'DEFINITELY' REGRETS PLAYING THROUGH HAMSTRING INJURY THAT ENDED HIS SEASON "It was a complete shift of what I had planned in my mind," Lendeborg said about gearing up for the game before hearing the Dončić news. Lendeborg is, however, a solid defender, winning Defensive Player of the Year in the AAC with UAB before becoming a first-team all-defense member in the Big Ten during his season at Michigan in 2025. Guarding Dončić is completely different than going up against even the best college players, but Lendeborg tried his best to play the part. "I tried to act all cool, but I was spooked," he admitted. "That was crazy." "I think [Vogel] said he averages like 30, 35. Nobody can stop him, so do your best. That was it. My mind was all over the place after that." No defender wants to be put through a clinic by his opponent, so it’s understandable how Lendeborg feels. But to Vogel’s point, Dončić is someone that can hit shots even with great defense, averaging 33.5 points per game last season, which led the NBA. In the end, Lendeborg held his own against Kessler, while also dropping 19 points on the other end of the floor. Looking ahead to the regular season, Lendeborg will likely be utilized by head coach Steve Kerr as a versatile defender, with the 6-foot-9 rookie able to handle multiple assignments, no matter his opponent’s position on the court. title: Colin Cowherd's analogy of the 2026 Dodgers to The Godfather Part III is brilliant
description: Colin Cowherd compares the Los Angeles Dodgers' stunning 0-3 postseason hole to "The Godfather Part III" — familiar names, but fading magic.
content: Perhaps the best analogy for the stunning 0-3 hole the Los Angeles Dodgers find themselves in comes from The Godfather – the third installment of the trilogy, that is. Credit FS1 host Colin Cowherd for the comparison Wednesday. "The Dodgers trying to win a third World Series is starting to have Godfather III vibes to it," he began. "Some of the names are familiar. Al Pacino. Diane Keaton. Francis Ford Coppola is still directing it. But it feels played. And the Dodgers feel played out." Brilliant. Now, for some ground rules before sharing the analogy widely. Before you start assigning Dodgers players to actors, understand that Pacino was still excellent in The Godfather Part III. Shohei Ohtani, universally recognized as the greatest baseball player in the world, has not been. Ohtani had batted under .200 in four straight postseason games. The Dodgers reportedly even considered benching him ahead of Game 3 because of his struggles and injuries. A DODGERS-LESS WORLD SERIES WOULD HURT NOW, BUT HELP MLB LATER | BOBBY BURACK But if the Dodgers don't somehow surge back from 0-3 and become just the second team in MLB history to overcome such a deficit in an LCS series, the Godfather analogy could hold up remarkably well. The Godfather and The Godfather Part II are two of the greatest films ever made. The opinion here is that the original is the greatest movie ever and the sequel – which is also partly a prequel – is somewhere in the top 10, maybe the top five. Part III isn't nearly as bad as some movie buffs sometimes portray it. However, it was undoubtedly a profound disappointment compared to the first two films. For one, Coppola cast his daughter Sofia as Mary Corleone. It didn't work. The romance between Mary and her first cousin Vincent consumed too much screen time for how little it ultimately contributed to the trilogy's conclusion. The absence of Tom Hagen is glaring, as is the loss of Sonny Corleone, whose death in the original film deprived the third installment of another defining character from the Corleone family. In sum, The Godfather trilogy would be remembered even more favorably had there never been a third film. There's a reason some Godfather marathons conveniently end after Part II. Likewise, if the Dodgers don't come back in this series, the 2026 team will be remembered as a stain on the legacy of the dynasty. Still, The Godfather Part III had excuses. The film was released 16 years after Part II. The principal cast had aged. Robert Duvall, who portrayed Hagen, did not return. And after nearly two decades, the first two films had been elevated to a standard that virtually no sequel could reasonably meet. The 2026 Dodgers have no such excuses. Their payroll exceeds that of the other three remaining teams combined. Los Angeles added Tarik Skubal and Kyle Tucker to a roster that was already considered one of the greatest ever assembled on paper. Granted, the cast, like in the film, is aging. They are trying to recapture old magic. It's not working. Nonetheless, we enjoyed the analogy. The Godfather Part III and the Dodgers' 2026 postseason are shaping up as two of the more memorable disappointments in their respective fields. Even depressed Dodgers superfan and OutKick reporter Ian Miller appreciated Cowherd's comparison. "There’s a case to be made that The Godfather Part 1 and Godfather Part 2 are two of the best movies ever made. Just like the 2024-2025 Dodgers are two of the best teams ever. If the price for that is getting pulled back in for the 2026 team, it was worth it," Miller said of Cowherd's analogy. title: Somalis in Minnesota unleash fury on Trump after feds raid Ilhan Omar's DC home
description: Minneapolis Somali community members say they feel personally attacked after federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home in a citizenship probe.
content: MINNEAPOLIS — Members of Minnesota's growing Somali community, including a city council member, tore into President Donald Trump and his administration when speaking with Fox News Digital after Monday's raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., residence. "Somalis — we all feel attacked by President Trump," Jamal Osman, the Somali-born vice president of the Minneapolis City Council, said of the impact of the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents. "Our president has broken the law many times. ICE [is] terrorizing our community ... and we're not surprised such action has taken place," Osman continued in reference to the search of Omar's home. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION "We have seen the threats, the horrific language he uses against my community. It's unacceptable, and we're hoping this could stop," Osman said. A 37-year-old social worker and Minneapolis resident named Abdi, who declined to give his last name or be interviewed on camera, had even harsher words for the president. He, like Osman, said he was born in Somalia. "I feel like raiding a congresswoman — it feels like Donald Trump and his regime wanted to use their power to dehumanize and also humiliate someone that is part of the Congress," Abdi said. He claimed that Trump "hates Somali people because of Ilhan Omar." Abdi said Trump created "hate" and a "fight" with Somalis in America and claimed that they are being followed and harassed in the streets because of the president. TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID "It's personal," he said. "And Ilhan Omar — he doesn't treat her as a congressmember — he treats her as someone who's below him." "If they take the citizenship away from her, then I will say, ‘Are we in a dictatorship?’ That's using power to use against an American citizen, then maybe the thinking we have for the United States is completely different." Osman said the raid is proof of what the Trump administration is willing to do. "We live in the United States, which is the land of the laws. I don't expect Trump or anyone in this matter to break the U.S. Constitution," he continued. "There's laws. He can, of course, threaten, but there's a court process, there's due process. He can't say he's gonna deport her, he's gonna deport me, thousands of Somalis." OMAR RAID OUTRAGE GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE WHEN INTERNET NOTICES HER PAST 6-WORD CLAIM: 'COULDN'T AGREE MORE' Osman's message to the president was simple: "Stop it." "We're American citizens like everyone else," he said. A third person, a 22-year-old Somali American woman who declined to be named or filmed, told Fox News Digital that she wasn't surprised about the raid on Omar's home. "I thought it was bound to happen soon enough," she said. "They've been talking about her in a negative manner. The government [has been] constantly questioning her immigration status and her naturalization in the country. So it was bound to happen for them to investigate her soon enough." When reached about the comments from the Minneapolis Somali community, the White House pointed Fox News Digital to the president's public reaction to the raid on Monday. "I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump brushed off. "I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is a non-country, and then she comes over here, and she complains about our Constitution." "I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the raid stems from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago. The investigation, the sources note, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Omar's phone, passport and computers were seized in the raid — it is not clear which other items or materials were taken from her residence, if any. Omar has not been seen since the raid, but offered her reaction to the unfolding investigation on social media Monday afternoon. "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," she said. LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES He continued, "The Biden people didn't want to go there. They were completely chicken about all that. title: Washington state's high school sports league puts onus for trans athlete controversy on state laws
description: The WIAA says Washington state law prevents it from banning males from girls' sports, even if members vote for change. Initiative 638 heads to voters.
content: Washington state has been rocked in recent weeks by a controversy involving a male cross-country runner who switched from a boys’ team to a girls’ team mid-season. The controversy culminated in a protest Tuesday, when about a dozen female runners for Camas High School walked off the course, refusing to compete with their new male teammate. The association governing Washington school sports says state law prevents it from implementing the proposed changes to its participation policy. In a statement to OutKick, the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA) said it cannot adopt a new policy to keep males out of girls’ sports, even if its members vote for a policy change, as it would be "in violation of Washington state law." DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER "In the last two years, through the association’s amendment process, three amendments have been proposed to alter the gender-identity participation policies. Those amendments did not meet the 60% threshold to pass. Nevertheless, even if the amendments had met the threshold and passed, the WIAA cannot implement a policy that is in violation of Washington state law and the amendments proposed would have violated state law. If state law changes, the WIAA Executive Board will revise policies as necessary to remain in compliance with state law," part of the WIAA’s statement read. Washington voters are set to decide whether to change the rules next month. Initiative 638, which would prohibit biological male students from competing in certain female-only school sports and require a healthcare provider's verification of biological sex, will be on the state ballot on Nov. 3. Democrats currently hold majorities in both chambers of the state legislature and control the governor’s office. Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson has expressed opposition to Initiative 638. WHERE TOP DEMOCRAT SENATE CANDIDATES AND THEIR GOP OPPONENTS STAND ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS "Washingtonians should know that I-638 won’t create opportunities for girls, but it will force them into invasive sex verification exams in order to participate in sports," Ferguson said in a statement published Sept. 29 by the opposition campaign, No Hate in WA State. The measure reached the ballot after lawmakers took no action on it during the 2026 session. Earlier this year, Democratic legislative leaders said they would leave the decision to voters. The vote will come as the state grapples with multiple controversies involving males in girls’ sports, including the Camas cross-country runner and a separate incident involving a transgender wrestler who allegedly sexually assaulted a female athlete during a match last December, according to the female athlete’s lawsuit. Prosecutors declined to file criminal charges in that case. In its statement to OutKick, the WIAA described itself as a membership-driven association whose members create its rules. It said its gender-identity participation policy has been in place since the 2007-08 school year and was adopted to align with Washington law. "The WIAA is a membership-driven association. The membership creates the rules found in the WIAA Handbook. The gender-identity participation policies found in the WIAA Handbook at Rule 18.16.0 have been in place for 20 years, since the 2007-08 school year. The rules were passed to align with Washington state law. The WIAA remains committed to following Washington state law … which permits student-athletes to participate in sports consistent with the gender with which they identify," the statement read. "WIAA Handbook 18.16.0 states that school personnel will work collaboratively with the student to determine eligibility, however, a timeline for switching teams is not designated. WIAA Handbook 17.11 establishes practice regulations, outlining the minimum number of practice requirements. WIAA Handbook 18.2.1 demonstrates that student’s must be deemed eligible by the respective sport’s 50% date in order to be eligible to participate in postseason competition. "The WIAA Handbook provides the framework for schools, leagues, and WIAA Districts to operate events throughout the year. The WIAA Office does not manage day-to-day league and WIAA District events and instead is tasked with running WIAA State Tournaments. For example, the WIAA Office establishes signage policies for WIAA State events, but not league or WIAA District contests. Once again, the WIAA is a membership-driven association." After the U.S. Supreme Court upheld other states’ laws restricting transgender athletes’ participation in girls’ and women’s sports in landmark rulings in June, Washington’s Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) said the decisions did not change Washington law. The agency said Superintendent Chris Reykdal would continue enforcing state law allowing students to compete consistent with their gender identity. "Today’s decision reinforces Washington state’s ability to adopt and implement our own laws in alignment with our values," Reykdal said in the June 30 statement. The distinction matters for families seeking a different policy: a ruling allowing states to restrict participation does not itself enact such a restriction in Washington. Initiative 638 would require school districts and covered athletic associations to prohibit students it defines as biologically male from competing with or against female students in certain competitions intended for female students only. It would apply to individual and team events. Students entering those competitions would have to provide a signed statement from a personal healthcare provider verifying biological sex through reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels. Backers, led by Let’s Go Washington, say the measure would preserve fair competition and opportunities for girls. They argue that transgender students would retain opportunities to participate in sports in categories corresponding to their sex. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Opponents say the measure would exclude transgender girls and create new medical and privacy burdens for girls seeking to play school sports. Supporters dispute Ferguson’s characterization of the verification requirement. Let’s Go Washington says the measure does not mandate genital examinations and that verification could occur through the existing sports-physical process. The political decision to leave the initiative for voters was clear months before the Camas protest. In January, Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen and House Speaker Laurie Jinkins said they did not plan to hold hearings on the sports initiative and a separate parental-rights measure, according to the Washington State Standard. "They’ll be up to the voters to decide."

title: Rep Andy Harris threatens to have student journalist prosecuted for recording news conference
description: University of Maryland's journalism school defended Cat Murphy after GOP Rep. Andy Harris wrongly claimed her recording violated Maryland consent law.
content: Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., incorrectly insisted that a University of Maryland student journalist was violating state law when she recorded him at a news conference, threatening to refer her to prosecutors during a heated exchange after a debate Tuesday. Speaking in a crowded hallway after an Oct. 13 debate with Democratic challenger Dan Schwartz, Harris demanded that University of Maryland student journalist Cat Murphy stop recording the news conference, arguing Maryland's two-party consent law required his permission. He was annoyed that she defended a reporter from The Baltimore Banner, who had irked him with a "silly" question about why he participated in the debate. "You do not have my permission to record. If you record, we will refer you to the prosecutor," Harris told Murphy, who responded that other journalists were already recording the news conference. PRESS FREEDOM GROUPS THAT BLASTED TRUMP TURN FIRE ON DEM GOVERNOR OVER ALLEGED MEDIA RETALIATION "But you are not allowed to. We are in a two-party state. You are not allowed to," an agitated Harris said while pointing in the student’s face. The student asked why she, specifically, wasn’t allowed to record and Harris continued to grow frustrated. "Because I refuse to give you permission to record," Harris said. "Do you know the law?" The student attempted to have a different journalist hold her recording device, and a separate reporter tried to explain to Harris that the interview was occurring in a public forum. "I’m a legislator. … I actually know the law well," Harris insisted. VIDEO SHOWS MAINE WIRE REPORTER NEARLY BEING RUN OVER BY CAR AFTER CONFRONTATION Murphy then tried to question Harris, who represents Maryland's 1st Congressional District, about the war in Iran. "You’re going to have to take her camera," Harris said to someone in the room. "She is violating the law. In fact, get an officer in here. She’s violating the law on two-party recording. We need an officer." Other reporters repeatedly told Harris they were "in public," but he responded that it "makes no difference whatsoever." LAWMAKER’S STUNNED FACE AND OTHER VIRAL MOMENTS CAP ROUGH WEEK FOR POLITICAL CLASS Harris continued to insist that Murphy needed his permission to record before ending the news conference and walking away. "She’s ruining all your chances to get an answer about anything. See y’all," he said while exiting. "Thank her profusely." In Maryland, the consent requirement only applies to "private conversation," according to the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP). Footage of the incident quickly went viral, and Harris was widely mocked for botching the law. "Cat Murphy is a master's student at the University of Maryland, credentialed as a reporter for our Capital News Service and doing the job we teach our students to do. Cat recorded openly in a public space alongside other news outlets, and that is her legal right," Dean Rafael Lorente said in a statement. Merrill College of Journalism did not immediately respond when asked for comment from Murphy. title: Comedian Bert Kreischer compares perfect burger to great sex: 'Doesn't need to be fancy'
description: Comedian Bert Kreischer shares his burger preference, his smash burger obsession and why Guy Fieri's Carnival cruise burger bar serves the best burger he's ever had.
content: Comedian Bert Kreischer knows a thing or two about burgers — and his recipe for the perfect one is surprisingly simple, even if his description is anything but family-friendly. title: College Football Playoff expanding to 24 teams in 2027, with more games coming to campuses across the country
description: ESPN is set to finalize a deal Thursday to broadcast the expanded 24-team College Football Playoff, featuring 19 at-large bids and campus games.
content: The College Football Playoff is doubling up. After what will be just three years of having a 12-team CFB Playoff, the field is being expanded to 24 teams beginning in 2027. Signs have long been pointing to an expansion, but now the final piece of the puzzle has all but fallen into place with ESPN reportedly jumping on board; this drastic change to the sport is taking shape in a hurry. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Sources have confirmed with OutKick's Trey Wallace that a meeting between representatives from ESPN and the College Football Playoff will take place on Thursday, in which the financial aspects of the deal will be presented between the two. title: Fort Hood survivors praise Trump for scrapping Hasan execution livestream: ‘We’re not barbaric’
description: Alonzo Lunsford, shot seven times by Nidal Hasan, called Trump's decision to cancel the firing squad livestream a "positive move" for the nation.
content: Survivors of the 2009 Fort Hood massacre praised President Donald Trump's decision not to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, after warning that broadcasting his death could turn the execution into a spectacle and hand terrorist groups a propaganda tool. Hasan is still set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, 2026, and Trump said the immediate families of his victims will be permitted to witness the execution in person. But it will no longer be broadcast to the general public as previously announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times by Hasan during the attack nearly 17 years ago, told Fox News Digital that Trump's decision is a "positive move." "It proves that we are a better people, a better nation, and that we're not barbaric," Lunsford said in immediate reaction to the walk-back by Trump on Thursday. "We don't glorify such actions." VETERAN SHOT 7 TIMES IN FORT HOOD MASSACRE HAS A WARNING FOR AMERICANS PLANNING TO WATCH EXECUTION Lunsford said he supports Hasan's death sentence and execution by firing squad but drew a line at broadcasting it to the public. "For it to be made a spectacle for everyone to witness how they're gonna do a tailgate or, 'Hey, we're gonna have a cookout and we're gonna watch this man be put to death.' No, it's not about that," Lunsford said. "It's not a spectacle. It's not a pay-per-view event or a WWE wrestling match or even a boxing match." He also warned that footage of Hasan's execution could be seized upon by terrorist organizations. "You don't want that to be used as a tool for ISIS or al-Qaeda to recruit and say, 'Hey, this is what happens to you if you do this against the infidel,'" Lunsford said. Julia Wilson was a civilian employee at Fort Hood when Hasan went on his rampage. She was nine months pregnant during the attack, which was carried out on her due date. FORT HOOD SHOOTER SHOULD BE EXECUTED '13 TIMES OVER' — BUT NOT ON LIVE STREAM, SURVIVOR SAYS She was slammed against a wall amid the chaos of the shooting and has said that it was only by the grace of God that she and her then-unborn son survived. Wilson was already against the livestreaming of Hasan's execution because she didn't want others to be traumatized like she was during the deadly attack. "I'm ecstatic about that," she told Fox News Digital, reacting to the news that the plan to livestream the event would not proceed. "I'm worried about other people's mental health," she continued. "I don't think the government… really put a lot of thought into how this was going to go down and how it was going to transpire until today." title: Heavy AI use linked to cognitive atrophy, MIT professor argues
description: Overreliance on artificial intelligence tools is making humans less capable of thinking through problems, remembering concepts and forming meaningful social bonds with other people, MIT Professor Eric So argues in his new book.
content:
The Meta exhibition stand at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Credit: Paulo Nunes dos Santos/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Meta released a powerful AI model Thursday that can run locally on two maxed-out Apple Mac Studios instead of relying on a data center.
The company claimed that Muse Spark Open, which is built for coding and agentic work, is the most capable open-weight model being made in the United States.
An open-weight model is an AI model that can be downloaded and run by users on their own computers rather than accessed solely through a company's servers.
Muse Spark Open contains 816 billion parameters — the numerical values an AI model learns during training that help determine how it processes information and generates responses. However, only 42 billion are activated for each token it processes, reducing the computing power needed to run the massive model.
One American competitor is Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra, which contains 550 billion total parameters and activates 55 billion per token. Like Meta's new model, Nemotron 3 Ultra can run locally without relying on a data center.
Chinese AI developers are also competing in the open-weight market. Z.ai's GLM-5.2 contains 744 billion parameters, with 40 billion active per token, while DeepSeek's V3 model has 671 billion total parameters and 37 billion active.
Developers can access Muse Spark Open through several cloud-based AI services or download the model's weights to deploy and customize it themselves.

title: Was your identity stolen? What to do in the first 24 hours
description: Identity theft recovery starts with securing bank accounts, freezing credit and enabling two-factor authentication within the first 24 hours.
content: Discovering that your identity has been stolen can leave you feeling angry, frightened and unsure where to begin. Maybe someone drained your bank account, opened a credit card in your name or filed a fraudulent tax return using your Social Security number. Whatever happened, your next steps can help limit the damage. The first 24 hours are especially important because identity thieves may continue using your information until you secure your accounts. Fortunately, you can take several steps right away to protect yourself and begin recovering. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT Why the first day is so important Identity theft can quickly spread beyond the account where you first discovered the problem. Someone who gains access to your email, for example, might use it to reset passwords for your banking, shopping or other accounts. That's why acting quickly can make a difference. However, you don't have to solve everything in one day. Identity theft recovery can take weeks or even months, depending on the circumstances. Your immediate goal is to stop additional fraud, protect your information and create a record of what happened. What to do in the first 24 hours after identity theft The following checklist breaks the process into manageable steps. The time frames are guidelines, so prioritize active fraud and compromised accounts rather than waiting for a particular hour. Hour 1: Stop the immediate damage Start with the accounts most likely to expose your money or personal information. Important: If money has been stolen, report it to your financial institution immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary by account and transaction type. Hours 2 to 4: Protect your credit Next, make it harder for criminals to open additional accounts using your personal information. You can freeze your credit even if you expect to apply for a loan or credit card soon. Simply lift the freeze temporarily when necessary. Hours 4 to 8: Report the identity theft Creating an official record can help you dispute fraudulent accounts and recover your identity. An FTC identity theft report can help you exercise certain rights under federal law, including requesting that credit bureaus block fraudulent information. However, you generally do not need to file an FTC report before notifying a bank about unauthorized transactions. A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO? Hours 8 to 16: Secure your other accounts Identity thieves sometimes try to use stolen information across multiple services. Hours 16 to 24: Document everything Once you've addressed the most urgent threats, organize your recovery efforts. Common identity theft recovery mistakes to avoid Even when you're moving quickly, certain mistakes can create additional problems. 9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE What can wait beyond the first day Some recovery tasks will continue beyond the first day, including disputing fraudulent accounts, correcting credit reports and following up with creditors. However, report unauthorized financial transactions immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary depending on the type of account and transaction. title: Country star Chris Janson admits he got 'a little cocky' before grueling Colorado elk hunt
description: With just 30 minutes left on his trip, Chris Janson finally tagged a bull elk after a humbling week in Colorado's high country during the rut.
content: Chris Janson has spent enough time chasing elk through the Colorado mountains that he figured he had the whole thing pretty well dialed in. Turns out, the elk had other plans. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS The country music star recently returned from a successful elk hunt in Colorado, where he's been making annual trips for the past six years. And while he ultimately came home with a beautiful bull, the hunt didn't exactly go according to plan. Usually, Janson said, he's able to fill his tag within the first day or two. This time, he figured he'd knock out the hunting early and spend the rest of the trip relaxing on the water. But one thing about chasing big game — it’ll humble you real fast. "I went in a little cocky," Janson told OutKick OutDoors. "I went in a little bit like, 'I got this, and I'll get this done, and I'll get an elk the first day, and then just fish the rest of the trip.' But it didn't happen that way." Watch Chris Janson's entire interview with OutKick OutDoors here: Instead, Janson and his hunting buddies spent the week trekking through the high country, encountering elk but struggling to get everything to come together. He suspects the unusually dry weather played a role. With little rain in the area, Janson said, the elk weren't behaving quite the way he'd come to expect during the September rut, when bulls are typically more active and vocal. "We were up in the high country a lot and just had a lot of opportunities that just didn't come together right at the last little bit," he explained. And as the days wore on, so did his patience. "I take hunting so damn serious that I'm almost not even fun to be around sometimes whenever it's not going my way," Janson admitted. "That's the hunter spirit in me. I hate to lose, and so I just want to get out there and get it done." Hey, at least he's self-aware. RILEY GREEN FILLS THE FREEZER AFTER SCORING MASSIVE BULL ELK WITH A BOW IN THE UTAH MOUNTAINS With their trip winding down and no elk to show for it, Janson and his group decided to change their strategy. After spending most of the week hunting at higher elevations, they headed for lower ground. And with just 30 minutes to spare, Janson finally got his bull. "We'd hunted high all week and hunted semi-high and then ended up being in the low country where we probably should have been from the very beginning," he said. "But that's hunting." Of course, chasing elk through the mountains is an entirely different animal than sitting in a tree stand waiting for a whitetail to wander by (not that there's anything wrong with that, by the way). It's a physically demanding pursuit that can involve miles of hiking, steep climbs and some pretty unforgiving terrain. And Janson isn't exactly spending his free time in the gym preparing for it. "I'm not really a training kind of guy. I don't work out," he said. "But I call that my workout for the year because it's all on foot, of course, and you're just climbing here and you're climbing there, and you walk mile after mile after mile." He said mental toughness is just as important as physical conditioning, especially when an elk is bugling a few hundred yards away and the only thing standing between you and that opportunity is another brutal climb. Some hunters might decide the trek isn't worth it. But if you want it badly enough... "I'll climb over any rock, crevice, mountain, river. It doesn't matter," Janson said. "If it gets the mission done, then I'm into it." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER For Janson, the exhausting week in the mountains was worth it. "Nice bull, and I've already eaten about half of it," he said. "And it's been really good." So much for all that fishing he was going to do, though. Love all things hunting, fishing and outdoors? title: RedZone host Scott Hanson defends NFL officiating, calls league 'best officiated' in America
description: Scott Hanson defends NFL officiating as the best of the four major sports despite an ESPN report showing accepted penalties at a 1978-era high.
content: Millions of NFL fans spend each Sunday of the season with Scott Hanson, host of the acclaimed "NFL RedZone." Few people are more aware of when flags are thrown—or missed—than Hanson, who checks in and out of the biggest moments from every Sunday afternoon game. An ESPN Insights report last week found that NFL officials had called more accepted penalties through Week 4 than during the same span of any season since 1978. Officials had also nullified 17 touchdowns, compared to just five through four weeks last season. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Hanson joined OutKick for a wide-ranging interview, and the state of NFL officiating was part of the discussion. "I believe the NFL just put out a statement about penalties. I don't know when people are going to watch this [we recorded on Friday, October 9], but as we are talking right here, the NFL says that penalties per game are actually down this year," Hanson said, citing the league's response disputing concerns about the number of flags in 2026. When we asked about the ESPN Insights report, Hanson said he tries to "err on the side of respect for all the professionals that are involved—players, coaches, support staff and officials." He continued, "I really believe that NFL football is the best—I know this will be controversial—is the best officiated of the major four sports." WWE'S MICHAEL COLE REFUSES TO DIP HIS TOE INTO POLITICAL WATERS, BUCKING TREND AMONG SPORTS BROADCASTERS We next asked Hanson whether he agreed that officials are throwing too many flags, particularly during the regular season. "I know people are going to say I'm a company man, but that's truly the way I feel. To answer your question, are there too many? The number is immaterial to me. The accuracy is what should matter." "Of course, there are calls that go the wrong way, that are not officiated the proper way. And it's not because of an interpretation of rules. It's because the human eye can only go so fast. And a lot of times, the human feet and hands and bodies can move quicker than what we can discern with our human eyes. And then there's error in judgment sometimes." Last week, OutKick argued that the NFL tones down the ticky-tack penalties during the postseason because it understands that an excessive number of flags bogs down the game. That apparent change in philosophy raises an obvious question: If the league is comfortable letting players play in January, why call the game so much tighter during the regular season? Hanson questioned that premise. "This might get me dismissed here, but I'm not even so sure that they do call it differently [in the playoffs]," he countered. "Every game is in a standalone window, so every call is extremely magnified. And so there's a narrative that gets developed, right? "We're all on the same page that the NFL does put all-star crews together, right?" he asked. "You're not getting a playoff game if you aren't great. Which, by the way, I also would have no problem with them making it public what grades the officials get, which would help the fandom understand, ' Okay, this crew or that crew might not be considered. They're not going to get a divisional game. They're not going to get the Super Bowl,' and whatnot." Do you agree? title: Weight-loss drugs may fight 7 serious health problems before the pounds even come off

title: LSU head coach Lane Kiffin is making the same mistake his predecessor did, will he suffer the same fate?
description: Lane Kiffin's LSU is losing top Louisiana five-star recruits to Florida, Alabama, and even Nebraska, eerily mirroring the failures that sank Brian Kelly.
content: It's probably fair to say that year one for Lane Kiffin at LSU isn't going quite how most people envisioned it when he was hired. The Tigers gave Kiffin a $93 million contract and one of the most expensive rosters in college football, and six games into his first campaign on the bayou, the Lane Train is 4-2 and staring down the barrel of missing the College Football Playoff if his team comes away with another loss during a brutal back half of the schedule. Even in today's day and age of instant roster upgrades, though, I tend to give most coaches a pass in their first year at a new school (within reason). WHAT DOES A REALISTICALLY SUCCESSFUL FIRST YEAR LOOK LIKE FOR HEAD COACH LANE KIFFIN AT LSU? Weird highs and lows can occur and players still need time to adapt to the culture and expectations set by the new staff, so going solely off of results on the field can leave fans ready to hit the eject button before enough data has been compiled. For that reason, I like to pay attention to what's happening off the field as much as on it, and there is a key thread throughout Kiffin's recruiting strategy that could be a tell for whether or not he will succeed in Baton Rouge. If we take a look at LSU's 2027 recruiting class as it stands right now, nothing looks too alarming. The Tigers sit at 11th in the 247Sports composite rankings, which is really good albeit not elite, but with only 16 commits, it still has plenty of room to grow. The ranking isn't necessarily the problem. The sticking point here is entirely geographical. Just to offer up a bit of a background note on Louisiana high school football before we continue, it has long been said that The Boot is one of the most talent rich states per capita in the entire country. Every successful LSU coach in the 21st century, from Nick Saban to Les Miles to Ed Orgeron, has made locking down the Tigers' home state a priority, and the results speak for themselves. Kiffin is letting the talent from Louisiana seep through his hands, and it's not an overreaction to say that could spell doom for him. Of the top ten prospects in the 2027 recruiting class from Louisiana according to 247Sports, LSU has four of them. Not bad, until you realize that, of the four prospects who carry a five-star rating only one of them is currently committed to the Tigers. The latest casualty came in the form of Easton Royal, a five-star, all-world wide receiver from literally right down the road at Brother Martin High School in New Orleans. Royal was committed to Texas for nearly a year, but everyone with any inside knowledge believed a flip to the instate Tigers was inevitable. The flip came this past Sunday, but instead of staying in The Boot, Royal opted to head to The Swamp instead to play for the Gators. What's even worse is that the lone composite five-star on from that list who is committed to LSU, Ahmad Hudson, has been getting courted heavily by Nebraska for several weeks now, and a flip to the Huskers seems imminent. LANE KIFFIN KNOWS THERE AREN’T EXCUSES AT LSU. NOW COMES THE TEST OF MAKING IT WORTH THE PRICE OF ADMISSION Losing instate five-stars to Florida (Royal), Alabama (quarterback Elijah Haven), and Notre Dame (o-lineman Albert Simien) is painful but excusable. Nebraska taking a five-star from the clutches of the Tigers is a different can of worms altogether. It's not 1996 anymore, and the Huskers are a shell of the once-dominant program they used to be. Over the summer, I wrote about how Kiffin adding former Tigers head coach Ed Orgeron to the staff was his way of addressing the shortcomings of his predecessor, Brian Kelly, but so far, that doesn't seem to be helping. Kelly famously failed to recruit the state of Louisiana to the likings of Tiger fans everywhere, and it ultimately sank his efforts and landed him on the unemployment line this past year. It's early, but Kiffin's classes are looking eerily similar to Kelly's first full class in Baton Rouge, when six of the top ten composite prospects in Louisiana left the friendly confines of The Boot. Although Kelly's 2024 class remedied this quite a bit (signing nine of the top ten composite prospects in the state), it was the only year in which Kelly landed a majority of the top homegrown talent. By that point, the damage had been done. Coaches like Orgeron in the past have eschewed recruiting the state when it made sense, such as during cycles when Louisiana lacked some of the top-end talent it normally possesses. But 2027 is a historically loaded cycle for the state, and Kiffin is failing to tap into the goldmine in his own backyard. Detractors of this theory will say things like "high school recruiting doesn't matter anymore" and "they can just use the portal," but will fail to mention that Kiffin leaned heavily on the portal this year to make up the bulk of his roster. Relying on the portal is volatile, and although most recruits are always a flight risk even after they sign at a school, kids from Louisiana have usually been fiercely loyal to their home state. Just look at the discourse surrounding LSU and Kiffin's recruiting efforts from Tiger fans and beat writers following the news of Royal's flip to Florida and Hudson's open flirtation with Nebraska. Recruiting and retaining the best players from The Boot matters to these people, and if Kiffin fails to show progress on the field, his leash could get that much tighter based solely on the fact that he isn't doing this the "LSU way." I've gone on record saying that Lane Kiffin will be wildly successful at LSU, and I still believe that. He's too talented a coach with too many resources behind him to fail. But if this trend continues, I could very well be wrong. title: Troy Aikman responds to report of tensions in the booth with Joe Buck over contract situation
description: Troy Aikman didn't deny tension with Monday Night Football partner Joe Buck this season, and left little room for possibility he sign new deal with ESPN.
content: Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback and ESPN Monday Night Football analyst Troy Aikman was given the opportunity on Thursday to refute there has been tension between himself and broadcast partner Joe Buck and he didn't take it. He didn't deny it. Actually, he kind of fed into it. So the broadcast team that has been together for more than two decades and is slated to broadcast Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14, the first ever on ESPN, apparently has beef. "There's probably a time and a place for all that to be discussed," Aikman said about the situation on Sportsradio 96.7 in Dallas on Thursday. "I don't know if now is the time. DOLPHINS CONSULTANT TROY AIKMAN WILL BE LIMITED IN MNF ROLE LIKE RAIDERS MINORITY OWNER TOM BRADY IS ON FOX "I don't know if it's hard to figure out kind of what's happened." Aikman was asked specifically whether a report of tension between him and Buck prior to Monday night's game between the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams is true. And that was his answer. The bright, articulate analyst who breaks down plays immediately after they happen didn't tear down a report by Front Office Sports that he and Buck had an argument before they worked the game together. And over what? The fact Buck has signed a new contract to remain with Disney/ ABC/ ESPN as the play-by-play man on Monday Night Football, and Aikman doesn't have any deal in place beyond this season. There has been ongoing tension between the longtime partners about this season and FOS reported Buck "broke the ice" on this tension, but he and Aikman had an argument as a result. Tensions obviously cooled and the two men broadcast the game and apparently intend to continue broadcasting together through the Super Bowl. But what happens after that remains uncertain. NFL ANALYST TONY ROMO PLACED ON LEAVE BY CBS SPORTS FOLLOWING DRUNK DRIVING ARREST IN WISCONSIN "I'll broadcast through this season and I'll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens," Aikman said. "I'm looking forward to whatever the rest of this year does hold and the Super Bowl and all that, and where my next landing spot might be." It's unknown what specifically has fed into this drama between Aikman and Buck. It could be that the pair had a gentleman's agreement to form a united front in their contract talks and Buck broke ranks. It could also be that Aikman is simply envious of his partner getting a new deal. Whatever it is, this incident puts both men in the crosshairs. Critics will now watch MNF for further signs of tension. And both ESPN and Buck will continue to be asked for comment on the issue, which neither has so far provided. ESPN declined comment. title: NBA Hall of Famer Amare Stoudemire is now a police officer after graduating from Miami academy
description: Amare Stoudemire graduated from the Miami police academy after a Hall of Fame NBA career, fulfilling a childhood dream rooted in family tradition.
content: After earning more than $161 million over his Hall of Fame career, Amare Stoudemire has more than enough money to never work again. But instead, his second act will be on the front lines. The former NBA big man, 43, recently graduated from the police academy in Miami and is now a police officer. "It’s something I always wanted to do since I was a kid. I remember back when I was in grade school, elementary school. They asked you on career day, 'What do you want to be when you grow up?' And my initial response was a police officer," Stoudemire told Sports Illustrated. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "It runs in the family. My uncle was a captain. His brother was a deputy. My cousin is a captain. My sister’s in the academy. So, it’s a family tradition, basically." Stoudemire took his lessons from the basketball court to the academy, where he endured physical tests and read thousands of pages on policy. "It’s a similar situation where you have to have discipline. You gotta have a sense of professionalism. You have to be able to communicate properly. I think as an athlete, all those things also are important. Being able to communicate with your fans and the media, but more so, as an officer, you communicate with the community. So I will be able to help steer the next generation in the proper way and catch them before they get in trouble and try to provide some guidance there," he said. Stoudemire said the "business" of "protect[ing] and serv[ing] the community" is what "drew" him to the line of work. "We’re able to somewhat help protect the community that really needs help and wants protection, and wants to live a comfortable lifestyle. To be hands-on with the young youth, and to steer them in the right direction, not only from an athletic standpoint, but also just from a successful, professional entrepreneur standpoint," Stoudemire said. title: Giant meat-eating crabs with crushing grip complicate Amelia Earhart expedition on remote island
description: The Purdue University expedition to find Amelia Earhart's Lockheed Electra has encountered massive coconut crabs while clearing trails on Nikumaroro Island.
content: Massive meat-eating coconut crabs are posing an unusual challenge for the team searching for Amelia Earhart's missing plane on the remote Pacific island of Nikumaroro. Purdue University confirmed on Monday that the crew would sleep aboard its vessel rather than on the island, citing the enormous crustaceans as one reason for the decision. The 17-person expedition team arrived off Nikumaroro on Monday evening after a five-day voyage across the Pacific, going ashore the following morning to begin investigating clues that could help solve Earhart's disappearance. AMELIA EARHART MYSTERY ENTERS CRITICAL PHASE AS EXPLORERS ZERO IN ON MYSTERIOUS OBJECT "The crew will sleep nightly aboard the Marin Mainiku for a number of reasons, one of which is the presence of coconut crabs, whose size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical," the university said. The team, which is 16 hours ahead of Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), has already encountered the massive crustaceans while working on the island. In a Tuesday statement, Purdue University officials said researchers came across at least four coconut crabs while clearing an overgrown trail to the island's lagoon. "The species is omnivorous and will scavenge carcasses, climb trees to access food or escape, and can live [for] over 40 years," added the USGS report. Coconut crabs are also equipped with two powerful pincers capable of cracking through the tough exterior of a coconut, according to London's Natural History Museum. Researchers testing 29 wild coconut crabs found that their pincers could generate more than 1,765 newtons of force. "For comparison, humans have a maximum bite force of between 1,100 and 1,300 newtons," the museum added. title: America's next war could reach US soil, top Army general warns
description: The Army's new "How the Army Fights" framework prepares American forces for contested deployments as drones and surveillance reshape the battlefield.
content: The American military has largely operated on a familiar premise: combat the enemy overseas before the fight reaches home. But as drones, cyberattacks and long-range weapons pose growing threats to U.S. military installations and critical infrastructure, Army leaders are preparing for a future in which American forces could come under attack before they ever deploy overseas. "If we're going against a pacing threat, power projection will be contested," Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's acting chief of staff, told Fox News Digital on Wednesday. He said the military is rethinking assumptions that were held during decades of fighting in Iraq and Afghanistan, when American forces could largely count on secure bases and supply lines at home. FBI WARNS BATTLEFIELD-STYLE DRONE ATTACKS COULD REACH US: 'ONLY A MATTER OF TIME' "During the Global War on Terror, we took a lot of things for granted, because we could," LaNeve said during a small-group roundtable at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington this week. In a potential conflict with China, disrupting American military bases, transportation networks and communications could delay U.S. forces from reaching the battlefield. The Pentagon's latest report on China's military capabilities warns that Beijing has positioned cyber capabilities inside U.S. critical infrastructure networks that could be used to disrupt American military mobilization during a conflict. The concerns come as the Pentagon places renewed emphasis on homeland defense and military installations as they prepare to potentially confront threats closer to home. U.S. officials have previously confirmed drone incursions over installations — including Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Virginia and Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey. Though those incidents have not been publicly attributed to China. The warning of a future fight on American soil comes amid the How the Army Fights rollout. The new operational framework places greater emphasis on preparing American forces to deploy, communicate and sustain operations even when military bases, supply lines and communications networks are under attack. The guidance places greater emphasis on the Army's ability to deploy and sustain forces under threat, including when communications, supply lines and military infrastructure are disrupted. US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING LaNeve said the Army is using the framework to establish clearer priorities for how its formations train, fight and incorporate new technology. "It was important to get this document out to provide a direction for our Army, a stake in the ground in where we're moving," LaNeve told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday. The changes are being led by an Army leadership team serving in acting capacities following the departures of former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll and Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George. LaNeve remains the Senate-confirmed vice chief of staff. LaNeve explained how the Army is preparing to keep fighting even when an adversary disrupts military communications. "I think what you would see inside this command and control capability is the ability to operate disconnected and then reconnect when you have that capability, but to continue to be able to maneuver," he said. The Army is also rethinking how it protects military installations at home. LaNeve pointed to Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which is working with federal and local law enforcement to strengthen counter-drone defenses around military bases and critical infrastructure. CARTELS USE DRONES TO SCOUT BORDER AGENTS AND MAP SMUGGLING ROUTES, EXPERT WARNS Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle pointed to the southern border as an example of how soldiers are already confronting drone threats closer to home. He said soldiers are using the mission to test new counter-drone technology against real-world threats, gaining experience they can bring back to their units as the Army prepares for future conflicts. The Army is also expanding its preparations for biological threats that could disrupt military operations. Officials announced this week that biological incidents will be incorporated into routine combat training as part of a broader effort to ensure soldiers can continue carrying out their missions through disease outbreaks or deliberate biological attacks. During a separate panel Wednesday, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink warned that advances in surveillance technology could soon make it increasingly difficult for military forces to operate anywhere without being detected. "We are rapidly heading to a point in time where, depending on what your signature is, how fast you're moving, the enemy is going to have some sense to where you are no matter where you are on the planet," Meink said. He suggested that level of surveillance could emerge within five years, potentially sooner, as China and other adversaries expand their ability to track and target military assets. Meink said the Pentagon is working to make its forces more survivable, including through autonomous systems capable of operating in dangerous environments where commanders might hesitate to send manned platforms. War Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking alongside Meink and the other service secretaries, criticized what he described as the Pentagon's failure to keep pace with technological advances under the Biden administration. "On hypersonics, they took a nap. On space, they took a nap. On weaponization of space, they took a nap. On drones, they took a nap," Hegseth said. LaNeve emphasized that despite the Army's growing reliance on advanced technology, soldiers must still be able to carry out their missions when those systems are unavailable. "Soldiers are our number one platform. It is the Army's platform," he told Fox News Digital.
