title: MORNING GLORY: The polls got Michigan badly wrong. Now Democrats may face a bigger reckoning
description: Here's why Abdul El-Sayed's ties to far-left streamer Hasan Piker and his refusal to call Israel an ally over Iran could cost him the Michigan Senate race against Mike Rogers.
content: The nationwide duel for the Senate is going on in the dark because polling this year has produced a series of spectacular busts, especially in Michigan, where polls on the primary battle between Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens posted double-digit lead after double-digit lead for El-Sayed. In fact, El-Sayed won by 1% — not the 10-18% that had been predicted. It turns out those polls may have suppressed voter turnout and encouraged some Stevens voters to stay home. It is doubtful anyone following the news will stay home in Michigan in the general election. El-Sayed is — at best! — an Islamist apologist. He cannot own his past statements or campaign rhetoric. He refuses to discuss his most prominent supporter in the primary: far-left streamer and YouTube personality Hasan Piker, who is part crazy and part extremist. Piker carried El-Sayed over the finish line in the primary, but now voters are supposed to accept El-Sayed’s deflections when questioned about him. HISTORIC NEWSPAPER GIVES EL-SAYED A SAVAGE REBUKE FOR HIDING HIS PAST WHILE ENDORSING HIS OPPONENT El-Sayed is a radical. He’s done very little to hide his antipathy toward America’s ally Israel, going so far as to equate Israel with the Islamic Republic of Iran. Iran has, of course, been at war with the United States since its revolution in 1979. That regime is responsible for the deaths of more than a thousand Americans, whether blown up at the U.S. Embassy or the Marine Corps barracks in Beirut in 1983 by Iran’s proxy in Lebanon, Hezbollah, or this past weekend, when another American was killed by another Iranian proxy, the Houthis, via a Houthi missile attack on the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Still, El-Sayed cannot simply declare that Israel is our ally and Iran is our enemy. That should tell everyone all they need to know about El-Sayed and cost him on November 3. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER All across the country, Democrats have nominated candidates from the fringe, from El-Sayed in Michigan to James Talarico in Texas, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Troy Jackson in Maine. It’s as though the Democratic National Committee put zero effort into candidate recruitment, or maybe they just threw darts at a board marked with "Guaranteed to Lose" at the top. But El-Sayed is the worst of the lot … by a lot. And the stories keep coming as opposition research reveals facts about El-Sayed’s past that he has tried to hide, including his claim of dual citizenship, which he has subsequently repudiated. With nearly three weeks left before polls close, it’s fair to expect that more such old tape and tweets will surface. FETTERMAN 'DARES' EL-SAYED TO STICK WITH PIKER, CLAIMS MICHIGAN NOMINEE HAS 'LITTLE MAN SYNDROME ENERGY' El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, is, by contrast, a mainstream and moderate Michigander, a former FBI agent and lieutenant in the Army before he went on to serve in the Michigan legislature and then for more than a decade in the House of Representatives, finishing there as chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. (That’s significant, by the way, as the Intelligence Committee is a select committee, with members selected by the speaker and the House minority leader, traditionally because of their national security chops.) Rogers v. El-Sayed ought not to be close. And chances are it won’t be because of El-Sayed’s reported difficulty connecting with Detroit’s Black community, on which Democrats traditionally rely to win in the Wolverine State. ROGERS OPENS DOOR TO DEMOCRATIC VOTERS AFTER EL-SAYED’S PRIMARY VICTORY: ‘THERE IS STILL HOPE’ Report after report hints at the long-standing estrangement between the Black and Arab American communities in and around Detroit, but hardly any pollster knows how to account for the antipathy felt toward El-Sayed by Black voters. Campaign drop-bys by former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Barack Obama are as close to "break glass, pull alarm" emergency signals as you can get, but they are not doing the trick. BLACK VOTERS, JEWISH DEMOCRATS IN MICHIGAN WARY OF VOTING FOR EL-SAYED, SAY 'HE'S TAKING ADVANTAGE' The trouble? Traditional Democrats know El-Sayed. He’s run for political office before. And lost before. "Winsome and gracious" is not on his resume. If anything, he’s the angriest major-party candidate we’ve seen in decades. His refusal to answer basic questions about Piker, about his family’s alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, and about the impact of "Medicare for All" on union-negotiated health care plans (the former would destroy the latter) marks El-Sayed as untrustworthy. An early call for Rogers on election night will secure the Senate majority for Republicans. (That result might have already been accomplished by victories for Sens. Susan Collins in Maine and John Sununu in New Hampshire, but Rogers getting the call early on November 3 would be a great relief.) CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Beyond simply having the far better man win an election, though, the victory of Rogers over El-Sayed will be a win for moderation and maturity and a rejection of the sort of extremism that Democrats have not flirted with outside of the deep-blue urban districts that sent AOC, Ilhan Omar and the rest of "The Squad" to D.C. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The United States needs two mainstream parties committed to playing between the 40-yard lines of American politics. Losing the Democrats to the control of extremists like El-Sayed would be terrible for everyone, including, and most especially, the Democratic Party. title: MARK HALPERIN: Republicans are bracing for a wipeout. Here's who they'll blame if it happens
description: Political strategists on both sides are already rehearsing recriminations weeks before Election Day, preparing to win the argument about why it was lost.
content: The political strategists I have known in my career are among the smartest, most interesting, most knowledgeable and most impressive people I have ever met. They are also capable of more white-hot animus for other people than anyone I have ever met. And I am not talking about Democrats hating Republicans, or vice versa. That is frequently a manageable relationship. Sometimes they even share a corporate client. BATTLEGROUND REPUBLICANS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON KEY ISSUES IN FINAL MIDTERM SPRINT The disgust to which I refer is intraparty. That is when the hatred becomes unmatched by all other human relationships. More than Glinda felt pure, unadulterated loathing for Elphaba at the beginning of "Wicked." More than a tenant despises her cruel and unusual landlord. More than the Red Sox detest the Yankees. These folks are experts at circular firing squads and shooting off bazookas inside the tent. Most political strategists detest two things: losing campaigns and losing money. The pair is connected. An election defeat can cost you your next client. Being blamed for an election defeat can cost you several. There is, therefore, a substantial professional incentive to establish that the catastrophe was foreseeable, preventable and definitely somebody else’s doing. With a few weeks to go before Election Day, Democratic strategists are feeling good or great, while Republicans range from uneasy and determined to absolutely horrible. The latter have begun rehearsing their recriminations with select audiences. Some of those audiences are reporters. Most political strategists detest two things: losing campaigns and losing money. The pair is connected. An election defeat can cost you your next client. Being blamed for an election defeat can cost you several. MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE The Democrats will not need a lengthy warm-up period if the election disappoints. There are two parallel campaigns underway: the one to win the election and the one to win the argument about why it was lost. LEE CARTER: TRUMP CAN STILL GET ATTENTION, CAN HE DISTRACT VOTERS FROM THEIR BILLS? On the Republican side, the simplest argument is also the hardest to refute. One man controls the party, and his name is Trump. His advisers can recommend a message, a schedule, a spending plan or a period of blessed silence. They cannot guarantee delivery. A Republican wipeout would thus produce a comprehensive Trump indictment: his unpopularity, his indiscipline, his economic decisions, his foreign entanglements, his family’s enrichment and his apparently inexhaustible interest in attaching his name to things. Trump’s cheerleading for AI and data centers is hurting Republicans, too, alienating voters who see higher electric bills and threats to their jobs where he sees a glorious future. The defense of the staff will be that they could not control him. The prosecution’s response will be that taking responsibility for the consequences of not managing him properly was rather prominently included in the job description. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS There had been a plausible Republican case for optimism late last year. Democrats were divided, the Senate map was favorable, the novel mid-decade redistricting plan seemed to be working, and Republicans could hope voters would tolerate an economic mixed bag if the promised benefits began arriving. Instead, a voter worried about groceries sees a president worried about building names. A family falling behind on retirement savings hears about a ballroom. A young adult unable to afford a house watches the president’s family make deals. IT’S NOT THE ECONOMY, STUPID. AMERICANS VOTE BASED ON THEIR PERSONAL ECONOMY Each story supplies the caption for the next one. The political damage requires voters to conclude that the president is spending more time on his surroundings than on theirs. "Why is he focused on a Washington arts building instead of my wallet?" is a question no Republican media buyer can answer with another video invoking Zohran Mamdani or AOC. The Iran conflict compounds the problem: higher energy costs, another foreign war that seems to be taking forever and a president who campaigned on avoiding precisely that sort of entanglement. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune will face a related accusation: that congressional Republicans produced too little voters could feel, understand or remember. A legislative accomplishment that requires a staff briefing to appreciate is difficult to sell in a 30-second spot. ONE MONTHLY BILL AMERICANS CAN’T AVOID IS QUIETLY SURGING THANKS TO EMERGING INDUSTRY: DATA Republicans have money. What they have lacked is a national message persuasive enough to make that money work. The consultants will say the committees commissioned stale spots and recycled attacks, and started airing them too late. If the spots fail, the people who approved them will explain that testing showed they worked. The people who opposed them will explain that they always knew the testing was wrong. The turnout people will be asked why they could not bring Trump-only voters back for an election without Trump on the ballot. The candidate recruiters will be asked why loyalty at times outranked electability. Individual candidates will be blamed for hugging him too tightly or abandoning him too quickly. Some may achieve the distinction of being blamed for both. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY And the media will occupy its customary place in the Republican explanation: burying accomplishments, magnifying liabilities and making every Republican candidate answer for Trump. The Democratic version will be less centered on one man and considerably more crowded. Suppose Democrats barely take the House and fail to win the Senate. What might once have been celebrated as a successful midterm could become an indictment of a party that persuaded itself it was entitled to a much bigger one. Once a wave becomes the assumed outcome, every seat it fails to wash ashore becomes evidence of malpractice. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries will be accused of weak leadership. The progressives will say the party offered voters too little to get excited about. The moderates will say the progressives offered Republicans entirely too much to get excited about. Strategists who made Trump the central issue will be accused of neglecting household costs. Strategists who emphasized household costs will be accused of failing to make voters understand the full danger of Trump. Republican billionaires will be accused of buying the final weeks, and their Democratic counterparts will be blamed for sitting on their wallets. The Democratic media complaint will be the inverse of the Republican one: Trump was normalized, and his opponents held to a higher standard. There is no neutral after-action report when the authors are competing for the next contract. That does not make the recriminations worthless. Sometimes the angriest person understands the failure best. Political strategists are very good at spotting other political strategists’ mistakes. They are less consistent about spotting their own. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP By the time the returns are in, both sides will have ready explanations, supporting anecdotes and witnesses who remember being ignored. The only thing they will not have is enough blame for themselves. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM MARK HALPERIN

title: San Jose girl, 8, dies after living in cockroach-infested home as mother, stepfather face charges
description: Aurora Williams lived in a cockroach-infested San Jose home with mold and pet feces before a fatal asthma attack, which prompted felony charges against her mother and stepfather.
content: An 8-year-old California girl died following a severe asthma attack after allegedly living for years in a filthy home infested with cockroaches, mold and pet feces, prompting felony child neglect charges against her mother and stepfather, prosecutors said. The Santa Clara County District Attorney's Office said this week that the girl's mother, Gabrielle Hanson, 32, and stepfather, Jacob Randolph, 39, knew about the dangerous conditions inside their San Jose home and had been repeatedly warned by medical professionals and social workers about the risks to their seven children. Despite the warnings, the couple allegedly waited eight hours before seeking medical help when their daughter, Aurora Williams, began experiencing serious medical distress in May. "It was too late," prosecutors said in a news release announcing the charges. title: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt opens up about Trump, motherhood

content: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt offered a glimpse into her relationship with President Donald Trump during a candid Instagram Q&A, praising her former boss as "kind and uplifting" while opening up about personal life decisions. Leavitt, 29, fielded a variety of questions from her Instagram followers while traveling Wednesday, touching on everything from Trump's personality to her career plans and life as a mother of two. When asked whether Trump was nice or kind, Leavitt offered insight into his personality. "Yes! He’s the best boss," she said. LEAVITT PULLS BACK THE CURTAIN ON TRUMP'S 'TENSE,' UNFILTERED PRIVATE TALKS WITH PUTIN, XI, STARMER "People don’t see this side of him because the media doesn’t show it but he has been nothing but kind and uplifting to me, even since departing," she continued. KAROLINE LEAVITT INVITED AS A GUEST ON ABC'S 'THE VIEW' AFTER LEAVING WHITE HOUSE ROLE Leavitt also confirmed that she would officially begin working as a Fox News Channel contributor next month. KAROLINE LEAVITT ANNOUNCES BIRTH OF SECOND CHILD, A GIRL "My advice to people who want to get into politics or comms is to get real world experience when you're in college," she said. Leavitt said she interned at NBC Sports Boston because she initially considered becoming a sideline sports reporter. She also worked at a local news station before securing a White House internship. "Just try to apply for internships, say yes to every opportunity that you can and don't spend your summers hanging out, spend your summers working and gaining that real world experience, which will help you later in your career." title: El Salvador's Bukele announces plan to free up to half of prisoners jailed in gang crackdown
description: Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele unveiled a plan to free up to half of 90,000 detainees arrested under the state of emergency targeting gangs.
content: Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has unveiled a plan that could allow the conditional early release of up to half of those detained under a state of emergency that authorities used to arrest more than 90,000 people in the past four and a half years as part of an effort to curb violent criminal gang activity. Bukele's plan to cut the prison population was announced on Tuesday night. It would focus on freeing prisoners who were deemed gang collaborators, a broad term that can include various people, including gang lookouts and those who make extortion payments. "There are many people who have indeed committed crimes, but their crime was collaborating with gangs," Bukele said. "They deserve to be in jail, but we come from a country where collaborating with gangs wasn’t so unusual, and if we were to arrest everyone who collaborated with gangs, we would have to arrest 20% of the population." Without offering details, the president indicated that authorities plan to analyze cases to determine potential early release with monitoring, which could apply to half of the people detained during the state of emergency. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SAYS FEDERAL AUTHORITIES HAVE ARRESTED MORE THAN 10,000 SUSPECTED GANG MEMBERS The state of emergency was declared in March 2022 after a surge in violence left more than 60 people dead in a single day. The measure was initially imposed for 30 days but has been repeatedly extended. The emergency declaration has coincided with a dramatic decline in the country's homicide rate and helped make El Salvador a more appealing tourist destination while also suspending or restricting certain constitutional protections, including the right to be informed of the reasons for detention, the right to access legal counsel and the right to visitation. El Salvador's president has maintained that the measure was needed to rein in rival gangs MS-13 and Barrio 18. Human rights groups, meanwhile, have denounced the declared emergency, arguing that it has sparked widespread arbitrary arrests. The groups have repeatedly demanded that Bukele scrap the measure. NICOLAS MADURO AND WIFE CILIA FLORES FACE NEW CHARGE OF CONSPIRACY TO TORTURE AMERICANS Human rights organizations have recorded more than 6,000 complaints during the emergency declaration and documented the deaths of at least 575 people in government custody. The potential release of thousands of prisoners, some argue, is not enough to repair the damage of their prolonged imprisonment. "The victims of arbitrary detentions don’t just deserve to recover their freedom, but they also deserve to be compensated for the harms caused by the State of El Salvador: the physical and mental harm that imprisonment causes, family suffering, loss of work or studies, reputational damage, among others," exiled Salvadoran lawyer Bertha Deleón wrote on X. Bukele dismissed widespread criticism from national and international human rights groups, suggesting that they should take the side of the victims of gang violence. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The president also defended the need to keep the state of emergency while also indicating his goal of ending it eventually. El Salvador's homicide rate has fallen dramatically over the past decade, including during Bukele's presidency, according to government figures. The rate dropped from a peak of more than 100 murders per 100,000 residents in 2015, four years before Bukele took office, to 1.3 per 100,000 in 2025. But the government has narrowed the definition of homicide to exclude killings by police, murders in prisons and bodies found in unmarked graves. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Pentagon sends hundreds of Army troops to Latin America for training as drug-trafficking campaign expands
description: Troops from the 10th Mountain Division are deploying to Panama for jungle training as the Pentagon expands military operations against drug traffickers.
content: The U.S. military is deploying several hundred Army soldiers to Latin America for training and joint exercises with regional forces as the Trump administration expands its campaign against drug-trafficking networks, Fox News confirmed. The deployment involves soldiers from the Army's 10th Mountain Division based at Fort Drum, New York, with the first troops from a roughly 600-soldier battalion expected to deploy to Panama, according to The New York Times, which first reported the deployment. A senior U.S. official confirmed to Fox News that the troops are being forward-staged under U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), which will determine where they are ultimately deployed. According to The Times, the troops will first deploy to a new jungle training facility in Panama before eventually training with local forces in Colombia and Honduras. EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S NEW SECURITY ALLIANCE FACES FIRST REAL-WORLD TEST DEEP IN SOUTH AMERICA AS TROOPS DEPLOY The troops could also support U.S. special operations personnel who are advising local militaries conducting raids against suspected drug traffickers, the outlet reported. Separately, several hundred soldiers from the 10th Mountain Division are expected to help staff a new Western Hemisphere military command based in Miami. The deployment comes as the Pentagon continues military operations targeting suspected drug traffickers across Latin America and the Caribbean. US MILITARY STRIKES ALLEGED NARCO-TRAFFICKING VESSEL IN CARIBBEAN, KILLING 4 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' Since the campaign began more than a year ago, U.S. forces have conducted dozens of strikes, with more than 235 people killed. Gen. Francis Donovan, commander of SOUTHCOM, previously said the military was considering operations against trafficking networks on land. "Do I see land strikes as options? Yes. We want all options at the table," Donovan said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal. "Those actions might be strikes, arrests, or the takedown of a safe house," he continued. "It could even be something as routine as increasing the use of cargo scanners at border checkpoints." TRUMP ADMIN'S LIST OF US-DESIGNATED 'FOREIGN TERRORIST' GROUPS IN LATIN AMERICA EXPANDS TO 21 Donovan added that the goal was to create "total systemic friction" for the cartels. The Trump administration has pursued agreements with allied nations that could allow it to expand military operations against trafficking networks onto land in multiple Latin American countries. title: Trump wishes Pope Leo speedy recovery after lung cancer diagnosis, speaks highly of pontiff's brother

content: President Donald Trump wished Pope Leo XIV a speedy recovery Wednesday following his lung cancer diagnosis, revealing that he is friends with the pontiff's brother, whom he described as an enthusiastic MAGA supporter. Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One while traveling from Arizona to Montana, Trump expressed optimism about the 71-year-old pontiff's recovery following surgery to remove part of his right lung. "I want to see Pope Leo get well. I hear the prognosis for that type of a problem. It's a cancer. It's big stuff. Anytime you have cancer," the president said. "But the prognosis seems to be good, I've watched. And we just want to wish him our love and our best wishes." POPE LEO XIV BEGINS HISTORIC 4-DAY VISIT TO FRANCE Trump then discussed his friendship with the pope's brother and his wife, describing them as enthusiastic supporters of the president. "His brother is a friend of mine, who's a great — he's a fantastic guy — and his wife. You know, they're big Trump supporters. They have MAGA all over their house," he continued. "And I can say that his brother loves him a lot. Loves the pope a lot, and that's good, but I just want to wish him well. Get better fast." The president's remarks came one day after the Vatican announced that Leo had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer, following surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital in Rome. According to the Holy See Press Office, doctors removed the lower lobe of the pontiff's right lung during a procedure that lasted approximately 90 minutes. Doctors reported no complications. TRUMP TAKES AIM AT POPE LEO XIV MEETING WITH 'USELESS' CHICAGO MAYOR BRANDON JOHNSON AT VATICAN The Vatican said the cancer diagnosis was confirmed through an examination of tissue collected during surgery, consistent with findings from tests conducted before the procedure. title: NFL says first regular-season game in France remains on track despite growing unrest in Paris
description: The Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints are set to meet at Stade de France on Oct. 25 despite weeks of protests roiling Paris streets.
content: Earlier this season, the NFL sanctioned its first regular-season game in Australia, extending the league’s international reach beyond its longstanding presence in England. The 2026-27 season is also set to feature a record number of games outside the United States. In addition to Australia and England, games will be played in France, Brazil, Spain, Germany and Mexico. As the NFL’s inaugural game in the Paris area approaches, social unrest and protests in France have entered their third week, creating a broader security backdrop for the event. However, the league said Wednesday that the game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints is still expected to take place as scheduled Oct. 25 at Stade de France in Saint-Denis, north of Paris. NFL OWNERS APPROVE RECORD 10 INTERNATIONAL GAMES FOR 2027 WITH SIGHTS ON MORE EXPANSION ABROAD There is precedent for the NFL relocating games, although past changes have typically been prompted by extreme weather or field conditions. "We're excited for the first-ever regular season game in Paris, and preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France on Oct. 25," the NFL said in a statement obtained by ESPN. "As we do for every NFL game, including our international games, we work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. We look forward to welcoming fans to Paris later this month." ROGER GOODELL DETAILS NFL EXPANSION POSSIBILITIES AND A TIMETABLE FOR A FULL SEASON OF INTERNATIONAL GAMES Calls for broad changes to France’s education system have been at the center of the unrest. content: Roughly a dozen high school girls took their spots at the starting line of a Washington cross-country meet and walked off the course in protest. DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER "I think if only a couple of girls had walked off it, they would have lost some opportunities. And I don't think it would have mattered so much. But so many of them," he added. "And I want you to remember that several of the girls, such as the team, team captains, had quit before this. So there really was a lot more girls than you see in the video that were protesting this." "You know, they should just be able to go out there and race and have fun and not deal with this adult issue." The friction carried straight onto the sidelines during the meet. WOMAN SAYS PUBLIC WAS FORCED TO LEAVE CALIFORNIA FORUM OVER HER 'SAVE GIRLS SPORTS' SHIRT "We've actually received a lot of support. “And it was in the New York Times, CNN they leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving.”
The president said he called Gen. Dan Caine , who assured him the military could proceed despite the leak.
“I said, let's change the time. “So I called off the raid,” Trump said, adding that the strikes took place two days later.
“Now we can do the raid. Let's leave it exactly the same time. That was the only time that they didn't expect us to be used.
“We used the exact same time, but they leaked. Leakers should be. In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump added.

title: White House punches back at Chicago Mayor Johnson over reparations demands
description: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson alleged Trump enriched the ultra-rich while ignoring descendants of the formerly enslaved, drawing a White House rebuke.
content: The White House punched back at Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson Wednesday after the progressive mayor claimed President Donald Trump neglected compensation for descendants of formerly enslaved Black Americans while favoring the wealthy. Johnson appeared on the "Native Land Pod" podcast Sunday to discuss his administration's crime reduction efforts in Chicago, where violent crime rates have fallen sharply, according to the Johnson administration and Chicago Police Department data. Speaking with hosts Angela Rye, Bakari Sellers and Andrew Gillum, Johnson argued that public safety "has to be something more than just policing," highlighting city investments in "mental behavioral healthcare, promoting detectives and expanding and investing in CVI (community violence intervention)." REPARATIONS ACTIVISTS CALL OUT BLUE STATES FOR USING SLAVERY HISTORY TO FUND BROADER AGENDA The podcast hosts turned to a recent Truth Social post by Trump targeting Illinois leadership over crime. "Chicago is suffering an unprecedented and particularly violent crime wave that is getting worse by the day," Trump posted on Oct. 6. "The Federal Government can extinguish it quickly and completely, but the Mayor of Chicago, or the Governor of Illinois, must ask for our help. What is wrong with them? Why aren’t they asking? TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE! President DJT." Johnson pushed back against the president’s statement, alleging Trump enriched wealthy Americans while ignoring the demands of "descendants of the formerly enslaved." "He's so sorry. It's real pathetic, right, because it's so disingenuous. … This is the president who just released the largest upward transfer of wealth into the hands of the ultrarich at the expense of the demands of those of us who are descendants of the formerly enslaved," Johnson said. "The largest upward transfer of wealth at the expense of education, housing, health care, transportation, good-paying jobs, which literally were all the demands of the formerly enslaved." TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF 'VIRTUE SIGNALING' TO GET 'VOTES' Johnson also said Trump "cut [the] violence prevention budget by $800 million," slamming the president for being concerned "about the wrong borders" as illegal weapons pour into Chicago. "He cut the ATF budget by 30%. My local police department has worked in tandem with the AFT to get illegal weapons off the streets of Chicago. This year alone, we have removed almost 9,000 illegal weapons off the street." The White House dismissed Johnson's claims and called on the mayor to focus on local public safety. "Government programs that dole out money based on race are illegal," a White House spokesperson told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "Chicago would be better served if Mayor Johnson focused more on lowering his city’s homicide rate instead of advocating for divisive, unconstitutional government action." BLACK CHICAGOANS CALL ON REPARATIONS FROM GOVERNMENT, MONEY DEPOSITS LIKE 'STIMULUS' CHECKS According to the mayor's office, Chicago has seen notable drops in violent crime since Johnson took office in May 2023, including double-digit decreases in homicides, shootings and overall violent crime. Chicago has "achieved historic double-digit decreases in crime and violence" in 2025, a spokesperson for Johnson told Fox News Digital, and is on track to see even further decreases in violent crime in 2026, with homicides down 3.8%, shootings down 1.3%and robberies down 20.9% from the same period last year. While Johnson did not explicitly use the word "reparations" during the interview, a spokesperson pointed Fox News Digital to the city’s reparations initiatives. Johnson previously signed an executive order establishing a 40-member reparations task force intended to address "historical harms committed against Black Chicagoans and their ancestors." In March, Johnson announced the Repair Chicago public engagement initiative aimed at gathering lived experiences from Black residents to inform future municipal policy and direct equity measures. The push for reparations in the region comes as the federal government ramps up legal scrutiny of local programs. Nearby Evanston, Illinois, launched a first-of-its-kind reparations program in 2021, offering $25,000 grants to eligible Black residents or their direct descendants for housing and home repairs, funded by local taxes on legal recreational marijuana sales. To date, Evanston has distributed more than $7 million of an allotted $20 million fund. Earlier this year, the city's Reparations Committee cleared an additional wave of funding for 44 residents. However, the Trump administration’s Department of Justice (DOJ) has signaled plans to challenge race-conscious distribution models. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division previously told Fox News Digital that local officials pushing these measures are "virtue signaling" to win votes. CHICAGO REPARATIONS ADVOCATES SAY FEDERAL GOV MORALLY OWES '7 QUADRILLION DOLLARS' IN SLAVE LABOR Federal intervention is expanding elsewhere as well. In September last year, the DOJ warned officials in Buncombe County, North Carolina, that it would investigate potential civil rights violations if local leaders approved recommendations from the Asheville-Buncombe Community Reparations Commission. Responding to Johnson's remarks on the podcast, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster emphasized that the administration remains committed to dismantling race-based initiatives. "DEI ran rampant during the Biden administration, and Americans ultimately paid the price for these destructive policies with a restricted labor pool, higher operational costs and workforce inefficiencies. The Trump administration will always promote equal treatment under the law for every American, regardless of race or ethnicity."

title: Canadian singer Joni Mitchell officially becomes American citizen after 62-year journey
description: Joni Mitchell shared a photo and video from her naturalization ceremony, becoming a U.S. citizen at 82 while retaining Canadian citizenship.
content: Joni Mitchell has officially become an American citizen at age 82, more than six decades after she first moved to the United States. The music icon, who hails from Canada, announced the news on Instagram, sharing a photo of herself beaming while holding an American flag along with a video from her naturalization ceremony. "A journey that began 62 years ago," Mitchell wrote in the caption of her post. ART GARFUNKEL JOINS GROWING LIST OF CELEBRITIES CONSIDERING A MOVE ABROAD OVER TRUMP PRESIDENCY Mitchell wore a red and navy blue floral cardigan that had an American flag pin along with a red beaded necklace, a red beret and black pants with black boots while posing in between an American flag and a Department of Homeland Security flag. In the video Mitchell uploaded, she was seated in the front row at the ceremony as the speaker announced, "And Joni Mitchell, Canada" to cheers and applause from the audience. According to KSL, Mitchell will also retain her Canadian citizenship because the U.S. and Canada legally permit dual citizenship. The legendary singer-songwriter was born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alberta, to Royal Canadian Air Force flight Lt. William Andrew Anderson and teacher Myrtle Marguerite. Mitchell's family lived on several bases during World War II before eventually settling in Saskatoon, which the singer has often referred to as her hometown. She went on to attend the Alberta College of Art in Calgary before dropping out and relocating to Toronto, where she played gigs at coffee houses and folk clubs. The "Both Sides Now" songstress moved to the United States in 1965 at age 21 after marrying American folk singer Chuck Mitchell. The former couple, who lived in Detroit, Michigan, performed together as a folk duo before divorcing in 1967. After their divorce, Mitchell left Detroit and moved to New York City, where she became part of the Greenwich Village folk scene and performed along the East Coast. By 1968, Mitchell moved to Los Angeles, settling in Laurel Canyon, which was becoming a hub for singer-songwriters including David Crosby, Graham Nash and others. In the mid-1970s, Mitchell moved to LA's Bel Air neighborhood, where she lived in a historic 1920s home for decades. Mitchell built her legendary music career while living in California, where she recorded many of her most acclaimed albums, including "Blue," "Court and Spark" and "Ladies of the Canyon." Mitchell has won 11 Grammy Awards and was inducted into both the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1997. She was also recognized with the Kennedy Center Honors in 2021 and received the prestigious Library of Congress Gershwin Prize for Popular Song in 2023. The musician lives in Santa Barbara, California. Mitchell is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and expressed frustration that she couldn't vote in U.S. elections because she was Canadian. CHRIS ROBINSON, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN FACE BACKLASH AS 'AMERICANS HAVE HAD ENOUGH' OF BEING LECTURED: EXPERT During a performance at the Hollywood Bowl in LA in October 2024, Mitchell slammed Trump while performing her 1985 song "Dog Eat Dog," according to Billboard. After singing a lyric about wealthy financiers, she added, "Like Donald Trump!" Following her performance of the song, Mitchell responded to an audience member who shouted an anti-Trump remark. "'F--- Donald Trump.' I love that song," she said, apparently referencing rapper YG's 2016 protest song "FDT (F--- Donald Trump)" featuring the late rapper and activist Nipsey Hussle. She then encouraged Americans to participate in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, in which Trump ran against Democratic nominee former Vice President Kamala Harris. "Everybody get out and vote. This is an important one. I wish I could vote . I'm Canadian. I'm one of those lousy immigrants," Mitchell said. Months before becoming an American citizen, Mitchell criticized the political climate in the U.S. while accepting a lifetime achievement award at Canada's Juno Awards in March. At the ceremony, Mitchell praised Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, saying, "I'm so glad to be back in Canada. This man is a blessing. You guys are so fortunate." title: Rogan warns Trump's voters feel betrayed by Iran war with 'no easy way out'
description: Joe Rogan told Michael Douglas the Iran war has infuriated President Donald Trump's voters who believed they were electing a president to prevent new conflicts.
content: Podcaster Joe Rogan discussed the war in Iran with actor Michael Douglas Wednesday, arguing the conflict has angered supporters of President Donald Trump, who voted for him in part because of his promises to avoid new wars. "I do not like this Iran war in any way, shape or form," Rogan said. "It doesn't make any sense for us. It seems like it's getting really out of hand. They were trying to get every single president, including Trump in his first term, to do this," Rogan said on his podcast. Douglas, who is both Jewish and a pro-Israel Democrat, agreed that the conflict was a mistake. ROGAN SAYS TRUMP ‘F---ED IT UP,’ MAY HAVE HANDED COUNTRY BACK TO THE DEMS IN 2028 WITH UNPOPULAR IRAN WAR "Now we've done it, and it's very clear it's a giant quagmire. It's very clear there's no easy way out. Not good," Rogan said. "And there's still a lot of people that insist that it had to happen, that Iran was the greatest funder of state terrorism in the world and that what they were doing was, you know, funding and arming these forces and having them do these — to commit these terrorist attacks. And I'm sure a lot of that's true." "I concur," Douglas said, noting his concern about the expansion of the conflict after an attack on an airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which he compared to attacks on major U.S. airports. "I'm surprised with all of our Western intelligence and Israelis’ intelligence that we have not had a better handle on the situation." Rogan responded to criticism that the Trump administration had been persuaded the conflict would be an easy victory, saying, "Well, look, obviously I'm not an expert on international relations, but I don't think the picture that they painted of how this was going to go down was even remotely accurate." "Yeah," Douglas agreed. After Rogan recalled Iran’s crackdowns on protesters and mass arrests, Douglas said there have been "tens of thousands" of arrests and appeared to suggest the war was instigated by Israel. "I think it was instigated by Israel by the fact that they had information that these key Iranian leaders would all be together and were persuaded that we take them all out. We can turn it over and, yeah, didn't turn out that way," the actor said. "I don't know how they convinced Trump to do it," Rogan said. "I do know that in any international conflict, I'm sure even during Vietnam, even after people kind of knew the Gulf of Tonkin was horses---, there was, I'm sure there's people even today that defend the Vietnam War," Rogan said, referring to U.S. claims of an attack on the USS Maddox in the waters off Vietnam on Aug. 4, 1964, that escalated the conflict. "You're going to get people that support this war," he continued. "But I think the majority of the United States felt like one of the things that we were voting for when we voted for Trump is, ‘No more wars.’ Stop this s---. Like, it's crazy. "You know, when I remember one of his speeches or one of his interviews, someone was asking him about Ukraine. ‘Do you want Ukraine to win? Do you want Russia to win?’ And he said, ‘I just want people to stop dying.’ And most people who voted for him based on that feel very upset that there's a new war going on." FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS OPPOSE THE IRAN WAR, SEE PROLONGED COMMITMENT "Yeah, yeah," Douglas agreed. Rogan also acknowledged that experts have warned about Iran's increasing missile production and the dangers of the country acquiring a nuclear weapon. Trita Parsi, the co-founder and executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, spoke to Fox News Digital about Rogan’s comments. "I fully agree that Trump's decision to start a war with Iran has deeply frustrated the anti-war component of his 2024 coalition and that it will be extremely difficult to get them back," he said. "The gap between what he so explicitly promised — no more wars — and what he has delivered — yet another war of choice in the Middle East that does not serve U.S. interests — could not be any wider." Like Rogan and Douglas, Parsi agreed that "the Israeli presentation of Iran could not have been further from the truth, as Iran's military capabilities and the theocracy's resilience were far more formidable than the Israelis had asserted." "Moreover, the GOP's ability to bring anti-war constituents to its side has been severely damaged. Many of them left the Democratic Party because of the wars in Ukraine and Gaza; now many of them will return to the Democratic Party due to the war in Iran. title: John Stamos says Beach Boys legend Mike Love is facing 'serious health challenges'
description: John Stamos revealed Mike Love is facing serious health challenges, but the Beach Boys legend insisted on performing at the Ryman over the weekend.
content: John Stamos performed with the Beach Boys on Sunday at the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville. Before the show, the actor was overcome with emotion talking about Beach Boys legend Mike Love, who is facing "serious health challenges." Stamos, 63, shared a carousel of images on social media with his "musical hero and mentor" before admitting he was "struggling" to put his feelings into words. ROD STEWART CONFIRMS FINAL TOUR AFTER HEART PROCEDURE AND HEALTH SCARES "My beloved friend, father figure, musical hero and mentor, Mike Love, is facing serious health challenges," he wrote. "We hope he’ll be doing what he loves for years to come, but we don’t know what the future holds. We have tonight." At Tuesday's Hot Cuisine fundraiser for the Scleroderma Research Foundation (SRF), Stamos told Fox News Digital it was his mission to get Love to the Ryman Auditorium for a performance of a lifetime. "Our goal was to get him up at the Ryman this weekend. He wanted it," Stamos said. "I've been spending a lot of time with him, you know, quiet time. We've been listening to music. … Doo-wop. He loves Doo-Wop. "And I said, ‘You gotta tell me, do you really think you can do these shows this weekend?’ He said, ‘Yes, and I really want to.’ I said, 'We'll make it happen.' "Everybody told him not to — doctors, his family — but it was something he wanted to do. He's made all my dreams come true and all my wishes. So, I had to fulfill his wish, and we made sure that he got there and did a good job." SRF presented John Stamos with the Bob Saget Legacy Award, recognizing his steadfast support for scleroderma research and his commitment to following in Bob’s footsteps by shining a spotlight on scleroderma and raising funds toward a cure. Love's representatives did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. It's unclear what health struggles Love faces. Stamos and Love's son, Brian Love, delivered speeches prior to the show. "One thing about him is he's stubborn, and he's steadfast, and he did not want to miss the Ryman. I mean, for good reason," Brian said, via Variety. "Look at this place. So, we are happy. We're going to be positive. We're gonna sing along. But I still remember something he told me when I was a child, and it stuck with me. I said, ‘Dad, why do you do so many shows?’ I mean, we are talking about a guy who's done over 100 concerts a year well up into his 80s." "That's just incredible, right? So, he told me, ‘Well, if you don’t do as many concerts, you don't see as many towns, and then that means less people get to hear the amazing Beach Boys personally.' So, he's always cared for the small towns, the fairs. … This is obviously a much more well-known, beautiful venue. But he cares about the listener, and I think it's such an honor to be part of that. And we've gotta live in the moment." Stamos said, "All we have is tonight really, and I think it's going to be very, very special. Mike, he insisted on being here. … He's done over 7,000 live shows. And tonight'll be 7,422, I think exactly. I think that's where we're at. He's counting. … We love you, and have the greatest night ever, and God bless you all." After the curtains opened, Love was already seated on stage, the outlet reported. He sang in his seat along with his bandmates but did not do his lead vocals. During the performance, the Beach Boys legend addressed concerns about his health, saying, "Obviously, I’ve been going through some health issues for quite a while. But I didn’t want to miss being at the Ryman with y’all." Variety reported that Love was helped up by Brian and Stamos at the end of the show as the song "We Are The Champions" by Queen played. JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK In his social media post, Stamos acknowledged that Love "is a fighter," and despite "doctors, family and friends urging him to focus on his health, he insists on being on stage." "He says he needs his band, the audience, his friends and drummer surrounding him to lift him up," Stamos wrote. "I’ve played with Mike for 41 years. I never imagined how deeply it would affect me to see someone larger than life face something so human and fragile." The Beach Boys have been touring in support of the 60th anniversary of their groundbreaking 11th studio album, "Pet Sounds." Stamos noted that "the Mike Love we see tonight may not be exactly the Mike we’ve always known. But he’s still every bit the Mike we love." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? He’s shared experiences with my family, and now my son." The "Full House" star noted that Love didn't only give him a spot in the band. He "gave me a place in his life." Stamos wanted to "be completely present" performing with Love at the Ryman over the weekend and "hear every harmony, familiar joke and cheer. title: Major airline abandons 3 key cities as passengers face shrinking flight choices
description: After all three routes failed to meet performance expectations, American Airlines has dropped nonstop flights to Santa Maria, Tijuana and Doha this year.
content: American Airlines has dropped flights to three destinations across the U.S., Mexico and the Middle East this year, leaving some travelers with fewer flight options. The airline has discontinued service to Santa Maria, California; Tijuana, Mexico; and Doha, Qatar, according to aviation outlet Simple Flying, which cited data from aviation analytics company Cirium. The cuts have left Santa Maria without service from a major U.S. legacy carrier, while Tijuana lost its only nonstop route operated by a U.S. airline. FURIOUS CROWDS PROTEST SKY-HIGH HOUSING COSTS AND MASS TOURISM IN MAJOR CITY By cutting its routes from Phoenix to Santa Maria and Tijuana, American Airlines has exited both destinations. At Santa Maria, Allegiant Air remains the only commercial airline serving the airport, with flights to Las Vegas, according to Simple Flying. Meanwhile, Qatar Airways has taken over the Philadelphia-to-Doha route, restoring nonstop service between the two cities after American's departure. Regarding the cancellation of service to Santa Maria, American Airlines said the decision was based on performance. American Airlines operated service to Santa Maria, California, under its American Eagle brand through a partnership with SkyWest Airlines, a spokesperson from the company told local outlet KEYT earlier this year. INNOCENT MISTAKE ON LONG FLIGHT COULD HAVE DEVASTATING CONSEQUENCES FOR TRAVELERS "Unfortunately, flights to SMX did not meet performance expectations, and SkyWest informed American it will discontinue service as of May 7," the official said. In June, American Airlines permanently cut its Philadelphia-to-Doha route after previously suspending flights due to regional hostilities, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer. The route failed to meet performance expectations. "As part of an optimization of our network and fleet, American has made the difficult decision to discontinue service to Doha, Qatar (DOH)," American Airlines spokesperson Bri Harper said in a statement to the outlet. In August, American Airlines discontinued service to Tijuana, Mexico, after the route failed to meet performance expectations. Elsewhere, the filing alleges that Kress knew she was a Republican who had voted for Trump and used those remarks to damage her relationship with players, excluded her from meetings and reduced coaching duties. The relationship at the center of the new complaint began well before the controversy. Batie-Smoose says she worked with Kress at Florida State in 2006 and again at Fairfield University from 2019 through 2022. When Kress moved to San Jose State, she accepted the associate head coaching position and relocated her family from Connecticut to California in January 2023. Batie-Smoose has previously alleged she learned that Fleming was transgender only after arriving in 2023. Over the next two seasons, Batie-Smoose says, disagreements about Fleming’s participation became entangled with her relationship with Kress, her responsibilities on the court and her standing inside the athletic department. One alleged confrontation described in the complaint began with a canceled recruiting visit. In approximately August 2023, a hurricane disrupted a recruit’s flight. Batie-Smoose says she returned from the airport to the gym to update Kress, who ignored her greeting twice. After she commented on his behavior, she alleges, he followed her into her office and closed the door. The complaint says he "cornered, yelled at, and berated her" and told her he could get her fired. Batie-Smoose describes feeling physically unsafe during the encounter. She says she reported the incident to athletics human resources and an administrator overseeing the program, but "in response, Plaintiff was told that Kress was her boss and that she needed to listen to him. Kress received no disciplinary action for his behavior towards Plaintiff." The filing also describes alleged confrontations involving players. OutKick is not disclosing the names of the players. The complaint alleges Kress berated one athlete "so harshly for not passing her running test that she experienced panic attacks. Plaintiff reported this mistreatment to Alexander. Upon information and belief, Kress was not disciplined." It described another alleged incident in which a player was "excoriated by Kress in front of the team for being a few minutes late to the locker room after a losing match. The ferocity of his interaction resulted in both Plaintiff and [the player] informing Alexander about the incident. Upon information and belief, Kress was not disciplined." The new complaint also separately cites an older accusation against Kress. Fox News Digital reported in July that a former Fairfield player had accused Kress of a 1998 hotel-room assault. Batie-Smoose’s filing alleges that the former player notified SJSU in October 2024 and that an official acknowledged her stated safety concern. It argues that the university’s handling of that report supports her claim of disparate treatment. "Plaintiff is further informed and believes, based on public reporting, that Defendant took no further action following this correspondence, and that Kress continued to coach and travel with the SJSU women’s volleyball team without interruption or restriction. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant’s handling of this report is consistent with, and corroborates, the pattern of disparate treatment against Plaintiff alleged throughout this Complaint," the lawsuit states. On Oct. 29, 2024, Batie-Smoose submitted a Title IX complaint alleging unequal treatment and failures to address concerns inside the program regarding the transgender athlete and the female players on that year's team. Days later, the university placed her on paid administrative leave. According to her new lawsuit, her punishment arrived on Nov. 2, about 90 minutes before a home match: a university administrator blocked her entry to the gym, required her to surrender her identification and keys, and instructed her to leave. She alleges she could not retrieve belongings from her office. The filing includes an attachment of her suspension letter. The letter referenced a complaint against Batie-Smoose dated Oct. 24 — five days before her own Title IX submission. The allegations included differential treatment based on a protected status, disclosure of confidential student information, drinking with athletes during team travel, unprofessional or insubordinate conduct, inappropriate language and a failure or refusal to coach athletes. The letter prohibited campus access and contact with student-athletes and imposed restrictions on discussing the investigation, with exceptions including legal counsel and a union representative. Batie-Smoose alleges the university used the accusations as a pretext and enforced its rules differently against her than against Kress. She denies improperly disclosing protected education records and says the information she discussed came from public sources or personal observations. Batie-Smoose acknowledged having a drink in an airport lounge while adult players were present, but says she neither purchased their drinks nor encouraged them to drink. She alleges another male coach was drinking there without facing the same consequences. She also denies directing inappropriate language at players or refusing to coach an athlete for whom she had responsibility. On Jan. 31, 2025, athletics director Jeff Konya notified her that her temporary coaching appointment would not be renewed, in a letter issued on behalf of President Cynthia Teniente-Matson. Batie-Smoose's latest lawsuit was filed Oct. 13 in the Northern District of California, the lawsuit names the California State University trustees and 11 university employees, including Kress, after a legal setback in September. On Sept. 4, Judge Noël Wise dismissed Batie-Smoose’s previous amended complaint, which asserted discrimination and retaliation under Title VII and Title IX. Wise found that the allegations did not plausibly connect the suspension or nonrenewal to Batie-Smoose’s sex or protected advocacy. The order emphasized the complaint’s account that the university acted after she disclosed student information to the media despite instructions to keep it confidential. "Plaintiff’s complaint supports that she was disciplined for violating a confidentiality law, not for opposing discrimination on the basis of sex," Wise wrote. The ruling granted leave to amend within 21 days. But now, Batie-Smoose and her attorneys have escalated their fight with a trove of new allegations. SJSU and CSU have declined to provide responses to Batie-Smoose's latest complaint. INSIDE THE FALLOUT OF THE SJSU VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL: ‘THIS IS AN OBVIOUS PROBLEM’ "Due to pending litigation, San Jose State is unable to comment," an SJSU spokesperson told OutKick. A CSU spokesperson responded, writing, "The CSU is not commenting at this time. We were made aware of the lawsuit yesterday and are still reviewing the claims." The new complaint comes as SJSU and CSU find themselves in the midst of a mult-front legal battle with Batie-Smoose, former athletes, and President Donald Trump's administration over the scandal. On Jan. 28, 2026, the Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights issued a findings letter addressing SJSU’s volleyball program. The letter, attached to Batie-Smoose’s new complaint, concluded that the university violated Title IX in its treatment of athletic participation, sex-separated facilities and the handling of discrimination complaints. On employment and scholarships, the letter expressed compliance concerns and identified evidence it considered indicative of unequal treatment, while acknowledging gaps in the records. Some of the most consequential passages concern the university’s handling of its two coaches. OCR reported that personnel investigations involving Batie-Smoose and Kress were opened on Nov. 12, 2024, and questioned why the university suspended her but not him. The letter cited investigator notes stating that Kress "crossed the FERPA line in his interview with ESPN," referring to the federal student privacy law. The letter also described internal records suggesting officials worried that suspending Kress could "spark more media attention" and "unduly disrupt the team." The lawsuit, citing those passages, argues that privacy and team stability were applied selectively. CSU disputes that comparison. Its March complaint against the Education Department argues that the coaches were not similarly situated, that Batie-Smoose disclosed protected information, and that an investigation found insufficient evidence that Kress retaliated against Slusser. The system also challenges the federal investigation’s procedures and conclusions. Meanwhile, CSU’s disagreement with Washington has become a lawsuit of its own. The university system sued the Education Department on March 6, arguing that the government was attempting to punish SJSU retroactively for conduct consistent with the law, federal guidance and NCAA rules in effect during the 2022–24 seasons. CSU declined the federal government’s proposed resolution agreement. It maintains that protecting transgender students and complying with then-governing rules did not amount to unlawful sex discrimination. Federal officials threatened enforcement that could put funding at risk. But a March 31 court order established protections against funding disruption based on the challenged findings. The legal landscape has also changed since the 2024 season. On Feb. 6, 2025, the NCAA changed its policy to restrict competition on women’s teams to athletes assigned female at birth, following Trump’s executive order the previous day. The policy permits athletes assigned male at birth to practice with women’s teams under specified conditions. On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the challenged restrictions in West Virginia and Idaho, ruling that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause permit schools to reserve female teams based on biological sex. The court expressly left unresolved a separate question: whether schools may allow transgender women and girls to participate on female teams. That limitation matters in the SJSU dispute, where permission to exclude and a legal obligation to exclude are different issues. In March, a Colorado federal judge dismissed the Mountain West defendants from the lawsuit brought by Slusser, Batie-Smoose and other volleyball players. The court found that the conference was not subject to Title IX and was not a state actor for the constitutional claims. It also dismissed several claims against university officials, while deferring a ruling on Title IX damages claims against the CSU trustees pending the Supreme Court’s decision. Supplemental briefing continued after that decision. For Batie-Smoose, the latest suit seeks both compensation and restoration of her professional standing. She requests reinstatement to her former job or a comparable position, back pay and other compensatory relief, punitive damages against individually liable defendants, legal fees and a jury trial. She also asks for removal or correction of adverse personnel records, including the suspension letter, the later evaluation and an October 2025 nondiscrimination-policy finding. The complaint specifies no total damages figure. She has returned to coaching elsewhere. Cisco College announced her appointment as head volleyball coach in April. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But her new filing asks a court to revisit the place she left: the gym entrance where she says her work was interrupted, the personnel file that followed, and the university decisions that she alleges converted a dispute over women’s sports into the loss of her job. CSU has disputed the broader accusations against SJSU. In its own litigation against the Department of Education, the university system says it followed the law and athletic eligibility rules applicable during the seasons at issue, protected student privacy and investigated complaints. It also says an investigation found that Batie-Smoose discriminated against Blaire Fleming because of sex and gender identity. Batie-Smoose contests the university’s findings and denies refusing to coach any athlete.

title: Minneapolis progressives turn on George Floyd-era public safety overhaul, push to dismantle office
description: Minneapolis Council leaders propose eliminating the Office of Community Safety over audit failures and wasteful spending, and Mayor Jacob Frey pushes back.
content: Minneapolis City Council leaders advanced a proposal Tuesday to eliminate the city's Office of Community Safety as part of a sweeping public safety restructuring, citing poor management and financial oversight concerns. Mayor Jacob Frey warned the move could jeopardize critical services. According to The Star Tribune, the office was created by Mayor Frey in 2022 in response to calls for police reform after the death of George Floyd. 3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING City Council President Elliott Payne and Council Member Robin Wonsley, who are spearheading the measure to eliminate the office, cited performance and cost concerns in a statement to FOX 9. "It is good governance to stop investing in things that are not producing meaningful outcomes and are wasting taxpayer dollars," Wonsley said. "The Office of Community Safety has also contributed to increased audit costs due to poor management. It’s our responsibility to cut unnecessary bureaucracy that does not contribute to public safety." The proposal marks a significant reversal for a city that reorganized public safety operations after Floyd's death. Frey, who established the office in 2022, criticized council members for seeking to dismantle a structure some had previously championed. In a statement to Fox News Digital, the mayor warned that the proposed elimination could threaten existing public safety programs. "This office — one that these council members advocated for — manages services like mental health response, violence prevention and police reform. If council members want these services in jeopardy, that’s on them. This wholesale elimination without a plan, combined with other proposed cuts to MPD, is not a serious proposal when it comes to public safety in our city," Frey said. According to the City of Minneapolis, the Office of Community Safety oversees five departments: police, fire, 911, emergency management and neighborhood safety. The office was designed to coordinate public safety services, improve communication between departments and establish a unified chain of command and accountability. GOP ACCUSES WALZ ALLIES OF BURYING $52M MEDICAID FRAUD REPORT BEFORE ELECTION The proposal comes amid mounting scrutiny of the city's violence prevention spending. A recent Minneapolis audit identified serious deficiencies in the Neighborhood Safety Department's oversight of community-based violence prevention contracts, including inadequate documentation and financial controls that increased the risk of fraud and misuse of taxpayer money. According to the investigation, the city failed to properly oversee millions of dollars awarded to violence prevention organizations. The audit examined a system that has directed more than $36 million to five major violence prevention programs since 2023. WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES Payne defended the proposed restructuring as a way to preserve services while reducing administrative expenses. "These proposed changes to the government structure ensure that progress on issues such as public safety and racial disparities is not impacted by unnecessary costs and bureaucratic bottlenecks," Payne told FOX 9. "Now more than ever, our city government must be responsive to the needs of residents, and its structure should reflect that." The city's published 2026 public safety budget allocated more than $16 million to the Office of Community Safety, nearly $10 million to Neighborhood Safety and more than $225 million to the Minneapolis Police Department. It remains unclear how much money eliminating the office would actually save. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Wonsley defended the proposal in comments to Fox News Digital, explaining that key non-police programs that continue to show success, such as the Behavioral Crisis Response team, predated the Office of Community Safety and would continue to operate without it. "The Office of Community Safety became administrative bloat that was a barrier to creating and expanding alternative responses rather than leading the development of a comprehensive public safety system," Wonsley said. She argued the $2 million office had become a "bureaucratic barrier" plagued by mismanagement by Mayor Frey and said taxpayers have paid the price. "The city can advance a comprehensive safety system and support police reform much more efficiently without unnecessary bureaucratic layers that have proven to be ineffective," Wonsley added. "Residents should not anticipate negative impacts because OCS was never able to effectively manage or oversee programs and services. The proposal does not eliminate any violence prevention or public safety programs that produce results. It simply removes administrative bloat."

title: Tomi Lahren suggests Tony Romo to listen to the advice he gave her during 2016 Trevor Noah backlash
description: Tomi Lahren revealed Tony Romo once gave her advice about handling online hate, words the former Dallas Cowboys signal caller now needs himself.
content: Former NFL quarterback Tony Romo's life has been a bit of a roller coaster these days. The four-time Pro Bowl selection recently parted ways with CBS, citing the need to take a mental health break. This came just a few short months after he was arrested on charges of OWI in Wisconsin back in July, and happened the same day he was booted from the Korn Ferry qualifier for signing an incorrect scorecard. It's probably safe to say that 2026 has not been Romo's year, but if anyone knows how to handle rough times amid public scrutiny, it's the former Dallas Cowboys signal-caller. JIM NANTZ SPEAKS OUT ON 'GREAT FRIEND' TONY ROMO'S OWI ARREST, SAYS HE WILL 'ALWAYS' BE THERE FOR HIM And OutKick's very own Tomi Lahren has proof. During an episode of "Tomi Lahren is Fearless," Lahren explained to her guest, Barstool's Kevin "KFC" Clancy, that Romo once offered up some sage advice about dealing with online hate. "It was actually Tony Romo at the time who told me, 'you think the whole world is talking about it, but really, nobody is,'" Lahren recounts. This came on the heels of Lahren receiving some hateful comments for her appearance on "The Daily Show with Trevor Noah" just after Donald Trump won in 2016. "Basically the message was, 'don't be so full of yourself that you think that everybody is talking about you,'" Lahren relayed. "Because most people aren't even on the internet." Clancy concurred and took things even one step further. "I think humans are not meant to be this connected and interact this much," he opined. "We can't handle it." The longtime Barstool employee goes on to explain that for 99.9% of human history, we as humans were only confined to interacting with our small community. COWBOYS OWNER JERRY JONES HAS TONY ROMO'S BACK, BELIEVES HE WILL 'WORK THROUGH' OWI ARREST "The fact that you have access to millions of people's opinions ... I don't think we are even wired to be able to handle that." It's great advice from all parties involved, and Romo would be wise to heed the words he offered up to Lahren nearly a decade ago. He's going through a rough patch, but he will come out on the other side. A guy as resilient as Romo is — undrafted from a small school in Eastern Illinois, coming back from a number of injuries — will be able to rebound just fine. No one knows what the future holds for the former CBS commentator, but as for the noise online in the present, 46-year-old Romo just needs to listen to the 36-year-old version of himself.
