And we just don't want her to miss out on the opportunity to compete in high school athletics," Frampton said.

title: Ethan Hawke blasts Hollywood's 'greedy bastards,' predicts massive rebellion against powerful elites
description: Ethan Hawke predicts massive rebellion in music and live theater against Hollywood's "greedy bastards" who he says control the entertainment industry.
content: Ethan Hawke isn't holding back when it comes to the powerful forces he believes are controlling the entertainment industry. During a new interview with GQ, the Oscar-nominated actor took aim at wealthy power players, blasting "greedy bastards" who think they control every aspect of Hollywood and predicting a major rebellion against the industry. "I believe in rebellion. And I think people are going to wake up and punch back and there’s going to be massive movements in music and massive movements in live theater and massive movements of people getting together," Hawke said. FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA "So don’t worry that the money and the greedy bastards that think they control everybody, they always lose in the end," he continued. "And they’re all going in the grave eventually. They think they’re winning, but they’re losing because their lives are worthless." Hawke also expressed frustration with the financial pressures shaping Hollywood, arguing that the projects actors care about most often come with the smallest paychecks. TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS "There's a direct correlation. I find that the more you love a project, the less you get paid," he said. "If you want to beat the algorithm, it's very difficult to do that and be paid." This isn't the first time Hawke has spoken about the pitfalls of Hollywood. ROBERT DOWNEY JR. SLAMS MODERN CELEBRITY CULTURE AS 'ABSOLUTE HORSES---' Last year, the actor called celebrity a "poison" for a young actor's brain. During an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience," Hawke got candid about his start in Hollywood as a young man and reflected on the psychological effect of becoming famous at a young age. "I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's poison. It's poison for your brain," the actor said. "To be a professional actor at a young age, it's dangerous in extremely insidious ways that are very, very hard to perceive when it's happening," Hawke said. Rogan compared the experience of becoming famous as a child to concrete. If concrete is made incorrectly, with the wrong amount of water or cement, that's it, he explained. Rogan added that once it dries there is no way to repair or fix it. DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH "That analogy works for all walks of life. Really. If you have something really traumatic happen in childhood, it's very hard to recover. It's a tremendous amount of work to recover. And I agree with you, like I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's a poison. It's a poison for your brain," Hawke said. During his GQ interview, Hawke expressed the same sentiment. "I wouldn’t be the first person to say that there’s an aspect of celebrity that is like a disease," he said. "And you can handle little bits of it, but too much of it — we can see what happened to Elvis and we can see Michael Jackson. It’s a form of isolation. It’s like being put in a zoo, and zoo animals go nuts. So do human beings." "And it seems like a kind of nice isolation because people are giving you money, and they’re telling you you’re wonderful, but nobody’s being real with you," he continued. "And that makes people insane. And they start scratching, trying to find some real life. And sometimes people do that with drugs, some people do that with acting out or getting in fights or whatever the ways that people do it." Last year, fellow actor Dakota Johnson also ripped into Hollywood, calling the industry an absolute "mess." During her appearance on the show "Hot Ones," Johnson was asked why "Hollywood is risk-averse." "I think it’s hard when creative decisions are made by a committee, and it’s hard when creative decisions are made by people who don’t even really watch movies or know anything about them … that tends to be what’s occurring a lot," Johnson shared with host Sean Evans. Johnson, who has grown up in the business as the daughter of actors Melanie Griffith and Don Johnson, is no stranger to the inner workings of Hollywood. The "Fifty Shades of Grey" actress’ comments come as studios continue to create sequels and remakes, with original storytelling often sidelined. "When something does well … studios want to keep that going so they remake the same things," she claimed. "But humans don’t want that. They want fresh. They want to feel new things, experience new things, see new things." She added, "So I don’t know, I guess it’s all just a bit of a mess right now, isn’t it?" title: ‘Paid for the bullets’: Dem challenger hits senator with stunning ICE accusation during fiery Senate debate
description: Troy Jackson accused Susan Collins of paying for the bullets that killed Johan Sebastián Guerrero, igniting a fierce clash over ICE funding.
content: Fierce disagreement broke out on the debate stage on Tuesday evening as Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, defended her record against accusations that she had enabled the death of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Troy Jackson, her Democratic opponent, argued Collins had facilitated the deadly encounter on the three-month anniversary of the incident by funding what he described as a "rogue agency." "Look, Senator Collins paid for the bullets and at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger," Jackson said, referring to the roughly $66 billion in funding for immigration enforcement agencies included in the Secure America Act, a party-line bill that extended provisions for the agency through the end of Trump’s term. TRUMP TAKES ICE SHUTDOWNS OFF THE TABLE WITH SIGNATURE ON KEY $70B BILL "That's the choice on this stage. A senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody who will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price." Notably, not all of the funding described by Jackson was set aside for ICE. The package set aside $26 billion for border security operations under Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and $38.5 for ICE. The package also included $5 billion for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) general funds. Guerrero’s shooting has become a flash point in Trump’s immigration enforcement push, especially in the Maine Senate race where Democrats have used his death to illustrate broader critiques of Collins: that her occasional willingness to break with the majority of the GOP hasn’t meaningfully curbed the administration’s policies. But at the debate on Tuesday evening, the third between Collins and Jackson, Collins pushed back on the narrative, arguing that her power as a Republican senator has been key to implementing a handful of safeguards on an agency that she described as critical to American safety. "After the Biddeford shooting, I called the Secretary of Homeland Security, [and] met with the acting director and suggested that they prioritize Maine for receipt of these body-worn cameras. And they did. And every ICE agent in the state of Maine and across the country now has the body-worn cameras," Collins said at the debate on Tuesday. "I increased by 17% the budget for the independent Office of Inspector General," Collins added. Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian national, was fatally shot in Biddeford on July 13 when he tried to flee ICE officers in a vehicle during an operation targeting an illegal immigrant with a final order of removal, according to the Department of Homeland Security. Guerrero was not the target of the operation. 'SQUAD' MEMBER CALLS DHS 'GREATEST THREAT TO OUR SAFETY' AFTER ICE-INVOLVED SHOOTING "The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and, fearing for public safety, an officer discharged his weapon. The driver of the vehicle was struck and emergency services were immediately contacted. He passed away from his injuries," DHS said in a statement at the time. In Jackson’s estimation, the moment is emblematic of what he described as an agency out of control. "That is why I believe that this agency is just a rogue agency that's doing Donald Trump's bidding," Jackson said. "I do believe it's important to get rid of it and take that money and prioritize it into existing law enforcement that actually people believe in." Like many progressives, Jackson has argued that the agency is beyond the scope of reform, sharing the view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group, which backed Jackson in his gubernatorial bid earlier this year before he became a candidate for Senate, calls the agency "a violent and illegitimate agency." Jackson has shared almost that exact framing, similarly stating that ICE "is not legitimate law enforcement," in a debate from last Thursday. Collins disagrees. On Tuesday, she argued that the agency, although flawed, serves an important role in American law enforcement, pointing out that its role overlaps with many other forms of law enforcement. "It investigates child trafficking, human trafficking and general child exploitation: drug smuggling, international cartels, financial scams. It recently helped shut down a child pornography ring in the state of Maine. I don't think any of us wants to go back to the days of completely open, uncontrolled borders. That is dangerous for us," Collins argued. But let us not forget the important work that ICE does, which is why it should be reformed and not abolished, as Troy has said." Having secured their parties’ respective nominations, Collins and Jackson will face off in the state’s Nov. 3 general election. Elaine Mallon contributed to this report.

title: Washington HS girls blast male athlete participating in track meet: 'Don't think that that's right or fair'
description: Charlie Garret and Sierra Retzlaff appeared on Fox News' "Fox & Friends" to discuss why they are protesting a male athlete competing in women's cross country events.

WASHINGTON GIRLS WALK OFF CROSS COUNTRY MEET IN PROTEST OF MALE ATHLETE, PARENTS REVEAL HOW IT CAME TO THIS Garret and Retzlaff both attend Skyview High, while the male runner attends Camas. During Tuesday's race, some members of the male runner's team joined the protest, refusing to compete. On Nov. 3, Washington voters will vote on Initiative 638, which would prohibit students defined as biologically male from competing in certain female-only interscholastic athletic competitions. The initiative would require students to provide verification of biological sex from a healthcare provider to enter those competitions. title: Rory McIlroy calls LIV Golf 'half a good idea' before saying he'd vote yes on having players return to Tour

title: James Talarico torches Biden border policies in stunning attack ad as progressive tries to flip Texas blue

content: Texas Democrat candidate for U.S. Senate James Talarico appears to be further moderating his previous left-wing stances as he slammed former President Joe Biden for ‘failing us’ on border security in a new campaign advertisement released Monday. But Talarico’s campaign couldn’t give Fox News Digital an example of him ever publicly criticizing Biden during his presidency. And the Texas Democrat explicitly made a call to put Texas’ entire $800 million two-year border security budget toward public education in a 2019 interview with The Austin Chronicle. JAMES TALARICO ADMITS DEMOCRATS TOOK ‘BORDER FOR GRANTED’ UNDER BIDEN "We're also sending about $800 million per biennium to the border with Mexico for ‘increased border security,’" Talarico said in the more than seven-year-old interview. The two-year deal allocating $400 million per year toward border security in the state of Texas was the state’s entire budget toward warding off illegal immigration at the time Talarico made the call to replace that funding. "I'd rather take that money and put it back into public education and help increase the basic allotment, for instance," he said in the interview. Talarico has ramped up his efforts to come off more moderate amid claims that he is too progressive to win a Senate seat in notoriously red Texas. His move to a more moderate stance on immigration only started during his Senate bid in the state with the highest rates of illegal immigration. "Putting a bunch of boats, planes and border patrol agents on the physical border is expensive and also does not solve the problem," he said in the interview. His 2019 criticism of border enforcement comes to the surface as border crossings under the Trump administration fell to a new record low level in 55 years in 2025, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The decline in illegal immigration followed a series of immigration enforcement measures implemented by the administration. "Everyone will admit it's just political grandstanding," Talarico said in the interview. "Certain lawmakers want to appease extreme parts of their base. And they do it by pumping money we don't have down to the border." EXCLUSIVE: TALARICO CAUGHT ON TAPE GIGGLING ABOUT HIS CHURCH HOUSING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS SET FOR DEPORTATION In his run for Senate, Talarico has now labeled himself a "border security" Democrat, despite an extensive history of pushing back on border security reform and authorities. A former member of the Texas legislature and a former school teacher, Talarico has been in the spotlight repeatedly for many of his far-left controversies, particularly comments regarding immigration enforcement. He has called to dismantle Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), claiming it was "time to tear down this secret police force." Talarico also referred to illegal aliens as his "constituents." He labeled Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s border security policies as "atrocities" and accused him of "hunting" illegal immigrants. The Senate candidate also said he "taught a lot of undocumented students," and that those illegal aliens were more patriotic than Americans. title: Pentagon appoints its own public affairs executive as acting Stars and Stripes publisher
description: Christian Devine, the Pentagon's public affairs executive director, takes over as acting publisher of Stars and Stripes newspaper as it aims to modernize.
content: The Pentagon has found a new publisher for Stars and Stripes, at least on an interim basis, appointing Christian Devine, executive director of the Pentagon's public affairs office, to lead the military newspaper. Stars and Stripes, which has published a newspaper continuously since World War II, describes itself as a source of "independent news and information to the U.S. military community, including active-duty servicemembers, DoD civilians, veterans, contractors, and their families" that is "governed by the principles of the First Amendment." "The Pentagon is proud to appoint Chris Devine to serve as acting publisher of Stars and Stripes," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told Fox News Digital. PENTAGON VOWS TO REFORM MILITARY NEWSPAPER STARS AND STRIPES, REMOVE 'WOKE DISTRACTIONS' "As a former Marine Corps colonel and a seasoned public affairs leader, Chris brings unmatched expertise, strategic vision and a commitment to ensuring Stars and Stripes maintains editorial independence while delivering exclusive, mission-focused reporting that directly serves America’s war fighters and their families," Parnell continued. "In this interim role, he will provide decisive leadership to modernize Stars and Stripes and to strengthen its mission." Devine will continue his role as executive director and principal advisor in the Pentagon’s public affairs office until a permanent Stars and Stripes publisher is found. He is expected to split time between the two gigs. "It’s a dynamic media organization with a prestigious history and purpose, and I hope I can lend a strong arm during the interim to the men and women who continue to contribute to its notable legacy," Devine said in a statement. The Pentagon, which funds roughly half of Stars and Stripes' annual budget, according to the newspaper's website, began 2026 by announcing plans to overhaul the long-running military publication. "The Department of War is returning Stars & Stripes to its original mission: reporting for our warfighters. We are bringing Stars & Stripes into the 21st century. We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members," Parnell posted on X in January. FIRED STARS AND STRIPES STAFFERS SUE PENTAGON, ALLEGE RETALIATION AND FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATION "Stars & Stripes will be custom tailored to our warfighters. It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability, and ALL THINGS MILITARY. No more repurposed DC gossip columns; no more Associated Press reprints," Parnell continued. "Stars & Stripes has a proud legacy of reporting news that’s important to our service members. The Department of War is committed to ensuring the outlet continues to reflect that proud legacy." As part of the shake-up, Stars and Stripes' longtime publisher Max Lederer, its editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte were fired in August. At the time, a source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital that the firings were a result of Slavin and Korte's unauthorized participation in a "CBS Sunday Morning" segment about the Pentagon's efforts to overhaul the paper and Lederer's refusal to fire them at the direction of Pentagon leadership. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE They have since filed a lawsuit against the Pentagon over their terminations, alleging they are facing "imminent retaliation and termination in violation of their First Amendment and statutory rights." In September, U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden denied a temporary restraining order filed by Stars and Stripes to reverse their firings, claiming they "ultimately fail to carry their significant burden to show that they are clearly entitled to a preliminary injunction." title: Wisconsin plane crash kills 5 adults, child as authorities probe final communications with air traffic control
description: A Piper PA-46 crashed in a wooded area in Sauk County, Wisconsin Tuesday night, killing all six people aboard including a child. The FAA is investigating.
content: A small plane carrying five adults and a child was in contact with air traffic control before crashing into a wooded area in Wisconsin Tuesday night, killing everyone aboard and leaving investigators searching for answers about the aircraft's final moments. The Piper PA-46 was on a return flight from Kenosha to Menomonie when it went down in the Town of Dellona in Sauk County, according to the Sauk County Sheriff's Office. Authorities received multiple reports of a downed aircraft around 9:31 p.m. Tuesday and dispatched emergency crews to the area of Park Lane, where first responders discovered the wreckage in a densely wooded area west of Herwig Road. SMALL PLANE CRASHES INTO SHALLOW WATER NEAR REMOTE ALASKA TOWN, KILLING ALL 4 PEOPLE ABOARD Rescue crews began searching for survivors while investigators worked to identify the aircraft and determine how many people were aboard. All six occupants were ultimately found dead at the scene, authorities said. Their identities have not been released. Investigators are now working to determine what communications took place between the aircraft and a nearby air traffic control tower before the crash, as well as whether weather conditions in the area may have played a role. "We know that they had contact with the tower prior to the crash and investigators are looking into that today to find out what that communication was," Sauk County Sheriff Chip Meister told FOX6 Milwaukee. FATHER, SON KILLED IN PLANE CRASH ON WAY HOME FROM BASEBALL GAME Meister said it remained unclear who owned the aircraft but confirmed that it was not a commercial plane. No structures were damaged, and no injuries were reported on the ground, according to the sheriff's office. The crash site remained secured Wednesday as investigators worked to piece together the circumstances surrounding the deadly flight. title: Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US amid looming Supreme Court battle

content: Jamaica began receiving third-country deportations from the U.S. this week, with the first flight of migrants arriving on Tuesday. President Donald Trump's administration has used the third-country policy to deport migrants who claim that their home countries are too dangerous to return to. Tuesday's flight saw 22 migrants land at Kingston’s Norman Manley International Airport in Jamaica. VENEZUELANS, CUBANS, COLOMBIANS ARRIVE IN AFRICAN NATION UNDER TRUMP DEPORTATION DEAL Jamaican authorities signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the U.S. in June to allow transfers to begin. The agreement caps the number of migrants arriving to 25 "per fortnight." LIBERIA AGREES TO ACCEPT 1,200 THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTEES FROM US WITHIN A YEAR "The government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of Third Country Nationals to their country of origin or other receiving countries, with the support of the IOM (International Organization for Migration)," the statement read. "The arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica," it continued. "No third-country national with criminal antecedents will be permitted to transit through Jamaica." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA Third-country deportations have faced heavy attacks from critics of the Trump administration, and the Supreme Court is set to consider the legality of the policy in December. The Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration in September to continue its deportations while the question is being litigated. title: Foul-mouthed anti-war protesters repeatedly derail Hegseth's remarks at Army event in DC
description: Protesters branded Pete Hegseth a "war criminal" and "coward" at his AUSA panel focused on Project Agincourt and autonomous weapons systems.
content: Protesters repeatedly interrupted War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s headline appearance at the Army’s biggest annual conference on Wednesday, calling him a "war criminal" and a "coward" in protest of the Iran war. At least five times in the first half hour of a panel, foul-mouthed anti-war protesters shouted at Hegseth, calling him a "f---ing Nazi" among other insults. Hegseth responded with chuckles and sarcastic comments, at first — but his reactions became increasingly short and irritated as he slammed the "semi-coordinated" attack as one-by-one protesters emerged among the crowd in Washington, D.C. PETE HEGSETH HEADS TO CAPITOL HILL TO DEFEND TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS 60-DAY CONGRESSIONAL DEADLINE LOOMS "You’re not a warrior you’re a coward!" one demonstrator shouted at Hegseth. "Children in Gaza are starving! He is a war criminal!" "She thinks highly of me," the Pentagon chief quipped after one outburst, which led to brief applause from the crowd. The protesters were spread among the room and waited a few minutes between outbursts to interrupt the panel with their anti-war messages. As Hegseth saw a pattern emerging among the outbreaks, he acknowledged: "Appears we have a bit of a tactic." "The protesters are spouting off slogans, Iran really will never have a nuclear weapon," he later added. The demonstrators were forcibly removed by security for the event — with at least one woman needing to be carried out of the room by multiple officers while she continued to scream her protest. "The First Amendment right to protest is fundamental. However, everyone who registers to attend the Annual Meeting and enters the convention center does so after agreeing to abide by a code of conduct, so the protestors’ outbursts were certainly not appropriate during today’s forum," the Association of the U.S. Army said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The acting Army Secretary organized, and we were honored to host, a historic forum to discuss a critical issue that directly affects national security. We’re grateful for the swift action of security and the Metropolitan Police Department to ensure this important discussion could continue." The panel with Hegseth included acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink and assistant Secretary for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict Derrick Anderson. As the disruptions continued, the speakers stopped pausing amid the din of shouting and tried to talk over the protesters. It’s unclear how the protesters received credentials to attend the event known as AUSA, which largely brings together Army brass and the defense contractors that service them. The event set an attendance record of 41,000 people this year. EMERGING TECH HAS NEW ARMY LEADERS WARNING TROOPS CAN'T ‘AI’ THEIR WAY TO VICTORY ON THE BATTLEFIELD The panel focused on Project Agincourt, the Pentagon’s initiative to accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous weapons and military systems. title: African nations on ‘knife’s edge’ as US embassy warns Americans of long-range attacks
description: With regional tensions mounting, the Horn of Africa risks war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Following attacks in Addis Ababa, the U.S. Embassy warned citizens of long-range threats.
content: The entire Horn of Africa region is said to be on a knife’s edge. As explosions reportedly claimed to be caused by drones hit Ethiopia's capital city in early October, the U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa warned U.S. citizens of the danger of "long-range attacks." Analysts say there’s a high probability that Ethiopia and Eritrea are about to erupt in a new war, with worrying regional backing for both sides. Former CIA analyst and National Security Council Africa Director Cameron Hudson says the Trump administration needs to become more involved. He told Fox News Digital, "Regional leaders will say privately that they don’t want a regional war. But with so many armed actors and so much meddling going on in each other’s countries, a regional conflagration becomes increasingly likely. It is this kind of miscalculation that the Trump administration needs to be working now to guard against." EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP ENVOY BLASTS SOUTH AFRICA OVER HATEFUL ‘KILL' CHANT, SAYS COUNTRY IS DRIFTING TOWARD US FOES The U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa took to its website to caution Americans in Ethiopia that it "is aware of reports of possible long-range attacks directed at Ethiopian military installations on several instances in October of this year. U.S. citizens should accordingly exercise caution and follow the advice of local authorities." The Embassy also hit out at reported disinformation, "some social media accounts contain false and misleading reports about the security situation in Ethiopia. U.S. citizens are urged to verify information using multiple sources or reliable information." Indeed, although explosions in and around Addis Ababa, mainly at military installations, can be confirmed as having taken place, it cannot be established that the frightening spectacle of drones crashing into buildings in a major African city which houses the headquarters of the African Union happened. Requests for comment to the Ethiopian government were not returned. TRUMP GETS MAJOR WIN AGAINST CHINA IN AFRICAN RARE EARTH MINERALS RACE Blen Mamo, executive director of the Ethiopian Horn Review think-tank, told Fox News Digital this is potentially a worrying development. "If identified as an aerial or drone attack, they exceed the capabilities of Ethiopia’s domestic insurgent groups, confirming Ethiopia's allegation of foreign state involvement." The rebel groups opposing Ethiopia’s government have joined together to form the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival. This coalition claimed responsibility for the Addis Ababa attacks, stating they used drones. Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, regional expert of the U.S.-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data research group, is also concerned about a new phase of conflict using drones. Birru told Fox News Digital, "should the Alliance for Survival possess drone capabilities, it could fundamentally alter the dynamics of the conflict, refocusing strategic control on aerial dominance." In early October, Ethiopian troops pushed out rebel groups who had occupied the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle. This operation ended a four-year-long ceasefire between Ethiopia and Tigray, the northernmost province of Ethiopia. Last week, reports claimed Eritrean troops had entered Ethiopia. Although the allegations have not been independently verified, Fox News Digital has seen multiple videos showing what appears to be large convoys of trucks carrying uniformed soldiers passing through the Ethiopian city of Adigrat. Addis Ababa is said to have subsequently launched drone attacks and pushed the Eritreans back over the border. The latest fighting was sparked principally by Ethiopia’s statements that it wants to get access to Red Sea ports. The country became landlocked when Eritrea became independent in 1993. In a speech as he was sworn in for a new five-year term Oct. 5, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said sea access was "of vital importance to Ethiopia’s civilization." He added, "Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea." US VISA CLASH EXPOSES SUDAN’S FORGOTTEN WAR AS FOREIGN POWERS COMPETE FOR STRATEGIC FOOTHOLD Possible regional expansion of any conflict also comes from the creation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Egypt and Sudan are at odds with Addis Ababa, after it built the dam across the Blue Nile, affecting access to water to these countries which are downstream. Egypt this month took up a formal position against Ethiopia, when it created a coalition with Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia. The State Department has been active diplomatically to try and resolve the situation. A spokesperson told Fox News Digital that Undersecretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker met this month with Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh and spoke with Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timotheos. Also, Assistant Secretary for African Affairs Frank Garcia met with Minister Saleh. The spokesperson added, "Both U.S. officials underscored the importance of respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity for all countries in the Horn of Africa." Following these discussions, State Department spokesman Thomas "Tommy" Piggott released a statement, saying, "Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region. The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis. A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries." Piggott added, "We strongly urge Ethiopia and Eritrea to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors, exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation as agreed in their 2018 peace framework. Peace through dialogue is the only path toward sustainable security, economic growth, and prosperity." The Horn Review’s Mamo told Fox News Digital the reality on the ground is "increasingly pointing toward a conflict that may prove impossible to avoid," and warned of Egypt’s motives: "Parallel military and technical cooperation with Asmara (the capital of Eritrea) also adds strategic depth along Ethiopia’s northern frontier, while Egypt’s expanding role in Somalia and Red Sea port initiatives extends its regional influence." "The situation in Ethiopia and in the region is extremely dynamic," analyst Cameron Hudson told Fox News Digital. Hudson added, "The question remains, given the weakness of the internal (rebel) coalition, will external forces attempt to step in and exert greater leverage against Abiy." He continued, "We are seeing Eritrea begin to move forces into Ethiopia, while a coalition of regional states including Somalia, Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea have issued a statement that amounts to a veiled threat against Ethiopia and its regional ambitions to establish a Red Sea naval presence and expand a series of hydroelectric dams on the Nile. The entire Horn of Africa region is on a knife’s edge and it is being made only more complicated by Houthi efforts to shut Red Sea shipping and the war in Iran." "Egypt would be happy to see Ethiopia bogged down in internal conflict and unable to pursue its ambitions on the Nile and in the Red Sea. Similarly, Sudan hopes that internal conflict in Ethiopia distracts Addis from its support of the rapid support forces militia in Sudan’s war." "Local disputes can quickly become regional and international disputes with global consequences very quickly in this corner of the world," Hudson added, "Closure of the Bab el Mandab Strait, owing to unchecked tensions and violence across the Red Sea, will quickly be felt in the U.S."

title: GOP lawmaker urges Johnson to scrutinize new socialist lawmakers' 'access to intelligence'
description: Nicole Malliotakis warns two Democratic Socialists of America members heading to the House of Representatives pose a "national security threat."
content: New York City's lone Republican in the House of Representatives is raising alarms about the far-left Democrats poised to serve alongside her on Capitol Hill next year. "These people are extreme, they're radical, they are dangerous, and they really have no business being in the United States House of Representatives," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "And it scares me that they're going to have access to intelligence." New York City was one of the largest fronts in the nationwide civil war that's gripped the Democratic Party this midterm election cycle. It's where two members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) scored upset primary victories against establishment-backed candidates — in deep-blue seats that mean they are virtually guaranteed to win their general elections in November. DEMOCRATIC CONGRESSMAN WARNS OF 'DANGEROUS' SOCIALIST AGENDA AFTER FAR-LEFT PRIMARY WINS Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chairman Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., in his Upper Manhattan and Bronx-area district, while New York State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez won an open race for the Brooklyn- and Queens-area district represented by retiring Rep. Nydia Velazquez, D-N.Y. Both Chevalier and Valdez have called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and have called Israel's war on Gaza a "genocide." DSA CO-CHAIR MOCKED FOR PROUDLY CONFIRMING SOCIALISTS WANT TO ABOLISH THE SENATE, NATIONAL BORDERS, PRISONS Malliotakis said their support of the DSA platform made both "un-American." "I think they want to undermine the country. I mean, anybody whose campaign is based on no jails, no cops, no borders, is a real detriment to the country," she said. "These are the people that are going to have access to intelligence? I think [Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.] really needs to look at that and see if they're a national security threat." JOHNSON WARNS COMMUNISM IS 'ON OUR OWN SHORES' AFTER FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES WIN NEW YORK PRIMARIES And if Republicans win the House majority in November, she called on Johnson to limit which committees the pair could serve on. "I do have a lot of concern about these members having access to sensitive information and intelligence that if put in the wrong hands, could be a detriment to our national security," Malliotakis said. DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’ The sentiment is just a preview of what is likely to be historic division within the House of Representatives next year, no matter who wins the midterms. The DSA has advocated for scrapping the U.S. Constitution in favor of a new system, as well as the abolition of prisons, the Supreme Court and the police. Malliotakis also pointed out that Chevalier once posted online, "I forgot to get napkins, so I just wiped my hand on the American flag behind me." But next year they are poised to be in the same congressional delegation, and the New York Republican, born to a Greek immigrant father and a Cuban immigrant mother, said she does not know how she could work with them. "They are so extreme, I don't see where we would find common ground," Malliotakis said. "I don't think I could work with somebody who wipes her hands on the American flag because she doesn't have a napkin." title: Stephen King's 'Carrie' gets updated spin with Mike Flanagan's bold take on classic story
description: Mike Flanagan's "Carrie" adapts Stephen King's horror classic with a social-media-age bullying twist and dual timelines that hint at tragedy.
content: Mike Flanagan's new project "Carrie" appears likely to make some waves. Below are his notable series: Flanagan reached a deal in 2022 to jump from Netflix to Amazon Studios ("The Fall of the House of Usher" was his final Netflix product), and "Carrie" is his first show for the company. Now, to be clear, I have never read the book written by Stephen King or seen any of the movies or TV products that were created. I know the 1976 film is considered a classic in the horror genre, and I understand the basic plot premise of a young woman ultimately terrorizing the people around her. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER I went into the premiere of "Carrie" more or less completely blind outside of the stated facts above, and as you all know, I prefer it that way most of the time. The series isn't a linear timeline through the premiere episode. It jumps between Carrie's introduction to being forced into a public school following her father's death and people being interviewed in a later timeline after some kind of horrific tragedy. In the school timeline Carrie is an isolated and shielded child struggling with her father's death and essentially thrown to the wolves at school. She's completely unprepared for the shift of not knowing much about the outside world to be bullied and traumatized by a school shooting drill. There's immediate signs of paranormal capabilities that nobody, Carrie included, have a handle on. In the later timeline, viewers don't see Carrie at all. There are only traumatized survivors, clear indications that a violent event has occurred and confirmed deaths of characters introduced in the premiere. Personally, I like the creative choice from Flanagan. It sets the stage to see Carrie's arc from innocent child to someone who plays a pivotal role (although, seemingly not alone based on what is shown in the premiere) of a live-altering event. One of the most interesting choices from Flanagan is that in the later timeline with the interviews, Carrie isn't painted as a villain by anyone. That would seem to indicate she will continue to be a sympathetic figure throughout season one. It will be fascinating to see that continue to unfold. title: Your phone may reveal doctor, church and pharmacy visits
description: Your phone's location data can expose visits to doctors, pharmacies and places of worship. The FTC took action against data brokers selling this data.
content: Nobody needs to follow you to know where you went this week. The phone in your pocket can already keep a record of your movements. And parts of that information can end up in the hands of other companies. Your pharmacy. Your cardiologist. The church you attend on Sunday morning. The support group you'd rather nobody knew about. None of it necessarily comes from hacking. It can come from ordinary apps you installed yourself and the permissions you gave them. Here's how your movements can get out, who buys location data and the settings that can limit how much gets shared. Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com. WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE Your phone can carry an advertising identifier Smartphones can use advertising identifiers that help advertisers and developers measure ads and activity. On Apple devices, the system advertising identifier is known as the IDFA. Android devices can use Google's advertising ID. Advertising identifiers can help connect activity across apps when apps and advertising systems are permitted to use them. Combined with location data and other signals, those identifiers can help companies build a much more detailed trail of where a device has been. And a trail stops being anonymous fast. A device that sleeps at your address every night and turns up at a dialysis center every Tuesday and Thursday isn't much of a mystery to anyone who can connect those locations with other identifying information. The apps hand it off, and it keeps moving An app asks for your location. Often for a fair reason, like providing a local forecast or showing the nearest pharmacy. What many people don't realize is that apps can include advertising and analytics software from outside companies. Depending on the app, its permissions and its privacy practices, that technology may collect or receive information about your device and location. Location information can also become part of the digital advertising ecosystem, where information about a device can pass among multiple companies. Once location data leaves your phone, controlling where it goes next becomes much harder. Federal regulators have already gone after this This isn't a theory about what could happen. The government spent years fighting one such case in court. On May 4, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission announced a settlement that bars the data broker Kochava and its subsidiary, Collective Data Solutions, from selling, sharing or disclosing sensitive location data without people's affirmative express consent, subject to the terms of the order. The FTC alleged Kochava sold location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices that could track people to health facilities, places of worship and other sensitive locations. Kochava did not admit wrongdoing. Kochava wasn't alone. In December 2024, the FTC took action against two more location data companies, Gravy Analytics and Mobilewalla, over allegations involving the sale of sensitive location data. Then one of them got robbed In January 2025, Gravy Analytics was breached. A hacker posted what they claimed was 17 terabytes of stolen data on a Russian cybercrime forum. Security researchers examining a sample found more than 30 million location points, including phones at the White House, the Kremlin and military bases around the world. The data reportedly came from everyday apps, including games and dating apps. Think about what that means. A company collects movements. Regulators take action over how sensitive location data gets handled. Then criminals allegedly obtain a massive collection of data anyway. What your movements actually tell a stranger Strip out the technical language. A few weeks of location data can potentially reveal: Those last few can turn a privacy problem into a safety concern. A device that regularly leaves a home at the same time and returns two hours later can reveal patterns about when someone may be away. Location information can also make a scam call more convincing. "I'm calling from the billing office at the clinic on Oak Street about your visit last week" is much harder to dismiss when the clinic and timing happen to be correct. And with Medicare Open Enrollment beginning October 15, a caller who seems to know your doctor or pharmacy may sound more convincing than a random scammer. 'But I never share my location' If you've ever tapped "Allow" on a weather app, a store app or a game, you may have shared it. You might have granted that permission years ago and forgotten about it. Even apps without precise location permission may be able to estimate your general area through information such as your internet connection. You can't make yourself invisible, but you can make your movements harder to track. What you can do about it You can't stop your phone from knowing where you are and still use every location-based feature. But you can limit which apps get that information and reduce some of the identifiers used for advertising and tracking. None of this takes technical skill, and you can tackle one part at a time. Start here: limit advertising tracking Advertising identifiers aren't the only way companies can recognize a device, but limiting them can remove one tool used to connect activity for advertising purposes. On iPhone First, control whether apps can request permission to track you across other companies' apps and websites: When this setting is off, apps that request permission to track are treated as though you selected Ask App Not to Track. They cannot access Apple's system advertising identifier, known as the IDFA. Apple also has a separate setting for ads that Apple itself delivers: This second setting limits how Apple personalizes the ads it delivers in services such as the App Store, Apple News and Stocks. It is separate from the app-tracking control above. THE SCAMMER AT YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE MAY ALREADY KNOW WHO YOU ARE On Samsung Galaxy To check your advertising ID controls: Depending on your Galaxy model and software configuration, you may also find Google's advertising controls through Settings > Google > All services > Ads. Deleting the advertising ID prevents apps from accessing that particular Google advertising identifier. It does not prevent every form of advertising, analytics or device identification. On Google Pixel Google says deleting the advertising ID removes that identifier. Apps that try to access it receive a string of zeros instead. Apps can still have their own privacy and advertising settings, so this does not eliminate every form of tracking. Next: tighten location permissions Now look at which apps can see where you are and whether they really need that access. On iPhone You don't have to turn Location Services off completely. Doing so can interfere with useful features. Instead, focus on apps that have more access than they need. On Samsung Galaxy Pay particular attention to apps allowed to access your location all the time. Weather, shopping and similar apps often don't need continuous background access. YOUR HOME IS EMPTY. DO BURGLARS ALREADY KNOW? On Google Pixel A weather app, for example, usually doesn't need to know exactly where you're standing. Navigation is one situation where precise location makes much more sense. Then: clear out what you're not using Delete dormant apps. Every unused app is another set of permissions and data practices you may have forgotten about. If you haven't opened an app since last year and no longer need it, consider deleting it. Finally: do it for your parents too If you have older relatives, their phones are worth checking next. They may be carrying years of old app permissions, and scammers frequently target older adults. Sit down with them for 10 minutes the next time you visit. Review location permissions, advertising controls and apps they no longer use. The half your phone settings can't reach Changing these settings can reduce future collection and sharing, but it doesn't erase information that companies may have already collected. And here's the piece many people miss. A location trail by itself may consist largely of coordinates and device information. It becomes much more revealing when someone can connect those movements with a name, home address, phone number or relatives. Some of that identifying information can come from people-search and data broker sites that publish or sell personal details. You can run a quick free scan to see what a scammer would see if they looked you up right now. If it shows details you never agreed to publish, you'll be able to take action and get them removed. Remove personal information that’s already out there This is where I strongly recommend using a personal data removal service. These services can automatically send removal requests to hundreds of data brokers, including people-search websites, on your behalf. They can also keep monitoring and resubmitting requests when your information reappears, which is important because data can return even after it has been removed. Kurt's key takeaways Your phone can reveal far more about your life than you may realize. Location data can expose visits to doctors, pharmacies, places of worship and other sensitive locations, especially when it gets combined with advertising identifiers and other information about you. The FTC's actions against location data brokers show this is not a hypothetical privacy problem. And the Gravy Analytics breach showed what can happen when enormous collections of location information fall into the wrong hands. I would start by reviewing which apps have access to your location and removing access from anything that doesn't truly need it. Then limit app tracking on your iPhone or delete your advertising ID on Android if that option is available. These changes won't make you invisible, but they can reduce the amount of information available to build a detailed trail of where you go. And don't forget the phones belonging to parents or older relatives. Years of forgotten app permissions can leave far more information exposed than they realize. title: LPGA commissioner shares sensible opinion on controversial Good Good Golf ad: 'Good people make mistakes'
description: LPGA commissioner Craig Kessler says Good Good Golf deserves forgiveness after the controversial Callaway ad that rocked the entire golf world.
content: LPGA commissioner Craig Kessler believes in something that has largely been lost, not only in sports, but across society as a whole: forgiveness. During the "Tuned In" summit hosted by Front Office Sports on Tuesday, Kessler was asked to share his take on the controversial Good Good Golf advertisement with Callaway that took over the golf world and social media back in August. Kessler's opinion on the ad — which featured Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark pushing member Alexis Miestowski to the ground — was one based in common sense. Like most, he couldn't believe the advertisement was greenlit to begin with, but he isn't on board with the idea of cancelling the brand over an admittedly huge mistake. FORMER PGA TOUR STAR HUNTER MAHAN SHARES HIS THOUGHTS ON CONTROVERSIAL GOOD GOOD AD, FALLOUT THAT FOLLOWED "The fact that someone thought that was a good idea and it came to life just shows you that while society has made enormous progress, we have a very, very long way to go," Kessler began. While his opening thoughts appeared to be him going down the path of completely bashing Good Good Golf and all that were involved, he later approached the topic from a forgivable point of view. "Good people make mistakes," Kessler continued. "And we have to leave room in society for someone to say, 'I made a massive mistake. Please forgive me. Here's what I learned, and it won't happen again.'" THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! title: SEC accuses LSU of defying its rules as Will Wade’s basketball roster adds fuel to a burning fire
description: The LSU Tigers filed a motion to dismiss, but the SEC fired back alleging school and Will Wade keep testing conference professionalism rules.
content: A legal battle between the LSU Tigers athletic department and the Southeastern Conference continues to play out in the Northern District Court of Alabama, with an explosive filing on Tuesday evening. If the SEC has its way, the case will linger until LSU acknowledges that it attempted to skirt the conference’s professionalism rules by recruiting — and potentially signing — athletes with professional experience in the NFL or NBA, or until LSU accepts some type of punishment without using a courtroom as a shield. The ongoing saga between one of the SEC’s biggest schools and the conference it resides in has pushed both sides toward a war over the limits of what LSU is permitted to do under league rules. INISDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN Dating back to before the college football season started, multiple athletes at first sued the NCAA for an additional year of eligibility based off the new guidelines that were enacted over how many years an athlete can play collegiate sports. When passed in June, the NCAA made it clear that while athletes would now have five years to play five seasons, they left out the 2022 class. This has led to a plethora of lawsuits being filed across the country, as some judges are granting athletes an additional season based on the NCAA's lack of grandfathering in the 2022 class, while the NCAA has been hellbent to fight each case presented in front of a local judge for consideration. But after a Louisiana district court judge ruled that Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris were eligible to play this season following their professional football experience, the SEC and other conferences adopted a rule barring athletes with professional experience from returning to college sports. LSU MIGHT HAVE TO SUE THE SEC IF THIS LEGAL WAR IS EXPEDITED, WHILE DABO SWINNEY IS STAYING IN HIS 'LANE' This led to attorneys for the plaintiffs adding the SEC to the ongoing lawsuit in a Baton Rouge court, which ultimately saw commissioner Greg Sankey taking the witness stand for over five hours on that Thursday before LSU would take the field against Clemson. It was not 20 minutes into his testimony that word started leaking from within the courtroom that the SEC had filed its own lawsuit against LSU, Lane Kiffin, President Wade Rousse and others within the Tigers administration for encroaching on their first amendment rights to govern themselves within the conference. LSU HOLDS OFF ON ADDING PLAYERS WITH NFL TIES AS SEC LAWSUIT LOOMS OVER PROGRAM, LANE KIFFIN If you were wondering why the SEC thought it would be best to file this type of lawsuit against a member institution, the conference is working under the impression that LSU would continue using the court system to maneuver around the enforcement of rules. "That threat is not hypothetical. Defendants have already shown they will use Louisiana’s courts to stop the Conference from governing itself," the SEC stated in a filing on Tuesday. "Working hand in glove with the Pyburn plaintiffs, they helped obtain state-court orders that bar the Conference from enforcing the Professionalism Rules." Just like a tale out of a John Grisham novel, the aftermath of that day in Baton Rouge has been nothing short of dramatic. LSU filed motion to dismiss lawsuit, while the SEC hits back with allegations After Lane Kiffin and the Tigers made the decision to not roster both Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, there were some who thought this lawsuit between the two sides would be dropped. "LSU’s eleventh-hour decision not to include two former professional athletes on its football roster does not moot the SEC’s claims," the conference said in a filing on Tuesday. "Nor does it matter that Defendants did not block or interfere with the September 10th meeting." NCAA HAS NO PLANS TO SURRENDER, AS ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS FOR 2022 CLASS TURN INTO AN ALL-OUT LEGAL WAR But, the fight between LSU and the SEC was essentially just getting started, which also came after subtle threats from the conference to kick the Tigers out of the league. In reality, this was not going to happen, but that hasn’t stopped the SEC from threatening punishment against the Tigers for continuing to recruit athletes with professional experience. Late Tuesday night, in a response to the SEC's response, Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill called the SEC's lawsuit "garbage". "The new response by SEC lawyers proves that the Commissioner was never acting in good faith," AG Murrill said. "LSU has broken no rules, and the case is moot. The lawsuit was garbage from the start and should be dismissed." While some were paying attention to what Lane Kiffin was doing with the football program, the real fight was already starting with LSU basketball coach Will Wade. Kiffin's roster moves were never the real threat in this battle, but more so how the Tigers were putting together a roster for the upcoming basketball season. It was never about football. The entire saga centered around college basketball Just a week ago, LSU technically had just four players on the current roster who were eligible, which came after former St. John's star RJ Luis Jr. was granted an injunction to play college basketball this season, though he has not been added to the Tigers roster. In their strategy to piece together a team, Will Wade has focused a majority of his time on players with professional experience, which was part of the SEC's filing on Tuesday in opposition of LSU's motion to dismiss. "LSU has openly recruited former NBA player RJ Luis Jr., has allowed him to practice with LSU’s men’s basketball team, and has refused to publicly and definitively state that he will not be included on LSU’s basketball roster, which is not due for several more weeks," the SEC's motion stated. For some minds, this strategy is of the same playbook that Lane Kiffin toyed with in the days leading up to LSU's season opener against Clemson. "We're going to follow all the SEC protocols with him," Wade said Tuesday during SEC Media Days. "I think it's been pretty clear what the SEC protocols are on all that. He didn't travel with us to McNeese, and he hasn't been rostered." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! title: AMB GORDON SONDLAND: Threading the needle on Ukraine, Russia and China
description: Trump's Ukraine strategy aims to reshape the global chessboard against China, but Volodymyr Zelensky must adapt his approach to survive it.
content: Let’s get the preliminaries out of the way. Ukraine has corruption problems and political dysfunction of its own. But in this war, Ukraine is unequivocally the good guy. Russia’s invasion was unprovoked, unjustified and indefensible. Vladimir Putin is the aggressor. Volodymyr Zelensky is defending his country. Period. Now let’s talk about geopolitical reality. Donald Trump is attempting something far more ambitious than ending the war in Ukraine. He is trying to rearrange the strategic chessboard for the next several decades. Understanding that objective is essential to understanding his seemingly contradictory decisions. The United States has one truly consequential long-term strategic competitor: China. Russia is dangerous, nuclear-armed and capable of wreaking havoc on its neighbors. But Russia is also a declining power with an economy dependent on natural resources, deteriorating demographics and ambitions that, while unacceptable, are largely regional. China is something else entirely. Beijing seeks to challenge American economic, technological and military leadership globally. It has the industrial capacity, financial resources and strategic patience to pursue that ambition for generations. China’s challenge is in a different category altogether. CHINA’S LONG-TERM FINANCES ARE ALL WET AS BILL TO MAINTAIN HUGE NAVY COMES DUE IN 2031 Here is Trump’s dilemma: Europe is not yet strong enough to contain Russia without substantial American support. Despite years of promises, too many NATO allies remain dependent on American military capabilities, intelligence, logistics and leadership. Until Europe can handle Russia largely on its own, the United States must continue devoting enormous resources to European security. Every additional weapons system, dollar and hour of strategic attention consumed by Moscow is a resource unavailable for deterring Beijing or addressing other threats around the world. Trump is trying to change that equation. His apparent objective is to create conditions under which Russia can eventually become a more normal, economically engaged country rather than a permanent adversary requiring America’s undivided attention. Think of it as strategic triage. In the long run, we want a fully economically engaged Russia that has something meaningful to lose, but still needs a good kick in the ass from time to time to remind Putin and his successors to stay the hell out of Europe. That is a far better outcome than a permanently isolated, militarized Russia driven ever deeper into China’s embrace. NATO'S EASTERN FLANK RACES TO REARM AS TRUMP PRESSURE EXPOSES WESTERN EUROPE'S DEFENSE GAP That doesn’t mean trusting Putin. It means understanding his incentives. Putin wants two things: money and real estate. He wants the economic benefits of international engagement and the territorial advantages of an empire. Trump is uniquely positioned to offer the former while making the latter prohibitively expensive. That is the needle Trump is trying to thread. But he is threading it while balancing competing global equities: keeping energy prices manageable, maintaining pressure on Iran, deterring China, supporting Israel, reassuring allies and protecting the American economy. Europe’s continued military dependence makes every calculation harder. And until Europe is genuinely capable of assuming primary responsibility for its own defense, America cannot simply disengage from Russia, however much we might wish to concentrate our resources elsewhere. Which brings us to Zelensky. I have enormous respect for his courage and determination. And when Ukraine strikes Russian oil refineries, the military logic is obvious. Petroleum revenues finance Putin’s war machine. Disrupting them is a legitimate strategic objective when conducted within the laws of war. Zelensky is right to hit Russia where it hurts. But being right is not always enough. An attack that makes perfect sense to Ukrainian military planners may complicate Trump’s larger negotiations, disrupt energy markets and create political problems at home. Zelensky’s first responsibility is Ukraine’s survival. Trump’s first responsibility is America’s interests. Those interests overlap enormously, but they are not identical. Here is what Zelensky must understand: Trump is not simply Ukraine’s principal supplier of weapons, intelligence and money. He is a strategic partner managing a far larger set of global obligations. Zelensky needs to stop approaching Washington principally with a shopping list and start asking a different question: Mr. President, what can Ukraine do to help you accomplish your broader objectives while protecting our sovereignty? TRUMP CALLS FOR UKRAINE TO REPLACE ZELENSKYY AFTER CLASH OVER RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL: 'GET A NEW PRESIDENT' That is not capitulation. It is sophisticated diplomacy. It means coordinating major military and economic initiatives before they become surprises. It means understanding American energy concerns and domestic political pressures. It means offering Trump practical ways to demonstrate progress rather than simply demanding more assistance. And it means recognizing that Trump’s ability to sustain American support depends partly on convincing Americans that his policies are working. There is another reality diplomats often prefer not to discuss: Donald Trump conducts foreign policy through personal relationships to an extraordinary degree. I worked for him. I know. The conventional diplomatic playbook emphasizes prepared meetings, formal communications and bureaucratic coordination. Trump places enormous weight on personal access and whether someone understands what he is trying to achieve. The late diplomat George Ball captured an enduring truth: "Nothing propinks like propinquity." In plain English, proximity matters. TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Zelensky needs to be talking to Trump constantly. Not once a month. Not only when he needs another weapons package. Almost every day. Sometimes to discuss the battlefield. Sometimes to share intelligence. Sometimes to float an idea. Sometimes just to tell him a joke or share some gossip. That may sound trivial when thousands are dying in Ukraine, but it isn’t. Personal familiarity creates trust. Trust creates access. Access creates influence. Even Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with their almost hourly access to Trump, can occasionally be surprised by a decision. That is the nature of his unusually fluid, personalized decision-making process. Imagine the disadvantage of a foreign leader relying exclusively on traditional diplomatic channels. Zelensky cannot afford that disadvantage. There is also the uncomfortable matter of American politics. Trump needs Republicans to retain control of the Senate in November. Zelensky needs Ukraine to survive the coming winter. To a neutral observer, those objectives are hardly equivalent. To each leader, however, they are critical. Should Zelensky intervene in an American election? Absolutely not. Should he understand Trump’s political pressures and help create conditions under which continued American support becomes easier to defend? Absolutely. There is a world of difference between helping a political party and helping an American president demonstrate that his foreign policy is producing results. Zelensky should be looking for opportunities to do the latter every day. Understanding Trump’s political constraints is not the same as surrendering Ukraine’s interests. It is recognizing that the most effective way to secure American support is to make Ukraine’s success part of Trump’s success. But this bargain must run both ways. Zelensky cannot be expected to restrain attacks on Russian energy infrastructure while Putin continues pounding Ukraine’s power plants, cities and civilian infrastructure. Ukraine has already demonstrated a willingness to consider reciprocal restraint. That willingness must be met by Russian action, not simply another American request for Ukrainian patience. If Trump wants Zelensky to accommodate his broader strategy, Trump must use America’s enormous economic leverage to make Putin accommodate it as well. That means no unilateral rewards for aggression, no permanent sanctions relief in exchange for temporary gestures and no settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless while Russia rearms. A temporary diesel arrangement or sanctions reprieve is not normalization. It is a tactic. Real normalization requires verifiable Russian behavior and meaningful consequences for renewed aggression. Putin wants economic engagement. Trump controls much of what makes that engagement possible. That leverage should be used to secure lasting concessions, not exchanged for another fleeting promise. Meanwhile, Europe must accelerate its military transformation. The United States cannot indefinitely remain Europe’s principal insurance policy while simultaneously preparing for the far greater strategic challenge posed by China. The ultimate prize is not a handshake with Putin or another White House announcement. It is a Europe capable of defending itself, a Russia with powerful incentives to stay within its borders and an America free to concentrate its strategic weight where the greatest long-term danger lies. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Until Europe reaches that point, Trump must balance competing military, economic and political demands that Zelensky cannot afford to ignore. And Trump must recognize that Ukraine’s survival is essential to making his larger strategy credible. Zelensky needs Trump’s leverage, weapons and economic power. Trump needs Zelensky’s cooperation to produce a sustainable settlement rather than a theatrical one. Putin must understand he cannot play them against each other indefinitely. The message to Zelensky is simple: Help Trump succeed in his larger geopolitical mission, and insist that Ukraine’s survival be part of that success. The message to Trump is equally simple: Give Zelensky a reason to trust that helping you will not cost him his country. Neither man needs to abandon his interests. Both need to understand the other’s. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That is how transactional diplomacy works when it works well. And that is how you thread the needle. title: Six Flags rider who fell to his death was in remission from cancer, survived 'crazy' car fire, sister says
description: Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath roller coaster remains under investigation after Hassan Kariem fell from the 200-foot-tall ride during a park visit.
content: A Georgia man who survived cancer and escaped a "crazy" car fire just a month ago died after falling from a Six Flags roller coaster, leaving his heartbroken sister struggling to comprehend how her brother could survive so much, only to lose his life in a tragic amusement park accident. Hassan Kariem, 42, died Monday after falling from the 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. His sister, Andrea Clark, 35, told the New York Post on Tuesday that her brother had been in remission from cancer since 2015 and had survived a car fire just weeks before his death. "He's an amazing person," Clark told the outlet through tears. "The coolest part about me was him." MAN DIES AFTER FALLING FROM GOLIATH ROLLER COASTER AT SIX FLAGS OVER GEORGIA Clark, who described her brother as "my hero," called his sudden death "unfair," saying she could not understand how someone who had overcome so much could be gone. "He had other issues, but he's healthy, he was able-bodied. I don't understand it," she said. Clark also recalled her brother's devotion to his loved ones, telling the Post that he worked hard to provide for his family and helped raise his fiancée's daughter, whom he had known since she was 3 years old. "He could do it all," she said. The grieving sister also condemned the circulation of disturbing images showing her brother's final moments as he fell from the roller coaster, urging people to stop sharing them. "That's just evil," Clark told the Post. "It's tragic, and I feel like we've gone too far as a society." ATTORNEY SAYS FATAL SIX FLAGS ROLLER COASTER ACCIDENT COULD RAISE BROADER SAFETY QUESTIONS AS 9 RIDES CLOSE Witnesses described a horrifying scene as Kariem reportedly fell from the ride, with one parkgoer telling local outlet WXIA that the victim appeared in a souvenir photo taken during the roller coaster's run. "He was in our pictures," the witness said. "He fell and hit the car three different times." The Goliath hypercoaster reaches speeds of up to 70 mph and features a 170-foot initial drop, a second 175-foot drop and a 540-degree spiral, according to the park's website. Atlanta Public Schools confirmed Tuesday that Kariem worked for the district as an IT manager and extended its condolences to his family. Six Flags said it was cooperating with authorities investigating the incident and temporarily closed similar roller coasters at other parks across the country as a precaution. title: State Department issues travel advisory as arrests and exit bans hit popular destination
description: The U.S. State Department's Level 3 Saudi Arabia travel advisory cites terrorism, missile attacks and strict social media laws as key concerns for those considering trips there.
content: Americans who may be planning an overseas trip are facing an updated warning from the U.S. State Department amid heightened safety and security concerns. The department issued a Level 3 "Reconsider Travel" advisory for Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12 — with certain parts of the country carrying the more severe Level 4 "Do Not Travel" designation. U.S. officials cited several concerns behind the warning — including regional conflict, terrorism, missile and drone attacks, exit bans and strict laws surrounding social media activity. AMERICANS WARNED AGAIN TO RETHINK TRAVEL AS MISSILE ATTACK RATTLES HISTORIC REGION The updated advisory comes after a series of attacks on Saudi airports by Iran-backed Houthi rebels reportedly killed at least 14 people, including an American, and injured more than 300 others, as Fox News Digital recently reported. "I would probably sit it out." Travel expert Lee Abbamonte told Fox News Digital, "Americans considering travel to Saudi Arabia should be aware of fresh attacks on Riyadh airport and threats of further action due to conflict with the Houthis and the ongoing Iran war." He added, "This is a very confusing time for Saudi travel, as we don’t currently know where this conflict will go. I would probably sit it out if I were thinking of traveling to the region" right now. The security concerns have also affected commercial air travel, according to the department. The threat of Iranian missile and drone attacks has continued since hostilities between the U.S. and Iran began in February, the State Department said. Commercial flights are still operating in Saudi Arabia, though service has faced major disruptions at times. Cities, airports, military bases, energy facilities and other infrastructure have been targeted, while debris from intercepted weapons can also pose a danger to people on the ground. Travelers are also being cautioned about what they capture on their phones during such incidents. "Do not photograph, film or share information about missile or drone interceptions or impact sites," the State Department warned — noting that Americans have been detained for taking photos of recent events. Terrorism remains another concern. Officials are warning that attacks could happen with little or no warning at tourist attractions, hotels, transportation hubs, shopping malls and other places visited by foreigners. The advisory also cautions Americans about what they post or interact with on social media. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "Some U.S. citizens have been arrested for past social media activity," the advisory states. That can include posts, reposts or likes viewed as critical of the Saudi government or its leaders, even if they were shared while outside the country, according to the department. The advisory warns that violating Saudi laws, even unintentionally, can carry serious consequences. "If you break laws in Saudi Arabia — even by mistake — you could be deported, fined, imprisoned or subject to an exit ban," the advisory states. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The strongest warning applies near the Yemen border, where Americans are advised not to travel due to terrorism. For those who do travel to Saudi Arabia, officials recommend staying alert, following local news and having a plan to leave in an emergency without depending on U.S. government assistance. Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for additional comment and details. A State Department spokesperson confirmed to The Travel that the U.S. Mission in Saudi Arabia issued a separate security alert on October 10, strongly urging all Americans to avoid King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the surrounding areas, the outlet reported.
