title: New York governor debate heats up as Blakeman, Hochul spar over Trump, sanctuary status, ICE shooting
description: The New York gubernatorial race heated up Tuesday as Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman clashed on the debate stage.
content: The New York gubernatorial race heated up Tuesday as Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman clashed on the debate stage, with the pair trading jabs over President Donald Trump, a recent ICE-involved shooting and inflation. The debate opened with the candidates being asked about the conduct of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which last week drew outrage in New York City following the shooting of a 28-year-old Dominican national whom the Department of Homeland Security said refused to comply with lawful orders during a targeted operation in the Bronx. A 5-year-old boy inside Oscar Bergal's vehicle was unharmed. "Kathy Hochul appealed to ICE to let this criminal out. The question that New Yorkers have to ask is what was this guy doing in New York in the first place? It's because Kathy Hochul has made us a sanctuary state," said Blakeman, a Republican. "Think about it. This guy came into the country illegally. He's been convicted of a crime. He's got pending charges for dealing drugs, poison to our children. And he's a gangbanger. This is who Kathy Hochul is defending?" Blakeman continued. "I have a cooperative agreement with ICE until Kathy Hochul said we could no longer cooperate with ICE. We got over 2,000 illegal migrants out of my county with criminal records ranging from rape, attempted murder, robbery, burglary, drug dealing, carjacking, gang activity. And that's because we cooperated with ICE, and we didn't raid one school, one hospital, one daycare center or one church. If you cooperate with federal law enforcement, it makes for a safer community. That's what I did. Kathy Hochul is taking that ability away from us. That's why things like this happen." Hochul called Blakeman's response a "non-answer," because "he refused to condemn what ICE did." "So he basically says in the state of New York, he'd be fine if ICE agents shoot into cars, shoot guns into vehicles, not knowing who's inside and could have killed a 5-year-old child. If that doesn't shock the conscience of everybody — and it should shock his conscience as well — that he says, that's OK, that's how ICE is supposed to do it," Hochul added. "I'll tell you what. I oversee over 500 policing agencies in the state of New York, over half a million arrests every year. That's not how you conduct yourself. ICE is out of control. It's out of control in Nassau County." Blakeman pushed back, saying, "it never would have happened" but for Hochul's "sanctuary policy." "You have invited criminals to come into our state and prey on our communities. And now you won't let local law enforcement cooperate with ICE in an orderly way, like we did in my county," Blakeman added. "We didn't have any incidents in my county because we were allowed to cooperate with local law enforcement. But you took that tool away. The reason why that happened is because of you, Kathy Hochul, and your immigration policies, where you actually invite people into our state, give them free everything, and you don't care whether they're criminals or not. That's a bad policy." As part of her rebuttal, Hochul said, "I have a right to answer this one because this is so absurd. I have said, from the president on down, I said, New York is not a sanctuary for criminals, not a sanctuary for criminals. Full stop." The two candidates also clashed over Trump and the state of the U.S. economy. "He promised to cut energy costs. He promised to cut down grocery costs. And you know what? Everything has happened under your friend, Donald Trump, who you are the president of the fan club for Donald Trump. It's absurd how adoring you are of him. My gosh," Hochul told Blakeman. "Well, what he has done is raise gasoline prices and energy prices and the cost of tariffs have driven up everything in the state. If you bought groceries lately, my God, the people are suffering. And that didn't have to be the case. Why are we at war with the rest of the world?" "You like to talk about Donald Trump all the time, because you don't want to talk about your record," Blakeman responded. "I'm talking about my record right now," Hochul said. "Because it's a record of misery and failure," Blakeman continued. "The highest taxes, utility rates that are 70% higher than the national average. But let me say something about Donald Trump. Donald Trump is my friend. He's endorsed me. But so is Bonnie Lautenberg, a liberal Democrat whose husband, Frank, served in the United States Senate and was a pillar of the Democratic Party. Actor Debra Messing, who is a liberal Democrat who supports me because she trusts me to make safer communities, improve the quality of life here in New York." "Alright, you got two votes," Hochul said. "Good for you."

title: 'Big Bang Theory' producer says societies who abandon God drift toward tyranny
description: Famous producer Chuck Lorre told Joe Rogan that societies replacing God with extreme ideologies like communism or fascism becoming tyrannical and dystopian
content: Hollywood producer Chuck Lorre, the creative force behind hit sitcoms such as "Two and a Half Men" and "The Big Bang Theory," discussed the importance of spirituality on Joe Rogan's podcast Tuesday. Lorre released his memoir, "Sitcom: A Memoir," on Tuesday, reflecting on his life and career. Lorre has previously discussed his religious background, having been raised Jewish before joining the Church of Scientology in his youth and later embracing Buddhism. In the most recent episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience," Lorre warned that worldly wealth and fame ultimately are not fulfilling and that "it's not the real solution. The real solution, you know, I'm going to say it and then regret it, but the real solution is a spiritual solution. You have to find something beyond this world." After Rogan asked why he might regret making the remark, including whether it had to do with working in Hollywood, Lorre replied that he didn't wish to be associated with "new age bulls---." RICHARD GERE CONFRONTS HOLLYWOOD FAME, EGO AND GREED AS 'DARK CLOUDS' THAT THREATEN INNER PEACE Rogan agreed, saying he believes the term "spirituality" has been co-opted by insincere people who have given it a "bad name." "I know some people that are like legitimately spiritual. Some of the nicest people that I know," Rogan said, describing a Christian acquaintance who built homes for homeless people and helped them overcome addiction. "It's like I know people like that too," Lorre agreed. "They're real, and they’re role models." Later on in the episode, Lorre marveled at how humans are unlike animals in that they create religions as a means of understanding and valuing the world around them, saying, "You wanna call it true or not, it's an organizing element that no other animal does." 'WIZARDS OF WAVERLY PLACE' STAR DAVID HENRIE SAYS HIS FAITH COST HIM AGENTS, MONEY AND FRIENDS IN HOLLYWOOD Lorre argued that it didn't matter if a particular religion was "true" but said that when a society abandons a belief in a supernatural god, it begins to worship extreme ideologies. "When civilizations or cultures that took God out of the picture, they replaced it, with the Communist Party, with a fascist dictator. You know, it's the same idea: ‘Organize around me. Doesn’t matter if I’m right or not, organize around me.’ And people will," he warned. Lorre compared shared religious beliefs to a tent pole holding society's understanding of reality together, suggesting that challenging those beliefs can provoke anger and uncertainty. "And if you take that away from them, they get angry. It freaks them out because it's like the tent pole. That tent pole moves, the tent comes down and everything, you know, if you believe that this is the truth and someone says, ‘No, it's not. It's bulls---.’ Everything else you believe is in fair play. Everything," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lorre himself is no stranger to political commentary. title: The Nobel Peace Prize has become a fig leaf for left-wing activism
description: Alfred Nobel created an award for world peace, but Navi Pillay's selection highlights how the committee rewards progressive causes over diplomacy.
content: Alfred Nobel intended the peace prize for those who had done the most to advance peace among nations. Instead, it is increasingly handed out to the international activist class: people who say the right things, back the right causes and appeal to the political instincts of a handful of parliamentarians in a rarefied progressive bubble. This year’s award to Navi Pillay is a case in point. Pillay is best known for chairing the U.N. commission of inquiry that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza. Her selection will inevitably be read as an endorsement of a U.N. culture in which hostility to Israel is not a liability but a badge of moral seriousness. NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA But there is more to Pillay’s record than the commission’s fixation on Israel. When Denmark’s embassy in Pakistan was bombed after Danish newspapers republished the Muhammad cartoons, former Foreign Minister Per Stig Møller reportedly said Pillay’s response was not to defend free speech, but to suggest censorship and restrictions on it. Her reaction to Charlie Hebdo was much the same. Pillay reportedly called the magazine "doubly irresponsible" for publishing Muhammad cartoons. She is said to have described them as "malicious and deliberately provocative" and said she "fully understands why people wish to protest strongly." When Islamists answer speech with threats, violence and murder, Pillay’s first instinct seems to be to scold those who exercised their right to speak. In 2022, she defended fellow U.N. commissioner Miloon Kothari after he referred to a "Jewish lobby" controlling social media and questioned whether Israel should even be a member of the United Nations. Kothari later apologized. An event in Pillay’s honor at Berlin City Hall was canceled after the mayor withdrew her support. WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM There are more reports of uncomfortable episodes. Pillay is said to have declined to attend the 2010 Nobel ceremony for the imprisoned Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo, citing a scheduling conflict in Geneva as Beijing pressured foreign governments to stay away. At Durban II the previous year, she remained seated while Mahmoud Ahmadinejad delivered an antisemitic tirade against Israel and Western delegations walked out. She condemned his speech later, but admitted that she had been "naive" about the Iranian president. A review of Pillay’s first two years as U.N. human-rights chief found no public statements from her on abuses in dictatorships such as Cuba, North Korea, Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Sudan or Belarus. This is the person the Nobel Committee now presents as a model of human rights, freedom and peace. The prize has a long history of such decisions. AMBASSADOR JEFF BARTOS: UN MUST ABANDON ANTI-AMERICAN, ANTI-WESTERN LEGACY OF DURBAN CONFERENCE In 1994, Yasser Arafat was awarded the Peace Prize despite a political career built around hijackings, murder and the glorification of violence against civilians. In 1973, Henry Kissinger and North Vietnam’s Le Duc Tho received it for negotiating a Vietnam ceasefire that quickly fell apart. Tho refused the award because peace had plainly not been achieved. In 2007, the prize went to Al Gore and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Climate change may be an important issue; it is not, however, what Nobel had in mind when he wrote of peace among nations. Barack Obama received the award in 2009, less than nine months into his presidency and before any significant diplomatic achievement. Even Obama seemed embarrassed by how premature it was. The European Union won in 2012, not for a particular peace agreement or diplomatic breakthrough, but for a lofty view of Europe that appealed to the Oslo establishment. None of this is an argument against human rights, international law or humanitarian work. It is an argument against pretending that every fashionable cause belongs under the heading of furthering world peace. There is a difference between speaking the language of peace and doing the hard work of making it. The latter involves deterrence, diplomacy, compromise, alliances and often dealing with people one does not like. It is not always glamorous and rarely produces applause in international conference halls. Consider the Abraham Accords. They normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states, creating embassies, direct flights, trade, investment and security cooperation. They replaced formal hostility with working relations between governments that had long treated one another as enemies. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Some may dislike Jared Kushner or the Trump administration. That is beside the point. Kushner did more to advance peace between states than many of the campaigners and organizations celebrated by the Nobel Committee in recent years. Yet it is almost impossible to imagine the committee rewarding such an achievement. Association with Trump alone would make Kushner unacceptable to the small political circle that controls the prize. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION That is the problem. The Nobel Peace Prize is decided by five people appointed by Norway’s parliament. They have the power to pronounce who represents the world’s highest moral ideals. Too often, they use it to reward people who share their own progressive assumptions. The Stockholm-based Nobel Foundation cannot simply reclaim the prize. Nobel’s will assigns responsibility to a committee appointed by Norway’s Parliament. But the committee can be criticized, and it should no longer be treated with the automatic reverence it enjoys. Alfred Nobel created an award for exceptional achievements that furthered world peace. The Norwegian committee has turned it into an annual seal of approval for causes it happens to favor. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A Peace Prize that cannot tell the difference no longer deserves the name — much less the respect it still receives.

title: Selma Blair's lawyer cites missed medication, head injury after in-flight arrest: What doctors say
description: Selma Blair's attorney claims she missed doses of a powerful MS medication, triggering severe neurological symptoms before her in-flight arrest.
content: Selma Blair’s recent in-flight arrest has raised questions about the potential effects when a person with multiple sclerosis misses prescribed medication. The actress, 54, was arraigned Monday on two counts of second-degree assault after allegedly attacking a police officer and nurse following an altercation with flight attendants aboard a Delta flight into New York City, The Associated Press reported. In court, Blair’s attorney, Shawn Barnes, said that Blair had missed several doses of Nuedexta, "a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms," according to multiple outlets. SELMA BLAIR ACCUSED OF KICKING NURSE HOURS AFTER JFK PLANE ARREST The attorney added that Blair hit her head during the flight, which departed from Los Angeles, and was in "a state of severe confusion and disorientation." He also suggested the altitude may have been a factor. The incident was the result of a "medical emergency" and not criminal misconduct, he claimed. Blair was diagnosed with MS in 2018. Fox News Digital reached out to Blair's representatives requesting comment. What to know about MS medications There are three primary treatment approaches for multiple sclerosis, according to Dr. Lee Murray, a board-certified neurologist practicing in Jackson, Tennessee, at West Tennessee Healthcare. "The first-line treatments we utilize try to prevent recurrent inflammatory attacks," Murray, who has not treated Blair, told Fox News Digital. 'HELICOPTER BRAIN' COULD BE MAKING YOU FEEL SICK: HOW TO SPOT IT AND WHAT TO DO These medications often involve IV infusions, but they can be in the form of pills or injections the patient gives themselves. "These are oftentimes medications folks take for several years," Murray said. "The hope of that is to keep the MS suppressed, to keep [the patient] from having MS attacks." When patients experience an MS relapse, doctors may prescribe high-dose steroids, either orally or intravenously, to reduce inflammation and help speed recovery, according to Cleveland Clinic. Patients with multiple sclerosis often have other health issues, Murray noted. "If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse." "For instance, patients with MS may have bladder difficulties, or they’ll develop depression or neuropathic pain," he said. "And so we prescribe medications that don't treat the MS itself, but they deal with the symptoms related to MS." Dr. Yoshua Quinones, board-certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, reiterated that there are different classes of MS medications. PARKINSON'S PATIENTS MAY PROTECT MEMORY AND MOVEMENT WITH ONE SIMPLE HABIT "Disease-modifying therapy reduces relapses, new MRI lesions and long-term disability accumulation," Quinones, who also did not treat Blair, told Fox News Digital. Other medications are used to treat acute relapses or manage symptoms such as fatigue, walking difficulties, spasticity and bladder problems. Disease-modifying therapies themselves fall into several categories, according to the doctor. Immunomodulators help regulate the immune system, while anti-trafficking drugs prevent certain immune cells from reaching the brain and spinal cord. Cell-depleting therapies, which are generally considered highly effective treatments, target and remove specific immune cells. Risks of skipping doses It’s essential for patients to be compliant with their MS medications, according to Murray. "If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse, which can result in acute or new changes neurologically," he said. "There's a host of different symptoms that can occur." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Potential effects of a relapse may include balance difficulties, vision loss, dizziness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or weakness, numbness or tingling on one side. In Blair's case, Murray said, "If the Nuedexta was being used to treat pseudobulbar palsy secondary to her MS, missed doses could result in uncontrolled crying or laughter and emotional lability (rapid or unpredictable changes in emotion or mood)." "I have never seen a missed dose of Nuedexta cause physical aggression," he added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES If a patient with multiple sclerosis has missed doses of medication and begins to develop new neurological deficits, they should seek medical attention to determine whether they are in an active MS flare, the neurologist advised. "Recognizing that and being able to quickly get on high-dose steroids can reverse some of the symptoms the patient may be experiencing," he said. Although steroids can speed recovery from an MS relapse, they have not been shown to improve long-term outcomes, according to the MS Society. Quinones agreed that skipping medications will reduce disease control. "Poor compliance will increase the risk of relapse and MS-related hospitalizations," he said. "For example, if you stop any anti-trafficking medication, it carries a high risk of rapid disease reactivation. Abrupt cessation of this class can even trigger a rebound worse than baseline." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Cell-depleting agents can act over months, so a single missed or delayed dose is less immediately impactful, Quinones added. "A single dose of disease-modifying therapy is not catastrophic — however, if constantly missed, it can raise a relapse risk." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The risks of missing medication depend on the specific drug, how long treatment is interrupted and the patient's individual circumstances, according to doctors. Fox News’ Tracy Wright contributed reporting.

title: Washington girls walk off cross country meet in protest of male athlete, parents reveal how it came to this
description: Holly Burns and teammates walked off a Washington cross-country race rather than compete against an athlete who switched from the boys' team.
content: Holly Burns and about a dozen other girls walked away from a cross-country race in Washington on Tuesday. They refused to compete against a male athlete who had started the season racing on the boys’ team. When the race began, half of the girls competing, and the male athlete, took off running. Burns and the other half of the girls slowly walked forward past the starting line, and then into the nearby tree line, sacrificing one of their high school competitions. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Footage of the protest has since gone viral across social media, igniting widespread awareness for one of the trans athlete incidents currently plaguing Washington state. For Burns, a Camas High School runner, the decision to protest was reinforced by strength in numbers. Her parents, Kevin and Sarah Burns, told OutKick their daughter initially wanted to avoid "making waves." "She wanted to kind of play it safe, so we, we weren't going to push it. We just kind of let her kind of feel it out. We told her that. We supported her whichever decision she tries to make," Kevins said. DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER But then her teammates began talking. The girls shared their concerns. They decided to act together. And her parents backed her. "The more I heard about her friends wanting to do something, the more I heard about her team wanting to do something, we definitely were in support of that," Kevin said. "We told her, do what you think is best." The Oct. 13 meet pitted Camas against Battle Ground. Camas hosted the event at the Underwriters Lab campus, where the girls’ race was scheduled for 4 p.m. The Burnses said they learned about the athlete’s move to girls’ competition recently. They worried about what it would mean for their daughter and her teammates. "You hear about it, but you just never think it’s going to be on your kid’s small cross-country team," Sarah said. ATTORNEY FOR ALLEGED VICTIM OF TRANS ATHLETE SEXUAL ASSAULT SAYS SCOTUS FIGHT CAN HELP SET TITLE IX PRECEDENT Camas School District has said it follows Washington law and Washington Interscholastic Activities Association eligibility rules. For the Burnses, that policy leaves their daughter’s concerns unresolved. "I don’t see how it’s OK to discriminate against my daughter and the daughters of everyone else that is trying to fairly compete," Kevin said. Their own protest began before the girls walked off. FEMALE ATHLETES, WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES SPEAK ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRANS ATHLETE ISSUE HOVERS OVER MIDTERMS They arrived with signs, and security challenged them, the parents said. "They said that we’re not allowed to hold up signs at this event today," Kevin Burns said. "I questioned them if that was constitutionally legal, if we could express ourselves by just holding a sign. And we kind of went back and forth about public versus private property. And in the end, it didn’t seem like they really had a grasp on what they could tell us to do or not. "So I just went ahead and held up my sign, and they had several security guards following me and pestering me and telling me that I would have to leave. And I just said, no, I’m not going to leave." Other parents approached, they said. Some offered support. Others said they agreed but feared the backlash that could follow speaking publicly. At one point, Sarah said she had a confrontation with a woman who identified herself as a psychiatric nurse. "I had a lady that came up to me and said she was a psychiatric nurse and that I was a disgusting human for holding up this sign and that I was doing psychological damage to these children," Sarah said. "I told her that one day I’m gonna have to stand before my Lord and Savior and I’m gonna feel good about this." The Burnses said they respected the girls who chose to race Tuesday. They believed some wanted to preserve their chances of competing in postseason meets. "I think they all have to make their own decision," they said. For Holly, they do not yet know what sitting out will mean. "Well, we don’t know that yet," they said when asked whether the protest cost her a chance at something she had worked toward. "But there’s cost to everything when you stand up for what you believe is right, I think. If there wasn’t, then you’re not really standing up for anything," they said. "Her goal this season was just to have fun and compete and do the best that she could." Now her parents hope she can keep pursuing those goals while standing alongside her teammates. More races remain. Camas lists its next championship meet for Oct. 21 at Lewisville Regional Park. Another decision awaits Washington voters on Nov. 3. Initiative 638 would prohibit students it defines as biologically male from competing in certain female-only interschool athletic competitions. It would require students seeking to enter those competitions to provide verification of biological sex from a healthcare provider. The Burnses support the measure. But even if voters approve it, the measure would take effect 30 days after the election. Washington’s state cross-country championships are scheduled for Nov. 7. The athlete at the center of the dispute had already competed in several girls’ races. On Sept. 5, the runner finished 76th in a boys’ junior varsity race at the Ultimook meet in Oregon. By Sept. 15, the runner was competing in the girls’ race at a Camas meet involving Skyview. The Burnses had not spoken with the athlete or the athlete’s family. Their position, they said, was that the runner should compete with boys. "Their child has every right to participate in the boys athletics, just like they did at the beginning of the season, but it’s not fair to the girls," they said during the interview. Holly’s parents rejected the idea that the stakes become insignificant because the athletes are in high school. "Some of these girls work really hard to compete. It’s most of what they do all summer long. It means a lot to them," they said. They argued that losing opportunities can undo the rewards of that effort. "Then that’s devastating to all the hard work. It erases everything they’ve done." The dispute unfolds against a broader conflict over Washington’s eligibility policies. President Donald Trump’s Feb. 5, 2025, executive order directed federal agencies to protect female athletic opportunities and prioritize Title IX enforcement against federally funded institutions that require female athletes to compete against males in women’s categories. Federal officials opened an investigation into Washington’s Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction in April 2025. State Superintendent Chris Reykdal defended Washington’s protections. He said the state had allowed students to participate in athletics consistent with their gender identity since 2007 and would continue enforcing its laws unless Congress or federal courts changed the legal requirements. A separate Washington sports dispute has also reached the Supreme Court. A high school wrestler identified in court filings as K.M.K. and her mother, Stephanie Brown, have requested emergency relief, including notice and an opportunity to decline competition against male athletes without penalties. The WIAA opposed the application in a filing Tuesday, arguing that the requested relief would conflict with state law and compromise other students’ privacy. The Supreme Court’s docket showed the responses filed Tuesday and no ruling on the application. The Burnses plan to keep showing up. "So we made a few contacts and we might go forward with that and have a more organized protest the next time," Kevin said. Asked whether they would return with more signs and shirts, the answer came quickly. "Definitely. Yeah, we will." They also said they were prepared for greater national attention if it helped bring change. Some friends disagree with their position. The couple hopes those relationships can survive the dispute. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "I think we can respect each other outside of the controversy," they said. Their fears extend beyond one race. They worry about what the policy means for college athletics, Olympic competition and other spaces reserved for women. "Women’s spaces will be erased," they said. For now, their daughter has chosen to stand with her teammates. Her parents want other families to know they can speak up, too. "Don’t be afraid." "Stand up for girls’ rights." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Girls need their own space. They need their sports. They need their athletics." Camas School District responded to the incident in a statement to OutKick. "Camas School District recognizes that students and community members hold differing views about athletic eligibility and have the right to express those views peacefully. Our responsibility is to ensure that school-sponsored events remain safe and respectful for all participants, staff, and spectators," the statement read. "As a Washington public school district and member of the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA), Camas follows applicable state law and WIAA eligibility rules. RCW 28A.642 prohibits discrimination in public schools based on gender identity and gender expression, and current WIAA rules permit students to participate in athletics consistent with their gender identity. The district does not set these eligibility standards independently. "We will continue to prioritize student safety, privacy, and well-being. We do not discuss individual students' eligibility, personal circumstances, or potential disciplinary matters." OutKick reached out to WIAA, Washington Superintendent for Public Instruction and Battle Ground for comment. Battle Ground hosted the race.

title: Bipartisan senators demand Trump scrap Russia diesel deal, call it 'betrayal' of US allies
description: A bipartisan group of United States senators joined together in a letter pressuring President Donald Trump to nix the diesel deal with Russia.
content: A bipartisan group of senators is urging Donald Trump to scrap his recently announced diesel deal with Russia, warning it could help President Vladimir Putin finance his war against Ukraine and calling the agreement "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies." "The Treasury Department’s General License No. 135, which lifts sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports, only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians. Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the senators asserted in the missive. The letter, which also includes a note of cc to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is signed by GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Susan Collins of Maine, Alan Stuart Armstrong of Oklahoma, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Cornyn of Texas, as well as Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Dick Durbin of Illinois, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Chris Coons of Delaware. REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON DIESEL DEAL WITH RUSSIA "We also recognize the urgent need to lower energy costs for American families and address the disruptions caused by the war with Iran. However, allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans. It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea. It will also endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury," the senators declared in their message. "Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world," they urged. TRUMP RUSSIA DEAL COULD FUEL PUTIN'S WAR, EX-NATO COMMANDER WARNS AS ZELENSKYY SAYS 'NYET' When asked during a gaggle on Tuesday whether he had been told that Russia would not utilize diesel money for bombs to use against Ukraine, Trump said no one "told me anything. That's a diesel deal not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's gonna be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices," he said. "But they're not releasing that to us, they're releasing it to the entire world." The senators' message to the president comes after Trump, in a Truth Social post on Friday, announced, "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel. Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement. Additionally, it must be understood, that Iran will not have a Nuclear Weapon!" the president declared in the post.

title: Battleground Republicans break with Trump on key issues in final midterm sprint
description: Battleground Republicans like Mike Lawler and Jen Kiggans are touting bipartisan credentials and conflict with Trump as midterm elections near.
content: Battleground Republicans are breaking from President Donald Trump with increasing frequency as Election Day draws closer and the party fights to protect its congressional majorities. With just three weeks until voters head to the polls to decide who controls Congress for the latter half of Trump’s term, some Republicans are putting distance between themselves and Trump as the party faces significant political headwinds. Veteran GOP strategist Doug Heye told Fox News Digital that such a strategy at this juncture was "not a surprise." "It happens in midterms when presidents aren’t popular," Heye said. "Add to that the more outlandish things he’s done — often on things that have nothing to do with lowering costs, ending the war with Iran, etc. — this was bound to happen." TRUMP VANISHES FROM GOP SENATOR'S CAMPAIGN WEBSITE AS POLL NUMBERS PLUNGE WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION It’s a similar situation to what’s played out with past presidents during a midterm election year, most recently with former President Joe Biden in 2022. And the Republican National Committee (RNC) is arguing that the party is united behind Trump, while conceding that GOP candidates have individual stakes. "Unlike the Democrats who are in a full-blown civil war with extremists, Republicans remain united behind the president's agenda of cutting taxes, lowering drug costs and securing our communities. We are laser-focused on winning, and our candidates will run the races necessary to best represent their districts and prevent Democrats from taking control," RNC spokeswoman Natalie Baldessarre said. And running their own races is what several are notably doing, balancing individuality with their support for Trump and the GOP base. At least two House Republicans, Reps. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., and Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., have touted conflict with Trump in advertisements. TRUMP-LINKED SUPER PAC PULLS FUNDING FROM 2 HOUSE REPUBLICANS AS GOP FIGHTS TO KEEP MAJORITY Kiggans is out with a new ad touting herself as "one of the most bipartisan members of Congress," who has taken on her "own party to protect jobs, and working with Democrats to save healthcare." One visual referenced a news article that said, "Kiggans bucks Trump on offshore wind." Meanwhile, Lawler recently released an advertisement in which he highlighted taking on "the left and the right," followed by a clip of Trump calling him a "pain in the a--" on state and local tax deduction issues. But for many, like Lawler, it’s a balancing act of trying to keep Trump and the GOP base happy, while courting independent voters. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said, "No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the president understands how to communicate with them." "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," Ingle told Fox News Digital. "The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs," Ingle continued. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Still, the political tightrope was on full display when Lawler appeared on stage at Trump’s midterm convention in September, when he noted he and the president didn't "always agree." He told Fox News Digital at the convention, "I fundamentally believe if you want to get things done, you have to be able to work with whoever the president is. And it's why I've consistently been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress." Former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., and Sen. John Husted, R-Ohio, also notably appeared at Trump’s convention in Dallas. They have, however, split from Trump on some key issues in an effort to show daylight between themselves and the president. CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION They have called for an end to the Iran war and have diverged from Trump on data centers — the president declared on Truth Social shortly after the midterm convention that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." But it’s a key sticking point for several Republicans on the trail who recognize the bad optics the hulking, windowless behemoths have with voters. Many, including Husted and Rogers, don’t believe it’s an issue that the federal government should have total dominion over. "What we've said is there should be a moratorium until we get all of the voters' decisions and questions answered," Rogers told Fox News Digital during the convention. "These are big decisions. I don't think there should be a federal ban, because if the federal government can ban it, it can also tell you have to have one." Another vulnerable GOP lawmaker who broke from Trump on the issue of data centers is Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., who has maintained that it should be a decision for local governments whether to allow such facilities in their backyards. "When you have people colluding with these corporations to come in and build a data center, before people in the community even know about it, because of these non-disclosure agreements, I think that violates the trust that people have or don't have with their local officials right now," Barrett said on Fox News’ "The Big Weekend Show." Barrett is also one of a small handful of House Republicans who has consistently voted against the U.S. operation in Iran without congressional approval. The Middle East conflict has gained a steady stream of GOP opposition the longer it’s gone on, as evidenced by the growing number of Republicans voting for Democrats’ war powers resolutions in the House. Among them is Rep. Marianette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who previously voted with the GOP on similar measures until the most recent such vote in mid-September. And Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, who voted against reining in Trump on Iran, noted on the Woo & WayCo podcast last week, "We need to get out of this war quickly." "What [Trump] did to stop a nuclear danger is a beautiful thing, but right now, you know, I don’t think anyone can cut a deal with Iranians, because you can’t trust them," Miller said. title: Mamdani, City Council move to end iconic NYC horse-drawn carriage industry as workers face uncertain future
description: Romanch's Law would phase out Central Park horse-drawn carriages by 2028, but Mayor Zohran Mamdani's transition plan guarantees no financial payouts.
content: New York City's iconic horse-drawn carriages could disappear from Central Park under an agreement reached Tuesday between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Council speaker Julie Menin, setting the stage for a vote to eliminate the historic industry. The agreement would ban horse-drawn carriage operations beginning June 1, 2028, if approved by the City Council on Oct. 22, ending a longtime tourist attraction amid concerns over animal welfare and public safety. The proposed legislation, known as Romanch's Law — named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who suffered fatal injuries in a horse-drawn carriage crash in June — would require city officials to develop a transition plan for carriage drivers, owners and stable workers, though financial compensation would not be guaranteed. MAMDANI'S LATEST FREEBIE SETS OFF ONLINE FURY AS CRITICS RIP CITY PRIORITIES: 'OPERA SOCIALISM' "The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected, and the horses are safe," Mamdani wrote on X. Animal rights group PETA celebrated the agreement after years of campaigning against the carriage industry. "This is long overdue, and it can't come quickly enough," PETA representative Ashley Byrne told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview Tuesday. Byrne cited incidents involving horses collapsing in city streets and colliding with vehicles, and said more than 70% of New Yorkers support a ban, a figure Fox News Digital has not independently verified. MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY The Central Park Conservancy also welcomed the agreement, emphasizing public safety. "We applaud the City Council for finally taking on this issue. For the Central Park Conservancy, this has always been a matter of public safety. We hope carriages can be phased out efficiently and humanely so that no one else ever suffers the fate of Romanch Mahajan," Conservancy President and CEO Betsy Smith said. But the Transport Workers Union sharply criticized the agreement, accusing city leaders of failing to provide meaningful financial protections for workers and carriage owners. "Council Speaker Menin's bill has no meaningful economic relief for workers," TWU International President John Samuelsen said in a statement. "It only says the city should prepare a worker transition plan by April 2027 and include weak measures like job fairs and job counseling." Samuelsen also accused Menin of exploiting the June death of 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan to advance the ban. MAMDANI'S 'THIS IS ONLY THE BEGINNING' ANNOUNCEMENT CRACKING DOWN ON FOOD DELIVERY TIPS SPARKS OUTRAGE "Council Speaker Menin used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis. This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed," he said. Under the legislation, city agencies would have until April 1, 2027, to develop a workforce transition plan that includes job placement, career counseling, training and referrals to other transportation and tourism jobs. Officials would also have to consider compensation for carriage owners and assistance with retiring horses, but no payouts are guaranteed. "We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," City Hall spokesperson Sneha Choudhary said. Fox News Digital reached out to Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents carriage drivers and owners, for comment. Menin, who would be the first sitting City Council speaker to support the legislation, according to the Council, said the city must balance tradition with public safety and workers' livelihoods. "We can honor our city's traditions while recognizing when it's time to move forward in the interest of public safety, protecting workers, and strengthening our city's economic vitality," Menin said. The legislation follows the June death of Mahajan, a tourist from India who suffered fatal injuries after a horse-drawn carriage bolted, collided with another carriage and overturned in Central Park. "The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable," Menin said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Central Park Conservancy previously reported that the fatal crash was the eighth horse-related incident in or around the park in approximately 13 months. Days earlier, a carriage horse named Deniz reportedly collapsed and died while pulling tourists. Following Mahajan's death, TWU Local 100 called for tougher driver examinations, enhanced training and additional safety regulations rather than an outright ban.Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

title: The Iran war's unexpected impact on US defenses against China threat downplayed by top Army leader
description: Gen. Ronald Clark says China's PLA continues preparing despite Trump-Xi diplomacy as U.S. Army Pacific expands deterrence across the Indo-Pacific.
content: Amid growing concerns that the Iran war is drawing away critical U.S. defenses from China's doorstep, the Army's top commander in the Pacific says the forces are using this unexpected opportunity to modernize. Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, provided his assessment that diverting Patriot missile defenses to the Iran war has not increased risk to forces in the Indo-Pacific despite concerns about deployments impacting America's readiness for potential conflict with China. "Actually, it's given us an opportunity to modernize our systems here," Clark told Fox News Digital during a small-group interview at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. Patriot systems have been redeployed from the Indo-Pacific to support operations in the Middle East, while U.S. forces in South Korea have also sent Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors to the region. An October Congressional Research Service report cited estimates that U.S. forces had expended roughly 1,700 Patriot and 200 THAAD interceptors during the conflict, while the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the military had used between half and two-thirds of certain interceptor inventories. The Pentagon's inspector general has cited strategic inventory shortfalls and manufacturing bottlenecks stemming from the conflict, raising questions about how quickly the U.S. could replenish its defenses in the event of another major confrontation. Clark said the deployments are giving Patriot crews firsthand experience defending against enemy attacks, while equipment upgrades are expanding what individual batteries can accomplish. He said an upgraded Patriot battery can now provide coverage that previously required an entire battalion, though he did not specify whether he was referring to geographic coverage or the number of threats the system can engage. Asked whether recent diplomatic progress between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had changed his assessment of the threat from China, Clark said he believes the People's Liberation Army (PLA) is continuing its build-up. "Well, I believe they're continuing to prepare," Clark said. XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT The assessment comes weeks after Trump welcomed Xi to Washington for a high-profile state visit that produced new trade agreements and commitments to improve military communications. But the diplomatic progress has not resolved tensions over Taiwan and China's growing military reach across the Indo-Pacific, where American commanders continue preparing for a potential conflict. Clark did not say whether China's military preparations had accelerated or whether diplomatic outreach had changed Beijing's intentions. He emphasized that the U.S. military's responsibility is to remain ready for a potential conflict while working to prevent one. TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD "Hopefully my legacy in this job is that when we walk away from command of USARPAC, that the deterrent posture of our command is such that we have not just prevented war, but we're preventing war in the future," Clark said. Clark said Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, recently discussed reviving disaster-management exchanges between the U.S. Army and China's PLA during talks with his Chinese counterpart. The exchanges would provide an opportunity for American and Chinese military personnel to work together on disaster response, restoring a channel of direct engagement that Clark said he hoped to see revived. "If you're able to have a conversation with your adversaries, you're able to share information with them in a way that makes them not want to fight," Clark said. He said U.S. Army Pacific would be responsible for coordinating the exchanges with its Chinese counterparts if the effort moves forward. He did not announce a date or say that Beijing had formally agreed to resume the program. The U.S. and Chinese militaries have periodically conducted disaster-management exchanges in the past, including an event hosted by the Army at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state in 2017. "The cost of going to war is just so high that it's our duty to, one, be absolutely prepared for that eventuality, but two, to prevent that from happening," Clark said. The diplomatic outreach comes amid continued confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces in the South China Sea. As Fox News Digital previously reported, the Philippines tracked 101 Chinese navy and coast guard vessels around disputed waters in September, nearly double the number recorded in August. More recently, Philippine authorities accused Chinese forces of obstructing maritime operations and carrying out dangerous maneuvers near Philippine aircraft. CHINESE MILITARY ACTIVITY NEARLY DOUBLES AROUND KEY US ALLY IN DISPUTED WATERS Meanwhile, the Army has been expanding its capabilities across the Indo-Pacific, positioning additional forces and equipment closer to potential flashpoints as part of its effort to deter Chinese aggression. Clark said the Army now has more resources committed to the region than at any previous point in his career, including additional divisions, a corps headquarters and specialized formations designed to conduct long-range strikes and operations across multiple domains. "The Army is now better resourced in the Pacific than I've ever seen it," he said. He pointed to the Army's growing ability to support naval and air operations, including land-based weapons capable of striking targets at sea. "It's really tied to existing capabilities we have," Clark said, citing the Army's ability to detect targets, conduct strikes, protect military assets and sustain operations from land.

title: Hooters restaurants keep closing even as CEO says there's more to the story
description: Hooters CEO Neil Kiefer told Fox News Digital that recent restaurant closures aren't a sign of brand weakness as the original founders rebuild after its 2025 bankruptcy.
content: Hooters restaurants continue to disappear across America, including several longtime locations in Florida — but the iconic chain's CEO insists the closures aren't a sign that the brand is losing its appeal. Neil Kiefer, CEO of Florida-based Hooters Inc., told Fox News Digital the company is focused on rebuilding the restaurant chain after its original founders regained control of the brand following its 2025 bankruptcy. "The number of stores will go up and down, but the longevity of our commitment will not," Kiefer said. "These store closures are not an indication of brand strength." HOOTERS RESTAURANTS KEEP DISAPPEARING AS ICONIC CHAIN LOSES LONGTIME LOCATIONS IN FOUNDING STATE His remarks come after Fox News Digital reported that Hooters closed its last remaining restaurant in Jacksonville, Florida, ending a 40-year presence in the city. The closure followed the September shutdown of a Hooters in Panama City Beach, which had operated for more than three decades. Other longtime locations have also disappeared, including a Hooters in Boca Raton, Florida, which closed earlier this year after 16 years when its landlord declined to renew the lease. But Kiefer said the recent closures need to be viewed in the context of the company's ownership changes. "In March 2025, Hooters of America filed for bankruptcy," he said. HISTORY OF HOOTERS: 5 FACTS YOU LIKELY NEVER KNEW ABOUT THE RESTAURANT CHAIN "Hooters of America was a separate corporate entity from the original Hooters team that first founded the brand and their first restaurant in Clearwater, Florida, in 1983," he went on. "While these two groups may have shared a name, they shared nothing else. The original founders saw an opportunity to step in and reclaim their brand, integrity and legacy. Since these acquisitions, we've learned some stores were in various stages of need." Kiefer also emphasized that the closures should not be viewed as a reflection of the restaurant chain's "beloved staff, community or sisterhood of the orange shorts." title: American-made goods also got more expensive under Trump tariffs, new research finds
description: Federal Reserve Bank of New York research shows Trump tariffs added 2.9 percentage points to consumer goods inflation through February 2026.
content: Americans aren't just seeing the price tag increase for imported goods. Thanks to President Donald Trump's tariffs, they are now paying more for products made in the U.S.A., according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In fact, the research finds that prices for many everyday goods would have fallen last year and into early 2026 without Trump's tariffs. The findings offer new evidence of how the sweeping tariff policy, a centerpiece of the president's economic agenda during his second term, have affected Americans’ wallets — and it's only getting worse with just one month until the midterm elections. TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS. NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK Economists had long warned that tariffs would drive up consumer prices, but measuring their precise impact has been difficult as trade policies shifted and companies made decisions about whether to absorb higher costs or pass them along to shoppers. Put simply, the New York Fed found that tariffs kept prices higher on many of the goods Americans buy every day. Without the tariffs, prices across the consumer goods examined for this study would have fallen by early 2026. Instead, they rose. The researchers estimated that tariffs added about 2.9 percentage points to prices across the goods they studied. And the impact, notably, was not limited to imported products facing the most fallout from tariffs. The New York Fed found that Trump's policies pushed up prices on American-made goods. Researchers estimated that about two-thirds of the tariff-related price increase came from imports, while roughly one-third came from products made in the United States. The White House pushed back, arguing that tariffs will ultimately benefit U.S. workers and be paid by foreign exporters. "President Trump’s America First trade agenda is reshaping the international economic order to reduce our trade deficit, revitalize American manufacturing, and deliver lasting benefits to our workers, farmers and producers," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital. The administration has maintained that foreign exporters reliant on access to the U.S. market will ultimately bear the cost of tariffs, Rogers added. A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, told Fox News Digital that consumers may not see significant relief as long as tariffs remain in place. "What we know is that the tariffs have increased prices a bit," Lincicome said. "What we don't know is whether the prices will stay where they are or go up even a little bit more as companies finally cave and start passing on more of the tariff costs onto consumers." "As long as the tariffs remain in place, it's unlikely we're going to see price declines," he added. The research also found that tariff-related price increases can take up to a year to fully reach consumers, particularly when American manufacturers face higher costs for imported materials and components. Although the researchers estimate that the inflationary impact of existing tariffs has largely peaked, they expect consumer goods prices to remain higher than they otherwise would have been. 5 STATES COULD BE THE BIGGEST LOSERS IN TRUMP'S TRADE WAR WITH CANADA, EXPERT WARNS The findings could carry political implications as Trump and Republicans face voters in November after campaigning on lowering the cost of living. "When you campaign on lowering prices, and then you actually actively increase prices, it's probably gonna hurt when voters go back to the polls and are mad about prices still being too high," Lincicome said. Meanwhile, higher energy costs are adding another layer of pressure on American households. "It's really a double whammy for American consumers because first you had the tariffs which increased the prices of a lot of products. And then you had energy prices spike because of the Iran war," Lincicome said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He warned that rising diesel costs could push prices higher beyond the gas pump, increasing transportation expenses for businesses that rely on trucks, trains and agricultural equipment. "Those things are going to act as kind of another tariff because they're gonna increase the cost of getting that product to you," he said.

title: Schumer warns of Republican advantage that could change the battle for Senate control
description: Senate Democrats face a Republican money tsunami as Chuck Schumer warns colleagues that massive GOP spending could overwhelm their candidates.
content: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer sees a path to victory for Democrats in November — but one major Republican advantage has him worried. In a letter to his Democratic colleagues, Schumer, D-N.Y., argued that his crop of candidates and Democrats running across the country are winning the messaging battle against the GOP, but asked, "Can Republicans buy the Senate?" "With just three weeks until Election Day, the battle for control of the Senate comes down to one defining question: Will the unprecedented tsunami of Republican money defeat the massive Democratic advantage in candidates, policies, and political climate," Schumer wrote. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS "There are 22 days until Election Day, and two enormous forces are on a collision course: deep voter dissatisfaction with Republicans and an unprecedented flood of money aimed at overcoming their political liabilities," he continued. "Which force prevails could determine control of the United States Senate." Republicans do have a distinct money advantage and have seen outside groups and President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. spending at eye-popping levels across the Senate map. MAGA Inc., for example, has over $400 million at its disposal, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings, and reportedly has plans to spend in key Senate races like Iowa, Ohio and Alaska in the waning weeks of the midterms. SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES Then there’s tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has contributed roughly $276 million to Republican-aligned political action committees (PACs) this cycle. Notably, he contributed $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC closely aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. Schumer lamented the funding, arguing that it was coming from a small field of deep-pocketed donors "looking to buy a pardon, curry favor, and move the needle in favor of their personal interests." He also charged that the influx of cash was thanks in part to the Supreme Court’s decision in June to eliminate federal limits on how much political parties can spend on candidates. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT "None of us are naïve; we’ve known this day would come ever since Justices Kennedy, Roberts, Scalia, Alito, and Thomas decided to give their billionaire and corporate friends permission to buy elections," Schumer said. But Democrats’ own super PAC, the Senate Majority PAC, which is closely aligned with Schumer, broke its own fundraising records in the third quarter of this year, raking in $151 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) announced shortly after the court’s decision that it would be pumping in $40 million in a slew of battleground states. "This pity pitch from Chuck Schumer is a testament to the enthusiasm of Republican grassroots donors who are re-engaging in full force to stop Democrats’ socialist march," NRSC spokeswoman Bernadette Breslin told Fox News Digital. title: Democrats have ‘dirty hands’ over complaints about Omar raid weeks before election, ex-prosecutor says
description: Former federal prosecutors say the Justice Department's 60-day rule that Democrats cite in the Ilhan Omar home search is unwritten, not a ban.
content: Former federal prosecutors are pushing back on Democrats' accusations that the Trump administration violated Justice Department policy by searching the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., just weeks before an election. "It's difficult to not point out the dirty hands of the people that might complain about election interference," Jim Trusty, a former federal prosecutor, said, pointing to former special counsel Jack Smith's prosecution of President Donald Trump ahead of the 2024 election. "Democrats definitely can't contend that it's a politicized investigation after everything that happened in the Trump era," Abhishek Kambil, a former federal prosecutor, told Fox News Digital. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, released a lengthy statement alleging that the Justice Department violated protocol by conducting "overt actions in politically-sensitive matters in the 60 days before an election." HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’ "Just 22 days before the elections, this is blatant political intimidation and an attempt to interfere with the Congresswoman’s reelection," Raskin wrote in his press release. But Kambil pointed out that the U.S. Department of Justice Manual, which outlines procedures for federal criminal investigations, does not explicitly impose a 60-day period before elections in which investigative actions can't be conducted. "The 60-day requirement is not something that's in the justice manual," Kambil told Fox News Digital. "That's basically an unwritten practice of what DOJ typically does, and the justice manual itself does not have the time frame on that." Kambil said that any actions which could be perceived as influencing an election will require prior approval from either the attorney general or the deputy attorney general. The Justice Department has long followed an unwritten practice known as the "60-day rule," which discourages politically sensitive investigative actions close to an election. The practice came under scrutiny in a 2018 DOJ inspector general report examining former FBI Director James Comey's decision to notify Congress of new developments in the Hillary Clinton email investigation just 11 days before the 2016 presidential election. The watchdog concluded that Comey had disregarded longstanding department policy and practice, calling his decision a "serious error of judgment." "It doesn't create a ban; it just creates effectively a consultation requirement to higher level leadership before it can happen, but there is no statute or anything else preventing this," Kambil told Fox News Digital. The Justice Department also was accused by President Donald Trump of ignoring its "60-day rule" when special counsel Jack Smith filed a revised indictment against Trump just 70 days before the 2024 presidential election. Weeks later, Smith submitted a 165-page brief outlining evidence against Trump in the federal election interference case, which was made public just 34 days before the election. Trump and Republican lawmakers accused Smith of attempting to influence the election, but Smith maintained that his office followed DOJ policy and complied with a court-ordered filing schedule. "For 60 days prior to an election, the Department of Injustice is supposed to do absolutely nothing that would taint or interfere with a case," Trump posted in all capital letters to his Truth Social. "They disobeyed their own rule in favor of complete and total election interference." BIDEN-ERA FBI’S ‘NIXONIAN’ TRUMP FAMILY SURVEILLANCE DRAWS SCRUTINY FROM UNLIKELY CORNER "Going back to Jack Smith, obviously trying to get a case tried — the January 6th case before the election — to affect the electorate," Trusty said. Trusty pointed out that the Justice Department needed approval from a magistrate judge in Washington, D.C., before executing its search warrant. "There's at least probable cause," Trusty said. "It's a long way off from proving a case at trial." "But keep in mind, in D.C. President Trump and his administration don't always have friendly treatment from the judges there," Trusty continued. "So this was a magistrate judge who looked at the sworn statement, said there's enough to justify a raid, and now we've had a raid." A judge can reject a search warrant application if investigators fail to establish probable cause. But approving a warrant does not necessarily resolve questions about whether the search complied with the Justice Department's election-year policies. TRUMP DOJ UNLEASHES LARGEST DENATURALIZATION EFFORT IN DEPARTMENT HISTORY — AND SAYS IT’S ‘ONLY THE BEGINNING’ "When you see Democrats challenging the warrant or what happened, they're not really going after the merits," Kambil said. "They're challenging the timing." The Homeland Security Investigations raid stems from an investigation into immigration paperwork Omar's father completed when she was a child. Omar, who fled Somalia's civil war, immigrated to the United States with her family in 1995 at age 12 and became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000. In response to the raid on her home, Omar accused Trump of engaging in "political intimidation" against her. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar posted on X. "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back." title: Ukraine showed Trump how easily an enemy could cripple an AI powerhouse
description: Ukraine's drone attacks on three Yandex data centers in four days exposed how adversaries can cripple artificial intelligence without defeating software.
content: An adversary can interrupt an artificial intelligence system without defeating its software. It need only strike the infrastructure that keeps the system running. Ukraine proved the point inside Russia this past week. President Trump and his national security team should take note before an enemy tries the same thing here. On October 8, a Ukrainian drone attack forced Yandex, the technology company often called "Russia’s Google," to suspend operations at its Sasovo data center. The next day, another strike knocked out several modules at its Kaluga facility, which Yandex had called its most powerful data center in Russia. On October 11, the company announced that its Vladimir-region data center had shut down completely after a drone attack. Ukraine disrupted three major Yandex computing facilities in four days. The Sasovo facility housed two of Yandex’s three supercomputers used to train its AI models, including YandexGPT. Yandex said it could not yet determine whether the equipment could be restored. Whatever the final damage assessment, Russia’s leading AI developer lost a major computing hub in a single night. AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR During my years as an Army officer and Pentagon strategist, I learned to judge a military capability by whether it would be there when needed. A weapon that dazzles on the test range becomes a liability when its supply line fails in combat. That standard should govern our dependence on AI. The word "cloud" hides the physical machinery behind computing services. Those services require buildings, processors, electricity, cooling equipment and communications networks. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency calls energy and communications "fundamental to the operation of practically every other critical infrastructure sector." THE AI REVOLUTION WILL GO WHEREVER THERE'S ELECTRICITY — AND CHINA KNOWS IT That vulnerability reaches well beyond Russia. Government missions, essential services and American businesses all run on advanced computing. When a privately operated facility supports an indispensable defense or intelligence function, its continued availability becomes a national security concern. That does not mean Washington should take these facilities over. A government nameplate on the gate would not stop a single drone. What matters is who defends these sites and how quickly they recover. An outage need not destroy equipment to cause serious harm. Intelligence that arrives after a commander must act may come too late to protect troops or shape the decision. A recovery plan that misses the mission’s deadline is no plan at all. US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING Russia is a war zone, and America is not. But consider Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, and neighboring Prince William County. Fences, cameras and guards protect those campuses on the ground. None of that stops a drone, and federal law reserves the authority to bring one down for federal agencies and certified state and local police. Ukraine’s strikes give Washington every reason to test whether our essential computing would survive an attack from the air. President Trump has already laid a policy foundation. His June 5 national security memorandum directed agencies to form partnerships with willing private companies to secure America’s most advanced AI technologies. It specifically contemplated threat intelligence sharing, joint AI red-team exercises and stronger physical and cybersecurity protections for the nation’s data centers. The memorandum gave agencies 120 days to develop those partnerships, a deadline that passed on October 3. The administration should now report what it has accomplished: which partnerships are operating, what protections they provide and whether essential missions can continue after a major facility becomes unavailable. Trump’s new Super Intelligence Task Force, announced October 4 and led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, is the right venue to demand those answers. Reuters reported October 8 that vice chair Scott Kupor expected the full committee to convene this week and to issue a charter afterward. Infrastructure readiness belongs in that charter. The president should direct four practical steps. First, identify the computing capabilities essential to national defense, intelligence and other indispensable government missions. Assess the cost of losing them, the availability of alternatives and the time required to restore operations. The mission, not a facility’s price tag or size, should determine its security priority. Second, assign responsibility. Private operators must harden their facilities and build redundancy. Defending the airspace above them is government’s job, so federal agencies and local police should plan counter-drone coverage for the most critical sites. Federal agencies must also provide timely threat information, define requirements for the missions they purchase and coordinate emergency assistance. The president should name a single official responsible for pulling those efforts together and closing gaps. Third, establish proportionate, enforceable security requirements. Government contracts can require protection and continuity arrangements for essential services, and Congress should close demonstrated gaps in authority. Requirements should cover power, cooling and communications as well as computing equipment. Fourth, test recovery the way Washington-area agencies have long exercised their continuity of operations plans in drills such as FEMA’s annual Eagle Horizon. Those tests should include the loss of more than one facility or a shared power or communications provider. Can another site accept the workload? Are the necessary data, equipment and personnel available? Can operations resume within the mission’s deadline? Where the answer is no, fix it before a crisis. Congress should receive classified reports on those results. A public summary can establish accountability without revealing sensitive facilities or defensive measures. The civilian nuclear industry offers a useful precedent. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission requires nuclear power plants to maintain armed security officers, physical barriers and intrusion detection, and it tests those defenses with force-on-force exercises. Most of those plants are privately owned. AI data centers pose different hazards, and Washington should not copy nuclear rules wholesale. The principle carries over: private ownership and enforceable federal security obligations can coexist. America should preserve the entrepreneurship that drives technological progress while requiring dependable service for essential national missions. Targeted protections can deliver both.
