content: NBC’s return to NBA coverage last season offered longtime basketball fans a dose of nostalgia. The venerable broadcast network regained the league’s rights as part of an 11-year media deal, reviving the iconic theme song that accompanied NBA broadcasts from 1990 to 2002. Disney-owned ESPN and Amazon Prime Video also joined the deal, which marked the NBA’s move away from longtime broadcast partner TNT. Some interpreted the announcement as a signal that Jordan would become a regular presence on the studio desk. title: Man who lived as woman for eight years warns surprising teen sexuality data may not tell full story
description: Walt Heyer says social media and peer pressure may explain why fewer teenagers now identify as gay or bisexual, casting doubt on CDC data trends.
content: A man who spent eight years identifying as a woman is casting doubt on reports of a dramatic decline in teenagers identifying as gay or bisexual, warning that social media and peer pressure may be influencing how young Americans describe their sexual orientation. Walt Heyer, who stopped identifying as a woman roughly 40 years ago and now serves as a senior fellow at the Family Research Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive video interview he remains skeptical of the apparent shift, suggesting some teenagers may be reluctant to openly identify as gay or bisexual because of social pressures. "I don't really believe that there's a big dramatic free fall," Heyer said, referring to recent reports about declining rates of gay and bisexual identification among some teenagers. LOG CABIN REPUBLICANS REMOVES 'T' FROM LGBT ADVOCACY, SAYS 'RADICAL' TRANS ACTIVISTS ARE ERODING GAY SUPPORT "I think what's happening is that, because of social media, there's a lot more influence on people who may not want to fall into that classification on a social media level and will withhold the fact that they are gay or bisexual but really don't want to openly admit it," Heyer said. The comments come after The Washington Post highlighted CDC data showing that the percentage of ninth grade girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual fell from 30% in 2021 to 17% in 2025. The share identifying as bisexual alone dropped from 26% to 13% over the same period. PRISHA MOSELY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME The percentage of boys identifying as gay or bisexual has remained largely unchanged over the past decade, while the share of high school girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual surged after the COVID-19 pandemic before beginning to decline, the Post reported. Heyer, an author and co-author of multiple books, including "Trans Life Survivors" and "Paper Genders," and has spent years working with people questioning their gender identities, argued that social dynamics among young people could complicate attempts to interpret the findings. "I've had actual people in school saying that they're bullied into identifying one way, or they're bullying and bullied to not identify that way," he said. BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS Heyer also said he believes peer and societal pressures are significant factors in kids choosing to identify with something else that is not their biological sex. "What's interesting about that is that many kids are sort of coerced by their peers to say things one way or the other, so I've been very skeptical about what the kids are saying, whether they're gay or bisexual," Heyer said. "I don't really believe that there's a big dramatic free fall. That was, I think, quoted as a free fall in the people identifying as gay or bisexual," he added. "I think what's happening is that, because of social media, there's a lot more influence on people who may not want to fall into that classification on a social media level and will withhold the fact that they are gay or bisexual but really don't want to openly admit it." A DETRANSITIONER CONFRONTED A CALIFORNIA LAWMAKER ON THE HARMS OF GENDER TRANSITION. HERE'S WHY HE SPOKE OUT Simply but perhaps most importantly, Heyer said he thinks adults should do a better job of only affirming what is true. "I think that what I've really discovered is that we know now and have evidence, factual evidence, that nobody has ever changed their gender," Heyer said. "I went through the hormones, had all the surgeries, identified that way. So far in all world history, nobody has actually biologically changed their gender. This is a cosmetic social appearance. It is not a biological change. "And when you come to that conclusion, you realize that really the procedures and these terminologies and labels, what I refer to as God rejecting labels, God rejecting procedures in every aspect. This is the way young people and adults reject God and say God doesn't exist by taking these labels on," he added. DETRANSITIONERS REVEAL HOW DOCTORS PUSHED THEM TOWARD LIFE-ALTERING TREATMENT AS TEENS Heyer also urged researchers to conduct additional studies before concluding that the numbers reflect a lasting shift in sexual identity. "I don't think we're there yet."

title: Former Chicago police detective linked by DNA to 8-year-old girl's cold-case murder, police say
description: DNA evidence and a fingerprint linked Thomas F. McInerney Jr., a former Chicago police detective, to the 1960 cold case murder of Gloria Kowalewicz.
content: A former Chicago homicide detective has been identified as the killer of an 8-year-old girl who disappeared while walking to church in 1960, with authorities now examining other cases that may have involved the officer. Thomas F. McInerney Jr. joined the Chicago Police Department in 1959, just one year before Gloria Kowalewicz was abducted and murdered. He later became a detective investigating violent crimes and remained with the department until retiring in 1987. More than 65 years after the killing, Chicago police confirmed to Fox News Digital that advances in DNA technology and a preserved fingerprint helped investigators identify McInerney, who died in 2006 at age 70. COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH SOLVES TEEN KILLING AFTER SUSPECT LIVED FREE FOR DECADES: 'BETTER BE AFRAID' Gloria disappeared Nov. 12, 1960, after leaving her home shortly before 8 a.m. to attend morning Mass at St. Mary of Mt. Carmel Church, just a few blocks away. Her body was discovered roughly four hours later in a ditch at a forest preserve southwest of Chicago. She had been shot and killed. The murder prompted an extensive investigation, with police interviewing more than 1,300 people and knocking on hundreds of doors. Despite those efforts, the case remained unsolved for decades. Investigators preserved evidence from the crime scene and surrounding area, including a bullet, Gloria's coat and shoes, and a white communion purse containing her prayer book. A fingerprint was also recovered from the purse's strap. DISCARDED TRASH UNCAPS 41-YEAR-OLD MURDER CASE IN RITZY SEASIDE RESORT TOWN, AUTHORITIES SAY Working with the FBI and Illinois State Police, investigators used modern forensic technology to link DNA and the preserved fingerprint to McInerney, according to the department. "McInerney should never have worn the CPD star, and it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive," Chicago police said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. The Cook County State's Attorney's Office is working to identify other cases that may have involved McInerney, according to The Associated Press. KILLER EX-COP EXECUTED FOR CHILD'S SLAYING AS SHERIFF SAYS HE’S SURE SAME MONSTER MURDERED ANOTHER GIRL Police said Gloria's parents died before learning who killed their daughter, but expressed hope that identifying McInerney would bring some closure to those who knew her. McInerney later worked for the Federal Public Defender's Office in Nevada before retiring in 2004, according to the AP. He died two years later without facing charges in Gloria's murder. title: Pentagon pushes hypersonic weapons production as startups slash costs

The cheap ones, the ones that are now the high-end like Patriot and then maybe some hypersonics," said Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marines colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department. The U.S. military is taking an increasing interest in hypersonic weapons, which are maneuverable and travel five times faster than the speed of sound. "These hypersonic systems are now seen as the novel revolutionary system and the ballistic missile is seen as the archaic one," said UC Berkeley Senior Research Scholar Cameron Tracy. US FALLS BEHIND IN HYPERSONIC RACE AS CHINA, RUSSIA GAIN EDGE But the weapons the military has traditionally invested in could come at a cost. Estimates from the Government Accountability Office show missiles for the Army’s long-range hypersonic weapon, the Dark Eagle, could cost more than $40 million each. As the Navy works to equip its Zumwalt Destroyers with hypersonics, the GAO puts estimates at $70 million per missile, which includes costs to develop and incorporate the necessary technologies. The GAO also notes the modernization project is two years behind schedule. "In the long run, for example, the Army thinks that the long-ranged hypersonic weapon will become cheaper as production ramps up," said Xiaodon Liang, arms control association senior policy analyst for Nuclear Weapons Policy and Disarmament. Tomahawk missiles cost around $2.6 million, according to the U.S. Navy. Army budget documents show Patriot missiles cost nearly $4 million. Precision Strike Missiles or PrSMs cost $1.6 million per unit. The U.S. Navy could buy almost 27 tomahawks for the price of one hypersonic missile aboard the Zumwalt Destroyers. The Army could buy around 25 PrSMs for the price of one Dark Eagle hypersonic weapon. "The U.S. has invested in recent years in several of the programs that are starting to become into fruition," said Liang. "These are exquisite weapons. And I think that the military is acquiring them for exquisite purposes." Hypersonic weapons travel up to 20 times faster than traditional missiles and an adversary’s reaction time is thought to be six times shorter. Hypersonic speeds are also vital for both evading enemy defense systems and executing strikes. The Atlantic Council estimates 75% fewer hypersonic weapons would be needed for a mission. US ARMY OFFERING DEFENSE FIRMS 'CONCIERGE ACCESS' TO TEST WEAPONS AT MILITARY RANGES Startups are hoping to bring down some of the costs to produce hypersonic weapons with more affordable missiles and increased testing capabilities. "The weapon itself is under $500,000, which, if you know about munitions, that's incredibly cheap," Castelion co-founder and CEO Bryon Hargis said. The Army and Navy are investing in Castelion's Blackbeard hypersonic weapon, which the company says is designed for mass production. "It is a story about hypersonics and what they can provide in terms of a weapon, but it's really a story of American manufacturing," Hargis said. "The company is focused on providing America options to have that middle deterrence layer, and we're doing that through production." This year, Castelion began building what it says will be the largest dedicated hypersonic weapon production factory in the U.S. Project Ranger is expected to produce thousands of Blackbeard weapons annually. Those will eventually be used to fill Castelion’s various contracts, such as integrating the weapons into the U.S. Navy's F/A-18 Super Hornet Jets, incorporating the system into the U.S. Army’s HIMARS and deploying Blackbeard on unmanned surface vessels. "The advantage of a hypersonic system is that it goes very far, it gets there quickly and it's highly survivable because of that maneuverability. And that's important for achieving deterrence because it's hard to shoot down," Hargis said. Hypersonic weapons remain mostly in Earth’s atmosphere. The missiles are maneuverable during flight and can strike a target quickly, in 15-30 minutes from around 1,725 miles away. US REBUILDING WEAPONS STOCKPILE COULD DELAY ORDERS FROM ALLIES "If you don't know what the target would be initially, unlike a ballistic missile where you can calculate where it'll land, you might misinterpret, for example, an incoming strike as a decapitation attempt. And that would be very concerning," Liang said. Developers say the U.S. speaks with other countries about missile launches and what the intended targets are. But there are other concerns that hypersonic maneuverability could lead to inaccuracy. "Technologies do tend to improve over time as testing and especially as experience with use builds up, but there are pretty important physical constraints on the performance of these systems," said Tracy. Defense contractor Rocket Lab is working with the War Department to improve hypersonic missile capabilities through an increasing number of test launches. INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH "With our HASTE program, what we have enabled is low-cost, high-frequency hypersonic and missile defense testing. And when you can say that you can get that cheaper and faster, now you're looking at more of a shots on goal approach to demonstrating capability of the technology insertion cycle," Rocket Lab Vice President of Global Launch Services Brian Rogers said. Rocket Lab’s HASTE is a suborbital test bed launch vehicle that provides flight test opportunities for the government to advance hypersonic and suborbital system technology development. The vehicle is derived from Rocket Lab’s Electron rocket, which has launched nearly 100 missions. "Rather than saying we need to be stuck in an analysis environment, and then it's a very rigorous test campaign that costs a lot of money and involves a lot people, now you can say we're planning 12 tests this year. We don't have to bet the farm on any one of them, which allows us to take more risk and really move the needle in terms of technology development," Rogers said. The U.S. military has never used a hypersonic weapon but has explored deploying its Dark Eagle to the Middle East. title: Major League Baseball is experimenting with new rules this fall to fundamentally change the sport
description: Beyond the infield shift ban, MLB is now testing outfield positioning rules in the Arizona Fall League to combat plunging fly ball batting averages.
content: Beyond the ill-informed effort to demand an unnecessary salary cap in baseball, one of the primary points of discussion around the sport have been the decline in offensive production. Strikeouts continue to increase, while league-wide batting averages have declined. There's an endless discussion around the importance of situational hitting, of putting the ball in play, and the supposed lack of talent among modern hitters. This "back in my day" thinking is wrong for any number of reasons, including the mountain of data we now have demonstrating it, but it ignores several key factors that have impacted the on-field product. Major League Baseball, though, realizes that the reduced run scoring environment doesn't always make for the most exciting viewing. And they're right. DODGERS DYNASTY ON THE BRINK AFTER THE MILWAUKEE BABIP MACHINE DIALS UP ANOTHER WIN FOR BREWERS One of their initial efforts to combat the surge in run prevention was to restrict infield shifting. For years, infielders were allowed to stand virtually anywhere, including in some extreme cases, in the middle of the outfield. Those shifts significantly reduced the likelihood of ground balls to the pull side turning into hits, as they had for most of baseball history. The league issued some specific guidelines about extreme positioning, essentially requiring shortstops and second basemen to remain on their side of second base, among other changes. Mostly, it worked. League-wide, batting averages on ground balls surged after baseball instituted new rules. Here's how it's looked since 2018: While still low, the mid-.240's represents a significant increase from the shift era. Fans though, might not have noticed more ground ball hits, and the data bears that out. For example, in 2018, there were nearly 54,000 at-bats that ended with a ground ball. In 2026, there were just over 51,000, but a similar number of hits. Ground ball batting average is up, but total overall hits haven't changed. Why would that be? More fly balls. Which is exactly what the league is hoping to address with its potential changes. Thanks to years of data analysis, baseball front offices know that the greatest likelihood of positive outcomes comes from hitting the ball in the air. Theoretically. The best hitters in the league hit the ball hard, and hit in the air. Thanks to the advent of pitch metrics, pitch shaping, and the endless parade of 100mph relievers, hitting in general has gotten harder than ever. Front offices then, have prioritized finding players who might not make contact as frequently, but generate high-quality contact when they do. The data bears that out; outcomes on fly balls and line drives are significantly better than grounders. In 2018, for example, the league hit .402 with a .770 slugging percentage when hitting the ball in the air, compared to .236 with a .258 slugging percentage on ground balls. Here's the problem though, which is what MLB is hoping to address: thanks to the advent of Statcast and the limitless data now available to teams on hitter propensities, defensive positioning is now so good that teams are dramatically reducing success rates on fly balls and liners. We'll get into the data in a minute, but here's a perfect example of this phenomenon from Monday night's NLCS game between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers. To set the scene, the Dodgers had a rally going against Logan Henderson, putting runners at first and second base with nobody out in the top of the third inning in a 1-1 game. Henderson threw Freddie Freeman an awful 0-1 changeup that wound up right in the perfect hitting zone for a left-handed batter. Freeman crushed it, 106.4 mph with a 22 degree launch angle, straight to the right center field gap. Balls put in play with those characteristics are hits 84% of the time, per the league's Statcast page. For the entirety of baseball history, it was a prototypical double. Instead, right fielder Sal Frelick was positioned perfectly, and ran the ball down without even needing to dive. Instead of a bases-clearing double that scores two runs and sets up a potential big inning, it's a fly ball out. Want to know why offense is down? That right there. Despite their reputation as a "play the game the right way" old-school, "back in my day" team, the Brewers use analytics as much, or more, than any team in baseball. title: Judi Dench blasts 'trigger warnings' ruining stories: 'Drives me wild'
description: Actress Judi Dench called trigger warnings in theater and movies "mollycoddling" in her upcoming memoir, arguing audiences should expect to be provoked.
content: Dame Judi Dench decried trigger warnings in theaters and movies as "mollycoddling," telling U.K. outlet The Times Friday that it "drives [her] wild" to see them. The 91-year-old English actress expressed the thoughts in an excerpt for Dench's upcoming memoir, "Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?" As a stage and screen veteran, Dench claimed that placing trigger warnings in front of productions has gone beyond age limits or sound effects. "I think they have gone too far," Dench said. "It's mollycoddling. If you're that sensitive, don't go to the theater. UNIVERSITY THAT PUT OVER 200 TRIGGER WARNINGS ON SHAKESPEARE WRITINGS SAYS REQUEST CAME FROM STUDENTS "By all means, keep the warnings about strobe lighting and gunshots, and obviously there should be age limits for children, but that's about it. Otherwise, where will it end?" Dench also joked that trigger warnings have potentially ruined classic stories by removing surprises and watering down provocative content. "The trigger warnings before 'Titus Andronicus' would be longer than the play. And if you overdo the warnings, doesn’t it take away from the audience’s enjoyment of the story? Do you tell them that the butler did it in an Agatha Christie play so as not to shock them? "Besides, in the safety of a theater or cinema, I want to be triggered, excited, stimulated, provoked and disturbed, to be taken out of my comfort zone. Isn’t that what makes theater and films so thrilling?" Dench said. ‘HOUSE OF THE DRAGON’ STAR MATT SMITH SLAMS TRIGGER WARNINGS ON TV SHOWS: ‘ISN’T BEING SHOCKED THE POINT?’ "And who knows what might trigger people? Balloons, clowns, buttons. ... I have a friend who doesn’t like bananas. She feels physically sick every time she sees one. Should supermarkets put up warning signs in the fruit and veg aisle? It drives me wild." Fox News Digital reached out to Dench's representative for comment. The English actress made similar comments about content advisories in a 2024 interview in which she expressed sympathy for some arguments but ultimately suggested those too sensitive should simply not go to the theater. "I can see why they exist, and it is preparing people, I suppose. But if you’re that sensitive, don’t go to the theater because you could be very shocked," Dench said. BILL MAHER RAILS AGAINST TRIGGER WARNINGS IN COLLEGES, ENTERTAINMENT: 'HOW WEAK MY COUNTRY HAS BECOME' In a comment to Fox News Digital, film critic and "Hollywood in Toto" podcast host Christian Toto called it a "sad state of affairs" that Dench's comments would be considered surprising but celebrated them regardless. "Dench's statement on trigger warnings is obvious, but it still needs to be said today. It's especially helpful coming from an artist. Almost anything in art can be triggering, all depending on the audience. If your beloved dog died last week, any story with a sick pup can be 'triggering.' Art is meant to challenge us, to question our beliefs and offer new perspectives on older ideas. All of the above might be triggering today," Toto said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So deal with it, or don't consume art. This kind of wisdom is rare in Hollywood. Kudos for Dench for lighting the way to sanity."

title: Woman accused of deadly revenge crash faces jury as boyfriend’s hospital account stays out of trial
description: Leigha Mumby's trial opened with prosecutors alleging she turned sharply into woods at nearly 100 mph after a fight over another girl's texts.
content: A Florida woman accused of deliberately crashing an SUV with her boyfriend inside was furious over another girl’s text messages before making a sharp turn into the woods at nearly 100 mph, prosecutors told jurors Tuesday. But Leigha Mumby’s defense attorney offered a different explanation as her trial opened, suggesting something happened inside the vehicle that she neither anticipated nor controlled. Mumby, 25, has pleaded not guilty to vehicular homicide and reckless driving causing serious bodily injury in the death of Daniel Waterman, 22, who survived the crash, but died eight months later. Assistant State Attorney Melissa Clark told jurors the couple had left a Super Bowl party before the Feb. 9, 2025, wreck on Interstate 95 in Flagler County, according to proceedings livestreamed by Court TV. OHIO SUPREME COURT DENIES MACKENZIE SHIRILLA'S LATEST APPEAL BID IN DOUBLE MURDER CASE Clark said the SUV traveled at speeds exceeding 100 mph before the crash. Vehicle data showed it was moving at 94 mph in the final seconds before an "abrupt, left-hand turn at 45 degrees" sent it off the highway and into the woods. The prosecutor described the turn as "a dangerous and reckless maneuver." Waterman suffered a broken neck that left him paralyzed from the neck down, Clark said. He fell into a coma and, after awakening, could not breathe on his own. His death on Oct. 8, 2025, was "directly related and caused by this crash," Clark told the jury, who will not hear Waterman's own account of the crash that he told detectives before he died. He told investigators from his hospital bed that Mumby deliberately swerved off the road following an argument over another woman's text message. A judge ruled those statements inadmissible, leaving prosecutors unable to present his version of events at trial. Defense attorney Reid Hart called the case a "pure and utter tragedy" and urged jurors to consider whether the SUV’s sudden change in direction resulted from something outside Mumby’s control. "The crux of this trial effectively comes down to one steering wheel input, and ultimately one question," Hart said, according to Court TV’s livestream. Hart questioned whether Mumby chose to drive off the road or whether something happened inside the vehicle that "she did not expect, she did not anticipate, and she did not control." He argued that once the vehicle began careening toward the woods, she could not stop it despite trying to avoid the crash. MACKENZIE SHIRILLA'S TEXTS SURFACE AS 'HELL ON WHEELS' DRIVER'S APPEAL COLLIDES WITH NETFLIX'S 'THE CRASH' Jurors also heard Tuesday from Sarah Stappenbeck, Waterman’s cousin and Mumby’s best friend, who hosted the Super Bowl gathering. Stappenbeck testified that Mumby announced earlier that day that she had learned she was pregnant. But the news came alongside concerns about Waterman’s contact with other women. Mumby "expressed concerns of Daniel talking to other girls and said that she wasn’t going to let Daniel cheat on her," Stappenbeck testified. The couple left before the game ended. Within about 20 minutes, Stappenbeck said, Mumby called her, yelling that Waterman was texting another girl and that she planned to bring him back to the house. "She’s yelling at me," Stappenbeck recalled. WATCH: MACKENZIE SHIRILLA’S FATHER CALLS HER ‘A DUMB 18-YEAR-OLD’ WHILE BERATING POLICE IN BODYCAM VIDEO Stappenbeck said she did not hear Waterman speaking in the background. She tried to calm Mumby and urged the couple to get home safely and address their disagreement the following day. "She just said that ‘You’re taking his side,’ and hung up with me," Stappenbeck testified. About 20 minutes later, Mumby called again, still angry, and repeated that she was bringing Waterman back, Stappenbeck said. They never arrived. Instead, Stappenbeck testified, Mumby’s roommate called and told her to go to the hospital because there had been a crash. The trial is unfolding without Waterman’s account to investigators of what happened inside the SUV. Before his death, Waterman told detectives Mumby deliberately caused the wreck after an argument over a text from another woman, according to charging documents previously reported by Court TV. He said the last thing he remembered was Mumby telling him, "I don’t care what happens, you’ll get what you deserve," before swerving off the road. Judge Dawn Nichols ruled those statements could not be introduced at trial. Prosecutors said they wanted jurors to hear Waterman’s account, but acknowledged the rules of evidence prevented them from using it at trial, Court TV previously reported. "The court is bound by the law and the court is bound by the rules of evidence," Nichols said when explaining the ruling. The first day of Mumby’s trial also brought an emotional moment for Waterman’s family. His mother, Heather Waterman, was seen wiping away tears as a photo of her son was shown in court. Court adjourned for the day following Tuesday’s proceedings. Mumby was initially arrested in July 2025 on charges of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. FAMILY OF FATHER-TO-BE WHOSE GIRLFRIEND ALLEGEDLY CRASHED CAR ON PURPOSE SPEAKS OUT THROUGH LAWYER After Waterman died, prosecutors upgraded her charges to include vehicular homicide. She was booked into the Flagler County Jail and released after posting a $150,000 bond. Waterman’s mother previously told Syracuse.com that he spent time in a coma before recovering enough to tell investigators what happened. Waterman’s aunt, Tiffany Waterman, expressed anguish over the exclusion of her nephew’s statements in a Facebook post Monday as jury selection began. She remembered his efforts to comfort a loved one watching a movie beside him in his hospital bed, smiling at her while trying to conceal his pain. "That’s who Daniel was. Protective, loving, and sweet," she wrote. "He had the biggest heart, even in those last moments of life." The family previously told Fox News Digital through attorney John Hager that they supported the charges filed following Waterman’s death. "There are no real winners in this situation. It’s a terrible, horrible situation," Hager said in November 2025, adding that the family believed the charges were "right and just." Mumby gave birth to a baby girl three days after Waterman died, according to WSYR. "Daniel was an excited, soon-to-be father of a baby girl," his obituary said. "He wanted nothing more than to come home to her and to the family who loved him so dearly." Similar case The trial comes amid renewed attention to another deadly crash involving a young woman convicted of intentionally driving into a building with her boyfriend inside. Mackenzie Shirilla is serving two concurrent sentences of 15 years to life for killing her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, 20, and their friend, Davion Flanagan, 19, in a 2022 crash in Strongsville, Ohio, Fox News Digital previously reported. Shirilla’s case became the subject of Netflix’s "The Crash." She was convicted in 2023 after prosecutors argued she deliberately drove into a brick building at nearly 100 mph to end her relationship with Russo. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Ohio Supreme Court recently rejected her request to reconsider its decision, declining to hear her latest appeal. Shirilla has maintained the crash was not intentional. Fox News Digital's Michael Sinkewicz, Greg Norman, and Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

If there is not significant structural change — whether it’s inequities, you know, income inequities or opportunities — the backlash, because, I said this: I got into politics because I said we’ll never find a worse president than George Bush. And I think now, if you think that this is the pinnacle of how bad things can get, I would caution you to rethink that. "And especially if Democrats do all of this, the public turns out, they vote for us and kids still can’t afford a college education, can’t afford housing. That’s going to be a problem." He then predicted that Democrats would regain control of the House, Senate and eventually the presidency in 2028. "This circular dynamic, whereby Democrats or Republicans enter into a narrow majority, only to focus on maintaining power, accumulates a kind of figurative debt against the challenges facing the American people," she said. title: Greta Thunberg joins massive French student protests as cars burn, police fire tear gas
description: Greta Thunberg joined student protesters in France amid over 6,100 arrests and widespread school closures as violent clashes with riot police escalate.
content: Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined student protesters in France on Tuesday after weeks of violent confrontations with police, thousands of arrests and widespread school closures over demands for education reform. The 23-year-old Swedish activist appeared outside a high school in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, where students were demanding more teachers, better facilities and shorter school days, Reuters reported. More than 6,800 people have been detained since the protests began in September, according to French authorities. Demonstrators have set fires, erected barricades and confronted riot police in cities across France, although many protests have remained peaceful. FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION Thunberg, who rose to prominence organizing school strikes over climate change, criticized the French government's response to the demonstrations. "We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," Thunberg told reporters, according to Reuters. She also described the police response as "extremely violent." About 161,500 people marched across France on Tuesday, including 41,500 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. The Education Ministry said 214 schools were closed. FRENCH SCHOOL RIOTS DEEPEN AS EXPERTS POINT TO FAR-LEFT ALLIANCE FUELING ‘BROADER CONFRONTATION’ President Donald Trump weighed in on the turmoil last week, blaming mass migration rather than complaints about education. "What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 6. The demonstrations have become a political flashpoint ahead of France's presidential election next May, with far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon accusing the government of excessive force against young protesters. FRANCE IS DEVOURING ITSELF AS SCHOOL RIOTS REVEAL A CRISIS FAR BIGGER THAN BROKEN CLASSROOMS Mélenchon joined demonstrators in Paris on Tuesday, while right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen has condemned violence by protesters and called for those responsible for damaging schools to pay for repairs. The police response has drawn criticism following an incident last week in which a 15-year-old boy lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade that detonated during a demonstration in Lens. French authorities subsequently suspended the use of the type of stun grenade involved in the incident.French President Emmanuel Macron has called for restraint and dialogue as the demonstrations continue. title: JIM GRAY: Mike Ditka did it his way. Football will never see another like him
description: Jim Gray honors Mike Ditka on SiriusXM NFL Radio with Tom Brady, Bill Belichick, Drew Brees and Matthew Stafford remembering America's Coach.
content: America knew him as a football legend. He became the NFL’s symbol of toughness and the emblem of Chicago. Mike Ditka was more than a Hall of Fame player and head coach who led the Bears to their unforgettable Super Bowl XX championship. He was a man who reached well beyond the football field. Coach Ditka was my partner on the radio for nearly a decade. On our show and podcast this week, "Let’s Go!," broadcast on SiriusXM NFL Radio, I paid tribute to and honored the life of Coach Ditka, along with my fellow co-hosts past and present — Tom Brady, Bill Belichick, Matthew Stafford, Drew Brees and Peter King. They joined me to speak about what Ditka meant to them and to the game of football. Here was our tribute. It's been a very difficult few days since we've learned of the passing of Mike Ditka on Oct. 9, at age 86. Guys like Ditka are very rare. He was a once in a lifetime man. He seemed indestructible. I thought he would beat everything and everyone, and that he just might live forever because a guy like Mike Ditka isn't supposed to die. NFL COACHES SHARE INCREDIBLE MIKE DITKA STORIES AS FOOTBALL WORLD MOURNS THE BEARS LEGEND America's Coach, that's what I called him, and that's who he was. He was my partner on the radio for many, many years. I truly loved him. He was so much fun. He lived his life to the absolute fullest. Tough yet tender. Generous, yet demanding. Funny as hell and a temper that was explosive. He could make you laugh, make you nervous, make you cry, and also feel like the most important person in the room, sometimes all in the same conversation. LIONS HEAD COACH PAYS TRIBUTE TO MIKE DITKA AFTER LEARNING OF HIS DEATH FROM A PRESS CONFERENCE QUESTION He was never polished, never predictable, never interested in being politically correct or being liked by everybody. But perhaps there was no one in sports more beloved by his teammates, by his players, by his colleagues, by his opponents, and even by his critics. MIKE DITKA TRIBUTES POUR IN FROM AROUND THE NFL INCLUDING FANS DRESSING LIKE HIM IN GREEN BAY He was Iron Mike. Da Coach. A man of character, who was, a character. The tombstone of Jackie Robinson reads, "A life is not important, except in the impact it has on other lives." Ditka's impact was enormous on Chicago, the NFL, sports, pop culture, and across the country. I thought he would beat everything and everyone, and that he just might live forever because a guy like Mike Ditka isn't supposed to die. He was bigger than life. Yet, he was always there and available for me personally. He traveled a great distance to introduce me and give the induction the day I was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. His words were heartfelt, helpful, and instructive. "I tell you what an honor this is when you really think about it. I don't know anybody else on this Walk of Fame, but I know you," Ditka said to me and the assembled audience. "What a great honor to be recognized by your peers for your achievements. And I know that you are a professional in everything you do, because when you do it, you do it right. Now I know that there's an art to everything in life. And if there is art to an interview, then you are Michelangelo, believe me, because you are good at that. Now, why is he good? Because he asks tough, hard, fair questions that you've got to answer. And the reason you've got to answer them is because the interview wouldn't work without your answer. And that's what makes him so good. I'm really proud to be your friend. We've been together for a long time," Ditka continued. "Let me tell you something that I know for a fact about life. If you have no critics, you have no successes. God bless you." That sentiment, is so enlightening and edifying to anyone in public life. He knew it, and he chose successes. Critics be damned. Ditka truly had it all. The mustache, cigar, volatility, the winning, the loyalty. He was one of a kind. And for the people who knew him beyond the public persona, there was another side. The one of extraordinary kindness. They saw the moments when the bluster disappeared. Mike Ditka helped, truly helped, so many people. Whether they were fellow players in need, youngsters in crisis, seniors in peril, families that were struggling, or strangers in distress. Ditka was the most generous person I've ever known. I saw his commitment to contribute, respond, and was constantly giving of his time and resources. And he wanted and expected absolutely nothing in return for his countless, truly endless acts of goodwill. That's the part you can't put in a highlight reel, and maybe that's the part that matters most. His life was lived to the lyrics of the song, "My Way." "For what is a man? What has he got? If not himself, then he has not. To say the things he truly feels, and not the words of one who kneels. The record shows I took the blows and did it my way." When somebody like that is gone, you don't just miss what he did. You miss his presence. There will never be another Mike Ditka because as Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, "When nature removes a great man, people explore the horizon for a successor; but none comes, and none will. His class is extinguished with him." Mike Ditka, my dear friend, America's coach, an institution and national treasure, was in a class all his own. Every time we ended a conversation, Mike would never say goodbye. His words would always be, "God bless, Jimmy." So, I won't say goodbye to Coach Ditka. I will follow his lead. God bless, Coach. May God rest your soul and bless your family. *** Here is what the all-time greats had to say during the show about Coach Ditka. This week’s episode of "Let’s Go!" can be heard here. Tom Brady, 7 time Super Bowl winning quarterback: "There are so many things I loved about Coach Ditka from watching from afar and getting to know him over the course of my NFL career. He was as tough as the city that he coached in and he was the first tight end ever in the Hall of Fame. I heard Gronk on the pregame show say he owed a lot to Coach Ditka. Without Coach Ditka, there are no players like Rob Gronkowski who revolutionized the tight end position. And without Rob Gronkowski, I'm down a bunch of Super Bowls. So I gotta thank Coach Ditka for a lot of reasons. He won a Super Bowl as a player, he won a Super Bowl as a head coach. And as a quarterback, I always know what a great tight end means to an offense. He is my safety valve. That's your third down answer. And every one I ever threw to owes something to Mike." Tom Brady: "On TV, he also revolutionized the game with his media career. He never softened on a word. There was never a filter. There was no fluff. It was just all football. Rest easy, Coach Ditka." Bill Belichick, 6 time Super Bowl winning head coach: "As a player, Mike was extremely tough, competitive, all business, a guy you certainly didn't wanna mess with and he set the tone for the teams that he played on. It was similar as a coach. He had that same toughness that transferred to his team and, and players. And you knew anytime you went up against him, like you were going to be in an absolute brawl and fight all the way to the finish because that's the way he and his teams competed. Loved Mike. Loved Mike and what he meant to the game. And we'll miss him." Matthew Stafford, NFL MVP Los Angeles Rams quarterback: "I had the pleasure of being on some of the NFL shows with him. You know, his presence was really something else. All these guys, they play football, they coach football, then they move to talking about football and they become just a guy that talks about football. But Ditka was always coach, right? I mean, and I remember, getting to do those shows with him. He had the cigar unlit under the table. He was just true to himself and that was such a cool thing to be a part of." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Drew Brees, Hall of Fame, Super Bowl-winning quarterback: "He was not only an incredible player, but an incredible coach. There's a type of leadership where you just see things happen before they happen. You just have a vision for what the way that things should be, and then your contributions to getting it to that point. It's a rare trait. I think Mike was no question, was certainly one of those guys and man, he's gonna be missed." Peter King, Award-winning NFL sportswriter: "Nothing ever about Mike Ditka was invented, was put on anything. He always was himself. Ditka, as a player, as a coach, as a broadcaster, was authentic and he was perfect and he was dedicated to be great at whatever he did at that moment." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

title: Coast Guard firefight puts US, Mexico at odds despite coordinated border operations
description: A U.S. Coast Guard firefight near the Rio Grande sparked a dispute with Claudia Sheinbaum, who demanded evidence that gunfire came from Mexico.
content: A firefight involving U.S. Coast Guard personnel along the Mexican border has sparked a dispute between Washington and Mexico City over where the gunfire originated, even as the two countries continue coordinating border security operations. The Coast Guard told Fox News Digital that personnel conducting joint interdiction operations near Garceno, Texas, came under fire from the Mexican side of the border Sept. 26 and returned fire. No injuries or damage to Coast Guard vessels or equipment were reported, and the incident remains under investigation. After U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson publicly announced that Coast Guard personnel had come under fire, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum demanded evidence that the shots originated from her country's territory. "We asked for all the evidence ​ because we have no evidence," Sheinbaum told reporters in Mexico City, saying Mexican security forces had not detected shots originating from their territory. MEXICO VOWS US WILL PAY AFTER ICE FATALLY SHOOTS ILLEGAL MIGRANT WHO ALLEGEDLY ATTEMPTED TO RAM AGENT WITH CAR The State Department, however, told Fox News Digital that information about the shooting had been shared with Mexican authorities. "U.S. Coast Guard personnel were fired upon from Mexican territory on September 26, and we have shared the available information with the Government of Mexico through official channels," a State Department spokesman said. The department did not specify what was shared or when, and U.S. officials have not publicly identified the shooters or detailed how they determined the gunfire's origin. TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER The incident occurred amid Operation River Wall, a Coast Guard initiative launched in October 2025 to deter illegal migration, drug smuggling and other threats along approximately 300 miles of the Rio Grande. "Over the past year, the Coast Guard has expanded operations in the region, deploying more than 1,000 personnel and more than 30 assets," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital, referring to "Operation Sable". Separately, Mexico's Navy Ministry, led by Secretary Raymundo Morales-Angeles, said 159 "Naval elements", 11 vehicles and two drones were deployed to the Tamaulipas sector. U.S. Northern Command (NORTHCOM) separately told Fox News Digital that American troops are being repositioned to the Rio Grande Valley in anticipation of a seasonal increase in attempted illegal border crossings. Asked whether Mexico had received evidence from U.S. authorities or launched its own investigation, a representative for Mexican Ambassador to the U.S. Roberto Lazzeri Montaño referred Fox News Digital on Monday to Sheinbaum's more recent remarks addressing the incident. Sheinbaum said Mexico's military ministry "maintains" communication with NORTHCOM and the Coast Guard and that a "mirror operation" coordinated with the U.S. remains active. "We want to have a good relationship with the United States within the framework of our sovereignty, our territorial integrity, mutual trust, and coordination without subordination," she said. Her response did not explicitly confirm whether Mexico had received the information Washington says it shared. Fox News Digital also contacted Sheinbaum's office for comment. LATIN AMERICA’S CONSERVATIVE SHIFT FACES ITS BIGGEST TEST YET IN BRAZIL ELECTION Santiago Vidal Calvo, a Venezuelan-born immigration analyst at the Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital that Sheinbaum's approach to border security is shaped by pressure from Washington and a broader Latin American shift toward right-wing governments. "She has that regional pressure [and] she has the international pressure from the United States" to cooperate on security matters, Calvo said. He suggested Sheinbaum's demand for evidence of the Coast Guard shooting could reflect pressure within her own political coalition to justify working with the Trump administration. "She has a high bar to meet if she wants to ally with the Trump administration internally within her own party and her own government," Calvo said. "We've got to understand this through the lens of what is going on in Latin America. I do think that Sheinbaum's position is substantially different today than it was when Trump got elected," Calvo said. His assessment reflects Sheinbaum's ties to the left-wing Morena Party and the political legacy of her predecessor, former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, commonly known as AMLO. Calvo characterized Sheinbaum as the "last bastion of Latin American socialism," arguing that she could face additional regional pressure if Flávio Bolsonaro defeats President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil's upcoming presidential runoff. Calvo suggested that the rightward shift among South American governments could increase pressure on Sheinbaum to cooperate with Washington on security matters. He said she may face questions about whether "you're the only president of Latin America who's not cooperating with the United States in terms of security?" "Both of those things do lead to a more serious border campaign for both countries," Calvo said. "I have no doubt that the change in South America from left-leaning governments to right-leaning governments has to do with the Trump administration's policy in Latin America," he added. US CHARGES MEXICAN GOVERNOR, TOP OFFICIALS IN CARTEL CONSPIRACY AS MEXICO FIRES BACK OVER PROOF Border security policy analyst Simon Hankinson told Fox News Digital that gunfire near the Rio Grande is not unprecedented, citing accounts he heard during previous visits to the border. Hankinson said cartel involvement was possible but expressed doubt that Mexican military personnel would deliberately fire across the border unless they were acting against orders. title: Massive fire destroys 400-year-old food market, leaving historic landmark in ruins
description: Flames tore through the Enfants Rouges market in Paris, destroying about 20 vendor stalls inside the historic market founded in 1615. It was the city's oldest covered food market.
content: Marché des Enfants Rouges, the oldest covered food market in Paris, was engulfed in flames in the early hours of Monday, Oct. 12, destroying vendor stalls and a piece of local history. The fire broke out around 3 a.m. Monday, with firefighters working for several hours to quell the flames, Reuters reported. The fire left the market in ruins, with about 20 merchants losing their stalls, according to Ariel Weil, the mayor of central Paris. CELEBRITY CHEF LEAVES ONE ICONIC INGREDIENT OUT OF HER COOKING AND DINERS CAN'T TELL "Fire brought under control but market totally devastated. Avoid the area around Rue de Bretagne," Weil said in a post on X on Monday morning. "9 hoses, including 2 high-powered ones, were required to bring the disaster under control," Brigade des Sapeurs-Pompiers de Paris (BSPP), the city's primary fire and rescue service, said in a post on X. "150 firefighters were mobilized tonight," Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire posted on X. "I want to express my full gratitude to them." He added that an investigation is underway to determine the cause of the fire. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We will find temporary locations for the businesses so that all their activities can be maintained," the post said. Located in the Marais district of Paris in the city's 3rd arrondissement, the market was founded in 1615 during the reign of King Louis XIII. A popular destination for both tourists and locals, the market drew people from all over the world, according to the website for the city of Paris. The name translates directly to "Market of the Red Children," a moniker that came from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges, where the children usually wore red, according to the city's website. Before its destruction, the market housed restaurants where people could sit down for a meal or a cocktail. ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME Omar’s husband is at the center of one of the congresswoman's most prominent controversies after her financial disclosure filings decreased significantly in reported worth within the span of one filing period. title: Actress Amanda Seyfried rejected TV role over nonstop sex scenes, refused to get 'naked with a stranger'

content: Actress Amanda Seyfried revealed during a Sunday conversation with Alec Baldwin at the Hamptons International Film Festival in East Hampton, New York, that she rejected a television series because of its frequent sex scenes, explaining that she has become increasingly uncomfortable performing intimate scenes as she gets older. "I passed on a show where I would have to have sex all the time because of the sex. Doesn't matter [who it's with]… I don't want to do it. I'm uncomfortable with it. I'm not into it right now," Seyfried said, according to People Magazine. Seyfried's decision echoes concerns raised by other Hollywood actresses, including Gina Gershon, who told Fox News Digital in March that she rejected a starring role in the 1981 horror film "Friday the 13th Part 2" after learning her character would appear topless. "I was offered a lead in that movie," Gershon said, adding that the nudity "definitely felt kind of exploitative to me." "Maybe if [the project] came along again [at a later point], maybe I'd be in a different space. But I don't want to deal with being naked with a stranger," Seyfried said. The Oscar-nominated actress previously acknowledged feeling pressured to participate in uncomfortable scenes when she was younger. In a 2022 interview with Porter magazine, Seyfried described participating in scenes without underwear at 19 because she feared upsetting people and jeopardizing her career. "Oh, I know why: I was 19, and I didn't want to upset anybody and I wanted to keep my job. That's why," Seyfried said. SYDNEY SWEENEY DEFENDS 'EUPHORIA' NUDITY AND REVEALS A POLE DANCING SCENE WAS CUT FROM SEASON THREE Other actresses have described similar experiences. "Someone threatened to sue me once because I didn't want to do this sex scene in a certain way," Ricci said. Keira Knightley previously revealed that becoming a mother changed her willingness to appear nude on camera. The actress incorporated a no-nudity clause into her contracts, allowing her greater control over intimate scenes. CATE BLANCHETT MOURNS HOW #METOO GOT 'KILLED VERY QUICKLY,' STILL 'SYSTEMIC LAYER OF ABUSE' Not every actress has taken the same approach. Hollywood has introduced additional protections for actors filming intimate scenes. Jessica Steinrock, an intimacy coordinator, told Fox News Digital that coordinators help establish expectations and consent during production. "[Intimacy Coordinator] is a relatively new role. It really hit its stride kind of in 2018 when HBO made their commitment to having an intimacy coordinator on all their film sets," she said. "An intimacy coordinator is there to provide safety and framework for scenes of intimacy. Those are scenes of simulated sex, simulated genital contact, or scenes of nudity." title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons remove part of right lung, Vatican says
description: Pope Leo XIV arrived at Gemelli Hospital in Rome for lung nodule removal after doctors said the growth was identified at a "very early stage." Doctors later confirmed he had a form of lung cancer.
content: Pope Leo XIV underwent a procedure at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital in Rome to remove a small nodule on his lung Tuesday, the Vatican said. The 71-year-old pontiff underwent thoracic surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung and doctors confirmed he had lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer, according to a statement released by the Holy See Press Office. The diagnosis was confirmed through a tissue examination conducted during the operation, consistent with findings from preoperative tests, the Vatican said. The pope spent approximately three hours in the operating room, although the surgery itself lasted about 90 minutes. Doctors said the procedure was successful and there were no complications. POPE LEO ANNOUNCES TUMOR ON LUNG, SURGERY PLANNED IN 'NEXT FEW DAYS' Leo awoke normally following surgery and, after a brief observation period, returned to his room on the hospital's 10th floor, according to the statement from Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora. "Doctors found a small lump in the lung," Leo said after an Angelus address at St. Peter's Square on Monday. "It was identified at a very early stage and well situated." "The doctors consider it appropriate to intervene and so, following their advice, I decided to have surgery to remove it," he continued. "The surgery is already scheduled for the next few days. I thank you for your spiritual closeness and I rely on your prayer." The Vatican's latest statement confirmed that the surgery involved the removal of the lower lobe of the pope's right lung using a video-assisted technique. POPE LEO XIV BEGINS HISTORIC 4-DAY VISIT TO FRANCE The announcement comes as a surprise for the American-born pontiff, who has no previously known health problems and is known for maintaining an active lifestyle. POPE LEO VISITS SITE OF MIRACLE CURES, MEETS PEOPLE WHOSE UNEXPLAINED HEALINGS STUNNED DOCTORS Leo regularly plays tennis and swims at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo, according to The Associated Press. Archbishop Ronald Hicks of New York offered his support to the pope, saying that the Holy Father is "in our prayers.""We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation," Archbishop Hicks said. "I know that I join with people from all corners of this archdiocese, across the country, and around the world in keeping the Holy Father in our prayers." The pope is also scheduled to embark on a major international trip from Nov. 6–17, with planned stops in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It remains unclear whether his surgery and recovery will affect those travel plans. UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS In addition to addressing his health, Leo used his Sunday remarks to renew his appeal for peace in war-torn Ukraine, warning that the conflict continues to inflict suffering far beyond the country's borders. title: A Dodgers-less World Series would hurt now, but help MLB later | Bobby Burack
description: The Milwaukee Brewers are now World Series betting favorites over the Los Angeles Dodgers after taking a commanding 2-0 lead in the NLCS.
content: For the first time this season, the Los Angeles Dodgers are not the betting favorites to win the World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers, who lead the Dodgers 2-0 in the NLCS, are the betting favorites to win the World Series. Despite the funeral arrangements demoralized Dodgers are making, Los Angeles isn't eliminated yet. The Blue Jays overcame a 2-0 deficit in the ALCS to defeat the Mariners just last season. Fifteen other teams have done the same. Those aren't great odds, but as Dodgers fans kept reminding everyone while assembling their superteam, baseball is inherently random. Teams get hot. Players go cold. Great lineups disappear for a week. Struggling pitchers suddenly look formidable. We are not writing off this Dodgers team until someone actually eliminates it. Even so, the prospect of a Dodgers-less World Series feels real for the first time in a while. DODGERS DYNASTY ON THE BRINK AFTER THE MILWAUKEE BABIP MACHINE DIALS UP ANOTHER WIN FOR BREWERS That said, the prospect of a Dodgers-less World Series feels real for the first time in a while. In the short term, a Brewers-Rays/Guardians World Series would hardly be MLB's dream matchup. As pure a form of baseball as those clubs play, they are small-market teams without much national appeal. For comparison, the past two World Series featuring the Dodgers, against the Yankees in 2024 and Blue Jays in 2025, averaged around 15.3 million viewers. In 2023, the Texas Rangers-Arizona Diamondbacks World Series averaged just 9 million. A Brewers-Rays/Guardians matchup would probably land much closer to the 2023 number, barring a long, dramatic seven-game series. However, the long-term gains off the Dodgers missing the World Series could prove worth the smaller viewership this season. The Dodgers have been World Series favorites for nearly the entirety of the past three years, dating back to the signing of Shohei Ohtani in December 2023. There was a brief stretch during Game 7 of last year's World Series when the Dodgers were trailing and the Toronto Blue Jays had shorter live odds. Los Angeles ultimately came back to win, clinching its second straight championship. The Dodgers entered 2026 as even heavier favorites than the past two years after adding Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in the offseason. Then, in August, they traded for Tarik Skubal, arguably the best pitcher in baseball. ESPN MLB insider Jeff Passan likened the 2026 Dodgers to the Avengers, citing their unprecedented collection of star power. The back-to-back champions adding more stars while much of the league declines to spend or trade aggressively has intensified discussion about a potential lockout and demands for a salary cap. Various outlets — including this one and this author — have argued that the growing disparity between the Dodgers and much of MLB is "ruining baseball." To be clear, the Dodgers are not at fault for relentlessly trying to improve. They are doing exactly what every fan should want their team to do. The criticism is directed at a system that allows such a competitive imbalance to develop in the first place. Or, at least, the perception of one. As the NFL has demonstrated, fans need to believe their team has a chance. It doesn't even have to be true. The same handful of franchises tend to contend for the Super Bowl every year. But constant roster turnover gives most fanbases enough reason to talk themselves into hope before each season. Jets and Dolphins fans are, of course, excluded from this demonstration. That becomes harder in baseball when fans suspect their franchise is more likely to trade its homegrown stars to the Dodgers than build around them. The Detroit Tigers' handling of Skubal is an example of that. There's a reason spoiling movies is considered so obnoxious. People don't want to know the ending before the story begins. If the Dodgers erase a 2-0 deficit, advance to the World Series and win a third consecutive championship — still the second-most likely outcome of the postseason, according to sportsbooks — MLB will have an increasingly difficult time convincing fans that the rest of the league isn't playing for second place. It will also become harder to argue that stricter payroll rules aren't necessary. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Technically, MLB's scriptwriters would prefer the Dodgers to come back, reach the World Series, and then dramatically lose Game 7. That would deliver the television audience in the short term without reinforcing the idea that baseball's richest superteam is inevitable in the long term. Still, if we're talking strictly about the long-term health of the sport, the small-market Brewers knocking off perhaps the greatest baseball team ever assembled on paper would suffice.

title: DAVID MARCUS: On the ground in Middle America, four issues will decide the senate, and none are affordability
description: Fraud in Minnesota, growth in Ohio, and culture in Texas are driving 2026 midterm election races more than affordability, ground reporting reveals.
content: For nearly a year now, the assumption from the chattering classes has been that the 2026 midterm election will be decided on the issue of affordability, but on the ground, in the mid-American states that will decide control of the senate, it is local issues that dominate, not the vague, overarching question of prices. Part of the problem with nationalizing the affordability issue is that it originated in New York City with the campaign of current socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani. But Gotham is a unique case that is always very expensive. The last time Manhattan was affordable was when the Dutch bought it from the Indians. In the middle of the country, including Michigan, Ohio, Minnesota, and Texas, all of which this column has visited in the past month, the economy is a major issue, as polls indicate, but it is not the same existential crisis that it was for voters we spoke with in 2022 or 2024. DAVID MARCUS: IN SPRINGFIELD, OHIO, ONLY TRUMP CAN MEND MAGA-CHAMBER OF COMMERCE RIFT I met Reggie at a restaurant in Springfield, Ohio. He’s recently married, reading self-help books, and in construction, he told Fox News Digital, "There’s work, wages are good, that’s not an issue, prices are prices, and gas has gone down with the tax holiday." Reggie was referring to Ohio’s decision to temporarily suspend gas tax, resulting in a price under four dollars in the Buckeye State. DAVID MARCUS: IN DAYTON, OHIO, BOTH PARTIES FACE BITTER POLITICAL DESPONDENCY In fact, in no state this column visited did it seem as if cost of living was the prime driver of the electorate. So what is it? Let’s take it state by state. Minnesota: Fraud The cleanest and clearest way to know what issue is driving any community of voters is when they bring something up before you do, and in Minnesota, almost everyone I spoke with brought up fraud with no coaxing. DAVID MARCUS: PEGGY FLANAGAN'S DEI RECORD AND FRAUD SCANDAL PUT MINNESOTA SENATE RACE IN THE SPOTLIGHT Over the past year, the scope and scale of fraud in Minnesota’s Somali community has come to shocking light and it is something that Democratic Lt. Gov. and Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan cannot escape, and that her GOP challenger, Michelle Tafoya is rightfully milking like a top-prize heifer at the Minnesota state fair. When it comes to the economy, Americans are not in fear, but they do have questions and doubts. This is a race that almost nobody expected to be competitive just a few months ago, but that is because pundits were reading the national mood, not the mood in Minnesota, which can only be found on the ground, and which is very angry. Ohio: Creating Growth Dayton, Ohio is full of absolutely lovely people, many of whom I spoke with, and I wish I could say kinder things about it, but it is an all but a dead city. Stunningly beautiful buildings sit abandoned, like coarse reminders of better days. What Daytonites, as well as Ohians in general, want and need is growth. It's not that they can’t afford their lives, it's that their communities do not thrive, do not grow, and they want to know if a once great state can be great again. THE BLUE WAVE LOOKS REAL UNTIL YOU LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER In the race between Republican incumbent Sen. John Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown, the winner will be the one who can convince Ohio voters that they have a plan to bring cities like Dayton back. Michigan: Sustaining Growth Compared to Dayton, Ohio, Grand Rapids, Michigan seems like Oz. As my Uber driver told me on the drive in, "Everyone I take back to the airport raves about the city. You will, too." And here we are. Like Detroit, which this column also recently visited, Grand Rapids is a buzzing town, neat-necktied producers of wealth roam the streets discussing deals and going to lunch. You also see kids in a downtown that screams not just wealth, but authenticity. LIZ PEEK: TWO TROUBLED SENATE RACES COULD SPOIL DEMOCRATS' BLUE-WAVE FANTASY In the race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for senate, the primary issue is who can sustain the growth that Michigan has experienced, and who gets the credit: Democrat Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, or President Donald Trump. Texas: Culture Texas is another state where the most pressing issue is not economic, but rather, in this case, cultural. Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton has universally been tagged as the worst candidate of 2026, and yet not only is he a successful attorney general, he is also undeniably Texan, for all his big faults. In James Talarico, Democrats have a once vegan, Unitarian-style Christian, who has admitted his biggest concern in life is making sure trans kids can get access to controversial surgical procedures. Now that Talerico is back from his two week bout of the flu, the cultural questions will be coming hot and heavy, and he has no good answer for them. EVERYONE IS WATCHING TEXAS AND MICHIGAN. title: 'Moonshiners' stars challenge notorious warning that outlaw liquor can make you go blind
description: Mark Ramsey and Digger Manes from "Moonshiners" challenge stereotypes about Appalachia's distillers as home distilling battles reach the Supreme Court.
content: Moonshine’s reputation is enough to make your eyes water. For generations, Americans have been warned that the notorious outlaw liquor could leave them blind. But "Moonshiners" stars Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes say there's more behind that warning than most people realize. "There's a huge different thought process behind moonshine than there was, say, in the '40s, '30s, early years," Manes told Fox News Digital. KENNY LAW, 'MOONSHINERS' STAR, DEAD AT 68 "There was a lot of propaganda out there. It was said that it could make you go blind, make you die, make you go crazy, make you get the jack leg. The government was the one that was poisoning the industrial alcohol the people were stealing to make bathtub gin." Historical records support part of Manes' account. During Prohibition, the federal government required industrial alcohol to contain toxic additives to discourage people from drinking it, according to the Smithsonian Channel. Some of that alcohol was diverted into the illegal liquor market and sold for consumption, although it was distinct from traditionally distilled moonshine. The consequences were deadly. According to the Smithsonian Channel, 66 people died in New York City on Christmas Day 1926 after consuming poisoned industrial alcohol. The city's medical examiner, Charles Norris, blamed the federal government's practice of adding toxic substances to industrial alcohol, including those involving methyl alcohol, also known as methanol, which can cause blindness and death. WATCH: ‘MOONSHINERS’ STARS REVEAL THE TRUTH BEHIND A MISUNDERSTOOD TRADITION But not every warning about illicit liquor was a scare tactic. Ramsey acknowledged that moonshine posed genuine health risks in earlier generations, particularly when distillers unknowingly used dangerous materials to build their equipment. "Back in the day, there were people who had health issues because of moonshine," Ramsey explained. "The solder that they used to build the pots had lead in it back in the day, and they didn't know that it was happening. So once it was discovered that the solder had lead in it, even the old timers here, when they built their stills, they no longer soldered their joints on the inside of the pots. All the solder connections were on the outside where the mash never touched the solder anymore." "So yeah, it caused some issues, but it was strictly an accident," he said. "They just didn’t know any better." While moonshine does not inherently cause blindness, improperly produced spirits can contain dangerous levels of methanol, a toxic form of alcohol. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that methanol poisoning can damage the optic nerve, causing permanent vision loss or death. "Moonshiners," which is now in its 16th season, premiered in 2011. The series follows "a diverse group of people living in Appalachia who carry on a 200-year-old tradition passed down from their forefathers, making moonshine," according to the show's synopsis. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Distillers can legally produce and sell spirits marketed as moonshine if they comply with federal, state and local licensing, taxation and other requirements. Federal law generally prohibits producing distilled spirits at home for personal consumption, according to the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, although recent court rulings have challenged the constitutionality of certain restrictions. According to The Washington Post, federal appeals courts have issued conflicting rulings on a federal restriction on home distilling dating back to 1868. In April 2026, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a federal restriction prohibiting distilled spirits plants from operating in homes and certain other locations was unconstitutional. Days later, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reached the opposite conclusion, upholding the restriction as a "necessary and proper means" of collecting liquor taxes, the outlet reported. The Hobby Distillers Association and four individual plaintiffs challenged the restriction in the 5th Circuit case, according to The Washington Post. Supporters of legal home distilling hope overturning the restriction could spark a "craft spirits revolution." The legal battle has since reached the Supreme Court. In July, John Ream, the plaintiff in the 6th Circuit case, asked the justices to review the ruling. The Justice Department filed a separate petition in August, seeking to overturn the 5th Circuit's decision. Ramsey also challenged longstanding stereotypes about "moonshiners." CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "A lot of times, people give it a bad name because they just see it as poison and a bunch of heathens out doing stuff they shouldn’t do," he said. "And moonshiners, as a rule, are very, very good people. They were just simply doing what they had to do to survive back in the day." "[Moonshine] didn't actually sell in Appalachia," Ramsey said. "It went farther north: Ohio, Detroit, New York, the East Coast. ... One of my friends told me ... he took a load of liquor to Ohio and said, 'Them fellas up there, they get it. And every one of them said, 'God bless them hillbillies.'" "The liquor business back in the day, the heyday of it, probably wouldn't have flourished here in Appalachia so prominently had it not been for our northern neighbors buying it," Ramsey said. "So we had a reason to make it, and they had a reason to want it." "We were broke, but could make liquor," Manes added. "And they had money and could buy it." Ramsey is also optimistic about the future of moonshine. He said a new generation of distillers is eager to carry on the tradition. "As we saw in previous seasons … we always want to know who's going to fill our shoes, who's going to carry the torch forward," he said. "[And] we have so many good distillers up and coming. I think it's got a future, a very healthy one. Things will change. It's been argued that the best drink of liquor hasn't been made yet, so they've got something to shoot for." "You make do with what you've got, and you don't let the situation you're standing in drag you down. You keep going forward." For Manes, preserving the tradition comes down to pride in his craft. "To me, it's more the pride," he said. "It's no different. I don't know what hobby you may have. It may be painting. You may paint pictures. Well, if you do a beautiful portrait, and you stand back, and you look at it, you think, 'Wow, that really does look good.'" Manes said he gets that same satisfaction from turning simple ingredients into moonshine. "We take what other people would consider slop — that’s the conglomeration of cornmeal and sugar — and make a crystal-clear product that tastes good," he said. "And we love it."
