If you were to tell me 15 months ago that Jr. would be where he's at with cross country, I would've called you insane, yet here we are. Guys, how are some of you still just finding out about Front Row Amy? In 2012, I came up with a bit called "Tweet Her Seat" where I bought Front Rom Amy's seat from her (she used to sell tickets to this seat on eBay) and I had a Playboy model friend sit in the seat and take over the Busted Coverage Twitter account to interact with fans. I'm talking the early days of Twitter. It helped build the account, there's no doubt about that. That feels like a lifetime ago. That's how long Amy has been sitting in this exact seat. Readers are still fired up over full integrity golf – Paul in La Crosse, WI shares how his group plays: First, some background. I've been in a golf league 20 years. The league was originally a church mens club league and has been active 52 years. It is no longer church men's club exclusive (they accepted me!). We play Tuesday afternoons at a small 32 par executive course. This is only the 2nd course the league has ever played on. The original, Hillview Golf Course, was a little par 27 course created on farm pasture. Thousands of kids learned to golf there. As some leagues go, we have hole prizes, side games and some non-standard golf rules. To keep the flow moving on the course (we play one group after another) gimmee's on putts were allowed but can only be offered by your playing partner that day. Some players started taking advantage and would assume the gimmee. A couple years ago, in another effort to "keep it movin", the gimmee rule changed to putter length. Hardly any of us are that good/consistant (50+ people in the league). Players have been complaining. Putter lengths obviously differ and matches could be won/lost. So, for next years golf season, the rule has reverted to playing partner gimmee only. – John in Murfreesboro, TN emails: I don't really have a full integrity golf story, but I will say I don't take gimmes unless they're inside 1 foot. Even then, I'll putt most of them, unless we're trying to keep pace. Hole out, that's how I was taught. But it is amazing how quick others are to give you a putt that's not a gimme at all. Having said that, I usually play just to have fun, so sometimes the rules get bent. Being against a tree and in danger of hitting a root? No thanks, move it out. Take an unplayable if you're being completely honest with yourself. In the middle of the fairway but in some idiot's divot? Uh uh. I don't report scores for handicap, never play tournaments, etc., so no one cares what my scorecard reads. I don't even tell my wife when I get home (she doesn't care anyway). I play to enjoy the game and sometimes the rules get in the way of that. I don't usually remember my score anyway, I remember the good shots I hit that day, and try to forget the bad ones! – Jonathan D. makes his Screencaps debut: I have never played 100% "down" because I feel if I m in the middle of the fairway and find a dead spot, I m going to roll in out. Not closer to the hole and not 3 feet away but within 18 inches back or lateral. That being said, the last 2 years I have played all my shots down and whether with my buddies or with my legit handicapped league (my dad's old man group that I play with during the summers), I play them down. It has been some of the most rewarding and frustrating rounds of my life. 50 rounds in just the last 2 summers. I am an elementary school teacher, so most of my golf is summer time. Happily divorced which is the reason I can play so much! I always hovered in the low to mid 80s when I improved my ball position or took mulligan (we often allow 1 on each 9). Over 2 summers, my legit handicap is 13 with some rounds near +18 and others at +8. Last summer I was consistently +18-20. This summer I got it consistently at +10-12. I am not a pro nor do I put in that time. But I take so much more pride in my game now than I ever have before. My dad was a legit scratch (played HS, college and some mini senior tours in his 50s). He is now a +6 (72 years old) and still kicks my ass on the regular. Lol! I'll out drive him by 40 yards and he'll birdie to my bogey. Golf is a special bond that we have. He told me how proud he is that I have gotten my game where it s at. I really don't care what I shoot when we play, as long as we play. Hard to go back to shaving strokes when it's laid out like that...at least for me it is. – Strat says he'll play whatever he wants to play: I play only if the other three guys will play best ball on every shot, on every hole; I always improve my lie; I play a "Mulligan" anywhere, anytime. It’s a social outing, not a competition. We have fun! – 13 handicap Kenny writes: I split my time between Texas and Colorado. In Tx, I play with guys for some money. 1$ skins, $5 gereenies on par 3s, lots of side bets, etc. we all play by the rules, because we r betting money. In CO, it’s a different story. I play with lots of retired folks and there is no betting. So, almost all folks take multiple mulligans (breakfast balls), move their golf ball around, kick it from behind trees , etc. i don’t mind since we’re not playing for money. However, one incident really pissed me off. On a par 4, i drove the ball well. Then, hit the approach on the green. Long downhill putt. I left myself an 8 foot par putt (uphill) and made the putt. Whew. Another guy in the group, hit his tee shot into the water. Re-teed, taking a mulligan. Then, hit his drive left of the cart path in a log of "fescue". He was in really rough stuff, embedded under a bush. He "placed" his ball on a tuft of grass away from the bush. Then, he hit a pretty good shot to the apron of the green. He putt from the apron to 3 1/2 feet. He then, gives the putt to himself and says "wow, That was a good par" to all of us. I couldn’t believe it. He had a 7 and then claimed he had a "great par". I would not mention this if he hadn’t been so proud of his "par". Just insane !!! HAHAHAHAHAHAHA...POLITICS IS REALLY HEATING UP! Please make it all end. Maybe that's the plan. Wear us down with stupidity. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! title: Birth tourism sells American citizenship, and Trump is shutting it down
description: Marco Rubio's new visa policy targets foreign operators and fixers who coach pregnant women to lie on applications as part of birth tourism schemes.
content: American citizenship is not a hotel amenity, yet a global industry markets access to it as part of an expensive travel package. Foreign operators recruit pregnant women, coach them to lie in visa applications and consular interviews, arrange their travel and housing, and then bank tens of thousands of dollars to arrange the birth of their child on American soil. President Donald Trump’s administration is changing the enforcement strategy by treating birth tourism as a business designed to circumvent U.S. immigration laws. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently announced a new visa policy targeting the people who knowingly sustain that business, including visa "fixers" who coach applicants to commit fraud and foreign medical providers who knowingly facilitate such travel or the fraudulent use of Medicaid. Rather than stopping with individual travelers who misrepresent their plans, this policy follows the money to the operators who recruit them, coach them to lie and profit from the deception. These fixers can simply move from one paying customer to the next unless enforcement dismantles the business behind the fraud. President Trump understands that ending this birth-tourism black market requires consequences for the people selling access to American citizenship. TRUMP ADMIN PUTS ALLEGED 'BIRTH TOURISM' SCHEME ON NOTICE AS EXPERT DELIVERS WARNING TO HOSPITALS It is important to note that traveling while pregnant or seeking legitimate medical treatment with the appropriate visa and truthful disclosures is not illegal. However, immigration fraud occurs when someone materially misrepresents the purpose, duration or destination of a trip to obtain admission under false pretenses. The State Department explicitly prohibits using a visitor visa when the traveler’s primary purpose is to give birth in the United States so that a child obtains U.S. citizenship. As an immigration attorney and an immigrant who came to America legally, I know firsthand that our immigration system relies on truthful representations in visa applications. A visitor visa permits temporary travel for a specific purpose. If we fail to enforce those limits, the visa process becomes a facade, and those who follow the rules are pushed behind those willing to manipulate them. BIRTH TOURISM CRACKDOWN EXPANDS AS HOUSE CHAIRMAN RAISES CRIMINAL CONSPIRACY CASE Commercial birth tourism is an organized, profit-driven industry that coaches applicants to deceive American officials. Federal prosecutions reveal just how extensive and brazen these operations have become. The Department of Justice secured jury convictions against two Southern California birth-tourism operators for conspiracy and international money laundering. Evidence showed that they coached customers to conceal pregnancies, misrepresent the length and purpose of their trips and enter through ports where they believed they would face less immigration scrutiny. Related indictments charged 19 people, including operators and clients, across three schemes. According to one indictment, an operation called You Win USA allegedly charged customers between $40,000 and $80,000, used 20 apartments and received Three million dollars in international wire transfers from China over two years. Another indictment charged a former Irvine resident with operating Star Baby Care, which claimed in its advertising to have served 8,000 pregnant women. US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR Operators advertised employment, education and public-benefit advantages of American citizenship while instructing customers to lie to consular officers. Some clients were allegedly advised to wear loose clothing to conceal their pregnancies, claim they were visiting for only a few weeks and stay in maternity houses. The indictments also alleged that some customers failed to pay all medical costs associated with their hospital births. To prevent the exploitation of U.S. citizenship, the Trump administration created a Birth Tourism and Prevention Task Force to identify visa abuse and dismantle fraudulent networks. Secretary Rubio’s new policy strengthens that effort by targeting the commercial infrastructure behind the applications. The task force has revoked more than 750 visas tied to suspected birth-tourism activity. The directive is clear: America will not issue visas to foreign operators who profit by coaching others to deceive American officials. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION President Trump and Secretary Rubio understand that immigration enforcement must extend beyond the airport to the recruiters and businesses that make deception profitable. America welcomes lawful visitors, including those seeking legitimate medical care, but that welcome does not extend to fraudulent schemes built on deception. By targeting the operators, the Trump administration is attaching consequences to those profits. The best way to deter fraudulent applications is to hold accountable the businesses that teach people to lie. American citizenship is a sacred national trust, not a cheap commodity sold to the highest bidder. President Trump is sending a clear message: The American Dream is not for sale. title: Fox News Power Rankings: As the House falls, the Senate stays in play
description: Democrats' generic ballot lead is wider than the 2018 blue wave, pushing the House forecast toward a potential 237-seat Democratic majority.
content: There are two big differences between the previous Trump-era midterms and this year’s contest. The first is the president’s approval rating, which is lower now than it was during President Donald Trump’s first term in 2018 or President Joe Biden’s term in 2022. The second is Democrats’ generic ballot lead, which is wider and more enduring than it was in the 2018 "blue wave" election and much larger than the edge the GOP had in 2022. Combined with Democrats’ candidate quality improvements and a Republican-led redistricting effort that could fall short of expectations, the House is likely out of reach for the GOP this year. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. Then there’s a similarity: in all three elections, the Senate has been in play right up until the finish line. In Trump’s first term, the Republicans ended up gaining two Senate seats despite a gloomy national environment. Four years ago, with inflation surging, the Democrats managed to add a Senate seat to their tally. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK The Democrats have plentiful paths to 51 seats on election night. Republicans keep plowing money into six toss-up states, plus Kansas, and those efforts haven’t much moved the needle. Yet the GOP’s paths to 50 are getting wider. That, plus a major update to the House forecast, in this week’s edition of the Power Rankings. House: Democrats set to take control with up to 237 seats The Democratic Party has enjoyed a lead in the House all year. Now, as another 20 races shift leftward, this forecast sees the Democrats taking control. THE BLUE WAVE LOOKS REAL UNTIL YOU LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER Democrats have an advantage in at least 219 seats, while Republicans should hold on to at least 198 seats. There are 18 toss-ups on the board. On a good night for the Democrats, the party will hold around 237 seats, or a gain of 22 from their current position. That’s because toss-up seats have mostly fallen in one party’s direction in previous elections. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG? (A "great night" for the Democrats, which would see the party take some Lean R seats as well, would mean a Democratic majority of up to 249.) If the toss-up seats go the other way, the GOP could make life hard for the left. A good night for Republicans would see the party end up with around 216 seats. That’s two short of a majority but also leaves the Democrats with a mere two-vote cushion in the House. In that scenario, a coalition of far-left Democrats, like the "Squad" of years past, could band together to put policy pressure on the next House speaker. That group is about to get bigger, thanks to the sure-thing victories of Democratic Socialists like Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez. Some of this week’s shifts are a product of polling. The Democrats’ generic ballot lead has pushed districts like Kentucky’s 6th District (Lexington and its suburbs) and Texas’ 15th District (Rio Grande Valley and Coastal Bend) away from the GOP. The party’s strength in statewide races also plays a role, especially in Iowa (the 1st and 3rd districts, which contain the state’s biggest cities), and in Pennsylvania (three districts have shifted to the left, thanks in part to Governor Josh Shapiro’s coattails). Other shifts are the result of Republican groups moving resources elsewhere, like from New York’s 19th District. Democratic Rep. Josh Riley lost this race by fewer than 5,000 votes four years ago, but as the GOP sends its money to more winnable races, it’s moving to Solid D. A more surprising theme is also emerging: the GOP is in trouble with rural voters. Sitting above Albany, New York’s 21st District contains some of the state’s most rural areas. Its voters delivered President Trump a 21-point victory over Vice President Harris two years ago. A survey last week had the Democratic candidate four points ahead of the Republican, 46%-42%. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS Maine’s 2nd District, which famously voted for President Trump three times in a row – and last time by nine points – is an open race this year after Rep. Jared Golden’s retirement. It was thought to be one of the best flip opportunities for the GOP. A new poll has the Democrat at 51% and the Republican at 45%. Even Virginia’s 5th District, stretching across the Southside region and home to a two-thirds rural population, is a six-point race in a recent survey (45%-51% with the Republican ahead). The Democrat, Tom Perriello, was recently endorsed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Gas, diesel and grocery prices are to blame. In dollar terms, the cost of living is higher in cities and suburbs, but voters across the country keep saying they are feeling the pressure of those increases and blame Republicans for them. Iowa, for example, has experienced the fourth-highest gas price hike in the nation. Kentucky, Ohio and Texas are all in the top five states for diesel increases. That has proven tough for GOP candidates to counter. New York’s 21st District moves from Solid R to Likely R. (Virginia’s 5th and Maine’s 2nd districts remain at Lean R and Toss-up, respectively.) Senate: Michele Tafoya plays offense in Minnesota The Senate is still a toss-up with Democrats and Republicans taking 47 seats apiece. Six toss-ups are the most likely to determine control. If Democrats win all six of those states, the party will take the majority with two seats to spare, for a total of 53. On the other hand, this forecast still sees a pathway for the GOP not to lose any seats. They’d accomplish that just by holding on to the same six states. The toss-ups have largely been locked in through summer. There’s been a lot more movement in the "lean" categories (Kansas in, Georgia and North Carolina out). Collectively, you can think of these as the election night battlegrounds. This week, a ninth state joins the list: Minnesota. The North Star State has been on the political radar since Republicans recruited Michele Tafoya, the former NFL sideline reporter. She has deftly navigated her foray into politics by focusing on fraud, crime, and the cultural issues that animate GOP voters. She also has a favorable matchup against Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s sitting lieutenant governor. It’s not clear whether Flanagan’s progressive politics or her proximity to the fraud issue is giving voters pause. Whatever the cause, there are signs that they are. A new gold-standard survey shows 47% of likely voters support Flanagan, while 43% back Tafoya. Another 9% are undecided. Republicans are fully united behind Tafoya, while 9-in-10 Democrats say they’ll support Flanagan’s bid. Independents are much less settled: 38% back Tafoya, 32% support Flanagan, and 29% haven’t decided. Minnesota’s voter profile and election history suggest that there are some left-of-center voters in the "independent" column. They may be wavering on Flanagan now, then show up to vote for her on election day. The Senate hopeful’s spot on the ballot next to Amy Klobuchar, the Democrats’ gubernatorial candidate and electoral over-performer, may also help push her over the line. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Either way, that poll can’t be ignored. Minnesota moves from Likely D to Lean D.

title: Jon Sumrall says teenage son sent him ruthless text before leaving Florida's loss to South Carolina early
description: Jon Sumrall's 13-year-old son texted him after Florida's shocking 38-19 home loss to South Carolina, declaring the defeat may not be "forgivable."
content: There were plenty of disappointed and angry members of Gator Nation on Saturday after Florida's surprising loss to South Carolina in Gainesville, but none may have been more distraught than a young member of Jon Sumrall's own household. With the Florida head coach pushing the Gators to a 4-0 record to start the season, both his new team's fanbase and the Sumrall family were in a comfortable situation. With Sumrall taking over the Gators this season after going 43-12 across four seasons at Troy and Tulane, his family hasn't necessarily been accustomed to losing, especially in games the coach's teams are heavily favored to win. Florida losing to what was a reeling South Carolina team in The Swamp, 38-19, was a shock to the entire college football world, including Sumrall's son, Sam, and the 13-year-old let his old man know exactly how he felt about the performance. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE During his weekly 'Gator Talk' show on Monday, Sumrall hilariously shared how passionate and unfiltered Sam is as a fan, and who was nowhere to be found when the coach's family greeted him on the field after the game. "I asked my wife, I said, ‘Where’s Sam?’ And she goes, ‘Oh, he left. He could not stay and watch y’all get your butt kicked.’ And I’m like, ‘What? The dude left?'" Sumrall recalled. After addressing his team in the locker room, Sumrall finally took a glance at his phone, and there it was, an infamous text from his teenage son. "I’m so pissed off. I don’t want to take a shower. I don’t want to do anything other than maybe punch something," Sumrall continued. "Finally, I grab my phone to just see, did my brother text, maybe check on Sam since he didn’t stay to the end of the game. "And Sam texts me and says, ‘Dad, I don’t know if this is forgivable.’ Like, I don’t know if I can forgive you for this. Choice words from your son after a bad loss are one thing, but the head coach also had to console his young daughter after the game, who was crying as the Florida band sent the team off the field. "My 13-year-old daughter, she comes up to me after the game. We go over to the band, and I look over and she is like in crocodile tears. She is balling," Sumrall explained. "And I’m like, sweetheart, it’s OK, we lost, we’re gonna bounce back. And she’s like, ‘Dad, I just hate losing for you.’ And I’m like, ‘Yeah, well, I do too.’" SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER While Florida's loss at home to the Gamecocks was a bit overshadowed by other upsets across the country in Week 6, it was certainly inexplicable. title: Pro wrestler goes on defense after airport attack rap lyric costs him job at TNA: 'It’s only to entertain'
description: Max Caster says he won't apologize for his Riyadh rap lyric at TNA Bound for Glory, claiming his intent was entertainment, not to offend anyone.
content: Pro wrestler Max Caster said in a video posted on social media Tuesday he wasn’t going to apologize for anyone being offended by his rap lyric that referenced the Houthis’ attack on a Saudi Arabian airport that left more than a dozen dead and several others injured. Caster appeared at Total Nonstop Action Wrestling’s (TNA) Bound for Glory pay-per-view to answer Moose’s open challenger. Caster, known for rapping over his entrance music and pushing the boundaries with some of his lyrics, said "… And it’s the firing squad. I drop bombs. You don’t even have to fly to Riyadh," as he made his way down to the ring. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE The line caused immediate outrage on social media. On Monday, TNA announced it had cut ties with Caster over the verse. Caster said he understood why TNA president Carlos Silva made the decision to part ways with him after just one match. He apologized to people who vouched for him, feeling like he let a lot of people down. He had a different message for those who were offended by the lyric. "For anyone who’s offended, I just want everybody to know that when I do these raps, it’s never to offend people," he said. "It’s only to entertain. So, in my mind, it’s entertainment value first. And then, if you’re offended by it, that’s your right. I can’t apologize for anyone being offended but just know that it’s not my intention to make people upset. If it gets a reaction, I think I did my job. It was a very relevant part of the show and highly talked about. I feel good about that but the consequences of everything – I’m accepting that. I can accept the facts of that. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "To anyone who’s asking if I’m good, I’m good. I’m just embarrassed how all this happened. You don’t want it to be one match and then that’s it. You get fired. But again, that’s the reality of the situation. I’m accepting it and that’s life and in life, sometimes, you gotta man up and just accept it and move on." TNA said Monday it deleted everything related to Caster from its social media and will no longer welcome Caster at its company. "During Sunday’s Bound for Glory pay-per-view, insensitive comments were made by Max Caster referencing attacks in Riyadh that killed and injured many people," the company said in a statement. "Making light of violent attacks is wrong. This should never have made it into the show, and that responsibility is ours. Our thoughts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected. We sincerely apologize. "We have removed the segment from replays and our social channels and are taking steps to ensure something like this never happens again. title: Metallica frontman James Hetfield blasts entertainers pushing political agendas at concerts
description: Metallica frontman James Hetfield took aim at concert politics amid Macklemore's removal from Ed Sheeran's tour over "Free Palestine" calls.
content: Metallica frontman James Hetfield is calling out performers who bring political agendas to the stage. During Metallica's show at the Las Vegas Sphere on Saturday night, the 63-year-old musician took a moment to express his gratitude to fans who traveled to see the heavy metal band and blasted entertainers who turn concerts into political platforms. "Unless you live in Vegas, you've come a long way to spend some time with Metallica," he said in a video shared on YouTube. "We're grateful for that — your travels, the money you spend, the time it took, thanks for coming to celebrate with us." GOO GOO DOLLS' JOHN RZEZNIK DRAWS LINE ON POLITICS AT CONCERTS: 'I'M NOT GOING TO LECTURE YOU' "I just gotta say, Metallica is not here, like some other entertainers, to influence you with their bulls---, OK?," Hetfield continued as the audience clapped and cheered. "We are here … no bulls--- … we're here to forget about all the outside s---, OK?" he added. "Metallica's agenda is love, energy and heavy music, baby!" ED SHEERAN CONCERTGOERS WARN ARTISTS ABOUT SHARING POLITICAL VIEWS: 'YOU'RE GOING TO ALIENATE' FANS Although Hetfield did not name any artists, several musicians have recently made political statements during their concerts. Last month, Macklemore was dropped from his remaining scheduled performances on Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour" after the rapper repeatedly called for a "Free Palestine" and performed his pro-Palestinian protest song "Hind's Hall" while opening for the "Shape of You" singer at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. MACKLEMORE'S LONG HISTORY OF CONTROVERSY FROM GRAMMY WINS TO 'FREE PALESTINE' CONCERT REMARKS At the time, Macklemore said Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, told Sheeran that the "Thrift Shop" hitmaker "would not be allowed" to perform at the stadium. Kraft later confirmed that he opposed Macklemore performing at Gillette Stadium, citing the rapper's "recent actions" and what he called a "broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery." ED SHEERAN APOLOGIZES FOR MACKLEMORE BACKLASH, ENCOURAGES UNITY AT FIRST CONCERT SINCE FALLOUT Following Macklemore's removal, all of Sheeran's remaining opening acts and supporting musicians, including Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga, pulled out in solidarity with the rapper. In an Instagram statement, Sheeran said he was not responsible for Macklemore's removal, explaining that the promoter and venues made the decision. READ IT: ED SHEERAN'S PRE-CONCERT SPEECH TO PHILLY CROWD ABOUT THE GAZA CONTROVERSY During his show in Philadelphia, Sheeran said he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine" and called the situation in Gaza "catastrophic and unjustifiable," while describing the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel as "horrific." Sheeran has also defended his decision to keep his concerts apolitical. The four-time Grammy winner said his audience includes children and fans from a wide range of backgrounds who "do not expect a political forum" when they attend his shows. MACKLEMORE SLAMMED AS 'PERFORMATIVE' AFTER ANNOUNCING 'FREE PALESTINE TOUR' Macklemore subsequently pledged to donate the $1 million he earned opening for Sheeran to organizations providing humanitarian aid to Palestinians. He also announced a three-date "Free Palestine Tour" scheduled for late October. During the controversy, country singer Zach Bryan wore a "Free Palestine" T-shirt during his sold-out concerts at Gillette Stadium in October. SPRINGSTEEN, OTHER STARS SHARE STAGE WITH HARDCORE LEFTIST GROUPS AT MUSIC FEST Other musicians who have made political statements during concerts include Bruce Springsteen, Rage Against the Machine's Tom Morello, Green Day's Billie Joe Armstrong and Kacey Musgraves. Meanwhile, Hetfield has long expressed his opposition to mixing music and politics. In a 2016 interview with the BBC, he explained that Metallica steered clear of divisive topics. MICK JAGGER DOESN'T WANT TO 'LECTURE' FANS, SAYS HIS JOB IS TO MAKE PEOPLE 'HAVE THE BEST TIME' "There's a lot of polarization going on in the States, and I see it in other places as well," he said. "But it just seems like you have to get more extreme to balance out the other extreme. We've got to find some balance in the middle here somewhere." "We stay away from politics [and] from religion," Hetfield added. "That just seems to polarize people even more. We all have our own beliefs, but at the end of the day, we're trying to connect with people, and it seems like political views don't do that as much as music does." In a 2017 interview with the Chilean newspaper La Tercera, Hetfield declined to share his opinion of Donald Trump, who was president at the time, and reiterated his opposition to mixing music and politics. title: Trump vanishes from GOP senator's campaign website as poll numbers plunge weeks before election
description: Sen. Mike Rounds' campaign scrubbed several Trump mentions from his website as the president's approval rating craters in South Dakota's Senate race.
content: A Senate Republican running for re-election in ruby-red South Dakota has joined a growing number of candidates putting distance between themselves and President Donald Trump. But it’s more subtle than Republicans opposing the Iran war or dodging Trump campaign visits as Election Day nears and his popularity struggles. Just last month, Trump’s name and endorsement were featured prominently on Republican South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds’ campaign website, but some mentions of the president have since been scrubbed, according to an older version of the website reviewed by Fox News Digital. SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Rounds’ campaign noted to Fox News Digital that not every mention of Trump has been removed. "The president’s endorsement is still front and center on the website in Mike’s announcement video," Rounds’ campaign advisor, Rob Skjonsberg, told Fox News Digital. "But, generally speaking, it’s not abnormal to hone in on general election messaging." Trump endorsed Rounds last year and lauded the lawmaker as an "incredibly strong advocate for the wonderful people of South Dakota, a State I love, and WON BIG, in 2016, 2020, and 2024!" "Mike Rounds has my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election — HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN," Trump said on Truth Social at the time. Still, Trump’s approval rating among voters has cratered — a Fox News poll last month found that overall, voters had a 39% approval rating of the president’s performance. Key issues like cost of living, cost of groceries and fuel, and the ongoing war in Iran were major sticking points for participants. FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS Rounds’ campaign website featured two mentions of Trump on its homepage, including "Endorsed by President Trump" and a photo of Rounds touting that "Mike is endorsed by President Trump and is working for South Dakota every single day." Those two mentions have since been removed, along with Trump’s name being removed in two places from the lawmaker's "Issues" page on his website — the president was previously included in Rounds’ "Put America First" and "Education" sections. The lawmaker is vying for a third term in deep-red South Dakota, where he previously served as the state’s governor and in the state Senate. He’s running against independent Brian Bengs, who previously ran as a Democrat against Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., in 2022. Thune easily defeated Bengs in the general election, securing over 70% of the vote. SCHUMER DIGS IN AS PROGRESSIVE CANDIDATES WITHHOLD SUPPORT FOR TOP SENATE DEM "I'm not running against the President," Bengs said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "But to me it says a lot that this didn't happen because of the Iran War that's raising our costs or the tariffs that are hurting us — it only happened when Mike's poll numbers went down and his big money allies are buying more ads to bail him out. I hope Mike finds the courage to debate me, so we can talk about it." title: Fiery discovery may finally unravel 2,000-year-old mystery involving Julius Caesar
description: A 66-foot stone-and-timber wall found near Notre Dame may belong to Lutetia, the ancient Gallic city described by Julius Caesar in his writings. The French Ministry of Culture announced the find.
content: Archaeologists in Paris recently unearthed an ancient wall that may belong to a long-lost city — potentially solving a centuries-old mystery dating back to the times of Julius Caesar. The discovery was recently announced by the French Ministry of Culture. In a translated statement, officials said a wall discovered in the courtyard of the Hôtel-Dieu hospital — just a stone's throw away from Notre Dame Cathedral in the city's 4th arrondissement — might have belonged to the ancient city of Lutetia. 'DIG OF THE CENTURY' BENEATH NOTRE DAME REVEALS MYSTERIOUS MARKINGS, ANCIENT SECRETS The excavation, which began in February, was conducted ahead of a "major redevelopment project," officials said. "Researchers initially expected to uncover traces of ancient dwellings, roads, or settlements dating to the medieval and early modern periods," the translated statement read. "Instead, alongside those remains, they discovered a stone-and-timber wall characteristic of ancient Gallic fortifications." The settlement was mentioned by Julius Caesar in his writings, particularly "The Gallic Wars" — but no conclusive archaeological evidence confirmed its location until now. ANCIENT CLUE CRACKS OPEN A 2,000-YEAR-OLD MYSTERY NEAR FAMED COLOSSEUM In a statement, French Culture Minister Catherine Pégard said officials "may be looking at one of the most important discoveries ever made in understanding Gallic Lutetia. "Scientific caution still requires us to verify its function and chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable," added Pégard. Photos from the excavation show large, weathered stone blocks stacked in uneven rows. The wall, which stretches roughly 66 feet, bears evidence of a major fire, while radiocarbon testing of wooden elements found at the site suggests they date to between 200 B.C. and 10 B.C. GRISLY DISCOVERY FROM LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR'S REIGN REVEALS SOLDIERS' REMAINS, WEAPONS Researchers believe the structure may have served as a defensive fortification for the Gauls. The wall's stonework showed signs of fire damage, while archaeologists also uncovered burned seeds and the remains of a charred wooden building nearby. Caesar's account indicated the Gallic Parisii tribe burned its own fortified settlement in 52 B.C. to prevent it from falling into Roman hands. "The architecture of the wall, with its large stone blocks and system of interlocking wooden beams, very quickly made us think of a wall built in the Gallic tradition," she said in the statement. title: Kelly Clarkson's store callout shows the 'power' of celebrity statements: expert
description: Kelly Clarkson's viral feud with Brooklyn store Art of Play over a singing bird automaton has PR experts weighing the risks and opportunities.
content: Kelly Clarkson's recent headline-making feud has public relations experts saying the viral attention brings risks for the store, but could create an opportunity if it handles the backlash well. Over the weekend, Clarkson called out Art of Play, a Brooklyn store known for its collection of toys, games, books, puzzles and other unique items, for allegedly denying her the ability to buy "Molly," a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton. "Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote. "Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale," she continued. KELLY CLARKSON SLAMS BROOKLYN STORE OVER ‘PRETTY WOMAN’ TREATMENT Clarkson then compared the encounter to a memorable scene from the 1990 movie "Pretty Woman," in which Julia Roberts’ character, Vivian Ward, is dismissed by a boutique saleswoman who assumes she cannot afford the store’s clothing. "But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in ‘Pretty Woman.’ For sure, check it out," Clarkson added. The singer’s description of the incident echoed the famous "Pretty Woman" scene, in which Vivian returns to the boutique after being rejected and tells the saleswoman, "Big mistake. Big. Huge." A source told People: "She’s usually very private and public drama like this isn’t her." "She’s clearly so ticked off that she couldn’t keep quiet about it. Everyone is surprised by how much this whole thing has escalated," the insider told the outlet. Doug Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, told Fox News Digital that this debacle speaks to three key points: "1. The power and presumptive veracity of celebrity statements and/or accusations; 2. The staggering pace and scale of social media as a tool of dissemination; 3. The critical need for a crisis communications plan, regardless of the size of your business." Art of Play posted a response to Clarkson's original social media callout, claiming that they have had "8 million people" bombarding them with hateful messages after the singer's accusations. "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It’s been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity. Thanks to all our friends for their support and welcome to all the curious folks who discovered us amidst the drama. We’re going to keep our heads down and hopefully, we can clear things up with Kelly someday. As a talented popular singer once said ‘what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger,’" the store posted to their Instagram page on Sunday afternoon. Eldridge continued, "Irrespective of which side you believe, this has proven Winston Churchill’s famous quip: 'A lie gets halfway around the world before the truth gets its pants on in the morning.'" After the store's Instagram post, Clarkson took to her X account and Instagram stories on Sunday afternoon to respond to their claims. "Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn't for sale. That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," Clarkson wrote, adding a thumbs up emoji. The singer continued: "So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn't happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone "yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can." That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it," adding a checkmark emoji. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t." Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer at International Services Inc. and creator of the Profit by Design Methodology, told Fox News Digital that there are two ways Art of Play could view Clarkson bringing millions of people's attention to their small business. The first effect is that you've seen people take up the banner in her name, and you see people posting bad reviews or, obviously, there's a lot of comments. So, there is a negativity that can have an effect. She's got a lot of social power. "But, if I were to make a counter, the counter is that all good press or all good heat or negative or positive heat, I guess is good and what the store does it with it right now I think can be quite eventful for them," Aldebert continued. Aldebert, who manages 1,000 people at his own firm, believes Clarkson should have taken her concerns about her treatment at the store to Art of Play's owner before blasting the whole business on social media. "If I'm Monday morning quarterback on this particular one, I'm going to say the first step you take is reach out to the owner, see if it can be resolved. If, obviously, it's treated as something where they just blow it off or they're rude, too, then I can kind of see, at least you wait out. You have a great weapon, which is your social media presence. title: Trump 'looking at' firing ambassador to Greece: 'We're not happy'
description: President Donald Trump says he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid allegations of improper conduct.
content: President Donald Trump is "looking at" firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after mounting reports alleging improper conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. "Well, we’re looking at it," Trump told reporters at the White House before leaving for an Ohio campaign rally Monday afternoon. "Yeah, we’re not happy." Trump’s comments came after a senior U.S. official said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by reports about Guilfoyle’s conduct and expected to make a decision on her future this week. TRUMP AND RUBIO WEIGH FIRING KIMBERLY GUILFOYLE AS MISCONDUCT AND DONOR BAILOUT ALLEGATIONS MOUNT The Wall Street Journal has reported a series of allegations involving Guilfoyle, including that she asked a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill before her confirmation hearing while allegedly promising access to administration officials. The Journal also reported claims that Guilfoyle made a threat involving the Greek government, promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company, allowed a lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings and accepted improper gifts or services. Rubio, who was in Greece last week, was frustrated by reporters repeatedly asking him to address the allegations publicly. RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on. "It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things." BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT A day earlier, Rubio said he would not discuss the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but defended the embassy’s work. "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job," Rubio said at a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister. "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here." TRUMP JR UNDER SCRUTINY FROM OWN PARTY OVER PUTIN-LINKED OLIGARCH'S LAVISH GIFT Vice President JD Vance also weighed in last week, saying he did not know the full details of the specific case but rejected the idea of selling access to government officials. "Of course, I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official," Vance told reporters. "I assume you’re talking about a specific case, and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of the way you’re describing it." HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing through her lawyers. In a statement released late Sunday, attorneys David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall said the money she sought from the Trump donor was payment for public appearances and speaking engagements that predated her nomination. "Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction," the lawyers said. "We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action." The attorneys also denied impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the department's travel regulations." BIDEN-ERA FBI TRACKED TRUMP FAMILY TRAVEL AND WILES’ CALLS WITH LAWYERS IN SECRET PROBE: DOCS A U.S. official told The Associated Press that the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, though it was not clear whether a formal investigation had been opened. The State Department declined to comment to the AP on a potential inspector general probe. Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Oversight Committee have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Donald Trump Jr. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Fake Facebook Marketplace listing uses your name
description: A fake Facebook Marketplace text scam uses your real name as the seller to trick you into replying, and Malwarebytes warns even one response helps.
content: You get a text message from a number you don't recognize asking a pretty normal question: "Is this still available for purchase?" Attached to the text is an image that appears to show a Facebook Marketplace listing. Maybe you're confused because you don't remember selling anything. Then you look at the seller's name. It's yours. That small detail could be enough to make you respond with something like, "That's not me." And that reaction may be exactly what the person behind the message wants. Security researchers at Malwarebytes are warning about a personalized text scam that uses fabricated Facebook Marketplace listings with the recipient's name as the seller. The message can create an immediate fear that someone is impersonating you online. Here's how this scam pulls you in and what you should do if one of these texts lands on your phone. Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com. THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET How the fake Facebook Marketplace listing works Malwarebytes analyzed an example sent through iMessage. The text asked whether an item was still available and included an image resembling a Facebook Marketplace listing. The clever part appears when you look at the supposed seller. The recipient's real name is there. However, Malwarebytes noticed something strange. The profile photo did not belong to the recipient. Researchers traced the picture to another Facebook user who happened to have the same name. That suggests the scammer may have started with a name and matching phone number. Those details could potentially come from breached data or another source. The attacker could then use the name to build a convincing fake Marketplace screenshot. Seeing your name creates an obvious question: "Is someone pretending to be me?" Before you know it, you're typing a reply. Why scammers want you to respond This technique is known as a conversation lure. Instead of immediately asking for a password or sending an obvious phishing link, the sender gives you a reason to start talking. In this case, the lure feels personal. Someone apparently put your name on a Marketplace listing. You may want to correct the buyer or find out what happened. You might also worry that someone has created a fake Facebook account in your name. The exact motive behind this particular campaign remains unclear because determining the next step would require engaging with the sender. Still, replying to suspicious texts carries its own risk. The Federal Trade Commission warns that even replying to an unexpected text can confirm that a scammer has reached a working telephone number. That could lead to more scam calls and texts. Your reply may tell scammers more than you realize Think about how harmless a response such as "wrong person" feels. You haven't shared a password or sent money. You haven't clicked a suspicious website. However, you've given the sender something useful: confirmation that someone is actively using the number and willing to respond. Malwarebytes reports that a live number can become more valuable to scammers and potentially be resold to others. The number could also be combined with additional information gathered from public profiles, breached databases or other sources. That can help set up another scam. You might later receive a fake delivery alert. Another message could pretend to come from your bank. A scammer might eventually try to steal a verification code, direct you to a malicious site or build a longer conversation designed to gain your trust. We recently looked at what a scammer can do with your name, phone number and address. Those details can become far more useful when criminals combine them with other personal information. How AI could make personalized scams easier to scale Creating individual Marketplace screenshots for thousands of people once would have required a lot of tedious work. AI and automation can change that equation. Malwarebytes says an attacker with a list containing names and phone numbers could potentially use an AI agent to help create personalized lures at scale. However, researchers have not established that AI created the specific example they examined. Still, automation makes this kind of personalization much easier to produce. That's an important shift in how we should judge suspicious messages. A text knowing your name provides little reassurance that the sender actually knows you. Personal information gets exposed through breaches, scraped from public sources and traded in criminal marketplaces. Once scammers connect a few pieces, they can make a random message feel surprisingly personal. Does this mean your Facebook account was hacked? No. Seeing your name on one of these fake Marketplace images does not, by itself, mean someone has accessed your Facebook account. The Marketplace screenshot may simply be fabricated. That's why I would resist the urge to reply to the sender asking what's going on. Instead, check Facebook yourself. What Apple says about suspicious iMessages Apple says this type of deceptive messaging uses social engineering, a tactic in which scammers rely on impersonation and manipulation to persuade people to share personal information. Criminals may pretend to represent a trusted company or organization while trying to obtain passwords, security codes or financial details. Apple also points to an important iMessage protection. By default, users cannot open links sent by an unknown iMessage sender until they add that person to their contacts or reply to the message. That gives you another reason to avoid responding to an unexpected text. Apple recommends treating suspicious, unexpected messages as potential scams and contacting the company directly through a trusted channel. The company also says users can filter unknown senders, report suspicious messages and block unwanted contacts through Messages. How to protect yourself from scam texts on iPhone Apple's Messages app includes tools to help filter unwanted texts, report suspicious messages and block senders. Since this Facebook Marketplace scam arrives through iMessage, here's how to use those protections on an iPhone. Turn on screening for unknown senders Messages from unknown senders will appear in a separate folder instead of your main conversation list. Apple says you won't receive notifications for these messages unless you've chosen to allow certain categories of unknown messages. SCAMMERS KNOW THE BEST TIME TO TEXT YOU Report a suspicious iMessage Apple says reporting an iMessage sends the sender's information and message content to Apple. The message is then permanently deleted from your iPhone. However, reporting does not automatically block the sender, so follow the blocking steps below. If you have already replied, the reporting option may no longer be available. For SMS, MMS or RCS messages that don't display a reporting option, Apple recommends contacting your wireless carrier directly. Block the scammer's number Blocking prevents messages from that number from reaching you. The sender won't receive a notification that you've blocked them. Check messages Apple has flagged as spam Important: These protections can reduce exposure to scam messages, but they cannot guarantee that every personalized phishing attempt will be detected. Don't reply to a suspicious Marketplace message simply because it contains your real name. How to stay safe from fake Facebook Marketplace texts A message like this is designed to make you react. Instead, give yourself a moment and investigate through channels you trust. 1) Don't reply to the text Even telling the sender they have the wrong person can confirm that somebody is actively using the number. The FTC recommends avoiding replies to unexpected messages from unknown numbers. 2) Don't use links or contact information in the message Don't click a link, call a number or scan a QR code supplied in the conversation. Never send the person a one-time security code or a screenshot containing security information. If you need to check Facebook, open the app yourself or type the address directly into your browser. 3) Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help protect you if a scammer eventually sends a malicious link or tries to get you to download malware. It can also warn you about some dangerous websites before they cause trouble. The best way to protect yourself from malicious links that install malware and potentially access your private information is to have antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, keeping your personal information and digital assets safe. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM 4) Check your Facebook account independently Open Facebook and review your Marketplace activity and messages. Look for anything you didn't post or send. You should also review your account security for unfamiliar logins, changed contact information or other activity you don't recognize. 5) Check with a known sender another way If a suspicious message appears to come from someone you actually know, contact that person through a different method. For example, call a number you already have saved rather than using contact information supplied in the suspicious message. 6) Report and block suspicious texts On an iPhone, follow the reporting and blocking steps above. Android users can use their messaging app's built-in spam reporting and blocking features. The FTC also recommends forwarding unwanted texts to 7726 (SPAM). These reports can help wireless providers identify and block similar messages. 7) Report a Facebook impersonator If you discover that someone really has created a Facebook profile pretending to be you, preserve the profile's URL and report it to Facebook. A fake screenshot alone does not prove that an impersonating Facebook profile actually exists. Check Facebook independently before assuming someone has created one. 8) Secure your Facebook account if something looks wrong If you discover an unfamiliar login, changed account information or other evidence of unauthorized access, start Facebook's account recovery process immediately. You should also review your password and enable two-factor authentication (2FA). Facebook currently places its two-factor authentication controls under Accounts Center > Password and security > Two-factor authentication. 9) Reduce the personal information scammers can find This scam shows why exposed personal information can be so useful to criminals. Your name and phone number may already appear on people-search sites or in data-broker databases. Removing that information won't erase data already exposed in a breach, but it can reduce what scammers can easily find and use to personalize future attacks. While no service can promise to remove all your data from the internet, a data removal service can monitor and automate the process of removing your information from hundreds of sites continuously over a longer period. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. What if you already replied? Don't assume a single response means your phone or Facebook account has been compromised. A reply alone does not give someone access to your Facebook account. What you should do next depends on how far the interaction went. Kurt's key takeaways What makes this scam so convincing is the personal detail. You see your own name on a Marketplace listing you never created, and, of course, you want to know what's going on. That's exactly why you should avoid replying to the stranger who sent it. Instead, open Facebook yourself and check your account. If you don't see the listing or any suspicious activity, report the text, block the sender and move on. If something looks wrong, secure your Facebook account right away. The bigger concern here is how easily scammers can use pieces of our personal information to make a random text feel legitimate. Your name and phone number may already be available through a data breach, data broker or another source. Seeing accurate information about yourself in an unexpected message should make you more cautious, not more trusting. Scammers keep finding new ways to use our personal information against us, so who should bear more responsibility for stopping these attacks before they reach our phones? title: Biggest waste of money in your home gym may surprise you, fitness expert says
description: Fitness coach Jacob Zemer reveals the three home gym essentials — bands, dumbbells and a bench — that let you train every muscle group on a budget.
content: Americans are spending more on health and wellness, research shows — and for some home gym enthusiasts, the cost can quickly climb into the thousands. A YouGov poll conducted in September 2026 found that 31% of Americans are spending more on health and wellness than a year ago, while 20% expect to spend more in the coming year. Meanwhile, a 2026 poll by Garage Gym Experiment, an online community for home fitness enthusiasts, found that 44% of respondents expected to spend at least $1,000 on their home gyms this year. FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG But building an effective home gym doesn’t have to break the bank, according to New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer. The biggest home gym money-waster may not be a particular piece of equipment, he said, but rather anything that takes up significant space and is difficult to set up or use consistently. Zemer spoke with Fox News Digital about the most worthwhile investments for working out at home — and which equipment may not deliver enough bang for the buck. The 3 home gym essentials "A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't," Zemer said. If someone is building a home gym from scratch, the fitness pro recommends starting with a few affordable pieces and adding equipment over time. 10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG "You can accomplish everything for every muscle group with just three items," he said. No. 1: Bands Exercise bands are a good first investment, Zemer said, "just because they're so incredibly affordable." They’re also very effective, he said, especially for those who are new to strength training. "You can do everything you need to with just those pieces of equipment — and you can travel with them, bring them on a plane and to a hotel, which makes them very versatile," Zemer said. No. 2: Dumbbells When choosing dumbbells, it’s important to consider how much floor space they’ll take up — especially if the home gym is in a room with multiple purposes, according to Zemer. "With adjustable dumbbells, you can have a very small floor print — however, they are a little bit more costly, and some of them are slightly fragile, so just be mindful of that," he advised. 4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS Beginners should first focus on learning the proper form and choosing a weight that makes the final repetitions challenging, according to Zemer. Progress doesn’t always mean moving to heavier dumbbells, he noted. "Pushing yourself doesn’t mean adding 20 pounds — it could mean doing one more rep," Zemer said. "You need to progressively get stronger, because your body will adapt to the stimulus you’re using." Once it becomes easy to complete a high number of repetitions, it may be time to increase the weight. No. 3: A bench With some exercises, it can be limiting if you have to lie on the floor or stand, Zemer said. "You can get quite an affordable bench online," he said. "I would look for one that both declines and inclines, maybe even perhaps sits completely upright. That will give you a lot of versatility." The biggest waste: equipment you won’t use Before buying a piece of home gym equipment, Zemer recommends considering how much space it requires, how many exercises it supports and whether it will be easy to use consistently. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Equipment that is bulky or difficult to move, or requires too much setup, may end up becoming an expensive waste of money. "The most important thing is that it’s quick and easy to set up, easy to grab and therefore more likely to be used," he said. "The more setup it requires, the less likely you will to be use it." Zemer learned that lesson after buying lever arms, attachments that connect to a power rack and move up and down for exercises such as presses, rows and squats. Because the equipment was cumbersome to move, he eventually sold it secondhand. "The secondhand market of gym equipment is brutal, so if you buy something, and you don't use it, the resale value is next to none," Zemer cautioned. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He recommends prioritizing items that serve multiple purposes, rather than devices designed to target just one body part. "I always look for equipment that can do multiple things," he said. "A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't." Do you need cardio equipment? Cardio equipment is not essential for everyone, according to the trainer, especially for those who are mobile. Many people can also raise their heart rate through activities such as walking, running or strength-training workouts performed at a faster pace, he said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For those who prefer a cardio machine, Zemer recommends choosing an option that is versatile and less likely to aggravate the knees or back, such as a stationary bike or ski erg (an indoor exercise machine that simulates the motion of cross-country skiing).

title: Traditional two-parent families vanish from big American cities as 'marriage deserts' expand
description: A new report from the Institute for Family Studies reveals a 70-point divide in traditional two-parent families, as urban marriage deserts expand across major U.S. cities.
content: The traditional two-parent nuclear family is far less common in parts of major American cities than in suburban communities, with fewer than a quarter of households with children headed by married couples in some neighborhoods in Cleveland, Washington, D.C., Milwaukee and Detroit, according to a new report. The study from the Institute for Family Studies showed that the share of households with children headed by married couples varies by roughly 70 percentage points across the areas studied, highlighting a divide between urban "married-family deserts" and suburban "married-family gardens." The findings revealed differences in family structure across the country, raising questions about how the neighborhoods where children grow up may influence their opportunities for upward mobility. DRIVEN BY PROGRESSIVE DOOMISM, LIBERALS ARE HAVING FEWER BABIES THAN CONSERVATIVE FAMILIES "Marriage and raising kids are both parts of your life that really force you to kind of die to yourself and live for others," Ken Burchfiel, a research fellow at the Institute for Family Studies, told Fox News Digital. "When you have lots of parents, lots of husbands and wives in a region, I imagine just overall the cultural focus is less on 'how can I get ahead in life' and more on 'what can I do for my family?’" The study analyzed 2020 Census data to identify where married and married-parent households are most and least common. It found that suburban neighborhoods tend to have higher marriage rates, while major urban centers often have lower rates. NORTH TEXAS DOMINATES IN POPULATION GROWTH AS BIG BLUE CITIES FAIL TO RECOVER TO PRE-PANDEMIC LEVELS Suburban Dallas-Fort Worth stands as the nation's largest grouped "marriage garden," while Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn form the largest grouped "marriage desert," covering nearly 686,000 householders, more than two-thirds of whom are unmarried. "This does not appear to describe small variations around shared national norms, but rather two distinct family-formation regimes, so stark it could even be described as family structure polarization," the IFS report stated. Burchfiel said high incomes do not necessarily translate into higher marriage rates either. In high-income Manhattan neighborhoods, including the Financial District and Greenwich Village, fewer than 28% of householders ages 15 to 64 are married. GEN Z IS WORKING HARD, BUT THE ECONOMY IS PUTTING THE AMERICAN DREAM OUT OF REACH FOR MANY "It’s clear that the decision to get married is not just due to financial concerns; it's also a matter of culture and, admittedly, perhaps a matter of affordability," Burchfiel said. "I recognize, having lived in New York for a few years, that having a high salary does not mean that it's easy to buy a house, raise a family. It can still be extremely difficult and probably many of the people in those areas who do get married find themselves moving out to the suburbs," he added. The IFS researchers said they examined the issue because of a large body of research showing that "family structure is closely associated with economic mobility and broader measures of social capital." They pointed to research by Harvard economist Raj Chetty that found the share of homes with two parents present was the strongest predictor of upward mobility in a community. "This represents a significant discrepancy in lived experience for children growing up in these distinct environments. Those in married-family gardens grow up with married parents, in neighborhoods, schools and after-school activities where most peers experience the same. These children will be observing marriage as a stable, ordinary feature of adult life," the study explained. US HURTLING TOWARD POPULATION DECLINE EVEN AS AMERICANS SAY THEY WANT BIGGER FAMILIES, NEW REPORT WARNS "By contrast, for children in married-family deserts, there is likely to be much greater churn in adult relationship stability, and greater inconsistency in supervision, where marriage and stable relationship bonds are atypical or distant from everyday norms — both for these children and their peers." Areas with some of the lowest shares of married-parent households nationwide included eastern Cleveland and nearby Bratenahl Village, Ohio, with only 18% of households with children headed by a married couple, followed closely by eastern Washington, D.C., at 20% and central Milwaukee at 22%. In suburban "married-family gardens" like Fremont City, California, Lakewood, New Jersey and parts of Utah County, Utah, up to 89% of households with children are headed by married couples. Burchfiel advised newlyweds and young couples evaluating where to settle down to look closely at these family maps alongside local job markets, but to also take into account their own personal circumstances, such as staying close to extended family. THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH "Living near other married couples can be really useful when you're settling down and raising a family," Burchfiel said. title: Trial in college student’s murder zeroes in on rum bottle, vulgar note and missing evidence
description: Miguel Enrique Salguero-Olivares faces murder, rape and burglary charges in the Faith Hedgepeth case as DNA and missing evidence clash in court.
content: Fourteen years after authorities found Faith Hedgepeth dead, the 19-year-old’s final hours have been unfolding in a North Carolina courtroom, where tearful testimony and questions about missing evidence marked the opening days of a murder trial. Miguel Enrique Salguero-Olivares, 33, is on trial in Durham County Superior Court on charges of first-degree murder, rape, sexual offense and burglary in the 2012 killing of Hedgepeth, a biology major at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill. Family members of Hedgepeth said they did not know her alleged killer and the two had no known prior interactions. The trial is in its second week, with Dr. Heather Waleski, a sexual assault nurse examiner with Atrium Health, testifying about forensic medical evidence. The first days of testimony brought tears from witnesses, spectators and jurors, the 9th Street Journal reported. A forensic technician showed the murder weapon to the jury. Close-up photographs of Hedgepeth’s face and body prompted some court spectators to cover their faces. SLAIN UNC STUDENT’S MOTHER HOPES NEW DOCUMENTARY WILL SHED LIGHT ON UNSOLVED MURDER: ‘I NEED TO KEEP GOING FOR HER’ The graphic descriptions of internal brain trauma overwhelmed the jury box, prompting the judge to call a recess Friday. Prosecutors and defense attorneys have clashed over whether DNA evidence revealed the killer or an unreliable investigation where key physical evidence vanished. A roommate's discovery Hedgepeth's roommate, Karena Rosario, now 34, sobbed Wednesday as she recalled finding Hedgepeth nude from the waist down in their shared bedroom at a nearby off-campus apartment, off Old Chapel Hill Road. "I walked around the bed and saw hair. I pulled the comforter down and saw she had a black eye," Rosario said, ABC 11 reported. Rosario took jurors back to Sept. 6, 2012, when she and Hedgepeth studied at a campus library before returning to their apartment to change. The pair then walked to The Thrill nightclub. MURDER SUSPECT ARRESTED 9 YEARS AFTER NORTH CAROLINA COLLEGE STUDENT FAITH HEDGEPETH KILLING They arrived back at the apartment at around 3:40 a.m. Rosario said she became sick from drinking before leaving at about 4:25 a.m. to stay with a friend. Rosario said Hedgepeth was conscious and breathing when she left. She later called Hedgepeth for a ride. Hedgepeth did not answer the call. Another friend, Marisol Rangel, drove Rosario home. They entered the apartment around 11 a.m. and found Hedgepeth beside her bed, Rosario said. Rosario described blood on the walls, the bed and Hedgepeth's arm. She told a 911 dispatcher that Hedgepeth felt cold to the touch. Rosario said she asked about an ambulance when police arrived. "I asked if they were still going to bring the ambulance, but they said she was gone," she testified. DNA testing Police collected DNA at the scene and tested hundreds of samples from people connected to Hedgepeth. None matched. DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON Investigators eventually turned to genetic genealogy, a technique that compares crime-scene DNA with profiles in public ancestry databases. The information led to Salguero-Olivares, a stranger to Hedgepeth’s loved ones. Authorities received a break nearly a decade later. On Sept. 16, 2021, police pulled Salguero-Olivares over during a DUI stop in Wake County, N.C. After obtaining a DNA sample, they charged him with murder. Prosecutors later added the rape, sexual offense and burglary charges. The evidence On Friday, prosecutors presented items recovered from the bedroom, including a Bacardi rum bottle, a wine bottle and a crumpled Time-Out restaurant biscuit bag. Investigators found a profanity-laced handwritten message on the fast-food bag that read, "I'm not stupid, b----. Jealous." Chapel Hill police forensic technician Tamika Price displayed the 1.75-liter rum bottle to the court, which prosecutors identified as the murder weapon used to deliver blows to Hedgepeth’s head. "When I put my hands on her head, I could feel where the side of her head was very soft. It was indented," Price testified, ABC 11 reported.
