title: Why verified social media accounts can still lead you into a scam
description: Microsoft's X account was hijacked to promote a crypto pump-and-dump scheme, exposing its more than 13 million followers to a scam campaign.
content: We have all developed little shortcuts for deciding whether something online looks legitimate. You check the account name. You recognize the company logo. Then you spot that verification badge and your guard comes down a little. That can be exactly what scammers are counting on. Microsoft’s official X account became the latest reminder after attackers gained unauthorized access and used the account in an apparent cryptocurrency pump-and-dump scheme. The account has more than 13 million followers, giving whoever controlled it access to a huge audience and the credibility that comes with Microsoft’s name. Here is what happened, why compromised verified accounts can be so convincing and what you should check before trusting the next surprising post that shows up in your feed. Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care . Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist . See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com 6 CRYPTO SCAM SCRIPTS CRIMINALS USE TO STEAL YOUR MONEY How Microsoft's X account got pulled into a crypto scheme BleepingComputer reported that Microsoft's @Microsoft account followed and reposted content from another X account that appeared to be Clippy-themed. That account was promoting a cryptocurrency called $Clippy. Microsoft tells CyberGuy that two unauthorized posts appeared during the period when its account was compromised. According to the company, the first was a quote repost of content from what appeared to be a Clippy-themed account and referenced bringing back Microsoft Office's old animated paperclip character. The second appeared to be an apology related to the earlier activity. Microsoft says neither post originated from the company. A Microsoft spokesperson provided CyberGuy with the following statement: "We have confirmed unauthorized access to our account on X, including posts that did not originate from Microsoft. The account has been secured, the unauthorized posts have been removed, and we are continuing to investigate the circumstances." Why a verified account can make a scam much harder to spot If an account you have never heard of suddenly tells you Microsoft launched a Clippy cryptocurrency, you might keep scrolling. When Microsoft’s actual account appears to amplify that same message, it becomes much easier to hesitate. You may assume someone at the company approved the post. You might click a link because you recognize the account. Someone interested in crypto could move even faster because they are worried about missing an opportunity. That is the advantage attackers get when they compromise a well-known account. They inherit trust that has already been built for them. We recently saw the same basic weakness after hackers hijacked HBO Max’s verified Reddit account. Researchers found that attackers used the compromised account to push 108 malicious ads over roughly 48 hours. Because those ads appeared under a familiar verified account, they had an extra layer of credibility. THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE Microsoft has dealt with a similar account takeover before This is also not Microsoft’s first encounter with a crypto scam involving one of its X accounts. In June 2024, scammers hijacked Microsoft India’s X account and used it to impersonate Keith Gill, better known online as Roaring Kitty. The attackers then promoted what appeared to be a GameStop cryptocurrency presale. People who followed the link and connected their cryptocurrency wallets risked having their assets stolen through wallet-draining malware. That example shows how quickly a social media takeover can turn into something much more expensive. A post may only be the beginning. The real danger often waits behind the link. Even the SEC’s official X account was hijacked One of the clearest examples happened in January 2024 when attackers took over the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s official X account. The compromised account falsely announced that the SEC had approved spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds. According to the Justice Department, Bitcoin jumped by more than $1,000 following the false post. After the SEC regained control and corrected the announcement, Bitcoin fell by more than $2,000. Investigators later determined that attackers gained control through a SIM swap involving the phone number associated with the SEC account. Eric Council Jr. pleaded guilty in February 2025 to conspiracy charges related to the attack and was sentenced in May 2025 to 14 months in prison. That case gives us a good example of how much influence one compromised account can have. An official-looking post can spread quickly before the real organization has time to warn everyone that something has gone wrong. A verification badge cannot guarantee who controls the account right now A verification badge can still be useful. It may help confirm that an account belongs to the person, company or organization it claims to represent. What it cannot tell you is whether that same organization still controls the account at the exact moment you are reading a post. Hackers can steal credentials through phishing or take advantage of other account takeover techniques. SIM swapping has also been used to intercept password reset codes and defeat some forms of two-factor authentication. CyberGuy has covered this problem before on X, where hackers have taken over verified accounts and then changed them to impersonate cryptocurrency projects. The account may look established because it is. The person controlling it may have changed. 7 ways to protect yourself from scams posted by trusted accounts You do not need to assume every surprising post is the work of a hacker. Still, when an account suddenly asks you to spend money or connect something valuable, a few extra checks can save you from a painful mistake. 1) Verify surprising announcements somewhere else If a company announces a cryptocurrency, giveaway or major investment opportunity on social media, go directly to the company’s website. Look for the same announcement in its newsroom or another official channel. If the only place you can find it is one social media post, wait before acting. 2) Pay attention when an account suddenly changes subjects If an account that normally talks about software suddenly starts pushing an obscure crypto token, treat that change as a warning sign. Scroll through its recent posts and check whether the promotion fits anything the company has announced elsewhere. 3) Do not connect your crypto wallet from a social media link Connecting a cryptocurrency wallet can expose you to malicious approvals that allow attackers to move assets. Navigate directly to a service you already trust instead. Never enter your recovery phrase or private key into a site because a social media post tells you to. 4) Use strong security software Strong antivirus software can help warn you about phishing sites, malicious downloads and other threats that may be waiting behind a suspicious link. Security software adds another layer of protection, but it should never replace slowing down and checking where a link came from. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 5) Slow down when money and urgency appear together Scammers love deadlines. You may be told a token is launching right now or that an offer disappears in a few minutes. That pressure is designed to get you moving before you verify what you are seeing. Give yourself time to check another source. 6) Check the destination before entering anything Even when the post comes from a legitimate account, the link inside it may lead somewhere dangerous. Look carefully at the web address before entering a password, payment information or crypto credentials. Small changes in a domain name can lead you to an entirely different site. 7) Protect your own social media accounts Use a unique password for important accounts and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). A password manager can help you create and store strong, unique passwords so you are less likely to reuse them across accounts. An authenticator app or passkey can provide stronger protection than relying only on texted security codes. Also check your account’s active sessions periodically and sign out any devices you do not recognize. What to do if you already clicked What you should do next depends on how far you got before realizing something looked suspicious. Kurt’s key takeaways The Microsoft attack is a good reminder of how quickly the signals we rely on can turn against us. We tell people to check the account name, look for the real profile and be cautious with impersonators. In this case, attackers briefly had control of the account people were supposed to trust. I would still use verification as one clue, but I would never let a checkmark do the thinking for me when money, passwords or a crypto wallet are involved. If a company suddenly posts something that feels out of character, verify it somewhere else before you act. Go to the company’s website, check another official channel and give yourself a minute before clicking. That extra pause can be the difference between spotting a scam and paying for one. title: Minnesota GOP chair blasts progressive group over KKK-themed sign shown during Black House speaker's remarks
description: Sunrise Movement Twin Cities said it disrupted a Minnesota Republican Party fundraiser, displaying a "RepubliKKKan Party" banner during Lisa Demuth's remarks.
content: Minnesota's Republican Party chairman is accusing protesters of racial intimidation after demonstrators disrupted a GOP dinner and displayed a sign invoking the Ku Klux Klan while the state's first Black female House speaker addressed the crowd. Minnesota GOP Chair Alex Plechash blasted the demonstrators in a statement after Friday night's Lincoln Reagan Dinner in Eagan, where protesters held a sign reading "RepubliKKKan Party" during remarks by House Speaker and Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth. "Last night, radical protesters stormed the stage at our Lincoln Reagan Dinner and held up a KKK symbol while Speaker Lisa Demuth spoke," Plechash said in a statement posted to X by the Republican Party of Minnesota. DAVID MARCUS: MINNESOTA GOP CANDIDATES KEEP TRUMP AT ARM'S LENGTH AS THEY EYE A POST-TRUMP PARTY FUTURE "Let's be clear about what happened. Left leaning protesters aimed a symbol of racial terror at a Black woman leader, at a dinner named for the president who ended slavery," he continued. Sunrise Movement Twin Cities, a progressive activist organization, claimed responsibility for the disruption and said the demonstration was intended to protest Republican policies it believes harm immigrants and marginalized communities, according to local news station KTSP. "We disrupted this fundraiser because we refuse to give a moment's peace to the people bankrolling racial violence," the group said in a statement cited by the outlet. The organization also said it was not affiliated with Minnesota's Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL). Video of the incident shows demonstrators moving toward the front of the room holding signs, including one with the letters "KKK" highlighted in red, according to outlet. One protester could be heard shouting, "You love Trump and you will not stand up for Minnesotans," as Demuth stood on stage holding a microphone. As security escorted the demonstrators away, attendees began chanting, "Lisa," followed by chants of, "USA." Plechash told the outlet that protesters gained access to the dinner by purchasing tickets and passing through security checkpoints. KLOBUCHAR'S FRAUD FIGHT CLAIM TAKES HIT AFTER GOP OPPONENT COMBS THROUGH RECEIPTS: 'WHERE WERE YOU?' The chairman said the event experienced two disruptions, the first during remarks by Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michele Tafoya and the second while Demuth was speaking. Plechash said roughly three or four protesters pushed toward the front of the room carrying banners during Demuth's remarks. He estimated the disruption lasted about 30 seconds and said he did not believe the demonstrators posed a physical threat. Plechash said in his X post that Eagan police issued trespass orders and that potential charges remained under investigation. The GOP chairman also called out Minnesota Democrats, specifically naming the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. "Intimidation, criminal behavior, and racist rhetoric have no place in Minnesota politics," Plechash wrote. "Republicans debate ideas, and we'd welcome the DFL to show up and do the same," he added. "Every hour they stay silent says something. Their silence is deafening." Tim Walz.

title: California city backs down on $20K daily fine threat against pastor's food pantry after outpouring of support
description: Matt Mahan says San Jose is offering relocation help to Lighthouse Food Rescue after a citation threatened daily fines of up to $20,000 a day.
content: A California pastor who provides free groceries to more than 1,000 people daily was ordered in September to shut down his food pantry after the city of San Jose cited zoning violations and blocked sidewalks, threatening fines of up to $20,000, just a day before officials changed course following an outpouring of social media support. Lighthouse Food Rescue & Distribution, operated by Pastfor Ralph Olmos, received a citation requiring the nonprofit to remove its food distribution operation from the public sidewalk within 10 days and cease operations at its longtime 17th Street location within 60 days. Olmos told Fox News Digital that despite the city's subsequent offer to help with relocation costs, he sees little possibility of keeping the pantry at its current location, pointing to the city's previous recognition of his charitable work. "I can tell you that this is definitely not my first rodeo with the City," Olmos told Fox News Digital. "But from being called a Beacon of hope, to get out or we will fine you. There really doesn't seem any way that the Lighthouse stays on 17th street." CALIFORNIA GOVERNOR CANDIDATE WARNS OF 'MAGA-LIKE' STATE MOVEMENT UNLESS DEMS 'WAKE UP' Following the backlash, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan and Councilmember Anthony Tordillos, who represent the district where Lighthouse operates, told Fox News Digital that the city was working to help relocate the pantry while addressing concerns about sidewalk accessibility for neighborhood residents. "Two things can be true at once – and they are in this case. Lighthouse is doing incredible work in the community and their neighbors deserve to be able to use the sidewalk," the officials said in a joint statement. "We’ve been working with our Housing Department and Code Compliance Team to find a place where the pastor can relocate and continue serving the community while ensuring that the mobility issues in the neighborhood are addressed so that elderly and disabled residents can get where they need to go," they added. The officials also addressed the potential financial penalties outlined in the city's original enforcement notice, emphasizing that no fines had been imposed and that San Jose was instead offering financial assistance to help the nonprofit relocate. "No fines have been assessed – in fact, the City has offered to help with relocation costs because we are committed to finding a solution that is not punitive but creates a better situation for everyone involved," Mahan and Tordillos said. DEM MAYOR FED UP WITH HOMELESS CRISIS PROPOSES JAILING VAGRANTS WHO REFUSE HOUSING The response followed a report from San Jose Spotlight, detailing a Sept. 25 citation ordering Lighthouse to remove its sidewalk food distribution operation and canopies within 10 days or face potential fines of up to $20,000 daily. The citation also directed the nonprofit to cease operations at its current location within 60 days. Pastor Ralph Olmos, the nonprofit's president and CEO, previously expressed concern about abandoning the families who depend on its services. "I'm up against the wall. It's almost like (the city is) telling me to stop. But my conviction says, 'How can I leave the people?'" Olmos told San Jose Spotlight. The pantry, located near East Julian and North 17th streets, distributes groceries five days a week to families, seniors, homeless residents and people with disabilities. Its offerings include milk, meat, eggs and specialized food packages. WATCH: CALIFORNIA DEMS RALLY AROUND HEALTHCARE FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS DURING FIERY DEBATE Mahan also addressed the controversy on Instagram, saying his administration was working to ensure the organization's charitable efforts continue. "Seeing the outpouring of advocacy and support for [Light House Food Rescue] has been amazing — and I’m right there with you. Pastor Olmos has been doing incredible work in our community and we’re going to make sure that work can continue. My team, alongside our Housing Department, has been in touch with the Pastor over the past week to help them relocate to a location that works for them, the people they serve and their neighbors. The city may even be able to help them with moving costs. Stay tuned!" Mahan said. The controversy marked another dispute between the Lighthouse and the city. In 2022, the nonprofit faced a special use permit requirement costing up to $15,500. Following community opposition, then-Mayor Sam Liccardo and Councilmember Raul Peralez proposed waiving or funding the fees. The City Council later voted unanimously to support relief for food pantries, according to the San Jose Spotlight. That same year, San Jose officially recognized Lighthouse through its Silicon Valley Strong Heroes initiative, praising Olmos and volunteers for feeding vulnerable residents during the pandemic. The city has not publicly confirmed a finalized relocation site or whether the original 60-day shutdown order has been rescinded.

title: Mysterious find beneath field leads man to massive treasure hidden for centuries
description: Marking the largest coin hoard from Emperor Hadrian's era ever found, a metal detector hobbyist unearthed 934 Roman silver denarii near Cologne, Germany.
content: A man searching a German field with a metal detector stumbled upon a remarkable discovery. He found 934 ancient Roman silver coins — and an expert says the nearly 2,000-year-old treasure and "huge hoard" may have been someone's life savings. The coins, found near Wesseling, south of Cologne, were uncovered by Oliver Riedl, according to The Associated Press (AP). Though the hoard was discovered last year, officials only recently announced the find, calling it the largest coin hoard from the reign of Roman Emperor Hadrian ever found in Germany. PUZZLING SOUND IN BACKYARD LEADS HOMEOWNER TO MASSIVE 1,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE A licensed metal detectorist, Riedl immediately alerted archaeological authorities after realizing more coins were buried beneath the surface. The hobbyist told the AP he suspected there were more coins beneath the surface after his metal detector continued picking up signals. "It was clear to me there was something bigger buried here," he said. Pictures show the ancient Roman silver denarii after they were carefully cleaned, some bearing portraits and inscriptions. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ANCIENT SITE DURING RAIL PROJECT, INCLUDING RARE ROMAN FIND The coins were likely buried intentionally between 125 and 150 A.D., according to the LVR Office for the Preservation of Archaeological Monuments in the Rhineland. The staggering hoard weighs 6.8 pounds and is currently on display at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn. The most striking aspect of the hoard was its unusual size, said Johannes Wienand, a professor of ancient history at the Technical University of Braunschweig in Germany. Wienand was not involved in the discovery or its research but told Fox News Digital the hoard is "a huge treasure." POLICE OFFICERS SPOT STRANGE OBJECTS UNDERWATER, THEN MAKE REMARKABLE ANCIENT DISCOVERY "It's certainly the largest Roman coin hoard of that sort from Hadrian's time," he said. "It's a time capsule of the money the people in that period actually used day by day." "A Roman soldier would need six, seven, eight, even more years to save this amount of money, maybe for his retirement." A Roman legionary would have earned a gross salary of around 300 denarii per year, Wienand said, meaning the hoard was roughly equivalent to three years of a soldier's gross salary. "A Roman soldier would need six, seven, eight, even more years to save this amount of money, maybe for his retirement," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The coins were discovered in a rural area near the Rhine frontier, which marked a border of the Roman Empire at the time, he noted. The Roman city of Cologne and a legionary fortress in Bonn were also nearby — raising the possibility of a military connection. While a military connection is possible, Wienand said the identity of the hoard's owner remains unknown. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "It seems to have been the life savings of one person who put this treasure together and put it in a pot, buried it in the soil to save it for later," Wienand said. "And obviously the owner was never able to recover this treasure." Above all, Wienand said the discovery highlights the importance of responsible metal detecting and reporting archaeological finds. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It's actually a story of how to do things right," he said. "The metal detectorist was licensed. He had permission to look for finds like that. He immediately called the heritage officers." Wienand added, "He reported the find, and he contributed to an orderly exploration of this remarkable find." The Associated Press contributed reporting.

title: Mike Elko calls out Texas A&M fans on community message board as Aggies continue to spiral after another loss

content: Things were already extremely grim in College Station after Texas A&M fell to 3-3 on the season with a 27-6 loss at Missouri on Saturday, but Aggies head coach Mike Elko found a way to make things far, far worse moments after the final whistle. Texas A&M began the season ranked eighth in the nation with aspirations of making the College Football Playoff for the second consecutive season. After going 11-1 in 2025 and returning senior quarterback Marcel Reed to one of the highest-paid NIL rosters in the sport, momentum for the Aggies to make noise in 2026 was legitimate. Before even making it to the midway point of October, that noise no longer exists, and that reality has understandably sunk in for one of the largest and most passionate fan bases in college sports. Elko, however, doesn't seem too concerned about his team's fan base, or at least a certain section of it. "There's a difference to me between the fan base and social media. So there's one group that I really don't care much about. Billy's cesspool can go be Billy's cesspool," Elko explained. "Our fan base, stay with us, be behind us. We're going to build something that we told you we were going to build. So we're in a really bad spot right now, but we'll work our way out of it." title: Kelly Clarkson slams Brooklyn store over ‘Pretty Woman’ treatment
description: Kelly Clarkson claims a Brooklyn store employee treated her like she couldn't afford the merchandise, comparing the experience to "Pretty Woman."
content: Kelly Clarkson is calling out a Brooklyn store after she claimed an employee mistreated her. "Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote. KELLY CLARKSON WON’T LET HER KIDS WATCH ‘FROM JUSTIN TO KELLY’ AFTER BRUTAL ADMISSION ABOUT 2003 FILM "Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale," she continued. Clarkson then compared the encounter to a memorable scene from the 1990 film "Pretty Woman," in which Julia Roberts’ character, Vivian Ward, is dismissed by a boutique saleswoman who assumes she cannot afford the store’s clothing. MICHAEL DOUGLAS' WILDEST HOLLYWOOD CONFESSIONS: FROM A-LIST ACTRESS BITE TO JULIA ROBERTS CLASH "But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in ‘Pretty Woman.’ For sure, check it out," Clarkson added. The singer’s description of the incident echoed the famous "Pretty Woman" scene, in which Vivian returns to the boutique after being rejected and tells the saleswoman, "Big mistake. Big. Huge." Clarkson’s post quickly drew attention from her followers, some of whom defended the singer and criticized the store on social media. The Instagram Story was later deleted, according to the outlet. The store posted a statement about Clarkson to their Instagram page on Sunday afternoon. "Yesterday, Kelly Clarkson visited us in Brooklyn and inquired about buying "Molly," a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here. Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale," the store wrote. Adding: "However, the negative experience Kelly described on twitter would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged in a shop. At Art of Play whether someone comes in to make a purchase or simply look around for a while, they are equally welcome. We greet everyone who walks in the door with the invitation to "pick things up and play." And they do, many stay for hours enjoying our puzzles, games and toys." "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It’s been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity. Thanks to all our friends for their support and welcome to all the curious folks who discovered us amidst the drama. We’re going to keep our heads down and hopefully, we can clear things up with Kelly someday. As a talented popular singer once said "what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger." That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," Clarkson wrote, adding a thumbs up emoji. The singer continued: "So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn't happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone "yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can." That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it," adding a checkmark emoji. Clarkson added: "And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things. I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. Art of Play took to social media to "clarify one additional detail" about Clarkson's visit. "During the 5 minutes she spent in the store, she inquired about our mechanical bird puppet named Molly. We explained that while Molly is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a de facto mascot for our shop, a nearly identical automaton is owned by the creator of the machines, a brilliant artist named Bliss Kolb who lives in Seattle. He told us he would be willing to part with Molly’s twin for $15,000. We explained all of this to Kelly Clarkson." title: Silent inflammation could be damaging your body — and 5 habits may help keep it in check
description: Jim LaValle reveals how the gut-immune-brain interface drives chronic inflammation, and why stress, blood sugar and environmental toxins play key roles.
content: Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but when it becomes chronic, it can pose a health threat, according to the National Institutes of Health. Over time, chronic inflammation can contribute to rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease. Keeping the condition in check can help protect healthy tissues and support overall health, experts say. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS Jim LaValle, a clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert based in Texas, told Fox News Digital that inflammation can be influenced by a variety of factors beyond injury or infection. LaValle first pointed to the gut-immune-brain connection — the communication between gut microbes, the immune system and the central nervous system — as one pathway that can influence the body's inflammatory response. Beyond gut health, he said several everyday lifestyle factors can play a role in preventing chronic inflammation. DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE No. 1: Manage stress Managing stress and anxiety can help support the gut-brain connection and keep inflammation in check, according to LaValle. He pointed to cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress, which he said can "wreak havoc on your chemistry" when levels remain elevated. Chronic stress can also affect the intestinal barrier, potentially allowing substances that would normally remain inside the gut to pass through more easily, LaValle said. This increased intestinal permeability is sometimes called "leaky gut." ZERO SUGAR, MORE PROBLEMS? STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING GUT HEALTH EFFECTS "So, it turns out that if I'm stressed out a lot, I can be more prone to irritable bowel," LaValle said, as stress can trigger or worsen digestive symptoms in some people. No. 2: Watch for food triggers Diets high in sugar, fat and ultraprocessed foods can also affect gut health. Paying attention to which foods trigger certain symptoms may help identify potential food sensitivities or intolerances, LaValle noted. Symptoms such as bloating, rashes or discomfort after eating certain foods may signal a food-related reaction, although they can have other causes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Certain medications, including antibiotics, may also alter the gut microbiome, but their effects vary depending on the drug and the individual, the expert said. No. 3: Keep blood sugar in check Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation, according to LaValle. LaValle noted that conditions such as diabetes and insulin resistance are often associated with chronic inflammation. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Research suggests that GLP-1 medications, commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, may have anti-inflammatory effects, while scientists are investigating other potential benefits beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. No. 4: Be aware of environmental exposures The "exposome," or the environmental exposures people experience throughout their lives, can influence inflammation and the risk of chronic disease, according to the National Institutes of Health. LaValle pointed to emerging research on how environmental exposures — including "forever chemicals," microplastics, metals and pesticides — may affect weight, blood sugar regulation and other aspects of health. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "A lot of us don't think about that kind of impact on our health and how that could trigger inflammation signaling," he added. No. 5: Don’t over-train Regular exercise supports overall health, but intense workouts without adequate recovery time can put additional stress on the body, LaValle cautioned. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "You’re not getting a good enough recovery," he said. "You’re training hard. And, in fact, you might be training hard every day to lower that cortisol, but you're not getting good recovery. And that could lead to silent inflammatory signaling as well." Anyone who is concerned about chronic inflammation or is experiencing persistent symptoms should consult a doctor to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment.

title: A child's question at a funeral reminded us death does not get the last word
description: A five-year-old's question at his great-grandmother's funeral sparked reflections on C. S. Lewis, hospice hymns, and the hope of eternity.
content: The question came unexpectedly from my five-year-old grandson. My late mom’s pastor had gathered our family to explain how her funeral service would go and asked if we had any final questions before we processed into the church. Raising his hand, my grandson inquired, "Will we see Momma Bettie again?" DOLLY PARTON'S PATH FROM NASHVILLE NEWCOMER TO BILLBOARD'S NO. 1 COUNTRY MUSIC ARTIST OF ALL TIME The poignancy of his request brought tears to the eyes of almost everyone in the room. As I pondered seeing my mom again in heaven, my grandson’s query brought to mind C. S. Lewis’s famous sermon, "The Weight of Glory." Given at Oxford in 1941, Lewis posed the thought-provoking statement, "There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal." This Christian belief — that we are both image-bearers of God and have eternal existence — was the basis from which Lewis preached. And for followers of Jesus — he provided an eternal perspective — not only that our life has purpose and a higher calling, but how we should truly love those around us. As Lewis concluded his sermon, "Next to the Blessed Sacrament itself, your neighbour is the holiest object presented to your senses. If he is your Christian neighbour he is holy in almost the same way, for in him also Christ vere latitat — the glorifier and the glorified, Glory Himself, is truly hidden." This conviction informed my mom as well. For she believed the Gospel changed everything. Spending time with her during the last week of her life in hospice was both deeply sad and amazingly redemptive and beautiful. It was such a blessing to witness her saying goodbye to family and friends — as she reflected on her life, gave advice, and let the light of Christ shine forth from her as she faced death with no fear. When I asked my children to reflect on a favorite memory of my mom, they reminisced about spending time in her home — including watching movies she selected for our evening entertainment. From To Kill a Mockingbird to Anne of Green Gables to an obscure black-and-white classic, we never knew what she'd planned for us to view together. One of the most memorable films we enjoyed was Coat of Many Colors — the story of a young Dolly Parton and her family growing up in poverty in the Great Smoky Mountains of Tennessee. In fact, 13 million viewers watched the premiere on December 10, 2015 —prompting NBC to re-air the film on Christmas night that year we visited. The film was powerful not only because it showed the real pain and trials of Dolly and her family, but also because it showed redemption and reconciliation. Reflecting on Dolly's recent passing, I thought these themes, in many ways, captured my mom's heart and approach to life as a wife, mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, and friend. Growing up in humble surroundings, she too looked for redemptive elements in life — whether it was family, church, community, literature, art, film, or music Along these lines, she kept an old Baptist Hymnal that she found at a garage sale with her Bible. As I was preparing for her eulogy, I found an inscription she wrote at the front: "There is great strength in these hymns. The words come to me even in my sleep. I love to wake up with a song already playing in my soul. The songs are planted in my heart through years of singing them." Flipping through the hymnal, I discovered that she had hearted the song "I Need Thee Every Hour." I now understood why, in her final days in hospice, when she barely opened her eyes, she started singing with me when I read the song "Lord I Need You, Oh I need you, Every hour I need you" from the timely Worship Initiative devotional that aired that week. It was a beautiful, powerful moment that demonstrated these songs sown in her spirit—and the hope and comfort they brought to her as she faced death. As a matter of fact, the last week in hospice showed me not only her deep love of the Lord, her family and friends, but also a heart for reconciliation. As I read through Gone From My Sight: The Dying Experience that week — provided by many hospice facilities around the country to walk through this process — I learned how "unfinished business" can be a big factor "in determining how much resistance we put into meeting death." Due to a challenging family situation, she had not seen two of her grandchildren since my father’s funeral eight years earlier. Nevertheless, when they heard about my mom’s condition, they arrived just in time to say their goodbyes. Knowing she had prayed to see them again and be reconciled, I was so thankful for the sweet time she had with both, leading her to tell my nephew that she could now die. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION It would be the last conversation she had before passing two days later. In regard to my grandson’s question the afternoon of my mom’s funeral, the pastor responded beautifully, explaining that we would one day see her again — not in the feeble, frail state she had left the world — but as St. Paul described to the Church of Corinth, in her heavenly body. For "in Christ all shall be made alive…[and] raised in glory," (I Corinthians 15). CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A great comfort as we ponder the weight of eternity.

title: Elon Musk's mom Maye nearly turned down SI Swimsuit cover over 'wrinkles and cellulite'
description: Maye Musk nearly turned down her Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover over wrinkle fears, but a phone call from her daughter changed everything.
content: Maye Musk nearly passed on the chance to make a splash in Sports Illustrated Swimsuit because she worried about looking "wrinkly" in the iconic magazine. The Canadian-born, South African-raised model made history in 2022 as the oldest Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover model at 74. Martha Stewart later broke the record at 81 in 2023. Now, Musk is looking back at the milestone and her journey from a single mother of three to a sought-after model in her new book, "Timeless." "At my age, you have wrinkles and cellulite on your arms and on your thighs, so I prefer to wear long sleeves," the mother of tech mogul Elon Musk told Fox News Digital. "So, the idea of wearing a swimsuit was very uncomfortable. But then my daughter called me. I told her they were going to be shooting in Belize. She instantly said, 'You've got to go. Belize is beautiful.' So, I did. I took a chance." MAYE MUSK DEFENDS SYDNEY SWEENEY'S NUDE SPORTS AD AND RECALLS 12-YEAR PATH TO CITIZENSHIP In the book, Musk wrote, "I was still 73. My skin showed the signs of my weight having cycled up and down so many times in my life, including for each of my pregnancies. I'm wrinkly and I have cellulite. Swimsuit model?" Despite her worries, Musk said she felt at ease when she began posing for photographer Yu Tsai. She even wore colorful two-pieces for the occasion. When you think of swimsuit models, you think of the Victoria's Secret models. Those are really special body shapes. So it was a challenge for me. But as I say, you have to take a chance in life. And I knew they're not going to publish ugly photos. At one point, I felt so at ease that I even started dancing with the local people. I was in awe of exploring a new country, a new culture. That's what I love doing. And I got to celebrate me." WATCH: MAYE MUSK DISCUSSES RAISING ELON MUSK, ESCAPING TOXIC MARRIAGE IN NEW MEMOIR ‘TIMELESS’ Looking back, Musk said she wonders why she was so nervous. "When women go to the beach, they wrap a towel around themselves," she said. "But men, they could be obese, and they're still strutting in Speedos with such confidence. We really have to make a change. And if any man insults your body, well, they can get lost. There's always going to be somebody who feels the need to trash on you. It's not fair. But it's all about embracing who you are and not apologizing for that." Musk didn't undergo a makeover to appear younger for the cover. Her signature silver hair remained untouched. "Why do I need to color my hair?" Musk said. "You have to do the roots every four weeks, and I used to do them myself. Your hair then becomes very brittle because it's so damaged. And it grows out. And then I decided to cut my hair short. Soon after, I had four billboards in Times Square. I didn't feel like a granny. I felt fashionable." It wasn't the first time Musk took a chance on a modeling gig. In her book, Musk describes a phone call she received from her agent: "Tomorrow, you pose naked for the cover of TIME magazine. You're the only model they want and they won't budge." Musk had never done a nude shoot because, as she wrote, "nobody had ever asked." "I picked up the phone to dial Elon first, then stopped myself," Musk wrote. "I already knew what he would say: 'Absolutely not.' He was not the kind of son who wanted his mother naked on magazine covers. Not prudish, but definitely more conservative when it came to nudity. So I called Tosca. I wasn't too surprised to find that she was not in love with the idea, either. 'You never do naked!' she said. Her instinct was protective, not wanting me to risk an uncomfortable experience." "Finally, I called Kimbal," she wrote. "Of my three children, he is the most relaxed and free-spirited. (He met his current wife at Burning Man.) He had a completely different perspective. ‘It’s TIME magazine. It’s journalism,’ he said. ‘Not some nudie magazine. It’ll be tasteful. You have nothing to worry about. Do it.’" Musk told Fox News Digital it was important for her to get her children's approval before posing nude. "Well, would you want your mother naked on the front cover of a magazine?" she said. "But it was Kimbal who encouraged me. He said it would be tasteful. He's always been a free spirit. And I trust him. When I arrived for the photoshoot, they were very careful with me. You have a makeup artist who has to go through your whole body. Then they did my hair and very plain makeup. Then they sat me with a mirror in front of me, so I could see exactly what the photographer sees." "The photographer came in for the shoot, and maybe five minutes later, it was over," she said. "It was really quick and very respectful. They immediately brought a robe for me. I got changed and went home. That's all there was to it." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS For Musk, aging with confidence isn't just about embracing wrinkles and silver hair. The longtime dietitian also believes that taking care of your health plays an important role in feeling your best at any age. "It gets harder to lose weight as you get older," Musk said. "With my patients, I always tell them to plan ahead. If you get hungry, there's no salad next to you. There's a donut. Also, only eat when you're hungry. And when you are hungry, make sure there is healthy food around, no desserts or chocolates. And if my patient didn't take the journey seriously, I would tell them, 'You can't come anymore.'" "Even 10 pounds can make you feel uncomfortable," she said. "Everything is tight and you don't have confidence. You have to track your food intake. If a patient goes off what I recommended, they need to explain why. You need to hold yourself accountable if you want to make smarter choices for your health." Musk said each decade of her life has been better than the last. At 78, she's happily embracing aging and hopes other women will do the same. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "When my mom was 86, she moved from South Africa to Canada and started all over," Musk said. "She was an artist. When she was nearing 90, her hands weren't strong enough to do the wood carvings she loved. So, by 94, she started doing computer art. My older sister taught her. She died at 98. But she always remained curious and busy. She was always exploring." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "You're never too old to start again," Musk said. "And don't worry about the wrinkles. A man doesn't care if he gets wrinkles. He still has his confidence. When you get insecure, you become less attractive. I didn't do anything to my face because I wanted to frown and have expression. But also, don't mix with people who make you feel insecure. They're not your friends. And there will be people who will push you down. You can't stay down. You just have to get up and show your talents, who you are."

title: Hollywood jobs flee overseas as Congress scrambles to stop production exodus — with Trump's blessing
description: A bipartisan bill aims to create a federal film tax credit to stop movie and TV production from fleeing overseas to Europe and Canada.
content: Congress is scrambling to stop one of the United States' most iconic industries from fleeing overseas and taking thousands of jobs along with it. The U.S. TV and film industry has been hemorrhaging work for years as production companies and movie studios flee to places like Europe and Canada for friendlier tax regimes and other attractive financial policies. It prompted President Donald Trump to publicly call on Congress to pass legislation aimed at incentivizing entertainment studios to bring their production back home — and an unlikely alliance of lawmakers is heeding the call. A new bill that could potentially end up in a bipartisan tax package at the end of this year would push film and TV studios to bring their productions back to the U.S. via new tax incentives, with extra support if they choose to bring development to rural communities. TRUMP CALLS HOLLYWOOD A 'TOTAL DISASTER,' PUSHES FEDERAL TAX INCENTIVE FOR FILM AFTER MEETING WITH JON VOIGHT "Since I was a child, I was moved and inspired by the stories of America's greatness, by living out the American dream, and by the notion that I could do and achieve anything in this world, if I set my mind to it, and most of that was driven by a whole lot of American-made movies," Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "I want this next generation to be inspired the same way, and I do not want American storytelling to go overseas, to be diluted by values from overseas." Moran's East Texas congressional district is largely rural and a far cry from the Sunset Strip that was home to much of America's filmmaking history. title: Abbas delays Palestinian elections again, making more than two decades without vote
description: Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas delayed elections to 2027, extending a nearly 20-year wait as Israel and Hamas clash over the blame.
content: More than two decades after being elected to what was supposed to be a four-year term, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has once again postponed elections, extending a nearly 20-year wait for voters to choose a new legislature. Abbas issued a decree Friday pushing Palestinian Legislative Council elections from next month to Sept. 11, 2027, according to the official Palestinian news agency WAFA. Presidential elections, which have not been held since Abbas' 2005 victory, are also scheduled for that date. The delay allows Palestinian leaders to remain in power without facing voters and could further damage the credibility of the Palestinian Authority, which has faced criticism over corruption and its security cooperation with Israel. NICARAGUA'S ORTEGA SAYS COUNTRY WILL 'NEVER AGAIN' HOLD ELECTIONS, SHUTTING OUT OPPOSITION The Palestinian Authority, dominated by Abbas' Fatah party, governs parts of the West Bank under agreements reached in the 1990s. Palestinian officials cited conditions in the West Bank, Gaza Strip and east Jerusalem as reasons for postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, claimed Israel had blocked election materials and international observers from entering Gaza, according to The Associated Press. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar rejected the claim, accusing Abbas of trying to shift blame for the delay. Abbas' "attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability," Saar wrote on X. Hamas, meanwhile, welcomed the postponement, calling it "a step in the right direction" and urging further talks on rebuilding Palestinian institutions before holding elections. Palestinians last held legislative elections in 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries subsequently boycotted the Hamas-led government, fueling unrest that ended with Hamas taking control of Gaza in 2007. IRAN REAFFIRMS SUPPORT FOR HAMAS AS TRUMP PUSHES TO DISARM TERROR GROUP Since then, Hamas has controlled Gaza while Abbas' Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority has governed parts of the West Bank. The postponed election also threatened to bring new challenges to Abbas' leadership. Before the delay, Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and a faction led by Mohammed Dahlan, a former Fatah security chief who fell out with Abbas, had been discussing an unlikely political alliance. "Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement. The decision comes as the Palestinian Authority's future role in Gaza remains uncertain under a U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year. Hamas continues to govern the territory, while a committee of Palestinian technocrats remains in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza and oversee a transition of power. title: WNBA Finals: Angel Reese headlines championship showdown as league seeks to draw viewers without Caitlin Clark
description: With Caitlin Clark and the Fever eliminated, Angel Reese's Atlanta Dream face the Golden State Valkyries in a huge WNBA Finals viewership test.
content: The WNBA didn't get Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham in the Finals, but it may have gotten the next best thing in terms of viewership hopes. Angel Reese’s Atlanta Dream face the Golden State Valkyries in a best-of-seven series beginning Oct. 17, matching a franchise seeking its first championship against an expansion team chasing a title in its second season. Both organizations also bring distinctive cultural identities. Atlanta’s players once campaigned against their own Republican co-owner, supporting Democrat Raphael Warnock. Golden State has embraced LGBTQ outreach through Pride celebrations, drag performances and community partnerships. Those histories offer another layer to a matchup with straightforward basketball questions: Can Golden State prevent Reese from creating second chances, and can Atlanta’s defense generate enough easy baskets to win the championship? The Angel Reese show CAITLIN CLARK'S LOWEST-RATED PLAYOFF GAME STILL OUTDREW EVERY NON-FEVER FIRST-ROUND BROADCAST These Finals could provide an indication of the WNBA’s current drawing power without Clark, and just how much star power Angel Reese has. Reese brings a substantial following of her own. Her Instagram account had approximately 5.3 million followers as of Oct. 10, which is the most of any WNBA player and more than one million more than Clark. Her visibility extends beyond basketball. She has a signature Reebok shoe and became the first female athlete featured in a national McDonald’s meal collaboration in 2025. Those partnerships have put her name before consumers who may not regularly watch the WNBA. Her first Finals appearance now offers an opportunity to see whether that recognition translates into viewers following her pursuit of a championship, with Clark and the Fever eliminated. There are substantial audiences to measure against. Indiana’s decisive first-round loss to Las Vegas averaged 2.25 million viewers across USA Network and CNBC. Atlanta’s semifinal opener against New York averaged 1.2 million on ABC, according to Sports Media Watch. The games aired on different networks and in different time slots, making them benchmarks rather than a direct measure of either player’s individual appeal. The league has already demonstrated that a Finals without either Clark or Reese can attract a sizable audience. Last year’s Las Vegas–Phoenix championship series averaged 1.5 million viewers across ABC and ESPN, the second-most-watched Finals on ESPN networks behind 2024. This year’s series will air across NBC, USA Network and Peacock, adding another consideration to comparisons with previous championships. One series cannot establish the league’s permanent audience ceiling. But Reese’s championship debut could help show how much of her substantial off-court following—and the broader interest surrounding the WNBA—will follow her onto its biggest stage. Both the Dream and Valkyries have histories of left-wing activism Atlanta brings a history of campaigning against a Republican co-owner, while Golden State has established prominent ties to LGBTQ advocacy. The Dream’s political activism drew national attention in 2020, when then-co-owner Republican Sen. Kelly Loeffler opposed the WNBA’s embrace of the Black Lives Matter movement. She urged the league to replace planned Black Lives Matter and "Say Her Name" warmup apparel with American flags. "The truth is, we need less — not more politics in sports," Loeffler wrote to then-Commissioner Cathy Engelbert. Dream players and others across the league responded by wearing "Vote Warnock" shirts, supporting Democrat Raphael Warnock in his challenge to Loeffler. Atlanta’s Elizabeth Williams described the effort as voluntary and driven by players. Warnock defeated Loeffler in the January 2021 runoff. AMERICANS CLASH OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES AS DEBATE HEATS UP: ‘JUST GETTING OUTRAGEOUS' The following month, the league approved the Dream’s sale to an ownership group comprising Larry Gottesdiener, Suzanne Abair and former Dream guard Renee Montgomery. Montgomery, who had sat out the 2020 season to focus on social justice work, remains a co-owner and vice president. The franchise’s official biography highlights her advocacy for social justice and equality in women’s sports. Those events preceded Reese’s arrival in Atlanta by several years. Golden State, which began playing in 2025, has a shorter organizational history but has made LGBTQ outreach a visible part of its identity. Its second annual Pride Game, against Atlanta on June 26, featured a surrounding celebration with drag performances, Pride merchandise and a halftime lineup featuring Sasha Colby. The franchise also announced participation in four regional Pride celebrations and sponsorship of the San Francisco International LGBTQ+ Film Festival. The Valkyries’ advocacy earned recognition from Equality California and the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, along with a Community Ally Award from the Harvey Milk LGBTQ Democratic Club. After Golden State’s victory over Atlanta that Pride Night, Gabby Williams celebrated toward a camera with the declaration, "For the gays!" Williams and Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase have also publicly supported transgender athletes participating in women’s sports. Before an Aug. 2 game, Nakase said her emphasis on inclusion extended to transgender women. "I’m all about women, little girls deserving to play, and that includes trans women," she said. Williams expressed a similar position during a May 19 media scrum, before clip resurfaced and spread widely in August. "I would welcome a trans athlete on my team or against my team, anytime," Williams told reporters. Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom subsequently cited Williams’ support as an inspiration for his announced bid to enter the 2027 WNBA draft. During an Aug. 14 interview with former Auburn coach Bruce Pearl, Freedom recalled seeing comments welcoming transgender teammates and opponents and deciding to pursue the opportunity himself. Freedom later confirmed to OutKick that it was Williams' comments that inspired him. "If they don’t have any problem with it, why not just go out there and take my shot?" Freedom said. Engelbert’s last Finals and the WNBA’s next chapter This championship series will also close a chapter for the WNBA’s leadership. Commissioner Cathy Engelbert announced in September that she will retire at the end of 2026, making Atlanta’s matchup with Golden State the last Finals of her tenure. Her final season began with uncertainty over whether labor negotiations would disrupt the league’s schedule. The eventual agreement delivered substantial raises for players and a seven-year deal running through 2032, giving her successor a foundation for the years ahead. Questions about officiating and player safety continued during the season. In June, Phoenix’s Alyssa Thomas received a one-game suspension after making contact with her fist to Clark’s throat. Officials did not call a foul during the play; the league imposed the punishment after reviewing it. Indiana coach Stephanie White publicly criticized the officiating afterward. Away from the court, league officials and players also confronted online harassment and a widening debate over transgender athletes in women’s sports. An August meeting of the league’s anti-hate task force addressed both subjects. The WNBA said there were no immediate eligibility matters affecting the league and pledged further discussions with teams and the players’ association. Some changes will arrive after Engelbert leaves. A centralized replay center is scheduled to launch in 2027, giving officials access to additional camera angles and assistance reviewing eligible plays. Its introduction will provide an early opportunity for the next commissioner to demonstrate progress on a recurring source of frustration. Expansion will also continue, with Cleveland beginning play in 2028, Detroit in 2029 and Philadelphia in 2030. That means more markets, more roster spots and more pressure to turn growing interest into sustained support. Against that backdrop, these Finals offer a look at the league Engelbert is leaving behind—and the task ahead: building lasting audiences for more teams and players while addressing the disputes that have accompanied the WNBA’s growth. The basketball And there will be some actual basketball being played too. Reese reached her first WNBA Finals after averaging 16.4 points and 12.1 rebounds during the regular season and winning Defensive Player of the Year. Golden State’s Kiah Stokes could make those opportunities harder to find. She helped defend A’ja Wilson during the semifinals and collected 14 rebounds in the opener. The battle near the basket will test whether Reese can establish position and create second chances against another experienced rebounder. At the other end, Gabby Williams has taken on a larger scoring role for Golden State. She enters the Finals averaging about 23 points in the playoffs, up from roughly 14 during the regular season. Atlanta must decide how much defensive attention to give her without leaving other Valkyries open. Williams has already shown she will trust those teammates. Late in the second semifinal game against Las Vegas, she passed to Veronica Burton, whose only basket of the night was a decisive 3-pointer. Tiffany Hayes added 21 points off the bench, demonstrating how Golden State can find scoring help beyond its starters. Atlanta has its own player capable of controlling a game without dominating the headlines. title: Real-life exorcist reveals eerie encounter, warns Hollywood misses most terrifying part of demonic possession
description: Father Carlos Martins reveals what Hollywood gets wrong about demonic possession and why the devil's mind is more terrifying than any spectacle.
content: Hollywood has spent decades frightening audiences with spinning heads, levitating bodies and priests shouting down demons. But Catholic exorcist Father Carlos Martins says the most terrifying part of alleged demonic possession isn't what the audience can see. It's what they can't. "The thing that Hollywood doesn't pick up well is the demonic mind," Fr. Martins told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview ahead of Halloween, as the third season of "The Exorcist Files" podcast gets underway. "It picks up [the devil's] demonic power well, throwing of chairs, the screaming, levitating and so on and so forth. But his rage, his inner anger, his disgust with humans and God, that it doesn't get well." FATHER CARLOS MARTINS RECOUNTS CHILLING EXORCISM, CLAIMS WOMAN MOVED OBJECTS WITHOUT TOUCHING THEM Fr. Martins, who co-hosts the podcast with co-creator Ryan Bethea, described what he believes Hollywood misses about the psychological dimension of alleged demonic encounters, including an incident in which he said a person undergoing an exorcism threatened to bomb a flight he was scheduled to take the following day. "Why are you here? You're not supposed to be here. I'm going to bomb your flight tomorrow," Fr. Martins recalled hearing while assisting another exorcist. The priest said he subsequently changed his flight, not because of the threat, but because the session had been so productive that he offered to remain for additional appointments. When he returned the next day, Fr. Martins said, the person appeared surprised by his presence. CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND "You weren't supposed to be here," he recalled the possessed person saying. Fr. Martins interpreted the encounter as evidence of what he believes is the extraordinary but imperfect intelligence of the devil and demonic beings. He said the apparent knowledge of his original flight contrasted with the alleged demonic entity's failure to anticipate his changed plans. For Fr. Martins, the encounter was a chilling example of why he believes the most frightening aspect of demonic possession has very little to do with the supernatural spectacles audiences see on-screen. The third season of "The Exorcist Files" launched Oct. 5, with new episodes scheduled to roll out over the next two months. Among the new cases is an especially complicated account involving multiple family members, according Bethea. IOWA CITY COUNCIL MEETING ERUPTS AFTER FORMER MEMBER OPENS WITH SATANIC PRAYER AND 'HAIL SATAN' "There is one particular episode this season that involves so many moving parts and multiple family members being demonized," Bethea told Fox News Digital. The case, he added, "actually spans hundreds of years." Bethea said the story may encourage listeners to examine unresolved trauma, mental health concerns and other personal struggles that he and Fr. Martins believe may contribute to spiritual vulnerability. The podcast, which dramatizes purported exorcism case files, has also challenged Bethea's own understanding of spiritual warfare. After working with Fr. Martins and hearing similar accounts from other exorcists, Bethea said he has become more confident in his Christian faith rather than more fearful of the supernatural. "I have walked away feeling, ironically, less scared and more confident than ever," he said. SACRED PAGES OF 1,000-YEAR-OLD GOSPEL REVEAL ANCIENT DNA SCIENTISTS NEVER EXPECTED Fr. Martins warned that what he considers the greatest danger of demonic influence is not necessarily its physical manifestations, but the intimate knowledge he believes the devil and evil forces possess about their targets. "When you're dealing with the devil, you're dealing with an entity that has observed you your whole life," Fr. Martins said. "He knows your weaknesses. He knows where your soft spots are. He knows what your preferences are." "So he knows exactly where to press and how hard to cause maximal damage," the priest added. Fr. Martins cautioned against attempting to confront demonic forces without spiritual preparation, arguing that human intelligence alone is no match for the adversary he describes as the "ancient serpent." The priest acknowledged that the 1973 horror classic "The Exorcist" remains, in his view, a compelling depiction of what can occur during an exorcism, although he singled out the film's famous head-spinning sequence as physically impossible. He also described witnessing what appeared to be a person's canine teeth growing several inches, an experience he attributed to a supernatural illusion rather than an actual physical transformation. POPE LEO VISITS SITE OF MIRACLE CURES, MEETS PEOPLE WHOSE UNEXPLAINED HEALINGS STUNNED DOCTORS For Fr. Martins, however, the disturbing imagery is secondary to what he described as the hatred and irrationality of the demonic mind. "Because that is the part of him that has no rational explanation," he said. Despite the dramatic subject matter, Fr. Martins said the actual practice of exorcism is considerably less theatrical than its Hollywood portrayal. "I never yell at the devil. I've never heard of an exorcist doing that," Fr. Martins said. He described exorcism as a generally calm process centered on prayer, spiritual reconciliation and helping the individual receiving assistance. "The job of the exorcist is not to cast out the devil," Fr. Martins said. Rather than attempting to overpower an alleged demon through increasingly forceful prayers, Fr. Martins said he seeks to understand why he believes the entity has gained influence over an individual and how that person can return to a state of reconciliation with Christ. The priest also described exorcist training as largely an apprenticeship process, with less experienced priests learning alongside seasoned practitioners before conducting sessions independently. FORMER TV ANCHOR WHO PLEADED GUILTY TO KILLING MOTHER LAST HALLOWEEN GETS LIFE SENTENCE With Halloween approaching, Fr. Martins and Bethea also addressed whether ordinary holiday traditions pose spiritual dangers. Fr. Martins said he does not oppose children dressing up or going trick-or-treating, although he would discourage costumes celebrating evil or demonic imagery. "Would I allow my children to go trick or treating? Yeah, I would," Fr. Martins said. "I would never let them go dressed as something sordid. As something evil, as something devilish or demonic." The priest said he would have no objection to children dressing as ordinary characters or participating in family-friendly Halloween traditions, provided the costumes did not celebrate something he considers contrary to his religious beliefs. Bethea similarly defended activities such as trick-or-treating and harvest festivals, recalling how his mother enthusiastically created Halloween costumes when he was a child. However, he cautioned against practices he associates with occult involvement. MASSIVE 2,000-YEAR-OLD DISCOVERY FROM TIME OF JESUS EMERGES REMARKABLY INTACT The podcast has featured several cases involving Ouija boards, including an account in which a grandmother reportedly gave her grandson a board so they could communicate after her death. Another case involved three children experimenting with a Ouija board, with one allegedly experiencing disturbing consequences, despite not having initiated the activity, according to Bethea. He also identified astrology and tarot cards among practices the hosts discourage, arguing that they can expose people to what he believes are spiritual dangers. "We would say there are plenty of fun, other games that you can play," Bethea said. He jokingly suggested Risk and Monopoly as alternatives, before noting that greed could also be considered a sin. Bethea emphasized that the show's accounts should not be interpreted as a reason to assume every unexplained experience has a supernatural cause, and pointed to psychological assessments and other scrutiny involved in determining whether someone should receive an exorcism. The co-host also acknowledged that he had not seen evidence establishing Halloween as a universally heightened period of supernatural activity, despite hearing such claims from people interviewed for the podcast. For both hosts, the larger message of "The Exorcist Files" is intended to be one of hope over fear. Bethea said producing the series has strengthened his Christian faith, and listeners have contacted the show describing renewed religious commitment after hearing its stories. Martins likewise said that although his work involves confronting what he believes to be demonic forces, he does not spend his personal life preoccupied with the devil. "You know, the devil has a plan for you. But the good news is, so does God," he said. "Am I afraid of the devil? No, I'm afraid of being separated from Jesus Christ."

title: ‘Big Balls’ of DOGE fame gives exclusive look at new Trump mission to overhaul government
description: Edward Coristine reveals plans to make passport applications fully digital through America.gov, the AI-powered platform replacing thousands of sites.
content: Edward Coristine, the former DOGE engineer better known as "Big Balls," is now helping build the Trump administration’s new digital front door to the federal government — an effort aimed at giving Americans one place to navigate information and, eventually, complete services now spread across thousands of government websites. "I think that the fact that there’s 29,000 government websites is pretty insane," Coristine told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview. "And it is the citizens’ objective to have to go figure out which government website they’re supposed to use for each specific thing." Coristine — better known around Washington by his attention-grabbing "Big Balls" nickname — sat down with Fox News Digital at the White House to talk about his new role helping build America.gov, what he learned during his time at DOGE, the administration’s plans to make more government services fully digital, his experience being attacked in Washington, and how the nickname that helped make him famous actually came from his dad. TRUMP UNVEILS AMERICA.GOV AS AI-POWERED HUB FOR PASSPORTS, MEDICARE ENROLLMENT AND MORE Coristine is now working with the National Design Studio on the administration’s revamped America.gov, which launched Sept. 29 as an AI-powered single point of entry for information drawn from thousands of government websites. President Donald Trump singled out Coristine during the launch, identifying him as the project’s lead engineer and thanking him for his work. Coristine said his time at DOGE gave him a firsthand look at the frustration Americans face when trying to navigate federal services and helped shape what he is working on now. "I think we got a lot of feedback that the American government is hard to interact with because you have to navigate the maze of bureaucratic services," Coristine said. The software engineer had already worked in Musk’s orbit before joining DOGE, spending several months at Neuralink, Musk’s brain-computer interface company, before later joining the government efficiency effort at 19. "What I think is really special about America.gov is it presents a single point of entry to find all the information that you need," he added, including finding government services tailored to the user and asking questions with answers sourced from the federal government. TRUMP TO USHER IN ‘GOLDEN AGE’ OF AMERICAN TECH WITH DC BASH SHOWCASING POWERFUL NEW TOOL Coristine pointed to Medicare as one example, saying Americans currently may have to move between Medicare.gov and the Social Security website to enroll in benefits. "Companies, generally speaking, only have one website and everything is easy to find," he said. "We should have the same vision for the government." The ambitions for America.gov also go beyond simply helping users find the right information. Coristine said the administration plans to make first-time passport applications fully digital, expanding beyond the online renewal system already available to eligible Americans. "Specifically with passports, what we’re going to do is we’re gonna make new passports online for the first time ever," Coristine said, describing the existing process as "very manual." TRUMP’S NEW HIGH-TECH GOVERNMENT HUB HOLDS SOME BIZARRE SURPRISES: ‘ENJOY FINDING THEM’ "You have to go in person, you have to get to the post office, you get your photo taken like a CVS or Walgreens," he said. Under the planned system, Coristine said users would be able to take their passport photo at home, preview how it would appear on the document and complete the process "without leaving the America.gov website." Coristine also offered a glimpse into how Trump has talked about the broader project, comparing the president’s approach to digital government with his background in hospitality. "I think the president has been a great host for his entire career. He’s been in the hospitality business, right?" Coristine said. "So any great host knows they have to make things easy, they have to make it all feel clean." ELON MUSK LANDS NEW TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ROLE SHAPING FUTURE OF AMERICAN WARFARE "President Trump is very focused on removing the potholes from the digital government that make it hard to get things done," he added. The role marks the latest chapter in a whirlwind stint in Washington that began at DOGE and quickly thrust the 20-year-old — and his now-famous "Big Balls" nickname — into the national spotlight. Coristine told Fox News Digital the "Big Balls" moniker had a far less dramatic origin than its eventual notoriety might suggest. "I got the nickname Big Balls from my dad," he said, explaining that he eventually made it his LinkedIn URL AND THIS IS WHAT DROVE IT INTO THE NATIONAL SPOTLIGHT, RIGHT? "It was actually, like, fairly underground, but I was discovered," Coristine said. "It’s been very funny ever since." EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE THE SECRETIVE MINE DOGE HELPED DRAG OUT OF A DECADES-OLD BUREAUCRATIC BLACK HOLE Coristine’s profile rose further in August 2025 after he was attacked while walking a female friend back to her car in Washington’s Logan Circle neighborhood, an incident that left him with a broken nose and concussion and drew national attention. Coristine has said he rushed his friend into the car before the group turned on him, slamming him against the vehicle and throwing punches. "I really thank President Trump for making D.C. safe again," Coristine said. "Like all my friends, they’re now able to walk outside." "Everyone is very calmed by the National Guard because it feels like the city is so much safer," he continued. "And the crime numbers totally represent that. The crime has been falling like a knife in D.C." Trump established the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force in March 2025 before launching an intensified federal crime crackdown in August, with the operation delivering more than 16,000 arrests, 3,200 narcotics arrests and nearly 2,000 illegal firearms seized in its first year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So I’m unbelievably grateful to the president for making the city safe and beautiful," Coristine said.
