content: President Donald Trump on Saturday criticized the Norwegian Nobel Committee for not selecting him for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, citing a long list of accomplishments. "I settled 8 WARS, am close to ending or settling 2 more, got all of the Israeli hostages back, including the final 28, both living and dead, had hundreds of hostages, from countries all over the World, released and sent back home, won a war in Venezuela, and captured the violent dictator who so viciously ran that country, and stopped the number one state sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, from obtaining a Nuclear Weapon — AND MUCH MORE! Yet, with all of that I, or the United States of America, did not get the Noble Peace Prize. WOW!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Saturday morning. Trump has long openly pined for the prize, first receiving a nomination in 2018 from Norwegian lawmakers for diplomatic efforts involving North Korea and nuclear disarmament. In 2019, he told reporters during a news conference, "I think I'm going to get a Nobel Prize for a lot of things if they gave it out fairly, which they don't." TRUMP TEASES POTENTIAL KIM JONG UN MEETING LATER THIS YEAR While the Norwegian Nobel Committee does not publicly release a list of nominees for the Peace Prize, Trump has been nominated at least five times, according to the people who nominated him. That list includes former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzō Abe, who nominated Trump in 2019, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who nominated him in 2025. NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA Despite being nominated again this year by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and others, Trump was passed over yet again, this time in favor of South African jurist Navi Pillay. The 85-year-old Pillay was the first non-White woman appointed to South Africa's high court, and she later served as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. title: Judicial Watch's Thomas Fitton slams FBI's 'drip-drip' release of 75,000 pages of Trump Butler shooting files

title: Stomach-turning sexually transmitted infection is on the rise, and standard medicines are failing
description: Shigella bacteria are becoming harder to treat as drug-resistant strains rise, and doctors warn Americans should be concerned but not panicked.
content: A highly contagious gut infection that can spread during sex is becoming harder to treat as antibiotic-resistant strains become more common. An April report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracked nearly 17,000 shigella samples, which causes shigellosis that can bring on diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps, collected between 2011 and 2023. In 2023, 8.5% of shigella samples with resistance data were classified as extensively drug-resistant, or XDR — resistant to all five antibiotics in the CDC’s definition — compared with none from 2011 to 2015. The findings point to a growing resistance problem, not a surge in overall infections, noted Dr. Tyler Evans, a California-based infectious disease physician and CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance. HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS STOMACH BUG SPREADS FAST, HITTING CERTAIN PATIENTS HARDEST "The infection is not surging. The bacteria are changing," Evans told Fox News Digital. "Case counts can hold steady while the treatment options quietly disappear." There is no FDA-approved oral antibiotic for XDR shigella, he said. Shigella bacteria can spread when tiny amounts of stool reach someone's mouth, including through contaminated food or water, unwashed hands or sexual activity. DANGEROUS DRUG-RESISTANT FUNGUS SPREADS ACROSS US, REACHING 27 STATES "Shigella is not considered to be a typical sexually transmitted infection," Dr. Andi Toufexis, a Texas-based family medicine physician who specializes in sexual health, told Fox News Digital. "However, this gastrointestinal bacteria can be spread through sex when one partner comes into contact with the other's fecal matter." Shigella is not new, and sexual transmission has been documented since the 1970s, Toufexis said. What is changing is the growing share of tested samples classified as XDR. MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000 The CDC report found that most people with XDR shigella were adult men. Sexual exposure data were not routinely collected, so the report could not establish exactly how each infection was contracted. But previous research has found sexual contact among men who have sex with men as an important transmission route. Eighty-six percent of XDR patients were men with a median age of 41, and of those with a known HIV status, nearly half were living with HIV, Evans noted. People experiencing homelessness and those with weakened immune systems may also face heightened risks, he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Children younger than 5 are especially likely to get shigella, according to the CDC, and many outbreaks in the U.S. have been linked to childcare and schools. Earlier U.S. outbreaks primarily affected children and involved strains that were susceptible to antibiotics. According to the CDC report, 37.6% of patients with hospitalization data were hospitalized for the antibiotic-resistant infection. The CDC reported no deaths among the XDR cases analyzed and said infections may be undercounted because not all positive specimens were cultured or tested for resistance. Most patients with available travel histories reported no recent international travel, though travel information was missing for many. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Evans said Americans should be "concerned, not panicked" about the infection. Most shigella infections resolve on their own, Toufexis added, but severe illness may need treatment. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City and author of "The Perfect 10 Diet" and "The Ageless Revolution," urged people who suspect shigella to seek medical advice before taking antidiarrheal medicine such as Imodium. "You want to flush out the bacteria, you want to get it out of your system," Aziz told Fox News Digital. To reduce the chance of infection, doctors recommend washing hands, genitals and the anal area before and after sex, using condoms or dental dams and cleaning sex toys after each use. If you or a partner has diarrhea, avoid sex and wait at least two weeks after symptoms end before resuming, Toufexis said. title: California Democrat 'deeply disappointed' after Newsom vetoes reparations tax break
description: Assemblymember Tina McKinnor says she is "deeply disappointed" after Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed her California reparations tax exemption.
content: A California lawmaker told Fox News Digital she is "deeply disappointed" after Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed her bill that would have exempted future reparations payments from California's personal income tax. "I am deeply disappointed that Governor Newsom vetoed AB 2186. Reparations are not a gift or a government handout," Assemblymember Tina McKinnor, D-Inglewood, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Reparations are meant to repair harm, not be partially taken back through taxation." Newsom vetoed the measure Sept. 30 while acting on a series of bills, including other reparations-related legislation. REPARATIONS ADVOCATES SLAM CASH COMPENSATION ‘HANDOUT’ LABEL, POINT TO PAST GOVERNMENT REMEDIES In his official veto message, Newsom acknowledged the bill's intent but cited fiscal uncertainty. "I thank the author for her continued work to redress the documented harms of slavery," Newsom wrote. "I was proud to sign into law last year legislation establishing the Bureau for Descendants of American Slavery, a first-in-the-nation law establishing a state agency that, among its key responsibilities, will advise on reparative justice programs for Black Americans. California's work on this important endeavor is just beginning." Newsom also cited uncertainty about the potential cost of the exemption. "Because the full scope of the proposed tax exclusion is unknown, fiscal caution is warranted," Newsom added. "The proposed exclusion for unspecified federal initiatives could be interpreted broadly, resulting in substantial fiscal uncertainty. Moreover, given the potentially significant General Fund implications, this measure should be considered as part of the annual budget process." CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS Despite rejecting the tax exemption, Newsom signed another reparations-related measure into law. The first-in-the-nation law requires large companies doing business in California to scour historical records and publicly disclose slavery-era transactions, advancing the state's broader reparations push through a new corporate mandate. Assembly Bill 2599, authored by Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, D-Ladera Heights, applies to businesses with more than $100 million in annual worldwide gross receipts that existed — or who have a predecessor entity — on or before Dec. 31, 1964. Once funded by the legislature, covered companies must submit sworn affidavits under penalty of perjury verifying searches for historical records involving the purchase or sale of enslaved people, their use as loan collateral, slave-related insurance policies and other transactions. Covered companies will have until January 2029 to submit their first affidavits. CASH PAYMENTS ARE NOT 'RULED OUT' AS CALIFORNIA COUNTY OFFICIALS PUSH REPARATIONS FOR BLACK LOCALS McKinnor's measure, Assembly Bill 2186, was designed to exempt future reparations payments or benefits from California's personal income tax if qualifying state, local or federal reparations programs were established. Under the text of AB 2186, gross income would not have included "any reparations benefit or payment received by a taxpayer during the taxable year" for taxable years beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2028, and before Jan. 1, 2033. The bill defined a "reparations benefit or payment" as any monetary payment, grant, trust distribution, debt forgiveness or other financial compensation provided through a qualifying reparations program. SOME BLACK NEW YORKERS DEMAND CASH PAYMENTS AS ONLY 'TRUE' FORM OF JUSTICE McKinnor emphasized that reparation payments are intended as compensation for generations of structural harm. "Reparations payments are compensation for generations of injustice, discrimination and economic harm," McKinnor said. "California cannot claim to support reparative justice while taxing the very compensation intended to repair that harm. I respect the Governor's concerns about fiscal responsibility, but justice must also be a priority. "We cannot continue to study injustice, acknowledge the harm, and then hesitate when it is time to act," she added. "I remain committed to working with my colleagues and the new Governor to bring this legislation back in 2027. Justice delayed should not become justice denied." California was the first state in the nation to establish a formal task force to study the legacy of slavery and recommend potential restitution measures. However, concrete direct cash payout initiatives at the state level have stalled over budget concerns and legal vulnerabilities. CHICAGO SUBURB EXPANDS CASH HANDOUTS AS RACE-BASED REPARATIONS PROGRAM FACES MAJOR LEGAL BATTLE Elsewhere in the country, localized reparations programs have moved forward with mixed success. Black residents in Evanston, Illinois, received $25,000 housing grants as part of a municipal program aimed at rectifying historic housing discrimination. Similar local and municipal initiatives seeking to provide direct compensation or economic aid are being debated nationwide. With Newsom vetoing multiple reparations proposals citing fiscal parameters and legal challenges, and with the upcoming gubernatorial race featuring candidates reluctant to endorse broad direct cash handouts, the state's path toward financial restitution remains uncertain. When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, Newsom's office said "the veto message speaks for itself."

title: Who is Sally Yates? Cornell rape-review pick was fired by Trump after refusing to defend travel ban
description: Sally Yates, fired by Trump as acting attorney general in 2017, will now lead Cornell University's independent review of sexual assault policies.
content: Cornell University has tapped Sally Yates, a former Obama administration deputy attorney general fired by President Donald Trump during his first term, to lead an independent review of the Ivy League school's handling of sexual assault allegations. Yates' appointment comes as Cornell faces scrutiny over its response to an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house in October 2024. As part of the independent review, Yates and her employer, King & Spalding, will have access to Cornell's internal documents, including case files, oversight records for Greek organizations, communications with law enforcement and disciplinary hearing records. Yates brings decades of Justice Department experience to Cornell's review, along with a public profile shaped by her confrontation with Trump and subsequent involvement in the Russia investigation. Sally Yates' career and clashes with Trump President Barack Obama nominated Yates as deputy attorney general in January 2015, and the Senate confirmed her four months later in an 84-12 vote. She previously served as U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Georgia, a position Obama appointed her to in 2010. CORNELL PRESIDENT SAYS UNIVERSITY 'MUST DO BETTER' ON HANDLING OF SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS During the presidential transition, Trump's incoming administration asked Yates to remain as acting attorney general while his nominee, Jeff Sessions, awaited Senate confirmation. But her tenure lasted just 10 days. Trump fired Yates on Jan. 30, 2017, after she instructed Justice Department lawyers not to defend his executive order restricting travel and refugee admissions from seven predominantly Muslim countries. "The acting Attorney General, Sally Yates, has betrayed the Department of Justice by refusing to enforce a legal order designed to protect the citizens of the United States," the White House said in a statement announcing her firing. Yates maintained that she was not convinced the directive was lawful. "My responsibility is to ensure that the position of the Department of Justice is not only legally defensible, but is informed by our best view of what the law is after consideration of all the facts," Yates said in a letter. "In addition, I am responsible for ensuring that the positions we take in court remain consistent with this institution’s solemn obligation to always seek justice and stand for what is right." Yates returned to the national spotlight in May 2017, testifying before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. Her testimony detailed warnings she had given White House Counsel Don McGahn about Trump's national security advisor at the time, Michael Flynn, shortly before her dismissal. CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS PROMPT NY ATTORNEY GENERAL LETITIA JAMES TO OPEN ‘ACTIVE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION’ Flynn had discussed Obama administration sanctions against Russia with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak in December 2016, despite Vice President-elect Mike Pence publicly denying that sanctions were discussed at the time. After reviewing FBI intelligence, Yates warned McGahn that Flynn had misled administration officials and could be vulnerable to Russian blackmail because Moscow knew what had actually been discussed. Flynn resigned in February 2017, 18 days after Yates' initial warning. He later pleaded guilty to making false statements to the FBI about his conversations with Kislyak. Before her confrontation with Trump, Yates spent 27 years at the Justice Department, prosecuting white-collar fraud and public corruption cases. She also served as lead prosecutor in the case against Olympic Park bomber Eric Rudolph, a prosecution then-Attorney General Eric Holder highlighted when Obama selected her as deputy attorney general. Yates returned to King & Spalding as a partner in May 2018, later leading an independent investigation into sexual misconduct and abuse in the National Women's Soccer League. Commissioned by the U.S. Soccer Federation in October 2021, the investigation included more than 200 interviews and uncovered widespread verbal and emotional abuse, sexual misconduct and repeated failures by teams and league officials to address complaints. The findings, released in October 2022, documented how coaches accused of misconduct continued working despite previous complaints. Yates' report recommended stronger background checks, clearer reporting procedures and greater accountability for teams and league officials. Cornell University investigations Cornell said it selected Yates and her firm because of "their expertise in higher education and extensive experience conducting independent investigations for boards and institutions." INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM Yates' involvement in the case brings another prominent Trump adversary into the controversy, days after New York Attorney General Letitia James, who previously brought a civil fraud case against Trump and has faced his calls for her prosecution, was appointed to oversee a separate state investigation. Cornell previously investigated the alleged assault and imposed suspensions and expulsions on several students accused of involvement. A lawsuit filed against the university by the alleged victim has since brought renewed national attention to the case and raised questions about the school's response. The two investigations have separate mandates. James' investigation will examine the case at the center of the controversy, while Yates' review will assess Cornell's broader policies and handling of sexual assault and dating violence allegations. "As part of that broader mandate, Yates and her team will conduct a detailed review of the university’s response to the allegations involving Jane Doe and members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter," the school said in a statement. title: Marvin Harrison Jr. informed he's being traded as Cardinals seek a second-round pick in return
description: Marvin Harrison Jr. was told the Arizona Cardinals are finalizing a trade, with the Texans, Chiefs, Eagles and Bills among teams pursuing him.
content: Marvin Harrison Jr.'s time with the Arizona Cardinals is coming to an end after it began only three seasons ago as a first-round draft pick with a Hall of Fame pedigree and high expectations. The team has informed Harrison it is finalizing a deal to trade him and he will be inactive for Sunday's game against the Detriot Lions, ESPN first reported and OutKick has confirmed. Harrison was not initially told what team he'd be traded to, perhaps, one NFL source said, because the Cardinals were open to the idea of having the news leak, and then other teams would raise their trade offers for Harrison. CARDINALS' MARVIN HARRISON JR LOOKS ENTIRELY DISINTERESTED AS SEASON GETS OFF TO A PUTRID START But he's definitely going somewhere else. Harrison, the son of Hall of Famer Marvin Harrison, was the fourth player taken in the 2024 NFL Draft ahead of multiple starting quarterbacks and more productive players such as Brock Bowers, but he has fallen out of favor over the last year as his production declined, his effort and even body language around the team has been questioned and other teams showed interest in acquiring him. CAN MARVIN HARRISON JR. AND TREY MCBRIDE CARRY THE CARDINALS OFFENSE UNDER NEW COACH MIKE LAFLEUR? New coach Mike LaFleur had defended Harrison's effort, saying, "I don’t see it that way. I think his running style is different than some other people’s," while adding that other players had increasingly more defined roles in an offense with limited weekly plays. LaFleur also said some opportunities for Harrison have been eliminated because defensive coverages have dictated he not get the ball while Arizona’s own subpar quarterback play also hasn't helped. The problem with that is the Cardinals have had great receivers who have dealt with similar issues and they were very much valued. Hall of Famer Larry Fitzgerald comes to mind. Except Fitzgerald was never inconsistent in his pass catching while Harrison has struggled with drops. And Fitzgerald simply played hard – all the time. Harrison? It's a lingering question. Rumors of a possible Harrison trade have persisted for weeks, fed by the fact he is eligible for a contract extension after this season and the Cardinals may not be convinced Harrison is worthy of a big contract. Also, Michael Wilson has emerged as a more productive receiver while Harrison currently ranks only fifth on the team in targets. General manager Monti Ossenfort said on Oct. 9 that Harrison "is a big part of what we’re doing," suggesting the team is still more interested in fixing his situation than moving him. Nope. Harrison Jr. wasn't immediately a bust after being drafted out of Ohio State. His rookie season showed both his talent and some inconsistency, but he finished with 62 receptions for 885 yards and eight touchdowns. The Cardinals expected a Year 2 jump from Harrison. That never came and didn't come this season, either. Multiple teams have contacted the Cardinals about Harrison. The Houston Texans have, the Kansas City Chiefs have, as have the Philadelphia Eagles, Buffalo Bills, New England Patriots, and even the San Francisco 49ers – although that last one is a long shot considering they play in the same division with the Cardinals. The Cardinals have been seeking a package that included a second-round pick in return for Harrison. And this is how bad teams stay bad: The Cardinals are essentially trading a 2024 first round pick for a second-rounder (maybe) years later after getting little in return for their initial investment. title: Letitia James faces new push to boot her from Cornell rape probe over alleged bias: court documents
description: A defense lawyer argues New York Attorney General Letitia James prejudged the Cornell University rape case and asks Tompkins County court to remove her.
content: A lawyer representing one of the men accused in a lawsuit of raping Cornell University's "Jane Doe" has formally requested that New York Attorney General Letitia James be removed from the criminal investigation, alleging she is biased and prejudged the case before being appointed as special prosecutor. Teny Geragos, daughter of prominent criminal defense attorney Mark Geragos, filed a motion Thursday in Tompkins County court arguing that James' previous public statements in support of the accuser have "prejudiced grand jurors." The motion cited a social media post made by James Sept. 28, the same day local prosecutor Matthew Van Houten announced he would be reopening the case. "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers," James wrote. "To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you." CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE Geragos argued that this showed James believed the seven men in the fraternity who were named in a prior lawsuit were guilty "despite not having examined a shred of evidence" up to that point. "The public cannot, and should not, have any confidence in the investigation or charging decisions of someone who has clearly prejudged the guilt of individuals who the law presumes are innocent," Geragos wrote in the filing. "The AG should be removed." She also accused New York Gov. Kathy Hochul of selecting James because of her "prejudicial public statements" about the case, arguing that the governor expects the investigation to produce a particular outcome. AOC'S DRAMATIC RETELLING OF CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS COLLIDES WITH COMPLAINT DETAILS When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Hochul referred Fox News Digital to the governor's answer to a reporter's question about James' social media post at an Oct. 2 press conference. "I will answer that. I have every confidence in our attorney general to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That's exactly what's going to happen in this case," Hochul said. The attorney general's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. Geragos' motion comes days after another one of the men named in the lawsuit filed a request in Albany State Supreme Court seeking James' removal, also citing alleged bias. The former Cornell student at the center of the investigation filed the lawsuit in September, accusing seven former Chi Phi fraternity members of drugging and raping her on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, and into the next morning. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. The fraternity was suspended Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe reported sexual assault allegations to campus police, according to Doe's civil complaint. Van Houten, who initially declined to pursue charges, has said Doe's November 2024 sworn statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped and, instead, described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

title: Inside Hasan Piker’s radical views on America, Israel and socialism
description: Hasan Piker's critics claimed his Marxist worldview goes beyond progressivism, casting America as fundamentally corrupt and worse than al Qaeda.
content: Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has built his online brand through intense commentary on political topics ranging from economics to foreign policy. During his daily streams, which last several hours, he gives his takes on the issues of the day, often through a combative left-wing lens. As Piker's influence has moved from his online audience and into the real world, including Democratic politics and campus events, critics argue his ideology deserves more scrutiny. To his supporters, Piker is an effective messenger for a generation looking for something outside traditional political structures. However, multiple critics who spoke with Fox News Digital described the streamer's worldview as going beyond typical progressive and anti-establishment outlooks. They claim his beliefs cast America as fundamentally corrupt, treat socialism as the answer to economic frustrations and frame Israel as uniquely immoral and illegitimate. WHO IS HASAN PIKER? MEET THE FAR-LEFT STREAMER WHO IS STIRRING UP CONTROVERSY AND DIVIDING DEMOCRATS Eli Lake, a senior reporter at The Free Press and host of the podcast "Breaking History," told Fox News Digital that Piker's belief system is "informed in many ways by a Marxist view of history" and that the streamer is part of "a tradition of the anti-American left." "There is a tradition of elements of the left that believes that the country and the republic are rotten to its core, and I think that that is a distinction from, you know, a more kind of hopeful version of progressivism," Lake told Fox News Digital. Lake contrasted Piker's beliefs with a reform-minded view in which the Declaration of Independence serves as a starting point from which the U.S. would progress. The goal, according to Lake, would be to hold the country to its stated ideals, an approach that he said is "distinct from the way that Hasan Piker understands the United States as sort of irredeemably evil." In one of Piker's more recent controversial statements, the streamer said in an interview with Axios that the U.S. was worse than al Qaeda. "Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker told Axios. "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world." Lake criticized Piker's remarks in an article for The Free Press, writing that the streamer's inability to "to grasp the distinction between intentionally and unintentionally killing civilians" showed his "moral illiteracy." HASAN PIKER ADMITS HE HAS 'DIALED DOWN' HIS OPINIONS AFTER PUBLIC AND DEMOCRATIC BACKLASH "I almost felt guilty writing a column because I could assume it was so obvious that America is nothing like al Qaeda. Al Qaeda deliberately is trying to kill as many civilians as it can," Lake told Fox News Digital. " If Hasan Piker cannot distinguish between America and its foreign policy and that of al Qaeda in a moral sense at least, or he thinks they're equal or 'pound for pound' America is worse, then he's helpless." Piker's critics argue that his moral framework also shapes his views of Israel. They say he goes beyond criticizing the Israeli government or its policies and frames the Jewish state's existence as being up for debate, something that Tanya Tsikanovsky, a first-generation American whose parents fled the Soviet Union, takes issue with. "I think that we can sit here and discuss the government of Israel, but we're not citizens of Israel. Certainly Hasan Piker is not, and we don't live there," Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital. "As a Zionist, and as someone who is a proud jew, I'm here to care about the existence of the state. I just want it to exist." She also pointed out that Piker does not apply the same standards he has for Israel to other countries. "You know we don't spend our time debating the existence of any other country. Like Hasan's not saying, 'Maybe Switzerland shouldn't really be a country.' No, like, we're good with every other country," she said, adding that, in her view, the reason for this singling out of Israel is antisemitism. Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital her immigrant parents view the country in an entirely different light from Piker. She said they see the U.S. as a place where they were finally able to be free and live as equals. "My parents came here from the USSR, and they kiss the ground of this country because we know that it's the best country on Earth," she said. "There really is no other place in the world that provides the same level of freedom, and Hassan Piker is using that freedom specifically to get everyone to want to lose it and without even realizing it." She argued that Piker's worldview is hostile to the American system and that it welcomes the exact things that families like hers fled. FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER DEFENDS HIMSELF FROM ANTISEMITISM ACCUSATIONS IN INTERVIEW WITH JEWISH OUTLET "[Piker] is aligning himself with an ideology that will embrace Sharia law, that will embrace communism," she said. Piker's critics say his worldview is not merely defined by what he opposes but also the economic system he promotes. Venezuelan-born economist Daniel Di Martino argued there is a hidden danger to Piker's economic stances, mainly the appeal of socialist promises to young people frustrated with capitalism. Di Martino, who grew up in Venezuela before immigrating to the U.S., said socialism was more than an abstract idea. It was a system that made ordinary life substantially worse. He described growing up under socialism as "feeling the constant deterioration of my quality of life in even the daily smallest things." Recently, Piker took the 12 Axes political test on one of his daily streams, and the results showed that he was closely aligned economically with late Venezuelan socialist leader Hugo Chávez, something Di Martino saw as a significant red flag. "Their economic policies are not those of Norway and Denmark. They're the ones of Venezuela. They are the ones that destroy the country I come from," Di Martino said. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA BACKS 'OUR TWITCH STREAMER' HASAN PIKER, RIPS ANTI-SOCIALISM HOUSE RESOLUTION He recalled Venezuela unraveling before his eyes as the government began using state resources to provide free goods and services. When oil money was no longer enough, Di Martino said, the government printed money, fueling inflation. Eventually, shortages came, and Di Martino recalled the government blaming business owners for being greedy and claiming that citizens were hoarding food. "They hailed bread lines and shortages as evidence that there was so much demand because Venezuelans were so well off. I mean, imagine how laughable these arguments [were]," Di Martino told Fox News Digital. "And, eventually, they said that inflation was imaginary. It was all made up in our heads. And then we had no electricity, and then we have no water," he added. "And then crime went up and it went unpunished. And then they jailed their political opponents when they tried to speak up. And then they rigged the elections because that is the only way for socialists to stay in power, because it always fails, so they have to rig the elections to stay in power." For Di Martino, the real danger of Piker's growing influence is not simply that he has a large online audience but that his ideas are moving into Democratic politics and could eventually shape U.S. government policy. "Even though he's not running, the people running on the socialist side, the democratic socialist candidates, listen to him and have his ideas, which are Marxist-Leninist ideas, are the ideas of the Chinese Communist Party — which is why he goes there — are the ideas of the socialist party of Venezuela, of the communist party of Cuba. That is what these people stand for," Di Martino said. "And, so, we should be worried, not because Hassan Piker is popular. He is not. We should be worried because his ideas are gonna make it to the Congress and to the state and local governments." title: Katie Zacharia hits ground running, promises Trump diesel deal delivers cheaper gas for Americans
description: Katie Zacharia says Trump's diesel deal with Vladimir Putin will lower gas and grocery prices as she prepares to take the White House podium Monday.
content: Incoming White House press secretary Katie Zacharia pledged to get to work immediately when she takes over the podium Monday, defending President Donald Trump's recent diesel deal as a move she says will help lower gas and grocery prices. TRUMP NAMES LEAVITT SUCCESSOR AFTER WEEKS OF SPECULATION — AND SHE'S NO STRANGER TO MAGA "President Donald Trump has never been unambiguous. He is an America-first president. TRUMP TELLS ZELENSKYY TO STOP DOING 'ONE THING' DURING ATTACKS ON RUSSIA Diesel prices have remained high as conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine continue, with rising fuel costs emerging as an issue ahead of November's midterm elections. title: ABC News quietly republishes gutted version of story on Trump sons it had deleted without explanation
description: ABC News issued an editor's note admitting errors in its report on Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump's investments tied to Pentagon contracts.
content: ABC News quietly republished a watered-down version of a previously deleted report scrutinizing the business dealings of President Donald Trump's oldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, Friday evening. The original report, published earlier in the week, was removed following criticism of its accuracy. The original report, which remains accessible through the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, was published Wednesday afternoon under the headline, "Trump sons' investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election." ABC News removed the report less than 24 hours later without a public explanation at the time. However, the revised report reappeared on ABC News' website Friday with an editor's note, factual corrections and a new headline: "New shipyard announced amid earlier Democratic concerns about potential conflicts of interest." ABC NEWS DELETES ‘HIT PIECE’ ON TRUMP SONS' PENTAGON-LINKED INVESTMENTS WITHOUT EXPLANATION The article's byline was also changed to "ABC News." The editor's note acknowledged errors involving descriptions of company investments, government contracts and the chronology of events. "Editor’s Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies," the statement read. "After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events." ABC News' decision to remove the report without an immediate public explanation drew criticism from media industry figures. ABC News' revisions followed public criticism from 1789 Capital spokesperson Alexa Henning, who disputed the original report's description of the firm's investments. Henning said "1789 Capital does not have a 'major stake' in Anduril" and challenged the article's characterization of the Trump brothers' involvement in other companies. "Here's a small lesson, that I also explained to ABC, the ‘reporter’ who is a complete idiot conflated raising funds with investment by 1789. Those are two separate actions," Henning wrote. 1789 Capital is the venture firm in which Trump Jr. serves as a partner. The initial report incorrectly attributed a $2.5 billion investment in Anduril to 1789 Capital. The revised article clarified that the figure represented the total funding Anduril raised last year. INSIDE TRUMP’S DEAL TO GIVE AMERICAN TAXPAYERS A MASSIVE STAKE IN NEW $6.6B SUBMARINE DEAL "1789 Capital — a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders — claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company," ABC News reported in the deleted story. The revised article also states that Trump Jr. does not sit on the three-person committee responsible for investment decisions, according to a spokesperson for 1789 Capital. The updated story states that 1789 Capital previously invested $50 million in defense contractor Anduril, which ABC valued at approximately $60 billion. The initial removal drew the attention of Trump Jr., who took to X to mock California Gov. Gavin Newsom after the story was taken down. "ABC deleted this article in less than 24 hours because it’s false. Sounds about as long as your presidential campaign would last," he wrote on X. Bill Ackman, founder and CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management, criticized ABC News on social media for removing the article without issuing a public correction at the time. "A quiet unexplained withdrawal of a false article does not constitute a proper error correction." Fox News Digital reached out to ABC News, Trump Jr. and 1789 Capital for comment. title: What WWE's Money in the Bank card says about the company's development of future superstars
description: Jacy Jayne and Joe Hendry reveal how the WWE Performance Center and NXT shaped nearly every superstar competing on the Money in the Bank card.
content: The Money in the Bank card is filled with major matches and WWE superstars, both who are rising through the roster and those who are already established. Looking deeper, there’s one thing that stands out among the more than two dozen wrestlers who will be involved in the matches – the NXT brand. NXT is billed as WWE’s developmental brand. It’s a way for those who either don’t know the art of professional wrestling to get hands-on training or those who don’t know the television side of the business to ingratiate themselves before, hopefully, moving to the Raw or SmackDown brands. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE Nearly everyone on the card has been in NXT before heading up to the main roster. The outliers include Roman Reigns, who got his start in Florida Championship Wrestling, which came before NXT was founded, and CM Punk, who made his mark outside the WWE before making his way to WWE’s Ohio Valley Wrestling. Penta never competed in NXT either. He became a legend in Mexico before receiving substantial face time on American programming. Everyone else got their feet wet in NXT, whose show takes place at the WWE Performance Center. The Money in the Bank card underscores how far WWE has come in creating the superstars of tomorrow in NXT. "The Performance Center is a very special place," women’s U.S. champion Jacy Jayne told OutKick Dropkick. "I feel like they, well, not I feel, I know they have the best coaches in the world. There's a coach that can help you with literally everything. There's someone for everybody. There's a lot of cooks in the kitchen, sometimes you gravitate more towards one or the other, but you definitely learn your craft, you learn how to talk, you learn how to be confident, you learn cameras, you learn everything. "So, they set you up for success. And I know it might not come as quick as some people want it to, and they get tired of being in the same routine, but it definitely pays off if you listen to what they have to say and you apply it." Hundreds of thousands tune into NXT on Tuesday nights and monitor the WWE Universe on social media on the daily. With the number of superstars who have come out of NXT and who have transcended sports entertainment, it’s worth wondering whether there was a "secret sauce" to the training that goes on behind the scenes in the Performance Center. Jayne agreed to a point. "There's so many people with experience that work there that you might not really know about, like people that used to be on NXT, people that were wrestlers or behind the scenes people," she said. "There's so much happening at the Performance Center every day. There's so many different classes that you can take, extra work, like ring work. It's a machine, really, and they're just pumping out superstars by the day." Jayne will be among the women contending in the Money in the Bank ladder match along with Lola Vice, Tiffany Stratton, Sol Ruca, Lash Legend and Roxanne Perez. Joe Hendry, a former NXT champion who joined WWE from Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA), isn’t involved in the Money in the Bank. He just put out an album titled "Beyond Belief." title: Rare coin bearing face of king with infamous nickname unearthed after 1,000 years
description: Marking the northernmost find of its kind, a 1,000-year-old Anglo-Saxon coin depicting King Ethelred the Unready was unearthed in the Shetland Islands.
content: Archaeologists in Scotland recently uncovered an Anglo-Saxon coin dating back 1,000 years that was minted under a king known as "the Unready." The coin was unearthed during an excavation in Nesting, a coastal community in Scotland's eastern Shetland Islands, according to Jam Press. Pictures show a thick, greenish-brown patina covering its surface, though some of the original markings remain visible. TEEN STUMBLES ON MYSTERIOUS COIN FROM LEGENDARY CITY, PUZZLING ARCHAEOLOGISTS OVER ITS JOURNEY The excavation was originally conducted to investigate prehistoric structures threatened by coastal erosion, according to Archaeology Shetland. The archaeological investigation included an examination of nearby Iron Age structures. The artifact was minted between 991 and 997 A.D., Jam Press noted. The coin's face depicts King Ethelred the Unready, who ruled England from 978 to 1013 A.D. DISCOVERY BENEATH SOCCER FIELD REVEALS MASSIVE MEDIEVAL CONVENT LOST FOR CENTURIES Ethelred, best known for his failed attempts to fend off Viking invasions, was eventually driven from the throne by Danish King Swein Forkbeard. He regained power in 1014 and ruled until his death in 1016, making him the longest-reigning Anglo-Saxon monarch. Elinor Graham, an archaeologist from the University of Aberdeen, was on vacation in Shetland when she participated in the excavation, according to Jam Press. MAN SEARCHING WITH METAL DETECTOR UNEARTHS MASSIVE VIKING AGE FORTUNE, SHATTERING RECORDS "This is exactly how I wanted to spend my holiday," Graham said. "The writing on the coin is still so sharp, and we knew immediately that it was extremely rare, actually unique, in this context." "We knew immediately that it was extremely rare, actually unique, in this context." The discovery could offer clues about ancient trade routes between Viking-controlled Shetland and Anglo-Saxon England, though researchers have not ruled out the possibility that the coin was taken during a Norse raid. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Scotland's Treasure Trove Unit will determine whether the artifact should be offered to a museum. Graham said she hopes the coin will eventually be added to the collections at the Shetland Museum and Archives, Jam Press reported. She said the discovery suggests the area may once have been home to a "well-connected cosmopolitan community" with trading links to Anglo-Saxon England. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It's an area with a huge amount of history through the Bronze Age, the Iron Age, the early medieval period and into the Viking Norse period," Graham said. The ancient coin is one of many that have surfaced across the United Kingdom. Earlier this year, archaeologists uncovered a nearly 1,750-year-old Roman coin during a railway construction project in England. title: Key American industry seeing blue-collar jobs boom as Trump's reshoring policies pay off
description: First on Fox: A CEA report says 72,000 manufacturing jobs were added in 2026 as reshoring and tariff policies reversed Biden-era offshoring.
content: FIRST ON FOX: Critical blue-collar manufacturing jobs in the U.S. are making inroads after years of Biden-era offshoring hollowed out the workforce, according to a new economic report. A Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) report says 72,000 manufacturing jobs have been added in 2026 alone, many of them due to a rise in the manufacturing of durable goods, like metal and transportation equipment. The advisors say this is a reverse of a Biden-era trend that saw 200,000 manufacturing jobs disappear in the last two years of the former president's administration. Not only is the current administration's focus on reshoring jobs contributing to the uptick, but so are his tariff policies, according to the CEA, a White House agency responsible for providing President Donald Trump with economic analysis. AMERICA’S NEW BLUE-COLLAR JOB BOOM IS ONE NOBODY SAW COMING, AND IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED In particular, Trump's landmark One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBB) has laid the groundwork for American companies to expand in the United States, instead of shipping jobs overseas, according to the report. The bill's provisions include allowing manufacturers an immediate 100% tax deduction on expenses related to new factory building and purchasing machinery and equipment. The report highlights success stories from corporations reinvesting in Americans and expanding their businesses. LARGEST-EVER US STEEL PLANT IS COMING TO A KEY RED STATE AS TRUMP UNVEILS $15B INVESTMENT For example, the 100% expensing provision in the OBBB has helped Jergens, a manufacturing company based in Ohio, expand to Illinois. "Since the passage of the bill [OBBB], our employees are voluntarily working additional hours," the company's CEO, Jack Schron, said. "They are keeping more of what they earn, putting more money back into the American economy, and Jergens has a ready workforce. It is a win-win-win: a win for the employee, for Jergens and for the United States economy." BESSENT CREDITS TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICIES WITH HELPING RETURN JOBS TO AMERICANS AS WAGE GAINS RESUME Schron added that 83% of his workers are picking up overtime after the OBBB provision established no taxes for overtime work. In another example touted in the CEA report, a company in North Carolina, Ketchie Inc., has expanded its workforce by 25% after taking advantage of the 100% expensing provision to purchase new machinery. The report says the company waited to buy the equipment until the OBBB passed. As for wages, manufacturing workers are seeing benefits, too, with their pay increasing by 7.9% since January 2025. "Adjusted for inflation, this means that blue-collar manufacturing workers are earning nearly $2,500 more per year, on average, since President Trump took office," the report says. It also touts figures from the construction industry, including 100,000 construction jobs added since Trump took office. Semiconductor chip manufacturing, an industry in which the United States typically competes with China, is on the rise in the United States too. Micron is building memory chip plants in Idaho, Virginia and New York, which the report says is a $250 billion investment in the United States. Apple is investing $600 billion in American semiconductor production, too. The report also says that major pharmaceutical companies like GSK and Gilead are investing billions of dollars in the United States, along with automakers like Stellantis. PESSIMISTS SAY THE ECONOMY IS WEAK. THE GOOD NEWS IS, THEY ARE WRONG All told, the reshoring and tariff policies have resulted in $11 trillion in investments in the United States during Trump's second term in office, according to the report. Meanwhile, the economy is on everyone's mind with only a few weeks left until the midterm elections. Inflation, particularly high gas and grocery prices, continue to impact Americans before they head to the polls. Majorities also view housing costs (54%, down from 60%) and grocery prices (62%, down from 66%) as major problems. "It means that American policing has always been bad, and it always will be," Clancy told a local outlet in 2023, alleging that American police forces have their roots in slave patrols. "It’s not like we can get back to this to the early days. … American policing … [is] epically racist and classist because that’s a dead end. That is the point of American policing." Clancy told Fox News Digital his comments concerned officers who abused their authority over sex workers, although his original remarks and subsequent 2023 interview criticized policing more broadly as an institution he argued was inherently racist and could not be reformed. He concurred with the RSLC's assertion that DSA-aligned candidates are shaping the future of the Democratic Party. State Rep. Eleanor Chávez, running with the DSA’s backing in New Mexico, has called Immigration and Customs Enforcement "fascist" and compared its agents to the KKK. Republicans in New Mexico have condemned such rhetoric, arguing it could spur people to commit violence against law enforcement officers. Despite its propensity to draw attention to its stances on social issues, the DSA bills itself as an economically motivated organization. NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’ To this end, some of its members running for state legislatures have called for reforms some have described as radical. New York Democratic Assemblywoman Sarahana Shrestha, who is running for re-election with the backing of the DSA, has pushed legislation that would allow the government to acquire the privately held Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp., potentially through eminent domain, if a negotiated purchase cannot be reached. Dylan Wegela, a DSA-backed state house candidate in Michigan, has similarly pushed for state acquisitions of utility companies. Shrestha agrees with the RSLC's assessment that DSA-aligned state lawmakers could influence the Democratic Party’s trajectory. "The things DSA-aligned state lawmakers are fighting for are things that are extremely popular with voters and have been for a long time," she told Fox News Digital. "A majority of our constituents believe the energy sector should not be for profit, healthcare should be single-payer and universal, the government should play a positive role in building necessary infrastructure such as permanently affordable housing and public transit and so on." The DSA-affiliated lawmaker also defended her plan to take over the Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp., citing a feasibility study commissioned by supporters of the bill that found it would lower costs for consumers. Sometimes, the stances of DSA clash with Democratic policy priorities. Gabriel Acevero, a DSA-backed lawmaker in Maryland, for instance, opposed a marijuana legalization measure he argued did not go far enough to address racial inequities, declaring that "cannabis legalization without reparations for communities harmed by the intentional drug war is not progressive policy." Scores of DSA-affiliated candidates running in states such as New York, Minnesota and Massachusetts have thrown their support behind reparations for racial minorities. SOCIALISTS ARE HELPING GOP CAMPAIGNS HEADING INTO NOVEMBER Republicans have a vested interest in tying the mainstream Democratic Party to the DSA. A Fox News poll from September found that 55% of registered voters had an unfavorable opinion of the DSA. While some in the Democratic Party argue that Republican attempts to tie the Democratic Party to socialism are bad-faith campaign tricks, party leadership has recently made significant concessions to its left-wing flank. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer backed Abdul El-Sayed's more moderate opponent in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, but a super PAC aligned with Schumer has since committed millions of dollars to supporting El-Sayed's general election campaign. El-Sayed is a progressive backed by prominent figures on the party's left but who has said he is not a socialist. Due to the disorganized nature of the DSA and the varying degrees of affiliation held by candidates, estimates of the number of socialist candidates running for state legislature vary across sources. The Brookings Institution, for instance, found at least 76 had advanced to the general election, while the RSLC’s analysis identified a minimum of 65 running in a total of 24 states. Though the DSA's gains have received significant attention, a Brookings Institution analysis found that candidates backed by the organization represent only a tiny fraction of the nation's state legislative seats, raising questions about how far the socialist movement's growing influence extends. "The RSLC has consistently said that socialism starts in the states and that is where we need to stop it," the RSLC’s memo reads. "The DSA’s growing presence in statehouse races could have dangerous impacts for state policy in the short-term, and it reflects a clearly orchestrated long-term effort to build political power from the state-level up." title: 5 marriage mistakes couples make without realizing it — and how to avoid them
description: Sex therapist Tammy Nelson identifies five relationship pitfalls that can quietly create distance between partners and shares ways to rebuild closeness.
content: The secret to a happier, longer-lasting marriage may involve much more than chemistry and compatibility. Recent research published in the journal Family Process found that improvements in communication and emotional safety were linked to greater relationship satisfaction. Maintaining that connection takes effort, particularly as couples settle into routines and begin to feel as though they already know everything about each other, according to Tammy Nelson, Ph.D., a board-certified sexologist, sex therapist and integrative relationship therapist in Los Angeles. ‘FOOD DIVORCE’ TREND AMONG COUPLES COULD DRIVE THEM APART, EXPERTS WARN "Compatibility can feel different to different people at different times," she told Fox News Digital. "The relationship will go through developmental stages just like you do." From losing curiosity to avoiding difficult conversations, Nelson shared five common mistakes that can weaken a couple’s connection and ways to avoid them. No. 1: Assuming you know everything about your partner Losing curiosity about a partner can chip away at attraction over time, according to Nelson. "That’s how we fall in love, when someone's curious about us," she said. "When they come along and say, 'I'm so interested in you. I'm curious about you.' WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY — PLUS THE ‘RED FLAG’ TO AVOID "We're attracted to something in the space in between us — not so much when it's sitting next to us on the couch every night, and so we tend to lose that curiosity." While someone may feel they know everything about their partner — "what they like to eat, what they'd like to watch on TV, what they might like in bed" — those preferences can evolve over time, Nelson said. "Don't put your partner in a box," Nelson said, urging couples to stay curious and ask questions. "Who are they becoming? What are they thinking? What do they desire? What's their vision for the future?" POLITICAL FIGHTS CAN RIP COUPLES APART: THERAPIST SHARES 3 WAYS TO SAVE A RELATIONSHIP The therapist suggested losing curiosity about a partner can sometimes make attention from someone outside the relationship particularly appealing. "That's why we have affairs, right? Somebody comes along, and they're fascinated by us," she said. "We love that. And it's why we pay a therapist, so someone will ask questions about us." No. 2: Avoiding difficult conversations Avoiding difficult conversations — and failing to pay attention to what goes unsaid — can create problems in a relationship, Nelson cautioned. "Pay attention to what you're not talking about and why," she advised. When it comes to relationship problems, couples who avoid conflict may be more vulnerable than those who openly disagree. "It's not the people who fight and communicate all the time. It's the people who aren't fighting, aren't arguing, aren't communicating," the expert said. COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS Nelson encouraged couples to notice which topics make them pull back or shut down during conflict — such as money or sex — and instead make an effort to lean into those difficult discussions. "You're probably avoiding it because you don't want to get into a conflict, which is totally legitimate, but maybe pay attention to those spaces where there could be more room for communicating," she advised. No. 3: Focusing on what’s wrong with your sex life When couples talk about sex, focusing on complaints rather than what is working can make intimacy more difficult, according to Nelson. "The key here is not to talk about what's not working or what your partner's not doing or why you’re not doing it more often," she said. The "magic formula," Nelson said, is for partners to share what they like and what is working. "The key to the universe is you get more of what you would appreciate," she said. "If you point out how your partner is not acting the way you want, then you're in conflict, you're defensive, you feel bad about yourself. That's not going to help. It’s not very sexy." "Expand on what’s already working." Instead, she recommends focusing on the positive by telling a partner what they've liked about their sex life, whether it is something happening now or a meaningful experience from years ago. "Whether you’re a new couple or you've been together forever, start with something you appreciate, and then something that you would like more of," she suggested. "Expand on what’s already working." No. 4: Getting stuck in ‘maintenance mode’ Another potential mistake is allowing the everyday responsibilities of life to crowd out opportunities for growth and excitement. Nelson encouraged couples to consider whether their relationship is primarily in "maintenance mode" or "expansion mode." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Maintenance mode involves managing the everyday responsibilities of a shared life, which Nelson said is essential. "You know, we need to pay the bills. We need to make sure the air conditioner is working," she said. "We need maintenance in a relationship, just like you need maintenance at a job or just in life. But you also need expansion." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Expansion mode, meanwhile, involves trying new things together and finding ways to keep the relationship exciting. If there’s too much maintenance and not enough expansion, one or both partners could get bored and feel stuck, Nelson cautioned. "On the other hand, if there’s too much expansion, you're going to feel like you’re always doing something new and there's no rest and maybe not enough connection. "All relationships need freedom and connection." No. 5: Keeping feelings of connection to yourself Couples may also miss opportunities for connection when they feel affection toward their partner but don't express it, according to Nelson. She encouraged couples to notice the positive emotions and physical sensations they experience when thinking about their partner and to share those feelings with each other. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Where in your heart or in your body are you feeling the most 'juice,' the most 'aliveness,' when you think about your partner?" she asked. Some people are more aware of these physical sensations than others, Nelson acknowledged. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "But if you can put your hand on your heart or on your stomach or your shoulders and say, ‘You know, when I think about you, I get this warm feeling in my heart,' that's all you have to share with your partner. And sometimes that means everything to them." Ultimately, Nelson emphasized that avoiding these common pitfalls comes down to ongoing attention, curiosity and a willingness to keep discovering new things about each other.

title: The storm is here: Georgia-Alabama set to write latest chapter after chaotic week around Hurricane Isaias
description: Hurricane Isaias forced Trump to cancel his Alabama trip, but the Georgia vs. Alabama SEC showdown at Bryant Denny Stadium rolls on tonight.
content: TUSCALOOSA, AL — There were two sides to the buildup between Georgia versus Alabama heading into tonight's showdown in Tuscaloosa. First, it was Hurricane Isaias barreling toward the Gulf Coast on Friday afternoon, as evacuations took place and preparations were well underway throughout the Southeast for what was going to be a long night of bad weather. Second, a massive SEC showdown that will set the tone for both teams moving forward this season, with Alabama hoping to make a statement about where it stands right now during the Kalen DeBoer era, while Kirby Smart hopes to start adding wins against the Tide in regular season play. ALABAMA FOOTBALL, DODGERS BASEBALL AND TWO NFL GAMES: INSIDE ONE GROUP'S INCREDIBLE SOUTHERN SPORTS TRIP A collision course for two teams, with a lot on the line. During the week, questions lingered about whether this game would actually take place with Hurricane Isaias making landfall and then heading on a northern track through the state of Alabama. University officials had met multiple times in the days and hours leading up to this weekend to discuss contingency plans in case the game needed to either be postponed a few hours, or moved. All the while, Alabama decided that fans would not be allowed to set up any type of tailgate until after 12 noon local time today in an abundance of caution for the wind and rain that would devour the area. FIVE IMPORTANT COLLEGE FOOTBALL QUESTIONS THAT WILL BE ANSWERED AFTER THIS WEEKEND'S SLATE This forced President Donald Trump, who was scheduled to attend the SEC showdown, to back out of traveling to Alabama, with a final decision coming on Friday afternoon. In reality, with everything taking place around Tuscaloosa over a 48-hour period, this turned out to be the most logical decision for all parties involved. Power trucks sat in the parking lot of the Tuscaloosa mall, while the campus started to slow down on Friday night, with so many unknowns leading up to this day. Can Georgia find a way to get Alabama during the regular season? On the field tonight, this is about two SEC teams looking to make a statement. Kirby Smart is hoping to exorcise some of the Crimson Tide demons that have followed him during his time as the Bulldogs head coach. Smart is 2-7 against Alabama during his time in Athens, which is a record he would prefer to start chipping away at. Sure, he's obviously had success against the Tide during the postseason, but there is obviously something different about rolling into Bryant Denny Stadium and beating the school that afforded him the chance to become a head coach. PAUL FINEBAUM’S PROCLAMATION ABOUT ALABAMA COACH KALEN DEBOER REIGNITES COLLEGE FOOTBALL ‘CULTURE FIT’ DEBATE To do that, the Dawgs might have to flip the script compared to what some are thinking. Can quarterback Gunner Stockton beat Alabama through the air? Sure, but this is also against a team that is starting to find its offensive wings behind Keelon Russell, along with a defense that has clearly found an aggressiveness that we haven’t seen on a consistent basis during DeBoer's tenure in Tuscaloosa. In reality, these two teams are finding their own identities. For Alabama, last week's dominant win against Mississippi State seems to have instilled a confidence within the fan base. "I'm not going to compare this type of aggression to the Saban era, but they look as though they're playing pissed off," Edward, from Cullman told OutKick. "I don't know what changed, but it's pretty obvious that Kane Wommack has found a cohesive group. "Hell, I don't care what it is. But, if we keep this up then who knows where this team could end up this season. We gotta get through the Dawgs, and I really want to see them beat Georgia with a strong defensive performance. I was kind of hoping the rain would at least stick around and allow us to get dirty in the trenches." Don't worry, it will be nasty inside Bryant Denny Stadium tonight The last time Kirby Smart led his team out of the visitors locker room in Tuscaloosa, he stood at the gate bouncing up and down as 'Thunderstruck' played over the stadium loudspeakers. If he could've, the Georgia head coach looked as though he was ready to throw on pads himself. What we will see tonight are two teams looking to create their own narrative around the 2026 season. This isn’t about last year, or the teams that came before them. All week, the college football world has drooled over a well-done Nick Saban documentary, while Kirby Smart smiled and complimented his former boss during a number of interviews. Around Alabama, it wouldn’t be surprising to hear that Kalen DeBoer has heard the tales being told about the guy he replaced. title: Angel Reese reveals 'embarrassing' training camp story after reaching WNBA Finals with Atlanta Dream
description: Angel Reese revealed a training camp drill where Coach Karl Smesko forced her to hit two consecutive 3-pointers before the team could continue.
content: Angel Reese has officially reached the WNBA Finals before Caitlin Clark, and gave fans a peek into the process that got her there after finishing off a three-game sweep of the New York Liberty in the semifinals on Friday, which included a training camp exercise that left her feeling "embarrassed' in front of her new Atlanta Dream teammates. In the postgame news conference, Reese spoke about a moment in training-camp when Coach Karl Smesko stopped a drill and made her hit two consecutive 3-pointers before her teammates could continue. Reese said the exercise left her upset with Smesko and worried about embarrassing herself in front of the team. "It's really hard for me to not want to rush success, and Karl told me how patient I had to be with it. I remember a very moment in training camp where we were going through drills and he stopped everybody and told me I had to make two in a row in front of everybody," Reese said. "And you never want to shutdown your teammates, you never want to let your teammates down, and we couldn't resume the drill until I made two in a row, and I was upset with him that day for sure. Because I didn't want to let the team down, I didn't want to feel embarrassed and in how long it coulda took me to make them. But now it's like so easy." ANGEL REESE SETS TWO WNBA RECORDS WITH HISTORIC REBOUNDING PERFORMANCE Reese is known as a poor shooter, and is often mocked for missing easy shots in games. She has even gotten in on the jokes herself by launching merchandise under the brand "Mebounds" in 2025. The term is a mocking play on "rebounds," referring to the rebounds she collects after missing her own shots. Later in Friday's postgame news conference, Reese was asked how many shots she needed to make two consecutively. "I don't know," Reese answered. "It wasn't that many," Smesko said. "My teammates are cheering for me on the sideline, and I was pretty embarrassed," Reese added. Now, months later, she made two 3-pointers in Atlanta’s 85-83 victory over the New York Liberty, which completed a semifinal sweep and sent the Dream to their first Finals since 2013. Her recollection addressed an area of her game that has attracted scrutiny throughout her professional career. Reese publicly pushed back against criticism of her missed layups in November 2024, following a rookie season in which she made 39.1% of her shots. Her shooting numbers since then show progress from that rookie season, with a more modest change during her first year in Atlanta. Reese made 45.1% of her shots this regular season, slightly below the 45.8% she made in her second season with Chicago. She attempted 3-pointers more frequently with the Dream, but still made fewer than one in five during the regular season. Her 19.3% success rate from beyond the arc was only slightly above last year’s 18.2%. She has made five of 13 playoff 3-point attempts (38.5%). That represents a stronger stretch across just five games. She averaged a career-high 16.4 points, again led the WNBA in rebounding and won her first Defensive Player of the Year award. She finished Friday’s clinching victory with 22 points and nine rebounds. The opportunity followed an April trade that sent Reese from Chicago to Atlanta for two first-round draft picks, with the Dream also receiving a future second-round pick swap. Chicago missed the playoffs in both of her seasons there and finished 10-34 in 2025. Atlanta already had a franchise-record 30-win season behind it and retained a core that included All-Star guards Allisha Gray and Rhyne Howard and two-time WNBA champion Jordin Canada. Sixth-seeded Indiana drew defending champion Las Vegas immediately and lost the deciding game on the road. The Finals berth came despite Atlanta losing center Brionna Jones to a season-ending leg injury and playing the final two games against New York without Gray, who had a left hand injury. Clark, who entered the WNBA alongside Reese in 2024, reached the playoffs first, during their rookie season. She missed the entire 2025 postseason with an injury, when Indiana eliminated Atlanta before falling one win short of the Finals against Las Vegas. title: Sophie Cunningham responds to column urging Fever to move on from her for sharing opinions
description: Sophie Cunningham fired back at The Athletic's column urging the Indiana Fever to move on, as her co-host disputed its basketball arguments.
content: Sophie Cunningham had a blunt response after a New York Times column urged the Indiana Fever to part ways with her: "Suck it." The Fever guard addressed the criticism on Friday’s episode of "No Hesitation with Sophie Cunningham & Drew Hanlen," pushing back against questions about her basketball value while saying she no longer lets outside opinions dictate how she lives. "That’s why I literally don’t even care what anyone says about me anymore," Cunningham said. "Because I’ve said this so many times, is if you’re going to live by the praise, you’re going to die by the hate." The discussion followed an Oct. 6 column by New York Times-owned The Athletic arguing that Indiana should move on from Cunningham. The column contended that the attention surrounding the guard’s outspoken views had overwhelmed the team’s basketball priorities, describing her as "too combustible." Cunningham is headed toward unrestricted free agency after two seasons with Indiana. Her opposition to transgender athletes competing in girls’ and women’s sports became a major flashpoint this season, prompting demonstrations supporting and opposing her position outside the Fever games. Cunningham previously said she was not concerned that those rallies would distract her team. Cunningham's co-host Hanlen called the column an "absolute hate piece," but said he wanted to focus his response on its basketball arguments. He disputed the suggestion that Cunningham’s scoring average diminished her appeal to other teams, saying she ranked fourth among the WNBA’s bench scorers and was a top-five three-point shooter. "So yes, a lot of teams would want a top five bench scorer that also happens to be a top five three-point shooter in the entire league, not just bench players," Hanlen said. He also challenged a passage discussing Cunningham’s effectiveness, citing her 60.8% effective field goal percentage and saying it ranked fourth in the league. "I understand if you just don’t like somebody and you try to write a hate piece, but don’t try to kind of put down the basketball stuff," Hanlen said. "At least keep it with the facts."
