title: Fetterman plays political maverick, but his voting record tells another story
description: John Fetterman votes with Democrats a majority of the time, yet his Israel stance and Republican friendships fuel intense party-switch speculation.
content: The Senate's most recognizable rogue Democrat has increasingly broken with his party since Republicans took control of the upper chamber, but he still votes with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., a majority of the time. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., is the Senate’s biggest enigma during a time of hyper-partisanship. He bucks his party on key issues, like the war in Iran and immigration, but continues to vote with Democrats an overwhelming amount of the time. Since joining the Senate in 2023, Fetterman has voted with Senate Democrats nearly 90% of the time, a figure that stacks up closely to some of the most staunch party liners in the caucus. Still, speculation has swirled about whether he'll jump the political shark and become a Republican. MAVERICK DEMOCRAT SURGES WITH REPUBLICANS AS HIS OWN PARTY TURNS ON HIM, STOKING TALK OF GOP SWITCH Despite that, Fetterman has set the terms clearly this year, arguing that if Democrats continued to turn their backs on Israel, he would leave the party. But some in the GOP believe that, no matter the swirl percolating in Washington, D.C., Fetterman isn’t swapping jerseys. He’s also keeping the speculation heavy about whether he will run for another term. "John Fetterman is a staunch Democrat that votes with his party 96% of the time. Anybody who seriously believes that he is going to switch to the Republican Party is thinking wishfully," a senior Republican aide told Fox News Digital. Fetterman’s national political career began as a politician armed with an endorsement for Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., running in a pivotal race in 2022 against Dr. Mehmet Oz. SEN JOHN FETTERMAN PLEDGES TO BE 'LAST MAN STANDING' IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN SUPPORT OF ISRAEL Sanders told The Associated Press at the time that "if there’s any candidate who was running more than anybody else, who identified with the working class, who made it clear that he was going to Washington to represent working people, it was John Fetterman." He flipped that seat, giving Democrats one of the slimmest majorities in history and cementing himself as a rock star in the party. Since then, he’s run away from Sanders’ ideals and often rejected Schumer and the caucus’ marching orders. But this year he’s leaned into that gray area, sometimes known as being a centrist, to support Republican ideals. During this session of Congress, Fetterman has broken from Democrats more than ever before, dropping to just under 81% along Democratic Party lines. And while that's happening, Fetterman is reportedly using Republican fundraising platforms to soak up precious donor dollars; is close friends with one of the GOP’s own rock stars, Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala.; made a video message introducing McCormick at the RNC and even accidentally called himself a lifelong Republican during an appearance at the Texas Tribune’s Tribfest last month. FETTERMAN TEASES WHERE HIS TRUE LOYALTY LIES AFTER SURPRISE APPEARANCE AT GOP CONVENTION But when asked about whether he’s considering leaving the party, even after drawing a line in the sand, he recoils. It’s become such a hot topic in the hallways of the Senate that Fetterman stopped taking questions. As to whether he would jump ship depending on the outcome of the upcoming election, Fetterman said during the event that "there are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community. That does not exist in the Republican Party." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So, wait until after the midterms and see what happens," Fetterman said. "And now, if we do win, and I'm 51, people can remember, 'Hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania." Fetterman’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Michael Douglas' wildest Hollywood confessions: From A-list actress bite to Julia Roberts clash
description: Michael Douglas alleges a confrontation with Julia Roberts, secret affairs and a cocaine-fueled evening with O.J. Simpson in his new memoir.
content: Michael Douglas is pulling back the curtain on the most explosive moments of his life, both in front of the camera and behind the scenes. In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the actor-producer also opens up about secret affairs; heavy cocaine and alcohol use; a "rehab or divorce" ultimatum from his first wife, Diandra; and the painful family struggles that followed him from childhood into fatherhood. Douglas details his volatile relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, his son Cameron’s addiction and imprisonment and the Stage 4 cancer diagnosis that forced him to confront his own mortality. Here are the top ten bombshells: MICHAEL DOUGLAS CONFIRMS SECRET AFFAIR WITH KATHLEEN TURNER ON 'ROMANCING THE STONE' SET An A-list actress bit him during casting dinner In the book, Douglas recalled he and filmmakers were trying to convince Debra Winger to star as Joan Wilder in "Romancing the Stone," but the meeting took an odd turn. "We took Debra to dinner and, once again, it was an epic meal. Any time you have dinner with Jack or Danny, it’s a riot. … But the real goal of the dinner was to get Debra on board to make Romancing the Stone, and no matter how hard we tried, she would not give us an answer, one way or the other. We were stuck in limbo. MICHAEL DOUGLAS ADMITS HE ALMOST LEFT HIS WIFE FOR HIS 'BASIC INSTINCT' CO-STAR AFTER AFFAIR "Stories had filtered back that Debra was delivering an incredible performance in Terms of Endearment, but also that she was difficult during shooting and had huge, blow-out fights with Shirley MacLaine. "We all left the restaurant and were walking down the street when, the way somebody might punch you in the arm as you part company, Debra leaned over and bit me. I mean, she really bit me. Jesus, I had a whole set of teeth marks dug into my arm. We still had no answer from her, but that bite sealed the deal for me. No, thank you!" MICHAEL DOUGLAS REVEALS HE MADE FIVE PHONE CALLS TO FIVE WOMEN THE DAY HE CHOSE CATHERINE ZETA-JONES Douglas said he later reenacted the moment for Fox executives, telling them, "She bit me. Hard. Look at the teeth marks in my arm." Although the studio pushed back because Winger was a major star, Douglas held his ground. Winger ultimately did not join the project, and Kathleen Turner was cast in the role. Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Winger for comment. Douglas confronted Julia Roberts over his teenage son Douglas experienced another tense moment involving Julia Roberts at a Golden Globes party. Douglas was at the event with his son Cameron, who was about 13 at the time. In the book, Douglas alleges that Roberts had her arm around Cameron and was "kind of nuzzling him." Douglas, who admits he was drunk, claims Cameron looked stunned. BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG "I told her, ‘Take your hands off my son and take that Golden Globe and stick it where the sun don’t shine,’" he wrote. Douglas later apologized to Roberts and her boyfriend at the time, Kiefer Sutherland. BRAD PITT ADMITS HE BEGAN DRINKING AGAIN AFTER YEARS OF SOBRIETY "I sent Julia roses with an apology for my behavior, and then, back in the production office, I apologized to her and Kiefer in person," he wrote. Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Roberts for comment. Douglas reveals secret affair with Lee Purcell While filming "Adam at 6 A.M." early in his career, Douglas says he and his married co-star Lee Purcell became lovers. However, our recall appears to differ. First, I remember the process of searching for his character of Adam after having already been hired by Steve McQueen for the role of Jerri Jo. Secondly, we had a strictly professional relationship during filming. The personal one came much later." Diandra gave him a ‘rehab or divorce’ ultimatum In the midst of his substance abuse and infidelity, Douglas said his first marriage to Diandra Luker eventually came to a head at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel. After Diandra initially declined to stay with him at the hotel, Douglas called a woman he had been seeing. The woman came to his room, where they had drinks. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? "The indiscretion, the drugs, the booze. I was in a constant state of temporary pleasure or temporary escape," he writes. "In my heart, I knew that I was heading down a very bad road at a very high speed, but I was trying my best to compartmentalize." Douglas entered the Sierra Tucson rehabilitation clinic in Arizona in 1992 for treatment for alcohol and substance abuse. According to Douglas, the story transformed his treatment for alcohol and drug abuse into a sensational headline portraying him as a sex addict. Douglas’ cancer was misdiagnosed for nine months Douglas says doctors initially treated his persistent throat pain as an infection and prescribed multiple rounds of antibiotics. A Canadian specialist eventually discovered a subtle swelling at the back of his tongue. A biopsy revealed squamous cell carcinoma. "It’s stage IV cancer," the doctor told him, according to Douglas, who says the tumor was the size of a walnut. Douglas writes that three doctors had missed the cancer and that he had been given the wrong diagnosis for nine months. He feared surgery would require removing part of his tongue and jaw, potentially ending his acting career. His doctors publicly referred to the disease as throat cancer rather than tongue cancer because they feared reports about possible disfigurement would become sensationalized. "When we came back, I asked to hold the leash. Cam figured it out. He looked at me, like, ‘Dad, how could you?’ Like I had broken his heart. Again." Cameron realized what was happening and resisted, so Douglas threw the plan out of the window. Cameron later served seven years in prison after a federal drug case. Douglas wrote that his son’s heroin relapse behind bars led a judge to add 4½ to his sentence, and Cameron also spent two years in solitary confinement. title: BROADCAST BIAS: Media skip Mamdani’s ‘genocide’ comment but love him bashing ICE
description: From "CBS Mornings" to NPR, Oct. 7 anniversary coverage revealed troubling media bias patterns in how outlets cover Israel, Gaza and Benjamin Netanyahu.
content: The third anniversary of the merciless slaughter of Israelis, as well as Americans, on Oct. 7 drew some solemn media coverage remembering the attack. If there’s a day that the news should display a pro-Israel bias, it would be on this anniversary. But on this subject, our broadcast networks have a disturbing tendency toward "both-sidesism." That’s the clunky word they use when they complain that it’s not moral to present pro-Trump and anti-Trump views as morally or factually equivalent. The best journalism should tilt toward the "right side" of our world. That generally means the liberal side in their view. On Oct. 7, "CBS Mornings" anchor Gayle King was Exhibit A in moral equivalence: "Three years ago today, Hamas unleashed a horrific attack on civilians in southern Israel, killing 1,200 people and taking another 250 hostage. Israel responded with an all-out military offensive in Gaza that killed more than 70,000 people, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry run by Hamas." NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK The impression that leaves is that Israel is 60 times worse than Hamas. The first problem here is using a terrorist group for your statistics. The left-wing media do this without blinking. Naturally, Hamas does not distinguish between its combatant casualties and civilian deaths, and the networks rarely note that Hamas routinely surrounds its soldiers and weapons with civilians with the aim of causing maximum civilian casualties. The other bias bubbling up on Oct. 7 was the bias against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom journalists dislike almost as much as President Donald Trump. CLINTON, BUSH RECEIVED MULTIPLE WARNINGS ON BIN LADEN HIJACK PLOTS BEFORE 9/11, DECLASSIFIED FILES SHOW ABC’s "Good Morning America" had just 75 seconds on the anniversary, which mostly focused on allegations that Netanyahu was warned in advance these attacks were coming. President George W. Bush faced this kind of partisan attack after 9/11 that there were warnings of an al Qaeda attack on America. Foreign correspondent James Longman summarized: "One claim, that the UAE warned the prime minister a week and a half before it happened, but those warnings were not passed on. Now, Benjamin Netanyahu has called all this lies and a smear campaign." BROADCAST BIAS: FROM FLYDUBAI TO BENGHAZI, THE MEDIA STRUGGLE TO KEEP POLITICS OUT OF TERRORISM On the homepage of National Public Radio on the morning of Oct. 7, its top headline announced: "3 years on, Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned before Oct. 7 attacks." They cited four anonymous sources with "direct knowledge." But we have no "direct knowledge" of their identities or motivations. They surely see that as the Trump playbook. NEW YORK TIMES ACCUSED OF FRAMING MUSLIMS AS TRUE VICTIMS OF 9/11 IN ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE The evening newscasts on ABC, CBS and NBC didn’t use any Hamas body counts. But ABC disposed of the subject in a cursory 13 seconds. The other two were somber stories marking the dark day. CBS anchor Tony Dokoupil added, "In the years since, more antisemitic violence has followed, targeting kids at Temple Israel in Michigan, a young couple outside the Israeli Embassy in Washington and a Hanukkah celebration on Australia's Bondi Beach." "The suffering did not begin nor end that day," Mamdani said. "It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza." The mayor added to the insult by showing up that night at a candlelight vigil in Union Square, where anti-Israel protesters, some of them with Hamas and Hezbollah flags, booed and yelled at him with jeers like, "Zohran, you can’t hide, we charge you with genocide." ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA' Then, Mamdani suddenly appeared on the broadcast networks after the anniversary, when the subject changed to an ICE shooting during an enforcement action in New York. title: Discarded trash uncaps 41-year-old murder case in ritzy seaside resort town, authorities say
description: A Rhode Island investigator trailed William Morton to a concert and seized a water bottle that allegedly links him to a 1985 Newport murder.
content: After sitting cold for more than 40 years, a Rhode Island murder case may have been solved with the recovery of a discarded water bottle in a theater. On Oct. 6, William "Billy" Morton was arrested and charged with first-degree murder for allegedly killing Hillary Hellewell in Newport in 1985. After four decades, investigators used new DNA technology that allegedly links 61-year-old Morton to the crime. DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON Since her death, investigators had slowly uncovered clues that suggested Morton might be a suspect. But they needed some of his DNA to confirm the connection. So, in late August, an investigator followed Morton to a Heart tribute band concert at a Rhode Island theater, court records show. FIANCÉE STICKS BY ACCUSED SERIAL RAPIST AS SPECIAL AGENTS DEFEND TAILING HIM FOR RESTAURANT DNA STAKEOUT Morton bought popcorn and bottled water for himself and his fiancée, investigators said. But when the couple left the concert early and Morton didn’t pick up his trash, an investigator collected it as potential evidence. DNA recovered from his water bottle was used to confirm the match to DNA found on Hellewell’s body, according to court documents. COVERT DNA SAMPLE FROM COLORADO MAN'S TRASH REVIVES 44-YEAR-OLD TEXAS MURDER CASE: REPORT Morton was taken into custody Oct. 6 and is being held without bond. The killing On May 19, 1985, the body of 22-year-old Hellewell was found in Newport, Rhode Island, by two brothers — 17 and 20 — who were on their way to work at 4:15 a.m. Hellewell’s body was lying on a sidewalk along Anthony Street. She was wearing white painter’s pants, a sweater and socks but no shoes. Her pulseless body was mostly "cold to the touch," with some areas still "slightly warm" when officers arrived, Morton’s arrest warrant shows. She died from asphyxia due to strangulation, a medical examiner reported. Her cause of death was homicide. KILLER UNDONE BY DECADES-OLD THREADS — GLOVE, TOWEL AND SHIRT STITCH TOGETHER COLD CASE JUSTICE Investigators found a blood stain on the back of Hellewell’s white pants,and a "heavily soiled" blue T-shirt near her head, the arrest warrant shows. Swabs taken from an internal exam of Hellewell’s body revealed spermatozoa, indicating sexual contact, the warrant shows. She was identified the next day when she was reported missing. Friends and family told investigators that she’d attended a gathering with friends in Newport the night before. Everyone there drank alcohol, investigators were told. Investigators learned that Hellewell had offered to walk home with one of her male friends, who’d become overly intoxicated. He made it home. She did not. The next day, he was still so intoxicated he couldn’t give many details to police. The men, who were close to Hellewell at the time of her death, were ruled out as being "potential donors" of the sperm, according to court records. But Newport Police were never able to develop a viable suspect. At the time of Hellewell's murder, DNA evidence was collected and preserved. Resurrecting a cold case The case was reviewed by state officials in 2004. They hoped new advancements in DNA technology could help. During that review, DNA profiles for Hellewell and the suspect were entered into the FBI's Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) database. Then, in 2023, the Rhode Island Attorney General's office formed the Cold Case Unit (CCU), and Hellewell’s case went under review again. With recent breakthroughs in technology used to evaluate DNA, the evidence was sent to a private lab. That work brought a new lead into sharp focus. Suddenly, Morton was a suspect. Investigators pinpointed Morton’s family line through the DNA found on Hellewell’s body. They later found Morton had been convicted in 1987 of a violent sexual assault in Newport 45 days after Hellewell's death. The assault took place a couple miles from where Hellewell’s body was found, court records show. Morton was sentenced to 20 years in prison. He spent seven years behind bars and served out the remainder of his sentence on probation. Date night DNA discovery FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X After the new DNA evaluation, investigators collected evidence and conducted interviews. New clues led them to Morton. They began to watch and trail him. On Aug. 21, Michael Nayor, a senior cold case investigator with the Rhode Island Office of the Attorney General, followed Morton and his fiancée, the arrest warrant shows. They pulled into a Burger King before heading to a theater in Woonsocket, Rhode Island. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS The investigator purchased a ticket to a show by Bad Animals, a Heart tribute band, and followed the couple inside. He watched as Morton bought popcorn and two bottled waters, the arrest warrant shows. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Naylor watched Morton sip his water throughout the show. And when he set the bottle on the seat next to him, Naylor took note, the warrant shows. SEND US A TIP When Morton and his fiancée left early, the bottle of water was left behind. Naylor seized it and submitted it for DNA testing. GOT A TIP? The DNA profile from the water bottle "is consistent with the previously reported partial profiles" from the sperm stain on Hellewell’s pants and a stain on the blue shirt found near her body, according to the Rhode Island Department of Health. He was charged with first-degree murder in the Rhode Island District Court Second Division. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL The case will go to a grand jury, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. title: Celebrity chef says people have Southern food all wrong, shares what her family ate
description: Tiffany Derry challenges Southern food stereotypes, pointing to her Louisiana farm roots and family meals built around fresh vegetables, peas and greens.
content: Southern food may have a reputation for being heavy and unhealthy, but celebrity chef Tiffany Derry says that stereotype misses a big part of what's traditionally been served on tables across the South. "I think a lot of times that criticism comes from folks who don't actually understand the South," Derry told Fox News Digital. The Texas-born chef and restaurateur, who competed on "Top Chef" and recently became a judge on "MasterChef," pointed to her own family's Louisiana roots as an example. 'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS "We had a farm," she said. "I ate from the farm very much." Derry said fresh vegetables were a routine part of meals growing up long before "farm-to-table" became a restaurant buzzword. "It wasn't this farm-to-table thing. It was what you did," she said. Neighbors would share what they grew, while meals featured relatively small amounts of protein alongside rice, peas, vegetables and beans, Derry recalled. DOLLY PARTON'S FAVORITE SOUTHERN DISHES, FROM CHICKEN AND DUMPLINGS TO BANANA PUDDING She said foods commonly associated with Southern cooking today don't tell the entire story. "It's important to not just tell the story of the country cooking where we talk about mac and cheese, and we talk about biscuits and biscuits and gravy," Derry said. "People don't really understand where food comes from." Those heavier dishes represented "such a very small amount of the cooking" and weren't "everyday" foods in her experience. Cooking was also a family affair. Derry said her grandmother had 11 children, and she has more than 50 cousins. As a child, Derry helped prepare greens, peas and green beans. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "People don't really understand where food comes from," she said. After 27 years in the restaurant industry, however, Derry believes she's seeing renewed interest in cooking at home. She recalled a period when Americans seemed to be cooking less, and some people "just didn't really know how to cook." Now, she said, younger generations are seeking out recipes on TikTok, entertaining at home and even embracing bread-making. "I love the fact that people are interested in sourdough. Like, are you kidding me?" Derry said. "People are back making bread." Derry sees the evolution firsthand on "MasterChef," where home cooks can progress to producing food that looks as though it came from professional chefs. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS She also noted that some younger cooks learned differently from previous generations. "So many of their parents didn't really cook," Derry said. "And, so, they learned on their own, and they learned through watching and through chefs and TV and reading books and magazines and all of that." Derry spoke with Fox News Digital while promoting a partnership with Tostitos and the brand's new Chunky Guacamole for football season. She said tailgating food has undergone its own transformation, ranging from traditional burgers to Kobe beef sliders and increasingly elaborate spreads made for Instagram. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Before, people weren't taking pictures of it. They were just eating it," Derry said. title: World Series champion says potential MLB lockout could 'absolutely' cause cancelled games next season
description: World Series champion Nick Swisher said games could "absolutely" be missed next season as MLB and the players association remain far apart on the thought of a salary cap.
content: In a normal year, most MLB teams would already be looking toward next year at this point in the season, as only a few teams remain alive. But what does next season even look like? Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association are all but guaranteed to have a lockout beginning Dec. 1 , as both sides have diametrically opposed positions on a salary cap. The owners are pushing hard to implement a salary cap, while the players are vehemently opposed. World Series champion Nick Swisher said that games could "absolutely" be missed next season due to a stalemate between the two sides. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "Absolutely, because just like yourself as me, is all of a sudden, you hear the players association speaking this language and the commissioner's office is speaking this language. I immediately knew out of the gate. Plus, just knowing a little bit more under the hood about the last couple of collective bargaining agreements, right?" Swisher told OutKick in a recent interview. The former New York Yankees star noted that Tony Clark is no longer the head of the MLBPA after resigning in February and that Bruce Meyer, who took over for Clark, will want everyone to know how he does business. Swisher said he hopes both sides go to the negotiating table in good faith. "When you get people going to the negotiation table, you're hoping that everyone's trying to go to negotiate a fair deal. You're hoping that both sides aren't trying to go to the negotiation table to win. Because if that's the case, we're in a lot of trouble. Because we're really, really far apart from each other right now, and the last thing we wanna do is slow this train down," Swisher said. Swisher said baseball is "absolutely crushing" right now, with revenue and attendance both up, going so far as to say that the game has never been in a better place. Yet, having spent 12 seasons in the big leagues, he understands just how tough the union is. "Pretty much all other sports are very salary cap-based, and that's kind of been the one thing for the players association and the players union. It's one of the strongest unions in the world for a reason, because they stand up for each other. And I was part of that before. I know the bond, I know the brothership, and, listen, it's a tough union," Swisher said. WILL MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL STILL LOCK PLAYERS OUT AFTER 2026 POSTSEASON PROVES OWNERS WRONG? Swisher, like the rest of the baseball world, hopes the two sides can reach an agreement before any games are lost . "I think at the end of the day, man, I'm praying that everything gets itself back on track come the end of the season because I wouldn't wanna slow this train down, man. It's moving too fast right now and we got too many things going on well in our game to be slowing it down right now," Swisher said. BASEBALL OR BABY? During the Division Series, two prominent players were forced to make an impossible decision: Miss their child's birth or leave their team during the postseason to attend the milestone event? About an hour before the San Diego Padres faced the Milwaukee Brewers with their season on the line, All-Star closer Mason Miller went on the paternity list to attend the birth of his child. The Padres won Game 3 and staved off elimination in his absence. New York Yankees starting pitcher Max Fried, on the other hand, said that despite his girlfriend being ready to give birth at any moment, he would pitch in Game 3 no matter what. The Yankees lost the game, so Fried is now free to support his girlfriend for the foreseeable future. Swisher, a father of two children , said he was fortunate to avoid the dilemma Miller and Fried faced . "I was very blessed that I had one child that was born at the beginning of the season and one child that was born in the middle of the season. So, I didn't get presented with this situation where both of these individuals are put in," Swisher said. LEGENDARY SPORTS AGENT WARNS MLB LOCKOUT WOULD BE 'REMARKABLY SELF-DESTRUCTIVE' WITH CBA SET TO EXPIRE "It's hard for me to say that as a father now of two beautiful young girls that I wouldn't want to be there for the birth of my daughter. But once again, I was never put in that position." Having played in numerous postseason games, the former All-Star outfielder said it would have been difficult to miss those opportunities . "At the end of the day, I will tell you this, it's not as often as you think that you get to compete for championships. And for myself, I played in a bunch of playoff games, and we had one great championship run. And it would be really hard for me also to say that I missed out on any of that as well," Swisher said. While it would be difficult to miss a postseason game, the 45-year-old said he couldn't reconcile missing the birth of one of his children. "For myself, at the end of the day, I've never been presented with something like that, so, I really wouldn't even know how to answer that because if I missed the birth of my daughters, either one of them. I feel like that would always bother me," Swisher said. "That would, I would just like – I wasn't there for you. And as a father, that's the one thing that you wanna do is you always wanna be there for your children. So, I can't blame Mason, I can't blame Max." Swisher praised Yankees equipment manager Rob Cucuzza and the entire clubhouse staff for their work. "At the end of the day, I think the unsung heroes are the clubhouse guys, right? The clubhouse, you know, people that, that clean our underwear, right? That wash our jerseys, right, that are up at 4 o'clock in the morning, just unpacking our bags, getting ourselves ready for the next day's worth of work," Swisher, who spoke on behalf of PAYDAY to highlight the low-key legends who helped shape his career, said. "If you don't have those people, if you don't have the engine of your organization, you're not gonna be any good. And the fact that we are so blessed to have someone in New York who does that, who does just that, has an amazing job."

title: Why Alabama, with its high-powered offense, could be the team to finally challenge unbeaten Georgia
description: College Football Week 6 features a massive SEC showdown as Keelon Russell and Alabama host second-ranked Georgia in a clash of unbeaten powers.
content: College Football Week 6 is here, and with it comes one of the biggest games of the season. It seems like the two schools square off each year, and it is always a great game. That’s what happens when two of the best teams in the country and two of the top programs in college football meet, and tonight we have Georgia taking on Alabama. This season, Georgia comes into the game as the second-ranked team in the country. They are a few years removed from being the best defense in the league. Now the team seems to have a better offense than defense. Still, the team hasn’t been bad on the defensive side of the ball, either. The Bulldogs haven’t allowed more than 20 points in a game this season, but they also haven’t faced anyone that impressive. In Week 1, the Bulldogs played Tennessee State and won by 60 points. In Week 2, they won by 50. Then in Week 3, they at least faced some more difficult opponents. They beat Arkansas on the road, but by "only" 28 points. Oklahoma came to face them in Week 4, and they won by 28 in this game as well. Last week, they played against Vanderbilt, and they won by 24 points. At no point in this season have they been tested or had to face a tough team. FIVE IMPORTANT COLLEGE FOOTBALL QUESTIONS THAT WILL BE ANSWERED AFTER THIS WEEKEND'S SLATE The Alabama Crimson Tide brings a 5-0 record of their own, and a rank of sixth in the nation. It has taken a while for the program to look good, but Alabama has been pretty solid through the first five weeks of the season. It isn’t like the Tide have faced anyone overly difficult outside of last week, but the team has looked good on offense, like it will be hard for anyone to stop. Georgia rocked Alabama in the SEC Championship Game last season, 28-7, but Alabama won the previous three meetings between the two teams. This game is in Tuscaloosa, so Alabama does get the edge. title: UCLA vs Oregon betting preview and spread analysis as undefeated squad eyes a major upset
description: No. 21 UCLA's ground-heavy rushing attack faces Oregon's 39th-ranked run defense in a college football playoff-shaping conference showdown.
content: Each week we get a little bit closer to the games that matter most. The College Football Playoffs are closer than you probably realize and we are essentially at the halfway mark for the year. We will still have the conference championships and a few of the lower-level bowl games, and plenty of great matchups in between. One of those great matchups happens today as UCLA takes on Oregon. UCLA comes into the game as the 21st-ranked team in the nation. The Bruins are 4-0 for the season and currently 2-0 in conference play. title: Sally Yates' Cornell review of alleged gang rape could scrutinize crucial police interview, attorney says
description: Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity case faces fresh scrutiny as Sally Yates examines a key police interview prosecutors never fully received.
content: A key campus police interview that local prosecutors say they never received in full before initially declining to bring charges in the Cornell University alleged rape case could face fresh scrutiny as former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates reviews the Ivy League school's handling of the allegations. Yates, who served as deputy attorney general during the Obama administration, has been tapped by Cornell's trustees to conduct a sweeping independent review of the October 2024 allegations involving members of its Chi Phi fraternity after the university's own investigation resulted in expulsions and suspensions. The woman, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, told Cornell University Police during a November 2024 interview, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," according to a transcript obtained by CBS News. She also described later sexual activity as coercive and said she had been "completely and totally incapacitated." INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, however, said his office reviewed a six-page sworn statement that described Doe's participation in the sexual activity and drug use as voluntary and consensual. Van Houten said his office did not initially receive the complete interview and told CBS News last week that the information in the fuller interview "changes the landscape for me." Scott Iseman, a New York attorney who has represented students accused of campus sexual misconduct, said Yates could review Doe's full police interview and compare it with her sworn statement, later testimony and other evidence gathered during Cornell's investigation. "Those full recorded interviews, I can tell you from experience, have a treasure trove of information that are really, really important to exactly what happened," Iseman said. "It wouldn't surprise me if there was additional information in there that would have changed the trajectory of this case because that happens all the time." The apparent differences between Doe's full interview and her shorter sworn statement could be particularly significant, Iseman said. "Law enforcement is supposed to make sure that all salient facts are included in that sworn statement," he said. Cornell said its police department provided prosecutors with Doe's sworn statement and a Snapchat screenshot in 2024, describing the evidence-sharing process as standard protocol when a possible crime has occurred. Iseman cautioned that he had not reviewed the complete interview, which has not been made publicly available, and could not determine whether any omitted information was material. It remains unclear why the full interview was not initially provided to Van Houten's office. Fox News Digital reached out to Cornell University Police and the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office for clarification. Cornell said Yates and her team will have access to relevant records, case files, university personnel and leadership as they review the school's response, under its original Title IX investigation, which determines whether students violated university sexual misconduct policies rather than criminal law. Beyond the police interview, Iseman said Yates could identify witnesses who were never questioned, overlooked text messages or social media evidence and other information that did not emerge during Cornell's original investigation. "There's a lot that potentially she could uncover," Iseman said. But he cautioned against assuming Cornell mishandled the allegations. "It may have all been done very appropriately by Cornell. We don't know yet," he said. CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE What Cornell's investigation found Cornell has defended its handling of the allegations, pointing to an extensive investigation that included more than 50 interviews and 12 days of disciplinary hearings. University President Michael Kotlikoff said two of the seven accused students were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had graduated before discipline could be imposed and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct. Cornell said both the accuser and accused students had opportunities to review evidence, testify and challenge the findings through an appeals process. What Yates' review could lead to Yates was brought in after the case erupted into a national firestorm following Doe's Sept. 16 lawsuit, which laid out graphic allegations that seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted her during a night involving alcohol, drugs and group sex at their fraternity house in October 2024. The allegations have since sparked protests on campus while New York Attorney General Letitia James' office is conducting a separate criminal investigation. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men. Yates' investigation extends beyond the Chi Phi case to examine how Cornell handles sexual misconduct allegations across campus, including its oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations. Her team at the law firm of King & Spalding will also assess Cornell's practices against federal and state laws and examine whether the university followed its own procedures in responding to the Chi Phi allegations. Any new or previously overlooked evidence identified during the review could potentially be shared with James' office, Iseman said, though Yates herself has no authority to bring charges. BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE Her findings could also lead to recommendations for improving Cornell's procedures, even if the university is found to have followed its existing rules. Cornell said Yates will report her findings and recommendations to a special committee of its Board of Trustees, which intends to share the results with the university community. Yates has tackled explosive misconduct allegations before. Her 2022 investigation into women's professional soccer exposed widespread sexual harassment, coercion and abuse by coaches, along with failures by league officials to act on complaints. What began as an investigation into individual coaches exposed much wider problems across women's soccer, prompting a series of recommendations for sweeping reforms that U.S. Soccer subsequently pledged to implement. Broader concerns The Cornell case also highlights a wider debate over the legal protections available to students accused of serious sexual misconduct, even as universities have the power to expel them. John R. Grasso, a Rhode Island criminal defense attorney and former police officer who has represented accused students for two decades, argued that campus disciplinary proceedings can carry life-altering consequences without offering the same legal protections available in criminal court. "When I defend a student on campus, we don't have any right to discovery. We can't compel the production of anything," Grasso said. He said those limitations can make it difficult for attorneys to obtain potentially important text messages, photographs and other evidence that might support an accused student's defense. Grasso also described the difficult choice students can face when university disciplinary proceedings and criminal investigations overlap: participating in campus proceedings and potentially making statements that could affect a criminal case or remaining silent and risking disciplinary consequences. "I have a right to remain silent, but if I don't participate, I'm getting found responsible," he said, describing the dilemma he has encountered representing students. The human toll Grasso said the consequences of campus sexual misconduct allegations can extend far beyond disciplinary hearings, describing students whose education, reputations and emotional well-being have suffered even when they were ultimately cleared. "Bad things happen to the accused the minute a complaint is filed against them on campus. Really bad things," he said. "Just because the allegations are salacious or dramatic does not mean that's what happened," Iseman said. "So, people need to keep an open mind."

title: Rahm Emanuel challenges DSA’s influence on Democrats, warns GOP ‘wing’ is disappearing
description: Rahm Emanuel warns the Republican Party faces a Mitt Romney and John McCain-style moderate exodus as the Democratic Party debates its left flank.
content: As democratic socialists, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, gain ground within the Democratic Party, former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel argued that socialists have less influence over his party than Republicans contend. Emanuel, the former mayor of Chicago and, at one point, President Barack Obama’s right-hand man, distanced himself from the more radical positions of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) while suggesting that the group could have a place within the party if it adopted more moderate positions. "I don't believe the socialists are a wing," he told the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "I think they are a separate party. They believe in defunding the police, which is not the party position. They believe in open borders and open prisons. That's not the party’s position." RAHM EMANUEL WARNS ‘BERNIE BROS’ COULD SINK DEMOCRATS BY SADDLING MODERATES WITH SOCIALIST AGENDA "When you switch that, we can talk," Emanuel added. Conservatives have expressed concern over the rise of far-left, progressive candidates within the Democratic Party, warning that socialist-leaning politicians like Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., could overtake party moderates. MAMDANI, TOUTING RI SOCIALIST’S VICTORY, ANSWERS QUESTION OF ‘WHAT IS THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY?’ Emanuel pushed back on the Republican Party’s characterization of the Democratic Party’s trajectory, pointing to New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger as examples of Democratic pragmatism. "I don't think that's where the party is," Emanuel said. "I think the party is in the pragmatic wing. You can see that in the governor of Virginia, you can see that in the governor of New Jersey, how they both won their primaries." FORMER DNC VICE CHAIR DAVID HOGG CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC MODERATES 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT VALUES' The longtime Clinton advisor argued it is healthy for the Democratic Party to have debate between its progressive and moderate factions. He also warned that the Republican Party faces an exodus of its moderate wing once spearheaded by Mitt Romney and John McCain. "I happen to think we're going to have a healthy debate in our party," Emanuel told host Sean Hannity. "We haven't had it for 20 years. That's what we should have," he continued. "In the same way that the Romney and McCain wing of your party is leaving. They have walked away, and that's what's going to tell the story of 2026." title: America's truckers issue dire warning as soaring diesel costs threaten 'domino effect'
description: Truckers say diesel at $6.32 per gallon is slashing profits and cutting routes, warning of a domino effect that could ripple through the supply chain.
content: American truckers are warning that sky-high diesel prices are eating into their profits and putting pressure on trucking companies to cut routes, raising concerns that some drivers could be forced off the road, and the pain could eventually reach Americans at the grocery store. "Fuel prices is going up. The rates are not going up," Miami-based trucker Suave Dorsett told Fox News Digital. "So, it's hurting our pockets real bad." The warnings come as the Iran war sends diesel prices soaring, squeezing American truckers even as President Donald Trump predicts oil prices will fall "like a stone" amid expectations that the conflict could soon end. Drivers told Fox News Digital the damage is already mounting, with routes being cut and smaller operators facing mounting financial pressure. Dorsett is among several truckers who told Fox News Digital that soaring fuel costs are cutting into their earnings and putting pressure on an industry responsible for moving goods across the country, with one driver reporting fewer routes and others warning that smaller operators could eventually be forced to park their rigs. THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE The national average for diesel stood at roughly $6.32 per gallon Monday, according to AAA, up from about $3.69 at the same time last year, a jump of more than 70%. The surge has also eclipsed the previous record of $5.816 per gallon, set in June 2022 under former President Joe Biden as Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent global energy prices soaring. For Dorsett, who has been driving for nine years, the price at the pump was even steeper. He told Fox News Digital he was seeing diesel at $7.40 per gallon while traveling through Ohio. Dorsett said the fuel spike comes as truckers are already shouldering a long list of expenses, including diesel exhaust fluid (DEF), which helps reduce harmful emissions, parking, showers, weighing and reweighing loads, repairs and towing. And if diesel prices remain elevated, Dorsett predicted smaller operators will be the first to buckle. BIDEN-ERA ENVIRO RULE ACCUSED OF STRANGLING TRUCKERS, SQUEEZING AMERICANS LANDS ON TRUMP CHOPPING BLOCK "Some of the smaller companies, like the smaller owner-ops, would slowly fall off, and it's going to create a chain effect," Dorsett said, predicting a "domino effect" that could eventually put pressure on larger carriers. Tyler Rinaldi, a Louisiana trucker with about a decade of experience who transports hazardous materials and other freight for an LTL company, said he has already seen weekend routes scaled back at his company. "I've seen a lot of routes get cut," Rinaldi told Fox News Digital. "They're not really running like they want to on the weekends right now." "I definitely see a lot of change because of it at my company, slowly, but it's starting to be more noticeable." TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS Rinaldi, who is married with two children, said fewer routes could eventually mean less money coming home. "When they start cutting routes and trying to limit the expenses on what routes they send out," Rinaldi said, "that takes away from the people that work in the company's pockets." Avante Jackson, an 11-year trucking veteran from Charlotte, North Carolina, who transports steel and other construction materials, said rising diesel prices are forcing truckers to take a harder look at whether the money they bring in is enough to keep their businesses running. "If I'm putting all of my profit in the tank," Jackson said, "at the end of the day, what do I have left to keep the doors open?" CUT THE BULL: THE REAL REASON BEEF COSTS SO MUCH — AND WHAT TRUMP IS TRYING TO DO Jackson cautioned against "fear-mongering" about potential shortages but said a widespread loss of drivers could ultimately reach consumers. "It really could hit the community," he said. The latest diesel spike mirrors a similar crunch in 2022 under former President Joe Biden, when the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent fuel prices flying. Diesel reached a then-record national average of $5.82 per gallon that June, squeezing truckers as operating expenses climbed. According to the American Transportation Research Institute, trucking fuel costs surged 53.7% in 2022, helping drive a 21.3% jump in overall operating costs to a then-record $2.25 per mile. The latest spike threatens to revive those pressures, particularly for smaller operators with less room to absorb rising fuel bills. As the Trump administration pushes international partners to release emergency fuel reserves in an effort to bring prices down, the truckers had their own message for the president: Don't forget about the drivers absorbing the costs on the road. "My message to President Trump would just be to think about who's keeping America moving," Jackson told Fox News Digital. "Think about the little guys out here each and every day." TRUMP JUST BROKERED A DEAL WITH THE COUNTRY SITTING ATOP THE WORLD’S LARGEST OIL RESERVES "We truly are the backbone of America. We keep America moving," he added. "We just want you just to think about us and put yourself in our shoes. ... Let's try to get the fuel prices down, and let's try to just make more of a change," he said. "We know we can do better." Trump described higher fuel prices Thursday as a temporary sacrifice in the fight to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, saying on Truth Social that rising gasoline costs were "a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon." Trump said last week that European countries had agreed to release diesel from their stockpiles after he pressed them to put more supply on the market. The G7 subsequently agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products from previously pledged emergency reserves over four months, including a substantial diesel release during the first 20 days, in an effort to ease pressure on global fuel markets. Trump predicted during a rally Wednesday night in San Antonio, Texas, that oil prices would "come down like a rock" once the war with Iran ends, insisting the conflict would be over "very soon." "This week, President Trump signed an executive order that will quickly cut diesel costs and put money directly back into the pockets of American truckers, saving them over $100 every time they refill at the gas pump. Last week, he negotiated a deal with our European counterparts to release 100 million barrels — mainly diesel — from their stockpiles to add supply to the market and lower costs," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital. "The president wants to see prices at the pump fall and continues to take historic action to ease temporary disruptions as oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz approaches pre-conflict levels."

title: Veteran shot 7 times in Fort Hood massacre has a warning for Americans planning to watch execution
description: A Fort Hood shooting survivor shot seven times by Nidal Hasan wants to witness the firing squad execution but warns against treating it as a spectacle.
content: On Dec. 3, 2026, the U.S. government intends to take Nidal Hasan to a firing range at Fort Hood and publicly execute him. Few condemned men could make a more difficult case for mercy. Seventeen years ago, Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time, walked into a soldier readiness center at the Texas Army post and opened fire, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. Now, after years of appeals, the Army is preparing to execute him by firing squad. And Americans will be able to watch on live stream. That last detail has transformed what might otherwise have been the long-delayed conclusion of one of the darkest chapters in the Army's history into a more uncomfortable question: How should a nation reckon with the gravity of taking a life, even when that life belongs to a mass murderer? For Alonzo Lunsford, a former Army staff sergeant who survived being shot seven times by Hasan, the answer is complicated. GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT Lunsford wants Hasan executed. He intends to witness it himself in December. He told Fox News Digital he would even prefer that one of Hasan's surviving victims or the relatives of those he killed be allowed to pull the trigger. Despite that, Lunsford says he has forgiven Hasan. "The weird thing about it, I've forgiven him because my faith does not allow me to heal and continue unless I forgive that man," Lunsford said. But forgiveness, for Lunsford, does not mean sparing Hasan from punishment. What troubles him is the prospect of turning that punishment into entertainment. "It's not a spectacle," he said. "There's nothing glorified in the smell of human flesh, blood and gunpowder. It's a smell you will never forget. It's a taste that you will never forget." "That's not something you sit around and say, hey, let's get some popcorn and look at this execution," he continued. "We as a people, we're better than that. This ain't no country where we do public beheadings and stonings and think it's fine." ARMY SERGEANT SENTENCED AFTER SHOOTING 5 SOLDIERS AND HIS MALE FIANCÉ AT FORT STEWART Lunsford was working at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center on Nov. 5, 2009, when Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, opened fire. He recalled watching Hasan kill a colleague before turning the weapon on him. Lunsford was shot above his left eye, fell to the floor and played dead before eventually escaping outside, where Hasan shot him again. "I've accepted the fact I'm gonna live with the pain for the rest of my life," Lunsford said. He has since found purpose in coaching basketball, mentoring young people and helping others struggling with their mental health. Lunsford said he doesn't want children watching the livestream, though he believes adults can decide for themselves whether to tune in. "This is not somewhere you all start throwing some meat on the grill, get outside and say, hey, we're gonna watch them unalive this guy by firing squad," he said. "Don't do that." "Don't do that because when you do that, you're dishonoring those that made the supreme sacrifice, those who are no longer here. Those are heroes." War Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended making the execution public, saying Americans should understand the consequences of Hasan's crimes. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said in an interview this week. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon would follow through with its plans to livestream Hasan's execution, saying he had no intention of watching it himself. "I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he told reporters Friday. The decision for the first U.S. Army death by firing squad in 86 years to be live streamed has drawn opposition even from Republicans who support putting Hasan to death. "I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote on X. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., likewise said Hasan "should face the death penalty," but called publicly streaming it "beyond disgusting." "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis wrote. "It should not be happening in America." The nation's Catholic bishops have gone further, opposing both Hasan's execution and the decision to make it public. "In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, said Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people." The decision has also raised a more immediate national security concern. Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot during the 2009 attack, has previously spoken about becoming a martyr. Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury counterterrorism official and director of the Washington Institute's Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence, warned that making footage of his death widely available could give terrorist groups material to exploit. "It seems like a poor decision to provide terrorist groups with a video clip they can effectively splice into radicalization propaganda," Levitt told Fox News Digital. "There's no tangible benefit to live streaming an execution, and it may, in fact, exacerbate the terrorist threat." For Lunsford, however, the execution remains deeply personal. During Hasan's 2013 court-martial, the two locked eyes. Lunsford wants Hasan to see him again before he dies. "I want to look at him in his eyes. I want him to see me — man to man," Lunsford said. title: ‘Donroe’ Doctrine and conservative victories squeeze cartels in Latin America
description: The Sinaloa cartel and CJNG are rapidly adapting as Trump's Shield of the Americas coalition squeezes drug trafficking routes across the hemisphere.
content: The cartels are losing political cover, and they know it. Colombia elected Abelardo de la Espriella, who ran opposed to negotiations with armed groups and won. Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Paraguay and others have aligned with Washington’s enforcement policies. The Shield of the Americas coalition now coordinates intelligence and operations against cartel networks, but with a handful of exceptions: Mexico, Brazil, Cuba and Nicaragua. EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S NEW SECURITY ALLIANCE FACES FIRST REAL-WORLD TEST DEEP IN SOUTH AMERICA AS TROOPS DEPLOY That is the Donroe Doctrine in practice: American predominance in the hemisphere, applied to migration, Chinese footholds and the drug trade. Cuba is the weakest link in the old arc. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the regime has already fallen as a functioning state. About a fifth of the population has left since 2021. The lights fail, the peso is worthless and the government that remains specializes in jailing people. Whether the Castro apparatus collapses by December is unknowable. What is knowable is that Havana is no longer a reliable logistics or intelligence partner for anyone who needs one. In Mexico, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Morena government is increasingly alone. It keeps bilateral contacts with Washington while refusing the regional coalition, citing fear of U.S. operations on Mexican soil. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins the Brazilian runoff, Sheinbaum’s remaining major left-of-center counterpart in the region is gone. Isolation raises the diplomatic cost of open sanctuary to the drug lords. But the cartels are already adjusting. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN In August, Spanish police rolled up a CJNG-linked cell that moved roughly 2½ tons of methamphetamine dissolved in vanilla aroma and finished it in a lab in Lleida. U.S. strikes on alleged drug-running fast boats have sharply reduced Eastern Caribbean drug traffic. Routes move. Chemistry is portable. Coca fields aren’t. TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT Violence is scaling with the same logic. Mexican authorities have arrested clusters of former Colombian soldiers — nine of 12 in one Michoacán case were ex-military — after mine attacks that killed Mexican troops. CRIME, KIDNAPPINGS AND DRONE ATTACKS FLAGGED IN US WARNING FOR BORDER REGION And a prosecutor’s office in Tijuana has already been hit by nail-packed drones. Avocado orchards, fuel theft, mining extortion and chemical import fronts are already balance-sheet items. European logistics firms and real estate laundering are the export version. Leadership disruption and route competition have historically produced spikes in ambushes, not quiet consolidation. Armored "monstruo" trucks, landmines and FPV drones lower the cost of killing rivals and local police. Expect more of it in Michoacán, Jalisco and the border plazas. title: Inside the protest playbook to vilify Israel on 'global day of action'
description: Global Alliance for Palestine distributed a detailed playbook urging groups to shut down city squares and blockade corporate hubs across continents.
content: WASHINGTON, D.C. — As demonstrators, including the headline-grabbing CodePink agitators, descend on the nation's capital late Saturday afternoon for a "coordinated global day of action" against Israel, they will join a worldwide wave of marches and planned disruptions that may appear to be unfolding independently. In Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on Friday, anti-Israel demonstrators carried signs deploying emotionally charged language against Israel, including one featuring a Palestinian flag and a bloodied hand with the message, "STOP GENOCIDE." Nearby, two women carrying mock machine guns flanked a cardboard image of a handcuffed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a noose around his neck. But a Fox News Digital investigation has found that, long before the first demonstrators gathered, the messages for the protest's "communications framing" and transnational action plan had already been written, the banners designed, the tactics circulated and the media strategy laid out to "turn public outrage into collective leverage." LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION The campaign documents reveal that coalition organizers instructed participating groups to direct protesters to "shut down city squares," "encircle government buildings" and "blockade complicit corporate hubs." The document declares, "This is not a symbolic march and not a routine protest." Fox News Digital identified 179 organizations in the coalition, while an interactive Google Map published by the network lists 322 events scheduled across three days through Sunday. They include a rally on an "Intifada Trail" in Saint John, New Brunswick, Canada; a protest in Bangladesh by the "Bangladesh Intifada Youth Collection"; and actions in South Africa by "Social Intifada." All three use "intifada," a term associated with Palestinian uprisings against Israel, including periods marked by deadly terrorist attacks. Activists describe the term as a call for resistance. The global coordination illustrates how contemporary protest movements combine international leadership, local activist networks, standardized visual branding, emotionally charged messaging and traditional news outreach into a single mobilization infrastructure in which professional political organizing amplifies the sincerely held convictions of individual demonstrators. Among the participating organizations is CodePink, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that has received $1.33 million from Neville Roy Singham, a Shanghai-based tech tycoon who has funneled $278 million into a network of nonprofits under scrutiny by the House Ways and Means Committee and its chairman, Rep. Jason Smith, over allegations that some operate as "Trojan horses" and proxies for the Chinese Communist Party and other malign foreign interests. CodePink and other organizations under scrutiny have denied wrongdoing. Two days ago, CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin and D.C. coordinator Olivia DiNucci dispatched a letter to members, directing them to join the "Feminist Contingent" at the Library of Congress for the "global day of action." "And don't forget to WEAR PINK!" they noted. The network's connections were also visible last week, when CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans, who married Singham in 2017, joined an anti-Israel protest in New York City, marching behind a band of activists from Revolutionary Communists of America as they chanted, "Long live the intifada." Evans told Fox News Digital Singham supports CodePink's efforts and the "amazing work" nonprofits are doing to "stand up when violent things are happening." Taken together, the documents reveal a coordinated protest and influence campaign spanning continents, combining accusations of Israeli "genocide," attacks on the news media, workplace and university walkouts, blockades, political lobbying and carefully orchestrated publicity. A review of the planning documents for the global protests reveals the machinery behind the wave of anti-Israel demonstrations across continents as not only a protest campaign but a psychological operation. At the center of the international mobilization are three organizations identified in the campaign documents: the Global Alliance for the Palestinian Territories, launched in July 2025 in London as a "truly international popular front for Palestinian liberation"; the Anti-Apartheid Movement for Palestine; and the Global Coalition to End the Occupation of Palestine. An online directory displays 179 organizational logos from participating groups worldwide. Fox News Digital extracted the names from the logos and built a database of the coalition. The same pattern of coordinated organizing has emerged in another international protest movement — the "student protests" rolling through France. A separate Fox News Digital investigation identified a network of 50 organizations coordinating and amplifying those demonstrations. Only 15 were classified as youth- or student-led groups, while the remaining 35 included communist organizations, labor groups, political organizations and professional protest coordinators. Organizers supplied participating groups with campaign materials, coordination and strategic support to "turn public outrage into collective leverage." In an August "Launch Statement," the alliance laid out a strategy to synchronize student demonstrations, workplace actions, rallies and civil disobedience across Asia, the Americas, Europe, Africa and the Middle East. The stated objective wasn't simply to organize demonstrations but to add Israel's war in Gaza to the international media agenda, turning separate protests into a coordinated communications effort intended to shape what audiences around the world see, hear and think about the conflict. But the most revealing aspect of the operation may be its stated objective of shaping what the world sees, hears and thinks about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In a "Launch Statement" in August, the alliance declared that the demonstrations are intended to return Israel's military campaign against Palestinians to the international media agenda. The campaign materials describe a strategy of synchronizing protests across continents, connecting student demonstrations, workplace actions, rallies and civil disobedience from Asia to the Americas, Europe, Africa and the Middle East. The result is a coordinated communications campaign designed to transform demonstrations organized by separate groups into the political impact of a single international mobilization. ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS Weeks before the demonstrations, the alliance had already prepared a collection of campaign posters in seven languages — English, Arabic, Turkish, Finnish, French, Portuguese and Spanish. They supplied graphics for a large street banner carrying carefully selected slogans, along with protest-sign designs from folders marked "HANDHELD PLACARDS" and "STREET DEMANDS." One of the downloadable images is a poster with the message "GAZA GENOCIDE" next to graphics of barbed wire and watermelon, both symbols of Palestinian "resistance" against Israel. In Malaysia, a woman wearing a black-and-white Palestinian keffiyeh raised her fist while holding a printed version of the watermelon and barbed-wire placard, with the organizers' branding in smaller letters on her sign: "GLOBAL ALLIANCE FOR PALESTINE." Behind her, other women carried the same sign and other signs featuring additional graphics from the same campaign materials. Other placards held by protesters in Malaysia yesterday read, "HUMANITY IS NOT A CRIME" and "STOP THE GENOCIDE WAR!" Another downloadable sign, carried in Malaysia, reads: "LET GAZA LIVE!" The campaign's "Communications Framing" employs familiar techniques of political persuasion: repetition, emotional imagery, collective identity, moral urgency and the portrayal of inaction as complicity. The materials offer a window into the battle for public attention that increasingly accompanies international conflicts. One poster declares, "You cannot erase a homeland." Another commands, "End the genocide. Defend the land." A third combines an image of a child with the message, "Defend the land. Protect its children." Another repeats the words "Silence normalises" across the background before presenting the word "genocide" in oversized red lettering. But the campaign's internal messaging guidance goes further, prescribing accusations against Israel and the news media in a section called "Slogans & Hashtags," with "Call to Action & Core Street Demands." Among its recommended slogans is the blunt declaration: "Israel Kills. The Media Justifies." Another declares, "1,100 Days of Israeli Genocide — The Killing Continues." Yet another calls for action under the message, "1,100 Days — From Every Street, One Demand: End Genocide, End Occupation." Together, the slogans strategically combine accusations of "genocide" with demands for political action, while claiming the media "justifies" Israel's conduct. In its "Concept Paper," the alliance describes Israel's actions as a "war of extermination" and calls for countries to stop providing weapons to the Israeli state. The same document instructs participating organizations in its "Communications Framing" to use language that is "disciplined, credible, urgent and impossible to ignore." It also directs organizers to portray "institutional silence" as part of the problem and public mobilization as necessary to confront what the alliance calls continuing complicity. The objective isn't simply to communicate a political position but to encourage audiences to emotionally identify with a movement and participate in its activities. The campaign presents its allegations of "genocide" and other violations of international law as established claims. On Friday, South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay received the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her work, which included arguing that Israel has committed a "genocide" against Palestinians. Israel disputes the "genocide" accusation. ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA' The organizing documents go beyond encouraging supporters to attend demonstrations. Instead, organizers describe a campaign intended to "interrupt business-as-usual" and organize "high-visibility rallies, marches, picket lines, sit-ins and peaceful blockades" at "civic sites, government offices, financial hubs and corporate locations" that its organizers have "identified as complicit in sustaining or normalising Israeli violence." They also recommend synchronized "workplace, campus and creative interruptions," including "silent walkouts," banner drops, nighttime projections, street theater, "die-ins" and "other highly visible public actions that interrupt normal routines and make the political demand impossible to ignore." A detailed logistical plan urges organizations to "allocate funds," arrange transportation and establish "legal, stewarding, and participant support." ISRAELI PM NETANYAHU ARGUES PUBLIC OPINION SHIFT ON ISRAEL 'CORRELATES ALMOST 100%' TO SOCIAL MEDIA The campaign's organizational structure brings together prominent political figures with longstanding backgrounds in international politics and anti-Israel activism in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia. A press release for the protests identifies seven members of the international steering committee, including former British Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn, who joined a coalition supporting the Communist Party of Cuba; pro-communist former Greek Finance Minister Yanis Varoufakis; former Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams; Palestinian political leader Mustafa Barghouti; former South African government minister Ronnie Kasrils; Indian activist Varsha Gandikota-Nellutla; and Italian politician Angelo Bonelli. Anas Altikriti serves as secretary-general. Jessica Breakey, the campaign's public relations officer, didn't respond to a request for comment. Beyond the streets, the alliance's strategy documents lay out a plan to convert the demonstrations' visibility into "sustained political pressure" on lawmakers and government institutions. In a separate advocacy document, organizers urge participating groups to mobilize protesters to write lawmakers, submit coordinated institutional letters and arrange meetings with elected representatives. The campaign calls for "immediate, total arms embargoes" and "comprehensive state sanctions" against Israel for alleged violations of international law. It also urges governments to suspend preferential trade agreements and institutional partnerships associated with Israeli policies. The alliance demands an end to what it calls Israel's "genocide and occupation," without specifying whether its reference to occupation encompasses Gaza, the West Bank or the entire State of Israel. The distinction takes on particular significance amid chants of "from the river to the sea" at anti-Israel demonstrations. Organizers encourage participating groups to use "targeted, template-driven letters" and "digital briefing toolkits" to support "localised political campaigning," adapting them to their national political systems. The documents provide direct instructions that participating organizations issue local press releases, distribute "ready-made social-media toolkits," share "graphics across digital channels" and hold briefing sessions to "ensure clear, aligned messaging ahead of the weekend." title: Former MN state trooper tears into Dems as Somali gang violence terrorizes Minnesota: ‘Where is Ilhan Omar?’

content: Former state trooper John Nagel pointed the finger at his opponent, Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and the Democratic Party for allowing Somali American gang-linked violence to escalate in the Twin Cities. Residents of Eden Prairie and surrounding Twin Cities suburbs have been left fearing for their safety after a string of gang-related incidents this month, including the shooting of two teens outside an Eden Prairie High School football game and more than 100 shell casings recovered in a Bloomington neighborhood. "Where is Ilhan Omar in all of this?" Nagel, a Minnesota native who spent 30 years as a state trooper, asked in an interview with Fox News Digital. "I would think that, as a congressman that represents this particular area, that she'd be at these meetings, or she'd have a statement, or she’d be sitting down and saying, ‘Hey, how can we help this? How could we stop this?’ And I don't see her." OMAR'S GOP CHALLENGER COMES OUT FIRING WITH VOW TO CLEAN UP 'MESS' IN DEEP BLUE DISTRICT: 'PEOPLE ARE FED UP' Nagel accused other Minnesota Democrats, including Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, of having their "heads in the sand" and preventing law enforcement from stopping the violence before it got out of control. "They're being restrained by politicians, people that are trying soft on crime, people that are trying to send somebody other than a police officer to take care of issues, and it's not working," Nagel said. Looking at the responses of statewide leaders, including Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison, Nagel said the majority of Democrats "don’t want enforcement." "The people do," he said. "They're tired of it." Democrats have been too lenient on crime for years, according to Nagel, which he said has "emboldened" gang members to break the law without serious consequences. "Because of how the Democrats have run Minnesota over the years, these gang members and then just crooks in general, they’re emboldened by this," he said. ILHAN OMAR ON TRACK FOR FIFTH TERM AS MINNESOTA VOTERS MAINTAIN FAR-LEFT STREAK Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher spoke at a news conference this week, highlighting that a "big chunk of the problem" is failing to hold gang members accountable, saying Moriarty's office needs to be more "aggressive" with prosecuting juveniles. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Daniel Borgertpoepping, a spokesperson for Moriarty’s office, said no cases related to the Bloomington incident have been submitted for charging consideration, but "they’ll be thoroughly reviewed" if they are. Adam Abdihakeem Adam, 18, was charged Friday in the Eden Prairie homecoming football game shooting with two counts of second-degree assault with a deadly weapon and second-degree riot. "Mr. Adam will be held accountable," Moriarty said in a press release Friday. "Violence in our communities is completely unacceptable, and it requires a professional, coordinated response, which happened here." Fletcher also pushed back on "East African" being used to generalize the gang members’ ethnicity, adding that "98% of these gang members are Somali" and that the broader label isn’t "fair." "I think we just have to say what it is and not run away from the term," he said. AMY KLOBUCHAR CALLS FOR MAJOR ANTI-TERRORISM INVESTMENTS AFTER ALLEGED MALL OF AMERICA PLOT Nagel said people are afraid of being called "racist" for referring to the gangs as Somalian, arguing that law enforcement is simply going after those committing the crimes rather than blaming an entire community. "I mean, we have Latino gangs and Asian gangs and Black gangs, and we have Somali gangs. This is not being prejudicial." He said it’s a "Somali problem" because that’s "who's showing up." "It's ridiculous," he said. "I'm a police officer. I don't care who you are. I don't care what color you are." Nagel said a "gang task force" could be part of the solution. "We don't need to pass any more laws," he argued. "We don't need any more people asking for money to help their group. We need to take the laws that we have and prosecute people." As gang violence spills into Minnesota communities, Nagel said it can’t continue to go on like it has. "We need enforcement, we need arrests and we need incarceration," he said. Nagel will face off against Omar and Independent candidate DeVelle Jackson in the upcoming midterm elections for the U.S. House seat representing Minnesota's 5th Congressional District.
