title: Plague mystery revives concerns over not-so-secret Russian bioweapons program
description: Marshall Billingslea reveals Soviet defector Ken Alibek exposed a massive biological weapons program involving antibiotic-resistant plague research.
content: Marshall Billingslea was a Senate Foreign Relations Committee staffer in the 1990s when he sat down with one of the highest-ranking defectors from the Soviet biological weapons program and began learning the extent of what Moscow had secretly built. And what he found out from Ken Alibek, the former No. 2 official in the Soviet biological weapons apparatus, is raising red flags for Billingslea over the Oct. 2, 2026, death linked to an anti-plague institute in Russia. "I think one of the most important things that Ken shed light on was the sheer scale of the Soviet program, which then Russia inherited," Billingslea told Fox News Digital. "Just mammoth." Three decades later, the mysterious death of a researcher at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East has put new attention on what became of that program, and Billingslea argues the world should be demanding answers from Moscow. MYSTERY DEATH AT RUSSIAN PLAGUE LAB TRIGGERS SWEEPING PRECAUTIONS AS US WATCHES CLOSELY "It's not acceptable in this day and age for the Russians to have a biological warfare program," said Billingslea, who previously served as President Donald Trump's special presidential envoy for arms control. "They need to cut it out, and they need to tell us. They need to come clean about what they're doing at this lab and whether this lab is still involved in their warfare program." The U.S. government says Russia's offensive biological weapons program did not disappear with the Soviet Union. "Russia maintains an offensive biological weapons program and is in violation of its obligations under the BWC," a State Department official told Fox News Digital this week. BWC, or Biological Weapons Convention, is an international treaty that prohibits the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons. State's 2025 arms control compliance report assessed that the Soviet-era program was "absorbed, not dismantled" by Russia after the collapse and has "continued and evolved" since then. There is no evidence linking the Irkutsk researcher's death to Russia's biological weapons program, and Billingslea told Fox News Digital he has seen no evidence that the institute remains involved in the program today. But the unexplained death has revived scrutiny of the Soviet program's work and the network of ostensibly civilian laboratories that Billingslea said Alibek identified as also performing classified work. Alibek's disclosures included Soviet efforts to alter pathogens to make them more lethal, transmissible or difficult to treat, Billingslea said, adding that some of the most troubling revelations involved plague. BIOWEAPON THREAT EXPOSED AS ANTHROPIC SOUNDS ALARM ON FOREIGN ACTORS PLOTTING VIRUS EXPERIMENTS "The goal was to render the plague bacteria far more resistant to antibiotics," he said. Billingslea said Soviet researchers also experimented with combining plague with toxin-producing pathogens, with the aim of making infections even harder to treat. "They took the plague bacteria, and they merged it with a non-dangerous bacteria," Billingslea said. "The goal was to render the plague bacteria far more resistant to antibiotics." According to Alibek's account, researchers also worked on combining plague with toxin-producing pathogens so that treating an infected person with antibiotics could trigger the release of toxins. Billingslea said U.S. officials were not relying solely on Alibek for their understanding of the program and that there were "multiple other sources of information" that made him "very confident in the basics" regarding the disclosures regarding Soviet-era research. "So, this doesn't all derive from Ken Alibek," he insisted when speaking with Fox News Digital. By the time Billingslea was interviewing Alibek in the mid-1990s, he said, Washington had already confronted Moscow over its biological weapons work. " We knew about the plague programs, we knew what they were up to and we knew where the sites were," he said. Among the sites Alibek identified were at least six Soviet Ministry of Health laboratories that had legitimate civilian public health missions while also performing classified work connected to the biological weapons program, according to Billingslea. The Irkutsk institute was among the facilities Alibek identified, but Billingslea cautioned he does not recall the Soviet defector saying that antibiotic-resistant plague or plague chimeras were specifically developed there. That distinction has become particularly important after the unexplained death of a 28-year-old researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute. Russian authorities have said they found no microorganism linked to the woman's professional activities, while the World Health Organization has sought additional information from Moscow about what caused her fatal pneumonia. Billingslea said the pressure for answers — and for Russia to end its offensive biological weapons program — should not come from Washington alone. "It's very, very important that this is not viewed as a U.S.-versus-Russia discussion," he said. "This is a topic of grave concern to the entire international community." He also said that Russia needs to release the genetic sequence of the pathogen that killed the researcher, along with information about contact testing, the timeline of her illness and the institute's biosafety procedures. The genetic sequence could allow outside experts to determine "what it was and whether it was modified," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Billingslea called on countries outside the traditional U.S. alliance system, including Brazil and Mexico, to press Moscow for greater transparency and pointed to a December meeting of parties to the Biological Weapons Convention as an opportunity for countries to confront Russia over the program. "At the December meeting, Russia is going to get grilled," he said. "And they should."

title: France is devouring itself as school riots reveal a crisis far bigger than broken classrooms
description: Student protests in France over crumbling schools expose deep tensions as Jean-Luc Mélenchon's La France Insoumise allegedly exploits the growing unrest.
content: Student protests over crumbling schools despite billions in public spending are fueling a broader crisis in France, and experts warn that the country's mounting financial troubles, President Emmanuel Macron's weakened political center and radical movements are pushing the unrest far beyond its original educational grievances. Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' senior envoy for Europe, told Fox News Digital in an interview from Paris that what began in September with legitimate complaints about school conditions has increasingly been exploited by political forces seeking confrontation with the state. "Overall, I'd say the anger is real, but the violence, I would say, is organized," she said, adding that destroying schools would do nothing to improve the education system. FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION Seventy-two percent of education expenditures went toward salaries, social contributions and pensions for teaching and non-teaching personnel, while just 8.5% went toward investment, including infrastructure and equipment. The figures cover the entire education system, not just high schools, according to France's Education Ministry's 2026 statistical overview. Harvey Feigenbaum, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University and an expert on French politics, told Fox News Digital that France's underlying problem is a government caught between expensive social commitments, sluggish economic growth and mounting pressure to cut spending. "France is in deep debt. It wants to cut its expenses," Feigenbaum said, explaining that years of financial pressure and neglected school facilities have fueled frustration among students. The scale of the financial predicament is striking. According to Eurostat, French public debt stood at 117.6% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, the third-highest ratio in the European Union, behind Greece and Italy. Reuters reported Oct. 8 that rising borrowing costs and investor concerns have severely limited the government's ability to resolve unrest through additional spending, a strategy employed during previous waves of French protests. The financial squeeze has collided with an increasingly fragmented political system, creating opportunities for parties at both ends of the political spectrum to capitalize on public dissatisfaction. FRENCH SCHOOL RIOTS DEEPEN AS EXPERTS POINT TO FAR-LEFT ALLIANCE FUELING ‘BROADER CONFRONTATION’ Macron's political center collapses For Feigenbaum, the long-term roots of the crisis lie in Macron's political legacy. When Macron won the presidency in 2017, he promised to move beyond France's traditional left-right divide, combining policies from both sides into a new centrist political movement. But Feigenbaum argues that the strategy produced an unintended consequence, weakening France's established moderate parties without creating a durable governing coalition to replace them. "What he ended up doing was attracting the moderate voters from the parties of the moderate left and the parties from the moderate right, and essentially destroyed those parties," Feigenbaum said. He argued that the collapse of the traditional political center helped create space for more ideologically polarized movements. "Macron is a smart man, but he's a terrible politician," the professor added. Macron's controversial pension reforms illustrate the difficulty of persuading French voters to accept reductions in longstanding public benefits, Feigenbaum argued. Those efforts triggered widespread protests, while implementation of the 2023 retirement changes has since been suspended until 2028. The situation became especially difficult after Macron called snap parliamentary elections in 2024, producing a deeply divided National Assembly without a governing majority. "Even if the government wanted to do something coherent, they simply don't have the votes to do it," Feigenbaum said. That paralysis has left Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu handling the immediate unrest while Macron faces questions about the stability of the political system he helped reshape. FRENCH PM REJECTS POLICE BRUTALITY CLAIMS AFTER TEENS SEVERELY INJURED IN PROTESTS: 'ACCIDENTS HAPPEN' Why are France's schools struggling despite billions in spending? The protests began in the Paris suburbs in September amid complaints about overcrowded classrooms, inadequate heating and cooling, aging buildings and teachers who were not replaced when absent. Rodan-Benzaquen said the anger reflected years of educational instability, frequent ministerial changes and reforms that have failed to resolve persistent school problems. She also pointed to a broader sense of anxiety among young people about their economic future, artificial intelligence, climate change and international conflicts. According to the OECD's September 2026 Education at a Glance report, France spent $16,674 in funding per student in general upper secondary education in 2023, compared with an OECD average of $12,421, adjusted for purchasing power. Yet teachers and students continue to complain about basic shortages. Responsibility for public high school buildings and equipment falls to regional authorities, while the national government oversees much of the education system, including teacher staffing. Feigenbaum said France's centralized education structure makes national leaders the focus of public anger when schools fail to deliver. The pressure has already forced a concession. Reuters reported Friday that Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced an emergency plan to deploy 3,000 qualified educators to particularly affected schools, costing several dozen million euros. Student unions welcomed the measure as an initial victory but pledged to continue demonstrating. The spending figures raise broader questions about whether France's financial and political priorities have left sufficient resources for maintaining school infrastructure and meeting students' needs. They do not, however, establish that teachers' unions or other organized constituencies have improperly diverted funding. TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT How the far left entered the unrest As the demonstrations expanded, the involvement of France's hard-left La France Insoumise party, known as LFI, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, became an increasingly contentious issue. Reuters reported Oct. 1 that French intelligence agencies had told a government crisis meeting that LFI and affiliated activists played a role in fomenting the unrest. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez also cited agitators moving between schools to encourage violence. LFI has denied responsibility and accused authorities of aggravating tensions through their response. Rodan-Benzaquen said far-left movements were capitalizing on students' frustration. "There is an obvious instrumentalization, obvious manipulation," she said, arguing that activists were seeking to push some protesters toward violence. She linked the unrest to what she described as Mélenchon's broader political strategy ahead of France's 2027 presidential election. "His idea is that, on the one hand, he will scare voters on the right and on the far right, who will then go to vote for the far right, and, on the other hand, he would mobilize his own camp," she said. Rodan-Benzaquen argued that intensifying political confrontation could help Mélenchon consolidate his support among younger voters and immigrant communities, while portraying the far right as an increasingly serious threat. She described it as a calculated political strategy rather than a spontaneous response to students' concerns. The involvement of LFI politicians has been documented by French media, although there is disagreement over whether the party helped initiate the demonstrations or became involved after the protests began. An Oct. 2 investigation by Le Monde examined a police intelligence assessment describing radical left activity around schools in Seine-Saint-Denis but questioned whether the evidence established that the movement itself was politically orchestrated. Feigenbaum offered a more cautious interpretation, describing some of the violent perpetrators as fringe provocateurs who exploit broader demonstrations without necessarily directing them. "They're not being organized by some, you know, some mastermind at the national level, at least as far as anyone knows," he said. FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE Islamist influence or political solidarity? The demonstrations have also raised questions about whether Islamist groups and pro-Palestinian activists are seeking to use the unrest to advance broader ideological causes. Rodan-Benzaquen argued that Mélenchon's emphasis on Gaza and the Palestinian cause has helped bring together political constituencies that might otherwise have little in common. "It's sort of the idea of sort of an intersection of different movements where they manage to bring together the different groups, the far left, Islamist movements, pro-Palestinian activists," she said. She pointed to Palestinian flags appearing during the demonstrations as an indication of how the movement has expanded beyond its original educational demands. The FDD expert argued that Islamist elements were attempting to capitalize on the turmoil, although she cautioned against reducing the entire crisis to immigration or religion. "But this goes far beyond the issue of immigration. It goes far beyond the issue of Islamism. It goes far beyond the issue of Islam," she said. EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT A crisis France cannot simply spend its way out of The government's latest concessions have not ended the protests. According to Reuters on Friday, 141 schools remained closed while students continued demanding broader reforms. Nearly 10% of teaching hours in French public high schools remained unstaffed. For Rodan-Benzaquen, one of the greatest dangers is that the demonstrations reflect a society increasingly divided into competing political realities. She described how her 17-year-old son created separate left-wing and right-wing Instagram accounts and encountered radically different portrayals of the same unrest, one emphasizing police violence and the other violence by protesters. "Now, if you live in two drastically different realities, it is very complicated to come to any form of dialog and end agreement," she said. Her warning extends beyond France's current protests. "We are in an extremely polarized environment," Rodan-Benzaquen said, noting that social media can deepen divisions and allow confrontations to escalate rapidly. Feigenbaum sees an additional structural danger of a government burdened by accumulated financial obligations and deprived of the political consensus needed to reform them. The result is a country spending heavily to sustain its public institutions while struggling to deliver the services citizens expect and a political system increasingly consumed by conflict over how to fix them. title: Ohio dog park shooting over Trump argument could end with two self-defense claims or none: legal expert
description: Both men in the Ohio dog park shootout over Donald Trump could claim self-defense or neither could, a legal expert says, creating a rare puzzle.
content: A shootout sparked by an argument over President Donald Trump at an Ohio dog park could end with a jury finding that both men acted in self-defense or that neither did, a legal expert told Fox News Digital. Emmanuel "Mike" Mathews, 81, was charged with felonious assault for shooting David Mattai, 55, April 21 at Centerville Mills Park in Bainbridge Township, according to authorities. Mathews has pleaded not guilty. Case Western Reserve University law professor Michael Benza said, under Ohio law, defendants lose the right to claim self-defense if they helped ignite the confrontation that led to the shooting. VIDEO SHOWS MOMENTS BEFORE ARMY VETERAN WAS FATALLY SHOT IN WALMART PARKING LOT DISPUTE Since both men allegedly took part in the escalation, he said, the case presents a unique legal puzzle. "They could both be found at fault, which means neither of them would get self-defense," Benza told Fox News Digital. Since self-defense relies heavily on subjective fear and perceived danger, Benza said, "It's also possible both get self-defense." Competing accounts Mathews' attorney, Ian Friedman, said the encounter began as an argument, which turned physical in the park before ending in gunfire in the park’s parking lot. "Mr. Mathews was attempting to leave," Friedman told Fox News Digital. "He was attempting to keep himself safe." Friedman said it started when Mattai, who overheard Mathews talking to an eyewitness about Trump, disagreed with Mathews' view that Trump is one of the country's greatest presidents. Bainbridge Township Patrolman Friedrich Kaufmann testified at Mathews’ May 5 preliminary hearing in Chardon Municipal Court that, after that initial argument, Mattai drove away, then returned to the park about five minutes later. FLORIDA MEN WIELDING HATCHET AND MACHETE CLASH IN PUBLIX PARKING LOT, POLICE SAY Mathews was still sitting at a picnic table with his dog when Mattai returned. Mathews gathered his belongings and began walking toward his vehicle, but after crossing to the other side of a park fence, an exchange of insults between the pair caused a physical confrontation. GUN-WIELDING COUPLE IN VIRAL BLM STANDOFF GOT FIREPOWER — AND 'A VOICE' — BACK AFTER LEGAL SAGA Friedman said Mattai grabbed Mathews by the hair and pulled him into the fence. Mathews also reported being headbutted. Mattai denied the headbutt allegation, but Friedman said an injury below Mathews' eye supports that account. After the physical altercation, both men retreated toward their vehicles after witness Jamie Jedlinsky, 70, reportedly stepped in to defuse the situation. OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO Mathews got into his vehicle and allegedly placed a .45-caliber gun on his dashboard, when Mattai, who stood in the parking area after loading his dog in his vehicle, saw the weapon. The men allegedly exchanged words before Mathews fired once. Mattai retrieved a 9 mm Taurus handgun from inside his Hyundai, then fired six shots "almost contemporaneously" near Mathews' head and body, according to Friedman. "We believe that Mattai was turning to retrieve his gun and coming back to aim at Mathews when the bullet struck the lower right portion of his back," Friedman added. Mathews was not injured in the gunfire exchange, but Mattai's return fire hit Mathews' vehicle at least four times. Mattai previously told The New York Times he did not physically touch Mathews after seeing Mathews’ weapon and fired back in fear of his own safety. Mattai’s wife, Sally Mattai, told the Times her husband almost died after suffering a severe gunshot wound to his lower back that damaged his spine and required two separate emergency surgeries. Mattai's attorney, Ryan Fisher, said he believes public opinions have convoluted the case and created confusion. "There are a great deal of differing opinions of what went on in the dog park that day," Fisher told Fox News Digital. Fisher's response did not address the defense's claims about the gun or the timing of the shots. Geauga County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Mattai Aug. 5. He’s facing misdemeanor charges of assault and disorderly conduct. 'You can't be the first one to draw the gun' Benza said introducing a gun changes the legal footing of a physical scuffle, but he emphasized that the order of events greatly matter. "You go from, OK, we're hitting each other. ... Physically, punches are being thrown. Now you've pulled a weapon. You have now escalated this fight, which then justifies me escalating my response by then pulling my own gun and defending myself," he said. "But you can't be the first one to draw the gun." Ohio law removes the duty to retreat when someone is lawfully in a location. Friedman said that since Mathews was legally allowed to be at the park, he had no obligation to flee. "He certainly had no duty to retreat," Friedman said. "Had he done anything different from what he did do in those seconds, he may not be here to talk about it today." Political challenges Friedman said, although the argument began over politics, his client acted out of fear for his safety, not political retaliation. "This was never about a political dispute for Mr. Mathews," he said. Benza, however, said the county’s politics could potentially complicate seating a jury, regardless of why the incident happened. "In Geauga County, where this happened, it is a very Republican-dominated county," Benza said. "The one defendant may be concerned that he will end up with jurors who are very pro-Republican or pro-Trump, which would create his concerns about a fair jury. "The other defendant may want a pro-Trump jury because they would be so, well, he got what he deserved or something to that effect." SEND US A TIP The case may come down to a jury deciding whether Mathews had a genuine, reasonable fear for his life when he was accused of shooting Mattai. GOT A TIP? Friedman predicted the evidence would show Mathews should never have been arrested, while Fisher said the case is "going to have to be flushed out by the jury in the upcoming trial." Mathews’ trial is scheduled to begin Feb. 16 at the Geauga County Court of Common Pleas. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL If convicted, he could face a minimum sentence of five years and a maximum potential sentence of 15 years in an Ohio state prison due to combined penalties of a second-degree felony assault charge and a mandatory gun specification. He told the Times he is "willing to plead guilty or no contest" if it means no jail time.

title: Comedians revolt against SiriusXM as 'middle class of comedy' fights corporate royalty cuts
description: SiriusXM’s Raw Dog rebrand cut 66% of its comedian roster, stripping vital royalty income from working stand-up. Rich Vos and top comics are pushing back against corporate cuts.
content: A programming change at SiriusXM has drawn criticism from comedians after the satellite radio company removed hundreds of working stand-up comedians from its comedy channel, cutting off a source of royalty income for affected performers. After SiriusXM replaced its Channel 99, Raw Dog Comedy, in April with comedian Sebastian Maniscalco’s new channel, Sebastian Maniscalco's Comedy Radio, veteran stand-up comedians began criticizing the move, warning it threatens an important source of income for independent comedians. According to the comedy industry advocacy group Stand Up for Stand Up, the channel's active roster had shrunk 66%, from 812 featured comedians in April to 275 by September, with more than 75% of plays going to the top 50 comedians. COMEDY STARS LASH OUT AT SEBASTIAN MANISCALCO OVER SIRIUSXM SHAKE-UP "Everything in life breaks down to money — numbers and money. That's what it breaks down to," comedian Rich Vos, who has performed stand-up for 40 years, told Fox News Digital. Vos was among the comedians who no longer received airplay on the channel, having ranked among the 20 most-played comedians on Channel 99 before the rebrand, according to Stand Up for Stand Up. Although Vos noted that his decades-long career and club relationships keep him busy, he said he decided to speak out because stand-up comedians lack a labor union. "I had a great run with Sirius. I appreciate how much they played me, for how long they played me and, you know, but there's a lot of comics that aren't doing as well as I do," Vos said. "I've been around for over 40 years. So, there's comics that have been doing it five, 10 years, and it's tougher for them. These are the comics that are really getting hurt by this." Comedians and industry advocates say the programming change has eliminated a reliable source of royalty income for many performers, including those still establishing their careers. Comedians can earn royalties when their recorded performances air on satellite radio, typically around $15 a play. But those removed from the rotation no longer receive payments from those broadcasts. WHITE HOUSE URGES SITCOM PRODUCER CHUCK LORRE TO SEEK 'PSYCHIATRIC HELP' AFTER HE TARGETED TRUMP, FIRST LADY According to Stand Up for Stand Up, the rebrand has hurt the "middle class of comedy," which the group describes as working comedians who earn their living performing but are not household names and often live paycheck to paycheck. The decision has drawn criticism from several prominent comedians, including Patton Oswalt and Michelle Wolf, who have called on Maniscalco to help restore airplay for affected performers. "The fact that you and I still get to tour and still get to work and still get to be as funny as we are is because comedy right now is so dynamic and has so many new, young voices that are coming up. But 500 of them have been booted off of Sirius," Oswalt said in an Instagram video addressed to Maniscalco. "I know you didn't mean to do anything bad by doing it. You can easily reverse this decision. Get those young comedians back on the Sirius channel. Let them get those checks. Let them keep working." The new lineup features established comedians, including Chris Rock, Jim Gaffigan, Jamie Foxx, Whitney Cummings and Kevin Hart, while also regularly airing recordings from late comedians like Joan Rivers and Bob Hope. CHRIS ROCK SHREDS 'WOKE 1.0' ERA, COMPARES MODERN OUTRAGE TO SALEM WITCH HUNTS SiriusXM said its decision to discontinue Raw Comedy was driven by the channel's "underperformance" and was made before Maniscalco joined the lineup. "We have been listening to comedians speak out this week and want to clarify that our decision to end Raw Comedy was due to the channel’s underperformance and came prior to Sebastian joining the SiriusXM lineup," the company said in a statement. "While the challenges facing working comedians are bigger than any one person or decision, we remain committed, as we have for more than two decades, to making SiriusXM a place where comedians at every stage of their careers can be heard."Fox News Digital reached out to Maniscalco for comment and was directed to the above statement by SiriusXM. Vos questioned SiriusXM's explanation for ending Raw Comedy. "I don't know what underperformance [means]. Obviously, that means not enough people are listening to it," Vos told Fox News Digital. "I just know funny is funny, and if that's your channel is to play funny, then maybe your marketing strategy is wrong. ... But funny's funny, and that's basically what a comedy channel is about, being funny." TURNING POINT USA TURNS THE TABLES ON 'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' AFTER LATE-NIGHT SKETCH MOCKS CAMPUS RECRUITERS Maniscalco has also faced criticism over the programming changes. In an Instagram video posted Wednesday, he asked fellow comedians for patience as he works to expand the channel's lineup. "This goes out to all my fellow comedians. I want to let you know that I heard you, I support you, I love you. I know how hard the grind is. Believe me, I've been there," he said, before adding that he had "nothing to do with removing Raw Comedy from SiriusXM." Maniscalco said he plans to work with SiriusXM to feature a wider range of comedians, from emerging performers to established acts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I just ask that you give me a little time, guys. I just got here, and I need a little time to build out the channel. So, I just want to let you know that I heard you, and just give me some time and be patient, and I think you'll like the result. God bless everybody," he added. In a statement to Fox News Digital earlier this week, SiriusXM said, "SiriusXM works together with our creative partners to program the best possible experience for our listeners. "The launch of Sebastian Maniscalco’s Comedy Radio introduced a new creative direction and a regularly evolving programming mix for the channel, and SiriusXM continues to invest in comedians more than any other audio platform to deliver a wide range of comedy offerings across our channels." Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

title: You’d never guess the crazy things cash welfare paid for; Nebraska is shutting that down
description: Nebraska and Florida are blocking cash welfare spending on alcohol, porn, tattoos and more, following Trump administration guidance on TANF reform.
content: Beer. Liquor. Cigarettes. Porn. This isn’t just a list of things that can be bad for you. This is a list of things that Americans are buying with cash welfare, thanks to a massive loophole in federal law. Thankfully, states are finally taking action to prevent this abuse and protect taxpayers with strong guidance from the Trump administration. It’s an overlooked — but important — new front in the ongoing War on Fraud. DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS The latest state to close this loophole is Nebraska. On Oct. 9, Republican Gov. Jim Pillen directed the state to stop recipients of cash welfare from spending money on items like tobacco, porn, tattoos, psychic and fortune-telling services, luxury watches and much more. Going forward, if you receive money under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program in Nebraska, you cannot spend the money on things the taxpayer shouldn’t be funding in the first place. Americans may be forgiven for wondering why people in Nebraska — or anywhere else — were ever able to buy these things with cash welfare. After all, most people assume that government assistance is only supposed to fund specific things that families need. Cash welfare, in particular, is explicitly designed to help low-income families "achieve economic security and stability." So, how did cigarettes and smut enter the picture? PRO-LIFE VS SOCIALISM: GOP LAWMAKERS DIVIDED OVER CONTROVERSIAL GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAMS It’s true that federal rules stop you from spending cash welfare at places like liquor stores. But you can still buy alcohol at plenty of other places, such as grocery stores. Similarly, you can’t spend cash welfare at casinos or strip clubs, but you can still gamble or buy pornography in plenty of other places. This loophole has existed for roughly 30 years, since TANF began, and it’s so large, it’s laughable. Did lawmakers not realize that alcohol isn’t just sold at the corner store? Do our nation’s leaders not know that "adult entertainment" is available outside of seedy clubs? WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE These are far from the only non-essential — and deeply questionable — things that cash welfare is funding. Taxpayers are also able to pay for things like concert tickets, streaming subscriptions, tattoos and luxury services like spa treatments. It’s enough to make you wonder: When Congress created cash welfare, did it put any meaningful restrictions on how the money could be used? Unfortunately, closing this loophole in one fell swoop would require another act of Congress. But, thankfully, the Trump administration has issued guidance explaining how states can close this loophole, one by one. States can’t change federal requirements for cash welfare. But they can ask the federal government to approve stronger requirements on a state-by-state basis, which explains the sudden and welcome progress. Before Nebraska, Florida took the first meaningful action to stop this abuse. In August, Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis announced that he was blocking cash welfare from being spent on tobacco products, drugs, porn, tattoos, video games, fortune-telling services and a slew of other obviously non-essential goods and services. The Trump administration quickly approved the Florida plan, which DeSantis rightly said will protect "Floridians who genuinely need assistance" while also guarding taxpayers from fraud and abuse. What are other state leaders waiting for? CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION It’s shocking that any state has allowed such blatant abuse of the taxpayer’s generosity for so long. Perhaps they’ve been waiting for Congress to act, but given the dysfunction in D.C., that was always a long shot. Regardless, now is the time for governors to act. The easiest thing to do is to follow Florida and Nebraska’s lead and simply amend their state plans for cash welfare. Governors could also work with state lawmakers if they want to ensure more permanent reforms, while holding retailers accountable for circumventing restrictions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bottom line: Every state must close this cash welfare loophole. No one should be using the taxpayer’s money to buy pre-mixed cocktails and porn. title: Workers erupt over DC plan to bring robotaxis to city streets: ‘This is bulls---’
description: Protesters rallied outside D.C.'s John Wilson Building as council members weighed legislation to allow Waymo robotaxis on Washington streets.
content: A new proposal that could bring driverless rideshare vehicles to the streets of the nation’s capital is causing an uproar among union workers, drivers and religious leaders who fear the technology could eliminate jobs. Protesters gathered outside the John Wilson Building as D.C. council members met to discuss legislation that would allow Waymo and other autonomous vehicle operators to offer commercial rides in Washington, D.C. The protesters urged the council to reject the legislation, arguing that an influx of robotaxis would displace rideshare drivers. "We came out here today strongly because we feel that these robotaxis will put people out of work," one protester told Fox News Digital. "And people need jobs." TERRIFIED PASSENGERS FILM WAYMO AUTONOMOUS VEHICLE DRIVING INTO LIVE FIREWORKS IN SAN FRANCISCO "I'm against robotaxis because it takes away from the community. It takes away from their jobs. It takes away food from their table," Frederick from Virginia said. "People need jobs to be able to support their family." "It's bulls---," Sabrina from Washington, D.C., said. "Let's not bring robots taking my neighbor's jobs. My folks that drive for a living, let's just not take their jobs." Another person at the protest acknowledged that autonomous vehicles could eliminate some driving jobs but argued the city should "take the offensive" by shortening the workweek without cutting pay and expanding employment elsewhere. "We should take the offensive on job issues," Michael from Washington, D.C., said. "We should shorten the workweek without a loss in pay. So, we'll create more jobs in public transportation, in hospitals, in service industries. So, we actually maybe will lose some jobs to taxi drivers, but we'll create better paying jobs." The Autonomous Vehicle Deployment Authorization Amendment Act of 2026 introduced by Councilmember Charles Allen in May would create a program for commercial autonomous vehicles in D.C. that would be run by the District Department of Transportation. TESLA ROBOTAXI MIAMI LAUNCH COMES WITH LIMITS Waymo says its latest safety data, covering more than 270 million miles of autonomous driving, shows its vehicles were involved in 82% fewer injury-causing crashes and 95% fewer crashes involving serious injuries or worse compared with human driver benchmarks in the same operating areas. Supporters of robotaxis have also pointed to the potential for lower fares without a human driver, although current comparisons have found Waymo's prices can vary widely and are not consistently cheaper than traditional rideshare services like Uber and Lyft. Protesters claimed that while prices may be lower as the driverless vehicles roll out, the rates will eventually spike. "That's just something just to … get our antennas up and have us saying, ‘Yeah, ooh, we're gonna get cheaper rides,’" Sabrina said. "It might be cheap for the trial periods, and then, all of a sudden, we'll be paying $50. So, no, I don't believe that. That's just some crap just to get people engaged with the Waymo." "They seem the same price to me," Helen from Maryland said. "They're in other cities, and it seems like not much of a difference in the pricing." ZOOX ROBOTAXI REDESIGN BRINGS BIG RIDER UPGRADES The proposed regulatory framework, which could bring robotaxis to the city by 2028, would initially limit operators to 200 vehicles. Companies seeking commercial permits would have to demonstrate at least 180 days and 250,000 miles of autonomous vehicle testing in the District and submit plans aimed at reducing disparities in service availability and wait times across the city's eight wards. There was a public hearing on the bill in July, but no vote has been scheduled. The bill would have to be approved by the entire council before self-driving cars start to hit the city’s streets. "A worker should be at the table," Metropolitan Washington Council, AFL-CIO President Samuel Epps told Fox News Digital at the protest. "We shouldn't rush this." title: Liberal hot spot residents can’t agree on what socialism means as far-left movement gains steam
description: A Gallup poll shows 43% of Americans view socialism positively, but festivalgoers in Takoma Park hesitated when asked about surrendering property.
content: Americans can't seem to get on the same page when it comes to what defines socialism even though new polling shows the movement's favorability is at an all-time high. Whether far-left factions are able to rally around the label could come down to understanding its principles. Fox News Digital took to the streets of a Maryland liberal hot spot, Takoma Park, for its annual street festival to talk with attendees about their definitions of socialism and how far they would be willing to go to embrace its ideals. LIBERAL HAVEN FESTIVALGOERS WEIGH GOVERNMENT SEIZURE OF THEIR HOMES: 'I'D BE SO GAME' "The fact is that there's no … one answer," Nina Gilden Seavey said when asked to define socialism. "Just the idea of, like, you've been paying all these things to set up these programs, and then you're actually giving them to the people," Jaw Blake said, describing his view of the political movement. "It's not a special group that gets to have them. It's just available." Jenny Sniderman had a more direct answer, claiming that "public libraries, the police department, the fire department, all our public services, utilities," are all part of what makes up socialism. A September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans have a positive image of socialism, the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010. But the survey asks respondents their image of socialism without providing a definition of the ideology or asking whether they would actually support adopting it in the U.S. The same festivalgoers were pressed on socialism as an economic system, questioning their favorability of collective ownership. They shared some skepticism when Fox News Digital asked whether they would personally surrender their private property to government or collective control. "Do I want to give up my private property? Of course, I don't want to give up my private property," Sniderman said. "Are they going to reimburse me fairly? That would be helpful in making my choice." "I don't know that I would necessarily love it," Blake said. "But, I mean, if it was something that was beneficial, I'd at least consider it. DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY' "Nobody wants what they have to be taken away from them," he continued. "But there is something to be said about … you can set up things so that they're available for everybody." "I think the government is not the greatest steward … of assets," Seavey said. "It's not to say that capitalism is somehow without flaw, but the fact is that there is an idealism that can come from thinking, 'Oh, if we had some more centrality, if … there was some kind of uber organization in charge of reallocation.'" Documentary filmmaker and self-described historian Seavey also questioned the idea of government control over private assets but argued that the growing democratic socialist movement in the U.S. should not be confused with traditional socialism. "This is not socialism. This is democratic socialism. It's different. There's socialism, there's communism, there are all kinds of 'isms.' Democratic socialism is essentially what we have a growing movement in this country," Seavey said. "Socialism is where there is a massive redistribution of wealth. We are not having redistribution of wealth in this country." But the Democratic Socialists of America, the largest socialist organization in the U.S., advocates redistributing wealth from wealthy individuals and corporations to workers and lower-income Americans. The DSA also calls for a public stake in major corporations and essential industries rather than private ownership. THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE; YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM The differing interpretations among festivalgoers reflect a broader debate over what socialism means in America, one that has taken on new political significance as socialist candidates gain ground within the Democratic Party heading into midterm elections. In a 2018 survey asking Americans to define socialism in their own words, just 17% described it in terms of government ownership or control of businesses or the means of production. Another 23% associated it with equality, while 10% pointed to social benefits and services. Nearly a quarter could not provide an answer. Seavey argued that political labels themselves have distorted the conversation. "Let's think about it differently, and let's take away these ridiculous stigmas that have to do with these crazy labels that we have allowed the right wing to foment onto the rest of America," Seavey said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But as socialist-aligned candidates compete for office, the growing movement raises a question that favorable polling alone cannot answer of whether voters are embracing its promises on affordability and equality or also support its broader proposals for economic ownership and control.

title: Trump rallies New York crowd for Republican Bruce Blakeman's bid to replace Gov Kathy Hochul
description: President Donald Trump rallied Syracuse supporters behind Bruce Blakeman's bid to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, promising tax cuts and cheaper energy for New York families.
content: President Donald Trump returned to his home state of New York on Friday night, showcasing America's "New Golden Age" and promising to help Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman flip the Empire State red as the GOP makes its final push toward November's midterm elections. Trump rallied supporters in Syracuse with a sweeping celebration of his administration's economic and immigration agenda, pledging to help New Yorkers secure lower taxes, cheaper energy and safer streets by electing Republicans up and down the ballot. "We're in the Golden Age of America," Trump told the crowd, urging supporters to deliver the same enthusiasm that powered his presidential campaigns. TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG "Please pretend I'm on the freaking ballot," Trump urged. "And in a really, in a certain way, I am on the ballot because they can take away everything that we, that we got." The president took Blakeman's challenge to Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul as the centerpiece of the rally, promising direct support from Washington if elected. "[Blakeman will] save this state. He'll turn the state around, and I'll help him from the White House," Trump said. "I'll be helping him for governor." Trump blasted Hochul over New York's taxes, utility bills and public safety, arguing that Blakeman could unleash the state's economic potential by embracing domestic energy production and cutting costs for families. DEBRA MESSING SAYS COST OF LIVING, SUBWAY VIOLENCE PUSHED HER TO BACK TRUMP-ENDORSED REPUBLICAN The president also hailed his administration's economic agenda as proof of what Trump described as a remarkable national turnaround. He singled out Micron's planned $100 billion semiconductor complex in central New York, a project the company says is expected to generate 50,000 jobs across the state, including 9,000 directly with Micron. "This will soon be the home to the largest semiconductor manufacturing facility ever built in the Western Hemisphere," Trump said. Blakeman joined Trump onstage and echoed the president's message of a Republican resurgence, promising to cut taxes and utility bills, focus on public safety and make New York more attractive to both businesses and families. "We have to create good jobs, good benefits to keep our young people here," Blakeman said. "We gotta look at business not as the enemy, but as a partner." Trump also threw his support behind Republican congressional candidates Kailee Buller, who is challenging Democrat Rep. John Mannion in New York's 22nd District, and Anthony Constantino, who is running for the state's open 21st District seat, pledging to help Republicans compete for both seats. The rally also notably featured a brief but memorable on-stage appearance by legendary former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson, whom Trump invited up before the crowd. "I'm just happy to be up here with my president, President Trump," Tyson said. "And there's no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn't for a president like Donald Trump. Thank you. Thank you very much." Trump responded with a laugh, recalling Tyson's notorious reputation. "I don't want to fight him," Trump joked, before complimenting the former champion. "You look good. Mike. What the h--- are you doing?" title: Gov Kathy Hochul signs New York onto Trump's school choice program despite teachers union opposition
description: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul joined President Donald Trump's Education Freedom Tax Credit despite fierce opposition from teachers unions and a petition to reject it.
content: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Friday signed on to join President Donald Trump’s school choice program despite opposition from teachers unions. "Every parent wants their child to have a great education and the best possible chance to succeed. That’s what guides my decisions as governor," Hochul announced Friday. "New York’s public schools are the backbone of communities across this state," she added. "That’s why I’ve made historic investments in public education, increasing school funding by more than $10 billion and fully funding Foundation Aid for the first time." GOV HOCHUL'S PLAN TO OPT NEW YORK INTO FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DRAWS UNION OPPOSITION Despite Hochul's stated intention to participate, major labor groups and teachers unions remain staunchly opposed. A coalition of teachers unions and other public school advocates launched a petition demanding that Hochul reject the program. "Gov. Hochul plans to opt New York in starting in 2027. But most New Yorkers haven’t even heard of this program or know how it will affect New York," the petition states. "Tax dollars would help pay private tuition for families who never used public schools." Sydney Altfield, Scholarships for All founder and Teach Coalition CEO, told Fox News Digital, "This is a tremendous day for New Yorkers. Millions of children across our state will now have access to scholarships that can help pay for tutoring, after-school programs and other educational needs. "Gov. Hochul has kept her promise to New York families, helping put money back into the pockets of hardworking parents while expanding educational opportunities for children across the state." PRO-TRUMP GROUP LEADS NEW COALITION TO UNDERCUT TEACHERS UNIONS Hochul’s announcement came after the Department of the Treasury and the IRS issued proposed regulations Oct. 1 to implement the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit (FSTC) program, paving the way for America's first nationwide school choice framework. The initiative, also referred to as the Education Freedom Tax Credit, allows individual taxpayers to receive up to a $1,700 dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for donations made to non-profit scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs). However, state governors must formally opt into the program for their residents and local educational organizations to participate and receive the funds. The IRS recently reported that more than half of U.S. states have already signed up to participate. Burke noted that "competitive pressure" will ultimately force blue states to capture the influx of private donations. Education Secretary Linda McMahon previously noted that some Democratic leaders have resisted the federal scholarship program simply because "it’s a Trump measure." Democratic governors who have traditionally opposed school choice initiatives will face mounting competitive pressure to join Trump's program as states weigh whether to participate and Hochul moves to formally opt in, a top Department of Education official told Fox News Digital. Kentucky has since formally joined the federal program after the state legislature overrode Gov. Andy Beshear's veto of opt-in legislation. Unlike traditional voucher programs that draw directly from municipal or state public education funds, tax credit scholarships allow taxpayers to redirect a portion of their federal tax liability toward non-profit funding for student scholarships. The federal framework leaves the opt-in decision to state governors, enabling local families to access federally incentivized scholarship dollars. "I’ve been clear from the start that New York would participate in the federal scholarship tax credit program if, and only if, all schools and students, including those in our public schools, could benefit," Hochul said. "After a careful review of the federal regulations, we believe this program has the potential to bring millions of additional dollars to New York students and families without taking a single dollar from public schools or our state or local budgets. "I’m not going to leave money on the table when it could help our kids," she added. "That’s why I have also been directly engaging with business leaders who have committed to use this program to support public school students and their academic needs. "I look forward to working with education leaders across the state to make sure these resources reach students in every community. My commitment to public education has not changed, and it never will." MORE THAN 400K NEW YORK CITY CHILDREN ENROLLED IN FAILING PUBLIC SCHOOLS: REPORT For decades, school choice initiatives have remained a third-rail issue for many Democrats, who contend that choice models weaken public school systems and undermine labor unions. However, growing parent demand for alternative education options — including charter schools, private schooling and homeschooling after the COVID-19 pandemic — has pushed several prominent Democrats to reevaluate their positions. title: James Talarico resurfaces after extended absence as his campaign pushes back

content: Texas Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico reappeared on the campaign trail Friday after a nearly two-week absence, ending days of speculation and criticism from political opponents regarding his whereabouts. title: Former Obama advisor tells divided Maine Democrats to 'get over your s---' and win the race
description: Former Obama strategists urge Maine Democrats to unite behind Troy Jackson, warning internal party feuds could cost them a critical Senate seat.
content: Former aides to President Barack Obama discussed divisions among Maine Democrats over the party's troubled U.S. Senate race against incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins, with a warning to Democrats to "get over your s---." Maine's Senate race has drawn national attention after Democrats replaced their initial candidate, Graham Platner, due to sexual assault allegations against him. His replacement, Troy Jackson, has faced controversies of his own. Even so, Obama, the former boss of the "Pod Save America" hosts, recently released an endorsement video urging Maine voters not to sit out the election. The hosts discussed why Obama might have chosen that message. Former Obama strategist Dan Pfeiffer told his co-hosts that "it is true, and we have — this has been sort of mysterious to both of us — that there are a significant number of people in Maine who seem not to like Troy Jackson, including some Democrats." DEM WHO ABANDONED PLATNER AFTER SEX ASSAULT CLAIM NOW SCRAMBLES FOR HIS VOTERS "Yeah," former Obama speechwriter Jon Favreau agreed. "That’s my biggest worry." Pfeiffer offered his assessment of the feuds between Democrats, saying, "And, so I think a little whether there are people who supported Platner who didn't like Platner being gone or the process by which we got here, or people who were supporting Mills who don't like any of this and Mills and Jackson do not like each other. And as of, like, two weeks ago, Mills had not endorsed Jackson and Jackson had not asked for the endorsement. "Everyone get over your s---, and let's try to win this race. "I think there is some sense or fear, maybe, that some of the people who are not enthusiastic about Jackson for some reason because of how this process played out may sit out and so just like ‘get in here, get in the fight,’" Pfeiffer added of Obama’s video. "I don't know if that's a real concern or not, but if I was trying to find a reason why that line would be in there, that would be it." "Yeah, I would say to all the Maine Democrats out there, I know it's been a rough one, but look to Michigan," Favreau said. "They had an extremely divisive primary, and you had Gretchen Whitmer … out there with Abdul [El-Sayed] this week. "Haley Stevens has been saying great things," he continued, noting Democrats in Michigan have been coming together after initially being divided. "And I really wish — I do think that Troy Jackson would probably benefit from more Maine Democrats and national Democrats kind of, you know, because, like, Maine is the kind of state that, again, it wants to go Democratic," Favreau added. "They want — those voters want a Democratic Senate. That's what they're telling. "Even The New York Times poll that showed Collins ahead, you had people — most people — wanting a Democratic Senate," he said. "So, like, I feel like the Democrats there just have to be reminded that, like, this is our guy, and this is our ticket to a Democratic Senate and not a Republican Senate." title: Trump gives raw reaction after finding out about Mike Ditka's death: 'A tough cookie'
description: Trump called Mike Ditka "a tough cookie" and "a winner" after learning of the Hall of Fame Chicago Bears coach's death on the South Lawn Friday.
content: President Donald Trump was caught by surprise on the South Lawn before heading to Syracuse on Friday. Before making the trip north with Mike Tyson and New York Yankees president Randy Levine, the press pool informed Trump that famed Chicago Bears head coach Mike Ditka had died. The news issued a raw reaction from the president. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "Oh, he did? He was a great guy. He was with me all the way. He was tough," Trump said. "Mike Ditka — that's a sad one." "He was great. He was a big supporter of mine, and he was a winner. He was a tough cookie." Ditka supported Trump ahead of the 2016 election. Ditka coached the famous 1985 Bears that rampaged through the NFL with an 18-1 record, losing only to the Miami Dolphins, and then going on to a Super Bowl title. The death of one of the NFL's greats was announced Friday morning by his family in a statement. "It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka," the statement said. "While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. LEGENDARY BEARS HEAD COACH MIKE DITKA DEAD AT 86 Ditka was a great tight end who won the Super Bowl with Dallas, and was a Super Bowl winning coach with the Chicago Bears. He also became something of an iconic figure as fans and celebrities copied his look and imitated his no-nonsense talk. Drafted by the Chicago Bears in 1961, he became the first modern receiving tight end and the first tight end selected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Ditka won NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year in 1961 and made five consecutive Pro Bowls from 1961-65 and earned five All-Pro selections. He played for the Bears from 1961-66, the Philadelphia Eagles from 1967-68 and the Dallas Cowboys from 1969-72, finishing with 427 receptions, 5,812 yards and 43 touchdowns. Ditka played on teams that won the 1963 NFL championship with Chicago and Super Bowl VI with Dallas following the 1971 season. He retired as a player after the 1972 season, entered the College Football Hall of Fame in 1986 and the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988. title: Hollywood feeling more hopeful amid a push for film tax credits and Paramount staying put, filmmaker says
description: California expands its film and television tax credits and launches a post-production incentive as Hollywood fights to keep jobs in Los Angeles.
content: Now that Paramount is staying put in Los Angeles and state and federal lawmakers are pushing for expanded film tax credits, Hollywood insiders are seeing a glimmer of hope. On Wednesday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom highlighted the state’s latest efforts to bolster its entertainment industry, including a new post-production tax credit, an expanded film and television tax credit and new protections for performers against the use of AI-generated content. "California is the home of entertainment, full stop," Newsom said in a statement. "We’re not just protecting that legacy; we’re investing in its future by expanding our film and television tax credit, launching a new post-production credit and standing up for performers in the age of AI. "We’re making sure independent filmmakers and the next generation of storytellers and creators have a real shot to build, hire and produce right here in California," he added. "More productions, more good jobs, more California stories told by California workers." CALIFORNIA LAW PUTS DIGITAL FINGERPRINTS ON AI FAKES At the federal level, a bipartisan coalition of lawmakers is working on a tax credit for film and television productions. The bill is expected to be introduced in Congress in early November, with its backers aiming to secure passage by Dec. 11, before the current Congress concludes its work. If passed, the credit would take effect in 2027 and could be used alongside state production incentives. Championed by President Donald Trump, the legislation has also received support from one of his most formidable political opponents, Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif. Schiff led the first impeachment effort against Trump and has remained a vocal critic of his leadership. "I am in strong agreement with the President," Schiff said on X. "Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we've lost to other countries." NETFLIX CHIEF ADMITS TRUMP IS HELPING SHOWBIZ INDUSTRY AS FEDERAL TAX CREDIT BILL AIMS TO FUEL HOLLYWOOD JOBS Filmmaker Paul Kampf, a 30-year veteran of the entertainment industry, described California’s incentives as "a really good start." "No matter where you make your film, whether it's Georgia, Delaware, Puerto Rico or Europe, if you can do your post-production in California, you're keeping jobs here, especially in independent films," Kampf told Fox News Digital. "We should be incentivizing filmmakers in America to stay in America. And we should also incentivize filmmakers who are outside of America to do their post here." Kampf, who has produced four feature films and a documentary in Serbia before embarking on his sixth project there, titled "Harvest," has also found himself embroiled in a situation in which a company owned by the Serbian government released the film in Eastern Europe without his permission. "This film is an example of what happens if we don't protect Americans and entice Americans to film here," Kampf said. In California, 35 films, including 28 independent projects, have received production incentives for filming in the state. The sequel to Lionsgate’s blockbuster 2026 hit "Michael" is among the projects, along with a new Pixar film. FILM PRODUCER SAYS 'MADE IN AMERICA' MOVIES CAN HELP REVIVE HOLLYWOOD'S STRUGGLING INDUSTRY All told, the projects are expected to generate more than $1 billion in direct production spending, according to the California Film Commission. "Through our tax credit program, we’re helping bring these stories to the screen while keeping the jobs, investment and production that bring them to life right here in California," Colleen Bell, director of the California Film Commission, said Wednesday in a statement. Kampf, who has made films in several countries, told Fox News Digital California had long been arrogant about its position in the industry, assuming it held a monopoly on filmmaking. "I've made movies all over the world. I don't make movies in LA. I live here. I lived the taxes of LA and California, and I live the sort of challenges of lifestyle here," he said. "I think Hollywood needs a facelift, and it's no pun intended. It needs to be seen as a place that is invigorating and investing in filmmaking again. title: Daniel Lurie argues progressivism led San Francisco astray on public safety, drug crisis
description: Daniel Lurie says San Francisco got "entrapped in our progressive values" and got to a point where the city wasn't taking stock of its problems.
content: San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said Thursday that the city had lost its way and was focused on the wrong things, arguing that the California city was "entrapped in our progressive values." "We lost our way as a city," he told CNN's Dana Bash in an interview. "We were focused on the wrong things, and today we're focused on common sense. We're focused on good governance. We're focused on delivering results for the people of San Francisco. I said from day one, public safety was going to be my number one priority. The crisis on our streets, the mental health and drug crisis is another top priority of mine. And I want to get the basics of governance right." Lurie, a moderate Democrat and heir to the Levi Strauss fortune, was elected in 2024 after defeating incumbent London Breed. "I mean, we got so entrapped in our progressive values and talking about progressivism, that we weren't taking stock of what was happening on our streets," he told Bash. "We had 810 people die of overdose in San Francisco three years ago. There's nothing progressive about that. There's nothing progressive about 30,000 car break-ins. Everyone had to deal with whether or not their car was going to be broken into," the mayor said, adding that the number of car break-ins had dropped 90%. SAN FRANCISCO STILL HASN'T RECOVERED SINCE PANDEMIC EXODUS: REPORT Bash asked Lurie about progressivism again, specifically how he defined the word. The mayor said he supported progressive values, such as taking care of the city's immigrants, and the LGBTQ+ community. "But, we got to a point where we said, 'Well, it's that person's right to be on the street using drugs,' or is that person — it's okay for someone to just go in and take what they want from a small business," he said. "In my mind, that's not progressive," Lurie continued. "There's nothing progressive about small businesses having to shutter up because they're a victim of crime over and over again. There's nothing progressive, as I said before, about 810 people dying of overdose. I'm not going to walk by somebody on the street and not do anything anymore." NEWSOM BLASTS DEMOCRATS FOR THEIR 'VICTIM MINDSET' THAT ENABLED HOMELESS CRISIS President Donald Trump praised Lurie during a cabinet meeting in March for "really trying" to improve San Francisco since taking office. "I know they have a mayor who’s trying very hard. He’s a Democrat, but he’s trying very hard," Trump said at the time. Socialism has been on the rise in the U.S., as several states have seen socialist candidates win their primary elections. In some places, progressive candidates were rejected for more moderate voices as well. Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital that even more liberal voices were calling out progressivism. "Lurie is right, and it’s not just more moderate voices like his calling this stuff out — we’ve seen AOC try to distance herself from ‘Woke 1’ as well," he said. "Some on the left have absolutely allowed themselves to get bullied into silence and, as funny and extreme a case as it was — that is how you get stories like that Massachusetts lesbian bar with the masking debacle." "Progressive policies are increasingly popular across the country, particularly on economic issues in these hard economic times," Shroff continued. "But there is also a sense that the DSA left can’t get out of its own way and can never be satisfied." "That is what Lurie is hitting on here and that is in some sense what happened in SF before his tenure. Yes, we want policies that are pro-family, pro-worker, pro-immigrant — that doesn’t mean letting the loudest voices dictate everything at the cost of a functioning city."

title: Tyreek Hill changes divorce battery trial testimony, claiming he didn't push wife but was verbally abusive
description: Tyreek Hill admitted to verbally abusing wife Lakeeta Vaccaro during intense cross-examination in their Miami-Dade County divorce battery trial.
content: NFL free agent wide receiver Tyreek Hill spent his second day on the stand of his divorce battery trial admitting to verbally abusing his wife Lakeeta Vaccaro but insisting he had not harmed her physically. And through the former player's testimony on Friday, the attorneys for Vaccaro have not yet produced incontrovertible evidence of physical violence by Hill against their client. Instead, what we saw on Friday was Hill on the stand trying to erase a significant problem he created for himself the day before, while Vaccaro's attorneys pressed the issue. TYREEK HILL DENIES MOST ABUSE CLAIMS BUT ADMITS TO SHOVING WIFE INTO WALL Hill on Friday morning changed his testimony from Thursday in which he admitted to pushing Vaccaro, which caused a hole in the wall of their Sunny Isle condominium. "I told her don't you ever touch me again in your life. I pushed her against the wall. And I tried to force her to get off me," Hill testified on Thursday. "I created a hole in the wall, trying to force her to get off me that night." His testimony on Friday changed to a door caused the hole. "The door, the main door," Hill told his attorney. "I was trying to evade [Vaccaro], but I'm not trying to harm her or push her against the wall or, like, do anything crazy. As I was trying to evade, I put a hole in the wall with the door." Hill's attorneys also made sure Hill explicitly denied ever hurting his wife's breasts, which Vaccaro alleged on the stand earlier in the trial. But Vaccaro's attorneys, on cross-examination, then tried to muddy up Hill further. The plaintiff attorneys got Hill to admit he spoke in an explicitly insulting manner about his wife to her and some of his friends. "The language, I'm gonna take that all on this end, I'm not proud of that," Hill testified. "I am ashamed. I don't even go back home because my marriage failed ... The language was terrible. Was terrible. I wish I could have been better in every single moment, but I'm not perfect. "The only thing I can do is learn from it and move forward and never talk to my co-parent like that again." Vaccaro's attorneys pointed to multiple instances in which Hill's testimony Thursday contradicted statements he made during his deposition. They impeached Hill on his testimony that Vaccaro may have had something to do with a house fire at the couple's Southwest Ranches home in Broward County when, in fact, the cause was determined to be a child playing with a lighter. They attempted to impeach Hill's contention on the stand Thursday that Vaccaro was "stealing" money from the family account. They impeached Hill on his suggestion on the stand Thursday that Vaccaro had something to do with him performing worse after the marriage than before, making the point it was Tua Tagovailoa throwing the passes and coach Mike McDaniel calling the plays. "She wasn't calling the plays on the field, but at home she was calling the plays" Hill said, sticking by his guns. "If you got a real good support system at home, that's what's important." title: Texas think tank accuses Houston parent coalition of using 'socialist' tactics to push radical agenda
description: The Texas Public Policy Foundation accuses a Houston education coalition of using socialist-aligned tactics to push radical policies in HISD schools.
content: Education policy experts are warning against a Houston education advocacy coalition, accusing the group of using socialist-aligned tactics to push radical policies in public schools. The Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF( warned that Community Voices for Public Education (CVPE) — which it said presents itself as a grassroots group of parents, teachers and community members — acts as a front for teachers' unions and far-left organizations working to preserve the status quo. "There are several policies that they're advocating for which are questionable at best, but very harmful," Kate Bierly, campaign director for TPPF's Next Generation Texas Campaign, told Fox News Digital. WATCHDOG REPORT EXPOSES TEACHERS UNION 'POLITICAL MACHINE' FUNNELING MORE THAN $1 BILLION TO LIBERAL CAUSES CVPE has been an outspoken opponent of the state's 2023 takeover of the Houston Independent School District (HISD), Texas's largest school district. The Texas Education Agency (TEA) intervened following years of academic underperformance at select campuses — a move that drew sharp accusations of political overreach from critics. State metrics, however, show noticeable academic gains since the intervention. Reading and math scores on the State of Texas Assessments of Academic Readiness (STAAR) improved among grades 3 through 8 over the past three school years, while the number of A- and B-rated campuses in HISD jumped from 93 to 197. SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' "F-rated campuses went from 56 to five, and the whole district moved from a C rating to a B rating," Bierly said. "The results were amazing. But from this, several critics emerged ... suggesting destructive replacement policies. One of the main groups behind these proposals is CVPE." The local group, Bierly said, uses tactics similar to those employed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which has gained traction in recent years as a political force with the election of several DSA-endorsed candidates across various levels of government. DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY' Beyond opposing the state takeover, CVPE advocates against mandatory STAAR testing and urges parents to boycott the exams. The group also calls for divesting from campus policing — ending student arrests except in severe cases such as murder — and encourages participation in walkouts and political protests. TPPF contends that CVPE actively instructs parents on how to organize student demonstrations outside schools, while CVPE maintains that peaceful advocacy is essential to improving school environments and curricula. "Some of the things they are advocating for is that parents should boycott the STAAR exam because the test allegedly supports racism and inequality," Bierly added.
