title: Jeff Bezos reveals his vision for America's next frontier — from AI to the moon
description: Blue Origin's Jeff Bezos unveiled plans for orbital data centers, a sustainable lunar base and launching rockets every minute from Cape Canaveral.
content: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos laid out a sweeping vision for America’s future Wednesday, telling Fox News the U.S. must beat China to the moon, artificial intelligence (AI) could help families get by with less work and data centers could one day operate in space. In an exclusive interview with chief political anchor Bret Baier on "Special Report," Bezos outlined his ambitions for Blue Origin and AI while pushing back on politicians who cast billionaires as villains. "Success is not villainy," Bezos said. The interview took place on Blue Origin’s factory floor in Cape Canaveral, Florida, as Fox News Channel marked its 30th anniversary. CHINA IS TAKING THE FIGHT TO THE STARS; AMERICA MUST RECLAIM SPACE SUPREMACY Bezos said the U.S. must prevail in the race against China to land humans on the moon, expressing confidence that an American landing is possible in 2028. "We have to beat China to the moon, and I believe we will beat China to the moon," he said. He said NASA and Blue Origin are focused on the goal, with cargo deliveries needed to support a sustained human presence. "We have to be able to land cargo routinely on the moon to support a lunar base on the moon," Bezos said. "So, there’s a lot of work to be done, but there’s every reason to believe that we can put humans on the moon in 2028." While Mars remains a destination, Bezos argued against skipping the moon, describing it as "a gift" because of its proximity to Earth and resources that could support future missions. "We’ll go to Mars. We’ll do all the other things. But we need to go to the moon first," he said. Bezos said lunar soil could be used to manufacture solar cells and oxygen produced on the moon could serve as rocket propellant. The goal, he said, should be to establish a lasting presence. NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND, OR CHINA WILL "It won’t just be a mission and leave," he said. "It’ll be a real sustainable lunar base." Blue Origin is also preparing to return its New Glenn rocket to flight in December, Bezos said, after an explosion during an engine test in May that Baier detailed during the broadcast. Bezos praised the team for repairing the launch pad, saying the next flight will carry Blue Ring, a vehicle designed to transport payloads into different orbits and farther into space. Asked about plans to increase launches from one pad from 12 to 50 annually, Bezos said Blue Origin is building three additional pads. His long-term ambitions are far greater. "Our goal is to fly every day," he said. "And, then, once we’re flying every day, we want to fly every hour. And then once we’re flying every hour, we want to fly every minute." That final goal, he acknowledged, draws skepticism from his own team. "They think I’m crazy," Bezos said. "But I’ve seen crazy things before come true." AMERICA CANNOT WIN THE GLOBAL AI RACE IF AMERICANS ARE AFRAID TO USE AI Bezos said he has personally invested $28 billion in Blue Origin and that the company recently raised $10 billion from outside investors for the first time. He also said an initial public offering could come several years from now. "I didn’t really want to take outside investors until I was sure that it would be a good investment for them," he said. His vision for AI is similarly ambitious, with Bezos predicting productivity gains could allow some families to live on one income or support themselves with a shorter workweek. "Some people will also decide, you know what? I can support my family by working three days a week," he said. "That’s what productivity in the economy means." BLUE ORIGIN LAUNCHES 38TH NEW SHEPHERD FLIGHT INTO SPACE Bezos argued those gains could create a labor shortage as Americans choose to work less. "It’s going to actually be difficult to hire people because the productivity in the economy is going to make it so that if people don’t want to work two jobs, they won’t have to," he said. Baier challenged that prediction, pointing to roughly 30,000 corporate roles Amazon had cut since late last year. Bezos said Amazon was in a "very special position" after substantially expanding its workforce during the COVID-19 pandemic. He acknowledged public fears about AI’s impact on jobs but said he disagreed with those predicting a more troubling outcome. At Prometheus, where Bezos is a co-founder and co-CEO, he said the goal is to develop an "artificial general engineer" that helps people turn ideas into physical products. "We’re going to make the tools so easy to use that anyone will be able to be an engineer," he said. Bezos said AI could generate double-digit productivity gains across the economy. Asked whether the industry is in an investment bubble, he said it is "very hard to know," but he argued that useful technology can survive even when investors lose money. "The inventions don’t disappear when the bubble pops," he said, pointing to lifesaving drugs developed during the biotechnology boom and fiber-optic cables laid during the internet boom. TRUMP'S AI RACE WITH CHINA COULD BECOME THE BIGGEST MISTAKE OF OUR TIME On government oversight, Bezos urged a light approach while the technology is developing, with rules focused on harmful uses. "In the beginning stages, when technologies are new, a light hand is appropriate," he said. "You don’t want to regulate knives. You want to regulate murder," Bezos added, arguing that policymakers should target dangerous applications and bad actors rather than restrict the underlying technology. Asked about concerns over data centers and electricity costs, Bezos pointed to Blue Origin’s Project Sunrise. He said the company has an application with the Federal Communications Commission to launch more than 50,000 satellites serving as orbital data centers. "Yes, we can put data centers in space," he said. "And there’s a good reason to do that." The conversation also turned to politics, with Baier asking about independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' criticism of billionaires. Bezos rejected the idea that building a successful business makes someone a villain, pointing to entrepreneurs who expand their companies while creating jobs. "There’s nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love," he said, citing the success of Raising Cane’s. "And it doesn’t make him a bad person." Asked why socialism is gaining traction in some quarters, Bezos acknowledged real affordability problems, particularly housing costs that leave young people struggling to live near their jobs. "You can’t pretend that there are no problems," he said. But he argued that politicians blaming landlords are overlooking the role of supply and demand. Government policies that subsidize demand while restricting construction drive prices higher, Bezos said, pointing to Austin as an example of a city making it easier to build housing. He urged voters to scrutinize politicians who spend their time assigning blame. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If there’s a politician who’s picking villains and pointing fingers, that probably means they don’t have a solution," Bezos said. He added that executives who behaved that way at his own companies would not last. "Those people wouldn’t be in our company for long."

title: Pro wrestler Karl Fredericks relishes opportunity to showcase who he truly is at Produce Wrestling's Skoden
description: Karl Fredricks opens up about his deep cultural identity struggles and why his Produce Wrestling match on Indigenous Peoples' Day means so much.
content: Karl Fredricks still has something to prove. The 36-year-old Reno, Nevada, native has already made a name for himself. He was the 2019 Young Lion Cup winner in New Japan Pro-Wrestling, he won titles at All Pro Wrestling, appeared in WWE NXT as Eddy Thorpe and was named one of the best 500 singles wrestlers by Pro Wrestling Illustrated in 2021. But one of his most meaningful accomplishments will come Monday when he appears at Produce Wrestling by Orange Crush’s Skoden event at Roulette Intermedium in New York. Fredricks will be one of the wrestlers with Native American ancestry on the card as the show celebrates Indigenous Peoples’ Day. He will be taking on Javi in a singles match. He talked about the upcoming event with OutKick Dropkick and suggested he wanted to show he was more than what he described facetiously as being a "cartoon Indian." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE "I'm a damn pro wrestler, and that's what Karl Fredericks is. That's what this has always been about. It was my love for pro wrestling, my love for performing, what I learned in Japan, that fighting spirit, the true heart and soul of professional wrestling and going out there, b---s to the wall. Not for four minutes, 4-7 minutes at a time," he explained. "That's what TV wrestling is. That's just playing the character I was (as Eddy Thorpe) being, being what I felt like was a cartoon Indian at times and doing all that stuff. "Working for a company like Produce is a blessing to be. I'm blessed to be here with people that give me a platform to be myself, to wrestle my match, to wrestle my style." Fredericks opened up about growing up with a Native American background and being unable to see anyone on television or in movies that looked like him. He lamented films portraying Native Americans as the bad guys. He said that being able to open up and be true to himself inside and outside of the ring has helped him get to where he is now – and he’s heard about it. He said he’s received messages from those of a similar background who were happy to see him on TV regardless of the role he was playing or the type of character he was asked to portray on television. "I would get messages all the time, and they did so much for me … Just the fact that we got a guy. Regardless of how they, I'm sure they had opinions on, you know, the way things were, but like they were just happy to have a guy. And so, I knew at the same time it was like, it was just important to be there giving my best effort regardless of what I was doing and I believe I did that, and now it's just it's going back out into the world as myself with a point to prove, and that's on both ends cause like I've experienced this struggle with cultural identity." Fredericks described a deep pain he felt growing up because, to some of his Native friends, he was a "White boy," but when he would be with his White friends, he would be the "native friend." "There are days when I'm, again, in the spirit of being facetious, and then there's a lot of pain in the experience behind it where it's just like, man, maybe I am just a f---ing Indian, whatever that means, and I don't know what that even means, because that's also, that's still something that, you know what I mean? Like I would, I wouldn't call myself (that). I do for the sake of the situation, essentially. So, I think it really is just up to me." Fredericks recalled one instance in the WWE Performance Center where tapping into his true self showed he was on the right path. He said the wrestlers he was with on one particular day got a chance to do promo work in front of John Cena. He said he grabbed his choker, jewelry and dressed up before bolting to the facility. He ended up cutting a promo on Roman Reigns. "I cut a promo on Roman Reigns, calling himself ‘The Tribal Chief, because culturally that's not in their vernacular and he was heel at the time, so I remember saying things like, ‘Where I come from, the chief is the wise man.’ The chief's a protector or provider, like the all of these good things, so I call out, I do this promo and John had no notes, said he loved it, said he understood who I was from top to bottom." Fredericks said, later in the session, he essentially asked Cena how he could stand out in the ring where nobody who was watching looked like him and didn’t feel like he was supposed to be to others unless he was "covered in animal bones." Fredericks said Cena described his question as "beautiful" and it clicked to him that whatever he was doing in the ring and whatever he was trying to portray was solely up to him and him alone, including saying no to a hair vs. hair match idea. "The last year and a half has been very tough mentally, just processing a couple years of my life, as well. title: Who's really played the best thus far through the first half of the college football season?
description: The Georgia Bulldogs top the SP+ rankings as college football's most efficient team, while Ohio State and Texas rank far differently than the AP Poll.
content: Most agree that the AP Top 25 Poll has become fatally flawed, thanks to a combination of human voter bias, time zone issues, mistakes and the sheer number of games, which makes following each one in detail virtually impossible. These issues start in the preseason polls, which are no more than lightly educated guessing based on recruiting rankings, coaches, the transfer portal, success in the previous season and conference affiliation. Even in season, the polls have become so unreliable and inaccurate that there's a case to be made that they might do more harm than good when the season hits crunch time and the selection committee starts their rankings. One way to solve for this is to look at rankings that are based not on preseason expectations, stadium size, jersey patches, or recruiting rankings, but actual on-field performance. Meaning, how efficient have you been on offense and defense, adjusted for the competition you've faced. What is the success rate you've had on offense, and allowed on defense, again adjusted for the competition you've faced. MIAMI HURRICANES COACH COMES OUT IN FAVOR OF ENDING PRESEASON COLLEGE FOOTBALL POLLS, BLASTS SEC The advantage to this? It filters out noise, like individual game results. Believe it or not, head-to-head matchups don't actually determine which team is better than the other, especially when the teams are closely matched. For example, look at the two games between the Alabama Crimson Tide and Georgia Bulldogs in 2025. In the first matchup, the Tide went into Athens and eked out a 24-21 win. The underlying performance, though, heavily favored Georgia. The Bulldogs averaged 6.7 yards per play, while allowing just 5.2 to Alabama. Georgia averaged a whopping 6.9 yards per rush, while the Tide could only muster 3.1. UGA missed opportunities too, only converting two of their red zone opportunities into points, losing a fumble, and only going 2-8 on third downs and 0-1 on fourth down. As a result, the postgame win expectancy heavily favored Georgia. Per ESPN's SP+, the adjusted scoring margin was Georgia by nearly seven points. The Bulldogs, based on their underlying performance, would win that game nearly 81% of the time. They didn't. Sure enough, when the two teams met again in the SEC Championship, the outcome was very different. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE To say Georgia dominated is a bit of an understatement. Alabama had -3 net rushing yards on 16 tries, a remarkable -0.2 yards per attempt. The third down success rate flipped, with the Tide going 3-14 and Georgia 6-16, plus 2-2 on fourth downs. Despite losing the penalty battle, the Bulldogs rolled, 28-7. The stats backed it up; UGA had 99.8% win expectancy with a +21.2 adjusted scoring margin. Looking at wins and losses is useful and necessary, but often deceiving as to which team is better. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! So what's happened thus far in 2026 that can give us some clues as to who's trending up and who's trending down? The latest SP+ ranking might be a better place to look than the AP Poll for who's truly elite in college football this year. Well, there's one team that somehow seems to have flown a bit under the radar, perhaps due to a lackluster schedule over the first few weeks. Once again, the Georgia Bulldogs are right back at it, with their dominance thus far making them the No. 1 team based on efficiency and success rate, combined with preseason expectations of team quality. Right behind them? Ohio State, a perfect example of on-field results not necessarily matching team quality. The Buckeyes lost to Texas, but the two teams played an essentially equal game, and the Buckeyes' other performances have been more impressive than the Longhorns. So while they've dropped to fifth in the poll, they're a far better team than their ranking suggests. Don't be stunned though if their game against Indiana is a lot closer than most expect. Mississippi State is No. 27 in SP+ and No. 17 in the poll, inexplicably. Kentucky just dropped out of the top-25, but SP+ has the Wildcats all the way down at No. 45. title: MIKE EMANUEL: I joined an unknown startup called Fox News; it gave me a front-row seat to history
description: Mike Emanuel reflects on nearly 30 years of covering war, elections and breaking news, from George W. Bush's Texas campaigns to the anchor chair.
content: I was hired at Fox News in the first year of its existence — 1997 — before the vast majority of America knew what it was. In fact, I was hired without a job interview. The network’s top executives at the time offered me a job as a correspondent based on my audition reel. It was an odd feeling to go to work for people I had never met at a network I had never seen. My career manager told me there were smart people at Fox who would likely figure out how to make it a success. So, I jumped at the chance to join the startup network. At that point, we were not available on cable TV in much of America. So, when I would call people about doing an interview for a story, they would ask if I was at the local Fox affiliate. Then they would ask where they could see Fox News. I told them we were working on it. But if they agreed to do a story with me, I would send them a VHS tape after it aired. About a month after I started, I was sent to London to work alongside the Fox team covering the death of Princess Diana. I thought that was going to be the story of my career. To be clear, it was a global story, but it was just the start of a truly extraordinary journey covering major national and international news of our time. JENNIFER GRIFFIN: I COVERED WARS, TERROR AND TRAGEDY FOR FOX NEWS. WHAT I FOUND WAS A FAMILY Evidently, my Princess Diana coverage was decent. When I returned to our bureau in Los Angeles, my boss essentially interviewed me about where I had worked before local news in Los Angeles. I told him I was at the Fox station in Austin, Texas, covering politics. His ears perked up, and he asked me if I knew then-Gov. George W. Bush. I told him the governor had nicknamed me "Mikey" since I covered his first campaign for governor in 1994 and his first couple of years in office. So, he asked if I could get a sit-down interview with Mr. Bush and instructed me to make it happen. After the governor did a couple of interviews with me in 1997, my bosses asked me to move to Dallas to open a bureau there to cover that whole region of the country. But the message was that if there was a Texas political story, they wanted me there to cover it. JIMMY FAILLA: I CAME TO FOX WITH MY TAXI DOUBLE-PARKED. THEN CAME THE RIDE OF MY LIFE I covered everything in that region and beyond from 1998 to just after President Bush’s 2001 inauguration. At one point, we were asked to come up with a story on a weekend because we needed more content for weekend shows. My team pitched going to the world’s largest rattlesnake roundup in Sweetwater, Texas. I think I nearly gave the folks in the control room in New York a stroke when I jumped into the pit with the rattlesnakes. I was wearing heavy boots and protective chaps, but the producers were scared to death I was going to end up in the hospital with snake bites. On election night 2000, I was on the platform in Austin, Texas, waiting to find out if George W. Bush had won or lost the election. We heard Vice President Gore had called to concede and then called back to say it was too close. Then, for six weeks, I camped out in Austin trying to figure out if Bush would be the 43rd president. Once that historic election was sorted out, my bosses asked me to move to Washington. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME When I arrived in D.C., I had no Washington experience, so my bosses used me to do all kinds of stories. When President Bush would return to his Crawford, Texas, ranch, they would send me since the president would typically call on me to ask a question if he saw me in the crowd of reporters. LAUREN GREEN: I WAS FOX NEWS CHANNEL'S FIRST ON-AIR HIRE. HERE'S HOW A DREAM BECAME A POWERHOUSE Six months after moving to Washington came Sept. 11, 2001. While the understandable focus of our coverage was on New York City, there was chaos in Washington, with concerns the White House and the U.S. Capitol could also be targets. My bosses sent me to the roof of our Washington bureau to do live updates on the situation here. From my position, we could see smoke behind me from the Pentagon. Later that day, I was doing reports at the Pentagon. A month later, I was sent to Islamabad, Pakistan, to cover the buildup to the war in Afghanistan. In early 2002, I was asked to go to Kabul to cover the war. Several of us went from being domestic correspondents to war correspondents virtually overnight. SANDRA SMITH: I WALKED INTO FOX NEWS 19 YEARS AGO. THE PEOPLE AND VIEWERS CHANGED MY LIFE Then, in 2005, I was asked to embed with 10th Mountain Division soldiers who were tasked with securing western Baghdad so the Iraqis would be safe going to vote in an election. It was an amazing experience being with those brave men and women responsible for such a strategic location in the Iraqi capital. I had the opportunity to be a White House correspondent in the final years of President Bush’s term and the first years of President Obama’s presidency. Traveling across the country and around the globe with two American presidents was beyond my dreams when I started out in local news in Midland-Odessa, Texas, years ago. Asking questions of both presidents in the Oval Office and at presidential news conferences was also the honor of a lifetime. I had the opportunity to interview President Bush about being a wartime commander in chief and did the final TV interview with then-Vice President Dick Cheney. In 2011, Fox executives asked me to move to Capitol Hill to be the chief congressional correspondent, a beat I had never covered before in my career. There I covered a decade’s worth of State of the Union addresses, Supreme Court confirmations, Cabinet confirmations and my share of government shutdowns. While I covered Capitol Hill, network leadership started asking me to fill in as an anchor. I had confidence about doing it, since, for 20 years, I had covered politics, war, natural disasters and more as a correspondent at the network. I felt like whatever news broke, I had probably covered it as a field correspondent before. I was grateful for the opportunity to fill in as an anchor on the network’s top news programs and became a regular anchor on weekends. While weekends are not typically as newsy as weekdays, massive stories break at any time. I was anchoring on Sunday, July 21, 2024, when then-President Joe Biden announced he was withdrawing from his re-election campaign. We were live and had the story first. We threw out the show rundown and went wall-to-wall for 90 minutes with the breaking news, totally unscripted. My producer, Eric Strain, would get in my ear to direct traffic. We would go from Kevin Corke reporting from the president’s weekend location in Delaware to Bret Baier on the phone to Brit Hume on the phone, back to Kevin, then to Martha MacCallum and Shannon Bream on the phone as the bosses rallied the weekday lineup to get into the office. At one point, Brit noted that this was history and congratulated me for being in the anchor chair to lead our coverage. I was also anchoring the weekend of June 21, 2025, when President Trump ordered Operation Midnight Hammer. That was a series of precision strikes on three major Iranian nuclear facilities. It was an opportunity for my experience reporting on Afghanistan and Iraq to help guide my questions from the anchor chair. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION And I was anchoring the weekend of Jan. 3, 2026, when President Trump ordered Operation Absolute Resolve, a raid in Venezuela to capture Nicolás Maduro. We canceled our scheduled guests and went all in on the breaking news. It feels like there have been thousands of adrenaline-rush stories in my nearly 30 years at Fox News. My dream as a young journalist was to make it back to New York, so my parents, family and friends could watch me on the local news. I’ve lived far beyond those dreams. My loved ones have watched me cover major stories across the country and around the globe, and I will be eternally grateful for the opportunities my bosses have given me at Fox. Needless to say, I’m so thankful I took that leap of faith to join this startup network all those years ago. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM MIKE EMANUEL

title: DNC lawsuit accuses Trump administration of diverting $20M in federal funds for 'propaganda' ads
description: The Democratic National Committee alleges the Trump administration directed $20 million in taxpayer funds toward ads designed to boost Republicans ahead of 2026 midterms.
content: The Democratic National Committee is suing the Trump administration, alleging it illegally diverted $20 million in federal funds to produce and broadcast partisan political advertisements. The ad campaign was designed to boost Republican prospects in the upcoming 2026 midterm elections and shore up President Donald Trump’s approval ratings, a move the DNC argues constitutes unlawful "publicity or propaganda," the lawsuit states. The lawsuit claims President Donald Trump personally directed the campaign, violating the longstanding statutory ban on using federal appropriations for "publicity or propaganda purposes." REPUBLICAN PARTY TO HOST HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION IN DALLAS, TRUMP ANNOUNCES ON TRUTH SOCIAL "President Trump’s political propaganda ads are an attempt to resuscitate his historically low approval ratings and avoid widespread Republican defeats in the 2026 midterm election," the lawsuit states. "The President has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day ‘midterm convention,’ and repeatedly directed voters to ‘pretend that I am on the ballot.’" The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) transferred the funds from money authorized under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to court filings. 2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN The OMB approved reallocating the funds into a U.S. Customs and Border Protection line item designated for "Commemorative Events," according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit also notes that congressional committee reports explicitly restricted that line item to line-of-duty death memorials, agency anniversaries and commendation ceremonies. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump wrote on Truth Social earlier this week. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!" The lawsuit highlights mounting pressure on Republicans, noting that polling numbers have dropped in traditional battlegrounds as well as in typically conservative states, which leaves Democrats "poised to take control of Congress, governor’s mansions, and state legislatures around the country." MADURO CLAIMS IMMUNITY, ASKS JUDGE TO DISMISS DRUG-TRAFFICKING CHARGES AGAINST HIM AND HIS WIFE Among the ads flagged in the filing is one featuring President Trump touting the capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. In another spot, Trump directly addresses the audience: "With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state. We will expel the warmongers from our government. We will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists." A third ad explicitly asks viewers to "pretend I'm on the ballot" to drive turnout. The lawsuit also targets ads featuring high-ranking administration officials praising Trump, including War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. FOX NEWS POLL: AS ECONOMIC PAIN DEEPENS, DISAPPROVAL OF TRUMP HITS NEW HIGH "Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November, so we’re suing him," DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement. "As gas and grocery costs rise and his approval numbers continue to crater, this president has stooped to taking money from a fund intended for memorials for Americans killed in the line of duty to promote his failed policies. "Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes." "Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction," a White House spokesperson told Fox News Digital, citing numerous examples. "The G.W. Bush Administration ran a national television campaign explaining the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act to seniors," they noted. "It also bought Super Bowl airtime for anti-drug and anti-terrorism public service announcements." Furthermore, "the Obama Administration used national advertising to promote Obamacare subsidies and open enrollment, and a digital campaign to sell its Waters of the United States rule," they said, adding that "the Biden Administration poured hundreds of millions of dollars into "We Can Do This" — television, digital, radio, and print spots — to drive a nationwide public health message." They also cited historical examples, naming the Wilson administration's Committee on Public Information and the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration's Office of War Information. SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES The lawsuit asks the court to declare that the Trump administration and affected federal agencies unlawfully produced and aired the advertisements using congressionally appropriated funds and seeks an immediate injunction to block further use of taxpayer dollars for the campaign. title: Fans are wondering if Florida Panthers are cursed as another star exits game Wednesday night
description: Aleksander Barkov's latest injury and Brad Marchand's scary exit have Florida Panthers fans wondering if the team is cursed after back-to-back Cups.
content: A little less than 16 months ago, the question surrounding the National Hockey League was whether or not the Florida Panthers were on the fast track to becoming the sport's next dynasty. They had just vanquished the Edmonton Oilers for the second year in a row to capture back-to-back Stanley Cups, and many fans were wondering if they had a chance to become the first team to three-peat since the New York Islanders won four straight from 1980-83. Then the injuries started to pile up, beginning right as the Cup celebration ended with star winger Matthew Tkachuk needing adductor surgery. OTTAWA SENATORS OWNER CLAIMS KEITH TKACHUK AND MATTHEW TKACHUK SWAYED BRADY'S TRADE REQUEST Tkachuk would be out for the first half of the season, but his injury was only the tip of the iceberg. The Panthers famously lost captain Aleksander Barkov for the year thanks to a torn ACL, and other key contributors like sniper Sam Reinhart, defender Seth Jones, and two-way wizard Anton Lundell also missed multiple weeks in the season with a bevy of injuries. 2026 was supposed to be the bounceback year for the Cats, as Barkov and the rest of his merry band of champions were thought to be fully healthy. Then, just two games into the season, the Panthers captain went down awkwardly in an eerily similar fashion to his ACL injury a little more than a year earlier, causing Florida fans to wince. Barkov was given a supremely positive diagnosis relative to what the news could have been — a 6-8 week recovery period — but before Panthers fans could even finish their sighs of relief, another integral piece to their 2025 Cup run went down in a heap. When it rains it pours, and Florida losing Brad Marchand for any stretch of time is less than ideal. The 38-year-old forward defied Father Time during the 2025 Stanley Cup Playoffs, scoring 10 goals and 10 assists in 23 postseason games, but this latest injury could be one that keeps him out for a while. Marchand was already recovering from an injury at the end of last season, and the fears are this could be serious given the fact he was unable to put any weight on his leg as he was helped off the ice Wednesday night (the most likely outcome seems to be an MCL injury). This rash of injuries over the past year plus has fans wondering whether the Panthers sold their souls for those back-to-back Cups. Fellow OutKick writer and hockey fanatic Matt Reigle even asked me if there were any electrical substations located near Amarant Bank Arena. While I'm not sure about that, I have opined for quite some time now that the Cats may be cursed, and the Marchy injury isn't exactly helping to assuage those concerns. If you're a Panthers fan looking for a positive, then consider the fact that the Barkov injury wasn't as bad as initially feared, and there is a world where Marchand gets a similar diagnosis. The Cats also went out and acquired Ottawa Senators captain Brady Tkachuk to help bolster the depth on the roster as well, so if anyone can withstand the injury bug early in the season, it's Florida. Also, we are only four games into the year, but the Panthers are leading the division even without their captain and their playoff ace. title: Dana Altman ends nearly four decade coaching career at Oregon: 'Stepping away is truly painful'
description: Dana Altman retires as Oregon Ducks basketball head coach after 16 seasons, with assistant Tony Stubblefield named interim for the upcoming campaign.
content: The coach who has manned the sideline for more Oregon men’s basketball games than any other coach is going off into the sunset. Dana Altman has decided to retire after 16 seasons with the Ducks and nearly four decades as a Division I coach, the school announced Wednesday. Altman, 68, first took over Oregon’s program in 2010. Assistant coach Tony Stubblefield will assume Altman’s responsibilities on an interim basis beginning next season. "I've loved every minute of coaching here, and stepping away is difficult and truly painful," Altman said in a statement. "I love coaching, it's what I know best and what I've been fortunate enough to do for almost five decades. "... It's been the honor of my life to coach the Ducks," he added. Oregon football coach Dan Lanning was among those offering praise for Altman. "A great mentor, sees the game, and obviously a Hall of Fame coach with what he’s been able to accomplish," Lanning said. "I love his story, and how grounded he is, and he’s as good as they come." BASKETBALL HALL OF FAMER DON NELSON DEAD AT 86 Altman’s announcement came as a surprise, but the Ducks have experienced some upheaval. title: Abdul El-Sayed reportedly called Hasan Piker warning his rhetoric was 'costing' votes
description: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed allegedly called Hasan Piker to warn that the Twitch streamer's Israel rhetoric was costing him votes in the Michigan Senate race.
content: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, allegedly called far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker and asked him to tone down his rhetoric, according to a CNN article published Wednesday. CNN reporter Edward-Isaac Dovere wrote that although the progressive candidate has denied attempting to modulate his positions ahead of November's election, El-Sayed has avoided discussing hot-button topics such as Israel and American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) funding. Another "concession" Dovere highlighted was El-Sayed distancing himself from Piker despite campaigning with the streamer during the primary election. The CNN reporter revealed that El-Sayed had, in fact, reached out to Piker as his comments regarding Israel caused more controversy. EL-SAYED TRIES TO PUT THE HASAN PIKER DEBATE BEHIND HIM AS MIDTERMS APPROACH "El-Sayed recently called Piker and warned his rhetoric was costing El-Sayed votes, asking him to stop, according to two people El-Sayed told about the conversation," Dovere reported, noting that Piker declined to comment on the issue. El-Sayed has faced backlash for campaigning with Piker, who has a history of making controversial statements such as suggesting America "deserved" 9/11. Though El-Sayed repeatedly said that he did not agree with all of Piker's beliefs, he declined to disavow Piker's comments. FATHER OF 9/11 HERO TODD BEAMER APPEARS IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE AD TO CONDEMN HASAN PIKER RHETORIC The Michigan Democrat eventually began distancing himself from Piker in August after Piker appeared to blame American Jews for antisemitic attacks based on their support for Israel. "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said during one of his streams. ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES Since then, El-Sayed has said he has no plans to appear with Piker and insisted that his campaign has nothing to do with a "Twitch streamer in California." "The question is not about a relationship I got with a streamer in California. There's not a relationship. The reason I have a conversation with him is the same reason I have a conversation with you. Because I want to talk to the folks out here who I want to have a conversation with. Do you think that you're better off now after two years of [President] Donald Trump?" title: Drink up, boys! NFL reverses course after meeting with NFLPA to allow all drinking celebrations without fines
description: The NFL and NFL Players Association now allow drinking celebrations after rescinding fines for Kyle Juszczyk and Jake Ferguson's touchdown moves.
content: It took nearly two weeks and a meeting of the minds from the NFL and NFL Players Association (NFLPA), but after all that high-priced talent hashed things out, we've come to a conclusion that will affect humanity. NFL players are allowed to celebrate big plays by simulating drinking. So, drink up, boys! NFL FINES PLAYER NICKNAMED 'JUICE' $14,926 FOR USING A DRINKING CELEBRATION, CALLING IT OFFENSIVE It no longer matters what's on a player's mind when he mimics drinking during a celebration. He might be thinking about sipping tea, as Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor apparently was after scoring a touchdown on Sunday in London. He might be thinking about drinking juice, as Kyle Juszczyk insisted he was doing when he was fined after Week 2. The player might be mimicking taking a drink from a Gatorade bottle as Cowboys tight end Jake Ferguson claimed he was doing when he was fined. 49ERS FULLBACK KYLE JUSZCZYK SUCCESSFULLY APPEALS NFL BEER FINE BY INVOKING HIS 'JUICE' NICKNAME And even this: The player could even be thinking he's shotgunning a beer. It's fine now rather than headed for a fine. That's because the path is now clear on all drinking, sipping, chugging and shotgunning beverages in the NFL. Peace on Earth! In a joint statement issued by the league and the NFLPA on Wednesday, it was explained that celebrations including "imitating drinking a beverage" will not be considered a violation. "Football is the greatest game in the world," the NFL and the NFLPA said in a statement released jointly. "NFL players are admired by millions of fans, including young people competing at every level of the sport. "The passion emotion, and personality players bring to the field are a big part of what makes the game special and connects them with fans worldwide. title: Popular US airport called out as 'most stressful' in America for travelers
description: Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport tops a new ranking of the "most stressful" U.S. airports, according to an analysis, with nearly 28% of all flights delayed in 2025.
content: Flight delays, cancellations and even the drive to terminals can add layers of frustration to already challenging travel experiences. A new analysis looked at some of the busiest airports across the U.S. to determine where travelers may encounter the most stress. Rightway Parking, an airport and cruise parking reservation company based in Tampa, Florida, analyzed 55 airports using federal flight data and Google Maps estimates. It weighed delays, cancellations, changes in delays, and the distance and travel time from downtown areas. TRAVEL NIGHTMARE UNFOLDS AS MAJOR AIRLINE SCRAPS FLIGHT AFTER HARROWING 12-HOUR DELAY After the analysis, Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) was ranked as the "most stressful" airport in the country in the study. Nearly 28% of flights at DFW were delayed, while 2.76% were canceled, according to the analysis, which used 2025 flight data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. The airport has also seen delays climb 33.67% since 2021, according to the report. Getting to the airport also added another factor to DFW's ranking. The airport sits about 20 miles or so from downtown Dallas. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The findings come after travelers at DFW faced a difficult day earlier this month. On Oct. 1, the airport recorded 390 delays and 155 cancellations, the most of any U.S. airport that day, according to NJ.com. DFW was followed by Chicago O'Hare International Airport, which took the No. 2 spot with 24.68% of flights delayed and a 42.77% increase in delays since 2021. Travel time also factored into O'Hare's position, with the drive from downtown Chicago to the airport estimated at about 50 minutes. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Rounding out the top three was Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. Reagan National recorded a 3.86% cancellation rate. It has seen delays increase 73.92% since 2021, according to the analysis. New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport and Philadelphia International Airport rounded out the top five, ranking fourth and fifth. Some airports fared much better when the same travel factors were taken into account. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Salt Lake City International Airport in Utah was ranked the "least stressful" airport — followed by San Jose International Airport in California and Daniel K. Inouye International Airport in Honolulu, Hawaii. All three recorded cancellation rates below 1% and had relatively shorter trips from downtown compared with many of the airports toward the top of the ranking. title: Woke Kansas City radio host admits OutKick is right, but asks his listeners to not read us
description: A Kansas City Chiefs radio host says he agrees with OutKick's Josh Simmons reporting but claims he doesn't respect the platform or its coverage.
content: A Kansas City sports radio host is unhappy with OutKick's coverage of the Chiefs. He says he doesn't disagree with anything we've written or reported, however. Instead, he claims he doesn't like that we're allowed to talk about his team while holding different views than he does. On Tuesday, Carrington Harrison criticized members of the Kansas City sports media for "spending any part of [their] day arguing with Bobby Burack about any subject." In doing so, he spent part of his day posting about me on social media – and discussing OutKick and me on his radio show. "I wouldn't get my [Chiefs] stories from OutKick," he said. "They are an underling of Clay Travis." He then said he doesn't "respect OutKick." Harrison later asked to appear on the conservative radio show Mundo in the Morning on KCMO in Kansas City. He claimed his issue with OutKick stemmed from a story we published last week about Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons, who has yet to play this season. In our story, we mentioned that ESPN had reported several "red flags" about Simmons' character and maturity before the 2024 draft. We also cited a Sports Illustrated report that Simmons left the team unannounced the night before a game last season, was unresponsive, and left the team unaware of his whereabouts for a period of time. Simmons then missed a month of games for what the team described as "personal" reasons. This season, Simmons has missed all four of the Chiefs' games. The team says he has a back injury, one that team sources told multiple reporters was a non-issue in August. ESPN's Jeremy Fowler has since described the injury as "mysterious." Most other national insiders won't discuss the injury, even during injury roundup segments in which they cover minor ailments involving players of far less consequence. We pointed out how the situation is unusual, that the team's lack of transparency is generating online theories, and that the secrecy suggests something more complicated than a simple back injury. So, what exactly does a radio host on the Kansas City Chiefs' official station dispute about our analysis? Well, nothing. "I don't fundamentally disagree with Bobby Burack," Harrison told a perplexed Pete Mundo on Wednesday. "I would define someone who is a hater, who is someone who is incapable of giving credit when credit should be due." Uh, okay. "The truth doesn't matter who says the truth. It's still the truth regardless of who says it," he added. So why the tweets, radio segments, and name-calling? According to Harrison, he doesn't like that OutKick told the truth. What does that mean? Didn't he just say the opposite? We'll let him explain. TOMI LAHREN DEFENDS OUTKICK'S ESPN SCOOP, TORCHES JEMELE HILL, BACKS SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM "I don't respect Bobby Burack's reporting," he said. "I don't respect the platform that he has created for himself. I believe that he is somebody who has cultivated an audience and a brand around insects, bots, trolls and racists. That's not someone that I'm super interested in getting on the internet and having to tussle with and going back and forth with." To recap, Carrington Harrison says he agrees with my reporting but doesn't respect it. He says he doesn't want to get into a back-and-forth with me, despite initiating a back-and-forth with me on X, his radio show, and another radio show. At this point, you have to wonder if there is something seriously wrong with this guy. He certainly doesn't appear to be operating with the highest IQ. Befuddled by Harrison's contradictions, Mundo questioned his premise. "But you are saying that he is absolutely onto something there with this Josh Simmons thing, but then saying on the other hand, he's not credible on this situation," Mundo said. "I've seen, I mean, I never said he's not credible on this situation. I've seen his work in reporting in other situations. That's just not somebody that I would align myself with," Harrison responded. Huh? Who asked him to align himself with anyone? He began by saying OutKick is not credible when it comes to the Chiefs, a point he now claims wasn't his intention. He then reiterated exactly what we wrote last week. "So in this situation, is there something greater going on with Josh Simmons? Yes, I 100% agree with that. Yes, I absolutely think there is something going on." Mundo again questioned why Harrison had made a point of telling his listeners not to trust OutKick when he now confirmed that he agreed with exactly what we had reported about the subject. "My sense of it is that you don't really disagree with Bobby. And I've only got about a minute here. You don't disagree with Bobby, but you kind of don't like Bobby and that's fine." "That's your prerogative. I'm not saying you have to like him or not, but because you don't like him, you kind of want to twist them here or tweak them a little bit here in this whole deal. Is that a fair analysis of this situation?" Harrison didn't deny it. Instead, he took more personal shots. "I mean, I wouldn't say that I want to tweak him a little bit, but I think Bobby's problem is, I think Bobby has stood on the shoulder of giants and thinks that he's now tall. Bobby Burack has never done anything outside of the success of Clay Travis. So I don't want him to come on here and on your show and act like he is a top-notch investigator or reporter. That's definitely not true." For the record, I did not claim to be an investigative reporter. My coverage of Josh Simmons is actually quite benign. I simply said the situation doesn't make much sense. I said that because the people covering the Chiefs daily, like Harrison, have been too afraid to do so at the risk of upsetting team public relations. Now that we've gotten that out of the way, Harrison's comments raise a broader issue. Why would a sports station in Kansas City tied to an NFL franchise want a host on the air who openly admits that he cannot tolerate the sports opinions of people who disagree with him politically? Harrison confirmed on multiple occasions since Tuesday that he told his listeners to ignore OutKick's accurate information because he thinks our readers are racist and because of our association with Clay Travis, one of the country's most prominent conservative radio talk show hosts. Imagine hosting a sports show in another city and saying something similar about a liberal outlet, while acknowledging their information is accurate. Harrison sent a message to sports fans across Kansas and Missouri: If you are not as liberal as he is, you are not welcome to listen to his show. Two points on that. One, based on his numbers, most people aren't listening to his show anyway. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Two, OutKick asked the program director of his station, Steven Spector, whether Harrison's views about conservatives and OutKick represent the views of 96.5 The Fan. Spector did not return our email in time for publication. We will update this story if he does. We also reached out to Harrison to see if he stands by his bizarre commentary. Anyway, we at OutKick do not believe you have to vote a certain way to have an opinion about sports. We also stand by our coverage of Josh Simmons. The starting left tackle for the NFL's most valuable asset playing in just eight games over two years, under two different sets of mysterious circumstances, is a story worth covering. title: Valerie Bertinelli hits back at trolls who say she's 'obsessed' with late ex Eddie Van Halen

title: 100-shot Somali gang gun battle rocks Minnesota as sheriff warns 'we're in trouble'

content: Violence tied to Somali-American gangs in the Twin Cities metro erupted in recent days, with law enforcement recovering nearly 100 casings after a gunfight captured on a resident’s surveillance camera — as officials warn they need help to contain the problem before it escalates. "We have the opportunity to fix it," Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher said of a surge in Somali gang violence across the Twin Cities — but warned authorities could be facing a much more difficult problem if the groups escalate the resources they use. 3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING "It’s early. TRUMP’S LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS, GUNS IN BLUE CITY "We need more people focused on this problem. title: 'The world is standing with you': Christian leaders from 122 countries unite in Jerusalem for Oct 7
description: The Friends of Zion summit drew delegations from 122 countries to Jerusalem, where released hostages and bereaved families shared their stories.
content: Christian community leaders and influencers from around the world gathered in Jerusalem Wednesday for an international memorial marking Oct. 7 as part of the Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit. The event also included Jewish leaders, released hostages, bereaved families, wounded Israelis, ambassadors and diplomatic representatives to commemorate the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre. "Oct. 7 is the worst day in Israel’s history, a day of hopelessness," Dr. Mike Evans, founder of the Friends of Zion Heritage Center in Jerusalem, told Fox News Digital. ON OCT 7, CHRISTIANS MUST REMEMBER AND STAND WITH ISRAEL "People talk a lot about the more than 1,200 people killed that day, but not enough about the more than 70,000 who lost their homes and loved ones. You have a nation going through unspeakable pain, not only because of Oct. 7, but also because of the feeling that they are alone and that the world has turned against them," Evans added. "What I’m sharing on Oct. 7 is this: ‘You’re wrong. The world is standing with you,’" he continued. "You see the faces, languages and songs of people from around the world united to comfort you and stand with you. It’s not political. It’s for the Jewish people: You are not alone. We’re with you. We love you." CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND Hosted by actor and influencer Nathaniel Buzolic and reporter Erin Molan, Wednesday’s event in the Israeli capital was broadcast live on dozens of television networks around the world. "When other minority or groups suffer, there tends to be some sort of acknowledgment of that suffering, but when it comes to Jewish suffering, particularly at the hands of radical Islamists, there is not only silence but also denial and an attempt to downgrade the atrocities we witnessed, and we really have witnessed atrocities not just on Oct. 7 but in the continuation of that," Buzolic told Fox News Digital. Buzolic said supporting Israel is a moral imperative given what he described as efforts to destroy the country. He argued that the hostility toward Israel is rooted in a radical Islamist ideology that rejects peace and coexistence not only with the Jewish state, but also with Western societies more broadly. Released hostages Agam Berger, Sagui Dekel-Chen, Bar Kupershtein and Evyatar David attended the event, along with Bar’s grandfather, Holocaust survivor Michael Kupershtein. Sylvan Adams, president of the World Jewish Congress Israel and a full partner in the event, also participated. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS Earlier in the day, participants visited Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust remembrance center. The Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit is being held for the second consecutive year and brings together over 1,000 participants from 122 countries. "The alliance is very strong. The vast majority of Zionists in the world are not Jewish; they are Bible-believing Christians," Evans told Fox News Digital. "The Christian Zionists worldwide don’t necessarily agree on the politics, but they agree on the people. They are uniting with the people of Israel." The delegation includes many young people as part of an effort to reach a generation that Evans said had been "poisoned" by countries such as Qatar at universities, as well as by artificial intelligence. The summit, held in cooperation with Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, opened Tuesday with an event on Jerusalem’s Mount of Olives. Evans said the site, which is associated with Jesus and his ascension, holds particular significance for participants and serves as a symbol of their faith. Israel’s Special Envoy to the Christian World George Deek said he was proud of the sustained support Israel has received from Jewish and Christian communities abroad since Oct. 7, 2023. LOST CITY WHERE JESUS PERFORMED MIRACLES HAS FINALLY BEEN IDENTIFIED, EXPERT SAYS "The arrival of Christian leaders carries a powerful message that Israel does not stand alone. They have come to bear witness, meet people whose lives were shattered on Oct. 7 and carry their stories back to communities around the world," Deek told Fox News Digital. Deek said the bond between Israel and the Christian world has been built on "truth, courage and sheer determination" to confront antisemitism and other forms of hatred wherever they arise. "This visit is a testament to the strength of the bond between Israel and Christian communities despite attempts by various groups, including paid actors and anti-Israel organizations, to drive a wedge between them," he added. Deek said the special relationship between Christians and Jews rests on three foundations: a shared biblical heritage; a commitment to ensuring Jews can live free from antisemitism and fear and the right of Christians in the Middle East and elsewhere to live without intimidation. "The future of the Jews in Israel and the future of Christians are connected because we have a shared history. We share the same historical land, the same values, kings and prophets, and we have to stand together, especially when it comes to this warfare against the soul of Christians, trying to drive them away from Israel," Deek told Fox News Digital. Influencer Oli London first visited Israel six weeks after the Oct. 7 attack, traveling to Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where residents were killed and kidnapped and homes were burned during the massacre. "I felt it was so important to come back to honor the memory of the victims, advocate for those still suffering from trauma, raise awareness of their suffering and take part in mass prayers," London told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "I think it’s also important to show Christians the holy sites in Israel. I’m visiting the Sea of Galilee, the Mount of Olives, the Garden Tomb and other biblical sites to encourage Christians to return because Israel has had a difficult time over the past few years," he continued. London also praised the resilience of the Jewish people and addressed rising antisemitism around the world since Oct. 7. "Sadly, many people are either staying silent or jumping on the bandwagon of the anti-Israel trend, fueling hatred and bringing out antisemitic views in many people. Jewish people need support and need to know they are loved and supported by so many Christians," he said. On Thursday, members of the delegation will visit the Nova music festival site, where one of the central massacres of Oct. 7 took place, and meet with released hostages Romi Gonen, Elkana Bohbot and Noa Argamani, who were abducted from the festival. On Friday, the delegation will visit the ancient site of Shiloh in Samaria for a special tour and prayer event. Hooman Khalili, who is participating in the summit, was born in Iran and has been an outspoken supporter of Israel. He said he has visited the country 17 times over 21 months to create "Woman, Life, Freedom" murals. title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges related to alleged torture of Americans
description: Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and wife Cilia Flores face new charges tied to alleged torture of Americans in Manhattan court Thursday.
author_name: Stepheny Price, David Spunt, Maria Paronich
content: Deposed Venezuelan Nicolás Maduro and his wife could face new charges tied to the alleged torture of Americans as prosecutors fight their efforts to have their criminal case thrown out. The additional charges are expected to be announced in Manhattan federal court, according to Fox News’ David Spunt and Jake Paronich. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald is expected to speak after a 10:30 a.m. hearing. That hearing was scheduled to address a request by Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores de Maduro, to be released from custody because of ongoing medical problems, including a heart condition. MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM The expected charges would add to a case already involving allegations of cocaine trafficking, narco-terrorism and weapons offenses. Maduro and Flores deny the allegations and have sought to dismiss the case on sovereign immunity grounds. Federal prosecutors pushed back in a recent court filing, arguing neither defendant is entitled to that protection and that Venezuela has not asserted immunity on their behalf. The government noted that the U.S. has not recognized Maduro as Venezuela’s head of state since January 2019. "The defendants are former rogue officials of a formerly rogue state with no entitlement to immunity," prosecutors wrote. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN They argued that foreign sovereign immunity is "a matter of grace and comity on the part of the U.S., and not a restriction imposed by the Constitution." Prosecutors also argued that the alleged cocaine trafficking, narco-terrorism and weapons offenses violated the law rather than served any legitimate government function. Maduro’s attorneys argued in their motion that the court lacks jurisdiction because he is recognized as Venezuela’s head of state. Flores separately filed a motion seeking dismissal on sovereign immunity grounds. Maduro is also challenging the narco-terrorism conspiracy count. title: DAVID MARCUS: In Dayton, Ohio, both parties face bitter political despondency
description: Dayton voters expressed deep skepticism toward Vivek Ramaswamy and Jon Husted, saying neither party delivers real change to struggling Ohio communities.
content: Generally, on reporting trips, the job begins once I land on the ground, hence, "on the ground reporting." But in Dayton, Ohio, I got my first tidbit of information in the air, looking out of my plane’s window to a large farm field below with the giant words, "Trump 28," blasted onto it like a crop circle. It was a reminder that President Donald Trump won the Buckeye State by 11 points in 2024, and, yet, both the Senate and gubernatorial races here are proving uphill climbs for the GOP’s respective nominees — Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy — even with Democratic challengers in former Sen. Sherrod Brown and Dr. Amy Acton whose support feels rather tepid. I spoke with Michael in the Oregon District neighborhood, one of few in this beat-down city of empty storefronts still brimming with life. His attitude seemed to be something akin to a pox on both political parties’ houses. FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC UNITY, REPUBLICAN CROSSOVERS SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE "It doesn’t seem like either candidate is going to be good for anybody," the young man said regarding Ramaswamy and Amy Acton. "It doesn’t matter who you vote for. Either way, they’re not going to represent what the people actually want." When I asked Michael if there was a politician these days who did inspire him, his answer was Texas GOP Congressman Brandon Gill, a far more populist figure than either the technocratic Ramaswamy or the establishment Husted, the latter of whom Michael admitted to knowing almost nothing about. At Blind Bob’s, I met Miss Barbara — as the men there all dotingly called her — a woman in her 70s who has lived in Dayton her entire life. She regaled me with tales of the busy metropolis she remembers from the 1970s and 1980s. "I suppose it was sometime in the '90s that things started going downhill," she told me, citing the loss of GM factories. On the elections, Miss Barbara told me, "I’ll start paying attention soon. I try to keep an open mind," adding in an echo of Michael. "Not much seems to change either way." Just down the road, I found Bonnett’s Book Shop, opened in 1939 by the grandfather of its current owner, Kevin. Once the world’s largest retailers of back-issue magazines, the shop has been a neighborhood fixture for generations. I asked Kevin what he was looking for from his state and federal governments. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS "In the last few decades, there’s been a big push for small businesses," Kevin told Fox News Digital. "There’s been a lot of help for new small businesses. ... We’re not a new business, we don’t get much attention." "We don’t get much attention," seemed to be a running theme from almost all the Daytonites I spoke with this week, very much directed at both political parties. There is a strong case to be made that no state in the union has suffered more grievously from the economic upheavals of the 21st century, from global trade to increased challenges in farming, than Ohio, where the emptiness of small-city America feels just a little more empty. It breaks one’s heart to see the monumental architecture of past glory, as intricate in detail as it is overpowering in scale, brought low, often literally empty shells of a once mighty Midwestern city. Sam, who runs a convenience store in the shadow of the abandoned stone and brick towers, told Fox News Digital, "It just feels like more of the same from both parties. Nothing much gets done." Given the dim view that many Ohioans take of traditional politics, it seems little wonder that Trump has consistently carried the state with big numbers on a message of rebirth and growth that, while it sometimes delivers less than it promises, at least it promises something. TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS Right now, there is not much indication that either Ramaswamy or Husted have the populist magic in a bottle that has rocketed Trump to victory, which explains why the president was in nearby Vandalia last weekend for a rally. Hopeless is too strong a word for Dayton, Ohio, but tired and skeptical are not; tired of a tame politics that cannot fix the big problems like massive amounts of empty commercial property, and skeptical that anyone running today can change that. But it can’t be with either party’s familiar bromides; rather, it must be done with new ideas.

title: Trail Blazers have 'set themselves up to fail' by firing Braiden Bell over teenage tweets, attorney says
description: Braiden Bell's attorney calls the Portland Trail Blazers' morals clause "immoral" for firing the announcer over social media posts he made at age 15.
content: Firing a grown man over social media posts he wrote as a 15-year-old kid has put the Portland Trail Blazers in hot water. Newly hired play-by-play announcer Braiden Bell was ousted shortly after taking the job when a local news report surfaced crude posts from 2012 and 2013. While Bell has navigated the situation with grace and issued an immediate public apology for his teenage posts, getting back into the Blazers' good graces remains a steep battle. Now, Bell's attorney, Arnie Herz, is pushing back against the franchise's approach. Speaking with OutKick, Herz addressed the societal shift toward retroactively punishing individuals for online posts. MEDIA SINKS TO NEW LOW BY DIGGING UP TWEETS THAT GOT ANNOUNCER FIRED BY COWARDLY BLAZERS "What we've become as a society is very much a gotcha and a teardown mindset," Herz explained. "If everything came to light of your most insensitive comments, your worst behaviors, you wouldn't be able to sustain this zero tolerance." Herz added that if the organization strictly enforced such a policy across the board, "I don't think there would be a single player, single member in the front office, a single coach, or a single fan who would be able to participate." Herz pointed out the utter absurdity of holding anyone to such a standard. "The only possible person who could be the play-by-play announcer based on a zero-tolerance standard is Mother Teresa," Herz added. "But there's three problems with that. One, she's not alive. Two, she knew nothing about basketball. And three, I don't think she'd want the job. So, that's it. There's no Saints, except in New Orleans, in football, and obviously, that's just the name." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! While morals clauses are common in sports, Herz argued applying them to teenage posts stretches the rule past common sense. "I'm a big fan of a morals clause," Herz noted. "I totally understand a team that has someone on their personnel who does something egregious, like being charged with a felony, making horrific comments as a grown-up in the course of their employment. ... But having a morals clause that's so broad that it is going to ensnare comments made by a teenage boy in early teenage years, 15, is immoral." "A morals clause properly drafted serves a very valuable moral purpose," Herz added. "And a morals clause overly broad becomes itself immoral. I think that's what we have here." Herz argued Portland's unyielding stance clashes directly with its own past. "Not only do they have no precedence, there's very few organizations in the world of sports that have shown greater leniency to giving second, third, fourth, and fifth chances than the Blazer organization," Herz stated. "This is an organization that's had significant issues in the past and have members on their staff on the court and off the court who have done far, far, far worse than what Mr. Bell did." He added that on-court value changes the rules entirely. NEW YORK TIMES LOSES DEFAMATION SUIT, ORDERED TO PAY $9.25M TO FORMER ALABAMA BASKETBALL PLAYER "When you're a big star, you make a lot of money, the team very much depends on you, the league depends on you, you get more slack," Herz admitted. "That's just the reality. If Braiden could hit a three and defend players like the starting five, we wouldn't be here right now." Herz warned that the franchise's stance sets a troublesome precedent for future hires. "If I'm legal counsel for the Blazers, I'm saying to the Blazers: 'You have to reinstate this guy. If you're gonna fire him for this, every single person on social media is gonna be scrutinizing every hire you make, every player you have on your roster, and it's going to consume you,'" Herz advised. "You've set yourself up to fail. Back off." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Herz urged both sides to acknowledge their mistakes and resolve the matter constructively. "Just like Braiden made a mistake, the Blazers made a mistake," Herz concluded. "Take responsibility, take accountability, let's move forward. title: Black voters, Jewish Democrats in Michigan wary of voting for El-Sayed, say 'he's taking advantage'

content: A group of Black voters and Jewish Democrats in Michigan both expressed reluctance to support Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in the state, during interviews on Monday. title: Flight passenger's odd appearance at major US airport leads officers to wild discovery
description: Photos show cylindrical containers holding 10 live birds allegedly sewn into a flight passenger's underwear on an airplane that arrived in Miami from Havana, Cuba.
content: A traveler's arrival at a Florida airport took an unusual turn after customs officers noticed something suspicious during an inspection. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers at Miami International Airport spotted what court documents described as an "unexplained bulge" around a passenger's waist and pelvic area after he arrived on a flight from Havana, Cuba, according to a federal complaint obtained by Fox News Digital. A closer inspection allegedly uncovered 10 live birds concealed beneath the traveler's clothing, the complaint said. AIRPORT X-RAY REVEALS SHOCKING ILLEGAL STASH CONCEALED BESIDE PASSENGER'S XBOX Alberto Hernandez Castillo, a native of Cuba and legal permanent resident of the United States, arrived in Miami Oct. 4. CBP officers selected him for a secondary inspection. Castillo signed a customs declaration indicating he was not bringing animals or wildlife into the United States, according to court documents. Officers first searched a carry-on bag and fanny pack belonging to Castillo but did not find any contraband. During routine questioning about his trip, officers noticed the bulge beneath his clothing and said Castillo "appeared nervous," prompting them to conduct a pat-down. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The search allegedly revealed six clear cylindrical containers holding live birds. The containers were wrapped in tape and tucked inside black pockets sewn into his underwear, according to the complaint. Officers recovered 10 birds from the containers, which were preliminarily identified as eight yellow-faced grassquits and two blue grosbeaks, court documents said. Photos included in the complaint show the containers after they were removed, as well as how they were allegedly concealed beneath the man's clothing. The man said the concealed items were for his "personal use." When questioned about the birds, Castillo allegedly told authorities they were for his "personal use." He later invoked his right to remain silent, according to the complaint. title: Jewish student sues New York school on Oct 7 anniversary over 'relentless antisemitic harassment'
description: Student Sophie Shabot alleged antisemitic assault and harassment at The New School's Parsons School of Design in a new lawsuit by The Lawfare Project.
content: The Lawfare Project announced on the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 Hamas attacks on Israel that it filed a lawsuit against The New School on behalf of a Jewish Israeli-American student it alleged faced "relentless antisemitic harassment, intimidation, and physical assault" as a student at the New York university. According to the legal group, New School student Sophie Shabot faced numerous instances of name-calling, intimidation and obstruction based on her religion and support for Israel at the Parsons School of Design. She was reportedly called names like "Zio b----" and "baby killer" and prevented from entering the University Center. In another instance, protesters allegedly vandalized and disrupted a Hillel event featuring an Israeli speaker in 2024. Shabot was among several Jewish students who were trapped in a dean's office as a group of protesters attempted to have them turn over the speaker. JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS According to The Lawfare Project, university officials failed to stop the harassment against Shabot and other Jewish students and even "at times rewarded those responsible." "There is no question in my mind that the New School violated its Title VI obligations and other obligations under the law in not intervening and taking meaningful action to stop the antisemitic, anti-Israeli harassment that my plaintiff endured while she was at the New School," Lawfare Project director of litigation Ziporah Reich told Fox News Digital. Reich, who also filed the lawsuit, added that more often than not, Jewish students like Shabot were the ones who faced consequences at universities following antisemitic actions by other students. "If the pro-Hamas protesters are essentially threatening your physical safety when you're trying to have a Jewish event, let's just shut down the event to make sure you're safe. When a group of pro-Hamas protesters occupy a space in which you're supposed to have an event, let's just move you somewhere else to a smaller, less accommodating place. In other words, she was bearing the brunt of the consequences for the negative harassment of the offenders," Reich said. JEWISH UCLA STUDENTS BEATEN WITH STICKS, PEPPER SPRAYED AND KNOCKED OUT BY ANTI-ISRAEL CAMPUS MOB: LAWSUIT Reich also acknowledged the significance of filing the lawsuit Wednesday on the anniversary of the attacks that killed more than 1,200 people in Israel and led to more than 250 people being abducted. "It's extremely important for the Jewish community to recognize that what happened immediately after Oct. 7 didn't end immediately after Oct. 7 because the harassment of Jewish students and Jews everywhere has continued and even if it has lessened to some extent in certain universities, it has not gone away. It's essentially in a quiet period where we know that at any minute it can rear its ugly head again. These students are activists without a cause," Reich said. The lawsuit brings claims under Title VI, New York state and city civil and human rights laws and claims for breach of contract and negligent infliction of emotional distress. It is seeking damages, statutory penalties, attorneys’ fees and costs, and other relief and demands a jury trial. Will Wilbur, Director of Communications at The New School, told Fox News Digital, "The New School does not tolerate antisemitism. We are dedicated to maintaining a campus environment where students can learn and grow free from harassment or discrimination of any kind." ANTI-ISRAEL NYC PROTESTERS CHANT SUPPORT FOR HAMAS, DEMAND MAMDANI MAKE MAJOR CHANGES AT RALLY The New School's Parsons School of Design was previously sued by the Dhillon Law Group in 2025 over similar allegations made by graduate Brandon White. White claimed that the school had opened a disciplinary investigation against him after he reported incidents of harassment while his assailants received no retaliation.
