title: Trump is fighting Obamacare fraud. Democrats are defending the numbers
description: Trump's CMS crackdown canceled 315,000 unauthorized Obamacare enrollments covering 760,000 people, targeting $2.2 billion in fraudulent subsidies.
content: Democrats love double-talk. They claim to defend affordable healthcare while taxpayers finance fraudulent enrollments that harm the very consumers Obamacare was supposed to protect. Right on cue, they turned the Trump administration’s fraud crackdown into cruelty. Chuck Schumer claims the administration is kicking hundreds of thousands of people off their plans, while former Speaker Nancy Pelosi calls fraud enforcement a "false pretext" for stripping away coverage. Before Democrats declare 760,000 people victims of Republican cruelty, they should explain why taxpayers were financing policies that some consumers never requested, used or knew existed. The Trump administration recently announced that CMS canceled approximately 315,000 unauthorized Obamacare enrollments covering more than 760,000 people and expected to recover approximately $2.2 billion in taxpayer-funded subsidies. An additional 419,000 enrollments are undergoing eligibility verification. Every taxpayer and every family struggling to afford health insurance should be alarmed. Instead, Rep. Richard Neal, the ranking Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, accused Republicans of "[doubling] down to take [coverage] away entirely," warning that the crackdown would increase medical debt and healthcare costs without acknowledging the fraudulent enrollment or the $2.2 billion in subsidies the administration expects to recover. GAO found that Biden-era controls failed to verify consumer consent, restrict broker access or notify patients when plans changed. Complaints involving confirmed unauthorized activity more than quadrupled from 2023 through 2025. Predatory brokers used basic personal information to enroll consumers or switch their plans without permission, changed their contact information to conceal the activity and then collected compensation from insurers. Victims risked losing doctors or medications, paying higher copayments and deductibles or repaying tax credits based on false information. BOMBSHELL REPORT EXPOSES HEALTHCARE FRAUD SCHEMES AS TAXPAYERS LOSE UP TO $521 BILLION ANNUALLY Democrats are defending enrollment numbers while President Trump is defending patients and taxpayers. Voters care about both fraud and affordability. Healthcare fraud is clearly an affordability issue. Every dollar lost to waste or fraud is a dollar unavailable to lower costs or provide care to a legitimate patient. President Trump’s fraud crackdown proves that protecting patients, safeguarding taxpayers and making healthcare affordable are all part of the same fight. Obamacare was sold as affordable healthcare, but affordability is measured by whether eligible patients knowingly receive coverage at a price they can afford, not by fraudulent enrollment numbers. Putting the patient first requires the administration to distinguish suspected fraud from legitimate patients caught in an eligibility review because of a missing document, outdated address or administrative error. Anyone wrongly removed should receive clear notice, a reasonable opportunity to verify eligibility and prompt restoration of coverage without losing care. Due process strengthens the crackdown by directing accountability toward fraud brokers who initiated questionable applications, enrolled consumers without consent and then pocketed compensation from unauthorized policies. Under CMS’s recent anti-fraud safeguards, brokers must reverify their identities and include verifiable Social Security numbers or immigration-document numbers. CMS also announced that electronic consumer authorization would be required before a broker makes changes to an application. GAO separately recommended stronger consent controls, including one-time passcodes, restrictions on broker access and notifications of broker activity. GAO also found that dishonest brokers could change consumers’ contact information and that CMS only sent notices to the newly submitted contact. To close that loophole, GAO recommended that CMS should alert both the old and new contacts whenever an email address or telephone number is changed, so a dishonest broker cannot conceal unauthorized activity. American families judge healthcare through whether they can afford premiums, see their doctors and fill their prescriptions. Republicans can win on affordability by following the Trump standard of care: Protect legitimate patients, provide due process and prosecute those who knowingly profited from abuse. title: Grocery shoppers may be relying on a 'misleading' clue when choosing healthy foods
description: Shoppers view foods with shorter shelf lives as more natural, but UBC Sauder research reveals packaging technology often explains the difference.
content: A shorter shelf life may make food seem fresher and healthier, but new research suggests that may be more perception than reality. A study from the University of British Columbia (UBC) Sauder School of Business in Canada found that many shoppers use a food's shelf life as a shortcut for judging how natural it is, even though longer shelf lives can reflect factors beyond heavy processing. The team, which included researchers from China, conducted a series of experiments in which participants compared foods with different shelf lives, including potato chips, pasta sauce, mayonnaise and granola bars. YOUR BRAIN MAY BE TRICKING YOU INTO LIKING ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS, STUDY FINDS Shoppers consistently viewed foods with shorter shelf lives as more natural and healthier, even when the ingredients and nutritional facts were nearly identical or the difference in shelf life was solely due to better packaging. In the case of the mayonnaise, the only difference between the two products was that one had a better seal, allowing it to stay fresh longer — it was no more processed than the other. Yet participants still viewed the shorter-shelf-life option as more natural. Even when they were given clear indications that a longer-lasting product just had better packaging, shoppers still used shelf life as a gauge, the researchers found. JUST ONE SMALL SERVING OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD A DAY LINKED TO HIGHER DISEASE RISK, MAJOR STUDY FINDS In other experiments, participants rated potato chips with a five-month shelf life as more natural and healthier than nearly identical chips with a nine-month shelf life. Nearly 70% of participants selected a pasta sauce with a one-year shelf life when they were encouraged to prioritize natural foods. That figure dropped to 43% when the emphasis shifted to reducing food waste and protecting the environment, as the researchers found that participants also associated longer shelf life with less waste because items wouldn't go bad as quickly. The findings, published in the Journal of Consumer Psychology earlier this year, suggest shoppers often use shelf life as a "mental shortcut" when making purchasing decisions, researchers said. AMERICANS ARE DITCHING ULTRA-PROCESSED SNACKS FOR AN ANCIENT FRUIT THAT'S EXPLODING IN POPULARITY "Our research shows consumers are using shelf life as a shortcut for judging whether foods are natural," co-author Yann Cornil, an associate professor at UBC Sauder, told Fox News Digital. "It sometimes can be diagnostic, but shelf life is also very much dependent on the quality of the packaging, which has nothing to do with food naturalness." Cornil added that the shortcut can be "misleading." THIS AMOUNT OF DELI MEAT ASSOCIATED WITH HIGHER DEMENTIA RISK IN COMPELLING NEW REVIEW Packaging has improved dramatically, he noted, just like refrigeration did 60 years ago, to improve food preservation. "Don't judge a food by its shelf life." The tendency to equate a shorter shelf life with less processing may have unintended consequences, according to the researchers. Buyers may therefore skip products that are just as healthy while choosing items that are more likely to spoil before they can be eaten. Products like canned beans, frozen fruits and vegetables and dried oats can stay fresh for months or even years thanks to preservation methods and packaging rather than added ingredients. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "A shorter shelf life does not automatically mean a food is healthier," Kelly Springer, a New York-based registered dietitian and founder and CEO of Kelly's Choice, told Fox News Digital. "Better seals, oxygen barriers and moisture-control packaging help foods stay fresh longer while maintaining quality and safety." Springer pointed to some packaged items such as guacamole, which can have a longer refrigerated shelf life because of high-pressure processing and packaging technology rather than added preservatives, yet are still healthy choices. Other items such as milk, yogurt and kefir can stay fresh longer due to pasteurization and fermentation — not necessarily added ingredients. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Don't judge a food by its shelf life," Springer, who was not involved in the research, added. "Turn the package over, read the nutrition label and make decisions based on what's inside." She recommends consumers focus on fiber, protein, added sugar and sodium rather than the expiration date alone. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Cornil added that saturated fat content can also be problematic. "Too many ingredients, in particular ingredients [such as] additives and preservatives that you can't recognize, or can't even pronounce, may be a signal of too much processing and unhealthiness," Cornil said. "It's not always true, but I would say that it is more diagnostic than shelf life information." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The findings are especially relevant as many seek to reduce how much ultra-processed food they eat. Roughly 55% of Americans' daily caloric intake is from ultra-processed foods, the researchers noted.

title: The Athletic column urging Indiana Fever to part ways with Sophie Cunningham draws widespread criticism
description: Martina Navratilova and thousands online fired back at Candace Buckner's column arguing the Indiana Fever should part ways with Sophie Cunningham.
content: The phrase "80-20 issue" is thrown out quite a bit in spaces such as these. But Tuesday, a 95-5 issue seems to have emerged. The 95% in this case? The people on the internet bashing a piece from The Athletic that attacked WNBA guard Sophie Cunningham. Columnist Candace Buckner argued that the soon-to-be free agent was a "combustible" figure whose "turbulent" opinions were a distraction to the Indiana Fever. Never mind that Cunningham's most publicized stance — that biological males shouldn't compete in female sports — is shared by the vast majority of the country. SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SENDS MESSAGE TO HER HATERS AFTER SAYING MEN DON'T BELONG IN WOMEN'S SPORTS Buckner's conclusion? That the Fever must part ways with Sophie so that they "can go back to being a basketball team." This sparked the public to break out their drivers. Among the most prominent critics teeing off was nine-time Wimbledon winner Martina Navratilova, a staunch advocate of keeping men out of women's spaces. Said the tennis legend on X: "Buckner seems to forget the W in @WNBA stand for women. There was nothing wrong with what Sophie said originally. It’s the response from WNBA that made it blow up. The policy is the problem, not Sophie Cunningham." This is hard to deny. The "circus" Buckner says surrounds Cunningham wouldn't exist if the WNBA could simply define what a woman is. Doing so would have kept former NBA players such as Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White from declaring their intent to enter the WNBA Draft. But the W doesn't want to have that discussion. Its leaders are too afraid of the internal blowback. They opt for the more widespread external blowback instead. Another Buckner critic was podcast host Stephen L. Miller, who focused less on the trans issue and more on the media's hypocrisy. Mocking the Athletic's post on X, Miller wrote: "If the San Francisco 49ers want to go back to being a football team, Colin Kaepernick has to go." KAEPERNICK TELLS 'THE VIEW' THAT NFL OWNERS KEPT HIM OUT OVER POLITICS AND POWER, CLAIMS THEY DONATE TO TRUMP Yes. I can make a Namath-esque guarantee that nobody in media decrying Cunningham as a distraction had that same energy for Kaepernick 10 years ago. Forget that Kaepernick made a conscious decision to enter the political fray whereas Sophie simply answered a question about trans athletes in an ESPN interview. The problem for media pundits isn't that Cunningham has "big opinions," as Buckner said — it's that she has the wrong opinions. But the disdain players and critics have for Sophie is often projected onto her fans as well. There seems to be this idea that Fever supporters are these backward hillbillies filled with hate because they back players embraced in conservative circles. So, you'll get players such as Angel Reese claiming that they heard racist comments from attendees in Indiana, or Brittney Griner saying that the league's "new fans" shouted racial slurs at her. Except, there hasn't been an ounce of evidence that any of this "hate" it taking place in real time. Which led to this rather on-the-nose post from the X account Veritas Explorer, which wrote "The real story was the anti-Fever, racist media campaign led by Jussie Smollett." SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS SPORTS All in all there were 1.3K comments on The Athletic's tweet linking to Buckner's column against 1.1K likes. That's a standard "ratio" — as the repulsed replies flooded in. What was interesting is that Buckner didn't tweet the column out on her personal account, which she often does. She likely knew what kind of reaction awaited her. To be fair, though, this is X — whose political tenor has shifted rightward since Elon Musk bought the platform four years ago. So maybe the readers over at The Athletic/New York Times were digging the take? Eh...not so much. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The most "liked" comment (by far) under her column read as follows. "Hold up. I clicked on this article because I wanted to see the basketball reasons why they should trade Cunningham. Turns out there are none, and the issue is because of off the court issues with something she said. And that is just stupid. I currently live in a city with a football team that employs Deshaun Watson, someone who is far far more destructive to the dignity of women and yet he plays and we don’t get constant columns how he should be. The WNBA should be about the top level of Women’s Basketball. Not the top level of women’s basketball who happen to agree with you. That alone will harm this league more than anything." The second-most "liked" comment was more succinct. "Candace had this one in the drafts for 6 months lol. Sophie did nothing wrong." title: Bassmaster pro Cooper Gallant says bass fishing is actually more fun without LiveScope sonar
description: Cooper Gallant uses Garmin LiveScope at the highest level of bass fishing but admits the sport might be more fun without forward-facing sonar.
content: There's no more divisive piece of equipment in bass fishing than forward-facing sonar. Depending on whom you ask, technology like Garmin LiveScope is either one of the greatest tools ever handed to an angler or the thing that's sucking the fun and skill out of fishing. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Cooper Gallant sees both sides. The Bassmaster Elite Series pro certainly isn't anti-technology. He uses LiveScope, knows how valuable it can be and understands that, at his level, refusing to adapt isn't really an option. But is fishing actually more fun without it? Yeah, maybe. B.A.S.S. flips a coin to determine LiveScope use in 2027 The timing of Gallant's comments is especially interesting now that we know exactly when Elite Series anglers will — and won't — have access to the technology next season. B.A.S.S. revealed the results of its 2027 live-sonar coin flips Tuesday, and perhaps the most intriguing result is Lake St. Clair. When the Elite Series visits the famed smallmouth fishery Aug. 5-8, forward-facing sonar will be prohibited. That's notable because St. Clair has become closely associated with the electronics-driven techniques that have transformed modern smallmouth fishing. It'll also be the eighth event of the season, with Angler of the Year points and Bassmaster Classic qualification increasingly important. The coin also determined that live sonar will be allowed at the 2027 Bassmaster Classic on Lake Hartwell, while the 2028 Classic will be contested without it. Gallant will have to compete under both sets of rules next season. And while he's certainly not giving up his electronics when they're allowed, he admitted there's something to be said for fishing without them. Cooper Gallant says fishing can be more fun without LiveScope Gallant gave me a crash course in LiveScope while we were fishing Table Rock Lake in Missouri last week. Watch the full video here: For those who don't know, forward-facing sonar allows anglers to see what's happening beneath the water in real time. Instead of simply casting toward a promising spot and hoping there's a fish hanging around, an angler can use the technology to locate fish and even watch how they react to a lure. "This transducer basically shoots wherever my trolling motor is facing," Gallant explained. "I have it set at 120 feet, so I can see 120 feet out in front of me." Fish, trees, rocks — whatever is down there, he can see it. And, more importantly, he can see what the fish does next. "You can see your bait, you can see the fish react to your bait," he said. "It's all in real time." That's obviously incredibly useful when you're trying to make a living catching bass. It's also a heck of a time-saver. Of course, not every tournament allows LiveScope. So I asked Gallant whether fishing without all that technology feels like a welcome challenge or a daunting task. Turns out, he actually enjoys it. "I think sometimes without it, it’s more fun," Gallant said. "There’s more unknown. You don’t know if there’s a fish there, and when you get a bite, it’s more of a surprise." That's a pretty interesting admission from someone who competes at the highest level of a sport that has spent the past several years arguing about this exact technology. Without LiveScope, you might know you're fishing a good-looking spot. You might have a pretty good idea there are bass nearby. But you don't get to watch the whole thing unfold on a screen before the bite ever happens. Gallant isn't saying he'd throw his electronics overboard. Far from it. "It's incredible technology," he said. He's simply acknowledging something plenty of recreational anglers probably understand. The most efficient way to catch a fish isn't necessarily the most fun way to catch one. Sometimes there's something to be said for chucking a lure into the water and having absolutely no idea what's about to happen. LiveScope isn't going anywhere in professional bass fishing Of course, Gallant doesn't have the luxury of approaching every day on the water like a casual Sunday fishing trip with a novice like me. For professional anglers, technology is part of the job. And when I asked him about some veteran anglers' reluctance to embrace forward-facing sonar, he was sympathetic — to a point. "I think the older generation, they're just hesitant to learn it," Gallant said. "But it's just like anything. The sport evolves." And so does the technology. Gallant said younger anglers may have an advantage simply because many of them grew up learning to fish with advanced electronics. But for anyone trying to compete at the highest level, ignoring that evolution isn't much of an option. "You have to learn it, or you're going to get left behind," he said. That's not a new position for Gallant, either. Before the 2025 Elite Series season, he wrote for Bassmaster that professional anglers had to adopt forward-facing sonar when LiveScope arrived to avoid falling behind their competition. Still, B.A.S.S. has spent the past year experimenting with what competition looks like when anglers don't have access to it. COOPER GALLANT SLEPT IN HIS TRUCK FOR YEARS CHASING PRO FISHING DREAM: 'I DIDN'T HAVE A PLAN B' In 2026, the organization introduced a split format for the Elite Series, with forward-facing sonar permitted at five of nine regular-season tournaments and prohibited at the other four. Lake Guntersville, where FFS was prohibited, became the most-watched Elite event of the regular season with more than 21 million minutes viewed across B.A.S.S. digital platforms. The St. Lawrence River finale, where anglers could use FFS, was second with more than 20 million minutes viewed. B.A.S.S. apparently liked the balance. The organization announced last month that the 50/50 format will return for 2027, with Tuesday's coin flip determining which events land on which side. For the first time, the Bassmaster Classic is getting the same treatment: One flip will determine whether forward-facing sonar is allowed at the 2027 Classic, with the opposite rules automatically applying in 2028. Now we know how that split will look in 2027. Live sonar will be permitted at Lake Okeechobee, Lake Fork, Santee Cooper Lakes, the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway and the Mississippi River. It will be prohibited at Kissimmee Chain of Lakes, the Sabine River, Lake Seminole and Lake St. Clair. And for the first time, the Classic will join the experiment. Live sonar will be allowed at the 2027 Bassmaster Classic on Lake Hartwell, while the technology will be banned at the 2028 Classic, regardless of where that tournament is ultimately held. It's an interesting compromise for a sport still figuring out exactly how much technology it wants at its highest level. And Gallant's perspective might be a pretty good summary of the whole debate. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER LiveScope can make you more efficient. It can show you fish you might never have known were there. At the professional level, learning how to use it can be the difference between keeping up and getting left behind. But take it away? And hey, you might just have a little more fun. title: Rubio sounds campaign-ready as he rails against open borders, globalism in speech from ancient Greek ruins
description: Marco Rubio will deliver a major address near the Acropolis calling on Americans and Europeans to reject decline and renew Western civilization.
content: Secretary of State Marco Rubio took aim at open borders and globalism Wednesday in a sweeping speech in Athens, Greece that at times sounded more like a campaign stump speech than a foreign policy address. "We opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay," Rubio said against the backdrop of the sun setting on the ancient citadel in Athens. "The word nationalism became a dirty word. And so we tore down our monuments, we condemned our own history, and in too many places we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit," he continued. "And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control." Rubio and Vice President JD Vance have both been widely discussed as potential successors to Trump in 2028, with the president himself repeatedly fueling speculation over which of the two could inherit his political mantle. Rubio argued the consequences were now playing out in an increasingly dangerous world. TRUMP’S COUNTERTERRORISM STRATEGY SCORES BIG WINS AGAINST GLOBAL TERROR THREATS "As the West's confidence faltered, its adversaries and rivals only grew more assertive," he said. Rubio called the current moment an "inflection point," warning that the threats facing the West are "every bit as real as they were during antiquity." "And now there is war again. There is competition between great powers again," he said. Rubio singled out Iran as he drew a sharp distinction between Western values and those of its adversaries. "Fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself," Rubio said. "Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but our heroes do not worship death," he went on. "It is precisely because we value life, that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles." The secretary of State delivered the address from the Acropolis, using the birthplace of Western civilization to trace America's own inheritance from Ancient Greece. "For twenty-five centuries since, the Parthenon has stood. Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow," Rubio said. "Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now, I stand here today – as the Secretary of State of that republic, and as the great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space, can ever extinguish." Rubio said he saw signs that Europe was beginning to reverse the trends he described. "We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago," Rubio said. "There are already signs. Across this continent, we are witnessing the beginning of what we hope will be a generational shift." During his visit, Rubio announced a new counterterrorism partnership between the U.S. and Greece. He emphasized the strategic importance of Greece on Wednesday, calling it a "source of stability in an unstable world." "As you see a world that faces these destabilizing events, you recognize how important this alliance with Greece is to the United States," Rubio said. "It is a source of stability in an unstable world." At the Munich Security Conference in Germany in February, Rubio delivered a speech on the topic that earned him a standing ovation from European leaders, and racked up millions of views online. One popular X user described it as "one of the greatest" speeches by a Secretary of State in decades. Many others insisted the speech upped Rubio's potential 2028 presidential chances. AS AMERICA MARKS 250 YEARS, OUR GREATEST CHAPTERS ARE STILL AHEAD OF US Rubio described the five centuries before the end of World War II, a time when the West had expanded across the globe, building "vast empires." But, he said, after the war, Europe was in ruins, and "godless communist revolutions" in Europe caused people to believe that the West's dominance was forever finished. "Against that backdrop, then, as now, many came to believe that the West's age of dominance had come to an end, and that our future was destined to be a faint and feeble echo of our past. But together, our predecessors recognized that decline was a choice, and it was a choice they refused to make," he said. Rubio urged the European leaders to reinvigorate that spirit. "This is why we do not want out allies to be shackled by guilt and shame," he continued. "We want allies that are proud of our culture and our heritage, and understand that we are heirs to the same great and noble civilization and who together with us, are willing and able to defend it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And this is why we don't want allies to rationalize the broken status quo, rather than what is necessary to reckon with what is necessary to fix it. For we in America have no interest in being polite and orderly caretakers of the West's managed decline. We do not seek to separate, but to revitalize an old friendship and renew the greatest civilization in human history."

title: Nolan Wells' friends sue Terrell Owens for defamation after he demanded their arrests
description: Three friends of Nolan Wells filed a defamation lawsuit against Terrell Owens over his X post demanding their arrest after the student's death.
content: Three friends of Nolan Wells, the college student who disappeared from a Fourth of July celebration on a Mississippi island and was later found dead, have sued former NFL star Terrell Owens for defamation. The friends — Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour — accused the Hall of Fame wide receiver of defaming them after he posted on X: "ARREST THEM IMMEDIATELY!!" The fathers of the three friends filed the federal lawsuit on their sons' behalf Monday. All three are under 21, making them minors under Mississippi law. Hudson, Pitalo and Seymour were among a large group of friends who traveled by boat with 18-year-old Wells to Horn Island on the Fourth of July. The three all said Wells did not return to mainland Mississippi with the group because he was talking to a girl, an account his family has disputed. Wells' body was found two days later off the island's coast. NOLAN WELLS' FRIENDS CLEARED BY GRAND JURY AS THEIR LAWYERS VOW TO HOLD ONLINE ACCUSERS ACCOUNTABLE Images showing Wells, who was Black, with his white friends before his disappearance circulated widely online, with some social media users viewing the circumstances surrounding his death through a racial lens and directing suspicion toward his friends. Owens joined the public criticism in a Sept. 26 post that remains online. The post links to an Instagram reel by content creator Trent Out Loud that accused the three young men of deleting Snapchat messages from Wells' phone after his death while also suggesting they may have been responsible for killing him. However, Andrew Garrett, a digital forensics expert hired by attorney Benjamin Crump, examined Wells' phone and concluded that no one accessed it between 2:18 p.m. on July 4, when Wells last unlocked it, and 3:14 a.m. on July 5, when his parents gained access to the device. Garrett also clarified that Snapchat messages can disappear from a recipient's phone when they are remotely deleted by the person who sent them. 'THE WIND AND DRIFT PATTERNS TELL A STORY,' CAJUN NAVY OFFICIAL SAYS OF MISSING MISSISSIPPI TEEN FOUND DEAD In the lawsuit, the friends say Owens, 52, circulated a false narrative about them and accused them of crimes they did not commit. "The Defamatory X Post also placed Warren, Jax, and Morgan before Owens’ audience in a false light, as murderers and participants in a murder coverup who had escaped justice," according to the lawsuit. "There was absolutely no evidence to prompt an arrest of the Plaintiffs because they had done nothing wrong, and there was no probable cause to arrest Plaintiffs because they had not committed a crime." Owens and SMAC Entertainment, which lists him as a client on its website, did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. GOVERNOR BLAMES ACTIVISTS IN NOLAN WELLS CASE FOR ‘STOKING DIVISION,’ OFFICIAL SAYS FBI PROBING THREATS On Sept. 22, days before Owens' post, a grand jury said Wells' death was "consistent with drowning" and declined to recommend charges against anyone. The grand jury did note that the state's autopsy report, which has not been made public, and an independent autopsy commissioned by the family found that Wells had bruising on the back of his head. The family's forensic pathologist, Roger A. Mitchell Jr., classified Wells' death as "undetermined," saying he could not rule out non-accidental factors because Wells did not appear too intoxicated to swim and had "apparent acute blunt force injuries to the head and body prior to his death." "Our son was found on ​federal ⁠land and we are asking the FBI to step in and do a full investigation," said Elmore Wonsley, Wells' father.

title: Imperiled House Democrat gets ripped by left and right after flip-flop on transgender sports

content: One of the most vulnerable House Democrats of the 2026 election cycle is being hammered from the left and right for her stance on transgender youth. Longtime Rep. Kaptur is in damage control, and she must remove herself as a co-sponsor of the Equality Act and disavow her previous votes or remove her lies from the airwaves," National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) spokesman Zach Bannon told Fox News Digital. That stance is creating political headaches for Kaptur on the other side of the aisle, as well. Ohio progressives are accusing Kaptur of throwing transgender kids under the bus to score electoral points. LGBTQ advocacy group Equality Ohio graded Kaptur a "D" for having "recently released anti-trans ads." Lucas County Stonewall Democrats wrote in an open letter to Kaptur, "Shame on you and your campaign staff for pushing this incredibly harmful anti-Trans rhetoric." Kaptur’s name on my resume. So much so that I removed it." Kaptur has survived prior redistricting bids by Republicans to serve her Toledo-area district for over four decades. title: Nickelodeon parent guides tackle gender identity, anti-racism and Islamophobia
description: Nickelodeon's parent resources page offers guides on gender identity, anti-racism, and countering Islamophobia, drawing sharp criticism online.
content: The popular children’s network Nickelodeon is facing criticism over its "Parent Resources" webpage, which provides guides for discussing anti-racism, gender identity, and other social issues with children. The resources touch upon various controversial topics, such as "countering Islamophobia" and "How to talk to kids about the attack on the Capitol," while providing talking points for parents and caregivers on how to approach each subject with their children, according to the website. In one 31-page document, Nickelodeon — in partnership with the LGBT organization Glisten, formerly known as GLSEN — lays out a step-by-step guide for teachers titled "Talk & Take Action: An Educators' Guide to Combating LGBTQIA+ Discrimination." "When preparing to talk about topics around identity, gender, and sexuality with students, it’s important to frame those discussions in ways that maximize opportunities to learn, while at the same time ensuring that students don’t leave the encounter confused, afraid, or traumatized," the guide reads. PORTLAND PARENT BANNED FROM SCHOOL EVENTS AFTER OPPOSING GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT FILES LAWSUIT "This guide delves into misgendering, discriminatory acts, and other forms of discrimination the LGBTQ+ community has endured, which can be challenging for all of us to read and talk about," it continues. The guide goes on to provide educators with a glossary of terms relating to the LGBTQ community and tips on how to "foster an inclusive classroom" for students — such as displaying LGBTQ flags and posters in their classrooms. Another resource titled "Talk and Take Action: Parents', Caregivers' and Educators' Guide to Countering Islamophobia" lays out the "history of activism against Islamophobia," while also providing parents with a discussion guide on educating children about the Muslim faith. "Explore the basic tenets of Islam. Similar to Judaism and Christianity, people who practice Islam believe in one God, called Allah," the guide states. The guide goes on to provide talking points for young children regarding how they can speak up if they encounter an individual who is being bullied for their faith, while encouraging the reader to be an "Upstander" for their peers. HARVARD OFFERS ‘ANTI-RACIST’ RESOURCES FOR PARENTS AS STUDENTS HEAD BACK TO SCHOOL It then lists examples of ways a child could respond if they encounter someone who is being bullied because of their Islamic faith, such as saying, "Hey, that is mean. Remember, your words can hurt people." Another Nickelodeon document, "Talking to Kids: Capitol Attack Resources," provides links for adults discussing the Capitol riot on Jan. 6, 2021, with children. The webpage and its resources have drawn criticism from social media users and a psychotherapist who told Fox News Digital that the guides go beyond the network's traditional entertainment role. In a reply to Libs of TikTok’s X post sharing the guides, one user wrote, "Kids network with a parent guide on gender and anti-racism. That’s not cartoons and that’s NOT fun. That’s recruitment. Keep them off it." MS RACHEL DEFENDS HER ACTIVISM BY POINTING TO MISTER ROGERS' POLITICAL LEGACY ON CHILDREN'S TV HOW MS RACHEL'S POLITICAL ACTIVISM IS SPARKING PUSHBACK FROM PARENTS Another user blasted the content, writing on X, "A kids’ network pushing ‘anti-racism,’ gender ideology, and the rest to parents as official resources. They’re not hiding it anymore. Parents, check what your kids’ shows are linking." Jonathan Alpert, a New York-based psychotherapist and author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital the guides could force children to begin looking at the world from a political lens prematurely, therefore harming their ability to relate to their peers. "There’s nothing controversial about teaching kids not to bully someone because of their religion. That’s basic decency and every parent should support and get behind that," Alpert told Fox News Digital. "But once you start teaching 7-year-olds about systemic discrimination and white supremacy, you’ve crossed into something very different." Alpert added that young children are not focused on "weighing different ideas about race and society," adding that "kids absorb what an adult in authority tells them is true." According to Alpert, the network’s encouragement of parents and educators discussing controversial — and often political — topics could have an unintended negative impact on the children they are teaching. "At an age when they should be learning how to get along with each other, adults are introducing complex ideas about power, privilege and oppression," Alpert said. "This may actually be teaching kids to focus on differences they otherwise wouldn’t be thinking much about." title: 'Saved by the Bell' star Dennis Haskins' cause of death revealed: report

"Dennis Haskins was a steady presence in my teenage years, the kind of figure who kept us in line while making sure we knew he was in our corner. title: Biden's 'weaponized' Mar-a-Lago raid slammed by White House as declassified docs reveal FBI's legal doubts
description: Declassified emails reveal the FBI's Washington Field Office told the DOJ it lacked probable cause for the Mar-a-Lago raid weeks before it happened.
content: The White House ripped Joe Biden after documents declassified by President Donald Trump on Monday revealed internal strife between the former president's Department of Justice (DOJ) and the FBI's Washington Field Office (WFO) before carrying out a raid on Mar-a-Lago in 2022. In the months leading up to the raid, internal emails between FBI agents in the field office expressed frustration that the DOJ, led by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland, was unresponsive to their requests and unwilling to consider alternative options to raiding Trump's estate in Palm Beach, Florida a year-and-a-half after he left office after his first term. Fox News Digital exclusively reported on the internal emails, which show the FBI didn't believe it had probable cause to execute the warrant, in December. "Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple," the White House said Tuesday. "This is further proof the Biden administration weaponized the DOJ to target political opponents. Those responsible must be held accountable." TODD BLANCHE REVEALS DOJ UNEARTHED CACHE OF JACK SMITH DOCUMENTS INSIDE FORGOTTEN ROOM An email dated May 24, 2022, with the subject line "PE (Plasma Echo) Next steps - timeline preference - UNCLASSIFIED," the special agent in charge of the counterintelligence division of the WFO sent an internal email detailing a proposed timeline for the investigation, ending with the execution of a search warrant. That target date was June 6 of that year. The raid would eventually take place on Aug. 8, 2022. Another agent replied asking the first to loop the DOJ in on the timeline. What followed was skepticism that the raid was even necessary. "[REDACTED] and I also agreed if there was a way to obtain the records via the [REDACTED], without the execution of the SW (search warrant), it would be preferable," the special agent in charge said. Another batch of internal emails from June 1-2, 2022, shows the FBI seeking a potential off-ramp from the investigation that was heading towards the execution of the raid. "Even as we continue down the path towards a search warrant, WFO believes that a reasonable conversation with the former President's attorney, [REDACTED], ought not to be discounted," the email said. "At a minimum, even if the former President's attorney is correct and that the documents were all declassified (or believed to be declassified), it can be reasonably argued that the documents remain sensitive and should be properly secured until the matter of classification is sorted out. This conversation could easily be accomplished at the same time that WFO presses forward with the investigation and continues building out the search warrant." JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS The emails noted that Trump's defense attorneys would likely argue that the president has the absolute authority to declassify documents and expressed frustration that the DOJ, despite being asked, had not provided the FBI with a list of the charges they might file. An internal email from July 13, 2022, less than a month before the raid, the assistant special agent in charge of the WFO said flatly that the FBI didn't believe there was probable cause for the raid. "WFO does not believe (and has articulated to DOJ CES), that we have established probable cause for the search warrant at Mar a Lago. DOJ has opined that they do, requesting the a wide scope including residence, office, storage space," that email says. The agent annoyedly continued by implying that the DOJ wasn't interested in recovering the allegedly mishandled classified documents, intimating that there may have been an ulterior motive. "Finally, if the goal is to identify and recover classified records quickly, so as to protect the information, the 5 weeks spent fixated on probable cause for a search warrant have been counterproductive," the email said. The agent offered other solutions to the raid, including re-interviewing Trump's attorney and attempting to find other material witnesses. BIDEN-ERA FBI TRACKED TRUMP FAMILY TRAVEL AND WILES' CALLS WITH LAWYERS IN SECRET PROBE: DOCS "A reasonable step would be to recontact the attorney and inquire about any further documents. WFO has made numerous suggestions to DOJ over the course of this investigation that the most expedient way to ensure recovery of all classified documents would be to go through [REDACTED]. DOJ has persistently disagreed. Other documents declassified by the White House Monday showed that the FBI tapped now-White House chief of staff Susie Wiles' phone and tracked the movements of Melania and Barron Trump. The raid on Trump's Florida estate was viewed as politically driven by many, as Trump was at the time mulling what became a successful bid for the presidency in 2024. DOJ-appointed special counsel Jack Smith investigated the alleged retention of classified materials. Trump pleaded not guilty to all 37 felony charges from Smith’s probe, including willful retention of national defense information, conspiracy to obstruct justice and false statements. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A superseding indictment charged Trump with three more alleged crimes: another count of willful retention of national defense information and two additional obstruction counts. Trump pleaded not guilty, and Smith dropped after Trump won the 2024 presidential election.

title: SCOTUS slams door on Dem judge’s career fight after years of pro-Biden Facebook posts
description: The Supreme Court declined to hear Mark Cohen's First Amendment appeal after the Pennsylvania judge was suspended over dozens of political Facebook posts.
content: The Supreme Court declined Monday to hear an appeal from a former Pennsylvania judge who was suspended after repeatedly posting partisan political content on Facebook, including praise for former President Joe Biden and his policies. Former Judge Mark Cohen, a former Democratic state lawmaker who began serving on the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas in 2018, made dozens of politically charged Facebook posts while on the bench, even after being warned to stop. Cohen appealed to the Supreme Court in April, with his lawyers arguing that the former judge’s First Amendment rights had been violated. "Allowing judges to be disciplined based on the perceived ‘tone’ or ‘volume’ of lawful speech promotes arbitrary enforcement, invites political interference in the judicial branch, and threatens to undermine the rule of law," Cohen’s lawyer told Law.com at the time. "This case presents an urgent opportunity for the court to restore constitutional clarity and reestablish the First Amendment’s protection of the rights of sitting judges to speak on matters of public concern." DOJ MOVES TO BOOT FEDERAL JUDGES FROM IMMIGRATION CASES OVER NYT INTERVIEW The Supreme Court declined to take up Cohen’s case, denying his petition without comment. Pennsylvania’s Judicial Conduct Board argued that the Supreme Court did not need to hear Cohen’s appeal because his social media activity amounted to "partisan cheerleading" and his suspension reflected a "straightforward application of familiar rules that judges around the country have followed for decades." FETTERMAN WEIGHS IN AFTER PA SUPREME COURT JUSTICE APPARENTLY SPLITS FROM DEMOCRATIC PARTY OVER ANTISEMITISM Pennsylvania’s highest court concluded that the volume and tone of Cohen’s posts made him appear to be an advocate for the Democratic Party. In November 2021, Cohen promoted Biden’s Build Back Better legislation, saying its passage would improve "many, many American lives." A year later, on Biden’s birthday, Cohen called him "an excellent President" and said he looked forward to "many more achievements." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS Cohen also made posts taking specific policy positions, including one in favor of higher minimum wage laws and another against restrictions on elective abortions. Cohen also highlighted his record on gun policy, including a post noting that he had consistently received an "F" rating from the National Rifle Association while serving in the state legislature. Cohen’s Supreme Court petition says the suspension also triggered the forfeiture of his judicial and prior public-service pensions. title: US, WHO request details from Russia amid reports of second pneumonia case
description: The WHO and the U.S. State Department have pressed Russia for more information about the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague institute.
content: Amid global public health concerns surrounding the death of an Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East worker, the World Health Organization noted in a statement issued Tuesday on the X account of Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus that it had requested more information from Russia regarding the matter, including on "media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause." "The individual died on 2 October 2026 after being hospitalized with severe pneumonia. Initial media reports suggested pneumonic plague following an alleged accidental laboratory exposure," the WHO statement noted. "In response to WHO’s verification request under the International Health Regulations, the Russian health authorities reported that no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk oblast. They informed WHO that an epidemiological investigation had been conducted, preventive and control measures implemented, and identified contacts placed under medical observation and tested. They reported that no high-threat pathogens had been detected among the contacts and that medical observation of all identified contacts had been completed," the statement explained. "WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause," the statement notes. Reuters reported that when questioned about the WHO's request to respond to reports of a second individual in Siberia allegedly becoming sick, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov called for caution when it comes to media reporting. "There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," Peskov said, according to the outlet. TRUMP SAYS PUTIN CALL COMING 'VERY SOON' AS US TRACKS SUSPECTED PLAGUE DEATH IN RUSSIA The U.S. State Department has formally requested more information from the Russian government regarding the death of the woman who worked at the anti-plague research facility, issuing what is known as a démarche, defined as a request or intercession with a foreign official. "We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government," a U.S. State Department spokesperson noted. "We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information." Fox News Channel senior foreign policy correspondent Gillian Turner reported that State Department health experts had been in touch with Russia's foreign ministry about the public health matter since Friday, but that the démarche arose due to Russian officials being unforthcoming via back channels. RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE 'FAR WORSE' THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) noted in a post on Tuesday that the "CDC is aware of and closely monitoring reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia that resulted in a death. We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available. "While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognized and treated early. Pneumonic plague can spread person-to-person through respiratory droplets during close contact, which is why rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals, are important public health measures. TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP' "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely," the CDC's post concluded. Fox News Channel's Nick Kalman and Gillian Turner contributed to this report.

title: Former CIA officer John Kiriakou's unexpected second act: From whistleblower to viral sensation
description: John Kiriakou discusses his transformation from whistleblower to viral sensation, gaining a younger audience through podcasts, social media and candid commentary.
content: John Kiriakou spent 15 years working in the shadows as a CIA officer. Today, at 62, he's walking the runway at New York Fashion Week, racking up millions of views across social media and becoming an unlikely Gen Z internet sensation. His videos regularly attract millions of views, and his audience of hundreds of thousands of followers has transformed the former intelligence officer into an unexpected voice for a generation that was too young to remember the events that once defined his life. "I never thought that I would be this figurehead for thousands and thousands of young men between 15 and 35," Kiriakou told Fox News Digital. That newfound popularity has opened doors he never imagined, including one into the fashion world. Kiriakou is the first to admit he has never considered himself fashionable. During the interview, he joked that the black T-shirt he was wearing cost about $12 and said he only occasionally flipped through GQ to see what men were wearing. Yet in September, he found himself walking the runway for designer Elena Velez at New York Fashion Week — an unexpected appearance for a man better known for the CIA, national security and exposing the agency's interrogation program. HOUSE GOP BILL MOVES TO CLOSE WHISTLEBLOWER GAPS EXPOSED BY MINNESOTA MEDICAID FRAUD SCANDAL "I'm 62 years old. When in life am I ever going to get the chance to be on the catwalk at New York Fashion Week?" he said. Velez, whose runway shows are known for avant-garde fashion and unconventional casting, reached out after hearing Kiriakou's appearances on several podcasts. But the runway is only one chapter in what has become an unlikely second act. His online popularity accelerated after appearing on Steven Bartlett's "The Diary of a CEO" podcast. Clips from the interview spread rapidly across social media, introducing millions of younger viewers to stories from his years inside the CIA. For many members of Gen Z, Kiriakou represents a world they never experienced firsthand. He joined the CIA in 1990, serving as both an analyst and counterterrorism officer before leaving the agency in 2004. His online reach now extends well beyond short-form videos. Kiriakou also connects directly with supporters through Cameo, where users can purchase personalized video messages. Long before he became an internet personality, Kiriakou was at the center of one of the most contentious national security controversies of the post-9/11 era. In 2007, he publicly discussed the CIA's use of waterboarding during the war on terror. He later pleaded guilty to one count of intentionally disclosing information identifying a covert CIA officer and was sentenced to 30 months in federal prison. CIA WHISTLEBLOWER CLAIMS OBAMA-ERA ESPIONAGE CHARGES AGAINST HIM WERE A TEST RUN FOR TARGETING TRUMP Many of the young people who now follow him, however, know him first through viral videos rather than the headlines that once defined his career. Most were born after the September 11 attacks and did not experience those events as they unfolded. Kiriakou believes that generational distance is part of what draws Gen Z to his story. "There is a special place in my heart for Gen Z," he said. "It's because of Gen Z that I’ve been able to turn my life around and to do things that I had, for the last 62 years, never thought I could do." Kiriakou believes his growing popularity reflects something larger than internet algorithms. He said many young Americans are increasingly skeptical of traditional politics and are searching for voices they view as more authentic. "Gen Z has the largest number of political independents of any generation," Kiriakou said. "They don't like the Democrats. They don’t like the Republicans because they feel like they’re being lied to." Kiriakou, who described himself as an "equal opportunity hater," said he believes frustration with both parties has made younger audiences more willing to listen to voices outside the political establishment. "I think that's why I’m popular with Gen Z — because I’m seen as somebody who’s telling them the truth," he said. He argues that his appeal isn't rooted in perfection, but in transparency. Rather than trying to present himself as flawless, Kiriakou said he speaks openly about government, politics and his own personal mistakes. "I have literally nothing to lose," he said. "I have nothing to gain by lying." That willingness to speak candidly, he said, has allowed him to build an audience that stretches across the political spectrum. Despite his criticism of modern politics, Kiriakou remains optimistic about the next generation. "I think that these are real leaders in waiting," he said. "I think they're the ones who are going to save the country." His confidence in Gen Z is shaped in part by his own improbable second act. The life Kiriakou leads today bears little resemblance to the one he expected after leaving the CIA. In addition to hosting a podcast, he has advised a royal family in the Persian Gulf and is set to appear in an upcoming movie. "I never thought that I would walk in New York Fashion Week, that I'd be an advisor to a royal family in the Persian Gulf, that I’d have my own podcast," he said. "I never thought that I’d act in a Hollywood movie." FORMER CIA AGENT JOHN KIRIAKOU REVEALS HOW SEX PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE IN ESPIONAGE AND SPYING Those experiences have reinforced a lesson he now tries to pass along to younger people: don't be afraid to pursue opportunities that fall outside the life you originally envisioned. "One of the things that I've learned, especially this year since February, is to embrace everything life has to offer," Kiriakou said. For young people uncertain about what comes next, he said the answer is often simpler than they think. "You just have to grab it," he said. "Grab it and do it. And have fun and enjoy yourself." Kiriakou's online following has also given him a new audience for issues he believes will shape the future, including artificial intelligence and national security. During his interview with Fox News Digital, he warned that AI is advancing faster than governments are prepared to manage. "This is the new frontier, AI," Kiriakou said. "It’s developing so quickly." TRUMP LAUNCHING 'SUPER INTELLIGENCE FORCE' TO ENSURE AMERICAN DOMINANCE From his perspective, the technology presents two major risks. One is the possibility that artificial intelligence eventually becomes difficult for humans to control. The other is the growing ability of foreign adversaries to weaponize AI against the United States. "There are two things to worry about here," he said. "One is that AI goes out of control, but two, it’s that our enemies use AI against us." Kiriakou said the United States has not kept pace with those emerging threats. "We’re not prepared. No, we’re not," he said. He pointed to one example that concerns him most: the impact AI could have on undercover intelligence operations. As facial recognition and biometric technology continue to improve, he questioned whether intelligence officers operating under aliases will be able to remain anonymous. title: Memphis City Council devolves into chaos after data center moratorium vote postponed
description: Memphis City Council delayed a vote on a data center moratorium as protesters chanted, police cleared the chamber and a fight broke out in the lobby.
content: A Memphis City Council meeting descended into chaos Tuesday night after lawmakers postponed a vote on a proposed yearlong moratorium on new data centers, as protesters chanted inside City Hall, police cleared the chamber and a fight broke out in the lobby. The proposal comes as Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI operates its massive Colossus supercomputer facilities in the Memphis area, where some residents have raised concerns about data centers' use of power and water, along with their effects on air quality, noise and nearby neighborhoods. The council voted 7-5 to delay the moratorium vote until Oct. 20. ERIC ADAMS BATTLES TENSE CROWD AS WISCONSIN AUDIENCE ERUPTS OVER AI DATA CENTER PROPOSAL After the vote was postponed, protesters chanted, "This is our city," and, "Show me what democracy looks like," as police moved to clear people from the chamber. A fight between two women also broke out in the lobby, with video showing punches being thrown, according to Action News 5. A Memphis Police Department spokesperson told the outlet that no one was detained or injured. It was unclear what sparked the fight or whether it was connected to the council meeting. Council members also clashed during the meeting. Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton exchanged words with protesters before turning her criticism toward Councilman J.B. Smiley Jr., the lead sponsor of the moratorium proposal, according to the outlet. "That’s all he does; he brings up mess," Cooper-Sutton said of Smiley. "That’s all you do, J.B. Smiley, confuse the people over, over, over and over!" Smiley had pushed the council to hold the final vote Tuesday, arguing that residents had shown up expecting a decision. DATA CENTERS COULD BE THE SLEEPER ISSUE OF THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS Seven council members voted to postpone the measure, while five opposed the delay. Councilman Edmund Ford Sr. was absent, according to Action News 5. The proposed ordinance would pause new data center projects for 12 months while the city studies their effects on health and Memphis' power, water and other infrastructure. Musk's SpaceXAI has established a major computing operation in the Memphis area with its Colossus facilities, raising concerns from some residents about air pollution, noise and the amount of electricity and water needed to run large data centers. Councilman Jeff Warren, who opposes the moratorium, warned that a year-long pause could push companies to build outside Memphis. "If we pass a moratorium, there’s no reason for them to think they need to come here," Warren said, according to WREG. "They get the same benefit from going to DeSoto County, Crittenden County, Fayette County, Tipton County." Memphis Mayor Paul Young has called for more rules governing data centers while also pointing to the tax revenue they generate. Young said the city should address their water and electricity use, air quality, noise and where the facilities can be built. "We need to keep the pressure high and make sure that we get the guardrails in place that we need for our community to feel protected," Young told WREG. "There’s a role for all of our agencies to play in ensuring we put the proper guardrails in place. The thing that I want to make sure is that we do it expeditiously." Smiley said council members should have done more to listen to residents who attended the meeting. "I’m disappointed that we didn’t listen with ears, okay, I hear you, I understand. Let’s figure out how we can do what you want, but also what we believe would be in the best interest of the community."

title: DHS orders deportation of illegal migrant who sold fraudulent DHS, FBI 'immunity' cards
description: A Brazilian illegal immigrant created a fake DHS branch and sold counterfeit Department of Homeland Security and FBI IDs promising deportation immunity.
content: FIRST ON FOX: A Brazilian illegal immigrant who admitted to creating a fake branch of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and selling counterfeit DHS and FBI identification cards — which he claimed would provide immunity from federal immigration officers — has been ordered deported. Mario Cesar Dos Santos Jr., 50, who entered the United States in 2016 and overstayed his visa, is currently in removal proceedings, according to DHS. He was arrested in February at Orlando International Airport after arriving on a flight from Boston. Dos Santos pleaded guilty to wire fraud and the fraudulent use of government seals. WOMAN EXPOSED RUNNING VISA FRAUD SCHEME SPANNING YEARS, POSING AS IMMIGRATION OFFICER As part of the scheme, Dos Santos claimed to be the president of the "Chaplain Emergency Management Agency" (CEMA), a fictitious federal agency he created to trick attendees at training seminars into paying for immunity from immigration enforcement. While the training courses were offered for free, participants were charged $400 to $450 for bogus certificates they believed would protect them from deportation, authorities said. Each seminar drew approximately 30 to 45 participants. FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME In addition to the counterfeit certificates, Dos Santos sold clothing, badges, stickers and other merchandise bearing official seals for DHS and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) — the agency responsible for coordinating federal responses to natural and human-made disasters. A confidential informant purchased several of these items at a training seminar last year, according to authorities. TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS The CEMA website, its social media accounts and a group chat — which had more than 750 members when the investigation launched in August 2025 — actively promoted upcoming courses and displayed an altered DHS seal, authorities said. The organization also falsely claimed to be accredited by the International Association for Continuing Education and the American Council on Education. Dos Santos faces up to 20 years in federal prison when he is sentenced on Dec. 18. title: MLW star Donovan Dijak talks tag team wrestling being a 'lost art,' partnering with Josh Bishop and growth
description: Donovan Dijak reveals why The Skyscrapers are banking on Killer Kross and Matt Riddle failing to coexist in their massive MLW tag team clash.
content: It has been more than two years since Donovan Dijak joined Major League Wrestling (MLW) and just as he was in WWE NXT, he continued to be a force to be reckoned with. The average pro wrestling might feast their eyes on the 6-foot-7, 270-pound Massachusetts native and believe he should be a singles competitor in the ring. However, Dijak has torn it up in MLW as part of The Skyscrapers tag team with Bishop Dyer and now Josh Bishop. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE Dijak and Bishop are set to have a massive tag team match against MLW world heavyweight champion Killer Kross and Matt Riddle. Kross and Riddle have had their differences in the past. Kross won the title in a Battle Riot earlier this year. Riddle had done the same in 2025. A win for Dijak and Bishop might catapult each of them into a shot at the world title down the line. "I'm banking on them not being able to coexist," Dijak told OutKick Dropkick. "Hopefully me and Josh can coexist. I know there's some volatility there. But he (Bishop) has all the potential in the world. He's just an incredible dude. Big, strong, exactly what you want in a tag team partner, especially in a tag team called The Skyscrapers. I'm very excited for his future. "I'm very excited to help mold his future and give him the path and the avenue and the direction and the instruction that is necessary for success at the level against guys like Killer Kross, against guys like Matt Riddle, who I've been wrestling for years and years and years, both of them. So, I'm super excited to get back in the ring with those guys and to be in the ring with Josh as well because he's just an unbelievable competitor." Dijak said he was a big fan of tag team wrestling as well as singles wrestling. He teamed with Mace in WWE and wrestler Mikey Webb. He also credited Tommaso Ciampa with helping him learn the psychology of a tag team match. Dijak held the MLW tag team titles with both Dyer and Bishop for nearly a year before dropping it to The Good Brothers – Karl Anderson and Doc Gallows. Pro wrestling fans have expressed some dismay about tag team wrestling over the years. OutKick Dropkick asked Dijak whether the style was a "lost art" in the sport. "Absolutely. There's so many points and purposes around tag team wrestling that I think kind of get lost in today's sort of system of professional wrestling. And I understand why, right? Because my perspective — and I teach a lot of this," Dijak said, pointing to his work at the New England Pro Wrestling Academy in Massachusetts and the course he offers online at Dijakwrestling.com. "A big piece of tag team psychology that kind of gets lost is how different and unique of a platform it is as opposed to a singles match or singles wrestling. People get so caught up — and I know this happens because it happened to me back in 2014, 2015, 2016 when I was a younger wrestler and I was really champing at the bit to prove myself as an elite wrestler — I would get put in tag team matches or triple threat matches, and my first thought would be, ‘I wish it was a singles match because I really want to show what I can do as a singles competitor.’ When you have that mindset, it can take away from a match because you get hyper-focused on, ‘Let me show them how good of a singles wrestler I am,’ and that doesn't fulfill the potential of the unique situation of what a tag team match is. It gives the fans a new experience because most cards have a ton of singles matches on them. It’s usually, singles, singles, singles, tag, singles, singles, triple threat, singles. title: Man hunting for gems at state park spots something 'glowing' in the gravel: 'I was shaking'
description: Navy reservist Jack Pearadin recently revealed how he spotted the rare yellow diamond glowing from a gravel pile during an icy Arkansas gem hunt trip.
content: A longtime gem hunter who struck it big with a rare yellow diamond is now opening up about the remarkable discovery — and what it may be worth. Jack Pearadin, a Navy reservist, found the gem at the Crater of Diamonds State Park earlier this year. The gem, which Pearadin named the "American Dream," weighs 6.03 carats. It has a striking golden-yellow color and an unusual, almost square shape. STUNNED COUPLE UNEARTHS 150-POUND MYSTERY HIDDEN BENEATH THEIR BACKYARD FOR DECADES Though the discovery was first announced earlier this year, Pearadin recently opened up about the find to The Associated Press. Arkansas state officials said Pearadin discovered the diamond during a Jan. 25 TikTok livestream while processing a bucket of gravel that he and his friend, Michael Schumacher, had collected from the park's search area in late December. Schumacher was traveling at the time. The hunt came shortly after a winter storm coated the area with more than an inch of ice, making it especially difficult to sift and wash the gravel. "I was about eight feet away, and for some reason I turned back and saw [the gem] glowing from the center of the pile," Pearadin said. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS FACE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES IN BOOK OF REVELATION CITY "I had to go almost to the bottom of the pile to pull it out, it was so big. I was shaking!" Pearadin's reaction was captured in real time during a TikTok livestream. "Oh my God! Oh my God!" he was recorded as saying. "We got a big one!" Pearadin told the AP that some collectors said the diamond could be worth as much as $1 million. Park officials previously told Fox News Digital that park employees "are not trained to grade or appraise diamonds or other rocks and minerals." POLICE OPERATION TAKES UNEXPECTED TURN WHEN OFFICERS STUMBLE UPON ANCIENT BURIAL CAVE "Our primary training involves properly identifying and registering diamonds for guests who find them," an Arkansas State Parks official said. "Anyone interested in having their diamonds graded or appraised can reach out to a certified gemologist, who has had special training to properly grade gemstone quality and estimate value." "It’s the only place in America where you can go find your own diamond, and you can’t compare that to a diamond from anywhere else." Laura Stanley, a certified gem appraiser in Little Rock, told the AP that a high-quality six-carat yellow diamond from the park could sell for about $250,000. "They are their own entity," Stanley said. title: WWE star Joe Hendry drops music album, stands by calling for Logan Paul's firing and not jumping to use AI
description: Joe Hendry's "Beyond Belief" album climbed as high as No. 2 on iTunes as the WWE and TNA champion reveals he wrote all 11 songs in just 34 days.
content: Joe Hendry was a WWE NXT champion, a Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) champion and made a surprise WrestleMania appearance in 2025 to take on Randy Orton. But did anyone have Hendry being a chart-topping musician on their bingo cards? Call it if you did. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE Hendry’s "Beyond Belief" was released this week, which includes 11 songs. He told OutKick Dropkick he had been performing live since he was a kid growing up in Scotland and before he started to pursue pro wrestling as a career. "It’s been an incredibly rewarding journey. It's very exciting. I had such fun when I released ‘I Believe in Joe Hendry’ as a single, but like an album is a whole different beast. That’s a big commitment for our fans and music listeners a full feature-length album," he said. "I appreciate people taking the time to listen to it and buy it, and it's just been very humbling to see the response." Hendry said he wrote the album in a span of about 34 days. At first, he said WWE Music wanted to put out a song about The Miz. The idea transformed into a possible EP and then into a full album. One of the songs on "Beyond Belief" is about firing Logan Paul, who Hendry has been in a feud with for a few months. He’s performed it live on "Monday Night Raw" multiple times and interrupted Judgment Day matches with his vocals. He said he had about a week’s notice before getting the song together because it was going to be about his Raw debut. But with a small storyline change, the lyrics changed with it. "I was told that I'd be debuting on the Raw after WrestleMania, so I had about a week's notice to come up with a song, but it was gonna be, ‘Raw, Raw, Joe Hendry signed to Raw,’ but then they announced my appearance, it was delayed, and they announced my appearance the following week, so me signing to Raw was no longer the story. And I needed to go after someone, and I've always been of the opinion you go after the biggest name in the building, and that's Logan Paul. "He's our most Googled WWE superstar. And so, to me, that was the person to go after and that's where ‘Fire Logan Paul’ came from. So, I'd say about a week for that one." Hendry said Paul hates the song, but he has no plans of backing off it. "Obviously, he hates it. He despises it. It tells the truth. It’s ‘Logan Paul should be fired.’ We all know this. This is a campaign that I've been on. It’s why it's an important part of the album. I think when you have a platform like mine, you have to use it for good, and that will probably involve trying to get Logan Paul fired, and that feels like a quest that I'll never stop." AI has been shown to create music, generate melodies and essentially creating a band when you have no instruments available. But Hendry told OutKick Dropkick he would trust himself before he trusts a machine. "For me and my songwriting, I feel like that's my skill, and I don't want to use AI to write songs because I don't know, I can just, I can personally tell the difference between a song that's been AI generated and that's been written by a human being and it's a skill that I've worked very hard on. "So I understand that we live in a world where there are tools that you can use. For example, there are amazing keyboard sounds and drum sounds that you can get just by pressing buttons on your keyboard, which obviously as musicians like those are amazing tools. But in terms of the actual creation of music, I think I'm going to trust Joe Hendry before I trust the machine." Hendry is far from the only one who has recorded songs on the WWE roster. Liv Morgan released "Trouble" before WrestleMania 42 and made it her entrance music. Alexa Bliss is set to release a song with her husband Ryan Cabrera later this week. Hendry said he was open to collaborations but might have to wait a bit on Morgan given her associations with The Judgment Day. "I'm always open to that. I'm always open to that. Right now, I will say, look, I'm open to collaborations, but right now myself and Liv Morgan are not on very good terms," he said. "She is obviously in the judgment Day who I have frequent problems with, so, I'm afraid that, I'm not going to lend my songwriting skills to the Judgment Day at this time." Hendry noted on X on Tuesday his album was rising on the iTunes, scoring as high as No. 2 on one chart.
