title: AI companies stop short of guaranteeing agents will always obey safeguards
description: Representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google declined to guarantee their AI agents will always follow safety guardrails, telling New York City lawmakers that eliminating risk or promising perfection is not possible.
content:
An anonymous nurse checks the vitals of a woman at a hospital. (iStock)
The American Hospital Association is pushing back on a Blue Cross Blue Shield Association report that linked hospitals’ growing use of artificial intelligence-enabled documentation tools to higher healthcare spending , arguing the analysis does not prove AI is driving improper billing.
The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association estimated that coding-related changes resulted in $942 million in additional spending for participating Blue plans between 2023 and 2025 as hospitals increasingly classified patients as having more complex conditions.
But the AHA said Monday that the analysis lacks critical context and does not establish that hospitals incorrectly coded patients or that AI tools were responsible for the changes.
“The central question is not whether hospitals are reporting more diagnoses,” the AHA said. “The question is whether the patient’s medical record supports those diagnoses.”
The hospital group argued that Americans are living longer with more chronic conditions, while lower-acuity procedures have increasingly shifted from hospitals to outpatient settings. That leaves hospitals treating a greater concentration of seriously ill and medically complex patients, according to the AHA.
AI-enabled documentation technology, the group said, can help clinicians identify and record conditions that may previously have been underreported while reducing administrative burdens and providing a fuller picture of patients’ health.
The AHA also challenged the methodology behind the insurer group's conclusions, saying the BCBSA analysis did not review underlying medical records to determine whether diagnoses were supported and did not appear to identify which claims actually involved AI tools rather than traditional coding practices.
“Without answering those questions, the analysis does not demonstrate that hospitals coded patients incorrectly,” the AHA said. “It may simply reflect more complete documentation of increasingly complex patients.”
The AHA further argued that the $942 million estimate should be viewed in the context of overall healthcare spending, contending that increased inpatient coding intensity represents only a small portion of broader growth in commercial healthcare costs.
The dispute comes as hospitals and insurers increasingly deploy AI across healthcare, raising questions about how the technology could affect everything from patient care and administrative workloads to billing and healthcare costs.

title: Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning ‘On the Waterfront’ and ‘North by Northwest’ star, dead at 102
description: Oscar winning actress Eva Marie Saint, who starred opposite Marlon Brando and Cary Grant, has died at 102 after a career spanning seven decades.
content: Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar- and Emmy-winning actress who became one of the defining stars of Hollywood’s Golden Era, has died. She was 102. Saint died Tuesday of natural causes at her Los Angeles home surrounded by family and loved ones, her representative confirmed to Fox News Digital. The actress made an extraordinary film debut opposite Marlon Brando in the 1954 classic "On the Waterfront," winning the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress in her performance as Edie Doyle. Directed by Elia Kazan, the landmark drama launched Saint onto the big screen after she had already established herself in television and on the New York stage. Her first movie role placed her opposite Brando at the apex of his fame. POST MALONE, EVA MARIE SAINT AND OTHER CELEBRITIES WHO SHARE A BIRTHDAY WITH THE FOURTH OF JULY Five years later, Saint then firmly cemented her place in Hollywood's Golden Era history while starring opposite the legendary Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s "North by Northwest," playing the mysterious "Hitchcock Blonde" Eve Kendall in the cult-classic 1959 thriller. The role offered a striking contrast to the vulnerable, angelic young woman she portrayed in "On the Waterfront." As Hitchcock’s elegant and enigmatic leading lady, Saint became part of one of the British director’s most enduring films, sharing the screen with Grant in a movie remembered for its sweeping romance, suspense and iconic Mount Rushmore climax. Saint’s two best-known films alone paired her with Brando, Kazan, Grant and Hitchcock, but represent only the start of a career that would stretch more than 70 years. Over an incredible career spanning more than seven decades, Saint worked alongside some of Hollywood’s most celebrated leading men, including Montgomery Clift, Henry Fonda, Paul Newman, Gregory Peck, Richard Burton, Warren Beatty, James Garner, George C. Scott, Burt Lancaster and Tom Hanks. OSCAR-WINNER BRENDA FRICKER, 'PIGEON LADY' FROM 'HOME ALONE 2,' DEAD AT 81 Her list of co-stars reads like a roll call of mid-century Hollywood. She appeared with Clift and Elizabeth Taylor in "Raintree County," Newman in "Exodus," Beatty in "All Fall Down," Burton in "The Sandpiper" and Garner in the racing epic "Grand Prix." Other notable films featuring the actress include "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "Exodus," "The Russians Are Coming the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," "Nothing in Common" and, later in her career, "Superman Returns." Saint was also a regular fixture of television and the stage. She earned five Emmy nominations, winning in 1990 for the miniseries "People Like Us," and appeared on Broadway in "The Trip to Bountiful" before director Elia Kazan cast her in "On the Waterfront." SHELLEY FABARES, STAR OF 'THE DONNA REED SHOW' AND 'COACH,' DEAD AT 82 Her career had actually begun during the golden age of live television. Saint earned early Emmy nominations for Paddy Chayefsky’s "Middle of the Night" and a live television musical adaptation of Thornton Wilder’s "Our Town," in which she played Emily alongside Frank Sinatra and Paul Newman. On Broadway, her performance in the Christian-themed "The Trip to Bountiful" earned her critical acclaim and caught Kazan’s attention. Saint's moves from radio and live television to Broadway and then an Oscar-winning movie debut uniquely placed her at the crossroads of several defining eras of 20th century American entertainment. Born in Newark, New Jersey, and raised in Albany and Delmar, New York, Saint attended Bowling Green State University in Ohio with plans to become a teacher before acting ultimately changed the course of her life. She tried out for a university play at the suggestion of a drama professor, won the leading role and abandoned her original plan to become a schoolteacher. After graduation, she moved to New York City, studying at the American Theatre Wing and with Lee Strasberg at the Actors Studio. Bowling Green later awarded Saint an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree and renamed its main campus theater the Eva Marie Saint Theatre. She returned to the Academy Awards as a presenter in 2009 and again in 2018, receiving a standing ovation from the stars gathered when she walked onto the stage at age 93. PAUL ANKA SLAMS MODERN SINGERS, SAYS FRANK SINATRA WOULD HAVE 'THROWN A CHAIR' Saint was married to director Jeffrey Hayden for 65 years until his death in 2016. She is survived by their two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren, Eli, Tyler, Molly and Stella, and two great-grandchildren, Arlo and Finley. From the docks of "On the Waterfront" to the intrigue and glamour of "North by Northwest," Saint became an undisputed face of Hollywood history while building a body of work that endured long after that era had passed. title: Trump says Putin call coming ‘very soon’ as US tracks suspected plague death in Russia
description: President Donald Trump says he'll speak with Vladimir Putin "very soon" as his administration tracks a suspected pneumonic plague death in Siberia.
content: President Donald Trump said Tuesday he will speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon" as his administration closely tracks reports of a suspected pneumonic plague death in Siberia that have prompted a U.S. health alert and heightened health precautions across several countries bordering Russia. Trump revealed the planned call while taking questions from reporters Tuesday. Asked whether he had spoken with Putin about the situation, Trump said he already had a call scheduled. "I have a call scheduled, yup," Trump said. TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP' Asked when the call would take place, the president responded, "Very soon." Trump said the administration was in "very deep discussions" when asked what U.S. intelligence agencies were saying about the reports. The president's comments came as the U.S. Embassy in Moscow issued a health alert Tuesday saying it was aware of press reports from Russia's Irkutsk region of "suspected pneumonic plague resulting in the death of an individual," along with associated quarantine measures and hospital closures. "We continue to track the situation closely," the embassy said. NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA A State Department spokesman told Fox News Digital that the department, along with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other interagency partners, is "closely monitoring the fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague" in Russia's Irkutsk Oblast. "The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," the spokesman said. The spokesman cautioned that "many details remain unconfirmed" and called on Moscow to provide greater clarity. "We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," the spokesman said. The alert advised Americans in the area to follow local health guidance, avoid affected medical facilities and seek prompt medical care if they develop fever or respiratory symptoms. Those who have traveled to an area experiencing an outbreak were advised to monitor their health for 14 days. The State Department's existing Level 4 "Do Not Travel" advisory for Russia remains unchanged. The embassy reiterated that Americans currently in Russia should depart and warned that the U.S. government's ability to assist citizens there is limited, particularly outside Moscow. UKRAINE STRIKES DEEP INTO RUSSIA’S ARCTIC GAS HEARTLAND AS TRUMP PUSHES PUTIN TOWARD PEACE Several countries bordering Russia are also implementing new health precautions in response to the reports. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan are moving to implement what their governments have described as "enhanced health and sanitary measures" in response to reports of pneumonic plague in Siberia. A 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East died last week from what Russian authorities described as pneumonia of undetermined origin. Russia has not said the woman died of plague and said testing found no microorganisms in her body linked to her work. Russian officials told the WHO that her contacts tested negative for dangerous infectious pathogens. The WHO has assessed the risk to the general population as low. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has also said it is closely monitoring the reports and working across the U.S. government as additional information becomes available. The agency said there is currently no indication of a broader threat to the United States. Pneumonic plague is a serious bacterial infection caused by Yersinia pestis. It can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact and can progress rapidly if untreated. The disease can be successfully treated with antibiotics, particularly when identified and treated early. For now, U.S. officials are continuing to seek additional information about what occurred in Irkutsk and whether the incident poses any wider threat. The president suggested his administration could have more to say as soon as Wednesday. "We'll be able to report about it probably tomorrow," Trump said. title: Drone strike sinks ship in NATO waters as Zelenskyy warns of looming ‘massive strike’
description: A cargo ship sank and a second vessel caught fire in a combined aerial and maritime drone attack inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
content: A commercial ship sank and its crew vanished Tuesday after an apparent coordinated air-and-sea drone attack off NATO member Bulgaria, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia before warning Moscow was preparing a broader "massive strike." A second vessel was also heavily damaged and set ablaze inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, with a drone expert warning the dual precision strikes signaled a dangerous escalation and possible "larger invasion posture" by Russia. "They were likely using the Geran-4 aerial drone to take the vessel out or the Maran surface vehicle to take it out," Cameron Chell, founder of drone manufacturer Draganfly, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday of the first strike. RUSSIA MAY BE USING HIDDEN 'LUNCHBOX-SIZE' DRONE DEVICES TO COUNTER UKRAINE DEFENSES: EXPERT "The reason it wasn't just an air vehicle or an air drone that took this ship out was that the Gerans generally come in at a pretty steep angle when they're on final attack," Chell said. "There are not really any precision drones that fly closely above the surface, which is where they would have had to hit in order to create an impact that would sink this ship fast enough," he added. "The nature of this strike suggests there was a combination of an air attack and surface attack," Chell said. The dual attack occurred roughly 70 nautical miles off the eastern Bulgarian coastal town of Byala, according to Reuters, bringing the conflict into the economic zone of a NATO member. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence and security services were working to determine the full circumstances surrounding the attack. US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS "Our intelligence and special services are now working to establish all available information about yet another attack in the Black Sea targeting civilian vessels," he wrote on X. "Our Navy contacted its counterparts in Bulgaria, and it has been established that this was a combined Russian attack using maritime and aerial drones." Chell suggested the attack’s location and hybrid nature could serve Russia by sowing greater uncertainty across the region. "We can see the amount of geopolitical chaos that's involved, and this is exactly the type of thing that would benefit Russia in the region," Chell said. "The hybrid element here is really blurring the lines between traditional military actions," he added, describing the attack as "an expansion of strategy and tactics." "This is indicative of this larger invasion posture that seems to be unfolding for Russia," Chell said. "And a real desire, what appears to be, for Russia to take things up a notch." RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev also confirmed that aerial and maritime drones targeted two commercial vessels in shipping lanes inside Bulgaria’s EEZ, calling the attack a "gross, flagrant violation of international law," according to Reuters. The sunken vessel, identified by British maritime risk group Vanguard as the cargo ship Alfa Watan, suffered catastrophic structural damage before submerging with an undisclosed cargo and an unknown number of crew members aboard. A nearby Bulgarian ferry, the Dioscuria, diverted to the scene after witnessing an explosion and receiving distress signals, Reuters reported. Rescuers found an overturned lifeboat, life rafts and life jackets floating in the debris field. RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS Search-and-rescue operations involving the Bulgarian Navy, Air Force and Border Police remained underway to locate the missing crew and monitor for environmental threats, the outlet said. Chell suggested the apparent coordination between the attacks was particularly significant. "Not only are you using pretty sophisticated equipment, but you're also doing it in a coordinated manner," Chell said. "These two ships were going opposite directions. One was actually just coming, and had left Ukraine the day before," he said. "These things coordinated and were struck relatively at the same time. So another level of coordination has unfolded here," Chell added. UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC The second ship, identified by Vanguard as the general cargo vessel ABLE, caught fire after being struck while carrying grain. A Bulgarian ferry crew evacuated all 18 seafarers aboard — 11 Turkish nationals and seven Indian nationals. Two crew members suffered severe injuries and were airlifted to a medical facility in Varna, while the remaining 16 were transported safely to shore. Radev convened an emergency government session following the strikes. While acknowledging it remained unclear whether the drones originated from Russia or Ukraine, he warned of the widening scope of the war. "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable," Radev told reporters. REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES "If this war is not ended in time, it will continue to expand its spatial scope and increase the risk of even a global conflict." Chell said striking the two ships inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone could also have the effect of disrupting a crucial shipping corridor and creating fear among commercial operators. "It all adds up to a perfect little scenario for the Russians to create chaos there, not just to disrupt the lane of economics for the region and in particular for Ukraine — a lifeline," Chell said. "The Russians are really taking a playbook out of the Iranians who have basically created enough chaos in the Strait of Hormuz where the operators can't take the chance to put their ships through there," he added. The strikes came amid a surge in attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident off Romania’s coast Monday in which two people died in a ship fire. Ambrey, a British firm specializing in global maritime risk, recorded more than 210 strikes on commercial ships between July and the end of September. "We’ve got updated intel on Russia’s preparations for a massive strike," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "I ask you, please, to take care of yourselves and respond to missile threat alerts." "Ukrainian services and our Air Force are ready to respond — as much as our defenses allow," Zelenskyy continued. "And a lot depends on our partners — every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us." title: Costco rolls out new Disneyland ticket deal but there's a catch for parkgoers
description: Costco's $329.99 Disneyland bundle includes a two-day Park Hopper ticket, Lightning Lane Multi Pass and a $60 dining card at select California stores.
content: Disneyland visitors have a new ticket option that bundles park admission with other perks — but there are some restrictions that travelers may want to know about. Costco is offering a two-day Disneyland Resort Park Hopper ticket with Lightning Lane Multi Pass and a $60 dining card for $329.99 at select locations in California. Disneyland Resort officials confirmed the offer to Fox News Digital, saying it rolled out last week at select Costco stores across the state. DISNEYLAND CRACKS DOWN ON GUESTS WITH SWEEPING NEW RESTRICTIONS, SPARKING BACKLASH The resort regularly makes limited-time ticket offers available throughout the year, including through third-party retailers, according to Disneyland Resort officials. The Costco package has since caught the attention of theme park fans online as travelers compare the price with the cost of purchasing tickets directly from Disneyland. In a recent Instagram post, one theme park content creator highlighted the $329.99 price and the included Lightning Lane access and dining card. "Costco has a Disneyland deal right now that is actually WORTH talking about!" the user wrote. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER By comparison, a two-day Park Hopper ticket is currently listed at $445 for one adult on Disneyland's website, before adding Lightning Lane — though pricing is subject to change. That puts the Costco package about $115 below the currently listed two-day Park Hopper price, although the two options come with different terms and restrictions. The offer also comes as Disneyland adjusted some of its ticket prices this week. Mid-tier single-day tickets increased by $5, while the least expensive $104 ticket and the highest-priced $224 ticket remained unchanged, according to the Los Angeles Times. The cost of Lightning Lane can now reach $38, up $1, while the Park Hopper add-on for single-day tickets increased by $5 to $10, depending on the date, the outlet reported. Multi-day ticket prices were unchanged. Hugh Johnston, CFO of The Walt Disney Company, speaking at the recent Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference in San Francisco, said the company is keeping ticket prices accessible for younger families by offering lower rates during off-peak value periods. "It's something that we're acutely sensitive to because we want to make sure we continue to bring young families, in particular, into the parks and develop that Disney love, right?" he said. "So we're super sensitive to the fact that, particularly in the value times of the year, we keep those ticket prices relatively low so that we can actually encourage those young families to come in," he added. "We want to make sure we continue to bring young families, in particular, into the parks." The Costco ticket can be used between Oct. 2 and Dec. 18, according to information shared by the Instagram user. Once a guest uses the ticket for the first time, the second park day must be used within 13 days, the video said. title: Iranian director decries Hollywood portrayal of foreign countries, calls American democracy 'a lie'
description: Director Asghar Farhadi slammed Ben Affleck's "Argo" at the Rio Film Festival, calling it a "Hollywood thing" that portrays Iran "like you're in hell."
content: Oscar-winning Iranian filmmaker Asghar Farhadi called out Hollywood's depiction of Iran and other foreign countries at the Rio Film Festival in Brazil on Friday, claiming it is a "lie" to call America a "democracy." While promoting his film "Parallel Tales," Farhadi was asked about the 2012 movie "Argo" winning Best Picture just one year after his film "A Separation" won Best Foreign Language Film at the Oscars. "Argo," directed by Ben Affleck, stars Affleck as CIA operative Tony Mendez in a loose adaptation of Mendez's memoir on the rescue of six U.S. diplomats from Iran by pretending to film a science-fiction movie in the nation. BEN AFFLECK REJECTS 'PROPAGANDA' OPPOSING AI, INSISTS EMERGING TECHNOLOGY WILL HELP FILMMAKERS Farhadi described the film as a "Hollywood thing" and suggested it was "not deep" based on its plot involving a "White guy" saving others, though Mendez in real life was of Mexican descent. "They make these movies for money; it’s a business," Farhadi said, according to Variety. "And in these films it’s always a [W]hite guy from the United States saving others. My question is: Why? Why does an American go to Cuba or Iran to save people? People understand they can save themselves. Who asked you to come and save us?" Farhadi also accused "Argo," which took place after the 1979 Iranian Revolution, of portraying Iran "like you're in hell." AMERICAN WHO FLED IRAN SAYS CITIZENS 'DESPERATE' FOR FREEDOM, PRAYING FOR ISLAMIC REGIME TO FALL "The problem with these kinds of films in Hollywood [and] some people in the United States [is that] they look at the world from up to down," Farhadi said. "Someday you should ask them: Why do you feel you’re up and we’re down? I don’t understand why they have this ego that they’re up." Farhadi also denied Americans' claim to "have democracy," saying he believed the "real America" exists among Black and foreign prisoners. "You don’t have democracy. It’s a lie," Farhadi said. Media Research Center President David Bozell called out Farhadi's negative view of America and American films in a comment to Fox News Digital. Maybe Hollywood makes movies about Americans saving the world for a reason," Bozell said.

title: Miami Hurricanes coach comes out in favor of ending preseason college football polls, blasts SEC
description: Shannon Dawson calls preseason rankings "the stupidest thing on the planet" and argues SEC teams get undeserved benefit of the doubt from voters.
content: There may not be a better season than 2026 to exemplify the problems with preseason polls in college football. The advent of NIL and the transfer portal has already made gauging the "best" teams in early August nearly impossible, and as the jaw-dropping 2025 Indiana Hoosiers championship season demonstrated, the modern era has created more surprise teams than in the past. Preseason polls then, despite being a part of the college football process for years, are less useful than ever before. And one prominent offensive coordinator thinks we should get rid of them entirely. He's probably right. Miami Hurricanes OC Shannon Dawson recently addressed the preseason polls, specifically addressing how they consistently seemingly favor one specific conference. A conference that already more often than not gets the benefit of the doubt from poll voters. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "First of all, there should be no such thing as preseason rankings," Dawson said during a press conference. "That’s the most ridiculous thing on the planet. That is the stupidest thing, because people weigh those things way heavier than they should. "You shouldn’t have a ranking until October. How do you know? (Texas) A&M was ranked in the top-five, but how does that look right now? If anything, it isn’t predictable for the future, it’s the past. Go look at the top-10 last year. I did. Five of them weren’t even in the (end of season) top-25." It's impossible to argue with that, because it's true. And despite A&M, and others, looking far worse than their preseason expectations, the first few weeks of games and rankings reflect that initial set. Texas A&M loses to LSU, which must mean LSU is good, because A&M was a preseason top-5 team. Missouri was ranked in the preseason, for some reason, which must mean Mississippi State is also good, because they beat a preseason top-25 team. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Obviously the preseason poll doesn't only affect one conference; Big Ten teams like Michigan, Penn State and Washington have looked far worse than preseason polls suggested. On the other hand, though, Nebraska and Wake Forest have received little attention and respect from voters, despite deserving it, because they didn't start the year in the top-25. Dawson continued, specifically calling out the SEC and how those teams fluctuate from week-to-week. "So we sit here and look at schedules, and obviously everything is SEC, SEC. Well look… they have all of their teams in the top-25. Guess what. Good for you. At the end of the year, half of them won’t be in the top-30. That’s just the way it is. We can’t sit here and say, ‘hey, we play X number of top-25 teams’. We don’t know that. We’ll count those chips up at the end of the year. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER "That’s why there shouldn’t be rankings, because you give people talking points that are idiots. They don’t know what they’re doing. Play the game. Play every week." It's like Dawson's been reading a certain OutKick writer's columns complaining about the polls each week. Ahem. Voters are humans, and humans are biased. They don't always watch all the games, and some have even forgotten to rank elite teams like Miami periodically. Some, like ESPN's Heather Dinich, post about the importance of winning "SEC road games," as if that some sort of remarkable achievement. Her specific example, Kentucky, beat a bad Texas A&M team and a bad South Carolina team. Great, so what? Why should that be rewarded by placing the Wildcats at No. 17, just because it's the SEC and those teams have big stadiums? OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD At the end of the day, using a blend of analytics and efficiency driven rankings would lead to a better result than trusting voters. Especially before anyone's even seen teams play on the field. But because there are vested interests who want preseason polls to continue, they will. Many valuable college football traditions have gone by the wayside in the modern game, but somehow not that one.

title: Unearthed social media posts contradict El-Sayed’s ‘capitalist’ narrative
description: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan, faces scrutiny over Detroit DSA ties as he prepares to face Mike Rogers.
content: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, recently embraced the "capitalist" label and pushed back against being called socialist, but unearthed social media posts contradict that narrative. Recently unearthed social media posts show the Detroit Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapter applauding his views on climate advocacy, going so far as to call him a "comrade" in its efforts. "Welcome to the team comrade," the group’s Detroit chapter wrote in a post in 2019 alongside a picture of El-Sayed, then a recent candidate for Michigan governor. Shortly after El-Sayed endorsed Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., in his presidential bid, the account again praised his support. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ENDORSED BY AOC AND BERNIE SANDERS INSISTS HE'S NOT A SOCIALIST "Thank you to our friend and ally Abdul El-Sayed for endorsing Bernie Sanders. Our movement is unstoppable," the group wrote. Although the DSA has not officially endorsed El-Sayed in his Senate bid or affirmed his platform, the DSA’s local support for him may raise questions of increased overlap between his platform and the DSA's official stances. In an interview with The New York Times, El-Sayed described his views on capitalism. "Capitalism is about leveraging the laws of supply and demand to efficiently allocate capital expenditure to maximize value. When capitalism works, it’s because you have free entry and exit into markets," El-Sayed said. "So if you believe in capitalism, you have to believe in government regulation to protect markets. In fact, right now, we have exactly the opposite. You don’t have to be a socialist to believe that you should be taxing billionaires their wealth," he continued. "In fact, if you are a capitalist, you should believe in that. So, I’m a capitalist who just knows about capitalism. I have a bad habit of reading; I’m so sorry." Among other stances, El-Sayed has championed policies like Medicare for All, increasing taxes on the country’s top earners and implementing more stringent penalties on businesses that, in his view, abuse natural resources like water supply and air quality. In his 2018 campaign for governor, El-Sayed espoused many of the same views, garnering support from the DSA — especially for his platform on climate. At one point, El-Sayed joined in calls to seize plants owned by General Motors after the company announced it would cut about 14,000 jobs from sites across the country. GREEN NEW DODGE: EL-SAYED RUNS FROM POLICY AS NEWLY SURFACED DELETED POSTS SHOW YEARS OF SUPPORT "Today, Abdul El-Sayed signed onto our bold demand to seize abandoned [General Motors] plants and convert them into green, public use. This is the courage and vision we need from our leaders to make the Green New Deal a reality. Thank you, Dr. El-Sayed! Onward!" The group wrote. El-Sayed was among 140 co-signers for the plan, including figures like Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Natasha Fernández-Silber, the co-chair of the Detroit DSA. "These facilities are not just the ‘property’ of a corporation. They belong to the workers who have contributed their labor, and the taxpayers who have provided enormous tax breaks, public subsidies and bailouts to GM," the resolution read. Between 2017 and 2020, the Michigan Democrat spoke at six events held by Democratic Socialists of America chapters, including a 2019 fundraiser where he served as the keynote speaker. Additionally, DSA officials told Politico in July that they were mobilizing resources to help El-Sayed win his Democratic primary election. "I'm not technically or practically DSA," El-Sayed told the Wall Street Journal in July. Socialist organizers, however, have called him "a longtime friend of Detroit DSA." "Our annual fundraiser is going to be [fire] this year. Chaired by the one and only Rashida Tlaib, with guest speaker Abdul El-Sayed," another post reads. "Our annual Douglas-Debs Dinner is THIS SATURDAY! The one and only Rashida Tlaib will give the keynote, with special guest speaker Abdul El-Sayed. Don’t miss out. Get your tickets today!" another stated. For its own part, the national platform for the DSA goes well beyond the proposals that El-Sayed has made a part of his Senate bid. JONATHAN TURLEY: ABDUL EL-SAYED’S WEALTH-TAX FANTASY COULD WRECK THE MICHIGAN ECONOMY Among other positions, the group has championed abolishing the U.S. Senate, establishing public ownership of the country’s largest corporations and defunding the Department of Defense — stances that El-Sayed has not voiced support for. El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether El-Sayed believes the past support from the Detroit DSA undermines his claims about what he believes about capitalism. Fox News' Robert Schmad contributed to this report

title: Transgender Washington state resident accused of fueling deadly Canadian school massacre that killed 8: DOJ
description: James Cody Bryant allegedly sent money, offered advice and agreed to livestream the Tumbler Ridge school shooting instead of alerting law enforcement.
content: A transgender Washington state resident allegedly helped fuel a Canadian school massacre that left children dead, choosing to aid the shooter, who also identified as a transgender, instead of sounding the alarm, federal officials said Tuesday. James Cody Bryant, 30, was arrested Tuesday morning in Bellingham north of Seattle, accused of sending money, offering advice and agreeing to broadcast the Feb. 10 attack at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in British Columbia. "Bryant had the information and ability to alert law enforcement, and even discussed that possibility with the shooter, but he chose not to," Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd said at a Seattle news conference. "Instead, he encouraged and offered assistance to a murderer." TRANSGEDNER EX-STUDENT IDENTIFIED AS ALLEGED SUSPECT IN DEADLY CANADA SCHOOL MASS SHOOTING Bryant faces a federal charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country. Prosecutors allege Bryant helped the shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, start a car to reach the school after the killings had begun. "So even after the shooter had already tragically killed two family members, Bryant assisted the shooter in successfully traveling to the second location to take even more lives," FBI Seattle Special Agent in Charge W. Mike Herrington said. "In the complaint, Bryant even admits to being maybe the only one who could stop the shooter." Herrington confirmed that Bryant and Van Rootselaar both identified as transgender, and said Bryant identifies as female. The two met through a random pairing on the online chat service Omegle roughly three years before the attack. Investigators have no indication what their transgender identities were, why they remained in contact, or that they ever met in person, Herrington said. TEEN PLANNED MIDDLE SCHOOL MASSACRE BEFORE MAKING DEADLY ‘LAST-MINUTE CHOICE’ TO KILL MOM: OFFICIAL Their online friendship developed into discussions of violence over at least six months, according to Herrington. "This complaint was particularly difficult to read, in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned," he said. Bryant allegedly agreed to record and broadcast a livestream to maximize the shooter’s notoriety. "Bryant even stayed awake after an overnight work shift to make sure this horrific act could be widely viewed online," Herrington said. FLORIDA MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING MASS SHOOTING TARGETING JEWISH EMPLOYEES AT ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION "We certainly know the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the livestream without Bryant broadcasting it, and was depending on Bryant to amplify the livestream because the shooter did not have many followers on social media." Floyd said the attempted livestream on Twitch lasted about 20 seconds before shutting down. Herrington said investigators do not know whether Van Rootselaar would have carried out the attack without Bryant’s willingness to operate it. Officials also described financial assistance, including a little more than $100 for shoes. An attempted transfer of roughly $15 for a lighter was ultimately reversed. NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS Floyd said Bryant and the shooter discussed sending weapons to Canada, but Bryant was uncomfortable doing so. Herrington said investigators had no indication the guns used in the attack came from the U.S. Asked about a possible political ideology or group affiliation, Floyd said investigators had no information indicating either. Herrington pointed to the shooter’s suffering and "a very keen focus on notoriety" as themes in the communications. The pair discussed other mass shootings, how the public reacted and a desire for the Tumbler Ridge attack to receive similar attention, he said. The investigation crossed the border within days of the massacre, when Canadian police received information from an online platform used by the shooter and contacted the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), British Columbia RCMP Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain said. Floyd said investigators obtained subpoenas and warrants and reviewed thousands of communications, many on Discord, before making the arrest. Canadian investigators have reviewed more than 90 statements from students, educators and first responders and continue to examine other online contacts, Rain said. GEORGIA HIGH SCHOOL SHOOTING SUSPECT COLT GRAY CHANGES PLEA TO GUILTY, NOW FACES LIFE IN PRISON "Our RCMP criminal investigation remains ongoing and the possibility of further charges being pursued in Canada remains under active consideration," he said. Herrington warned that assisting a mass shooting from afar does not shield someone from prosecution. "If you think you are safe from prosecution because you did not pull the trigger, or were not physically present at the scene of the crime, think again," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The FBI and our partners will use all of the considerable investigative tools at our disposal to hold accountable those who enable or assist in acts of mass violence." The Feb. 10 attack killed eight victims, including five students, an educator and the shooter’s mother and 11-year-old stepbrother, according to Canadian authorities. Van Rootselaar was found dead inside the school from an apparent self-inflicted injury.

title: ‘Digger’ bombs: A rare box-office misfire for Tom Cruise
description: Tom Cruise's dark comedy "Digger" earned just $8 million domestically despite a reported budget of up to $150 million, marking a rare career low.
content: You can’t win ’em all. That’s a phrase Hollywood’s global cinematic icon and producer Tom Cruise isn’t likely to hear often. But this past weekend, what many consider Hollywood’s biggest movie star in history suffered one of the worst debuts of his career. The painful performance at the box office of the dark comedy "Digger" was one for the headlines. Cruise earned legendary praise for keeping Paramount’s "Top Gun: Maverick" out of streaming services during the pandemic, forcing a theatrical-only release that grossed $1.5 billion worldwide, and has long been viewed as the studio’s "golden boy," anchoring multibillion-dollar intellectual properties and protecting the traditional theatrical experience. TOM CRUISE UNVEILS DRAMATIC TRANSFORMATION IN FIRST LOOK AT ALEJANDRO IÑÁRRITU’S HIGHLY-ANTICIPATED 'DIGGER' The Alejandro G. Iñárritu-directed "Digger," however, delivered a disappointing farewell note for Warner Bros. as a standalone studio. It grossed only $8 million domestically and $12 million internationally, where Cruise is ordinarily a big draw. That’s despite the film reportedly costing between $125 million and $150 million to make, with marketing expenses estimated at $100 million. "Given his extraordinary history with Paramount, the timing certainly adds an interesting layer to the story, but one movie doesn’t erase decades of success or the value he brings to a studio," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends for global media measurement and data analytics company Rentrak, told Fox News Digital. "There are lessons to be learned from ‘Digger,’ particularly around budget, positioning and expectations, but I don’t see this changing the fact that studios will continue to want to work with him." Meanwhile, the weekend’s No. 1 box office draw, debuting with $32.6 million, went to Amazon MGM’s erotic psychological thriller "Verity," directed by Michael Showalter and starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett. The film’s strong showing extends a winning streak for adaptations of author Colleen Hoover’s work at the box office. SAUDI-BACKED 'DESERT WARRIOR' GROSSES JUST $472K ON A $150M BUDGET IN HISTORIC BOX OFFICE DISASTER Following "Verity," Zach Cregger’s video game adaptation "Resident Evil" came in second for Sony Pictures with $12.5 million, while Paramount’s "Heart of the Beast," starring Brad Pitt as a former special forces soldier trapped in the Alaskan wilderness with his combat dog, grossed $11 million. That was followed by director Lance Oppenheim’s "Primetime" and "Digger." In the case of "Digger," critics weren’t especially kind, with the film earning a 51% score on Rotten Tomatoes. Cruise pulled out all the stops, giving a rare one-on-one interview with GQ magazine as part of the promotional campaign for the climate satire. The film’s London premiere on Sept. 22 at the ODEON Luxe Leicester Square brought out Prince William and Princess Catherine, as the event also served as this year’s royal charity screening benefiting the UK’s Film and TV Charity. While Cruise welcomed the two on the red carpet, David Beckham also made an appearance with his two sons, Cruz and Romeo. TOM CRUISE ADMITS RUMORS ABOUT HIS 'INTENSE' BEHAVIOR ON MOVIE SETS ARE TRUE The underwhelming opening comes as Paramount Skydance closes its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery in a $110 billion deal. Despite "Digger’s" poor showing, Dergarabedian said it won’t ultimately affect Cruise as a Hollywood powerhouse. "I think the interesting thing here is that the result really doesn’t change the fundamental reality that every studio wants to be in the Tom Cruise business," he said. "‘Digger’ was always a much tougher commercial proposition than the kind of broad, action-driven, franchise-oriented films audiences traditionally associate with Cruise." content: The Puyallup School District in Washington state, which has been embroiled in a national scandal after its transgender wrestler allegedly sexually assaulted a female opponent during a match, has responded after the female opponent's family filed a request for an injunction with the U.S. Supreme Court. The WIAA also defended current state policy on Monday after Keeler's SCOTUS appeal. "The WIAA remains committed to following Washington State law which permits student-athletes to participate in sports consistent with the gender with which they identify," the association said. title: NFL refs have set all-time record for flags this season, and it's changing the outcome of games
description: NFL officials have thrown more accepted penalties through Week 4 than any season since 1978, with 17 nullified touchdowns compared to five last year.
content: Each year, NFL fans complain that officials are throwing more flags than ever before. Most years, the perception exceeds the evidence. This year, the evidence supports the complaint. The NFL is on a historically high penalty pace. According to ESPN Insights, the league has recorded more accepted penalties through Week 4 this season than in any other season since play-by-play data became available in 1978. Week 4 was especially severe. Officials assessed 271 accepted penalties, the second-highest total for any week over that span. That's around 17 accepted penalties per game. BOMANI JONES CALLS JOSH ALLEN A 'MORON' FOR COSTLY INTERCEPTION, WHILE DEFENDING LAMAR JACKSON FOR SAME THING Sharp Football Analysis provided additional context on Tuesday. According to its analysis, officials are flagging offenses at the highest per-snap rate through four weeks of any season since 2000, at 6.18 penalties per 100 snaps. The increase is also occurring at particularly consequential points in games. Officials have set early-season records for accepted flags thrown in the red zone and on third and fourth downs in the second half. These penalties aren't merely disrupting drives. They are erasing points. So far this season, penalties have nullified 17 touchdowns. At the same point last year, that number was five. In 2024, it was four. To be clear, an accepted penalty does not mean officials made the correct call. Last week, Rams coach Sean McVay said the NFL privately acknowledged that officials incorrectly called defensive pass interference against Los Angeles in the closing moments of its Week 3 loss to Denver, nullifying an interception. Without the flag, the interception would've won the Rams the game. Instead, Denver retained possession and capitalized on the erroneous call to win. That example illustrates the larger problem. The proliferation of flags has become one of the defining features of the 2026 season. Fans don't watch football to see officials determine the outcome of drives. Yet listen to almost any broadcast after a significant play, and you'll hear an announcer quickly add, "No flags." There's a reason for that. MICHELE TAFOYA DEFENDS HOLLY ROWE AMID ARCH MANNING, STEVE SARKISIAN INCIDENT Viewers have become conditioned not to trust the initial result of a play. A touchdown, long completion, turnover, or critical stop now routinely produces a moment of hesitation as everyone scans the field for yellow. Waiting to find out whether a play counts has become part of the viewing experience. It shouldn't be. It's a problem. Which raises a more important question: Why are officials throwing flags at such a historic rate? One possibility is that teams are simply playing sloppier football. Reduced offseason work and lighter practice schedules could plausibly contribute to more procedural errors, poor technique, and legitimate penalties. But football has always operated under an inconvenient reality: officials could probably identify some technical violation on nearly every play. Some infractions are obvious and materially affect the play. Others occupy a gray area where enforcement depends largely on judgment and discretion. The distinction matters because officials plainly exercise that discretion later in the season. The same officiating crews that produce flag-heavy games during the regular season generally adopt a more permissive standard in the playoffs. Officials are more inclined to "let them play" in the postseason, particularly in high-leverage situations where a marginal call could dictate the outcome. By effectively raising the threshold in the playoffs, the NFL acknowledges that over-officiating diminishes the product and that marginal penalties should not decide its most important games. That also suggests the league accepts, or at least tolerates, the flag-heavy officiating that has come to define the early months of the season. If it didn't, it would instruct officials to exercise the same restraint in September and October that they routinely exercise in January. Perhaps the league sees officiating controversy as a marketing tool. Questionable calls generate scrutiny, debate, television segments, social-media engagement, and another news cycle surrounding the NFL. Or perhaps the increase reflects an institutional tendency toward over-enforcement. Officiating gives referees considerable authority over the game. It stokes their egos. Whatever the explanation, the league should intervene and stop this immediately. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Obvious infractions should be called. Marginal violations that require slow-motion examination or have no meaningful effect on the play should face a much higher threshold. What's happening this season is bad for fans, broadcasters, teams and the quality of the sport itself. There are too many flags, too many erased touchdowns, and too many pivotal possessions altered by officiating. That's particularly difficult to defend at a time when the NFL has never been more expensive or complicated to watch. Between expanded national windows, streaming exclusives, multiple subscriptions, and an increasingly fragmented broadcast schedule, the league is already asking more of consumers than ever before. title: Loyalty be damned: Did these coaches stick around a season too long and blow their chances at a big gig?
description: Kenny Dillingham, Jedd Fisch, and Brent Key were among college football's hottest coaching names. Now all three programs are struggling in 2025.
content: I want to take you all back to January 2025. The Arizona State Sun Devils just completed an improbable run to the College Football Playoff only two years removed from the disastrous Herm Edwards era. Head coach Kenny Dillingham, in only his second year on the job, had guided the program through NCAA sanctions and three-win seasons to a Big 12 championship and had his team on the precipice of a Playoff win over Texas thanks to the contributions of exciting players like Cam Skattebo, Jordyn Tyson, and Sam Leavitt. SLEEPER TEAMS FROM EACH POWER 4 CONFERENCE: WHO WILL EXCEED EXPECTATIONS THIS COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON? Just two years later and the Sun Devils now sit at 2-2 with an anemic offense, fresh off a beatdown at the hands of Baylor, a team currently employing a coach who was on a ridiculously hot seat himself just a month earlier. Less than a year after Arizona State's magical CFP appearance, two more coaches were making names for themselves at schools on opposite ends of the country. Jedd Fisch inherited a Washington program in 2024 that had just competed for a national championship the season prior to his arrival, but had to replace almost 100% of the team's production from a year earlier. After a 6-7 campaign that year showed promise, Fisch followed that up with a nine-win season that included a bowl win over Boise State and featured a quarterback by the name of Demond Williams who was the toast of college football. LINCOLN RILEY HOT SEAT RUMORS GET LOUDER AFTER 'FIRE LINCOLN' CHANTS DURING USC-WASHINGTON Meanwhile, more than 2,600 miles to the southeast, Brent Key was turning Georgia Tech into a legitimate threat in the ACC with a super innovative offense and a Heisman hopeful by the name of Haynes King at quarterback. The Yellow Jackets climbed to as high as number seven in the AP Poll, their highest mark in nearly two decades, and even finished the season ranked for the first time since 2014. Ten months later, and both Washington and Georgia Tech - along with the aforementioned Sun Devils - look like shells of their former selves from just a season ago. It happens. These schools are not built to contend for more than a season or two in a row without sharp fluctuations year-to-year. THERE'S A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN COACHES WHO 'CAN'T' WIN A NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP AND COACHES WHO 'HAVEN'T' While programs like Ohio State, Texas, Oregon, and Georgia have the infrastructure, funding, and talent pipelines to be consistently great year in and year out, the Washingtons, Georgia Techs, and Arizona States of the world need to capitalize on razor thin windows and go "all in" whenever they recognize those windows are approaching. That goes for their coaches, too. There was a time when Dillingham, Fisch, and Key were being linked to every major job in college football following their respective "window years." Dillingham was talked about as Mike Norvell's potential replacement at Florida State following their abysmal 2024 season, and the 36-year-old head coach was even discussed for the Michigan job shortly after they fired Sherrone Moore. WHICH HEAD COACH'S SEAT IS HOTTER HEADING INTO 2026 SEASON: SHANE BEAMER OR MIKE NORVELL? Speaking of the Maize and Blue, Fisch was also thought to be the leader in the clubhouse to take the job in Ann Arbor, and both he and Key were heavily considered as candidates for the opening at Florida, with Fisch getting extra attention given his alumni status in Gainesville. These three coaches were some of the hottest names in the last two hiring cycles, and for whatever reason, they chose to stay at their respective spots. There's no shame in that, and for Dillingham and Key, it could also come down to the fact that they are coaching at their alma maters. But the question remains: did they miss their chance to parlay their successful seasons into jobs at bigger, more established programs? If Washington, Arizona State, and Georgia Tech all finish with six or seven losses each this season, their respective coaches likely won't be fielding many calls when high-level jobs come open in November. Perhaps they're happy where they are now, although Dillingham has specifically called out Arizona State's fanbase and booster clubs about a lack of funding in the past, and based on conversations I've had with people close to the Gators' football program regarding the Florida job, it's one that Fisch would readily take under the right circumstances. Time will tell for all three of these coaches, as well as others who are making a name for themselves at the "mid-tier" Power 4 programs. COLLEGE FOOTBALL WEEK 4 CONTENDERS, PRETENDERS: TEXAS SURVIVES, MICHIGAN'S KARMA AND COACHES ARE SWEATING Maybe one of these three will win 10 or 11 games in 2027 and land a tier-one job to make me look like a fool. It worked for Matt Campbell, who had multiple historic seasons at Iowa State in 2020 and 2024 only to turn down other offers. It was only after Penn State came calling a year later that Campbell finally decided to leave the comfort of Ames. Patience is a virtue, as is loyalty, but when it comes to being a college football coach, sometimes those things can come back to bite you in the rear end. You're only as good as your latest season, and a lot of these hiring athletic directors have a bad case of recency bias when it comes to selecting their next football coach. I'll be interested to see where Kenny Dillingham, Brent Key, and Jedd Fisch are a year from today. Will they be settling in at cushy new jobs in Tallahassee, Los Angeles, and Norman? Or will they be the latest victims of the "what have you done for me lately" league that is Power 4 college football? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There's only one way to find out.

title: Mother, son among six identified after Boston-bound medevac jet vanishes off Nantucket
description: The six people aboard the Latitude Air Ambulance medevac jet that vanished over the Atlantic near Nantucket while en route to Boston have been identified.
content: The six people aboard a Boston-bound medical jet that disappeared over the Atlantic have been identified as a Bermudian mother and son and a four-person Canadian flight and medical crew. Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, was being transported for treatment related to a stroke, with her son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, accompanying her aboard the medevac flight. The U.S. Coast Guard identified the four Canadians aboard as Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir. 1 MISSING, 4 RUSHED TO HOSPITAL AFTER HELICOPTER CRASHES OFF SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ISLAND Childerhose was the captain and Farquhar was the first officer, while Paton served as the flight nurse and Weir as the respiratory therapist, according to Latitude Air Ambulance. The Gulfstream G100 disappeared early Saturday while traveling from Bermuda to Boston, triggering a major Coast Guard search off Nantucket. The Coast Guard suspended the search Sunday after debris associated with the aircraft was located. Lottimore was senior vice president and head of specialty reinsurance at Hamilton Re, according to the Bermuda-based company. "The entire Hamilton team is heartbroken by the loss of a respected leader, colleague and friend," Hamilton Re said in a statement. 4 FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS FOUND DEAD AFTER SMALL PLANE GOES DOWN OFF THE BAHAMAS Lottimore was also a 2002 graduate of Warwick Academy, where he had served as a prefect. The school remembered him as an "outstanding person." Bermuda Police said a family liaison officer had been assigned to assist the family. The aircraft was operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, a Canadian medical transport company. Latitude previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that the Gulfstream was operating as a medevac flight and was expected to make the journey from Bermuda to Boston in approximately two hours. Latitude Air Ambulance President Peter Byl said the company was mourning an "unimaginable loss." "Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities," Byl said. "We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day." The flight departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport late Friday night and was bound for Boston Logan International Airport. COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN ON BOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE The Transportation Safety Board of Canada said the crew reported electrical difficulties as the aircraft approached the Boston area before the jet descended rapidly and air traffic control lost contact south of Nantucket. FlightAware data previously reviewed by Fox News Digital showed the aircraft descending from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in roughly three minutes around 1 a.m. Saturday. The Federal Aviation Administration previously told Fox News Digital that it issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice at approximately 1:20 a.m. ET. Massport later confirmed the aircraft never arrived at Boston Logan. A civilian vessel located debris associated with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. "During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard Northeast District, said Monday. "We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation," Lake added. Canada is leading the investigation because the aircraft was registered there, in accordance with international agreements, according to the TSB. The National Transportation Safety Board is assisting as an accredited representative for the United States. The cause has not yet been determined. title: US could play role in united Ireland push after Trump's backing, Irish PM says
description: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the United States could potentially help in a future push for a united Ireland after Trump backed it.
content: NEW YORK — Nearly three decades after the Good Friday Agreement transformed Northern Ireland, Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the United States could potentially play a role in a future push for a united Ireland following President Donald Trump's backing for reunification. Martin, whose Fianna Fáil party supports Irish unity, said the landmark 1998 agreement – which largely ended 30 years of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland known as "the Troubles" – created a peaceful mechanism for deciding Northern Ireland's constitutional future, but cautioned that the deep divide between Northern Ireland's nationalist and unionist communities must first be bridged. "I believe in unity and my party believes in unity, but we have to work on it," Martin told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "We have to build reconciliation among the different traditions on the island of Ireland." "The U.S. were critical to the success of peace and conflict resolution in Ireland," Martin added. IRISH PM REJECTS ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS IN IRELAND AMID DRAMATIC VOTE OVER BOYCOTTING ISRAEL GAME Martin spoke to Fox News Digital during the U.N. General Assembly in New York at what he described as a global "crossroad," with war raging in Ukraine, conflict across the Middle East and negotiations underway over Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. Throughout the interview, he repeatedly returned to Ireland's own experience of conflict and peace as a guide to how the country approaches crises abroad, while defending the country's long-standing policy of military neutrality despite its growing support for Ukraine. The constitutional question of Irish unity gained renewed attention during Trump's recent visit to Ireland last month, when the president said he would "love" to see Ireland unified and predicted it would eventually happen. Asked during the Fox News Digital whether Washington could play a role again if Ireland eventually moves toward reunification, Martin replied: "To a degree maybe, potentially, yeah." Martin spoke before the latest confrontation over Garvaghy Road erupted in Portadown, reviving one of Northern Ireland's most bitter marching disputes and underscoring how potent nationalist-unionist divisions remain. The Parades Commission last month approved a limited Orange Order march along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road for the first time in 28 years. Residents and supporters blocked the route, while police declined to force the parade through amid fears of serious disorder. The Orange Order is a Protestant organization whose members generally support Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, while many residents of the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road community, who are predominantly Catholic, favor a united Ireland. The standoff has since spilled into the courts and Stormont, where parliament meets, as efforts to broker a compromise continue. Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum can be called if it appears a majority in Northern Ireland would support reunification. But Martin said more work is needed to define what a united Ireland would look like and deepen engagement on both sides of the border. IRISH PM SAYS IRELAND ‘NOT OVERRUN’ BY IMMIGRANTS, LEGAL MIGRATION TIED TO ECONOMIC SUCCESS UKRAINE AND THE SEARCH FOR PEACE For Martin, however, the lessons of Northern Ireland's peace process extend far beyond the island. "Because of our conflict in Northern Ireland, we feel we can make a contribution to that conflict resolution pathway," Martin said. He said Ireland's experience ending decades of violence now shapes how it approaches Russia's war in Ukraine, the conflict in the Middle East and Europe's increasingly uncertain security environment. "We don't get a sense that Russia is really interested at this particular stage," Martin said of efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Martin, who had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy the previous evening, nevertheless argued that continued channels between Washington and Moscow were important. Asked whether a realistic peace settlement would ultimately require Ukraine to surrender territory to Russia, Martin rejected the premise. "Ukraine can't cede territory that Russia hasn't even conquered, despite four years of war," Martin said. But he said a ceasefire along existing battle lines could provide a starting point for negotiations. "If we even could get a ceasefire on existing lines, and then negotiations to start," Martin said, adding that Kyiv would need protections against renewed Russian aggression. "Ukraine needs security guarantees." Martin also pointed to Ukraine's path toward European Union membership as potentially providing an additional layer of security and said the broader security architecture between Europe and Russia would ultimately have to be addressed in negotiations. "From our perspective, no one has the right to go into another country and take its territory," Martin said. HOW NEUTRAL IS IRELAND? Ireland's extensive support for Kyiv, however, raises a more contentious question at home: how far can a militarily neutral country support one side in a war while maintaining that neutrality? Ireland has committed more than $754 million in humanitarian assistance, military training and other non-lethal support to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 while stopping short of providing lethal weapons. Fox News Digital asked Martin whether that level of support undermined Ireland's neutrality. "No, because we don't give lethal aid, we haven't given military weaponry, but we have given non-lethal assistance in terms of training and so on like that, and also humanitarian aid to Ukraine," Martin said. Ireland has also taken in large numbers of Ukrainians fleeing the war. Martin said more than 120,000 had arrived at one point, with roughly 80,000 remaining in the country at the time of the interview. "That's not taking sides, that's taking a humanitarian response to a war," Martin said. "And many are contributing, many are working in the economy." Ireland's neutrality has also faced scrutiny over the long-standing use of Shannon Airport by the U.S. military. NATO's top military commander, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, described Shannon in August as a "very important logistics hub" for the United States and said withdrawing American military access would probably damage U.S.-Irish relations. The airport's role has long drawn protests from Irish neutrality campaigners, who argue that allowing U.S. military personnel and aircraft to transit through a civilian airport undermines the country's neutral status. Despite differing approaches to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, Martin described the U.S.-Ireland relationship in almost familial terms. "There's a very strong bond between Ireland and the United States," Martin said. He pointed to the long-standing tradition of Irish leaders visiting the White House on St. Patrick's Day and the enormous Irish American diaspora, which he estimated at roughly 30 million people. "It's just family, there's kinship ties," Martin said. MIDDLE EAST Martin said Ireland's peace-process experience also informs its approach to the Middle East, where Dublin has emerged as one of Israel's strongest European critics. He condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack and defended Israel's right to security while arguing that the subsequent Israeli military campaign in Gaza had been "absolutely disproportionate." "We believe in a two-state solution," Martin said. "We believe that Israel, of course, has a right to exist in security and its people need to be guaranteed of security. But likewise, Palestinians should have a right to live in their homeland in a peaceful way." Martin said Ireland's strongly anti-Israel position was shaped partly by its own history and what he described as a "sense of right and justice and fairness." WATCH: Irish PM explains Ireland's position on Israel, rejects antisemitism concerns amid controversial soccer match TRUMP'S INVESTMENT PUSH HITS EUROPE AS IRISH PM EYES NEXT TARIFF BREAK EUROPE'S SECURITY Ireland currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union, placing Martin at the center of negotiations as Europe confronts its biggest security challenges in decades. "There's a big realization in Europe that we have to do more to provide greater security to Europe, particularly because of the Russian-Ukrainian war," Martin said. He pointed particularly to Baltic and Nordic countries, whose governments have increased defense spending amid fears about Russia. "Many have an existential fear of Russia," Martin said. Martin said Europe was also tightening its approach to immigration, echoing comments he made elsewhere in the interview that asylum applications had fallen across Ireland and that governments across the continent were responding to mounting political pressure. "The world needs to try and turn a page toward a more peaceful sort of coexistence," Martin said. WATCH: Irish PM explains how Ireland is responding to Trump's 'America First' agenda

title: Former Hamas hostage counters Hasan Piker’s UT Austin event with her story of survival
description: Former Hamas hostage Maya Regev spoke at UT Austin on the same night Twitch streamer Hasan Piker addressed the University Democrats on campus.
content: Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker made waves with his visit to the University of Texas at Austin before he even made it into the Lone Star State. While he was speaking at an event last week hosted by University Democrats, a student group, another speaker with a much different point of view was telling her story of survival. Former Hamas hostage Maya Regev spoke to students with the goal of ensuring that they hear from someone who witnessed the horrors of Oct. 7, 2023, firsthand. In a recent conversation with Fox News Digital, Regev took issue with one of Piker's infamous remarks that "It doesn’t matter if rapes f---ing happened on Oct. 7, like that doesn’t change the dynamic for me." HAMAS USED SEXUAL VIOLENCE 'DELIBERATELY AND SYSTEMATICALLY' ON OCT 7, COMMISSION REPORT FINDS Regev said students concerned about cases like the sexual assault allegations against Cornell fraternity members may be listening to a person who's said "rape doesn't matter." Asked about his controversial remarks about the reported rapes committed by Hamas on Oct. 7, Piker told The New Republic that there was "definitely testimony of sexual violence that had taken place amongst the hostages. But that doesn’t change the dynamic of Israel committing a genocide against the Palestinians, and my opposing that genocide." Regev told Fox News Digital that Chabad, a Jewish organization with representatives across the globe, reached out to her about speaking at UT Austin after Piker's visit to the university was announced. "I'm not here to silence anyone," Regev told Fox News Digital. "I came there to let people hear what I've been through, like the other side of the story, with facts, with pictures, with records." UNIVERSITY EVENT WITH HASAN PIKER IN TEXAS DRAWS BACKLASH FROM BOTH SIDES OF THE AISLE The Anti-Defamation League has criticized Piker for what it calls his "antisemitic conspiracy theories and tropes," and has a list of some of his remarks about Oct. 7, including posting that Hamas hostage and American-Israeli soldier Edan Alexander had volunteered for the "Nazi army." Regev said that while Piker has freedom of speech and "can say whatever he wants," it was important for her to make sure students were getting more than one point of view. Regev also emphasized the fact that she was speaking from her own experience, not things she read about from others. "For me, Oct. 7, it's not a debate, it's not something I read online. It's something that I've lived through, something that will forever be inside me, something that I will have to live with for the rest of my life," Regev told Fox News Digital. "I just think that it's important for them to understand that behind every story there are real human beings." "I was a hostage. I was a Hamas hostage," Regev told Fox News Digital. "I was being held by Hamas, by those monsters, and I think that students might, you know, forget that they are actually real human beings, real families that lost their lives, real women that got raped, men, lives were destroyed on Oct. 7." Regev pushed back on Piker and other online influencers shaping students' opinions without firsthand knowledge. "When they hear an influencer post something, when they read something, it's important for them to check the facts before they are repeating a slogan or celebrating death of innocent people," Regev said. She later added, "I sat with those people. I lived with them for two months, with Hamas people... I think that people should listen to a person who was really there and not to a person who just sees stuff online and has millions of followers." When asked what influencers like Piker get wrong about the situation in Gaza, she said that they overlook the realities on the ground, particularly Hamas' use of Palestinian civilians as human shields. "Hamas is using children and women and elderly women as a human shield," Regev said. "I think, again, people should know the facts before they're talking, and especially when you're very influencing." HASAN PIKER'S DEFENSE OF HAMAS HAVING 'RIGHT TO RESIST MILITARILY' DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM HUMAN RIGHTS GROUPS On Oct. 7, 2023, Regev went to the Nova Music Festival with her brother Itay Regev and her friend Omer Shem Tov. When the rocket alerts began sounding at 6:29 a.m., Regev was not so alarmed, explaining, as someone who grew up in Israel, it was something she had experienced several times before that day. "We thought it was just a matter of time before everything will calm down, and we can keep on partying, but after some time we understood that it [was] a lot more serious than what we thought," she said. Regev explained that the group headed toward their cars before being told by police officers to abandon their vehicles and that terrorists had invaded the country. That's when Regev, her brother and Shem Tov began running for what she estimated to be 60 to 90 minutes. They then got a call from Ori Danino, a friend of a friend who was also at the festival. Danino had already gotten out of the danger zone, but decided to turn around and pick up the group to get them to safety. Unfortunately, all of them would be abducted and taken to Gaza. The group drove for about five minutes before "a big pickup truck" with terrorists began shooting at them, hitting Regev in both of her legs. Her brother was also shot. The terrorists dragged Regev, her brother and Shem Tov out of the vehicle before loading them into the pickup truck and driving them into Gaza. While Danino was initially able to escape, he was later caught by another group of terrorists and taken into the Strip. The Regev siblings were released from captivity in late November 2023, within a few days of each other. Regev described her release from Gaza as bittersweet, feeling grateful to be home while worrying about her friends who were left behind. "It was a total shock. I thought that Omer will return home, like, a few days after me, but then the ceasefire was stopped. So, it was very hard for me. I couldn't believe that I escaped this hell, and they are still there being held, Ori, Omer, all the other hostages," Regev told Fox News Digital. HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA "I felt very guilty that I was saved, that I'm back home with my family. I can get the medical treatment that I needed to receive and there are people there suffering, still hostages suffering, not eating, being abused physically and mentally. But I understood that I have a voice now, and I have to use it, and I'll do anything in my [power] to bring them back home," she added. Danino would survive 11 months in captivity before terrorists executed him, along with Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Eden Yerushalmi, Carmel Gat, Almog Sarusi and Alexander Lobanov. Shem Tov endured 505 days in Hamas captivity and was released on Feb. 22, 2025. With her brother and Shem Tov back home, Regev is finally able to look to the future, something she wasn't mentally ready to do until all the hostages were returned. Now, she's enjoying the simple things in life, walking outside, looking up at the sky. "When I was there in captivity, I promised myself that I will live life. I told myself that if I'll ever be home again, I'll live life, and I'll study, and I'll go travel the world, and I'd be with friends and my family. And it's what I'm doing now, you know, I'm just doing whatever makes me happy." "I think that the only thing I wish for myself is to be happy forever and grateful for everything that I have." title: Comeback canceled: Seahawks ditch plan to sign veteran RB Joe Mixon after failed physical
description: Joe Mixon's NFL comeback stalled after the Seattle Seahawks declined to sign him following a failed physical, turning to Robert Henry Jr. instead.
content: So much for Joe Mixon’s NFL return. After bringing the 30-year-old running back in for a workout, the Seattle Seahawks decided not to sign Mixon to their practice squad after his physical, multiple reports said early Tuesday. Instead, the reigning Super Bowl champions plan to sign Robert Henry Jr. off the Washington Commanders' practice squad.
