title: America’s Arctic war machine roars to life as commander reveals chilling new reality on Russia’s doorstep
description: U.S. and Canadian forces deploy HIMARS, F-35s and F-16s across western Alaska as Tundra Merlin tests rapid American Arctic combat readiness.
content: Across one of the coldest, most remote and strategically exposed corners of the United States, American forces are practicing how to fight on land, at sea and in the air — rapidly moving rocket systems into western Alaska, sending F-35s and F-16s toward simulated threats, and coordinating U.S. and Canadian warships in the Bering Sea. The operations are part of Tundra Merlin, an enduring U.S. military campaign aimed at proving that even across Alaska’s vast distances and extreme Arctic conditions, American and allied forces can rapidly assemble combat power to defend the northern approaches to the homeland. And behind that show of force is a changing security environment increasingly shaped by Russia and China. TWO ICEBREAKERS HEADED TO ALASKA AS US COMBATS RUSSIAN, CHINESE INFLUENCE IN ARCTIC "I think what’s changed is primarily two things," Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, told Fox News Digital. "One is that the melting sea ice has made the Arctic more accessible. And we’re seeing increased activity both commercially and militarily in the Arctic, particularly during the summer months." "The other factor is that China and Russia and others are continuing to advance their military capabilities and capacity with an interest in showing that they can use them in the Arctic as well," Davis said. The Pentagon has reached a similar conclusion. Its 2024 Arctic Strategy warned that growing Russia-China cooperation could "alter the Arctic’s stability and threat picture," and called for greater U.S. presence, exercises and military preparedness in a region becoming increasingly accessible. Defense officials have said forces operating there must be able not merely to train in extreme conditions, but survive them. RUSSIA PULLED BACK FROM THE ARCTIC, FOR NOW. NATO MUST ACT BEFORE THOSE TROOPS RETURN Few places illustrate the stakes better than Alaska. The state sits at the intersection of the Arctic and Pacific and serves as a critical hub for homeland defense and a platform for projecting U.S. military power toward the Indo-Pacific and beyond. The Russian and American mainlands are only about 55 miles apart at their closest points across the Bering Strait, while Russia’s Big Diomede Island and Alaska’s Little Diomede Island are separated by roughly 2.5 miles. Alaska also hosts major air bases, early-warning and missile-defense infrastructure, and tens of thousands of military personnel. U.S. Northern Command says Alaskan Command has more than 22,000 active-duty personnel from across the services, along with approximately 4,700 Guard and Reserve members. Air Force officials have described Alaska as the "crossroads of the Arctic and the Pacific," providing U.S. forces with reach and domain awareness for both homeland defense and global power projection. Davis put that geography in even starker terms. Pointing to the fifth-generation fighters positioned in Alaska, he told Fox News Digital that U.S. forces can "project from the Arctic to almost anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere in about 10 hours of flight time." RUSSIA’S QUIETER NUCLEAR SUBMARINES THREATEN NATO, FORMER COMMANDER WARNS Tundra Merlin is designed to turn that geographic advantage into combat capability. Davis described the operation as a collection of military options — essentially "plays in a playbook" — that can be activated either to deter an adversary or respond if one begins acting aggressively. "Our hope is that we don’t have any adversarial activity because we’ve effectively deterred it," Davis said. "But if we do see it and we have kind of a play in the playbook ready to go. For a response." One of the most striking demonstrations came recently, on Alaska’s western edge. U.S. and Canadian forces rapidly moved a U.S. Army HIMARS mobile rocket system and an AN/TPQ-53 radar into western Alaska aboard a Royal Canadian Air Force C-17, then connected those ground forces with American F-35s, F-16s and a KC-135 tanker operating overhead. CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS The mission brought air defense and long-range offensive firepower together in a single operation. F-35s and HIMARS synchronized against a simulated ground target approximately 135 miles away, while F-16s simultaneously intercepted F-35s acting as simulated incoming aerial threats, according to U.S. Northern Command. Davis said the point was not simply to prove the individual weapons worked, but to show how quickly forces could be moved into a remote part of Alaska and linked together. The operation demonstrated that U.S. forces can rapidly move capabilities into Alaska "both to defend Alaska, but also, if necessary, to put other adversary targets at risk," he told Fox News Digital. Tundra Merlin pushed that same concept out to sea in September. From Sept. 18–22, U.S. and Canadian forces conducted a joint maritime strike scenario roughly 100 nautical miles north of Dutch Harbor, integrating U.S. Coast Guard and Royal Canadian Navy surface and subsurface vessels with Canadian maritime patrol aircraft and Alaska-based U.S. Air Force F-35 fighters and E-3 airborne warning and control aircraft. The forces practiced multiple simulated maritime target engagements, testing whether information collected by different ships and aircraft could be rapidly passed across the force and used to identify, track and engage a potential threat. "The most impressive part to me was seeing the high degree of cooperation and integration among units that day in and day out don't necessarily operate together," Davis said. "To see the joint nature on the U.S. side integrated together with the inter-agency of the U.S. Coast Guard and with our allies, with Canada as an example, was just an amazing thing to see," he added. That ability to operate at scale is complicated by Alaska itself. Extreme cold can affect equipment and personnel, while the enormous distances and limited infrastructure of the North American Arctic make moving and sustaining forces unusually difficult. The Pentagon’s Arctic Strategy specifically identifies those distances and the region’s infrastructure limitations as obstacles to military operations and says maintaining infrastructure in Alaska is essential for missile defense, surveillance and rapid power projection. Davis said military equipment brought into Alaska cannot simply be expected to function as it would elsewhere. "It needs to be conditioned. It needs to be properly outfitted to operate in sub-zero temperatures for a long period of time," he said, adding that troops also require specialized clothing, training and procedures to avoid cold-weather injuries and continue fighting in Arctic conditions. The pressure to master that environment comes as Russia and China increasingly demonstrate their own ability to operate near North America. In July 2024, the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, detected and intercepted two Russian Tu-95 bombers and two Chinese H-6 bombers flying together in the Alaskan Air Defense Identification Zone. It was the first time NORAD had intercepted Russian and Chinese military aircraft operating together in the zone. The aircraft remained in international airspace and did not enter U.S. or Canadian sovereign territory, and NORAD said the flight itself was not considered a threat. The episode nevertheless highlighted the very kind of cooperation U.S. defense planners are watching. For now, Davis said Alaska is positioned to deal with the military threats commanders expect under normal conditions. "We're postured very well for any of the anticipated threats that we think would come our way in the very near term," he said. But if commanders saw indications of a significant escalation, Davis said Alaskan Command would likely request additional forces and capabilities. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That, ultimately, is what Tundra Merlin is intended to prove: that in a theater defined by enormous distances, punishing weather and growing Russian and Chinese activity, the United States can move forces across Alaska, connect them across land, sea and air, and have combat power ready before a potential adversary decides to test the northern edge of the homeland.

title: Woman's routine Uber ride takes alarming turn after her driver misses the exit
description: A viral TikTok video describes an Uber passenger's 3 a.m. ride turning alarming when her driver asked to stop at a parking garage to charge his EV. Experts weigh in.
content: A late-night ride experience is raising questions about what passengers should do when a routine trip begins to feel uncomfortable. In a recent TikTok video, a woman said she was riding in an Uber at around 3 a.m. when her driver asked to stop at a parking garage for 15 to 20 minutes to charge his electric vehicle. The woman, according to her video, said the vehicle was at 43% charge — and that she was about 25 minutes from home at the time. FRIGHTENING OBJECT CAUGHT BY TSA INSIDE PASSENGER'S BASEBALL BAT-SHAPED FLASHLIGHT Her concern grew after the driver reportedly missed an exit, prompting her to question exactly where they were headed. "I don't want to get into a random parking lot with you," the woman can be heard telling the driver. "You also just missed the exit." Fox News Digital reached out to the woman who posted the TikTok video for additional details. The woman ultimately ended the trip and contacted police, according to the video. In a statement, Uber told Fox News Digital that it investigated the report and took action. SKYDIVERS WATCH PLANE VANISH FROM SIGHT, MAKE SPLIT-SECOND DECISION TO JUMP "Everyone deserves to feel safe and comfortable when using the Uber platform," an Uber spokesperson said. "We have investigated this report and taken appropriate action." The company pointed to safety features available through its app, including an emergency button, GPS tracking and the ability to share trip details with others. The incident has raised broader questions about what passengers can do if they feel uneasy during a rideshare trip. 'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS Dillon Abend, a recent college graduate and the founder and CEO of rideshare safety app 3rd-i, based in New Jersey, told Fox News Digital that an unexpected change in route can quickly raise concerns, particularly for someone traveling alone late at night. "Your heart just drops," he said. Abend said he's heard from hundreds of college students about situations that left them feeling uncomfortable during various rideshare trips. For passengers who begin feeling uncomfortable, seeking help can be challenging. "Almost everyone's reasoning in this situation is, 'I didn't want the driver three feet away to hear me call the police and have them act,'" Abend said. Technology can provide passengers with additional ways to stay connected or seek help during a ride-hailing trip, according to Abend. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Ideally, you want to share your location with people," he said. "Let a core group of three to five people know where you're going and the details of it." Before getting into a vehicle, check the license plate and confirm that the driver and vehicle match the information displayed in the rideshare app, he advised. New Jersey-based Seymour Josephson, co-president of the What's My Name Foundation, has been working with Uber and Lyft since July 2020 to promote rideshare safety on college campuses. He and his wife, Marci Josephson, established the foundation after their 21-year-old daughter, Samantha, was killed on March 29, 2019, when she mistakenly entered a vehicle she thought was the Uber she had hailed. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The What's My Name Foundation encourages passengers to follow four steps before entering a ride-hailed vehicle: stop, ask, match and inform — known as the "SAMI" steps. People should stop before they enter the vehicle, ask the driver, "What's my name?" and match the vehicle's license plate with the information provided in the app. Fox News Digital reached out to Lyft for comment and details. "We want to make sure that we're not just getting into a car, but we're getting into the right car, the right Uber," Josephson said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Seymour Josephson said he is not looking to discourage people from using rideshare services, but to make the experience safer for everyone — both rider and driver. "We also helped bring forward the four-digit PIN with Uber and now Lyft," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "All it is," he continued, "is a two-step authentication. And it's securing that it is your ride by giving that pin to the driver before you get in."

title: Matthew McConaughey says Woody Harrelson’s wild antics include 2 am visits, inviting strangers on vacations
description: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson share outrageous stories from their decades-long friendship, including a possible DNA test revelation.
content: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson's friendship has put both of them in some wild situations. While promoting their new show, "Brothers," the two actors, and close friends, have shared many anecdotes from their years-long friendship, which have sent the internet buzzing. Whether it be finding out they might be brothers to Harrelson surprising McConaughey in bed in the middle of the night, these two Hollywood icons have made it clear they have an interesting friendship. Here are some of the most outrageous stories the two shared during recent interviews. MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY'S PIECE OF RELATIONSHIP ADVICE THAT KEEPS HIS MARRIAGE TO CAMILA ALVES STRONG Late-night surprise During an appearance on the "Glass Half Full" podcast, McConaughey described some of the oddities that come with being Harrelson's friend, saying "he's never gone through a front door in his life." He explained that no matter how long it has been since they last saw each other, Harrelson has "never called or sent a message" to make plans, adding, "he just shows up." "We hadn't seen each other for a year at the time when I was living out in LA. I hadn't seen him for a year. Guess my introduction to him," he said. "My wife goes 'ah.' And I go, 'Woah.' Two in the morning, wake up, Woody's in between us in bed! He had jumped the fence, picked the window, snuck in, and got in bed with us." When host Craig Melvin told Harrelson that "people have been shot for less," the actor replied, "Well, I was hoping he didn't have a gun." "But what a good way to wake up a friend, you know what I mean, and get to be next to Camila [Alves, McConaughey's wife]," Harrelson added. "Like, that was nice. She was warm to me." Anniversary confusion When speaking to Melvin, the celebrity duo also shared how they first met, although they admit they have different recollections. McConaughey admits Harrelson "believes we've known each other one year longer" than he does, because "I don't remember the first time we met." He blames it on the idea that they began taking shots together at 1 p.m., but when Harrelson corrected him on a detail in the story, McConaughey told him, "I don't remember. You tell me." "I already knew of him and I liked him from a distance," Harrelson said. "And then I met him, and I'm like, 'Hey, let's do a shot,' and he's like, 'Man, I got a lot of work to do today.' I said, 'One shot's gonna stop you from all the work you got?'" McConaughey then chimed in adding, "Hence, I don't remember meeting that day. It doesn't sound like that was the beginning and the end of the story." Living on the edge While telling Melvin about Harrelson's many talents, McConaughey casually mentioned that the actor once "did a handstand 18 inches away from the edge of the Grand Canyon." "The stuff this guy pulls off because he didn't know better is still amazing," McConaughey said. "Most people do that stuff when they're a kid, and they lose it as they get older, because you know better. This kid, what are you, 60 what now... 65 and he's still doing handstands on the edge of the Grand Canyon." While Harrelson tried to downplay the achievement by saying he was farther away than McConaughey is saying and that it wasn't the Grand Canyon, the "Dallas Buyers Club" star continued to praise him. "I'm probably exaggerating less than from the edge on his hand, the Grand Canyon," McConaughey said. "The photographer freaks out. Never got a picture of it." He added that had the photographer been able to take a photo, "it would have been the most epic shot." Vacation antics While promoting the new show, the two actors also sat down with Conan O'Brien on his podcast, "Conan O'Brien Needs A Friend." During the interview, McConaughey shared an unbelievable story about the time Harrelson met a couple on their honeymoon while waiting for his luggage at baggage claim in Greece, and invited them to stay with him and McConaughey in the house McConaughey had rented for them and their families. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "You have a consistent habit of having an open heart and inviting people into your future life or yours or mine," McConaughey told Harrelson during the interview. "He's doing this routinely. He's, he's very consistent. We go on a Greek holiday and my family… we rent the place... We rent the place and they… we fly over, but they get there before us and we show up and there's two people sitting on the tailgate of a truck right in front of our rental." He went on to say that at first he thought it was Harrelson and his wife Laura, but soon found out it was two strangers who told him, "We met Woody and Laura at the airport getting our luggage and… they're great." When he confronted Harrelson, who had already claimed the primary bedroom in the rental, he told him, "They're great, man. They're going to be with us for a week." Break-in When speaking with People, McConaughey expanded on the idea that Harrelson would show up at his home "unannounced," calling it "one of Woody's great traits." "He never comes through a front door. And he’ll swing by for an hour to say, ‘Howdy!’" McConaughey said. "It might turn into, ‘I’ve moved in for three months.’ It’s a beautiful trait how he makes himself at home." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Harrelson confirmed he does make a habit of making McConaughey's house his own, noting, McConaughey "tolerates it." McConaughey went on to explain that often during these months-long stays, he will approach Harrelson after a while asking him to leave, and his kids will fight back. "There are times when I’m like, ‘Man, Woody, I need some space,’ and my whole family’s like, ‘No, don’t let Woody go. We’ve been staying up later having more milkshakes,’ whatever," McConaughey said. "The laughter’s been in the house a while." Brothers? PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE In their new show, McConaughey and Harrelson play fictionalized versions of themselves who find out they could potentially be brothers. The premise for the show seems outrageous. However, it is closer to the truth than it may seem, as the two actors found out during a trip to Greece with their families that there is a possibility the two may actually be brothers. "In Greece a few years ago, we’re sitting around talking about how close we are and our families and et cetera and my mom is there. And she says, ‘Woody, I knew your dad,’" McConaughey told Kelly Ripa on her podcast in 2023. McConaughey explained to Ripa that his mother and father were divorced before he was born, so there is a possibility that she and Harrelson's father met during that time period. Harrelson also told the story while on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" in 2023 that McConaughey's mom's story was "filled with innuendo," implying she and his father may have had a romance when they knew each other. "The year of his birth, nine months before, she was on a sabbatical from her relationship with his supposed father, Jim," Harrelson joked about McConaughey’s birthday. title: WATCH: Dem senators dodge backing Kamala Harris in potential 2028 run: ‘Very messy’
description: Democratic senators aren't rallying behind Kamala Harris despite her frontrunner status, with a wide open primary looming for the 2028 race.
content: Former Vice President Kamala Harris is leaving the door open to another White House bid in 2028, but Democratic senators aren’t rushing to line up behind their party’s 2024 nominee. "Well, I've backed her before, but there'll be other contenders this time," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "I've made no decisions about who I would support." "I think we're going to have a very, very, very messy and very big primary," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said. "It's going to be every Tom, Dick and Harry. And that's probably where it should be." HARRIS KEEPS 2028 DOOR OPEN AS SHE HITS MIDTERM CAMPAIGN TRAIL, WARNS ‘28 WON’T MATTER’ WITHOUT 2026 "We've got a lot of people who are going to run, and I think we should sort that out after the midterms," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., said. Harris returned to the campaign trail last week alongside Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, while continuing to leave open the possibility of another White House bid. Asked in Detroit whether she would run in 2028, Harris said she had not decided and urged Democrats to focus on November, warning that "'28 won't matter" without success in 2026. "We're focused on 2026," said Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md. "We're gonna win back the House and the Senate." She continued, "I love Kamala Harris. I have a very personal friendship and relationship. She's amazing. I think anybody who wants to run should. She's obviously very well qualified. We need to focus on '26." DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 "This is going to be a wide open primary, and again, that's democracy at its best," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said. "Everyone who wants to run should be able to run for office here." Another potential 2028 contender is Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who represents the party’s progressive wing. title: NFL legend warns more rulebook tweaks won't save signal-callers from getting hurt
description: Dan Fouts says more rules won't fix NFL quarterback injuries, arguing offensive line play matters more than roughing the passer protections.
content: "Well, it might be a good idea to put dresses on all of them," Hall of Fame linebacker Jack Lambert said in response to the NFL tightening rules on roughing the passer calls in 1979. The Pittsburgh Steelers legend said that in 1979. Imagine what Lambert would say now with all the rules the league has added and altered to protect quarterbacks. Yet, despite all the changes, the players who play the most important position in all of sports are still getting injured. Heading into Week 4, six starting quarterbacks have already dealt with injuries. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback Dan Fouts said that more rules changes aren’t the answer to limiting quarterback injuries. "Jack (Lambert)’s famous quote was, well, let's just put (dresses) on all those quarterbacks. And I thought that was a good idea 'cause I got really good-looking legs," Fouts told OutKick in a recent interview. "As far as today and the quarterbacks and getting hurt, it’s a violent, violent game. Defenders are very, very good. They are more athletic than offensive linemen, and that's no rip on offensive linemen. But you look at the number of different blitzes that you are throwing at quarterbacks these days with corners off the slot and linebackers and the whole, the whole nine yards." As the sport has evolved, players have gotten bigger, stronger and faster. While the NFL can try to protect quarterbacks as much as it can by changing the rulebook, the nature of the game leads to injuries. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. All the other quarterbacks have already returned — Sam Darnold and Kyler Murray — or are expected to return this season — Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels and Baker Mayfield. title: Cowboys legend Randy White endorses Ken Paxton, warns James Talarico ‘can’t be trusted’
description: Dallas Cowboys legend Randy White endorsed Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, citing concerns over transgender athletes in girls' sports and bathrooms.
content: FIRST ON FOX: Dallas Cowboys legend and Pro Football Hall of Famer Randy White has endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the state’s consequential U.S. Senate race. "Ken Paxton will get in there and get things done. He’s not afraid," White told OutKick in an exclusive interview. "That’s one thing I really like about Ken. He will get in there and say what needs to be said. He doesn’t hold back. He tells the truth. He’s not trying to win a popularity contest when he’s working. It’s what’s right for the people." White said his endorsement grew out of his personal relationship with Paxton and their shared work on issues involving children and the opioid crisis. "I like his attitude, the things that he does, the way he does them." White highlighted Paxton’s support for the National Child Identification Program, which provides parents with kits to preserve their children’s fingerprints, DNA and other identifying information at home. Paxton previously joined a coalition supporting federal funding for the program, while White has served as one of its Hall of Fame ambassadors. "He is a big supporter of the Child ID program, which is something I’m a big supporter of — helping kids," White said. White also lost his son-in-law to an accidental opioid overdose, a personal tragedy that prompted him to become an advocate for drug-awareness initiatives. In 2024, White joined Paxton and Texas parents who had lost children to fentanyl-laced drugs in a public service announcement released by the attorney general’s office. EXCLUSIVE: FENTANYL DEATHS PLUNGE 22% AS TRUMP WHITE HOUSE TOUTS CRACKDOWN ON DEADLY DRUG CRISIS "This opioid stuff — I lost a son-in-law to opioids, accidental," White said. "He’s been right on top of that ever since that happened. Everything he does is kind of the way I think it should be done." TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS White drew a stark contrast between Paxton and Talarico, whom he said he does not trust. "I know Ken Paxton," White said. "I know he’s going to do what he says he’s going to do. I know he’s going to go to work every day, and he’s going to help the people of Texas. This other guy, I don’t know him. But I hear what he says, and it’s different from what I believe." Asked whether he considered Talarico "too woke," White answered, "Yes." "I don’t want to go into each specific thing, but, yeah, he’s different than what I think is right," White said. "If this guy gets elected in Texas, I’m going to pull my hair out, and I don’t have many left. So, we’ve got to get out and vote so this doesn’t happen." White specifically cited transgender participation in girls’ sports and access to girls’ bathrooms among the issues on which he disagreed with Democrats and Talarico. Talarico voted against Republican-backed restrictions on transgender athletes while serving in the Texas House. In September, however, he told Fox News that he would "oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness." Talarico later said his position had not changed, arguing that he opposes a blanket statewide prohibition and believes local education and sports officials should make decisions on an athlete-by-athlete and sport-by-sport basis. White said Talarico’s recent comments reinforced his doubts about the Democrat. "I think that’s a sign that we can’t trust him," White said. "He’s going to go with the way the wind flows, whatever he feels like is the best thing for him and what his goals are. We don’t need somebody like that. "We need somebody like Ken Paxton who is going to stick to his guns, who is not afraid to stand up for what he believes is right." The general-election race has become unexpectedly competitive. A Fox News Poll conducted Sept. 24-28 found Talarico leading Paxton 51%-49% among likely voters, a result within the poll’s three-point margin of sampling error. It’s just something that’s part of the process of getting America back where it needs to be and making it safe." title: Fever star Sophie Cunningham tells Aces' A'ja Wilson to 'grow up' in response to her playoff meltdown
description: Sophie Cunningham blasted A'ja Wilson on her "No Hesitation" podcast for confronting a Fever fan who was simply pointing during the WNBA playoffs.
content: If you know anything about Indiana Fever forward Sophie Cunningham, you know she's not going to mince words. She famously stated, "I said what I said," while speaking to the media following relentless backlash for saying men should not compete in women's sports. That’s why it shouldn’t shock anyone that Cunningham went off on WNBA MVP and Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson for confronting a Fever fan and verbally berating him in Game 2 at Gainbridge Fieldhouse for simply pointing at her. In the latest episode of "No Hesitation," hosted by Cunningham and elite basketball trainer Drew Hanlen, the Fever forward gave her long-awaited take on the now-infamous incident involving the controversial blocking call. "Oh my God! I have so many thoughts," Cunningham stated after her and Hanlen watched a clip from the "Pat McAfee Show" where one of the hosts (Boston Connor) confirmed, just as I did in my reporting following the incident, that the fan said, "It (the foul) is on you," while pointing. CRAIG CARTON BLASTS WNBA, A'JA WILSON OVER FAN CONFRONTATION: 'THIS LEAGUE CAN'T GET OUT OF ITS OWN WAY' While explaining that she held back from giving her reaction to the incident on X and saving it "for the pod," Cunningham went off on Wilson. "Us women in sport, and I'm just gonna say women in sport because that's my occupation and I have lived this, we yell from the rooftops that we want equality. We want to be treated like the men," she stated, prefacing her blunt comments. "We're gonna go for them for just pointing and saying, 'You fouled!'? Like grow up! What are we doing?" Cunningham said. She also took exception to the idea that Wilson, and seemingly other players, should be allowed to attack fans, claiming, "Us athletes need to be treated better" and "These fans need to be more supportive and not say anything negative." Cunningham pointed out that she has a unique perspective on this as one of the most, if not the most, hated WNBA players simply because she doesn’t believe men should be in women's sports and spaces. "I can say this, because I, hands down, have probably got s--- on the entire season, maybe sometimes two seasons — people coming after who I am, my character, what I stand for, x, y, z, I could go on and on." WHO IS SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM? FOX NATION CHRONICLES THE WNBA STAR'S RISE FROM FARM GIRL TO WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATE "I've heard the worst of the worst. It's part of it," Cunningham said. "You should be grateful to be on this platform. You should be grateful to be playing basketball for a living and inspiring the next generation. If you really want sports fans, then you're gonna get sports fans. That includes pointing. That includes getting yelled at. Probably [will] be getting called names." "I don't think [the Fever fan] did absolutely anything wrong," Cunningham said definitively. Maybe Cunningham's most controversial take was saying, "If you want to get technical, that (Wilson's actions) could've called for a suspension, but she's like the LeBron James of our league so of course they're (WNBA) not going to suspend her." Not only was Wilson not suspended, she was neither ejected, nor was she fined for her actions. Cunningham seems to say players of Wilson's caliber will be treated far less harshly and get away with clear violations. Cunningham also said there should have been repercussions for former Fever guard and Amazon Prime commentator Sydney Colson, as well as fellow Amazon analyst Theresa Plaisance, who left their courtside seats to insert themselves in the altercation. That says a lot more about your mental status to anything the fans are doing," Cunningham said in response to both Wilson and viewers upset over her poking fun at the situation on TikTok. title: More Gen Z college freshmen are quitting school early and moving back home with mom and dad
description: Just weeks into the fall semester, some Gen Z college freshmen have left campus and headed back home to take online classes — creating viral debates about the reasons.
content: Some Gen Z freshmen have already decided — just weeks into the fall semester — to abandon their college campuses, head back home and take classes online. title: Dems hand GOP fresh midterm weapon by opposing widely used voter ID
description: Senate Democrats blocked a voter ID and insider trading ban bill as Chuck Schumer's caucus faces accusations from Republicans of denying Trump a win.
content: Senate Democrats’ recent rejection of voter ID is giving Republicans fresh ammunition in the midterm fight, putting them on the opposite side of a practice that is common across the country and broadly popular with voters in both parties. Republicans have developed a cynical view of why Democrats won’t play ball with voter ID, arguing that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his caucus don’t want to give the GOP a win heading into the midterm elections. "Democrats are gonna vote against it because they don't want to give the president a win," Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital. "They don’t want to give Republicans a win. They'll screw the country and stuff." DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID Republicans' latest attempt to pass a federal voter ID law, which was paired with another popular issue to ban insider trading in Congress, comes months after initially launching their push to pass the SAVE America Act, a high priority for President Donald Trump that Schumer and Democrats have time and again rejected. Earlier this year, Democrats argued that voter ID isn’t so bad, it’s just how Republicans were approaching it that they disagreed with — Schumer dubbed the SAVE America Act "Jim Crow 2.0" and contended it would disenfranchise Black and Brown voters. "Democrats support voter ID," Schumer said on a press call earlier this year. "In fact, we included it, and it is included, in our Freedom to Vote legislation several years ago." INSIDE THE SENATE'S CHAOTIC ALL-NIGHTER THAT LEFT TRUMP'S SAVE AMERICA ACT ON THE SHELF But as the months have dragged on, an issue that voters overwhelmingly support has become a place for Democrats to dig their heels into the dirt against. title: DR MARC SIEGEL: The angels behind Alcoholics Anonymous still inspire hope
description: Middle-aged adults are drinking more and dying at alarming rates from alcohol use disorder, but a faith-based cure from the 1930s still works.
content: Alcohol is still something to be worried about. Granted, national data shows a decline coming out of the pandemic, but the overall numbers are still higher than they were in 2018. Not only that, but though Gen Zers and millennials are drinking less, middle-aged adults are drinking more, with an increase in heavy drinking since 2018. Some of this is because middle-aged adults face increased pressures as they try to manage both aging parents and children who are in adolescence or early adulthood and are just finding themselves. But though drinking may temporarily ease stress, the long-term health risks are significant. A recent study from Colorado determined that older adults are more likely to drink alone, which carries with it additional health risks, including cognitive decline. There are an estimated 28 million Americans who suffer from alcohol use disorder, with a substantial portion of them being middle-aged. Not only that, but about 50% of the deaths due to alcohol in the U.S. occur among middle-aged adults. HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK Faith-based cures remain highly effective for alcoholism, with none more effective than Alcoholics Anonymous, which was developed in the 1930s by Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith after a chance meeting, the kind that the famed psychiatrist Carl Jung called synchronicity, or meaningful coincidence. They became messengers of God for each other and ultimately, for millions of other alcoholics with their 12-step program based largely on making a spiritual connection. In my new book, "The Angels Among Us," I devote a chapter to the miracle recovery of Bill Wilson and his consequential friendship with Dr. Bob. Bill is admitted to Towns Hospital in New York City in 1934 for the fourth time because of alcohol intoxication followed by withdrawal. He is in the depths of despair and is not sure if he will survive. And then he experiences the central miracle of his life as he demands that God show Himself. CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND "The room lights up with a blinding glare of light. Wilson is seized by an ecstasy he has never known. He stands on a mountaintop with a great wind blowing. He thinks to himself, 'This is not a wind of air. This is spirit. This is the God of the preachers.' "Bill feels that a great, clean strength is blowing through him, that he is now free." Bill Wilson tells about his experience to his medical angel, Dr. Silkworth, who is tending to him there in the hospital, who decides he is not crazy, but that a great psychic event has occurred. This changes Bill's life, as the doctor/"angel" advises him to hang on to this experience and to share it. By meeting other alcoholics where they live, and not speaking down to them, by not preaching, Wilson and later Dr. Bob spread faith, goodwill, and ultimately sobriety. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In today's world, this lesson remains crucial. It is the in-person exchange of peer-to-peer kindness and caring that gives us all the chance to heal. It doesn't work the same way on social media, and self-destructive behavior (including alcohol addiction) is much more likely to occur in isolation. title: 10-minute fitness habit can help adults over 40 maintain muscle and stay strong
description: CEO Carl Daikeler compares metabolism to a furnace: Muscle is the coal and cardio stokes it, urging a balance of strength training and cardiovascular work.
content: Adults over 40 may not need to spend hours in the gym to maintain muscle, preserve mobility and stay strong. According to Los Angeles fitness entrepreneur Carl Daikeler, just 10 minutes of targeted resistance exercise each day can help preserve muscle, mobility and long-term function. Daikeler, 63, who has spent 28 years leading BODi, the fitness brand formerly known as Beachbody, says his approach to exercise stems from a practical desire to stay healthy without having to be a dedicated fitness enthusiast. 4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS "I don't like to eat healthy, I don't like to work out," Daikeler told Fox News Digital at the Strong New York conference in September. "I'm just constantly trying to figure out how I can hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of these diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that." For adults looking to stay healthy in midlife, Daikeler recommends what he considers a "minimum effective dose" — short, targeted resistance workouts at home instead of lengthy gym sessions. "Ten minutes a day, and you can establish and build and maintain muscle," he said. WANT TO AGE BETTER? RESEARCHERS SAY 4-MINUTE ROUTINE MAY HELP PREVENT DANGEROUS FALLS Federal physical activity guidelines say that adults should perform muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups at least two days per week, in addition to regular aerobic activity. Rather than doing a full-body workout every day, Daikeler recommends rotating muscle groups — focusing on the chest one day, upper body the next, then legs and glutes — to build consistency without requiring lengthy gym sessions. "Ten minutes a day, and you can establish and build and maintain muscle." "Do that consistently, and you're going to find your strength return, your muscles return, your joints will start to respond appropriately," he said. The 10-minute approach can be especially valuable for people taking GLP-1 medications, who may be trying to preserve muscle mass and bone density while losing weight but may feel intimidated by traditional gyms, Daikeler said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES For individuals seeking more significant weight loss, he recommends extending daily activity to 20 or 30 minutes, incorporating a balance of strength training and cardiovascular exercise. The balancing act Daikeler cautioned against focusing exclusively on either cardio or resistance training, noting that different exercise types serve distinct functions in the body. "Your body's like a furnace," Daikeler said. "The coal in that furnace is muscle. So you want to build muscle. But then you want to stoke that coal, and that's cardio. So, you need a balance of both things." While resistance training builds muscle and strengthens bones and connective tissue, cardiovascular exercise challenges the heart and lungs, helping to maintain overall fitness, he said. Shifting focus to function As adults age, Daikeler says the primary motivation for maintaining physical activity should shift away from aesthetic goals and toward functional mobility and independence. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Reflecting on his personal experience visiting his father in an assisted living facility, Daikeler observed how residents struggled with basic movement and balance. Many residents relied on walkers and canes, and often stopped walking before talking to one another because they feared tripping over cracks in the pavement, he recalled. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "This is no longer about my abs," Daikeler added. "I need to work out in order to be able to walk and talk at the same time into my 90s ... It's no longer about aesthetics and vanity. It's really about mobility." Maintaining healthy physical habits means accepting daily short-term discomfort to protect long-term independence, Daikeler noted. title: Trump launching 'Super Intelligence Force' to ensure American dominance

title: US Marine arrested in Japan over suspected killing of woman as Tokyo lodges 'strong protest'
description: Surveillance footage showed Anna Yagi entering a Naha hotel with Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard before he later left alone, police reported.
content: A U.S. Marine stationed in Japan has been arrested on suspicion of robbing and killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Okinawa, prompting Japanese officials to lodge a formal protest with the United States. Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa Prefecture, early Saturday and taking her wallet and backpack, according to Japanese police. Ballard has denied the allegations, police said. SERVICE MEMBER AMONG 2 ARRESTED AFTER MISSING MAN PROBE LEADS COPS TO BODY DUMP SITE ON ARMY BASE Ballard is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, according to the Marine Corps. Surveillance footage showed Yagi entering the hotel with Ballard before he later left alone, Stars and Stripes reported, citing Okinawa police. A hotel employee later found Yagi unresponsive after she failed to check out. Police subsequently located Ballard in Okinawa City and arrested him, according to the outlet. Fox News Digital has reached out to the Okinawa Prefectural Police for additional information. THAI RESORT CITY CRACKS DOWN ON PROSTITUTION AHEAD OF USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN ARRIVAL The Marine Corps said it was cooperating with Japanese authorities and that Ballard remained in Japanese custody. "The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior," the service said in a statement obtained by Reuters. The arrest prompted swift condemnation from senior Japanese officials. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi offered condolences to Yagi's family and said her government had lodged a "strong protest" with the United States. "The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret," Takaichi said in an English translation of her Japanese-language statement. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass and called for full U.S. cooperation with the investigation, stricter discipline among American military personnel and measures to prevent similar incidents. Glass expressed regret over the loss of life and pledged U.S. cooperation with Japanese authorities. title: GOP Senate candidate's estranged wife confirms who she's voting for amid divorce proceedings

Angela Paxton is addressing the "elephant in the room," saying she’ll vote Republican this November without mentioning one GOP candidate by name: her estranged husband, Ken Paxton. Angela Paxton, who filed for divorce from the Texas Republican Senate candidate last year on "biblical grounds," says in a new political ad that she will back the Republican ticket on Nov. 3, arguing that keeping the seat in GOP hands outweighs concerns about any individual candidate. "People have asked my thoughts about this election, and turns out, I have some," she says in the ad. "Let’s talk about the elephant in the room." GOP FORTRESS IS UNDER THREAT IN ONE KEY RED STATE, AND THESE VOTERS COULD DECIDE WHETHER IT FALLS "In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team; it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line," she continues. "Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team." "That’s why I’m voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3," she adds. "Let’s hold the line together." The ad does not mention Ken Paxton by name, but its message comes as the Republican Senate candidate faces a tight general election contest against Democrat James Talarico. The latest Fox News Poll, released Thursday, found Talarico with 51% support among Texas likely voters and Paxton with 49%, a difference within the poll’s margin of sampling error. The same poll found 50% of likely voters preferred Republican control of the U.S. Senate, compared with 49% who preferred Democratic control. Angela Paxton has previously signaled that maintaining Republican control of the seat takes precedence over her feelings about the individual candidate. During an address to the Texas Federation of Republican Women in September, she similarly framed the issue as the "elephant in the room" and told the audience that "it’s not the people, it’s the seat." title: ‘Addiction Economy’ is a bad gamble for young men. Here’s their way out
description: Roughly 35% of young men gamble daily or weekly as the "Addiction Economy" exploits their isolation. But their ambitions reveal a path forward.
content: You cannot scroll on social media, watch television or even make a purchase online without being inundated with advertisements for sports gambling and prediction markets. Companies are spending millions to make sure we see them, and their primary target audience is young men. Data from the Institute for Family Studies confirms just how deeply this has taken hold: roughly one-third (35%) of young men gamble daily or weekly. This is not the only digital habit growing among young men today. Nearly half (42%) watch pornography daily or weekly, and most young men (86%) play video games daily or weekly. This is what some people refer to as the "addiction economy." As a pastor, I know young men who engage in these things every day. And, to be honest, I’m not surprised. More than half (61%) of young men say they often feel they have little control over the things happening to them. Coping with this pervasive felt lack of agency drives them toward digital escapes that offer a temporary illusion of control, thrill or connection. DAVID MARCUS: BRAVE NEW WORLD OF PREDICTION MARKETS CAN MAKE US ALL INSIDE TRADERS Yet, we know two crucial things about today’s young men: they’re ambitious — and they’re vulnerable. An overwhelming majority (84%) of young men say they have ambitious plans for their future. They want to grow. They want to succeed, and in some sense feel that they’re capable of doing so. But they’re also profoundly isolated and frustrated. They’re facing a world where the paths to traditional success — like career success, homeownership, marriage, children and more — feel washed away or blocked. They struggle with the ability to make friends with other young men or relate to young women. AI IS CHANGING MODERN DATING, BUT EXPERTS WARN IT'S MAKING PEOPLE 'RELATIONALLY STUPID' The addiction economy demands young men’s attention, time and money, and undermines their vision for a successful life. Left unchecked, society and commercial forces will continue to exploit or ignore their tendency at early ages to use things to numb pain, deal with anxiety, or cope with discouragement. But the true role of society should be to help them fulfill their aspirations for good and build lives of purpose. If we don’t offer them a better vision for their lives, the addiction economy will gladly fill the void. Older generations are quick to notice and criticize young men for retreating into digital vices, but scolding and shaming have never produced excellence. Young men may be demoralized, but they haven’t given up. What they need is a guide and a path forward. They need to know they can build a life they actually want and can inhabit. POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT' Young men need formation and support if they are to develop their open-ended sense of potential and ambition into real success and healthy relationships with peers, colleagues and romantic partners. They are capable of building good and desirable lives for themselves, and of attaining real excellence. But they need help to do so. And any invested, stable adult is capable of providing the support they need. Their needs are ultimately simple, though urgent. So, go out of your way to establish strong, authentic, transparent relationships with the young men in your life. Show them they’re not alone, that they’re not unique in their struggles. Provide relatability and accountability, hand in hand. These relationships will help remove the burden of guilt, of embarrassment, of shame for young men. This is part of being a human. We’re all going to struggle, often with the same things. These common struggles allow us to encourage and remind young men that they have the ability to overcome them. DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE It’s also important to help young men feel like they have agency in their own lives, and that their lives have meaning. They have a lot of questions: how to be successful, find a fulfilling job, make friends and navigate dating. Often, we have to help them find answers and take practical steps to feel more in control of their future. Make sure they have the space they need to ask important questions and share vulnerable feelings or experiences, without feeling judged, dismissed or doubted. Young men also need a clear vision for their lives, and a clear vision of how they fit into their own communities. Help them develop their ambitions into specific plans. Help them come to know and understand how much impact they can have, just by showing up to serve. Whether at work, at church, in their friendships or in their families, young men need opportunities to contribute, make a difference and see that their lives matter to the people around them. I WORRY LESS ABOUT SCREENS THAN ABOUT THE CHALLENGES TODAY’S TEENS NEVER FACE We as their mentors have to help them build lives they want to live. And in order to help them build those lives, we must step into their present lives without fear, without judgment and without hesitation. They want to succeed — they just need our support. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The addiction economy that has them firmly in its grasp isn’t something to be feared. It is one of the most profound opportunities for us to enter and help change the course of the lives of young men. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It’s time we stepped in.

title: GOP rising star helped topple Trump-backed incumbent. Now he's caught leadership's eye
description: Mike Haridopolos is emerging as a behind-the-scenes force on the East Coast, helping secure billions for NASA and Kennedy Space Center's future.
content: It’s June 2026 and the summer’s intense heat is slowly creeping across the East Coast. In Florida, a different kind of heat is threatening to burn Republicans — a firestorm of political backlash that could at best force the GOP to spend millions more in the midterms, and at worst cost the party what should be a safely red House seat. Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., was one of the first to sound the alarm publicly about embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., and the scandals that could have sandbagged his re-election chances. It’s an unusually bold move for a first-term congressman, particularly when the House GOP leadership and the White House were still publicly backing Mills. But Haridopolos’ plan was well-executed — and with the help of Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., Mills went down as one of only four Republican incumbents to lose a primary in the 2026 midterm cycle. Republican election watchers saw the loss with some relief, privately feeling better about their chances with former journalist Ryan Elijah, who Haridopolos recruited to run, against Democratic former NASA official Bale Dalton. And Haridopolos was there with Elijah both figuratively and literally. The former local news anchor said he was "right there in the front row" during the primary debate. REPUBLICANS MOVE TO OUST EMBATTLED FLORIDA GOP LAWMAKER IN BITTER PRIMARY FIGHT "Not only was he there, he was kind of like the spin room. He did a lot of the media interviews, and that was huge for us," Elijah told Fox News Digital. TRUMP'S SUPPORT DOESN'T SAVE SCANDAL-PLAGUED LAWMAKER IN PRIMARY Haridopolos told Fox News Digital, "I recognized that Cory Mills was absolutely going to lose a general election against a solid Democrat candidate. And so I went to the leadership and, of course, the president's team and said, ‘Look, we need to find a way for Mills to step aside.’" "Unfortunately, Mr. Mills was not willing to step aside. And so I let the leadership and the president know that I'd be helping someone else in the primary," he continued. "It was not the easiest thing to do, taking on a colleague. But… this is a team sport and all of us need to work together." WATCH: CORY MILLS BLASTS DOJ PROBE AS ‘POLITICAL OP' AHEAD OF FLORIDA PRIMARY "Team sport" is an analogy that the Florida Republican has used frequently, and one that he’s used to try and define his tenure in the House. It’s paid off for him so far, with Haridopolos forging close relationships with both House GOP leaders and his peers. "He’s a trusted ally and somebody you can count on. He delivers. You never have to worry about where he’s going to be," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., who has known Haridopolos for roughly two decades, told Fox News Digital. The two politicos first forged a relationship in their respective state houses. When Haridopolos said he would launch a campaign for Congress, Scalise said he told him, "I want to be your first check… I want to support you." And in his short time so far, he's already been entrusted to lead a House panel. Haridopolos is chair of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee’s space subcommittee, a fitting position for someone whose district is home to the Kennedy Space Center despite his junior status. The Florida freshman said space has long been a passion of his, dating back to his efforts as a state lawmaker to bring the shuttle program back to his backyard. NASA'S ARTEMIS FOLLOW-UP MISSION 'RIGHT AROUND THE CORNER' AFTER SUCCESSFUL LUNAR FLIGHT "So many people were concerned that we'd go back to the post-Apollo days, which are very detrimental to the economy of Central Florida. And so at that time, Rick Scott was governor… We decided that we needed to not just rely on NASA but start pushing for public-private partnerships," Haridopolos said. The U.S. has seen an unprecedented resurgence of success in space in the last two years, partly propelled by the public-private partnerships that Haridopolos is pushing. NASA completed its historic Artemis II mission just this year, sending four astronauts around the moon and back in the first such mission in decades. PETER NAVARRO: TRUMP'S ARTEMIS VISION IS NOW FLYING — AND CHINA IS PAYING ATTENTION "I'm really confident that in two years we'll be landing back on the moon," Haridopolos said. That’s also due in no small part to the federal government investing in the new space race, after the Trump administration initially proposed a roughly 24% cut to NASA’s budget in May 2025. Haridopolos, seeing space as another frontier for national security, was alarmed. He told Fox News Digital at the time that he would seek a "constructive conversation with the White House" about a higher figure. "I’m not sure what that number will be in the end, but in my conversations with the president about space, he’s absolutely committed to it," he said in May 2025. Eventually, President Donald Trump signed into law a spending bill that included $24.4 billion for NASA — rather than the initial $18.8 billion proposal — and approved an additional $9.9 billion in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that Haridopolos "understands that so much of America’s future in space runs through Florida and Kennedy Space Center." "He is serious about the mission, willing to engage on the hard issues, and always focused on how we can move the ball forward," Isaacman said. Before his political career began, Haridopolos was a history professor at what is now Eastern Florida State College. He was born to an American mother and Greek immigrant father, and is currently married to Stephanie Haridopolos — a physician by profession who has spent the last several months as acting surgeon general. But despite his accomplishments and connections, Haridopolos’ name is not one that has garnered headlines in the way that more bombastic House Republicans have in their public defiance of GOP leaders or criticism of Trump. That’s because he prefers to settle disputes behind closed doors, a hallmark of politics that has largely been abandoned in an age where attention is seen as political currency. "When you hear members of Congress saying, like, ‘Oh, I want you to get me on TV,’ it's usually like, ‘Uh-oh, someone’s about to do something crazy here to get on TV.’ He was like… I’m going to earn my spot on there legitimately by being a good, reliable messenger for the party," a Republican aide familiar with Haridopolos’ operation told Fox News Digital. The aide said that could pose a challenge in times when television networks were looking for dramatic tales of discord, but that his communication skills still got him a "high volume" of press. That aide said they also witnessed Haridopolos turn down media interviews that did not fit his schedule, but offer to help fellow House Republicans secure that spot instead. "He was just finding ways to help out leadership, but also just his fellow members, especially his fellow freshman members," the aide said. Haridopolos told Fox News Digital of the chaos that’s become a regular facet of Republicans' majority, "One of my goals is to tell those folks who always stand [in front of cameras] after we finish the session, you know, what we need to do more is spend time in the caucus having these knock-down, drag-outs. Not through the press, but as a family, and come out there unified. I think it's the best way to solve problems." He’s also been known to offer help on the fundraising side — as Scalise put it, "He raises a lot of money." The political maneuvering has raised questions for some about where Haridopolos sees his future and what he’s looking to get out of the relationships he is building in a largely transactional world. "He knows how to work with people and how to advance what he wants," the Republican aide said. "I could see him in senior leadership… and sooner than people expect." Scalise said, "Mike has a bright future, because he's a natural leader." But Haridopolos has insisted that his efforts are all dedicated to the greater good of the Republican Party. "A lot of people have asked me if I'm going to pursue a leadership position after the elections this year. I'm absolutely not going to pursue one of those leadership positions," he said. "There's people who have been in Congress for three, four, or five terms who I think have really put that effort in." He named members like fellow freshman Rep. Brian Jack, R-Ga., Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, and Rep. Rudy Yakym, R-Ind. title: Smartwatch AFib alert sends dad to ER before heart surgery
description: Joseph Holycross dismissed his racing heart for nearly two years until his Samsung Galaxy Watch detected atrial fibrillation and changed everything.
content: When Joseph Holycross came home from work feeling off, he had plenty of reasons to brush it aside. He was a busy father of four, worked long hours and had grown accustomed to blaming a racing heart on caffeine and exhaustion. His wife, Jamie, saw something that worried her. She urged Joseph to use the ECG feature on his Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic. Seconds later, the result gave him a reason to stop making excuses and head to the emergency room. What doctors discovered would lead to a week in the hospital, open-heart surgery and new health concerns for Joseph's family. It also completely changed the way he looks at the smartwatch on his wrist. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed. Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist. Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA Joseph thought his racing heart had an explanation Joseph says the elevated heart rate had been happening on and off for roughly a year and a half to two years. At the time, just weeks before his 40th birthday, he did not see it as a warning sign. "I tend to fuel with caffeine. I'm a father of four, so, you know, we tend to drink coffee and things like that when we're tired to kind of push through the day," Joseph told CyberGuy. That made the symptoms easier to explain away. If his heart was racing, Joseph could point to coffee, exercise or a long day and keep going. Then Jamie noticed something different. "She had made the comment that I looked like I was short of breath, like I was breathing strangely," Joseph recalled. Jamie works as a respiratory therapist, so her concern carried weight. This time, Joseph agreed to check his heart with the ECG feature on his Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic. His Galaxy Watch showed AFib Joseph had owned his Galaxy Watch4 Classic for about three years. Before this happened, health monitoring was hardly the reason he wore it. He mainly liked being able to receive messages or answer calls while he worked without carrying his phone around the shop. He had tried the ECG feature perhaps once about a year earlier, mostly to see what the watch could do. This time was different. Joseph scrolled to the ECG feature, tapped the option to record and followed the directions on the screen. He says the watch instructed him to remain still and keep his finger on the sensor while it recorded for about 30 seconds. "It came up and told me immediately at the top in bold letters, atrial fibrillation," Joseph said. His reaction was immediate too, but it was not fear. "Denial," Joseph said. "I just thought it had to be a malfunction. I wasn't even 40 yet." He wondered whether the watch could be wrong, especially because it was an older model. So he ran the ECG again and then repeated it several more times. Jamie was not interested in continuing to test it at home. Joseph recalls her telling him, "We need to go to the ER and have an actual EKG done just to make sure." AI MAY SPOT DEADLY HEART RISK IN A ROUTINE ECG The watch changed Joseph's mind about going to the ER When I asked Joseph whether he would have gone to the emergency room that day without the watch, he did not hesitate. "Nope," he said. That answer gets to the heart of this story. The Galaxy Watch did not determine everything that was happening inside Joseph's heart. It gave him information that made his symptoms much harder to dismiss. Joseph sent the watch's ECG recording to his phone and brought it with him to the hospital. He says an ER doctor reviewed the tracing and confirmed that he was in AFib. Jamie remembers being struck by how closely the watch's result resembled what doctors were seeing. "The doctor was kind of impressed that it actually even looked like the rhythm that it showed looked like atrial fib," she said. Joseph expected to get checked out. Instead, he stayed in the hospital for about a week while doctors worked to understand the problems affecting his heart. Then came another major turn. About 10 days later, Joseph says he returned for open-heart surgery. "They had several things on my heart that they had to repair," he said. Jamie says doctors warned them what could have happened For Jamie, the experience reinforced something she had already seen through her work in healthcare. Wearable health data can give people useful information, but they have to take concerning results seriously and seek professional medical care. She says doctors warned the couple about what Joseph could have faced had he continued attributing his symptoms to caffeine or exercise. "He probably would have had a stroke, heart attack, or both," Jamie said. The family also says one of Joseph's doctors told them that without medical intervention, he likely would not have lived to see 45. That warning carries additional weight because Joseph had not considered himself someone with serious health problems. He was still 39 when his watch recorded the AFib reading. "It can happen to anyone," Jamie said. She hopes their experience encourages people to learn what the health features on their devices can actually do instead of waiting until something feels wrong. Hospital monitors gave Jamie another reason to trust the data Jamie had another perspective during Joseph's hospital stay because of her medical background. She says they compared the heart rate information on Joseph's watch with the hospital equipment while he was being monitored. According to Jamie, the readings were sometimes within about one beat per minute of the hospital monitor. That does not make a smartwatch a replacement for hospital equipment, but seeing the numbers track so closely left an impression on both of them. "I would definitely encourage people to take it seriously for sure," Jamie said. She views the watch as a tool that can give someone a reason to seek a professional opinion rather than something that should make medical decisions for them. Doctors raised concerns for Joseph's children and siblings Joseph's medical journey also created new questions for the rest of his family. He says doctors told him that some of the problems involving his heart could have a genetic component and that some may have been present since birth before gradually becoming more noticeable. That prompted doctors to recommend additional screening within the family. Joseph says his siblings have been encouraged to get checked for the same issues. His children will also need to undergo screening when they are adults. "It brought up a lot of concern," Joseph said. For a father of four, the discovery suddenly extended beyond his own recovery. The medical information doctors uncovered could potentially help his siblings and children watch for similar problems earlier. What the Samsung Galaxy Watch ECG can tell you Samsung says the ECG feature in its Samsung Health Monitor app records the electrical activity of the heart using a compatible Galaxy Watch. The recording takes about 30 seconds. Depending on the recording, Samsung says the app can return results including sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, high heart rate, AFib with a high heart rate, an inconclusive result or a poor recording. Samsung says an AFib result means the watch detected an irregular rhythm during the recording and advises users who receive that result to contact their doctor for guidance. Anyone who receives an AFib result with a high heart rate should contact a doctor as soon as possible. However, Samsung also cautions that its ECG feature does not replace traditional methods of diagnosis or treatment. Users should not interpret the device's output or take clinical action based on it without consulting a qualified healthcare professional. That difference is important in Joseph's case. His watch gave him an AFib result. Medical professionals then evaluated him and determined what treatment he needed. How to take an ECG on a compatible Galaxy Watch On Samsung's current software, the ECG feature works through the Samsung Health Monitor app on compatible Galaxy Watches paired with a compatible Galaxy phone. Availability and requirements can vary by device and region. To record an ECG, Samsung says to wear the watch snugly and rest your forearms comfortably on a table. Open Samsung Health Monitor on the watch and select ECG. Lightly rest a finger from your opposite hand on the watch's top button without pressing it, remain still and avoid talking while the watch records for 30 seconds. For the best reading, Samsung recommends sitting still beforehand, making sure the sensor is clean and dry and wearing the watch snugly so it lies flat against your wrist. Movement or poor skin contact can lead to a poor recording. Once the recording finishes, the result appears on the watch and can sync to the Samsung Health Monitor app on the paired phone. You can then review your ECG history and share a report with a healthcare professional. If you have symptoms that could indicate a medical emergency, do not wait for a smartwatch result before seeking emergency care. For Joseph, the watch now brings peace of mind After open-heart surgery, every strange feeling can carry more weight than it did before. Joseph described how even a small pain can make him wonder whether something is wrong again. Being able to check his heart rate and rhythm does not eliminate that concern, but he says it gives him reassurance. "You don't have to sit and worry, 'Oh, am I in AFib again?'" Joseph said. "I can check and, you know, it's a reliable source. It kind of puts you at peace." He has also been using the watch during his recovery to track his walking, steps and exercise. Before his medical ordeal, many of those health tools went unused. Now Joseph says the watch leaves his wrist mainly when he needs to charge it. "It's really been a peace of mind type" of device, Joseph said. Jamie hopes people learn what their watches can do Jamie says one of the lessons she wants other people to take away is surprisingly simple: If you already own a smartwatch with health features, learn how to use them. She sees people, including some who work in healthcare, use smartwatches primarily for steps or everyday notifications while ignoring other available tools. "I think the reassurance it gives people is amazing for anyone who even has, you know, cardiac issues," Jamie said. Joseph agrees. Before this happened, he knew his watch had additional capabilities, but he had little reason to explore them. Now he wants people to understand what may already be sitting on their wrists. "You've got to know that it's a lot more than just a watch," he said. For Joseph, that lesson became deeply personal. The watch did not perform his surgery or replace the doctors who diagnosed and treated him. What it did was give a busy 39-year-old father information that finally persuaded him to stop explaining away how he felt and head to the hospital. Kurt's key takeaways What stays with me about Joseph's story is that he came incredibly close to doing what many of us have done at one time or another: convincing himself there was a perfectly reasonable explanation for feeling off. He was working hard, drinking caffeine and raising four kids. A racing heart fit easily into the story he was already telling himself. Jamie noticed something different and pushed him to check. Then the watch gave Joseph a result he could no longer comfortably ignore. That combination ultimately got him through the doors of an emergency room. No smartwatch can tell you that you are healthy, and a reassuring reading should never override symptoms that concern you. Samsung makes that limitation clear. But Joseph's experience shows why the information these devices collect can be useful when it prompts someone to pay closer attention and talk to a healthcare professional. There is also a powerful family piece to his story. What doctors discovered led to new screening concerns for Joseph's siblings and, eventually, his children. A health scare that started with a 30-second reading on his wrist may now give other members of his family an opportunity to ask questions earlier. If your smartwatch warned you about a possible health problem but you felt fine, would you head to the doctor or be tempted to dismiss the alert?
