title: Dems demanding Venezuela brief face State Department fury as senators leave town before meeting
description: Senate Democrats have challenged the legality of a Pentagon equity stake in Venezuelan oil company NABEP, but the State Department fires back sharply.
content: The State Department is accusing Democrats of performative "grandstanding" by demanding a sweeping Venezuela oil deal briefing then postponing it so the Senate could leave town early. Four senior Senate Democrats demanded documents they already knew were coming, according to material reviewed by Fox News Digital. Then, the Senate rescheduled a congressional briefing on the agreement planned for Oct. 1, 2026, so it could break for fall recess. The group of lawmakers were seeking more information on the Pentagon's involvement in an agreement with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) that gives the Department of War a 35% stake in one of Venezuela’s largest oil producers. TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES State says the lawmakers had known for weeks that administration officials planned to brief the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and provide documents on the deal on Thursday. The department went forward with delivering copies of the U.S. government’s strategic partnership agreement with NABEP to the committee, claiming it did so despite the briefing being pulled down "as a courtesy." "Copies of the USG Strategic Partnership Agreement with NABEP for your Members are in the SFRC front office," a senior State Department official wrote. "Each Member has a folder with their copy." State Department Assistant Secretary for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson claimed Senate Democrats canceled the briefing so they could "skip town and go on vacation." "This is pure grandstanding," Johnson wrote on X. "When they sent this letter, they had known for weeks that we planned to brief them and provide the documents today, on October 1." A congressional source familiar with the planned briefing disputed State’s characterization, telling Fox News Digital that lawmakers had not been told the written NABEP agreement would be provided before writing the letter and that the briefing was intended as a broader update on U.S. policy toward Venezuela, not specifically the oil deal. And emails reviewed by Fox News Digital show the briefing postponement request itself came from a Republican majority staffer on the Foreign Relations Committee, who told State early Oct. 1 that "the Senate has left town" and asked to move the briefing until November. A State Department official told Fox News Digital the staffer was acting on behalf of the full committee. The congressional source said Republican leadership had ended legislative business for the week, with senators on both sides of the aisle preparing to leave Washington ahead of next month’s midterm elections. The group of Democrat lawmakers demanding the briefing are challenging the legality and prudence of the Trump administration’s agreement with NABEP, which would give the Pentagon rights to a 35% stake in one of Venezuela’s largest oil producers. Under the arrangement, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital would receive rights to the stake through so-called penny warrants, while the State Department would receive preferential rights to purchase 20% of the company’s production at cost. The unusual structure is part of the administration’s broader effort to revive Venezuelan oil production and expand U.S. economic influence after Nicolás Maduro’s ouster. Democrats argue the Pentagon may lack legal authority to take the stake and have raised questions about the administration’s vetting of NABEP and its leadership. The administration argues the structure could generate substantial returns for the U.S. without requiring taxpayers to buy the stake up front. The White House has said the government’s 35% position could ultimately be worth hundreds of billions of dollars in equity and dividends if NABEP succeeds in developing the fields. The deal could also give Washington a new source of relatively low-cost crude at a time when the administration is trying to increase global supply and bring down fuel prices. State would have the right to buy 20% of NABEP’s production at cost and the right of first refusal on the remaining output, which the administration says could help replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and supply U.S. military and other sensitive needs. The White House also says millions of barrels of additional Venezuelan production could eventually flow through U.S. refineries and be developed using American drilling equipment and infrastructure, generating investment and jobs in the United States. NABEP produces roughly 220,000 barrels a day and has said it plans to more than double production to 500,000 barrels a day by late 2028. The administration is betting that private investment can revive fields that have suffered years of underinvestment and mismanagement. The agreement is part of a much broader U.S. effort to remake Venezuela’s economy after the dramatic removal of Nicolás Maduro earlier this year. On Jan. 3, U.S. forces carried out a military operation in Venezuela to capture Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and transport them to the United States to face federal charges. The administration has characterized the operation as a law enforcement mission supported by the military and has since made rebuilding Venezuela’s oil sector a central part of its stabilization strategy. Interim leader Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s former vice president, has remained in power while cooperating with Washington, even as Venezuela’s political transition remains unsettled and opposition figures continue pressing for elections. The White House has described the NABEP agreement as part of a three-part strategy of stabilization, reconstruction and eventual democratic transition, arguing that restoring oil production is necessary to rebuild Venezuela’s economy and reduce the influence of China, Russia and other U.S. adversaries in its energy sector. TRUMP 'SERIOUSLY CONSIDERING' PLAN TO MAKE VENEZUELA AND ITS $40 TRILLION IN OIL PERMANENT PART OF USA Senators Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H.; Jack Reed, D-R.I.; Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.; and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., challenged both the legality and prudence of the deal in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Among their central questions is whether the Pentagon office being used to structure the investment has the legal authority to acquire an equity position in a foreign oil company. The senators also demanded the agreement itself, details about how State would pay for oil and information about the administration’s vetting of NABEP and its leadership. "The proposed agreement is unlikely to reduce high energy costs for Americans, and it risks undermining the Venezuelan people’s transition away from a dictatorship," the senators wrote. Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of all four senators who signed the letter for comment. The unusual Pentagon role has drawn scrutiny since the deal was announced. Rather than immediately purchasing shares with taxpayer money, the Office of Strategic Capital’s position is structured through penny warrants that give the government the right to acquire equity for a nominal price. The Democratic senators argue that structure does not resolve the underlying legal question. They contend the statute establishing the Office of Strategic Capital authorizes loans and loan guarantees but does not explicitly empower the Pentagon to acquire equity stakes in private foreign companies. "It is unclear," the lawmakers wrote, "why the American public should support this attempt to entangle the United States with a relatively unknown foreign oil company that lacks the capacity or credibility to develop oil fields of the magnitude described." The senators also raised concerns about NABEP Chairman Alejandro Betancourt, noting past money-laundering investigations involving the Venezuelan businessman. Betancourt has not been charged with a crime, and Rubio has previously said he is not under active U.S. investigation. title: JUAN WILLIAMS: My wife thought I was crazy to join Fox News. I'm glad I did
description: Juan Williams reflects on leaving CNN to join Rupert Murdoch's startup Fox News Channel 30 years ago and the friendships that defined his career.
content: My wife said I was crazy. This was 1996, thirty years ago. I worked for the established brand name in cable television, CNN. FOX NEWS CHANNEL TOPS NBC, ABC AND CBS IN KEY RATINGS MEASURABLE FOR SECOND STRAIGHT SUMMER Why then, she asked, with three young school-age children still at home, was I willing to give up that prime seat to join a start-up cable network being launched by a controversial Australian media mogul, Rupert Murdoch? And this start-up Fox News Channel faced an uphill fight just to get on cable systems in big cities, including New York. "Crazy!" Yes! But I told her they were going to be scrappy, innovative, and give me a foothold on the ground floor of the next era of news. So, I went with the new kids in cable news. And Fox delivered over the last 30 years by doing news for people who did not watch news. Fox is now often the number one channel of any kind on cable. From the early days, the screen has been full of colorful graphics. Stories come and go fast. Heroes and villains are clear-cut. Crime stories and war stories took center stage — no matter where they occurred. The on-air people did not speak down to the audience as experts. They talked to them as friends and neighbors, always shaking their heads at a crazy world. As Brit Hume, now Fox's chief political analyst, told me at the start, Fox was willing to do stories being ignored by the news networks and cable outlets. He said Fox News was picking up money others left on the street. DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE On top of being daring, Fox had the novel idea of featuring right-of-center voices, Republican political players who generally felt like outsiders on the other networks. Roger Ailes, the first head of the network, knew politics. He was a top GOP consultant. And his top programming aide, Chet Collier, a Democrat, had been Ailes' mentor at the popular daytime talk show, "The Mike Douglas Show." They sold me on Fox, and they knew exactly what they were getting with me. I'd worked at The Washington Post and CNN. In bestselling books, I called out politicians on the right and the left. And as a Black journalist, I was known to trade punches with Black politicians. Fox's founders wanted me to trade punches with their right-wing media personalities. I was happy to get in on the action. From the start, Fox made good television. Ratings slowly climbed as viewers discovered turn-up-the-volume debates among finger-pointing, smirking, laughing, and eye-rolling personalities. Fox was in the right place as bombshell revelations hit the air about the president of the United States having a sexual relationship with a White House intern. DR. MARC SIEGEL: WHAT 18 YEARS AT FOX TAUGHT ME ABOUT COURAGE AND FAITH The impeachment of a president included nightly stories about the popular President Clinton facing a hard-edged prosecutor, Kenneth Starr. And then came provocative reports about a blue dress and cigars. The ratings climbed. What I remember most about those early years of Fox is being on set in the D.C. bureau with Brit Hume, then the managing editor. He held the air for hours of hearings and press conferences. I was by his side as we struggled with new equipment, technicians discovering buttons, and producers shouting breaking news into our earpieces. I think about the amazing Fox audience — the countless people who treat me as a friend when we meet in diners, airports, supermarkets, campaign rallies, ball games, convention halls, studios and green rooms across America. The same chaos followed when "Fox News Sunday" hit the air. No studio was ready. So, Tony Snow, the show's first moderator, and Marty Ryan, the top producer, had to hunt for historic homes, even gardens, in Washington, D.C. For Snow, Hume, and an all-star panel of D.C. commentators, including Fred Barnes, Mort Kondracke — hail to the Beltway Boys — Mara Liasson, Bill Kristol, and Charles Krauthammer, every show was about speaking directly to the hot, populist passions in politics. It was about being sharp with each other and giving no quarter to political guests. Creating the best show for the people at home has remained the goal for Fox. Krauthammer would win laughs and applause on the lecture circuit by beginning his speeches by saying he was grateful to be invited anywhere Juan Williams could not interrupt him. By 2000, Fox was perfectly positioned to offer 24/7 news and analysis of the disputed presidential election, the Florida recount, and the 5–4 Supreme Court decision that gave the White House to an underdog Republican who lost the popular vote. And when terrorists struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001 — 25 years ago this month — Fox was there with an established news-gathering operation and unique access to the new Republican administration of President George W. Bush. Then came Fox News' coverage of the war in Iraq and the fight against terrorist cells in Afghanistan. Fox's ratings grew as more and more viewers trusted that, no matter their politics, Fox delivered the most compelling take on the sizzling stories defining each election, especially the 2008 race that saw a little-known Black senator running against former First Lady Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination. GREGG JARRETT: MY MOTHER’S ADVICE LED ME TO THE CAREER OF A LIFETIME It was a freezing night in Des Moines when the "All-Star" panel realized Barack Obama, a Black man, was about to win the Iowa caucuses. On the air, I started crying. My emotion got to me as I tried to explain to the Fox audience what that moment meant to our nation's history, and especially to Black American history. Another memory is being lustily booed by an auditorium full of South Carolina Republican voters in 2012. The booing started when, while asking questions at a Fox-sponsored GOP primary debate, I questioned Newt Gingrich about his use of racially loaded rhetoric concerning President Obama and the poor. Years later, I would joke with the Speaker that he had me to thank for his upset victory in the Palmetto State primary. That exchange became one of the first viral moments of a presidential campaign in the early internet age. FOX NEWS DIGITAL LEADS IN UNIQUE VISITORS, OTHER KEY METRICS AGAINST CNN, NY TIMES DURING AUGUST By Obama's second term, I was spending more time in the New York studios as a co-host of "The Five." By 2015, I began nearly a decade of living in New York to co-host the show. My role was described by Ailes as a center-left foil to the conservatives on the show. Politico summed up my role this way: "Fox's Lone-Wolf Liberal Had a Tough Job. But It Made for Better TV." "Juan Williams was particularly good at what might be the hardest, least appreciated, and most important job in cable news," the outlet wrote. "The Five" became the number one show on the number one cable channel and delivered a robust message about debate in America. No matter your politics, no matter if you are with conservatives or liberals, and no matter racial and religious lines, "We the People" — Americans of all stripes — can find common ground in defense of honest debate, even with rants and occasional posturing. "You cut a path through the jungle," a friend recently told me as we reminisced about the state of the media and the dearth today of conservative media platforms where liberals feel comfortable appearing, as well as liberal platforms where conservatives feel comfortable appearing. I told him that since Fox became the number one cable news channel, it is often the case that more Democrats are watching Fox than any other cable news channel. I've written more than a dozen books over the last 30 years. And on book tours, hard-right conservatives show up to tell me they disagree with me but love hearing a different point of view from someone they trust and, sometimes grudgingly, even like. In truth, working with Brit, Shannon Bream, Bret Baier, Bill O'Reilly, Sean Hannity, and so many others almost always ended with more conversation, then dinner, a ballgame, or a beer. Brit once said the two of us are like TV's pro wrestlers. We fight like hell tonight, and the next night we go to another town and do it again. At its best, Fox News is a reminder that social media and the internet are not real life. The bitterness we see online is produced by computer algorithms designed to divide Americans. Fox is about the audience. There's a bond. That is why, on Fox News' 30th anniversary, I find myself thinking less about ratings or political fights than about friendships. I think about Charles. I think about Tony. I think about Roger and Chet. I think about Brit, Mara, Bill, Fred, Chris, and Bret. I think about people like Cherie Grzech, who directed politics, and Porter Berry, who ran shows before taking control of FoxNews.com. I think about former television producer Nate Fredman. I think about Lynne Jordal Martin, who edits for FoxNews.com. I shared offices with Mike Emanuel and Leland Vittert. I think about the amazing Fox audience — the countless people who treat me as a friend when we meet in diners, airports, supermarkets, campaign rallies, ball games, convention halls, studios, and green rooms across America. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION And I think about the people viewers rarely see: editors, producers, bookers, tech operators, directors, hair and makeup artists, security guards, and janitors. So, three cheers for Fox News — one for each decade we have been on the air. Thank you to the viewers and FoxNews.com readers who made our success possible. Thirty years ago, my wife thought I was crazy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She still thinks I am, and maybe she's right. But I'm awfully glad I took the chance. title: Karine Jean-Pierre admits Biden admin failed on economic, age messaging, but claims Trump making same mistake
description: Karine Jean-Pierre argued President Donald Trump is repeating former President Joe Biden's messaging failures on the economy, warning that grocery and gas prices remain undefeated.
content: Former White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre argued in an opinion piece published Friday that President Donald Trump was making the same messaging mistakes as her former boss, former President Joe Biden. "Mr. Biden wanted his team to highlight his domestic agenda," she wrote in The New York Times guest essay. "His policies were working, and he wanted the country to understand what he was doing and why. But the polling was clear: Our economic message didn’t land. "Too many people were struggling with the prices of groceries, rent, child care and gas. Their lived experience did not match the encouraging economic news, and that disconnect shaped the entire public conversation." FOX NEWS POLL: AS ECONOMIC PAIN DEEPENS, DISAPPROVAL OF TRUMP HITS NEW HIGH Jean-Pierre pointed to the president's messaging on gas prices, inflation and the war in Iran in the piece and said, "When leaders neglect lived experience, the message collapses." "The truth is, we had a stale message and outdated models for delivering it. It cost Mr. Biden and, eventually, Vice President Kamala Harris dearly. President Trump is now making a mistake even more damaging," she wrote. When asked about Jean-Pierre's argument, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Biden’s policies destroyed our economy by creating the worst inflation crisis in history, instituting burdensome red tape and stifling American energy dominance. "President Trump has fixed the disaster that Joe Biden created by cooling inflation, signing the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowering drug prices and reshoring our manufacturing industry. The fake news won’t, so President Trump will continue to tout his economic wins to Americans." Jean-Pierre admitted the Biden administration misread the public and said her press briefings fueled much of the debate surrounding Biden's age, in addition to the economic messaging. "We learned that lesson with the economy and again with the debate around Mr. Biden’s age. Looking back, we misread the public mood, thinking the age conversation would fade. At best, my responses from the podium about Mr. Biden’s age failed to put out the fire; at worst, they fueled it," she conceded. TRUMP VS HISTORY: HOW PRESIDENT'S POLL NUMBERS COMPARE TO BIDEN, OBAMA, BUSH AHEAD OF MIDTERMS She also pointed to the changing media ecosystem and said a "TikTok about high prices, filmed with a phone in a grocery store aisle or in front of a gas pump" would get more attention than her press briefings or a Cabinet official on the Sunday news programs. "The Trump White House should realize that over the next two years, there will be only more, not less, scrutiny when the president appears to drift off during meetings, is cagey about the results of his medical exams or goes on one of his erratic, late-night social media screeds," Jean-Pierre wrote. "His communications team should know by now that the prices at the pump and the self-checkout line are undefeated. "Once people believe their government is not speaking to their reality, it becomes incredibly difficult to earn that trust back. I felt that tension every day in the White House briefing room. I see it happening again now." KAROLINE LEAVITT REVEALS SHE’S ADVISED TRUMP ON WHITE HOUSE REPLACEMENT IN FINAL INTERVIEW AS PRESS SECRETARY Jean-Pierre released a book in 2025, "Independent," about her time in the White House. Ahead of its release, she revealed she was leaving the Democratic Party and registering as an Independent. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The Democratic Party had defined my life, my career," Jean-Pierre wrote. "Everything I’d done to make people’s lives better had been connected to it. The party was the vehicle that allowed me not just to have a front seat to history, working first on [Barack] Obama’s presidential campaign then in his administration, but also to make some history of my own as the first Black woman and openly queer person to ever be a White House press secretary. Never had I considered leaving the party until now."

title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s partner, Ken Urker, found dead inside his Louisiana home: sheriff
description: Ken Urker was found dead in his Louisiana home after loved ones couldn't reach him. Gypsy Rose Blanchard says she believes it was a drug overdose.
content: The Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office confirmed Kenan "Ken" Urker, the partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, was found dead inside his Louisiana home Thursday after loved ones requested a welfare check. Anita Blanchard told authorities that she and her husband, who is Gypsy Rose Blanchard's half-brother, went to the 34-year-old's home and spotted Urker lying unconscious from an outside window, according to an incident report. A man accompanying Anita Blanchard and her husband then entered the house through a window and found Urker, who was not breathing and cold to the touch, according to the report. GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD IS ENGAGED TO MAN WHO CONTACTED HER IN PRISON, REPORT SAYS Investigators recovered syringes and a spoon next to a brown powdery substance in the bathroom, as well as a handgun, two shot glasses, and a syringe on a nightstand next to the bed, the report states. Deputies noted Urker "appeared to have been there for an extended period of time." Anita Blanchard told authorities that Urker had been with her and her husband at church the previous evening around 8:45 p.m., where he mentioned feeling depressed and upset. GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD SAYS SHE 'FELT LIKE A PRISONER' BEFORE MOTHER'S FATAL STABBING "They advised he made a TikTok live video at approximately 2300 hours," deputies wrote. "They advised that he just had the video going while he was driving without him saying anything." Urker had amassed more than 36,000 followers on the platform. After Urker failed to show up for work the following day, Anita Blanchard and Urker's employer decided to check on him, ultimately prompting them to contact law enforcement. The sheriff's office told Fox News Digital the case remains under investigation, but there are "no signs of foul play." Thursday was Urker's 34th birthday. "If that would change at any point, or there would be any major update in this investigation, we would issue a new statement," the sheriff's office said. HAYDEN PANETTIERE CAUSE OF DEATH REVEALED Gypsy Rose Blanchard was sentenced to 10 years in prison for second-degree murder in 2016 for her role in the fatal stabbing of her mother, Clauddine "Dee Dee" Blanchard, alongside her then-boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn. The killing inspired the 2019 TV series "The Act" on Hulu. Godejohn was sentenced to life in prison without parole. Blanchard was released on parole in December 2023 after serving 85% of her sentence. Urker and Gypsy Rose Blanchard got engaged in 2018 while she was incarcerated, but later separated. The couple rekindled after her first marriage and welcomed their daughter, Aurora, on Dec. 28, 2024. In a statement to PEOPLE, Blanchard said she believes Urker died of a drug overdose. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I don’t know if it was intentional or not," Gypsy Rose Blanchard told the outlet. "He was not in a good state of mind lately." She shared a photo of Urker on Instagram Friday, writing, "You will always be my greatest love story. You will be remembered and loved forever." Gypsy Rose Blanchard also shared an Instagram Story detailing his struggle with cyberbullying. "Ken endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit," she wrote. "The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure. I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline, and every comment." "I will make sure [Aurora] grows up knowing how deeply her father loved her and who he was beyond what strangers on the internet chose to say about him," she added. The post, shared with her one million followers, garnered nearly 100,000 likes within hours.

title: Social media reacts to excruciatingly awkward moment between Devils Jack Hughes and ESPN analyst
description: Jack Hughes' interview with ESPN's AJ Mleczko is already a frontrunner for awkward moment of the year after her injury joke fell completely flat.
content: The NHL season is just a few days old, and it's safe to say that we have a frontrunner for "Awkward Moment of the Year" already. This one comes courtesy of New Jersey Devils star Jack Hughes and ESPN analyst AJ Mleczko. The Devils hosted the Philadelphia Flyers for their season opener at the Prudential Center. After the first period, the Devils were down 1-0, and Hughes was called over to do an interview with Mleczko, who was stationed between the benches. AVALANCHE FORWARD NATHAN MACKINNON SCORES A PAIR THEN DROPS GLOVES, MIGHT BE THE BEST PLAYER IN THE WORLD Hughes offered the usual interview platitudes and seemed to be pleased with how his team was playing. But then Mleczko decided to make a joke about the Team USA golden goal scorer's injury history, including an infamous moment in which he sustained a cut during a team dinner. WYNDHAM CLARK TROLLS CANADIAN OPEN CROWD WITH TEAM USA JACK HUGHES JERSEY, GETS SHOWERED WITH BOOS How did it go? Well, about as well as a dog fart at a wake. Cue the "Curb Your Enthusiasm" music. It's a rough one, and you've got a clear line of demarcation, with some going after Mleczko for making the joke. Others said criticism of her was misogynistic or saw it as an opportunity to go after Hughes for laughing at a joke the president made after the gold medal game. Personally, I think it was a perfect storm of awkwardness. Just an accidental mixing of social bleach and ammonia. I think Mleczko is a really solid broadcaster, and everyone has moments where they say something they wish they could grab out of the air and pretend it never happened. Any analyst who tried to make that joke would've ended up with egg on their face too. Buuuuuuut... Hughes is not known to be one of the more gregarious NHLers. If you make a joke like that, someone like the Flyers' Trevor Zegras or Florida's Brad Marchand would field it and probably volley one back in the other direction. I think Mleczko's biggest mistake was taking the wrong approach with the wrong player. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Who cares? Everyone goofs up. But it is also weird to take an awkward moment, tie it back to an unrelated and overblown moment from months earlier, in a vain attempt to build a narrative that just doesn't seem to be there.

title: Android malware can steal your PIN and bank logins
description: RatHat Android malware uses AI to steal banking credentials, intercept two-factor authentication codes and reconstruct your PIN from touch inputs.
content: Your Android phone probably holds far more sensitive information than you realize. Banking apps, passwords and security codes can all pass through that little screen in your hand. A newly uncovered Android threat called RatHat wants access to all of it. Security researchers at Zimperium discovered the malware, which uses generative AI as part of its attack, and found that it can turn permissions you approve into surprisingly deep control of your phone. RatHat can steal banking credentials, intercept authentication codes and even reconstruct a PIN or unlock pattern from where your finger touches the screen. It can also create a persistent connection that may survive after you remove the malicious app. The attack still needs help from the person holding the phone. RatHat relies heavily on tricking someone into installing a malicious Android app and approving powerful permissions. That gives you several opportunities to stop it before the malware takes over. AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover five ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com How RatHat Android malware gets onto your phone RatHat starts with social engineering. Zimperium says attackers primarily spread it through SMS phishing, malicious advertising and deceptive third-party download sites. The malicious APK may pose as familiar software, including a streaming app or Chrome. That familiar name can lower your guard. A download page might look convincing enough to make you think you are installing a normal app. However, RatHat relies on you manually installing an APK outside Google Play. Once installed, the malicious app pushes you to enable Android's Accessibility service. The excuse can vary by region. In some cases, the malware claims the permission will solve a network problem or unlock a financial benefit. Accessibility services perform important legitimate functions on Android. However, they can also give an approved app the ability to inspect what appears on your screen and interact with the interface. RatHat takes advantage of that power to begin changing settings without you doing the work yourself. How RatHat uses AI to gain deeper access Once RatHat gets Accessibility access, it can tap through Android settings to enable Developer Options and Wireless Debugging. It can then read the six-digit ADB pairing code displayed on the phone and connect to the device's own Android Debug Bridge. No separate computer has to complete the connection. ADB, short for Android Debug Bridge, gives developers powerful tools to test and manage Android devices. RatHat abuses that legitimate feature to establish shell-level access outside the normal Android app sandbox. From there, the malware launches a Go-based agent that can execute system commands. It also starts a reverse-proxy client that creates a persistent connection back to the attacker. Zimperium says that connection can give an operator continued access to the phone's ADB service. RatHat also brings AI into the process. The malware sends information from Android's live Accessibility tree to a generative AI assistant. The AI can help determine where an item appears on the screen, read displayed text and tell the malware when to scroll. That makes the attack more adaptable than automation that follows the same fixed sequence every time. We recently saw another Android threat abuse Wireless Debugging in a similar way. RatHat adds AI-assisted navigation and another persistence mechanism to the mix. RatHat can steal bank logins and security codes After gaining access, RatHat can watch for financial apps and display fake screens over legitimate ones. Those overlays can trick you into entering banking credentials directly into a page controlled by the attacker. Zimperium found RatHat targeting banking and cryptocurrency apps. It also specifically identified overlays aimed at payment services such as WeChat and Alipay. The malware can intercept SMS messages and notification content as well, giving attackers another way to capture one-time passwords and two-factor authentication codes. Then there is the way RatHat watches your fingers. The malware can monitor raw touch coordinates and compare those locations with known keypad layouts. That allows it to reconstruct PINs from where you tap. It can use a similar method to recover Android pattern-lock sequences. Because the malware reads those touch coordinates at a low level, protections that normally hide PIN digits from screen readers do not stop this technique. That means a criminal may never need to see your PIN displayed as text. Your finger movements can give it away. RatHat can fight attempts to remove it RatHat also tries to make leaving your phone much harder than getting onto it. Zimperium found that the malware can interfere when you try to uninstall the malicious app. It can cancel the real uninstall process and place a fake Google Play error message on top of the screen. Even if you successfully remove the visible app, another problem remains. RatHat launches a separate native service outside the normal app life cycle. That service can stay behind after the original app disappears. It can then reinstall the malware and restore its permissions. Zimperium also found that RatHat can request Device Admin rights. Those rights give it additional control, including the ability to wipe the device if someone tries to uninstall it. That persistence is why deleting a suspicious app may not be enough once RatHat fully compromises a phone. What Google says about RatHat Google responded to CyberGuy and says it has not found RatHat on Google Play based on its current detection. The company also says Android users already have protection against known versions of the malware through Google Play Protect. "Based on our current detection, no apps containing this malware are found on Google Play. Android users are automatically protected against known versions of this malware by Google Play Protect, which is on by default on Android devices with Google Play Services," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy. That is reassuring for people who download their apps through Google Play. It also reinforces why keeping Play Protect enabled can add an important layer of defense if a harmful app reaches your phone from another source. How to protect your Android phone from RatHat RatHat becomes dangerous after it gains several layers of access. Fortunately, you can break that chain at several points. These steps can reduce your risk and help you respond if something has already gone wrong. HACKERS HIJACK VERIFIED STREAMING ACCOUNT TO SPREAD MALWARE, RESEARCHERS FIND 1) Install apps through Google Play Avoid installing APK files that arrive through text messages, online ads or unfamiliar websites. RatHat relies heavily on persuading people to sideload malicious apps. If a page looks like Google Play, but you can see a browser address bar, you are still on a website. Close it and open the actual Google Play Store app. Also question any message that tells you to reinstall Chrome or another app already on your phone. Open Google Play yourself and check the app there instead. 2) Be extremely careful with Accessibility permissions Accessibility access plays a central role in RatHat's attack. Therefore, treat an unexpected request for that permission as a serious warning. Open Settings and search for Accessibility. Review apps with Accessibility access and remove permission from anything you do not recognize or no longer use. Menu names can vary by Android phone. If a streaming app, browser update or other unrelated app suddenly tells you that Accessibility access is required, do not approve it until you know exactly why. 3) Keep Wireless Debugging off Most Android users never need Wireless Debugging. RatHat uses it to establish its powerful ADB shell connection. Open Settings and search for Developer options or Wireless debugging. Leave Wireless Debugging turned off unless you have a specific reason to use it. If you discover Developer Options or Wireless Debugging enabled and you do not remember turning them on, take a closer look at the apps and security settings on your phone. 4) Use strong antivirus software Install strong antivirus software and keep real-time protection enabled. Security software can help detect malicious apps and suspicious activity before they get deeper access to your phone. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. However, detecting RatHat and completely removing it are two different things. Because the malware can leave behind a persistent service after the visible app is removed, we recommend a factory reset if a security scan confirms RatHat has fully infected your phone. 5) Keep Google Play Protect turned on Google says Android users are automatically protected against known versions of RatHat through Google Play Protect, which comes turned on by default on Android devices with Google Play Services. You can still check that it is enabled. Open the Google Play Store > tap your profile picture > Play Protect > Settings. Make sure Scan apps with Play Protect is turned on. You can also enable Improve harmful app detection. This gives Google additional information about unfamiliar apps installed outside Google Play so they can be checked for harmful behavior. 6) Consider Android Advanced Protection Android's Advanced Protection can provide another useful barrier on supported devices. Google says it blocks app installations from unknown sources and restricts Accessibility services to verified accessibility tools. It also prevents Play Protect from being turned off while Device protection is active. To turn it on, open Settings > Security & privacy > Advanced Protection > turn on Device protection. Google notes that your phone may need to restart. For someone who rarely sideloads apps, those extra restrictions can remove two of the avenues RatHat relies on. THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE 7) Keep Android and your apps updated Install Android security updates and app updates when they become available. Updates fix known vulnerabilities and strengthen protections across your phone. RatHat's documented infection chain depends primarily on malicious downloads and permission abuse, so an Android update alone will not solve the problem. Even so, running current software closes other security gaps that attackers could try to exploit. 8) Treat unexpected texts and app links with suspicion RatHat spreads partly through smishing, which is phishing delivered by text message. An urgent message can push you toward a malicious download before you stop to question it. Avoid tapping links in unexpected texts that tell you to install an app or fix a problem on your phone. Instead, open the company's official app or visit its known website yourself. The same advice applies to online ads offering apps. Malvertising can lead to convincing download pages that have nothing to do with the company they appear to represent. 9) If you suspect RatHat, stop using that phone for sensitive accounts If antivirus software flags RatHat or you have strong reason to think your phone has been compromised, stop entering passwords and financial information on it. Use another trusted device to change important passwords. Start with your primary email account since access to email can help an attacker reset other accounts. Then check your bank and credit card accounts for activity you do not recognize. If you spot anything suspicious, contact the financial institution using the number on the back of your card or through its official app. 10) Factory reset a confirmed infection If RatHat is confirmed, we recommend a factory reset rather than relying on a normal uninstall. RatHat's separate background component can survive after the visible malicious app disappears. Before resetting the phone, preserve personal photos or documents you know are safe. After the reset, install apps again through Google Play. Avoid reinstalling unfamiliar APK files from an old backup. You should also change credentials from another trusted device before returning to sensitive accounts on the reset phone. 11) Keep watching your accounts afterward RatHat can target banking credentials and authentication codes, so cleaning the phone should not be the end of your response. Continue reviewing bank statements and login alerts. Also watch for password reset messages or authentication requests you did not initiate. If you believe personal information beyond your login credentials may have been exposed, consider an identity theft protection service that can help monitor for suspicious activity. Acting quickly can limit the damage if stolen information gets used later. Kurt's key takeaways The AI component makes RatHat unusual, but the attack still begins with something very familiar: getting someone to trust the wrong download and approve a powerful permission. That gives Android users a chance to stop RatHat before it reaches the most damaging stages. Google's response adds another important piece of reassurance. The company says no apps containing RatHat are showing up on Google Play based on its detection, and Play Protect already guards Android users against known versions of the malware. Still, that protection works best when you avoid sideloading questionable apps and pay close attention to powerful permission requests. Keep Play Protect running and add strong antivirus protection to your phone. Wireless Debugging should stay off unless you know exactly why you need it. If RatHat does make it onto a device, do not assume deleting the app solves the problem. A confirmed infection calls for a much more serious cleanup. title: Florida Gators, Georgia Bulldogs caught in social media standoff over origins of 'Bloody Tuesday' practice
description: Jon Sumrall's "Bloody Tuesday" practice ritual sparked a heated debate between Florida Gators and Georgia Bulldogs fans over who coined it first.
content: Things could not be going much better for the Florida Gators to start the Jon Sumrall era. Sumrall and his team are 4-0 with a 24-point beatdown of a top-five Ole Miss team less than one week ago. Recruiting is on fire and the whole program looks like a completely different monster than they did this time a year ago. FLORIDA DROPS IMPRESSIVE OFFENSIVE PERFORMANCE TO PULL OFF MASSIVE WIN OVER NO. 4 OLE MISS A lot of that is due to Sumrall's intensity as a head coach. The 44-year-old first-time SEC coach has taken great pride in returning the edge that has been missing from Gainesville since Urban Meyer exited Alachua County back in December 2010. Just hearing the man talk for more than 60 seconds confirms this, and in keeping with the theme of being an absolute psychopath (in the best way possible, of course), Sumrall is instituting a ritual for his Tuesday practices which will ensure maximum violence and physicality. He's calling it "Bloody Tuesday." FLORIDA COACH JON SUMRALL REVEALS EARLY CAREER STRUGGLES, LIVING IN SLUMS OF SAN DIEGO AND 'CARRYING A GLOCK' "We got a great indoor (practice facility) here," Sumrall said on The Triple Option Podcast. "On Tuesdays, we don’t use the damn indoor. I don’t want anybody going in the indoor on Tuesday. We’re going to be outside. I hope it’s hot. Tuesdays have to be physical and violent, and you gotta strain, or you don’t know how to play way on Saturday." If you're a Gator fan, you have to be pumped hearing that. After years and years of milquetoast scrimmages run by mealy mouthed head coaches, it's refreshing to see Sumrall bringing some much-needed juice back to Ben Hill Griffin Stadium. But not everyone is impressed with Sumrall's "Bloody Tuesday," particularly fans of Florida's archrivals, the Georgia Bulldogs. Dawg fans on social media have pointed out that Kirby Smart has been using the term "Bloody Tuesday" to describe his weekday practices since arriving in Athens in 2016. HIGH STAKES, SOCIAL MEDIA BARBS REMIND COLLEGE FOOTBALL FANS THAT AUBURN AND FLORIDA SHARE HISTORY OF HATRED Uh-oh! Is Sumrall guilty of copying Kirby's homework and turning it in as his own? Well, it's a little more complicated than that. As Gator fans were quick to point out, the aforementioned Urban Meyer started calling his Tuesday practices "Bloody Tuesday" all the way back in 2009, and it perhaps dates back to an even earlier period in the Meyer era. Georgia fans responded with articles from 2003 showing that former head coach Mark Richt used the phrase early in his tenure, creating a good old fashioned social media standoff. So who's right here? The truth of the matter is, both of these fanbases are wasting their breath. The term "Bloody Tuesday" isn't some revelatory concept; it's literally an adjective followed by a day of the week. None of these coaches invented the printing press or discovered penicillin, and if you really want to get historical, Richt wasn't even the first one to start using the term "Bloody Tuesday." Not by a long shot. A quick Google search shows that legendary Penn State coach Hugo Bezdek coined the phrase back in the 1920s to describe his physical weekday practices with the Nittany Lions. So, if anyone has a right to be upset with both of these programs, it's the Penn State faithful, though I doubt any of those fans who were alive for Bezdek's reign have an X account to be able to weigh in. Much of coaching football is taking ideas from your predecessors and adopting them as your own with a personal twist. Sumrall likely got the idea from Meyer, and Smart likely got the idea from Richt, who in turn adopted it from legendary Georgia coach Vince Dooley. It's like getting mad at Metallica for using power chords because Black Sabbath did it first. There's plenty of productive things to argue about between these two fanbases, and "Bloody Tuesday" is pretty far down the list. Then again, this is part of what makes college football rivalries so great. Hopefully at their press conferences next week, both Sumrall and Smart pay homage to the true originator of "Bloody Tuesday" so we can all just move on with our lives. title: Murdaugh lawyers allege prosecutors withheld witness claim that police chief handled murder weapons: filing
description: Alex Murdaugh's defense claims prosecutors withheld a witness statement alleging a police chief handled the murder weapons after the 2021 killings.
content: Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh accused prosecutors Wednesday of withholding a witness statement alleging a South Carolina police chief handled the weapons used to kill Murdaugh's wife and son and arranged a change of clothes for him after the 2021 killings. And they're asking a judge to intervene. Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County. The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury. His retrial is scheduled to begin April 5, 2027. The new allegations come as Murdaugh's team said "all urgent evidentiary issues" in the case will be heard at a hearing on Oct. 16. ALEX MURDAUGH DEMANDS NEW EVIDENCE SEARCH IN HUNT FOR CRACKS IN CASE A spokeswoman for Murdaugh's defense team told Fox News Digital that Judge Debra McCaslin notified them that "DNA, cell phone extraction, ballistic data, and FARO scan data will be addressed at the hearing." All other motions will be heard at a Nov. 13 hearing. Police chief allegations The motion, filed by Murdaugh's attorneys Wednesday, cites press reports that a state grand jury heard testimony alleging Yemassee Police Chief Greg Alexander was seen with the murder weapons shortly after the June 7, 2021, killings. "According to those reports, witnesses have testified that the Chief of Police of the Town of Yemassee, Greg Alexander, was seen with the murder weapons in the immediate aftermath of the June 7, 2021, killings, and that second Yemassee officer is under investigation for transporting and concealing weapons and clothing," the filing states. It also cites a story from The Post and Courier, which reported that "a Lowcountry official told SLED agents that Chief Alexander 'spoke of arriving early to the murder scene and talked about providing a change of clothes to Murdaugh,' and that the official believed the guns and clothing were brought into the police station and stored there." MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS DETECTIVES FOUND MALE DNA UNDER VICTIM'S NAILS BUT SKIPPED KEY TESTING Notably, the allegations couldn't be corroborated by The Post and Courier. SEND US A TIP At Murdaugh's first murder trial in 2023, prosecutors contended that he killed his family members using two different types of weapons, then used a nearby water hose to clean up, changed his clothes and drove to his parents' house, where he allegedly left the murder weapons before returning a week later to dispose of them. Prosecutors had previously acknowledged that police never recovered the weapons. "The same explanation has been provided to SLED," McCulloch told Fox News Digital. "That truth will outlive any ridiculous rumors and gossip." title: Harvard Medical School artist-in-residence calls to ‘Free Luigi’ Mangione during ‘fat liberation’ panel
description: Roxane Gay said "Free Luigi" at a Harvard Medical School event before admitting she uses concierge medicine to avoid ordinary healthcare costs.
content: Roxane Gay, Rutgers University professor artist-in-residence for Harvard's Master of Science in Media, Medicine and Health and Media and Medicine Certificiate Program at Harvard Medical School, called for the release of Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty in August to federal stalking charges resulting in death in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, during a Harvard panel Wednesday examining fatness and healthcare. When the discussion turned to the health insurance industry, Gay responded, "Free Luigi, for one," and then Gay went on to call the health insurance industry "equal opportunity evil," The College Fix reported. In a Wednesday post on X from Stu Smith, an investigative analyst at the Manhattan Institute, Smith wrote, "At tonight’s Harvard Medical School event, artist-in-residence Roxane Gay responded to a question about the health insurance industry with ‘Free Luigi.’" HASAN PIKER SPARKS BACKLASH WITH LUIGI MANGIONE REMARKS, CLAIMS SLAIN CEO ENGAGED IN 'SOCIAL MURDER' Smith continued, "Minutes earlier, Gay admitted she uses concierge medicine after deciding to ‘throw money at this problem’ and ‘buy my way out’ of ordinary healthcare. Gay, incidentally, is former Harvard president Claudine Gay’s first cousin. We all know Harvard is morally bankrupt at this point, but this was a great reminder." Gay made the remarks during the Harvard Medical School's "Against the Pathology of Unruly Bodies" event, which focused on what organizers described as the "intersection of fatness and healthcare" and how medical professionals treat overweight patients. The event also examined, according to a listing advertising the event, "the way fat bodies are pathologized by medical professionals with grave consequences, and how medical professionals can more ethically treat fat patients as people rather than as problems to be solved." Gay holds the Gloria Steinem Endowed Chair in Media, Culture and Feminist Studies at Rutgers. LUIGI MANGIONE PLEADS GUILTY IN FEDERAL COURT TO STALKING AND KILLING UNITEDHEALTHCARE CEO BRIAN THOMPSON Mangione, who faces a second-degree murder charge, several weapons charges and a forged-instrument charge in New York state court, pleaded guilty Aug. 14 to two federal stalking charges resulting in death. He is scheduled to be sentenced in federal court Dec. 18 and faces a maximum potential sentence of life in prison. His state case remains pending. LUIGI MANGIONE MUSICAL SET TO MAKE NEW YORK CITY DEBUT IN THE SUMMER In a statement to Fox News Digital, Gay said, "I said Free Luigi out of utter frustration, and this is a frustration most Americans have about the health insurance industry. That industry is far more focused on profit than actually providing people with the healthcare they need, healthcare that should be covered by the health insurance we pay quite a lot of money for." Gay continued, "Luigi Mangione was clearly dealing with mental health issues when he committed murder. Murder is wrong, in all cases, including the death penalty. I don't think his mental health issues will be addressed in a carceral setting. He should be in a setting where he can get actual help, not in a place that might exacerbate the mental illness that drove him to commit murder. Unfortunately, our justice system doesn't really care about rehabilitation, so I doubt he will get the help he needs. Whatever his sentence ends up being, I hope he is able to get the help he needs while pays his debt to society and I hope Brian Thompson's family feels justice is served even though nothing will bring back their loved one." "I condemn the killing of Brian Thompson," Gay said further. "I condemn all killing. Murder doesn't solve anything. Thompson's murder didn't improve the health insurance system. It only created a cavern of grief for his loved ones. You know that. The health insurance industry is absolutely equal opportunity evil. Millions and millions of Americans feel this way. It is not a unique sentiment. I would love for the American health insurance system to evolve into a single payer system so we have universal healthcare like a significant percentage of the rest of the world. At the very, very least, it would be great if health insurance companies didn't make healthcare decisions for patients that should be made by their physicians." title: Taking daily supplement may help preserve muscle as you age — even without exercise
description: New research in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition links daily creatine to memory gains and sarcopenia prevention.
content: Daily creatine supplementation could help middle-aged and older adults preserve lean muscle mass, gain strength and support cognitive function, whether it's paired with exercise or not, according to a study published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. The 12-week study, conducted by researchers at Texas A&M University’s Exercise & Sport Nutrition Lab, evaluated 64 men and women ages 45 to 65. Participants were divided into non-exercise and exercise-plus-diet groups, then randomly assigned to take either 10 grams of creatine monohydrate per day — administered in two 5-gram doses — or a placebo. ONE MUSCLE PROTEIN MAY HOLD THE KEY TO STAYING STRONGER AS YOU AGE, STUDY FINDS Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that helps cells regenerate adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy source for cellular activity in both muscle and brain tissue, according to Cleveland Clinic. Creatine monohydrate is a dietary supplement that helps muscles produce quick energy during activities like strength training. Adults naturally lose muscle mass and strength as they age, a condition known as sarcopenia. While dieting can accelerate that muscle loss, the new study found that creatine monohydrate helped counter the effect. FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG Adding creatine to an exercise and diet intervention resulted in greater reductions in body fat percentage, better preservation of lean body mass, and marked improvements in upper- and lower-body strength compared to a placebo. Even among participants who did not engage in exercise or dietary changes, daily creatine supplementation increased lean tissue mass and improved muscular strength and endurance, according to the study. "The fact that you can increase lean muscle mass even without exercise is remarkable, especially as we age," New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer told Fox News Digital. "Between the physical and mental benefits, most people should be considering creatine supplementation." The expert, who was not involved in the study, noted that even participants who did not exercise saw an increase in their bench press and leg press. "The fact that you can increase lean muscle mass even without exercise is remarkable." Zemer said the findings suggest creatine may help build actual muscle tissue that generates strength, rather than simply increasing the amount of water stored in muscle cells. Beyond physical performance, the researchers found that the 10-gram daily dose of creatine supported improvements in select tests of memory and cognitive processing. "My main takeaway from the study is that the benefits of creatine extend far beyond just athletes and bodybuilders," Zemer said. "Creatine continues to be the most scientifically studied and validated supplement on the market." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ However, the trainer emphasized that supplementation should not replace regular physical activity. "Just because you can increase lean muscle mass by taking creatine without exercise does not mean that it is optimal or a replacement for exercise," Zemer cautioned. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "The benefits of exercise will always supersede those of creatine alone, and when the two are combined, they are both enhanced." The study authors noted several limitations to their findings. Participants chose whether to join the exercise or non-exercise groups before being randomly assigned to receive either creatine or a placebo, which could have introduced lifestyle differences between the groups. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Additionally, because the study lasted just 12 weeks and included only healthy adults, researchers don't yet know whether the benefits would be long-term or whether they would apply to people with serious metabolic or neurological conditions. For those considering taking creatine, Zemer advised consulting a healthcare professional to determine whether it's right for them, then choosing a reputable brand, staying hydrated and taking it consistently. "Recommended minimum dosages for creatine are typically 3 grams for women and 5 grams for men," he said. "This study used higher dosages. Creatine is about consistency rather than when you take it, so find a time you can consistently take it daily." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER According to the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, creatine is generally considered safe for healthy adults, although some people may experience bloating, stomach discomfort or water retention. Experts recommend talking with a healthcare provider before beginning supplementation, particularly for those with kidney disease or other chronic health conditions.

title: Aces' fans spew unfounded claims that Fever fans are 'racist' while defending A'ja Wilson
description: Las Vegas Aces fans accused Indiana Fever supporters of racism and slurs at Gainbridge Fieldhouse, but their claims crumbled under scrutiny.
content: There's a glaring problem in the WNBA. From media, to the players, and the league's dedicated fan base full of left-wing political activists, far too many people have been unfairly characterizing Indiana Fever and Caitlin Clark fans. Since Clark's rookie season, the claims of racism have been leveled at an astounding rate. My conversations with Las Vegas Aces' fans proved just how hostile and unfair, to say the least, that rhetoric has become. When controversies arise in the WNBA, and across sports in general, I want to do my due diligence by asking fans what they think in person. I want to hear the thoughts and opinions from people who are invested and aware in what is going on, whether they are left, right, or center. I've done that at the Sophie Cunningham rallies and protests outside arenas across the country. I've interviewed fans in the aftermath of flagrant fouls on Caitlin Clark and Cunningham. I've covered a lot of the issues the league has faced and brought upon themselves. As you know, the WNBA is no stranger to controversies. It's engrained in the fabric of the league. So when A'ja Wilson walked over 20 feet away into the seating area during Game 2 to confront a fan in Indiana for simply pointing at her from the second row of the baseline courtside seats, I wanted to hear fans thoughts about it. I wanted their thoughts on the WNBA refusing to reprimand the league's MVP or have Wilson face any repercussions whatsoever for her actions. Those questions triggered some insane accusations from Aces fans regarding the Fever fan and their fanbase. PRIME VIDEO WNBA BROADCAST CREW EMBARRASSES ITSELF WITH COVERAGE OF A'JA WILSON FAN INCIDENT About an hour before gametime, I spoke with a female Aces fan, who said, "I think it (the A'ja Wilson incident) is bigger than that moment. I think it's more about racism and the concerns regarding the Fever fans being racist." That's the way this incident was framed from the beginning, unfortunately. It was a Black athlete confronting a White fan, so people jumped at the idea there must have been a slur thrown in Wilson's direction. That was obviously not the case.She then continued by disagreeing with A'ja Wilson's actions, but justified them due to claims of racism: "She was out of line to approach a fan like that, but by the same token, racism in our country is also out of line." When I asked if she thought the fan was racist she responded, "No. Not at all." I was now a little confused, so I asked if she was claiming the fan wasn't racist, but that race played a factor in A'ja Wilson losing her cool. "I do," she said definitively. "I think as a Black athlete, in a state where there's a history of racism, and where this team has been accused of having racist fans," she continued before I cut her off to ask if there's validity to those claims. "I think there's validity to racism," she responded. "Well, of course, but [I'm asking about] Indiana Fever fans," I responded. FORMER ESPN ANCHOR SMEARS CAITLIN CLARK FANS WITH SWEEPING, FALSE ACCUSATIONS OF RACISM | MATT CALKINS "No, I can't say that," she humbly responded, realizing she was assigning labels to a fanbase without proper proof. The conversation went on for another minute or so where I respectfully pressed her on her characterization of the Fever fan base and how they've been labeled as racists, bigots, you name it. I even mentioned that Wilson even stated in the postgame interview that her actions weren't because of anything he said, but the fact that a man pointed at her. If anything, she was claiming some form of misogyny. The fan still speculated that race could've played a part in Wilson's thinking, leading her to lose her cool. In another conversation, an Aces fan unashamedly said that she believes Indiana Fever fans are "racist." She claimed, "It's (Gainbridge Fieldhouse) a hard place and the way they treat us up there. I've sat there and watched games and watched them yell slurs." When I asked her if she believed a slur was said by the fan towards Wilson, knowing good and well that no slur was stated because both I and Pat McAfee Show personality, Boston Connor, who was seated by the fan, have confirmed the fan simply said, "It (the foul) is on you," she responded by saying, "It's kinda hard to say. He did something to provoke her because that's not A'ja and that's not her demeanor." This is where I let her know that multiple sources have confirmed nothing racial was said to Wilson. "But then, the way he came [at her], he left his seat, he left his area, and he stepped towards her," she responded trying to find a way to justify Wilson's unsportsmanlike actions, though she was just proven to be ignorant about the facts. She continued by saying the Fever fan was "provoking" Wilson and seemingly questioned his intentions as a threat to Wilson's safety. Here's where things went completely off the rails. LET'S HAVE AN HONEST CONVERSATION ABOUT CAITLIN CLARK, RACISM, AND MEDIA COWARDICE| BOBBY BURACK She then claimed the WNBA made the right decision to not eject, fine, or suspend Wilson, because Indiana Fever fans are "racists." I'm not kidding. This was actually her argument. "If you've never been to Cambridge Fieldhouse and seen the demeanor of the Indiana Fever fans," she mistakenly said while referring to Gainbridge Fieldhouse. "If we did half of what they did up there, the WNBA would be fining the Aces." So now was the time to get the clarification we are all looking for. I asked, "Do you believe Indiana Fever fans are racist?" She responded with a resounding, "Yes! By all means! By all means! By all means! Yes, they are racists." So here is the problem. Fans like this, making outlandish claims that aren't based in facts or reality, are what is wrong with the WNBA. They spew unfounded talking points about Fever fans. It's been that way since Clark entered the league three seasons ago. The millions of people who have flocked to the league because of Caitlin Clark, helping players like A'ja Wilson sign million dollar contracts, assisted in teams now flying private, and who may be the fans who help make the league profitable for the first time in the league's 30-year history, are labeled as the scum of the earth. They might as well be considered the KKK of WNBA fanbases. An insane, divisive, unfair label that echoes the claims of even A'ja Wilson's mom, who paraded around the arena with a "Love Beats Hate" sign following the Aces' Game 3 win. There is still racism in America, and it's not just White people discriminating against Blacks, but we have to stop making claims like this, if they can't be substantiated. All you're doing is insulting your paying customers and fellow fans in the most vile way.

title: Obama judge halts Trump firing bid as decades-old legal authority tees up possible major reversal
description: President Donald Trump's firing of court-appointed U.S. attorney Roger Rogoff was blocked by Judge Stanley Bastian, sparking a separation of powers clash.
content: An Obama-appointed judge blocked President Donald Trump from firing court-appointed U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Washington Roger Rogoff, ordering the Justice Department to recognize Rogoff as the rightful officeholder and restore his ability to serve. "This is yet another ruling from an activist judge trying to thwart President Trump’s agenda and undermine his constitutional authority. U.S. attorneys serve at the pleasure of the President," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. Judge Stanley Bastian, who was first nominated by Obama in 2013, issued a preliminary injunction reinstating Rogoff and barring the administration from treating him as having been lawfully removed. The ruling sets up a legal fight over whether a president can fire a U.S. attorney appointed by federal judges. A 1979 Justice Department opinion and a 2000 federal appeals court ruling both concluded that the president has that authority. "We disagree with the decision and intend to seek an immediate stay and will appeal," the DOJ Rapid Response account wrote. TRUMP ADMIN FIRES US ATTORNEY IN SEATTLE MINUTES AFTER HE WAS APPOINTED Some legal experts and conservative attorneys took to social media to sharply criticize the ruling, arguing it infringes on the president's constitutional authority over the executive branch. "Another lawless and dangerous ruling. Violating the separation of powers. By another Democrat activist judge. This time? Seattle Obama Judge Stanley Bastian," wrote Article III founder and president Mike Davis. "Democrat judges handpicked their own U.S. attorney. The President, through his attorney general, fired him. Under Article II of the Constitution, the President clearly has the executive power to fire Justice Department officials," Davis added. Davis also noted Bastian’s first name was misspelled in the order, missing the "e" in Stanley. 'ROGUE' OBAMA JUDGE'S SMACKDOWN OF TRUMP ELECTION RULES PROVOKES OMINOUS WARNING FROM WHITE HOUSE DEPUTY "The Federal Judge misspelled his own name in his order. That's how you know it's quality legal work," wrote one user. "Now Judge Bastian created an unnecessary constitutional crisis by essentially ordering a coup at the Justice Department, by ordering the removal of the President’s pick and putting in Bastian’s judicial puppet. The Ninth Circuit must fix this. Or the Supreme Court will have to step in. Again," Davis concluded. "The President's power to remove U.S. Attorneys must be unfettered consistent with Article II of the Constitution. Judge Stanley Bastian is wrong here to order Rogoff reinstated. I predict Judge Bastian will eventually be reversed, whether at the Ninth Circuit or by the Supreme Court," said Oversight Project litigation vice president Jeff Clark. WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER "Judicial overreach, plain and simple. The judiciary does not get to run the Executive Branch. Period," said Holtzman Vogel partner Brian Nieves. In Myers v. United States (1926), which centered on President Woodrow Wilson's firing of a postmaster without Senate consent, the Supreme Court ruled that the president generally has constitutional authority to remove executive branch officers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP More recently, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel concluded in a 1979 opinion that the president’s statutory authority to remove "each United States attorney" also extends to prosecutors appointed by federal judges. The case is the latest in a string of legal fights over President Trump's U.S. attorney appointments, following similar disputes in New Jersey, Virginia and New York. A similar dispute unfolded in New Jersey after the administration sought to keep Alina Habba leading the U.S. attorney’s office after her interim term ended. Federal courts ultimately rejected the administration’s effort to maintain her authority, although the judges’ original appointee, Desiree Grace, did not simply take over the office. Rogoff’s case goes a step further, directly testing whether a president can remove a U.S. attorney appointed by federal judges under the statutory process for filling a vacancy.

title: Socialist streamer Hasan Piker faces fury after pressuring Talarico to enact far-left policy if elected
description: Hasan Piker's remarks about holding James Talarico accountable drew sharp rebukes from Ken Paxton and Ted Cruz ahead of the Texas Senate race.
content: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker is getting dragged online after calling for Texas Senate nominee James Talarico to "play ball" by governing as a leftist if elected in this year's midterms. Talarico, running to be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas in more than three decades, has publicly realigned on some of his more radical stances and tried to campaign on a more moderate platform despite his previous comments. But Piker, who has gained prominence through his relationship with socialist-aligned Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, appears to want Talarico to pull a bait-and-switch if he wins in November. "Hopefully, after James Talarico wins, we’ve got to hold him to account," Piker said during a campus event at the University of Texas at Austin. "We've got to make sure that he doesn’t become another, ‘do nothing Democrat’ ‘business as usual,’ and we've got to keep up that pressure. HASAN PIKER SPEAKS TO UT AUSTIN STUDENTS AFTER BACKLASH FROM TEXAS LAWMAKERS As his campaign has progressed, Talarico has rolled back on some of his controversial statements like his claim that "God is non-binary." But he continues to back progressive policies like universal healthcare, arguing his beliefs stem from "biblical grounds." Piker's recent remarks quickly became ammunition for Republicans. Talarico’s opponent, GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton, and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, pounced, claiming that Piker is saying the quiet part out loud and showing the pressure Talarico could face from the party's left flank if he were to ascend to the U.S. Senate representing the Lone Star State. "James Talarico is bought and paid for by the Democratic Socialists," Paxton posted in response to Piker’s comments on Talarico. "And if he wins, they'll cash in at YOUR expense: raising your taxes and making life more expensive to pay for their radical agenda. Texas can't afford Talarico." Ted Cruz said on X: "When they tell you who they are…believe them." EL-SAYED TRIES TO PUT THE HASAN PIKER DEBATE BEHIND HIM AS MIDTERMS APPROACH "James Talarico will be nothing more than a puppet of the radical left," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas posted. Piker erupted in the left-wing party over the past couple years, most notably campaigning with El-Sayed. Democrats, including El-Sayed, are now distancing themselves from Piker after many of his controversial statements caught heat — like his claim that "America deserved 9/11." "Hasan ‘America Deserved 9/11’ Piker expects James Talarico would support his extreme agenda & be beholden to his base," Fox News Political Analyst Guy Benson warned. "He think he’s a mafia boss, and with the psychotic state of today’s Democrat party, he’s kinda right…" Dave Rubin posted. New York City Council member Vickie Paladino said, "Hasan Piker says he’s the one actually in charge of the Democrat party." Piker’s comments, mixed with Talarico’s back-and-forth from progressive to moderate rhetoric, have sparked skepticism about the direction the Texas Democrat would take in governing if elected. "Here we have Hasan Piker—an outspoken socialist, hater of Israel and opponent of capitalism — telling us exactly what he expects from James Talarico if elected," one user posted. "He says, ‘We gotta remind [James] that we are the force that backed him…’ and got him elected and that we expect him to remember that and fall in line. Every Republican, Independent and even common-sense Democrat even thinking about voting for Talarico needs to see this and think deeply about it." "A huge reason not to vote for Talarico he has to answer to the Fascist wing of his party," another posted. "No thanks." TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS Other users on social media argued Piker’s comments are irrelevant to Talarico’s campaign, and would not impact the agenda he would bring to the Senate if elected. Talarico’s campaign is the success of Talarico’s morals, policies and his hard working team’s outreach to the people of Texas." "What is Hasan even talking about," another user posted. "Talarico isn’t DSA and doesn’t owe DSA anything. He will be a senator that represents Texans, not California Socialists like Hasan."
