title: EXCLUSIVE: Supreme Court prayer grotto case could impact 'every single zoning law' in America, attorney says
description: The Supreme Court agreed to hear a Kentucky Catholic church's fight over a prayer grotto, a case that could reshape RLUIPA zoning law nationwide.
content: FIRST ON FOX — The Supreme Court agreed Thursday to hear a Kentucky church’s fight to build a prayer grotto on its property, taking up a dispute over what constitutes a "substantial burden" on religious exercise under federal land-use law. Ryan Gardner, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, which represents the Missionaries of St. John the Baptist, told Fox News Digital the implications stretch far beyond the proposed Catholic shrine in Park Hills, Kentucky. "This is a massive case for religious liberty because it has the potential to impact every single zoning law in this country," Gardner told Fox News Digital. ORTHODOX JEW FIGHTS BACK, SAYS CALIFORNIA CITY FINED HIM FOR HOME PRAYER MEETINGS At the center of the case is a proposed 16-by-39-foot grotto that court records say would include a shrine to the Virgin Mary, a plaza, walking path and retaining wall. Gardner compared its roughly 600-square-foot footprint to the size of a swimming pool. The church applied in March 2021 for a conditional-use permit and variance to build the grotto behind its building in honor of the Virgin Mary’s apparition to Saint Bernadette in Lourdes, France. The church building itself has stood on the property for nearly a century, predating Park Hills’ zoning ordinance adopted in 1974. The property history is a bit more complicated than the case’s shorthand description may suggest. The proposed grotto involved an adjacent parcel that was initially subject to a perpetual lease that would be transferred to the religious organization as a condition of the project’s approval. But unlike many religious land-use disputes, Gardner said, the church’s initial fight in this case was not with the local government. The Park Hills Board of Adjustment approved the church’s permit in April 2021. Two neighboring property owners, however, Joel and Elizabeth Frederic, objected and challenged the board’s decision in Kentucky state court. AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’ A trial court ruled in the church’s favor, but the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed, concluding the board exceeded its authority in approving the project and finding no violation of federal religious land-use law. The Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed the RLUIPA ruling in December 2025, prompting the church to seek Supreme Court review. The case centers on the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, known as RLUIPA, a federal law enacted to protect religious institutions from certain burdens on the use of their property. "RLUIPA is at the intersection of two very critical rights in this country: the rights of religious liberty and property rights," Gardner told Fox News Digital. The church asked the justices to review two questions under RLUIPA, but the Supreme Court agreed to hear only one about whether prohibiting a religious institution from building a religious structure on its own property constitutes a "substantial burden" on religious exercise under the law. SUPREME COURT SHOWDOWN LOOMS OVER ST MICHAEL STATUE BLOCKED FROM PUBLIC SAFETY BUILDING Gardner said lower courts have developed different approaches to the law since Congress enacted it in 2000, leaving religious organizations with different levels of protection depending on where a dispute arises. He argues the Supreme Court now has an opportunity to establish a clearer standard nationwide. The missionaries similarly argued in their Supreme Court petition that federal and state courts are divided over how to determine whether a land-use restriction creates a "substantial burden" under RLUIPA. The Frederics disputed that characterization in their opposition brief, arguing appellate courts generally consider similar factors and that differing outcomes can reflect differing facts. The Frederics also argued that the Missionaries failed to show that alternative locations for the grotto were unavailable. An attorney for the Frederics did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The case also puts two constitutionally significant areas of law alongside one another — religious exercise and the authority of local governments to regulate property use. While Gardner acknowledged that zoning serves a legitimate role in how local governments organize, he argued those same regulations remain subject to federal-level protections for religious exercise. That question, he said, reaches well beyond one prayer grotto in Kentucky. The SCOTUS ruling could affect disputes involving churches, synagogues, ministries and other religious organizations seeking to use their properties for worship or religious activities, according to Gardner. He warned that an overly narrow interpretation of the federal law could have "dire consequences" for religious land use around the country. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For the Missionaries of St. John the Baptist, however, the case that could shape religious land-use law across the country began with something much smaller, a roughly 600-square-foot place of prayer.

title: Fox News Poll: It’s a Lone Star Senate showdown between Talarico and Paxton
description: Democrat James Talarico holds a slim 2-point edge over Republican Ken Paxton as GOP enthusiasm gaps and crossover voters reshape the Texas Senate race.
content: Weeks before Election Day, Democratic engagement and positive ratings give Democrat James Talarico a razor-thin edge over Republican Ken Paxton in what is, so far, shaping up to be a photo finish for the Lone Star State’s U.S. Senate seat. This analysis, released Thursday, is among Texas likely voters, unless otherwise noted. Talarico enjoys a net positive personal rating of 8 points (52% favorable vs. 44% unfavorable), while Paxton’s is underwater by 18 points (40% vs. 58%). Republicans are six times more likely to view Paxton unfavorably (32%) than Democrats do Talarico (5%). The GOP also has an enthusiasm gap. More MAGA than non-MAGA Republicans are extremely interested in the midterms (64% vs. 50%) and certain they will vote (76% vs. 65%). By contrast, two-thirds of DSA and non-DSA Democrats are extremely interested, and nearly three-quarters of both groups are certain they will vote. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS Overall, Texas likely voters split on control of the Senate: 49% prefer a Democratic Senate while 50% favor a Republican upper chamber. Eight percent of self-identified Republicans prefer the Democrats in power versus 1% of Democrats crossing over to pick the GOP. All this gives Talarico a slim 2-point edge over Paxton (51-49%) in the first Fox News Poll among Texas likely voters (so no comparisons are available). These matchup results are within the margin of sampling error. Among the larger sample of registered voters, Talarico’s advantage widens to 7 points (just outside the margin of error). That’s up from a 3-point edge in July. GOP ambivalence is further reflected in Senate preferences because non-MAGA Republicans are more than five times more likely to back Talarico than their MAGA counterparts (22% to 4%). The crossover echoes lingering divisions from the competitive GOP primary and runoff: 20% of likely voters who backed Republican incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the March primary back Talarico. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI'S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISK Fully 100% of DSA Democrats and 98% of non-DSA Democrats back Talarico, and slightly more of his backers are certain of their support (89%) than Paxton backers (85%). In addition, Talarico also gets strong backing from Black voters (79%), moderates (65%), Hispanic voters (64%) and voters under age 35 (62%). Paxton’s best groups are White evangelical Christians (74%), White men without a college degree (65%), rural voters (57%) and voters ages 65 and over (55%). Both candidates face ideological concerns. Roughly equal numbers are concerned Talarico is too liberal on the issues (53% concerned) and Paxton is too close to President Trump (51%). In 2024, President Donald Trump won Texas by nearly 14 percentage points. Today, his job rating is underwater by 11 points: 44% approve vs. 55% disapprove. Fifteen percent of those disapproving still back Paxton compared to 9% of Trump approvers backing Talarico. Economic hardships continue to dominate the narrative. Seven in 10 Texans say the cost of living will be extremely important to their Senate vote, and this is another problem for the Republicans because twice as many voters say they are falling behind financially (35%) as getting ahead (16%). Those falling behind back Talarico by 32 points, while those getting ahead favor Paxton by 48 points. Those holding steady (48%), the largest group, narrowly back Paxton by 3 points. Nearly half say Trump (48%) and immigration (47%) will be extremely important to their vote, while one-third say the same about artificial intelligence technology (34%). Talarico holds wide leads among those saying the cost of living (Talarico +19), artificial intelligence (+18) and Trump (+6) will be extremely important to their Senate vote, while immigration-focused voters back Paxton (+20). In the governor’s race, incumbent Republican Greg Abbott’s positive job ratings give him an edge over Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa. The three-time incumbent has a 52%-47% advantage over the Texas state House representative. Over half, 52%, approve of the job Abbott is doing as governor, and that same share backs him in the race. Another 47% disapprove, the same number who back Hinojosa. Abbott fares better than Paxton because he has slightly higher support among men, Republicans and moderates. Women are more evenly divided in the governor’s race. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Abbott also has a modest crossover advantage: 10% of Talarico supporters back Abbott for governor while just 3% of Paxton supporters do the same for Hinojosa. "Democrats in Texas will walk across broken glass to vote against Trump, so the question is whether the average Republican will vote in an election without Trump and where the Senate race features a controversial GOP candidate," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts Fox News Polls with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Ironically, Paxton may owe his political life to Abbott, who is doing most of the get-out-the-vote work for the Republicans." Conducted September 24-28, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,203 Texas registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (127) and cellphones (789) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (287). Results based on the registered voter sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2.5 percentage points, and for the subsample of 881 likely voters it is ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling errors, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Likely voters are based on a probabilistic statistical model that relies on past vote history, interest in the current election, intention to vote, age, education, race, ethnicity and marital status. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.

title: Gavin Newsom signs Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha into law as new California state holidays
description: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the Muslim days Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha into law as California state holidays before signing bills protecting Jewish holidays.
content: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law a bill that formally recognizes two Muslim holidays as state holidays on Sunday, making it the second state to formally recognize both holidays statewide. California Assembly Bill 2017 officially added Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha to the list of state holidays, which would permit public schools and colleges to close and allow state employees to be eligible to observe the holidays. However, schools and businesses will not be required to close on these days, and courts will be required to stay open. This makes California the second state in the country, after Washington state, to pass statewide legislation recognizing the Muslim holidays. DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH Before signing AB 2017, Newsom had multiple bills on his desk that provided protections and exceptions for other religious observances, including Jewish holidays such as Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. For example, AB 395, which reached the governor days before AB 2017, would codify these Jewish holidays, among others, into state law and require state agencies and facilities like schools to "make every reasonable effort" to avoid scheduling significant functions for those days. Another bill, AB 1763, would also guarantee students in K-12 be allowed excused absences for religious holidays. Though these bills were introduced and presented to the governor before AB 2017, Newsom did not sign the additional bills into law until Wednesday, prior to the midnight deadline. Republican opponents criticized Newsom for appearing to prioritize bills recognizing Muslim holidays over bills allowing for equal treatment for Jewish holidays. SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT "The fact that Newsom chose to sign the Eid law before the law that protected other religious observance speaks volumes about the direction he is moving as he eyes a 2028 run for the presidency," Elizabeth Barcohana, chair of Jewish engagement for the California Republican Party, told the Jerusalem News Syndicate (JNS). She also warned that these laws would give Muslim holidays additional privileges not afforded to other religions, which could include closing schools. "People may think this is alarmist, but this is an example of American laws adopting a Sharia law framework," Barcohana told JNS. "Special protections no other religious observance receives, the option to shut down public institutions to observe the holiday that, until now, only Christian holidays received and curriculum in public schools that is religious in nature notably about a religion that emphasizes conversion." However, David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, supported Newsom's actions, saying he was not concerned about the order in which the bills were signed because all three became law. CALIFORNIA LAWMAKERS' PUSH TO MAKE MUSLIM HOLY DAYS STATE HOLIDAYS SPARKS DEBATE OVER SCHOOL NEUTRALITY "With more than 1,000 bills in front of him this past month, we aren't concerned with the sequencing of Assembly Bill 395 and Assembly Bill 1763, as long as they got signed, and they did. We're thrilled to see these two critical religious freedom protections become law and to recognize three Jewish holidays in California statute for the first time," Bocarsly told Fox News Digital. His organization also celebrated Newsom signing into law SB 1387, which recognizes Jewish identity as an ethnicity. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. A spokesperson for Newsom's office told Fox News Digital, "This is not about manufacturing a scorecard among faiths. The Governor signs bills based on the substance of the legislation and the constitutional process governing when he receives and acts on bills. California is proud to continue strengthening its religious freedom – something our nation’s founders strongly believed in, too."

title: Angel Reese's Defensive Player of the Year win looks like WNBA media rewarding its own hype
description: Angel Reese earned 46 WNBA Defensive Player of the Year votes, but the Atlanta Dream's unchanged 30-14 record raises some serious questions.
content: Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese deserved consideration for the WNBA’s Defensive Player of the Year award. Her rebounding, effort and ability to force turnovers gave voters plenty of reasons to put her in the conversation. Apparently, putting her in the conversation wasn’t enough. Reese received 46 of the 74 votes for the award announced Thursday. Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams finished second with 20. Las Vegas Aces center A’ja Wilson, the best defender in the WNBA as far as I’m concerned, received four. Four. Reese received more than 11 times as many votes as Wilson and more than twice as many as Williams. The result fits a suspicion I’ve had about Reese’s coverage for a long time: too many members of the media want her to be an elite player so badly that they oversell what she actually does. ESPN TURNS ANGEL REESE’S 49 ‘MEBOUNDS’ INTO PROOF THAT SHE’S A LEGENDARY WNBA REBOUNDER An award decided by sportswriters and broadcasters gives them something convenient to point to when anyone questions that assessment. "Of course she’s elite. Look at the award we gave her." Atlanta was already winning 30 games and playing elite defense The Dream finished 30-14 this season. They ranked third in defensive rating, allowing 103.5 points per 100 possessions. A very good season. But how much better did Atlanta get after adding Reese this past offseason? Last year, the Dream finished... 30-14. The exact same record as this season. Surely the team's defense improved by adding the Defensive Player of the Year, right? Well, not exactly. The Dream ranked second in defensive rating, allowing 98.9 points per 100 possessions in 2025. Atlanta already had one of the league’s best defenses before Reese arrived, and the team was actually a little worse defensively this year. That doesn’t mean Reese made Atlanta worse. Rosters change, opponents change and comparing defensive ratings across seasons requires accounting for many variables. But anyone selling her arrival as a dramatic transformation has to explain why the Dream finished with the same number of wins and a slightly worse defensive rating. Reese helped Atlanta allow a league-low 9.5 second-chance points per game, she averaged an impressive 1.8 steals and she led the league in defensive win shares. But she also joined a 30-win team that already played elite defense. A’ja Wilson deserved a lot more than four votes Wilson gives a defense options that Reese doesn’t provide at the same level. She can protect the basket, switch onto a guard and defend a possession that takes her well away from the paint. Against Indiana in August, Wilson guarded Caitlin Clark with the game on the line in overtime and forced the turnover that set up Chelsea Gray’s winning 3-pointer. Aces coach Becky Hammon said after the game: "I’ll take that matchup … any day." I don't think the Atlanta Dream want Reese trying to defend Clark on the perimeter with the game on the line. In fact, if that matchup happened, it would mean some very poor coaching and execution from the Dream. Reese’s activity around the basket is valuable, but Wilson’s ability to handle that assignment is a major reason she's the league's best defender. Wilson led the league in blocks for the fifth consecutive season, averaging 1.9 blocks per game, while Reese averaged just 0.7. Wilson actually averaged more defensive rebounds per game (7.5) than Reese (7.3), while adding 1.4 steals per game. ANGEL REESE’S LATEST WNBA CONTROVERSY SHOWS HOW VICTIMHOOD BECAME CENTRAL TO HER BRAND The defensive rebounding comparison tends to get lost amid the celebration of Reese’s rebounding records. Of her 521 rebounds this season, 206 came on offense. Those are valuable possessions to create, but they aren’t defensive stops and shouldn't factor into a Defensive Player of the Year conversation. And, of course, there are the "mebounds" Reese gets when she misses a layup and rebounds her own shot. Wilson has advanced statistics supporting her case, too. CBS Sports’ Jack Maloney explained that he voted for Reese while acknowledging that Wilson led the league in defensive VPM, an advanced metric estimating a player’s impact on preventing points. Gabby Williams had a serious argument, too. She regularly took the opponent’s toughest scoring assignment for Golden State’s top-ranked defense. The WNBA’s own awards preview cited Synergy tracking that placed her first in points allowed per possession across tracked play types. Some of the explanations sound a little too eager Consider how Swish Appeal’s Edwin Garcia, an official awards voter, described Reese’s defense. "At the rim, she was a black hole, devouring everything that even attempts to enter the paint," Garcia wrote. He also called her a "shoo-in" for the award. A player averaging fewer than one block per game was supposedly devouring everything near the basket. Protecting the rim involves more than blocking shots, but Garcia’s description makes Reese sound like an overwhelming shot-blocking force. She wasn’t. Garcia also leaned on Atlanta’s defensive on/off numbers, citing a 15.5-point difference with Reese off the floor. CBS Sports’ Jack Maloney used on/off figures, too, but he cited a 13-point gap in his explanation for choosing Reese. Atlanta’s own award announcement said 7.9. That’s an awful lot of confidence in a number that changes considerably depending on where it came from and when it was pulled. And it still measures the performance of five players together, not Reese’s individual defense. ANGEL REESE GOT A BARBIE DOLL, SIGNATURE SHOE AND WNBA THEME NIGHT, THEN PLAYED VICTIM AGAIN Hoops Junkie’s version raises another question. Its defensive on/off comparison puts Aces guard Jackie Young at 15.1 points and A’ja Wilson at 7.0, giving Young a much larger apparent impact on the Aces’ defense. Are we supposed to believe Young is more important to Las Vegas’ defense than Wilson? Watch the Aces play and try making that argument. Young is a good defender, but Wilson is the player protecting the basket, grabbing rebounds and handling assignments most centers couldn’t handle. A number that puts Young so far ahead of Wilson deserves some scrutiny before it becomes the deciding argument for a defensive award. The numbers don’t make Reese the obvious choice SB Nation voter Noa Dalzell cited opponents’ worse shooting numbers with Reese on the floor and wrote: "if Angel Reese is guarding you, your team starts missing shots." Except being on the floor and guarding the shooter are two different things. Reese gets credit in that comparison when a teammate forces a difficult shot or an opponent simply misses an open one. Translating the team’s shooting numbers into a claim about Reese personally shutting down opponents overstates what those numbers establish. Dalzell, like Maloney, acknowledged that Wilson led the league in DVPM and noted that Reese also trailed Gabby Williams and Aliyah Boston in that metric. Two voters openly noted an important individual defensive metric that favored Wilson but decided to push forward using team on/off figures. Unsurprisingly, they leaned more heavily on stats favoring Reese, even if those stats aren't the best barometer for defensive performance. Reese’s on/off advantage is fair game when making her Defensive Player of the Year case. But it doesn’t explain why Wilson barely registered in the voting, or why Williams received fewer than half as many votes as Reese. That’s been my issue with the coverage of Reese for a long time. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD She’s a very good player with limitations that too many people covering her seem determined to overlook. Now, a strong defensive season has become a runaway award victory, and the same media that handed her the trophy can point to it as proof that their assessment was right. It’s a vicious little cycle of self-validation. Reese deserved consideration. But 46 votes to Williams’ 20 and Wilson’s four looks like a media corps that was awfully eager to give itself something to celebrate.

title: Mamdani pledges millions to combat antisemitism while leaving key question unresolved
description: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's antisemitism task force boosts funding from $3 million to $29 million but refuses to adopt a formal definition of anti-Jewish hate.
content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced plans to combat antisemitism Tuesday afternoon despite leaving out a definition for what separates it from other forms of racial or religious prejudice. He also did not formally recognize the existence of Israel as he unveiled plans to create the Interagency Task Force to Combat Antisemitism. The plan’s announcement puts renewed scrutiny on Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, as he looks to undercut allegations that he lacks support for the Jewish community amid a rising number of hate crimes against the Jewish community. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS "My administration has a responsibility to ensure New York City remains a place where Jewish New Yorkers can live their lives peacefully and safely, where they can walk down the street, enter their houses of worship and build their lives knowing that this city will stand with them," Mamdani said in a strategy document. "But too many Jewish New Yorkers have told me that they are no longer certain that promise can be taken for granted." Antisemitic acts make up the greatest slice of the city’s tracking for hate crimes in 2026, accounting for roughly 9% of the picture, according to NYPD reporting. In the first eight months of 2026, the city has recorded a hate crime uptick of 16% over last year’s levels. Recorded hate crimes in the "homosexual" category, for instance, make up 29 incidents, and those against Muslims make up another 21. Hate crimes against Jews have reached 181. One hundred and thirty-one of those are felony offenses. DOMINICAN REPUBLIC JOINS GLOBAL FIGHT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM WITH LANDMARK MOVE The strategy document, which lays out a number of policy proposals, notes the numerous "useful" definitions for antisemitism that already exist but also stipulates that the Mamdani administration would not adopt any of them. "New York City can and will leverage all of the tools at its disposal to combat antisemitism effectively without needing to adopt a definition for this specific form of hate," the framework states. "Federal hate crimes statutes — which criminalize conduct motivated by bias against protected characteristics, such as race, national origin and religion — do not adopt a standalone definition of discrimination." In practical terms, the proposal outlines a substantial increase in its funding to combat hate crimes, a jump from $3 million to $29 million annually. It further creates cooperation pathways between the NYPD, the Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes and the Commission on Human Rights, among other agencies. It also designates $2 million for the Queens Holocaust memorial and $2.5 million for the Center for New Jewish Culture in Brooklyn. Mamdani framed the proposal as the beginning of larger efforts to ensure the safety of the Jewish community. "We will fight antisemitism with urgency and resolve. And we will do so in relentless solidarity with the many communities who also know what it means to be targeted, marginalized or made to question their safety," he said. "This Strategy is neither the beginning nor the end of this work. But it is an important milestone: a clear commitment from New York City government and a roadmap for the meaningful work ahead." However, the plan ignited backlash from Jewish New Yorkers. "I sat with the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism in July and told them what Jewish teachers and families need: a definition of the hate, an honest reckoning with anti-Zionism, and real security for synagogues and schools. What the mayor announced today does none of that," Moshe Spern, president of United Jewish Teachers, told the New York Post. "Quoting the Talmud while refusing to name Zionism and putting $1 million in security across every house of worship in New York City is not a strategy. It is a disappointment." ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Moshe Davis, the executive director of the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism, gave Mamdani some credit for using some of his proposals but said, "It seems to make a conscious effort to erase the connection between the violence against Jews we are seeing in our city and the anti-Israel propaganda clearly fueling it," according to the New York Post. "A report on antisemitism that ignores what is driving much of the hate and violence against Jews is tone-deaf and dangerous." Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

title: Kratom industry warns synthetic opioids should not be called 'kratom'
description: The American Kratom Association claims products found near two dead Ole Miss students were synthetic opioids, not natural kratom, amid pending toxicology.
content: Amid the ongoing investigation into the deaths of two Ole Miss students, representatives of the kratom industry are speaking out about how the product may have been mischaracterized. Court documents show that Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were discovered dead on Sept. 21 at separate locations. Initial reports stated that products described as "packaged kratom" or "synthetic kratom" were found near both students. In a Sept. 30 statement, however, investigators said only that "packaging associated with kratom-related products" had been recovered at both locations. WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS "During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations," Lafayette County Metro Narcotics, a department in the sheriff's office, said in the statement Wednesday. Toxicology results from the medical examiner are still pending. Packaging found near both students bears the name Modus, according to court documents. The affidavit describes the tablets as Smax Pseudo-DHM, and lists pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15(DHM) among the ingredients on the pack found near Hamilton. Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy at the American Kratom Association in Virginia, spoke with Fox News Digital Thursday about the initial reports of packaged kratom at the two locations where the students were discovered. OLE MISS NAMES STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS OFFICIAL ADDRESSES POTENTIAL FOR FOUL PLAY "We were deeply concerned with that characterization because it is highly unlikely, if not statistically improbable, that a natural kratom leaf product would be the cause of two deaths independently, let alone one," he said. After attempting to contact the Oxford Police Department, Haddow said the association held a news conference in Oxford asking for clarification on why officials would have disclosed a packaged kratom product. The clarification showed that the products recovered were "chemically manipulated opioids, not kratom," Haddow added. "We are grateful for the clarification because what they have told us and disclosed is that these, in fact, were highly synthetic and importantly controlled substances under the Federal Controlled Substances Act," he said. HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK "Those products never should have been on the market in the first place in those locations." The Mississippi Kratom Consumer Protection Act (KCPA) is a state law that regulates the sale of kratom rather than banning it. In 2012, the FDA issued an import alert on kratom products, and the DEA sought to temporarily classify kratom's primary alkaloids as Schedule I substances in 2016 before withdrawing the proposal following public comment. More recently, the agencies have raised concerns about concentrated and chemically modified kratom products, including those containing high levels of 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH). title: Virginia State University accused of suppressing Christian student ministries while Muslim groups are exempt
description: Alliance Defending Freedom sued Virginia State University over a policy allegedly forcing Christian student groups under a university-appointed minister.
content: Virginia State University (VSU) is facing a federal lawsuit from two Christian student organizations that say the school stripped them of their official campus status and placed them under the direct authority of a university-appointed minister. "Higher education has really broke from its long-standing desire to promote intellectual diversity and to actually seek truth, and, instead, they are essentially telling students that any disagreement, that certain speech is violence and that hearing difference of opinions on important topics is actually not encouraged. It's actually discouraged," Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF) Senior Counsel Tyson Langhofer told Fox News Digital. "I think that higher education is really failing in its primary role, which is to educate the next generation … how to deal with living in a pluralistic society with people who have different opinions." 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS Attorneys with ADF filed the lawsuit on behalf of campus chapters for Women of Victory and Bethel Campus Fellowship. The lawsuit challenges VSU’s updated Campus Ministries Policy, which plaintiffs argue violates the First Amendment by forcing Christian student groups under university control while granting exemptions to non-Christian religious groups. According to the policy, all Christian student-led ministries must operate under the "governance and influence" of VSU Campus Minister Thomas Wynn and an advisory board made up of faculty and university personnel. Additionally, the rule bans student ministries from affiliating with their national parent organizations. Langhofer told Fox News Digital the policy unconstitutionally penalizes Christian students for their religious beliefs. "The message that it would send is that the First Amendment means what it says: that you can't treat secular groups better than religious groups," Langhofer said. "You can't treat one religious group worse than another religious group, regardless of your motives. "It doesn't matter whether your motives are unity or things like that. You can't have one single campus pastor on campus that is able to control all Christian groups and then exclude the Muslim group and allow them to receive all of the benefits." GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS Non-Christian and Muslim student organizations remain exempt from the mandate, according to the legal filing. The lawsuit alleged that the policy targets Women of Victory and Bethel Campus Fellowship, both local chapters of national organizations that host Bible studies, leadership training and spiritual development events for students on and off campus. Although both groups remain listed on VSU’s official website, ADF representatives noted that the online directory does not reflect their current operational status on campus. The student organizations are seeking a court order restoring their status as fully recognized registered student organizations (RSOs). Langhofer pointed to "theological differences" between the campus pastor and the student organizations as a core issue created by the university's mandate. "I don't know whether that's the fruit of this or not," Langhofer said regarding the policy's origins. "What it ultimately comes down to is an attempt to control what these groups are doing by the university, rather than allowing these groups to continue to operate in the same fashion as they've operated for a long time." VERMONT PAYS $566K IN DAMAGES, LEGAL FEES TO CHRISTIAN SCHOOL IT BANNED FROM ALL SPORTS COMPETITIONS FOR YEARS He emphasized that decades of legal precedent prohibit public universities from targeting groups based on religious viewpoints. "The Supreme Court has held for a very long time that all student groups on campus must be treated equally, and you can't single some out simply because of what they believe," Langhofer told Fox News Digital. title: College football moves closer to 24-game playoff and the destruction of the best regular season in sports
description: The college football playoff expansion to 24 teams appears all but certain after key executives met this week, potentially reshaping the regular season.
content: For a sport that spent decades with effectively the same system, structure and configuration, the rate of change in modern college football is jaw-dropping. The first iteration of the College Football Playoff was in 2014, not too long ago, in the grand scheme of things. Four teams, picked by a selection committee, played two rounds to win a title. For a decade, despite a long list of controversial choices by that committee, it stayed at four teams. Then, the expansion. After a wave of criticism from Florida State's exclusion from the 2023 edition and administrators realizing that there was a massive reservoir of revenue available if the sport added playoff games, the sport moved to 12. Just a few years later, here we are and most of the major players involved seem set to blow tradition up further and move to a whopping 24 teams. Seriously. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The execs who control the playoff format met this week outside Chicago, with several new reports saying that the 24-team playoff is all but a done deal. "We've worked through a lot of the other issues associated with [a 24-team] expansion and those things needed to happen before we started any kind of negotiation [over money]," said executive director Rich Clark, per Yahoo!'s Ross Dellenger. There's a widespread assumption that the money will be there to make an expansion possible, whether that's with the current network, ESPN or another broadcast partner. And Clark seemed confident enough to publicly explain some details of how the new format would work. Eight first-round games would start two weeks after the end of the regular season, essentially one week after the current conference championship game window. This would eliminate conference championships, long viewed as a necessary consequence of further expansion. Second-round games, another eight, would follow in late December, "most likely" played at the home stadium of the lower seeded team. Similar to the current first-round format. Dellenger also quoted a "confident stakeholder," who is adamant that if the money materializes through a TV deal, "we are definitely going to 24." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE There are two ways to react to this news, but a few things seem certain about a 24-team field: traditional bowl games are all but dead, with reaching a 24-team field all that matters. The other? That the college football regular season, long the best in sports, will be irreparably changed. There’s no question that three-loss teams will be part of a 24-team playoff. It’s a near certainty that four-loss teams will be too. Those close losses between rivals or top programs that were once so meaningful will now just be another week in the schedule, particularly in the era of superconferences, where strength of schedule will guarantee spots for some three-loss teams and four-loss teams. There is another possibility, as unlikely as it is, that big teams are more willing to schedule each other in non-conference weeks, given that losses are less harmful on an overall resume. For example, when the Texas Longhorns lost to Ohio State in 2025 and missed the playoff, head coach Steve Sarkisian went ballistic. He called it a "disservice" to the sport, and ranted about the importance of schedules while threatening to reevaluate future matchups to give the Longhorns an easier path to the tournament. Obviously, he had a different tune after winning in 2026, but the underlying point he made still stands. Easier schedules means a greater likelihood of a 10-2 season and a playoff berth. But if three losses isn't a death sentence, are programs more likely to risk it with higher-profile matchups? Particularly with ratings on the decline thus far in 2026, as well as even traditional powerhouses like Penn State struggling to sell out their stadiums, teams could sell season ticket packages on the promise of seeing big games. Even if losing doesn't carry the same penalty as it used to. USC had ~50,000 fans at the San Jose State game in miserable weather at 12 p.m., but sold out against Oregon. With ever-increasing competition for entertainment dollars, rapidly growing ticket prices, and the ease of following and watching games on smartphones, the best way to keep fans in the building is giving them a reason to come in the first place. That said, even in a sport now infamous for quick cash grabs, this feels like the most blatant of them all. Conference championships and the bragging rights they bring are done. Revenue matters most, rather than competition or truly rewarding exceptional teams. Few fans, if any, have demanded or even wanted a 24-team playoff. But what fans prefer was already at the bottom of the list in terms of importance, and somehow it's sinking even lower. Get ready for 8-4 Missouri playing 8-4 Wisconsin in the first round of the playoff, coming soon to a television near you.

title: Le'Veon Bell accuses Pittsburgh Steelers of racial bias in comparing treatment of Black and White draftees
description: Le'Veon Bell claims the Pittsburgh Steelers don't pay their black draft picks while paying white ones, but the facts tell a very different story.
content: Le'Veon Bell is among the Pittsburgh Steelers most productive running backs of all time, joining a list that includes multiple Hall of Famers. But as an observer of how his former teams do business, Bell put himself in the Hall of Shame on Thursday. Bell, who played for the Steelers from 2013-17, saw his former team trade cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to the Dallas Cowboys overnight after a contract dispute and decided it was all about race. Because Porter is Black. No, seriously. JERRY JONES GOES ALL IN AS COWBOYS TRADE FOR STEELERS' JOEY PORTER JR IN HOPES OF SUPER BOWL PUSH "I wish Pittsburgh paid their black superstars they drafted just like they pay their white ones they draft," Bell posted on X on Thursday afternoon. " ... hate to see porter get traded .. I thought same thing with [George] pickens? TJ Watt is worth every penny tho, so let's not get it confused .. but something needs to change." Now, Bell has said some wild stuff in the past. But someone needs to jar Bell's memory and adjust his grasp of facts to get him off this race-baiting narrative. Bell, you see, is not an honest broker. He was drafted in the second round by the Steelers in 2013 and after three 1,000-yard-plus seasons, the Steelers tried to pay him. A lot. And that led to a contract dispute that ultimately ended his career in Pittsburgh. But before that happened, the Steelers offered to pay him $70 million on a five-year contract before the 2018 season. That offer from eight years ago, before the NFL salary cap jumped seven times, would be competitive with most running back contracts today. But Bell, who has admitted he came close to accepting the offer, ultimately turned it down based on his desire for greater guarantees. Those details aren't primary. What matters is that Bell lived through a negotiation where he, as a Black Steelers draft pick, was offered a lucrative contract by the Steelers. And still on Thursday he's saying the Steelers don't pay their Black draft picks like they do their White ones. The racist undertones of Bell's post also flies in the face of the fact that the Steelers, at the time of his offer, were coached by Mike Tomlin, who coached the team for 19 years until he stepped away this year. Mike Tomlin is Black. The team's general manager now is Omar Khan. He is a first-generation American of South Asian and Hispanic descent, with an Indian father and a Honduran mother. And those are the people who only want to pay White players? Pittsburgh's two-highest-paid players today are Watt and quarterback Aaron Rodgers. They are both White. But that has nothing to do with their pay because Watt is the team's best and most accomplished player and Rodgers is the quarterback who has earned the right to be highly-paid after winning four MVP awards ... and, did we mention he's the quarterback? But Pittsburgh's next seven highest-paid players are Black. And Pittsburgh's next nine of 10 highest-paid players are Black. The team has shown zero compunction about paying Black players. Receiver DK Metcalf got a big contract from the Steelers. He's Black. Defensive back Jalen Ramsey got a big contract extension from the Steelers. He's Black. Linebacker Patrick Queen got a big contract from the Steelers. He's Black. Receiver Michael Pittman has gotten two big contract extensions from the Steelers. He's Black. Someone challenged Bell about these facts beneath his post. And the former running back, who may be suffering from too many blows to the head, shot back that none of those players were drafted by the Steelers. Except, running back Jaylen Warren got a big contract from the Steelers, as did defensive lineman Keeanu Benton, as did tight end Darnell Washington. All were drafted by the Steelers. All are Black. All got paid. And then there's defensive lineman Cam Heyward. He was drafted by the team in 2011, so he was there when Bell was on the team. The Steelers renegotiated Heyward's rookie deal, rewarding him with more money before that initial contract expired. Then they paid him again in 2015, 2020, 2024 and before this season. Cam Heyward is Black. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

title: Sleeper Senate race emerges as unexpected headache for Republicans ahead of midterms
description: JD Vance rallied for Roger Marshall as the Kansas Senate race against Adam Hamilton tightens with Election Day political headwinds battering the GOP.
content: Republicans fully acknowledge they are facing political headwinds going into the midterm elections in November, and those winds are swirling in a race that has become quietly competitive as Election Day nears. Kansas has, for nearly a century, consistently elected Republicans to the Senate. But in a midterm election year when voters are unhappy with the Trump administration’s actions and its impact on the economy, the race between Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and megachurch Pastor Adam Hamilton has tightened more than some in the GOP would have liked. Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., the Senate GOP’s campaign chief, acknowledged that the race is close but remained confident Marshall would hold on. WOKE MEGACHURCH PASTOR, DEM NOMINEE CALLED ON CONGREGATION TO REPENT FOR DRIVING, EATING BEEF "Listen, I think if you look at Kansas, it's a very competitive state, more competitive than I'd like to see it. But the fact of the matter is that we're gonna win in Kansas," Scott said. Republicans are trying to maintain and expand their 53-seat majority but face many toss-up contests across the map and voters that are frustrated with high fuel prices, tariffs and the war in Iran, which could threaten that grip on power. Kansas isn’t in that toss-up category, but it was recently downgraded by "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican" by the Cook Political Report and in Fox News’ election power rankings. "No one should be surprised that Adam’s message of leading from the middle and working together is resonating across Kansas," Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton told Fox News Digital. KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’ "Roger Marshall has spent the past 18 months hiding from his constituents, voting to slash health care and supporting and endless war that’s led to skyrocketing gas and grocery prices," he continued. "Kansans are ready for something different, and that’s why we’ll vote to elect Adam in November." Still, Scott gave Marshall and others some advice that could be the recipe for success, even in close contests. "I told Roger Marshall the same thing I told all the candidates nearly two years ago: "You do one of two things. You either run afraid or you run unopposed,’" Scott said. "And, frankly, it's not unopposed. "And, therefore, you can't run to the tape. You have to run through the tape. I believe that Kansas is a competitive state," he continued. "I will, however, say that, as I look at all the data, it tells me that Roger Marshall will be successful." GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS He has already gotten reinforcements in the form of Vice President JD Vance, who earlier this month rallied for the lawmaker and pitched to voters that Marshall, a former obstetrician, was a man who devoted his life to delivering babies and making sure that moms and children from every walk of life were safe and had the healthcare that they need." "Let’s stand for Doc Marshall and send the crazy people packing, ladies and gentlemen," Vance said. He will get more backup soon, too. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital as he exited the Senate late Wednesday night he planned to travel to Kansas. When asked if Republicans would keep the majority, Thune said, "Of course we are." Marshall is eying a second term in the Senate against Hamilton, a political newcomer who was previously registered as a Republican now running a centrist-aligned campaign. Marshall was first elected to the upper chamber in 2020, cruising to an 11-point victory while Republicans across the country took hits as Trump’s first term came to an end. Since then, he has aligned himself with Trump as many Republicans did during their time in total control of Washington. But in recent weeks and months, Marshall has started to distance himself from the administration, like pushing for ICE to coordinate with local law enforcement as agents descended upon southern Kansas or vowing to fight for jobs at Bombardier, a Canadian aircraft maintenance center that employs nearly 1,500 Kansans as Trump’s trade wars ensues. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hamilton has his own headaches, too. Marshall has consistently painted Hamilton as a "woke" pastor who has delivered sermons to Kansas’ largest United Methodist congregation on Black Lives Matter and climate change, among others. "As voters continue to learn more about Democrat Adam Hamilton, they are realizing his views are just a carbon copy of every other woke liberal in Washington," Brent Robertson, a longtime senior advisor to Marshall, told Fox News Digital. "Voters are turning on this guy quicker than cider." During one sermon six years ago, Hamilton called on his congregation to repent for eating and producing beef. Notably, Kansas is the third-largest cattle producer in the country. "Some of the things that we grow, because we like to eat them, like cattle, end up producing more carbon dioxide than other crops that we could grow, other forms of food that we could have," Hamilton said. "And, so, in all of these ways, we are creating or adding to the amount of greenhouse gases in our world."

title: Norwegian soccer star files lawsuit against airline that photoshopped his hair onto an airplane
description: Manchester City's Erling Haaland sued Norwegian Air Shuttle over a since-deleted social media post featuring his signature ponytail hairdo on a plane.
content: Manchester City's Erling Haaland is one of the biggest soccer stars on the planet, and the Norwegian seems to want to make sure that no one capitalizes on that fame. And that includes taking his signature hairdo and slapping it on an airline. One Norwegian air carrier is reportedly learning that firsthand. SHOULD ERLING HAALAND GET HONORARY US CITIZENSHIP FOR CRUSHING TEE SHOTS OFF A BOAT AND BLASTING ELLA LANGLEY? According to Norwegian outlet VG, a lawsuit has been filed against Norwegian Air Shuttle ASA by Haaland and York Promotions Ltd. that has to do with a post the airline made on social media. The company posted a photo of one of their planes with Haaland's ponytail with shaved sides — which he recently cut — plopped on top and the caption, "We've never looked more Norwegian." POLICE SEIZE COCAINE BRICKS WITH STICKERS OF NORWEGIAN SOCCER STAR ERLING HAALAND ALL OVER THEM That post has since been deleted, but there's a hearing scheduled for October 9 in Oslo. "It is true that we have received a lawsuit that we do not understand," Norwegian press officer Eivind Hammer Myhre said. "We, like almost all of Norway, have been involved in cheering on the national team this summer through a few spontaneous posts based on trends in social media." This is interesting. I'm far from a trademark law expert — I dabble, though — but I could see this going either way. On one hand, I get wanting to protect your brand, and that extends to a signature hairdo like the one Haaland has become known for. Buuuuuut... Social media has made stuff like this so weird, because trends pop up, and then companies (for some reason, I kind of wish it would stop) feel the need to hop on board and toss up a hastily photoshopped image. title: Disney chief Dana Walden dodges when asked about Jimmy Kimmel's future as ABC's late-night host
description: Disney content chief Dana Walden refrained from commenting on Jimmy Kimmel's future at ABC during her appearance at Bloomberg Screentime 2026.
content: LOS ANGELES — A top Disney executive refrained from weighing in on Jimmy Kimmel's future at ABC as his role as a late-night host for the long term remains in question. Dana Walden, The Walt Disney Company's president and chief creative officer, appeared Thursday at the Bloomberg Screentime summit and was asked by Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw whether Kimmel will be hosting his late-night show "a year from now." "Well, I'm certainly not going to make that announcement with you here today," Walden awkwardly responded with a grin. CONAN O'BRIEN COMPARES DECLINING LATE-NIGHT TV LANDSCAPE TO DETROIT Shaw then asked why it isn't a "no-brainer" for Disney to keep Kimmel on air, pointing to a boost in ratings and his status as a "free speech hero" following his clashes with President Donald Trump and Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr. "The truth is, it's a very challenging day part, late night," Walden responded. "That's not to say that Jimmy is not doing a phenomenal job, and his ratings are up, but they're up relative to a smaller audience that's watching late night on broadcast television." "Obviously, there's a YouTube channel. Millions of people are watching On Demand, the parts of that show — that is not a lucrative opportunity for a very premium talk show. So we're trying to make sense of the business while also honoring a deep partnership," she continued. "I love Jimmy. We have a great friendship," Walden continued. "He's close to a number of the people at Disney. And again, we're trying to work through it and make sense of both what does Jimmy want, what's the right thing to do and what's right thing for our business." JIMMY KIMMEL RETURNS FROM LENGTHY HIATUS WITH DEFIANT MESSAGE TO FCC CHAIR BRENDAN CARR There has been unconfirmed speculation that the current season of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" will be its last and officially bow out in 2027. It would come following a tumultuous year for Kimmel, including when Disney briefly suspended his show in September 2025 after he sparked backlash for comments he made about the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk. He also clashed with the White House earlier this year after he joked that first lady Melania Trump had "a glow like an expectant widow." At the same event on Wednesday, comedian Conan O'Brien lamented the decline in the late-night TV landscape. "I saw over my 17 years with NBC ... I started to see, oh, this is really changing. This is really changing," O'Brien said. "They're asking us to be much more cost-conscious. And it was for a good reason, which is that, you know, HBO, Cinemax, these are the things [that] are coming up. There's more networks — instead of one late night show, 'The Tonight Show,' there's now 'Tonight Show' and there's David Letterman's show, then there are other shows." "It's a little like Detroit and automobiles," he added, referencing the decline in the U.S. auto industry as competition increased from Japan and Europe. CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS O'Brien spent decades on late-night television between his stints on NBC and TBS before transitioning into podcasts, now hosting "Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend." TBS ultimately scrapped its late-night programming in 2022 following the cancellation of "Full Frontal with Samantha Bee." Earlier this year, CBS pulled the plug on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert," replacing it with Byron Allen's syndicated comic talk show "Comics Unleashed." "The Late Show" reportedly was losing CBS $40 million a year and had been running on a whopping $100 million budget per season. title: Fox News Poll: Turek, Hinson in close Iowa Senate race
description: Josh Turek holds a slim edge over Ashley Hinson in Iowa's U.S. Senate race as cost of living dominates voter concerns and independents break heavily.
content: Economic concerns and party loyalty are key factors shaping Iowa’s U.S. Senate matchup. A Fox News statewide survey of Iowa likely voters finds Democrat Josh Turek with a two-point edge over Republican Ashley Hinson, 49% to 47%, well within the margin of error. Among registered voters, Turek is ahead by 4 points, 50% to 46%. That also falls within the range of sampling error and has been unchanged since June. The analysis below is based on likely voter results. Democrats are more unified behind state representative Turek (96%) than Republicans are of current Congresswoman Hinson (87%). Independents favor Turek by two-to-one, and 10% of Republicans back him. It’s Iowa’s partisan structure that keeps the race tight, as more voters identify as Republicans than Democrats. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS Iowa voters are split on control of the Senate: 49% prefer Democratic control and 48% favor Republican. With those numbers nearly matching the Senate matchup, both candidates are performing close to their party’s ceiling. Turek is preferred by 11 points among women, 16 points in the suburbs, 17 points among voters with a college degree, and 32 points among independents. Hinson is up by 7 points among men, 6 points among those without a college degree, 14 points among rural voters, and 41 points among White evangelical Christians. Economic pressure influences the contest. In the 2024 Fox News Voter Analysis, 3 in 10 Iowans described their families as falling behind financially. That share has risen to 4 in 10 today, and they back Turek by a 38-point margin. Meanwhile, those holding steady (45%) and getting ahead (13%) favor Hinson (by 14 and 53 points respectively). FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI'S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS In addition, 6 in 10 say the cost of living will be extremely important to their Senate vote decision. That outpaces other top issues, like President Donald Trump (43% extremely), immigration (39% extremely), and AI technology (27% extremely). Turek has the advantage among voters who say the cost of living, Trump, and AI technology are each extremely important to their vote, while voters prioritizing immigration favor Hinson. Trump won Iowa with nearly 56% of the vote in 2024. Today, that’s how many Iowa voters disapprove of his job performance as president (57%), while far fewer, 42%, approve. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE The president’s ratings are only part of Hinson’s challenge. While 42% view her positively, 50% have an unfavorable view, including nearly 4 in 10 who are "strongly" unfavorable. In contrast, Turek’s ratings are net positive: 48% favorable to 40% unfavorable (24% "strongly" unfavorable). By a 9-point margin, more voters are concerned Hinson is too close to Trump than are worried Turek’s views are too liberal (52% vs. 43%). Among those "extremely" concerned, that gap widens to 14 points: 36% say Hinson is too tied to Trump, while 22% say Turek is too liberal. More of Turek’s backers are certain of their choice: 88% are committed to him compared to 77% for Hinson. Twice as many Hinson supporters say they might change their mind (20% vs. 10%). "Recent history and the state’s partisan makeup suggest Hinson can pull this out," says GOP pollster Daron Shaw, who works on the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But the warning signs are clear: Iowa Republicans seem ambivalent, independents prefer Turek, and even her supporters say they aren’t sure." Iowa hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate in 18 years (when Sen. Tom Harkin won his final term), and it's been 20 years since they elected a Democrat as governor. In the Iowa governor’s contest, Democrat Rob Sand outperforms Republican Zach Lahn among likely voters by 53-44%. The race has been steady since June. Sand’s lead comes not only from getting the support of nearly all Democrats (97%), but also 14% of Republicans and 66% of independents (vs. 16% of independents for Lahn). Plus, 11% of voters backing Hinson for Senate switched parties to support Sand for governor. Conducted September 24-28, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,204 Iowa registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (183) and cellphones (733) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (288). Results based on the registered voter sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2.5 percentage points and for the subsample of 1,008 likely voters it is ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Likely voters are based on a probabilistic statistical model that relies on past vote history, interest in the current election, intention to vote, age, education, race, ethnicity, and marital status. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100. Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

title: Larry Fitzgerald Q&A: NFL icon talks breast cancer awareness for his late mother, friendship with John McCain
description: Larry Fitzgerald revealed how losing his mother to breast cancer in 2003 inspired the DraftKings Pink 'Em campaign, which has raised over $700,000.
content: Former Arizona Cardinals star Larry Fitzgerald has turned the personal pain of losing his mother to breast cancer into a mission to help families confronting the disease. Fitzgerald’s mother, Carol, died from breast cancer in 2003. His foundation has since partnered with DraftKings on its annual Pink ’Em campaign, which has raised more than $700,000 for breast cancer awareness, research and patient support since launching in 2019. Fitzgerald spoke with OutKick about the campaign, the influence of his mother, his friendship with the late Sen. John McCain, the relationships that defined his 17 seasons with the Cardinals and the current NFL season. Questions and answers have been shortened for brevity and focus. Q: Your foundation’s partnership with DraftKings through the Pink ’Em campaign has raised more than $700,000 for breast cancer awareness. What does that mean to you personally? Larry Fitzgerald: Well, it means a lot that you can raise this type of awareness together in a partnership. And I think that’s what makes partnerships so special, especially when you have one as longstanding as this. Every single year, obviously, we’re raising money for a wonderful cause, but also getting people on our platform to play in our Pink ’Em campaign. And it’s a win-win for everybody. We get to raise awareness, and it’s a beautiful thing. Q: When did you first become passionate about this cause? Fitzgerald: In 2003, I lost my mother to breast cancer. And so this has been something that’s near and dear to my heart. I have a couple other family members who’ve battled it. People in my organization at our foundation have done it as well. And so it’s something that I live with, I think about, I hear about often in terms of treatments and cutting-edge results that are happening from some of the life sciences that are occurring now. And so this is something, I live this every single day. Q: When you think back on your mother, what do you think she would think of where your career has gone and how you’ve created this foundation and championed this cause? Fitzgerald: My mom was in the nonprofit space. So I know that it would be something that she would be happy about. As a child, I was always going to events that she was either a part of, or she was a part of organizations that supported them. So it was always a part of the fabric of who we were as a family. My hope is that she would be proud of the work that we’re continuing to do. And I think she would want me to continue to stay motivated, to not take my foot off the gas and keep my focus on serving. Q: What’s the biggest thing your mother taught you while you were growing up that you’ve carried throughout your life? Fitzgerald: Well, just to be thoughtful and compassionate. There’s a lot of people out there that are in need. And sometimes somebody needs just a helping hand, a hello, a thank you, "How are you doing?" Just to be seen and thought about. Those things are really important. They were important to her. And I always saw that she would always do that. And it’s something that I tried to implement when I was a youngster and still to this day. SAM ACHO Q&A: FORMER NFL PLAYER AND ESPN ANALYST SPEAKS OUT ON CIVILITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN SPORTS AND MEDIA Q: How do you think that helped shape you during your football career? Fitzgerald: It’s something that I think is a part of you no matter what you do. It doesn’t matter if it’s in my current occupation or my former occupation. Being thoughtful, caring, really enjoying cultivating relationships and developing relationships is something that is important in anything that you do in life. It doesn’t matter if you’re on TV, if you’re a garbage man, if you’re a doctor. Having that human connectivity is important. Q: One of the friendships you made during your career that really stood out was with the late John McCain. Fitzgerald: Yeah, I mean, Senator McCain was a wonderful man and influence in my life. He’s one of the people that I credit with helping me mature and seeing the world in a different light. Traveling to Vietnam and doing a lot of his events with him opened my eyes and my world up to things I never would have thought I’d been exposed to. And so, really, really thankful and appreciative of the relationship that I’ve had with him and so many others. It doesn’t have to be one of the greatest U.S. senators and patriots that we’ve had in our country. It could be anybody that you meet in an elevator. That’s what I really enjoy about fostering relationships. Q: How did he help you change your worldview? Fitzgerald: Well, I mean, he just opened his world to me, showed me different things, gave me tours of the Senate, let me sit in hearings and confirmation hearings and things that I would have never experienced without him allowing me to be a part of it. And so I think that’s huge. It says a lot about who he is to take somebody in that didn’t necessarily have a view into that type of life. Q: Did you agree with Senator McCain politically? Fitzgerald: I don’t know if I would say I agree with everything Senator McCain — I don’t know if I agree with everything that any senator or politician believes in. I kind of have my own political views that I keep to myself. But I can attest to the quality of man that he was and the contributions that he made to our country. Q: What does it say about the connection you had that, even if you disagreed on some political views, you were still open to letting him help shape your worldview? Fitzgerald: Well, I think that’s something I talked about when he gave me one of the best honors of my life, to be able to speak at his funeral, is that he embraced the differences. And it would be really nice to be able to see that thoughtfulness in the way that our country is governed like it was when he was around. And so I’m very thankful that he poured into me and poured into so many of his other constituents. Q: Nowadays, there are a lot of people who don’t agree politically, including athletes and politicians. What do you think people could learn from your friendship with John McCain? Fitzgerald: I don’t know if I would say I did not agree with him politically. I did say I didn’t agree with everything politically. I really enjoyed my relationship with him. It would be nice to be able to see people have civil discourse without heartburn or hard feelings for somebody who doesn’t necessarily see eye to eye with them on something. So I think that’s something that we can all learn. I still look back at when he was running for president and somebody at one of his political rallies said something that wasn’t true about President Obama. And then he quickly debunked it. And that was a very powerful message, like, "Hey, he’s an opponent, an opponent that I really want to beat, but I’m not going to allow you to say things that are not true." And I think that was something that I really admired about him. Q: Do you see yourself cultivating any friendships with politicians nowadays? Fitzgerald: Yeah, I’m friendly with a lot of people. Friendly with people that are politicians. I’m friendly with people that are doctors. I’m friendly with people that are lawyers. I’m friendly with most people. Q: Another thing about you that fascinated a lot of people throughout your career is how loyal you stayed to the Arizona Cardinals. Looking back on it, what grounded you there and kept you in Arizona? Fitzgerald: Well, I’ve always been one of those people who likes to finish what they started. They brought me there to do a job, and I wanted to make sure I did the job that I was brought there to do. And a lot of times there’s other opportunities that might be more attractive, but I really like to kind of do the things that I want to do in the places that I’m at. And the grass is not always greener on the other side. Q: Were you ever tempted to consider an offer from another team? Fitzgerald: Not seriously. No, not seriously. No. Q: What was your best moment with the Cardinals? Fitzgerald: I mean, to take one moment from 17 years, I would say probably playing in a Super Bowl. But that’s not what I think about the most. I look back in those times, I think about the relationships with the coaches, support staff, my teammates, management, ownership. Those are the things that I think I take the most joy from. It’s just the wonderful people I was able to work with. Q: Who are some of the people specifically from the Cardinals whom you remember most fondly? Fitzgerald: Mark Dalton, Lisa Manning, Steve Ryan. Obviously, Michael Bidwill was — he gave me my job, he drafted me. Rod Graves, Dennis Green, Bruce Arians, Ken Whisenhunt and so many teammates as well. I mean, I could be here all day naming people who influenced my life in a positive way. Q: Bruce Arians is famous for having a personality that is a little different from other coaches, at least in terms of what fans and the media could see. In your experience, was he unique compared to the other coaches you played for? Fitzgerald: I wouldn’t say he was too much different than any other coaches. He never bit his tongue. He told you what he thought. I think that was really cool, to be able to have somebody that was so transparent. You never had to worry about or wonder what he was thinking. And that made it a lot easier to play for him. When you know exactly what the expectations are going to be every day. But all the coaches are different, and they’re effective in their own right. Q: What was your favorite memory with Coach Arians that people may not know about? Fitzgerald: I would say just seeing his heart. Him and his wife, Chris, were really big on adoption and foster parents. And I had no idea how many thousands of kids are in the foster care system in Arizona. And the work that he would do through his foundation would do a really good job of pairing foster parents with foster children, trying to give stability to so many of our young people that are in need. And so, seeing that human, compassionate side of him was something that really resonated with me. Q: Do you think he could make a coaching comeback today? Fitzgerald: I think so. If that was something he wanted to do and his wife allowed him to do it, I think he would be really good. I mean, he’s one of the best play-callers I’ve ever been around. He has a way to really connect with his players. And also, I think he really does a good job with quarterbacks. You look at what he did with Ben Roethlisberger, what he did with Andrew Luck, what he did with Carson Palmer and everywhere that he’s gone. Tom Brady won a championship down there in Tampa. He’s done a hell of a job every single stop he’s made. Q: The Cardinals have a big game this week against the Giants. Both teams are dealing with veteran backups. As someone who has played with a lot of veteran quarterbacks, sometimes backup quarterbacks, what do you expect from this game and the two teams moving forward as they navigate their quarterback situations? Fitzgerald: Yeah, the Giants have unfortunately got kind of bit with a rash of injuries. They lost Brian Burns, their best edge rusher, and then losing Jaxson Dart to a season injury. It’s a tough thing to deal with, but injuries are part of the game. I think the Cardinals are a much healthier, fresher team. They played their last two opponents in the Seahawks and the 49ers, who I think are both playoff teams, really, really hard. And so, I like their chances to be able to get a win this week in the Meadowlands. Q: Do you stay in touch with any of the players and coaches currently on the Cardinals? Do you ever give them advice or coaching? Fitzgerald: No, not advice. I’m not one to give unsolicited advice, but still have great relationships with a few of the players. I played with guys like Budda Baker, and so I have a really good relationship with guys on the squad still. Q: Who are your top five wide receivers in the NFL this year? Fitzgerald: It’s hard. I haven’t had a chance to watch every single team play. But they got some terrific play in the game right now. And even guys who you thought their skill set started to diminish, you watch guys like Davante Adams still had an amazing game last week against the Broncos, eight catches, 140 yards receiving. So, I mean, any given week, somebody can rise to the occasion and be special. Q: What about quarterbacks? Fitzgerald: Again, that’s tough, man. Obviously, Josh Allen’s coming off an MVP season and Patrick Mahomes coming off a knee injury and still looking just as good as he’s ever looked. And the throw that Lamar Jackson made last week to put his team in position against the Cowboys to get that game-winning field goal was great. You got to throw — let me think who else you put in that conversation. Joe Burrow’s looked really good statistically. He’s been throwing around and making a lot of plays. Bo Nix is playing good ball. So, I mean, there’s a lot of good players out there. Q: Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart looked very good in Week 1 before going down. What should fans expect from him when he returns from injury? Fitzgerald: Yeah, I mean, he’s really showed a lot of promise. I really like the way he leads. I enjoyed watching him at Ole Miss when he was down there. And then every single year, it looks like he’s just taking more steps in the right direction. So it sucks to see him go down the way he did and affect his team the way that that’s going to affect him. But I think he’s got a really, really bright future. And I think anybody who’s a Giants fan or football fan in general should be excited about it. Q: As a star wide receiver who played with many different quarterbacks, what kind of impact will Malik Nabers have to make for the Giants to have a good season? Fitzgerald: Well, Malik is coming off an injury himself, and so it’s really cool to be able to see him take that ownership and leadership position. He’s the best player on that offense now, and I think he can still go out there and win regardless. Jameis Winston is a veteran guy. He’s been in the league a really long time. And so, will there be a drop-off? Possibly. But I don’t think it will be one that would hurt him in a negative way. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. As someone who had a friendship with a politician, what was your reaction when you saw that? Fitzgerald: Yeah, I don’t know what his relationship was or is with President Trump. And I don’t know how that came about. But he made a decision that he felt was best for himself. And that’s what we all do as human beings. We make decisions based on the information that we have.
