title: College football ratings are down double digits so far this season
description: Ohio State vs. Texas drew 14 million viewers, down from 16.6 million last year, as college football viewership drops 11% through four weeks.
content: Overall viewership for the 2026 college football season is down 11% compared to the first four weeks of 2025. FBS broadcasts have averaged 1.7 million viewers this season, according to Nielsen data. By comparison, NFL ratings are essentially flat through three weeks. Some networks are up slightly, while others are down slightly. The league's decision to open on a Wednesday instead of a Thursday this season has also weighed on the overall average. So this isn't because of declining interest in football this season. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The reason for the decline in college football is less obvious than when sports viewership typically falls. Ratings drops are often tied to weaker matchups, political controversy, increased television competition, changes in measurement or shifts in network distribution. None of those explanations clearly apply to college football this season. Each of the first four weeks featured at least one marquee matchup: LSU vs. Clemson in Week 1, Ohio State vs. Texas in Week 2, LSU vs. Ole Miss in Week 3, and Texas vs. Tennessee in Week 4. Here are the 10 most-watched games of the 2026 season so far: The number for Ohio State vs. Texas is particularly notable. The same matchup drew 16.6 million viewers a year ago. Several factors may have contributed to the decline. Last season, the teams met in Week 1, when anticipation was arguably higher. There was also greater hype surrounding Arch Manning, and Ohio State entered the game as the defending national champion. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Just as important, last year's game kicked off at noon ET. This year's matchup didn't begin until 7:49 p.m. ET on ABC. Late kickoff times have become a trend this season. Because of multiple weather delays in Baton Rouge, ABC's Week 1 matchup between LSU and Clemson didn't begin until 9:40 p.m. ET. The delay almost certainly hurt the audience, with the game drawing fewer than 6 million viewers despite Lane Kiffin making his head coaching debut at LSU. Another possible factor is the expanded College Football Playoff. The 12-team format has reduced the consequences of early-season losses. Ohio State's defeat to Texas, for example, is unlikely to significantly damage its postseason chances. At 3-1, the Buckeyes are ranked No. 5 in the nation, ahead of several undefeated teams, including Indiana, Alabama and Florida. Longtime college football fans may also point to broader changes that have altered the sport's appeal, including conference realignment and the NIL era, which some believe has diminished the traditional connection between fans and players. Those factors are worth considering, though it's difficult to determine how much they have actually affected television viewership. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Whatever the explanation, expanding the playoff to 24 teams would hardly address the issues. If the double-digit decline persists, television executives and conference officials ought to take a closer look at why. The biggest matchup this weekend features No. 4 Ohio State against No. 14 Iowa on CBS at 3:30 p.m. ET. Ratings will also face stiffer competition as the MLB postseason continues.

title: Conan O'Brien compares declining late-night TV landscape to Detroit
description: Comedian Conan O'Brien compared late-night TV's decline to Detroit and discussed his transition into podcasts during an interview at Bloomberg Screentime.
content: LOS ANGELES — Veteran funnyman Conan O'Brien spoke in blunt terms about what he's observed in the late-night television landscape Wednesday, comparing its decline to Detroit. Speaking at Bloomberg Screentime 2026, O'Brien was asked by Bloomberg's Ashley Carman whether he believed late-night TV "made sense economically," prompting him to look back at the evolution of late-night from its origins. The former NBC host first pointed to how networks in the late 1940s would go off the air at 10:30 and just have the American flag and music playing overnight, until his ex-employer was the first to fill the empty airtime with more television. JIMMY KIMMEL ERUPTS OVER QUESTIONS ABOUT LATE-NIGHT TV'S RELEVANCE IN STAR-STUDDED 'LATE SHOW' EPISODE "And my analogy has always been, you own a nice house, kind of like 'It's a Wonderful Life' house, you fix it up, the kids live there, it's the nice old drafty Victorian, and then you realize, hey, there's an attic," O'Brien said. "What you do is you go up there, and you just put down some basic flooring and put some beds in there, and suddenly you have all this room you didn't know you had." "That's what networks did," he continued. "They found room that was not being used. NBC, in particular, capitalized on it. You have an early show, then you have Steve Allen, then Jack [Paar], then Johnny Carson, and you're off and running." He said late-night TV quickly became "a giant machine that fires out cash" and remained so when he began hosting "Late Night with Conan O'Brien" in 1993. "And then I saw over my 17 years with NBC ... I started to see, oh, this is really changing. This is really changing," O'Brien said. "They're asking us to be much more cost-conscious. And it was for a good reason, which is that HBO, Cinemax, these are the things [that] are coming up. There's more networks — instead of one late-night show, 'The Tonight Show,' there's now 'Tonight Show' and there's David Letterman's show, then there are other shows." COLBERT LASHES OUT AT CBS, SAYS CANCELLATION ‘REINFORCED A NARRATIVE’ OF ‘KNEE BENDING’ TO TRUMP "It's a little like Detroit and automobiles. Like, the things just started to change, and you can get really upset about it," he continued. "But then streamers come along. And then I'm not even mentioning the internet. For years, we were working really hard to do something innovative and creative at night. Now you're competing with how many people in America are posting videos every day, or worldwide. Hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of millions of people are making funny videos." "If you do the math, nine of them are going to be one of the funniest things you've ever seen. Those come out every day. That's what you're competing against." O'Brien spent decades on late-night television between his stints on NBC and TBS before transitioning into podcasts; he now hosts "Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend." TBS ultimately scrapped its late-night programming in 2022 following the cancellation of "Full Frontal with Samantha Bee." Earlier this year, CBS pulled the plug on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert," replacing it with Byron Allen's syndicated comic talk show "Comics Unleashed." "The Late Show" reportedly was losing CBS $40 million a year and had been running on a whopping $100 million budget per season. title: Judge permanently dismisses Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandalism case against former Olympian
description: Judge Todd Edelman's ruling prevents the Justice Department from refiling charges against Hearn, who was accused of damaging the pool’s peeling coating.
content: A judge on Thursday permanently dismissed the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandalism case against former Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of damaging the costly $14 million renovation project in June. D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman’s ruling marks the end of a monthslong legal battle that included President Donald Trump criticizing U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro after she moved to voluntarily dismiss the federal charges in late July. Unlike Pirro’s decision, Thursday’s ruling was made with prejudice, meaning the Department of Justice (DOJ) cannot refile the same charges against Hearn. Edelman rejected prosecutors’ request to preserve the possibility of recharging Hearn if new evidence surfaced, finding that existing investigative findings were sufficient to show the damage stemmed from a flawed renovation job. TRUMP SAYS HE 'DISAGREES 100%' WITH U.S. ATTORNEY JEANINE PIRRO OVER REFLECTING POOL CASE "In the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense," Edelman said. "This case must be dismissed with prejudice, and the government must thus be barred from reinstituting this charge against Mr. Hearn." Hearn’s counsel described the decision as a victory for "an innocent American seeking justice." "This case never should have been brought in the first place. This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American," Hearn’s counsel said in a statement. "This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted." Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment. WHITE HOUSE ASKS DOJ TO CONSIDER NEW PROSECUTION IN REFLECTING POOL CASE Hearn was arrested June 19 and later indicted on one felony count of destruction of property for allegedly damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s lining. Prosecutors alleged that Hearn was seen grabbing and tugging on a loose section of the pool’s coating, reportedly causing about $1,000 in damage. Officials added that he continued to do so even after National Park Service employees urged him to stop. TRUMP DOUBLES DOWN ON REFLECTING POOL VANDALISM ALLEGATIONS, CITES NEW WITNESS ACCOUNT Trump has strictly maintained that the pool was vandalized, criticizing Pirro’s decision to drop the case as "hastily made." "Anybody who thinks the Reflecting Pool wasn’t vandalized should go back to Law School!" Trump previously said in a post on Truth Social. "People were on their knees with their hands in the water at the exact location of the ‘slashes.’ Additionally, there were witnesses to the VANDALISM, and the flexible areas of the material were cut with a knife." The DOJ moved to dismiss the indictment after evidence from the Department of the Interior revealed that the damage was caused by a "rushed and botched" installation by contractor Atlantic Industrial Coatings ahead of the America 250 celebrations, court filings said. Hearn subsequently requested that the case be dismissed with prejudice, permanently barring the government from refiling the charges.

title: Amish face New York vaccine mandate in Supreme Court fight, might have to ‘pack their wagons’
description: First Liberty Institute is urging the Supreme Court to intervene as Amish families face crushing fines under New York's school vaccine mandate.
content: New York’s elimination of religious exemptions for school vaccine mandates is threatening to drive Amish families from the state, according to First Liberty Institute attorney Hiram Sasser, who is urging the Supreme Court to intervene in the ongoing legal battle. For decades, New York allowed religious exemptions for schoolchildren. But the state repealed that exemption in 2019, leaving Amish families and their small private schools facing vaccination requirements and potentially crippling fines. The 2nd Circuit upheld the law in June, and the Amish have since asked the Supreme Court to take up the case. "For decades, New York had a religious exemption for their vaccine mandate that they had on the books, and it protected the Amish who've been there for over 200 years," Sasser told Fox News Digital Wednesday. ‘COVID 2.0’: LAWMAKERS PUSH BACK ON SWEEPING HEALTH 'POLICE POWER' IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE "And it's just such a shame that New York is one of the only states in America that decided that they wanted to get rid of their vaccine religious exemption and to try to impose it on everybody, including private schools and, unfortunately, hitting the Amish who have their own ‘Little House on the Prairie’-style schools that they have on their farms," Sasser said. "And, for whatever reason, New York decided that they were going to start enforcing this requirement on the Amish who, frankly, just don't participate in these kinds of things. And instead of just leaving the Amish alone, New York decided to enforce it." Sasser said the state has put "crushing fines" on the Amish, which are endangering their farms and even the ability to stay in New York. CATHOLIC NUNS CARING FOR DYING PATIENTS FIGHT NEW YORK TRANS RULE, FACE JAIL TIME "We're representing the Amish, and I got to tell you, when they filed their declaration with the court, it was, it's handwritten because that's how they do it, and they work as a community together. … They want to be really good citizens. They want to do their part for the state of New York, for America," Sasser said. "They want to live quiet, humble lives, be good neighbors, but New York is putting them to a religious test that we should never put the Amish to." Sasser said the dispute is about more than vaccines and could determine whether the Amish can continue living out their faith and traditional way of life in New York. DOJ BACKS NUNS CARING FOR DYING CANCER PATIENTS IN FIGHT AGAINST NEW YORK TRANS IDEOLOGY MANDATE "These are the Amish schools like ‘Little House on the Prairie,’ if you've ever seen that show. It's like that, and they're carrying out a way of life that was, that predominated across America for a long time, but we've all sort of moved on with modern things. But they're holding the fort, so to speak, of a way of life that we all used to live," Sasser said. "I have no idea why the state of New York wants to go in there and shut them down," Sasser continued. "Frankly, the Amish would just like to be left alone, but they still really want to be positive members of the community. They want to serve their neighbors, they want to be good citizens, and New York just won't seem to let them do that unless they violate their religious beliefs." While we cannot comment on pending litigation, the department is committed to eliminating serious illness and unnecessary deaths caused by vaccine-preventable diseases. "The department continues to provide community outreach and education on the safety of immunizations. New York’s school immunization requirements are based in science and protect the health and well-being of all New Yorkers." Fox News Digital reached out to New York Gov. title: Marine turned homeschool mom sues Oregon district over denied reimbursement for Christian curriculum
description: Tessa Bulzan said Hillsboro School District approved her Christian curriculum academically but denied reimbursement over the author's biblical worldview.
content: A Marine veteran and mother of five is suing an Oregon school district, alleging officials denied reimbursement for academic curriculum solely because the books reflected a Christian worldview. She says the district initially approved her Christian curriculum as academically valid before denying reimbursement months later. "There was an incident where a teacher said something against our moral and biblical beliefs, and it was so convicting and, after a lot of prayer, my husband and I decided that I would quit my six-figure job and I would become a stay-at-home mother and start homeschooling our children," Bulzan told Fox News Digital on Wednesday. She said the family was encouraged to learn that the Christian curriculum they were already using, including Abeka and Classical Conversations, met the district’s academic requirements. "Then in January, when we went to go reimburse or seek reimbursement for that curriculum, we were denied solely on its author's biblical world beliefs," Bulzan said. Bulzan said she was shocked and devastated when her reimbursement request was denied because the family had planned to use the money for extracurricular activities and additional curriculum. WISCONSIN STUDENT ALLEGES SCHOOL BARRED HER FROM USING BIBLE VERSE AT GRADUATION She said she questioned an administrator about why the district would reject academically rigorous core materials, including a cursive book used to help her daughter, who has dyslexia. According to Bulzan, the administrator acknowledged that there was no comparable alternative at the same academic level but said the materials could not be funded because of the author’s biblical worldview, references to God and incidental Scripture. "One-hundred percent, it was discrimination," Bulzan said. "When I first started the program, I was told that all of my curriculum not only met the standards of the school board and the state of Oregon, but it excelled and went past most of their standards for all of their core." "So, math, arithmetic, writing, grammar, all of these books that I was using to satisfy their academic requirements were all being accepted and there was no argument, there was no denial of that," she continued. "When I was denied, I wanted to understand, is it just because it's the Bible or and my Christian beliefs, or is it because they just are trying to be neutral? They're trying to make sure that everybody has a fair play in the reimbursement process?" SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT Bulzan said that after some investigation on her part, she felt as if she was being singled out. "What I quickly realized is that that's not true, that they were singling me out as a Christian because I bought two different books with very, very secular and very opposing worldviews that I, in my opinion, should not be taught or be within the school district," she said. "One of them is of Indian or ancestral nature where they're worshiping water spirits, and they believe that as you drink water, these spirits become part of you," Bulzan added. "And so they're allowing other forms of worship for reimbursement, but they won't allow my grammar book because it references God." VERMONT PAYS $566K IN DAMAGES, LEGAL FEES TO CHRISTIAN SCHOOL IT BANNED FROM ALL SPORTS COMPETITIONS FOR YEARS In September, ADF attorneys filed suit against the Hillsboro School District in federal court. "We just filed this case in federal court in Oregon, so it's very early stages, but the case is really clear here," ADF attorney Kate Anderson told Fox News Digital. "This is religious discrimination, and it's discrimination that the Supreme Court and the Constitution does not stand for," she added. "Over the last decade, the Supreme Court has over and over again said that when a government sets out a public benefit program like this funding that can go to any person, it cannot exclude religious conduct, religious content." "In this case, it's religious curriculum," Anderson added. "Religious families need to be treated on equal footing with secular families and the same with their curriculum. title: Tennessee death row inmate survives 2 lethal injection doses in failed execution attempt
description: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike remained alive after two doses of a lethal injection drug, prompting Gov. Bill Lee to halt the state’s remaining execution this year and order an outside review
author_name: Landon Mion, Michael Ruiz, Brittany Miller
content: Tennessee officials were unable to execute death row inmate Christa Pike on Wednesday night after she remained alive following two doses of a lethal injection drug, according to court filings from her attorneys. The failed execution prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to halt the state’s remaining scheduled execution this year and order "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred." Pike was taken to a hospital by ambulance for treatment, her attorneys said. "Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective," Lee said in a statement. In what were expected to be her final words, Pike said she was "at peace." But the execution did not proceed as expected. Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head, asking prison officials whether her arm was supposed to feel that way. At 8:26 p.m. local time, witnesses said the executioners had "injected both syringes of lethal injection chemicals and Pike is still alive and snoring," her lawyers said in a federal court filing, according to The Associated Press. Pike’s attorneys said in emergency court filings that she "has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat," arguing that the attempted execution was causing "unnecessary agony." At 8:53 p.m., media witnesses were escorted from the area after Pike could still be heard snoring behind the closed curtain. The state’s protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. The protocol does not specify what should happen if the inmate remains alive after the second set. The Supreme Court granted Tennessee's application to vacate the stay issued Wednesday morning by the U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals, clearing the way for the state to carry out Pike's execution. In a 2-1 split decision, the Sixth Circuit issued a stay "until further notice" as the court weighed motions filed by Pike's attorneys and the Tennessee Attorney General's Office. The state immediately appealed to the Supreme Court, seeking to have the stay lifted. Justice Sonia Sotomayor dissented from the Supreme Court's decision, joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.Sotomayor argued that the Sixth Circuit should have been given time to consider Pike's pending legal challenge before the execution proceeded. Read the Court of Appeals order: "In capital cases, "[a]ppreciation of our own fallibility, and respect for the judgment of an appellate tribunal," demand caution before "acting irretrievably."" She added that the Supreme Court "chooses to overlook that principle precisely when it matters most." title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress dodged a fall shutdown, but the real fight looms

That epitomizes the customary fall tension in the halls of Congress when lawmakers are on the precipice of a shutdown. But this year is different. TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS No shutdown. That’s a good thing, considering last year’s 43-day shutdown odyssey which crawled from October 1 into mid-November. Everything is funded through December 11. So at least members and journalists can enjoy some of those autumnal fall trappings and dash to the pumpkin patch. That’s because we don’t know what’s going to await everyone for the next spending round in mid-December. Lawmakers are recovering from the battle scars of last fall. So with the midterms approaching, no one wanted to return to the 2025 contretemps. The sides are willing to tussle over spending. But only after the midterms. Does that mean a shutdown in December? Unclear. If Democrats seize control of the House or Senate — or both — that could compel House and Senate Republicans to fund the government the way they want through the fall of 2027 right away. They won’t want an interim spending bill which punts things into early next year when Democrats may have power. That said, if Democrats capture either the House or Senate, they will argue that the voters have spoken and it’s incumbent on them to decide how to spend taxpayer money next year. Under those scenarios, Democrats will push for a stopgap bill, hoping to tangle with President Trump in the early days of 2027. The only thing which is known is that President Trump will in fact still be in office come January. This scenario could spark a shut down next year – if not December. The reason? You still need 60 votes to clear a filibuster (and probably two) in the U.S. Senate. That means Republicans just can’t ram through whatever spending package they want. That may work in the House. And the GOP could even test the willingness of Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., to buck their party and assist passing a GOP-favored spending measure in the lame duck. FETTERMAN STRONGLY SUPPORTS THE FILIBUSTER AS TRUMP URGES SENATE REPUBLICANS TO SCRAP IT But in the Senate, Republicans will certainly need the cooperation of at least seven Democrats to help them hit the 60 vote threshold. Those Democrats won’t be anxious to assist unless they won the majority and think they can apply their stamp on federal spending in the first quarter of next year. This is the same problem which vexed the Senate during the shutdown of 2025. The House passed a partisan spending bill to re-up all current funding on an interim basis. But Senate Republicans could never break a filibuster to lug that spending package across the finish line. The same circumstances may be true in December. So could the 120th Congress begin in January with a shutdown? It’s happened before. In fact, under very similar circumstances. Democrats flipped control of the House during the 2018 midterms – two years into President Trump’s first term. But the President and outgoing House Speaker Paul Ryan, R-Wis., balked at a bipartisan spending package the Senate cleared just before Christmas that year. So the government closed. There was no way to resuscitate the Senate-approved package. So the 116th Congress began with a shutdown. It ran a then-record 35 days. A possible government shutdown over spending disputes frankly serves as a symptom for what could be ahead if voters flip either or both bodies of Congress. Democrats will convulse at spending plans made by Republicans and the President. Plus, House Democrats likely add several progressives and Democratic Socialists to their ranks in November in solidly blue districts. Granted, those left-wing politicians won’t take office until January. But House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., must court the support of candidates Melat Kiros in Colorado along with Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York to win the Speaker’s gavel. Any missteps by the Democratic brain trust in the lame duck could ignite an internecine firestorm – before Democrats potentially seize the majority in January. Republicans could face their own issues, too. SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS Some rank-and-file Republicans are ready to move on from House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA). Granted, it is said that Johnson is Speaker as long as President Trump wants him in the job. But what’s not clear is what happens if Republicans lose control of the House. Will the President and others support Johnson for Minority Leader? Does Johnson want that job? What happens to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA) and House Minority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn.? There are signals that House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, is interested in moving into leadership. Especially if the GOP loses the majority. Jordan is tight with President Trump. He lost a bid to become Speaker three years ago after Republicans unceremoniously ousted former Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif. If Republicans lose the majority, it’s not clear that some Republicans will back Johnson for the top GOP job in the House – regardless of what President Trump says. Some House Republicans will blame the President if the party loses the House. Especially since they believe he’s responsible for the toxic political climate they face right now. It’s unknown if a Republican party out of power might begin pushing back against President Trump, frustrated by the economy, tariffs, the price of gasoline and the war in Iran. Most GOPers have shown a reluctance to break with the President so far. But that could change if voters hand Congressional Republicans their head in the midterms. We haven’t even raised the question about the future of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. – although the New York Democrat insists he isn’t going anywhere. But questions would emerge if Democrats don’t flip the Senate, considering that progressives and younger activists want to move on from the 75-year-old Schumer. The same with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. President Trump and Thune have never been close. If Republicans lose the Senate, would the President use that as a reason to call for the removal of the South Dakota Republican? All of this will color those questions about spending bills, maybe renewing FISA – or even getting the House to sync up with the Senate on the college sports bill during the lame duck Congress. Summer collapsed into fall. Capitol Hill was bereft of the usual autumnal mayhem. So go pick out some pumpkins. Sip a cinnamon spice latte. Prepare for trick or treating. Fall is here. title: Make unknown callers explain why they're calling
description: iPhone, Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones now offer call screening that asks unknown callers to identify themselves before your phone rings.
content: You know the feeling. Your phone rings, you look down and see a number you do not recognize. Now you have to decide whether to answer or let it go to voicemail. That choice gets harder when you are expecting a call from a doctor, repair person or someone else who may not be in your contacts. Fortunately, your phone can now help figure out who is on the other end before you get involved. With iOS 27, your iPhone can ask an unknown caller for their name and why they are calling. Google Pixel phones have their own Call Screen feature. Compatible Samsung Galaxy phones can also use AI-powered call screening. Here is how each one works on the latest software. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com ANDROID FAKE CALL DETECTION WARNS YOU ABOUT SCAMS How to screen unknown callers on iPhone Apple's Call Screening feature can automatically answer calls from unknown numbers without interrupting you. The caller gets asked for their name and the reason for the call. After they respond, your iPhone rings and shows you what they said. That gives you a little more information before deciding whether to answer. How to turn on Call Screening on iPhone Once you turn it on, calls from unknown numbers are asked for more information before your iPhone rings. Apple also gives you two other options in the same section. Never turn Call Screening off. Silence sends calls from unsaved numbers directly to voicemail and keeps them in your Recents list. For many people, Ask Reason for Calling may offer a useful middle ground. You can still hear from someone important without immediately answering every unfamiliar number. You can filter suspected spam calls too While you are in the Phone settings, you can also review Apple's call filtering options. Go to Settings → Apps → Phone, then scroll to the call filtering section. Turning on Spam lets your carrier identify potential spam or fraud calls. Those calls can then be silenced, sent to voicemail and moved into the Spam list. You can also turn on Unknown Callers. That moves calls from unknown numbers out of your main Recents list and into a separate Unknown Callers list. FAKE VERIZON FRAUD CALL NEARLY STOLE HIS ACCOUNT How Samsung Galaxy screens unknown calls Samsung has also brought call screening to compatible Galaxy phones. Samsung says the feature is available on supported Galaxy phones running One UI 8.5 or later. However, feature availability can still vary by Galaxy model, carrier and region. Galaxy Call screening can answer the caller and ask why they are calling. You can then read the caller's response as a live transcription. How to turn on Call screening on Samsung Galaxy Samsung also lets you choose a transcription language and customize the assistant's voice. If you prefer to decide which calls get screened, you can do that manually. When an incoming call appears, tap Call assist, then tap Call screening. The AI assistant answers for you and asks the caller to state the purpose of the call. Their response then appears as text on your screen. If you do not see Call screening, check for the latest Galaxy software update. You should also make sure the Samsung Phone app is current. Some Galaxy models may not support the feature. How to screen unknown calls on a Google Pixel Google Pixel phones take a slightly different approach with Call Screen. The feature can answer certain calls for you and ask the caller why they are calling. Depending on your Pixel and settings, Google can also screen some calls automatically. How to turn on Call Screen on Pixel On newer Pixel phones, you may see Maximum protection, Medium protection and Basic protection. Medium protection is Google's recommended setting and screens suspicious calls while declining known spam. Maximum protection screens unknown numbers more aggressively, while Basic protection mainly declines known spam. You can still screen a call manually. When an unfamiliar number comes in, tap Screen call. Call Assist will ask who is calling and why while you watch the response appear as a live transcript. From there, you can answer the call, hang up or use one of the suggested responses. Why screening can beat automatically silencing every unknown caller Sending every unfamiliar number straight to voicemail certainly cuts down on interruptions. However, it can also send legitimate callers there. Maybe you are waiting for a medical office to call from a number you have never seen. Perhaps a service technician needs to reach you from a work phone. Call screening gives that person a chance to explain why they are trying to reach you. You can then make the call about whether to answer. There is also a security benefit. Scam callers often count on getting someone on the phone quickly. Screening puts another step between the caller and you. However, do not assume someone is legitimate simply because they answered the screening question. Scammers can still lie about who they are. Caller ID can also be spoofed. Do not let a convincing answer lower your guard Call screening gives you information. It does not verify someone's identity. If a caller claims to represent your bank or another company and suddenly asks for money or login information, end the call. The same advice applies if someone asks for a one-time security code. Instead, contact the organization yourself through its official app or website. For financial accounts, you can also use the phone number printed on your card or statement. This is especially important because phone scams continue to get more convincing. Scammers can spoof familiar numbers and create a sense of urgency to push you into acting quickly. Kurt's key takeaways I like the idea of making an unknown caller explain themselves before they get my attention. With iOS 27, iPhone owners can have unfamiliar callers provide a name and reason before the phone rings. Pixel owners can use Google's Call Screen, while compatible Galaxy phones offer their own call screening feature. For me, screening makes more sense than automatically silencing every unfamiliar number. There are plenty of legitimate reasons someone outside your contacts may need to reach you. Still, treat the screening response as information rather than proof. If the conversation turns to passwords, money or account access, hang up and contact the company yourself. Would you rather have your phone screen every unknown caller first, or do you still prefer sending unfamiliar numbers straight to voicemail? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. title: Joe Burrow's girlfriend shares cheating hot take, woman's sister hooked up with her date & regaining the spark
description: Olivia Ponton reveals on her podcast that cheating plagued all her past relationships, while Brooke Hogan opens up about Hulk Hogan's betrayal.
content: Welcome to the latest edition of True Romance. For whatever reason, this week we're being hit from all sorts of angles with tales of cheating. I don't know if that's the type of mood fall sets or what, but it's everywhere. I try my best to steer us back towards hope. I don't know that I'm successful. I take a deep dive into why it's time for a woman to forgive her sister for hooking up with a guy she went on a date with, and we bring the spark back before all is said and done this week. MAN IN TROUBLE FOR USING ROBOT VACUUM TO RECORD WIFE'S AFFAIR, FRIENDS WITH BENEFITS LEASE UP & HALL PASS WINS Is that enough? I can't say. I put it out there, hope for the best and let you decide. I don't look to the stars for answers. Unfortunately for Tom Brady, that's what Gisele Bundchen did, according to a new book about the legendary quarterback, reports Page Six. The stars allegedly told her they weren’t compatible. From one quarterback and model relationship to another. As far as we know, the stars haven't told Olivia Ponton that she and Joe Burrow aren't compatible. Although, she's had other relationships that didn’t work out. In fact, she revealed during a recent episode of her Booked, Blonde & Busy podcast that she had been cheated on in all of her past relationships. But she finally realized after the third time it happened that she wasn't the problem. Forget that common denominator nonsense. Ponton has it figured out. "I think cheating is a sign of insecurity," she said. "If you feel the need to be in a happy, healthy relationship with somebody, and go to get outside validation that you are attractive, that is not a reflection of this perfectly great person that could be in your life. That is a reflection on them. That’s my hot take." She's the perfectly great person that you're now missing out on. Well, not the Cincinnati Bengals quarterback. He presumably isn't seeking outside validation that he's attractive. Good for him. INNOCENT WRESTLING WITH SISTER OF WIFE'S BEST FRIEND REVEALS CHEATING WITH A TWIST, MCDONALD'S WEDDING & SIGNS Go follow True Romance on Twitter and Facebook and keep sending your emails here: sean.joseph@outkick.com (anonymously if you prefer). If you can believe it, Brooke Hogan says her dad sleeping with her friend changed their relationship I think you're just going to have to trust me on this one. Call me crazy, but I believe Brooke Hogan when she says her relationship with Hulk Hogan changed after she says he slept with her friend. She's a forgiving person, so that wasn’t the issue. She forgave her dad, but the relationship they had prior to him sleeping with one of her best friends was gone. How you ask? It's one of life's mysteries. "A major turning point came after he slept with my friend Christiane [Plante]," Brooke told Us Magazine. "I forgive people very easily — sometimes probably too easily — and I forgave him, but something between us changed afterward. I don’t think he ever related to me in quite the same way again." The Hulkster was known to run wild on occasion. This relationship with her friend might have been one of those times. But all wasn’t lost. Hooking up with her friend, her parent's divorce, and everything that went along with it, didn’t mean she didn’t still care for Hulk. "I can love my father profoundly and still tell the truth about where he hurt me," Brooke added. "I can acknowledge the wonderful things my family gave me while also acknowledging that eventually the dynamic became something I could no longer live inside. Both things can be true." Exactly. It's all about forgiveness. I think this is a lesson that a lot of us can learn from, including another of the stories we're going to get into. Woman's sister hooked up with a guy she went on a date with How long is too long to hold a grudge with your sister just because she slept with a guy that you went on a date with? A week? A month? A year? How about six years? This wasn’t a guy that she was in a serious relationship with. This was a guy she really liked is all. Yet she still hasn't gotten over it. "My sister and I lived together and I went on a date with a guy I really liked. I introduced them before he and I went out and I thought we had a great time. She wasn't home when I got back but we texted a little and I told her I had the best time, etc. She told me not to wait up for her so I didn't," she wrote on Reddit. "The next morning I was making breakfast when I heard her coming in and I saw my date from the day before with her. He ran away once he saw me but she couldn't hide what they did. She was giggling and it was clear she had been with someone. I made breakfast and then hid in my room from her for the rest of the day and texted my brothers." She's off to a decent start. She sees her sister coming in after a night out and her date is there. She knows by the look on her sister's face that they slept together and instead of a confrontation right there, she stuffs her feelings deep inside and hides out in her room. "When I was still avoiding her the next day she barged into my room and asked me what was wrong and why I was avoiding her and I broke down and told her she hurt me when she slept with my date. Her whole demeanor changed and it was like she had no idea that might have hurt my feelings," she continued. "She apologized but I didn't want to hear it and I told her to leave me alone. She asked me what she could do and she promised she'd never sleep with him again and she'd tell him to take me out again but that made it worse. I stayed a few more days but moved in with my brother when I realized I couldn't keep living with her and I didn't forgive her just because she said she was sorry." Since then, she's been "civil" with her sister, but they’re not hanging out or doing anything together. Those days are gone. Things came to a head recently when one of their brothers told the sister's boyfriend, who she was in a serious relationship with, about the incident. The sister thinks it's time to get over it. "She was upset with our brother but then she told me I needed to get over what she did because it was one stupid decision and she is too damn good of a sister to let one thing ruin us," she added. "She also defended what she did because she doesn't think what she did was bad, which honestly was what I suspected all along." The reason she suspected it all along is because that's the truth. This wasn’t a guy she was planning to marry. It was one date, and sure the timing wasn't great, but better to find out what this guy is all about immediately. She should be thanking her sister, not dragging this out for this long. Couples who have been together 10–20+ years: what brought the spark back? This one proves there's not a single way that couples who have put time in together keep the spark going or bring it back. You really have to find what works for you. I think that's the lesson here. There are things like losing weight and trying to stay healthy that work for some. Others point to communication. Hormones do the trick for couples too. title: Jayden Daniels does not dismiss playing Sunday against the Colts in London after ugly elbow dislocation injury
description: Jayden Daniels spoke to reporters in London and hinted he could return Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts after his elbow dislocation injury.
content: Jayden Daniels' journey through his elbow dislocation 11 days ago has been a rollercoaster ride, especially if you saw how the injury happened, and the concern that it ended his season prematurely. But we've reached the point where the Washington Commanders quarterback is talking to the media again and even suggesting he might play on Sunday. Daniels, in London with his teammates for the game against the Indianapolis Colts, faced reporters for the first time since his injury on Sept. 20 and was almost immediately asked if he could play this week. "It feels good," Daniels said of his left elbow, which was also dislocated last season. "Feels good to be back and, you know, taking it day by day." WASHINGTON COMMANDERS FACE SEASON-DEFINING CRISIS AS JAYDEN DANIELS SUFFERS ANOTHER SERIOUS ELBOW INJURY Daniels has practiced the past two days to varying degrees. Is he surprised that he's been able to get back on the field this soon? "What you think?" Daniels playfully responded to the question. "I'm not surprised. No, everything I went through, you know, everybody said, I'd be good to go if I'm able to go out there on Sunday, but again, just taking it day by day." So, um, the money question: Is he indeed playing on Sunday? Daniels smiled. " Just taking the day by day," he replied. COMMANDERS PLAYERS PUSH BACK ON THE NARRATIVE THEY DIDN'T CARE ABOUT JAYDEN DANIELS INJURY Looking for a no, in that response. Not there. In fact, a source close to Daniels told OutKick that while he is "not pushing coaches" to play on Sunday, that is exactly what he wants to do. But it's not ultimately his decision. Coach Dan Quinn on Wednesday said the team wants to gauge how Daniels looks in practices this week before making a final decision on whether to start backup Marcus Mariota or return Daniels to the lineup. "As we're working through the week, he'll get more [repetitions in practice]," Quinn said. "It's part of our return-to-play process where guys do individual, that kind of limited portion, then some of the team reps and then more. "As we get into Thursday and Friday, we'll see what that load looks like. And by Friday, we'll have a definite determination of where we're at." Looking for the part where Quinn says Daniels is out. Not there. It does not take Sherlock Holmes to figure out that while in London, the Commanders are sounding almost hopeful about their starting quarterback's status. And part of that is leaving the door ajar for his return this week. This is a bit surprising because in the days after the elbow injury, there was a real possibility Daniels could require surgery and be out the remainder of the season. Then Daniels met with multiple medical experts and decided wearing a brace, while affecting the functionality to his non-throwing arm, would be acceptable. His return to play is not a pain tolerance issue. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! So, Daniels decided to return – be that this week or the next, barring a setback. "I love football. I play football," Daniels said in explaining his reason for returning. "I mean, I get paid to play football, so, I went to my teammates and stuff like that to see that everybody's hurting. Something's wrong with everybody on this team. "So, I just feel like just for me, just being a leader, being a guy, just going out there and, give it my shot to go out there and play and obviously protect myself, you know, stuff like that. "But, you know, I just love football. I have a passion for it." FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

title: John Calipari shares boneheaded message about players earning more money than coaches while calling for reform
description: John Calipari says nine Arkansas basketball players earn more than his assistants, fueling the debate over NIL deals and athlete compensation.
content: It is undeniable that the current landscape in college athletics is completely broken. There are seemingly no rules, there are no leaders, and the exorbitant amount of money being distributed is entirely unsustainable. The Protect College Sports Act, recently passed in the Senate, could — emphasis on the word could — establish some form of ground rules when it comes to name, image, and likeness (NIL) deals, athlete compensation, eligibility, and the transfer portal, which has turned into the Wild Wild West. While everyone can agree that a uniform framework across collegiate sports is long overdue, what that framework entails for athlete compensation is where government officials, athletic directors, coaches, and athletes themselves will never agree. "The other three make more than all my staff, and we are not one of the highest payers." "All the coaches on this campus in every sport make less than the rev share, which is $22 million, and it's much less. So the players are getting more than the coaches; I just don't understand who could be against it," he continued, while referring to reform across collegiate sports. Calipari, who earns approximately $8 million per season, is by no means sharing an Earth-shattering discovery here about players earning more than staffers. However, specifically knowing exactly nine of his players earn more than his assistants and then sharing that exact number unprompted with reporters can only be perceived one way, and it's not positively. In Calipari's defense, he can not stand in front of the media and say, 'college athletes should be making less money than they are' despite the majority of the public agreeing that NIL deals have gotten way too hefty. title: WNBA reveals why A'ja Wilson was not ejected for approaching Fever fan during playoff game
description: Aces star A'ja Wilson avoided ejection against the Fever because officials ruled she stood in a player escape lane during the fan confrontation.
content: Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson wasn’t ejected for confronting an Indiana Fever fan during Game 2 of their WNBA first-round playoff series because officials determined she remained in an area beside the basket that they considered part of the court area, OutKick has learned. Following an in-game review during Tuesday’s Aces-Fever playoff game, officials concluded that Wilson was in a player escape lane adjacent to the basket stanchion. That determination was the basis for allowing the Las Vegas star to remain in the game, according to a league source. The WNBA also reviewed the incident and found that the fan had not violated its Fan Code of Conduct. OutKick asked the league whether Wilson would face additional discipline, including a fine or suspension, but did not receive an answer to that question before publication. The Athletic reported Thursday that Wilson would not face further league discipline and would be available for Game 3 against the Fever. PRIME VIDEO WNBA BROADCAST CREW EMBARRASSES ITSELF WITH COVERAGE OF A'JA WILSON FAN INCIDENT The explanation addresses a question OutKick raised with the league after the confrontation: Why wasn’t Wilson ejected under a rule requiring players to be removed for deliberately entering the stands? Rule 12A, Section V, subsection l(4) of the 2026 WNBA Official Rule Book requires an ejection for "Deliberately entering the stands other than as a continuance of play." The rulebook’s player conduct section also specifies where the stands begin. "The first row of seats is considered the beginning of the stands." Despite Wilson walking into an area where fans were seated, officials determined that she had remained in the court area. They classified the space she occupied as a player escape lane rather than part of the stands, according to the league source. Wilson received a technical foul for unsportsmanlike conduct following the fourth-quarter incident at Gainbridge Fieldhouse. She approached the fan near the baseline, and teammates intervened during the confrontation. Afterward, Wilson defended her reaction, saying she believed the fan had stepped toward her and pointed at her. "I don’t give a damn what you said. I don’t give a damn how you said it, the tone, that is unacceptable," Wilson said. She also apologized to her teammates for receiving the technical. The Fever had already determined that the spectator had not broken the arena’s rules. In a postgame statement, the team said security personnel had spoken with the fan and witnesses, found no code-of-conduct violation and considered the matter closed. There is an important distinction between additional discipline and the standard consequences of a technical foul. The rulebook provides for fines for unsportsmanlike technical fouls. It also gives the commissioner discretion to impose a fine or suspension regardless of whether a player was ejected. In other words, the game officials’ ruling on Wilson’s location did not prevent the league from imposing additional punishment. title: What to know about pentobarbital after death row inmate survives 2 lethal injection doses
description: A look at pentobarbital reveals why the barbiturate used in Christa Gail Pike's failed lethal injection may not have reached fatal concentrations.
content: A high-profile execution attempt in Nashville ended in chaos and raised urgent medical questions after Tennessee death row inmate Christa Gail Pike survived two separate doses of lethal pentobarbital, the Associated Press reported. Pentobarbital is a short-acting barbiturate, according to medical authorities at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Historically prescribed as a sedative, anti-seizure medication or sleep aid, pentobarbital enhances the activity of GABA, the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, slowing activity throughout the central nervous system. TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT In clinical medicine, pentobarbital has been used for several purposes, including: Because newer, safer drugs with lower risks of overdose have largely replaced barbiturates in hospital settings, pentobarbital is now rarely used in routine patient care. However, it remains a primary agent in veterinary euthanasia and lethal injection protocols across several U.S. states, according to the National Library of Medicine, FDA-approved veterinary drug labeling and the Death Penalty Information Center. How pentobarbital is used in lethal injections In a high-dose lethal injection protocol, pentobarbital is administered intravenously in large, ultra-lethal quantities — typically 2.5 to 5 grams (far exceeding clinical therapeutic doses). JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA'S NITROGEN GAS EXECUTION METHOD, RULES IT IS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY CRUEL When injected directly into a vein, the progression follows three stages, according to medical sources. What happened in the Christa Pike execution? Media witnesses observed her asking if her arm was supposed to feel that way (burning), breathing raggedly, and audibly snoring behind closed curtains over an hour-long span. The incident prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to halt all remaining executions in the state pending an independent investigation. title: France rocked by student riots as hundreds arrested, violence spreads nationwide
description: Violent student protests continue to spread across France, with school blockades, clashes with police and officials warning of outside agitators.
content: More than 625 people, mostly students, have been arrested over two days of violent protests near schools and universities across France over what students say are staffing shortages, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classes, government budget cuts and long schedules. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting Thursday, canceling ministers’ trips to focus on the protests, which began last week in Paris-region schools and have snowballed. EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT Reports say over 350 high schools and about 30 university campuses were affected by the movement on Thursday alone. RFI reported 83 police and gendarmes were wounded today, with 119 students and school staffers injured since the start of unrest last week. Reuters reported the principal of Marseille’s Victor Hugo high school was doused in gasoline and injured, while two other principals were injured in attacks in Rouen and Petit-Quevilly. Police used tear gas in several cities, with Reuters reporting students accusing authorities of heavy‑handed tactics. Meanwhile, authorities are warning of "urban violence" and attempted arson at multiple schools. The protests coincide with the government announcing a series of unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget two weeks ago and have become a political flashpoint at a ​sensitive moment for the French government. GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM LEAVES JEWISH COMMUNITY ISOLATED; RABBI SAYS WORLD AT 'A TIPPING POINT' Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told Reuters that, "in certain places, there were individuals acting as agitators — people who moved from one school to another to stir up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence." Education Minister Edouard Geffray called for schools to hold classes remotely if protesters were blocking their premises, posting on X: "Violence will not keep our students from their fundamental right to ​an education." Senior Envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies Simone Rodan-Benzaquen told Fox News Digital, "The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first. But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government." The Associated Press reported the protests are quickly blowing up as a hot topic in the election campaign to replace President Emmanuel Macron next May. Far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon has decried the government response to the protests as repressive. Critics have accused his party, La France Insoumise, (LFI), of seeking to use the unrest to score points in the presidential campaign and of inciting violence. GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS Rodan-Benzaquen says the LFI has "actively supported the mobilization. Activists circulate footage of clashes, party accounts amplify it and elected officials present themselves as the students’ defenders." With an election next year, she said, "Mélenchon sees these mobilizations as a way to consolidate young voters and marginalize the moderate left. At a time of deep political, geopolitical and economic challenges, this is a very dangerous situation for France." title: Supreme Court to scrutinize key pillar of Trump deportation machine in blockbuster case
description: The Supreme Court will hear a major case over whether certain immigrants held in ICE detention must receive bond hearings while awaiting deportation.
content: The Supreme Court agreed Thursday to hear a blockbuster challenge to ICE's mandatory detention policy after the Trump administration asked the justices to review the case. The outcome of this case will determine whether certain noncitizens held in immigration detention while awaiting deportation are entitled to bond hearings, an issue that has divided the federal appeals courts. Nine federal appeals courts have rejected the Trump administration's interpretation of the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act. The case now before the Supreme Court stems from a ruling by the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The 5th and 8th U.S. Circuits have taken the opposite view, ruling that the Trump administration may require the mandatory detention of certain noncitizens without offering them bond hearings. Barbosa da Cunha challenged the government's interpretation of federal immigration law, arguing his detention was governed by a different provision that permits immigration judges to hold bond hearings. The district court agreed, and the 2nd U.S. Circuit affirmed. The district court ruled Barbosa da Cunha was entitled to a bond hearing because his detention was governed by a different provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act. title: Netflix chief admits Trump is helping showbiz industry as federal tax credit bill aims to fuel Hollywood jobs
description: Ted Sarandos praised Donald Trump's push for a federal film tax credit, saying the president "really cares" about creating entertainment industry jobs in America.
content: LOS ANGELES — One of Hollywood's top executives offered praise for President Donald Trump as he rallied behind a proposed federal tax credit aimed to bringing back American jobs in the entertainment industry. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos was asked Wednesday by Bloomberg News' Lucas Shaw what his relationship with Trump is like as the two of them became more acquainted as the streaming giant pursued a buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery, ultimately losing to Paramount. "Well... for everything else you wanna think, he's a guy who really cares about the entertainment business," Sarandos said at the outlet's annual Bloomberg Screentime summit. "And he cares about protecting the industry and creating jobs. And he loves creating jobs in the entertainment business in America." TRUMP CALLS HOLLYWOOD A 'TOTAL DISASTER,' PUSHED FEDERAL TAX INCENTIVE FOR A FILM AFTER MEETING JON VOIGHT In August, Trump expressed support for the federal tax incentive to keep film and television productions within the U.S. versus overseas. Over the past several years, countries like the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada have lured major Hollywood projects using tax credits, and the result was that it could become less expensive to shoot a production across the ocean than to film on the backlot of a legacy studio. The proposed bill, formally introduced last week, has bipartisan support with Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C. and Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., co-sponsoring the legislation. TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS When asked whether he believed the bill will become law, Sarandos expressed some skepticism, citing "a couple of wild card things," such as the result of next month's midterms. "I think it's a bipartisan approach, which helps a lot. I think it's completely sound, and it has a working model that's proven, that you can put a dollar in and get six to nine dollars out, depending on how well you administer the incentive," Sarandos said. "The problem is, is you have, depending on what's going to happen in a couple of weeks, you've got a lame duck session, and if you have a change in control and who wants to champion what, who wants to give you a win. The win for America is if that — if we got it. That would be a win for the country." title: 10 Democrat-held House seats Republicans could flip to save their majority
description: President Donald Trump's margins in redrawn districts fuel Republican hopes of flipping 10 Democratic House seats in the battle for Congress.
content: The battle for control of Congress is entering its final sprint, with Republicans and Democrats just over a month away from learning who will wield power for the final two years of President Donald Trump's presidency. House Democrats lead House Republicans in the most recent Fox News Power Rankings, with the left projected to win 215 seats in the lower chamber compared to 201 for the GOP. But 19 seats are still ranked as toss-ups, meaning the final majority is still anyone's to claim. One issue that's given Republicans a glimmer of hope in an otherwise bleak cycle is the far-left insurgency that's gripped the Democratic Party. Several key victories by socialist candidates could threaten to push the party further left than most Americans are, a warning that GOP candidates across the country have shared. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME Below is a list of 10 House districts currently held by Democrats where Republicans could see key victories that help them retain control. Alabama's 2nd Congressional District Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., is running for re-election in a congressional district that's been redrawn to significantly favor Republicans. SUPREME COURT ALLOWS ALABAMA GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAP FOR MIDTERMS A 2023 Supreme Court decision ordered Alabama to create a second Black opportunity district ahead of the 2024 election, meaning Black voters there would have meaningful sway in the general election. The resulting boundaries helped Figures win his seat, which was previously held by Rep. Barry Moore, R-Ala., who ran in a neighboring district that cycle. But the Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais earlier this year significantly curbed the Voting Rights Act's enforcement of racial considerations in congressional maps, paving the way for southern states to alter district boundaries that were drawn to give minorities more representation. BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES That hit Figures particularly hard. The new district would have voted for President Donald Trump by roughly 14% in 2024, according to 270ToWin. Both Fox News Power Rankings and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report (CPR) rate it as "likely Republican." Florida's 9th Congressional District Florida lawmakers also altered their state's map ahead of November, aimed at giving Republicans a slight edge in the already-red state. Rep. Darren Soto, D-Fla., who is running for a sixth term representing his district, was one of the Democrats whose seat was hit the hardest. His newly redrawn district voted for Trump by nearly 18%, 270ToWin's analysis states. REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS Fox News Power Rankings rates it as "lean Republican" while CPR ranks the seat as a "likely" Republican pickup. Florida's 14th Congressional District The Tampa-area House seat held by Rep. Kathy Castor, D-Fla., was also among the blue seats redrawn by the Sunshine State's government to make it more competitive for Republicans. The longtime moderate Democrat has served in Congress since 2007 and represented her current district since 2013. She's facing off against a former Florida state lawmaker, Republican Mike Beltran, who also has name recognition in the area. Under its new lines, which remove more Democrat-leaning places around the city of St. Petersburg in favor of more rural and suburban areas in the south and east, Trump would have won the district by 10.5% in 2024, according to 270ToWin. Both Fox News Power Rankings and CPR rate it a "toss-up," meaning it's anyone's game. Florida's 22nd Congressional District Republicans redrew Florida's 22nd Congressional District in a way that could have pitted incumbent Reps. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., and Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla., against each other in a likely expensive and bruising primary. But both opted to run in other districts, leaving the seat currently occupied by retiring Rep. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., as a potential opportunity for both parties. Under Florida's new map, 270ToWin projects Trump would have won the district by roughly 10% in 2024. Democrat Pia Dandiya, a political newcomer, is running against Republican businessman and Marine Casey Askar. Both Fox News and CPR rank the district a "toss-up." Florida's 25th Congressional District Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., is running in Florida's 25th Congressional District after the GOP's aforementioned redistricting play, a seat that on paper was amended to give Republicans a slight edge. Redistricting shifted the seat from one that ex-Vice President Kamala Harris won by single digits to one that Trump would have won by nearly 10 points. Moskowitz has long touted his bipartisan work in Congress and as Florida's emergency management director under Gov. Ron DeSantis, giving Democrats some confidence that he could overcome the political shift in Republicans' favor. Fox News' latest projections have the seat leaning Democrat, while CPR ranks it a "toss-up." Louisiana’s 6th Congressional District Rep. Cleo Fields, D-La., is retiring at the end of this year, making his seat another open race. But the same 2023 and 2026 Supreme Court decisions that affected Figures in Alabama are at play in the Bayou State this year. After the most recent decision rolling back the Voting Rights Act, Republicans were able to redraw the 6th district in a way that diluted the Black population, who primarily voted Democrat in 2024, to factor in more red-leaning areas. Because of the Supreme Court’s ruling earlier this year, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry signed legislation delaying the state’s House primary races to Nov. 3 and the general election to Dec. 12. Both Fox News’ and CPR’s rankings project the seat to fall into Republican hands. Maine’s 2nd Congressional District The retirement of moderate Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, has opened up a rare opportunity for a GOP pickup in the American Northeast. Golden, who is known for frequently breaking from his own party on key issues like immigration and tariffs, represents a district that Trump won by 9% in 2024, according to 270ToWin. Republicans have a particularly strong candidate in that open race, former Gov. Paul LePage. Fox News rates the district a "toss-up," while CPR projects it as a likely Republican victory. North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District Perennial battleground Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., is facing one of his toughest re-election battles yet thanks to North Carolina also joining the nationwide redistricting fight ahead of November. Like Golden, Davis also won a district that went to Trump over Harris in 2024. But under the state’s new maps, Trump’s margin of victory in that state widened considerably — and with it, Republicans’ chances of winning. Davis is facing Republican Laurie Buckhout, who he defeated in 2024 by less than 2%. Fox News rates the district a "toss-up," while CPR’s rankings say it leans slightly for Republicans. Texas’ 35th Congressional District Lone Star State Republicans kicked off the nationwide redistricting fight ahead of the 2026 midterms with a map that was redrawn to win the GOP up to five more seats in November. Among those is a district currently represented by Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar, D-Texas. But Casar is now running in the nearby 37th Congressional District, leaving the 35th a wide-open race that both parties see opportunity in. Under the new boundaries, Trump would have won the district by roughly 10%, according to 270ToWin. A GOP victory there, however, will depend heavily on its considerable Hispanic population shifting to the right again this year. Both Fox News and CPR project the district leaning slightly in favor of Republicans. Ohio’s 9th Congressional District Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, is also running a tougher race this year thanks to her state’s new congressional map. Kaptur’s battleground district was shifted slightly to include more Republican-leaning areas, making an already difficult re-election bid even more of an uphill battle. Trump would have won the district by 10.5% under its new lines, according to 270ToWin. But Kaptur has survived several attempts at redistricting by Republicans since her first victory in 1982. She is the longest-serving woman in congressional history and the longest currently-serving House member from Ohio. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Both Fox News and CPR rated the district a "toss-up" in November. Fox News' Remy Numa contributed to this report.

title: Trump’s new high-tech government hub holds some bizarre surprises: ‘Enjoy finding them’
description: America.gov developers planted Easter eggs across Trump's new AI-powered site, including a Minecraft "End Poem" parody and a hot dog search bar.
content: Users digging into President Donald Trump’s new AI-powered America.gov discovered a series of hidden features embedded across the federal platform, including a "Minecraft"-inspired response and a search bar that transforms into a hot dog. The Trump administration unveiled the revamped America.gov on Tuesday, consolidating information from more than 29,000 government websites into a single AI- powered search platform. Some of the site's more unusual features quickly began circulating on social media, with users posting screenshots of AI responses and hidden interactive elements. Users who entered "Play Minecraft," for example, were met with a lengthy, surreal response appearing to be modeled by the video game’s "End Poem," swapping its original language for references to government bureaucracy, privacy and federal programs. TRUMP TO USHER IN ‘GOLDEN AGE’ OF AMERICAN TECH WITH DC BASH SHOWCASING POWERFUL NEW TOOL The "End Poem" is text written by Julian Gough that shows up as rolling credits when a user completes the video game. "This constituent dreamed of sunlight and trees. Of fire and water. It dreamed it created a small business. And it dreamed it destroyed a password. It dreamed it hunted a job, and was hunted by a recertification. It dreamed of shelter that would take a voucher," the response read in part when tested by Fox News Digital Wednesday. "Hah, the original interface. A million years old, and it still works. By Thursday, however, Fox News Digital could no longer trigger the response using the same prompt. "America.gov will continue to be updated to provide Americans the most accurate and reliable federal information and resources," a White House official told Fox News Digital Wednesday when asked about the unusual responses. National Design Studio (NDS) developers indicated that hidden surprises, such as a hot dog, were intentionally built into America.gov. "We put Easter eggs all over https://America.gov Enjoy finding them," wrote NDS team member Adam Bhaloo. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS In another scenario, typing "hotdog" transformed the chatbot’s input bar into a frankfurter when tested by Fox News Digital Thursday. "29,000 agencies. One glizzy," wrote one user who tested it out. "Apparently @POTUS loves hotdog. type hotdog in https://america.gov and you will see hotdog mode lol," said another user. "I went to https://america.gov and asked it ‘Is a hotdog considered a sandwich?’ and as I typed the word hotdog, the prompt turned into an actual hotdog," wrote one person. TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS If users type in Lincoln Memorial, Washington Monument, Jefferson Memorial, Statue of Liberty or Gateway Arch, the logo on the top left changes from an American flag to the monument prompted. Along with the logo change, the AI-powered platform sends visitation instructions. The website is expected to eventually let users complete government forms and track their progress through America.gov, with the administration planning to integrate additional federal services into the platform. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia, who helped create America.gov, said Tuesday that by 2027, citizens will be able to use the site to complete government forms and track the status of various applications. "Very soon, all she'll have to do is ask America.gov and it'll fill out the forms, track the progress and send her a new Social Security card, passport and insurance card in the mail," Trump said. "Whether you're a scout leader who wants to reserve a campsite at a national park, a senior citizen trying to choose a Medicare plan, or an American veteran trying to get the benefits that you've earned and so justly deserve, America.gov will be there to help," Trump added. title: Police near Ole Miss respond to suspected overdose, say 'not student-related'
