title: Hasan Piker speaks to UT Austin students after backlash from Texas lawmakers
description: Hasan Piker took the stage at UT Austin despite bipartisan backlash from Greg Abbott, Ted Cruz and others, drawing a packed venue of cheering students.
content: After much scrutiny, controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker spoke to students at the University of Texas in Austin. Sporting a Longhorn orange tie and pin, Piker began the stream in his hotel room and continued it backstage at UT Austin before he finally took the stage. On Sunday, the University Democrats said they were forced to "return tickets to thousands of students," claiming that UT Austin refused to give them a larger space and an off-campus venue decided it would not host the event after "internal discussions." The student group declared it would not cancel the event despite outside pressure to do so. Piker was welcomed into the event Wednesday evening with loud cheers and applause. The venue looked almost entirely filled. A UT Austin spokesperson later told Fox News Digital that there were 301 people at the event, including media and non-ticketed attendees. The spokesperson said the school estimated there were 50–60 non-ticketed attendees. Piker opened his speech with "Hook 'Em Horns," garnering another wave of cheers. The streamer went on to thank the students for attending the event despite the backlash it received. CONTROVERSIAL STREAMER HASAN PIKER'S LECTURE AXED BY UNIVERSITY OF WASHINGTON AMID FREE SPEECH QUESTIONS "There was supposed to be 3,000 people here today. Three thousand. It's a real testament to how much progress can be made in even a state like Texas that the people in the national Democratic Party have left behind," Piker told the crowd. "That's why I wanted to come here today, not just because of the pushback, not in spite of the pushback, but because I know for a fact that there are people who want their voices to be heard." At the top of his speech, Piker addressed allegations he hates the U.S., saying, "I always tell people that if I hated America, I'd be a Republican." He went on to accuse President Donald Trump of "destroying" the country. In his remarks, Piker focused much of his ire on Republicans, Trump, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Israel. The event was hosted by the University Democrats, a student group at UT Austin, and it drew backlash soon after it was announced. Ahead of the event, Texas lawmakers from both sides of the aisle, including Gov. Greg Abbott, Sen. Ted Cruz and Rep. Henry Cuellar condemned Piker's appearance in the Lone Star State. And Piker condemned all of them at the beginning of his remarks at the university. HASAN PIKER DOUBLES DOWN, DEFENDS HIS 'GOD-GIVEN RIGHT' TO SAY HOW MUCH HE HATES AMERICA Cuellar raised concerns on X about Jewish students at UT Austin being made to feel unsafe due to Piker's presence. The Twitch streamer approached their criticism by speaking about the First Amendment and the importance of freedom of speech. However, he argued that those on the left are not given the same freedom as their ideological counterparts on the right. Additionally, Andrew Mahaleris, press secretary for Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, also chimed in, telling Jewish News Syndicate (JNS), "Terrorist sympathizers have no place in Texas." In a statement provided to Fox News Digital Sept. 16, Cruz said the event was a statement about the status of the Democratic Party. "Hasan Piker is an America-hating Marxist who has said that America deserved 9/11 and celebrates political violence against Republicans," Cruz's statement said. "Americans are entitled to free speech, but it is incumbent upon good people to condemn Piker's incitement. Instead, some Democrats are bringing him to college campuses, while almost all other Democrats are conspicuously silent or worse. It says everything about the state of their party." In his criticism of the Texas lawmakers, Piker spoke about the First Amendment, claiming that those on the right are often given more freedom than those on the left. HASAN PIKER POINTS THE FINGER AT AIPAC AS DEMOCRATS SPEAK OUT AGAINST HIM "I want to talk about the hypocrisy of free speech," Piker said. "It seems to only go in one direction, right? You can't have an opinion that's outside of the permission structure, and the permission structure year over year seems to swing wide in the right direction." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Despite the bipartisan backlash, the event at UT Austin was relatively smooth and proceeded without any major disruptions. After his speech wrapped, Piker thanked the audience on his livestream and admitted that while he was apprehensive about being in Texas, the turnout proved the demand for progressive voices even in a red state.

title: Reparations advocates slam cash compensation ‘handout’ label, point to past government remedies
description: Reparations advocates demand direct cash payments to descendants of enslaved Americans, warning broader eligibility risks are diluting the movement.
content: Reparations advocates are insisting that the federal government provide direct cash payments to Black descendants of American slavery, warning that broadening the eligibility scope risks diluting the movement amid growing resistance from conservatives and the Trump administration. "Cash payments — that’s just a little solution to it, but it’s a big solution because without cash payments, there’s no reparations," Rev. Phyllis Coachman, a supporter of the U.S. Freedmen Project, told Fox News Digital. "[Slavery] ended in 1865, but so many other things happened after that," Coachman added. "After slavery, the collapse of Reconstruction. We had Jim Crow. We had legal segregation, disenfranchisement. We had lynching. "We had racial terror, destruction of Black property and communities, housing discrimination, redlining, discriminatory lending, barriers to wealth building …. the war on drugs and mass incarceration." CHAOS ERUPTS AT NY REPARATIONS HEARING AS ‘FOUNDATIONAL’ BLACK AMERICANS CLASH WITH LEFT-LEANING GROUPS The U.S. Freedmen Project, an organization representing self-identified "foundational Black Americans," works to educate the public on the distinctions between Black Americans who are direct descendants of enslaved persons in the U.S. and those who immigrated to the country voluntarily. According to its official website, the group is a nonpartisan organization seeking to fulfill the abandoned missions of the 19th-century Freedmen’s Bureau and the Freedmen’s Savings and Trust Company. Supporters argue that broader reparations bills risk violating constitutional principles, contending instead that state and federal officials must base eligibility criteria strictly on lineage. The debate comes as several state and local governments explore reparations initiatives intended to compensate Black residents for historic racial injustice. Evanston, Illinois, a Chicago suburb, became the first U.S. city to offer direct remedies, providing up to $25,000 in homeownership grants and cash payments to eligible Black residents to address legacy housing discrimination. Reparations advocate Annette Wilcox pushed back against critics who frame direct monetary payouts as government handouts, arguing the term is used selectively to delegitimize Black claims. "My thoughts about people who say cash payments are handouts is this is a government that has given trillions of dollars to all sorts of people as reparations," Wilcox told Fox News Digital. "We have reparations for 9/11. We've had — even things that aren't reparations after the crash and the Depression, there was an estimated $5 trillion in programs, money and remedies given to people — 90% went to White people at that time. So, handouts are, you know, just, frankly, an insult that people give to Black people. "The government has a responsibility for what it did to the citizens — the Black people who were enslaved in this country — and it needs to own up to it just like it owned up to what it did to the Native Americans, the Japanese and many other groups that it has given reparations to." SOME BLACK NEW YORKERS DEMAND CASH PAYMENTS AS ONLY 'TRUE' FORM OF JUSTICE Fox News Digital previously attended a public hearing hosted by the New York State Community Commission on Reparations Remedies at Hempstead High School on Long Island. During the hearing, residents warned panel officials that expanding the definition of reparations to include recent immigrants or other marginalized groups risks co-opting the movement. The New York commission was established after Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation in December 2023 creating a state panel to examine the legacy of slavery in New York and evaluate potential remedies. Among those who testified in Long Island, U.S. Freedmen movement supporter Aubrey Muhammad called for an explicit payout amount of $800,000 per eligible individual. "We need $800,000 for each foundational Black American. That's simple," Muhammad told Fox News Digital. "In New York, that's about the cost of living that'll get you a home, a small business, or help you recover from financial duress." CHICAGO SUBURB LOCALS HOPE REPARATIONS ADDRESSES 'AFFORDABILITY PRESSURES' AS BLACK POPULATION DWINDLES However, Devine Prince, president of the U.S. Freedmen Project, noted that such figures reflect broader efforts to address the national wealth gap rather than standard baseline figures. Still, Prince maintained that direct compensation remains non-negotiable. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If you count yourself as a true American, then there should be no pushback and no rebuttals for direct monetary compensation for the harm that was done," Prince said. "That needs to be repaired through direct monetary compensation to American freedmen."

NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK California’s latest official assessment results lend context to Shaw’s criticism of Los Angeles Unified’s academic performance. That meant roughly 53.5% did not meet the ELA standard and 63.2% did not meet the math standard. Shaw said the criticism described in the video would not change her approach to the statewide race. title: ‘We beat Disney, Fauci, Soros’: Ron DeSantis unleashes ‘Florida model’ in hard-hitting midterm rally
description: Ron DeSantis headlined a rally for Navy veteran Dan Green, a GOP candidate in Florida's 9th district seeking to oust incumbent Darren Soto
content: Pitching his administration’s conservative record as a national blueprint for Capitol Hill, Gov. Ron DeSantis rallied Republicans in Osceola County Tuesday night, portraying Navy veteran Dan Green’s bid for Florida’s 9th Congressional District as part of a broader push to bring aggressive Florida-style governance to Washington. Speaking before a crowd in St. Cloud, south of Orlando, DeSantis pointed to his administration's high-profile battles on education policy, state spending reductions and corporate pushback and urged voters to bring that same combative, policy-driven mandate to the halls of Congress. SOCIAL MEDIA ERUPTS AFTER DESANTIS GIVES ‘SOROS’ PROTESTER A PIECE OF HIS MIND: ‘AIN’T MY FIRST RODEO’ "I will say that I'm looking forward to y'all getting the congressman elected that has served this country and that has served for the right reasons. Now, I am a big believer that we need term limits for members of Congress. But until we do that, you can show your current guy the term limit by kicking him out of office. "So, I think what we need is what we've done in Florida. It can be a model for people like Dan going to Washington, other states, you name it, because it's not just about peacocking and putting social media press releases out and never getting anything done. We have fought every big fight that there has been to fight in the state of Florida, and we have won every big fight that there is to fight in Florida." DeSantis rallied the conservative faithful with a recap, alleging major victories over left-wing institutions, agencies and agendas. "Just think about it. We beat Dr. Fauci on COVID. We beat Disney on gender ideology. We beat Soros on crime by removing two of his prosecutors. We beat Martha's Vineyard on illegal immigration. "We just beat the Muslim Brotherhood by banning Sharia law. We beat the teachers unions by enacting universal school choice for all Florida families. We beat SEIU by doing paycheck protection. "Every single time there was a fight, we would beat and win the fights. And that's ultimately what it's all about. Because leadership — when it's popular, when it's easy — anyone can do that. 'I'll just go with the flow,' all this other stuff. It really matters when it is tough and when you're going to face arrows." TRUMP'S HANDPICKED DESANTIS SUCCESSOR WINS CROWDED GOP PRIMARY FOR FLORIDA GOVERNOR DeSantis repeatedly emphasized that his top priority was sticking to the courage of his convictions, not seeking political expediency or going along to get along. "I remember during COVID, I was doing things, and people said, 'Oh, he's not shutting down the beaches. Why does he have these people in school?' And all this other stuff. You know, people come after you, and a lot of people told me that I was frittering away my governorship, that I wouldn't be able to win in '22, and all this other stuff. I don't know if that was true. Who knows, right? "But when you get in a position to lead, you either do it or you should just sit down. My job was not to be worried about my own political hide. My job was to be worried about protecting the liberty, jobs, and businesses of the people I was elected to serve. So, we started the fire, and we gave them his right." It is clear that the two-term governor considers his famed battle with Disney to be a particular feather in his cap. "Nobody in the history of the state had ever taken on Disney in anything. A lot of people told me I was making a mistake," DeSantis said. "But the reality is, do we want a society in which our 6-year-olds are being told they can change genders, or do we want a society rooted in truth? If you want a society rooted in truth, even if the biggest, most powerful corporation in the state is against you, you've got to stand up and you've got to fight. And we fought, and we won." As the federal debt has topped a staggering $40 trillion, DeSantis made the case that he has taken the state on a markedly divergent course. "Just look at the results. For four straight years, Florida has reduced its budget. Is any other state in the country reducing spending? We've done it four years in a row," DeSantis said. "I was just able to announce today if you take all of Florida's debt for all of our history up until the time I became governor, just in my tenure, we will retire 54% of the state's debt, more than cutting it in half. "We've been ranked No. 1 for education freedom, and our public university system is ranked No. 1. We have the lowest in-state tuition of any state in the United States, and it's the exact same cost today to students and families that it was the day I took office. "It did not go up one penny under my tenure. Is there anything else that didn't go up? The dollar menu at McDonald's is all $2.99 now. Everything else has gone up, but that has not gone up." And DeSantis touts Florida as a national leader in lowering taxes for its citizens and called for voters to back Amendment 3 in Florida, which would pave the way for elimination of non-school property taxes. "If you look at tax relief, we've done $10 billion over my tenure — more than anyone. Some of it is permanent, like no tax on baby items, back-to-school items and no tax on business rent. But, really, the big enchilada is going to be on the ballot in November when you have a chance on Amendment 3 to vote yourself more control over your own home and not let them tax you to death. So vote yes on 3. As Republicans face headwinds heading into the midterms in a little over a month, DeSantis drew a parallel between this year's election, and the 2018 election, which propelled him to the governor's mansion by a narrow margin. "We've done all this stuff, but I think the lesson is this: When I won eight years ago, it was kind of similar to how it is now. People were saying it was a ‘blue year.’ There was a lot of wind in the face of Republican candidates," DeSantis recalled. "A lot of people thought Florida was a swing state — that we were purple — where one point had decided all these races for the previous decade. A lot of people didn't think I could even win given those circumstances. And even if I won, they said, 'Well, the state's going to go blue. You've got all these people moving from Puerto Rico, the Northeast, anything.' So, I'm running. It wasn't easy, and we won." DeSantis maintains he has never taken a poll as a means to determine a position on an issue. Or do I say, 'You know what? I won the election. I got 100% of the executive power, and I didn't get elected to follow. I got elected to lead,'" DeSantis said. title: Fetal tissue supplier billed $765 procurement fee per organ, warns records could imply illegal sales: records
description: Records obtained by David Daleiden’s Center for Medical Progress show UCLA purchase orders tied $765 procurement service fees to individual liver and thymus specimens
content: FIRST ON FOX: Newly obtained public records show Cercle Allocation Services billed a UCLA research operation a $765 procurement service fee tied to each individual liver and thymus specimen, while warning in internal correspondence that certain billing language could improperly imply the tissue itself was being sold. The records, obtained from UCLA through a California Public Records Act request made on behalf of Center for Medical Progress founder David Daleiden, include purchase orders and correspondence between the university and Cercle Allocation Services. An internal UCLA order form identifies the purchasing operation as part of the David Geffen School of Medicine’s Division of Hematology-Oncology and references the "Mouse Core." UCLA redacted the names and other identifying information of researchers from the record. The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that UCLA or its researchers, procurement personnel or other employees engaged in illegal or unethical conduct with the transactions. 'DRUG-DEALING' NETWORK SHIELDED BY BLUE STATES TARGETED IN SCOTUS CHALLENGE One UCLA purchase order lists seven individually numbered liver and thymus specimens at a $765 unit amount apiece, totaling $5,355. Another lists five specimens from Aug. 18, 2023, each carrying the same $765 amount, for a total of $3,825. Additional purchase orders reflect the same per-specimen amount. Cercle objected to the purchase orders’ tax treatment and asked UCLA to reissue them, telling the university that the charges reflected procurement services and that sales tax should not be applied. Cercle said tax language could improperly imply that the specimens themselves were being sold. Cercle does supply human fetal tissue for biomedical research. Peer-reviewed scientific literature has identified the company as the source of human fetal liver tissue used by researchers, providing independent evidence of the type of procurement business described by CMP. SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY SLAPS DOWN BLUE STATE TARGETING PRO-LIFE GROUP CMP identified the liver and thymus specimens in the UCLA purchase orders as fetal tissue. Fox News Digital has not independently verified that the tissue associated with these specific purchase orders was fetal. The purchase orders identify the organs by type, sample number and date but do not describe them as fetal. The records do not establish that the payments were illegal. Cercle characterized the money as fees for procurement services rather than payments for the tissue itself. But correspondence shows the company was particularly concerned about how those payments were described. "The overriding issue is the use of terminology that we must not use due to their improper implication that we are selling taxable items, which we are not," a Cercle accounts manager wrote in September 2023. "Due to the nature of our business, we must be very careful and clear that we invoice fees for our procurement services." The same email said notations referring to sales tax would imply Cercle was "selling the items received," which the company said were "illegal to sell." Cercle instead instructed UCLA that purchase orders should authorize payment for its services while tying individual sample numbers and dates to a unit amount of $765. The correspondence shows UCLA subsequently prepared revised purchase orders after Cercle objected to the tax language. One Cercle email said a July invoice totaling $5,355 for procurements on three dates had already been "processed and paid." The company also asked UCLA to replace other purchase orders containing tax language, including one covering five procurements from Aug. 18 worth a combined $3,825. Federal law prohibits knowingly acquiring, receiving or otherwise transferring human fetal tissue for "valuable consideration," if the transfer affects interstate commerce, while allowing "reasonable payments" associated with transportation, implantation, processing, preservation, quality control or storage. The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that Cercle or UCLA violated that prohibition. Daleiden contends the documents raise questions about whether the uniform $765 charges represented permissible reimbursement for procurement-related costs. HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS He pointed to the uniform $765 amount UCLA assigned to individual specimens on the purchase orders, including multiple organs listed on the same date. Daleiden told Fox News Digital he believes the structure raises questions about whether the payments reflected the procurement-related costs permitted under federal law. Documents reviewed by Fox News Digital do not contain Cercle’s invoices or underlying cost calculations and do not establish whether the $765 amount exceeded reasonable procurement-related expenses. Daleiden also said UCLA did not produce Cercle’s invoices in response to the public records request. The May 2025 request sought the original and most recent materials associated with UCLA IRB No. 11-002504 and records and communications from 2023 forward between the authors of a specified UCLA study and Advanced Bioscience Resources or Cercle. The request covered records, including emails, text messages, notes and fetal tissue logs. UCLA later said its departments had completed their search and that the September 2026 production represented the final batch of non-exempt responsive records. The university said it redacted certain researcher identities because of concerns about threats and harassment involving sensitive research. title: Gavin Newsom seeks counsel from ‘master’ Bill Clinton as he plots Project 2029

I’ve been a student of his from day one," he told the outlet. Newsom said the relationship extends beyond admiration from afar, revealing that he and Clinton frequently speak late at night about policy, political strategy and how to address California's challenges. "He calls me late at night, wanting to talk about it, and he goes, ‘I’ve been thinking just nonstop about this. I just think you represent what they fear,’" Newsom said. He praised Clinton as an exceptional problem solver despite scrutiny surrounding the former president’s past association with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and a sex scandal with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton has denied knowing about Epstein’s crimes or engaging in wrongdoing. BILL CLINTON REVEALS HOW HE FEELS ABOUT UPCOMING MIDTERMS AFTER SOCIALIST VICTORIES "[There is] no greater problem solver in that respect than Bill Clinton, in my mind. Master of his craft. title: Sean McVay says NFL has admitted officials made major mistake that probably cost the Rams a loss vs Denver
description: Sometimes NFL officials get it wrong. Sean McVay says the league admitted the pass interference penalty on Josh Wallace was not the right call.
content: Sometimes NFL officials get it right. Sometimes they get it wrong. And when that happens, the NFL often acknowledges the mistake to its teams, as it did with the Los Angeles Rams and their controversial pass interference call against the Denver Broncos. The NFL has apparently admitted its officials were wrong to call pass interference on Rams defensive back Josh Wallace in the Sunday Night Football game. NFL'S MOST DEBATED WEEK 3 CALL HAS PEOPLE WONDERING HOW TO DEFY GRAVITY WHEN HITTING PATRICK MAHOMES That call almost certainly cost the Rams the game. The NFL did not immediately respond to an email from OutKick seeking confirmation that the league acknowledged the officiating mistake to McVay. So we're going on his word only. But the coach has no reason to lie. The penalty against Wallace was a double whammy. It negated what would have been a potential game-sealing interception with 1:09 remaining to play and the Rams leading 26-23. The blown call instead resulted in pass interference against Wallace and the Rams. That gave the Broncos a first-and-goal situation at the Los Angeles 7-yard line, setting up a touchdown six plays later and a 30-26 Broncos win. It should be noted that Wallace did indeed make contact with Broncos wide receiver Pat Bryant. But in a league that often prefers to let players decide games in the final minutes rather than having officials determine the outcome, referee Bill Vinovich's crew stepped in, and they pretty much helped decide the game. Regardless of the mistake, the NFL is not awarding the Rams anything other than maybe some satisfaction. The Rams still carry the loss in the standings and the Broncos keep their victory. title: Mamdani's taxpayer-funded influencer army accused of plotting pressure campaign against NYC CEOs
description: Senior aides to Mayor Zohran Mamdani reportedly discussed mobilizing a 200-plus influencer network against top CEOs and business leaders in New York City.
content: Senior officials in New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration are reportedly plotting a coordinated social media pressure campaign against some of the city's most powerful business leaders, looking to mobilize a 200-plus influencer network run through City Hall. Mamdani's network of social media creators working for him first drew scrutiny earlier this month after the Columbia Journalism Review revealed that City Hall was communicating with more than 200 influencers through an encrypted Signal group called "NYC Creators Announcements." Fox News Digital subsequently reported that members receive daily talking points, videos and other updates from the administration, while also being offered access to events and city officials. MAMDANI’S ‘MASS ENGAGEMENT’ OFFICE DRAWS FIRE OVER PLANS TO BUILD INFLUENCE BEYOND CITY HALL: ‘NYC IS DONE’ Now, two sources briefed on the effort told the New York Post that senior City Hall aides have discussed mobilizing the influencer network against New York business executives, including leaders of the Partnership for New York City, an influential nonprofit representing the city's business leaders and largest employers. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla and Related Companies CEO Jeff Blau have also been floated as potential targets, according to the Post. The reported strategy centers on "blindsid[ing]" Partnership for New York City President and CEO Steven Fulop, who took over the organization earlier this year, with one source telling the Post that aides viewed the leadership transition as an opportunity to "go at CEOs." "They want to punch Fulop in the face," the source told The Post. Fulop, however, told Fox News he personally spoke with Mamdani after the report and that the mayor, his communications director and political director all denied plans to target business executives. Fulop said the Partnership would take Mamdani "at his word" while remaining "vigilant and watchful" but noted if he continued down this path there could be "huge repercussions in a bad way." Mamdani spokesperson Dora Pekec, meanwhile, called the Post's report "categorically false" and "a complete lie," though the Post reported that she declined to identify specific inaccuracies in its account. The Mamdani administration's use of influencers and Signal had already drawn scrutiny before the latest report this week from the New York Post. Reinvent Albany, a government watchdog focused on transparency and accountability, has said it supports city agencies using paid social media influencers to promote government programs but opposes city officials using instant-messaging apps such as Signal for official communications. MAMDANI SPARKS FEARS OF VIOLENCE AFTER DOXING WEALTHY NYC PROPERTY OWNERS: 'OUTRIGHT DANGEROUS' In testimony before the New York City Council earlier this month, the group warned that the city still lacks a practical way for agency Freedom of Information Law officers to archive or retrieve official records created on apps such as Signal. "Even now, in 2026, the City of New York has not developed a practical way for official records created by these apps to be archived or retrieved by agency FOIL officers," Reinvent Albany testified. The watchdog has called for legislation clarifying that electronic and instant messages constituting public records must be preserved and easily retrievable, while also proposing disclosure requirements for influencers paid to promote city messaging. NYC MAYOR MAMDANI CALLS THREAT OF RICH PEOPLE LEAVING NYC OVER TAXES 'IMAGINED' The alleged effort to go after NYC's CEOs comes as Mamdani continues to push for higher taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and corporations to fund his agenda and address the city's budget challenges. Mamdani called earlier this year for a 2% personal income tax increase on New Yorkers earning $1 million or more, alongside an increase in the corporate tax rate. While those proposals did not make it into this year's budget, Mamdani has continued to publicly back both. "I've been very open and honest about my vision, whether it be fast and free buses or whether it be higher personal income taxes on the wealthiest New Yorkers or the most profitable corporations," Mamdani said in May. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The mayor did secure a new pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes owned by non-city residents, which his administration projects will generate roughly $500 million annually. The measure was dealt a legal setback Tuesday, however, when a Staten Island judge ordered the administration to scrap its initial rollout and restart the process after finding the city failed to follow required procedures before sending tax notices. The ruling did not strike down the tax itself, and Mamdani's administration vowed to continue fighting for the surcharge. Matt Rauschenbach, a Mamdani spokesman, defended the surcharge as a "basic principle of fairness," arguing that owners of luxury second homes should contribute toward the city services they benefit from.

title: Arizona State hockey coach placed on paid leave as investigation into tragic workout continues
description: Arizona State University placed hockey coach Greg Powers on paid leave as the investigation into a workout that left a player in a coma continues.
content: Arizona State University has placed head coach of the men's hockey program Greg Powers on paid administrative leave as the school continues to investigate a workout that left a player in a coma. Sophomore and St. Louis Blues prospect Matthew Mayich has been in a coma since the August 20 workout the team held, run by an ex-Army Green Beret. On Wednesday, ASU athletic director Graham Rossini announced that Powers — who has led the program since it debuted at the D-1 level for the 2015-16 season — had been placed on leave the previous day. Assistant coach Mike Corbett will be behind the bench when the Sun Devils open their season on the road against Lindenwood University. An interim head coach will be named at a later date. Powers' leave comes just days after seven members of the Sun Devil hockey program released a letter through an attorney that disputed certain findings of the school's initial review into the incident. The Sept. 23 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General report reviewed a sample of 678 asylum applications filed by Afghan nationals admitted through Operation Allies Welcome, the Biden administration initiative launched after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan. Inspectors identified 303 missing aliases, 23 missing security checks and more than 150 additional documentation deficiencies, including two cases involving applicants who may have been inadmissible on terrorism-related grounds. FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME The findings come as Operation Allies Welcome has faced renewed scrutiny following several high-profile arrests of Afghan nationals admitted under the program. Fox News Digital has previously reported on the arrests of an alleged ISIS-K supporter, an Afghan national charged with making terroristic threats and another Afghan national admitted under Operation Allies Welcome who was later arrested after being convicted of indecent exposure to a minor. In a press release, DHS argued the report demonstrated the Biden administration "dangerously mismanaged" Operation Allies Welcome, saying a lawsuit settlement that required USCIS to adjudicate 90% of asylum applications within 150 days forced the agency to prioritize speed over more thorough reviews. The DHS inspector general report, which noted hundreds of aliases had not been recorded for applicants, underscored the importance of accurate record keeping, pointing out one applicant had 124 known aliases. The report said that "missed FBI name checks" accounted for nearly 60% of the absent security checks that the report identified. The report also flagged two asylum applications involving applicants with potential terrorism-related concerns. In one case, required paperwork documenting the government's review was missing entirely. In another, supervisors began the approval process but never completed the final step, leaving no clear record that the review had been finished. ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE' Mark Krikorian, executive director of the conservative Center for Immigration Studies, said the inspector general's findings reinforce concerns critics have raised since the chaotic Kabul evacuation in 2021. "The fact that 40% of these applications have errors is alarming," Krikorian told Fox News Digital. "This IG report just underlines how superficial and even frivolous the vetting that we were assured was going on was." Krikorian said many evacuees were first flown to temporary processing hubs, sometimes referred to as "lily pads," in third countries before ultimately being admitted to the United States. While those locations allowed U.S. officials to conduct additional processing, he argued the practical reality was that partner countries were not going to permanently accept the evacuees, leaving the United States effectively committed to resettling them. HOMELAND SECURITY OFFICIAL'S KILLING LEAVES AGENCY 'DEVASTATED' AS VETTING BREAKDOWN EXPOSED "As soon as that cargo bay door closed, we're stuck with those people," Krikorian said, noting how the United States effectively committed itself to resettling evacuees once they boarded evacuation flights during the chaotic Kabul withdrawal. Krikorian argued the inspector general's report likely understated the scope of the problem because inspectors could only identify documentation deficiencies visible in the files they reviewed, not determine whether every applicant had been thoroughly vetted. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The inspector general ultimately made five recommendations aimed at strengthening USCIS' review of Operation Allies Welcome asylum applications, including improving documentation of applicant aliases, ensuring required security checks are properly recorded and enhancing oversight of adjudication files. USCIS agreed with all five recommendations, according to the report.

title: Fox News Poll: Michigan voters split between El-Sayed and Rogers
description: Abdul El-Sayed holds a slim 1-point edge over Mike Rogers in the Michigan senate race as voter concerns about both candidates keep it tight.
content: Michigan voters have concerns about both candidates in the U.S. Senate race and that leads to a tight contest, according to a new Fox News poll. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has a slim 1-point edge against Republican Mike Rogers, 50-49%, among Michigan likely voters. The survey, released on Wednesday, is the first Fox News Poll this season among likely voters, so a direct comparison can’t be made to previous polls. Yet among registered voters, the preference is almost identical, 51% El-Sayed vs. 48% Rogers. That’s a reversal since August, when Rogers was ahead by 4 points among registered voters, 51% to El-Sayed’s 47%. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI’S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS The analysis below is among likely voters, unless otherwise noted. More of El-Sayed’s backers feel certain of their choice (87%) than Rogers’ (80%). Overall, 15% say they could switch their pick before voting, including 18% of Rogers’ supporters and 12% of El-Sayed’s. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Here’s why the race is tight. Roughly equal numbers of Michiganders say they are extremely concerned Rogers is too close to President Donald Trump (39%) as say El-Sayed’s views are too liberal (36%). And their favorable ratings are also close: 47% view El-Sayed positively compared to 44% for Rogers. Among registered voters, positive views of El-Sayed increased by 5 points since August while Rogers’ declined by four points. El-Sayed’s best groups include those who traditionally go Democratic: women, Black voters and those with a college degree. He’s also ahead with voters under age 45 and the small subgroup of union households. The groups giving Rogers some of his strongest support include men, rural voters, White evangelical Christians, married voters and Whites without a college degree. Both candidates receive near-universal backing from their party. Rogers receives 95% among Republicans, while it’s 93% for El-Sayed among Democrats. In addition, Rogers gets 99% of MAGA Republicans and 88% of non-MAGA Republicans, while El-Sayed garners 98% of DSA Democrats and 90% of non-DSA Democrats. The small number of independents narrowly favor El-Sayed. This year’s political landscape favors El-Sayed. The Democrats hold a 5-point advantage when voters are asked which party they want to control the Senate, 52% to 47%. But to capitalize on that, he’ll need to consolidate Democratic support after a contentious primary because 11% of likely voters who backed his primary opponent Haley Stevens say they plan to vote for Rogers. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE "The Michigan Senate race is unique in that short-term political forces favoring the Democrats are somewhat offset by concerns about the Democratic candidate," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "The bad news for Rogers is El-Sayed has made progress shoring up Democratic support and has room to grow given voter concerns about the economy." Four in ten Michiganders say they are falling behind financially, and they back El-Sayed by 25 points. But the largest share, nearly half, describe their family as holding steady, and they favor Rogers by 13 points, while the small number who are getting ahead prefer Rogers by 36 points. Still, for 7 in 10 voters, the cost of living will be extremely important to their Senate vote, and they back El-Sayed by 13 points. He also has advantages among the 4 in 10 focused on U.S. policy toward Israel (+8 points) and AI technology (+17 points). Conversely, Rogers is favored by 26 points among the 44% focused on immigration. Half of Michigan voters consider Trump extremely important to their Senate vote, and they favor El-Sayed by 22 points. In 2024, Trump won Michigan by less than two percentage points, while Rogers lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by less than half a point. Voter frustration with the administration is a drag on Rogers, as nearly 6 in 10 disapprove of the president’s performance. While 40% approve, not all support Rogers (93%). He remains competitive with support from 19% of Trump disapprovers overall, even as 28% who only "somewhat" disapprove of Trump prefer El-Sayed. In the gubernatorial race to replace term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Democrat Jocelyn Benson leads Republican John James 54% to 45% among likely voters. Twelve percent of those backing Rogers in the Senate race cross-party lines to favor Benson. Conducted September 24-28, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,203 Michigan registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (794) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (295). Results based on the registered voter sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2.5 percentage points and for the subsample of 1,028 likely voters it is ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Likely voters are based on a probabilistic statistical model that relies on past vote history, interest in the current election, intention to vote, age, education, race, ethnicity and marital status. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100. Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

title: Riley Gaines speaks out on dismissal of her lawsuit vs NCAA, hopes to take case to SCOTUS
description: Riley Gaines says she and fellow plaintiffs plan to appeal the NCAA lawsuit dismissal, hoping the Title IX case reaches the U.S. Supreme Court.
content: Riley Gaines said the dismissal of her lawsuit against the NCAA could move the legal battle closer to what she hopes is its ultimate destination: the U.S. Supreme Court. Gaines, joined by Independent Council on Women’s Sports co-founders Kim Jones and Marshi Smith, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive group interview that the plaintiffs will appeal after a federal judge granted summary judgment to the NCAA on their remaining Title IX claims. "No instance of defeat or what is perceived or deemed as defeat feels good," Gaines said. "There [were] feelings of frustration, obviously, with the basis of what the grounds for dismissal was, indicating that the NCAA was not subject to Title IX." RILEY GAINES' LAWSUIT VS NCAA DISMISSED BY BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE, APPEAL PLANNED Smith said the first reaction among the other women involved in the lawsuit was "shock," particularly because the NCAA has frequently celebrated Title IX and its role in the growth of women’s college sports. "The year that Riley was confronting this at the swim championships in 2022, it was the 50th-year anniversary of Title IX," Smith said. "The number of Title IX parties that the NCAA and each individual university threw for themselves, celebrating themselves for the success and triumph of Title IX." Smith said the plaintiffs were stunned to see the NCAA successfully argue that it was not covered by the law it had publicly celebrated. "To watch Riley compete against a 6-foot-4 male athlete that same year and have the NCAA celebrate him and his success in women’s sports, fast-forwarding to now, their complete denial of having any responsibility to Title IX — it’s mind-blowing," Smith said. Jones described the other athletes as "bewildered" and "shell-shocked" by the outcome. "This is an institution that we, as female athletes, have always believed had our backs, were bound by federal law [and] could not violate the rights of female athletes across the country," Jones said. "Even when I was going through school, the NCAA helped schools to ensure compliance to Title IX." Jones argued that the NCAA’s structure makes the ruling especially difficult for the plaintiffs to accept. The organization is governed by representatives of its member institutions, many of which receive federal funding and are independently subject to Title IX. "The NCAA is the controlling authority for collegiate athletics. They set nationwide policy. And the NCAA is composed of the schools," Jones said. "Their board of directors is presidents of universities." WHAT THE SCOTUS TITLE IX RULING COULD MEAN FOR LAWSUITS SEEKING DAMAGES FOR WOMEN IMPACTED BY TRANS ATHLETES However, Gaines said the athletes became more optimistic after considering the path ahead. "Ultimately, this is something that I think myself and the dozens of other plaintiffs involved in the lawsuit would like to see before the Supreme Court," Gaines said. "That way it can be established, the law of the land once and for all, when it comes to female athletes and how large institutions like the NCAA are able to harm us with, at this point, little to zero accountability." U.S. District Judge Tiffany R. Johnson ruled Monday that the evidence did not establish the NCAA as a recipient of federal financial assistance through its concussion-research collaboration with the Department of Defense. Because receiving federal assistance is required for liability under Title IX, Johnson entered judgment for the NCAA and closed the case. The Biden-appointed judge did not determine whether the NCAA’s former transgender-athlete policy constituted sex discrimination. The lawsuit was filed in 2024 by Gaines and more than a dozen other current and former female college athletes. It challenged NCAA policies that permitted biological males who met certain eligibility requirements to compete in women’s events. The case focused heavily on the 2022 NCAA Division I Women’s Swimming and Diving Championships, where Gaines tied former University of Pennsylvania swimmer Lia Thomas for fifth place in the 200-yard freestyle. Thomas won the 500-yard freestyle national championship and used a women’s locker room during the event. NCAA PRESIDENT CHARLIE BAKER REACTS TO SUPREME COURT RULING ON TRANSGENDER ATHLETES That championship coincided with the 50th anniversary of Title IX, a detail Gaines and Smith said made the NCAA’s successful legal position particularly jarring. "At that national championship, the NCAA was handing out shirts that said, you know, ‘50 years of Title IX creating opportunities for women,’" Gaines said. "The irony at the time, of course, being that they were making us compete against a 6-foot-4 man. But now here we are in this position, understanding that the NCAA is arguing that they’re not subject to Title IX." Smith called the contrast "mind-blowing." "The number of Title IX parties that the NCAA and each individual university threw for themselves, celebrating themselves for the success and triumph of Title IX," Smith said. "Fast-forwarding to now, their complete denial of having any responsibility to Title IX — it’s mind-blowing." The NCAA responded to the dismissal by defending its current record on women’s athletics. "The NCAA is proud to continually invest in and expand women’s sports and the NCAA is in full compliance with the Trump administration’s executive order on women’s sports," the organization said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Gaines dismissed the response as "total hogwash" and accused the organization of invoking women’s sports only when convenient. "It’s just a way to kind of wink at everyone, act as if they’re doing the right thing, the upstanding thing," Gaines said. "Again, pretending as if they care about women and their female athletes." The NCAA changed its transgender participation policy in February 2025, one day after President Donald Trump signed his "Keeping Men Out of Women’s Sports" executive order. Its current rules prohibit athletes assigned male at birth from competing on women’s teams or receiving scholarships designated for women. However, the policy permits those athletes to practice with women’s teams and receive other benefits available to athletes eligible for practice. Smith argued that the NCAA’s statement did not offer female athletes a durable guarantee independent of the current administration. "They have made absolutely no guarantees to women," Smith said. "They have not said, ‘We support female athletes and will not put men into women’s sports again.’" Jones said the legal fight has left the plaintiffs feeling betrayed by an organization they once believed was responsible for protecting college athletes and promoting Title IX compliance, and hopes to take the lawsuit to the highest court. "The goal of the young women is to — exactly what Riley said — take this all the way. There’s got to be accountability here." Jones said. The plaintiffs have 30 days from the entry of judgment to file their notice of appeal with the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. Gaines said she remains confident that the case can eventually reach the nation’s highest court. "There is light at the end of the tunnel," she said. "There is some optimism thinking forward about this case." The dispute has also become intertwined with the 2026 midterm elections and the broader political fight over transgender participation in women’s sports. Gaines said she expected Democrats to distance themselves from transgender-athlete policies after Republicans’ success in the 2024 election. Instead, she argued, the party has remained committed to positions she believes contributed to its electoral losses. "I really was under the impression that we would begin to see Democrats slowly start to recant, or distance themselves from their previous voting records, or statements, or things, that they’ve said when it comes to women’s rights and our safety and privacy and equal opportunities in our sports and beyond," Gaines said. "But that’s just not at all what they’ve done." Gaines cited Democratic proposals to expand the Supreme Court as one political development that could affect the lawsuit if it takes several years to reach the justices. "Even beyond this issue, that concerns me. Of course it does," Gaines said. "That’s just one of many things across many different issues that the Democrats have promised to do and have campaigned on doing, which is why I believe there is such an emphasis on this November and what midterms really look like." She urged parents to consider issues involving school sports, parental rights, education and student privacy when they vote. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "If you have daughters, if you have kids, if you’re a parent, and you care about your parental rights and your children and their education and their success and their well-being and their health and their safety and their privacy and their opportunities, that enough should be a motivating factor to get out to the ballot box in November," Gaines said. Gaines acknowledged that the debate has become heavily partisan, but said the athletes challenging the NCAA did not originally view the protection of women’s sports as an inherently political cause. "We don’t view this issue as a political issue," Gaines said. "We have called on those on the other side of the aisle to link arms, to stand with us, but that just hasn’t been the case." She characterized policies allowing biological males to enter women’s sports as a reversal of the progress female athletes secured through Title IX. title: Staggering drug haul found at major airport after bizarre attempt to hide evidence
description: Orlando International Airport police and K-9s intercepted over 200 pounds of marijuana allegedly smuggled on commercial flights from Los Angeles. A security expert shares context.
content: More than 200 pounds of marijuana reportedly made its way onto commercial flights from Los Angeles to Orlando International Airport (MCO) this summer — before police intercepted the drugs in two separate airport busts. The smugglers allegedly attempted to bring hundreds of pounds of bulk marijuana into Central Florida from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), according to police records recently obtained by FOX 35 Orlando. The drugs were intercepted by undercover officers with the Orlando Police Department (OPD) and drug-sniffing K-9s, FOX 35 reported. ONE CANNABIS MISTAKE AT AIRPORT COULD BRING 10 YEARS IN PRISON AND $15,000 FINE Investigators said the suspects used superglue and ripped-off luggage tags to try to evade police, as well as dryer sheets to conceal the smell of marijuana. During one bust, which occurred on May 7, officers found 57.6 pounds of marijuana packed inside 50 vacuum-sealed bags, wrapped in blankets and stuffed with dryer sheets, according to the report. In a second bust on July 1, police found 144.4 pounds of marijuana in suitcases with locks that had been completely glued shut. FOX 35 identified the suspects as individuals in their 20s who are now facing felony drug trafficking charges. TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS Keith Jeffries, vice president of K2 Security Screening Group, told Fox News Digital that drug smuggling on commercial flights "can happen in multiple ways." Investigators said the suspects used superglue and ripped-off luggage tags to try to evade police. Those scenarios could include airport or airline employees assisting smugglers or traffickers using drug mules, he said — though he cautioned that it remains unclear how the drugs made it onto the flights in these cases. Jeffries also said law enforcement may have been tipped off about certain individuals or bags by a confidential informant. "It's unknown at this time without talking to law enforcement and getting the specifics," he said. Jeffries, who previously served as TSA's federal security director at LAX and deputy federal security director at MCO, added that drug trafficking "can happen on any domestic route — and it does." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER He said Orlando's status as a major tourist destination, in particular, could make the city attractive to traffickers. "The illegal perpetrators in this [situation] may think and believe that, well, the security must be lax there, which is not the case," Jeffries said. He also noted that TSA officers do not specifically search for illegal drugs, and that suspected narcotics discovered during screening are referred to law enforcement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "The TSA's administrative search authority is very, very narrow and very specific," Jeffries said. "TSA does not look for illegal narcotics," he added. "They simply say, 'We've got an unknown substance, and we need law enforcement's attention so that law enforcement can validate what it is or is not.'" TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Fox News Digital reached out to the Orlando Police Department for additional information. While the Orlando marijuana was intercepted by local law enforcement, TSA officers have made other unusual discoveries during airport screenings in recent weeks. Earlier in September, TSA officers at Dallas Love Field Airport in Texas discovered a pocketknife concealed inside a tube of toothpaste during routine carry-on screening. title: Major League Baseball desperately needs to fix its terrible postseason scheduling practices
description: Austin Riley's three-run homer off Jhoan Duran gave the Braves a wild card series lead, but thousands of empty seats exposed MLB's scheduling problem.
content: Tuesday afternoon was a tremendous showcase for postseason baseball, with two division rivals squaring off in a best-of-three playoff series at a home stadium. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies are playing a wild card series in Atlanta, with each game taking on tremendous importance as both look to advance to the NLDS and later rounds. Tuesday's matchup was playoff baseball at its best, with a tight, closely-fought game between two elite starters in Jesus Luzardo and Chris Sale. Phillies manager Don Mattingly made the decision to win or lose with closer Jhoan Duran, sending him out for multiple innings to try and secure a 3-2 lead. Instead, the move backfired, with Braves third baseman Austin Riley launching a massive, two-out three-run homer to give Atlanta a 5-3 lead. Raisel Iglesias got the final three outs to take a 1-0 series lead and make Wednesday's contest a possible elimination game for Philadelphia. ASTROS PLAYERS CALL OUT FANS FOR BOOING DURING GAME 1 LOSS TO WHITE SOX: 'EXTREMELY FRUSTRATING' That's exactly what Major League Baseball wants to showcase about the postseason. A late, game-changing homer involving two of the game's stars. Dramatic finishes to conclude tight matchups. Massive stakes and incredible crowd reactions. There's just one problem. As the camera panned across the field as Riley rounded the bases, showing the stands in left field, there were thousands of open seats. Some fans huddled in the concourses to avoid the late-September Atlanta heat, but entire sections were effectively completely empty. A huge, game-changing postseason moment at a home stadium with a star player launching a homer off one of baseball's best closers. And there are thousands of open seats visible on the broadcast. Not exactly the best look for a sport working hard to grow and showcase its popularity against the all-powerful NFL. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE This isn't a criticism of Braves fans. The high temperature on Tuesday approached 90 degrees. First pitch wast at 2pm local time in the middle of a school and work day. It's criticism of Major League Baseball's scheduling strategy, which was always inexplicable and is now bordering on insane. MLB's best-of-three wild card format now means that there are four games for the first two games of the playoffs, a necessity to allow the division series round to start on time. The league's plan for this scheduling issue has been to stagger start times throughout the day. This year, for example, the first game starts at 2pm Eastern, then 5pm, then 8pm, then 10pm. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! In theory, this makes some sense. Instead of the games stepping on each other and limiting potential viewership, each is separated to allow fans to watch all four without flipping back and forth. In practice, it's a disaster. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The 2pm Eastern start time on a weekday doesn't work for many fans who'd otherwise love to attend or watch games. Which is what leads to the scores of empty seats at a playoff game for a team with a massive, dedicated fanbase like Atlanta. Even for those watching on television, say, west coast fans, an 11am start time puts first pitch squarely in the middle of a workday. Following the game on a phone is one thing, watching it in an office or at a job that requires manual labor is another. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD The league may have decided that it's worth these sacrifices in order to space out the games, but anecdotally, they're wrong. Before the advent of streaming television, it was harder to watch multiple games at once. In the modern world though, YouTube TV, as just one example, will automatically create multi-view setups. Or fans can create their own. Individual apps have built their own multi-view experiences too, useful with several games broadcast exclusively on Peacock. Meanwhile, Tuesday night's game in San Diego was completely packed, with a raucous, sold out crowd celebrating wildly when Fernando Tatis Jr. hit a leadoff homer, then again when Manny Machado hit one of his own. That game started at 7pm local time. What a surprise. This issue isn't exclusive to the wild card series either. The league already announced that if the Padres advance in their wild card series, game one of the NLDS between the Dodgers and winner of the Braves-Phillies series will start at 1pm local time. It's on a Saturday, at least, but with LA expected to face an extreme heat wave pushing temperatures to near or over 100 degrees, a 1pm start time would guarantee open seats at Dodger Stadium. Even in Houston, Astros players spoke about the frustrations with poor attendance for a game that started at 4pm local time. "The fans here are definitely spoiled with a lot of ALCS and World Series runs, and we have to earn that right to bring this team back to that position," said pitcher Bennett Sousa after the game. "That being said, when this team was in their first (playoff) series 10 years ago, Minute Maid Park was probably packed. It makes a big difference. If we were in Chicago, it’d probably be loud as s—." Again, there's an easy solution to this. Start the games at a time that makes sense for local fans; 5pm-7pm. The league will get the big moments and crowd reactions they want to highlight, television networks likely won't see a meaningful dip in viewership, and fans and players will be happier. It's easy and simple, which means it won't happen.

title: 'The View' panel blasts Lindsay Clancy defense attorney for 'moving the goalposts' on evidence
description: "The View" co-hosts slammed Lindsay Clancy's lawyer Kevin Reddington on Wednesday for shifting from a postpartum psychosis defense to claiming no evidence exists Clancy murdered her children.
content: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800-273-TALK (8255). "The View" co-hosts criticized Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington on Wednesday for seemingly "moving the goalposts" by suggesting a lack of evidence that she killed her children. During the show, the women of the ABC daytime talk show discussed Reddington appearing to change strategies after he submitted a motion for a required finding of not guilty on the grounds that the prosecution did not provide sufficient evidence to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy killed her three kids. "Where’s the evidence that she did this?" Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan in court Tuesday. "Where is the evidence she did this?" LINDSAY CLANCY'S ATTORNEY ASKS JUDGE TO ACQUIT HER OUTRIGHT, ENDING CASE AND BARRING A RETRIAL This marked a significant shift in Reddington's legal argument. During the trial, Reddington did not dispute that Clancy killed her children, but argued that she was not criminally responsible due to postpartum psychosis. "The View" panel was skeptical of this new claim considering Reddington's previous argument already presumed that Clancy had, in fact, killed her children. "My jaw was on the floor because the defense’s entire argument hinged on she had postpartum psychosis. She wasn’t responsible by reason of insanity but she — in a psychotic state — did this crime, and now he’s like, ‘We don’t even know if she did it,’" Alyssa Farah Griffin remarked. Co-host Sara Haines suggested Reddington reasonably pointed out holes in the evidence but added that she knows no one who believes there should be no accountability. "Now I feel like the lawyer is moving the goalposts a bit, but if you read his description ... there were a lot of holes. Everything was decided on that it was assumed she did it. But there was a question then about everything that she was repeating had been recounted to her because she had no memory in the hospital," Haines said. ROGAN SHREDS SUPPORTERS OF LINDSAY CLANCY, SAYS THEY WOULDN'T RALLY IF A FATHER WERE ON TRIAL FOR SAME CRIME Sunny Hostin, a former lawyer, had the harshest criticism against Reddington, calling his argument "a terrible take." "I don’t understand how you can spend an entire trial arguing that she did it but she is not criminally responsible because she was suffering from a psychotic episode and postpartum psychosis and then turn around in front of the very same judge and say there’s no evidence she did it. I think that is a terrible take," Hostin said. "I’m not convinced he’s not on TikTok," Haines replied. "It feels very conspiracy theory and not grounded in the law and I don’t love this new position," Hostin added. In a comment to Fox News Digital, George Washington University professor and Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley likewise criticized Reddington's new strategy. "Kevin Reddington appears to be crafting a criminal defense like the 1985 screenplay of ‘Clue’ with different endings for different audiences. After insisting that Clancy did kill her children, he is now arguing that there is no evidence showing that she killed her children," Turley said. He added, "Reddington says that the judge effectively prevented him from arguing that Clancy may not have committed the crime. If so, he should thank Judge Sullivan. His insanity defense built on a clearly sympathetic jury. Arguing this alternative theory would likely have alienated many jurors by insulting their intelligence." SUNNY HOSTIN'S HOLDOUT JUROR CLAIM COMPLICATED BY CONFLICTING REPORTS FROM INFAMOUS 1991 MURDER TRIAL Fellow Fox News contributor Gregg Jarrett also said Reddington has lost all credibility. "At trial, he openly conceded that his client strangled her three young children. It was never in doubt or dispute. Now he's contradicting himself by saying something that's demonstrably untrue and utterly absurd. When you do that as a lawyer, you undermine the very argument you're making to the judge. And you've damaged your client in the process. But given the outrageous conduct of Reddington in publicly attacking the holdout juror, no one should be surprised." Clancy is due back in court on Nov. 2 for another motion hearing. She has pending motions to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds and to open an inquiry into the holdout juror. title: Pentagon data breach exposes Social Security numbers, personal info of 2.76M US military, civilian personnel
description: A Pentagon personnel data breach exposed employment information belonging to both living and deceased U.S. military and civilian personnel.
content: A Pentagon personnel database breach exposed sensitive personal information belonging to 2.76 million living U.S. military and civilian personnel, and 294,000 deceased individuals, a Pentagon official confirmed to Fox News. Unauthorized users accessed unencrypted files containing Social Security numbers and military or civilian employment information between October 2025 and July 2026. The Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) discovered the vulnerability in a file-sharing system on July 16 and notified affected individuals Sept. 18. FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER A Pentagon official said a few unauthorized users accessed personally identifiable information through the DMDC system during the roughly nine-month period. Upon discovering the vulnerability, the DMDC immediately remediated it, according to the official. The Pentagon said it has no indication the information was misused. PENTAGON REVEALS SECRET SPACE WEAPONS ARE ALREADY IN ORBIT — BUT WON'T SAY WHAT THEY DO Affected individuals are being notified by postal mail through Identity Theft Guard Solutions, or IDX, a provider contracted by the Department of Defense. IDX will provide credit monitoring and identity restoration support to affected individuals based on the types of personal information impacted in each case, according to the Pentagon. The Pentagon directed individuals with questions about the breach to contact IDX through its website or by calling 1-855-744-4556. The DMDC maintains personnel and workforce information for the Defense Department and provides data and services supporting military personnel, their families and other Defense Department operations. FORMER SECRET SERVICE CYBERCRIME EXPERT WEIGHS IN ON PRIVACY AFTER HACKERS BREACH STOLEN FLOCK CAMERA The breach exposed information belonging to more than 3 million living and deceased individuals overall, though the Pentagon said it has not identified evidence that the accessed information has been misused. title: Jemele Hill says we can't blame A'ja Wilson for charging at fans because of what 'men' have done
description: Jemele Hill defended A'ja Wilson's confrontation with a courtside fan during the WNBA playoffs, citing broader incidents involving men at league games.
content: Jemele Hill says we cannot blame WNBA star A'ja Wilson for charging at a fan Tuesday night because of what other "men" have done at league games. For background, Wilson received a technical foul during Game 2 of the Aces' first-round playoff series against the Indiana Fever after confronting a courtside fan. According to reports, the male fan pointed at Wilson and told her she had committed a foul on Sophie Cunningham. Teammates restrained Wilson as arena security intervened. After reviewing the incident, the Fever determined the fan had not violated the arena's code of conduct and allowed him to return to his seat. WNBA REFS MISS OPPORTUNITY TO EJECT A'JA WILSON OVER MELTDOWN, ENTERING STANDS Wilson defended her actions after the game. "I don't really get into the bulls---. I try to play my game. But if I'm just walking and I just got the foul, I'm chilling. If I see a man coming at me, taking steps toward me and pointing at me. I don't give a damn what you said. I don't give a damn how you said, the tone. That is unacceptable," Wilson said. "You don't step towards me. You should never step and point at me. I'm not for that s--- ... that there is unacceptable. They said he didn't do anything and that's fine. ... There's certain things I'm not going to allow because it's unacceptable. You don't know me at all to step toward me and say anything." Wilson's behavior was unprofessional. Imagine a star athlete charging at a fan for acting like, well, a fan. SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SENDS MESSAGE AFTER PATHETIC FINGER-POINTING TANTRUM & SOX-YANKS ANNOUNCERS WON'T SHUT UP! You would never see Patrick Mahomes, LeBron James, Shohei Ohtani or even Caitlin Clark react that way. Had they done so, the criticism would have been swift and nearly universal. Instead, many of the usual suspects have downplayed Wilson's behavior or defended it outright. Here's what Jemele Hill wrote on Threads: "While A’ja could have handled it better and I’m sure it was partially fueled by the frustration losing, let’s look at the broader context: The W has had to deal with men showing up dressed as women to mock them. Men throwing dildos on the court creating an unsafe environment. Can’t blame the players for being on high alert," Hill posted. Apparently, losing the game and previous incidents involving other fans are enough to excuse charging at someone who, by the league's own determination, did not violate the rules. Hill's broader argument is also remarkably weak. Excusing Wilson's conduct because of what other "men" have done at other games effectively holds one fan responsible for the actions of unrelated people. By that logic, no player could ever be expected to distinguish between acceptable and unacceptable fan behavior. Once again, this reflects a recurring problem in the WNBA. Many of the league's biggest stars want the benefits that come with greater fame and visibility but struggle with the scrutiny and interaction that accompany it. Wilson's supporters have long argued she should be marketed as the face of the league. Her play certainly warrants that conversation. Her composure in moments like this does not. Hill's response is unsurprising. She doesn't care what Wilson and the fan did. A'ja Wilson is a Black woman in the WNBA. That is enough for Hill to defend her no matter what. Rather than evaluating the specific incident on its own merits, she shifts the discussion elsewhere to justify Wilson's actions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If Caitlin Clark or Sophie Cunningham had charged toward a Black fan under similar circumstances, it is difficult to imagine Hill responding with the same level of understanding. The WNBA, its players, and its media once again failed to meet the moment.

title: Country hitmaker reveals how faith carried him through son's murder — and toward compassion for his killer
description: Casey Beathard reveals how faith led him to reconcile with his son Clay's killer in the Fox Nation special, "Chords of Faith," narrated by Ainsley Earhardt.
content: Legendary country music songwriter and former college football player Casey Beathard opened up about the tragic stabbing death of his son, Clay, revealing how his faith helped guide him through the unimaginable event. In the new Fox Nation special, "Chords of Faith," narrated by "Fox & Friends" co-host Ainsley Earhardt, Beathard explained how his trust in God allowed him to forgive the convicted killer Michael Mosley for his actions on that fateful December night in Nashville. "It was just going to kill me to carry all this weight, all this stuff," he said. "You know, I realized in the wake of this whole process that the more you dig into the Word of God, that he could be trusted with justice. And vengeance, you know, it's not mine, because that was just gonna weigh on me. Vengeance was God, it helped me [be] free and let me let it go." MICHAEL MONSOOR HAD AN ESCAPE ROUTE — THE MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT CHOSE TO SAVE HIS TEAMMATES INSTEAD Beathard described the great pain he felt for Mosley, explaining that he "wasn't loved growing up" and expressed his sympathy for the Tennessee man convicted of killing his son. "Because this kid, honestly, when I looked across the room at this kid, it was so sad for a young kid to have to spend his whole entire life in prison," he said. "His parents weren't there, and I think he was looking for love and found love in the wrong, wrong, wrong places." Clay, a 22-year-old quarterback for the Long Island University Sharks football team, and his friend Paul Trapeni III, 21, were killed in December 2019 outside The Dogwood bar in Nashville. Attorneys said Mosley pulled a knife during a fistfight, resulting in the deaths. Mosley was charged and convicted of first-degree murder in March 2022 and sentenced to two consecutive life sentences plus 40 years. RILEY GREEN THOUGHT HE'D 'FRAME HOUSES FOR THE REST OF MY LIFE' BEFORE BECOMING A COUNTRY MUSIC STAR "Chords of Faith" goes beyond Beathard's family tragedy and into his storied music career. After playing college football at Elon University, in 1991, he moved to the Music City and never looked back, working at the Country Music Hall of Fame and the Bluebird Café before signing a songwriting contract that launched his success. Beathard wrote songs for some of the most prolific country music artists, including Kenny Chesney, Eric Church and George Strait. Many of his hit songs topped the Billboard Hot Country and Country Airplay charts, including Tracy Byrd's "Ten Rounds with Jose Cuervo," Chesney's "Don't Blink" and Church's "Hell of a View." "Casey's one of the best songwriters this town's ever known," Chesney said on the show. "[He] changed my life." ELLA LANGLEY SAYS 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SUCCESS IS 'CHANGING MY LIFE' AFTER HER SONG BREAKS MARIAH CAREY'S RECORD Church credited Beathard for writing relatable music, boasting that he does it "probably better than anyone at incorporating what we all experience in everyday life." Beathard remains an inspiration to his children, not only for his chart-topping hits but also for his unwavering dedication to fatherhood, especially in the wake of Clay's death. His eldest son, C.J., an NFL quarterback, praised both his father and mother, Susan, for their strength and resilience through the tragedy — maintaining they set a lasting example for their children. "It was hard on us, but for the parents, it's tough," C.J. said. "And to see the way my mom and dad handled that was very inspiring for us all as siblings."
