title: FBI hack claim raises fears over sensitive personal data
description: ShinyHunters claims it breached FBIJobs.gov and stole Social Security numbers, home addresses and sensitive assignment details of FBI personnel.
content: If you have ever filled out a job application, handed over your Social Security number for a background check or trusted an organization with information about your family, pay attention to what happened at the FBI. The cybercriminal group ShinyHunters claims it compromised FBIJobs.gov and stole highly sensitive information connected to current and former FBI personnel and people who applied for jobs at the bureau. The group says its haul reaches far beyond basic contact information. On Sept. 23, the FBI acknowledged the group's claims and said it was "actively and aggressively investigating" the incident. The bureau said investigators had not yet determined whether the point of breach involved an FBI system or a third-party provider supporting FBIJobs.gov. That uncertainty is important. At the same time, samples provided to journalists contain enough real-world information to make the situation difficult to dismiss. For anyone whose details may be included, the potential fallout goes well beyond having an email address leaked. FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED Since that statement, the FBI has struck back by announcing the arrest of an alleged ShinyHunters leader in the Netherlands after a joint operation with Dutch authorities. Dutch police said a 24-year-old Amsterdam man was arrested Sept. 15. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com What the FBI said about the FBIJobs.gov incident In its Sept. 23 statement, the FBI addressed both the alleged compromise and the uncertainty surrounding where the attackers may have gained access. "The FBI is aware of a cybercriminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the fbijobs.gov portal," the bureau said. It added that the point of breach remained undetermined and said it was "actively and aggressively investigating this matter." The FBI also said investigators were working closely with third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to reduce potential risk. The FBI confirmed the investigation and the unresolved question about where the breach occurred. It did not verify ShinyHunters' full account of what the group says it stole. The FBI's Special Agent Applicant Portal also became unavailable as the incident unfolded. A notice posted Sept. 22 said FBIJobs.gov and the Special Agent Applicant Portal were unavailable. The applicant portal supports people who have progressed through portions of the special-agent hiring process, making the type of information potentially involved especially sensitive. CyberGuy reached out to the FBI for an update on the incident, including whether employee or applicant data was accessed and whether affected individuals are being notified or offered identity protection. We did not hear back before our deadline. The data sample raises much bigger concerns ShinyHunters provided journalists with a spreadsheet containing about 5,000 alleged FBI personnel records. Reuters reported that the spreadsheet included names, home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers and emergency contact information. It also included information about field office assignments and, in some cases, sensitive intelligence or counterespionage work. Reuters said it could not authenticate the entire spreadsheet. However, reporters independently verified details belonging to more than 22 people by comparing the information with credit records and earlier leaked data. Reuters also matched career information or job titles for eight people against court filings, news reports, public profiles and online posts. That still does not establish where every record came from. Real information can appear in several databases or previous breaches. Yet the matches add credibility to at least portions of the sample. 404 Media separately reported that the 5,000-person sample contained names, home addresses, phone numbers and information involving FBI employees' spouses. Sensitive FBI assignments reportedly appeared in the data The personal information alone creates obvious privacy concerns. The reported job information raises another level of risk. Reuters found records identifying people connected to China-related investigations, Russian intelligence work, human intelligence operations and electronic surveillance. Other entries referenced covert access, clandestine technical operations and telecommunications interception. Reuters said it could not verify that every assignment was authentic or up to date. On Sept. 23, 404 Media also reported that the data appeared to expose members of the FBI's Remote Operations Unit. The outlet describes the ROU as a secretive FBI team involved in developing and using hacking tools to gain access to target devices. Think about what that combination of information could provide to someone with bad intentions. A name may lead to a home address. An emergency contact could identify a spouse or child. Job information might reveal the kind of investigations someone works on. For an FBI employee working in a sensitive position, that creates risks far beyond ordinary financial fraud. IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB? What ShinyHunters claims happened ShinyHunters says it breached the FBI and stole between 2 and 3 terabytes of information connected to FBI personnel and job applicants. The group has also claimed that Justice Department worker data was obtained. The hackers claim they exploited a previously unknown vulnerability involving Oracle PeopleSoft, software used for human resources and other enterprise functions. FBI documents reportedly show its recruiting operation uses PeopleSoft and AWS GovCloud. However, that does not prove the hackers' claimed method of attack. The alleged PeopleSoft vulnerability, the claimed 2-to-3-terabyte haul and a broader compromise of FBI systems had not been independently verified. Reuters also reported that ShinyHunters claimed to possess files involving employee and applicant vetting, contracted background investigations and sensitive medical information. Reuters said it could not verify what additional information the hackers actually possessed. That caveat is critical. ShinyHunters has an obvious interest in making its access sound as extensive as possible. For now, there are signs that portions of the information supplied by the hackers correspond to real people. Major questions about the source, scope and attack path remain unresolved in the FBI's public statement. Why ShinyHunters says it targeted the FBI ShinyHunters says retaliation, rather than a demand for money, motivated the attack. The group points to warnings the FBI issued about ShinyHunters-related cyber activity earlier in 2026. On May 15, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center published an advisory describing ShinyHunters as a cybercriminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion. The advisory warned that actors using the name may use real or exaggerated claims about stolen information to pressure victims. It also described threatening communications, harassment of family members and swatting among tactics associated with ShinyHunters actors. ShinyHunters disputes portions of the FBI's description of its activities. Reuters reported that the group said it targeted the FBI because of the May warning and said it was holding the allegedly stolen data while demanding that the bureau rescind the statement. Why you should care even if you never worked for the FBI You may read a headline about FBI employees and assume this has little to do with you. Yet the way the alleged data could be abused should feel familiar to anyone who has handed personal information to an employer, bank, health provider, insurance company or government agency. Organizations often collect far more than your name and email address. They may hold your home address, Social Security number, birthdate, employment history and emergency contacts. Job applications can contain years of background information. You may have done everything right and still have that information exposed because the organization holding it or one of its technology providers was attacked. That third-party piece deserves attention here. In its Sept. 23 statement, the FBI specifically said investigators had not determined whether the breach point involved its own enterprise or a third party. The same setup exists throughout everyday life. Your employer might use an outside payroll provider. Your doctor's office may rely on billing software from another company. Retailers routinely send information through outside payment systems. Once you hand over your personal data, you often have little visibility into how many systems eventually store or process it. Stolen personal details make scams much harder to spot Suppose someone emails you and knows your full name, employer and home address. Then the person mentions your spouse or a job application you actually submitted. That message feels very different from a generic scam email. This is why personal data can be so useful to attackers. They can combine stolen records with information already available from data brokers, social media or previous breaches. The result can be a phishing message tailored closely enough to make you hesitate before questioning it. Cybercriminals could pose as an FBI recruiter or someone from an employer's human resources department. They could even claim they are contacting you to help protect information exposed in the breach. The FBI's May advisory warned that stolen personal information can help attackers create targeted campaigns and pressure victims. What FBI applicants, employees and families should do now Even while investigators work to establish the full scope, anyone who believes their information may be involved can take precautions. 1) Verify every unexpected FBI-related message If you applied for an FBI job, be suspicious of calls, texts or emails claiming you need to reenter information because of the portal incident. Do not use a link or phone number contained in an unexpected message. Contact your existing applicant coordinator or reach the FBI through a channel you already know. The FBI's own ShinyHunters guidance recommends verifying unusual requests through another method before responding. 2) Warn family members and emergency contacts This step becomes particularly important because the reported sample included spouses and emergency contacts. Tell people listed on employment or application records to be cautious if someone suddenly knows their connection to you. Criminals may target a relative because they expect that person to have fewer security safeguards. If someone claims there is an urgent problem involving you, an employer or law enforcement, verify the story independently before sharing information or sending money. 3) Freeze your credit if your Social Security number may be exposed A credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name. You need to place the freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. The FTC says credit freezes are free and remain in place until you lift them. A freeze will not prevent every form of identity theft. Continue monitoring accounts you already have. 4) Consider getting an IRS Identity Protection PIN If your Social Security number may have been exposed, an IRS Identity Protection PIN can help protect you from tax identity theft. The six-digit IP PIN prevents someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number. Anyone with an SSN or ITIN who can verify their identity can request one. Keep the number private. The IRS says it will never call, email or text you asking for your IP PIN. 5) Watch financial, tax and medical activity Look for new accounts you do not recognize, unfamiliar charges or changes to existing accounts. Also pay attention to unexpected IRS notices, rejected tax filings and medical bills or insurance explanations of benefits for treatment you never received. These can signal types of identity theft that a credit freeze alone may not stop. If you discover identity theft, report it through IdentityTheft.gov and follow the recovery plan for the information that was compromised. 6) Strengthen your online accounts before phishing begins Neither Reuters nor the FBI's Sept. 23 statement said passwords were included in the 5,000-record sample. Still, exposed personal details can make attempts to steal your passwords much more convincing. Use a unique password for every important account. A password manager can help keep track of them. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) or passkeys wherever available. Also be cautious about unexpected password-reset requests. 7) Keep strong antivirus protection running on your devices A personalized phishing message can still contain a malicious link or infected attachment. Strong antivirus software can help detect known phishing websites, malicious downloads and malware before they compromise your device. That gives you another layer of protection if a convincing email or text gets through. Security software cannot replace careful clicking, but it can help when a scam looks unusually believable. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 8) Reduce how much personal information strangers can find If your home address, phone number and relatives already appear on people search sites, leaked records can give criminals even more information to work with. Search for yourself online and review what is publicly visible. You can request removal from many data broker and people search sites yourself or use a personal data removal service to handle recurring opt-out requests. Reducing what is publicly available gives a criminal fewer pieces to combine with information from a breach. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 9) Use dark web monitoring as an early warning Dark web monitoring can alert you when information tied to your email address, phone number, Social Security number or other identifiers appears in known breach collections. Some identity theft companies include Dark Web Monitoring that searches for exposed personal information and alerts you when it is found. However, treat an alert as a warning rather than proof that someone has stolen your identity. Monitoring cannot prevent information from circulating once criminals obtain it. Its value comes from giving you an opportunity to secure affected accounts, watch for fraud and take action sooner. See my tips and best picks on best identity theft protection at CyberGuy.com. 10) Do not pay someone who claims to have your data The FBI's guidance involving ShinyHunters recommends against paying or engaging with threat actors making demands. Save threatening communications instead. Preserve screenshots, email addresses, phone numbers and other identifying information. You can report cybercrime through the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. If someone appears to face an immediate physical threat, contact emergency services. Kurt's key takeaways There are still major unanswered questions about the FBIJobs.gov incident. The FBI's Sept. 23 statement left the point of breach unresolved, and the bureau had not publicly validated ShinyHunters' claim that it stole between 2 and 3 terabytes of data. Still, the data samples deserve serious attention. Reuters verified details belonging to more than 22 people and reported that the spreadsheet contained Social Security numbers, home addresses, dates of birth, emergency contacts and information about sensitive assignments. What concerns me most is how useful those pieces become when they are connected. A criminal who knows where you work, where you live and who your spouse is has a much easier time building a scam that feels authentic. For FBI personnel tied to intelligence or covert technical work, the exposure could create security concerns that reach well beyond financial fraud. The takeaway for the rest of us is practical. You cannot control the security of every employer, government agency or company holding your information. You can control how much information about you remains publicly available, how strongly your accounts are protected and how quickly you respond when something suspicious appears. title: MIKE DAVIS: The American gun-free zone you didn't know about
description: The High Court of American Samoa ruled the Second Amendment doesn't apply in the unincorporated territory, allowing a near-total gun ban to take effect.
content: In October 2024, the High Court of American Samoa, an unincorporated territory of the United States, issued a staggering ruling that received little media attention. The justices ruled that, since American Samoa is unincorporated, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms does not apply there. The ruling allowed a near-total gun ban to take effect. President Donald Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum can and must reverse this immediately. The issue of territories is obscure, so some background is helpful. The United States has 50 states and several territories, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa. The District of Columbia also is not a state; however, unlike the other territories, it receives three electoral votes for the presidency pursuant to the 23rd Amendment. None of these territories receives voting representation in Congress, though delegates from the territories can sit on congressional committees and, for instance, serve as managers for the House during a Senate impeachment trial. These territories generally have courts, such as the U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico and the U.S. District Court for the District of the Virgin Islands. Presidents nominate judges to these courts, and the Senate confirms them. As Article IV judges, those on these courts serve with a tenure of 10 years, and litigants may appeal their rulings through the relevant circuits. When territories violate constitutional rights, individual litigants or the Justice Department can sue them in federal court. President Trump's Justice Department did precisely that last year, accusing the U.S. Virgin Islands of enacting gun restrictions that run afoul of the Second Amendment. LAWYER WHO BEAT HAWAII GUN LAW CALLS STATE’S RELIANCE ON BLACK CODE ‘DISGRACEFUL’ American Samoa differs judicially and in other ways from the other territories. No statute grants birthright citizenship to those born in American Samoa, unlike every other territory. American Samoa also has no federal court, unlike other territories. The High Court of American Samoa serves as the ultimate judicial authority in that territory. 48 U.S.C. § 1661 vests the president with civil, military and judicial control over American Samoa. A 1951 executive order by President Harry Truman delegated authority over the territory to the secretary of the interior. Article III, Section 3 of American Samoa's territorial constitution grants the secretary of the interior the power to appoint justices to the High Court. These justices serve no life tenure, unlike federal judges who serve during good behavior. The secretary can remove American Samoa justices without cause and appoint replacements without Senate confirmation. President Trump and Secretary Burgum must act in light of the court's ruling against the Second Amendment. That amendment stands as a cornerstone of the Republic, and the Supreme Court reaffirmed its vitality recently in Wolford v. Lopez. Hawaii decided that it did not wish to comply with the Supreme Court's recent Second Amendment precedents. It implemented an absurdly restrictive concealed-carry regime under which gun owners could bring their weapons onto properties only where signs expressly permitted them. The Hawaii Supreme Court relied on, among other ridiculous rationales, the so-called "Aloha Spirit" to justify this infringement. Hawaii argued that, prior to statehood, no right to gun ownership existed. The Supreme Court, over a dissent from its three liberal justices, rejected that rationale. The Second Amendment applies just as much in Hawaii as it does in Chicago, New York and the District of Columbia. DOJ TARGETS SPANBERGER, NEWSOM GUN LAWS WITH TWIN LAWSUITS AFTER SCOTUS AFFIRMS SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS No lawsuit is even necessary in American Samoa. The broad authority Congress granted the president under Section 1661 empowers President Trump and Secretary Burgum to overrule this egregious decision. Federal courts have upheld this overruling authority in several cases, though the Supreme Court has never addressed the question squarely. Beyond firing the justices and appointing new ones who respect the Constitution, President Trump should make clear in an executive order that the Second Amendment applies with equal force in American Samoa as it does in states and other territories. The First Amendment is foundational to the Republic. The Second Amendment is no different, no matter how hard anti-gun zealots work to obscure that truth. The current justices of the High Court of American Samoa have stripped it of any force whatsoever. The administration holds a simple, swift and lawful remedy, and they must use it. title: 'Drug-dealing' network shielded by blue states targeted in SCOTUS challenge
description: Louisiana Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill filed two lawsuits targeting blue-state shield laws and the online abortion pill pipeline.
content: Louisiana Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill is escalating her fight against abortion pills entering states that ban abortions through two lawsuits — one targeting the providers accused of distributing the drugs and another challenging the blue-state laws shielding them from prosecution. Murrill, along with Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin, sued New York, California and Massachusetts at the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging their shield laws block cooperation with investigations into abortion-pill providers. The attorneys general also filed a separate lawsuit in Louisiana against more than 30 people and organizations accused of advertising, prescribing, dispensing or shipping abortion pills into their states. "This is drug dealing and it's illegal," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "And we're going to continue to do everything that we can to enforce the laws in our states." The two lawsuits, filed Wednesday, are the latest move in a widening state-by-state fight over abortion. That conflict has grown since the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, which struck down Roe v. Wade and gave elected officials the power to set abortion policy in their states. HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS Murrill said the Supreme Court case targets the blue states' legal protections that have thwarted Louisiana's previous efforts to prosecute out-of-state doctors. "These shield laws are very comprehensive," Murrill said, arguing that California and New York prohibit officials from assisting other states seeking to enforce judgments stemming from abortion-related conduct. Louisiana has already indicted New York physician Margaret Carpenter and California physician Remy Coeytaux over allegations that they prescribed abortion drugs that were sent into Louisiana. New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom have refused to extradite the doctors. The Supreme Court complaint cited Louisiana's unsuccessful effort to extradite Carpenter, saying Hochul declared there was "no way in hell" she would comply with Louisiana's request. The filing said New York later strengthened its shield law, including by allowing prescribers of abortion drugs to keep their names off prescription labels. In response to the lawsuit, Hochul said she will continue fighting to ensure New York remains a "safe haven for reproductive rights." "No one should have to fear being punished for seeking or providing reproductive care," Hochul said in a statement. "As anti-abortion extremists in other states try to reach across our borders and threaten patients and providers, New York will stand up for them. Our shield laws are there to protect that freedom." Newsom similarly rejected Louisiana's request to extradite Coeytaux in January, saying California would not help other states punish doctors for providing abortion access that is legal in California. CALIFORNIA ABORTION PILL SUPPLIERS PLOT WORKAROUNDS AHEAD OF SUPREME COURT MIFEPRISTONE DECISION When Murrill vowed to sue, Newsom responded on X telling her to "Go f--- yourself. California will never help you criminalize healthcare." "I think that if I sent guns into their states illegally, they would certainly try to come after me," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "I said specifically at the time that we would be coming for them and we are." "We are going to take down those laws using every tool that we have at our disposal," she continued. The second lawsuit directly targets what Murrill calls the "pill pipeline." The 100-page complaint alleges providers used online questionnaires to obtain information from customers before abortion drugs were mailed into states where their distribution is prohibited. The states allege some organizations openly acknowledged that their conduct violated those states' laws while relying on shield laws to protect themselves from legal consequences. Murrill said investigators have conducted controlled purchases and received pills packaged in small bags, sometimes in quantities she said exceeded what would ordinarily be prescribed. "We've seen it for ourselves," Murrill said. "There's no supervision, there's no healthcare, there's no communication whatsoever. It's all done online." Murrill argued that the system can allow people other than pregnant women to obtain the drugs, pointing to cases Louisiana authorities said involved women being pressured or deceived into taking abortion medication. PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND "We have a situation in one town in Louisiana that we've documented and investigated where a father did not want his teenage daughter to keep a pregnancy," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "And so he basically put the medication in a smoothie, forced her to drink it. She did ultimately give birth to that baby at 23 weeks and is still in a NICU fighting for its life." The attorney general also said Louisiana wants more help from the Trump administration. "Obviously we think the FDA could be doing more and we've asked them to do that," Murrill said. Louisiana has separately challenged federal rules that eliminated an in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone. Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser backed the litigation, accusing blue states of using their laws "to obstruct justice" and urging the Justice Department to settle Louisiana's separate FDA litigation. Abortion activists flagrantly sell dangerous drugs across state lines and women and children pay the price, with more and more survivors of ‘death in a pill’ bravely coming forward," Dannenfelser said in a statement. title: Trump admin’s proposed ‘English-only’ Head Start rule draws fire from Los Angeles mayoral candidate
description: Nithya Raman vows to fight the Trump administration's proposed Head Start English-only mandate, threatening a lawsuit to protect LA families.
content: Los Angeles City Councilmember and mayoral candidate Nithya Raman criticized the Trump administration Tuesday over a proposed federal rule that would require Head Start programs nationwide to conduct all education in English, taking aim at the policy as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) considers a sweeping overhaul of the federal preschool program. Raman said in an X thread that the proposed change would move Head Start away from multilingual instruction and disproportionately affect communities such as Los Angeles, where large numbers of children enter classrooms speaking a language other than English at home. The proposal comes as California Head Start programs serve tens of thousands of dual-language learners. "As mayor, I will fight back against Trump’s plan to gut a program that gives every LA child a strong start," she said. "I'll bring the full weight of the mayor's office to fight this cruel mandate and work with our school district to call for a joint lawsuit if needed to protect our families' rights." LA MAYORAL RACE HEADS TO NOVEMBER RUNOFF AS KAREN BASS FACES MAMDANI-STYLE SOCIALIST Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation, responded to Raman’s criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing the debate over language instruction underscored broader problems with the federal program. "Head Start should be sunset," he said. "The gold-standard federal evaluation found it does not improve student outcomes in any lasting way, and it costs taxpayers a ton of money." The Trump administration's proposed Head Start overhaul, announced by HHS in August, would require programs to "conduct all education to children in English." Children whose native language is not English and who do not speak English would have to receive priority for English instruction. Certain American Indian and Alaska Native Head Start programs using Tribal languages would be exempt. AMERICAN SCHOOLS COST MORE THAN EVER BUT OUR STUDENTS STILL KEEP FAILING DeAngelis pushed back on Raman's criticism, arguing the administration's proposal would better prepare Head Start children for English-language classrooms. "Nithya Raman is attacking the Trump administration for requiring Head Start to teach English," he said. "English is the language of American schools. If the program won’t teach it, American families with English-speaking kids pay the price when those classrooms get dumbed down." HHS said the change is intended to prepare children for school and align Head Start with President Donald Trump's executive order designating English as the official language of the United States. An HHS spokesperson said Head Start is designed to prepare children to enter school and described a strong foundation in English as an important part of that preparation. "Head Start is designed to prepare young children to be ready to enter school, and providing a firm foundation in the English language is a critical part of that preparation," an HHS spokesperson told The Los Angeles Times. PRO-TRUMP GROUP LEADS NEW COALITION TO UNDERCUT TEACHERS UNIONS The proposed rule represents a reversal from existing Head Start regulations that call on programs to support both English acquisition and children’s home languages. Federal officials estimated roughly one-third of non-Tribal Head Start classrooms could be affected by the language change. California received nearly $1.5 billion in annual operations funding for Head Start Preschool and Early Head Start in fiscal year 2024, according to the federal Office of Head Start. The state had 68,126 federally funded enrollment slots across those two programs, excluding American Indian and Alaska Native and Migrant and Seasonal Head Start programs. Nationally, Office of Head Start data for the 2024-25 program year show more than 283,000 participants either lived in households where a language other than English was primarily spoken or were learning another language in addition to English. Roxanne Hoge, chairwoman of the Los Angeles County Republican Party, also criticized Raman’s opposition to the proposed English-language requirement, arguing the federal government has an interest in ensuring children receiving taxpayer-funded Head Start services become proficient in English. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I find it fascinating that Nithya Raman is making demands of a gift bestowed by American taxpayers," she said. "English is the way Americans communicate with each other, and the government has an interest in everyone becoming proficient in our country's language." "Parents can and do have a variety of school options for their children to learn the plethora of languages we speak in LA — from Armenian to Hebrew to Spanish and beyond. Stop demanding and start adapting. I am a mother of four and also an immigrant, since she thinks that's relevant." title: Blanche announces charges against 10 permanent residents accused of Minnesota voter fraud
description: Attorney General Todd Blanche announced indictments of 10 lawful permanent residents accused of noncitizen voting in Minnesota elections since 2022.
content: Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Wednesday that a federal grand jury had indicted ten lawful permanent residents accused of voting illegally or attempting to do so in multiple Minnesota elections, including the state’s August 2026 primary. The ten defendants, originally from Liberia, Canada, South Africa, Brazil, Bosnia, Germany, Ghana and Lithuania, allegedly lied to election officials and told them they were U.S. citizens so they could register to vote. They were accused of voting in the 2022 and 2024 general elections, according to court records. "Voter fraud erodes the public's trust in our electoral system, and it's vital to our democratic process that we do everything that we can to restore that trust," Blanche said at a news conference announcing the charges. FEDERAL INDICTMENT HANDED DOWN IN MINNESOTA RELATED TO ISSUE SOME DEMS CLAIM NEVER HAPPENS: 'HOTBED FOR FRAUD' "The most basic way the Department of Justice can accomplish this restoration of trust is by working to make sure the only people voting in an election in the United States are American citizens who are eligible to vote." The 10 defendants were charged separately. They are Bhator Konah Bryant, 61, of Liberia; Edvile Vaidoto Edmunds, 59, of Lithuania; Joshua Frederick Kofi Edzie, 63, of Ghana; Alan Barbu Kargbo, 48, of Liberia; Paul Kras, 78, of Germany; Fadil Rasim Ozegovic, 58, of Bosnia; Aparecido Donizetti Padovan, 62, of Brazil; Chris Adam Pettiquoi, 43, of Liberia; Christian Liam Schenk, 47, of Canada; and Hester Sophia Weihmann, 69, of South Africa. Bryant appears to be the only defendant who wasn't charged with voting illegally, only falsely claiming citizenship in 2024 to register. Making a false citizenship claim to vote is a felony punishable by up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, while voting by a noncitizen is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in prison and a $100,000 fine. Blanche also expressed frustration that the media has, in his view, not taken the Justice Department's work prosecuting election fraud cases seriously to this point. BIDEN ADMINISTRATION GRANTED WOMAN GREEN CARD MONTHS BEFORE SHE ILLEGALLY VOTED IN 2024 ELECTION: DHS "I don't know what the number is that will work for you guys. Whether it's 106, maybe it's 120," he said, referring to a hypothetical number of investigations. "At some point, it has to become meaningful to to the media." Blanche said since President Donald Trump has returned to office, the Justice Department has charged more than 90 people with voter fraud offenses, including 50 illegal immigrants in the past five weeks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there have been 10 voter fraud-related convictions and that there are more than 1,600 active investigations into similar conduct across the country. Mullin did not answer a reporter’s question about how the department plans to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database, known as SAVE, to identify voters who may be ineligible ahead of the midterms. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS The Supreme Court ruled Friday that the administration may use the database for voter-eligibility checks while litigation continues. SAVE has historically been used to help government agencies verify whether noncitizens applying for public benefits are eligible to receive them. States’ use of the SAVE database is voluntary, but federal law generally bars states from conducting systematic voter-roll purges within 90 days of a federal election. With the midterms less than a month away, the Supreme Court’s ruling is expected to have limited immediate impact. During the same news conference Wednesday, Blanche also announced that the Justice Department had filed a judicial misconduct complaint with the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals against several Minnesota federal judges who spoke with The New York Times about cases the department said were still pending. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The article, published Sept. 17, centered on an interview with Judge Patrick J. Schiltz, who said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violated nearly 100 orders from the federal district court in Minnesota during the height of Operation Metro Surge, which saw hundreds of federal agents in the streets of Minneapolis throughout January of this year. Schiltz, a George W. Bush appointee, told the Times that the alleged violation of these orders likely came down to incompetence and staffing shortages at the Justice Department. Blanche said Schiltz airing various complaints about the Trump administration to the Times was a violation of judicial canons and his ethical duties. "We have asked the 8th Circuit to conduct an investigation, and in the meantime, we ask that these judges recuse themselves from every case involving DHS, either criminal or civil in nature, because of the obvious bias they have shown in this article," Blanche said. Shiltz issued this response to Fox News, "As legal ethics experts have confirmed, I was acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times. Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may ‘speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.’ That is exactly what I did."

description: A White House graph shows a 96% drop in legal immigration from Muslim-majority nations since 2024, but the Cato researcher behind it pushed back.
content: The political right celebrated after a White House X account posted a graph showing that legal immigration to the U.S. from nations with Muslim majority populations has all but halted. The account highlighted a 96 percent cut in legal immigration from majority-Muslim countries since 2024 and attached a graph from the Cato Institute, a notoriously pro-immigration think tank. The graph showed a drastic decline in quarterly admissions of immigrants from those countries beginning in January 2025, when President Donald Trump officially took office. It also declined in late 2024, the last year of former President Joe Biden's tenure in office. AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION At its peak, immigration from Muslim-majority nations was over 22,000 people per month between July and October of 2024, according to the graph. But by the beginning of January of this year, that number had dropped to almost zero. Online, the political right cheered the drastic shift. "Absolutely incredible victory for the American people, thanks to POTUS," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, said. "These are the wins we need to continue to deliver on," said Brandon Herrera, the GOP nominee for Congress in Texas' 23rd District. "4 percent to go! Thank you, President Trump," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "Let’s pump up those rookie numbers for every category of immigrant," columnist Kurt Schlichter said. 100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY Some turned the graph into a referendum on the results of Republican leadership, and urged conservatives to vote during the 2026 midterm elections despite concerns about cost-of-living, the Iran war, and other issues for which Trump has been knocked by members of his own party. "I voted for this—and will again," said user David Harrison. "The next time you get the urge to 'punish the GOP.' Remember that Democrats will reverse this overnight," said Turning Point Action's Ben Larrabee. "People screaming that Trump and the GOP aren't doing anything about this problem [are] hardest hit, like squarely between the eyes," online personality James Lindsay said of the graph. JONATHAN TURLEY: SUPREME COURT HANDS TRUMP A BORDER VICTORY LIBERALS CAN'T SPIN "Vote like Western Civilization depends on it, because it does," said Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet. Not everyone was thrilled with the decline in legal immigration from this demographic, though, including David J. Bier, who is the director of immigration studies at Cato and who took credit for the research behind the graph. "Thanks for citing my work. You are violating the law and harming Americans while making the country less safe, less free, and less prosperous," he said in reply. Despite Bier's claim, no court has decided that Trump's move to reduce immigration from Muslim-majority countries is "illegal," though there have been challenges in district courts. The policy was enjoined by the federal district court for the District of Hawaii, and upheld by two federal appellate courts. However, the Supreme Court ultimately decided in Hawaii vs. Trump that Trump's policy was legal.

title: Dems kill Republican's chances of lowering Americans' electricity bills in key election flashpoint
description: Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill aimed at making AI data centers bear rising electricity costs that Jon Husted championed.
content: Democrats blocked a push to tackle one of the key issues driving this midterm election cycle, and may have given a vulnerable Republican a political lifeline in the process. Republicans’ effort to crack down on rising electricity costs caused by the boom in data centers across the country was stifled on Wednesday by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats, despite cruising through the House in a massive bipartisan vote. Schumer’s blockade, however, wasn't unanimous among Democrats, with four — Sens. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Maggie Hassan, D-N.H. — breaking ranks to support the bill. The Ratepayer Protection Act, would have created a standard for AI companies and the data centers they run to bear the brunt of electricity costs — an issue that has become a predominant concern for voters this midterm cycle. FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY But Democrats argued it was a toothless effort that lacked any real enforcement mechanism, and merely a political ploy to give vulnerable Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, a boost. "The Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud. It does not require any protections at all," Schumer said. "While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill." "We need real action on data centers. And what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push force forward a bill that is totally optional?" While the U.S. continues its arms race with China for AI dominance, voters want to see tech companies cool their jets and slow the rapid construction of data centers. A Fox News poll from July found that 70% of voters, both Republicans and Democrats, opposed the construction of new data centers. SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS Republicans, including Husted, hoped that voter concerns could persuade Democrats to break from Schumer and vote in favor of the bill heading into Wednesday’s test. "We all know that people would like to see us do something to lower their prices," Husted said. We have the opportunity to do that." Data centers have become a political cudgel against Husted in his race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who has labeled him the "face of data centers" in a battle that could determine who wins the majority in November. Husted argued that the bill passed the House with only three Democrats voting against it, and that this push didn’t need to be labeled a "partisan victory." Killing the bill, however, could give Husted a needed boost to campaign on, given that Democrats stopped one of the main issues voters have going into the election, particularly in Ohio. "It's like, look, this can be an opportunity for the Democrats to join us and say, ‘yeah, we agree. We're gonna work with them to get something done,’ and I hope they will," Husted said. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER But Democrats countered the legislation was just a stunt to give Husted political ammunition. Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital that voters could see through the politics being played with by the GOP, and that the bill is "good for Senator Husted, but not necessarily for them." "Because it's not, it doesn't have anything that would actually force change," Kim said. "And so that's what we need. We need something that is actually gonna be substantial and meet the moment rather than things that are just designed to be able to help with political elections." "I just think, if you’re looking at issues that we want to get at the heart of what everybody seems to be saying, the Democrats and others are saying, are important, we're concerned about," Thune said. "And it's a chance to actually make the law, it’s not just making a point here."

title: Packers receiver Jayden Reed gets bad news about neck injury after leaving Week 2 game on spine board
description: Jayden Reed will require neck surgery after a frightening hit at MetLife Stadium, and Matt LaFleur confirmed the injury is season-ending for the Packers.
content: The last time everyone saw Green Bay Packers wide receiver Jayden Reed, he was lying motionless on the MetLife Stadium turf after suffering a vicious hit that prompted trainers, doctors and stadium emergency personnel to spring into action, fearing the worst. The worst, thankfully, did not happen. Reed was hospitalized overnight and eventually posted on his Instagram account that he was "doing much better." He had movement in his extremities. SCARY SCENE AS JAYDEN REED CARTED OFF ON SPINE BOARD DURING PACKERS GAME AGAINST THE JETS But it's not all good news. title: Moscow threatens nuclear response over tiny fortress wedged between US allies as clash fears grow
description: Russia's nuclear threat over Kaliningrad raises alarm as experts warn the Baltic exclave is already a hub for hybrid warfare against NATO allies.
content: Russia’s warning that it could resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempts to isolate Kaliningrad is raising new concerns that the heavily militarized Russian exclave could become a flashpoint between Moscow and the alliance, as experts warn the territory is already being used to pressure Europe through hybrid warfare. Moscow warned NATO in a diplomatic document that it was prepared to use "the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" if alliance members attempted to isolate Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia, Reuters reported Wednesday. Kaliningrad, a Russian territory geographically separated from the Russian mainland, sits on the Baltic Sea between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and hosts significant Russian military assets, including elements of Moscow’s Baltic Fleet. RUSSIA THREATENS STRIKES ON UK MILITARY TARGETS, ‘CATASTROPHIC CONSEQUENCES’ OVER UKRAINE The Russian document also raised the possibility of strikes against "decision-making centers" in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict. NATO rejected Moscow’s allegations in a response reviewed by Fox News Digital, saying the alliance is defensive and that none of its exercises or activities threaten Russian territory. The alliance also urged Russia to stop its "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric." Carrie Filipetti, executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, a nonpartisan network of foreign policy leaders, told Fox News Digital that Moscow has repeatedly used nuclear threats as a means of trying to deter Western support for Ukraine. "Russia has threatened to use nuclear weapons in the past, including veiled references to tactical nuclear attacks at the beginning of Putin's invasion of Ukraine, lowering their formal threshold for launching a nuclear attack in 2024, placing Russia's nuclear forces on high alert, and restarting nuclear testing," Filipetti said. "It is very common for Putin to use these threats, because he sees it as a way to deter Europe and the United States from continuing to support Ukraine." SHE GREW UP UNDER SOVIET RULE. NOW EU'S TOP DIPLOMAT WARNS EUROPE AGAINST GIVING RUSSIA WHAT IT WANTS "The threat about a nuclear attack if Kaliningrad is threatened or isolated comes on the heels of a few developments," she added, pointing to NATO jets being scrambled over Russian aircraft, U.S. and NATO air drills near Kaliningrad last month, and heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine. Filipetti, who also served as a deputy assistant secretary at the State Department and as a senior policy advisor for the United States Mission to the United Nations (USUN), argued that the timing also reflects mounting pressure on Moscow as the war continues. "Putin seems to understand that the tide is turning against him, and he's resorting to aggressive rhetoric to try to stop European support for Ukraine as he has tried to do in the past," she said. Dr. Azeem Ibrahim, a research professor at the Strategic Studies Institute at the U.S. Army War College and chief strategy officer at the New Lines Institute, told Fox News Digital that NATO should take the warning seriously, particularly because of the broader role Kaliningrad is already playing in Moscow’s confrontation with Europe. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT Ibrahim argued that while NATO has traditionally prepared for conventional military conflict involving "tanks and troops and divisions," Russia is increasingly using methods designed to disrupt the infrastructure and systems on which civilian societies depend. "Russia is actually adopting a very different approach," he said, describing a strategy of hybrid warfare targeting "infrastructure" and "societies in general — what keeps societies functioning." Ibrahim described Kaliningrad as the "front line" of that effort. "It’s essentially become a Russian fortress," he said. "This is essentially a front-line operation of the Russians in terms of signals intelligence, signals interference and essentially mechanisms by which to carry out this hybrid warfare." Such interference, Ibrahim said, could play a role in the broader confrontation by disrupting civilian communications and infrastructure before or alongside a conventional military attack. "All of that would be preceded by interference operations like this to ensure that societies are not functioning, are not able to respond to emergency services, the news information services, etc.," Ibrahim said. "So governments lose control over what actually makes societies function." RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT The challenge for NATO, he said, is that such operations can be more difficult to attribute than a conventional assault. "Many times, you cannot trace exactly where a lot of this interference is actually coming from — attacks on power stations or internet and telecommunications, et cetera," Ibrahim said. "There’s always some sort of plausible deniability if it’s done by an actor who's very capable." The ambiguity, Ibrahim argued, presents a challenge for an alliance built around collective defense against armed attack. "NATO really does have to kind of reconfigure its posture to understand that these kinds of attacks are equivalent to essentially any sort of kinetic attack," he said. Asked what NATO and neighboring Poland and Lithuania should do following Russia’s warning, Ibrahim called for the alliance to establish clearer consequences for hybrid attacks. "We now need to start going on the offensive in terms of hybrid warfare and understanding the threat and pushing back and sending a very clear signal to Moscow that such threats will not stand," he said, arguing that a sufficiently serious hybrid attack should be considered capable of triggering NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense clause. Lithuania, which directly borders Kaliningrad, rejected Moscow’s warning and accused Russia of trying to undermine NATO unity and Western support for Ukraine. "Russia’s insinuations and threats have no basis. NATO is a defensive alliance and poses no threat to Russia or any other country," Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry told Fox News Digital. "Russia’s threatening is intended to fracture transatlantic unity and impede our support to Ukraine. Russia will not achieve its goals." The ministry added: "We strongly condemn any threats to use force and irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. Russia must stop its aggression against Ukraine… Lithuania is strengthening its national defense system and capabilities, including air defense," the ministry said. "We train with our allies and work alongside NATO forces deployed in Lithuania. We are prepared to defend every inch of NATO territory and respond to any threats." The ministry said Lithuania would also continue providing "comprehensive support to Ukraine and its fight against the aggressor Russia." Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton told Fox News Digital, "In the weeks leading up to February 2022, many officials and commentators (myself included) weren't sure Putin would actually invade Ukraine, even though there were a number of warnings and indicators he would do so. And then on that Feb. 24, Putin launched the largest land invasion against Ukraine since World War II." US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS "NATO should take Russia's warning seriously that it could resort to employing nuclear weapons against the alliance should Kaliningrad be cut off from Russia. We are in the midst of Russia employing ‘gray zone’ coercive actions against NATO nations, so this pronouncement should not surprise the West," he added. Filipetti cautioned that regardless of whether Moscow intends to follow through, nuclear threats themselves carry risks. "NATO is a defensive organization that is in no way threatening Russia's position on Kaliningrad," she said. "That said, any time there is a public threat of nuclear attack it must be taken seriously, especially with someone like Putin." "Nuclear bombs are a potentially world-altering technology," Filipetti added. "It is not only their use, but the threat of their use, that could cause significant miscalculations and escalations." Russia has denied Western accusations that it is conducting hybrid warfare against European states and has said it has no intention of attacking NATO countries. Moscow says NATO military activity around Kaliningrad is instead contributing to an increasingly dangerous confrontation. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov characterized recent Russian warnings as diplomatic reminders to "hotheads in Europe," Reuters reported Wednesday. Reuters contributed to this story.

title: FlyDubai passenger says co-pilot stabbed captain before terrifying plunge, emergency landing
description: A passenger says a FlyDubai co-pilot stabbed the captain before the Israel-bound flight plunged, triggering hijacking fears and an emergency diversion.
content: A FlyDubai passenger said the co-pilot apparently stabbed the captain during a cockpit altercation before the Israel-bound jet plunged thousands of feet, triggering a terrifying scene aboard the aircraft and an emergency diversion to Saudi Arabia Wednesday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later said one of the pilots stabbed the other and apparently attempted to crash the aircraft, which was carrying mostly Israeli passengers. Netanyahu said a passenger and crew member managed to enter the cockpit and overpower the alleged attacker as he tried to sabotage the aircraft's systems, allowing another crew member to stabilize the plane. "I salute the heroes who showed extraordinary bravery and, according to the passenger's account, saved many lives," Netanyahu said, according to an unofficial translation of his remarks. He added that the pilot accused of carrying out the stabbing was arrested and was being investigated by Saudi authorities. The passenger told Fox News that accounts of what happened remained conflicting, but said passengers understood that the co-pilot had stabbed the captain and then collapsed onto the controls. "There are many different accounts, but apparently the co-pilot stabbed the captain and collapsed onto the controls, shutting down the entire instrument panel. We began plunging downward for several minutes. Everyone on the plane was screaming, the overhead compartments opened, and the power went out. We were sure we were going to die. It was very scary," the passenger said. FlyDubai later confirmed that an "altercation occurred in the flight deck," saying on-duty FlyDubai crew traveling aboard the flight secured the aircraft, diverted it and landed safely in Tabuk. The airline did not confirm the reported stabbing and said the underlying reasons and motives remained under formal investigation. LIVE UPDATES: FLYDUBAI PILOT STABS FELLOW PILOT, ATTEMPTS TO CRASH PLANE, NETANYAHU SAYS Saudi Arabia's Tabuk airport said both pilots were hospitalized after suffering injuries, according to Reuters. An investigation into the incident remains underway. The Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and everyone aboard was reported safe, according to officials. A regional official briefed on the incident said an altercation broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved the pilots, though it was not immediately clear what sparked the confrontation. Israeli media, citing security officials, also reported that a dispute between the two pilots was behind the emergency. "The crew have been questioned as part of the investigation," the regional official said, according to The Associated Press. A U.S. official later told Fox News that the alleged attacker was taken into custody when the plane landed in Saudi Arabia. The incident prompted an immediate security response in Israel, where authorities initially feared the plane — carrying more than 100 Israeli passengers, according to The Jerusalem Post — could have been hijacked. Israel scrambled fighter jets as the situation unfolded. AMERICANS WARNED AGAINST TRAVEL PLANS AS TERRORISM THREATENS POPULAR DESTINATION Two Israeli officials told Reuters that Israel's assessment was that the incident may have been an attempted "terror attack." The Jerusalem Post separately reported that the growing assessment among Israel's security establishment, including the IDF, Mossad and Shin Bet, was that the incident was intended as an act of terror. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz went further, calling the incident an "attempted jihadist terrorist attack" that was thwarted by Israeli passengers who entered the cockpit and overpowered the alleged attacker. "According to the preliminary information available to us, the terrorist had one intention: to crash the aircraft with everyone on board," Katz said. The aircraft transmitted an emergency alert during the flight, according to publicly available flight-tracking information. Flight FZ1073 had departed Dubai and was headed for Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv before diverting to Tabuk. Flightradar24 data showed the aircraft suddenly plunging nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the first emergency signal, according to Reuters. "The flight from Dubai was a very calm one for the first two hours. And when we were at the Jordanian border, suddenly the aircraft dropped, like a massive drop, like a massive turbulence for 20-30 seconds. Then balanced, and then once again dropped for 10 seconds and balanced again," passenger Almog Italie said in a video obtained by Reuters. "And then we saw that in the front of the aircraft there was a riot. Many people rushed over there. Apparently, one pilot stabbed the other." Capt. Meidan Barr, former chairman of the Israel Airline Pilot Association, told Fox News Channel that such a rapid loss of altitude would ordinarily resemble an emergency descent, such as one performed following a loss of cabin pressure. "Losing like 15,000 feet in two or three minutes, that is something that you do in, like, an emergency descent when you lose pressure," Barr said, adding that the aircraft's safe landing was significant and would allow investigators to determine what went wrong. Flight-tracking data also showed the aircraft transmitting emergency transponder code 7700 before briefly switching to 7500, a code used to signal unlawful interference with an aircraft, and later returning to 7700. Passengers described a tense scene aboard the aircraft as the emergency unfolded. Travelers told Israel's Channel 12 by phone that they heard shouting from passengers near the front of the plane who had apparently heard the cockpit altercation. They also said the aircraft dipped steeply before landing in Saudi Arabia. IRISH SOCCER PLAYERS WEAR BLACK ARMBANDS, REFUSE TO SHAKE HANDS AHEAD OF CONTENTIOUS MATCH VS ISRAEL The account provided directly to Fox News offered a more harrowing description of the sudden descent, with the passenger saying people screamed as overhead compartments opened and power aboard the aircraft went out. Yasmin Abukasis, whose daughter was aboard the flight, told Fox News at Ben Gurion International Airport that her daughter described passengers rushing to intervene during the cockpit confrontation. Abukasis said her daughter told her that a man had a knife and that passengers grabbed his hand and forced him to the floor amid significant bleeding. She also said two other pilots subsequently took control of the aircraft. After landing, passengers remained aboard the plane as a heavy Saudi security presence surrounded the aircraft, according to their accounts to the Israeli outlet. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office later said the situation was under control. The scare came as Netanyahu has warned in recent days about unspecified heightened security threats facing Israel. Netanyahu convened security consultations over the incident and cleared the remainder of his schedule to manage the crisis, according to Reuters. The Jerusalem Post reported that Israeli airspace was temporarily closed before reopening after the aircraft landed in Saudi Arabia. FlyDubai said it deployed two replacement aircraft to Tabuk to relieve the passengers and crew and that the incident had no impact on its other scheduled operations. A FlyDubai plane carrying the passengers later landed safely in Tel Aviv on Wednesday evening local time. "The plane was falling down... and then I felt that I am losing it, and I am going to lose all of my family. My wife was beside me, my little boy was also beside me and I was separated from them... it was very, very terrifying," passenger Haim Lazarovich said at the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport after landing. "There was a group of young people and they fought with the second pilot," Lazarovich added, noting that he sat at the front of the plane. "Thank God I’m alive." A FlyDubai spokesperson said "at this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," and, "we urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts." The exact circumstances surrounding the reported cockpit confrontation remained unclear Wednesday. While disputes between pilots serious enough to affect a flight are rare, similar incidents have occurred. Two Air France pilots were suspended in 2022 after fighting in the cockpit during a flight from Geneva to Paris. That aircraft did not divert and landed as scheduled. The initial hijacking fears carried particular weight in Israel, where aviation security has long been shaped by a history of attacks on Israeli travelers and aircraft. Palestinian militants carried out a series of hijackings and attacks involving Israelis during the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced an aircraft hijacking in decades and maintains stringent security procedures for Israel-bound flights. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP FlyDubai is a lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates. Flights between Israel and the United Arab Emirates began after the two countries normalized relations in 2020, opening the UAE as a major destination for Israeli travelers. Fox News' Yonat Friling, Greg Norman-Diamond, David Spunt, Jake Gibson, Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Irish PM says Ireland ‘not overrun’ by immigrants, legal migration tied to economic success
description: Micheál Martin addresses Ireland's demographic change as nearly one in four in Ireland are born abroad as the government moves to tighten asylum, citizenship and immigration rules.
content: NEW YORK — Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin pushed back on the notion that Ireland has been "overrun" by immigrants as nearly one in four residents is now foreign-born, arguing that the country's dramatic demographic change has been driven largely by legal migration tied to its economic success story. Martin, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, acknowledged failures in Ireland's asylum system after a record surge in applications, saying it "was too slow" in recent years. He also addressed moves to tighten citizenship rules and opened the door to publishing crime statistics by nationality amid a heated debate over immigration and crime. The issue has become a political flashpoint across Europe and the U.S. and comes weeks after President Donald Trump warned about Europe's approach while appearing alongside Martin in Dublin. "That immigration, what you're doing to yourselves, you're just killing yourselves," Trump said. TRUMP SAYS HE WOULD 'LOVE' TO SEE IRELAND UNIFIED AS ONE NATION "Ireland is not overrun in any shape or form," Martin told Fox News Digital. "But we are conscious that it is an issue that has to be addressed robustly, firmly, fairly as well in terms of those seeking asylum." "All over Europe it's tightening up because of the pressures and migration has created significant political pressures across Europe," he added. "Obviously, illegal migration is the more potent issue. And our system was too slow in processing those seeking asylum. That has changed. We've accelerated the application and the consideration of applications, and we've also now accelerated the appeals process." Martin said his government is developing a new migration strategy that includes proposals to increase residency requirements for citizenship from five to eight years and introduce language and economic self-sufficiency requirements. Migration and crime Immigration has become increasingly intertwined in Ireland's political debate with concerns over housing, crime and rapidly changing demographics in a country that was drastically more homogeneous a generation ago. The issue burst into international view in November 2023, after Algerian-born Irish citizen Riad Bouchaker stabbed three young children and a childcare worker outside a school in Dublin, triggering riots as anger among some opponents of mass immigration spilled into violence on the streets of the capital. The unrest was followed by sustained opposition to government efforts to house asylum seekers in communities across the country, with some protests also descending into violent clashes. Immigration returned to the spotlight this summer following the violent killing of Jamey Carney, a 43-year-old American mother from New York who was found dead at her home in County Kerry. Her Jordanian boyfriend, the suspect in the case, had applied for asylum in Ireland but was rejected and was appealing the decision while remaining in the country. He fled Ireland for Turkey shortly after the killing, later traveling to Jordan and Irish police are now seeking his extradition. Fox News Digital asked Martin whether the case exposed weaknesses in Ireland's immigration system and whether laws needed to be changed. "We're looking at all of that in terms of tightening up the laws," Martin said. "We will make sure that, particularly if people's applications are rejected, that there's fast movement in terms of the consequences of that." MIGRANT WHO FLED IRELAND AFTER AMERICAN MOTHER'S MURDER IS ARRESTED IN JORDAN Crime data Critics of Ireland's immigration policies have argued that migrants are disproportionately responsible for crime, while opponents of that view say such claims unfairly stigmatize the country's growing foreign-born population. But the debate has been difficult to settle because Irish national crime statistics do not routinely publish nationality breakdowns, leaving limited public data to test competing claims. The lack of data has prompted calls for greater transparency from women's advocates and some Irish lawmakers, including proposals to publish crime statistics broken down by nationality. "I've no issue with data ... because that can inform, because sometimes you get a kind of distorted picture," Martin said when asked whether crime statistics should include the nationality of alleged suspects. "So as far as I'm concerned, data is important." But Martin pushed back on the argument that nationality itself drives crime. "I don't think crime is specific to any nationality," he said. "But there are issues there, and in some cases, yes, there's been horrific crimes committed, but not all by illegal migrants either." Housing pressures Housing has become another flashpoint as Ireland struggles to build enough homes to keep pace with its growing population. Martin acknowledged that workers arriving legally in Ireland add to housing demand but said his government’s answer is to increase supply, with about 36,000 homes built last year, up more than 20% from the previous year and the highest annual total since 2011. The Irish government's reliance on hotels and other properties to house asylum seekers has itself become a flashpoint. The state spent about $1.4 billion on asylum accommodation and related services in 2025, while also buying properties outright, including the sprawling Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre for about $175 million. The allocation of scarce public housing has further fueled the immigration debate. The pressure is particularly acute in Dublin, where figures released by the city council this month showed 42% of the 15,005 households on its social-housing waiting list were categorized as non-Irish, fueling anger online as Ireland's homeless population hit a record high last month. Nationally, 28.7% of social housing applicants — nearly 18,000 households — were non-Irish citizens in 2025, according to government figures provided to Fox News Digital. That included nearly 3,200 applicants from outside the EU with refugee status, up 64% from the previous year. Asked whether Irish citizens should receive preferential treatment for social housing amid pressure on waiting lists, Martin backed the idea, saying that "our position is basically its citizens get priority." WATCH: Irish PM Micheál Martin addresses immigration's impact on Ireland's housing crisis A country transformed Ireland's demographic transformation has been rapid. Nearly one in four people living in Ireland was born abroad, up from about one in seven two decades ago. At 23.3%, Ireland now has the fourth-highest percentage of foreign-born residents in the European Union, according to Eurostat. The transformation accelerated after the EU expanded eastward in 2004, a decision that helped fuel a sharp rise in immigration during Ireland's "Celtic Tiger" economic boom, when years of rapid growth transformed the country from one of Western Europe's poorer economies into one of its wealthiest. "It's a bit like America really, free movement for the states here," Martin said. "Our economy's expanded hugely." Martin pointed to financial services and medical devices as industries that rely on skilled foreign workers, including non-EU workers arriving on work permits. More than half a million non-EU citizens were living in Ireland at the start of 2025, accounting for 9.3% of the population, according to Eurostat. "It has been very dramatic, I agree, in the last three decades, largely because of the economic growth of Ireland," Martin said. "You can't switch off an economy either." WATCH: Irish PM says legal immigration fueled Ireland's economic success story Ireland's economy has undergone a remarkable turnaround since the economic stagnation of the 1980s, through the "Celtic Tiger" boom and a devastating crash in 2008, before rebounding strongly. Over those decades, Ireland became a major European base for U.S. multinationals including Apple, Meta, Pfizer and Johnson & Johnson. Martin has been at the center of Irish politics through much of that period, serving in successive Fianna Fáil-led governments from 1997 before becoming prime minister, or Taoiseach, in 2020 and returning to the post in 2025. Ireland's economy continued to expand in 2025, with GDP growing 8%, according to Ireland's Central Statistics Office (CSO). But prosperity has not eliminated pressure on households: nearly 45% reported difficulty making ends meet, while 64% identified housing and the same share identified inflation and the cost of living as among Ireland's most pressing problems, according to the CSO. Ireland's more recent migration pressures have included a post-pandemic surge in asylum applicants, including people arriving from Africa, the Middle East and elsewhere. Applications jumped from roughly 3,500 a year before COVID to a record 18,561 in 2024, before falling nearly 30% last year and continuing to decline in 2026. Separately, more than 120,000 Ukrainians fleeing Russia's invasion arrived under the EU's Temporary Protection system rather than the asylum system. Martin said roughly 80,000 remain in Ireland, with many now working and contributing to the economy. "Irish people are working and living all over Europe," Martin said. "That's the other side of that story and that is something perhaps that we're not as conscious of, but it is reality." Martin also placed Ireland's modern demographic transformation within the country's much longer history of emigration, pointing to the exodus that followed the Irish Famine. "Ireland had 8 million people in 1845 before the Great Famine. That led to the big wave of Irish people migrating to come to America," Martin said. "We're not at that level yet on the island of Ireland, so we need to look at it through the broad sweep of history in a historical perspective."
