title: Ex-NFL player Jack Brewer leads charge to end fines for players using religous, political eyeblack messaging
description: Jack Brewer met with EEOC officials over the NFL's $6,651 fine on a Cardinals cornerback for wearing "Glory Be 2 God" on his eye black strip.
content: Former NFL player Jack Brewer met with officials from the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday as he seeks federal scrutiny of the league’s decision to fine Arizona Cardinals cornerback Kei’Trel Clark for displaying a religious message on his eye black. Clark was fined $6,651 after wearing eye black bearing the message "Glory Be 2 God" during Arizona’s Week 1 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. Brewer, an ordained Christian minister and member of the federal Commission on the Social Status of Black Men and Boys, told OutKick that his meeting was intended to determine whether the NFL’s treatment of Clark could raise an employment-discrimination issue. DOJ CRACKING DOWN ON MLB FOR POTENTIAL RELIGIOUS DISCRIMINATION AFTER PRIDE NIGHT CAPS CONTROVERSY "When you start talking about freedom of speech in this country and you start talking about employees’ rights in this country, it’s a big deal," Brewer said. "As a Christian man, I’m not going to stand for that. And as a former NFL player, I’m not going to stand for that." Brewer said the meeting was "very well received" and left him confident that further conversations with the agency would take place. "The goal was to first understand: Do we have a potential case? What does that look like? What would the player’s rights be?" Brewer said. "My goal was just to establish some communication and talk about next steps, which we did. And so now we’ll start to work to gather information and get a deeper understanding of really what goes on in the minds of a league like the National Football League." Brewer initially raised the issue in a Sept. 25 letter to EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, requesting a meeting about the fine and the league’s policies governing religious expression. "The NFL treated Clark’s gratitude to God, as expressed in four words, as a punishable personal message," Brewer wrote in the letter obtained by OutKick. "This fine represents an action that strikes at the heart of religious liberty and sends a chilling message to every person of faith in professional sports." Brewer asked the EEOC to consider whether the NFL would be required to accommodate a player’s sincere religious expression when doing so would not impose an undue hardship on the league or its teams. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act requires covered employers to reasonably accommodate employees’ sincerely held religious beliefs and practices unless an accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the employer’s business. In its 2023 decision in Groff v. DeJoy , the Supreme Court held that an employer must demonstrate that an accommodation would create "substantial increased costs" in relation to its particular business. However, Brewer’s meeting does not mean the EEOC has opened an investigation or concluded that the NFL violated federal law. Any potential case would require a fact-specific examination that could include Clark’s employment relationship with the Cardinals and NFL, whether he requested a religious accommodation, and the effect an exception to the uniform rule would have on the league’s operations. NFL TOLD AZEEZ AL-SHAAIR HE'D BE PULLED FROM TEXANS GAME OVER PRO-PALESTINIAN EYEBLACK MESSAGE An individual or organization may file an EEOC charge on another person’s behalf, according to the agency, but Brewer did not say that a formal charge had been filed. The NFL cited Rule 5, Section 4, Article 8 in its disciplinary letter to Clark. The rule prohibits players from displaying personal messages in writing or illustration on game day unless the message has received advance approval from the league's office. Clark posted the fine notice on social media and wrote that he "needed answers." "I got to report to God at the end of my days on the day of judgment," Clark wrote. "I’ll always give God the glory and out loud. All good." Brewer argued that allowing four words on a player’s eye black would place little apparent burden on a multibillion-dollar sports league. "If someone’s writing things across their uniform or putting it out there on top of their helmet, that’s a different story," Brewer said. "But the eye black — think back to Tim Tebow and many, many other athletes, myself. We would write stuff on our tapes, on our forearms. We would write stuff on our eye black. "To think about fining someone for doing that, it’s unconscionable," he added. "It’s disgusting." The NFL’s rule does not distinguish between religious and political messages. Houston Texans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair, a practicing Muslim, was fined $11,492 this month after wearing eye black bearing the name "Hind Rajab," a Palestinian girl killed in Gaza in 2024. Al-Shaair was also fined $11,593 after displaying the message "Stop the genocide" during the previous postseason. When asked whether Al-Shaair should receive the same protection he is seeking for Clark, Brewer initially distinguished between expressions of faith and political statements. But he ultimately said the NFL must apply its restrictions consistently, particularly while promoting league-approved social messages. "I think he should be just as protected," Brewer said of Al-Shaair. "If you’re going to pull down the messaging, pull it all down, but don’t pick and choose." The NFL has continued to display league-approved social justice messages in stadium end zones and on players’ helmets. Teams have been permitted to select from phrases including "End Racism," "Stop Hate," "Choose Love" and "Inspire Change," while the league has also promoted LGBTQ inclusion through team and league initiatives. Brewer contended that the difference between league-selected messages and unauthorized player expression creates a double standard. "You cannot treat people differently based upon whatever it is you want to promote," Brewer said. "If you are an organization like the National Football League, you cannot pick and choose the messaging that you want your players to play underneath." Brewer said his immediate objective is to build support among current and former players and ultimately force the NFL to address the treatment of religious expression. "I want players across the National Football League, current and former, to take a stand, to show unity on something," he said. "As a National Football League player, you should be able to use your platform to profess the gospel, to profess your God and to write it on your eye black." Brewer emphasized that he would support the right of players from other faiths to seek the same accommodation. title: UCF Knights salute Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo programs with slick new Space U uniforms
description: UCF Knights unveil Mission X Space Game uniforms honoring the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo programs with stunning details from the 1960s space race.
content: Thanks to the modern Artemis Missions, mankind is headed back to the Moon in the next few years, but for their annual Space Game uniforms, the UCF Knights are throwing it back to the pioneers who got us there in the first place. The Knights have been throwing on special space-themed getups for a decade now, and they're pretty much always a feast for the eyes with unique designs, nods to the space program, and of course, the Citronaut. However, I think this year's batch, which pays homage to the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo programs of the 1960s, is tough to top. This is the school's tenth Space Game, which they've dubbed "Mission X," and there is so much cool symbolism in everything. UCF opened its doors in 1963 — right around the time the Space Race was heating up — as Florida Technological University, and ever since, it has long served as a pipeline to the nearby Kennedy Space Center. ANCIENT ARTIFACTS FOUND BENEATH CAPE CANAVERAL SPACE FORCE STATION AS ONE MYSTERY STILL STUMPS RESEARCHERS That's why this year, the team is celebrating that particular era and, man, are there some cool details. The black stitching that criss-crosses the jersey is a nod to the Mercury program's space suits, which featured black stitching and prominent zippers. NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND—OR CHINA WILL If you look at the cuffs, one is "Canaveral blue" — which has become the go-to Space Game color for UCF — and the other is red, just like the cuffs were on the Gemini program's space suits. The collar is Canaveral blue, just like the inside of the suits worn throughout the 1960s. On the shoulders, the patches mimic those worn during the Gemini missions, while this year's Space Game patch is modeled after the patch from the Gemini X mission. The pants feature the school's old Citronaut mascot (which, as a UCF alum, I wouldn't hate seeing back full-time; I love it), and a striping pattern like the one that appeared on Apollo program rockets and space suits. Finally, the helmets have a bold red stripe on them, which is a reference to the similar stripe worn on the helmets of Apollo mission commanders. Alright, I've seen enough: ten out of ten. No notes. What an absolute home run on all fronts. There are Easter eggs everywhere you look, but the entire uniform still looks killer in its own right. title: Arizona lawmakers demand independent investigation into ASU hockey workout that left player in coma
description: Arizona lawmakers demanded an independent probe into the Arizona State Sun Devils hockey workout that left Matthew Mayich hospitalized in a coma.
content: As seven anonymous Arizona State Sun Devils hockey players called for their coaching staff to be placed on administrative leave, the House and Senate education chairs have also called for an independent investigation into the team’s workout that left a player hospitalized, still fighting for his life in a coma. Matthew Mayich remains on life support after an Aug. 20 workout in the blazing Arizona heat left him unconscious, and far worse than the players who wrote a 26-page letter that said they were initially told by head coach Greg Powers and the staff. On Monday, House Education Committee Chairman Matt Gress and Senate Education Committee Chairman Hildy Angius called on the Arizona Board of Regents to retain an independent investigator to examine the workout. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE In a letter sent on Monday to Board Chairman Doug Goodyear, Gress and Angius cited unresolved questions about whether the school followed its own policies and allegations from the anonymous players, who all fear retaliation by the current staff for speaking up about their account of the incident. Arizona State conducted an initial review, which acknowledged the hockey team’s staff didn’t submit a plan of training activities as part of the investigation. Also, the review’s findings were that Mayich didn’t receive proper hydration and had inadequate medical care after collapsing. ARIZONA STATE HOCKEY PLAYER, BLUES DRAFT PICK HOSPITALIZED AFTER COLLAPSING DURING TRAINING "Seven players who were on that field have raised serious questions that ASU’s own review does not answer," Gress said in a press release. "We need an independent investigation to determine whether ASU followed its own rules, who was responsible for protecting these athletes, and what happened when Matthew Mayich showed signs of distress. ASU should not be left to investigate its own conduct and decide whether anyone should be held accountable." The lawmakers are asking the Board of Regents to figure out who authorized the workout, which the players said was led by an ex-U.S. Army Green Beret, as well as "whether required vetting and heat-safety procedures were followed, why ASU’s strength and conditioning professionals did not review the workout, and why the final exercise proceeded after the outside consultant left." They also wish to have protection against retaliation for student-athletes and witnesses in this case. "Student-athletes should never have to choose between telling the truth and protecting their scholarship, roster spot, or playing time," Angius said. "If players fear retaliation for speaking about what happened to a teammate, the Regents need to act. They should protect these students and appoint an investigator who answers to the Board, not ASU." A response by Gress and Angius was requested from the Board of Regents by Oct. 9. In the 26-page letter from the players, which was obtained by The Athletic, the players said they were put through a "grueling" workout by the Green Beret that day, but while the ASU review said players were given a water break about 20 minutes into the workout, that wasn’t the case, they claimed. They said that the water break was around 40 minutes into the 75-minute activity, but it was just a few seconds. The players added that only about eight players actually drank water because they were the first to finish a bear crawl drill beforehand. "The first of us to finish had a few seconds at the bottles before being ordered back while others, including Matthew, were still crawling," the players’ letter read. "This was the only water break." The players also wrote that the ex-Green Beret admitted forgetting they needed a water break, but added he didn’t drink water during combat missions. As for Mayich, a draft pick of the NHL’s St. Louis Blues, the players wrote that their teammate showed signs of distress early on in the workout, saying he started to become disoriented during the bear crawl. Also, he was unable to carry a teammate during a buddy carry exercise. "No one at ASU properly monitored him during the workout and no one intervened," the letter read. title: Michael Monsoor had an escape route — the Medal of Honor recipient chose to save his teammates instead
description: Fox Nation's "Man of Honor" documentary tells the story of Petty Officer Michael A. Monsoor, who shielded fellow SEALs from a grenade on a rooftop.
content: On September 29, 2006, Petty Officer Michael A. Monsoor of the United States Navy sacrificed his life to save his fellow sailors. Fox Nation's new documentary, "Man of Honor: The Michael Monsoor Story" premieres Tuesday, exactly twenty years later, telling the story of the sailor behind the medal of honor. Monsoor received the award posthumously in a ceremony at the White House April 8, 2008, according to the Navy's website. Monsoor "distinguished himself through conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty," the site reads. While serving as an automatic weapons gunner in a combined SEAL and Iraqi Army sniper overwatch element during Operation Iraqi Freedom, Monsoor was placed in a confined sniper hide-sight between two SEAL snipers on an outcropping of a roof, which allowed the three SEALs maximum coverage of the area. MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH' An enemy fighter hurled a hand grenade onto the roof, which hit Monsoor in the chest and fell to the ground. He was located closest to the exit from their position, but he did not run. Instead, he immediately leaped to his feet and yelled, "Grenade!" to alert his teammates, who would have been unable to evacuate before the explosion. "Without hesitation and showing no regard for his own life, he threw himself onto the grenade, smothering it to protect his teammates who were lying in close proximity. The grenade detonated as he came down on top of it, mortally wounding him," the Navy wrote. HEGSETH UPGRADES ABBEY GATE MARINES' VALOR AWARDS AFTER 5-YEAR DELAY: 'THOSE DAYS ARE OVER' "Petty Officer Monsoor's actions could not have been more selfless or clearly intentional. Of the three SEALs on that rooftop corner, he had the only avenue of escape away from the blast, and if he had so chosen, he could have easily escaped. Instead, Monsoor chose to protect his comrades by the sacrifice of his own life. By his courageous and selfless actions, he saved the lives of his two fellow SEALs and he is the most deserving of the special recognition afforded by awarding the Medal of Honor." Monsoor was survived by his mother Sally, his father George, his sister Sara, and his two brothers, James and Joseph. title: Paul Finebaum roasts Lincoln Riley, says he's a 'complete fraud' as hot seat rumors swirl
description: Gary Patterson's USC defense allowed 504 yards and six touchdowns against the Oregon Ducks as Paul Finebaum called Lincoln Riley a "complete fraud."
content: The marketing coming out of the USC football program over the offseason was that the time for the Trojans to return to the national stage was "now." This time would be different, thanks to bringing in the number one recruiting class in the country and the hire of former TCU head coach Gary Patterson to run the defense. SC invested heavily in NIL, the coaching staff, and spectacular, state-of-the-art football facilities on campus to attract recruits and enhance their rest and recovery. A vital step as the Trojans travel nearly 20,000 round trip miles for road games this year in the Big Ten Conference. After years of middling-to-poor performances, this was supposed to be head coach Lincoln Riley's statement to the rest of college football that the Trojans were back. SC's first four games provided little opportunity, coming against overmatched opponents like San Jose State, Fresno State, Louisiana, and Rutgers. Still, SC's defense, always a topic of discussion, did little to show fans that the changes had "worked." DAN LANNING BLASTS USC AFTER OREGON'S WIN, AS LINCOLN RILEY OFFICIALLY ENTERS HOT SEAT IN LA While the first unit mostly played well in the first three games, the backups put up little resistance against overmatched offenses. Rutgers moved the ball at will, racking up 460 yards on offense while averaging 6.7 yards per play. That set up a gigantic matchup Saturday afternoon in Los Angeles against the Oregon Ducks. Oregon, expected to be one of the top few teams in the country, had shown some vulnerability with a blowout loss to Oklahoma State. The game was in Los Angeles, seemingly giving the Trojans an advantage. For a team with aspirations of reaching the College Football Playoff, it was a golden opportunity to make the case to a national audience while giving themselves some breathing room with tough games coming up against Ohio State and Indiana. Instead, it was more of the same for USC. The offense mostly held up their end of the bargain, racking up 446 yards and ripping off several explosive plays. But the SC defense was, well, awful. Oregon, despite playing most of the game with backup quarterback Dylan Raiola, punted only twice, gained 504 yards on offense with 7.4 yards per play, scored six touchdowns in six red zone visits and averaged over 10 yards per pass attempt. title: MLB putting playoff games exclusively on a streaming service is officially too far
description: MLB's Wild Card round moves two series exclusively to Peacock, frustrating baseball fans who must pay up to $19.99 monthly to watch postseason games.
content: This year, for the first time, several MLB postseason games will not air on television. As part of NBC's acquisition of the entire Wild Card round, the White Sox-Astros and Cubs-Padres series will air exclusively on the Peacock streaming service. One note for YouTube TV subscribers: you can stream the games through NBCSN on the YouTube TV app. It's not television, but it could save you the cost of a separate Peacock subscription. WATCHING THE NFL WILL COST MORE, REQUIRE MORE STREAMING SERVICES THAN EVER THIS SEASON The decision to air two postseason series exclusively on Peacock is unlikely to sit well with baseball fans, a demographic that has traditionally been slower to embrace streaming than fans of other major sports. In fact, many are still unhappy that MLB required Netflix subscriptions for Opening Night and the Home Run Derby. Wait until they discover Peacock isn't free, either. Peacock subscriptions range from $8.99 to $19.99 per month, or $89.99 to $199.99 per year. For years, the prevailing assumption across the industry was that MLB would be more reluctant than leagues like the NFL to move playoff games behind a streaming paywall. The viewership data has largely supported that belief. While streaming-exclusive NFL games still trail comparable broadcasts on traditional television, Amazon has shown that football fans are increasingly willing to follow the sport wherever it airs. Last season, Amazon Prime Video set an NFL streaming record by averaging 31.61 million viewers for the Packers-Bears Wild Card game. The broadcast also generated the highest single-day global viewership and the most concurrent streams in Prime Video history. HAVE YOU PAID FOR ALL THE SERVICES YOU NEED FOR THE NFL YET? MLB and the NBA must remember where they stand relative to the NFL. For context, the viewership for the Home Run Derby in June set a 20-plus-year low as it aired on Netflix for the first time. Still, fans frustrated by the limited availability of the Wild Card round should not blame NBC. The decision ultimately belongs to MLB. In previous years, ESPN aired the Wild Card round across ESPN and ESPN2. NBC no longer operates a national cable sports network and must reserve its broadcast network for local news, national news, and other daytime programming. Peacock was the only practical home for the remaining games. MLB could have sold NBC only half of the Wild Card round—the portion that will air on NBC—and licensed the remaining series to another television partner. Fox and TBS, both existing MLB rights holders, would have been logical candidates. Even ESPN, which retained a smaller package this season, could have aired the games. Instead, MLB determined that Peacock carrying the series exclusively was an acceptable trade-off. We suspect many baseball fans disagree. Streamers can also watch the games on FOX One (all the Fox and FS1 games) and HBO Max (all the TBS games). It shouldn't be this hard, confusing and expensive to watch live sports from home.

title: Congressman Joe Wilson praises NHL response to Ovechkin's Putin party ad, urges Capitals to follow suit

content: Rep. "I am grateful Commissioner Bettman took the opportunity to condemn war criminal Putin’s illegal invasion of Ukraine," Wilson said in a statement to OutKick/Fox News Digital. "At this point the League has done everything reasonable to make it clear they do not endorse the regrettable position held by Mr. Ovechkin. I hope the Capitals organization takes the opportunity to do the same." ALEX OVECHKIN SIGNS A ONE-YEAR DEAL TO RETURN FOR ANOTHER NHL SEASON WITH THE CAPITALS In a Sept. 28 letter to the South Carolina Republican, NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said Ovechkin participated in the video in a "personal capacity" and reiterated the NHL's opposition to Russia's invasion. "The NHL's position on Russia's invasion of Ukraine is clear and remains unchanged," Bettman wrote. "Since the outset of the war, the League has condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine and called for a peaceful resolution as quickly as possible." Ovechkin's campaign appearance prompted Wilson's letter The controversy centered on a United Russia campaign video featuring Ovechkin standing behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of Russian state-controlled network RT, also appeared in the advertisement, which aired ahead of Russia's Sept. 18-20 parliamentary elections. Wilson sent Bettman a letter Sept. 15, copying Capitals owner Ted Leonsis. He called Ovechkin's participation "shameful" and asked the league to review the matter. Wilson wanted the NHL to explain whether it had policies governing active players' participation in political advertisements for foreign parties or regimes. He also asked the league and Capitals to make clear that Ovechkin's participation did not represent either organization's position. His letter did not request a suspension or fine. Bettman's response drew a distinction between the political activities of individual players and the NHL's position. "Mr. Ovechkin is a Russian citizen, and his participation in the video was in his personal capacity," Bettman wrote. "The NHL is an international league, with players from many countries who bring with them their own individual views and perspectives. The League does not speak for its players on political matters, just as individual players do not speak for the League." Bettman's letter does not announce disciplinary action or identify a policy governing players' participation in foreign political advertisements. It also does not say whether the Capitals knew about or approved Ovechkin’s participation. content: Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre (CMLL) is one of the most historic pro wrestling promotions on the planet. title: Canadian broadcaster reportedly pulled after recording anti-Israel protest outside service
description: Newsreader Neil Herland's viral video of an anti-Israel protest outside a Toronto synagogue service on Yom Kippur reportedly led CBC to pull him off-air.
content: Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) newsreader Neil Herland was reportedly pulled off the air and faced an internal investigation after posting a video of an anti-Israel protest outside a synagogue service last week. Herland documented himself attempting to enter a service held by The Song Shul at the Meridian Arts Centre that was protested by about two dozen demonstrators holding signs and noisemakers while chanting, "Free, Free Palestine." "I'm a journalist. And I happen to be Jewish. On Yom Kippur I went to a synagogue service in Toronto and was met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building," Herland wrote on X. ANTI-ISRAEL AGITATORS CLASH WITH NYPD OFFICERS NEAR SYNAGOGUE In the video, a man shouted "Zionist alert" as Herland approached the building, and Herland was accosted by a man shouting, "You're going to hell" for attending the service, which featured Israeli diplomat and former Benjamin Netanyahu advisor Mark Regev as a speaker. In follow-up comments, Herland emphasized his growing concerns that Canada itself may no longer be safe for Jewish people. "My late father was an Austrian Jew who survived the Holocaust in Romania. And came to Canada as a refugee. This year I got an Austrian passport, in case Canada becomes unsafe for me as a Jew. I fear that moment is approaching, here in Canada and elsewhere," Herland wrote. "Jewish Canadians are living in a parallel world," he added. "Where police stand guard with guns outside synagogues. And Jewish schools, religious sites and businesses are targeted with bullets. And most Canadians have no awareness or understanding." CANADA'S CARNEY PLEDGES ACTION ON ANTISEMITISM AMID BACKLASH OVER NEW ANTI-HATE COUNCIL MEMBERS The video has since received 3.8 million views. After Herland posted his comments, The Toronto Sun reported Thursday that the veteran journalist was pulled from his on-air job and informed that he would be investigated based on complaints made to the company. Herland himself has not posted anything from his X account since Friday. Though it is unclear what complaints could have led to this decision, the organization Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) encouraged followers on X to send in complaints, claiming that Herland was purposefully misleading people about the situation. "On September 21, @CBC National Radio News Reader @NEWSneil Neil Herland posted on X that was 'met by [pro-Palestine] protesters trying to taunt and intimidate [him] from entering [a synagogue service in Toronto].' He shared an accompanying video of Palestine solidarity protesters." "However, Herland was on his way to the Meridian Arts Centre, not a synogogue, to see Mark Regev. Regev was not merely a teacher and former Israeli ambassador, but served in multiple high-ranking positions in the Israeli government, including as the Prime Minister’s Senior Advisor for Foreign Affairs and International Communications and the International Spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office," the CJPME's post read. CBC TELLS JOURNALISTS NOT TO CALL 9/11 ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’ IN INTERNAL GUIDANCE The post continued, "The reality is that Herland was telling a demonstrable lie to defame pro-Palestine activists. Join us in writing to the Values and Ethics Commissioner for CBC/Radio-Canada, Sherry Perreault, to express serious concerns about apparent ethics violations by Neil Herland." When reached for comment, CBC spokesperson Chuck Thompson told Fox News Digital that CBC would not comment on the matter but claimed that reporting has been filled with "errors and mischaracterizations." title: NCAA responds after Riley Gaines' lawsuit is dismissed, affirms compliance with Trump's executive order
description: Riley Gaines and fellow athletes plan to appeal after a federal judge dismissed their Title IX lawsuit, ruling the NCAA isn't a federal funding recipient.
content: The NCAA defended its record on women’s sports after a federal judge dismissed Riley Gaines’ Title IX lawsuit against the organization, emphasizing its current compliance with President Donald Trump’s executive order without directly addressing the allegations underlying the case. "The NCAA is proud to continually invest in and expand women’s sports and the NCAA is in full compliance with the Trump administration’s executive order on women’s sports," the organization said in a statement. The Independent Council on Women's Sports (ICONS) responded to the NCAA statement in a social media post later on Tuesday. "No promises to women. No assurances. No accountability. The weakest possible response: empty words on a page," the organization wrote. The response came one day after U.S. District Judge Tiffany R. Johnson granted summary judgment to the NCAA on the lawsuit’s remaining Title IX claims and directed the clerk to close the case. SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS Johnson did not determine whether the NCAA’s former transgender-athlete policies discriminated against female athletes. Instead, the Biden-appointed judge concluded that the evidence did not establish the NCAA as a recipient of federal financial assistance, a requirement for liability under Title IX. Gaines and more than a dozen other current and former female college athletes sued the NCAA in March 2024. They alleged the organization violated their Title IX rights through policies that allowed biological males to compete in women’s events and enter women’s locker rooms. The case focused heavily on the 2022 NCAA Division I Women’s Swimming and Diving Championships, where former University of Pennsylvania swimmer Lia Thomas won the 500-yard freestyle and shared a locker room with female competitors. Gaines, then representing Kentucky, tied Thomas for fifth place in the 200-yard freestyle. Gaines and the Independent Council on Women’s Sports, which funded the lawsuit, announced Monday that the plaintiffs intend to appeal the ruling to the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. "This momentary setback will not deter me or other women athletes in the least," Gaines said. "Rest assured, we will be appealing this decision." The NCAA’s statement did not address the planned appeal, the plaintiffs’ criticism of its previous policy or whether the organization maintains that it is categorically beyond Title IX’s reach. FEDERAL JUDGE DISMISSES DOJ LAWSUIT CHALLENGING CALIFORNIA POLICY ALLOWING BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS’ SPORTS The ruling centered on the NCAA’s concussion-research collaboration with the Department of Defense. The plaintiffs argued that the arrangement made the organization an indirect recipient of federal funding. Johnson found that the NCAA and the Defense Department maintained separate funding streams, with both contributing money to Indiana University for research conducted through the Concussion Assessment, Research and Education Consortium. "Here, there is no evidence that the NCAA ever received, or could have received, federal funds," Johnson wrote. "Thus, Plaintiffs’ Title IX claims cannot proceed." The policy challenged by Gaines and the other athletes is no longer in effect. Trump signed his "Keeping Men Out of Women’s Sports" executive order on Feb. 5, 2025, directing federal agencies to enforce Title IX based on biological sex. The NCAA changed its participation policy the following day, limiting competition on women’s teams to athletes assigned female at birth. The current rules contain no waiver allowing athletes assigned male at birth to compete on women’s teams, although they may practice with those teams and receive benefits such as medical care while practicing. See ncaa.org. ICONS co-founders Kim Jones and Marshi Smith have argued that the NCAA’s successful position that it was not covered by Title IX demonstrates that Congress should not provide the organization with additional authority through the Protect College Sports Act. Smith said the NCAA "cannot be trusted to regulate anyone’s sports — men’s or women’s" and urged members of Congress to oppose the legislation after it passed the Senate on Monday. title: Wyoming man kicks mountain lion in the face to save his dog, then fights it off bare-handed
description: Adam Borkhus kicked a mountain lion in the face to save his dog Diesel near Cody, Wyoming, but the predator then pounced and knocked him down.
content: Earlier this month, a Wyoming man found himself in a situation no dog owner ever wants to imagine. His Labrador was being attacked by a mountain lion. So he did the only thing he could think to do. He kicked the big cat in the face. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Adam Borkhus, a 33-year-old amateur wildlife photographer, was out looking for elk near Cody, Wyo., on Sept. 19 when he stopped along a remote road to change camera lenses and let his 2-year-old Lab, Diesel, out of the vehicle. Seconds later, he heard his dog yelp. Borkhus ran into the brush and found a mountain lion on top of Diesel. He had both a firearm and bear spray with him, but with his dog tangled up with the cat, he didn't want to risk hitting Diesel with either. So Borkhus went with Plan C: his foot. A swift kick square in the mountain lion’s face successfully got the cat off Diesel. Unfortunately, it also got the cat's attention. "The lion spun around and looked at me," Borkhus told Outside. "Then it pounced and hit me in the chest." Borkhus — who stands 6-foot-3 and weighs roughly 300 pounds — was knocked onto his back by the approximately 70-pound cat. He said he tried to keep its teeth away from his face and neck while punching it with his free hand before eventually grabbing its ear and wrenching it hard enough that the lion took off. The whole thing lasted somewhere around 20 to 30 seconds. Borkhus escaped with scratches to his hands, arm and face. Diesel somehow came out of the ordeal without any injuries. And, while his owner was busy throwing hands with a mountain lion, he retreated to the vehicle. BIG SKY, MONTANA WILDLIFE ENCOUNTER CAUGHT ON VIDEO AS MOOSE CHARGES TOWARD WOMAN AND HER DOGS He was waiting for Borkhus at the tailgate. Not much of a protective instinct there, but we’re sure Diesel is still a good boy anyway. What should you actually do if you encounter a mountain lion? Kicking a mountain lion in the face worked out remarkably well for Borkhus. But it probably shouldn't be your first line of defense. Wyoming Game and Fish says conflicts between humans and mountain lions are rare, but there are several things people should know when recreating in lion country. For starters, don't approach one — which should be obvious. Give the animal room to escape and remain calm if you encounter one. The department recommends speaking calmly and firmly rather than running away. Traveling in groups can also reduce the chances of surprising a mountain lion in the first place. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER And if things go sideways? Fight back. That's the official advice from Wyoming Game and Fish: "If a mountain lion attacks you, fight back and defend yourself." Outside also spoke with Mountain Lion Foundation researcher Joshua Lisbon, who recommended keeping dogs leashed or under strong voice control while in the wilderness. If a lion does grab your dog, Lisbon recommends using bear spray rather than physically jumping into the fight — even if your dog gets sprayed in the process. Obviously, that's much easier advice to process while sitting safely at home than when your best friend is underneath a mountain lion. But thank goodness for Borkhus and Diesel, it worked out this time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Love all things wildlife and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

title: Supreme Court takes up fight over Trump’s third-country illegal alien deportation policy
description: The Supreme Court cleared Trump's third-country deportation policy to proceed while justices prepare to hear the full legal challenge in December.
author_name: Jasmine Baehr, Shannon Bream, Bill Mears
content: The Supreme Court on Tuesday handed the Trump administration an interim victory in its ongoing immigration crackdown, clearing the way for officials to continue deporting illegal aliens to third countries while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. The justices granted the administration's request to stay a February ruling from a federal district court in Massachusetts that imposed additional procedural requirements before illegal immigrants could be removed to countries other than their own. The high court also agreed to hear the administration's challenge, treating its emergency application as a petition for review and ordering the parties to prepare for arguments during the court's December session. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson said they would have denied the administration's request for a stay. The decision gives the administration the immediate relief it sought as it presses ahead with third-country removals, even as the Supreme Court has yet to decide whether the policy remains. The dispute centers on the Trump administration's efforts to remove illegal aliens to third countries. Lower courts have not categorically prohibited those removals but have required procedures intended to give aliens an opportunity to raise claims that they could face persecution or torture in the destination country. The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, arguing that those requirements were interfering with its ability to carry out removals and disrupting sensitive diplomatic negotiations with countries willing to accept deportees. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY "The order below also undermines our standing abroad," the administration argued in its filing, according to the ruling. "Finding third countries willing and able to accept aliens is a delicate diplomatic endeavor." The government also argued that judicial intervention in those arrangements could cause "significant and irreparable harm to U.S. foreign policy." Attorneys challenging their policy pushed back, arguing that the lower court's ruling did not prevent the administration from conducting third-country removals but instead required the government to provide notice and an opportunity for illegal aliens to raise protection claims before they were sent abroad. "The judgment does not require release from detention, prohibit third-country removals, or undo existing arrangements," the challengers argued in their response. DHS' TOP LAWYER THREATENS PENALTIES FOR ATTORNEYS CLOGGING ASYLUM SYSTEM They alleged that illegal aliens removed without meaningful notice or an opportunity to raise country-specific protection claims had faced "prolonged and arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual assault, disappearance, and chain refoulement." Tuesday's order puts the February district court judgment on hold while the Supreme Court considers the case. The stay will remain in effect until the high court sends down its judgment. The decision gives the administration the immediate relief it sought as it presses ahead with third-country removals, even as the Supreme Court has yet to decide. "For the third time in 18 months, the Supreme Court has been called upon to stay the same local district judge’s campaign to halt the Trump Administration from removing illegal aliens including many of the worst-of-the-worst criminals to countries willing to receive them," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "The President will stop at nothing in his effort to make America safe again," Bis added. "Today’s ruling from the Supreme Court yet again affirms the lawfulness of the President’s homeland security agenda." title: Aaron Judge's calf strain could cascade into hamstring or Achilles injuries if rushed back, surgeon warns
description: Aaron Judge's soleus strain could lead to an Achilles rupture if he returned too soon, a surgeon warns, explaining the risks behind the New York Yankees' decision.
content: Aaron Judge desperately tried to return for the postseason after straining his calf, but the New York Yankees captain was wisely left off the Wild Card series roster. Judge sustained a moderate soleus muscle strain in his calf and received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection to try to speed up his rehab, but it wasn’t enough for him to make the roster for the team’s best-of-three series against the Boston Red Sox. Former college football quarterback-turned-foot-and-ankle surgeon Dr. Drew Burdi said if Judge came back too soon, he could leave himself exposed to further injury. "If you do go too fast, too soon, you could just make it a more severe injury. It's a soleus, so that could lead to overstraining (the) hamstring, up and down. So that's your calf muscle, or part of the calf muscle. You could put more strain on your Achilles, you could put more strain on your hamstrings, and that could lead to other injuries," Burdi told OutKick in a recent interview. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Burdi explained that strains involve varying degrees of muscle tearing and that a premature return to play could cause Judge’s strain to go from moderate to severe. A more severe tear could lead to a much longer recovery time, regardless of the treatment used. "If you're not ready to go back in yet, you tear it more, you can get to a point where the advanced conservative therapies like PRP injections, shock wave therapy, these guys are getting oxygen chamber therapy. This stuff can only go so far. The body can only adapt so much, can only heal so quickly," Burdi said. The worst potential outcome of Judge returning too soon could be an Achilles rupture. Burdi said such an injury is a possibility. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "Possibly, yeah, I mean, that's always a risk. Again, it, it kind of depends how he feels, but it's always a risk, and Achilles is always so scary because a lot of people, you see it in football, guys are jumping up on the sidelines and they come down weird and they rupture their Achilles. You're just like, wow, they don't even feel it before it happens," Burdi said. "That's tough because those are tough injuries to come back from. Guys do do it, but they're never quite the same." Burdi said that while Achilles injuries aren’t necessarily career killers, they are career changers. title: FBI's Andrew Bailey blasts exit 'lies' as he reveals real reason he's leaving agency
description: Andrew Bailey defends FBI Director Kash Patel and calls reports about his departure "lies," saying his exit is solely about raising his four children.
content: EXCLUSIVE — Andrew Bailey is heading home to Missouri, and the outgoing FBI co-deputy director has a blunt message for anyone suggesting turmoil at the bureau pushed him out. "This was 100% about my need to get home and raise my four small children," Bailey told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "I love my kids." Bailey, who announced Monday that he is leaving the FBI after just over a year, rejected suggestions that problems at the bureau played a part in his decision. KASH PATEL TO TOUT 'LARGEST' YEAR-TO-YEAR VIOLENT CRIME DROP IN US HISTORY "My decision to go home is based solely upon my need to be a parent to my four children," he said. He accused some news outlets of spreading "lies" about the reason for his departure and offered a forceful defense of FBI Director Kash Patel amid scrutiny of the bureau's leadership. "Any accusation that Director Patel has focused on anything other than fulfilling the president's promise to make America safe again are bold-faced lies," Bailey said. "We wake up every day and work early every morning and stay up late, oftentimes without sleep, to ensure mission accomplishment." ‘WORSE THAN WATERGATE’ NEW FBI FILES DETAIL AGENT’S PUSH TO JOIN TRUMP PROBE, INVESTIGATE ELON MUSK Patel, in his own statement Monday, said Bailey was leaving to return to his family in Missouri and praised his role in the FBI's overhaul. "Andrew's leadership at the FBI will be missed but we are grateful he answered the call to serve!" Patel wrote. He said Bailey had helped institute "critical reforms" and thanked him for his dedication to the bureau's mission. EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY' Bailey had left his post as Missouri attorney general to join the bureau in 2025. Asked whether anything about the job factored into the timing of his exit, Bailey insisted it did not. He said protecting children had been central to his work as Missouri attorney general and remained a priority at the FBI. FBI NABS MORE THAN 350 ALLEGED CHILD SEX ABUSE OFFENDERS According to Bailey, the bureau added 55 agents to child protection efforts and increased the number of victim service providers in field offices nationwide. During field office reviews, Bailey said he pressed staff on whether the bureau was "fulfilling our moral and legal obligation for victim notification and quality victim services." He called the FBI's victim services program "top-notch." FBI AND TEXAS AUTHORITIES ARREST 276 SUSPECTED CHILD PREDATORS, RESCUE 89 CHILDREN IN SWEEPING OPERATION Bailey portrayed his time in Washington as part of what he called a "truly historic transformation" of federal law enforcement under President Donald Trump and Patel. He credited the administration's creation of homeland security task forces and designation of Mexican drug cartels as foreign terrorist organizations with helping law enforcement pursue its mission. He also said the FBI had made it easier for state, tribal and local officers to join its task forces, adding more than 2,000 task force officers in a year. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SAYS FEDERAL AUTHORITIES HAVE ARRESTED MORE THAN 10,000 SUSPECTED GANG MEMBERS Bailey also pointed to what he described as a 20% reduction in homicides, more than 5,000 violent offenders arrested by the FBI and thousands of child victims identified and rescued as evidence that the administration's approach is working. The outgoing official also said the bureau had seized 3,258 kilograms of fentanyl in one year and arrested more than 4,200 members of foreign terrorist organizations. He cited 11,000 child victims located and identified, without specifying a time period for those latter two figures. Asked what the public might misunderstand about the FBI, Bailey described the scale of an agency with roughly 38,000 employees and 11,000 armed agents, charged with both criminal investigations and national security work. He said the leadership team had pushed resources from headquarters to field offices, where agents could have a greater impact. KASH PATEL REVEALS FBI'S CAPTURE OF ALL 10 MEMBERS OF MOST WANTED FUGITIVE'S LIST DURING HEARING "We've done so much to push resources out of headquarters back to the field where they can maximize their impact," he said. PROSECUTOR JOSEPH DIGENOVA RESIGNS FROM DOJ ROLE INVESTIGATING TRUMP-RUSSIA PROBES Bailey said more than 1,500 positions had been shifted from headquarters to field offices and that reducing layers of approval allowed agents to follow leads more quickly. He said the FBI processed more than 1.8 million DNA samples and reduced its backlog to zero for the first time in bureau history. Asked about political considerations at the FBI, Bailey said protecting the American people and upholding the Constitution were "the only considerations." When asked how he protected agents' ability to follow the facts, he pointed to those staffing and approval changes. He did not address whether he had seen politics influence a specific investigation or personnel decision. He rejected criticism of Patel's approach as resistance to change inside an organization accustomed to the status quo. Bailey alleged that the FBI had previously been "weaponized" against Trump and his family and said Patel wanted to return it to its core mission of protecting Americans and upholding the Constitution. "That is going to anger those sacred guardians of the status quo," Bailey said. As for what comes next, Bailey said he expects to return to public service someday, though he did not name a role. He traced a career that took him from the Army and two deployments to Iraq through Missouri state government and the FBI before returning to the reason he is leaving now. title: Supreme Court climate showdown jolted by Alito's last-minute decision
description: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from Suncor v. Boulder without explanation, while Elena Kagan faces separate recusal calls.
content: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from a closely watched case over climate change liability less than a week before oral arguments were scheduled to begin. Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, informed the parties' lawyers in a letter Monday that Alito had recused himself from Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County without providing an explanation. "Justice Alito does not take his duty to sit lightly. We do not know why he recused himself, as the reason has not been made public, but I do not expect his recusal to ultimately change the outcome of Suncor v. Boulder," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, told Fox News Digital. LAWSUITS COST EVERY AMERICAN HOUSEHOLD THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS. SUPREME COURT CAN HELP The justices were scheduled to kick off the 2026-27 term by hearing oral arguments in Suncor v. Boulder on Monday. The case centers on whether Boulder, Colorado, can use its state-law tort claims to sue oil and gas companies over their alleged role in contributing to climate change. The case has drawn scrutiny from Republicans, who argue Colorado officials are weaponizing the court system to get their environmental agenda enacted. "What they're doing is they're going around to these cities and these states, and using tort litigation, mass tort litigation, public nuisance lawsuits in state courts, and in a coordinated way to effectuate the same kind of a result, but just without having to go through their democratically elected officials," Steve Cox, former Alaska attorney general and current counsel to Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy , said in a Tuesday conference call. "It's not a fight about climate change," O.H. Skinner, former Arizona solicitor general and executive director of the Alliance for Consumers, said during a Tuesday conference call. "It's not a fight about climate science." "It's a fight about whether we're going to allow this maneuver to be what reshapes American society, and that's why I think everybody should care, irrespective of their views on climate change or their views on how to fix this problem or that problem. Do you want courts as our primary policymakers?" Skinner acknowledged that Alito did not come to his decision lightly, but said its "never good for the court" when a justice is missing from a ruling. CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION "This is part of why the left constantly screaming at the justices about recusal and other things is counterproductive for the country," Skinner said. "It doesn't help the court when they don't have their full complement." "At the same time, he made that decision knowing all of that and based on his own personal considerations, and we will never know all of the details of that. At the end of the day, it does not help the court to not have their full complement, but it is also not something that we think will be dispositive of the case, and it's not something that we think is noteworthy, other than that he made that decision based on his own considerations and didn't do it lightly, and he is making the right choice in his mind," Skinner continued. Alito's last-minute decision to recuse himself from the high-stakes climate case follows his January recusal in Chevron USA Inc. v. Plaquemines Parish, a Louisiana coastal erosion dispute, because he owned stock in ConocoPhillips, the parent company of one of the parties in the related litigation, Burlington Resources Oil and Gas Company. SUPREME COURT FINANCIAL DISCLOSURES REVEAL CONCERT TICKETS FROM BAD BUNNY'S LABEL, MILLIONS IN BOOK PAYMENTS Meanwhile, Justice Elena Kagan has faced calls to recuse herself from Suncor v. Boulder because she wrote the foreword to the Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence, which included a climate science chapter that was later criticized by Congress and Republican attorneys general as biased and was eventually removed. title: 'American Idol' alum Caleb Flynn convicted of murdering his wife

content: Former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn was convicted Tuesday of murdering his wife, Ashley Flynn, following an Ohio trial that exposed his secret affair and a series of messages about wanting his wife dead. Flynn was found guilty on all counts. Jurors also considered firearm specifications attached to several charges. Flynn broke down as the guilty counts came one after another, visibly shaking and wiping tears from his face. He repeatedly dropped his head toward the defense table, his eyes red and tear-filled when he looked back up. Sentencing is scheduled for 3 p.m. on Oct. 5. Flynn's lead attorney, Patrick Mulligan, said after the verdict that he expects the conviction to be appealed. "While we respect the system, certainly, we're disappointed," Mulligan told reporters. "I fully anticipate that there will be a notice of appeal filed, and this decision will be tested thoroughly in the Court of Appeals." Mulligan said Flynn faces possible sentences on the aggravated murder conviction ranging from 20 years to life, to life without parole, with an additional three years tied to the firearm specification. He said the first six counts will merge for sentencing. While speaking with reporters after the verdict, Miami County Prosecutor Paul Watkins thanked jurors and law enforcement before urging attention to shift away from Flynn. "To be quite honest, I'm tired of talking about Caleb Flynn," Watkins said. "It's time for the community, the media and everyone else to turn their focus on to Ashley." FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON FOUND GUILTY OF MURDERING ATTORNEY WHO VANISHED FROM BLOODY OFFICE Watkins then read a statement from Ashley's family, who said the verdict brought "justice and accountability" but could not bring Ashley back or "give the girls back their mother." "The cruelty of what happened to Ashley and the things we've been forced to hear and relive have at times felt unbearable," the family said. "But through all of it, we've held tightly to this truth: Ashley's life will not be defined by the way it ended. She'll be remembered for the way she lived." The family described Ashley's faith and devotion to her daughters before asking for privacy as they continue to grieve. "Please remember Ashley not for how she died, but for how beautifully she lived," the statement read. Prosecutors alleged Flynn shot Ashley in the back of the head inside their Tipp City home before staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. WATCH: Caleb Flynn prosecutors argued the evidence did not line up with his account FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Flynn pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges. Prosecutors built a largely circumstantial case against Flynn. Investigators never recovered the gun they alleged was used to kill Ashley, there was no eyewitness to the shooting and testimony showed no gunshot residue was found on Flynn. WATCH: Prosecutor argues Ashley Flynn was ‘executed’ in her sleep during closing arguments Jurors also heard two days of testimony from Flynn's former mistress, Alleigha Botner, who detailed their roughly year-and-a-half affair and walked them through many of the more than 107,000 messages the pair exchanged, including explicit discussions about Ashley's death. In one May 2025 message, Flynn allegedly wrote, "If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB The pair's communications in the hours before Ashley was killed also became a focus of the trial. SEND US A TIP Shortly after midnight Feb. 16, Flynn allegedly told Botner, "It's happening." GOT A TIP? He later wrote, "February 16th – day I'll never forget." "You're about to be free," Botner responded. "I choose you," Flynn replied. Botner testified she understood Flynn's plans at the time to mean he intended to finally leave Ashley and seek a divorce – not kill her. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Flynn's attorneys argued prosecutors failed to prove he killed Ashley, pointing to the missing murder weapon, lack of eyewitnesses and absence of gunshot residue while accusing investigators of rushing to judgment. "This simply is proven versus not proven," Mulligan told jurors during closing arguments Tuesday. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL While speaking with reporters after the verdict was read, Mulligan defended the decision to rest without calling witnesses. "It's simply a matter of them not showing the elements," Mulligan said of prosecutors. Asked why Flynn did not testify, Mulligan pointed to the three recorded police interviews jurors had already watched. "You heard his statement three times with the police," Mulligan said. "There wasn't any reason to put him on for a fourth time." Before the verdict, Laura Niemi, a jury consultant with Magna Legal Services and assistant research professor of psychology at Cornell University, told Fox News Digital that jurors faced two tasks: deciding which side's story best explained the evidence, then determining whether prosecutors proved each of the nine charges beyond a reasonable doubt. "The prosecution presented a cohesive circumstantial case. The defense challenged the links holding that case together," Niemi said. "The verdict is going to depend on whether jurors can see one reliable chain of evidence or unsupported leaps." Niemi said Flynn's affair and messages could make him appear "dishonest, callous, dangerous, even," but cautioned that "bad character is not proof of murder." Their significance, she said, depended on whether other evidence connected Flynn's words to Ashley's killing. Jurors deliberated for roughly three hours Tuesday before returning guilty verdicts on all nine charges.

title: Dengue fever outbreak triggers states of emergency in 3 southern counties
description: Three Florida counties declared emergencies as 190 locally acquired dengue fever cases were confirmed, with Hillsborough County reporting 170 infections.
content: Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency amid the spread of dengue fever in the state. As of Sept. 23, Pasco County, Hillsborough County and Pinellas County have made the declarations due to a spread of the mosquito-borne disease, according to each county’s news release. The local emergency declarations allow county officials to expedite mosquito-control operations, make emergency purchases, coordinate response efforts and, where applicable, seek state or federal assistance or reimbursement, the releases state. TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE Under Florida law, local emergency declarations expire after seven days unless they are renewed. A total of 190 locally acquired dengue cases have been confirmed across six Florida counties, according to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance report, which covered cases with onset through Sept. 19. Of the 190 locally acquired cases, 170 were reported in Hillsborough County, seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties, three in Orange County, two in Pasco County and one in Palm Beach County. The 190 locally acquired infections are separate from travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year. TICK-BORNE 'RABBIT FEVER' SPREADS WITH CASES REPORTED NEAR MAJOR METRO AREA Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida." Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health, makers of OFF!, said in a statement sent to Fox News Digital. "As dengue cases continue to be reported in the Tampa area, taking steps to help prevent mosquito bites is especially important," the expert went on. "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk." Stopping the spread The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) previously said crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to reports. FMCA has urged residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say. The FMCA also advises people to dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors. Symptoms and treatment Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition. Symptoms typically begin four to 10 days after the bite of an infected mosquito. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness. People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

title: Is your personal data changing what you pay online?
description: The FTC proposed a new enforcement policy on personalized pricing, warning companies that hide how personal data shapes the prices shoppers see.
content: Retailers and the companies working behind the scenes can collect information about where you are, what you search for, what you buy and how you behave online. The FTC says pricing systems can use personal data to estimate how much an individual consumer may be willing to spend. That concern is now getting serious attention in Washington. On Aug. 19, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission published a proposed enforcement policy statement aimed at personalized pricing. The FTC says it cannot ban the practice in every situation, but companies that fail to clearly tell consumers how personal data affects the prices they see could violate federal consumer protection law. So, could the information companies collect about you actually change the price, discount or product you see? Here's what the research shows and what you can do before your next online purchase. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com Dynamic pricing and personalized pricing work differently You've probably encountered dynamic pricing already. Dynamic pricing adjusts prices based on broader conditions such as supply, demand, available inventory, time or location. Rideshare fares may rise when lots of people need cars at once. Airline tickets and hotel rooms can also change as availability and demand shift. That does not mean every shopper will always see the exact same dynamic price. Timing, location and other market conditions can change quickly. Personalized pricing is different because information about a particular consumer helps determine the price or offer that person receives. That means two people looking for the same product could potentially receive different offers because of information connected to them. There's also price steering. A retailer may leave the actual prices alone while changing the order of the products shown to you. FTC research found that pricing tools can use consumer data to give certain products more prominent placement, including potentially showing higher-priced products first. The FTC says consumers generally expect prices to change because of supply and demand. What can come as a surprise is a price influenced by someone's browsing habits, buying history or other personal information. What companies can potentially learn about you FTC research into surveillance pricing found that third-party pricing companies can use surprisingly detailed information when helping retailers tailor prices, promotions or product rankings. That information can include: The FTC found that the pricing intermediaries it examined worked with at least 250 clients selling goods and services ranging from groceries to clothing. The FTC's research also found that companies can combine first-party information with data from outside sources. Those sources can include loyalty programs, reservation systems, e-commerce platforms and data brokers. That does not show that every one of those clients charges individualized prices. It does show that technology exists to combine detailed consumer information and use it to influence prices, discounts and which products shoppers see. A 2026 rideshare test found big price differences A newer investigation brings the Uber example much closer to today. In June 2026, Consumer Reports published results from a months-long study of Uber and Lyft pricing. The investigation used 174 volunteers who checked more than 40 routes across the U.S. For the 30 virtual routes in its analysis, Consumer Reports found a median gap of 42.4% between the lowest and highest price groups. On some routes, people checking the same trip within minutes of one another received several different prices. Consumer Reports designed the study to reduce the effects of time-based pricing by having volunteers check routes at roughly the same time. However, the investigation could not control for every factor inside Uber's and Lyft's pricing systems, including driver supply, estimated arrival times, traffic, routing differences and network delays. Uber and Lyft disputed Consumer Reports' conclusions. Both companies said they do not use personal data to personalize base fares and do not engage in behavioral or surveillance pricing. So, the study shows that riders can receive significantly different prices for similar trips checked around the same time. It does not prove those price differences were caused by personal data. WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE Shoppers have also seen different grocery prices online Online groceries have produced another eye-opening example. In December 2025, Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union reported that nearly three-quarters of the grocery items they tested on Instacart were offered at different prices to different shoppers. The investigation involved 437 shoppers across four U.S. cities. Some items showed differences of as much as 23% between the lowest and highest prices. Researchers also found that totals for identical baskets varied by an average of about 7%. Using an Instacart figure for how much a household of four spends on groceries, the researchers estimated that a similar difference over a year could amount to roughly $1,200. Instacart strongly disputed that annual extrapolation and said the limited tests should not be treated as though a household would continually pay higher prices throughout an entire year. The company also said the pricing tests were randomized and did not use personal information, demographics, shopping history or individual behavior to decide who received each price. Instacart ended the item price tests in December 2025. The company now says customers shopping for the same item at the same store location at the same time will see the same item price. So, the investigation showed that Instacart shoppers could receive different prices during those tests. It did not prove that Instacart used personal profiles to select those prices. Online price personalization goes back years Researchers were finding customized shopping experiences long before today's AI-powered pricing systems. In 2014, Northeastern University researchers studied 16 major retail and travel websites and found evidence of price discrimination or personalized search results on nine of them. CheapTickets and Orbitz offered reduced hotel prices to members. Expedia and Hotels.com steered some users toward more expensive hotels. Home Depot and Travelocity personalized search results for mobile users. Priceline personalized the order of hotel search results based on a user's history of clicks and purchases. However, the researchers said those different result orders did not correlate with price, so they did not classify that Priceline example as price steering. The researchers also emphasized that most of their experiments on the 16 sites did not uncover price steering or price discrimination. Then, in 2015, ProPublica found that The Princeton Review charged different prices for an online SAT tutoring package depending on a customer's ZIP Code. Prices for its Premier package ranged from $6,600 to $8,400. ProPublica found that people living in ZIP Codes with larger Asian populations were 1.8 times as likely to be offered a higher price, regardless of income. The Princeton Review said its pricing was based on the costs of running its business and competitive conditions in each market. It said its prices were set by geographic region rather than a customer's race. That example was geographic pricing rather than a retailer setting a unique price for each individual shopper. It still shows how data connected to where someone lives can lead different groups of consumers to receive different prices. 13 ways to reduce personalized tracking when you shop There is no guaranteed trick for getting the lowest online price. However, you can reduce some of the information retailers, data brokers and tracking companies can connect to you while giving yourself more ways to compare offers. 1) Check the price before signing in Look at a product while signed out before logging into a retailer or loyalty account. Then compare the price or promotion after signing in. A difference does not automatically mean personalized pricing. Membership discounts and other promotions can also explain a change. Still, comparing both views gives you more information before you buy. 2) Use guest checkout when you can If you do not need a retailer account, consider checking out as a guest. That keeps the purchase from automatically becoming another entry in a logged-in shopping history. Guest checkout does not make you anonymous. A retailer may still receive information such as your email address, payment details, shipping address, browser data or device information. 3) Reject optional tracking cookies When a website gives you the choice, reject optional advertising and tracking cookies. The site may still need essential cookies for things such as your shopping cart, security and payment. Rejecting optional cookies mainly reduces some tracking and advertising activity. 4) Reduce the data brokers have about you Retailers are only one source of personal information. Data brokers and people ssearch companies collect information from numerous sources and combine it into profiles. FTC research found that pricing systems can incorporate third-party data, including information from data brokers. Reducing what's available through those companies may shrink one part of your broader data footprint. It does not guarantee a lower price or prevent a retailer from using information it collects directly from you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. HOW SCAMMERS BUILD A PROFILE ON YOU USING DATA BROKERS 5) Compare prices in a private browsing window A private browsing window generally creates a separate browsing session that does not use the normal session history and most existing cookies from your regular browsing window. It does not make you anonymous. Websites may still see information such as your IP address and information you provide directly. The FTC specifically points to private browsing as one step consumers might use when trying to avoid higher personalized prices. 6) Use privacy opt-outs when they are offered Look for choices such as Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information, Your Privacy Choices or controls for targeted advertising. The options available depend on the retailer and the privacy laws that apply where you live. 7) Limit precise location access Review which shopping apps can access your precise location. If an app does not need your exact location, consider switching to approximate location or turning location access off. Keep in mind that websites and apps may still estimate your general location from other information, including your IP address. 8) Review app tracking permissions Your phone may let you limit how apps track activity across other apps and websites. Turning off unnecessary tracking can reduce some third-party data collection. It will not stop a retailer from using information you provide directly through its own app, website or account. For step-by-step instructions on iPhone and Android, see our guide to improving your digital privacy. 9) Clear cookies and stored site data periodically Cookies can help websites recognize the same browser when you return. Clearing them can remove some of those stored identifiers. However, other tracking methods may still recognize your device, and signing back into an account reconnects your activity to that account. 10) Compare the app and website Before making an expensive purchase, check the retailer's website and app. Then compare the same product with other sellers. Any difference you find may have a simple explanation, but comparison shopping gives you a better picture of the available prices. 11) Use price-history tools For products supported by price-history services, check whether today's deal really is lower than recent prices. A retailer's sale banner only tells you what it wants to advertise. Historical pricing can give you additional context before you buy. 12) Read the fine print on discounts A lower price may require a loyalty membership, subscription, automatic renewal or another commitment. Make sure the offer actually saves you money after those conditions are included. 13) Consider using a VPN A VPN can hide the public IP address assigned by your internet provider and replace it with the address of the VPN server. That can make your IP-based location appear different. The FTC specifically lists VPN use as something consumers might try when they are concerned about personalized prices. A VPN cannot erase your retailer account, purchase history, cookies or location information that an app already has permission to access. Websites may also use other signals to recognize you. For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. Kurt's key takeaways What gets my attention here is how much information can now go into deciding what we see when we shop online. We do not have evidence that every retailer is quietly setting a different price for each person, and seeing two different prices does not automatically prove personal data caused the change. What we do know is that companies have technology capable of using location, browsing behavior, shopping history and other information to shape prices, discounts and product rankings. My advice is to compare prices before you buy, limit tracking you do not need and avoid assuming the first offer on your screen is the best one available. The less unnecessary information you hand over, the less there is to feed into a detailed profile about how you shop.
