title: Stephen A Smith and ESPN should consider a full-time reunion with Skip Bayless
description: Skip Bayless returned to "First Take" for a monthly role, but a full-time reunion with Stephen A. Smith could revitalize ESPN's debate show.
content: Last week, Skip Bayless returned to ESPN to reunite with his former debate partner, Stephen A. Smith, on "First Take." Under a new agreement, Bayless will appear on the program on the final Friday of every month. The history between Bayless and the show is significant. ESPN built "First Take," its daily debate program, around Bayless in 2007. Like Smith today, Bayless initially debated a rotating cast of analysts. He pushed the network to give Smith a recurring role, but executives initially resisted after Smith's previous, unsuccessful stint at ESPN. SKIP BAYLESS BOOSTS STEPHEN A'S SLUGGISH "FIRST TAKE" RATINGS BY 24% ON THEIR REUNION SHOW Smith eventually joined the show on a weekly basis and became Bayless' full-time debate partner in 2012. Together, Bayless and Smith drew an average audience that well exceeded ESPN2's typical viewership, often outperforming the main ESPN channel during the same time slot. Bayless left ESPN for FS1 in 2016 to launch "Undisputed," a similarly formatted debate program designed to compete directly with "First Take." Bayless partnered with Shannon Sharpe at FS1, while Max Kellerman replaced him at ESPN. Comparing the success of the two programs warrants context. ESPN reached three to five times as many morning viewers as FS1 at the time. Even so, "First Take" lost more than 20% of its audience after Bayless departed. ESPN responded by moving the program from ESPN2 to ESPN. After the move, "First Take" attracted roughly twice the audience of "Undisputed." The gap widened after Kellerman left "First Take" and Sharpe exited "Undisputed." By 2023, "First Take" regularly drew three to four times as many viewers as its FS1 rival. Bayless ultimately left the network in 2024. Smith and Bayless are in different positions than they were in 2012. At the time, Bayless was one of ESPN's most viral personalities. Smith had been relegated to local radio. Today, Smith is among the most influential figures in sports media, having recently signed a five-year, $100 million contract with ESPN. Until recently, Bayless was the one without a television platform. Bayless' transition to digital media has been rocky. His weekly show with his wife averages about 1,000 views per episode on YouTube. He has not uploaded a new episode of his eponymous podcast in nearly a year. He has, however, recently gained traction through a venture with former NFL cornerback Aqib Talib called "Gridiron." Although Bayless accepted an invitation to become a monthly contributor to "First Take," the arrangement is undoubtedly awkward. Returning to the program you built, alongside the co-host whose career you helped build, in a limited role cannot be easy. It is also reasonable to wonder whether Bayless believes Smith owes him the same full-time opportunity that he extended in 2012. OutKick asked Bayless about that possibility following Friday's show. He did not respond. Honestly, Smith should consider it. The current version of "First Take" has grown stale. The format of pairing Smith with two rotating panelists produces inconsistent results. Michael Irvin, Dan Orlovsky, Chris "Mad Dog" Russo and Marcus Spears are strong contributors. Much of the remaining rotation, however, consists of interchangeable ESPN personalities, including Chris Canty, Kimberley Martin and Domonique Foxworth. Perhaps a more effective approach would be to reduce the size of the rotation and feature only the program's strongest personalities alongside Smith and perhaps Bayless. On Friday, Spears joined Smith and Bayless for most of the show. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "First Take" is still one of ESPN's highest-rated programs, but its growth lags behind the network's other studio shows. ESPN's monthly press releases routinely emphasize year-over-year gains for "Get Up," "The Pat McAfee Show," "NFL Live" and other programs, but not "First Take's." Smith himself has acknowledged the importance of evolving the program. Explaining why he wanted Kellerman removed from the program, Smith said it was necessary "to keep things fresh and make changes every three years." It has now been five years since Kellerman's departure. Bayless also brings out a different side of Smith, one that is generally more appealing to viewers. The formula is simple but effective: Bayless makes a provocative claim, Smith responds with theatrical indignation, Bayless defends his position and the segment often ends in good fun. While not the most intellectually rigorous form of television, it's better than the pandering, faux sophistication that has come to define too much of sports television. Despite his branding, Smith rarely offers a profound opinion on sports. He believes the Cowboys underachieve, Stephen Curry is the greatest shooter in NBA history and LeBron James is the second-greatest player in basketball history. Those are conventional positions. In fact, Smith tends to expose a lack of depth when he tries to offer a unique opinion. His recent commentary on LSU, Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson suggested a limited familiarity with those subjects. Smith performs best opposite a contrarian, like Bayless. The same dynamic explains why his appearances with Will Cain and Sean Hannity on Fox News often generate more interest than his solo political monologues. Smith, who has frequently responded to criticism from OutKick, may view that comparison as a slight. It is not. Michael Wilbon and Tony Kornheiser remain the gold standard of sports television because their partnership is stronger than either host individually. The same principle applies to Smith and Bayless. With Pat McAfee surpassing Smith as ESPN's most relevant personality, a full-time reunion with Bayless would represent an opportunity to regain momentum. Debating Chris Canty one day and Gerald McCoy the next does not. ESPN may be reluctant to approve a broader reunion for Bayless. Our understanding is that there was pushback about bringing him back even in a limited role. Executive Mike Foss, who oversees the network's daily studio programming, has emphasized a shift away from "embrace debate," the slogan that once defined "First Take," in favor of authenticity and conversation. Ratings trends suggest that approach has benefited much of ESPN's daytime lineup. But not "First Take." "First Take" is a debate show. The program has never fully recaptured the cultural relevance and virality it reached with Bayless and Smith together. It is also 2026. As Hollywood continues to demonstrate, nostalgia remains a more reliable commercial strategy than reinvention.

title: Dumping stocks after Trump’s 2016 win was ‘stupid,’ NYU professor admits
description: Scott Galloway reveals his emotional reaction to Trump's 2016 election victory led to what he calls his biggest investment mistake, costing him dearly.
content: NYU professor Scott Galloway said Monday on "The Prof G Pod" that he sold all of his stocks in an emotional reaction to President Donald Trump’s 2016 election victory, taking a major tax hit before buying back into a more expensive market months later, a decision he estimated cost him 40% of his liquid net worth in stocks. Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU Stern, called the move his "biggest investment mistake" during the "Office Hours" edition of the podcast as he warned listeners about allowing emotions to drive investment decisions. "So when he was elected in 2016, I sold all my stocks," he said. "That was stupid. The market ripped for the next year. There was so much insecurity about him actually winning that the fear had been priced in. Stocks ripped up." THE RICH HAVE ONE FINANCIAL HABIT MOST AMERICANS IGNORE AT THEIR PERIL Galloway said the selloff also triggered taxes on significant capital gains while he was living in New York. He said he returned to the market about six months later after stocks had risen between 10% and 20%, compounding what he described as the cost of the decision. "So you could argue, at least notionally, that decision cost me 40% of my liquid net worth in stocks," Galloway said. White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital Tuesday that Galloway’s continued criticism of Trump reflected what he characterized as an obsession with the president. "Scott Galloway should immediately seek psychiatric help to treat his severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain," Ingle said. GOVERNMENTS CAN TAKE YOUR STOCKS WITHOUT YOUR PERMISSION. IT HAPPENS ALL THE TIME Galloway criticized Trump, saying he believed the president's economic and foreign policies could ultimately damage the U.S. economy. "I think the president is a f---ing idiot and a stain on the American experience and that the grand sum of all of these head up your a-- economic and foreign policy decisions will eventually crash this economy or result in long-term structural damage that will take decades if not generations to repair," Galloway said. The stock market rose substantially following Trump's 2016 presidential victory. According to the federal government's 2017 Economic Report of the President, the S&P 500 climbed 3.4% in November 2016 and reached a then-record high later that month. The 2018 report said the index went on to gain 19.4% in 2017, posting increases in 11 of the year's 12 months. DAVID MARCUS: TRUMP DERANGEMENT SYNDROME ISN'T MENTAL ILLNESS, IT'S MASS HYSTERIA Galloway said his experience reinforced his view that investors should remain in the market rather than attempt to anticipate political or economic turning points. While discussing current elevated valuations, he recommended diversification instead of trying to predict exactly when stocks will decline. "Trying to guess when the top happens is dangerous," Galloway said. "Probably my biggest investment mistake was the emotional reaction I had to the 2016 election of Donald Trump." "And what the government does matter, but the majority of the economy just grinds on regardless of who is tweeting what or not tweeting what," he continued. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Galloway predicted Trump would ultimately abandon his 2024 presidential campaign as part of a plea agreement that would keep him out of jail. Trump remained in the race and returned to the White House after winning the 2024 presidential election. title: Hero K-9 sniffs out hidden $6M cocaine shipment along US-Canada border
description: Customs and Border Protection officers and a canine unit uncovered 174 vacuum-sealed cocaine packages hidden in a tractor-trailer's modified floor.
content: FIRST ON FOX: Officers with Customs and Border Protection (CBP) seized a shipment of 450 pounds of cocaine worth an estimated $6 million at a port along the U.S. northern border with Canada last Tuesday, the agency revealed to Fox News Digital. After CBP conducted a routine inspection on a northbound commercial tractor-trailer driven by a 21-year-old Canadian man, a physical inspection revealed modifications to the floor, leading to a K-9 inspection. Agents soon uncovered 174 vacuum-sealed packages carrying cocaine. "This significant seizure highlights the exceptional vigilance, advanced training and relentless dedication of our CBP officers and canine teams at the Lewiston Bridge border crossing," Sharon Swiatek, acting port director for the Area Port of Buffalo, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. BORDER AGENTS UNCOVER $20M COCAINE STASH HIDDEN BENEATH TRUCK FLOORBOARDS IN MASSIVE BUST The seizure follows other recent cases involving drugs concealed in commercial trucks caught by CBP in recent months, demonstrating the continued challenge federal agencies face in stopping the flow of narcotics across both the U.S. southern and northern borders despite greatly reduced illegal crossings. Since President Donald Trump returned to office at the outset of 2025, border crossings have plummeted at the southern border — an issue that captured much public attention in the 2024 presidential election. Since October 2024, illegal border crossings have dropped from over 240,000 to just 12,200 this past August, a reduction of over 94%. The drop also extends to the northern border. There, encounters have plummeted from over 17,000 to under 6,100, a 64% decrease. TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER Even so, CBP has continued to battle the smuggling of drugs, weapons and human trafficking rings into — and out of — the U.S. While the majority of CBP’s work focuses on securing the American border, a number of its busts have centered on preventing dangerous shipments from entering neighboring countries as well. According to Swiatek, the CBP acting port director, it’s a mission that carries the same gravity as its southern counterpart. "While a large focus of our border security mission is on inbound threats, our officers remain equally sharp during outbound operations to dismantle transborder criminal networks, disrupt the flow of dangerous narcotics and protect communities on both sides of the border," Swiatek said. NEVADA MAN FUNNELED 140 GUNS TO VIOLENT MEXICAN DRUG CARTELS, INCLUDING POWERFUL 'MILITARY-STYLE' RIFLES: DOJ In April, for example, CBP announced it had prevented a car carrying a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, 16 AK rifles, 24 rifle magazines, 16 rifle stocks, 20 pistol grips and other weapon parts from crossing the border into Mexico. "CBP prevented these dangerous weapons from wreaking havoc on the good people of Mexico," Acting Deputy Commissioner Ron Vitiello said at the time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With respect to the Tuesday cocaine seizure, the shipment has been referred to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Buffalo for investigational review, according to CBP.

title: Foiled terror plot at bomber base signals wider threat to US military installations: expert
description: Five men arrested near RAF Fairford may have planned a complex, coordinated VBIED attack on U.S. strategic bombers, a former intelligence official says.
content: Five men arrested near a key U.S. bomber base in the U.K. on Sunday may have planned a "complex," coordinated attack with potentially far-reaching security implications for American military installations globally, a former U.S. intelligence officer warned. As counterterrorism police investigated after officers detained the suspects near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, a former Pentagon official also said President Donald Trump would ultimately be the one to decide the consequences if indeed the "trail leads to Tehran." The men were initially held on suspicion of offenses under Britain’s Explosives Act before being arrested on terrorism charges in connection with the airfield, a key U.S. Air Force hub and the primary European base for American strategic bombers. On Sunday, Trump said U.S. authorities had been monitoring the suspects prior to their capture. FORMER UK PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR WARNS EUROPE ‘WE DON’T WIN’ IN WAR WITHOUT US SUPPORT "We had them under investigation," Trump told reporters in Chicago. "They were looking to do big damage to our fort." "It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know. We worked with a lot of them. We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," Trump added. According to Sky News, counterterrorism police were investigating whether Iran is linked to the suspected bomb plot. Former Trump White House official Morgan Murphy also told Fox News Digital that British authorities are leading the investigation alongside U.S. law enforcement and intelligence. "Every phone, bank record and rental receipt will be run through British and American intelligence, and if the trail leads to Tehran, it will be found," Murphy clarified. "But as American airmen and bombers seem to have been the target, Air Force investigators on the base, the FBI in London, and American intelligence will likely all work the case." "If conclusive evidence proves Iran is behind an attempted attack on U.S. forces, the American president will ultimately decide how Tehran pays," Murphy added. BRITAIN INTRODUCES SWEEPING NEW POWERS TO TARGET FOREIGN STATE-LINKED GROUPS INCLUDING IRAN'S IRGC Former Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) officer Andrew Badger told Fox News Digital the number of suspects and vehicles involved raised the possibility of a sophisticated operation. "We are going to see elevated security protocols across Europe, across the U.K., and across the entire world for any U.S. installation," the former case officer said. "This is a very significant threat, and again, seeing that we had five individuals involved and three different reported vans at the scene, this could have been a very complex, highly orchestrated operation," Badger, who teaches on grey-zone warfare at the University of Oxford, added. "This isn't just some type of amateur lone wolf operation," he said, noting Fairford’s strategic importance to the U.S. military. "Fairford is also where the U.S. houses its strategic bombers for Europe as well as the rest of the world." He said a potential attack posed broader risks beyond the airfield itself, which he said "could have had significant security implications. It could have damaged the nearby area." HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY "They could have tried to use a VBIED or a vehicle-borne explosive device where the first van could have gone off at the front gate, and then the other vans would have gone in and tried to go for the strategic bombers," Badger said. British authorities have not publicly identified who they believe was behind the suspected plot or announced a motive, but RAF Fairford had taken on greater strategic importance during the war with Iran. The U.K. government previously authorized U.S. forces to use the Royal Air Force bases Fairford and Diego Garcia for limited defensive operations, including destroying Iranian missiles and launchers at source. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later warned that any base used to attack Iranian territory would be considered a legitimate target. "Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory is a legitimate target for our forces," the IRGC said, according to reports. "Tehran warned London in July to keep American bombers off Fairford, and if this plot traces back to Iran, the answer must be more bombers, not fewer," Murphy said. IRAN EXPERT BRANDS ISLAMIC CENTER OF ENGLAND IRAN'S 'UK OFFICE,' URGES IMMEDIATE CLOSURE A local councilor told Reuters there had been a recent security alert at Fairford and surveillance had been stepped up. "So there was a specific threat about six weeks ago from the Iranians on this base. At the time, there was increased surveillance around the area," he told the outlet. Badger, however, cautioned against assuming Iran was responsible while pointing to other potential threats. "This could be Iran trying to gain strategic leverage in negotiations, but there are other actors as well," the co-author of The Great Heist, added. "There's Russia, who has been launching a campaign of gray zone or hybrid warfare attacks across Europe, as well as Islamic extremists, which are still a significant threat here in the U.K." "Was this some type of retaliation by Iran to perhaps try to gain leverage or to try to inflict a cost on the U.S. for withdrawing from these negotiations? Again, we don't know for sure, but it is a possibility," Badger said. Badger also pointed to RAF Welford, a major U.S. ammunition storage facility that primarily supports operations at RAF Fairford. US EMBASSIES IN MIDDLE EAST WARN AMERICANS OF 'UNFORESEEN ESCALATION' AS LATEST STRIKES HIT IRAN "Welford is the second-largest weapons and ammunition depot in all of Europe," Badger said, noting that the facility where the U.S. stores ammunition "could have been a target as well." "Other bases across Europe, including European and U.S. partners, have already been on a heightened state of alert," Badger continued. "But of course, after this attack, they're going to be in an even more heightened state. You're going to have more frequent security patrols." "There are reports that RAF Fairford was put onto what's called the Delta alert, which is the highest state of security alert within the military base system," Badger said. "So this is basically that 'an imminent terrorist attack is inbound,'" he concluded. Iran's Embassy in London denied any connection with the incident in a public statement on Monday. title: Lindsay Clancy's defense says 'complete lack of evidence' amid retrial delay
description: Lindsay Clancy returned to court for the first time since her trial ended in a deadlocked jury and the judge declared a mistrial on Sept. 4. Several motions were addressed, with Massachusetts Judge Kevin Sullivan scheduling another hearing for Nov. 2 to discuss matters further, including a potential retrial that could be months away.
content:
Speaking to reporters outside the courthouse following today's hearing, Lindsay Clancy's civil attorney Andrew Meyer issued a sharp warning about how hospitals treat postpartum mental health crises.
When asked by Fox News Digital whether there is a "public danger” that hospitals are still treating people in these situations, Meyer asserted that the danger stems from a lack of proper treatment and adequate follow-up for severe conditions.
"I think there's a public danger when we don't have a proper response to women who have postpartum depression, ultimately psychosis," Meyer said.
"And when they're simply given medication to treat the problem and there's no follow up, they're treated over some type of, it was a Zoom-type of treatment. And there wasn't, it wasn't taken seriously. There were no, there was not adequate communication between the doctors."
“The various people who were basically writing her off, telling her to go about her way and when in fact, she was a danger,” he added. “She was screaming for help for months and she wasn't getting it. And that's what leads to this kind of tragedy. It never should have happened. This entire matter could have been avoided. All the lives that have been tragically affected by these failures are going to be addressed.”

title: Sunny Hostin addresses resurfaced reports questioning her claim she was a holdout juror in 1991 murder trial
description: Sunny Hostin addressed claims she wasn't the holdout juror on a 1990s murder case, clarifying she held out on a different count than the man cited in the reporting did.
content: "The View" co-host Sunny Hostin addressed reporting about her identifying herself as a holdout juror in a gruesome murder case in the 1990s during the show's podcast Monday after resurfaced reports from multiple outlets said it was a man who was the holdout juror. "Someone on the internet dug up a Daily News article from 1991 that profiled another, different person that was a holdout juror. You were quoted in this article too, but they were talking about a man that other people pointed to as saying this is the reason we couldn't come to a verdict," Brian Teta, the producer of "The View," noted during the "Behind the Table" podcast. Hostin said she remembered him and explained that there were different counts in the case. ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW "So, as I recall, and look it up for yourselves, there were three counts, I believe. One was second-degree murder, but it was intentional. Then there was the defense to that was, we could consider the insanity defense, meaning that he committed the crime, but he was not criminally responsible because of a mental disease or defect. And there was a third count, or a third issue that we dealt with, and that issue was the desecration of Monika Beerle's remains," Hostin said. The co-host of "The View" said she felt strongly that he tried to hide the fact that he killed Beerle by dismembering her remains and that he should be found guilty of that count. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM "He was insane when he killed her," Hostin said. "And he said that, he confessed that he didn't realize that she was even dead. But then he decides to dismember her. I just thought that was so clear and gruesome and despicable to do that to someone's remains. I thought that he should be found guilty of that. And everyone else did too, except for this one guy. And we were, like, kind of looking at him, like, 'That was the easy one.' It was always the easy one. But we could not reach a unanimous verdict on that count." Teta noted that Hostin didn't mention this male juror on the show when she identified herself as the holdout juror in this trial. She clarified during the podcast that she was the holdout on a different count, the count related to the insanity defense. During the liberal talk show earlier this month, Hostin said she was a holdout juror on a case in which a man murdered his roommate and dismembered her. Hostin felt strongly that the man, Daniel Rakowitz, also known as "Butcher of Tompkins Square Park," was insane. The co-host shared an excerpt from a report in The New York Times about the trial, which was held in 1991. Rakowitz was acquitted by reason of insanity. Hostin, whose maiden name is Cummings and whose first name is Asunción, was quoted in a Feb. 23, 1991, New York Times report about the trial, which said, "Several jurors questioned afterward said one holdout juror was principally responsible for preventing them from returning a guilty verdict." LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN "The View" co-host presented the article on the show while explaining the case. "That was me. It was because I saw clearly that he was psychotic," Hostin said during the show Sept. 22. After revealing she was the holdout juror on the case, the New York Post reported that other contemporaneous accounts identified an unemployed man as the principal holdout. The Post wrote that "Jurors told The Post, Newsday, the Daily News and the Associated Press that the actual holdout was an unemployed man who wanted to keep the trial going so he could continue getting paid by the court for his civic duty." title: California college lecturer removed after erupting at student over question on Native Americans

content: A California college lecturer is "no longer in the classroom" after a viral video showed her ordering a student out of class during a heated exchange over his question about alcoholism rates among Native Americans, according to a comment posted by the university on TikTok on Sept. 18. The confrontation unfolded at California State University San Marcos and spread rapidly online after clips posted to TikTok showed the lecturer repeatedly telling the student to leave the classroom. She later became emotional after students asked why she removed the student. "So get up and get the f--- out of my class right now," the lecturer said in one clip. In another, she said, "You did this s--- on purpose, you are out of my class. I am dropping you." CSUSM is committed to providing a safe and welcoming space where all members of our community can learn, grow and thrive." In a statement to Fox News Digital, Cal State University San Marcos said, "Cal State San Marcos is aware of the situation involving a lecturer and a student in a classroom. title: Bombshell report exposes healthcare fraud schemes as taxpayers lose up to $521 billion annually
description: House GOP lawmakers unveil 14 bills targeting Medicaid fraud after a report warns billions in taxpayer dollars are lost annually.
content: FIRST ON FOX: House GOP lawmakers are rolling out a slew of new bills after a bombshell report found that hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars are potentially being targeted by fraudsters every year. As people across the U.S. are battling high costs that make it hard to make ends meet, a report released Tuesday by the House Energy & Commerce Committee warns that federally subsidized healthcare programs are rife with fraud and abuse — "impacting every single American, in one way or another." While no estimate for Medicare and Medicaid fraud exists specifically, the report noted, a 2024 estimate by the Government Accountability Office said $233 billion to $521 billion taxpayer dollars going to federal programs are lost to fraud every year. Federal healthcare programs accounted for 24% of federal spending in 2024, according to the Center on Budget Policy and Priorities. Medicaid specifically is rife with vulnerabilities making it susceptible to fraud, the report said, which is why House Republicans are rolling out 14 bills aimed at closing loopholes in the system, shrinking bureaucracy, and making it easier for states to recoup lost dollars while also incentivizing them to go after potential fraudsters. "Taxpayers that fund benefit programs with federal and state taxpayer dollars are cheated by fraud, inflating healthcare costs that are passed along to everyone," the committee's report states. "Every dollar stolen from federal health care programs is a dollar that is not spent on high quality healthcare for those that need it most." WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE "The amount of fraud that the Biden-Harris Administration allowed to go unchecked in government health programs is unacceptable. Every dollar stolen by fraudsters or wasted on improper payments is a dollar that cannot be used to support families in need who rely on these programs," House Energy & Commerce Committee Chairman Brett Guthrie, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital. REPUBLICANS DECLARE WAR ON 'ORGANIZED THEFT' WITH GOVERNMENT FRAUD CRACKDOWN Republicans' new bills can be lumped into three categories: legislation aimed at improving identification of fraud in state and federal health programs, legislation aimed at enforcing anti-fraud rules, and legislation to hold states that allow fraud to run rampant accountable. One bill led by Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, for example, would force states to designate a single role for internal financial controls of state Medicaid programs. READ: DR. OZ PUTS ALL 50 GOVERNORS ON NOTICE OVER BILLIONS LOST TO MEDICAID FRAUD A bill by Rep. Mike Rulli, R-Ohio, would force each state to annually report to the federal government on any potential Medicaid fraud vulnerabilities and their plan to fix it. And legislation by Rep. Nick Langworthy, R-N.Y., would require states to check whether someone enrolling for Medicaid was removed from another taxpayer-funded healthcare program. The report released on Tuesday said that Medicaid spending accounts for an average 30.7% of states' budgets, and that those outlays have increased exponentially in recent years. States like New York and California are also projected to see costs spike, the report said. TOP FEDERAL PROSECUTOR CALLS CALIFORNIA A 'FRAUDSTER'S PARADISE,' WARNS STATE OFFICIALS COULD FACE CHARGES The Golden State is expected to see annual Medi-Cal spending, its state healthcare program, rise from $83 billion per year in 2014 to $219.7 billion by 2027, the report said, adding, "New York is projected to spend 11% more on Medicaid from all funding sources in 2027 — a total of $124 billion." The report noted that federal healthcare is ripe for fraud given its size and complexity, as well as the traditional enforcement model of "pay and chase," which relies on law enforcement to investigate fraud suspicions after a false claim has already been settled. Provider fraud is also a common area of losing tax dollars, with healthcare providers being known to submit multiple claims for a single service or bill services and equipment for patients that they have never seen at all, the report said. Transnational criminal groups have also profited from U.S. healthcare fraud, the report said, alleging that hardworking Americans are seeing their tax dollars not only lost to fraud at home but overseas as well. TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS The Department of Justice's (DOJ) "Operation Gold Rush" uncovered that Russian organized crime actors billed over $10 million in false claims made via 30 medical supply companies they purchased in a years-long scheme, the report said. It highlighted further foreign healthcare schemes that saw malign actors in Hong Kong, Georgia, Estonia, Pakistan and elsewhere attempt to steal billions more in U.S. taxpayer dollars. The fraud reports come at a time when millions of Americans across the country are struggling with high living costs that have made it a challenge to make ends meet. Guthrie said the House GOP legislative package amounted to "commonsense steps" to ensure states can recoup lost fraud dollars and incentivize them to close loopholes in the future. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It comes as the Trump administration is also prioritizing healthcare fraud crackdowns. Vice President JD Vance announced last week that 760,000 enrollees under the Affordable Care Act, also known as ObamaCare, would be removed over fraud claims.

title: Mike Tomlin's coach criticism makes him better TV analyst but raises question whether he's eyeing Cowboys job
description: Mike Tomlin called the Dallas Cowboys' end-of-game sequence against the Baltimore Ravens "negligent," drawing parallels to Jimmy Johnson's coaching path.
content: Mike Tomlin knows how to win in the NFL because he never suffered a losing season in any of his 19 years as the Pittsburgh Steelers head coach. He's also winning as a TV analyst on NBC's Sunday Night Football pregame show. And it could be he's winning so much that he's using the latter to return to the former. Tomlin on Sunday night did something most former-coaches-turned-broadcasters not named Rex Ryan rarely do: He criticized a current coach. SUPER BOWL-WINNING COACH MIKE TOMLIN LANDS NBC ROLE ON 'FOOTBALL NIGHT IN AMERICA' BROADCAST Tomlin analyzed the end of the Baltimore Ravens 34-31 victory over the Dallas Cowboys and laid the loss at the feet of the coaching staff, which obviously is led by head coach Brian Schottenheimer. "The sequence played by the Dallas Cowboys at the end of the game in Rio was somewhat negligent, to be quite honest with you," Tomlin said. Tomlin explained how a game that was tied at 31 with seven seconds remaining in regulation should not have turned into a loss until "strategically, Dallas helped [Baltimore] in that circumstance." How? The Cowboys' disaster began with the fact their kickoff went into the end zone for a touchback rather than remaining on the field, where precious seconds would have ticked off the clock. "Baltimore gets the ball on the 35-yard-line, and they had this really significant play down the middle of the field to their No. 1 receiver, Zay Flowers," Tomlin said. "But let's really analyze it for a minute. Man, the Dallas Cowboys are playing outside leverage man-to-man. "They got caught in some one-on-ones, Zay Flowers won, and they put them in position to kick that game-winning field goal." The ultimate decision on what coverage the defense plays and whether to avoid coverage that doesn't make sense, falls on Schottenheimer. DEBUT OF FORMER STEELERS COACH MIKE TOMLIN ON NBC HAD HIGHLIGHT MOMENTS Following the loss, Cowboys owner Jerry Jones requested (demanded?) an explanation of what exactly his coach was thinking. Is Jones satisfied with the explanation he got? "Well, there is no explanation you're satisfied with," Jones said during his regular Tuesday appearance on 105.3 The Fan in the Metroplex. "None. Let's be sure that we all understand that." Uh-oh. "They don't have one that they're satisfied with. We made mistakes during that time. There's no question about it. So there is no explanation..." This is where the possibility that Tomlin highlighting his fellow coach's mistake to millions of people on TV's most popular weekly broadcast makes him look good. Because being able to explain what should have happened, sends the message that's how he would have handled it as the Cowboys coach. We are not reporting that Tomlin is focused on putting himself in position to be the next Cowboys coach. But he surely didn't hurt himself with this segment, if that is his intent. Tomlin hasn't said he wants to get back into coaching next year. Then again, he hasn't said he doesn't. But if he does eventually want a coaching comeback, one way to help, is by highlighting that he wouldn't lose a game another coach, who displeased ownership, just lost. Anyone reading this might doubt a former coach would use his position as a broadcaster to help himself land a job he covets. Except, it has happened before. In 1995, former Cowboys coach Jimmy Johnson would often comment on the Fox pregame show about how talented the Miami Dolphins were and how they should be performing better and winning more. The obvious implication was that then-coach Don Shula should be doing better than the 9-5 record he eventually milked out of his team. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! People in Miami saw through it. They understood Johnson, who had coached at the University of Miami and lived in Key West, liked the idea of returning to coaching with the Dolphins. And it worked. Johnson's work on TV fed a public relations campaign that painted him as an upgrade. Shula was ultimately forced out in January 1996 and Johnson was hired one week later. Shula, believing he had been undermined, never forgave Johnson. The question now is whether Tomlin will continue to critique Schottenheimer and his staff, adding to more speculation that he's focused on their job. That would make him a more interesting analyst and maybe even the next Dallas Cowboys coach. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

title: Chris Hansen rips Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ as ‘complete fiction,’ reveals how he’s fighting back
description: Chris Hansen accuses A24's "Primetime" of fictionalizing his "To Catch a Predator" investigations and says he bought ads running on 3,500 screens.
content: Chris Hansen is pushing back against Hollywood's portrayal of his career in the new A24 film, "Primetime," saying the movie fictionalizes the work that made "To Catch a Predator" a television phenomenon. "Nothing in that trailer except for the actor saying my name and ‘have a seat’ ever happened in real life. It’s complete fiction," Hansen said during an interview on the "Planet Tyrus" podcast. The A24 feature, released Friday, offers a dramatization inspired by Hansen's hit "To Catch a Predator" investigations, including events surrounding the death of Bill Conradt, a Texas chief felony assistant district attorney who died by suicide as police arrived at his home to execute search and arrest warrants stemming from an online sting. The film stars Robert Pattinson as Hansen, portraying the television host as he pursues greater exposure for the program while its increasingly high-stakes investigations propel him toward greater fame and, ultimately, the Conradt incident. 'PRIMETIME' STAR ROBERT PATTINSON SHOCKS FANS WITH CHRIS HANSEN TRANSFORMATION IN 'UNSETTLING' TRAILER Hansen said the film distorts the work he and others have done to expose adults seeking to sexually exploit children, arguing that Hollywood is using his name and the popularity of the franchise to sell a fictionalized version of events. "It’s shocking and a bit of an insult, based upon what I’ve seen in the trailer, based upon what other people have told me about the film… It’s an insult to turn something that’s been so positive and so important into a dark, over-dramatized [portrayal]…" he told Tyrus. "It's Hollywood twisting what happened..." he added. Hansen said he had not seen the film at the time of the interview and had no input in its production. He said he had no issue with Pattinson, adding that he considers him a "good actor" who has been "very gracious" to him. Instead, Hansen directed his criticism at the filmmakers and Hollywood more broadly, invoking former film producer and convicted sex offender Harvey Weinstein. "What do you expect out of an industry that was led for years by one of the most prolific predators to walk the face of the earth, Harvey Weinstein?" he asked. To combat what he views as an inaccurate portrayal, Hansen said he purchased ad slots before showings of "Primetime," in which he will "walk into [a] kitchen, tell everybody in the theater to have a seat" and remind them that the "real work continues every day" on his true-crime streaming service, TruBlu. CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS Hansen said the 30-second ads will run on 3,500 screens nationwide during the film's first month, which he said will allow him to use the movie's release to direct audiences toward the work he says Hollywood misrepresented. Meanwhile, Hansen is also preparing to tell his side of the story through a documentary titled "I’m Chris Hansen," which he said recently finished production and is being shopped to streaming platforms. Unlike "Primetime," Hansen said he cooperated with that project and knew the filmmakers involved. Director Lance Oppenheim has defended his decision not to involve Hansen in the production of "Primetime." When asked by W Magazine why he did not consult Hansen while making the film, Oppenheim said he believed Hansen's existing work and public record provided what he needed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I felt like I had everything I needed with the Cameo," Oppenheim said, referring to a $30 personalized video Hansen recorded for him in 2024 after the director's wife purchased it as a gift. Oppenheim said he also read Hansen's book and blog and spoke with Mitchell Wagenberg, a hidden-camera operator who worked with Hansen on "To Catch a Predator." "It almost felt like we were adapting the Internet's version of Chris Hansen rather than the real Chris Hansen," Oppenheim said. "You can self-mythologize all you want, but at a certain point it becomes part of culture." "The Odyssey wasn’t told by Odysseus. This movie shouldn’t be told by Chris Hansen. It should be told by the fans of Chris Hansen, which is us," he added.

An ultrasound revealed that he had "a mass that had to come out." After undergoing surgery to remove the testicle (an orchiectomy), Reeve discovered the mass was embryonal carcinoma. The aggressive subtype of testicular cancer can spread more quickly than some other forms, according to the American Cancer Society. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PLAY SURPRISING ROLE IN CANCER OUTCOMES Reeve later underwent a second surgery to remove lymph nodes from his abdomen after some cancer cells had spread there. The surgery took place at Memorial Sloan Kettering, which is where his mother, Dana Reeve, died from lung cancer in 2006 at age 44. His father died in 2004 at the age of 52. Reeve shared that he also underwent two rounds of chemotherapy to lower the risk that the cancer would return. He said he experienced several side effects from the medication, including ringing in the ears, bone pain, night sweats, blood clots and constant headaches. He did not lose his hair because he used a method called "cold capping," which is used during certain chemotherapy treatments to help reduce hair loss by cooling the scalp and constricting blood vessels. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES After finishing his second round of chemotherapy on July 31, Reeve said he received "clean scans" on Sept. 8. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER In an interview with People, Reeve said he is "going to be fine," although it has been "one heck of a chapter." "I’m fortunate that I caught this early," he said. "Yes, I had to jump through some flaming hoops to get to the other side, but it could have been much worse had I ignored it or delayed going to the doctor." Reeve also praised his wife for serving as his "caregiver," similar to how his mother helped care for his father after a 1995 horseback-riding accident left him paralyzed. "I learn[ed] more about what it was like to be my dad in the final nine years of his life, where he had my mom and our family taking care of him," Reeve said. title: Office of Personnel Management uncovers $500M in fraud and waste in federal health benefits programs
description: The Trump administration's Office of Personnel Management uncovered $510 million in fraud and waste across federal employee health benefits programs.
content: FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration announced $500 million in waste and fraud findings at the Office of Personnel Management – revealing a recovery of potentially fraudulent funds for federal health benefits programs. Health insurance carriers in the Federal Employees Health Benefits and Postal Service Health Benefits programs reported preventing nearly $510 million in losses before or during payment and recovering an additional $21.9 million after claims were paid, according to the Office of Personnel Management. "OPM runs health insurance for about 8.9 million retirees and federal employees, and we spend about $80 billion a year," Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor told Fox News Digital. "The $500 million, a little more than half percent, is a good number, but certainly we have a long way to go here to root out more fraud, waste and abuse." FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP ADMIN OPENS NEW FRONT IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETING HEALTH INSURERS, DRUG MIDDLEMEN The White House anti-fraud task force led by Vice President JD Vance has reported $260.7 billion in fraud uncovered since Trump took office, and $72 billion in fraud stopped on an annualized basis. Kupor said his agency is conducting its own review of health insurance claims data for the first time, allowing the agency to analyze billing patterns across providers and health plans to identify unusual prescribing habits, surgery rates and other anomalies that could signal overuse, misuse or potential fraud. TRUMP ADMIN BLOCKS MORE THAN $1.6B IN POTENTIALLY IMPROPER MEDICARE LAB PAYMENTS, AGENCY SAYS He said the agency will use those findings to remove providers from federal health programs when warranted and will refer cases involving suspected criminal conduct to the agency’s Office of Inspector General and the Justice Department for further investigation. Kupor leads the agency responsible for overseeing the federal workforce while managing key employment and benefits programs for millions of current and former federal employees. One of the most prominent examples of his work stems from Elon Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) targeting of a mine in Pennsylvania. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE THE SECRETIVE MINE DOGE HELPED DRAG OUT OF A DECADES-OLD BUREAUCRATIC BLACK HOLE Last April, Fox News Digital first reported that the United States government applied the use of artificial intelligence for federal employee recordkeeping – the first time the federal government implemented AI at scale. The movement was led by Kupor and Musk, and Musk didn’t hide his shock that federal records were being stored and managed solely on paper at the time. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ "The speed at which the mine shaft elevator can move determines how many people can retire... And the elevator breaks down and then nobody can retire," Musk said last February. "Doesn't that sound crazy?" When asked for an update on progress made on modernizing the mine, Kupor said it is now fully operational on an electronic system. "This past year, we did 180,000 electronic online applications for retirement, which is just unprecedented," he said. "That's almost double the production that we've had in any prior year. Electronic applications can get solved in less than half the time today that a paper one does." "We will take something that has been a six-month, nine-month, 12-month horrendous process for retirees, and I think we will be able to do it in as little as 15 days with the continued development of technology." WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE Kupor’s previous experience working with artificial intelligence has led to his name being floated to serve as the AI czar in the Trump administration – a role cast into the spotlight as data center development and artificial intelligence have become midterm election talking points. After working as an investment banker at Credit Suisse, Kupor worked at Loudcloud, which was co-founded by Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, in 1999. He was then hired as the first employee by Andreessen and Horowitz at the duo’s venture capital firm. Kupor also served as the chair of the National Venture Capital Association from May 2017 to May 2018. TRUMP SAYS ANTI-FRAUD EFFORTS ARE UNCOVERING BILLIONS IN WASTE, CLAIMS SAVINGS COULD BALANCE BUDGET When asked about whether he has had any conversations with the White House about the role, Kupor said he had seen the reports he was being floated, and discussed President Donald Trump’s views on artificial intelligence broadly. "I’ve read all the same reports you've read and don't have anything to add there," he said. "What the president has said is exactly 100% right, which is that AI is the most important piece of technology that will determine economic growth for us, national security, sovereignty for our country." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION UNCOVERS $1.2B IN SUSPECTED COVID CONTRACT FRAUD TIED TO BIDEN-ERA SPENDING "One of the things that I know, again, having spent all my life in the venture world, is there is no limit to the intellect and inventiveness of entrepreneurs in this country. And we just need to make sure that the conditions around, you know, regulatory controls and others continue to allow the U.S. to flourish in the way that it's always done." Kupor did not rule out accepting the role if Trump should offer it to him, saying that while he is focused on his job as director of the agency, he serves "at the will of the president." title: Ross Chastain calls Ryan Blaney's fight with Carson Hocevar at Bristol Motor Speedway 'NASCAR 101'
description: Ross Chastain called the Ryan Blaney and Carson Hocevar fight at Bristol Motor Speedway "NASCAR 101," referenced it to the 1979 Daytona 500 brawl.

content: FIRST ON FOX: Jeffrey Soros, the wealthy nephew of billionaire Democrat mega-donor George Soros, detailed his yearslong connection to Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed during a Monday night fundraiser, according to footage obtained by Fox News Digital. The Soros nephew, a wealthy Hollywood producer, hosted El-Sayed at his home Monday night for a fundraiser that attracted controversy given the emphasis the candidate has placed on getting money out of politics. During remarks, Soros noted that he played a key role in helping El-Sayed get his career off the ground, according to footage obtained by Fox News Digital. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS The financial and political ties come as El-Sayed has made the influence of wealthy donors a recurring theme of his campaign. title: ICE confusion ignites MAGA backlash: ‘I would have called for impeachment’
description: Verbal guidance telling some ICE offices to stop arresting illegal immigrants without criminal histories was rescinded within hours amid fierce backlash.
content: Reported guidance directing some ICE offices to pull back on arrests of illegal immigrants without criminal histories triggered backlash from policy hawks, raising questions whether the Trump administration is sending conflicting signals on enforcement. The guidance was rescinded within hours, and Trump told Fox News there had been no change in an enforcement posture that prioritizes — but is not limited to — the "worst first." The verbal guidance had been relayed to ICE field offices around the country, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter, though it remains unclear who initially issued the instruction. Administration officials later characterized it as a misunderstanding rather than a formal policy change, and new guidance reaffirming there had been no change in enforcement policy was sent within hours. The episode nevertheless reinforced concerns among some immigration hawks who say recent public messaging from administration officials has suggested a narrower approach to interior enforcement than Trump campaigned on. Mike Howell, a leader of the Mass Deportation Coalition and president of The Oversight Project, argued public criticism helped force the reversal but said the episode also fit what he views as a broader pattern of mixed messaging from DHS on interior immigration enforcement. "[The guidance] was walked back, allegedly, which is great, and I think it was in large part walked back because people spoke out very, very loudly," Howell said, while adding there is a troubling undercurrent to some of DHS' messaging on the greater matter: WHITE HOUSE BRINGS RECEIPTS AFTER MEDIA CLAIMS NONCRIMINAL ICE ARRESTS ‘SOARING’: ‘FALSE NARRATIVES’ As an example, Howell pointed to a tweet from DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin posted one day before the ICE guidance news broke, in which the secretary said the department was "not conducting worksite operations in Kansas" but was targeting criminal illegal immigrants and those facing removal. The post followed ICE operations in Kansas that prompted complaints from Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., who said DHS had failed to coordinate with local authorities during operations in cities including Liberal. "I've never seen a secretary put anything like that in writing," Howell said. "[If it were] an Obama or Clinton or Biden DHS secretary, we would have called for impeachment if they said that." 'GONE TOO FAR:' GOP CANDIDATE RUNS TO TRUMP’S LEFT ON SIGNATURE ISSUE IN DEEP RED DISTRICT Asked to put a finer point on it, Howell stated outright: "If Mayorkas tweeted that, I would have immediately called for his impeachment: for flagrant admission that they are not enforcing the laws and faithfully executing them -- It was amnesty by another means." Howell emphasized that he was not calling for Mullin’s impeachment, but using the comparison to underscore how seriously he views any pullback from broad immigration enforcement. He further argued that shifting signals are unfair to rank-and-file ICE agents who served during the Biden administration. It remained unclear who originated the guidance, but Fox News was told it was a "misunderstanding" and that the person responsible would likely face reprimand. A source told Fox News Digital on Sunday evening that the order "definitely went out" and that some immigrant-heavy Republican districts have seen anger over family members being caught up in worksite-enforcement removals. The source pointed to Kansas as an illustration. "This type of ping-pong is deeply unfair to ICE, the men and women there tasked with actually deporting these people," he said. "They watch the news, they read X, they see these mixed signals and it's affected operations." EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis pushed back, saying Trump has been clear that "no one is off the table." "DHS continues to deliver results for the American people including the most secure border in history and three straight months of a record number of ICE arrests," she said, citing more than 3 million deportations thus far. An ICE report also put arrests-per-month at a record high of 51,000 in August, while a source familiar confirmed that ICE guidance that went out was a "miscommunication" and not from the top. Mark Krikorian, executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for tighter immigration controls, said the situation is uniquely instructive because it comes at a time when factions of the Republican Party are at odds, whether silently or not, over the immigration enforcement issue. "All of this comes on the backdrop of conflicting goals and messages within the administration on immigration," he said. Krikorian said the administration may have contributed to that confusion by repeatedly emphasizing its focus on the "worst of the worst," even as officials including border czar Tom Homan have said immigrants without criminal records are not exempt from enforcement. "The administration does need to get its story straight internally so that they can then present a consistent message externally," Krikorian said. He argued the larger unresolved issue is worksite enforcement, which he said is critical to encouraging self-deportation but creates political tension between business interests seeking labor and working-class Republicans demanding tighter enforcement. Republican donors who favor the "loose labor market" that low-wage migrants bring clash with the working-class Republican bloc demanding tighter labor markets and stricter enforcement, Krikorian said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Krikorian said he had hoped Trump or Mullin would clarify after the Kansas controversy that the administration was not "randomly" cracking down on employers, but conducting worksite enforcement based on intelligence about businesses employing illegal immigrants. Several Republicans, including Marshall and Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., have criticized aspects of the administration’s immigration push ahead of the midterms. Krikorian argued that conflicting signals could also carry political consequences with Trump voters focused on enforcement – citing competing pressures between big-business and the base. "You don’t tweet out that you’re not doing what voters want you to do," he said. Krikorian praised the administration’s border policies but argued interior and worksite enforcement create more complicated political tradeoffs for the Trump coalition. After the Wire report broke, DHS responded in part "this is false. No one is off the table." title: Hollywood actress’s performative rant about son’s sexuality at LGBT gala fuels online backlash frenzy
description: Camryn Manheim told the Human Rights Campaign dinner she "always wanted a gay son," but her boy turned out straight despite her very best efforts.
content: A Hollywood actress used her platform on stage at a far-left Human Rights Campaign (HRC) event to performatively joke that despite her best efforts, her son turned out to be heterosexual. Camryn Manheim, best known for her role as Ellenor Frutt in the late 1990s and early 2000s drama series "The Practice," introduced and presented her friend and fellow actress Marcia Gay Harden with the Ally for Equality Award at the HRC's National Dinner on Sunday. "For Marcia, of course, this is deeply personal to her," said Manheim of this year's recipient of the prestigious award. "She has three remarkable children who all align with the LGBTQ+ community, which is another thing that deeply irritates me about her, because I always wanted a gay son." GLAAD RELEASES 'PARTICULARLY CONCERNING' REPORT SHOWING SHRINKING LGBTQ REPRESENTATION THIRD YEAR IN A ROW She then launched into a tirade about how her son is heterosexual. "I love that relationship between gay sons and their mothers," she said from the stage. "I wanted to be the picket sign-holding mom who would beat the s--- out of somebody for her kid. I mean, let's just admit it, gay sons are the best, right? Right!" "I have photographs of my son in high heels, in full drag, he knows every word to every musical ever written, his fairy godfather, Aaron Walton, is here with us tonight. I mean, truly, I thought I had this f---ing thing locked up, but no, no, he's the only straight guy in his entire musical theater company," Manheim complained. Manheim's only child, Milo Manheim, 25, is an actor best known for his starring role as Zed in the Disney Channel film franchise "Zombies." He played Joseph in the 2023 Christmas musical, "Journey to Bethlehem," and in 2018 came in second place on season 27 of "Dancing with the Stars." LOG CABIN REPUBLICANS REMOVES 'T' FROM LGBT ADVOCACY, SAYS 'RADICAL' TRANS ACTIVISTS ARE ERODING GAY SUPPORT Manheim, during her recorded remarks, relayed a story about Harden, a 2021 Oscar winner for best supporting actress in the 2000 film "Pollock," calling her a decade ago to tell her that her son was gay. "All I said was, 'Oh my God, you are so f---ing lucky!" Manheim said, yelling into the microphone and drawing a round of applause from the crowd. And about a week later, I was at Marcia's house for dinner when an Amazon package was delivered, and inside, I'm not kidding you, was a pair of thigh-high patent leather boots, like kinky boots," Manheim continued. "And I thought, 'oh come on, now she is just showing off!" DEMOCRATS TURN ON CONGRESSIONAL HOPEFUL AFTER 'HIDING' LGBTQ+ VIEWS FROM MUSLIM VOTERS HRC is America's largest civil rights group dedicated to "engaging and mobilizing millions of pro-equality voters and supporters to elect pro-equality leaders and to demand equity-based policies and legislation." The organization was founded in 1980 by gay rights lobbyist Steve Endean and today boasts 4 million members. Sunday night's dinner was part of the Human Rights Campaign's events program, which it says reaches more than 20,000 people each year through 30 fundraising dinner events. It allows the group to "elevate LGBTQ+ candidates around the country, keep volunteers engaged, amplify our work in the local community, and solicit corporate sponsorships and donations through our auctions." Online, reactions ranged from dismayed to disgusted. "How do any straight males survive mothers like this? It's a miracle some of them come out normal," said a right-wing commentator who goes by Peachy Keenan. "These people are mentally ill. They need to be institutionalized or thrown in prison for trying to groom children," said Andy Froemel. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It’s the entertainment industry mothers who are the psychos," online personality @shipwreckedcrew, who boasts more than 180,000 followers, said. "These people are sick," radio show host Joe Pagliarulo said. "Liberalism is a performative sickness," said Jon Nanjarian. Fox News Digital reached out to HRC and representatives for Manheim but did not hear back at time of publication.

title: Which college football coaches improved or tanked their hot seat status four games into the season?
description: Lincoln Riley's USC tenure lacks a College Football Playoff appearance through five years, and a home loss to Oregon has the heat rising fast.
content: If you're not in a headspace to receive sensitive information then plug your ears, but the college football season is officially a third of the way through. As hard as that is to believe, it also means that we have some significant data to draw from that will help paint a clearer picture of the landscape of college football for 2026. Some teams are already outperforming their preseason expectations while others are greatly disappointing thus far, as is the case with every season. COLLEGE FOOTBALL WEEK 4 CONTENDERS, PRETENDERS: TEXAS SURVIVES, MICHIGAN'S KARMA AND COACHES ARE SWEATING With that, we also have four games worth of data on head coaches and where they stand on the "hot seat" conversation, so I thought it would be interesting to look at a few coaches who entered 2026 with a target on their back and how they've done to either improve or worsen their standing. Think of it as a "hot seat report card." KEEP AN EYE ON THESE UNDER-THE-RADAR NAMES DURING THIS SEASON'S COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHING CAROUSEL With all the preamble out of the way, let's begin. Dave Aranda - Baylor Dave Aranda's path at Baylor has been a circuitous one, to say the least. It was looking like a classic rags to riches story for the former LSU defensive coordinator early on, as he guided the Bears to a Big 12 championship and a 12-win season in just his second year on the job. Since then, the results have fluctuated between middling and downright putrid, and entering this year, Aranda was said to be on his last leg. So far, though, I don't really think he's done anything to change that for better or for worse, but he has set himself up nicely to buy a little more time in Waco. Outside of a neutral site opener against Auburn, in which the Bears had a chance to win on the last play even with a hobbled DJ Lagway, Baylor has taken care of business and is 3-1 through four weeks. Their next few conference games are winnable though not automatic, which sets up an absolutely brutal last three games where they have to play BYU, Texas Tech, and Houston, essentially the best the Big 12 has to offer. If he can hold serve and maybe even steal one of those three games at the end of the year, I believe 8-4 or 9-3 will land Aranda in the "safe for now" category as 2026 comes to a close. Status: Hold Luke Fickell - Wisconsin Coming into the season, it was basically a forgone conclusion that Wisconsin head coach Luke Fickell would be gone by the end of the year; essentially a dead man walking. After getting blasted pretty handily by Notre Dame to start the season, it looked like nothing would change, and maybe he's still gone by the end of the year, but Saturday's massive win on the road against a top-15 Penn State might go a long way in determining Fickell's fate. It was the Badgers' first road win over a ranked opponent under Fickell, and with a more manageable schedule - Wisconsin avoids having to play Indiana, Oregon, and Ohio State this season - a bowl game could be well within range for their embattled head coach. RANKING THE TEN BEST COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES IN THE COUNTRY AHEAD OF THE 2026 SEASON I'm not confident simply making a bowl game will save Fickell, but an 8-4 record is certainly on the table and I'm sure that would give boosters some pause about paying his nearly $20 million buyout. It's still "wait and see" for Fickell, but Saturday might have been his first attempt at digging out of a massive hole in Madison. Status: Trending slightly up Lincoln Riley - USC This might surprise a lot of people who just paid attention to the preseason polls, but Lincoln Riley was under a lot of scrutiny heading into his fifth year in Los Angeles. The Trojans have yet to make a College Football Playoff under Riley's watch, causing some of the natives in Southern Cal to stir a bit. This was seen as the year it could all come together for USC and Riley, and after holding serve the first few weeks of the season, their week four showdown with Oregon was supposed to be the first test of that theory. Consider that test failed, as the Trojans dropped one at home to a Ducks squad playing with a backup quarterback for the majority of the contest. Losing to a stacked Oregon team in a vacuum is nothing to hang your head about, but the fact that this was supposed to be a Playoff season for USC means the magnifying glass gets brought out after every result. There's still plenty of season left to get it right, but things aren't getting any easier for Riley and the Trojans with teams like Ohio State, Penn State, Indiana, and a resurgent UCLA still on the schedule. Until USC can wash the taste of this one out of their mouth, the temperature on Riley's office chair will feel uncomfortably warm moving forward. Status: Trending down Mike Norvell - Florida State It could be argued that no one had a hotter seat coming into 2026 than Mike Norvell, and the Florida State Seminoles didn't exactly do anything to change that through the first third of the season. The Noles are 2-2 through four games, and their two losses might actually be more inspiring than their two wins. A three-point home loss to then-ranked SMU and a competitive road loss to Alabama might signify progress, but the fans in Tallahassee have long run out of patience. Luckily for Norvell and unfortunately for those fans, they don't make the decisions, and after firing athletic director Mike Alford a few weeks ago, the prevailing theory coming out of the Florida panhandle is that their coach is likely safe for 2026. That might seem almost unfathomable to anyone familiar with the last few years of FSU football, but there's still the lingering questions of Norvell's buyout now coupled with a new AD trying to get his footing in an absolute mess of a situation. The Seminoles still have a shot at a winning season and a bowl game, and there is some talent at spots on this roster. I wouldn't be shocked at all to see the Noles pull a 6-6 or 7-5 season out of their hats and keep their lame duck coach in Tally for another season. I'm sorry, FSU fans. Even you don't deserve a fate this cruel. Status: Hold Shane Beamer - South Carolina Back in July, I wrote an article about the hot seat status of every coach in the SEC, and South Carolina coach Shane Beamer's seat was so radioactive that it needed its own section all by itself. Not to toot my own horn, but that is looking downright prophetic four games into the 2026 season. The Gamecocks took care of the two scrubs on their schedule to start the year before getting their tail feathers handed to them in back to back weeks to begin SEC play. First, the world was finally introduced to the magic of Mississippi State's Kamario Taylor, as the Bulldogs hung a 41-spot on South Carolina's head in Williams Brice Stadium. Then Beamer and his boys went on the road and got clobbered by Alabama to the tune of a 49-18 beatdown. What's worse, their best player, edge rusher Dylan Stewart, had a generational crashout on the field and was sent to the locker room with his status with the team in question, prompting many to opine whether Beamer had "lost the locker room." Regardless of what becomes of the Stewart situation, the schedule doesn't lighten up at all for South Carolina. Kentucky, Florida, Tennessee, Oklahoma, and Georgia all await in conference play, and the Gamecocks also have to travel to Clemson to play the Tigers to end the season. A schedule like that presents opportunities to land some impressive wins, but it also acts as a minefield that could sink the goodship Beamer in the process. I have a hard time seeing Beamer surviving this season barring a miracle from above. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Status: Trending down

title: Motorcycle patrols swarm Iranian cities, checkpoints rise as regime braces for unrest
description: Sources told Fox News Digital that IRGC, Basij and police have flooded Tehran with checkpoints and patrols as student protests over compulsory hijab grow.
content: Iranian security forces have stepped up their presence in Tehran and other cities, with motorcycle patrols, checkpoints and forces positioned across major urban areas as authorities brace for possible unrest, multiple sources inside Iran told Fox News Digital. The security buildup comes as university students have returned to the streets in Tehran, protesting compulsory hijab rules, rising education costs and political repression, videos published on Iran International show. Sources inside Iran confirmed to Fox News Digital that motorcycle units have been operating across Tehran and other cities during events surrounding Iran’s annual "Sacred Defense Week," while members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Basij and law enforcement have been positioned at major squares and other locations. IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS The sources also said security personnel have stopped pedestrians, searched some individuals and examined mobile phones, including material authorities consider "anti-regime." The accounts follow a report from the National Council of Resistance of Iran’s (NCRI's) Committee on Security and Counterterrorism alleging that Iranian authorities ordered a "100%" state of readiness for the Army, IRGC, Basij and law enforcement and canceled leave through Sept. 27. The NCRI also claimed 51,000 personnel had been deployed across Greater Tehran, including 30,000 IRGC and Basij members and 21,000 law enforcement personnel. The reported preparations are taking place as signs of public unrest have begun resurfacing on university campuses. Fox News Digital has not independently confirmed those claims. One source in Tehran told Fox News Digital that the heightened security presence extends beyond what is visible on the streets. INSIDE TEHRAN: IRANIANS DESCRIBE IRGC'S BRUTAL RULE, POVERTY — ASK TRUMP TO 'STAY THE COURSE' "Motorcyclists taking photos of shops, and prisoners being threatened and forced to tell their families not to physically participate in any protests that might arise," the source said. The source said Basij members who previously received military training have been placed on alert and are being housed or assembled at educational facilities and large properties on the outskirts of Tehran. The measures were not limited to the capital. "This situation exists in all cities, but the nature of the presence and the way things are organized differ," the source told Fox News Digital, citing information received from Borujen, Isfahan and other cities. IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP "In those places, plainclothes agents are more prevalent and try to remain out of public view; however, in Tehran, they appear openly on the streets in military uniforms and gear specifically to instill fear and terror," the source said, adding that leave had also been canceled in smaller cities and claimed shops, telephone communications and everyday activities were under increased surveillance. Iranian journalist Mehdi Ghadimi, who lives outside Iran after years of opposition activity, separately told Fox News Digital that he had received similar accounts. "I’ve received reports of new checkpoints being set up in Tehran, and there have also been reports of military forces being put on alert, as well as civilians who had previously been trained by the regime for urban repression being called up," Ghadimi added that people are being detained on espionage charges simply because they communicate with people outside of Iran. IRAN INMATES SEW LIPS SHUT IN MASS HUNGER STRIKE AT NOTORIOUS US-SANCTIONED JAIL: REPORT Ghadimi also said he had received reports that individuals with serious criminal records had been released from prison in exchange for reporting to local Basij bases and participating in the suppression of demonstrations. Students at Allameh Tabataba’i University in Tehran held a protest Monday against compulsory hijab, rising tuition and university living conditions, according to videos reported by Iran International on Sept. 28 and 29. Students were recorded chanting against the morality police and political repression. Iran International reported that the protest began over tuition, dormitory and food costs before expanding into broader political chants. The outlet, citing the student publication Amirkabir, reported that Basij members attempted to disrupt the gathering and threatened students. IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN The protests also come amid renewed pressure over compulsory hijab rules on university campuses. On Sept. 8, Iran International reported that a senior official in the office representing Iran’s supreme leader at universities said a new compulsory-hijab directive for universities had been drafted and was expected to be issued by the ministries overseeing higher education. Separately, the IRGC escalated its rhetoric toward Washington on Tuesday, with spokesman Hossein Mohebbi calling on Americans to pressure President Donald Trump’s administration. "This lying administration must be changed," Mohebbi said at a Tehran press conference, according to Reuters video distributed Sept. 29. His remarks came as U.S. and Iranian officials continued indirect contacts through mediators in an effort to end the seven-month conflict, Reuters reported. The combination of visible security preparations and renewed demonstrations is fueling speculation among Iranians about whether the country could face another broader wave of unrest.
