title: Trump unveils America.gov as AI-powered hub for passports, Medicare enrollment and more
description: President Donald Trump launched America.gov, an AI-powered site that consolidates federal services from passport applications to Medicare enrollment in one place.
content: President Donald Trump on Tuesday unveiled America.gov, an AI-powered website designed to consolidate information from tens of thousands of federal webpages into a single searchable database. After delivering brief remarks at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C., Trump signed an executive order that directs all federal agencies to make their websites "integrate directly" with America.gov as soon as possible. The site is live as of Tuesday and allows users to type questions into a search bar that generates AI chatbot-style responses. "Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov," Trump said. TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS Currently, the site can only answer questions and direct users on how to complete various tasks themselves. U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia, who helped create America.gov, said that by 2027, citizens will be able to use the site to complete government forms and track the status of various applications. In his speech, Trump highlighted several ways the site could streamline interactions with the federal government, including simplifying the paperwork involved when a woman changes her last name after getting married. "Very soon, all she'll have to do is ask America.gov and it'll fill out the forms, track the progress and send her a new Social Security card, passport and insurance card in the mail," Trump said. UNITED ARAB EMIRATES PLANS AI-RUN GOVERNMENT WITHIN TWO YEARS "Whether you're a scout leader who wants to reserve a campsite at a national park, a senior citizen trying to choose a Medicare plan, or an American veteran trying to get the benefits that you've earned and so justly deserve, America.gov will be there to help," he added. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz followed Trump's remarks with a demonstration of how America.gov could simplify prescription ordering and other services. Oz brought a woman named Lisa onstage who said she had spent more than a year trying to enroll in Medicare before revealing her newly issued beneficiary card on a large banner. Oz said America.gov "explains what applies to Lisa's situation and guides her through the decisions." At the same event Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that beginning in 2027, Americans will be able to use America.gov to apply for their first U.S. passport. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Today, if you need your first passport, you start at the State Department's website," Rubio said. "There's a lot of information up there, but if you actually want to apply, that is where the maze starts." Rubio said the site will allow users to upload their own passport photos, eliminating the need to visit a pharmacy or retail store to have one taken. "No printing forms, no drugstore hostage photo, no appointment, no line, no middleman that you're paying to do something that should be available to you," Rubio said. "You tell America.gov what you're trying to do and it walks you through every single step." More federal services are expected to be added over the coming months as agencies begin to integrate with America.gov.

title: Vape store clerk near Ole Miss campus warned buyer 'people were dying' from kratom pills, affidavit says
description: A vape store clerk allegedly warned that "people were dying" from kratom sold at the Oxford, Mississippi, shop where an Ole Miss student bought products.
content: An Oxford, Mississippi vape store clerk told a confidential informant that "people were dying" from the kratom being sold there, according to court records showing that one of the two Ole Miss students found dead had bought products from the same store. Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were found dead on Sept. 21, both with similar packages of kratom or synthetic kratom found to be in their possession, according to the court documents. Officials detailed that Hamilton "could have died due to a Pulmonary Edema," which would be consistent with a drug overdose. Strang was found "cold to the touch" when first responders arrived at his house near campus. In a statement Wednesday, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics, a department in the sheriff's office, stopped short of declaring that investigators found kratom itself near either student. "During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations," part of the statement read. The Sept. 25 affidavit reported toxicology results from the medical examiner were still pending.American Kratom Association Senior Fellow on Public Policy Mac Haddow said Wednesday during a press conference that the specific drug found near both students is illegal. OLE MISS NAMES STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS OFFICIAL ADDRESSES POTENTIAL FOR FOUL PLAY Haddow pointed out the sale and possession of kratom has been illegal federally as of August and illegal to sell or possess in Oxford, Mississippi since 2019, and illegal in Lafayette County, where Oxford is located, since 2021. Packaging on the kratom items found near both men were labeled "Smax, Pseudo-DHM" tablets, which is a "Kratom like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops" that people buy for the "narcotic like effect," according to the court documents. Hamilton made several purchases in September at Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford, where workers Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18, were arrested and face a charge of possession of a controlled substances with intent to distribute. Officials did not say in the court documents that the kratom found near him when he died came from that store. One of the purchases was made one day before Hamilton was found dead. A confidential informant to law enforcement went to Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store and asked if they sold "7 O Kratom based pills," to which a store clerk said "yes" and opened a drawer from under the register and pulled out a package of kratom, according to the court records. Mosleh allegedly told the informant to "be quiet" about the pills and to be careful taking them because "people were dying from them." SEND US A TIP Over 500 units of kratom was seized from the vape store along with THC cartridges, gummies, pre rolls, and other suspected THC substances. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Hamilton's roommate told officers that Hamilton often smoked marijuana but that he did not know him to use any hard drugs. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST One hour after finding Hamilton dead, police were dispatched to a house near campus and found Strang dead. A package of the "Smax, Pseudo-DHM" tablets were found on his night stand, along with 20 to 30 Nitrous Oxide cans, known as "whippets," which Strang's roommates said he used daily. Strang's roommates told officers that he was watching football and took a Xanax bar the day before being found dead. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Officials said the synthetic kratom-derived product Strang had bought was purchased at a gas station about 30 minutes away from Oxford. title: Drug cartel kingpin among targets in sweeping Trump crackdown on alleged Mexican corruption network
description: The Sinaloa cartel's Los Mayos faction faces sweeping Treasury sanctions targeting Mayito Flaco, a fugitive born in Anaheim accused of ordering hits.
content: FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is seeking to disrupt with a sweeping set of sanctions a sprawling Sinaloa cartel network accused of corrupting Mexican officials just across the U.S. border. Los Mayos, a powerful faction of the Sinaloa cartel, and its U.S.-born leader are accused of funneling fentanyl and drug money through California and hiring hitmen to kill rivals on American soil. The Treasury Department, according to material exclusively obtained by Fox News Digital ahead of their public release on Tuesday, will sanction 21 individuals and 25 entities in a crackdown against Los Mayos and their alleged illegal activity within U.S. borders. The targets of the sanctions include Ismael Zambada Sicairos, known as "Mayito Flaco," a dual U.S.-Mexican citizen born in Anaheim, California, whom Treasury describes as the "undisputed head" of Los Mayos. MEXICAN GOVERNOR FACING US DRUG CHARGES SEEKS LEAVE JUST ONE DAY AFTER RETURNING TO OFFICE The action lays out how one of Mexico’s most powerful cartel factions allegedly maintains its grip on two critical trafficking corridors along the U.S. border — through political and police corruption, money laundering and violence that Treasury says has extended into Southern California. It also exposes what Treasury describes as deep cartel penetration of government and law enforcement in Baja California, the Mexican state bordering California. The Treasury says Sinaloa-linked "narco-corruption has reached the highest levels" of the state government, alleging that the ex-husband of Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila Olmeda used his political influence to protect cartel operations and that a former Mexicali public security chief accepted bribes to allow the cartel to exert control over municipal police. The allegations shed new light on a controversy that erupted last year when the U.S. revoked the visas of both Ávila and her then-husband, Carlos Torres Torres. The State Department revoked Torres’ U.S. visa in May 2025 over what Treasury now describes as his "cartel affiliation and work on behalf of the Sinaloa cartel." Olmeda’s U.S. visa was also revoked around the same time, though U.S. officials did not publicly disclose a reason for the action against her. The Department of War also played a role in the effort through Joint Interagency Task Force-Counter Cartel, which works with federal law enforcement, intelligence agencies and Treasury to identify cartel financial and facilitation networks. "These sanctions reflect the impact of sustained interagency collaboration and intelligence fusion in identifying and disrupting the networks that enable violent transnational cartels," Brig. Gen. Maurizio Calabrese, director of JIATF-Counter Cartel, told Fox News Digital. Calabrese said the task force contributed analysis and operational insight on cartel-linked financial and facilitation networks to support the broader effort behind the sanctions. POTENTIAL SECURITY THREAT PROMPTS US TRAVEL SUSPENSION FOR BORDER CITY ON ALERT Treasury also alleges the cartel’s reach extended directly into California. Lorenzo Castillo Maldonado, an associate in Mayito Flaco’s network, allegedly hired hitmen on the cartel leader’s orders to kill rival cartel members in Southern California. Another part of the network allegedly worked with complicit Southern California money exchanges to collect bulk cash from U.S. drug sales and move the proceeds back to Mexico. The sanctions are aimed in part at disrupting Los Mayos’ grip on the Tijuana and Mexicali "plazas," strategic corridors Treasury says the cartel uses to move fentanyl and other narcotics into the U.S. "Today’s action underscores that no cartel kingpin, corrupt Mexican government official, or financial facilitator is beyond the reach of Treasury’s authorities," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. "Our message is clear: the Trump administration will identify and disrupt any cartel actor who threatens our security or the integrity of our financial system." The designations effectively cut the targets off from the U.S. financial system, blocking property and assets under U.S. jurisdiction and generally barring Americans from doing business with them. Foreign financial institutions that knowingly facilitate significant transactions for sanctioned individuals could also face U.S. sanctions. At the center of Tuesday’s action is Mayito Flaco, who Treasury says has emerged as the undisputed leader of Los Mayos following the July 2024 arrest of his father, longtime Sinaloa cartel kingpin Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada Garcia. SINALOA CARTEL BOSS 'EL MAYO' SENTENCED TO LIFE, ORDERED TO PAY $15B IN DRUG TRAFFICKING PROFITS El Mayo’s arrest set off a violent struggle between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos, the Sinaloa faction led by sons of Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman. Treasury says the two factions remain locked in a costly internal war that has forced both sides to rebuild their leadership and alliances. Mayito Flaco, 44, was born in Anaheim in 1982 and later filed a U.S. name change to Fernando Sicairos Aispuro, according to Treasury. He was federally indicted in California in 2014 on drug trafficking and money laundering charges and remains a fugitive in Mexico. The Treasury says he now commands Los Mayos’ drug trafficking, murder, extortion, corruption and kidnapping operations. The sanctions also target Torres’ brother, Luis Alfonso Torres Torres, whom Treasury accuses of collecting bribes and laundering illicit funds through companies and political campaigns. The Treasury alleges Mendivil accepted bribes from Los Rusos leader Juan Jose Ponce Felix, known as "El Ruso," in exchange for allowing the cartel to exert control over municipal police, facilitate drug trafficking and carry out enforcement operations.

title: Cam Schlittler and Payton Tolle set up a potential pitching masterclass as MLB playoffs open at Yankee Stadium
description: Payton Tolle and likely American League Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler face off as the Red Sox and Yankees open their MLB postseason at Yankee Stadium.
content: As a fan, I'm bummed that football is over until Thursday, but as a sports bettor, I'm happy to see it go after a brutal NFL week. title: Men who claim they experienced hell reveal terrifying encounters with demons and the afterlife
description: Three men describe terrifying visions of hell, demons and the afterlife in an exclusive conversation with Sean Hannity about their experiences.
content: Three men who say they visited hell are sharing chilling accounts of what they believe they encountered, sitting down with Fox News host Sean Hannity to describe their terrifying experiences with the afterlife. "I had no idea how I got there, why. Nothing was explained until the way back," said Bill Wiese, author of "23 Minutes in Hell," on Tuesday's episode of the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "But I was in this actual dungeon, and there were demons in this cell, reptilish in appearance, bumps and scales all over the one's body, huge jaw, sunken in eyes, claws about a foot long. And these particular two are about 12 or 13 feet tall," he recalled. COLTON BURPO DESCRIBES MEETING JESUS AND HEARING ANGELS SING DURING NEAR-DEATH EXPERIENCE Wiese joined pilot Jim Woodford, author of "Heaven, an Unexpected Journey," and former Buddhist monk Steve Kang, now a pastor and author of "Eight Hours in Hell," for an exclusive conversation with Hannity about their accounts of the afterlife. Wiese said he experienced a vision. "I got up at three o'clock in the morning to get a glass of water and, suddenly, I was pulled out of my body... and I found myself falling through the air down this long tunnel, and I was getting hotter and hotter, and I landed on an actual stone floor in a prison cell in hell... a dungeon..." he said. "I never asked for this. I've never gone to dark movies. I have never drank. I've never taken drugs, and I had never had a vision before." After the experience, Wiese said he consulted Scripture, eager to learn whether it described what he said he had seen. FATHER CARLOS MARTINS RECOUNTS CHILLING EXORCISM, CLAIMS WOMAN MOVED OBJECTS WITHOUT TOUCHING THEM "It doesn't matter if people believe my experience. I'm just a signpost to point them to the scriptures and by those be persuaded," he said. "There's 132 verses in the Bible about hell. Jesus mentioned hell [in] 46 different verses, and because it's a message of warning. He's letting people know there really is a hell, and it's far worse than our minds can even conceive." Woodford said his experience began after he took more than the prescribed amount of pain medication he was using to manage severe pain from Guillain-Barré syndrome. He said his previous ambivalence toward faith changed dramatically. Woodford said he believed he was dying inside his truck one evening and called out for God's forgiveness, which he later credited with helping lead to his survival. Woodford recalled being above his truck and traveling through what he described as a tunnel of light before arriving at a place of extraordinary beauty. He said he then approached a chasm where he encountered a towering creature that appeared to emerge from what he believed was hell. "It knew me," Woodford said of an alleged demon. "It said my name. ‘Jim, Jim, this is your time with us. Come to us, Jim. We have been waiting.’" Terrified, Woodford said he cried out three words: "God help me." SITE WHERE JESUS WAS CRUCIFIED AND BURIED REVEALS NEW EVIDENCE THAT BACKS BIBLICAL ACCOUNT Woodford said Jesus spoke to him and told him to "go back" before he eventually regained consciousness in a hospital. Kang's story was different still. The former Buddhist monk was 19 when, after using marijuana that he said was laced with heroin, cocaine and PCP, he attempted suicide and underwent an eight-hour operation. Kang said he experienced what felt like an eternity in hell. "Anything is better on earth," Kang said. "Any suffering on earth is better than the pain I felt in hell." Kang said he awoke after the ordeal surrounded by Christian prayer warriors who had come to pray for him. He later converted to Christianity, became a pastor and said he has devoted his life to sharing his faith. Though Wiese, Woodford and Kang described different circumstances surrounding their experiences, all three said they came away believing they had been given another chance at life for a reason and felt a responsibility to tell others about what they believe lies beyond. title: FBI strikes back at hacking group with overseas arrest of alleged leader
description: A 24-year-old Amsterdam man was arrested by Dutch police and the FBI for allegedly leading the ShinyHunters global hacking syndicate network.
content: An alleged leader of the notorious global hacking syndicate ShinyHunters has been arrested in the Netherlands following a joint operation between the FBI and Dutch authorities, targeting a cybercrime network linked to high-profile attacks across the U.S. and worldwide. Dutch police announced the arrest of a 24-year-old Amsterdam man Sept. 15 for his alleged role in the ShinyHunters hacking group and for attempting to incite two murders, with authorities noting that further arrests remain possible as they investigate seized electronic devices. "This morning @FBI and our partners the Dutch National Police are announcing the arrest of one of the alleged leaders of ShinyHunters – a global cybercrime and threat actor group linked to cyberattacks in the United States, the Netherlands, and around the world," FBI Director Kash Patel wrote Tuesday morning on X. FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS "In coordination with FBI investigators the Dutch High-Tech Crime Unit arrested the suspect under Dutch law. As we speak FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest. "Thank you to our Dutch National Police partners for their continued work with us in this case and the industry partners who shared information with us. The investigation continues." "The man is also suspected of attempted incitement to commit two murders," according to a Dutch police release. "Various data carriers have been seized and are being investigated further. Further arrests are not ruled out." Brett Leatherman, assistant director of ​the FBI's ⁠Cyber Division, made an unusually public address to the hacking group ShinyHunters, telling the cybercriminals that "we know how to find you." FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS "To the remaining members of ShinyHunters: You've heard about the arrest of your colleague," Leatherman's video statement warned. "We're confident you've seen or heard things in recent days that the public has not."Other groups believed anonymity or their friends would protect them, and they were wrong. Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk. And seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who's left."The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us and we know how find you. I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours." Benjamin Korper of Amsterdam-based cybersecurity company Neo Security named the arrested man as Pepijn van der Stap, the company's offensive security lead. FBI EXTRADITES CHINESE HACKER ACCUSED OF STEALING COVID-19 RESEARCH "Since last year, this cyber criminal and his co-conspirators have allegedly breached more than 140 organizations and taken at least $70 million in extortion payments," Leatherman said in his video statement, which did not name the suspect. "They often target third-party vendors and cloud-based platforms, stealing sensitive data in extorting victims with threats to publish it."In a telephone interview with Reuters, Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office Sept. 15, the night Van der Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that involved flash bang grenades. ShinyHunters is a hacking group known for large-scale data breaches and extortion and had announced its recent theft of what it said was terabytes of sensitive personnel data from U.S. FBI servers, including intelligence assignments and medical records of employees, according to Reuters. An internal memo circulated to staffers said the FBI was operating under the presumption that hackers stole data pertaining to all bureau employees, a source told Reuters. FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED In a statement, ShinyHunters said Van der Stap had "no association" with the group and that Dutch police were incompetent. News of Van der Stap's arrest caused a stir in the cybersecurity community. Van der Stap's 2023 convictions of data theft and extortion had already received widespread publicity, as did his subsequent public disavowal of cybercrime. On his personal website, Van der Stap acknowledged his journey "hasn't been a straight line" but said his experience had taught him that "knowledge is for building and protecting, not breaking." Korper said he had carefully vetted Van der Stap before hiring him, monitored him during his employment, and was shocked by the arrest. "I truly believe that people deserve a second chance, but in this case I was not thanked for it," Korper said. "Absolutely everybody I talked to is flabbergasted." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The executive said he had hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but so far investigators have found no evidence that he acted against his employer or its clients. Korper and Van der Stap have not been in touch since the arrest, Korper said. Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Jack Smith's Trump probe swept up Fox News, other media communications as investigation went beyond lawmakers
description: Jack Smith's investigators obtained records containing communications between nearly 50 journalists and government officials during the Trump probe.
content: FIRST ON FOX: Former special counsel Jack Smith's investigators obtained records containing communications between nearly 50 journalists and Trump administration officials — including Fox News personnel — after subpoenaing text-message records associated with dozens of White House phones during the federal election investigation of President Donald Trump, Fox News Digital has learned ahead of Tuesday's Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. Previous congressional disclosures showed investigators obtained records involving members of Congress. The latest records reveal the production also included communications between government officials and journalists working for some of the country's largest news organizations. The communications appeared in records produced by the National Archives in response to a subpoena seeking material associated with 87 White House phones from Trump's first administration, according to a spokesperson for Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, citing whistleblower disclosures made to the chairman. "What will the partisan media say about this disgraceful government overreach? This wasn’t a normal prosecution by any means," Grassley challenged in comments to Fox News Digital on Tuesday, as critics have highlighted the lack of concern or coverage given to Smith’s probe by legacy media. EXPLOSIVE NEW REPORT PUTS JACK SMITH BACK IN HOT SEAT AS JIM JORDAN ALLEGES HE TRIED TO 'SWAY' 2024 ELECTION One organization identified Tuesday as having been swept up in the probe was the Media Research Center. Its president, David Bozell, announced in 2025 that "not one single broadcast network aired one solitary second" about Smith’s alleged spying on conservative organizations and senators following a tranche of public disclosures. Fox News is among the organizations whose journalists appear in the records, along with CNN, CBS News — including its newsmagazine "60 Minutes" — NBC News and CNBC. The records also include communications involving journalists from the Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, Bloomberg, Los Angeles Times, New York Magazine, Reuters, the Associated Press and NPR, as well as The Federalist and Washington Times. READ THE LIST: 44 LAWMAKERS SWEPT INTO JACK SMITH TEXT SWEEP AS HIS LEGAL RECKONING GROWS The nationally syndicated "The Mark Levin Show," hosted by Fox News host and former Reagan Justice Department chief of staff Mark Levin, also appears in the records. The records stem from a June 2, 2023, subpoena issued by Smith’s office to the National Archives seeking text messages from phones associated with numerous officials who served in the first Trump White House. JACK SMITH HIT WITH CRIMINAL REFERRAL AS GOP MOVES TESTIMONY FIGHT TOWARD PROSECUTION The Archives produced responsive records on Aug. 21, 2023, according to documents previously disclosed through congressional oversight by Grassley and Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., of Arctic Frost. Grassley and Johnson pressed the Justice Department and FBI in May for information about how potentially privileged material in that production was screened before investigators could review it. An Aug. 21, 2023 email from assistant special counsel Thomas Windom instructed members of Smith’s team, including prosecutors and FBI personnel, to download documents associated with text messages from the White House phones. "We are writing to determine what procedures and protocols, if any, Smith and his team used to filter privileged or potentially privileged materials from being impermissibly accessed, reviewed and/or used," Grassley and Johnson wrote. The senators requested DOJ’s filtering protocols and the names of officials assigned to review material for privilege before it reached investigators. The committee has identified the individual journalists whose communications appear in the records but does not plan to release their names because of privacy concerns, a Grassley spokesperson told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The disclosure broadens questions surrounding Smith’s handling of the White House records ahead of Tuesday’s Senate hearing, including what safeguards governed investigators’ access to communications involving lawmakers, journalists and other third parties. The Judiciary Committee is expected to examine Smith’s investigative practices and the broader scope of Arctic Frost. Grassley also pressed Smith about another revelation from the senator's recent investigation into the former special counsel's probe. The Iowa Republican asked whether Smith's operation obtained donor data, including the financial and personal information of rank-and-file civilians who gave even small sums to political candidates. Smith acknowledged the claim, saying he could not recite "every subpoena we issued" but that the purpose was "to conduct a criminal investigation of one of the most serious crimes that's ever happened in our nation's history," referring to the allegations against Trump. "Indeed, you did," Grassley fumed in reply, citing disclosures to his office that Smith "obtained at least 4,782 donor[s'] checks. Many of those checks were $5 to $10. The list includes checks from constituents in every state of every single member of this committee, both Republicans and Democrats. It included 42 checks from Iowans who dared to donate money to Republicans," he said. Grassley argued there was "no legitimate basis" for what he described as a violation of donors' privacy. title: Hero cop stopped synagogue massacre in Canada as Jewish group calls for armed guards
description: The Yom Kippur attack outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville has intensified demands for armed security at Jewish institutions across Canada.
content: When a gunman approached a police cruiser outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, during Yom Kippur, approximately two dozen people were praying inside. The armed officer sitting outside was not part of a permanent security system available to every synagogue in Canada. Police had dispatched him after receiving a report about a suspicious vehicle. That decision may have prevented a massacre. "The only thing that stood in the way of every congregant of that shul being murdered was the presence of an armed police officer," Simon Wolle, CEO of B’nai Brith Canada, told Fox News Digital. ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH Police said last week's shooting was a deliberate, hate-motivated attack targeting the Jewish community. According to authorities, 29-year-old Sean Ward approached Belleville Police Constable Jeff Smith and allegedly shouted, "You are going to die for the Jews," before firing a shotgun at him. Smith was struck multiple times while still inside his vehicle. Despite his injuries, he emerged from the cruiser and returned fire. A second officer arrived within minutes and joined the confrontation. Ward later died at a hospital. Smith remains hospitalized after suffering multiple gunshot wounds to his head and body and serious head trauma. Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said Smith faces multiple surgeries and a "lengthy and challenging" recovery, but said the officer is "making progress every day." Smith’s wife, Ashley, has also spoken publicly about her husband’s recovery, describing the shooting as "the scariest and darkest day of our lives." "My words aren’t strong or steady yet, but I knew I needed to find them," she wrote. "I needed to use my voice for my dear Jeff, until he is able to use his." MAN CHARGED WITH ASSAULT, HATE CRIMES AFTER ALLEGEDLY DISRUPTING SHABBAT SERVICES AT NYC SYNAGOGUE Ashley Smith also addressed the Jewish community directly, thanking those who have supported her husband and their family. "Please know that your love, your prayers and your support have reached us," she wrote. "We are deeply grateful. We love you, we see you, we pray for you." She said her husband still faces "a very long, difficult road ahead," but added that he is surrounded by what she called "an army of love." The worshipers inside the synagogue were not physically injured. Investigators later disclosed that the gunman possessed what Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd described as the "means, motive and mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue." Police also reported discovering combustible materials inside the suspect’s vehicle. "This individual had the means, the intention, the deliberate plans and the capacity to conduct a murderous massacre," Wolle said. For Wolle, the attack exposed more than a violent act of antisemitism. It revealed a legal and security system that he believes leaves Canadian Jewish institutions dangerously vulnerable. B’nai Brith Canada is calling for changes to federal and provincial laws that would allow synagogues, Jewish schools and other vulnerable institutions to hire qualified armed security guards. "There is currently no legislation in place that allows for Jewish institutions to hire the kind of armed protection that may be necessary," Wolle said. Canada’s firearms regulations are controlled at the federal level, while private security is also governed through separate provincial rules. Wolle said those frameworks must be aligned so institutions confronting credible threats have a lawful way to employ trained, licensed armed guards. FLORIDA MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING MASS SHOOTING TARGETING JEWISH EMPLOYEES AT ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION At present, he said, Jewish institutions can ask police departments to increase patrols, although departments cannot always guarantee that an officer will be stationed outside. Communities can also try to hire paid-duty police officers, but availability remains limited. "So the only option right now for the Jewish community to protect itself from the unprecedented amount of violent attacks taking place all across this country is to plead with local police services to come by if they can," Wolle said. "They will not guarantee that they will do so in most circumstances." That leaves Jewish communities spending their own money to reinforce buildings, install surveillance systems and hire officers when available. "Right now, the Jewish community is using its own money primarily to build walls, put up stronger fences, add cameras and then pay for the privilege of having an armed police officer," Wolle said. "Our lives are being threatened across the country, and the government hasn’t taken the steps to offer the necessary protection." B’nai Brith has made two requests. It wants laws amended to permit qualified armed private security at vulnerable Jewish institutions, and it wants the government to fund an increased police presence at those locations. Wolle said the burden of protecting Jewish Canadians from targeted violence should not rest solely on the people being threatened. "The government needs to meet its most basic obligation and responsibility, which is to protect its citizens," he said. The numbers provide a stark context for his concerns. Statistics Canada recorded 788 police-reported hate crimes targeting Jewish people in 2025, representing more than 70% of all reported religiously motivated hate crimes that year. Wolle said Jewish Canadians constitute approximately 1% to 2% of the country’s population, yet remain overwhelmingly affected by religiously motivated hate crimes. Preliminary data from B’nai Brith’s 2026 annual audit indicate that violent antisemitic incidents have already more than tripled compared with the total recorded throughout 2025. "There is a national crisis of Jew hatred in Canada," Wolle said. B’nai Brith has been warning for months that antisemitic violence is accelerating. Wolle said the organization submitted recommendations and concrete plans to different levels of government before the Belleville attack. "We’ve been calling for many things from all levels of government," he said. "We provided concrete action plans to each." The shooting has intensified the organization’s demand that lawmakers treat the security of Jewish institutions as an emergency rather than another subject for future discussion. "The most urgent thing that is needed is a mechanism for there to be armed protection of Jewish institutions that are under attack right now in Canada," Wolle said. He emphasized that B’nai Brith is not calling for firearms to be placed indiscriminately inside synagogues and schools. Its proposal concerns trained, vetted and qualified security professionals operating under a clearly defined legal framework. "If we don’t have enough armed officers, then we need legislative frameworks changed to allow for alternative armed guards to protect Jewish institutions," Wolle said. Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the Belleville attack and called on anyone with information to contact law enforcement. RECORD ANTISEMITIC INCIDENTS IN CANADA FUEL CRITICISM OF CARNEY GOVERNMENT RESPONSE SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "On the holiest night of the Jewish calendar, a shooting took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville," Carney said. "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives." Wolle welcomes expressions of support and said Canadian Jews now need their government to move beyond statements. "The government gives us words and no action," he added. Belleville offered a disturbing picture of what could have happened without an armed officer outside. The congregants did not know that a man police say was driven by hatred had allegedly arrived with weapons and the capacity to cause mass casualties. One report of a suspicious vehicle led to one officer being placed outside. That officer, Wolle stressed, became the barrier between the gunman and the people praying inside. "In the wake of these harrowing events, Canada’s Jewish community cannot wait any longer for the government to act," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The people inside the synagogue, Sons of Jacob, survived. Wolle’s warning is that Canada cannot depend on chance, a suspicious-vehicle report or the availability of a single officer the next time a Jewish institution is targeted. "This is not a Jewish community problem," he said. "This is a Canadian problem."

title: Apple's $250M Siri settlement: How to claim up to $95
description: The $250 million Apple Siri AI settlement is now accepting claims, with eligible iPhone owners potentially receiving up to $95 per device.
content: If you bought one of Apple's AI-ready iPhones because you expected the smarter Siri Apple had been talking about, check when you purchased it. You could have some money coming your way. A proposed $250 million Apple Siri settlement now has an open claims process for qualifying iPhone owners. The case centers on allegations that consumers bought certain iPhones expecting Siri features powered by Apple Intelligence that they did not receive during the period covered by the lawsuit. Apple denies the allegations and says it did nothing improper or unlawful. The amount may sound small next to the price of a new iPhone, but filing a claim could put as much as $95 per eligible device back in your pocket. There are a few important catches, though, including exactly which iPhone you bought and when you bought it. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com 8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT Why Apple agreed to a $250 million Siri settlement The lawsuit is called Landsheft, et al. v. Apple Inc. and is pending in federal court in Northern California. The plaintiffs alleged that Apple promoted certain Siri features powered by Apple Intelligence, leading buyers to expect capabilities that were not delivered during the class period. Apple denies those allegations. The company agreed to put $250 million into a settlement fund rather than continue litigating the case. The agreement received preliminary court approval on July 17, 2026. The court has scheduled a final approval hearing for Feb. 24, 2027. That timing is especially interesting because Apple finally began rolling out its long-awaited Siri AI beta with iOS 27 in September 2026. The updated Siri can use personal context from information on your device, handle follow-up questions and take more actions inside supported apps. We recently took a closer look at iOS 27 and the new Siri AI features. Which iPhones qualify for the Apple Siri settlement? The settlement covers seven models: iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro and iPhone 16 Pro Max. The regular iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus are excluded. Owning one of those eligible models alone does not qualify you. You must be the original purchaser and live in the United States. You also must have purchased the phone in the United States between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025. The purchase had to be for personal or business use rather than resale. There is another important requirement. When you submit the claim, you must confirm that you expected to receive certain Siri Apple Intelligence features when you bought the device and did not receive those features as expected. Businesses can qualify, too. The official settlement site has separate filing options for individuals and organizations that purchased eligible devices for business use. How much could you receive from the Apple settlement? The settlement sets the payment at $25 per eligible device, but the final amount can change. If fewer valid claims come in, the payment may increase to as much as $95 per eligible device. If more claims come in, the payment can fall below $25. Administrative costs, approved attorneys' fees and other court-approved expenses also come out of the $250 million fund. You can submit a claim for each eligible device you purchased. That could make the payout more meaningful for someone who bought multiple qualifying iPhones during the class period. However, nobody knows the final payment yet. The settlement administrator has to count and validate the claims before that figure can be determined. 12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW How to file your Apple Siri settlement claim The claims period officially opened on Sept. 21, 2026. You can file through the official Smartphone AI Settlement website at smartphoneaisettlement.com. The deadline is Dec. 21, 2026. The claim form asks for your contact information and information that can confirm your eligible purchase or ownership. You also need to certify that you expected the covered Siri Apple Intelligence features when you purchased your iPhone and did not receive them as expected. I would have your iPhone's serial number handy before you start. On your iPhone, open Settings, tap General, then tap About. Your serial number appears near the top of that screen. You can press and hold it to copy it. The settlement site also says you may find the serial number on the phone's original packaging or purchase documentation. Do you need to have received a settlement notice? The official site says people who received an email or postcard can file a claim. It also says people who believe they belong to the settlement class can submit a valid claim even if they did not receive a notice. So, I would not automatically write this off because nothing showed up in your mailbox or inbox. Instead, compare your purchase with the eligibility requirements and use the official settlement site. Be careful with links arriving through unexpected texts or emails. Large settlements often attract phishing attempts because scammers know people are looking for claim information. I recommend going directly to the official settlement website rather than clicking a claim link in an unsolicited message. When will iPhone owners actually get paid? Do not expect a payment right after submitting your claim. The court has scheduled its final approval hearing for Feb. 24, 2027. The judge will decide whether to give the settlement final approval. Appeals could delay the process further. The official settlement administrator says payments will be processed after the settlement becomes effective, assuming the court approves it and any appeals are resolved. In other words, filing now secures your claim before the deadline. The check or digital payment could come much later. YOU COULD GET PAID FROM GOOGLE’S ANDROID DATA LAWSUIT What if you do nothing? If you qualify but do nothing, you will not receive a settlement payment. You will also remain bound by the settlement if the court gives it final approval, which affects your ability to pursue your own case against Apple over the claims covered by this lawsuit. The deadline to request exclusion from the settlement or formally object is also Dec. 21, 2026. Anyone considering those options should read the official settlement notice carefully because the legal consequences differ from simply submitting a claim. CyberGuy reached out to Apple for additional comment but did not hear back before our deadline. Kurt's key takeaways Apple spent a lot of time building excitement around what Apple Intelligence would bring to Siri. If you bought one of these iPhones expecting those promised features, you may have been left waiting much longer than expected. Apple has now agreed to put $250 million into a settlement fund while continuing to deny the allegations. If your iPhone and purchase date qualify, I would take a few minutes to check your eligibility and file a claim. You could receive as much as $95 per device, depending on how many valid claims come in. This is also a good reminder to pay close attention when a company promotes upcoming software features as part of the reason to buy new hardware. What you are promised at launch and what you can actually use on day one may be very different. Did you buy an iPhone expecting Apple's new AI-powered Siri, and do you think a payment of up to $95 per device fairly reflects how long buyers had to wait? title: Skydivers watch plane vanish from sight, make split-second decision to jump
description: Skydive Milwaukee jumpers spotted a single-engine plane vanish behind trees near East Troy, then leaped from their own aircraft to reach victims and try to help.
content: A group of professional skydivers who witnessed a plane crash took an extraordinary route to the scene — jumping from their own aircraft to reach the victims. The men, all experienced skydivers with Skydive Milwaukee, were preparing for a jump when they spotted a small plane near East Troy Municipal Airport on Sunday, according to the Town of East Troy Police Department. John Bechtel, one of the skydivers, told local outlet WSMV the plane appeared to be flying unusually before disappearing behind a line of trees. MIDAIR SCARE FORCES PACKED PASSENGER JET INTO EMERGENCY LANDING, TRAVELERS HOSPITALIZED "He kind of banked up a little bit, and then, he disappeared behind the trees," Bechtel recalled. "We were all sitting there waiting for him to show back up somewhere, and [he] never did," he added. "We all just kind of looked at each other like, ‘Did we just see a plane crash?’" The single-engine plane had crashed in a cornfield near the airport. The group quickly asked their pilot to identify a safe place for them to jump so that they could help. PROBE UNDERWAY AS 7 FLIGHT ATTENDANTS SICKENED BY BAFFLING ODOR ON MAJOR AIRLINE Air traffic control told the pilot it was his call whether to drop the skydivers over the area. "It is your discretion if you want to drop jumpers over the area," air traffic control told the pilot, according to WSMV. "Yes, I am going to drop a couple of them. Yeah, we are going to drop ‘em right now," the pilot reportedly replied. The skydivers were the first to reach the crash site. One of the jumpers, a former paramedic, treated a person with a serious head injury until emergency service workers arrived. title: Forgotten coffee brands Americans grew up with — and what happened to them
description: Starbucks and Dunkin' Donuts reshaped coffee culture, but brands like Gold Shield and Savarin still stir powerful nostalgia this National Coffee Day.
content: Long before Starbucks became shorthand for coffee culture, Americans were opening cans of coffee from brands like Gold Shield, Savarin and Schilling. This National Coffee Day, many of those once-familiar names exist mostly in memory. But that may be exactly why they still resonate. "I think there's a lot of nostalgia and romance around coffee because I do think it's such an important part of daily life," said Wendy Pojmann, a professor of history at Siena University who has studied coffee culture and wrote "Espresso: The Art and Soul of Italy." 6 ICONIC AMERICAN RESTAURANTS STILL SERVING UP NOSTALGIA AND CLASSIC FLAVORS For people who grew up with those brands, Pojmann said the connection often goes beyond what was in the cup. "So, I do think that, especially if you grew up and you smelled the coffee in the kitchen and maybe your mom and dad or your grandparents were preparing a certain kind of coffee, those memories are important, and we associate memory with smell," she told Fox News Digital. Coffee culture looked different then, too. Convenience helped define the American coffee routine, from instant coffee to the automatic drip machines that became fixtures in American kitchens. "Americans, again, were interested in ease, efficiency, things being relatively quick," Pojmann said, describing a routine that might include grabbing a big can of Folgers from the grocery store and brewing it at home. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Folgers and Maxwell House endured, but plenty of other familiar names did not. Smaller regional and local coffee brands were often acquired by larger companies, Pojmann said, part of a cycle of consolidation that has played out repeatedly in the coffee business. Gold Shield, a once-popular West Coast brand, and Savarin, a longtime East Coast favorite, were among the coffee labels that eventually disappeared after changing hands. Their fate reflected a broader consolidation in the coffee business, as larger companies acquired smaller regional and local brands, Pojmann said. Then came another shift. Chains such as Starbucks and Dunkin' helped reshape American coffee culture, followed by the rise of specialty coffee and a new generation of small roasters and boutique brands. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ More recently, specialty coffee has created another generation of small roasters and boutique brands. Pojmann said today's coffee market includes everything from huge national brands to tiny small-batch roasters. Still, a coffee brand doesn't necessarily disappear when its cans leave supermarket shelves. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Pojmann said she sometimes spots tins from bygone brands in vintage and antique stores, where an old label can unexpectedly reconnect someone with the past. "Maybe you hadn't thought of it in years and then you see that label on the can and you think, 'Oh yeah, I remembered my grandfather used to make that coffee for us,'" Pojmann said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For some coffee drinkers, a favorite old brand may be long gone from the supermarket aisle. But the smell of a pot brewing can still bring back memories of the people who once poured it.

content: Iowa wide receiver Reece Vander Zee hauled in the catch of a lifetime as time expired in The Big House, but don't ask him to recount what exactly went down on the field. It was one of those magical moments, at least if you're an Iowa fan, that portrays the magic of college football, and while Vander Zee explained that the Hawkeyes routinely run that exact play during practice, he doesn't remember any of the exact details about the game-winner. It’s just great to see everybody having a good time. You know, coach Ferentz is just as happy as anyone, and just great to be great to play for him and great to have this opportunity, so it’s awesome." title: Republicans fear they ‘haven’t done a damn thing’ to lower prices ahead of midterm reckoning
description: Senate Republicans spent weeks passing the Protect College Sports Act while Sen. Josh Hawley and others warn affordability concerns are being ignored.
content: The key focus of this election, like many before it, is the economy, but the Senate has spent its waning weeks in Washington focusing on something else: college sports. And that has proven a sticking point for some Republicans who are eager to maintain power in the upper chamber and worried that they aren’t meeting the moment to address voters’ concerns over the cost-of-living. "I'm just hoping that this will be the best bill ever passed by the United States Senate considering the ungodly amount of time we've spent on it," Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told Fox News Digital. "So maybe this will be the most perfect and pristine piece of legislation ever," he quipped. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS "There's a lot of things we could be doing and should be doing," the senator added. "So I hope we'll do those before we leave. We'll see." Hawley rattled off those issues that he hoped lawmakers would tackle that all ended in one word, costs — be it for fuel, prescription drugs, health care or the financial burden of the artificial intelligence boom. The Senate is expected to leave the nation’s capital on Wednesday to hit the campaign trail for the homestretch of the fast-approaching midterm elections. But from the summer of 2025 to now, with several shutdowns and partisan fights in between, the sting on voters’ wallets, to some concerned Republicans, has become an afterthought. Still, Republicans are quick to tout their accomplishments from last year, notably the "big, beautiful bill," as their signature achievement to tackle the growing issue of affordability in the country — it was a predominant pitch during the midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month, and can be heard increasingly in the halls of the Senate as Nov. 3 nears. SENATE MOVES TO REIN IN COLLEGE SPORTS 'WILD WEST' WITH SWEEPING NEW RULES FOR PLAYERS, SCHOOLS The concern over inaction in the recent weeks and months has intensified as the main business in the Senate has been devoted to passing the Protect College Sports Act from Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, which cruised through the upper chamber late Monday night. "We've been spending all week on trying to make the football coaches happy," Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said. "I'm voting for the bill, but I can assure that moms and dads out there across America, when they lie down to sleep at night … they're not worried about the football coaches." Kennedy said that he and others have been pressuring Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., to take another shot at reconciliation tailored exclusively toward affordability issues, or at the very least to put a bill that would shield consumers from increasing electricity costs as part of the AI boom. "Because we haven't done a damn thing," Kennedy said. "And it's biting us in the ass right now." ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER Thune did tee up what will likely be the Senate’s last attempt at dealing with affordability for a vote this week on a bill that would require AI companies to bear the brunt of rising utility costs from data centers. That bill, from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is expected to be blocked by Democrats, however, who aren’t eager to give Republicans or Trump a victory — especially so close to the midterm elections. But for some Republicans, it’s too little too late when it comes to actually trying to address voters’ worries. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., recalled a story when he won the North Carolina House and became speaker. He ran to fix the economy, and once he won the power to do so, he and Republicans in the state would have to own the issue, regardless of the previous administration’s actions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "That's how you actually show some leadership and get it done. You can't rationalize that we're here because of a problem caused by the prior administration," Tillis told Fox News Digital. "That's how we got elected. But you gotta fix it if you promise to. And that's what we have to work on. I just think rationalizing away, that's just not good politics." Still, Republicans are asking for a second chance this fall, specifically Vice President JD Vance, who earlier this month asked voters to "give us another chance." When asked about Vance’s plea, Tillis said, "You know what? If it works, it'll be a first."

title: I've battled gangs for decades. Now I'm fighting a threat that's even harder
description: Drill rap livestreams on smartphones are leading to shootings and funerals on Chicago's South Side, where location tags become deadly dares.
content: In my time on the South Side of Chicago, I’ve asked people to look at what we’re losing. I have pointed out the root causes of gun violence, set up programs to counter it, confronted gangsters and brought them to truces, and helped many enter mainstream society as productive citizens. I’ve created after-school programs to counter our failing public schools so that kids won’t give up on themselves. But lately, I’ve been looking at another problem that may just be equally dangerous: the smartphone. When you look at a smartphone, it doesn’t look like a threat. It looks like a tool for connection and even for opportunity. And for a lot of young people in my neighborhood, it has been exactly that — a way to make music, create an online following and learn about worlds outside of this block. I don’t want to discount what they have done because some have built real careers with nothing but a phone and its many tools. That’s a genuine way out of poverty, and I have no desire to shut that door. But I can’t ignore the dark side of the phone. AMERICA MOCKED THE AMISH AND OTHER GROUPS OVER TECHNOLOGY. MAYBE THEY WERE RIGHT What I feel is that far too few of us acknowledge the full power of the phone. I once watched a documentary that said the power of all the computers needed to put the first man on the moon now existed in our tiny little phones. I don’t know if that’s true, but there is no doubt about the phone’s power. It puts the entire world at a kid’s fingertips. Where I’ve seen the most devastating impact of the smartphone is in the world of drill rap, which began on O-Block, where my church and community center sit. Drill rap means "kill rap." Some of it is honest storytelling about a life that most of the country has never seen. But some of it has become a weapon. A phone cannot love a child. It can only hold their eyes through the trickery of the algorithm. Fights that we used to see on corners have now moved onto livestreams. What happens is that a location tag is then dropped. Sometimes it’s dropped when a drill rap crew chooses to film in the wrong neighborhood as a dare. This dropping of a location is not an accident but a challenge: Come and get us. INDIANA REPUBLICAN SENATOR MOVES TO BLOCK KIDS FROM ACCESSING PORN ONLINE So we have kids watching these livestreams, half listening to the rap and half waiting for that burst of gunfire to come. When the latter happens, it is me or one of the nearby pastors who has to host the funeral. We then have to send our violence impact teams to the hospitals and homes of families to prevent retaliatory shootings. All from a livestream playing out on the phones of 10-, 12-, 14- and 17-year-olds. So the same phone that can build a young artist up — and, man, some of these kids are so talented — that same phone can bring them down. When there is a shooting, the police and prosecutors comb through all these livestreams, and any comments may be treated as confessions. Whatever you think of this legal strategy, some of these kids get locked up. But the phone isn’t only a problem on the streets. Parents here struggle with the problem of the phone in their homes. I see this in good families that are far removed from the life of gangs or drill rap. Their kids simply cannot put the phone down. Kids can access pornography even before they’ve had a chance to form healthy relationships. Our communities don’t teach courtship much anymore, and for the last several decades, we’ve lived in this hookup culture. So what does a child wired by pornography think when he or she encounters the other sex? Parents are not always right, but the phone deprives the child and parent of the process of working through that misunderstanding and, in turn, weakens the fabric of their relationship. Parents often tell me the same thing, and I’m struck by how similar the wording is. It goes something like this: "I don’t know how to take the phone away from my child. It’s like I’m ending their world. I don’t know if I even have the authority to do it. They tell me that if I do, I’m cutting them off. It just becomes an endless battle." WHAT META'S NEW TEEN RESTRICTIONS MEAN FOR YOUNG PEOPLE The reality is that the phone often turns into a weapon that the child uses against the authority of the parent. I’ve heard kids tell their parents that they are smarter than them. That’s nothing but an illusion. When a child Googles or uses AI while arguing against a parent, that’s not the same thing as learning or processing the actual argument. That’s using a machine to speak for oneself. And what this ultimately does is stop the child from respecting the authority and knowledge of the parent. Parents are not always right, but the phone deprives the child and parent of the process of working through that misunderstanding and, in turn, weakens the fabric of their relationship. That’s the real crisis. Not the technology itself — the erosion of the adult’s ability to set a limit on it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The solution is not a ban. What I’m calling for is a shift in the culture. We need to return to the basic authority that parents used to take for granted. Yes, take that phone away at night. Yes, put limits on the phone. Yes, tell your child to sit at the table and do homework. Go to church. Look people in the eye when talking. Make them look at reality instead of a screen. And one thing that we need to do is support these parents. We adults who make up this community must echo this pushback against the phone, so the kids understand that it is not just their parents but the entire community pushing back. title: Rahm Emanuel expresses support for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race

content: AUSTIN, TEXAS — Former U.S. ambassador and lifelong Democrat Rahm Emanuel doubled down on his declaration that democratic socialists don't belong in his party while expressing support for a far-left candidate competing in one of the most highly contested Senate races in the midterms. "Democratic Socialists are a separate party. I'll see you in November," Emanuel told Fox News Digital at the Texas Tribune Festival. Emanuel, who has been mulling a 2028 presidential bid, has been outspoken against the far-left. Democratic socialists have won several congressional Democratic primaries across the country, including three candidates in New York City who were endorsed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, as well as Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros in Colorado and Florida Senate hopeful Angie Dixon. title: EXCLUSIVE: Hegseth to double cuts to generals, admirals in major Pentagon shakeup

content: War Secretary Pete Hegseth will announce plans to reduce by 20% the number of positions reserved for generals and admirals during his State of the Force address on Wednesday. Hegseth approved reduction plans for the Army, Navy, Air Force and the military's joint pool earlier this month, according to memos seen by Fox News Digital. Wednesday's address in Quantico, Va. is expected to lay out Hegseth's priorities for the military in the year ahead, with the reduction in senior leadership positions among the changes he will unveil. At least some of the positions will be downgraded rather than eliminated altogether. title: Nikole Hannah-Jones' daughter asks why her education was sacrificed for ideology, says 'it makes no sense'
description: Nikole Hannah-Jones and her daughter Najya clashed on a podcast over the 1619 Project founder's decision to send her to a majority-Black public school.
content: New York Times journalist and 1619 Project founder Nikole Hannah-Jones and her daughter Najya revisited their disagreement over Hannah-Jones' decision to send Najya to predominantly Black public schools, a choice Hannah-Jones now says she regrets aspects of, in a recent episode of "This American Life." Both Hannah-Jones and her 16-year-old daughter appeared on the podcast, where Najya expressed her thoughts about her mother's viral New York Times Magazine essay, in which Hannah-Jones revisited her decision to choose her daughter's school in an effort to challenge school segregation. Though Najya told the podcast that she had never read her mother's original essay, she called out her mother's reasoning for sending her to what she considered a lesser-quality school. KAROL MARKOWICZ: 1619 PROJECT FOUNDER NIKOLE HANNAH-JONES LEARNED THE HARD TRUTH ABOUT SCHOOLS "I didn't ever agree with her response," Najya said. "All I know is that I wasn't having it. I was just like, ‘why? Why am I here?’" Najya was later allowed to choose her own high school, which was majority White and Asian. While she described the students as "too bougie" with "high egos," she struggled academically at first, and her parents arranged tutoring and other support as she caught up with her classmates. During the podcast, Hannah-Jones and her daughter revisited their argument as Najya questioned why her education had to be sacrificed because other Black children were suffering. "What do we then do? Do we just say, well, there's nothing I can do? Or do you try in some way to make some intervention? It's like, why should my child be the one that's rescued? You should escape what we consign so many other kids just like you to. I just will never feel right about that," Hannah-Jones said. 'THE VIEW' HOST SUNNY HOSTIN CLAIMS HER CHILDREN EXPERIENCED RACISM AT PRIVATE SCHOOLS "Why? It makes no sense. You're talking about, 'Oh, I'm just going to give you the worst just because it's not fair that you' ... I didn't ask to be born. All you're supposed to do is just put me in a good school. Like, 'oh, well, I didn't want to put you in a great school and have you have advantages over other kids.' Isn't that what you want? Isn't that what you want me to have? Is that not a normal thing you want me to have?" Najya responded. Najya also told Hannah-Jones that "everyone's not your kid" and that she "can't save everyone who doesn't want to be saved." She denied there were any benefits either to her or the school for being sent there. "I wanted better. All the kids in my school that wanted better, wanted better. There's no benefit that came out of you putting me in those schools. There's no benefit at all. Could you tell me a benefit?" Najya said. In Hannah-Jones' essay, she apologized to her daughter for her decision, writing that she felt Najya had been cheated educationally. "Now I felt overcome with regret. Najya deserved better," Hannah-Jones wrote. "They all did. But she was mine. This girl, my only child, looked to me to protect her, to give her what she needed to thrive. And I had not chosen her." Fox News Digital reached out to Hannah-Jones for comment. OAKLAND SCHOOL DISTRICT VOWED REPARATIONS FOR BLACK STUDENTS, YET OUTCOMES APPEAR STAGNANT AFTER 5 YEARS Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation and longtime school choice advocate, previously responded to Hannah-Jones' essay in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing parents should prioritize their children's individual educational needs. "Parents should put their children first. They should not sacrifice them to a failing government school system in the name of ideology," DeAngelis said. "Nikole Hannah-Jones now says she regrets putting her ideals ahead of her daughter’s education. That admission is long overdue." Hannah-Jones originally told Fox News Digital on Sunday after her essay was published that the broader focus should remain on families who lack the resources to pursue better educational options for their children. title: Riley Gaines' lawsuit vs NCAA dismissed by Biden-appointed judge, appeal planned
description: Riley Gaines vows to appeal after a federal judge ruled the NCAA is not subject to Title IX, dismissing her landmark transgender athlete lawsuit.
content: FIRST ON FOX: A federal judge dismissed Riley Gaines’ lawsuit against the NCAA on Monday after concluding that the evidence did not establish the NCAA as a recipient of federal financial assistance subject to Title IX. Gaines and the Independent Council on Women’s Sports (ICONS) plan to appeal. Gaines and more than a dozen other current and former female college athletes filed the lawsuit in March 2024, alleging the NCAA violated their Title IX rights by adopting and enforcing policies that permitted biological males to compete in women’s events and use women’s locker rooms. "This momentary setback will not deter me or other women athletes in the least," Gaines said in a statement. "Rest assured, we will be appealing this decision. We are on the side of truth. I am confident Americans will rally to our side to fight the NCAA." The plaintiffs have 30 days to file a notice of appeal with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit, U.S. District Judge Tiffany R. Johnson of the Northern District of Georgia granted the NCAA’s motion for summary judgment on the lawsuit’s remaining Title IX claims. Johnson was nominated to the federal bench by former President Joe Biden in 2024. Johnson found that the NCAA and the Defense Department maintained separate funding streams for the research. Both contributed money to Indiana University, but the department’s money went to the university and other research participants rather than to the NCAA, according to the order. The judge also rejected the athletes’ arguments that the NCAA indirectly received federal funding, controlled entities that received the money or became a federal-funding recipient through reimbursements for certain employee travel expenses. "Here, there is no evidence that the NCAA ever received, or could have received, federal funds," Johnson wrote. "Thus, Plaintiffs’ Title IX claims cannot proceed." The ruling turned on whether the NCAA qualifies as a recipient of federal financial assistance, a prerequisite for liability under Title IX. It did not decide whether the NCAA’s former transgender-athlete policy constituted sex discrimination. The case centered heavily on the 2022 NCAA Division I Women’s Swimming and Diving Championships at Georgia Tech, where former University of Pennsylvania swimmer Lia Thomas became the first openly transgender athlete to win an NCAA Division I championship. Gaines, then swimming for the University of Kentucky, tied Thomas for fifth place in the 200-yard freestyle final. Gaines has also said she and other female swimmers were required to share a locker room with Thomas during the championships. The lawsuit named athletes from multiple sports, including swimmers Kylee Alons, Reka Gyorgy, Kaitlynn Wheeler and Grace Countie, former San Jose State volleyball player Brooke Slusser and former Roanoke College swimmer Lily Mullens. Johnson previously dismissed the plaintiffs’ constitutional and bodily-privacy claims, as well as their claims against the University System of Georgia, Georgia Tech and other state defendants. However, in September 2025 she allowed the Title IX claims against the NCAA to survive temporarily, finding that the athletes had plausibly alleged that the organization received federal assistance through a concussion-research partnership with the Department of Defense. The court then authorized limited discovery specifically addressing the NCAA’s relationship with the Defense Department. RILEY GAINES AND WOMEN'S SPORTS ACTIVISTS SHARE HONEST REACTIONS, EMOTIONS TO SCOTUS TITLE IX RULING The decision follows the framework established by the Supreme Court’s 1999 ruling in NCAA v. Smith. In that case, the high court held that the NCAA was not subjected to Title IX merely because it collected dues from member institutions that received federal funds. ICONS co-founder Kim Jones said the organization believes Johnson erred and predicted the appeals court would conclude that the NCAA, which governs more than 1,100 member colleges and universities, is covered by Title IX. "We will not give up our fight for women and girls’ rights in sports," Jones said. "ICONS will support an appeal by Riley Gaines, Brooke Slusser, Kylee Alons, Reka Gyorgy, Kaitlynn Wheeler, Grace Countie, Ainsley Erzen, Lily Mullens and the many other young women who depended on the NCAA to protect their equal opportunities but were let down by the NCAA." The NCAA no longer uses the eligibility policy challenged in the lawsuit. In February 2025, following an executive order from President Donald Trump, the organization changed its rules to prohibit athletes assigned male at birth from competing on women’s teams. Such athletes may still practice with women’s teams and receive certain benefits associated with practicing. ICONS co-founder Marshi Smith responded to Monday’s decision by urging members of Congress to oppose the Protect College Sports Act, a sweeping bill backed by the NCAA that would establish national rules governing athlete compensation, transfers and eligibility while providing certain antitrust protections to the NCAA, conferences and schools. The Senate passed the legislation Monday by a 77-22 vote, sending it to the House. The bipartisan proposal is led by Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash. "The NCAA’s refusal to recognize its responsibility to uphold women’s rights means the NCAA cannot be trusted to regulate anyone’s sports — men’s or women’s," Smith said. Smith argued that Congress should not grant the NCAA additional authority after the organization successfully maintained that it was not covered by Title IX. "The NCAA cannot be trusted to receive broad new powers that it will only use to inflict further harm upon women," she said. title: New York Magazine's first 'Men's Style' issue features shirtless trans actor Elliot Page
description: Elliot Page appears shirtless in New York Magazine's first-ever men's style issue, sparking fierce debate over masculinity and fashion coverage.
content: New York Magazine has released a new men’s style issue, a first for the company, and decided to feature the transgender actor and biological female Elliot Page. In an article headlined "The Men’s Style Issue," the magazine recalled its history covering men's fashion. "Over the years, we have often returned to the subject of men’s style. There was the 1971 cover story wondering if men would get into high heels for fall and the 1996 profile of male supermodels (‘They’re hot, they’re rich, they’re openly straight,’ read the cover line)," the magazine wrote. "For several seasons starting in 2006, the back half of the women’s fashion issue was a mini men’s magazine and featured a baby Thom Browne fresh off his first CFDA Award win and metrosexuals done up in their aughts finery sipping Peronis at Bungalow 8." "Now, 20 years later — when even 15-year-olds are ‘hype’ about Ralph, Armani’s got a brand-new designer, and a pair of worn Chrome Hearts jeans can go for $100,000 — feels like the right moment to devote a special issue to men’s style: the power players shaping the business, the new characters shaking up the scene, the old ‘semi-supermodels’ who are still around," the magazine continued. "We stopped short of announcing another revolution in men’s clothes, though you may soon find guys sauntering through the city in sarongs." ELLIOT PAGE CLAIMS NO ACTING OFFERS ARISE AFTER 'THE ODYSSEY,' HINTS TRANSITION MAY BE WHY The issue featured multiple covers, including one with Page, and linked to an article headlined "The Boys in the Baths." The magazine described the piece as "Shvitzing and kibitzing with some of New York's most stylish men at the East Village's Russian & Turkish Baths." Page was among numerous others featured largely unclothed and described the bathhouse experience. "I went to a bathhouse recently. I’ve only in the past couple of years been like, 'Yeah, that sounds nice, to like go somewhere and sit around in your body like that.' I do sing in the shower sometimes," Page said. "The same songs and lyrics will get stuck in my head, and I don’t know why. Like ‘Do you believe in life after love?’ That’s one I’ll belt out. Or ‘The Sound of Music’: I’ve never seen the movie, which seems crazy, but for some reason I find myself belting out that song in the shower. I can’t explain it." Political commentator Link Lauren criticized the magazine for promoting a biological female in a male space, arguing that displays of masculinity are already rare in the media. "There is a shortage of masculinity in mainstream media, and for years masculinity itself has been degraded and dismissed as ‘toxic.’ Now New York Magazine launches its first-ever men’s style issue with Elliot Page shirtless, wearing little more than a flimsy necklace with visible mastectomy scars. It’s supposedly about fashion, yet there are barely any clothes. They knew this cover would generate attention and controversy. I don’t think they actually care about men or style — they care about clicks. If it weren’t for 'transitioning' we wouldn’t even be talking about this actor. They hadn’t been relevant in years." DANA WHITE MOCKS CONCERNS ABOUT SO-CALLED 'TOXIC MASCULINITY,' WARNS SOCIETY HAS 'DISPLACED' YOUNG MEN Tim Graham, executive editor of media watchdog NewsBusters, blasted the magazine for its choice. "My first reaction is this: I thought these New York Magazine people are the smartest graduates from the best journalism schools, and they can't figure out who is a man and who is a woman for a ‘Men's Style’ feature. They want to pretend that this guy is a slightly thinner Channing Tatum who could dance in a Magic Mike sequel. They want to pretend none of [us] remember Ellen Page playing pregnant in ‘Juno.’" He concluded by saying that this is part of a larger phenomenon: "Obviously, they seem like they're borrowing from Glamour magazine making a ‘trans woman’ model one of their ‘Women of the Year’ a while back. They're striking a woke pose and they expect a round of progressive applause."
