title: Judge Judy passed the torch to son Adam Levy with one blunt piece of advice
description: Adam Levy reveals the blunt advice his mother Judge Judy Sheindlin gave him before he took the bench on "Adam's Law" and how he confronts nepo-baby pressure.
content: Judge Judy Sheindlin's son Adam Levy recalled how his famous mother displayed her trademark bluntness while encouraging him before he took the bench for his new syndicated reality court series "Adam's Law." Levy, 58, is the presiding judge on the show, which was created by Sheindlin, 83, who also serves as an executive producer through her company Queen Bee Productions. "Adam's Law" is also produced and distributed in national syndication by CBS Media Ventures. During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, Levy shared the advice that Sheindlin gave him before the television icon handed off the gavel to her son. JUDGE JUDY'S SON ADAM LEVY SAYS HE COULD FIX LOS ANGELES ‘IN A MONTH’ "She said, 'You've got this. I know you've got this. Have fun, do what you do, don't let people lead you to places where you don't feel comfortable, be true to yourself, and don't screw this up,'" Levy said with a laugh. "That's what she said." Prior to her TV fame, Sheindlin was a New York Family Court judge known for her no-nonsense courtroom style. She was appointed to The Family Court in 1982 by then Mayor Ed Koch. Sheindlin skyrocketed to fame after she was featured in a 1993 "60 Minutes" segment that introduced viewers to her tough, outspoken courtroom demeanor. She went on to star in the syndicated courtroom hit "Judge Judy" for 25 seasons from 1996 to 2021. During its run, "Judge Judy" was the highest-rated courtroom show on television, regularly drawing millions of viewers and at one point attracting an audience of 10 million. It became one of the most successful syndicated programs in TV history. After wrapping "Judge Judy" in July 2021, Sheindlin returned to the courtroom that November with the Amazon streaming series "Judy Justice." HAYDEN PANETTIERE AND THE CHILD STARS WHOSE RELATIONSHIPS WITH THEIR MOMAGERS TURNED COMPLICATED Earlier this month, Sheindlin announced that the October finale of "Judy Justice" would mark her retirement from appearing on TV, and she was passing the torch to Levy. Levy is the son of Sheindlin and her ex-husband Ronald Levy, who also share daughter Jamie. He has practiced law for 25 years and previously served two terms as the Putnam County District Attorney in New York. JUDGE ADAM LEVY PREVIEWS HIS ‘NITTY-GRITTY’ NEW SHOW – AND HOW HIS STYLE COMPARES TO HIS MOM JUDGE JUDY Before launching "Adam's Law" on Sept. 14, Levy appeared as a presiding judge on Prime Video's "Tribunal Justice" and "Justice on Trial," two courtroom series created by Sheindlin. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Levy confessed that he was worried about how his mother would judge his performance when he made his TV debut on "Tribunal Justice." He admitted to feeling pressure to live up to her legacy, and he was anxious over being labeled a "nepo baby." KAIA GERBER OWNS 'NEPO BABY' STATUS WHILE QUESTIONING OTHER CELEBRITY KIDS: 'SHOW ME WHY YOU DESERVE THIS JOB' "I was nervous," he recalled. "Not doing what I was doing, that was in my wheelhouse. I didn't want to disappoint her. And I knew that there were a lot of other people, a lot of other lawyers and judges that were just as qualified, if not more so, to be in the seat I was in." "And, but for my DNA, I would still be trying cases someplace else," he continued. "So there was a lot of pressure to prove that, and it wasn't even to myself — because I knew that, again, it was in my wheelhouse — but to show everyone, ‘Listen, I get it. I get this whole nepo baby stuff. I do.’ And I can understand why people sometimes are disappointed and angry and upset and at the offspring of famous people." "But at the same time, I just wanted people to give me a fair shot, a chance," Levy added. Levy recalled feeling relieved when Sheindlin told him that he was "a natural" after watching him on "Tribunal Justice." "When she saw me for the first time, she said, 'There, now you know. Now you've got nothing to worry about.' And that was nice to hear," he said. Levy told Fox News Digital that while Sheindlin has never criticized the rulings that he makes on his shows, she has sometimes shared how she would have handled the cases differently. He explained that the two regularly discuss his cases and Sheindlin is continuing to actively mentor him. JUDGE JUDY PREPARING TO END DECADES-LONG RUN AS TV'S TOUGHEST JUDGE "She's hands-on," he said. "She's not retired. She is rewired. So, while she may not be in front of the camera anymore, that does not mean that she has removed herself from the courtroom genre." "She and I discussed many of the cases before they are tried and when they are taped," Levy continued. "We will go over the facts of the case. We will go all over the legal issues, the moral issues, we will go over the background information that I have uncovered and how, if at all, to use it during the trial." Levy said that his discussions with Sheindlin were in keeping with a tradition that his family members, many of whom include prosecutors and defense attorneys, carried on for 30 years. "Whenever we had cases, we would go out to dinner as a family," he recalled. "And we would — whoever was on trial, we would bring our case file, and we would throw it in the middle of the table." "Everyone would take a piece, and we'd review it," Levy continued. "We would find the strengths and the weaknesses and how to go about arguing the issues before — whether it was a bench trial with a judge or a jury. I mean, that's what we did." JUDGE JUDY WARNS OF 'DANGER' IF PROSECUTORS DON'T RETRY LINDSAY CLANCY AFTER MURDER TRIAL ENDS IN MISTRIAL "And that's what I do now with Judy," he added. "So I think it's seamless. The process is seamless. That's what we do." Levy explained that his judicial style is "a bit different" than that of his mother, though viewers will also recognize certain similarities. "It is still about taking personal responsibility for yourself, doing the right thing, telling the truth when you're in court — all of those things are the same," he said. "The way that I go about it though is my own style. It's a little more understanding at times, I think, but when someone comes in to court and misrepresents their case or lies, that's when you'll see the DNA come out." Levy also shared that his approach to the litigants who appear before him in court was influenced by his upbringing under Sheindlin's watchful eye. He told Fox News Digital that he and his sister Jamie could "never" get away with anything while they were growing up. JUDGE JUDY SAYS THOSE WHO DON'T LIKE AMERICA SHOULD 'GO SOMEWHERE ELSE' "I kid around, and I say, hundreds of millions of people have watched her over the last 30 years. And they see a tough lady, a tough judge, cutting through the nonsense, and they see it every day," he said. "I, when I saw her on TV, would say, 'Yeah, that's exactly who I grew up with. Exactly.'" "And when the litigants would say something that offended her sense of common sense, or said something that was demonstrably false, I could sympathize with that litigant because I, as a kid, would try to do the same thing," Levy continued. "And when they would say it, I would just close my eyes and wince because I knew what was coming. And she never disappointed me while watching her on the show." "But in all fairness, at the same time, I also remember when things would happen, and I would tell the truth as a child, as a teenager, and she did not believe something I said that was the truth," he shared. "And I remembered how that felt. And so with that in mind, as I'm doing the show now, as part of my own style, is not to so quickly reject something someone says if it sounds or if it would seem to be inconsistent with common sense." "Sometimes, things happen that are inconsistent with commonsense," Levy noted. "Everyday life, things just — you get a curveball. And just because you get a curveball, and you respond to that curveball in a certain way doesn't mean that — and you tell about it — doesn't mean that you're lying." Levy explained that his childhood experiences led him to make a major format change to "Adam's Law" that differentiated the series from his mother's courtroom shows. On "Judge Judy," Sheindlin generally questioned litigants and reviewed the case file as the proceedings unfolded on camera. She would receive the case materials at the start of each hearing, summarize the dispute, and then question the parties, with much of the evidence being introduced during the televised proceeding. However, Levy said that he built more time into his process so he could thoroughly vet each case before litigants stepped into his courtroom. "I insisted on changing the format to requiring the litigant to provide their evidence before they come to the show so that I could review it," he said. "And if something did seem off, I was able to examine it, do a background check on it." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "I was able to spend a little more time or no — I could spend a lot more time," Levy continued. "Sometimes it would take me a day, one full day, to review one case that would end up 17 minutes on TV." "It would take me 48 hours sometimes to go through it to make sure that, at least to me, I got it right. Because I didn't want to accuse someone of being a liar, where they were really telling the truth." When asked who between himself and his mother would be more likely to show mercy if they heard the exact same case separately, Levy had a definitive answer. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "I would," Levy said. "Because she has never been on the other end of her takedown. I have." title: 2 Navy aviators eject during landing 'mishap' aboard USS Eisenhower, injuring 4 sailors

content: Two U.S. Navy aviators ejected while trying to land their aircraft on USS Dwight D. Eisenhower off the coast of Virginia Monday evening in what the Navy described as a "mishap" that also injured four sailors. The sailors were on board the aircraft carrier at the time. One sailor is being treated for non-life-threatening injuries at a Norfolk-area hospital, the Navy said. The aviators, assigned to Carrier Air Wing 3, were successfully brought back to the ship by search and rescue personnel. They are being evaluated by medical personnel, the Navy said. ONE CREW MEMBER MISSING AFTER US NAVY HELICOPTER MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING IN ARABIAN SEA The Navy did not reveal which type of two-seater plane was involved in the accident. It also did not specify what happened to the plane or what could have happened to cause the accident. The Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, a nuclear-powered Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, entered service in 1977. The incident follows several recent mishaps in which military aviators had to eject. PILOT EJECTS AS F-35 CRASHES AT MCAS MIRAMAR, SPARKING FIRE In May, four Navy crew members ejected safely after two EA-18G Growlers collided during an aerial demonstration at Mountain Home Air Force Base in Idaho. title: School tied to history's greatest ruler reveals clues about his life before he rose to power
description: Archaeologists at Mieza in ancient Macedonia uncovered lecture rooms and mosaic floors within Royal Gymnasium complex long tied to Aristotle and Alexander the Great.
content: New discoveries at an ancient site in Greece are revealing the remains of a sprawling royal complex where young Macedonians studied and trained — offering new clues about a school tied to one of history's most legendary rulers. The recent finds were announced by the Hellenic Ministry of Culture, part of the Greek government, in early September. The excavation centers on Mieza, an ancient Macedonian city in northern Greece, where archaeologists have been uncovering a sprawling complex known as the Royal Gymnasium. ANCIENT PALACE DISCOVERY CHALLENGES THE MYTH BEHIND SPARTA'S RISE TO POWER It has long been believed, based on ancient accounts, that a young Alexander the Great was taught by Aristotle at Mieza. The site dates to the reign of Philip II, Alexander the Great's father, in the fourth century B.C. Archaeologists began excavating the site in 2024, gradually uncovering evidence of an expansive complex where young Macedonians studied, trained and dined. This year's excavation has focused on the eastern side of the complex, including the palaestra and the "Didaskaleion," or teaching area, where archaeologists identified lecture rooms with stone benches. 'DIG OF THE CENTURY' BENEATH NOTRE DAME REVEALS MYSTERIOUS MARKINGS, ANCIENT SECRETS One of the most significant discoveries was a three-part complex spanning more than 1,700 square feet within the Didaskaleion, or teaching area, according to the Hellenic Ministry of Culture. The space includes a central entry room and two banquet rooms with surviving mosaic floors and raised platforms that once held dining couches. Though the buildings were destroyed by the Romans after the second Battle of Pydna in 148 B.C., officials noted that "significant architectural remains have survived." Those remains are now giving researchers a clearer picture of what education may have looked like for young Macedonian elites. DAMAGED FRAGMENT DEEMED 'UNREMARKABLE' TURNS OUT TO BE RARE PIECE OF HOMER'S 'ODYSSEY' HISTORY Alexandra F. Morris, a lecturer in ancient history at Queen's University Belfast, told Fox News Digital that ancient texts link Alexander and Aristotle to Mieza, while the archaeological discoveries are providing a physical setting for those accounts. "What we have in the ancient text is writers like Plutarch, basically just a line in the text saying that Alexander was taught by Aristotle at Mieza," Morris told Fox News Digital. "The case seems to be getting stronger." "But now we have an actual building to put that story to, which is really exciting." The evidence makes the identification increasingly compelling, the historian said, though she cautioned that researchers cannot yet definitively say Aristotle taught Alexander in this particular complex. "I think the identification we have right now is a strong argument, but it’s still only an argument that Aristotle potentially taught Alexander here." "But the case seems to be getting stronger." Education at an ancient gymnasium looked far different from a typical school day today, Morris also noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "You would go there to train physically as part of your day," Morris said. "So you would compete in sports games like pankration, which was a form of wrestling. You would then go and listen to lectures." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Students would also dine and drink together — giving young Macedonian elites an opportunity to forge relationships with their peers. "You were there to learn, but you were also there to learn how to build loyalty with other elite men who were there," the historian added. title: Rubio confirms 'foreign actor' involved in UK terror plot
description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed a "foreign actor" was behind the thwarted terror plot near RAF Fairford, warning of repercussions tied to Iran.
content: Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that a recent thwarted terror plot near a United Kingdom military base used by the United States involved a "foreign actor," linking the incident to global threats from adversaries such as Iran. "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the U.K. over the weekend is a very serious situation," Rubio told Fox News' "Hannity" on Monday night. "It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor." "I won't get into great detail about that yet." RUBIO QUESTIONS ‘POINT’ OF NATO AFTER ALLIES BLOCKED US FROM USING BASES DURING IRAN CONFLICT Rubio added there would be "repercussions" for threats against U.S. interests. "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is, we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," he continued. "We're going to always take that very seriously. There will be repercussions for that, if it ever were to happen or even attempted." Rubio thanked the partners in the U.K. for helping thwart the "very serious threat" of an attack. TRUMP WARNS US WOULD 'DECIMATE AND DESTROY' IRAN OVER ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT "I want to thank the U.K. for their cooperation and their help on it," he said. "There's a lot more news that will come out on this in the days to come. But there's only so much I can say right now at this point about it, other than this was a very serious thing, and it was responded to appropriately." British police declared a major incident at the RAF Fairford base in western England following the arrests early Sunday, and the government held a national emergency meeting. Police, however, released the five on bail Monday but said the investigation was not over, and they were examining whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved. BRITAIN INTRODUCES SWEEPING NEW POWERS TO TARGET FOREIGN STATE-LINKED GROUPS INCLUDING IRAN'S IRGC President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that the incident "might be" connected to Iran, which the United States has been at war with since late February, and that he would not have released the suspects on bail. "I wouldn't have done that," he said. A source familiar with the situation told Reuters that three large white vans the men appeared to travel in had not contained viable explosives. TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS The Reuters source said Sunday's police response had not been intelligence-led — an indication that the five were not under direct surveillance — but security had been beefed up at the base, suggesting there was information it was being targeted. The five arrested are all British nationals in their early 20s from London. They were detained in the early hours on Sunday after police were alerted by a local farmer to the three white vans parked near RAF Fairford. Local residents have said security was significantly beefed up at the base in the days leading up to Sunday. The local farmer told reporters that one neighbor, driving past the base on Saturday night, had been ordered by U.S. security personnel to stop and put their hands out of their car. AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. A large cordon remained around the base Tuesday morning and roadblocks were in place, although local media reports said residents from nearby homes which had been evacuated were returning. title: Real winner of Xi summit revealed as Trump looks to usher in new era with China
description: Trump's red-carpet welcome for Xi Jinping yielded fentanyl and tariff progress, but critical minerals, cyber threats and Taiwan remain unresolved.
content: For years, being "soft" on China was a political insult hurled across the aisle. Great-power competition ruled. Washington increasingly prepared for the possibility of war with Beijing as the national security world pivoted toward the Indo-Pacific. The scene in D.C. last week looked markedly different as President Donald Trump attempts to welcome in a new era with the world's second-biggest superpower and growing adversary — especially when it comes to the ever-changing tech landscape. Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping with a red carpet and the pomp of a state visit last week, speaking warmly about his relationship with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) leader as the two sides looked for new areas of cooperation. "The summit went great — for Xi Jinping," Scott Kennedy, a China economics expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. 'RED CARPET FOR A DESPOT': TRUMP'S LAVISH XI WELCOME COLLIDES WITH GOP ANTI-COMMUNISM MESSAGE The reception was striking given how Washington's leaders have spent years describing the challenge posed by Beijing: Chinese hackers penetrating American networks, state-backed efforts to steal U.S. technology and trade secrets, unfair trade practices and a rapidly expanding military with its sights set on Taiwan. Gordon Chang, a China analyst and author who has long advocated a harder line toward Beijing, said there was a distinction between keeping lines of communication open with a rival and giving Xi the reception he received in Washington. "I understand that you have a need for dialogue, but when you have that dialogue, you don't necessarily have to have all of the ceremony and all the legitimization," Chang told Fox News Digital. "We can talk to the Chinese, but we don't need to do it in the way that occurred last week." Trump, however, is betting that a warmer relationship with Xi can produce results despite those enduring disputes. The question is how much Beijing's behavior has actually changed — and what Washington is willing to live with in pursuit of a more stable relationship. Kennedy explained that "the U.S. got a few small things — agreement to lower tariffs on $60B worth of goods, some purchases of specific items (such as agricultural and coal), the standing up of an AI dialogue, and alignment on major goals with regard to Iran and the Strait of Hormuz." "But Xi came away the winner because the current commercial ceasefire works mainly to Beijing’s advantage," he added. "It gives them time to continue unabated their drive for tech self-reliance, narrow the lead in various sectors, including AI, and maintain an imbalanced commercial relationship with its trading partners." TRUMP'S QUIET CHINA WINS ARE MORE IMPORTANT THAN XI'S EMPTY STATE VISIT Chang identified the same commodity as particularly valuable to Beijing: time. "While we talk, we defer taking action," Chang said. "So China got delay. And that is, I think, absolutely critical." The administration has gotten movement from Beijing on some long-running disputes. China has tightened controls on chemicals used to make fentanyl and, according to the White House, arrested 21 Chinese nationals in August based on information supplied by U.S. law enforcement. Trump is still pressing Xi to permanently restrict additional precursor chemicals, but the steps mark tangible progress on an issue that has bedeviled Washington for years. Trade is more complicated. Trump and Xi emerged from last week's talks with a new list of $30 billion in American products and $30 billion in Chinese products recommended for lower tariffs. For U.S. exporters, that could mean better access to the Chinese market for agricultural products, seafood, timber, cosmetics and medical devices. But there is a gap between the announcement and its impact. The two countries have agreed to consider favorable tariff treatment for the products — they have not yet put all of those lower tariffs into effect. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD And Washington is still trying to get Beijing to make good on commitments it already made. Nowhere is that more consequential than critical minerals, where China's dominance over global supply chains gives it enormous leverage over industries ranging from automobiles to weapons production. After his May summit with Xi, Trump announced that China had agreed to address U.S. concerns over shortages of rare earths and other critical minerals. Four months later, the issue remains unresolved. The White House said after last week's summit that Washington and Beijing "continue to work" on restoring adequate shipments. No new comprehensive critical-minerals agreement was announced. "China has not been living up to its commitments on supplying those minerals," Chang said. The gap between Washington's warmer posture and its longstanding concerns about Beijing extends beyond trade. Ahead of Xi's visit, Trump was asked about Chinese spying and cyber activity — an issue U.S. officials have spent years describing as one of the most persistent threats from Beijing. "When they say China spies on us, I say you’re right, and we spy on them too," Trump said. "They basically do what we do." Trump's own intelligence community describes the threat in markedly different terms. The intelligence community's 2026 Annual Threat Assessment calls China the "most active and persistent cyber threat" to U.S. government, private-sector and critical infrastructure networks. U.S. officials have accused Beijing-linked hackers of burrowing into telecommunications networks through the Salt Typhoon campaign and pre-positioning inside critical infrastructure through Volt Typhoon — activity officials have warned could give China the ability to disrupt communications, energy, transportation and water systems in a future crisis. "Yes, we do spy on each other, but there's a difference in the spying world," Chang said. "There are so-called legitimate targets. That's the governments of each state, defense contractors. What is not considered legitimate is spying on civilian institutions, NGOs, universities, all the rest of it. China does that. "I don't think it's his job to make excuses for China. His job is to protect the United States." Taiwan offers another test of the new relationship. A roughly $14 billion weapons package for the self-governed island remains in limbo months after Trump described it as a "very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. China claims Taiwan as its territory and has continued military activity around the island even as relations with Washington have warmed. "My sense is that Taiwan is nervous," Chang said, pointing to the still-pending package. "We still have not had that package green lighted." Trump has also looked to Xi for help beyond the Indo-Pacific. U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue said Trump warned Xi against Chinese intelligence, components or military assistance reaching Tehran amid the war with Iran and suggested Beijing subsequently took action, saying, "They pulled some things down." Perdue did not publicly specify what China curtailed. The emerging relationship, then, is not simply a story of rapprochement. It is a test of Trump's wager that engagement with Xi can produce concrete results while managing threats that Washington still considers serious. So far, that record is mixed. Beijing has taken steps on fentanyl, and the two countries are exploring lower tariffs on billions of dollars in goods. But China's critical-minerals commitments remain unresolved. Its cyber operations remain a top U.S. intelligence concern. U.S. defense strategy remains heavily focused on deterring China in the Indo-Pacific, and Taiwan remains one of the most dangerous potential flashpoints between the two powers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What has changed most dramatically, at least so far, is the relationship at the top — and Trump's willingness to bet that engagement with Xi can manage those risks better than confrontation alone.

title: 4 simple habits can help slow muscle loss as you age, fitness expert says
description: A fitness coach reveals four key strategies to slow age-related muscle loss, from daily protein intake to strength training and sleep habits.
content: As Americans increasingly turn to GLP-1 medications — which have been linked to a loss of lean muscle, especially during rapid weight loss — experts say preserving strength and mobility should be a priority as people age. Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said that beyond GLP-1s, there are several other reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older. "The biggest change is lifestyle," he told Fox News Digital. "When you're in your teen years or your 20s, you're running around, you're doing activities that lend themselves to building muscle." FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG That tends to change as people shift focus to career and family, the expert said. "You simply become more sedentary, which lowers your metabolism and your level of activity, so you're going to have less muscle." As people approach their 40s, hormone levels begin to change for both men and women, Zemer noted. "That means we partition the calories we're using less and less for protein and building muscle, and more and more for simply storing as fat," he said. THIS EXERCISE HABIT MAY SLASH DEMENTIA RISK AND HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, STUDY FINDS "We see this all the time … people start to store fat in their tummies, and they start have less muscle." Zemer said he believes that everyone should be "very mindful" about building muscle, starting from a young age. "All the way up into your 50s, your goal should be to build muscle so that when you enter your golden years — your 60s, 70s, 80s — it's kind of like your 401K," he said. "You're going to be depleting from it as you go through life. So in your 30s and 40s, you just have to be more strategic about it, because your lifestyle has changed. You need to go to the gym and train in order to have that muscle later in life." Zemer shared the following strategies that can help people slow down muscle loss as they age. No. 1: Get adequate protein Protein helps to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, the body's process of repairing and building muscle, according to Zemer. EATING TOO MUCH PROTEIN COULD BACKFIRE, EXPERTS WARN AFTER LONGEVITY REVIEW Including enough protein in your daily diet can help reduce the risk of sarcopenia, which is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. While people’s protein needs will vary based on age, activity level and fitness goals, Zemer said people who regularly strength-train generally benefit from higher intake. "If you're a sedentary person, you don't need to be obsessed with protein," he told Fox News Digital. "Very few people aren't getting enough protein in terms of macronutrients. But if you're training and going to the gym, you want to be getting somewhere between 0.8 to 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight." No. 2: Strength-train regularly For general health, the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend that adults strength train at least two days per week, working all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises using moderate or greater intensity until it's difficult to complete another repetition with good form. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The guidelines also recommend pairing the strength training with 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity) each week. Lifting weights isn’t just about building muscle, but also preserving muscle, according to Zemer. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Even if you have a busy week, and you went to the gym and you lifted weights 30 minutes twice a week, that may not be enough to build new muscle, but that is certainly enough to maintain muscle," he said. "So it's very important that you lift weights a couple of times a week as you age." For beginners, Zemer recommends focusing on a few basic functional movements. Body-weight exercises like squats, lunges, push-ups and pulling movements help build strength for everyday activities, while carrying weighted objects — known as a farmer's carry, Zemer said — can improve grip, balance and overall stability. For people who feel intimidated by the gym, working with a qualified trainer for a few sessions can help boost confidence and refine technique, according to Zemer. No. 3: Get sufficient sleep Perhaps the most difficult strategy for maintaining muscle is to get enough quality sleep — seven to nine hours, Zemer emphasized. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Now, if you don't get that every night, you're not going to lose muscle," he noted. "But when you start to look at actual serious sleep deficiency, like we're talking five hours consistently, that is when you see rapid muscle loss." No. 4: Find alternatives if necessary "The worst thing you can do, even if you're injured, is to stop doing anything," Zemer said. "Find things you can do. Even if something hurts you, even if your knees aren't like what they used to be." Even without structured workouts, regular movement can help slow age-related muscle loss, while being sedentary is associated with rapid declines in muscle mass and strength, the expert cautioned. GLP-1s and muscle loss The above strategies are especially important for people who are taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, Zemer noted, as these drugs can lead to muscle loss in the absence of strength training or adequate protein. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If you are on a GLP-1, just remember you're accelerating the rate of fat loss, but you're also accelerating the rate of lean muscle," he said. "You want to make sure you're getting that protein and training, so that you are not losing muscle on top of the fat loss."

title: Cheryl Reeve's WNBA Coach of the Year win shouldn't distract from her dangerous accusations
description: Cheryl Reeve earned a historic fifth WNBA Coach of the Year honor while her comments on "transgender people" in sports fueled growing controversy.
content: Cheryl Reeve added another WNBA Coach of the Year award to her collection Monday. Unfortunately, winning basketball games hasn't stopped her from treating disagreement with her politics as evidence of hatred. The Minnesota Lynx coach received 40 of 74 votes from a national panel of sportswriters and broadcasters, earning the honor for a record fifth time. Her team finished with the WNBA's best record at 33-11, so there is an obvious basketball argument for the selection. But it's worth remembering who votes on this award. I've written repeatedly about the largely left-wing women's basketball media and its tendency to celebrate progressive activism, while treating dissent as something that needs to be shut down. I doubt Reeve's politics hurt her standing with that crowd. WNBA FIGHT OVER MALES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS EXPOSES HOW THE LEFT KEEPS ANSWERING A QUESTION NOBODY ASKED Before anyone explains that Reeve deserved to win simply because Minnesota finished with the best record in the WNBA, let's check that theory against, well, last season. The best record doesn't guarantee Coach of the Year The Lynx went 34-10 in 2025, four games ahead of second-seeded Las Vegas, and Reeve received just two Coach of the Year votes. This season, Minnesota won one fewer game and finished one game ahead of Golden State. Reeve's previous award came in 2024, when Minnesota finished second. In fact, she is the first coach of the No. 1 seed to win since Becky Hammon in 2022, when Las Vegas tied Chicago for the best record and held the tiebreaker. Reeve had a legitimate case this season, including guiding Minnesota through Napheesa Collier's extended absence. But her team lucking into Rookie of the Year Olivia Miles in the 2026 WNBA Draft definitely didn't hurt. The Dallas Wings could have (and should have) taken Miles, but elected to draft Paige Bueckers' girlfriend, Azzi Fudd, with the No. 1 pick instead. WNBA MEDIA PREDICTABLY EMBARRASSES ITSELF AGAIN BY IGNORING SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM STORY OVER ALL-STAR WEEKEND And Reeve's politics certainly don't make her an outsider among the largely left-wing women's basketball media, a culture I've written about from firsthand experience. Neither do Natalie Nakase's – the Golden State coach, who won the award last year, finished second with 20 votes. "I’m all about women, little girls deserving to play, and that includes trans women. So I’m all about inclusivity," Nakase said in August. "Deserving to play" is a convenient way to dodge the actual disagreement. The argument for protecting the female category is that male athletes should compete in the male category, regardless of "gender identity." Nakase presents the choice as including people or excluding them from sports altogether. Cheryl Reeve puts words in her critics' mouths After Thursday's regular-season finale, Reeve discussed her advocacy for "transgender people" and the response to the "Trans Kids Belong" shirt she wore earlier this season. As OutKick previously reported, she portrayed the controversy as something much larger than sports. "They don't want transgender people to exist," Reeve said. That's a strong and sweeping accusation. The dispute that brought this issue to the WNBA involved whether males should compete in girls' and women's sports and have access to female locker rooms. But Reeve turned that into a claim that opponents want "transgender people" erased from existence. Those are wildly different arguments. IF GENDER DYSPHORIA IS A SOCIAL CONTAGION, WHAT'S THE REMEDY? I believe women's sports should be reserved for females and that girls deserve privacy in their locker rooms. Neither position requires me to hate anyone, much less wish that person would stop existing. That's a classic straw man. Reeve should be able to defend her position without pretending she doesn't understand mine. The irony is that Reeve makes her living coaching in a league that exists because there is a separate category for female athletes. She also knows that the presence of a boundary doesn't establish hatred of the people outside it. If she wants to argue for a different boundary, she can explain why. Accusing opponents of wanting people not to exist is a way to avoid the tougher position of arguing why males should be allowed in women's sports. Anecdotal gratitude isn't scientific evidence Reeve also discussed the response to her advocacy. "With the platform that we have in professional sports, it was a small gesture by me, it’s something I believe in obviously wholeheartedly and so if I could have helped just one to feel differently about themselves because for the transgender community this really is about life and death for them," Reeve said about wearing a "Trans Kids Belong" shirt during a game against Sophie Cunningham and the Indiana Fever earlier this season. "The number of parents of transgender kids that I heard from and how it helped them and their families, it helped their child think differently about themselves and that there is someone in our position like we have as a leader. To know that there are people out there that believe in them, that they belong." First, find someone who pats you on the back as hard as Cheryl Reeve pats herself on the back. My goodness, you can practically feel the self-congratulations through the camera. But listen carefully to what she's saying. People thanking her for agreeing with them doesn't establish that her position is correct. It definitely doesn't establish that the people who disagree with her are a threat to their children. The most telling part of her comments was this: "for the transgender community this really is about life and death." While Reeve didn't openly say it, her implication is clear. A major left-wing talking point is that children will commit suicide without "gender-affirming care." Some parents say they've even heard that warning from their children's doctors. In written testimony submitted to Connecticut lawmakers last year, Simon Amaya Price said a doctor asked his father: "Would you like a dead son, or a trans daughter?" Imagine hearing that as a parent from a trusted physician. You're worried about your child, and now you're being told the choice could be between agreeing with the doctor and burying your son. Of course that language is powerful. Pro-woman advocate Riley Gaines has described similar pressure on female athletes who object to males competing in women's sports. "They told us that we would be murderers if we spoke out because we would be complicit in a potential death," Gaines said. Gaines has called this "emotional blackmail," and she's right. Tell people they'll be responsible for someone's death if they speak up, and plenty will keep their mouths shut. That doesn't make their concerns go away. It makes them afraid to raise them. title: Lindsay Clancy's push to probe holdout juror hits snag before pivotal retrial hearing
description: Lindsay Clancy returns to court in person as her defense pushes a double jeopardy motion and seeks to investigate holdout juror Michael Desronvil.
content: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — A Massachusetts judge overseeing the Lindsay Clancy case is expected to hear arguments on her double jeopardy motion Tuesday, while another push to investigate the lone holdout juror in her mistrial may be on hold — for now. Clancy is expected in court in person for the first time since her trial ended in a deadlocked jury and the judge declared a mistrial on Sept. 4. In the weeks since her mistrial, Clancy's case has remained a topic of national interest, with fellow jurors and Clancy's defense attorney attacking the lone holdout. At the same time, Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz's office has been relatively quiet about their plans for a potential retrial. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR ASKS FOR ONE THING IN NEW VIDEO AFTER MISTRIAL DRAMA LINDSAY CLANCY'S PUSH TO INVESTIGATE HOLDOUT JUROR COULD BE PAUSED AS DEFENSE, PROSECUTORS AGREE TO ADJOURN Here's a roundup of what to expect as she returns to court: Defense calls to investigate the holdout juror Clancy's defense lawyer Kevin Reddington had called for an inquiry into the lone holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, whom he has dubbed "the obstructionist juror." Desronvil opposed 11 others on the panel and was the only one who wanted to find her guilty until the end. Michael Desronvil, who is said to be hiding out at an undisclosed location, spoke out publicly for the first time in a video exclusively shared with Fox News' "Hannity" Monday evening. "I know the whole focus has been on me, but we want to reel everything back and put the focus on the three angels," he said. "The ones that can't speak for themselves, the ones that can't defend themselves, and the ones that can't fight the battles — and those are Cora, Dawson and Callan." WATCH: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror thanks supporters after mistrial in exclusive video LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR'S LAWYER TORCHES 'LOONEY TUNES MOTION' TO INVESTIGATE HIM According to Desronvil's attorney, Edward Paltzik, both Reddington and Plymouth County prosecutors agreed to adjourn that motion after counsel for the holdout raised an objection because they didn't yet have access to impounded materials necessary to file a response. "The DA and Reddington consent to adjourn the motion to investigate Michael," Paltzik told Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Monday. ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW "If Judge Sullivan signs an order today, much of it could be adjourned," he said. "Either way, a status conference is still likely." Reddington pushed back, forcefully, while conceding that he and the district attorney's office had agreed to continue the motion out of professional courtesy to local counsel now representing the juror. LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON FIRES BACK AT LONE HOLDOUT JUROR'S ATTORNEY AFTER FIERY INTERVIEW "Earlier today, both the government and I were contacted by a professional local attorney who represents Juror Doe," he said, not using the juror's name due to an impoundment order from the court. "That attorney requested — as any qualified counsel would — adequate time to review our motion and reply." He added, "As is professional courtesy, both the government and I agreed to continue this specific motion to a later date at their request. The motion remains active, fully alive, and is currently pending a ruling from Judge Sullivan. We will not allow a publicity-seeking opportunist to twist simple courtroom courtesy into a victory that does not exist." The terms adjourned and continued are similar but have distinct meanings. "Adjournment generally signifies that something like a hearing is off indefinitely especially because no date is specified," explained retired Massachusetts Judge Carol Erskine. "A continuance is a simple request by a party or two parties to get a new date. [Reddington] objects because adjournment is a misrepresentation of what is happening." CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR TAPS FORMER TRUMP LAWYER TO FIGHT BACK AS HE’S ‘DRAGGED THROUGH THE MUD’: ATTORNEY If Reddington ultimately prevails, the court could hold a Fidler hearing, where the judge would question Desronvil. "There are three phases to a hearing like that," said Erskine, who is also a child welfare advocate and has been closely following the case. "This is something that could result in a strong manifest necessity claim but hard to tell until it happens." LINDSAY CLANCY'S ATTORNEY ASKS JUDGE TO ACQUIT HER OUTRIGHT, ENDING CASE AND BARRING A RETRIAL Manifest necessity is the legal standard required to hold a second trial. Erskine said the motion is a long-shot but Reddington is likely laying the foundation for an appeal in the future. "The big issue, in my opinion, is whether outside information came into the jury room and whether a judge can find that any 'hypothetical juror' would let it influence his decision," she told Fox News Digital. "It’s definitely more complicated than that, but there is case law about it." Could the holdout sue Reddington? "This is a strange new world in which disagreeing jurors and their surrogates conduct a public debate after the trial in the media and social media," said Jack Lu, another retired Massachusetts judge. Reddington's request for an inquiry into Desronvil is largely based on allegations from other jurors who accused him of having reasonable doubt about the case and ignoring it. He is seeking phone records, his confidential juror questionnaire and police records. However, he's also called him an "obstructionist" outside the courtroom and accused him of having an "agenda." "[The other jurors] know that they were robbed — by one man — for whatever his agenda was, who stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors that were so attentive, so beautiful, so wonderful and listened to this evidence," he told reporters after leaving the courthouse on Sept. 4, the day the mistrial was declared. Still, he downplayed speculation from legal analysts about a potential defamation lawsuit from the holdout against Clancy's team. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "Defamation law is textbook complex," he told Fox News Digital. "Statements made in court proceedings are privileged." Statements made out of court that could appear to be "false statements of fact" may end up being considered opinions, he added. "If a person says X happened, and we all know that person was not present, then it may be deemed to be an opinion," he said. "This might apply to any alleged statements about what happened in the jury room." SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS What's next? "I don’t think any of the legal maneuvering, double jeopardy, all that stuff, a hearing in the trial court with the juror, I don't think it’s going anywhere," said Mark Bederow, a New York-based criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor who is following the case. title: Mass migration eroding Western sovereignty, immigration expert warns
description: President Donald Trump challenged the United Nations General Assembly on mass migration, but an expert says the sovereignty crisis runs deeper.
content: Unchecked mass migration, particularly in Western nations where millions have settled after leaving third-world countries, tends to erode national sovereignty, one expert said — an issue President Donald Trump highlighted during his speech last week in front of other world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly. As migrants continue to reach Western shores, those countries are grappling with stretched resources and tensions between newly arrived immigrants, some here illegally, and the native population, many of whom feel their best interests and cultural identity are being overlooked by government bureaucrats. The pushback stands in contrast to the vision of "global citizenship" advocated by entities like the World Economic Forum and U.N. initiatives, set against the rise of nationalist opposition led by figures like Trump. Much of the push for illegal migration comes from non-governmental groups and other grant-making networks, Lora Ries, director of the Border Security and Immigration Center at The Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital. LIZ PEEK: CAN TRUMP MAKE THE UN GREAT AGAIN DESPITE ITS GLOBALIST AGENDA? "It's no coincidence that we've seen the same tactics in a handful of countries at the same time, whether that's to the U.K., to France, to Germany, other parts of Western Europe, or to the U.S., particularly during Biden's four years," said Ries. "And what that does is it erodes the sovereignty of the nation-state. So no longer do people in a nation get to decide who's coming, how many, for what reason, and for how long, and whether people are complying with our laws." Groups like the U.N., World Economic Forum and International Organization for Migration (IOM) all advocate for managed, regular and lawful migration while treating mobility as a natural economic and demographic reality. However, European countries are being stretched thin as migrants continue to change the demographic and cultural landscape within their borders, critics of mass migration say. Ries cited the lack of assimilation among some migrants, the formation of ethnic enclaves, language shifts, and hesitation by law enforcement and elected officials to address the matter driven by political correctness. TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS "And now we've got Western countries like the U.K. and France really teetering on, are they still the same countries?" said Ries. "The U.S. is on the same path — we're just further behind. And so now … we have to ask ourselves, ‘Do we want to continue down the same path that the U.K. has been on? Or do we want to get off this path?’" During Trump's speech last week at the United Nations General Assembly, he reiterated his administration's hardline position on defending American borders while criticizing the U.N. TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH "It is deeply ironic that the United Nations has an entire institution, the UNESCO group of people and countries, devoted to protecting cultural heritage — yet, with their ceaseless promotion of mass migration, these globalists are actively destroying the greatest cultures and most extraordinary heritage in history," he said. "There is no human right to illegal immigration, but there is a right to remain a sovereign nation." The IOM, an arm of the U.N., states that it's committed to the principle that humane and orderly migration benefits migrants and society. Ries cited the U.N. 2030 agenda, the universal action plan adopted in 2015 by its member states to combat poverty and fight climate change. At the heart of the plan are 17 sustainable development goals. "They view mass migration as a way to achieve some … all of those 17 goals of sustainable development. But it's certainly not sustainable for the nation-states that are being overrun," Ries said. DHS' TOP LAWYER THREATENS PENALTIES FOR ATTORNEYS CLOGGING ASYLUM SYSTEM One aspect of the mass migration crisis is the asylum process, which critics say is ripe for abuse, allowing people into countries despite not having a valid claim and rendering asylum and refugee protection meaningless. "We need to get back to the original objective grounds for persecution, which is it has to be a government actor persecuting you on account of your race, your religion, your nationality or political opinion," Ries said. "And really get the meaning of persecution back into a box, because right now it is so watered down." It takes a lot of political courage, a lot of political will, and the ability to say no to this global funding and these major donors that are involved in this racket." title: Lobster roll war erupts in New England over controversial ingredient in 'die-hard' divide
description: Maine-style with mayo or Connecticut-style with butter? A Portland lobster roll shop reveals the surprising split among customers ordering each.
content: Ordering a lobster roll "Connecticut-style" in Maine might garner a dirty look — or worse, a side of mayonnaise instead of butter. A recent debate has heated up in Maine over how a proper lobster roll should be served: warm, with butter, or cold, with mayo. Maine-style lobster rolls traditionally consist of cold lobster meat, either tossed in mayo or served with mayo on the side. RED LOBSTER'S 37-YEAR-OLD CEO BETTING ON NOSTALGIA, AI TO FUEL CHAIN'S COMEBACK AFTER BANKRUPTCY A Connecticut-style roll typically includes warm lobster meat, poached in butter or served with warm butter on the side. In both variations, the lobster is piled onto a warm, toasted split-top bun, usually brioche. Despite the discourse over which style of lobster roll reigns supreme, Peter Bissell, co-owner of Highroller Lobster Co. in Portland, Maine, believes there's room for both. SPINY LOBSTER MINI SEASON KICKS OFF IN FLORIDA, DRAWING EAGER DIVERS TO THE WATER "We just want to make people happy with fresh, never frozen, Maine lobster meat, and our specialty mayos was sort of our differentiating factor," he told Fox News Digital. "But we're not dying on any of these hills. It's really good either way." Highroller Lobster Co. is known for its specialty mayos, which come in flavors like roasted red pepper, fresh lime and roasted garlic. Instead of tossing the meat in mayo, the restaurant drizzles the mayo on top of the lobster roll in a zigzag pattern. Those who opt for Maine-style lobster rolls tend to appreciate the tangy mayo combined with "the cool, refreshing interior of the sandwich [and] the crisp, warmed bread on the outside," Bissell mentioned. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER For guests who prefer butter, it's available at Highroller and always has been, Bissell said. It has offered warm butter on cold meat from day one, but warm lobster meat with butter is a relatively recent menu addition. "We added Connecticut-style," Bissell said. "It's a $1 upcharge because the cooks, they poach it in butter for 45 seconds to one minute on the line, so now customers can order fully warmed meat with butter if they choose." Of all the lobster rolls sold this past summer, about 50% were ordered with mayo and 50% were ordered with butter. Of the 50% with butter, 25% were Connecticut-style, according to Bissell. Connecticut-based chef and restaurant owner Robert Marcarelli's approach to lobster rolls is not quite as flexible as Bissell's. His restaurants only sell Connecticut-style lobster, warmed with butter. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Connecticut is very die-hard butter, no mayo. As you head a little bit north, mayo starts coming into the picture," Marcarelli told Fox News Digital. "I will try the mayonnaise ones here and there, but my favorite is just hot lobster with butter," he noted. title: Could Trump revoke Ilhan Omar's citizenship for alleged brother marriage? Ex federal prosecutor breaks it down
description: DHS is conducting a criminal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, but a former federal prosecutor warns of "very high bars" to prove marriage fraud.
content: The Trump administration's recent effort to bring the law down on Rep. Ilhan Omar could go as far as seeking to strip the Minnesota congresswoman of her citizenship for alleged immigration fraud. But a criminal investigation is unlikely to yield the results the president wants, according to a former federal prosecutor. Michael Wildes, an immigration attorney, told Fox News Digital that investigators face a "very high bar" to build a case against Omar after White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is conducting a "criminal" investigation against the progressive "Squad" member. It all stems from claims that Omar married her brother to gain U.S. citizenship, which she has repeatedly denied. President Donald Trump has a longstanding feud with Omar going back to when she was first elected in the middle of his first term, and quickly became one of his most vocal critics in Congress. Trump has repeatedly called for Omar to be sent back to Somalia because of her alleged fraudulent activity. The Trump administration continues to ramp up efforts to denaturalize and deport individuals accused of immigration fraud. And Vice President JD Vance claimed earlier this year that the Department of Justice is investigating Omar for alleged fraud and immigration violations. But questions remain over what a potential prosecution and denaturalization case against the Somali-born lawmaker would require. Wildes said that investigators would need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Omar knowingly entered her marriage — to a man critics allege is her brother — for the sole purpose of evading U.S. immigration laws. DOJ MOVES TO STRIP CITIZENSHIP FROM 17 PEOPLE ACCUSED OF HIDING DISTURBING CRIMES "In order to establish a successful marriage fraud case, the government would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt… that the defendant knowingly entered into a marriage with the primary purpose to evade immigration laws and get a benefit," Wildes said. Wildes noted that even if Omar and her husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, decided after getting married that their partnership could be a scheme for Elmi to fast pass America’s immigration process, this would not be considered marriage fraud in court. He continued, "Those are very high bars and thresholds that they would have to surmount. The immigration benefit cannot be a byproduct or secondary consideration. This is not deemed to be illegal." If evidence was presented to prove Omar and Elmi committed marriage fraud, the Minnesota Democrat could face up to five years in jail, a maximum fine of $250,000, or both. Wildes also pointed out that there are statutes of limitations that could hinder a potential prosecution and make it more difficult to prosecute Omar for marriage fraud, as that marriage was in 2009. But there is still a pathway for Omar to be denaturalized, which Homan described as a "very serious process" while discussing the investigation into the congresswoman. "The question is: Do they have it factually, and is it the right thing to do?" Wildes said. "The question is whether or not inadvertences were made not purposefully and whether or not it's over the top to then denaturalize somebody," he said. "We're talking about taking away a benefit and then banishing them from the United States." FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME For Omar to be denaturalized, the process would have to be related to allegations that she falsified information when obtaining her own citizenship in 2000. Omar claims she was granted automatic citizenship because she was a minor when her father was naturalized. Congressional records state Omar became a citizen at age 17, but speculation that she was older at the time of her naturalization began after former Minnesota congressional candidate AJ Kern accused Omar’s birth year of being revised on the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library website. This caused allegations to circulate on social media that she was not a minor at the time, which, if ever proven true, could lead to her denaturalization. Even if her father lied in his citizenship paperwork, this could also potentially lead to Omar being stripped of her citizenship. Wildes also explained that the government makes a "case-by-case" decision when it comes to pursuing denaturalization cases. He also pointed out the relevancy of an intentional lie as opposed to a mistake. "If the government were to prosecute for document fraud, we would also want to know whether or not she was represented by counsel, and if there were simple mistakes on her application or inadvertences that may be deemed to be fraudulent," Wildes said. "Whether or not [these] things are truthful, hypothesized, or can be backed up in fact, will play heavily in that prosecution." Homan didn't answer whether the federal government has evidence that Omar committed either marriage or immigration fraud, while also declining to go into detail about what particularly DHS is investigating Omar for. Omar told Fox News Digital just last week that she has not been contacted by DHS or made aware of any ongoing investigation into her marriage or immigration status, saying she isn’t worried about it because "the right wing always had this s--- going." 'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP But Wildes said her being unaware that she is being investigated is not unusual and doesn’t invalidate Homan’s confirmation of a "criminal" investigation against her. "The congresswoman's not being aware doesn't change anything," Wildes said. "There is no obligation for the government to show their hand, and they're going to want to make sure that they have a good prosecution, and they don't give anything up in the interim because of the politics that this presents as well." "I haven't seen anything that I think is worthy of a prosecution," Wildes said. "This is a member of Congress. It may not be your politics, but we have to also make sure that we engage in prosecutions properly and not frivolously." title: New audit in Walz's backyard exposes massive fraud risk tied to post-George Floyd activism
description: A Minneapolis audit reveals weak oversight of $36 million in violence prevention contracts tied to programs launched after George Floyd's death.
content: As Minnesota’s massive fraud problems continue to gain nationwide attention, an audit is now sounding the alarm about potential fraud in a new area in the state related to contracts doled out by the city of Minneapolis in response to the death of George Floyd. More than 100 contracts were handed out to community groups as alternatives to policing in 2020 and the lax oversight of those contracts, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune report, was found by an audit to be susceptible to fraud and favoritism. The new Neighborhood Safety Contract Management Audit Report, which reviews spending from 2020-2025, shows the city is "not providing sufficient contract oversight or managing contracts effectively" in order to properly manage the more than $36 million that has been spent since 2023 on five major violence-prevention programs. The report warns that Minneapolis’ weak contract controls created a heightened risk of fraud and improper payments. Auditors found contractors often submitted invoices with limited supporting documentation, while the city sometimes continued making payments despite missing records or unresolved concerns. The department is also said to have lacked a standardized process for conducting and documenting site visits to verify that contracted services were actually being performed. FINAL WALZ FRAUD REPORT RIPS ‘CULTURE OF TOLERANCE’ AS MINNESOTA TAXPAYERS FACE BILLIONS IN ALLEGED LOSSES Additionally, auditors found the city still needs to improve invoice reviews, preserve contract records, document contractor communications and establish clearer procedures for escalating concerns. "Based on my past reporting on this and other city grant programs, any diligent audit of any city-administered grant programs would produce similar results," Center of the American Experiment policy fellow Bill Glahn told Fox News Digital, pointing to his 2023 reporting on the matter. Glahn’s reporting raised questions about whether Minneapolis’ violence-interrupter program was producing measurable results. In a 2023 analysis, Glahn noted that the city had committed up to $7.5 million to the initiative for 2022–23, with another $13 million included in its budget for 2024–28, while the city had not published substantive evidence demonstrating that the program was reducing violent crime. Glahn also examined the backgrounds and finances of participating organizations, finding that several had annual revenues or staffing levels far below the size of the grants they received. One participant, We Push for Peace, had staffers involved in violent incidents outside St. Paul grocery stores in 2021, including one violence interrupter captured on video beating a homeless man. "The city seems primarily interested in shoveling money out the door to ‘address’ urgent problems," Glahn added. "Little if any care is given to ensuring that the grant recipients are capable of or have a track record of doing the work, are actually doing the work contracted for, or whether that work is resulting in net benefit for city residents and taxpayers." MINNESOTA'S ANTI-ICE AID FUND BECOMES LATEST CASUALTY OF STATE'S EMBARRASSING FRAUD PROBLEM The state has faced heavy criticism in recent years for not conducting enough onsite visits to combat fraud in the Feeding Our Future program along with fraudulent Medicaid programs. "If they would have just gone to the facilities, you know, you hear of the thousands of people being served out of an apartment twice a day, all they would have to do is show up and look at it," Minnesota Republican state Sen. Mark Koran told Fox News Digital in December as the fraud scandal was unfolding. "There was a legislative auditor report that showed that 30 property owners where these businesses claim to operate out of, contacted the Department of Education who manage it, who managed that program, and they told them one, the businesses don't exist in their facilities, so they don't exist, period, and one of them I think was a city park," Koran said. Glahn told Fox News Digital that site visits are "generally helpful" but he suspects that "even a cursory, front-end review of tax records and financial statements would have disqualified many of these vendors from the get-go." "We have not slowed down, there is no sense in which the fraud has been stopped in Minnesota," Glahn told Fox News Digital last month. The audit did not identify a specific instance of fraud, but it warned that Minneapolis’ weak oversight controls created a heightened risk of fraud and improper payments, and many social media users weren't willing to give the state the benefit of the doubt. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Call it what it is," retired Navy intelligence officer Phillip C. Parrish posted on X. "This isn’t a tracking glitch. It’s the same business model that looted child-nutrition money, Medicaid housing, autism therapy, and daycare: stand up a moral emergency, pour cash through politically connected nonprofits, skip site visits and receipts, then scream 'livelihoods' when anyone asks where the money went." Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment. A Minneapolis city spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement, "We appreciate the support of the auditor to make thoughtful, strategic recommendations to improve our department. In fact, the auditor expanded the scope of the report to be more thorough and holistic." The spokesperson added, "The Neighborhood Safety Department has a lot to be proud of. Our work is meaningful, and every day we’re working to make our City safer through innovative safety services, like violence prevention and human trafficking prevention, among others. We’ve taken several steps since the audit report to improve our processes and contract oversight. We are in the business of helping people and improving lives – and that means improving how we do it. It’s that simple."

title: The AI revolution will go wherever there's electricity — and China knows it
description: President Donald Trump's solar and battery storage push aims to secure energy dominance and fuel the AI data centers America needs to outpace China.
content: Despite the recent surge in AI doomerism, President Donald Trump is right to maintain his strong support for data centers. As he notes: "China couldn’t be happier" if we were to turn our backs on these centers as a nation, which would effectively let the Chinese Communist Party win the AI race. As Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in July, "The country that leads in artificial intelligence in the coming years and decades ahead will be the global superpower." Victory means capturing trillions of dollars in national wealth, securing an advantage in military technology and gaining enormous leverage in international affairs. An energy bottleneck could pose a serious risk to America’s AI lead. We need data centers to train and run top-tier AI models, and those centers need a lot of electricity. In 2024, they accounted for over 4% of electricity use, and their consumption is expected to more than double by 2030. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE Ensuring there is sufficient supply and generation to meet the soaring demand is imperative to staying in the lead. Solar should be a key part of that equation. New data centers need energy right now. New gas turbines and other large power projects can take years to bring online. Solar and battery projects can generally be deployed much faster, making them especially useful for meeting the near-term surge in electricity demand. Solar power has been closely associated with the environmental left, because for decades, Democrats largely sold solar as a climate policy, often with no concern for cost, for whether the panels themselves were made in America or whether deployment strengthened a supply chain dominated by China. However, the strategic equation has changed. Under the Trump Administration, the case for solar isn’t about "going green." It’s about reindustrialization, energy security, technological leadership and the national interest. The Trump Administration recognizes the value that producing more domestic batteries brings to our energy security. That’s why the Energy Department recently backed 220 megawatts of new battery storage in Puerto Rico, which is enough to provide backup electricity for more than 100,000 customers during power shortages. This project will use American-made battery technology — strengthening the grid and our domestic energy supply chain at the same time. Thanks in large part to the work of the Trump administration, a very different picture of solar has emerged from the one encountered a decade ago. By creating the conditions for investment in Made in America panels and components, Washington is turning what was once a China-dependent industry into another source of American energy security and industrial strength. In fact, private industry has poured $18.2 billion into building a domestic solar supply chain since 2022, and cell production was recently reshored for the first time in five years. Battery storage in the U.S. just topped 52 gigawatts of capacity, and it's been growing about 70% a year for three years straight. Thanks to these batteries, the American people now have significant access to this power not just when the sun is out at midday, but also in the evenings when America’s workers return home and turn on their lights and air conditioning. President Trump’s agenda has created an opportunity to support the domestic U.S. solar industry that we should take advantage of. By emphasizing solar as part of a broader all of the above energy dominance strategy, we can reinvigorate the domestic supply chains and spur U.S. production necessary to support our national interests, in both energy and AI policy. CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS Building up secure domestic supply chains for solar has the added advantage of insulating the U.S. against future energy shocks because the fuel these panels run on doesn’t require pipelines or tankers. Iran might be able to mine the Strait of Hormuz, but it can’t block out the sun. Call it an Arsenal of Democracy for the AI age. At a moment when the country needs vastly more electricity, American companies are answering with real capital and real factories, and Washington is finally clearing a path for them to build here at home. As one of the fastest sources of new power backed by an increasingly domestic supply chain, solar is a vital asset. America must bring solar online to continue driving AI development and U.S. technological leadership.

title: At least 40 rescued, 2 dead as boat capsizes after machete fight near Puerto Rico
description: A machete fight aboard a makeshift migrant boat near Mona Island caused it to capsize, leaving survivors stranded in open waters for over 12 hours.
content: At least 40 people were rescued in open waters by the U.S. Coast Guard, and two people died after their boat capsized several miles from a tiny, uninhabited island west of Puerto Rico following a fight that involved a machete, officials said on Monday. Survivors said there were an estimated 60 people aboard, according to the Coast Guard. The Coast Guard said the makeshift boat capsized late Sunday after a fight in which some people were severely injured by a machete, forcing the group to jump into the water despite not wearing life vests. Survivors had spent more than 12 hours in the water when someone on a boat passing near Mona Island noticed them at around noon on Monday. CBP, COAST GUARD INTERCEPT MIGRANT VESSEL HEADING FOR PUERTO RICO; 40 APPREHENDED INCLUDING UZBEK NATIONAL The person alerted authorities and helped rescue four people at that moment. Rescue efforts were still ongoing as of Monday evening. The Coast Guard said it was not immediately known where the people who were on the capsized boat were from. Migrants fleeing poverty and violence have long traveled from Hispaniola, the island shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, to Puerto Rico and other islands, moving through the Mona Passage. Many of these migrants navigate the passage on makeshift boats that can capsize in treacherous waters. This incident marked only the latest deadly voyage. In June 2022, 11 Haitian women and girls were buried in Puerto Rico after their grossly overloaded boat capsized in open waters northwest of the U.S. territory. In June, 240 Haitian migrants were detained near the Turks and Caicos Islands. Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,000 people were reportedly killed between January and June, according to U.N. data. Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and portions of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: State Department considers sharing passport records for voter citizenship checks
description: The State Department is assessing how to share passport records with state and local officials to verify citizenship on voter registration rolls.
content: The State Department is assessing how it could grant state and local officials access to federal passport records to verify voters' citizenship status ahead of the midterm elections in November. The department is weighing how to share passport information with state and local officials, as well as some nonprofit groups, as part of the initiative that aims to ensure registered voters are U.S. citizens. The objective of the plan is to share the information in a way that "protects Americans' data, deters fraud and supports the integrity of U.S. citizenship," a department spokesperson said in a statement to NewsNation. The Justice Department disclosed the plan in a court filing last week, saying federal officials plan to use passport records to identify potential noncitizens on voter registration rolls. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL According to the filing, the State Department will publish a notice in the Federal Register proposing to share information contained in the Passport Services Records system with other federal agencies. The notice would permit "information sharing with various entities utilizing federal government verification platforms, for the purpose of verifying the identity or citizenship for users accessing government websites and applications, voter eligibility, and other governmental services," according to the filing. The records the Trump administration plans to share include personally identifiable information contained in the State Department's Passport Services Records system. The 1974 Privacy Act requires the federal government to provide public notice establishing a new "routine use" for records maintained in a federal records system. The DOJ filing said the notice could be published in the Federal Register as early as Oct. 22. The filing came just days before a 6-3 Supreme Court decision on Friday that allowed the Department of Homeland Security to share citizenship information, so local governments can verify whether registered voters are U.S. citizens. DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED Earlier attempts by the administration to use federal records to verify voter eligibility primarily relied on records from the Social Security Administration and DHS, with several of those efforts halted by successful court challenges. The filing was submitted in a lawsuit brought by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee against President Trump over his executive order on mail voting. The Supreme Court recently blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing parts of that order, though other provisions remain in effect.
