title: Senate passes Protect College Sports Act with decisive vote
description: The Protect College Sports Act, which would set national rules for NIL deals, the transfer portal and more, was passed by the Senate on Monday night.
content: The Senate has passed the Protect College Sports Act, establishing national rules for college athletics, which includes standards for Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) deals, athlete compensation, recruiting, eligibility, transferring and more. The bill, led by Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., was passed by a vote of 77-22 on Monday night. President Donald Trump has urged lawmakers to pass the bill, saying "we have to get that done" prior to Congress' summer recess. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "I’m urging the House and the Senate to come together, bipartisan if possible and it looks like they have done, to send the bill to my desk and I will sign it," he said the night he hosted members of Team USA from the Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games, who performed well earlier this year. "I think we have no choice. We have to get that done. If we don’t, we’re very foolish. Nobody knows what will happen. We’re in Never-Never Land. We’re not going to let that be happening. We’re not going to let that happen to these great people and others." The bill finally got pushed to the next phase earlier this month, giving the Senate the opportunity to advance the bipartisan bill. Now, the bill will go to the House of Representatives, and Trump may see it on his desk to sign into law if it goes through there. RAND PAUL: POLITICIANS SHOULD STAY OUT OF COLLEGE SPORTS AND LET ATHLETES COMPETE FREELY "I think most people acknowledge that the current landscape of college sports is a mess," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said ahead of the vote. "It needs to be addressed." The Protect College Sports Act would provide the collegiate governing body with greater antitrust legal protections while also establishing a uniform framework for college athletics in terms of NIL compensation, the transfer portal and more. Cruz was the one pitching the bill since the NCAA made its decision to allow student-athletes the opportunity to benefit financially while playing college sports. However, there were no boundaries, and despite the NCAA attempting to clean up after the landmark decision in 2021, its asked lawmakers to step in for help. "Some have asked why should Congress get in the middle of this? The answer is simple: because Congress screwed it up in the first place," Cruz said during a news conference on Monday. "It has been the federal antitrust laws applied in litigation after litigation after litigation that have had the effect of tearing down essentially all the rules," he continued. "So right now it is the Wild West." The bill would broadly add restrictions to the transfer portal for athletes, while creating a uniform eligibility framework of five years. Recruiting and tampering guardrails would be established, where schools or agents will have to follow specified timeframes when they’re allowed to contact or recruit an athlete. title: Kentucky trooper, father of 3, gunned down during traffic stop as suspect captured after manhunt
description: Hayden Phillips, a 30-year-old Kentucky state trooper, leaves behind a wife and three sons after being killed during a routine stop on Interstate 65.
content: A routine traffic stop on a Kentucky interstate turned deadly Monday when a state trooper was gunned down, launching a statewide manhunt that ended with a suspect in custody. Trooper Hayden Phillips, 30, was killed along Interstate 65 in Warren County. He leaves behind a wife and three young sons. "He was senselessly murdered," U.S. Attorney Kyle Bumgarner said at a Monday night news conference. "We have a wife that expected her husband to come home. We have three little boys who don’t have a dad." SUSPECTS AT LARGE AFTER TUCSON POLICE RECRUIT KILLED, PIMA COUNTY CORRECTIONS OFFICER WOUNDED IN SHOOTING Phillips was a three-year veteran of Kentucky State Police, assigned to Post 3 in Bowling Green. He graduated from Cadet Class 103 and was known to fellow troopers as Unit 369. "Because he served us, because he served our community, because he wanted to keep each of us safe," Bumgarner said. "He gave the ultimate sacrifice." Kentucky State Police Commissioner Col. Phillip Burnett Jr. pledged to pursue justice for Phillips. "We will seek justice for Hayden," Burnett said. "Let me repeat that, we will seek justice for Hayden. We will not rest until this happens." JURY CONVICTS KEVIN SALAZAR IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING OF LA DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER Burnett called Phillips’ death one of the most difficult moments the agency could endure. "His dedication to duty and commitment to the Commonwealth will never be forgotten," Burnett said. "Our hearts break for Trooper Phillips’ family, loved ones and fellow troopers as we grieve this tremendous loss." State police initially announced a trooper-involved shooting on northbound I-65 near the 38-mile marker. They then asked the public to watch for a bluish-gray Honda Civic with an Alabama tag that had been present during the shooting. A Blue Alert identified Emonnie Branch as the wanted person. Louisville Metro Police took Branch into custody, and state police canceled the alert. Burnett said Branch was being charged with the murder of a first responder. Bumgarner said Branch would be returned to Warren County to face state murder charges. Authorities have not said why Phillips stopped the vehicle or whether Branch had a prior criminal record. "One of our own was gunned down and murdered on the side of the road," Bumgarner said. He pledged that the Justice Department would give Kentucky prosecutors and investigators "every tool" and "every bit of support" it could provide. Burnett addressed Phillips’ family directly, promising that state police would stand beside them. "You will not walk this path alone," he said. "Rest Easy U/369. We have it from here," state police wrote in a tribute to Phillips. AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND Gov. Morgan McGarvey, D-Ky., also offered prayers for Phillips’ family and said Kentucky would not forget his service. title: Will the College Football Playoff selection committee's new rules make their rankings better?
description: The College Football Playoff committee is adding strength of conference as a new metric, but questions about transparency and bias remain unanswered.
content: There's no question that the College Football Playoff selection committee has a difficult job. And one where it's virtually impossible to please all interested parties. In the current format, just 12 college football teams reach the playoffs, which has become the ultimate sign of success or failure for a program's season. Coaching changes are decided based on playoff appearances. Conference bragging rights, both in the public discourse and in deliberations, are determined based on playoff appearances. Given the competing priorities at play, there's little chance of keeping everyone happy. There will always be a 13th best team in the country. Or a Power 4 school that feels like they missed out to allow a Group of 6 school to reach the tournament. Conferences will advocate for more of their member teams to be included. Group of 6 schools will argue that they deserve to be included after a good season, even if their schedules can't match up to top teams. FLORIDA GATORS, MISSISSIPPI STATE SOAR, USC TUMBLES IN LATEST INEXPLICABLE AP TOP 25 POLL It's a guarantee that their choices will lead to disagreement, debate, and some level of unhappiness. Especially because the rankings are based on human evaluation, and humans make mistakes, are biased, or have their own individual priorities and valuations. Which is what makes the opacity of the committee's process and evaluation tools so frustrating. For years, committee members have spoken about how they incorporate strength of schedule and resume into their deliberations and their top 25 poll. But there's little transparency as to how they determine the strength of schedule and resume. It's nice to say it, it's another to show your work. Are they creating their own metrics based on wins and losses against, say, AP ranked teams? Or is it just eye test? Or do they use more advanced, computer-driven analytics? Who knows? Well, the committee revealed recently that they're now adding another metric to help inform their discussions: strength of conference. Oh good, more metrics with little transparency that will lead to more debate and disagreement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Heather Dinich from ESPN reported that the committee would now incorporate this new metric to help separate teams within the league. "The CFP selection committee will incorporate another data point in late November that helps determine the strength of each conference based on the schedule strength of each team in its league,' she posted on X. "It will help separate teams in the SAME LEAGUE with similar records based on the strength of their conference opponents. (Ex: PSU doesn’t play Oregon, Ohio State or IU) It will also help separate teams with comparable records in different conferences based on how tough their league opponents were." How are they evaluating which teams have faced the "strongest" conference opponents? Win-loss record? AP Top 25 poll appearances? Random eye test? Computer analytics? How do they determine how to separate teams with comparable records in different conferences? Again, the questions that the committee wants answers to, evaluating different schedules and conferences, are all valuable and important debates. title: Caleb Williams, limited by a hamstring injury, seen casually pacing Bears sideline during national anthem
description: Caleb Williams was caught pacing the Bears sideline during the national anthem before Monday Night Football despite being out with a hamstring strain.
content: There was a lot going on during the national anthem prior to the Monday Night Football game between the Chicago Bears and Philadelphia Eagles , and the strangest part was how Caleb Williams handled the moment. The Mariachi Herencia de México, a Mexican mariachi band, performed the "Star-Spangled Banner". And while the anthem played , the two teams' players, coaches and others stood along the sidelines. But Williams was an exception. CALEB WILLIAMS AVOIDS MAJOR HAMSTRING INJURY AS MRI REVEALS A STRAIN BUT NO TEAR AFTER VIKINGS GAME SCARE While the anthem was playing, Williams was seen on the ESPN national broadcast pacing along the Bears sideline as if he had somewhere else important to get to. Williams , in fact, didn't have anywhere important to go because he isn't playing in this game – or possibly in a couple of others – while he recovers from a hamstring strain suffered in last week's loss to the Minnesota Vikings. And yet, the guy who cannot move well enough to play because a soft tissue injury is walking around during the national anthem. Maybe Williams doesn't know or doesn't care, but this is a ceremonial no-no at best and disrespectful at worst. The patriotic Code of Conduct for the national anthem is available online, through a government website. It reads: "During rendition of the national anthem when the flag is displayed, all present except those in uniform should stand at attention facing the flag with the right hand over the heart." That, believe it or not, has been the code since 1942. In 1976, the code was amended to insert the requirement that "during the rendition of the national anthem when the flag is displayed, all persons present except those in uniform should stand at attention, face the flag, and place the right hand over the heart and men with headdress should remove the headdress and hold it at the left shoulder, the hand being over the heart and when the flag is not displayed, those present should face the music and act in the same manner they would if the flag were displayed." This is not debatable. It's the universal code of conduct for Americans. Maybe Williams isn't aware. The educational system today is not renowned for teaching traditional American values and traditions any more, and Williams, 24, is a product of that system. Or maybe Williams doesn't really like to be bothered by the traditions of the national anthem. He was seen last season trying to chat with a teammate on the sideline during the national anthem. More than a few reacted negatively on social media about the behavior. Other people will simply shrug it off as an oversight or not worthy of attention. title: Reparations activist does not expect compensation from New York officials as action is delayed for years
description: The U.S. Freedmen Project said New York's reparations commission delay proves the system is designed to stall, not deliver, for descendants.
content: A reparations activist with a grassroots organization called the U.S. Freedmen Project told Fox News Digital that their group expects no financial compensation from New York state officials after lawmakers quietly delayed a high-profile study into historic remedies. "What the mainstream reparations movement is really about ... is spinning your wheels until [those] to whom the debt is owed tire out, give up, and give in," U.S. Freedmen Project President Devine Prince told Fox News Digital. "That's the only reason why you would pursue race-based policies within a system and within a country that has the 14th Amendment, which bans and prohibits race-based policies." The U.S. Freedmen Project — a group of self-identified "Foundational Black Americans" — aims to educate the public on the legal and historical distinctions between African Americans who are direct descendants of enslaved people in the U.S. and immigrants from Africa or the Caribbean who arrived voluntarily in recent decades. CHAOS ERUPTS AT NY REPARATIONS HEARING AS ‘FOUNDATIONAL’ BLACK AMERICANS CLASH WITH LEFT-LEANING GROUPS Prince’s comments follow sharp backlash after state leaders extended the timeline for the New York State Community Commission on Reparations Remedies to issue its final report. A provision embedded in the recently passed state budget pushed the commission's deadline back two years — from 2027 to 2029 — nearly four years beyond its original 2025 deadline. The New York Civil Liberties Union (NYCLU) publicly criticized the delay in June. "The state’s decision to spend an additional three years before it takes any action to address these harms raises a lot of questions about when Black New Yorkers will receive reparations," said Chantelle Williams, assistant director of the NYCLU’s Racial Justice Center. "Meanwhile, the impact of discrimination continues to harm Black individuals and communities across the state. This delay is not just a bureaucratic inconvenience. It is a disservice to those who have suffered the profound and lasting consequences of inequality," Williams added. NEW YORK FAR-LEFT GROUP CLAIMS REPARATIONS 'OWED' AS BLACKS' MEDIAN WEALTH 'NEARLY 15 TIMES LESS' THAN WHITES The nine-member state commission, established by legislation signed by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul in late 2023, was tasked with examining the Empire State's historical ties to slavery, Jim Crow-era discrimination, and economic disparities like redlining. The panel was charged with delivering recommendations for potential state-level financial compensation and policy reforms. The commission recently concluded a series of statewide public hearings, culminating in a May 30 forum in Harlem titled "From Extraction to Repair: Closing the Racial Wealth Gap." However, state lawmakers opted to move back the commission's deadline. Assemblymember Michaelle C. Solages, D-N.Y., who sponsored the original legislation, acknowledged the extension was requested to navigate a shifting national legal environment. Solages cited conservative legal challenges targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and the broader erosion of race-conscious policies. The budget measure also included a provision shielding commissioners from personal legal liability if targeted by lawsuits over their findings. Lineage advocates with the U.S. Freedmen Project, who attended the Harlem hearing, pushed back strongly against both the delay and the commission's framework. They argue that reparations should be strictly limited to direct descendants of individuals enslaved within the United States rather than broader race-based categories. Activists with the group contend that progressive organizations like the NYCLU fail to represent the distinct legal and historical claims of descendant Black Americans by attempting to include recent Black immigrants under the same umbrella. Prince claimed that members of the New York commission were appointed to preserve the status quo rather than deliver tangible results. "These are individuals that have been put in place to keep the status quo intact while pretending they're working to undo it," Prince said. "There's a bunch of things moving around in the background that tie them to this ideology that benefits them if we keep the status quo of race-based advocacy alive." "What we are focused on is true repair — and, unfortunately, true repair means repairing those who were truly harmed. Not everyone who comes in and says, 'Hey, I'm included in that, too,'" he added. Supporters of the Freedmen Project maintain that any state-level reparations bill based on race rather than direct lineage would violate the U.S. Constitution's Equal Protection Clause. They urged state officials to adopt strict lineage-based criteria to reduce the program's exposure to legal challenges. New York is part of a broader wave of blue states and municipalities attempting to construct local reparative frameworks. In Illinois, the Chicago suburb of Evanston, Illinois made headlines as the first U.S. city to distribute reparations, offering $25,000 housing grants to eligible Black residents. Despite public hearings and ongoing research, Prince expressed skepticism that New York state will ever deliver payments to descendants. TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF 'VIRTUE SIGNALING' TO GET 'VOTES' "Realistically, I'm expecting the same thing that I expected going into this: nothing," Prince said. "Based on all the advocacy we did before this was even signed into law — all the recommendations we suggested and experts we brought to the New York Legislature to inform them on how to get this right — once all those things were ignored, I knew it would end up right where it is now. Realistically, I'm expecting them to find a way to distance themselves from this." title: ABC's 'The View' co-host Ana Navarro urges viewers to vote for Dem in key Florida congressional race

title: Be like Sophie Cunningham, not Chris Simms — never give in to the outrage mob
description: Sophie Cunningham's refusal to back down after WNBA backlash stands in stark contrast to Chris Simms and other sports figures who caved to outrage.
content: Sophie Cunningham understands something that very few others in the sports world seem to. You never, ever cave to the mob if you haven't done anything wrong. The Indiana Fever guard proved as much this summer after she came out against biological males competing against females in sports. SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPARKS SOCIAL MEDIA MELTDOWN BY SPEAKING OUT TO PROTECT WOMEN'S SPORTS Her stance prompted her to garner the title "MAGA Barbie." It sparked fans to boo her when she entered the game in cities such as Seattle. It caused a sports reporter to say that she is "unafraid to be blatantly transphobic" and fans to call for her suspension. Did Cunningham buckle? Hell no. She doubled down with an Instagram post that declared she isn't backing down for anyone. "I said what I said," she wrote. This is the only way to do it. If there's one thing the mob hates more than anything, it's courage. You show it to them, they go away. It's just sad that so few seem to possess it. NBC Sports football analyst Chris Simms was the latest to bow to online outrage over some perfectly reasonable comments. After Oregon quarterback Dante Moore was knocked out of Saturday's game due to a helmet-to-helmet hit by USC's Desman Stephens II, Simms did what an analyst is paid to do: analyze. At halftime, Simms said that Moore's injury was a "Debbie Downer" moment because fans want to see teams at full strength. He then shared some advice his father told him about how to "make sure you get down in time and don't take any big hits." He added how Moore's late slide put Stephens in a "no-win situation." DAN DAKICH CALLS CHRIS SIMMS' APOLOGY OVER DANTE MOORE SLIDE ANALYSIS 'SOFT A-- BULLS--T' This is an ex-football player talking football. But apparently all Oregon fans wanted to hear was that this was the dirtiest hit in the history of the sport, so Sunday, Simms took to social media to write "I clearly did not show enough sympathy for the situation. I mishandled the situation and I was wrong. I'm sorry for that." It seems like we see a new one of these every week. Earlier this month, Texas quarterback Arch Manning laughed at an AI meme of ESPN reporter Holly Rowe getting slapped by Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian. He was shamed into apologizing two days later. In July, Sandy Brondello, coach of the WNBA's Toronto Tempo, wanted a foul to be called on Atlanta's Angel Reese, and could be heard telling refs that Reese was a "protected species." This is common lingo in Australia — Brondello's home country — where it's meant to express frustration over a player getting special treatment. But Brondello still issued a written apology to Reese, saying "I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that." title: Dan Wilson announces his own firing as Seattle Mariners manager in rare postgame moment
description: Dan Wilson broke MLB protocol by personally announcing his own dismissal as Seattle Mariners manager, delivering an emotional postgame address.
content: Seattle Mariners manager Dan Wilson personally broke the news to his team and the media Sunday that he will not return for the 2027 season. Before Game 162 against the Los Angeles Angels, Wilson held a closed-door meeting to inform players and staff. Postgame, he stepped to the podium to deliver the news publicly and face questions before front-office executives addressed reporters. Standard MLB protocol calls for front-office executives to issue a news release or hold a solo news conference while the ousted manager stays out of sight. A manager taking the microphone to announce his own dismissal is virtually unheard of in modern sports. "This season has been very difficult, and of course, the results have not been what any of us have expected," Wilson said. "As a result, it's concluded that today is my last day as manager of the Seattle Mariners." Wilson, a former Mariners catcher who took over as manager in August 2024, acknowledged his deep roots in the organization. "I'm still processing this with my family, and it's a very difficult day," Wilson said. "We love this city. We love this community and we appreciate the organization for what it has meant to the family since coming here as a player in '94. We feel extremely blessed by all the opportunities we've been afforded." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Expectations were sky-high entering 2026. Coming off a 2025 AL West title and reaching Game 7 of the ALCS, Seattle fell just one win short of the World Series. Instead, the club collapsed to a 76-86 third-place finish. The downward spiral was driven by offensive regression among core players, inconsistent starting pitching, a second-half bullpen collapse and some of the worst defensive metrics in Major League Baseball. Late-season comments from players highlighted a lack of clubhouse accountability as a core failure. Pressed on whether leadership failed to enforce standards, Wilson faced the criticism directly. "That's always a necessary component, and I think accountability comes in a lot of different ways," Wilson said. title: Trump CMS faces bipartisan pushback over Medicare proposal tied to Biden-era drug pricing law
description: Lawmakers say the proposed Medicare policy could make it harder for patients to access newer cancer treatments by discouraging medical innovation.
content: EXCLUSIVE: A bipartisan group of more than 50 lawmakers is urging the Trump administration not to finalize a proposed Medicare policy tied to the Biden-era drug price negotiation program, arguing it could discourage development of improved cancer treatments. In a Sept. 21 letter obtained by Fox News Digital, the lawmakers called on Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz to remove the agency's proposed fixed-dose combination policy from its final rule implementing Medicare's Drug Price Negotiation Program. The Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program was created under the Inflation Reduction Act, which former President Joe Biden signed into law in 2022. The Trump administration proposed the policy in June as part of implementing that program. At the center of the dispute is how Medicare would treat newer versions of existing drugs for price negotiation purposes. DR OZ WARNS MEDICARE SCAMMERS ARE STEALING BILLIONS — AND YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION COULD BE NEXT The lawmakers argue the proposal would cause some improved treatments to face Medicare price negotiations much sooner after receiving Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval. They say that would reduce incentives for drugmakers to develop better versions of existing medicines. "If finalized, the proposed fixed-dose combination policy would subject these advancements to negotiation almost immediately after FDA approval, harming patient access as well as incentives to develop these improved therapies," the lawmakers wrote. CMS, meanwhile, said the proposal is designed to prevent drugmakers from avoiding or delaying negotiated Medicare prices by making only limited changes to existing drugs and introducing them as new products. DR OZ NAMES 5 STATES IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TARGETS MEDICAID ABUSE The lawmakers pointed to advances in cancer immunotherapy that allow some patients to receive a quick injection instead of spending hours receiving an intravenous infusion. They said those improvements can make treatment faster, easier and more accessible, particularly for patients in rural areas. "Patients fighting cancer deserve access to the most advanced new therapies, and if CMS finalizes this proposal, those advances are less likely to reach those who need it the most," the letter states. The lawmakers also argued the FDA already evaluates the therapies as separate medicines, requiring separate clinical trials and approvals. They said CMS should treat those therapies as separate medicines under the Medicare drug price negotiation program. The lawmakers also argued that CMS actuaries "have not been able to show this policy would produce meaningful savings for taxpayers." DR OZ REVEALS THE HEALTHY RETIREMENT HABIT THAT COULD MAKE AMERICA $1 TRILLION RICHER "We strongly urge CMS to withdraw the fixed-dose combination proposal from the final rule," the letter states. "The patients we represent need policies that expand access to lifesaving care and reward medical progress and innovation in the treatment of deadly diseases." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The letter was signed by more than 50 lawmakers from both parties, including Reps. John Joyce, R-Pa., Darin LaHood, R-Ill., Mike Kennedy, R-Utah, Tim Moore, R-N.C., Jim Costa, D-Calif., Donald Davis, D-N.C., and more. CMS could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

title: Grandmother sues after alleged AI facial recognition error led to months in jail, experts sound alarm
description: Angela Lipps was arrested at gunpoint and jailed for nearly six months after Fargo police allegedly relied on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match.
content: A Tennessee grandmother has filed a lawsuit against a North Dakota city and police department, accusing officials of wrongfully detaining her for nearly six months after allegedly misusing artificial intelligence facial recognition technology to investigate a bank theft case. Angela Lipps, now 50, of Elizabethton, Tennessee, said she was caring for her neighbor's four young children when police showed up at the home and arrested her at gunpoint in July 2025. The complaint, filed Sept. 15, 2026, alleges that authorities relied exclusively on a flawed AI facial recognition match to extradite Lipps from Tennessee to North Dakota, despite her having no connection to the crime or the state. Experts on police technology told Fox News Digital that the case is among more than a dozen known instances involving alleged police mishandling of facial recognition technology. "I sat in a county jail in Tennessee for 108 days," Lipps said in a GoFundMe post. "They said I was fugitive from justice. I had no bail. No one interviewed me. I just sat and waited." FRAUD EXPERT WARNS AI IS HELPING CRIMINALS OUTPACE THE GOVERNMENT: 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT TOOLS' The bank theft case stemmed from April and May 2025, when an unknown woman allegedly used fake IDs and stolen identities to perpetrate bank fraud in Fargo and West Fargo, North Dakota, according to the lawsuit. Officials then used a photo from a fraudulent ID card presented by the suspect, rather than surveillance footage, to conduct facial recognition searches using Clearview AI, plaintiffs alleged. While Clearview AI explicitly requires facial recognition matches to be treated as potential leads, Fargo police allegedly characterized the AI match as a positive identification without disclosing that it had not been independently corroborated, according to the complaint. Meanwhile, the West Fargo Police Department reportedly declined to seek charges because the AI match was uncorroborated. A West Fargo police captain reportedly characterized AI facial recognition as "close to a last-ditch effort" in police investigations, the lawsuit said. FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES According to the complaint, Detective Lucas Heck did not review Lipps’ financial or travel records that showed she was in Tennessee during the bank thefts and failed to conduct photo lineups with bank tellers. Surveillance video reportedly showed physical differences between Lipps and the suspect, including a different build and a neck tattoo on Lipps that was absent from the suspect. "Heck ignored, concealed, and misrepresented exculpatory evidence that Lipps did not commit the bank thefts," the complaint alleged. On July 14, 2025, U.S. Marshals surrounded a neighbor’s house in Tennessee and arrested Lipps at gunpoint on a nationwide warrant, plaintiffs said. Lipps was extradited to North Dakota and reportedly held on a $100,000 bond while facing eight felony counts, the most severe of which carried maximum sentences of up to 10 years in prison. Prosecutors dismissed all charges on Dec. 24, 2025, after Lipps produced bank records showing that she was in Tennessee when the bank thefts occurred, plaintiffs said. "When she was released, she found that her residence, car, and personal property were lost while she was absent," the complaint said. FLOCK SAFETY CEO CALLS FOR NATIONAL 'COMPROMISE' AMID CAMERA SABOTAGE AND PUBLIC REVOLT Following public scrutiny, the Fargo Police Department and city of Fargo acknowledged at a March 2026 press conference that the department had made investigative errors. "When chief found some errors that were made in this area of where we got our facial recognition and how that worked, we immediately addressed it," Mayor Tim Mahoney said. Clare Garvie, the deputy director of Technology Law & Policy with the Policing Project, told Fox News Digital that incidents involving the alleged mishandling of AI have increased as law enforcement agencies adjust to "integrate AI and additional tools into police investigations." "We are aware of 16 misidentifications stemming from a face recognition match where someone was wrongfully arrested and spent time in jail because of that misidentification, and in many of these cases, it was because additional investigative steps weren't taken to prove, or in these cases to disprove, the face recognition match," Garvie said in an interview. "We're asking officers to do a different job now, such that we need to update how we think about these workflows," she added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In an interview with Fox News Digital, Nate Freed-Wessler, a deputy director at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the rise of artificial intelligence in law enforcement has fueled wrongful arrests across the country. "We've been seeing these kinds of wrongful arrests happening for at least five or six years now out of this kind of AI technology. And the rate of them seems to be increasing," he said. "We've seen cases where police intentionally avoid making any notes about their use of facial recognition technology or other AI."

title: Dem Senate nominee breaks silence after Susan Collins' office was vandalized with vulgar message

content: Republican Sen. Our Biddeford constituent service office remains open, and we will continue serving the people of Maine," Collins Chief of Staff Katie Brown said in a statement to Fox News Digital. SUSAN COLLINS DEFIES BLUE-STATE HEADWINDS IN CRUCIAL SENATE BATTLE AS NEW POLL REVEALS STRIKING SPLIT Collins is running for re-election this year for a sixth six-year term representing blue-leaning Maine in the Senate, and is locked in a competitive contest with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president. title: Former Obama aides claim Democratic donors are still holding back after being burned by 2024 loss
description: "Pod Save America" hosts say Democratic donors are holding back despite what they call a generational midterm election opportunity for the party.
content: Former Obama advisers who host the "Pod Save America" podcast spoke Friday about the purported reasons some major Democratic donors are holding back money as the party sees encouraging signs ahead in November's midterm elections. At the Texas Tribune Festival last week, the podcast hosts shared their optimism over Texas turning blue because of Republican struggles in purple states. Dan Pfeiffer spoke about numerous factors working against Republicans, even in rural areas, but still warned that Democrats have far less money to work with, compared to the GOP. Tommy Vietor replied, "I think those spending restraints compared to the opportunity are why you're starting to hear some, you know, sort of operatives and candidates like voicing concern and frustration that some of the traditional like big, big donors of the Democratic Party, are not viewing this as the generational opportunity that it could be." THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES "Because I was talking to someone today who was like, ‘Let me paint for you the like extreme optimistic picture,’ which is Democrats are not only winning on the generic ballot, but if you look at the top like most salient issues, we are crushing in those areas as well, which was not the case in 2024, right?," he continued. Vietor proposed that if the results of this midterm election resemble recent special elections where Democrats overperformed, "it is like truly a historic opportunity to win statewide races, congressional races, down-ballot, up and down. And it just feels like a moment when all the biggest donors in the party should be pushing all their chips in the table as aggressively as possible and not holding back for — I don't know what reason — Trump bothering them?" "Yeah, I think there has been a huge shift in the funding approach ... in the large donor community since 2024," Pfeiffer said. "Part of it is people still angry about how that election went and feeling like they lit a billion dollars on fire in that election, which is a fair quibble in some ways." "There are a lot of people who are very afraid of being targeted by Trump like that just that your business is going to be targeted," he continued. "You're going to have all of a sudden, you're going to the FBI is going to show up at your door. You're going to have regulatory scrutiny you wouldn't have before. And so that has limited money." CASH-STRAPPED DNC SHELLED OUT MORE THAN $800K TO NON-VOTING TERRITORIES LIKE VIRGIN ISLANDS WHILE IN DEBT Pfeiffer argued further that this midterm election could possibly lead to a scenario where "you're looking at one of the largest swings in American history, something where Democrats could pick up races we've never even thought possible," he said. "We've been using 2006 as like the most relevant example of an election because it's you know, it's an unpopular president, unpopular war, all of that. But it very well could be a little more like '94, where everything changes where it's a realigning election." Democratic consultant Julian Epstein rejected the podcasters' comments. "It's always funny to me how these group think 'insiders' parrot one another, even when their 'consensus' is obviously wrong. The truth is that the so-called 'blue tsunami' is very likely overstated. The margin of error in the 40 battleground congressional districts is more like 2% right now, and we've consistently seen Republicans being undersampled in recent years," he told Fox News Digital. "Donors are holding back because the Democrats don't have any attractive, positive agenda," he continued. "Democrats have an even lower approval rating than the president. Democrats used to be about building; today they are about tax-and-spend redistributionist big government welfare. They are about the victim Olympics." "Try going out on the street and ask 10 voters to name three things Democrats stand [for] today. I doubt you'll find any that can," Epstein added. "Yes, major Democratic donors are holding back, still frustrated by the fallout from the 2024 cycle and increasingly concerned about the party's direction," Marslender told Fox News Digital. "Kamala Harris’ failed presidential campaign spent a staggering $1.5 billion in just 15 weeks, losing the popular vote, the Electoral College, the Senate, the White female vote, and support among both Latino and working-class voters," she continued. title: Texas player's vulgar sack celebration was inexcusable for an athlete who promotes Christianity
description: Colin Simmons' vulgar sack celebration against Tennessee sparked backlash, raising questions about his faith after once bringing a Bible onto the field.
content: Texas Longhorn defensive end Colin Simmons is arguably the best d-end in college football. He looks like a man among boys in the way he manhandles offensive tackles and sacks quarterbacks, but his antics in the Longhorns thrilling victory over Tennessee on Saturday showcased why he's still very much a boy in maturity. Simmons, who claims to be a Christian, used to be best known for what he did following winning the Texas 6A Division I state championship with Duncanville High School. He brought a Bible onto the field and boldly proclaimed, "It ain't nobody but God!" In the biggest moment of his high school career, he pointed people to God. He deferred the glory, honor, and praise from himself and gave it to his Creator. It was refreshing to witness, just like it is every time we hear a player or coach do in their brightest moments. Now, Simmons is unfortunately known for one of college football's most vulgar sack celebrations ever. Following a clutch third down sack, deep in the Tennessee side of the field, Simmons simulated pulling his penis out and peeing on the field. It wasn't just immature; it was utterly disgusting. Kirk Herbstreit called it "idiotic" on the broadcast and Chris Fowler, also calling the game, said it "it doesn't much [more] vulgar" than what Simmons did. TEXAS DROPPED SOME CELEBRATIONS AGAINST TENNESSEE THAT WERE ABOUT AS UNHINGED AS THEY COME What Simmons did wasn't just wrong as an athlete in a public setting. He was representing much more than just the Longhorns on national television. As a professing Christian, he's always representing Jesus Christ and the faith as a whole. No, thankfully the Christian faith isn't based on the moral failings of Simmons and I, but what we say and do are undoubtedly a reflection of our faith. That makes what he did much worse, in my opinion. No, that's also not to say an atheist athlete should be able to get away with this and shouldn't have to apologize. I'm simply stating that an athlete who has purposely linked his Christian faith with his public persona, should hold himself to the highest moral and ethical standards. That's why I believe Trinindad Chambliss dropping an f-bomb in the postgame interview following Ole Miss' upset win over LSU, where he spent much of the interview praising God, was a bad look as well and worth apologizing over. It's unbecoming of a Jesus follower and showcased a blatant hypocrisy and major lack of control and discernment. SAM ACHO Q&A: FORMER NFL PLAYER AND ESPN ANALYST SPEAKS OUT ON CIVILITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN SPORTS AND MEDIA Chambliss ended up apologizing postgame while wearing a "Jesus Won" T-shirt, showing true remorse for allowing the heat of the moment to cause himself to be a poor reflection of his faith saying, ""That’s not who I am. I’m deeply, deeply apologetic to Holly Rowe & everyone who was listening." Houston Texans QB CJ Stroud addressed the problem with Christians cussing in an interview with Sports Spectrum in 2024. He said, "I can't proclaim I love God and have a wild mouth… it's hypocritical." He said this while references James 3, a biblical chapter focusing on the power and discipline of taming the tongue. BUCS' EMEKA EGBUKA, WHOSE INSTAGRAM NAME IS 'CHRIST FOLLOWER,' EXPLAINS HOW FAITH HELPS DRIVE HIS CAREER But what Simmons did was something that was incredibly difficult to imagine a professing Christian athlete ever doing. We all have trouble taming our tongue. I know I've had trouble with that over the years playing sports, and in times of frustration, but having a premeditated sack celebration with that level of vulgarity is inexcusable. Simmons did apologize postgame, but saying you're remorseful and actually being remorseful are two very different things. Seemingly excusing his actions, Simmons stated, "I was definitely in that mode, feeling myself. It happens." That's not a valid excuse, in my opinion. It portrays a lack of understanding of the severity of his suggestive actions, especially as a Christian. Cussing happens. Losing our patience happens. Pretending to whip out your penis and pee on an opposing team's field doesn't just happen. That is a premeditated, unsportsmanlike, vulgar action that makes him look like a degenerate. NO. 1 TEXAS ESCAPES TENNESSEE WITH THRILLING SEC VICTORY AS PRESIDENT TRUMP WATCHES ON FROM NEYLAND STADIUM In the Bible, 1 Peter 4 addresses the Christians of the early church, who are called, just as Christians of this day and age, to hold themselves to a higher standard than they once did when they weren't Christians. As believers, we are to pursue holiness and encourage each other to pursue it, too. That is why I'm calling my professed brother in Christ, Colin Simmons, to hold himself to that standard. I'm calling his Christian teammates, family members, coaches, and more, to help hold him accountable. Lord knows I need accountability too. Proverbs 17:7 says, "As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another." We can't do this Christian walk alone, and when money, status, and fame cause us to stumble, and lose sight of who we are, we need others to call us to repentance and get back on the straight and narrow pathway. CLEVELAND BROWNS PLAYERS PUBLICLY BAPTIZED AT CLEVELAND FOR CHRIST EVENT IN POWERFUL DISPLAY OF FAITH Christians have a moral framework from which we draw and are expected to live out. The unbelieving world and other Christians don't expect us to be perfect, but they certainly have every right to call us out on hypocrisy. I believe there is a moral standard embedded in every human and society, giving us an innate understanding of right and wrong to an extent, but there's no question whether actions like this by Simmons are wrong. It has no place in football. That's for sure. Simmons tweeted after the game, "All Glory To God 🙏🏾 Thank you for listening to my prayers and forgive me for my actions." LOUISIANA FOOTBALL PHENOM PEYTON HOUSTON CREDITS FAITH, FAMILY FOR HIS REMARKABLE SUCCESS Here was my reply to him: "This is a great learning experience, Colin. You have a lot of eye balls on you. Please use the platform & abilities God has given to be a good representation of Him. Don’t be like the world. Live like a man renewed through Christ. Thank God for His grace & forgiveness."Let this be a message to all Christians, not just athletes with a platform playing on national television: You're under a microscope. People are watching. Kids are watching. As it says in James 3, which Stroud referenced, they hear us praise God with the same tongue we curse with. That shouldn't be the case. But more than anything, this isn't about appealing to the world, fellow Christians, coaches, boosters, athletic directors, or even family, this is about living a moral life in our words and deeds for the one we profess as a Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. title: Lindsay Clancy's 'Shooter McGavin' unloads on 'hoodie-wearing lawyer' amid war of words over holdout juror
description: Kevin Reddington's motion to investigate holdout juror Michael Desronvil in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial may not be on the agenda at key status conference Tuesday.
author_name: Michael Ruiz, Kayleigh McEnany, Bryan Llenas
content: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy's legal team and Massachusetts prosecutors have agreed to delay defense attorney Kevin Reddington’s motion to investigate the lone holdout juror in her mistrial, his attorney Edward Paltzik told Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Monday. "The DA and Reddington consent to adjourn the motion to investigate Michael," Paltzik said. "If Judge Sullivan signs an order today, much of it could be adjourned. Either way, a status conference is still likely. But the motion about Michael is likely not on tomorrow." Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington, however, fired back a short time later in a fiery statement of his own, calling Paltzik's statement "pure nonsense" while conceding that he and county prosecutors had agreed to a continuation as a "professional courtesy" to local counsel now working with the holdout juror. A final decision is subject to Judge William Sullivan, but the judge has not yet announced a decision one way or the other. The delay agreement comes as the juror's new local counsel informed the parties that he does not have access to impounded information necessary to prepare a response. LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON FIRES BACK AT LONE HOLDOUT JUROR'S ATTORNEY AFTER FIERY INTERVIEW "Earlier today, both the government and I were contacted by a professional local attorney who represents Juror Doe," Reddington said, not naming Desronvil due to an impoundment order from the court. "That attorney requested — as any qualified counsel would — adequate time to review our motion and reply. As is professional courtesy, both the government and I agreed to continue this specific motion to a later date at their request." title: US visa clash exposes Sudan’s forgotten war as foreign powers compete for strategic foothold
description: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan struck a defiant tone after Washington withheld his visa amid a dispute over a proposed 90-day humanitarian truce in Sudan.
content: UNITED NATIONS — Sudan’s military leader is openly defying a U.S.-backed ceasefire push after Washington withheld his visa to attend the U.N. General Assembly, exposing a widening rift over a war that has become not only one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters, but also a regional struggle for influence stretching to the Red Sea. Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of Sudan’s armed forces and de facto leader, had been expected in New York during UNGA before the Trump administration withheld his visa amid a dispute over a proposed 90-day humanitarian truce. Days later, Burhan struck a defiant tone from Khartoum. "We will keep our heads high. We will not accept bargaining, sell ourselves cheaply to anyone or bow to anyone," Burhan said Saturday, according to Anadolu Agency. "We do not need a visa to any country or anyone’s permission." WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR? The State Department has accused both Burhan’s Sudanese Armed Forces, or SAF, and the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, of failing to make serious commitments to an immediate truce. "Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said Sept. 22, adding that the conduct of both leaders renders them "ineligible to govern the country." The State Department said both sides had instead intensified combat operations and drone strikes that killed civilians and said Washington had repeatedly asked them to accept a humanitarian truce "without preconditions" and commit to an inclusive political dialogue leading to civilian government. But a senior advisor to Burhan disputed Washington’s account in an on-camera interview with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of UNGA. SUDAN'S FORGOTTEN WAR LEAVES MILLIONS HUNGRY AS GLOBAL ATTENTION REMAINS ELSEWHERE Dr. Amjad Farid Al-Tayyib, the foreign affairs advisor to Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council, said Sudan never rejected the American ceasefire proposal and instead submitted technical comments on it. "We never rejected this proposal," Farid said. "The Sudanese government wants war with no one." Farid said a negotiating team had intended to accompany Burhan and accused Washington of undermining the very diplomatic process it was seeking to advance by preventing the delegation from traveling. The State Department declined to comment on Burhan’s specific visa case, citing its policy of not discussing individual visa decisions. A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital on background that Washington is instead focused on a broader diplomatic framework with Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through the Quad, linking a humanitarian truce and sustained aid access to a permanent ceasefire, civilian transition and reconstruction. "We are working with our partners to encourage the parties to agree to the humanitarian truce and guarantee humanitarian access, and to also ensure external military or financial support to the warring parties is cut off," the spokesperson said. The spokesperson added that the Quad supports the Quintet-led civilian political track and rejects parallel diplomatic processes that could fragment negotiations. The United Nations also challenged Washington over the visa decision. "We immediately raised with the U.S. authorities the issue regarding the denial of visa to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of the Sudan, who was scheduled to address the General Assembly this week," U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric told Fox News Digital. PUTIN USING AFRICA AS ‘PURSE’ FOR UKRAINE WAR WHILE US FACES ‘INTELLIGENCE BLACK HOLE’: COMMANDER Cameron Hudson, a former director for African affairs on the National Security Council who also served as chief of staff to successive U.S. presidential special envoys for Sudan, said his understanding was that Washington had asked the Sudanese to send a delegation both to the U.N. and to Washington for talks on a ceasefire. He said the Sudanese were preparing to do so before Washington, in his understanding, made Burhan’s visa contingent on signing the ceasefire agreement before traveling. "It doesn’t fully make sense why the United States took this decision at the last minute," Hudson told Fox News Digital. Farid said the central dispute is whether the RSF would be required to withdraw from civilian areas it controls. He argued that freezing current lines of control risks turning a temporary ceasefire into a de facto partition of Sudan. The dispute comes against the backdrop of a brutal civil war that erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti. Both sides have been accused of serious violations, but Hudson told Fox News Digital that treating their records as interchangeable obscures an important distinction. "The RSF is committing war crimes on a scale and with an intention that the army does not," Hudson said. Hudson said SAF has struck civilian targets and committed war crimes, including through drone attacks, but said the RSF’s record goes significantly further. "They have committed mass rape, mass killing, torture, sexual enslavement," Hudson said, arguing that Western descriptions of "both sides" can create the impression that the two forces are committing the same crimes "on the same scale or with the same intention." U.N. investigators have also drawn distinctions while documenting abuses by both forces. AS WORLD FIXATES ON OTHER WARS, SUDAN SEES 12 MILLION FORCIBLY DISPLACED IN DEVASTATING CONFLICT A U.N. fact-finding mission reported in September 2025 that both SAF and RSF were responsible for direct, large-scale attacks against civilians and the destruction of critical civilian infrastructure. But it found that the RSF, particularly during its siege of El Fasher and surrounding areas, committed crimes against humanity including murder, torture, enslavement, rape, sexual slavery, forced displacement and persecution on ethnic, gender and political grounds. A separate U.N. Human Rights Office report released in February documented more than 6,000 killings during the first three days of the RSF’s final offensive on El Fasher and found that the violations could amount to war crimes and possible crimes against humanity. Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a ‘false equivalence’ between Sudan’s military and the RSF. "The U.N. is not staying neutral," he told Fox News Digital, arguing that international institutions have documented RSF atrocities without taking sufficient action against the group or those supporting it. Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a false equivalence between Sudan’s military and the RSF. U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric rejected the allegation that the organization was equating the two sides. "This is not about equating two sides," Dujarric told Fox News Digital. "We focus on the facts, the violations that have been documented, and above all, the devastating toll this war has taken on civilians since 15 April 2023." Dujarric said both the RSF and SAF have used explosive weapons in densely populated areas and that the U.N. Human Rights Office has documented attacks affecting schools, hospitals, markets and religious sites. He pointed specifically to what he described as "particularly grave violations" by the RSF and affiliated forces in Darfur, including mass killings, sexual violence, torture, abductions and forced displacement, while noting that serious abuses have also been documented in SAF-controlled areas, including arbitrary detention, torture, ill-treatment and summary executions. The war, meanwhile, increasingly extends beyond Sudan’s borders. Foreign backing has become a central feature of the conflict. A July 2026 UK government assessment, drawing on U.N. and other reporting, said the RSF had benefited from support networks involving the UAE and neighboring countries, while SAF had received backing from states including Egypt, Iran, Pakistan and Turkey. The UAE has repeatedly denied providing military support to the RSF. Fox News Digital reached out to the UAE Embassy in Washington and the UAE mission to the U.N. but did not receive a response in time for publication. BAB EL-MANDEB STRAIT FACES GROWING THREAT AS HOUTHI ATTACKS RAISE FEARS OF A SECOND HORMUZ Hudson said the RSF’s foreign relationships are only part of a much larger regional competition. He said Egypt, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Qatar have supported the army to varying degrees, while outside powers pursue their own strategic interests in Sudan. That competition increasingly centers on Sudan’s Red Sea coastline. "There is a regional battle of influence among neighboring states and regional states who want to be able to control Sudan’s Red Sea coastline," Hudson said, pointing to potential military, port and economic access. "Superimposed on top of the conflict inside Sudan is a regional proxy conflict for influence in Sudan and in the wider Horn of Africa, Red Sea region," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also said foreign powers are central to prolonging the war. "What’s happening in Sudan would not be happening were it not for external actors supporting one side or the other," Rubio told reporters during UNGA week, describing U.S. efforts to secure even limited humanitarian agreements as "very frustrating." Rubio said the parties have repeatedly agreed to commitments only to abandon them when one side believes it is gaining the upper hand. "There are external actors. I’m not going to single them out. You know who they are," Rubio said. "That war and that conflict and that crisis would not be happening were it not for the active participation of external actors that are feeding one side of that conflict or another." He said meaningful progress would depend on those states pressuring their respective partners in Sudan. "Until those external actors are prepared to use influence and pressure their respective proxies to live up to the commitments that they’re making, we’re not going to make progress," Rubio said. WORLD'S HUMANITARIAN SYSTEM BUCKLING, 'NO LONGER FIT FOR PURPOSE,' US-BASED RESEARCHERS SAY Sudan’s strategic value goes beyond geography. The country has significant gold, agricultural and livestock resources and sits at the crossroads of Africa and the Middle East. The World Bank has described Sudan as rich in fertile land, water and minerals, while noting its substantial gold production and agricultural potential. Sudan also controls critical infrastructure used to transport South Sudanese crude oil to the Red Sea. A World Bank assessment says South Sudan’s oil has historically traveled through pipelines across Sudan to Port Sudan, its key export route. Hudson said that broader regional competition helps explain why Washington has struggled to force Sudan’s outside backers to pull away. "The United States is not going to use the limited political capital that it has with Saudi Arabia or Egypt or Turkey or UAE to get them to control their support to one side or the other in this conflict," he said. Hudson also questioned Washington’s diplomatic strategy, arguing that pressure on Burhan has not been matched by sufficient direct engagement inside Sudan. He said Massad Boulos, President Donald Trump’s senior advisor for Arab and African affairs, has never traveled to Sudan while attempting to mediate the conflict. "He’s trying to mediate peace in a country that he’s never been to," Hudson said, arguing that Washington needs more "personal diplomacy" and less reliance on public statements and social media. "If we want these people to sign a ceasefire deal, then they have to trust us," Hudson said. "And right now we’ve given them no reason to do so." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The U.N. acknowledged that international efforts have so far failed to stop the fighting. "Unfortunately, we are not seeing the war abating," Dujarric said, reiterating the U.N. position that "there is no military solution to the conflict," and noting Washington’s diplomatic role as the US and African Union co-chaired a Sept. 23 meeting bringing together the Quad and Quintet diplomatic groupings. "The immediate priority is to stop the killing and secure a cessation of hostilities, while creating the conditions for a credible political process," he said. Fox News' Sydney Finver contributed to this report.

title: 'Insulting': Ex-Trump official's 'dishonest' campaign ad triggers conservative revolt

content: Republican Arkansas Gov. You pay taxes to cover welfare for guys like Brad who just choose not to work." title: Once again, no one knows when Josh Simmons will return — perhaps including the Chiefs
description: Josh Simmons has played just eight of 20 games since being drafted, and Andy Reid's vague updates on the Chiefs left tackle only deepen the mystery.
content: Kansas City Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons is mysteriously absent from the team — again. Simmons holds one of the most important jobs in football. He is paid to protect the blindside of Patrick Mahomes, the central figure of the NFL’s defining dynasty and one of the most valuable assets in American sports. Yet Simmons has played in just eight of 20 games since the Chiefs drafted him two seasons ago. Khali Benson, an undrafted rookie right tackle who played exclusively on the right side in college, has filled in for Simmons this season. The Chiefs are 3-0, but Benson showed clear limitations on Sunday against the Dolphins. The team’s own highlights package of the victory is marred by defenders beating him almost immediately off the line of scrimmage. The Chiefs offense misses Simmons' stability. And yet, there is still no information regarding when he might return, or whether he will return at all this season. How does that happen in a league where highly paid insiders compete to deliver minute-by-minute injury updates on even the most obscure players in the NFL? To understand how, we have to return to the 2025 pre-draft process. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE In October 2024, Simmons suffered a season-ending patellar tendon injury at Ohio State. After the season, reports indicated that he was well ahead of schedule in his recovery. The Chiefs selected him 32nd overall. A week after the draft, Simmons was active for rookie minicamp. According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, the national reporter most connected to the Chiefs, the injury did not cause Simmons to fall to the final pick of the first round. The concern was something less clinical and more ominous: his character. "Several teams agree: Josh Simmons had best tape of any OT last year. And they aren't very concerned with recovery on the torn patella tendon. More of the concern is maturity/character. But he's going to the ideal, veteran-laden place," Fowler posted on X on April 24, 2025. It remains unclear what those "character concerns" were. But they had to be substantial for nearly every team in the league to pass on a left tackle with elite tape who had already been cleared for contact by draft night. For the first month of last season, it appeared the Chiefs had taken advantage of the rest of the league’s hesitation. Simmons looked like the long-term answer to Kansas City’s chronic left tackle problem. That reading no longer holds. On Oct. 6, 2025, two hours before the Chiefs’ Monday Night Football game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, the team abruptly listed Simmons as questionable due to an "illness." He ultimately played and played well. The episode would have disappeared into the weekly churn of NFL oddities if not for what happened days later. After a full week of practice, Simmons did not show up for his pregame responsibilities the following Sunday against the Lions. It was reported that players and members of the staff were unsure of his whereabouts. After the game, head coach Andy Reid suggested he knew where Simmons was. Reid and the Chiefs offered almost no explanation afterward. The silence continued throughout much of Simmons’ four-game absence, which the team described only as a personal/family issue. Reporters provided no real clarity over the past year about what happened or why members of the organization were apparently unaware of Simmons’ absence until close to game time. Last month, Sports Illustrated’s Matt Verderame provided the first substantive report on the matter, saying Simmons left the team without approval the Saturday before the Lions game and that there was a period of time in which the "team didn't know where he was." That is also the version of the story OutKick has heard but have been unable to independantly verify. The team will not confirm, deny, or comment on the matter. OutKick emailed Chiefs general manager Brett Veach and Simmons’ agent Drew Rosenhaus before Verderame’s report to ask whether those details were accurate. Neither responded. Which brings us back to the present. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! After a full training camp, Simmons missed his first practice of the season on Aug. 18. Verderame reported afterward that Simmons was "fine." "On Chiefs LT Josh Simmons missing practice with a back injury, I’m told 'he’s fine.' Don’t sense any concern about the second-year star," Verderame posted on X. It is now Sept. 28. Simmons has not practiced since. He has missed the first three games of the season. Though the team says he has been in the building, he's clearly not "fine." However, we have already established that Verdemran's sources with the team are strong. There is reason to believe that the team did consider Simmons' injury minor at the time. Something changed. On Monday, Reid offered a vague, almost eerie update. "I’ll tell you what," Reid told Chiefs Digest reporter Matt Derrick. "I will let you guys know when Josh [Simmons] is coming back. I’ll be the first to tell you. So we’ll just see how that all works out." The contrast with Reid’s other injury updates is difficult to ignore. Asked about safety Chamarris Connor, who, like Simmons, is the only other starter to miss the team’s first three games, Reid sounded far more direct. "Yeah, so he practiced last week, and he’ll get going this week, too," Reid said. "So there’s a good chance he’ll be out there. We’ll just see how the week goes, but it looks like it’ll be a pretty decent chance." Now consider the reporting around other injured Chiefs players. When rookie Mansoor Delane injured his shoulder in Week 1, Adam Schefter, Ian Rapoport, and Tom Pelissero quickly reported that the injury was minor and continued providing updates throughout the week. ESPN, Fox, NFL Network, NBC and Amazon devote weekly pregame segments to injury news. They inform viewers about the availability of backup linebackers and rotational defensive backs. Yet we cannot find a single example of them discussing the status of the player tasked with protecting Patrick Mahomes. Over the past month, there has been one national report about Simmons. It came from Fowler, who, fittingly, described the injury as "mysterious." We keep coming back to that word. At minimum, we can establish this: the NFL’s top reporters either do not know the story behind Simmons’ absence or are choosing not to pursue it publicly. Likewise, the Chiefs either do not know when Simmons will return or are deliberately withholding information they routinely provide about other players. That is unusual, to use a term. Simmons’ absence has naturally invited speculation about whether it is connected to last year’s disappearance from the team. Yahoo NFL analyst Hayden Winks is among those asking. "So Josh Simmons is going to miss more time than what he would've on IR, which could mean he's missing longer than the Chiefs expected based on this back injury. title: Lane Kiffin is already somehow blaming the SEC's new conference schedule for LSU's injuries
description: Lane Kiffin is already blaming LSU's injuries on the SEC's new nine-game conference schedule, despite the Tigers having played just two league games.
content: For years, the SEC has enjoyed a bit of an advantage over other conferences when it comes to record, rankings, and strength of schedule: they played fewer conference games. The Pac-12, when that conference existed in its previous form, for example, played nine games against other conference teams. So did the Big Ten. The SEC, however, had just eight. With four non-conference opponents, some schools could choose to schedule four likely wins, before entering SEC play. An ideal example is the 2025 Missouri Tigers. Missouri's non-conference slate was Central Arkansas, Kansas, Louisiana, and Massachusetts. Four games in which they'd be overwhelming favorites, four wins secured before conference play started. FLORIDA GATORS, MISSISSIPPI STATE SOAR, USC TUMBLES IN LATEST INEXPLICABLE AP TOP 25 POLL Missouri proceeded to win just four conference games, 29-20 over South Carolina, 23-17 over Auburn in double overtime, a 49-27 win over Mississippi State, and 31-17 over Arkansas. But, thanks in large part to their four scheduled wins, the Tigers remained in the AP Poll for most of the season, providing a "ranked" opponent for Texas A&M, Vanderbilt, Alabama, and Oklahoma. They did not beat a team that finished the season with a winning record on their way to finishing 8-4. Incredibly, with this resume, the Tigers were ranked in 12 of 16 polls during the regular season. And why not? 8-4 doesn't look bad, does it? That's a solid season in a tough conference, if you aren't paying close attention. Now remove one of those scheduled non-conference wins, and suddenly the road to 8-4 looks a lot harder. Which is the point other conferences made when arguing against the SEC's endless complaints about strength of schedule. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Well, for 2026, the SEC finally moved to nine conference games and eliminated the "extra" win many of the member programs used to their advantage. And even through just a few weeks of conference play, new LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin is already using it as an excuse. Ahead of last weekend's matchup against Texas A&M, Kiffin complained sarcastically, and inaccurately, about the perceived scheduling issues hurting the Tigers with Marcel "Obviously we just played the best one in the country last week thinking he can hurt you even when you have the right call on and everybody covered and a guy comes free," he said. "Obviously he (Chambliss) played great a year ago here in the stadium, so this is one of those scheduling quirks just like last week where never in that LSU-Ole Miss series had it ever been played two times in a row." That was, of course, incorrect, but Kiffin wasn't done there in going after the SEC for its scheduling practices. LSU is dealing with its fair share of injuries through the first few weeks of the season, including to star linebacker Whit Wheeks and tight end Trey'Dez Green. Per ESPN's Marty Smith, LSU's injuries are a direct result of the SEC's nine-game conference schedule. Which is odd because his team has played just two conference games so far. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Smith posted that Kiffin explained that it's an indication of the differences "versus other conferences, and how (they) don’t have to play players or play them as long." "Be careful what you wish for, SEC," Kiffin said. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP Ah. Yes. Classic Lane Kiffin. There is no outcome that doesn't have a predetermined excuse. No other schools face injuries. No other games require playing starters. When the SEC had eight conference games, it wasn't an advantage, but with nine, they're at a significant disadvantage. Even when they've only played two conference games so far. One of those games was against a very bad Texas A&M team, where the score was 35-6 in the fourth quarter and the outcome was never in much doubt. The Tigers shouldn't have much to worry about with powerhouse McNeese State coming into town next weekend either. Curiously, Kiffin never addresses the impact of travel, rest, and recovery on other conferences. Like, for example, USC, which played a road game in New Jersey, then turned around and played a home game in LA a week later. That's a ~6,000 mile round trip road game. LSU's longest road trip of the season is Lexington, Kentucky. Their entire travel schedule is less than one USC road game. That stuff matters as Kiffin would say if it were impacting his team. UCLA has road games traveling 8,120 one-way miles. USC is 9,500 miles. Just a few examples. The "woe is me" act Kiffin puts on might be effective for the SEC boosters in friendly media outlets. It's just not backed up by any reality we live in. But it's a near-certainty he'll be running the same playbook after the season to try and get the SEC back to eight conference games. Then he'll find something else to complain about.

title: DR. MARC SIEGEL: What 18 years at Fox taught me about courage and faith
description: Benjamin Hall recalls the Ukraine war attack that killed his crew and the miraculous Ukrainian special forces rescue that he believes was a sign from God.
content: I joined Fox in early 2008 as a contributor. I was struck from the beginning by the network's flexibility and creativity, allowing me to expand my role from expertise in infectious diseases to health policy and Obamacare. I was able to flex various journalistic muscles, too. I was sent to Phoenix to examine Sen. John McCain’s health records but ended up with the opportunity to deliver on-air reports. I began to report for the network in earnest in 2012, and then in the spring of 2013, during the Boston Marathon, when two self-radicalized brothers executed the largest terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11, I managed to get permission from our top executives to head up there. DR MARC SIEGEL: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AFTER 9/11, THE DEADLY HEALTH CRISIS IS STILL CLAIMING LIVES On the way, I somehow convinced the PR team at Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) to grant me the very first interview with a survivor — a woman. Our excellent production team wasn’t expecting me, as we had our top reporters already in the field, but they quickly transitioned to supporting and guiding me. She had been blown off her feet and badly wounded her leg. Her would-be boyfriend had carried her down one-way streets (going in the opposite direction of the cars) to MGH. We were ready. She looked straight into the camera and said, "We can’t let the terrorists win. We must stay strong and not be afraid. Boston is a great city." Ten years later, another top Fox executive sent me to East Palestine, Ohio, following the train wreck there. One of the best field producers in the business came with me, and while I was in the neighborhood doughnut shop sampling the best doughnuts I’d ever had, she was assembling an array of guests who had all been injured or affected by the toxic smoke. FOX NEWS MEDIA'S SPOTLIGHT AWARDS CELEBRATE BEHIND-THE-SCENES STARS AS NETWORK NEARS 30 YEARS The ERs in the area were calling it "situational anxiety," but outside the temporary state health facility, I interviewed patients who were having trouble breathing while the smoke in the air gave everyone, myself included, a sore throat. People who swam in the river developed rashes, and the long-term health risks remained unknown. The angels of Fox are the executives, producers, and bookers who have the vision and work ethic to seek out and present stories that would otherwise be missed. We are a family that has developed strong bonds, and we look out for each other. When my father died earlier this year at age 102, the entire Fox management team, from the CEO on down, came to the funeral. The angels of Fox are the executives, producers, and bookers who have the vision and work ethic to seek out and present stories that would otherwise be missed. BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES Senior Correspondent Ben Hall brings out the best in the Fox team, and they inspire him. Chief National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffin was crucial to arranging his extraction from Ukraine after a horrific near-death experience when his car was bombed and his cameraman and producer were killed in 2022. He survived, thanks to many angels, messengers from God, as I write in my new book, "THE ANGELS AMONG US." Here’s what Benjamin Hall shared with me about what he was thinking on the day he and his team were attacked in Ukraine: "At this moment of trying to stay strong, I think of how I am going to get home. I think of my children. Our car has burned totally to pieces, and we are down on the road, down a slight little dip in the road where we are lying, and this one car comes out of nowhere, and it drives past us. And I am shouting at it, ‘We’re here! We’re here!’ And it doesn’t see us, and it keeps driving. And it is a car of Ukrainian special forces, and this same car, amazingly, has engine trouble ten minutes or so down the road, and they have to stop to figure that out. And because of that, they drive back again!" Hall believes this event is a sign directly from God. DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE "I have pulled myself further up by this time, dragging myself along, up toward the road, and as the car comes back again, I don’t know it’s coming. There it is… The last thing I remember is this guy jumping out. He grabs my body armor, grabs the back of my arm, and pulls me along the ground, running to his car." Is the vision of his daughter that he sees after the missile hits actually an angel? It’s the question everyone has, and I ask it of Hall. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME "Yeah, 100%, either she is an angel that comes to me when I need her, and she gives me the strength I need, and she brings me back, or it is because my body and my mind are calling for her. It’s after the first and then the second shell, when I go into this other world, that’s when I get shrapnel in the eye, and it takes out part of my skull. So, I am already pretty badly injured at this point. Then the third shell takes off my leg, my foot. But I’ve no doubt that my daughter is sent to me, and either it is God who sends her or my body needs it, and my mind goes to the place it has to go to find the right strength." Hall can feel his father is there with him as well. It’s as if his father’s life has joined with his own now that his spirit has moved on to the next world, into heaven. His father gives him strength. His daughter is there with him, and so is his father. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News loves Ben Hall, and his courage and strength inspire all of us. title: 'Nobody Wants This' star accuses Israel of 'genocide'

content: On Friday, Jewish actor Adam Brody joined the growing list of progressive celebrities accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza while suggesting that Hollywood has grown more "conservative" under President Donald Trump.
