Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. EMPTY ENVELOPES IN YOUR MAILBOX? DO NOT SCAN THAT CODE How QR code clothing works The basic idea is simple. ShareAScan prints a unique QR code on products such as T-shirts, hoodies, hats, mugs and other merchandise. A person scans the code using the camera already built into a smartphone. No special scanning app is required. However, the interesting part happens behind that code. Instead of permanently tying the printed QR code to one piece of content, ShareAScan lets the owner change what appears later. The physical code stays the same while the digital experience behind it changes. For example, someone could use a shirt to share a portfolio at a conference and later update the content to promote a project or event. The company describes its technology as a patent-pending platform connecting physical products with dynamic, user-controlled digital identities. Its September announcement says a single product can become a changing introduction, portfolio, personal message or business card. That makes the concept more interesting than simply printing a website address across your chest. The idea recently made its way to the Emmys ShareAScan was founded by sisters Shara and Kailey Zuckerman. Shara is a college student studying business, finance and artificial intelligence, while Kailey is still in high school. The company got a major dose of exposure this month when its QR merchandise was included in gift bags distributed around the 78th Emmy Awards. ShareAScan merchandise went into gift bags for nominees, presenters and performers. Still, the bigger story goes beyond an awards-show gift bag. It is another example of physical products gaining a digital layer that can change long after you buy them. Your shirt could become a changing digital business card There are plenty of ways people could use this. A business owner could wear a shirt that introduces a company. A creator could share recent work. Someone at a conference could use it as a digital introduction. Meanwhile, a musician could share new content or an organization could promote an event. Because the material behind the QR code can change, the same physical product can serve different purposes over time. ShareAScan says purchases start at $19 and current customers do not pay an ongoing subscription fee. The company also tells CyberGuy that customers who buy under the current model will not later face a subscription charge even if its terms change for future customers. That gives the physical product something most ordinary clothing never had before: content that can keep changing after you take it home. What happens when someone scans your shirt? ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that scans are anonymous. The company says it collects no information about the scanner unless an owner's access restrictions require it to check whether that scanner is allowed to view the content. If someone does not have permission, the company says that person simply does not receive access. ShareAScan also says it does not currently give the wearer scan analytics. In other words, wearing one of these products does not give you a dashboard showing who walked by and scanned your code. The company says owners can choose who gets access to their content and can completely delete their account and associated data. However, there is still another side to privacy: what you decide to reveal. If you make your full name, workplace, photos, social accounts or other personal information publicly available, someone who scans you may learn quite a bit. That is why anyone using connected clothing should look at the experience from a stranger's point of view before wearing it in public. QR CODE EMAIL SCAM TARGETS EMPLOYEE REVIEWS Can a ShareAScan QR code send you to a malicious website? This required an important clarification from the company. ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that its QR codes cannot point directly to an outside website. Instead, scanning the code first opens the experience hosted through its platform. However, content within that experience can include links. The company says it scans uploads for malicious links, phishing links, pornography and other inappropriate material. It also says people review flagged material. ShareAScan acknowledges that its screening cannot catch everything. That makes its setup different from a random QR sticker that directly sends your browser to an unknown website. Even so, you should never treat every QR code as automatically safe simply because scanning has become second nature. The FTC continues to warn about criminals using QR codes to send people to fake websites designed to steal passwords, financial information and other personal data. In a fresh warning published Sept. 3, the agency again advised people to inspect the destination before opening a QR link. So, the familiar security advice still applies whenever you pick up your phone to scan something. ShareAScan requires users to be 18 or older Connected clothing could naturally catch the attention of younger users, especially when it links fashion with social content. ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that account holders must be at least 18 years old. At the same time, the company acknowledges that an age requirement cannot completely stop someone younger from trying to create an account. That makes conversations about public sharing especially important for families. A QR code someone wears outside can potentially expose information to people they have never met. What happens after you wash the shirt? A scannable shirt also has to hold up to everyday wear. ShareAScan says its QR codes have been tested through repeated washing and continue to scan after normal use. Of course, a QR code still needs to remain physically readable. Heavy damage, fading or distortion could eventually interfere with any printed code. There is another longevity issue too. Unlike a normal graphic on a shirt, this feature depends on the online platform behind it. ShareAScan says it plans to keep the platform operating and has purchased insurance intended to help support continued operation. That is worth keeping in mind with any connected product that depends on a company's servers long after the initial purchase. QR codes are becoming part of the physical world QR codes are already everywhere, from tickets and restaurant tables to payment screens and packages. Now, they are starting to show up on the things we wear. ShareAScan takes that familiar technology and gives it a more personal use. Instead of linking to one fixed piece of information, the code can connect to content that the owner changes over time. That means a sweatshirt could introduce your business at a conference, while a T-shirt could share your latest project, interests or something you simply want people to know about you. A quick scan could even become an easy way to start a conversation. But once your clothing can share information about you, it is worth thinking about exactly what you are putting out there. Anything you make public could potentially be seen by someone you have never met. AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU 6 ways to use QR code clothing more safely If clothing is going to become scannable, a few simple precautions can help you share without giving away too much. 1) Check what strangers can see Start with your public profile. Look at exactly what appears to someone who does not know you. Avoid exposing your home address, private phone number, personal email or other sensitive information. 2) Use the privacy controls Review who can access your content. ShareAScan says owners can limit access, so use those controls when you want to share something with a smaller group. 3) Separate public and private information Create content specifically for public sharing. That can help you avoid giving strangers access to personal accounts filled with years of photos, posts or identifying information. 4) Think before opening anything after a scan Treat QR codes like links. ShareAScan says it screens content on its platform, but QR codes in general can still lead to trouble. If anything asks for a password, payment information or other sensitive data unexpectedly, stop. 5) Check the destination Look at the address your phone shows before opening a QR link. The FTC recommends checking for misspellings and switched letters that can signal an impersonation site. 6) Keep strong antivirus protection active Install and keep strong antivirus software active on your devices. It can help detect malicious links, phishing pages, dangerous downloads and other threats you may encounter after scanning a QR code. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. Also, keep your phone's built-in security protections and software updates turned on too. No security tool can make every QR code safe, so always check where a code is taking you before entering passwords, payment information or other sensitive data. Kurt's key takeaways What I like about this idea is how simple it is. There is no battery, Bluetooth or complicated hardware inside the shirt. The QR code does the work, and the person wearing it can keep changing what people see after they scan. ShareAScan also says it has built in some useful controls. Scans are anonymous, owners can limit who sees their content and the code itself does not send you straight to an outside website. The company also says it checks uploaded content for malicious material. The bigger question is how much of yourself you want to make scannable. If your shirt becomes part of your digital identity, take a minute to look at exactly what a stranger could learn about you before you wear it out the door. title: AEW star Pac's death leaves pro wrestling world in disbelief
description: AEW star Pac died at age 40 just one day after he wrestled Andrade El Idolo at All Out, leaving the entire pro wrestling world in disbelief.

title: Fox News Media's Spotlight Awards celebrate behind-the-scenes stars as network nears 30 years
description: Suzanne Scott and Jay Wallace celebrated the 2025 FOX News Media Spotlight Award winners at an intimate luncheon hosted by anchor Bill Hemmer.
content: FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott and President & Executive Editor Jay Wallace honored the 2025 FOX News Media Spotlight Award winners on Thursday during an intimate luncheon. The FOX News Media Spotlight Awards are an annual tradition for the organization, and management received hundreds of nominations from staff members passionate about celebrating colleagues who earned special recognition. Winners were announced at a network-wide town hall, and they gathered at Avra in midtown Manhattan just blocks away from FOX News Media’s headquarters to celebrate alongside their families and colleagues. FOX News anchor Bill Hemmer, who hosted the event, welcomed guests before introducing Scott to the stage. "In a couple of weeks, Fox News Channel will mark 30 years. When we started, we didn’t have a system for recognizing extraordinary people, and there were many," Scott said. "We were just figuring out how to not lose a satellite and keep a guest on the air from remote locations, forget about competing with MSNBC, which had just launched a few months prior, and CNN, which was the national leader in cable news at the time," Scott added. "But a lot has changed since then." FOX NEWS CHANNEL TOPS NBC, ABC AND CBS IN KEY RATINGS MEASURABLE FOR SECOND STRAIGHT SUMMER Scott noted that nowadays, Fox News Channel dominates cable news and regularly competes with and beats the broadcast networks. "We’ve also come up with a way to celebrate our most extraordinary performers," Scott said. The Spotlight Awards launched in 2020, and prizes have since been handed out to staffers on dozens of teams. The annual event gives FOX News Media leaders a chance to show appreciation for individuals who show up every day and keep the company on top. Wallace then took the stage to hand out the first award, where he was joined by Executive Vice President Scott Wilder and "FOX & Friends" co-hosts Ainsley Earhardt and Lawrence Jones. Unsung Hero Award The Unsung Hero Award goes to employees who consistently go above and beyond with work that is vital to FOX News Media but often goes unnoticed. This award recognizes those behind-the-scenes stars who keep everything running, often without fanfare, but always with excellence. Director of broadcast contribution Pat Butler "I think Pat preceded maybe everybody in this room because he’s been here since 1995, and he’s got some good stories," Wilder said before sharing Butler’s astonishing role in covering the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. "Pat drove the truck down there on 9/11, he communicated with our assignment desk by dialing an 800-number from a phone booth because cell phones didn’t work, he told them where he was parking the truck," Wilder said. "He shot all of those live shots that morning… he’s been an unsung hero for a very long time." FOX NEWS TOUTED AT ANNUAL UPFRONT PRESENTATION TO ADVERTISERS: ‘WE’RE NOT JUST COMPETING, WE ARE DOMINATING’ FOX Nation producer Tania Joseph "Tania has been with Fox for seven years, working hard and working her way up. She launched ‘The Sean Hannity Show’ podcast and now handles every single episode. She ensures Fox Nation’s content stays at the highest quality. Her recognition is especially well-deserved, because not only does she have an incredible work ethic, she’s also one of the most likable people you’ll ever meet," Wilder said. Field Engineering and Scenic Design Specialist Tiger Stanley "If you’re ever stranded on an island, Tiger is the one you want with you. He’ll have a shelter, a theme park, maybe a bar, and he’ll build it by the end of the day. None of us have any idea how he gets it done… impossible challenges are met all the time. Tiger is there to handle anything," Wilder said. Rising Star Award The Rising Star Award goes to employees who have shown exemplary work ethic and growth during the early stages of their careers. Assignment editor Matthew Donnell "We’re starting with two Assignment Desk staffers from Washington, who have done such good work, that both of them have earned gigs with the politics unit. First, Matthew Donnell, who has begun working as a Political Embed, covering campaigns through the midterm elections," Earhardt said. "Matt always looks for ways to move stories forward, and now he’s going to do it from the field, interviewing candidates, and breaking news in primaries across the country," she added. Associate producer Jessica Sonkin "Second, also from the D.C. desk, associate producer Jessica Sonkin. Jessica was already known for her incredible work ethic, and it was an easy call to make her a political embed," Earhardt said. "Jessica, you and Matt have a lot of long days ahead on the trail, so I hope you’re all caught up on sleep," she continued. "We very much look forward to your dispatches from across the country during this exciting election season." ‘FOX & Friends’ associate producer Carey Gallagher "I personally know firsthand how hard Carey works, never complains, stays under the radar. She produces segments and handles our research packets. We can always count on her to come up with talking points, good intros and important graphics. Like so many of our Rising Stars, she puts in long hours and is always ready to take on more responsibility. Because of that dedication, Carey has earned the trust of both the ‘FOX & Friends’ hosts and the production team," Earhardt said. FOX Nation associate producer Sabrina Baker "Colleagues say Sabrina is exceptionally creative, and reliable. She routinely juggles at least six shows at the same time, and she’s currently leading the production of ‘Park’d’ Season 10. Sabrina adds that she’s excited to keep growing in her role at Fox. We’re excited as well," Earhardt said. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME Community Service Award This award goes to an employee that has dedicated time and energy to his or her local community and is active in company volunteer efforts. ‘FOX and Friends First’ stage manager Matt Rodriguez "Matt has worked overnights for 13 years. Despite working the graveyard shift, he still has enough energy to volunteer for his Cub Scouts. He’s a Unit Commissioner for them, and that’s a big job. He works with many different packs of Scouts. And he recently completed the Wood Badge course, which is focused on advanced leadership, so that he can continue to help children grow into the best versions of themselves," Jones said. Washington, D.C., assignment manager Lillian LeCroy "She volunteers with American Corporate Partners, a nonprofit that connects veterans with mentors for career guidance. It’s an organization Fox has been proud to support and partner with for more than a decade, and we’re so proud of Lillian for her dedication to the community," Jones said. Innovator of the Year Lead technical director Rich Cozzi "Rich Cozzi is someone I’ve worked with for years, obviously working at Fox, we’re leaner, meaner, better and more experimentative than any other network … he exemplifies this," Wallace said. "I could not be more proud of him… he’s driving automation across all parts of FOX News Media, from Business to Weather," Wallace added. "Rich Cozzi, you earned this." "Innovation at Fox means finding better, faster, smarter ways to get the job done," Wallace said. The Impact Award Director Brianne Bombara and recruiter Veronica Baker The Impact Award goes to those who have had some of the most positive overall effects on FOX News Media. This year, a pair of colleagues from the campus recruitment team shared the award for building a first-class recruiting program. "People ask me all the time, I’ve worked for 30 years, and it’s no secret I started entry level, ‘How do you continue to have a successful culture and develop great people?’ That’s because we bring in the best and brightest at the university level, and we design a way to offer the best, top-rated jobs before they leave. These two have done an incredible job, I couldn’t be prouder of you," Scott said. "This year, the team has overseen three intern cycles with nearly 700 participants, made 34 campus visits… they spent 53 days on the road recruiting top talent," Scott continued. "Brianne and Veronica, I’m so proud of this program you have built and, because of your dedication, our internship program is ranked among the best in the country." title: AOC gives major hint about 2028 as Democrat civil war looms
description: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she's weighing a 2028 presidential run or a challenge to Chuck Schumer's New York Senate seat after midterm elections.
author_name: Paul Steinhauser, Elizabeth Elkind, Alex Miller
content: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's political future has remained a topic of discussion within the left wing — and there's increasing speculation that she could be set for a collision course with Democrats' top leader in Congress. The progressive rock star says she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a 2028 presidential run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker. "I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a recent fundraising email to supporters. The 36-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a recent New York Times interview that her decision, which could happen sometime after this year's midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?" OCASIO-CORTEZ OPENS UP ABOUT 2028 If she decides on a statewide rather than a national run, it could set up a titanic Democratic Party and generational battle between her and the soon-to-be 76-year-old Schumer, who was first elected to Congress nearly half a century ago and has served in the Senate since 1999. Ocasio-Cortez, in her interview, made clear that her decision about 2028 would not be dictated by someone else. "I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference," she said. Meanwhile, a campaign swing the past few days throughout upstate New York by Ocasio-Cortez raised some eyebrows. While the trip was aimed at boosting fellow Democrats on the ballot in this year's elections, it sparked speculation that it was also a move by Ocasio-Cortez to build relationships far from her base in New York City. Schumer has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for yet another term. When asked about re-election, he's repeatedly said his "first focus is winning in 2026, getting back the Senate in 2026." Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's office regarding his thinking on a potential 2028 re-election run, but didn't receive a response by the time this story was published. "Everyone has an expiration date," said one strategist, who like the others asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely. And referring to Ocasio-Cortez, the strategist told Fox News Digital, "I think she’s in a good position to win statewide." Another operative, pointing to Schumer, speculated, "I think Schumer wants to go out on top and with a good legacy and one way to do that is to hand the reins over to this inspiring generational leader. At the same time, New York politics are insane and there are lots of people gunning for that spot and he may feel like he can’t do that." title: Walz's 'exit interview' reflecting on his tenure sparks lawmaker debate about his legacy: 'Never serious'
description: Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz says fraud shouldn't define his legacy, but Republican lawmakers fire back with a list of grievances beyond the scandal.
content: Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz reflected on his legacy in a recent interview and his comments sparked immediate pushback both online and from Republican lawmakers in the state who spoke to Fox News Digital. "Fraud — should have stopped it sooner," Walz told the Minnesota Star-Tribune in a discussion that is being dubbed an "exit interview" with the headline "Walz accepts blame for fraud but says it shouldn’t define his legacy" as he prepares to leave office in January. "We didn’t stop them. I accept that. I think there does need to be accountability with that. And part of it is that, yep, that’s with me, I’ll step aside." Walz claimed the state "immediately" took action on the fraud and then went on to suggest the true cost of the fraud, estimated at $9 billion by federal prosecutors, has been overstated and claimed President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, expected to cost taxpayers around $300 million, was more expensive than the Minnesota fraud. WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT' "I should have been down on those agencies a little more, but I will tell you this, in the scheme of things, all the fraud that's been prosecuted, by the way, and all the fraud that's probably out there is less than the ballroom at the White House," Walz said. "So it puts it into perspective. It doesn't make it right. Doesn't make it right." The outgoing governor then explained his hope that people will remember his other accomplishments when talking about his legacy. "Those are legacy things to address climate. They’re legacy things to address livability," Walz said. "And I get it, that fraud tainted a lot of that. It doesn’t change the fundamentals underneath it. This is the best state in the country to raise a child, and it will continue to be so because of those investments." Three Republican lawmakers in Minnesota who spoke to Fox News Digital had a different take. "Governor Walz is correct, he shouldn’t only be remembered for fraud," Minnesota state Sen. Julia Coleman told Fox News Digital. "We should remember him spending our $18 billion surplus, raising taxes $10 billion, creating an unsustainable budget, letting rioters burn down Minneapolis, hurting our students and businesses with lockdowns and pardoning a child rapist." 'WE HAVE NOT SLOWED DOWN': MINNESOTA NOT OUT OF THE WOODS ON MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL, EXPERT WARNS Walz has faced fierce criticism for helping approve a full pardon for Tue Lue Vang, a Laotian national convicted of repeatedly raping a girl beginning when she was 10. Critics argued the decision prioritized Vang’s immigration concerns and family ties over the severity of his crimes, with a DHS official calling it "disgusting." Minnesota Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth is running to replace Walz in November as she heads into a matchup with Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar to be the state’s next top executive. Demuth told Fox News Digital Walz’s legacy won’t be able to overcome the fraud scandal and pointed to Klobuchar’s tight association with him. "Tim Walz's legacy will always be defined by the out-of-control fraud crisis that occurred on his watch," Demuth said. "Yet Amy Klobuchar praised him as ‘an incredible leader who delivers for the people of Minnesota.’ As the senior member of our state’s congressional delegation, Sen. Klobuchar likewise failed to address the fraud crisis and even skipped hearings on the matter in D.C. Minnesotans deserve better than four more years of Walz-style failure." Republican State Rep. Kristin Robbins chaired the last legislative session’s Fraud Prevention and State Agency Oversight Policy Committee, and she told Fox News Digital that "no matter how hard he tries to spin it, Tim Walz’s legacy will be that he allowed rampant fraud." "He has been silent on fraud for months instead of taking the actions that are STILL under his control." Robbins said Walz could have taken several steps to combat fraud, including firing senior DHS official Shireen Gandhi to send a message that abuse would not be tolerated, blocking Minnesota from seeking a SNAP waiver that allows applicants to attest to eligibility by phone without recording the call, and asking Attorney General Keith Ellison to prosecute Partners in Nutrition, a nonprofit that administered federally funded meal programs, rather than approve a settlement. "His legacy will be fraud because he continues to enable fraud, despite two years of hearings, investigative journalists, and Office of the Legislative Auditor (OLA) reports," Robbins said. "He was never serious about stopping it and still isn’t." Walz's comments not only drew scrutiny from Republican lawmakers but also sparked backlash on social media. "Walz accepts blame for fraud, but believes his loss of $9 billion in taxpayer dollars 'shouldn't define his legacy,'" the X account for Minnesota House Republicans posted on X. title: Far-left legal 'cartel' in the hot seat as Trump admin decides its law school gatekeeper status
description: The Trump Education Department now has 90 days to decide whether to strip the American Bar Association of its decades-long law school accreditation monopoly.
content: The future of the nation's primary law school accreditor now rests in the hands of the Trump Education Department after a federal panel deadlocked 8-8 on whether to strip the American Bar Association (ABA) of its gatekeeper status following dozens of federal compliance failures. The deadlock hands the decision to Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent, who has up to 90 days to decide whether to revoke the ABA’s decades-long accreditation monopoly over roughly 200 law schools nationwide. In a statement to Fox News Digital, a Department of Education spokesperson confirmed that staff had already recommended stripping the ABA's gatekeeper status after finding the group out of compliance with "more than 26 recognition criteria." The advisory body — known formally as the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI) — advises the Education Department on whether higher education accreditors meet federal standards. NACIQI Chairman Jay Greene told Fox News Digital that while the panel split 8-8 on what action to take, committee members across the board shared a core concern over how the ABA is structured. "The primary issue that troubled all members of NACIQI is that the ABA accrediting body is clearly not separate and independent from the ABA as a whole," Greene said, noting that federal law requires institutional accreditors to operate independently of trade associations. "Everyone on the committee agreed that this was a problem that required changes. The main divide was over whether the ABA was willing and able to take those steps to remedy the problem or not." WATCH: BRANDON GILL CORNERS LAW SCHOOL GATEKEEPER WITH DEI QUESTION SHE WON'T ANSWER Responding to panel criticisms of chronic noncompliance, Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA Accreditation Council, defended the organization's historic track record. "The Council has been continuously recognized by the Department of Education since 1952, being found in compliance during every regular recognition cycle for the past 74 years," Hart said in a statement. "We take accreditation and our recognition as an accreditor very seriously, and we continue to be a reliable authority for accrediting J.D. programs." However, legal advocacy groups argue the ABA's structural defects and recent policy shifts render it unfit to serve as an industry gatekeeper. Reed Rubinstein, senior vice president of America First Legal and former general counsel at the Department of Education, told Fox News Digital that the ABA has "disqualified itself and undermined public faith and trust in the legal profession." EXPLOSIVE REPORT EXPOSES ‘DANGEROUS IMBALANCE’ IN LAW SCHOOL PIPELINE SHAPING HOW ELECTION CASES ARE DECIDED Rubinstein also dismissed the ABA's recent move to repeal its controversial diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) accreditation standard as a "ruse to retain power," arguing it does not cure the underlying legal flaws. "The DEI accreditation standard, from the moment it was adopted, conflicted with controlling Supreme Court rulings and the plain text of the Civil Rights Act," Rubinstein said, urging the Trump administration to permanently strip the ABA of its federal status. "The ABA's leadership has made it clear, publicly and otherwise, that it will return to its unlawful ideological agenda at its first opportunity." For more than 70 years, the ABA has operated as the sole federally recognized accreditor for U.S. law schools, granting the organization a near-monopoly over the legal profession. In almost every state, students must graduate from an ABA-accredited law school to be eligible to sit for the bar exam. Furthermore, the federal government uses the ABA's accreditation as the gatekeeper for Title IV federal student aid, meaning law schools must secure the group's stamp of approval for their students to receive federal loans. BEAUTY SCHOOL MOMS CAUGHT IN ACCREDITATION CROSSFIRE AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION WEIGHS CONSEQUENTIAL DECISION If Under Secretary Kent ultimately moves to strip the ABA of its recognition, the decision would effectively break that national monopoly. While law schools affiliated with larger universities could rely on their broader institutional accreditors to maintain access to federal financial aid, roughly a dozen stand-alone law schools would be forced to scramble for alternative accreditation. State supreme courts would also face immediate pressure to rewrite their bar admission rules to allow graduates from non-ABA schools to take the exam. Some states have already begun taking matters into their own hands to bypass the ABA's grip. Because the legal profession is regulated directly by the judicial branch, state supreme courts hold the ultimate authority to set educational requirements for bar admission. TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES In January, Texas became the first state in the nation to eliminate its reliance on the ABA for law school accreditation, with the Texas Supreme Court finalizing a rule to take over the approval process itself. Just nine days later, the Florida Supreme Court followed suit. By cutting ties with the organization, the Texas high court announced it would judge law schools on "simple, objective, and ideologically neutral criteria" rather than the ABA's mandates deemed by many as politically-driven. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Other states are now catching on to the rebellion against the ABA. The Ohio Supreme Court formally proposed amendments in May to establish a state-run accreditation process, while supreme courts in Tennessee, Alabama and Washington have all recently taken steps to bypass the organization's monopoly. "The ABA’s cartel-like control over law school accreditation drives up costs, limits access, and pushes ridiculous ideological mandates over merit," Trump's DOJ said earlier this year. "Ending the Tennessee Supreme Court’s exclusive reliance will expand opportunity AND lower costs." Rubinstein noted that transferring authority back to the states marks a long-overdue correction for legal education. "State supreme courts are ultimately responsible for certifying and disciplining attorneys—there is arguably no need for a middleman," Rubinstein told Fox News Digital. "By returning actual authority over legal education directly to the courts themselves... the result should be a better-quality education for attorneys and more accountability and transparency for the public."

title: Education Department rescinds Biden Title IX rule, restores Trump-era regulations
description: Linda McMahon announced the formal rescission of Biden's 2024 Title IX rule, restoring Trump-era regulations on girls sports and gender identity.
content: EXCLUSIVE: The U.S. Department of Education is formally rescinding the Biden administration's 2024 Title IX rule, Education Secretary Linda McMahon announced in an interview with OutKick. McMahon said the action reinforces the administration's position that girls' and women's sports should be reserved for females. "We're just acknowledging that boys and men are in boys and men's sports and girls are in theirs," McMahon told OutKick. The action restores the 2020 regulatory text in the Code of Federal Regulations. Courts had already invalidated the Biden rule, and the department announced in January 2025 that it would enforce the first Trump administration's regulations. EDUCATION SECRETARY LINDA MCMAHON RIPS CALIFORNIA TRANS ATHLETE ‘COMPROMISE,’ TELLS NEWSOM TO ‘PICK A SIDE’ OutKick asked McMahon what this step accomplishes, given that her department was already enforcing those rules. "Well, it just gives clarification to students, teachers, schools, parents," she said. "Everyone now knows what the rule is and how everyone is going to abide by it." Asked whether schools face new obligations or deadlines, McMahon said they should return to the Trump-era rules. She did not identify a new compliance deadline. "Title IX was set up to give everyone, including women, equal opportunity to sports. And then under the Biden regulations, many of those rights had been taken away," McMahon said. "And so now this is just returned to Title IX as it was originally intended." The Biden administration's 2024 rule expanded Title IX's sex-discrimination protections to include gender identity. Its separate proposal addressing eligibility for athletic teams was withdrawn in December 2024. The Trump administration has pursued its interpretation of Title IX through investigations, funding restrictions and referrals to the Department of Justice. As OutKick has reported, the departments of Education and Justice announced the Title IX Special Investigations Team on April 4, 2025. The federal government also filed a lawsuit against Maine over the state's policy allowing trans-identifying males to compete in girls' sports. Asked about consequences for states including Maine, California and Minnesota, McMahon described the department's use of reimbursement requirements for funding recipients designated as high risk. THE STATES THAT STILL ALLOW TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS FACE QUESTIONS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING "What that means is that they don't get their funding in advance. They have to produce receipts to us," McMahon said. "We therefore can confirm that they are spending the money in ways that it should be spent." She also cited her department's referral of the Maine case to the Justice Department. "So there are many kinds of consequences that can come to states and schools that are not abiding by Title IX," she said. McMahon also addressed what recourse is available to female athletes who have already lost records, titles or opportunities. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. That agreement required Penn to restore records and titles to female athletes and issue apologies following Lia Thomas' participation on the women's swimming team. "Not only were apologies extended, but the titles were then given to the women who had rightfully won," McMahon told OutKick. Asked whether the Penn agreement provides a framework for other cases, McMahon said the department would consider each circumstance individually. For parents whose daughters are told to compete against a male athlete or share a locker room with one, McMahon advised raising the issue with the responsible school officials, including the superintendent, and reporting it to federal authorities. She did not specify how quickly the department could intervene. On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court upheld laws in Idaho and West Virginia restricting girls' and women's sports to females. title: Rising NASCAR star jumped, attacked & beaten at America's most famous hot dog shack
description: NASCAR driver Corey Heim ate punches near the famous Martinsville hot dog stand after going airborne over Treyten Lapcevich's hood in a wild wreck.
content: Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists. I tell you what, if NASCAR's big idea to stay relevant during the fall is to just start throwing punches every weekend ... I think I'm in. It's not the worst idea in the world. Frankly, it just might work. That's right. Another weekend, another viral fight in the racing world. This one didn't take place during a Cup race, but it did involve a NASCAR driver. Heck, it involved a NASCAR winner! NASCAR DRIVER SAYS QUIET PART OUT LOUD ABOUT SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM, THE WNBA LOOKS EVEN WORSE & CAR GOES AIRBORNE! Wait till you see this beatdown poor Corey Heim took at Martinsville Saturday night. Just a brutal attack. And right in front of a hot dog stand, no less! Disgusting stuff. You'll see. As for the NASCAR Cup Series ... Kyle Larson won at Kansas in a race that featured a handful of green flag passes for the lead, which is always a sign of a great race! At least it was a halfway decent finish. We've also got more fallout from Carson Hocevar giving Ryan Blaney a black eye last weekend at Bristol, but that rivalry is pretty much dead on arrival, folks. Those two spent all week basically dating each other through the media. So much for that storyline. The good news? Carson's already been wrecked again! I'm not sure this one was intentional, though. You'll see. Four tires, enough fuel to get us through the final full month of the 2026 season, and maybe a free Martinsville hot dog for poor Corey Heim ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'Grown Men Acting Like a Bunch Of Weiners' edition — is LIVE! Corey Heim attacked by a hot dog stand So, this is the wreck that everyone and their mother is talking about from this past weekend. Corey Heim — who won Cup races at San Diego and Indy this season — was racing in a late model event in Martinsville. He battled hard over the final few laps as folks tend to do at Martinsville, and got into Treyten Lapcevich after the checkered flag. And by "got into," I mean ... well, he went up the track, spun Lapcevich, and promptly went airborne over his hood. Lordy. What a wreck! You don't see that very often in Martinsville. But, this is also a late model race. These ain't your modern day NASCAR stock cars. They're actually way better, but that's a story for another time. Anyway, this was a big race. A big event. The ValleyStar Credit Union 300 is often described as the Daytona 500 for these drivers. It's been around for over five decades. It's a big deal. Emotions were running HOT after this race, especially after Heim parked himself on Lapcevich's hood. One thing led to another, and, as Corey was trying to cool off with a nice, Martinsville hot dog ... he started eating helmets and fists: Corey Heim eats a couple punches, but why? Goodness gracious. What a fight! Well, it wasn't really a fight. Like last weekend's "fight" between Hocevar and Blaney, this "fight" was really just one person(s) beating the hell out of another. It was pretty lopsided. Corey just ate punch after punch. He had a helmet, and didn't even use it! Again, all of this right in front of the famous Martinsville hot dog shack. Disgusting. PS: Ever had a Martinsville hot dog? Amazing. No, they're not regular hot dogs. The first time I saw one, I was floored. They're these tiny, little, bright red hot dogs and buddy, they will change your life. And I'm not even a big hot dog guy. Anyway, back to Corey ... "Solid effort, but at least make it count next time," Heim said via his X account on Saturday, with an accompanying picture of him looking completely normal. Well done, Corey. Solid response. As for the fight ... Heim was clearly in the wrong ... on the track. I don't know exactly what he was doing after the checkered flag, but it's tough to pin any of that on Treyten Lapcevich. That being said, it's a pretty embarrassing look for the Chad Bryant Racing team — including Chad Bryant himself — to just gang up on a kid and start beating the piss out of him when he clearly has no intention of fighting back. Now, why didn't he fight back, you might ask? I would assume because A) he's got a full-time Cup ride with 23XI lined up for next season, and B) he was wearing a 23XI firesuit. Would Michael Jordan really care that much if one of his future drivers defended himself? I doubt it. He'd probably prefer it. But, Corey wasn't gonna take that chance. That's my guess. Dale Earnhardt Jr ... thoughts on this? Larson, Blaney & Carson, oh my! "The thing of it is, those are some damn good hotdogs," Junior tweeted out Saturday night. Couldn't agree more, brother! It's important to keep things in perspective. Thanks, Dale. OK, let's put the pedal to the floor and kick this thing into high gear on this final Monday of September. First up? We DID have a NASCAR Cup Series race this weekend, and it was the Kyle Larson show. Larson led 235 of the 267 laps, scored 76 points on the day, and is now your Chase leader with six races to go. Yeah, Chase Briscoe briefly took the lead late in the race, but it was never going to hold up. Larson was, by far, the most dominant car yesterday. Barring a freak wreck, he was always going to win — mainly because it's nearly impossible to pass in these cars. Speaking of wrecks ... let's go ahead and check in on Carson Hocevar! Eh. I don't know. The announcers try to make it sound like Brad Keselowski did it on purpose, but I don't see that. Yes, Brad is going to wreck Carson this season after what happened a few weeks ago. It's gonna happen. He said as much. But not like that. NASCAR'S MOST POPULAR DRIVER HAS A TIKTOK GIRLFRIEND THAT'S CAUSING A STIR, AND HE DOESN'T CARE Brad Keselowski is a vet. He's not gonna wreck someone intentionally and put others cars in peril. That took out a ton of drivers. It wasn't payback. It was Brad getting Carson loose right in the middle of the pack on a restart. Bad recipe. But not a nefarious one. Finally ... while we're talking about Carson Hocevar ... it appears last weekend's fight with Ryan Blaney was a one-off, because these two fellas couldn't have been nicer to each other this week. Frankly, it was a bit much: Blaney admitting defeat — "I went over there and I got my a– kicked" — and Hocevar in turn talking about how much of a "stand-up guy" Blaney is doesn't exactly scream RIVALRY! So, yeah, this one is dead, folks. Blaney went on Denny Hamlin's podcast and talked about eating "two-piece," and Hocevar spent 10 minutes in the media center this weekend talking about how much he respected him. We can go ahead and put a bow on this one. It was fun while it lasted, though! CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Let's have a big week and end September with a bang. Here's Carson's TikTok girlfriend, Tabitha Swatosh, sending the HATERS a postcard from Italy on the way out. See y'all at Vegas.

title: JASON CHAFFETZ: Fox News has never let DC scandals become mere footnotes
description: Fox kept Brian Terry's name on the air after Fast and Furious guns walked into criminal hands and other newsrooms dismissed it as a botched sting.
content: Long after the rest of the media passed on exposing the corruption in D.C., Fox knew when there was a real story. In December 2009, I sat down with Neil Cavuto. It was one of my earliest national interviews. As a freshman who had been in Congress less than a year, I was sleeping on a $45 cot in my closet in Longworth at the time. Cavuto didn’t book me because I had a famous name. He booked me because a member who refused to load pork into an omnibus was news. Fox was willing to bring on a back-bencher from Utah because the story mattered. As a junior member of the House Oversight Committee, I did not know then that this would become the only place some of our hearings got traction after the initial press release died down. Viewers who wanted the whole story knew they could find it on Fox. JASON CHAFFETZ: A DECADE OF SECRET SERVICE FAILURE PROVES THE AGENCY IS STILL IN CRISIS Start with Fast & Furious. The Obama Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives deliberately let guns walk into the hands of criminals so the agency could "build a bigger case." On Dec. 14, 2010, Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry was shot and killed in Arizona. Two of those walked guns were found at the scene. The Justice Department’s first instinct was to minimize it. Other newsrooms were happy to call it a botched sting and move on. Fox kept Agent Terry’s name on the air. We kept asking who authorized a program that ended with an American lawman dead and thousands of firearms unaccounted for. I was not yet chairman. I was a member, but I had been down on that border. Without a network willing to stay on the story, Fast & Furious becomes a footnote and Brian Terry becomes a statistic. Then the Secret Service. By 2015, I was chairman, and the agency charged with protecting the president had become an agency in crisis: a fence jumper with a knife inside the White House, a prostitution scandal in Cartagena, supervisors crashing a crime scene after a night of drinking. We looked into all of it. We held the hearings. Called out the problems. The agency’s response was not to fix the protection mission. It was to open my old job application and pass around "information he might find embarrassing." Forty-five employees accessed my file. A senior official wrote that the information needed to "get out. Just to be fair." This was not a personnel spat. It was a federal agency using private information to punish the committee investigating it. Other outlets covered the fence jumper for a news cycle. Fox stayed on the pattern — and on the retaliation — long enough for an inspector general to put it in writing. 3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT Let’s not forget the IRS. Lois Lerner’s shop slow-walked conservative groups before an election. When Congress asked for the emails, we were told they were gone — hard drive crash, backup tapes that "didn’t exist." It took an inspector general two weeks to find tapes the agency swore were unrecoverable. The White House called the scandal phony. The Justice Department declined to prosecute Lerner’s contempt. A lot of newsrooms took the cue. Fox did not. As chairman I told the country the commissioner had failed to comply with a subpoena, failed to tell the truth about what had been destroyed and failed to notify Congress until after the evidence was gone. You can argue with the politics of that fight. You cannot argue with missing emails and a tax agency picking targets by ideology. That story stays buried if the only cameras left in the room have already declared it over. I’ve been honored to know and interact with so many great Fox personalities over the last two decades. I got to know Charles Krauthammer in the Fox green room, and on the air when he talked about investigations we were running. We did not always agree. I was in awe of his strength. His was a voice I actually listened to, day after day. FOX NEWS DIGITAL HITS 165 MILLION UNIQUE VISITORS IN MAY TO CRUSH BROADCAST NETWORKS, NEWS COMPETITORS One day I said, "Charles, how are you? You’re my favorite person on the planet." He said, "Good to see you, Jason. You’re my favorite person on the Oversight Committee." I said, "My universe is bigger than your universe." He said, "Yeah, well, I’m being generous." Fox News Channel went on the air Oct. 7, 1996. Thirty years later the scandals have different names. The instinct to look away does not. A chairman can issue a subpoena. He cannot make the country watch. For a lot of the years I spent on that committee, Fox was the network that still would. title: Rosie O’Donnell rips Ed Sheeran for ‘siding with billionaire elite,’ accuses him of ‘supporting genocide’
description: Rosie O'Donnell accused Ed Sheeran of siding with Robert Kraft and of "supporting genocide" after Macklemore was dropped from the "Loop Tour."
content: Rosie O'Donnell blasted New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and singer Ed Sheeran on Friday during an appearance on Ireland's "The Late Late Show," accusing Sheeran of making a "very bad mistake" after Macklemore was removed from his U.S. tour following the rapper's pro-Palestinian performances. "I think Ed Sheeran made a very bad mistake and that he will come to understand the ramifications of siding with a billionaire elite, in supporting genocide rather than the people who are saying, 'This is wrong. We will not stand for it. We are human beings and each human life matters and that's what's the most important thing,'" O’Donnell said. LIBERAL LAWMAKERS, ACTIVISTS RALLY BEHIND MACKLEMORE AFTER SHEERAN TOUR REMOVAL OVER 'FREE PALESTINE' STANCE "Hollywood in Toto" host Christian Toto said celebrities face pressure within the entertainment industry to adopt a particular position on the Israel-Palestinian conflict and compared the dynamic to the entertainment industry’s response to Black Lives Matter. "There is only one acceptable answer for celebrities when it comes to the ongoing Israel/Palestinian conflict. Say 'Free Palestine' and nothing else," Toto told Fox News Digital in comments Sunday. "It's the new BLM, a contentious issue where celebrities know they'll gain approval within their circle by repeating that mantra. They also understand they won't be pressured to defend their point of view by the vast majority of entertainment reporters. It's a safe space for them. Journalists now know they can pepper stars with similar questions and get a similar response (and lots of clicks for their interviews)." "Most artists know better than to alienate audiences with their political views," he continued. "The Springsteens, Morellos and Macklemores remain the exception. Concert ticket prices are too high for most bands to get on their soapbox and risk dooming repeat business. Actors don't make the connection between their divisive words and audience reaction. They simply want to appease their fellow actors and make nice with potential directors and casting directors. So they read from the approved script." ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL O'Donnell directly targeted Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium and founded the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, after Kielty referenced Kraft's role in opposing Macklemore's appearance at the venue. "Well, he's part of the billionaire elite," she said. "Those are the most corrupt people in the United States right now. And they have sort of performed a coup on the American government. And it's very tragic." Nick Fondacaro, associate editor for NewsBusters, reacted to O'Donnell's comments, saying, "Are we surprised that an unabashed 9/11-truther took an irrational and unhinged position?" "It’s irresponsible and incendiary to claim a coup has taken place in America, especially when political violence is on the rise. Given that people like Charlie Kirk and Brian Thompson have been killed by leftists for their political causes, Rosie’s prediction that Sheeran will come to learn a lesson sounded like a warning or threat," he continued. "It’s hypocritical that a multimillionaire like Rosie things that Robert Kraft didn’t have the same rights as she and Macklemore. The stadium is his property, and he can decide who to allow in or not, just like they can bar Kraft from their multimillion-dollar mansions." Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran's "Loop Tour" after repeatedly saying "Free Palestine" and performing "Hind's Hall" during shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The rapper alleged Kraft told Sheeran he would not be permitted to perform at Gillette Stadium and rallied other venue owners against his continued participation. Tour promoter Messina Touring Group said venues had informed them they would not allow concerts to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup. ROBERT KRAFT, GILLETTE STADIUM BOOT MACKLEMORE FROM ED SHEERAN TOUR OVER ‘FREE PALESTINE’ RANT Kraft defended his position by citing what he described as Macklemore's "broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery," while stressing that his decision was not intended to dismiss Palestinian suffering. Kraft said support for Palestinians and opposition to Hamas and antisemitism were compatible positions. "Standing with the Palestinian people and standing against Hamas, antisemitism and hate should not be mutually exclusive," Kraft said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Sheeran has also publicly rejected the implication that he supports the suffering of Palestinians. During his first concert after the controversy, Fox News Digital reported from Philadelphia that Sheeran condemned Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack while also criticizing the scale of civilian suffering in Gaza. "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate," Sheeran said. Sheeran also pledged $2 million toward humanitarian relief and asked Kraft to match the contribution. Kraft agreed, saying he had spent decades supporting programs bringing Palestinians and Israelis together. Macklemore separately pledged the $1 million he said he earned from the tour to Palestinian aid organizations. title: I'm 25 with a terminal disease. We need an FDA commissioner that hears people like me
description: A 25-year-old living with Duchenne muscular dystrophy explains why the Senate confirmation fight over FDA nominee Dr. Heidi Overton is personal.
content: I just turned 25. People with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) aren't expected to see another birthday after this one. DMD is a progressive disease; my muscles weaken over time and things that used to be automatic now take planning, assistance, or simply aren't possible anymore. Even sleeping can be hard. Bed sores are now an issue. Basic physical function takes work most people never have to think about. I know what the statistics say. I am not ready to let them write the ending of my story. TRUMP FDA PICK REPEATEDLY SIDESTEPS SANDERS' UNIVERSAL HEALTHCARE DEMANDS IN HEATED CLASH I want to grow my career, I want to get married and start a family. I want to wake up decades from now and realize that turning 25 wasn't the beginning of the end — it was just another birthday I was blessed enough to reach. That's why I'm watching the Senate confirmation fight over Dr. Heidi Overton, the nominee to lead the FDA, more closely than most 25-year-olds ever watch Washington. For most Americans, an FDA commissioner is just another name in the news. For the 30 million Americans like me living with a rare disease, that person can decide how many options I have and how much time I have to use them. To be clear: I'm not asking the FDA to abandon science. I respect doctors, clinical trials and hard evidence. I know some drugs don't work and some carry real risk. But there's a question Washington doesn't ask often enough: who gets to decide how much risk a patient is willing to accept? If I understand the risks, my doctor understands the risks, and there's real evidence a treatment could help, why does a regulator in Washington get the final word on whether I'm allowed to try? Congress already recognized part of this principle when President Trump signed the Right to Try Act into law in 2018. That law was a major step forward because it affirmed something patients facing life-threatening diseases have always known: when approved options are exhausted, and a doctor believes an investigational treatment may help, patients should not be treated as passive observers in their own survival. Right to Try was not the end of that idea. It was the beginning of a patient-centered philosophy that should shape the FDA’s culture more broadly. The same principle should apply when the agency weighs evidence, risk, urgency and access for rare-disease patients. If the patient understands the risk, the physician understands the risk, and there is real evidence that a treatment could help, the system should lean toward partnership instead of paternalism. That’s why Senator Ron Johnson and Representative Diana Harshbarger introduced Right to Try 2.0: to carry that same principle into the next era of medicine, including individualized treatments that do not fit neatly into the FDA’s traditional approval model. They are right to press the issue. But the next leader at the FDA should not have to wait for Congress to force a more patient-centered approach. The FDA already knows that time matters. Its accelerated approval pathway exists precisely because making patients with serious, life-threatening diseases wait years for a traditional clinical endpoint can cost them the thing they can't get back. The agency has used that pathway for multiple DMD treatments already. FIRST-EVER GENE THERAPY FOR HEARING LOSS GETS FDA APPROVAL: 'GROUNDBREAKING' Because waiting is never neutral when you have Duchenne. Every year can mean another loss of strength, another limitation, another piece of independence gone for good. My brother, who also lives with DMD, has seen the other side of this fight, too. Even when a treatment exists, actually getting it can be its own battle. Traveling hours away from home for a multiyear clinical trial sounds manageable in a Washington conference room. It looks very different when you're the one making that trip while your body is working against you as opposed to having access to the therapy at your own hospital. CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’ That's why I want the next FDA commissioner to listen to patients like me. We don’t just read about the disease in books or look at it through a microscope — we live with it every day. It’s in us — woven into our DNA. Living with Duchenne has forced me to learn more about drug development and regulatory pathways than I ever expected to know. I want an FDA that works with patients, physicians and rare-disease experts. That's also why I'm going to say something people will have opinions about: I hope whoever leads the FDA brings on Dr. Houman Hemmati as deputy commissioner. He has spent his career in biotech, not politics, building treatments for rare and degenerative diseases instead of just regulating them from the outside. He's also my friend. I know what that sentence invites. Critics will say I'm just trying to get someone I know into the room. They're right that I know him. What they're missing is: he doesn't just know my disease, he's lived it with me. I'm not asking anyone to promise me forever. I'm asking for the chance to fight for the future I still see. I've already outlived what a lot of people expected. I'm not ready to stop. It's time. And I'd like Washington to finally understand what mine is worth.

title: Woke megachurch pastor, Dem nominee called on congregation to repent for driving, eating beef
description: Adam Hamilton, the Democrat seeking to be the first Kansans sent to the Senate in nearly a century, once asked his church congregation to repent for eating beef.
content: FIRST ON FOX: In Kansas, cows are king, but a Democrat trying to seize power once told his congregation to repent for eating beef and raising cattle. Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee running to unseat Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in the Sunflower State, for years led the largest United Methodist church in the nation. He would give sermons that Marshall charged were "woke," and counter to Kansans' values. One such sermon, reviewed by Fox News Digital, saw Hamilton call on his congregation to repent over their carbon footprints. GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS "That's what repentance means — I saw things differently, it changed my heart, and it changed my behavior," Hamilton said during a January 2020 sermon called, "What would Jesus say about climate change?" "So what I'm calling you to today, and I'm calling myself to it, because I've been wasteful, I've done things that wasn't, you know, I didn't think about it, how it wasn't really good stewardship of the earth around me," he continued. "I'm calling us to repentance to say, ‘I realize that this has impact, even if it seems small, it has an impact on the world and future generations. And I feel badly about that, and I'm going to do something different from this time forward.’" Despite Kansas’ 94-year history of being a ruby-red bastion for the GOP in the Senate, the race between Hamilton and Marshall has unexpectedly tightened in recent months as Republicans across the country face a sobering political environment. BIG MONEY PROPELS DEM MEGACHURCH PASTOR TO VICTORY IN LONGSHOT KANSAS SENATE BID Kansas slipped from "Likely R" in Fox News’ Power Rankings to "Lean R," and Cook Political Report echoed the same shift, too. "In a state with more cattle than people, Hamilton saying that Kansans need repent for eating too much beef and flip flopping on the Farm Bill proves he’d be just like every other liberal Democrat in the Senate," Marshall told Fox News Digital in a statement. High fuel prices, particularly diesel in an agriculture-centric state like Kansas, spurred by President Donald Trump’s Iran war are giving voters anxiety, and expanding the map of battleground states that Republicans need to defend to maintain their majority in the Senate. Hamilton's campaign countered to Fox News Digital that Marshall has "repeatedly introduced legislation to reduce emissions from cattle and claimed 'everyone's concerned about the methane production in the cattle industry.'" "Marshall even bragged how the decline of the herd 'eliminated half of the methane gas produced from cattle already,'" Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton, said. "As Adam said at the debate, Roger should repent for failing to stand up for Kansas cattle producers on tariffs, foreign imports, and skyrocketing diesel prices, and now he should repent for attacking Adam for something Roger Marshall said himself in the Senate. Kansas producers don't need lectures from someone who voted to put warning labels on hot dogs and bacon." Meanwhile, Hamilton’s sermon was part scripture, part PowerPoint presentation on how greenhouse gases occur and their impact on the environment. And during his 44-minute talk, Hamilton suggested that one of Kansas’ staple economic drivers, beef, was a major contributor to the problem. 'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN "Some of the things that we grow, because we like to eat them, like cattle, end up producing more carbon dioxide than other crops that we could grow, other forms of food that we could have," Hamilton said. "And so, in all of these ways, we are creating or adding to the amount of greenhouse gases in our world." Cattle is a major industry for Kansas, which is the nation’s third-largest producer of beef, according to the Kansas Livestock Association. There are more heads of cattle in the state, just over 5.8 million, than people, with the state’s population sitting at roughly 2.9 million. It provides a major cash influx for the state’s economy, too, with cattle farming and ranching producing tens of billions of dollars and employing over tens of thousands of Kansans. "It is disappointing that a candidate for the U.S. Senate in Kansas, one of the nation’s top beef-producing states, would make a statement like this to his parishioners about beef’s impact on the climate," Kansas Livestock Association Chief Executive Officer Matt Teagarden told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Beef is an important, nutritious part of the American diet, and cattle play a significant role in maintaining grassland health and conservation, while accounting for only 2% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Still, six years ago, Hamilton was calling on his congregation to change their habits to reduce their carbon footprint. "Now, you got to do everything you can to reduce your own usage of fossil fuels, but maybe changing your diet so that the things that you eat are requiring less production that creates methane and carbon dioxide and everything else," Hamilton said.

title: Malicious browser extensions can hijack AI assistants
description: BragJack research reveals how a single malicious browser extension could hijack Gemini, Perplexity Comet and Edge AI agents with zero clicks.
content: AI assistants are moving deeper into the browsers we use every day. They can summarize a webpage, explain what you are looking at and, in some cases, take action on websites for you. That convenience also gives these tools access that a normal webpage would never have. Now, security researcher Gal Weizman of Forever Security has shown how a malicious browser extension could potentially turn those powerful AI capabilities against you. His research, called BragJack, targeted Gemini Live in Chrome, Perplexity Comet, Microsoft Edge Actions, Opera Neon and Anthropic's Claude in Chrome. The findings resulted in more than $20,000 in bug bounties and two CVEs. There is one important detail before you panic. The attack still required the malicious extension to be installed first. After that, Weizman demonstrated attacks that needed zero additional clicks from the victim. So how could one extension get that far inside the browser? It comes down to how these AI assistants are built. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION How a malicious extension can reach your browser's AI Weizman describes these AI systems as having a "brain" and a "body." The AI model works out what should happen. A privileged component inside the browser then carries out the request. Depending on the product, that privileged component might read webpage content, capture a screenshot or interact with a website. That setup becomes risky if something else inside the browser can manipulate the connection between those pieces. The proof-of-concept attacks relied heavily on Chromium's declarativeNetRequest, or DNR, system. Browser extensions can use DNR to modify how network requests work. That can include changing response headers or redirecting resources. Forever Security showed how those capabilities could let an extension interfere with web content trusted by a browser's AI features. Chrome's Gemini flaw exposed files and screenshots Chrome was one of the more striking examples. Google's Gemini side panel essentially has two pieces. Gemini handles the intelligence behind the request while Chrome provides the browser-level abilities needed to carry it out. Researchers found that Chrome already prevented extensions from directly injecting scripts into the Gemini page. However, the researchers discovered that an extension could still manipulate certain network requests used inside the Gemini experience. That gap allowed Weizman to demonstrate access to browser capabilities that the extension itself should never have received. According to the research, he could access local files, capture screenshots and obtain browser profile information. The researcher says the flaw also let him turn on the camera and microphone with zero clicks from the user. Google awarded the researchers a $7,000 bounty for reporting the vulnerability, which received the identifier CVE-2026-0628. Google has since confirmed to CyberGuy that it has closed this specific attack path. A Google spokesperson told us, "Confirming we've released a patch in Chrome so this method no longer works on the Gemini side panel." That means the technique demonstrated by the researchers should no longer work against the Gemini side panel in an updated version of Chrome. Perplexity Comet could take the attack further Perplexity Comet raised a different concern because its AI agent can take actions inside websites. Weizman found that Comet's built-in agent trusted several Perplexity domains. One testing domain lacked the same extension protections used on the main Perplexity site. Normally, that testing address redirected elsewhere. The proof-of-concept used DNR to remove the redirect and load the page instead. That gave the extension a path to communicate with Comet's built-in agent. The demonstrated access included browsing history, screenshots and local files. Then things became more personal. Weizman demonstrated sending an instruction that told the agent to access Perplexity, summarize the victim's recent emails and send the information to another email address. The AI agent performed the browser actions using capabilities it already had. Microsoft Edge had safeguards that researchers bypassed Microsoft built safeguards into Edge to keep outside prompts from easily controlling what its AI agent could do. Researchers still found a way around them. Weizman discovered a timing flaw known as a race condition. In simple terms, his test extension could feed the AI a prompt and then quickly switch on its ability to take action before Edge finished checking whether the request should be allowed. That opened the door for the AI agent to carry out a command it should not have accepted. Microsoft tracked the flaw as CVE-2026-55945 and rated it medium severity. The company says Edge versions before 150.0.4078.48 were affected. Updating Edge closes this particular security hole. Opera Neon and Claude in Chrome were vulnerable too Forever Security also demonstrated related attacks against Opera Neon and Claude in Chrome. There is an important difference with Claude. Claude in Chrome is itself a browser extension, rather than a complete browser. The researcher found that a page on Claude's domain could send prompts to the extension's side panel. Another extension could manipulate that trusted page and force prompts into Claude. Forever Security says Anthropic awarded a bounty for the finding and classified it as medium severity. Opera Neon also allowed the proof-of-concept extension to reach its AI agent. According to the researcher, that access could force the agent to carry out instructions on websites. All five demonstrations were Chromium-based, which helped the researcher reuse the same basic attack approach. We reached out to Google, Microsoft, Perplexity, Opera and Anthropic for comment on the research. Google responded with the update included above. Microsoft pointed us to its CVE-2026-55945 security advisory and said it had nothing further to share. We did not hear back from Perplexity, Opera or Anthropic before our deadline. LOCK DOWN YOUR CHATGPT ACCOUNT BEFORE THE NEXT AI ATTACK Prompt Forcing gives attackers another way to abuse AI You may already have heard about prompt injection. That usually involves hiding malicious instructions in something an AI reads. Weizman calls this new approach Prompt Forcing. Here, the attacker does not need to hide instructions inside a webpage and hope the AI follows them. The attacker can force a complete prompt into the agent through a channel that the browser or assistant trusts. The AI can then turn that plain-English instruction into legitimate browser actions. That creates an interesting problem for security software. A suspicious program stealing an email may be easier to spot. An approved AI agent opening a website and clicking a button can look like normal browser activity. The published BragJack research describes proof-of-concept attacks and does not report that these techniques have been exploited in the wild. Still, the research shows how the security equation changes as AI agents receive deeper access to browsers and computers. Why you should take another look at your browser extensions The attack starts with something many of us barely think about anymore: a browser extension. CyberGuy has covered malicious extensions that pretended to be AI assistants, hijacked online accounts and even turned trusted extensions into data-stealing spyware. That makes extension cleanup one of the easiest steps you can take right now. Maybe you installed a coupon extension two years ago and forgot about it. Perhaps you tested an AI sidebar once and never opened it again. If you no longer need an extension, there is little reason to keep giving it access to your browser. 8 ways to protect yourself from malicious browser extensions 1) Keep your browser updated Browsers receive security fixes regularly, so install updates as soon as they become available. Google's response makes that especially relevant here. The company says it has already released the Chrome patch that blocks the Gemini side-panel method demonstrated by the researchers. Restart Chrome after an update if prompted so the newest version can finish installing. 2) Remove extensions you no longer use Open your browser's extension manager and remove anything you do not recognize or no longer use. Here is the quickest way to check: Chrome and Claude in Chrome: Click the three-dot menu → Extensions → Manage extensions → find the extension → Remove. Google confirms this path in its current Chrome instructions. Microsoft Edge: Click the Extensions puzzle-piece icon → Manage extensions → find the extension → Remove. Opera Neon: Open the Extensions area from the browser sidebar or menu → review your installed extensions → remove anything you no longer trust or use. Opera documents its extensions manager through the Extensions icon and menu. Perplexity Comet: Open the browser's extensions manager and review imported or installed Chrome extensions. Comet supports Chrome extensions and can import them from Chrome. Pro tip: If you are unsure about an extension, disable it first and research the developer before removing it. THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE 3) Check permissions before installing Look carefully when an extension asks for broad access to websites or browser activity. The permission should make sense for what the extension actually does. 4) Limit an extension's access when possible Some browsers let you decide whether an extension can run on every website or only certain sites. Give an extension the narrowest access it needs to work. 5) Be careful with AI extensions An extension that uses a familiar AI name may have no connection to the company behind that AI service. Check the publisher before installing it. 6) Turn off AI browser features you do not use If your browser gives you the option to disable an AI assistant or agent you never use, consider turning it off. That reduces the number of powerful browser features available if another component gets compromised. 7) Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help flag malicious downloads and suspicious activity connected to bad extensions. It adds another layer of protection if something slips past you. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. 8) Treat extensions like apps Do not install one because it sounds useful for five minutes. Every extension adds code and permissions to the browser you use for email, banking, shopping and other private activity. Kurt's key takeaways What gets my attention here is how much more powerful a bad browser extension can become when an AI agent enters the picture. We already knew extensions could spy on browsing or steal account data. This research shows a possible path to something with much broader privileges. There is also a practical takeaway. These demonstrations still required the attacker-controlled extension to get inside the browser first. Once it was there, however, the researcher showed that the attack could continue without another click from the victim. I would take five minutes and look through your extensions today. If you cannot remember why you installed one, find out what it does. If you stopped using it months ago, remove it. As browser AI grows more capable, the companies building these tools also need strong barriers between ordinary extensions and the privileged systems that let AI act for us. Would you still let an AI assistant control parts of your browser if a malicious extension could potentially turn that access against you? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com. title: Josh Duhamel credits controversial routine for feeling better than in his 30s

content: Josh Duhamel is crediting taking testosterone with helping him feel better at 53 than he did 20 years ago. JOSH DUHAMEL SAYS HIS HEART RATE DROPS 25% AT OFF-GRID MINNESOTA CABIN "I feel better now than I did in my early to mid-30s," Duhamel said. "I'm not even kidding you. My joints, my back, my knees, everything. I just feel stronger." "I won't tell you the agency that I'm no longer with, but they said, 'Don't do it. It's bad for your image.' And I was like, 'Alright, watch,'" Duhamel recalled. "It took me a while," he admitted.
