"I had low T in my early 40s," Duhamel shared. "And so, I really started looking into it. FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG "But I found that I was feeling better," he continued. Duhamel said he injects testosterone three times a week, explaining that the schedule helps keep his levels consistent. title: Irish national soccer team should be ashamed for not shaking hands with Israeli opponents
description: Ireland's soccer players refused to shake hands with Israeli opponents before their Nations League match, sparking fierce debate over the protest.
content: Irish national soccer team players bowed their heads in protest Sunday. They should be hanging their heads in shame. This is a country known for its love of throwing a few back when the moment strikes. But it's disconcerting to see that their drink of choice is the Kool-Aid. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Ireland's players opted not to shake the hands of their Israeli opponents before Sunday's Nations League match in Hungary, and their goalkeeper, Gavin Banzunu, refused to play against Israel because of his "personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong." It was one giant virtue signal in the team's attempt to announce its moral superiority, but upon a closer look, it was the Irishmen who fell short. Some background. The Irish soccer team had faced pressure to boycott Sunday's game against Israel due to the country's response to the Hamas terror attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed nearly 1,200 Israelis. The narrative pushed by much of the media is that the counter-attacks have been akin to a "genocide," which has no basis in reality. Nevertheless, the Irish soccer team has seemed to deem Israel the villain in this conflict, and took out their resentment on the Israeli players. They wouldn't even shake their hands??? Pathetic. ISRAELI OFFICIAL SAYS EU SANCTIONS REVEAL ANTISEMITISM HIDING BEHIND 'SOCIALLY ACCEPTABLE MASK' Let's pretend for a second that Israel was, indeed, the "bad guy" in this conflict — something I don't believe to be true. Does that mean it's OK to shun the athletes representing the country? Where else could you apply that logic? Should opponents of North Korea's teams refuse to shake their players' hands because of a brutal dictatorship responsible for an innumerable amount of human rights abuses? Should opponents of Russian teams refuse to shake their players' hands because of Vladimir Putin's government invading Ukraine? KUWAITI MUSLIM JIU-JITSU CHAMPION REFUSES ISRAELI ATHLETE’S HANDSHAKE: ‘WE DO NOT RESPECT THEM AT ALL’ I was on hand in Seattle when Iran took on Egypt in a World Cup group play match. I didn't see Egyptians deny handshakes with Iranian players due to their government's extermination of protesters against the Tehran regime. I never saw players at the World Baseball Classic snub the Venezuelans because of Nicolás Maduro's brutal regime, either. I could go on and on. The world is brutal. Conflict is everywhere. But there's a big difference between protesting a country's government and treating players from said country as pariahs. The Irish soccer team doesn't seem to understand that. Never mind that Israel's attacks have essentially always been in response to attacks brought upon its country. Innocent people die tragically because Hamas uses them as human shields, embedding its fighters and military infrastructure among civilians in schools, hospitals and residential areas. The Israeli government regularly gives warnings that these attacks are coming, and provides aid to the Palestinian people. title: The NFL is America's most God-centered professional sports league and Sunday's games continued to prove it
description: Bo Nix and Talanoa Hufanga praised God on national TV after the Denver Broncos beat the Cowboys, highlighting the NFL's deep culture of faith.
content: Sunday's most compelling game was over and now it was time for the Denver Broncos stars to discuss their stirring victory over the Dallas Cowboys on NBC's national broadcast. And that's when quarterback Bo Nix and safety Talanoa Hufanga told everyone where the credit goes: To God. "Honestly man, all praise to God, just to come out here, believe in myself, believe in my teammates to be in the right spot," Hufanga said after collecting two interceptions, including a Pick Six. "Man, all glory to God that I go out there and play and have some fun." CARDINALS BACKUP CORNERBACK FINED BY NFL FOR WRITING 'GLORY BE 2 GOD' ON HIS EYEBLACK NBC's Melissa Stark turned to Nix and asked something about what was discussed at halftime. And the quarterback gave her 10 seconds of fluff football talk then said this: "But like he said, all glory to God," Nix said. "He's really good. He's given us this platform. He's given us this opportunity and our job is just to make the most of it." "Believe," Hufanga then added, as if imploring the audience to join them. And this is example 1,403,285 (more or less) that the NFL is the most God-centered professional sports league in America. CLEVELAND BROWNS PLAYERS PUBLICLY BAPTIZED AT CLEVELAND FOR CHRIST EVENT IN POWERFUL DISPLAY OF FAITH Every game day the most popular league playing the country's most popular sport shows up publicly thanking, praising and worshiping God. Unapologetically. No shame. No embarrassment. Out in the open, regardless how fans, media, or the league itself may feel about people of faith. So, how could this secular, oftentimes super liberal monolith of a business preach God so often? Well, let's understand there is a difference between the mostly faceless, nameless, Godless league that is headquartered in New York, and the people that fans actually come to see and cheer — the players and coaches. THE JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS OPENED TRAINING CAMP WITH AN AMAZING MESSAGE ABOUT GOD ON THEIR SOCIAL MEDIA While we think of the NFL as a sterile office bent on making gobs of profit, you've got people in uniform or wearing headsets that sometimes speak like prophets. Consider: The Baltimore Ravens beat the Dallas Cowboys in stunning, last-second fashion in Brazil. Quarterback Lamar Jackson completed a long pass with one second remaining to set up a final kick. So he stepped off the field and went to work. "The crazy thing about it [was] I had no doubt in my mind," Jackson told an international group of reporters afterward. "I prayed to Jesus. I prayed to God. "I am like, ‘Man, I feel like we already won.’ I could not show it, but I am like, I have all my faith in [kicker Tyler Loop] right now, man." In Washington, the Commanders lost linebacker Leo Chenal to a neck injury in the first half. He was taken to a local hospital where doctors saw he had movement in all his extremities. Back at the Northwest Stadium, Kain Medrano stepped in for Chenal. Medrano intercepted a pass in the fourth-quarter. And returned it for a touchdown and the game-deciding points. And afterward was thinking about his fallen teammate. "Yeah, obviously, we lost a brother," Medrano said, "but we're all praying for him." The Giants, like the Commanders, won on Sunday despite not having their starting quarterback because both Jaylen Daniels and Jaxson Dart are out injured. title: Workers renovating major city street stumble on ancient discovery buried 20 feet below
description: Ancient pottery dating back 1,000 years was unearthed 20 feet beneath Tbilisi's Rustaveli Avenue during routine roadwork on the city's main boulevard.
content: Workers renovating a bustling city boulevard stumbled across a piece of the ancient past — a cache of pottery dating back roughly 1,000 years. The discovery was made amid ongoing excavations in Tbilisi, the capital city of Georgia in the Caucasus region, south of Russia. The artifacts were found roughly 20 feet beneath Rustaveli Avenue, Tbilisi's main thoroughfare. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ANCIENT SITE DURING RAIL PROJECT, INCLUDING RARE ROMAN FIND Pictures show archaeologists examining the intricately decorated pottery fragments, as well as centuries-old jugs and various shards. The roadwork is part of a larger project to upgrade Rustaveli Avenue with new pedestrian crossings, improved signage and other improvements, according to Reuters. David Lordkipanidze, director of the Georgian National Museum, told Reuters the discovery was not entirely unexpected given Tbilisi's history. "Tbilisi is very rich with archaeological material ... so it's very logical to find workshops of different periods," he said. ANCIENT SHIPWRECK GIVES UP DAZZLING TREASURES AFTER MORE THAN 1,300 YEARS UNDERWATER Lordkipanidze also pointed to Tbilisi's long history as a crossroads for cultures and commerce. "Tbilisi was always multicultural," he said. "[It's been] a real center for the region, particularly an economic center." title: Rahm Emanuel lays out five-point ethics plan, says Democrats should learn from GOP-led states on education

content: AUSTIN, Texas — Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel insists his five-point plan would clean up ethics in government, and whoever emerges as the 2028 Democratic nominee could learn from Republican-led states if they want to help fix America’s education system. During an interview with Fox News Digital following his appearance at the 2026 Texas Tribune Festival, the high-powered Democrat, who has floated a potential 2028 White House run, insisted Americans need "five simple things" to ensure elected officials work for the people instead of themselves. "Across all three branches of government, ban all stock trading. Two, ban all participation in the prediction market. Three, when you hit the age of 75, mandatory retirement. Four, if your net worth is north of a million dollars… mandatory blind trust. Five, tighten up legally, not constitutionally, the foreign gifts and foreign investments and participation," Emanuel told Fox News Digital. DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID "For all three branches of government," he said. "Every one of those applies." title: Data centers could be the sleeper issue of the 2026 midterm elections
description: Data centers may be the sleeper issue of the midterms as a Gallup survey found 70% of Americans oppose new AI facilities in their communities.
content: Data centers may be the sleeper issue of the midterm elections. Fox News reported that Senate candidates are confronting growing voter anger over the electricity costs, water consumption and sprawling developments associated with artificial intelligence. One recent Gallup survey found that 70% of Americans oppose the construction of new AI data centers in their own communities. Politicians are paying attention. Some are calling for moratoriums. Others are targeting tax incentives or demanding that projects generate their own power. The political temptation is obvious: When voters are worried about higher utility bills and rapid changes in their communities, blaming large technology companies is easier than explaining a complicated energy and infrastructure problem. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER The concerns are real. They should not be dismissed by industry, and they cannot be ignored by elected officials. No family should be forced to subsidize the grid upgrades required by one of the world’s wealthiest companies. Communities deserve honest answers about water use, noise, land, electricity demand, tax incentives and who will pay for new infrastructure. But, legitimate concerns are quickly hardening into something far more dangerous: a political campaign against the physical infrastructure of American artificial intelligence. If that happens, we will repeat one of the most damaging patterns in modern American history. For decades, the United States surrendered factories, critical supply chains, mineral production and industrial capacity to foreign competitors. Communities lost jobs, our national security became dependent on adversaries, and Washington eventually spent billions trying to rebuild industries that should never have left. THE AI REVOLUTION COULD BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY DISASTER IF WE AREN'T CAREFUL We cannot make the same mistake with AI. Artificial intelligence does not exist somewhere in the cloud. It requires chips, servers, power plants, transmission lines, cooling systems, construction workers, electricians, pipefitters, engineers and data centers. These facilities are not incidental to the AI economy. They are the factories of the next industrial age. AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL China understands this. Beijing is not debating whether it should possess the energy and computing infrastructure necessary to dominate artificial intelligence. It is building. The International Energy Agency projects that data-center electricity consumption will increase substantially in both China and the United States through 2030. If America decides that data centers are too politically difficult to construct, the demand for AI will not disappear. The investment, jobs, technical expertise and strategic advantage will simply move elsewhere. That would be a profound failure of American competitiveness. It would also create a serious political problem for Democrats. Data-center construction has become an important source of work for the building trades. The Associated Press recently reported that data centers account for at least 40% of the work hours performed by members of the Columbus-Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council and at least 50% for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 26 in the Washington metropolitan area. WELDER TURNED LAWMAKER SEES A ‘NUCLEAR BOMB FOR WORK’ — AND A CHANCE TO HELP BLUE COLLAR AMERICANS Those are not theoretical jobs promised years from now. They are jobs for electricians, laborers, operating engineers, pipefitters and other skilled workers today. Democrats cannot claim to represent organized labor while allowing progressive activists to shut down the projects employing union members. Republicans should resist a similar temptation. Conservatives have spent years arguing for reshoring, energy dominance, permitting reform, American manufacturing and competition with China. Those commitments mean very little if they disappear when building the next American industry becomes locally controversial. The answer is not to wave every project through without conditions. It is to build responsibly and communicate honestly. Data-center developers should be expected to explain what they are building, how much electricity and water it will require, how they will protect residential ratepayers and what the surrounding community will receive in return. Utilities and regulators should ensure that large customers pay the costs created by their demand. Projects should pursue closed-loop cooling, on-site generation, long-term power agreements and other options that reduce pressure on local systems. TO BEAT CHINA IN AI, AMERICA MUST WORK WITH COMMUNITIES — NOT AROUND THEM Most importantly, America needs more energy. Data centers are exposing a problem that existed before the AI boom. Electricity demand from data centers has tripled over the past decade and could double or triple again by 2028. Electricity demand is rising after years of stagnant generation, premature plant retirements, congested transmission systems and permitting processes that make major infrastructure nearly impossible to build on time. Stopping data centers will not modernize the grid. Building more reliable generation, accelerating transmission, preserving existing nuclear capacity, expanding natural gas infrastructure and deploying advanced nuclear power will. Industry also needs to recognize that silence is no longer a strategy. As Sen. Jon Husted told Fox News, data-center companies have not done a good enough job explaining why they should be allowed to develop in communities. He is right. Americans hear about enormous power consumption, water use and tax incentives. They need to hear, in plain language, what data centers make possible, which jobs they create, how they support national security and why domestic computing capacity matters in the competition with China. That education must happen before a project is announced, not after opposition has already formed. Political leadership means taking voters’ concerns seriously without allowing fear to determine America’s economic future. We can protect ratepayers, demand transparency, give communities a meaningful voice and still build the infrastructure required to compete. title: NFL's most debated Week 3 call has people wondering how to defy gravity when hitting Patrick Mahomes
description: Miami Dolphins edge rusher Chop Robinson's hit on Patrick Mahomes drew a roughing the passer flag that reignited debate over NFL quarterback rules.
content: The Miami Dolphins are winless, which isn't good, but it gets worse because they also don't have a sack this season, making them the NFL's only team bearing that stigma. And all that made Sunday's controversial call sting all the more. The Dolphins today are going to dissect the fact they thought edge rusher Chop Robinson hurried Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes to throw the football out of the end zone for a big fourth-quarter stop. The ball fell harmlessly incomplete. PATRICK MAHOMES ANSWERS TROUBLING QUESTIONS ABOUT HIS SERIOUS KNEE INJURY ON FIRST DRIVE OF THE CHIEFS SEASON The way Mahomes fell was much more harmful in the view of the officials, who promptly called Robinson for roughing the passer. And why did Robinson get called for the controversial penalty? Because he landed on Mahomes without somehow sufficiently showing that he was trying to avoid stuffing the great quarterback into the Hard Rock Stadium grass. Remember that word – stuffing – because, believe it or not, it's an actual NFL rulebook standard for calling roughing the passer. (But first, full transparency: This penalty didn't change the outcome of the game. It didn't really affect the Chiefs at all because there was another Dolphins penalty on the play that would have extended the possession anyway.) But this penalty speaks to what lengths the NFL is going to protect its quarterbacks., how much latitude flawed officials get in making a call, and to what degree defenders are supposed go to avoid hurting QBs. That degree perhaps includes floating in air. Maybe levitating for a beat or two. Or simply defying gravity. Robinson didn't do any of those. He hit Mahomes and the quarterback went down. "No, he got me," Mahomes said afterward. "He got me for sure pretty good. But that’s part of playing football." Part of playing football is requiring pass rushers to somehow tackle the quarterback but "not unnecessarily or violently throw him down or land on top of him with all or most of the [defender's] weight," per the NFL rules book. And here's the problem 1: It's in the official's sole judgment if the defensive player did his best to not land with full weight on the quarterback. Problem 2: Defenders cannot typically hit the quarterback square and then stop their progress while in mid air. "Those are tough, man. Those are tough," Dolphins linebacker Jordyn Brooks said. "... I personally don't think that Chop was wrong in anything he did, and so that's something that we can't control." It's understandable the Dolphins cannot control this because neither can anyone else. It's physically impossible for a 280-pound dude to stop falling once he's in the air. He also cannot change the trajectory of his fall so as to avoid the guy he just hit. NEW NFL FINE SCHEDULE IS GOING TO A POINT SYSTEM THAT COULD LEAD TO SUSPENSIONS BUT ALSO REFUNDS The only way coaches have figured out to coach this is for rushers to try to cushion their fall with their arms and hands. You know, act like they didn't fall as hard as gravity demanded. That's what this call left Robinson thinking about – how to put his hands out with such drama as to allay the referee's fear that the face of the NFL was on the ground. "Put my hands out earlier," Robinson told reporters at his locker stall after the game. "I did what I was taught to do..." What makes this so difficult is the rule itself. NFL Rule 12, Section 2, Article 11 defines roughing the passer, and protecting any player in a passing posture from unnecessary, late, or violent contact. It states: "The Referee has principal responsibility for enforcing these rules. Any physical acts against a player who is in a passing posture (i.e. before, during, or after a pass) which, in the Referee’s judgment, are unwarranted by the circumstances of the play will be called as fouls." So, yes, this is all "the referee's judgment." And then the weight-bearing problem that brings the stuffing action into play... "A rushing defender is prohibited from committing such intimidating and punishing acts as 'stuffing' a passer into the ground or unnecessarily wrestling or driving him down after the passer has thrown the ball," the rule reads. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "When tackling a passer who is in a defenseless posture (e.g., during or just after throwing a pass), a defensive player must not unnecessarily or violently throw him down or land on top of him with all or most of the defender’s weight. "Instead, the defensive player must strive to fall to the side of the quarterback’s body, or to brace his fall with his arms to avoid landing on the quarterback with all or most of his body weight." Robinson braced his fall with his arm. But apparently the referee weighed the defender's fall and decided he followed through with all or most of his body weight. Or maybe it's just an faulty rule that needs more work. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

title: Our closing argument: The midterms are a referendum on who runs your life

content: The coming midterms lay bare a divide that runs deeper than policy and older than any party platform. Beneath every debate sits a single question, and it is the question on which this election turns: Who do you trust to run your life, you or the government? House Republicans' answer is our closing argument. The current Republican majority arrived in Congress in January 2025 and spent the next 20 months answering that question. After record highs of hundreds of thousands of illegals streaming over the southwest border into the country under President Joe Biden, we’ve slammed the door shut. We now have the most secure border in modern American history. Families in El Paso, Texas, no longer worry about migrants roaming the streets at night. We’ve funded and empowered law enforcement for the first time since 2020, resulting in the largest recorded drop in violent crime in FBI history. Now a mother in Chicago can let her son play outside after school without worry. SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' The Working Families Tax Cuts delivered the largest tax cut for the middle class in American history, putting money where it belongs: back in the pockets of those who earned it. By delivering "No Tax on Tips," "No Tax on Overtime" and a tax break for seniors, Republicans put real money back into the hands of the waitress closing out a double shift, the lineman working and the retiree who spent a lifetime building this country. We lifted Washington's weight off your backs, shrinking the federal government to its smallest level since 1966. We rolled back red tape that drove up the price of a car and many appliances and stood between ambitious Americans and the businesses they dreamed of starting. That is what small government with big results looks like. Our record rests on a conviction the Founders would immediately recognize: Free people, left alone to build, will build something worth keeping. The other side makes its convictions just as plain. Prominent Democrats demand that we defund the police. Democrats speak openly of abolishing the Senate, packing the Supreme Court and stripping away Second Amendment rights. When the Working Families Tax Cuts came to a vote, every Democrat in Congress opposed them, voting to take more money out of your pocket. That’s not government serving its people; that’s Washington grabbing your wallet with both hands and calling it help. The Democrats’ ideas grow from the belief that government belongs above the individual, an idea that found fertile soil in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The DSA calls for collective ownership of major parts of the economy and works to elect more socialists. Its goal is the end of capitalism. BRANDON GILL UNLOADS ON DEMOCRATS OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH RAPING TEEN: 'COLLATERAL DAMAGE' You might think the DSA is some marginal group in this country. Unfortunately, you’d be wrong. This is a national organization with more than 120,000 members. More than 250 DSA-backed Democrats hold office across the country today. The Democratic Party is fully locked in with the radical group. We should be clear-eyed about the DSA’s goal. Socialism and communism are twin evils, bound by a shared conviction that a central, all-powerful government must be trusted. In fact, socialism is a waypoint on the road to communism. Both Karl Marx’s 1875 "Critique of the Gotha Programme" and Vladimir Lenin’s 1917 "The State and Revolution" make clear that socialism is the first phase of a social transition to communism. And history offers many warnings about what happens after that transition. In Havana, Cuba, the pastel mansions of a once-glittering city have spent six decades dissolving into the salt air. Seen from orbit at night, North Korea is a vast patch of darkness where a nation of millions ought to be glowing. In the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s, people stood for hours in the winter dark outside shops whose shelves had been stripped long before they reached the door. SEN TOM COTTON: DEMOCRATS SAY SOCIALISM WILL HELP. HISTORY SAYS IT WILL HURT Each time the promise was paradise, financial equality for all working men and women, an escape from capitalism’s worst impulses. Each time the ending arrived in the same form. It came in neighborhoods where people had learned to lower their voices to avoid punishment for criticizing the all-powerful government. It came in cities where no one expected the lights to come back on. It came in lines formed where families waited for hours for meager subsistence for the dinner table. This is a conflict with common sense and the burden of history and responsibility on one side. And on the other is a group of individuals prepared to ignore the whole of history to embrace a politics that sets aside the element that has always underpinned the American experiment: human agency. Prominent Democrats demand that we defund the police. Democrats speak openly of abolishing the Senate, packing the Supreme Court and stripping away Second Amendment rights. We’ve clung tight to that beautiful individualism through 250 years. That’s the vision behind the Revolution that birthed this country. We’ve leaned on that ideal through a war fought to end the evil of slavery, a Great Depression that swallowed the poor and middle class, a war in Indochina that ripped the country apart, a stunning and catastrophic terror attack and multiple technological revolutions. Through it all, the radical ideal of human liberty has stayed lit like a lighthouse a ship finds on the darkest nights. title: King Charles, Prince William 'furious' as Princess Diana's brother unleashes explosive claims: experts
description: Charles Spencer's "Swan Song" reopens royal family wounds with claims about Princess Diana's funeral that have rattled Buckingham Palace insiders.
content: King Charles III and Prince William are said to be furious at Charles Spencer's new book, which makes damning allegations about the monarch and reopens decades-old wounds within the royal family. The claim was made by several royal experts who spoke to Fox News Digital after "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" was published on Tuesday. In it, Princess Diana's brother says he argued with then-Prince Charles over palace plans to have William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, walk behind their mother's coffin during her 1997 funeral procession. Most notably, Spencer alleged that after Diana died at age 36 in a car crash, Charles "sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner." He wrote that Charles "went ballistic" during an argument they had over William and Harry. Spencer said Charles then hissed, "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." KING CHARLES RESPONDS TO CHARLES SPENCER'S CLAIMS ABOUT PRINCESS DIANA IN A RARE STATEMENT "What I am hearing concerning the reaction around both households is frustration and anger, but for slightly different reasons," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "For the king, I think there is genuine anger at what amounts to an attack on his character almost 30 years after Diana's death," she explained. "But Charles has also lived with being cast as the villain in the Diana story for decades. Unfortunately, being portrayed as the bad guy in somebody else's version of this story is not new territory for him. For Prince William, there is an additional sense of betrayal. This is his uncle, who famously stood at Diana's funeral and promised that her 'blood family' would protect William and Harry." Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links. "William now has to watch that same uncle reopen some of the most traumatic events of his childhood and hear extremely damaging allegations against his father," Schofield said. WATCH: KING CHARLES FACES RENEWED ROYAL DRAMA OVER SPENCER MEMOIR: EXPERT "And William isn't just Charles' son. He is the future king. The monarchy Charles Spencer is attacking is the institution William will inherit. William is also reasonably questioning how dredging up disputed private conversations from 30 years ago, attacking the current king and reigniting the ugliest chapters of the Charles and Diana story could be in his nephew's best interests." After excerpts from the book were published last week, Buckingham Palace issued a rare, strongly worded statement. "His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said. A spokesperson for Buckingham Palace told Fox News Digital it had no comment. A spokesperson for Kensington Palace previously told Fox News Digital the palace does not comment on books. Spencer has stood by his account, insisting to the BBC that he is telling the truth. He asked, "Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" Some critics have questioned why Spencer felt the need to revisit the pain and trauma nearly 30 years later, The Associated Press reported. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Spencer said he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories about Diana, "once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths." Author Christopher Andersen told Fox News Digital he was surprised by Spencer's allegations. "Just weeks after Diana was killed, I interviewed hundreds of sources in London and Paris for my book 'The Day Diana Died,'" he said. "They all remembered that Charles was absolutely devastated. 'Crushed' was a word I heard repeatedly when he first learned the news of Diana's death. After years of famously battling as a married couple, they had finally found a kind of peace with each other following their 1996 divorce. They actually became friends." "When Charles got the call at Balmoral that Diana had been killed, a staffer told me that the king let out a howl that sounded like a wounded animal, then burst into tears. Others described Charles at the time as being racked with sobs, his face streaked with tears." "I also interviewed the nurses at the Paris hospital who witnessed the moment Charles saw Diana's body for the first time," Andersen continued. "He fell back, one of them told me, as if he had been struck by an unseen hand. They thought he was going to pass out. He then began to weep openly. Everyone was very surprised at how emotional King Charles was because they believed members of the royal family, and especially Charles, were cold and aloof. They did not doubt in their minds that he was shattered by his ex-wife's tragic death." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Andersen said he wonders whether the words Spencer says he heard from Charles over the phone were those of "a man on the verge of a nervous breakdown." "King Charles' world was crumbling all around him," Andersen said. "Not only was the mother of his children suddenly gone, but at the time, Queen Elizabeth did not want the princess to have a public funeral. She refused to fly the flag at half-staff over Buckingham Palace in Diana's honor. She did not even want to come back from her summer vacation at Balmoral. It fell on Charles' shoulders to force his mother to show Diana the respect the British people felt she deserved." Still, Andersen said he would not be surprised if the king had shouted hurtful words at Spencer in anger. "Charles has a long history of lashing out, making rash and sometimes cruel, offhand statements," Andersen said. "The king always resented being overshadowed by Diana during her lifetime, and now he was being totally eclipsed by her in death. There was lingering resentment there. It's also clear the king knew that the public would blame him and Camilla for making Diana so desperately unhappy during her lifetime and, to some extent, for the extent, for the events leading up to her death." Andersen noted that the late queen "was in no mood" to see her eldest son remarry anytime soon. Any hopes Charles may have had of marrying Camilla, with whom he had previously had an affair, were dashed. Eight years passed before the queen permitted Charles to marry Camilla. A source told Radar Online that Queen Camilla is trying to "lower the temperature" behind palace doors. "Camilla is particularly conscious that there are different memories of what happened during an extraordinarily difficult period for the family. People experienced those events from very different perspectives, and she recognizes that emotions surrounding Diana are still exceptionally powerful." British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that William isn't close to his uncle and that sources have told her he is "absolutely furious." "His public silence regarding this matter is admirable," she said. "The pain Spencer is causing William has backfired as he’s being accused of monetizing his sister’s memory." British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that Buckingham Palace is "rattled, but they're not panicking" over Spencer's "verbal grenades straight at the palace gates." She said the royal family is privately presenting a united front as its members focus on their duties. "The strategy is clear: let the book have a few weeks of noisy publicity and just plow on with the job," Chard said. It's trauma stirred anew. Palace aides say his focus is on public work and protecting the family." PRINCESS DIANA'S BROTHER CHARLES SPENCER SAYS KING CHARLES 'GASLIT' HIM OVER MEMOIR CLAIMS "Whatever you think of Prince Harry's memoir, Harry was King Charles' son, Prince William's brother and a central participant in the family life he was describing," Schofield said. "Charles Spencer simply did not have that same proximity to the royal family or even, according to multiple accounts, to Diana throughout the final years of her life. There have been people within Diana's circle who have challenged the impression that Charles Spencer was this constant, intimate presence in her life." Spencer has stood by his account as the book rolls out globally and is translated into 12 languages.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs can become an ‘atomic bomb’ at high doses, doctor warns
description: Dr. Will Cole warns that macro-dosing GLP-1s isn't the answer to metabolic health, advocating for micro-dosing peptides paired with lifestyle changes.
content: As interest in peptides continues to grow, experts are increasingly looking beyond weight loss to their potential role in healthy aging. Functional medicine expert Dr. Will Cole told Fox News Digital that peptides are "intimately connected" with longevity, cellular healing and metabolic health. "[Peptides] help with cellular communication," said Cole, co-author of the upcoming book "Heal Your Cells." The recommendations for peptides depend on the context in which they're used, he said, noting that the answer often falls "somewhere in the middle." THINKING ABOUT PEPTIDES? DOCTORS REVEAL KEY DOS AND DON’TS AS ‘WILD WEST’ MARKET GROWS Citing previous research, Cole noted that an estimated 93% of U.S. adults are metabolically unhealthy, leaving only about 7% who meet the criteria for optimal metabolic health — a figure he described as "wild." "That's common, but not normal," Cole said. He added that while GLP-1 medications can be beneficial, improving metabolic health also requires addressing lifestyle and other underlying factors. FDA TO REVIEW 7 POPULAR PEPTIDES TOUTED FOR WEIGHT LOSS, HEALING AND LONGEVITY Cole shared that he does not believe "macro-dosing" GLP-1s "forever and ever in perpetuity" is the solution to improving metabolic health. While GLP-1s can reduce food cravings — often referred to as "food noise" — and promote weight loss, Cole said he’d like to see more research on how decreasing the desire for food could also decrease cravings for love, relationships and other mood-boosting factors. Cole questioned whether suppressing food cravings could have unintended effects on other reward-related behaviors, including social relationships. "So, are we circumventing pathways and pathologizing things that don't have to be pathologized?" CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Cole argued that some degree of hunger signaling is healthy. "Food noise is actually a decent thing in balance, so shutting down your hunger cues with an 'atomic bomb' peptide dose is not the solution." He added that he believes overreliance on GLP-1 medications may contribute to disordered eating patterns and a growing fear of hunger. Cole attributed the trend to a culture that favors simple, fast solutions over sustained lifestyle changes. "We want a magic pill," he said. "And the truth is somewhere in the middle: Can we micro-dose? Can we do it cyclically? And can we pair it with lifestyle?" CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The expert questioned why there has been an "epidemic rise" of metabolic problems, pointing to factors such as diets high in ultraprocessed foods, nutrient deficiencies, environmental toxins and the presence of stress and trauma. "That is why we're seeing a rise of chronic health problems, not a pharmaceutical deficiency," he said. Cole said he supports wider access to peptides, but emphasized the importance of transparency, product purity and clear labeling so healthcare professionals and consumers can make informed decisions. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Despite those concerns, Cole said he believes GLP-1s also hold significant therapeutic promise, citing their potential to reduce inflammation, help manage autoimmune conditions and improve gut health. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But again, what's the lowest dose that yields a beneficial result paired with lifestyle? I think that's where peptides can really shine," he said. "And I am actually more excited about some of these other [peptides], like the inflammation ones or the longevity peptides."

title: NFL Week 3 Sunday takeaways: Patriots have a Maye problem, Chargers hit rock bottom and Cowboys crumble
description: Biggest Week 3 NFL takeaways incldue Drake Maye struggling with six interceptions, and Brock Bowers returning from knee surgery in stunning fashion.
content: We spend all offseason waiting for football to come back and somehow we're already three weeks into the NFL season. I'd appreciate it if things could slow down a little. Although, if you're a fan of the Dolphins, Titans or Chargers, you probably think the season can't go by fast enough. Week 3 gave us plenty to talk about, and I have some thoughts. Here’s my biggest takeaway from each of Sunday’s games. Bills 24, Chargers 16 Takeaway: It was a good week for Buffalo to come out flat. Buffalo's offense came out of the gate with a 36-point output against a stout Houston defense in Week 1 and then followed it up by dropping 41 on Detroit in Week 2. But the unit struggled mightily on Sunday, turning the ball over three times on its first four possessions. After managing to get the game tied at 10 going into halftime, the Bills turned it over on their first two possessions of the second half. Lucky for them, they were playing the awful winless Chargers, who couldn't even beat a team that turned the ball over five times. Buffalo can't play like that against good teams. Browns 21, Panthers 18 Takeaway: Sorry, Deshaun Watson, I wasn't really familiar with your game. Insert Shaq meme here. Yeah, so, I buried Watson after a horrendous performance in Week 1 (following a terrible preseason). But he played pretty well against the Bucs in a Week 2 win and did enough to lead the Browns to a shocking 2-1 record. Watson's numbers don't look great (16-30, 144 yards, 2 TD), but he kept making big throws when the team needed them and added some important runs to keep the chains moving. Watson isn't great, obviously, but he's at least playing like a serviceable NFL quarterback and that's more than I expected from him after Week 1. DESHAUN WATSON GOES FROM CLEVELAND VILLAIN TO HERO IN BROWNS UPSET WIN, AS HOME CROWD TURNS JEERS TO CHEERS Lions 31, Jets 24 Takeaway: The Jets really aren't that bad. Speaking of teams for which I didn't have high expectations, the Jets have been much better than I expected. Yes, they're 1-2. But they should have beaten the Packers in Week 2 and they were tied with the Lions with under three minutes left. Now, great teams win those games. The Jets aren't great. But given that the bar was set at, like, below average, Jets fans have a reason to at least have some hope for the first time in years. Colts 19, Texans 17 Takeaway: The AFC South is bad again. You know, for a minute it looked like the AFC South might be good again instead of being relegated to that Saturday afternoon Wild Card slot (the one that goes to the least interesting first-round playoff matchup). But here we are with the Colts and Texans both not looking particularly good. C.J. Stroud has never regained his rookie season form and Daniel Jones turned the ball over three times. Plus, these teams just aren't even fun to watch (the Jaguars really aren't, either, and don't get me started on the Titans). Just put the winner of this division at 4:30 on Wild Card Saturday now and be done with it. Jaguars 35, Patriots 6 Takeaway: Drake Maye looks like a one-hit wonder. I'm trying not to overreact but Maye keeps making it harder and harder. He's made some of the worst throws of any quarterback so far this season, and that's saying something. The Patriots offense has generated just two touchdowns in three games and Maye has thrown six interceptions and has lost a fumble. With a game in Buffalo next week, it could start getting late early for the reigning AFC champions. TREVOR LAWRENCE FANTASY OWNERS ARE BESIDE THEMSELVES AFTER INEXPLICABLE DECISION IN FOURTH QUARTER BLOWOUT Chiefs 24, Dolphins 10 Takeaway: The Dolphins showed some fight? I don't know, what do you want me to say? The Chiefs beat the Dolphins, as literally everyone expected. Miami hung around for a while and was only down four heading to the fourth quarter. But Kansas City still won by two touchdowns. Dolphins fans have only one date on their minds: April 29, 2027 (the first round of the 2027 NFL Draft). Giants 12, Titans 7 Takeaway: Two bad offenses playing in bad weather is a recipe for a bad game. I have four TVs in my living room and thanks to multiview, I can essentially watch every NFL game simultaneously. I do my best to keep my eyes moving so I can watch as much of each one as possible. But I'm not going to pretend I spent much time watching Jameis Winston and Cam Ward battle on a wet field to see who could get to double-digit points first. It was the Giants, by the way, and they won. Woo-hoo. Steelers 30, Bengals 27 Takeaway: I tried to warn you. I wrote in my NFL picks column this week that the Bengals were due for a letdown and the Steelers were likely to show up at home and finally play a solid offensive game. There was no chance I was going to let this perfect "I told you so" moment pass. That being said, this doesn't change my opinion: The Bengals are still good, the Steelers still aren't very good. It was one game and I'm not reading too much into it. Commanders 33, Seahawks 31 Takeaway: Turnovers matter a lot, folks. No, I don't think the Commanders are better than the Seahawks. No, I don't think the Commanders are better with Marcus Mariota at quarterback instead of Jayden Daniels. But I do think that winning the turnover battle is massively important (unless you're the Chargers) and Washington had 3 takeaways to Seattle's 0. That's why the Seahawks lost despite outgaining the Commanders 437 to 258. 49ers 36, Cardinals 30 Takeaway: What a weird game this was. The 49ers appeared to be on their way to an easy victory after taking a 23-6 lead four minutes into the second half. But give credit to the Cardinals, who just never quit. At the same time, San Francisco never trailed and every time Arizona got within one score, the 49ers would score a touchdown (except the final time, but the game was over at that point). The bigger concern is that San Francisco saw three key players leave the game with injuries: Mike Evans, Trent Williams and Dre Greenlaw. Vikings 23, Buccaneers 16 Takeaway: Kevin O'Connell is a magician. The Vikings are 3-0 because O'Connell is legitimately a top-five coach in the NFL (maybe top three). It almost doesn't even matter who the quarterback is because KOC will scheme his way into victories. More importantly, though, the Bucs screwed me over this week and I'm not going to miss an opportunity to whine about that. I'm officially over Tampa Bay. BAKER MAYFIELD LEAVES GAME AFTER WRITHING IN PAIN ON TURF IN TAMPA BAY WHEN THUMB ON THROWING HAND INJURED Raiders 35, Saints 27 Takeaway: Welcome back, Brock Bowers. Bowers angered fantasy football managers (including myself) by undergoing knee surgery just before the start of the season (without any major indication there was a problem prior to most fantasy drafts), but he reminded everyone that he's not really human. Not only did he return from meniscus surgery in less than 20 days, but he immediately went out and caught 10 passes for 116 yards and a touchdown. Don't look now, but the Raiders are 3-0 with a showdown against the Chiefs coming in Week 4. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Ravens 34, Cowboys 31 Takeaway: Ball don't lie. The referees nearly gifted the Dallas Cowboys a win with an awful pass interference call that set the Cowboys up on the Ravens 2-yard line trailing by 3 points with 23 seconds left in the game. Dallas ultimately didn't score a touchdown, kicked a field goal to tie, then inexplicably allowed the Ravens to easily pick up 27 yards in 6 seconds to give Tyler Loop the opportunity to boot a game-winning 56-yard field goal, which he did. The team that should have won did win, and that doesn't always happen in the NFL so we should be grateful for that. Broncos 30, Rams 26 Takeaway: Sean Payton remains the most overrated and luckiest coach in the NFL. If you've read my NFL columns before, you probably saw this one coming. If you're new, welcome! I'm Dan and I think Sean Payton is the NFL's most overrated head coach. Once again, Payton benefited from something outside his control, this time a terrible pass interference call on what should have been a game-winning interception by the Rams. Instead, Denver kept the ball and scored a game-winning touchdown a few plays later. Payton is a good coach that the media treats like an elite coach because he's nice to them. But that reputation glosses over his up-and-down record, the Bountygate scandal that no one seems to talk about anymore and just how much he benefited from landing Drew Brees (only because the Dolphins medical staff screwed up royally). Denver won despite Nix completing just 50% of his passes for under 200 yards with an interception.

title: White House reporters float some surprise choices on which Republicans could run for president after Trump
description: White House reporters were asked who among Republicans may enter the 2028 presidential race during a panel discussion at the Texas Tribune Festival.
content: AUSTIN, Texas — Three prominent White House reporters discussed which Republicans could run to succeed President Donald Trump in 2028 — and floated a wide range of names. Politico White House bureau chief Dasha Burns, NBC News chief White House correspondent Garrett Haake and New York Times White House correspondent Maggie Haberman sat down for a panel discussion about covering the Trump presidency Friday at the Texas Tribune Festival. While much of the discussion focused on Trump's current term in office, moderator Annah Aschbrenner of The Washington Post finished the conversation by asking how the "competition" will shape up in the next election. RAHM EMANUEL TOUTS WHAT SEPARATES HIM FROM OTHER DEMS AS HE MULLS 2028 PRESIDENTIAL BID "I think there are four lanes to the Republican Party," Haake responded. "I think one lane is the Trump successor, the sort of like, from the inside of the White House, who's the person who gets blessed... Presumably, that's JD Vance. Unless JD Vance decides, for whatever reason, [he] doesn't want it, or is somehow disqualified, then maybe it's Marco Rubio." "Then I think there's the 'I tried to help you, but you didn't listen' lane, which is like Ted Cruz, somebody who's going to spend the next two years making Trump's closest ally, fight real hard, but then when it comes around saying, you know, it didn't work, [Trump's] approval rate is 25%, here's what I told him to do, he didn't listen," he continued. "Then I'd think there is this explicitly anti-Trump lane, which is somebody like if Chris Christie... maybe it's [outgoing Nebraska Congressman] Don Bacon or somebody like that." Haake then shared what he called his "fourth wild card," which was HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., sparking gasps and groans from the largely liberal audience. Burns jumped in, adding former DNI Tulsi Gabbard to Haake's fourth lane of candidates. TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028 Haake theorized that if the MAGA coalition is fractured by 2028, the "MAHA group" — the Make America Healthy Again movement that helped fuel RFK Jr.'s independent run for president in 2024 and ultimately rallied behind Trump could rally behind the ex-Democrat, who he said "owns" that constituency more than Trump. Haberman seemed to agree with Haake's assessment, adding the "asterisk" that it's "likely JD Vance's nomination if he wants it" but that the war with Iran could also impact his chances. While she stopped short of adding his name to the list of GOP hopefuls, Burns stressed the major influence Donald Trump Jr. has within the Republican Party, telling the crowd that Vance would not have been vice president without him. "He speaks the language of conservatives more," Haberman chimed in. The Politico Playbook co-author then recalled Trump Jr. introducing his father at campaign rallies and how he'd receive "massive ovations" to the point that Trump would come out and remark on the enthusiasm for his son. Burns said Trump Jr. eventually stopped introducing his father as a result. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So there's a world where Don Jr. really brings a ton of the coalition to JD Vance, and that will, I think, largely be positive for him," Burns said. "I think that what is happening with these midterms, if it is the bloodbath that all the numbers are saying will be . . . I think the floodgates open, and it really changes the 2028 dynamics." Burns added that a "ton of people" from Trump's cabinet could throw their hat in the ring in addition to RFK Jr. and Gabbard, also citing Secretary of War Pete Hegseth as a potential contender.

title: MARTHA MACCALLUM: After 22 years, here's why I'm grateful to call Fox home
description: From the 2004 Democratic convention floor to the beaches of Normandy, two decades of reporting shaped a career.
content: Twenty-two years ago, I made the best move of my career. My early years were spent at The Wall Street Journal and CNBC. But coming here changed my life in so many positive ways that I can’t imagine what any other path would have looked like. I am deeply grateful that I trusted the gut feeling that told me I belonged here. On my first day, Jeff Hark, who was overseeing the scheduling of reporters and anchors, asked me about my family. He knew I had three young children, and he wanted to assure me that Fox understood the pressures of young professionals raising kids. Defensive at first, I insisted I could handle it and wouldn’t be bothering him with requests for time off, but then I realized he actually meant it. It was such a smart company perspective that it made me want to work even harder, knowing they would have my back. Fox liberated me to grow and take on so many new challenges. The environment was still scrappy, and the growth was exponential. Every opportunity I leaned into opened a door. That first year, I asked to be part of the election team covering the November 2004 presidential race. I offered to stand on a street corner in Boston and report on how the DNC was affecting traffic. Kidding, but not kidding — I just wanted to be in the "room where it was happening"! I soon found myself reporting from the floor of the Democratic convention alongside correspondents Carl Cameron and Major Garrett, two of our most seasoned political reporters. I was exuberant and terrified. But I survived, and it was the beginning of 20 years of covering elections for Fox News. I have traveled the world, covered presidents and kings, and perhaps most rewarding of all, I have had the honor of walking the beaches of Normandy with our war heroes and sharing their stories, from Berlin, Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan. At Fox, a deep respect for our veterans was encouraged in a way that would not have happened anywhere else. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION I am forever grateful for our Fox family here. For Lachlan, Suzanne and Jay, and everyone else who feels like home. We are bonded by a love for our country. We are driven to hold it to the highest standard. To hold those who govern it accountable. And to pray for its continued success. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Happy 30th birthday, Fox. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM MARTHA MACCALLUM

title: Restaurants lock up customers' phones as devices become the 'new cigarettes'
description: Locked pouches, free wine bottles and no-Wi-Fi policies are how bars and restaurants are pushing back against phones at the dinner table.
content: Cigarette smoke may be gone from restaurant dining rooms, but some owners say a new distraction is affecting the experience: customers glued to their phones. Bars and restaurants are finding increasingly creative ways to get diners to focus more on the experience and less on their screens, from locked pouches like those used in schools to a free bottle of wine. At Antagonist, a cocktail bar in Charlotte, North Carolina, guests receive a lockable pouch for their phones upon entry — one example of devices becoming the "new cigarettes" in restaurants, as The Wall Street Journal recently put it. RESTAURANTS BAN DINERS' PHONES DURING MEALS AS NO-SCROLL TREND GROWS: PUT IT AWAY OR ELSE The goal is "to bring back a little slice of human connection that we all feel has been lost with technology," Adam Horner, Antagonist's general manager, told the outlet. The Saloon, a Washington, D.C., bar with no televisions, prohibits phone use altogether. A regular told the Journal the policy pushes back against a bar culture that has become "very insular and not very fun" because of phones. Eulalie, a bistro in Manhattan, states its no-phone policy at the entrance and on its handwritten menus. Co-owner Tina Vaughn told the Journal that diners welcome it. MORE AMERICANS ARE DINING ALONE AS SOLO RESTAURANT RESERVATIONS SOAR, DATA SHOWS "People want an excuse," she said. "They're dying for someone to say, 'You can get off that. It’s OK.'" Philadelphia's Hop Sing Laundromat also bans calls, texting, photos and selfies as part of its tightly controlled speakeasy experience, according to reports, and guests are briefed on the rules upon arrival. Other spots, meanwhile, are taking a more subtle approach. The Edge Harlem in New York City does not offer Wi-Fi and displays a sign on the bar that says, "No Wi-Fi. No Screens. Connect With Each Other," the Journal reported. RESTAURANT OWNER SAYS DINING ROOM IS 'NOT A PLAYGROUND' AS ETIQUETTE EXPERTS WEIGH IN ON VIRAL DEBATE Across the Atlantic, restaurants are trying different approaches, according to The Guardian. Spy Bar in London places stickers over phone camera lenses, while AI Condominio in Verona, Italy, offers diners a free bottle of wine if patrons hand over their phones before eating. The practice appears most common at curated, higher-end experiences such as tasting-menu restaurants, cocktail lounges and listening bars, Fox News Digital previously reported, but even some major chains are experimenting with phone limitations. Chick-fil-A offers a "Cellphone Coops Challenge" at select locations, so groups can stash their phones in a box while they eat in exchange for free ice cream. AMERICANS ARE PAYING PEOPLE TO WAIT IN LINE FOR TIKTOK-FAMOUS FOOD The movement comes as phones have become as common as place settings, with people snapping food photos, taking videos, making loud calls and scrolling through social media during meals. Phones can disrupt the carefully timed rhythm of service, especially when a drink or dish is meant to be served at a certain temperature or with an explanation, Sanwar Mal Khokhar, a Dallas-based mixologist and beverage program leader, told Fox News Digital. title: DANA PERINO: The untold story of the remarkable people who make Fox News possible
description: Anchor Dana Perino marks Fox News Channel's 30 years with a tribute to the behind-the-scenes producers, crews and teams who power every breaking news moment.
content: FOX NEWS ALERT! You’re joining our coverage live as Fox News Channel celebrates 30 years of on-air excellence. Thirty years? It went by so fast. And yet, a 30th anniversary doesn’t happen by accident. Fox News makes it look easy. It’s not. The work behind the scenes is incredible to witness. FOX NEWS TOUTED AT ANNUAL UPFRONT PRESENTATION TO ADVERTISERS: ‘WE’RE NOT JUST COMPETING, WE ARE DOMINATING’ Let’s take a moment to recognize the people our viewers never see — the ones who make it possible for the shows to get on the air and for those of us in front of the camera to have complete confidence that the product reaching our viewers is informative and entertaining. Having that confidence matters to the anchors, hosts and guests. It’s critical to know the research is solid, the technology is working, the pictures are right, and, if something changes in an instant, that the team has your back. Nearly the entire building is organized around making that possible. FOX NEWS DIGITAL THUMPS ALL NEWS BRANDS INCLUDING BROADCAST NETWORKS IN KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS DURING JULY Aside from the hours I’m on air, I walk into work so happy. I love my routine — and knowing that the plan could change in an instant. It keeps me on my toes. My day begins with a security guard who likes to announce, "Talent is in the building!" precisely because he knows the word "talent" makes me cringe. I blush, walk faster, and we laugh about it every single morning. I often see one of the custodial staff on my way up to my office, and one joins me in trying to get a tradition going of saying, "Morning morning!" every day. We have a streak — we never miss. Long before I arrive, the producers have already been working. They get up hours before we do, thinking about what would make a good show — not simply what we are going to say, but what the audience is going to experience. They’re looking for the best and latest video that captures an event, making graphics to help explain the story (I love charts!) and writing scripts that grab the viewer and keep them watching. And then, at a moment’s notice, they may have to tear up the entire rundown when breaking news changes everything. Suddenly, the carefully planned show is gone, and the team is shifting to something happening across the country or around the world. They have to gather information, verify it, find the right pictures, reach the right correspondents and guests, and help us understand what matters — fast. That kind of flexibility only looks effortless when the people doing it are exceptionally good at their jobs. My day begins with a security guard who likes to announce, ‘Talent is in the building!’ precisely because he knows the word 'talent' makes me cringe. I blush, walk faster, and we laugh about it every single morning. I remember once interviewing an Afghan man who witnessed the Abbey Gate airport bombing in August 2021, when President Joe Biden pulled our troops out. This man picked up an injured child, carried her to safety and then came on air with us. He was a man with no hope. And while I am usually very stoic on air, I was about to cry. WOUNDED MARINES RELIVE THE HARROWING KABUL AIRPORT ATTACK IN EXPLOSIVE NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY I will never forget the reassuring voice in my ear from the line producer: "You’re OK. You’re OK." My tears dried up. The interview continued. Assistants are a lifeline for us — they produce our lives. They do the research, keep the schedule, block and tackle, and get in front of problems. The scope and scale of their talents are immense, and without them, we’d be lost. Our technology teams keep us connected to breaking news and events around the world in real time — something we all take for granted right up until the second something doesn’t work. And then, of course, there are those who help us look our best. The wardrobe department has a great eye and is always there with a pin or a piece of tape when we need it. The hair and makeup team is by far the best in the business. Name another? You can’t. FOX NEWS LEADS ALL NEWS BRANDS IN YOUTUBE VIDEO VIEWS AND SOCIAL ENGAGEMENT FOR SECOND QUARTER 2026 They’re also our confidants — I’ve worked with the same team for almost 15 years, and they’ve become my sister-friends. Sure, they make sure I’m camera-ready at an hour when most reasonable people are still in pajamas, but they also know when I’ve had a tough night, could use some encouragement, need to laugh and when it’s better just to let me sit quietly for a few minutes. I can’t wait to see them every day and catch up. So many others to mention — the directors who know how to get the best reaction shots, the cameramen who never miss an angle, and the lighting technicians we wish we could take with us everywhere. And there’s a special relationship with a stage manager who can communicate an entire paragraph with one glance. There are also those who laugh at our jokes — it’s very gratifying to hear those chuckles. On the road, another kind of magic happens. Our crews can take a barn, a convention hall, a parking lot or almost anywhere else and turn it into a beautiful television set. Hollywood should be so lucky to know these people. And amid the enormous logistical challenge of covering an election or a breaking-news event, someone still remembers the little things: Dana likes warm water in her cup. Dana would love a yoga mat in her room if we’re going to be here for a very long time. Dana needs a footstool (always!). Those things may sound small, but they make all the difference. They say: We know you. We’ve got you. Go do your job. That same support extends far beyond the studio. Our media relations team promotes our work, tells our stories and, when we need it, defends us vigorously. They are in the arena with us and knowing they are there matters. The same is true of our radio, podcast and digital teams, which have evolved right alongside the technology and opened up more and more ways for us to reach people. What once lived mostly on a television screen now lives in earbuds, phones, websites and across platforms that did not even exist when Fox News began. The technology changes, but the mission remains the same: Find the audience and serve them well. And there are so many others whose names never appear on the screen. You don’t just work alongside people — you live a lot of life alongside them. These are not just colleagues. After enough years, they become deep friendships, and all the while, I have laughed so much. FOX NEWS DIGITAL HITS 165 MILLION UNIQUE VISITORS IN MAY TO CRUSH BROADCAST NETWORKS, NEWS COMPETITORS I have also leaned on this group for comfort during some of life’s hardest moments, including when my dad passed away earlier this year. And I have had the privilege of sharing in the joy, too — marriages, babies and now, after all these years, even grandbabies. That is what longevity really looks like. You don’t just work alongside people — you live a lot of life alongside them. We have celebrated, mourned, adapted and endured more than a few difficult seasons. And I think we are stronger because of it. I’ve been at Fox for nearly 17 years, and somehow I still feel new compared with the OGs who built this network and made it what it is today. But excellence still comes down to people and our corporate culture. Without their singular focus on getting it right, we would not be number one, and we would not have lasted 30 years. Because of them — along with the vision and leadership from the top, including our founders — I have tremendous confidence in the years ahead.
