title: HUD’s homelessness reforms put human lives ahead of housing bureaucracy
description: HUD reforms shift homelessness policy away from Housing First toward measuring recovery and self-sufficiency after a 27% surge in homelessness.
content: On Sept. 16, the First Circuit Court of Appeals cleared the way for the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to move forward with desperately needed reforms to the nation’s homelessness system. After months of litigation by the Homeless Industrial Complex to repeatedly block these reforms, the decision allows HUD to redefine success and fund the programs that generate the greatest success in moving the homeless toward recovery, restoration and self-sufficiency. And not a moment too soon. TRUMP WANTS TO HELP 146,000 MENTALLY ILL WHO ARE HOMELESS. DEMOCRATS WANT TO STOP HIM For more than a decade, federal homelessness policy has centered heavily on permanent housing placement, while the measures used to define and count homelessness have often obscured important differences between who is counted as homeless and who is being served through homelessness programs. Success will now be measured by whether people are getting better: recovering, working, reconnecting and reclaiming their lives. Getting here required that HUD officials confront a series of gimmicks that helped sustain the old system — promises, definitions and measures of success that painted a very different picture than what was happening on America’s streets. SEATTLE MAYOR SAYS SOBRIETY WON'T BE REQUIRED AT NEW HOMELESS SHELTER The first gimmick was in 2013 when President Barack Obama declared Housing First the predominant federal approach, promising to end homelessness in a decade by prioritizing permanent housing placement without requiring treatment, sobriety or other preconditions. The promised end never came. By 2025, despite a 151% increase in taxpayer-funded beds, homelessness surged 27% and chronic homelessness by 81% — reaching the highest levels ever recorded in our nation’s history. The problem was that we defined success as housing placements and system growth rather than recovery, self-sufficiency and restored lives. Spending soared, the system expanded and homelessness grew with it. LETITIA JAMES FACES SCRUTINY AFTER NEW YORK CITY SPENDS $81,700 PER HOMELESS PERSON AMID SHELTER SCANDALS That brings us to gimmick No. 2: housing people and then removing them from the homelessness count. HUD’s Point-in-Time count excludes people already living in taxpayer-funded permanent housing for the homeless even though roughly 83% of HUD’s homelessness resources are devoted to housing them. That exposes a fundamental contradiction: If they are no longer counted as homeless, why does the nation’s largest homelessness agency continue devoting the majority of its resources to housing them? SEATTLE CLEANED UP FOR THE WORLD CUP BUT ONLY WHILE THE WORLD WAS WATCHING, COMMENTATOR SAYS Then came another statistical sleight of hand: rapid rehousing. Success will now be measured by whether people are getting better: recovering, working, reconnecting and reclaiming their lives. HUD classified rapid rehousing as permanent housing even though its rental assistance is time-limited to 24 months. Move a family into rapid rehousing, and they disappear from the point-in-time count. Move that same family into transitional housing — which can also last up to 24 months — and they remain officially homeless. TAXPAYER-FUNDED 'METH MANSION' UNDER FIRE AS CRIME CONCERNS MOUNT AROUND HOMELESS CAMPUS Same potential 24-month horizon. Two radically different statistical outcomes. And the distinction mattered. As HUD steered communities away from transitional housing and toward rapid rehousing, HUD itself attributed declines in reported family homelessness in 2018 "largely" to that shift. FURIOUS RESIDENTS CONFRONT HOMELESS HOUSING LEADERS AS POPULAR BEACH COMMUNITY HITS BREAKING POINT Put the populations together and the picture changes dramatically: 1,456,923 Americans were either homeless or living in taxpayer-subsidized housing in 2025 — nearly twice the 745,652 captured by the headline point-in-time count. That is one of the flaws in defining success primarily through housing status: The statistic can improve the moment someone crosses into a program classified as permanent housing, long before we know whether that person has achieved lasting stability or self-sufficiency. Housing matters, but recovery, stability and self-sufficiency must be the finish line. Then there is the "chronic" definition gimmick. Under 12 years of Housing First rule, HUD has repeatedly changed how it defines and calculates chronic homelessness, making apples-to-apples comparisons across years increasingly difficult. Some changes temporarily altered who qualified as chronically homeless and therefore who appeared in federal statistics. But this year, this HUD administration did the calculation and reports chronic homelessness is 81% higher than it was in 2013. Perhaps the most consequential gimmick, however, involves homeless children and families. In 2011, HUD made the decision to apply a far narrower standard than the Congress-codified McKinney-Vento definition to identify homeless children and youth in our nation’s schools. The result is a stunning federal contradiction: a child can be officially homeless under federal law while at school, yet that same child and family is moved into the shadows under HUD’s narrow definition simply because, after losing their housing, they are sleeping on someone else’s couch or in a motel room the government is not funding. The definition disparity is staggering. And the distinction mattered. As HUD steered communities away from transitional housing and toward rapid rehousing, HUD itself attributed declines in reported family homelessness in 2018 "largely" to that shift. The Department of Education identified roughly 1.5 million homeless K–12 students in the 2023–24 school year, a number that includes only students. It does not count their parent(s), younger siblings not yet enrolled in school or other family members experiencing homelessness alongside them. Applying a conservative household adjustment suggests those students could represent more than 2.3 million Americans experiencing homelessness within families. The result is that most homeless families are excluded from HUD’s homelessness count, and those excluded families do not qualify for HUD-funded homelessness assistance. HUD simply defined them out of the system that was supposed to support them. Pushing them into the shadows will have consequences reverberate for generations. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Under the Trump administration, HUD now recognizes a basic truth: America cannot solve homelessness by narrowing definitions until millions disappear from the numbers — or by declaring success based simply on where someone sleeps. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The era of statistical gimmicks and lowered expectations must end. It is time to measure what matters: lives recovered, restored and returned to self-sufficiency. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM MICHELE STEEB

title: Trump’s Greenland bases could change Arctic defense. I learned why at 76 below zero
description: Trump's Greenland deal expands Arctic Ocean defense, but a veteran of 76-below-zero Alaska warns that cold-weather bases demand far more.
content: I spent four years as an Army infantry officer in Alaska, where our operational responsibilities stretched from Prudhoe Bay on the Arctic Ocean to the Aleutian Islands reaching toward Russia. During Exercise Brim Frost ’89, some 26,000 American and Canadian troops took the field, and I served as a brigade operations officer. As we maneuvered across Alaska’s interior, temperatures plunged as low as 76 degrees below zero. The exercise produced more than 250 cold-weather injuries, including 88 cases of frostbite. At those temperatures, fuel systems become unreliable, batteries lose power, lubricants thicken, and weapons and vehicles can fail in ways soldiers from warmer climates rarely encounter. And no, a week on the slopes at Vail does not prepare anyone for that. The Arctic punishes amateurs. TRUMP’S GREENLAND DEAL SET FOR SIGNING AFTER MONTHS-LONG FIGHT OVER US CONTROL That experience is why President Donald Trump’s Greenland announcement at the United Nations on Tuesday deserves attention beyond the political headlines. "We’ll be building two very major military bases," the president told the General Assembly. The agreement Trump signed with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen amends the 1951 defense pact. It allows the United States to modernize and expand the existing Pituffik Space Base in the northwest and to establish new defense areas at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the northeast. It also grants U.S. forces broad access by land, air and sea, including undersea access for American public vessels within Greenland’s territorial waters. TRUMP DECLARES VICTORY IN HISTORIC DEAL WITH GREENLAND AS HE SECURES 'PERMANENT' US MILITARY RIGHTS Announcing an Arctic base, however, is a long way from making one operational. Frederiksen said no decision has been made on the specifics of Golden Dome, and Washington has yet to say which forces will occupy the new sites or when. Forget the flat map and look at the globe from over the North Pole. Alaska, northern Canada and Greenland form the northern approaches to North America, and Greenland sits astride the routes connecting the Arctic Ocean, the North Atlantic and Europe. WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS The Pentagon’s 2024 Arctic Strategy calls the North American Arctic vital to homeland defense because it hosts NORAD’s aerospace and maritime warning. Greenland has been strategic terrain for generations. Narsarsuaq itself was an American air base, Bluie West One, until the United States closed it in 1958. At the height of the Cold War, Washington operated 17 military facilities with more than 10,000 troops on the island. Today only Pituffik remains, with about 150 service members. TRUMP’S MASSIVE GREENLAND DEAL MAKES CLEAR WHO CONTROLS THE ARCTIC’S STRATEGIC FUTURE Pituffik supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance. The new agreement recognizes American access to defend Greenland, the NATO area and the American continent, including through the Golden Dome, Trump’s planned missile-defense system. Add Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, and the United States could build a distributed Arctic network. Pituffik is already the northern sensor and space node. Narsarsuaq could strengthen access to Greenland’s southern approaches and the North Atlantic, while Mestersvig could extend American and allied reach toward the Greenland Sea. ARCTIC POWER PLAY GIVES TOP US ADVERSARY NEW OPENING WITH RUSSIA AS US STAKES GROW That geography matters most against Russia. The Pentagon’s 2024 Arctic Strategy calls the North American Arctic vital to homeland defense because it hosts NORAD’s aerospace and maritime warning. Russia fields the most developed military presence in the Arctic. Its Kola Peninsula hosts the Northern Fleet and important strategic nuclear forces. The Pentagon warns that Russian Arctic capabilities could place the American homeland and allied territory at risk and complicate U.S. power projection. SECURITY EXPERT HAILS TRUMP'S GREENLAND PACT AS A 'BIG DEAL' ON PAR WITH ALASKA PURCHASE Russia does not have to invade Greenland for Greenland to matter. Russian submarines, long-range aircraft and missiles make the island important because of where it sits. More American sites could improve warning, surveillance, reinforcement and resilience while reducing our dependence on a single installation. China presents a different problem. Beijing is not an Arctic nation, yet it has spent years seeking influence there. The Pentagon strategy documents Chinese icebreaker operations, dual-use research and growing military cooperation with Russia. CHINA ‘WIRETAPPED RED SEA’ WITH SPY HUB 6 MILES FROM US BASE: EX PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS Against China, the agreement’s most consequential provision may involve no runway at all. No non-NATO country may establish a manned or unmanned military installation or maintain a persistent military presence in Greenland without the parties’ agreement. The pact also bars non-allied control of, or significant influence over, critical infrastructure, resource extraction and other sensitive sectors. It has no expiration date, and it requires Denmark and Greenland to ensure that any future independent Greenland remains in NATO and assumes the pact’s defense obligations. "No U.S. adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland," Trump said. That closes one path to a Chinese foothold in the Arctic. TWO ICEBREAKERS HEADED TO ALASKA AS US COMBATS RUSSIAN, CHINESE INFLUENCE IN ARCTIC None of this changes the lesson I learned at 76 below zero. An Arctic base is a supply chain that has to survive January. And an Arctic force is more than troops flown north on short notice. The people operating those bases must know how to live, maintain equipment and perform their missions where routine mistakes quickly turn deadly. Fuel must arrive. Aircraft must fly. Vehicles must start. Communications must work. Soldiers must function outdoors without becoming cold-weather casualties. Spare parts must travel thousands of miles from America’s industrial base. The Army’s Arctic strategy says the service must "man, train, equip, and organize to win in the Arctic." The Pentagon calls for better communications above 65 degrees north, where satellite coverage thins. Pituffik and Mestersvig both sit well north of that line. Can two additional U.S. defense areas strengthen deterrence against Russia and China? They can, but concrete and runways alone deter no one. Deterrence exists when an adversary believes America and its allies can see what is coming, move forces, sustain them and respond effectively. Greenland strengthens each of those against Russia. Against China, denying military access and strategic investment may matter just as much. The agreement provides geography and access. The hard work is converting them into enduring capability. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Alaska taught me long ago that the Arctic has little patience for PowerPoint plans or optimistic assumptions. At 76 below zero, strategy meets reality fast. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The adversaries have changed since World War II and the Cold War. The geography has not. Neither has the Arctic’s unforgiving nature. title: Trump won't rule out more Iran strikes as Pezeshkian touts path back to nuclear talks

title: Houston Astros secure the most embarrassing kind of Major League Baseball history with AL West win
description: The Houston Astros clinched the AL West at 81-81, becoming the worst division-winning team in Major League Baseball history over a full season.
content: When Major League Baseball changed the schedule to ensure that the final day of the regular season featured all 15 games starting within a few minutes of each other, Sunday is what they envisioned. Mostly. While most postseason spots and seeds were decided either within the last week or the last few days, there were two races that came down to the final day of the year. The American League West race featured the Houston Astros and Texas Rangers entering the day tied at 80-81, remarkably, and the third wild card spot in the National League between the Philadelphia Phillies and Arizona Diamondbacks. The Phillies, who as recently as last week had a 99.1% chance of reaching the postseason, per FanGraphs, avoided a historic collapse and clinched a wild card series appearance with a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays. WITH ONE MONTH LEFT, AMERICAN LEAGUE TEAMS ARE HEADING TOWARDS AN EMBARRASSING, HISTORIC LOW But the Astros, even with a win, did in fact make an embarrassing type of history: they are officially the worst division-winning team in baseball history. The previous low-water mark was the 2005 San Diego Padres, who won the NL West with an 82-80 record. And while the Astros won 9-0 over the long-eliminated Athletics to avoid the 80-82 record, 81–81 marks a new low winning percentage for a division winner over a full season. While wins and losses are what decide the standings and outcomes, run differential has proven over time to be a significantly better predictor of future win and loss records than the previous standings. Essentially, the better you are at outscoring the opposition, the more likely it is that you'll win more games moving forward. One-run outcomes are not sustainable, but blowouts are illustrative of team quality. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Run differentials are also used to build "expected" records. Meaning that in the history of baseball, a specific run differential is expected to result in a given number of wins and losses. The Miami Marlins, for example, outscored the opposition by just three runs over the course of the season, which is an "expected" record of 81-81. Makes sense, they were even with the other teams in the league, they should finish at an even .500. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER By contrast, the Milwaukee Brewers finished with a league-best +214 run differential, good for an "expected" record of 103-59. They finished 103-59. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD But teams frequently over perform or underperform against their expected win-loss record, for any number of reasons. A bad bullpen could mean a team wins blowouts, but loses more than their fair share of close games. Bad luck. Poorly timed injuries. Poor defense. Inconsistent hitting with runners in scoring position. The randomness of baseball. Or a dominant closer who shuts the door consistently in close games. This year's 81-81 division winning Astros team was so bad they were outscored 32 runs over the course of the season, good for just an 78-84 expected win-loss record. While the Rangers and their fans are sure to be disappointed with the outcome, missing out on the final day, they were even worse. Texas had a -46 run differential, and a 76-86 expected record. These are not good baseball teams. So it's a near-certainty that Houston will make a quick postseason exit, right? Yeah, no, not at all. Houston plays the Chicago White Sox in the best-of-three wild card series, which the Astros now host as division winners. Chicago's a better team, but the randomness inherent in the small sample size of a playoff series makes the result effectively a toss up. In fact, FanGraphs gives the Astros a 55% chance of advancing to the ALDS. Should Houston win that series, they'd play the extremely mediocre Cleveland Guardians, who finished with a +11 run differential and 85-77 record. Cleveland may be slight favorites in that series, maybe 57-43, but hardly a foregone conclusion. Which means we could be staring down the barrel of an 81-81 team reaching the ALCS. MLB always hoped for last-minute drama by starting every game around the same time on the final day of the regular season. They got it. They also got the worst-ever division winning team because the league's financial incentives and playoff structure encourage owners to do the bare minimum and spend as little as possible to win 85 games and hope for the best. Or in Houston's case, 81. The Astros benefited, and fans were forced to watch the AL West "battle" lost.

title: Kathy Griffin says Ed Sheeran should have told Robert Kraft to 'go f--- yourself' over Macklemore
description: Kathy Griffin said Ed Sheeran should have told Robert Kraft to back off after Macklemore was barred from Gillette Stadium over his "Free Palestine" chants.
content: Comedian Kathy Griffin said on Wednesday that singer Ed Sheeran should have told Gillette Stadium owner and billionaire Robert Kraft to "go f--- yourself" after barring Macklemore from performing as his opening act over his "Free Palestine" stunt. In an interview with Queerty, Griffin commented on Macklemore being pulled from the rest of Sheeran's tour earlier this month after he repeatedly pushed for a "Free Palestine" during his act and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind's Hall." The decision came after Kraft barred Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium. Though Sheeran has said that the decision ultimately came from the concert promoter and venues rather than him, Griffin argued that Sheeran could have, and should have, defended Macklemore at the time. MACKLEMORE'S LONG HISTORY OF CONTROVERSY FROM GRAMMY WINS TO 'FREE PALESTINE' CONCERT REMARKS "I wish that Ed Sheeran had not taken the advice of the ones who told him to fire Macklemore," Griffin said. When Robert Kraft says I’ve called all the other stadium owners, and they’re not gonna let you do the show with Macklemore either, Ed Sheeran should’ve said go f--- yourself, I can go to Brazil and perform for 250,000 people. He had more options." Griffin added that Macklemore's comments were protected under the First Amendment and professed her own support for a "Free Palestine." "I don't think 'Free Palestine' is such a controversial thing to say, because that's a genuine genocide that is happening there, in my opinion. I don't want Israel to be eradicated. I love the Israeli people as I hope the rest of the world likes the American people but hates [President Donald] Trump and his cabinet and our current SCOTUS. So I can't stand [Israeli Prime Minister] Bibi Netanyahu. I think he's ruined the Knesset which is their Congress. But I certainly don't have a beef with the Jewish people or the Palestinian people. They're both trying to survive. I personally think that Palestine should be its own country," Griffin said. title: Team USA captain thanks Trump after massive Presidents Cup comeback: ‘He gets all the credit’
description: Trump told captain Brandt Snedeker he'd bring energy to the Presidents Cup, and the U.S. rallied from a three-point deficit in Sunday singles.
content: U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker credited President Donald Trump after the Americans rallied for a 17-13 victory over the International team at the Presidents Cup on Sunday. "One last shoutout: Donald Trump. President Trump. He told me, 'I [am] going to bring energy today for you. You guys need it,'" Snedeker said. "I told him if we did this, he gets all the credit. So, thank you, President Trump." With Trump in attendance, the United States team found itself in uncharted territory heading into Sunday singles at Medinah Country Club. For the first time in the event's history, Team USA trailed on home soil entering the final session. TEAM USA GOLFERS WELCOME TRUMP’S EXPECTED PRESIDENTS CUP VISIT, SHARE PRIDE IN REPRESENTING AMERICA Trump, the event's honorary chairman, briefly addressed the crowd from the first tee before play began. "You know, the fake news media will say I get a very bad reception," Trump said as the crowd laughed. "But we get a good reception." "[PGA Tour CEO] Brian [Rolapp] said, 'Could you make a short speech?' I said, 'No, I don't have the courage to make a speech. These people wanna see golf. They don't wanna hear speeches.' I'll only say this: Our country is doing great, better than ever before." The Americans entered the week having won all eight Presidents Cups played on home soil and 10 straight overall. But Team USA was also coming off a 15-13 loss to Europe at last year's Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black. The last thing American golf needed was another visiting team celebrating a victory on U.S. soil. Instead, the Americans erased a 10½-7½ deficit by winning nine of the 12 singles matches and outscoring the Internationals 9½-2½. Presidents Cup rookie Jacob Bridgeman delivered the winning point with a par putt on the 18th green. USA sent an early message on Sunday Snedeker sent out some of his best players in the first few matches, hoping to swing the event and put pressure on the Internationals. Cameron Young led off, with Justin Thomas and Scottie Scheffler going out third and fourth. The plan worked. Young did his job as the leadoff man, despite falling 2 down to Ryo Hisatsune after four holes. He won five of the next 12 holes to close out a 3&2 victory. Match play specialist Justin Thomas, who entered Sunday with a 20-10-5 career record in Ryder Cups and Presidents Cups, won five of the first six holes against Corey Conners before coasting to a 5&3 win. Nico Echavarria gave Scheffler a little more trouble than many might have expected, but the world's No. 1 player ultimately closed out the 32-year-old Colombian, 2&1. However, the International team wasn't going down easily. Tom Kim capped an incredible week by beating world No. 5 Wyndham Clark, finishing as the tournament's leading scorer with four points. Sungjae Im also took down world No. 8 Sam Burns. Chris Gotterup was a major bright spot for the Americans all tournament. The 27-year-old Presidents Cup rookie defeated Christiaan Bezuidenhout 1 up and finished 3-1 for the week. He made a strong case for a spot on the 2027 Ryder Cup team in the process. US PRESIDENTS CUP PLAYERS EXPLAIN HOW CHRISTIAN FAITH BUILDS FRIENDSHIPS AND PUTS GOLF IN PERSPECTIVE Arguably the best match of the day featured Collin Morikawa and Japan's Hideki Matsuyama. Matsuyama jumped out to a 2-up lead through six holes, but Morikawa battled back and took the lead by winning the 10th. Matsuyama won two straight holes to move back in front, only for Morikawa to square the match again at 15. The pair tied 16 and 17, sending them to the 18th all square. On 18, Matsuyama drove into the rough and could only advance his second shot short of the green. His pitch ran 15 feet past the hole, while Morikawa cozied a long birdie putt to within 2½ feet. Matsuyama missed his par putt, giving Morikawa a 1-up win and the Americans a much-needed full point. Cantlay makes a major statement Patrick Cantlay delivered one of the afternoon's biggest moments in his match against Adam Scott, burying a 57-foot birdie putt from just off the 16th green. The usually reserved Cantlay pumped his fist hard and yelled, "YES! YES!" to the crowd, which was going wild, sensing the gravity of the moment. Cantlay closed out Scott on 17, 2&1. His victory and Morikawa's came moments apart, putting the U.S. ahead 13½-12½ with four matches still on the course. With Xander Schauffele holding a commanding lead, the Americans looked set for another point. That put the pressure on rookies Jackson Koivun and Bridgeman, along with the steady veteran Russell Henley, to finish the comeback. Koivun, a 21-year-old Presidents Cup rookie, was 2 down at the turn against Si Woo Kim, who entered Sunday tied for the tournament lead with three points. But Koivun completely flipped the match on the back nine, winning holes 11, 12, 13 and 15. Koivun took a 1-up lead to 18, where Kim hit his approach to 15 feet. But the rookie wasn't intimidated. After driving it down the middle of the fairway, the Auburn product stuck his approach to eight feet. Kim lipped out his birdie putt, and Koivun secured another crucial point to push the U.S. total to 14½. CANADIANS NICK TAYLOR AND COREY CONNERS LAUGH OFF LAKE ONTARIO RENAMING AHEAD OF PRESIDENTS CUP Bridgeman delivered another clutch moment from an American rookie, burying an eight-foot par putt on 16. Min Woo Lee missed his four-footer for par, squaring their match with two holes to play. With Schauffele guaranteed at least a half-point, the Americans could do no worse than a tie and needed just another half-point beyond that to win the Cup outright. Schauffele had been 4 up with four holes to play, but lost 15 and 16, keeping the Americans waiting a little longer. Apparently, the afternoon hadn't been dramatic enough. Schauffele's delay left the honor to Bridgeman. Fittingly, the rookie delivered, sinking his par putt on 18 to beat Lee 1 up and give the Americans the 15½ points they needed. A "U-S-A!" chant broke out from the crowd as Bridgeman's putt dropped, and the Americans celebrated on the 18th green. Schauffele eventually closed out Ryan Fox, 2&1, while Henley halved his match with Nick Taylor to complete the 17-13 victory. The win was the Americans' 11th straight in the Presidents Cup and ninth in nine tries at home, improving their overall record to 14-1-1. USA still has work to do before the Ryder Cup Of course, the Americans never should have put themselves in this position. Eight U.S. players entered the week ranked higher than Si Woo Kim, the International team's highest-ranked player at No. 14. Seven Americans were inside the world's top 10. The visitors didn't have one. At home, against that roster, this should have been a blowout. It certainly shouldn't have required a three-point comeback on Sunday. Instead, the International team swept Friday's foursomes 5-0, just as it did at Royal Montreal in 2024. That turned a 3-2 U.S. lead after Thursday into a 7-3 deficit heading into Saturday. Saturday offered opportunities to regain control. The Americans led all four matches at one point in each of the day's two sessions, but finished with just a 4½-3½ edge. That still left them down three entering Sunday. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Clark finished 1-4 for the week, while Henley went winless in three matches, earning just a half-point. That followed last year's embarrassing Ryder Cup loss at Bethpage Black. And the next Ryder Cup sends Team USA to Adare Manor in Ireland in 2027, tasked with doing something the Americans haven't done since 1993: winning on European soil. Sunday singles should give the Americans some confidence heading to Ireland. They won that session 7½-4½ at the 2024 Presidents Cup and 8½-3½ at last year's Ryder Cup before hammering the Internationals 9½-2½ at Medinah. But Bethpage already showed that even a great Sunday might not be enough. title: Police hunt sexually violent predator who vanished after GPS 'tamper mode' alert
description: Merle Wakefield had been on conditional release since November 2024 with GPS monitoring. Now, the convicted sex offender is missing in San Diego County.
content: A convicted child sex offender was still missing Sunday, two days after his GPS monitor sounded a tamper alert at a San Diego worksite and supervisors arrived to find him gone, authorities said. Merle Wakefield, 69, was working in Rancho Bernardo when his device alerted to "Tamper Mode" at about 3:30 a.m. Friday, according to the San Diego County Sheriff’s Office. Liberty Healthcare, the state contractor supervising him, responded to the location and found the device removed and Wakefield gone. The company notified the sheriff’s office and San Diego police. ACCUSED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT MURDERER WHO FLED US DURING 48-HOUR PASS HAD ACCESS TO TAXPAYER-FUNDED APARTMENT The sheriff’s office said Sunday it "shares the community’s concerns over Merle Wakefield’s disappearance" and was still actively looking for him. "We have been working diligently to locate him," the agency said. It asked the public to report any sightings or information that could help find Wakefield. CALIFORNIA DEMS TRIGGER OUTRAGE AFTER SIDING WITH CONVICTED CHILD SEX OFFENDERS IN SHOCKING VOTE "It’s been more than 48 hours since Merle Wakefield took off his GPS monitor and walked away. He’s still out there," San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond wrote Sunday on Facebook. He called Wakefield "a convicted child molester and violent rapist" and accused the state of saying nothing publicly about his disappearance. Wakefield is wanted for violating the terms of his conditional release, the sheriff’s office said. He was convicted in 1980 and 1991 of lewd or lascivious acts with a child under 14 and rape by force, according to the agency. He has been on conditional release since November 2024. MACHETE-WIELDING MS-13 GANGSTER WANTED FOR MURDER WALKS FREE AFTER BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE RELEASES HIM: DHS Desmond said Wakefield was gone by the time Liberty Healthcare arrived after the GPS alert. "That’s how easy it was," he wrote in an earlier post. "The state released him into our community in November 2024 and promised he’d be monitored and supervised. Less than two years later, he’s missing and wanted." DHS UNLOADS ON 'SANCTUARY CALAMITY' VIRGINIA AFTER ILLEGAL ALIEN ACCUSED OF HEINOUS CRIME RELEASED: 'SICKO' Local officials had warned about Wakefield’s release before it happened. A San Diego judge granted him a transient release in October 2024 rather than placing him in a designated home, Fox 5/KUSI reported at the time. It was the third attempt to place him in San Diego County. An earlier proposal would have placed Wakefield in a Poway home near a school and park, prompting residents to rally against it, according to the outlet. Poway Mayor Steve Vaus opposed that location and argued that allowing Wakefield to live without a fixed address would make it harder for the public to know where he was. BIDEN ADMIN'S 'PREDATOR' RELEASE PUTS VIRGINIA'S SANCTUARY POLICIES BACK IN THE SPOTLIGHT "It’s a shell game that puts a community at risk," Vaus told Fox 5/KUSI about the transient release. The San Diego County District Attorney’s Office also opposed releasing Wakefield without a fixed residence, citing concerns about limited monitoring and supervision. Spokesperson Tanya Sierra told the outlet that the Department of State Hospitals and Liberty Healthcare needed to find suitable housing where people granted conditional release could be closely monitored. SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS State Sen. Brian Jones raised his own concerns about where Wakefield would stay. He told Fox 5/KUSI that Wakefield might end up on the streets or in a hotel at taxpayer expense. "Supposedly, he’s going to have a tracking device," Jones said at the time. NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN Jones had also called for an audit of California’s sexually violent predator program, the outlet reported. The audit found that about 36% of participants had violated the terms of their release. Jones criticized the program’s cost and argued that the state should keep sexually violent predators in hospitals rather than place them in communities. The California Department of State Hospitals pushed back on criticism of the release process, telling Fox 5/KUSI that the court ultimately decides whether someone designated a sexually violent predator can be conditionally released. SEXUAL PREDATOR ‘COOKIE MONSTER’ CAUGHT IN TERRIFIED CHILD’S BED DURING MIDNIGHT BREAK-IN, POLICE SAY The department said its supervision program used GPS monitoring, unannounced home visits and surveillance, and that breaking the rules could send someone back to a state hospital. The outlet also reported that Wakefield’s court order called for 24-hour in-person supervision wherever he stayed. That report was published before the hearing to finalize his release. Desmond renewed his objection after Wakefield disappeared. "I’ve fought these placements from day one," he wrote. "These people do not belong back out in the community. title: Deshaun Watson goes from Cleveland villain to hero in Browns upset win, as home crowd turns jeers to cheers

title: Florida Gators, Mississippi State soar, USC tumbles in latest inexplicable AP Top 25 Poll

content: One of college football's greatest traditions got another entry on Sunday, as the week four edition of the AP Top 25 Poll was released to mostly bemused reactions from confused fans. And if there was any doubt that the SEC continues to enjoy some, uh, questionable, benefits based on preseason polling and perceived strength, this week's voting should put that to rest. Unsurprisingly, one of the biggest gainers of the week was the Florida Gators, coming off an impressive 52-28 win over the Ole Miss Rebels. Florida racked up over 300 yards on the ground, forced two turnovers, and kept the ball away from Trinidad Chambliss and the powerful Ole Miss offense. The Mississippi State Bulldogs, who held on to beat Missouri and moved up eight spots to No. 16. But speaking of Missouri, they exemplify the problem that the preseason poll and voters' pre-conceived biases have with these rankings. The Tigers entered the season as the No. 25 team in the preseason poll and proceeded to do literally nothing of importance in the first three weeks. title: 'Home Improvement' star says Patricia Richardson got 'tired' of fighting for sitcom
description: Taran Noah Smith reveals Patricia Richardson fought to keep "Home Improvement" realistic as new writers pushed scripts in a different direction.
content: "Home Improvement" star Taran Noah Smith is shedding new light on why the hit 1990s sitcom came to an end. The 42-year-old former actor was seven-years-old when he landed the role of Mark Taylor, the youngest son of Tim "The Tool Man" Taylor (Tim Allen) and his wife Jill Taylor (Patricia Richardson) in 1991. The sitcom, which was based on Allen's stand-up comedy persona, centered on Tim, a television host known for his home improvement show, "Tool Time," and his family life with Jill, Mark and older sons Brad (Zachery Ty Bryan) and Randy (Jonathan Taylor Thomas). 'HOME IMPROVEMENT' STAR JONATHAN TAYLOR THOMAS ARRESTED FOR ALLEGED PUBLIC INTOXICATION, RESISTING DEPUTY "Home Improvement" became one of the highest-rated shows of the '90s and ran for eight seasons and aired 204 episodes. However, the show concluded in 1999 after Richardson declined to return for a proposed ninth season. During a recent appearance on Tom Scharpling and Julia Vickerman's podcast "Outgrown" podcast, Smith reflected on his time starring on the show and weighed in on the reasons behind Richardson's departure. TIM ALLEN SAYS HE 'NEVER REALLY WANTED' TO BE A DAD AND OPENS UP ABOUT SOBRIETY AND FATHERHOOD REGRETS Smith recalled that Richardson joined the cast as Jill just days before the pilot was taped after producers replaced Frances Fisher, the actress originally cast as Tim's wife, during rehearsals. "When they brought Patricia in, there was just a much better chemistry," he said. "And she had her own kid. She had just given birth to twins, and she had one older kid who was about my age. She really brought a lot more of a realistic mom energy to her, and she fought throughout the whole show to keep the show more realistic." "She would tell the writers, ‘A mother would never say this,’ and get them to change it," he added. Smith said he "definitely" agreed with Richardson's input though he acknowledged that he and the show's other child stars weren't really involved in conversations about the script. "They'd do a run-through of the script on Monday and then the kids would go to school usually, and they would continue to discuss the script," he said. Smith recalled that there were creative disagreements on set after a new creative team replaced the show's original writers and producers. ROSEANNE BARR HASN’T SPOKEN TO TV SISTER LAURIE METCALF SINCE SHOW’S CANCELLATION "The original creators only did the first couple seasons, and then they moved on, and they brought in a whole other group of writer/producers," he remembered. "Those guys, very few of them had kids, and the show kind of started to go in a different direction, at least the scripts we'd get on Monday." "It was really Pat, the mom, who fought the good fight to make it more realistic because oftentimes it would just be something that was very out of character just to sell a joke, just to set up a joke," he continued. "It's like, ‘Wait, this is not what the characters are about.’" ROSEANNE BARR CALLS FORMER CO-STAR A 'BRAINWASHED BIGOT' AFTER HE SAID REBOOT WAS 'RIGHTFULLY CANCELED' Smith speculated that Allen was reluctant to appear overly controlling after witnessing what happened on another sitcom, "Roseanne." "Roseanne," which became an instant hit after it premiered in 1988, was created by "Home Improvement" co-creator Matt Williams. Like "Home Improvement," Roseanne was built around its star's stand-up comedy voice and persona. However, Barr clashed behind-the-scenes with producers and writers, including Williams, over the direction and tone of the show. The tensions between the two led to Williams leaving after the first season. Barr later gained more influence and was credited as a creator in later seasons. ‘THE OFFICE’ STAR JENNA FISCHER EXPOSES THE GRUELING REALITY THAT FORCED HER OFF TV "I think Tim was overall maybe a bit worried about being a tyrant because the same creators created ‘Roseanne,’ and Roseanne took over the show and fired the creators, fired everybody," Smith recalled. "Actually, all our camera crew had been fired in one day from ‘Roseanne’ and came over to us. So, Tim was always, I think, more hands-off with that, not wanting to be tyrannical, which meant that it was a lot more on Pat to push." "That's one of the reasons why the show ended up eventually ending, because she was just tired of it, of having to fight to make it realistic all the time," he continued. JODIE SWEETIN SHARES SHOCKING 'FULL HOUSE' RESIDUAL CHECK AMOUNT DESPITE SHOW'S MEGA SUCCESS "And Tim was getting far more money than she was," Smith added. "That was her actual way of stopping. She said she'd do a ninth season if she got paid the same amount as Tim, knowing they wouldn't do it." Smith's recollection of why Richardson left "Home Improvement" echoes what the actress has said for years about her experience on the show and the reasons for her departure. During a May 2024 interview with the Los Angeles Times, Richardson recalled that the creators emphasized the importance of the character of Jill and her relationship with Tim. "When I took the job, they said it wasn’t meant to be the Tim Allen show. It was meant to be our show," she said. "I’ve always said, I don’t want to play the thankless wife." Richardson recalled having creative disagreements with male writers over how Jill would react to specific situations, remembering one instance in which she was told, "Pat, it’s not like we don’t understand women. We’re married to them." The actress, who earned four Primetime Emmy Award nominations for her performance as Jill, told the LA Times that she made the decision to leave the show. Richardson told the LA Times she decided during the eighth season that it would be her last, citing a desire to spend more time with her children after her divorce and her belief that the sitcom had run its course, pointing to Jonathan Taylor Thomas' departure and declining ratings. "I told everybody, there’s not enough money in the world to get me to do a ninth year. This show is over. It needs to end," Richardson recalled. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? She said the network's parent company, Disney, proposed paying her a salary of $1 million an episode, while Allen would be paid $2 million an episode. title: Susie Wiles reveals brutal toll of fighting cancer while running Trump’s White House
description: Susie Wiles reveals what it was like to undergo chemotherapy while leading the White House staff, saying some days just getting out of bed was a test.
content: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is opening up about the grueling reality of fighting breast cancer while holding one of Washington's most demanding jobs, revealing that some days simply getting out of bed and going to work took all the strength she had. In an op-ed published Sunday in USA Today, Wiles described what it was like to undergo chemotherapy while continuing to lead the White House staff for President Donald Trump. The disease occupied her thoughts from the moment she woke up and sometimes even while she slept, she wrote. "Fighting cancer is brutal and unrelenting," Wiles wrote. Questions about treatment, test results and what might come next could overtake even a strong mind. At times, she acknowledged, they overtook hers. CANCER-RELATED BRAIN FOG MAY IMPROVE WITH 2 SIMPLE TREATMENTS, SCIENTISTS SAY Some days, Wiles said, she poured her strength into fighting the disease. On others, getting out of bed, getting dressed and going to work was its own test. "Most days, I carried the full weight of both," she wrote. Work gave her a purpose beyond appointments, scans and side effects. "Cancer can make your world very small," Wiles wrote. She said she pushed herself to stay focused on the people who depended on her, even as she knew others might question whether she could still lead effectively. KAI TRUMP REVEALS HOW FAMILY RALLIED AROUND MOM VANESSA AMID BREAST CANCER BATTLE: ‘IT’S A LONG JOURNEY’ The treatment did take a toll on her stamina, mobility and, at times, her focus. Wiles said she could not always be everywhere she wanted to be. Colleagues inside and outside the White House stepped in, while her two daughters, extended family, friends and medical team helped carry her through the illness. Wiles made clear that working through treatment would not be right or possible for everyone. For her, she wrote, the job helped her hold on to a sense of who she was beyond the disease. CANCER SURVIVORS MAY SEE SURPRISING BENEFITS FROM ONE SPECIFIC EXERCISE, STUDY SAYS After successful surgery, pathology showed no residual cancer, Wiles wrote. She said she now faces the work of rebuilding what treatment took from her. "Chemotherapy is, in a word, a b----," she wrote. DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES In a post on X Sunday, Wiles said she rarely writes about herself but wanted to share what it was like to fight cancer while continuing to do a job she loves. "Cancer tried to make my world smaller. I was determined not to let it," she wrote, adding that she hoped her account could offer strength to someone still fighting the disease. VANESSA TRUMP REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN EMOTIONAL STATEMENT: 'I AM STAYING FOCUSED AND HOPEFUL' Wiles announced Sept. 16 that she was cancer free after receiving clear pathology results following an appointment at the Mayo Clinic. She had disclosed her early-stage breast cancer diagnosis in March. Trump praised Wiles during her treatment, saying in a prerecorded May tribute that she was winning her cancer battle. Wiles thanked him for his kindness and compassion, and credited her family, friends, colleagues and doctors with helping her through the ordeal. For others going through treatment, Wiles offered a message of hope. "Cancer does not have to take away who you are," she wrote. She said that for her, life beyond the disease includes serving Trump and the country and being a mother, grandmother and friend. "A strong woman isn’t loud in her strength; she’s steady and unshakable," she wrote. "You are our champion. So incredibly proud of you, Mom."

title: Florida Gators may or may not be ‘back,’ but one thing is certain, football is finally fun in The Swamp again
description: Jon Sumrall's Florida Gators crushed No. 4 Ole Miss and surged to 8th in the AP Poll, but the new coach says the beast hasn't fully awakened yet.
content: December 5, 2009. I remember it like it was yesterday. It was the date of the SEC Championship, the supposed "Game of the Century" in college football. Florida vs. Alabama. Number one against number two. A rematch of last season's thriller between the two teams and a matchup thought to be a "de facto" national championship game. FLORIDA GATORS, OLE MISS REBELS FIND THEMSELVES IN GOOD OLD FASHIONED 'RESPECT OFF' AHEAD OF SATURDAY'S GAME It was also the night the Gators' budding dynasty came crumbling down before our very eyes. Oh sure, Florida would go on to eviscerate Cincinnati in the Sugar Bowl less than a month later, and they even managed to cobble together a few impressive seasons in the years since. JAMES MADISON COACH BILLY NAPIER CONTINUES SELF PITY TOUR, REFUSES TO TAKE ACCOUNTABILITY FOR PAST FAILURES But as far as being the nationally relevant powerhouse they had become under head coaches Steve Spurrier and Urban Meyer in the 90s and 2000s, those days were long gone. The Gators would stumble their way through myriad coaching searches, hiring flawed candidate after flawed candidate. If Florida landed a defensive wizard (Will Muschamp), the offense would suffer under his watch. Conversely, if the Gators nabbed an offensive guru (Dan Mullen), the defense would inevitably fail to live up to their end of the bargain. FLORIDA GATORS COACH JON SUMRALL SAYS HE WOULDN'T HAVE LEFT TULANE IF HE WASN'T ALLOWED TO COACH PLAYOFF TEAM And if they happened to get a guy who was a relentless recruiter (Billy Napier), neither side of the ball would look up to snuff. Big wins were short-lived, usually followed by a cataclysmic event that would tank any shot at a successful season after the fact. In 2015, the Gators welcomed a top-three Ole Miss team to The Swamp in an eerily similar scenario to Saturday's game, and handled them from the opening whistle. Just weeks later, rising second-year signal caller Will Grier would be suspended for testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs, and the Jim McElwain era was never able to replicate the magic of those first six games. COLLEGE FOOTBALL WEEK 4 CONTENDERS, PRETENDERS: TEXAS SURVIVES, MICHIGAN'S KARMA AND COACHES ARE SWEATING Five years later, during the fog of the COVID-19-shortened season of 2020, Florida had a legitimate championship-level offense under head coach Dan Mullen's tutelage, and even with a porous defense, were able to knock Georgia off its perch and take the inside track to the SEC Championship Game. A month after their win over their fiercest rival, the Gators lost as a three-touchdown favorite at home to LSU thanks to the now infamous "shoe toss" from defensive back Marco Wilson. HOW A PODCAST COMMUNITY HELPED RESTORE THE CONTROVERSIAL 'GATOR BAIT' CHANT FOR FLORIDA FOOTBALL TEAM Mullen was relieved of his duties as head coach less than a year afterwards. My point is that any time the Gators seemed to gain a foothold in the "we're back" conversation, something would jump up and drag them back to reality. I'm not sure if Saturday's domination over number four Ole Miss means the Gators are "back," but for the first time in a very long time, the picture is looking clearer than ever. The offense looks as dangerous as it did six years ago, when that aforementioned 2020 team ran roughshod over a 10-game SEC schedule thanks to the aerial assault provided by Kyle Trask, Kyle Pitts and Kadarius Toney, among others. And the crazy thing is, this year's offense might be deeper and even more balanced. Consider the fact that Florida had Eric Singleton Jr., Vernell Brown III and Bailey Stockton, three of their top four wideouts, all hobbled for large portions of the game, and still put up 52 points and nearly 500 yards of total offense against a top-five SEC team. That 2020 offense was lethal, but they couldn't run the ball as effectively and certainly didn't have a tailback of Jadan Baugh's magnitude. The defense was the Achilles heel of that COVID-19-year team, and while this year's unit doesn't look elite, they certainly play a more cohesive brand than their predecessors did in 2020. Florida fans (myself included) begged on their hands and knees for Lane Kiffin to come to Gainesville. Ultimately, that didn't work out, and when it was announced that Jon Sumrall was the hire, Gator Nation revolted. For 24 hours, that is. After hearing the man speak and seeing the plan he had in place for the orange and blue, many of the Florida faithful started to have hope. It's early on in the process, but Sumrall and his staff have already started to show proof of concept, winning a road SEC game and then clobbering one of the best teams in the country in back-to-back weeks. I can't say for certain if Jon Sumrall will ever win anything of significance while coaching the Florida Gators. This season is only four games old, and it's year one of his tenure. But with the way things are trending, both on and off the field, it's safe to say football is, at the very least, fun again in The Swamp. I try to be as objective as possible in my writing, but you can read it for yourself in my bio: I'm an unabashed Florida fan. This was an article 17 years in the making, and I want to reiterate that the job is far from finished. The Gators moved all the way up to 8th in the AP Poll on Sunday, their highest position in any poll since the end of the 2020 regular season. No one is going to hang a banner about where you are ranked in week five, and there are plenty more tests still on the schedule. This feels different, though. Will the Gators win an SEC Championship or national title in 2026? Not likely, but I see the vision from Sumrall and trust this is a sustainable approach to building a consistent winner. Florida labored in finding an explosive offense outside of a few years with Mullen, so Sumrall went out and hired the best offensive coordinator in the country in Buster Faulkner. Offensive line play has been downright putrid for large swathes of the last decade and a half, so Sumrall brought offensive line coach and UF alum Phil Trautwein, widely considered the best O-line teacher and recruiter in college football, back to Gainesville. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The man gets it. Sumrall said in his postgame press conference that the beast hasn't been fully awakened yet, a nod to his comments from his introductory press conference back in December, but he acknowledged that they are getting there. And if what I'm hearing from those close to the program is true about the recruits in attendance, the beast might be waking up sooner rather than later. Saying the Gators are "back" feels a bit premature and might be an oversimplification of things, but the fact that they are even in the conversation means things are trending in the right direction. title: Bill Gates warns artificial intelligence 'powerful enough' to cause 'a billion deaths' if unchecked
description: Bill Gates warned on NBC's "Meet the Press" that AI could drive events causing a billion deaths, calling it irresponsible not to require more safeguards.
content: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could cause "a billion deaths" if left unchecked in the latest push to regulate AI on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday. During his interview, Gates, who previously warned that AI could be the "greatest equalizer" or "worst source of injustice" without some level of human regulation, stopped short of answering whether the technology could "end all of humanity" but argued that it could drive events that would lead to significant deaths. "AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths," Gates said. "You know, so even though it’s pretty hard to get to 100%, there’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools." AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST Gates is among several tech giants who have put forth warnings about AI, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Despite this, President Donald Trump has rejected calls to ease back on AI development in an effort to compete with other global powers like China. Gates disagreed, saying there "absolutely" needed to be more focus on regulation and legislation passed by Congress rather than concerns about global competition. WATCH: AI SAFETY SCARE SPARKS CAP HILL FIGHT OVER GUARDRAILS: 'CHINA'S GOING TO EAT OUR LUNCH' "The problem is that the rest of the world is either discounting this or just thinking of this as a competition. And it’s very scary that we don’t have all of the thinkers saying, 'How do we want to shape this?'" Gates said. When host Kristen Welker compared the situation to limitations around nuclear weapons development between the U.S. and U.S.S.R. during the Cold War, Gates called AI "more difficult," particularly if there is less effort to work with allies. "And, you know, because it’s cast in this nationalistic, you know, us versus them type thing, you have people who are saying, 'Well, let’s just go full-speed ahead.' It’s completely irresponsible not to require every AI to have these safeguards and monitoring capabilities. And it only is a question of do you do it now?" Gates said. Fox News Digital reached out to the Gates Foundation for comment. RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS Though Trump has downplayed concerns over AI, some Republicans have called for the government to take action, including Republican National Committee member and Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer. "Even Bill Gates, one of the most influential figures in the history of technology, is now admitting the dangers of artificial intelligence. He warns that AI could drive events causing a billion deaths and that people with ill intent have never held a more powerful weapon. At this point, the only people still denying the reality of the situation are those being paid by Big AI to gaslight the American people," Kremer told Fox News Digital. However, Laffer Tengler Investments CEO Nancy Tengler called out Gates' comments, claiming that he was belittling his critics with no clear evidence. "To say that 'there's never been a weapon as powerful' is an absolute statement rich in irony as the [Trump] Administration seeks to keep nuclear weapons out of the hands of the Iranian regime. The U.S. needs to win the AI race just as we sought to win the arms race during the Cold War," Tengler told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In another comment, Julia Cartwright, senior research fellow in law and economics at the American Institute for Economic Research, also offered Fox News Digital a more optimistic view on AI development. "Economically, what Gates is describing is a catastrophic negative externality. AI is sharply lowering the cost of causing harm, whether that's bioweapons design, cyberattacks or large-scale fraud, while the companies building these tools don't bear the full cost when things go wrong," Cartwright said. She added, "A way to combat this is clear liability and clear rules of the game, so developers internalize the risks they create. Done right, that doesn't slow American innovation it strengthens it, because firms can build and invest with confidence when they know what's expected of them, and the public can trust what they're building."

title: Pope Leo visits site of miracle cures, meets people whose unexplained healings stunned doctors

content: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lourdes from Paris on Saturday evening for his first-ever visit to the renowned place of miracle cures. I spoke with Dr. Alessandro de Franciscis, who recently retired as president of the Lourdes Office of Medical Observation after 17 years of reviewing treatments and possible miracle cures. He discussed his upcoming meeting with the pope, who he said was visiting Lourdes in the name of purification and healing, including healing from the Church's recent sexual abuse scandals. "These so-called spiritual cures are so, so much more numerous than the physical ones that we know." title: Supersonic Russian jets trigger joint scramble by NATO allies amid Putin 'clowns' jab
description: Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish Gripens scrambled jointly for the first time to intercept supersonic Russian military jets over the Gulf of Finland.
content: Finnish and Swedish fighter jets scrambled for the first time on Sept. 24 to intercept supersonic Russian military aircraft flying over the Gulf of Finland, marking a major milestone in Nordic defense cooperation amid heightened tensions with Moscow. The mission also came one day before Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed European warnings about the threat from Moscow in the region and mocked Estonia's new defense minister over the Baltic state's preparations for a potential Russian attack. Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish JAS 39 Gripens were scrambled after Russian aircraft were detected in the international airspace, according to the Swedish Armed Forces. US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS The Russian formation included a Tu-134 transport plane, a high-altitude, supersonic MiG-31 interceptors designed to detect and engage long-range threats; and Su-30 multirole fighter jets which are designed for air-to-air and air-to-ground combat. "This is what close cooperation looks like in practice," Maj. Gen. Jonas Wikman, commander of the Swedish Air Force, said in a statement following the joint operation. "Built over years on trust and strong personal relationships, we can now operate seamlessly together — as air forces, as nations and as Allies." Concern over Russian military activity along NATO’s eastern flank has grown following a string of airspace violations. These include Russian drones entering Polish airspace, a Mi-8 helicopter crossing from Kaliningrad into Poland, drones crashing in Romania and Moldova, and armed Russian jets entering Estonian airspace before being intercepted by NATO aircraft on Sept. 18. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT In Estonia, Defense Minister Martin Herem warned that Russia could be capable of using military force against Estonia within a year and argued that Tallinn must determine whether its defenses are sufficient for such a scenario. Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that the government is ready to shut down border crossing points on short notice if threat assessments change, according to reports. Speaking at the St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum on Friday, Putin pushed back against such warnings. "Many people in Europe say they expect an attack from Russia and therefore claim they must prepare for war with Russia," Putin said. "I want to emphasize once again: we are not preparing for military action against Europe. We have no such plans, no basis for them, and, most importantly, no real motive to escalate the situation with Europe." Putin then mocked Herem's warnings: "As we jokingly say in Russia: 'The circus has left, but the clowns remain.' It is political clowning. ... Clearly, these statements are complete nonsense and absurdity," Putin said, according to EurAsia Daily. FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE Estonia sits across the Gulf of Finland from Finland, with the three countries forming part of NATO's increasingly integrated northern and eastern defenses amid concerns about Russian military activity. Finland formally joined NATO as its 31st member in April 2023, roughly doubling the alliance's land border with Russia. Sweden followed as the 32nd member in March 2024. Estonia, which regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, has been a NATO member since 2004. The Baltic Sea region has also remained on heightened alert following incidents involving gas pipelines, sabotage and hybrid threats since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters has reported. NATO said in June that it was enhancing protection of its eastern members in the cyber and space domains while helping countries build resilience against what it describes as hostile Russian actions, including cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace violations. NATO says its military activities along the eastern flank are entirely defensive and that it is "ready, willing and able to defend every Ally." FINLAND'S STUBB CREDITS TRUMP FOR PUSHING UKRAINE PEACE TALKS WHILE DISMISSING RUSSIAN INVASION FEARS The alliance has said an attack against any member would be met with a "resounding response." NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently underscored Washington's role in the alliance during a visit to Iowa, telling The Associated Press that Putin "knows that the United States and Europe are totally intertwined." "We have to make sure that we are prepared, we are strong, and he knows it," Rutte said. "And if he does anything silly, he knows our reaction will be tough," he warned. European intelligence officials said Sept. 24 that Russia could test NATO's defenses. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service assessed the risk of a limited Russian military attack against a NATO country in the coming months as "low but growing" and said Moscow is expected to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and the West. title: Popular pantry product can't legally be called peanut butter — here's why
description: Skippy must add the word "spread" to its natural peanut butter label due to FDA regulations requiring at least 90% peanut content in every single jar.
content: Peanut butter is a spread by definition, but when the word "spread" appears on a peanut butter jar label, it's most likely satisfying a legal requirement rather than acting as a simple descriptor. Skippy, a well-known name in the peanut butter world, must label its Natural Peanut Butter Spread as such because it contains palm oil. Regulations set by the U.S. Food & Drug Administration (FDA) state that, in order to be classified as peanut butter, a product must contain at least 90% peanuts — otherwise, the word "spread" needs to be included on the label. REESE'S FAMILY MEMBER ESCALATES BATTLE WITH HERSHEY OVER CHOCOLATE INGREDIENTS, BLASTS 'PR STUNT' The Skippy website acknowledges this FDA regulation, saying: "Natural Peanut Butter Spreads can include additional ingredients like palm oil or other oils, which are not hydrogenated." "These spreads may still contain at least 90% peanuts but include other ingredients that place them outside the standard definition of 'peanut butter,'" the website notes. It wasn't the smoothest journey to get this regulation set in stone. Back in 1959, an FDA press release included the findings of a survey which showed that "products labeled 'peanut butter' had reduced their peanut content as much as 20 percent by substituting cheaper hydrogenated or vegetable oils for expensive peanuts and peanut oil," according to the FDA. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER When manufacturers asked about adding glycerin to peanut butter in order to fight oil separation, the FDA responded by stating that, "if glycerin could be added without rendering the food adulterated, its addition would have to be set forth prominently on the product label." It became apparent that customers liked peanut butter that spread easily and had a bit of sweetener. So, in 1961, the FDA proposed a new standard which maintained products consisting of 90 percent peanuts and additional sweeteners would be classified as peanut butter. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Upon this proposal, three peanut butter brands — Skippy, Jif and Peter Pan — began a 20-week public hearing to argue what peanut percentage the new standard would dictate. Eventually, the U.S. Appeals Court approved the FDA proposal to set peanut butter standards "at no less than 90 percent for peanuts and no more than 55 percent fat," according to the FDA. title: Forgetting names and losing keys may signal something other than dementia

content: Everyday memory lapses, like misplaced keys or forgotten names, are often overinterpreted as early signs of dementia, but neuroscience experts say actual early cognitive changes may be reversible if addressed promptly. Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said minor forgetfulness is often caused by fatigue or stress rather than the beginnings of a neurodegenerative disease. "For most people, it's just because you're stressed or you're tired and weren't paying attention," Wood told Fox News Digital at Strong New York, the city's largest annual fitness and wellness festival. DOCTOR REVEALS '10-YEAR RULE' FOR EVALUATING BRAIN FOG AND DEMENTIA SYMPTOMS "If you want to remember something ... you need to actually be focused, be paying attention. You need to tell your brain it's important to remember it." Understanding memory loss Wood said memory formation works in three stages: encoding (forming a memory), consolidation (storing it) and retrieval (accessing it). When someone is stressed or sleep-deprived, the issue is typically retrieval, he said — the memory exists in the brain, but the individual struggles to access it in the moment. In contrast, people experiencing a neurodegenerative disease often fail to encode the memory in the first place. ‘MIRACLE ON THE HUDSON’ HERO SULLY SULLENBERGER REVEALS ALZHEIMER’S WARNING SIGNS HE MISSED YEARS AGO "They don't even remember or notice that there's something going on," Wood said. "If you're noticing something's not quite right, that's usually a good sign." Preventable risk factors and reversibility Dementia is clinically defined as the loss of cognitive function that's severe enough to impair an individual's ability to manage daily life independently. Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia account for 70% to 90% of cases, with many individuals showing signs of both. Research indicates that at least 50% of dementia cases can be prevented by modifying lifestyle and health risk factors. Key preventable risk factors include heart and metabolic health problems, as well as hearing and vision loss. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "If you expect decline, you won't do the things that will prevent decline from happening," Wood told Fox News Digital. "Believing that it's possible means you'll actually engage in these processes, and then through that, you can prevent a lot of this decline." Wood's focus on reversible causes of cognitive symptoms aligns with guidance from Mayo Clinic and Cleveland Clinic, which note that several treatable medical conditions can mimic early dementia symptoms or contribute to subjective cognitive decline. title: RNC rips Beshear's 'woke trans record' over veto of Kentucky girls' sports bill
description: Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear defended his veto of a transgender athletes ban, saying his party doesn't "throw anybody under the bus."
content: Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear defended his record on transgender issues Sunday during an appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," saying his party does not "throw anybody under the bus," as host Jake Tapper pressed him over his veto of a bill barring transgender students from girls' and women's sports. Tapper confronted Beshear about his 2022 veto of Kentucky's Senate Bill 83, which prohibited male students from participating on girls' athletic teams from sixth grade through college. The Republican-controlled legislature later overrode Beshear's veto. The governor pointed to what he described as Kentucky's lone transgender athlete at the time before defending his broader approach. FEMALE ATHLETES, WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES SPEAK ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRANS ATHLETE ISSUE HOVERS OVER MIDTERMS "Here's my take. We don't throw anybody under the bus," Beshear said, "That is not the party that we are. We start as a party of compassion and empathy. And I tell you what. If we want to ruin sports, put government in charge of them." RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre ripped Beshear's record in an exclusive statement to Fox News Digital, accusing the potential 2028 presidential contender of putting transgender policies ahead of female athletes. "Democrats claim to be the party of women," she said. "But they can't define what a woman is and have no issues when men expose themselves in locker rooms or take over women’s sports. Andy Beshear can pretend he’s for fairness, but his woke trans record shows he traded girls' safety for applause from men in dresses." DEMOCRAT POLITICIANS ARE BETRAYING THEIR OWN VOTERS ON TRANS SPORTS ISSUE Beshear told Tapper that he believed athletic competition should be fair but rejected abandoning transgender Americans as Democrats face political attacks over the issue. "Sports need to be fair, and there should be no unfair advantage," Beshear said. "But, in Kentucky, we already had rules in place with our Kentucky High School Athletic Association that prevented any of the things that you saw ultimately in colleges or the rest." Kentucky legislative records show the 2022 legislation, Senate Bill 83, known as the "Save Women's Sports Act," dealt with athletics and did not include restrictions on transgender medical treatments for minors. The measure required girls' and women's athletic teams to be based on biological sex and prohibited male students from participating in them. SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS Those healthcare and school-facility provisions instead appeared in Senate Bill 150, a separate measure Beshear vetoed in 2023. The legislation restricted transgender medical treatments for minors and required school policies limiting students from using restrooms, locker rooms or showers reserved for the opposite biological sex. Republican lawmakers also overrode that veto. Beshear had argued in his 2022 veto message that existing Kentucky High School Athletic Association rules were sufficient to protect competitive fairness. The rules at the time generally required athletes to participate according to the sex listed on their birth certificate, while providing a pathway for transgender athletes who met specified medical requirements. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Beshear defended his separate SB 150 veto on parental-rights and mental-health grounds. His campaign said in 2023 that his opposition was based on multiple provisions in the legislation and was not specifically about its prohibition on sex-change surgeries for minors. Fox News Digital reached out to Beshear for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

title: AG Blanche rejects calls for new AI laws after rogue agents target US government websites

content: Attorney General Todd Blanche rejected calls for additional artificial intelligence regulation Sunday on "Fox & Friends Weekend," arguing that existing laws already give the government the tools it needs to pursue bad actors after reports allege that rogue AI agents targeted U.S. government websites. "Everybody's saying more laws, more laws, more regulation, but we don't need it. We don't need it right now," he said. OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION Blanche's remarks come as top AI firms, like OpenAI and Anthropic, are probing tens of thousands of security incidents in which models took "problematic" steps. title: NFL field expert says playing international game on Brazil field 'challenging' and included trim with scissors
description: Workers used scissors to trim Maracanã Stadium's grass as Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys prepared for the NFL's Brazil game amid safety concerns.
content: The NFL is going to play international games come hell or high grass, or slippery, dangerous grass. That's the message the league is sending on Sunday when the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys play in Brazil's Maracanã Stadium in Rio de Janeiro. All week long, the NFL has had its field experts and groundskeepers on the, um, ground to make sure Lamar Jackson can run and cut like he typically can. They want Dak Prescott knowing his receivers will come out of their breaks without breaking their necks. And that required some extreme work. NFL COMMISSIONER ROGER GOODELL CONFIRMS LEAGUE WANTS MULTIPLE TEAMS BASED OUTSIDE THE US: 'NO DOUBT' Workers were still trimming the turf on Saturday. The Associated Press reported some were using scissors to level the high grass. No, seriously. Scissors. The NFL also gave the field an application of fiber using the new GrassMaster Stitch Machine. So, these guys are trying everything. Earlier reports had players from both teams showing concern about the field and the NFL Players Association issuing a statement expressing its concern. Sounds like a player injury waiting to happen. Ultimately, NFL Field Director Nick Pappas said Saturday, "Things check out. No need to worry." He even posted a video of the field at 12:54 Sunday morning that shows how nice it looks. But even that video is problematic. Posting it at that time is evidence of how late it was before the league thought the field ready for play. And, of course, the field looking good before a player steps on it on Sunday is not a predictor of how well it will hold up. Earlier this week, Pappas offered a more sobering message about this field in particular and international fields in general. "Our fields are where they are today in America because of how long we’ve worked at it," Pappas told reporters. "Not everywhere we travel is going to have the same resources, same climate, same available type of grass, same tools at their beck and call like we have in the United States. "It becomes challenging. How can we put it on a plane and fly it there? Just like the rest of the game: what can we put on a plane, what can we put on a ship, and how do we execute to make it a successful Sunday?" NFL PUSHES DEEPER INTO STREAMING AS NETFLIX LANDS AUSTRALIA GAME AMID FCC, DOJ SCRUTINY At minimum, Pappas is admitting playing these NFL games internationally, and specifically in Brazil, is a challenge. At worst, he's fueling the idea that some fields are a hazard to players. That was obviously one of NFLPA Executive Director JC Tretter's concerns when he released a statement about the situation. "Two of the three games played in Brazil have had field-related issues. That's not a coincidence. This time of year makes it extremely challenging to maintain the kind of grass surface we expect at the NFL level. "Our guys are exceptional at what they do, and I'm confident they'll put on a terrific game in Rio this week. They always do.
