title: Pope Leo calls out ‘false compassion’ of medically assisted suicide during French hospital visit
description: Pope Leo XIV condemned assisted suicide as "false compassion" during a Mass in Lourdes, France, urging the healthcare community to reject causing death.
content: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800-273-TALK (8255). Pope Leo XIV called for an end to medically assisted suicide during a visit to medical facilities in Lourdes, France, on Sunday. The pope gave Mass in Lourdes before addressing a large crowd who cheered as he emphatically affirmed the dignity of all human lives and admonished listeners to reject the "false compassion" of assisted suicide. POPE LEO XIV BEGINS HISTORIC 4-DAY VISIT TO FRANCE "It is precisely in the name of this inalienable dignity of the human person that we must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," the pope said, speaking in French. "It is impossible to regard causing death as something normal. What is legal is not necessarily moral," he continued. "Here in Lourdes, the city of the sick and of hope, I appeal to the entire healthcare community to remember the profound meaning of your vocation, which is to care for a suffering person, not to eliminate that person." CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH "No one ever has the right based on laboratory algorithms to decide the life of a given embryo or elderly person. Medicine must never become the servant of programmed death," he said. Assisted suicide is legal in many Western countries, including France. MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS PROPOSE PACKAGE SEEKING TO LEGALIZE ASSISTED SUICIDE The practice has come under heavy criticism, particularly in Canada where it has seen widespread use. Last week, the family of an 83-year-old Canadian woman demanded answers after she died through the country's medical assistance in dying program despite allegedly becoming distraught when told the procedure would end her life. ASSISTED LIVING CENTER SENT RESIDENT TO DOCTOR'S APPOINTMENT AFTER GIVING HIM 18 SHOTS, 5 AM BEER: OFFICIALS The Daily Mail reported that 83-year-old Christian grandmother Brigitte Stegemann was killed under Canada’s physician-assisted suicide program, called Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID), on July 10. Her granddaughter, Brigitte Kranendonk, said that she was her grandmother’s primary caregiver and that her family had decided to place Stegemann at The Pearl care home in Cannifton due to physical and mental decline. ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS But according to Kranendonk, her grandmother still had a good appetite even following a stomach cancer diagnosis, and rejected the idea of using MAID when it was presented as an option. Kranendonk said she was present for Stegemann's second MAID assessment, and said that the doctor used "really loose terms, never using the words death or dying." NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS "She explains MAID to my grandmother by saying: 'We’re going to give you medicine, you’re going to feel at peace. And I just want you to know that you won’t have a bowel movement,'" Kranendonk said. When Kranendonk interjected and said, "She doesn’t understand what you’re saying," the doctor allegedly looked at Stegemann and said, "We’re going to make sure you won’t have any more pain." CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND According to a doctor, Stegemann was "deemed fit for MAID, and we're going to proceed," The Daily Mail reported. Kranendonk said that two days before Stegemann's death, she asked her grandmother directly whether she understood that the scheduled procedure meant she would die. title: DAVID MARCUS: Why JD Vance's reshoring message is a perfect fit for struggling small towns like St. Cloud
description: St. Cloud, Minnesota's struggling downtown could be revitalized by JD Vance's reshoring agenda, but Somali immigration and fraud concerns loom large.
content: Three weeks ago in Dallas, at the midterm convention, Republicans chose to put Vice President JD Vance in the spotlight, to lead the troops to November. His speech, about the future of the nation, could have been addressed directly to the town of St. Cloud, Minnesota, and its environs. In those remarks, referring to the future of his own kids, Vance said, "I want, whether they work in tech or manufacturing, American businesses to hire American workers, to rely on American people and to ensure that we build the next generation of great American products with American hands." You can almost hear those words echoing around the historic downtown of 19th century red brick, and it is a bit of a puzzle, because usually it is fairly obvious whether a city of this size — about 80,000 souls — is ascending or descending. But St. Cloud seems, well, stuck in the middle. THE ONE LINE FROM JD VANCE’S GOP KEYNOTE THAT REVEALS HIS VISION FOR AMERICA On the positive side of the civic ledger is the fact that the businesses that are open seem to be thriving. It's not in every minor metro downtown that you see packed restaurants for lunch on a Tuesday. There were also volunteers out painting the planters that line the sidewalk, another very positive sign of civic engagement. On the downside, almost half of the available commercial space is empty — like a handsome hockey player with some missing teeth — and foot traffic, at least for now, is not heavy enough to support many more retailers. Rob, now in his 40s, went to college at the nearby university in the early 2000s and told Fox News Digital, "Back then downtown was packed every night, you could barely move, I don’t think it's ever getting back to that." When I asked how he thought the town was doing, he said, "Better these days, better since COVID, but it's kind of plateaued," and he was not the only person I spoke to who used that particular word. One that can also be applied to much of the broader nation. Janice, another long-time resident dating back to the 1990s who works in real estate, set the date of the town’s downturn a bit earlier, with the closing of Herberger's department store — which opened in 1927 and shut down for good in 2018. "It’s a huge hole, right in the heart of downtown," she said, "and there isn’t anything to fill it." It was around this time that several factories in the area also closed down. To add insult to injury, in 2019, St. Cloud State University dropped its football program, never a great sign for a college town. But there are seeds of growth as well, and one of the planters, Chad O’Brien, opened a vintage store downtown in March 2025, just after Trump’s inauguration, and now has two on the same block, as businesses bubble up to life. "I think that the way the downtown works, the way that it draws people in, our business model and structure and the things that we sell seems like a really good fit," O’Brien told Fox News Digital, though he also said that more people living in the area would certainly help. Ultimately, this is why Vance’s mission to reshore manufacturing and reward firms that stay in America is such a perfect fit for St. Cloud. Honestly, a handful of businesses, with a few thousand jobs, could easily bring some of the hustle and bustle back. Perhaps one big plant with 1,500 factory jobs that can fill the single-family homes that semicircle the city, and a big tech firm hiring 300 to 500 younger workers to live downtown in walking distance to the bars and eateries. In a city this small, that's all it takes to make a difference. The biggest concerns you hear in St. Cloud surround the Somali immigrant community, but this issue is actually two distinct problems — both of which are firmly in the Vice President’s portfolio, the first being the massive fraud scandal. VICE PRESIDENT VANCE SAYS MIGRANT COMMUNITIES SHOW 'CLEAR PATTERN' IN FEDERAL FRAUD AS INVESTIGATIONS WIDEN Even on the ride back to the airport, Lynn, who also works in the beauty industry, told me of a ride she had given recently where an immigrant woman was bragging to her friend that she had just secured government-subsidized housing — but her boyfriend already had it, so they were going to rent hers out for cash. I could see Lynn’s knuckles whiten on the steering wheel as she said, "It just makes me so mad, I want to help the poor, but this can’t be the way." Everyone can agree that the fraud is bad, and hopefully, that the efforts spearheaded by Vance to stop it are good. But, the second part of the Somali issue is trickier and more intractable. It is the cultural component, another strong theme in Vance’s convention speech, and here opinions vary. Several people I spoke with expressed deep frustration at the seeming unwillingness of Somalis to assimilate, but not everyone. Trey, in his late 20s, is the sales manager at a local phone store who hired a Somali to help with customers of Somali descent. "He’s worried that their kids are becoming too Americanized and losing their roots," Trey said, adding, "I do see some of that, a lot of the teenagers don’t even speak their language now." Another gentleman in his 60s, who I met at a fairly high-end lounge told me, "There is no downside to these immigrants, it is all upside and the only reason to be against it is racism." I gently suggested that there are certainly people who think they have non-bigoted objections, but he doubled down, "It’s only racism." Downtown, though, is the place where the cultural and economic concerns meet, or, in this case, do not meet, because just as is true with the Haitian community in Springfield, Ohio, the Somalis in St. Cloud are not to be seen downtown — living instead, almost exclusively in their own enclave. The influx of Somali immigrants has not revitalized downtown because they don’t go there. A few thousand blue and white collared native-born workers absolutely would. More broadly, the Somali community sends so much of its income back to Somalia, money not being reinvested in St Cloud, that their overall economic contribution has to be questioned. Just northwest of St. Cloud is Sauk Centre, Minnesota, the real-life inspiration for Sinclair Lewis’ seminal novel Main Street, which over a century ago captured the uniqueness of the American small town — something that still charmed so many foreign World Cup travelers this past summer. His blend of America first and reshoring jobs to small communities truly does resonate, and makes sense. Just as Vance and his muscular populist message kicked off the midterms for the GOP, in October, it must carry it through. In other words, Mr. Vice President, are you ready for your close-up?

title: Texas clinic owner convicted in $26M military health fraud tied to gold-plated Cybertruck
description: Kevin D. Curry used TRICARE kickbacks to fund a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck and lavish parties after billing $26 million in fake TMS therapy claims.
content: A Texas mental health clinic owner was convicted by a federal jury after prosecutors said he orchestrated a $26 million scheme to defraud the military's health care program, using some of the proceeds to fund luxury purchases, including a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck worth more than $100,000. Kevin D. Curry, 64, of Frisco, was found guilty Thursday in federal court in Fort Worth on three counts of health care fraud, three counts of offering and paying illegal health care kickbacks and three counts of engaging in monetary transactions in criminally derived property, according to the Justice Department. Federal prosecutors said Curry exploited TRICARE, the health care program serving active-duty servicemembers, retirees and their families, by billing for transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, therapy that was medically unnecessary or, in many cases, never provided. FBI LAUNCHES 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AS DOJ CHARGES OHIO DEFENDANTS IN $30M MEDICAID SCHEME FOR KIDS According to evidence presented at trial, Curry owned and operated mental health clinics in Plano and Fort Worth, Texas, as well as Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Prosecutors said he paid more than $5.5 million in illegal kickbacks to persuade active-duty servicemembers, veterans and their family members to consent to TMS therapy they did not qualify for and, in many instances, did not receive. The Justice Department said Curry falsely represented himself as a medical doctor, used licensed doctors' credentials without their knowledge or consent to submit claims to TRICARE, and directed employees to fabricate medical records to justify fraudulent billings. FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD, OTHER MAJOR SCAMS: 'CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE' Authorities said Curry's clinics submitted more than $26 million in false, fraudulent or kickback-tainted claims to TRICARE, which ultimately paid approximately $17 million. Prosecutors said Curry laundered some of the proceeds by spending the money on luxury hotel stays, a lavish casino-themed party and a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck valued at more than $100,000. TAXPAYER FUNDS MEANT FOR LA HOMELESS ALLEGEDLY SPENT ON TAHITI TRIP, NIGHTCLUB, LUXURY CARS: FEDS "This defendant exploited a critical health care program serving active-duty servicemembers and their families, diverting taxpayer dollars to bankroll personal luxuries ranging from hotel stays to a casino-themed party and even a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald said in a statement. U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said Curry "shamelessly preyed on the trust of servicemembers, veterans, and their families," accusing him of fabricating medical records, stealing doctors' identities and submitting fraudulent claims while profiting from kickback-tainted money. A federal district court judge will determine his sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

title: 'Gilmore Girls' star Lauren Graham reveals her go-to fall coffee order — and it's not pumpkin spice
description: The "Gilmore Girls" star told Parade she gets a sweeter coffee craving each fall but won't reach for a pumpkin spice latte during the season.
content: Autumn has officially arrived, and fall coffee drinks are back for another season. Lauren Graham, who starred as Lorelai Gilmore in the TV show "Gilmore Girls," recently revealed her favorite fall coffee order. Many episodes in the "Gilmore Girls" series are set during autumn in New England, and the show lends itself well to the season. Many viewers associate the show with crisp air and coziness, with The New York Times even calling it a "fall tradition." STARBUCKS BRINGING BACK VIRAL MENU ITEM DESPITE 2017 BARISTA REVOLT: 'MAY GOD SAVE US ALL' Graham enjoys a seasonal drink, especially one on the sweeter side. "I do get more sweet-tooth coffee-ish in the fall," she told Parade. However, the actress and author doesn't typically reach for beverages featuring pumpkin or warm spices. "I won't really get a pumpkin spice latte, but I'll go chocolate mint, like a peppermint mocha," she said. In 2025, Starbucks released its peppermint mocha, a holiday menu item, on Nov. 6. title: 81-year-old refuses to stop working as wife battles cancer, then strangers try to help
description: Don Johnson, 81, of Texas delivered lost luggage to cover his wife's cancer costs until a viral fundraiser begun by his daughter raised $700,000. Now, the GoFundMe campaign has been pulled.
content: An encounter with an elderly delivery driver in Texas has captured attention after the reason he was still working came to light. Donald Johnson, 81, was delivering lost luggage to a home when Erin Howell, a resident at The Colony, saw him struggling to carry a heavy bag up a steep set of stairs — a moment captured by her doorbell camera, according to reports. Howell went outside to help and learned that Johnson had been making luggage deliveries as an independent contractor for the past three years to help cover medical expenses for his wife, Josephine Johnson, who is battling cancer, FOX 4 Dallas-Fort Worth reported. MILITARY VETERAN’S PAINFUL WALK ACROSS AIRPORT TARMAC SPARKS STRANGERS TO RAISE OVER $135K The couple has been married for 57 years. Donald Johnson continued to work during his wife's medical treatment. He was continuing to make deliveries because he had struggled to find other work, he told Howell during their encounter. "It's the only job that will hire me," Johnson told her, according to the outlet. Howell shared the elderly man's story online and even started a fundraiser to help with medical expenses and give him the chance to stop working and care for his wife. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER As his story spread, thousands of strangers responded with donations and messages of support. "I think I'm going to be able to stop working, and that's amazing," Johnson told FOX 4. "So we're not quite totally over the hump yet, but we're getting there very quickly." The outpouring of support and prayers had given her encouragement as she continued her cancer battle, Josephine Johnson told FOX 4. "I can face it. I think that's the big difference," she said. "Some have made comments and they're praying for us. And it's just — it's a joyful feeling." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The family's circumstances, however, took another turn after the fundraiser was eventually removed from GoFundMe. In a recent TikTok video, the couple's daughter, Amy Johnson, said the campaign had collected more than $700,000 — but that her parents would not receive the money because the donations were being refunded due to "a technicality." Sitting alongside her parents in the TikTok, the daughter said the money that was raised was intended to help cover her mother's medical expenses as she battles pancreatic cancer and would also give her 81-year-old father the opportunity to stop working. The company did not specify the exact reason for the decision. It said its policies require "authenticity and transparency for donors." title: Ukraine's attacks on Russia are pushing Putin closer to negotiating table, Trump NATO ambassador says
description: Matt Whitaker says Ukrainian attacks inside Russia are pushing both sides closer to peace talks as Trump presses Putin and Zelenskyy to negotiate.
content: Ukrainian attacks inside Russia are helping push Moscow and Kyiv closer to the negotiating table, U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matt Whitaker said on Saturday, as President Donald Trump continues pressing Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to negotiate an end to the war. Whitaker emphasized during "The Big Weekend Show" that it would take the cooperation of both adversaries to end the war, but said Ukraine "continuing to make strong attacks on Russia... is helping to, I think, bring the sides closer together." The ambassador cautioned that Moscow and Kyiv still remain "a long way apart" on key issues, adding that the resolution would not come through hostilities. UKRAINE STRIKES DEEP INTO RUSSIA’S ARCTIC GAS HEARTLAND AS TRUMP PUSHES PUTIN TOWARD PEACE "This conflict is not going to be resolved on the battlefield. It's only going to [be resolved] through diplomacy and negotiation," he said. "That's why President Trump and his team continue to talk to both sides to find any similarities between the positions to bring them together." ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE If Putin is unwilling to compromise, striking a deal will be "impossible," said Whitaker. "But I think if there's a deal to be made, President Trump is a businessman, he's a dealmaker, and I think he'll make the deal." Trump said Saturday that 25,000 people were killed last month and another 32,000 the month before in the war between Ukraine and Russia. FINLAND'S STUBB CREDITS TRUMP FOR PUSHING UKRAINE PEACE TALKS WHILE DISMISSING RUSSIAN INVASION FEARS "Last month, 25,000 people died in the Ukraine-Russia war, okay? Twenty-five thousand," Trump told reporters on the White House lawn. "The month before that, 32,000 people died … mostly soldiers, 97% soldiers," he added. "But whether they're soldiers or civilians, think of it: 32,000. Two months ago, 33,000 people; this month, 25,000 people died. What a shame." title: Bass angler couldn't use LiveScope, so he followed whitetail deer to find the fish instead
description: Kaden Buchmann used deer sightings to gauge fishing pressure at Norfork Lake, going wire-to-wire without forward-facing sonar to win $71,317.
content: What do you do when you can't use LiveScope to find the bass? You ask the deer, obviously. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Kaden Buchmann went wire-to-wire to win the first Bassmaster Elite Qualifier of the season Friday at Norfork Lake in Arkansas, finishing the three-day tournament with 42 pounds, 7 ounces. But the fun part is how the 22-year-old found some of those fish. Forward-facing sonar was not allowed for the Norfork event, one of three Elite Qualifiers that will ultimately determine which 10 anglers earn invitations to the 2027 Bassmaster Elite Series. So Buchmann had to find another way to figure out where bass might be hiding — and, more importantly, where 130-plus other anglers hadn't already been. His solution was to ask the locals. Well, the four-legged locals. With so many boats working a relatively small reservoir, Buchmann started watching the shoreline for deer. If deer were hanging out close to the water, chances were pretty good another angler hadn't just come ripping through that pocket and scared them off. "If I saw 15 deer in a pocket, I'd say, 'I'm getting bit here,'" Buchmann told Bassmaster. And, somehow, it worked. Buchmann spotted more than 30 deer during the opening day of competition — including a 9-point buck — and used their presence as a clue for finding areas that hadn't seen as much fishing pressure. He weighed 16 pounds, 7 ounces that day to take the tournament lead. TREY MCKINNEY SAYS BASSMASTER VETERANS MADE HIM EARN THEIR RESPECT BEFORE HISTORIC AOY SEASON Then he did it again. On Day 2, Buchmann once again spent part of his morning looking for deer and said he caught two quality bass in a pocket where he had spotted them. "We can't use (forward-facing sonar) this week, so you just have to fish where you think they're gonna be," he told Bassmaster. Simple enough. But not easy. To be clear, Buchmann did a whole lot more than follow deer around Norfork Lake. Bassmaster credited his speed, mental toughness and ability to stay away from other competitors as major factors in the win. He covered enormous stretches of the lake, kept his trolling motor running high and targeted everything from docks to shaded shoreline with a topwater bait and skipping jig. On the final day alone, he said four of the fish he weighed came from places he had never previously fished. "I fished the whole lake," Buchmann said after the win. "I fished from about 3 miles from Missouri, all the way down to a pocket by the Norfork Dam." It all added up to a wire-to-wire victory. Buchmann opened with 16-7, added 14 pounds on Day 2 and survived a tougher final round with another 12 pounds. His 42-7 total beat runner-up Cody Stahl by 1 pound, 14 ounces and earned Buchmann $71,317 along with an invitation to compete in the 2027 Bassmaster Classic at Lake Hartwell. But now that his deer-scouting secret is out, don’t be surprised if there are a few more anglers watching the shoreline next time. Love all things fishing and outdoors? title: Why the New Orleans Saints can cover the spread against the Las Vegas Raiders in NFL Week 3
description: The Las Vegas Raiders face the New Orleans Saints in Week 3 as both teams look to prove their early-season success wasn't a fluke against each other.
content: Each NFL season has its own story and uniqueness. Discovering it is part of the fun, but it can also be a point of contention when you’re a sports bettor. You don’t have a ton of time to determine who is a good team and who is bad. You have to constantly evaluate and change your opinions on things. I’ve already changed my opinion on both of these teams – the Raiders and the Saints, and now they face each other in Week 3. The Las Vegas Raiders cost me some money last week, or maybe I should say the Chargers cost me money once again. After backing them in Week 1, I took the Chargers to beat them in Week 2 and cover the spread. The Raiders looked like a fairly well-oiled machine against Los Angeles, getting three touchdown passes from Kirk Cousins on 19-for-29 passing. Part of the key for the Raiders will be keeping Cousins upright, and he was only sacked twice. The other key to the Raiders' success is getting Ashton Jeanty to effectively run the ball. What I liked about the Raiders game is that despite him not having a very good game, they stuck with it. Jeanty had just 48 yards on 21 attempts. He did haul in four of his seven targets, but added just 15 yards. Before we crown the Raiders as being elite, let’s realize that the Chargers were also part of their problem. Sure, some of this can be attributed to Las Vegas, but Los Angeles fumbling six times was also ridiculous. The New Orleans Saints have put together some decent games to start their season. They almost came back and beat the Lions in Week 1 after bringing them to overtime. In the first two quarters of the season, the Saints scored zero total points. Since about the middle of the third quarter of that game, they have scored 54 points. All of their touchdowns have come through the air as well, relying on Tyler Shough to lead the way. Maybe it is Shough taking too long to figure out opposing defenses. Maybe there is some other reason, but they are playing with fire by waiting until the last quarter to try and come back. The Saints have played two rather difficult teams and now get to play at home. The Raiders had an easy game to open the season, and their second game wasn’t exactly a challenge considering how bad the Chargers look. Again, some of that was certainly self-inflicted, but I don’t want to take a ton away from the Raiders. I just don’t think this is a great situation for the Raiders. I don’t think their offense will be able to be quite as effective in this one. I like the Saints to win and cover the -3 spread. title: Panthers favored at -2.5 over Browns as Bryce Young's offense faces Cleveland's home opener
description: Bryce Young has thrown six touchdown passes through two weeks, and now the Panthers face a Cleveland Browns team coming off a lightning-aided upset.
content: You can go ahead and tell me I’m a glutton for punishment, and maybe I’m a fool, but there are some games that stood out to me this weekend, and both involved teams that hurt me last weekend. I’m not chasing any sort of win; I just feel like this one is the correct angle for the game. Today we start with two teams that both got back on track last weekend as the Panthers take on the Browns. Lost in the mess that was Week 1 was how good the Panthers offense looked against the Chicago Bears. Of course, the main story was that the Panthers allowed 59 points, but they put up 37 of their own. Bryce Young looked solid in the contest with 361 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception. That’s a game typically good enough to beat most teams. His defense just gave him no help. Even the running game was performing well, but they had to somewhat abandon it. Last week the team was dominant in a road victory over the Falcons. It wasn’t just an offensive victory; the defense adjusted and held Atlanta to just a field goal in the game. Before you anoint the defense completely back on track, just keep in mind that the Falcons turned the ball over three times. They had almost 100 yards more on the ground, meaning the Panthers have given up a many of yards through two games to opponents' rushing attacks. The offense with Young was still rolling. He threw for another three touchdowns in the game. The Cleveland Browns broke the hearts of a lot of people last week. That’s nothing new for a franchise that seems to thrive on hurting people’s hearts. However, this time it was because the Browns took down the Buccaneers on the road in Week 2. That knocked out another 30% of the remaining Circa Survivor entries (including mine). But was this the Browns playing great, the Bucs playing bad, or both? It probably lies somewhere in between. Deshaun Watson played a strong game. After a terrible Week 1, Watson went 24-for-30 through the air with two touchdown passes. He added 22 yards on the ground, which was a team high for the Browns. There also was an act of God that helped the Browns capture the victory. The Buccaneers were mounting a comeback and working the ball downfield when lightning struck. That suspended the game and took away any momentum that Tampa had. The Buccaneers' penalties after the play resumed cost the Bucs the game and put Cleveland at 1-1 after a terrible opener against Jacksonville. title: Bruce Campbell says Hollywood studios left ‘very sour’ taste after he was 'kicked out' of lead role
description: After a cancer diagnosis and decades in Hollywood, Bruce Campbell and wife Ida Gearon filmed "Ernie & Emma" entirely in their home state of Oregon.
content: Bruce Campbell is taking a chainsaw to the Hollywood playbook. The "Evil Dead" star is ditching the traditional studio system for "Ernie & Emma," his new independent film that puts him firmly in the driver's seat after decades of navigating Hollywood — and after one early studio experience left a bad taste. "The first studio film I ever did, I got kicked out of the lead," Campbell told Fox News Digital. "The movie was re-edited, retitled and never came out. So, the taste in my mouth from studios is very sour." KEVIN SORBO BLASTS HOLLYWOOD 'BLACKLISTING' OF CONSERVATIVES AS 'SEVENTH GRADE MEAN GIRLS' CULTURE That experience stuck with the cult-favorite actor, who said he has long wanted to make a project without studio executives calling the shots. "It was time to be unbridled in my life," Campbell said. Campbell said earlier this month on "The Adam Carolla Show" podcast that doctors had given him an estimated five years to live, but he remains focused on treatment and continuing his work. title: Irish PM rejects antisemitism concerns in Ireland amid dramatic vote over boycotting Israel game
description: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin rejected antisemitism claims as Ireland's soccer players held a dramatic last-minute vote on playing against Israel.
content: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin rejected claims that Ireland's sharp criticism of Israel has crossed into antisemitism as tensions flared around a politically charged soccer match between the countries Sunday, with Irish players holding a last-minute vote over whether to boycott the game. Martin, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital this week in New York, outlined why Ireland has taken such a staunch position against the Israeli government's conduct of the war in Gaza, calling its military response "absolutely disproportionate" while pressing Israel to "change strategy" and calling for increased humanitarian aid to Gaza. Martin argued that Ireland's own history — particularly its experience ending decades of conflict in Northern Ireland — gives the country a role to play as a voice for peace on the international stage, a theme he returned to while discussing Ukraine and the ongoing debate over Irish reunification. "I think for the vast majority of people it does not," Martin said when asked directly whether anti-Israel sentiment in Ireland had crossed the line into antisemitism. "We have no toleration for antisemitism, none," Martin added. NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK The extraordinary player vote came after months of pressure surrounding the UEFA Nations League fixture on Sunday, with more than 160 Irish sports figures calling for a boycott and players themselves publicly questioning whether the match should go ahead. A "significant majority" of players ultimately voted on Saturday to play the game, while one player left the squad after expressing his wish not to take part. In the interview, Martin strongly condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack and defended Israel's right to exist in security. "First of all, we condemned, absolutely, the outrageous terrorist attack by Hamas in October," Martin told Fox News Digital. "We believe in a two-state solution," Martin said. "We believe that Israel, of course, has a right to exist in security and its people need to be guaranteed of security. But likewise, Palestinians should have a right to live in their homeland in a peaceful way." "There are many peaceful voices in Palestine that I've met who want peaceful coexistence with Israel." Martin said Ireland's strongly pro-Palestinian position was rooted partly in its own history. "There's a very strong pro-Palestinian position in Ireland," Martin said. "Ireland, the Irish government and the Irish people, probably because of our own history, but also because of a sense of right and justice and fairness." Thousands have taken to the streets across Ireland since the war began, while national broadcaster RTÉ refused to air this year's Eurovision Song Contest after Israel's participation was confirmed. Ireland spent centuries under British rule before most of the island gained independence a little more than a century ago, while Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom. He said Israel's military response to the Oct. 7 attack had resonated deeply in Ireland and called for increased humanitarian aid into Gaza. "We want humanitarian aid going into Gaza. There's not enough humanitarian aid going in," Martin said, pointing to the conditions facing roughly 2 million people there, including shortages of food and shelter and children without access to education. Martin said Ireland wanted Israel to reconsider its conduct of the war, asking whether it would "change strategy" and "change its approach to the whole issue." "So that's the background to the Irish position," he said. "People are angry in terms of what's going on in the Middle East and that's the manifestation of it." ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS Soccer flashpoint Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson said his players were uncomfortable with the games, declaring: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide." The Israeli Football Association accused him of "stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy," prompting Martin to call the remarks "unacceptable." The FAI previously sought Israel's suspension from international competition. Separately, Irish soccer officials later voted to fulfill the Israel fixtures after being warned a boycott could cost the association at least $6.3 million and trigger UEFA sanctions. Sunday's game will be played in Hungary, while Ireland's Oct. 4 home fixture has been moved to Serbia and will be played behind closed doors. Irish supporters will not have access to either game. An organized campaign dubbed #StopTheGame has, meanwhile, spent months pressuring Irish soccer officials and players not to fulfill the Israel fixtures, staging protests and urging the national team to refuse to play. The campaign has also spilled onto the field. During a friendly against Qatar in May, protesters threw tennis balls bearing "Stop The Game" messages onto the pitch in opposition to the Israel fixtures. Martin has resisted calls for Ireland to boycott Israel, arguing that unilateral action could be "self-defeating" and may hurt Irish soccer without having any effect on Israel. Antisemitism concerns The dispute over the games reflects a broader debate over whether Ireland's criticism of Israel has crossed a line. The American Jewish Committee raised concerns directly with Martin in Washington in March 2025 about antisemitism and what it called the "vilification of Israel in Ireland." An Anti-Defamation League official also participated in the meeting. The AJC alleged that antisemitism had become "pervasive" in Ireland. Martin pointed to Ireland's annual Holocaust commemorations and the historic contribution of Jewish communities in Dublin, Cork and elsewhere in rejecting the suggestion that antisemitism was broadly tolerated in Ireland. He also pointed to Ireland's participation in international efforts against antisemitism and said the country campaigns against it globally. "We cherish that contribution that the Jewish community has made to Ireland," Martin said. Martin's defense of Ireland's position came before he addressed world leaders at the United Nations on Thursday, where he delivered a sharply critical assessment of Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, declaring that the international community had "failed Palestine." "When the full truth of what has happened, what is still happening in Gaza, is finally known, when the evidence is gathered, when the testimonies are heard, when the true horrors are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world," he said. "Nobody will be able to say that we did not know." Martin accused violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank of acting with "near-total impunity" and said Palestinian communities faced displacement and destruction "amounting to ethnic cleansing." He reiterated his support for a two-state solution, saying the only viable outcome was for "a State of Palestine and a State of Israel" to live side by side "in peace, security and dignity." Ireland as a peacemaker During his Fox News Digital interview, Martin connected Ireland's position on the Middle East to its experience ending decades of violence in Northern Ireland, saying "we feel we can make a contribution to that conflict resolution pathway." That role has taken on added significance as Ireland holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union, giving it an elevated diplomatic role at a time of multiple international conflicts. Martin also pointed to a personal experience that shaped his thinking, recalling meeting Israeli Rami Elhanan and Palestinian Bassam Aramin in Israel, two fathers who each lost a daughter in the conflict and later worked together for peace. Their stories are told in Colum McCann's novel "Apeirogon." "That's an inspiration to me," Martin said, adding that he had met both men in Israel. He said their work reflected Ireland's own efforts to reconcile communities divided by generations of conflict. Ukraine and a united Ireland Beyond the Middle East, Martin addressed Russia's war in Ukraine, saying a ceasefire along existing battle lines could provide a starting point for negotiations while rejecting territorial gains by force. "Ukraine can't cede territory that Russia hasn't even conquered, despite four years of war," Martin said. "From our perspective, no one has the right to go into another country and take its territory." Ireland has maintained its military neutrality while providing humanitarian and non-lethal assistance to Ukraine and taking in more than 120,000 Ukrainians since Russia's invasion. Martin rejected suggestions that such support compromised Ireland's neutrality, noting that Dublin has not supplied lethal weapons. "We want the war to end," he said. Martin's focus on ending long-running conflicts also extends to Ireland's own divided island. He and his Fianna Fáil party support reunification with Northern Ireland, but he said greater trust between the two communities must come first. "I believe in unity and my party believes in unity, but we have to work on it," Martin said. "We have to build reconciliation amongst the different traditions on the island of Ireland." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum would be called if it appeared likely that a majority in Northern Ireland supported reunification — an issue that gained fresh attention when Trump said during his recent visit to the country that he would "love" to see a united Ireland. Martin also pointed to Ireland's unique relationship with the United States, crediting Washington with playing a "critical" role in the Northern Ireland peace process in the 1990s. Asked whether Washington could play a role again in a future reunification process, he replied: "To a degree maybe, potentially, yeah."

title: Hugh Hefner's 'most sexy' Playboy model reveals how Anna Nicole Smith changed her life
description: Sandra Taylor shares stories of dating Fabio, shooting romance novel covers and Dan Aykroyd buying her SAG card after her Playboy career launched.
content: Anna Nicole Smith unknowingly transformed the life of the woman Hugh Hefner once called his "most sexy model." Sandra Taylor, who made hearts race as a Playboy cover girl during the '90s, is now the head sommelier at Allegiant Stadium, home of the Las Vegas Raiders. But long before then, her friendship with the 1993 Playmate of the Year changed the course of her life. "We shared two makeup artists. One was in New York, one was in LA. And they introduced us very, very early on to her coming here from Texas, and we became friends. She needed a place to stay when she first came out here." A visit to Smith on the set of "Naked Gun 33 1/3: The Final Insult" changed the course of Taylor's career. After Smith's makeup artist urged her to meet with Playboy during its 40th anniversary search, Smith encouraged her friend to go for it. The opportunity led Taylor to Playboy and launched a new chapter in her life. "I never, in a million years growing up, thought I would ever be in Playboy," she said. "It just seemed so out of the realm of reality. I was full speed ahead to be a mathematician just like my dad. ... I studied macroeconomics, microeconomics, statistics, differential equations, and I was a dream dancer." "I was only 19 years old when my dad passed away," she continued. "It was on my college campus at SUNY Purchase. He was walking with my mom, and he had a heart attack just out of the blue and passed away. And then I never went back to that campus again. Books in locker; never went back. Never looked back. I always used to joke, 'I wonder if my books are still in my locker,' because I never cleared it out. But after that, when he passed away, the math died along with him, and I just didn't want to do it anymore." After her father's sudden death, Taylor abandoned her plans to pursue math and embraced a career in modeling. Looking back, she remains grateful for her friendship with Smith, whom she credits with helping open the door to Playboy before Smith died in 2007 at 39. "I remember how sweet she was," said Taylor. "She was really, really a sweet girl and loved her son so much. She really wanted to be a great mom. She was really a sweetheart, just a really nice girl. I don't think she could hurt a fly." Brunettes, blondes ... every single walk of life you want to represent in the magazine. But I always thought he favored blondes. So, when she told me that, it was so beautiful. ... We dated a few times, and he was lovely. He said, 'Have you ever thought about doing a romance novel cover?' And I was like, 'No, but I would love to.'" title: Noise cameras are spreading across America
description: Noise cameras are popping up in at least 10 U.S. cities, using microphones and license plate readers to catch loud vehicles and issue big fines.
content: If you have ever been jolted awake by a car roaring down your street, you know how quickly the sound disappears. By the time someone calls the police, the driver could already be several blocks away. Now cities are turning to technology for help. We've repeatedly reported on Flock license plate readers popping up along roads and in parking lots. Another type of roadside camera is gaining ground, and this one listens. Noise cameras use microphones, cameras and software to pinpoint a loud vehicle. Some also capture its license plate. Depending on the program, that can lead to a warning, a review by an official or a citation. At least 10 U.S. jurisdictions have deployed or piloted noise-camera technology in recent years. More communities are preparing programs or looking at whether to follow. New York City has one of the most established enforcement programs, while places from Iowa to Hawaii have taken very different approaches. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN' Noise cameras are already handing out tickets New York City gives us one of the clearest looks at how far noise-camera enforcement can go. The city's Department of Environmental Protection operated 12 cameras in 2025. Those cameras recorded 15,994 noise events and generated 1,691 summonses. The system can target excessive engine or muffler noise. It can also capture certain horn and vehicle-music violations. A muffler violation carries a minimum penalty of $800, while the maximum can reach $2,625. New York's cameras combine microphones with video and a license plate reader. When the microphones detect noise above a preset level, the system attempts to pinpoint which vehicle produced it. City staff can then review the evidence before issuing a summons. The company behind New York's equipment is Intelligent Instruments Ltd., a U.K. company that makes the SoundVue noise-camera system. New York paid the company for equipment, calibration and service during 2025. One company keeps showing up in U.S. noise-camera programs Intelligent Instruments is becoming a familiar name in this space. SoundVue combines an array of microphones with cameras and software designed to locate the loudest vehicle. It can also connect with automatic license plate recognition technology. Knoxville, Tennessee, has used the technology in a mobile noise-camera program. The camera records information tied to excessive-noise events, including the time, location, type of vehicle and license plate. Knoxville says the camera can support warnings, but the city currently does not use it to issue camera-generated citations. The system originally came from 24 Acoustics, another Southampton, U.K.-based company. Knoxville's current city page says that camera technology now trades through Intelligent Instruments. Miami Beach also tested three Intelligent Instruments systems. The city launched its noise-meter and camera pilot to see whether the equipment could identify the correct vehicle under different traffic conditions. Florida law prevented Miami Beach from using camera evidence to issue automated noise citations during that pilot. Miami Beach has since taken another approach. In July 2026, the city launched a year-long Quiet Zone pilot in the South of Fifth neighborhood. Police officers handle enforcement there under existing laws rather than relying on automated noise-camera citations. LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS AT HOME DEPOT AND LOWE’S SPARK PRIVACY FEARS A small Iowa city is using noise cameras for trucks You do not have to live in a major city to encounter this technology. Avoca, Iowa, moved ahead with a noise-camera program along Highway 59 after testing the technology in spring 2025. The city was dealing with complaints about loud engine-compression braking from trucks, often called Jake braking. During the one-month pilot, Avoca recorded 183 violations involving 83 vehicles. The city later announced a full implementation using technology from Intelligent Instruments with backend services from Sitestream. Hawaii is listening but not writing tickets Hawaii launched a two-year noise-camera pilot on Oʻahu in September 2025. The state planned 10 locations around the island, beginning with the H-3 Freeway and Ala Moana Boulevard. However, drivers are not receiving camera-generated tickets through the pilot. The Hawaii Department of Transportation says the cameras collect information about vehicle noise levels and where the sound originates. The agency plans to use that data to help guide future legislation and enforcement decisions. The systems flag events exceeding 90 decibels and help identify the type of vehicle noise involved. That could include an engine or muffler. Washington tested whether cameras could find the right car Kirkland, Washington, also used noise cameras as a test rather than a ticket machine. The city's Street Racing Noise Pilot Program placed equipment at two locations with a history of complaints about racing and modified exhausts. The system used a camera with an array of sensitive microphones. When a vehicle crossed the noise threshold, software created a heat map showing where the sound came from. Kirkland did not issue tickets or warnings during the pilot. Instead, the city wanted to see whether the system could reliably separate one noisy vehicle from everything else happening around it. That question becomes important on a busy street. A motorcycle may be next to a truck while another car accelerates through the intersection. The camera has to figure out which one created the sound before anyone can confidently connect that event to a plate. Another major player can actually make sound visible Intelligent Instruments is not alone in this market. Sorama, a Dutch acoustic technology company, has also supplied equipment for U.S. noise-camera programs. Sorama's technology uses microphone arrays to locate a sound source and display it visually over an image or video. In simple terms, the system can show where the noise came from instead of only telling you how loud it was. Newport, Rhode Island, uses Sorama technology in mobile equipment that can move between problem areas. The city wanted flexibility because its loud-vehicle complaints can shift between traffic hot spots. Sorama says Newport expanded the program after its initial deployment. Newport's program has gone beyond data collection. Drivers can receive $250 citations for excessive vehicle noise, according to reporting on the city's system. Albuquerque, New Mexico, also partnered with Sorama for a three-camera pilot that began in 2025. Two units went to designated areas, while a mobile camera could move around the city. The six-month test collected noise data without issuing fines. Albuquerque officials were still asking for analysis of the program in early 2026. Santa Fe is taking noise cameras further Santa Fe, New Mexico, is one of the newest cities to move from a pilot-style concept toward a broader enforcement program. The city signed a five-year contract worth up to $4 million with Jenoptik Smart Mobility Solutions for automated speed and noise enforcement. City records show the agreement covers automated speed and noise enforcement services. Santa Fe's initial plan called for six mobile enforcement devices. Three would serve the north side and three would serve the south. One device on each side would include both speed and sound enforcement. The other four would focus on speed. Jenoptik says the systems capture a violator's license plate and send the event for law enforcement review. The city also planned a warning period before moving into citations. Maryland has put another noise camera on the road University Park, Maryland, activated a noise-enforcement camera at Adelphi Road and Van Buren Road on Jan. 7, 2026. The town says the device is part of a larger county and state effort to deal with excessive vehicle noise. University Park secured one of two noise cameras authorized for Prince George's County through the pilot. Maryland's experience is another sign that these systems are spreading through state and local pilot programs rather than through one national rollout. West Haven is preparing to join the list West Haven, Connecticut, is one of the latest communities moving toward noise-camera enforcement. The city plans to add four noise-detection devices along its shoreline, an area where residents have complained about loud vehicles. As of mid-September 2026, the broader program had not gone live. WFSB reported that the devices were expected to be installed within about a month. Connecticut law allows municipalities to use photo noise violation monitoring devices if they adopt an ordinance. The state sets the threshold at 80 decibels for qualifying violations, excluding certain horn sounds. State law also lays out the penalty structure. A first violation brings a written warning. A second carries a $100 fine, while a third or later violation carries a $250 fine. A police officer or municipal employee must review the images before the city mails a citation. East Hartford has also authorized noise cameras, although the town has not implemented them yet. Boston and Providence are looking at noise cameras too The trend could spread further. Boston City Council approved a request in August 2026 to explore a noise-camera program. The discussion grew out of complaints about loud cars and street takeovers. Boston had not launched a program at that point. Providence, Rhode Island, has gone a step further in its planning. The city issued a request for proposals seeking companies for a 16-month acoustic-camera pilot. The specifications call for equipment that can detect and document potential violations. They also call for a system capable of producing evidence that could support citations. Who makes these noise cameras? There is no single Flock Safety equivalent controlling this market. Several companies are developing acoustic roadside enforcement systems. California Highway Patrol has tested technology from Intelligent Instruments, Jenoptik and Dutch mobility company TNL. That evaluation also exposed one of the biggest challenges facing the entire industry. How does a noise camera know which car was loud? This is the tricky part. A regular sound meter can tell you how loud something is. That does not necessarily tell you which moving vehicle caused the noise. Noise cameras try to solve that problem with multiple microphones. Software compares the sound reaching each microphone and calculates where it came from. A camera then provides the visual evidence. For example, SoundVue says its Halo microphone array can identify the dominant vehicle even when other vehicles are nearby. The system then combines that acoustic information with video and a license plate image. New York describes a similar process. Its panoramic camera places a marker over the source identified by the microphone array. A separate plate reader captures the vehicle's license plate. That sounds impressive. However, California's testing shows why cities still need to be careful. California found accuracy problems worth watching The California Highway Patrol evaluated sound-activated enforcement systems from TNL, Intelligent Instruments and Jenoptik. Technical problems prevented CHP from fully evaluating all three systems. Only the Intelligent Instruments device produced enough usable data for a detailed analysis. CHP found that the technology could detect excessive exhaust noise. However, the agency concluded that the systems it evaluated were not adequate as standalone enforcement tools. One challenge involved reliably tying the noise to the correct vehicle. Lighting, license plate visibility and traffic conditions could also affect the evidence. The study covered specific equipment under specific testing conditions, so it does not prove that every noise-camera system will make the same mistakes. Still, it explains why human review plays such a big role in many of these programs. A microphone can detect a loud event. Turning that event into a fine requires a higher level of confidence. Noise cameras also create another license plate record The privacy conversation goes beyond whether a microphone can hear your exhaust. Many of these systems capture a license plate after a noise event. New York says its camera positioning allows the plate to appear while keeping occupants and the vehicle's interior out of the video. Connecticut law also restricts how noise-camera information can be collected and used. It requires human review before a citation and sets rules around the recorded images. Still, those protections can vary depending on where you drive. A city considering noise cameras should be able to explain what it records, who can access the information and how long that data stays on file. We have already seen why that deserves attention with other roadside camera systems. We recently covered how a Flock camera hit helped send the wrong woman to jail. Prosecutors later dropped the charges, and the case showed what can happen when investigators treat camera information as a conclusion instead of one piece of evidence. What this means to you For most drivers, a noise camera may never trigger anything. However, where you drive can change the rules considerably. One city may use the technology to issue fines. Another may send warnings. Somewhere else, the camera may collect data without identifying drivers for enforcement. The sound being targeted can differ as well. New York looks for several types of excessive vehicle noise. Avoca focuses on loud engine braking. Other communities are mainly concerned about modified exhausts or street racing. If you receive a noise-camera citation, review the evidence that comes with it. Check the location, time and vehicle information. Find out whether a person reviewed the event before the citation went out. You can also look at the local process for challenging the citation if you believe the system picked the wrong vehicle. If your town announces a noise-camera program, ask who supplies the equipment. Then look at what the system records and how long officials keep that information. Those details can tell you much more than the words "noise camera" on a city agenda. Kurt's key takeaways Noise cameras feel like the next chapter in a much bigger change happening along American roads. Cameras started by watching traffic. License plate readers made vehicles searchable. Now acoustic systems can listen for one particular car as it passes. I can understand why people who hear roaring exhausts outside their homes at 2 a.m. want a better way to deal with the problem. An officer cannot sit on every noisy street waiting for the next car to come through. Still, California's testing gives me pause about treating a noise reading as automatic proof. A busy roadway can be a complicated place to figure out exactly where a sound came from. Human review and a clear appeals process become especially important when a machine-generated event can cost someone hundreds of dollars. I would also watch the companies behind these systems. Intelligent Instruments, Sorama and Jenoptik are building a new category of roadside technology. As more cities sign contracts, we should know what their equipment collects, how accurate it is and what happens to the information after the car drives away. Would you want a noise camera on your street if it stopped loud cars from waking you up at 2 a.m., or does tying roadside microphones to license plate technology go too far? title: 4 killed, 4 wounded in mass shooting near capital of Caribbean luxury tourism destination
description: Four people were killed and four others were wounded in a shooting near Kingstown in St. Vincent and the Grenadines as police search for those responsible.
content: A shooting near the capital of St. Vincent and the Grenadines left four people dead and four others wounded Friday night, prompting an intensified police response in the Caribbean island nation as authorities search for those responsible. Gunfire erupted shortly before 10:30 p.m. in the Green Hill community near Kingstown, according to Acting Commissioner of Police Trevor Bailey, who addressed the killings during a Saturday news conference. Officers responding to the scene found two bodies on a public road, while a woman was found dead inside a vehicle parked nearby, Bailey said. ROBBERIES, ASSAULTS AND RAPES SPUR NEW US TRAVEL WARNING FOR POPULAR CARIBBEAN GETAWAY A fourth victim was discovered on an adjacent piece of land. All four appeared to have suffered gunshot wounds. Four additional people were taken to Milton Cato Memorial Hospital with gunshot injuries. Two were treated and released, while two remained hospitalized at the time of the police briefing. Assistant Commissioner of Police Brenton Smith said investigators were working to identify whoever was responsible and cautioned against speculation while the investigation remained active. Police were also investigating a separate shooting in Ottley Hall early Saturday and had not determined whether the two incidents were connected. "That determination must be made by investigators based on the evidence and not on rumors or assumptions," Smith said. The killings come as authorities grapple with gun and gang violence across the small island nation. Smith said 37 murders have been recorded in St. Vincent and the Grenadines so far this year. US UPDATES TRAVEL WARNING FOR QUAKE-HIT NATION, CITING DISASTER RISKS AND VIOLENT CRIME Bailey acknowledged that police have seen instances of retaliatory violence involving rival groups but did not link the Green Hill killings to gang activity. Asked whether criminal groups could be connected to the latest violence, police said the investigation had not reached a point where they could make such a determination. Authorities said additional patrols, random searches and intelligence operations were underway in Kingstown and surrounding communities as police attempt to recover illegal firearms and prevent further violence. Local outlet iWitness News reported that the Green Hill attack was one of several shootings in recent years in which multiple people were killed, including a July shooting in Kingstown that left three people dead. The outlet reported the identities of Friday's four victims based on its own sources, though police had not officially released their names when the report was published. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The violence occurred in a country heavily promoted for its secluded Caribbean setting and high-end tourism. St. Vincent and the Grenadines consists of 32 islands and cays and is promoted by the country's tourism authority as a destination for sailing, beaches, coral reefs and secluded getaways. Mustique, one of its inhabited islands, is known for private villas and celebrity visitors, while the broader archipelago is a major destination for yachts and sailing. title: First-ever images reveal mysterious remains of town swallowed by sea 700 years ago
description: Divers captured the first known images of Shipden, a medieval village lost to the North Sea for some 700 years. The pictures reveal massive flint structures.
content: Divers recently captured the first-known images of mysterious underwater structures believed to be remnants of a village swallowed by the sea some 700 years ago. The images and video were recently taken off the coast of Norfolk in the United Kingdom, as news agency Jam Press reported. The remains are believed to be the lost town of Shipden, a medieval settlement that was eventually consumed by the North Sea in the 14th century. MYSTERIOUS SETTLEMENT DISCOVERED AFTER RESIDENTS SEEMINGLY PACKED UP AND VANISHED At the site, divers photographed and mapped 25 man-made features. Pictures show massive, marine-covered stone structures jutting from the sandy seabed as divers explored the centuries-old site. Volunteer divers from the East Anglian branch of the British Sub-Aqua Club (BSAC) helped survey and map the underwater site as part of the Alfred Savin Project's investigation. Despite the North Sea's reputation for rough and dangerous conditions, the water was unusually still during the summer dives — which helped the team photograph and map features on the seabed. FAINT SIGNAL LEADS TREASURE HUNTERS TO MASSIVE DISCOVERY AT LEGENDARY 400-YEAR-OLD WRECK The divers found structures made of flint — a popular building material in medieval Norfolk — as well as other pieces of cut stone and the remains of stone foundation structures known as caissons. The caissons may have been part of a 14th-century attempt to hold back the sea, but researchers have yet to determine their exact purpose. Some structures remain eight to 10 layers of stone high despite spending centuries underwater. The effort marks the first time the features are believed to have been photographed. UNDERWATER ROBOTICS EXPERT REVEALS 'SHIPWRECK CITY' HIDING BENEATH MAJOR URBAN LAKE Once a thriving village, Shipden was home to a modest population in the High Middle Ages. The Domesday Book — the survey that recorded land and populations across England following the Norman Conquest — noted that Shipden had just 117 residents in 1086. The town also boasted three acres of meadow, a harbor, two churches and "woodland capable of supporting 36 pigs," Jam Press noted. By the 14th century, its name gradually disappeared from records and the area became known as Cromer. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Historical records confirm that a church was lost to the sea, but divers have yet to find any remains that can be definitively identified as the building. Legend holds that the tower of St. Peter's Church survived beneath the waves on a formation known as Church Rock. "For the present, we’re putting forward ideas rather than conclusions." Lead diver Nick Schiller told Jam Press the team initially set out to search for additional remains of the Victoria, a vessel that wrecked on Church Rock in 1888. "However, it’s been a bonus to help the Cromer team to take some steps forward in understanding the town of Shipden and the port of Cromer," said Schiller. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS He said the findings suggest that Church Rock, long believed to be connected to the lost church, may instead be the remains of medieval sea defenses. For now, the location of the church remains a mystery. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Looking ahead, Peter Stibbons, chair of the Friends of Cromer Museum and director of the project, said researchers are examining medieval records alongside the physical discoveries to gain a better understanding of the area. "Those of us brought up in Cromer have always known the story of Church Rock, so it’s a big step to saying the legend may be incorrect," Stibbons told Jam Press. content: It's Sunday, and I am back after taking a couple of days off last week. More on that in a minute. But first up on the Screencaps agenda today is the transition from summer to fall. It's about putting the swimsuits and short shorts away and reaching for the sweatshirts and warmer clothing. It's also about properly paying your respects to the summer that was. When you're in the content game and considered one of the best, like golf's top influencer Paige Spiranac, bidding adieu to summer while looking forward to fall shouldn't be difficult. SYDNEY THOMAS MOCKS LANE KIFFIN AFTER LOSS WITH BRUTAL HALLOWEEN COSTUME IDEA, LSU FANS FIGHT & NATE'S SHORTS That is, of course, if you're not overthinking it. Any up-and-coming influencers out there, take a page from Paige's playbook and revisit summer with a highlight package of some of your best work. This isn't about trying to outproduce anyone with the content. It's about respect. When you give it, you receive it. Here's how one of the best to ever do it approached it. "Saying goodbye to summer golf and hello to fall golf😍," Paige wrote. "but first wanted to revisit some summer golf fun⛳️" There's another lesson to be learned from this and that's to keep your foot on the gas. You won't see Paige Spiranac blowing many leads at home. She keeps at it no matter how far out in front she is. PAIGE SPIRANAC GIVES PEOPLE WHAT THEY DIDN'T KNOW THEY NEEDED: HER YOGURT BOWL RECIPE The same can't be said for Michigan It was a tough day for some Big Ten teams at home on Saturday. Most notably for No. 12 USC, who ended up losing 41-27 to No. 20 Oregon. And for No. 18 Michigan, who didn't have any extra time available during their 20-19 walk-off loss to No. 17 Iowa. The Michigan loss, which you really hate to see, produced real art. Take a look at this touchdown and the reaction from the Wolverine student section. The shock. The horror. I'm well aware of No. 13 ranked Penn State losing to unranked Wisconsin at home and blowing a 17-point lead. But I was under the impression that James Franklin was no longer the head coach and that ugly losses were a thing of the past. Although to be fair to Franklin, up until his last season, he didn’t lose these types of games all that often. It's the wakeup call Penn State needed. title: NFL told Azeez Al-Shaair he'd be pulled from Texans game over pro-Palestinian eyeblack message
description: Azeez Al-Shaair wore pro-Palestinian eyeblack again in Week 2 against the Cincinnati Bengals but was told he'd be removed from the Houston Texans game.
content: Azeez Al-Shaair tried for the second consecutive week to mark his eyeblack with an anti-Israel and pro-Palestinian message last week, but backed down when an NFL official told him he'd be removed from the game if he persisted, an NFL source told OutKick. Al-Shaair, a linebacker for the Houston Texans, was fined $11,492 in Week 1 when he inscribed the name of slain Palestinian girl Hind Rajab on his eyeblack to highlight her death during a bombing in Gaza by the Israeli Defense Force. The NFL prohibits the display of personal messages by players throughout game day. NFL FINES PLAYER NICKNAMED 'JUICE' $14,926 FOR USING A DRINKING CELEBRATION, CALLING IT OFFENSIVE Al-Shaair, who is Muslim, was undeterred by the cost of the Week 1 fine because he came out for warmups before the Week 2 game against the Cincinnati Bengals wearing the name of another Palestinian girl – Wafaa Akila – on his eyeblack. The eyeblack inscription remained even when the game began but then an NFL official spotted it, according to the league source, and informed the Texans and Al-Shaair he must remove it or he'd be removed from the game altogether. NEW NFL FINE SCHEDULE IS GOING TO A POINT SYSTEM THAT COULD LEAD TO SUSPENSIONS BUT ALSO REFUNDS The threat of not being able to play apparently convinced Al-Shaair to do something the threat of being fined again obviously did not. He removed the eyeblack and played the entire rest of the game without any eyeblack. The threat of fines is not important to Al-Shaair. He signed a three-year contract extension worth $54 million in April. He also did not appeal last week's fine. NBA STAR KYRIE IRVING JUMPS INTO NFL DRAMA, OFFERS TO PAY PLAYER'S FINE FOR GAZA-THEMED EYE BLACK "What’s a life worth?" Al-Shaair told reporters last week when questioned about the fine and his anti-Israel campaign. "Is a life worth $11,000? I think it’s priceless. So, to sit there and say that, ‘Oh man, the money’ and whatever, that wasn’t relevant to me." PRO-PALESTINE PROTESTER WHO INTERRUPTED SUPER BOWL LIX HALFTIME SHOW FOUND GUILTY IN COURT But playing time obviously is relevant to Al-Shaair, who is now basically on the NFL's radar for repeatedly trying to amplify pro-Palestine and anti-Israeli messages on game days. In January, the linebacker was fined $11,593 for wearing eyeblack on which he inscribed the slogan "Stop the Genocide." So is the NFL cracking down on Al-Shaair personally? No. The league has a long history of not allowing players to share personal messaging. And it has a long history of cautioning players that if they persist, they will be removed from games. Chicago Bears quarterback Jim McMahon was told prior to Super Bowl XX in 1986 that he must abstain from wearing a headband with messages or would not be allowed to play. Maxx Crosby, Odell Beckham and A.J. Brown have been told during various times they must change out of personalized cleats or be removed from a game. Last week, Arizona Cardinals defensive back Kei'Trel Clark was fined when he inscribed his eyeblack with the message "Glory B 2 God." NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE SLOGANS ON FIELDS WHILE ITS BATTLING DRUNK DRIVING, DOMESTIC ABUSE, PROSTITUTION ARREST OFF THE FIELD Why does the NFL have this policy when it actually inscribes messages on its fields every game day? Simple: The league wants to maintain consistency in how its teams and players look and avoid, as one source put it, "the wild west out there." That is clearly the right approach. If the NFL allowed players to express their individualism by marking up their uniforms, helmets, eyeblack, cleats, or themselves, it's impossible to predict in what direction those personalized messages would go. Al-Shaair is an example of that. He is not an honest broker about what is happening in Gaza or in the Hamas-Israel conflict. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! He has a certain worldview about the Middle East and that's what he's trying to amplify on the NFL stage. He has highlighted, what is in the case of Rajab, the death of an innocent Palestinian girl. But he has never mentioned the death of all the innocent Israeli boys and girls that preceded it on Oct. 7, 2023. And he has never mentioned the way Hamas uses children as shields, couriers, and even as weapons transporters while the IDF holds fire. The Houston Texans play visit the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday. The NFL will be watching. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

title: Human vs. ChatGPT NFL Week 3 betting picks: can AI recover from its ugly 2-8 start to the season?

THREE WORD GAME: THREE WORDS TO DESCRIBE EVERY NFL TEAM SO FAR THIS SEASON AHEAD OF WEEK 3 Every wager is sized to win one unit, which means a bet at -110 risks 1.10 units to win one, while a bet at +110 risks 0.91 units to win one. Jacksonville lost by seven, the Giants got blown out by 22 and Kansas City needed overtime to beat Indianapolis by three. GPT is now 0-7 on spread and moneyline picks through two weeks. SEASON REPORT CARD DAN: 5-5, -0.24 units GPT: 2-8, -6.50 units Dan’s Week 3 NFL Betting Card 1. New York Giants -2½ (-110) Tennessee Titans at New York Giants, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET Dan’s analysis: This is what's known as a "plug your nose" bet. title: I lost a state championship to a boy. I refuse to lose my voice
description: A Minnesota softball player describes losing her state championship semifinal to a team with a transgender pitcher and her fight for female athletes.
content: I have never been much of a crier. So when my softball team lost in the semifinals of the Minnesota state tournament, I surprised even myself. I sobbed to my parents and family. I was devastated, confused, and hurt. But underneath it all was a sense of helplessness. I was a senior, and my biggest goal was to make the state tournament and play alongside my younger sister. We made it. We battled through the tournament as underdogs. And then our season ended because the opposing team was allowed to put a boy in as the pitcher on a girls' team. His team went on to win the girls' high school state championship. WE WERE FORCED TO COMPETE AGAINST A MALE. THE SUPREME COURT HAD OUR BACKS I wasn't crying because we had simply lost a softball game. I was crying because I couldn't understand how the adults who were supposed to protect girls like me had allowed this to happen. I later learned that his parents had changed his legal documents to reflect the opposite sex when he was a young boy. What shocked me even more was the realization that the adults around us—administrators, policymakers and legislators—had allowed it and left girls like me tossed aside, hurt and abandoned. WHAT'S NEXT IN THE BATTLE TO 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' AFTER SCOTUS RULING — AND THE HIDDEN DAMAGE DRIVING IT We were expected to accept it, play through it and remain quiet. But the consequences didn't stop with my team. When a male athlete advances through a girls' state tournament, every girl who might have faced that team is affected. Every roster spot, inning, championship, award and recruiting opportunity matters. At the elite level, one tournament can change a player's future. The impact extends across girls' teams throughout an entire state. RILEY GAINES: SUPREME COURT HANDS WOMEN AN IMPORTANT WIN, BUT THE FIGHT ISN’T OVER After our loss, I decided I wasn't going to stay quiet. I never imagined that decision, or that loss on a softball field in Minnesota, would eventually bring me to Washington, D.C. On Wednesday, I spoke at a press conference on Capitol Hill following a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on opportunity, fairness and safety for female athletes. Getting to this point has not been easy. My decision to openly share my experience has come at a price. DEMOCRAT SENATORS FLEE OR NO-SHOW JUDICIARY COMMITTEE HEARING ON PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS I was recruited to play Division I softball at Western Michigan University. I entered college hoping to find my voice and pursue my dreams as a student-athlete. Instead, I felt isolated and shamed for speaking publicly about what I had experienced. I was even directed not to identify my university to the media. The message was clear: Keep quiet. I believed then, and still believe now, that girls should not have to surrender roster spots, playing time or championships to boys because some adults have decided that the feelings of boys mean more than the feelings and opportunities of girls. JONATHAN ALPERT: WOMEN WERE TOLD TO SPEAK UP. EXCEPT ABOUT WOMEN’S SPORTS In an introductory sociology class, I was assigned a paper explaining the difference between sex and gender. I received a zero. My professor told me to "remove any bias and dive deeper into the difference between the two." She was telling me I was wrong to treat sex and gender as synonyms and that a person could identify as another gender by adopting stereotypes associated with the opposite sex. Confusing? Yeah, I know. I felt like I was being asked to erase my own perspective and accept something I believed was untrue as fact. I won't accept that women can be defined by sexist stereotypes. This wasn't just a classroom debate. I had lived it. The lack of support from my coaches and the pressure in my coursework led me to transfer after my freshman season. THESE FEMALE ATHLETES NEED TO SPEAK UP ABOUT KEEPING WOMEN'S SPORTS FOR WOMEN, LIKE SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DID Today, I play softball at Colorado Christian University. I feel supported, encouraged to speak out and, most importantly, unashamed to tell the truth about what happened to me. I am now a sophomore in college, but I still think about that girl crying after the state tournament. I think about my younger sister, my cousins and all the girls coming after us. I WAS A FEMALE ATHLETE, NOW I FIGHT FOR THEM IN COURT. WE NEED MORE SOPHIE CUNNINGHAMS I can't change what happened on that field or give my team back the opportunity we lost. But I can refuse to let that loss teach the next generation of girls that they have to accept being pushed aside. I want my sister and little cousins to grow up knowing that when adults fail to protect girls, girls can still find the courage to protect one another.
