title: Trump's Greenland obsession isn’t random. Here’s what’s at stake
description: Greenland's untapped rare earth minerals, oil and gas reserves could reshape U.S. energy security as Trump's Denmark deal expands military presence.
content: Greenland may be covered in ice, but beneath its surface could be resources critical to the global economy — including rare earth minerals, nickel, copper, palladium, cobalt, oil and natural gas. The Arctic island’s location is just as valuable. Positioned between North America and Europe, Greenland sits along key military and shipping routes. As conflicts in Ukraine and Iran expose vulnerabilities in global energy and supply chains, the island has become increasingly important to the United States and other world powers. WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS Those factors help explain why President Donald Trump has spent years pushing for greater American control and influence in Greenland and why his administration recently reached a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland. The deal, which Trump signed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, will expand the U.S. military presence on the island while keeping Greenland under Danish sovereignty. Here are three reasons Greenland has become one of the world’s most strategically important places. 1. Greenland could hold critical minerals the U.S. needs The United States is seeking to reduce its dependence on China and Russia for critical minerals used in electronics, batteries, energy infrastructure and defense technology. "We don’t want to be dependent on China for our rare earth minerals, and we don’t want to be dependent on Russia for them either," Robert Price, CEO of Greenland Energy Company and president of USFM Corporation, told Fox News Digital. FLOURISH CHART EMBED HERE: 30309299 Price’s USFM is exploring nickel, copper, palladium and cobalt deposits around Disko Island in western Greenland. He said the region could eventually rival Russia’s mineral-rich Norilsk district, though its potential remains unproven as drilling continues. 2. Greenland could become an energy source Greenland’s potential riches extend beyond minerals. Price’s Greenland Energy Company is pursuing permits for an exploratory oil well planned for 2027 on the island’s eastern side, where he said the geology resembles the petroleum-producing North Sea. "Our licenses are similar to the same petroleum system as the North Sea," Price said, adding that the company has sampled oil on and below the surface. TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER The project comes as the Iran war disrupts global energy markets and threatens shipping through the Strait of Hormuz a critical artery for the world’s oil supply. "One of the reasons that we are exploring for oil in Greenland is because of what’s going on in the Strait of Hormuz right now," Price said. Greenland’s oil and gas potential remains unproven and would require additional permits, exploration and investment. 3. Greenland occupies a critical military position Greenland’s strategic value also comes from its location between North America and Europe, near key air, sea and missile routes connecting the United States, Russia and Europe. The U.S. has maintained a military presence on the island for decades. Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, is the northernmost Defense Department installation and supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance. Melting Arctic ice is opening new shipping routes and increasing interest from the United States, Russia and China. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump’s agreement with Denmark and Greenland would expand the U.S. military presence while preserving Danish sovereignty, according to the administration. Price said the deal could also boost investor confidence in long-term oil, gas and mineral projects. "What it does is it shores up long-term investment in Greenland, and that’s what our projects are," Price said. "They’re long-term investments from oil, gas and minerals."

title: Four American tourists among 6 killed after explosion levels building near Athens’ Acropolis
description: A suspected gas leak caused an explosions that leveled a residential building in Athens' Plaka district near the Acropolis, killing four American tourists and two residents.
content: Four American tourists were among six people killed in Greece when a devastating explosion leveled a residential building near Athens’ famed Acropolis, according to officials. The four Americans — two men and two women believed to be two couples — were staying in the two-story building in the historic Plaka district, the historic neighborhood at the foot of the Acropolis and close to some of Athens’ most heavily visited landmarks, when the blast struck Friday. The two couples had been expected to catch a flight from Athens airport at 3 p.m. Friday but never showed up, a police source told Reuters. Documents and belongings recovered with the four victims indicated they were U.S. citizens, according to Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media. AMERICAN TOURISTS STABBED OUTSIDE ATHENS' ACROPOLIS AS POLICE DETAIN SUSPECT IN APPARENT RANDOM ATTACK U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle mourned the victims in a post on X. "I am deeply saddened to learn of the death of four American citizens in yesterday’s explosion in central Athens," Guilfoyle wrote. Emergency crews searching through the rubble recovered six bodies from the collapsed building Saturday, authorities said. Firefighters had been searching for an elderly couple who lived in one apartment and four tourists staying in another as crews painstakingly removed debris, fire brigade spokesman Vassilis Vathrakogiannis said in a televised briefing. EXPLOSION NEAR GERMAN TRAIN STATION INJURES 2 UKRAINIAN CITIZENS The explosion was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Authorities were investigating the cause after reports of a gas smell in the area. The powerful blast destroyed the building and damaged nearby homes, shops and vehicles, sending rubble and shattered glass as far as three blocks away, Reuters reported. Video from the scene showed debris strewn across the street and parked cars crushed beneath falling rubble. The destroyed building was reduced to twisted metal, broken tiles and concrete, with clothing and household belongings scattered among the wreckage. The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs, while crews also used cameras and sensors to comb through the debris. title: Popular food could boost heart health, but the amount you need to eat may surprise you
description: A major meta-analysis of 87 trials reveals that 60 to 100 grams of whole grains daily may lower cholesterol, blood pressure and blood sugar levels.
content: A bowl of oatmeal, a sandwich on whole-grain bread and a side of brown rice may do more for your heart and overall health than you think, according to a new study. Eating four to six servings of whole grains each day may offer the greatest benefits for heart health, lowering body weight, cholesterol, blood sugar and blood pressure, a large meta-analysis published in the European Heart Journal found. The analysis reviewed data from 87 randomized trials involving more than 6,500 people across Asia, Europe, the United States, Canada, Australia and Brazil. MAN SAYS MEAT-ONLY 'LION DIET' CLEARED PSORIASIS COVERING 90% OF HIS BODY, ENDED DECADES OF DEPRESSION It found that many of the greatest benefits occurred when people ate about 60 to 100 grams of whole grains daily — about what you would get from a bowl of oatmeal, two slices of whole-grain bread and a serving of brown rice, according to the researchers. "This is the largest and most comprehensive meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on whole-grain intake and cardiovascular risk factors," lead author Helda Tutunchi, of Tabriz University of Medical Sciences in Iran, said in a statement. People who consumed more whole grains had lower body weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, total cholesterol, LDL ("bad") cholesterol, triglycerides, blood glucose and levels of interleukin-6, an inflammatory marker, the study also found. One key finding, Tutunchi noted, was that whole grains appeared to boost heart health through "several modest improvements acting together, rather than through one large effect on a single factor." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The researchers cautioned, however, that most of the studies they looked at were short and did not measure heart attacks or strokes directly. Longer-term research is still needed, they said. Four to six servings of whole grains is more than the two to four servings the current Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend — and many Americans don't even hit that, said Lauren Manaker, a South Carolina-based registered dietitian nutritionist. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Going from zero to six is a lot," Manaker, who wasn't involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "My recommendation is to start slow. Two servings is better than zero servings." Simple swaps can include starting the day with oatmeal or overnight oats, or replacing refined grains with whole-grain sides such as sorghum or brown rice, she said. Consumers should also be careful not to assume every brown-colored loaf at the supermarket is whole grain, Manaker added. "We want to look at the ingredient list and make sure one of the first ingredients is a whole grain," she said. "We also want to look at the nutrition panel and make sure there's some fiber in there." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Whole grains contain all three parts of the grain kernel — the bran, germ and endosperm — rather than having some parts removed during processing, the researchers noted. While researchers say more studies are needed, they concluded that increasing whole-grain intake is "a relatively simple, accessible and affordable dietary strategy" that can complement other heart-healthy habits. In an editorial that accompanied the report, Cecilie Kyro of the Danish Cancer Institute in Copenhagen and her colleagues encouraged policies that make minimally processed whole-grain staples accessible, affordable and culturally acceptable while also "avoiding a drift towards ultra-processed products." title: College football week 4 contenders, pretenders: Texas survives, Michigan's karma and coaches are sweating
description: Iowa stunned Michigan on a last-second touchdown, and LSU's Lane Kiffin sent Texas A&M fans into panic mode on a wild college football Saturday.
content: KNOXVILLE, TN - It only took four weeks of action to immerse ourselves in the madness of college football, with upsets and teams already up against the ropes heading into the month of October. Are schools already looking to make changes at the head coaching position? Sure, and some leaders might end up making the decision pretty easy for their bosses. But what we witnessed on Saturday will go down as one of the wildest weekends of this early season, and there will be ramifications. ARCH MANNING REVELS IN CIGAR SMOKE: TEXAS LEAVES NEYLAND WITH WIN—AND A WARNING FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL Heck, Texas led Tennessee by ten points late in the fourth quarter, but had to withstand a last minute drive by the Vols to get out of Knoxville with the win. There wasn’t even a touchdown pass thrown by Arch Manning on Saturday, but the defense ended up with over ten sacks on Vols quarterback Faizon Brandon, in what felt like a Will Muschamp defensive revival. We're only getting started on this wild weekend in college football. Oregon lost quarterback Dante Moore to a head injury in the first half, thanks to a dirty hit. But, that did not end their hopes of beating USC. Two weeks after losing to Oklahoma State, the Ducks rolled into Southern Cal and once again left Trojan fans wondering when Lincoln Riley was going to win a few meaningful games. We don't know when Moore will return, but backup Dylan Raiola took the reigns on Saturday night and never looked back. Throwing for over 280 yards against USC, this might be the start of Raiola's redemption tour, at least until Dante Moore returns. But, a massive 41-27 win for the Ducks have put their season back on track, while USC fans are left wondering what else Lincoln Riley feels like putting them through. Who would of thought before the season started that Oklahoma would already be regretting that contract extension for Brent Venables. But just four games into the 2026 season, the Sooners have a major problem on their hands, thanks in part to the 41-13 drumming by the Georgia Bulldogs on Saturday afternoon in Athens. Not a trap, Florida earned Ole Miss' respect. Beamer in trouble. Hey, Kamario Taylor Oh, and if you were wondering whether Ole Miss was walking into a trap this week in Gainesville after defeating LSU last weekend, I think that would be disrespecting what Jon Sumrall is doing with the Florida Gators. A 52-28 loss on the road brought the Rebels back down to reality, with Pete Golding having to regroup his team this week after a rollercoaster two-week stretch. But make no mistake about it, the Florida Gators look nothing like the team we witnessed during the Billy Napier era. FLORIDA DROPS IMPRESSIVE OFFENSIVE PERFORMANCE TO PULL OFF MASSIVE WIN OVER NO. 4 OLE MISS And, speaking of teams we thought could get things back on track in 2026, South Carolina has itself a major problem moving forward under head coach Shane Beamer. Not only were they beaten 49-18 by Alabama, the Gamecocks feel like a rudderless ship, with such high expectations for quarterback LaNorris Sellers before the season began. Now? The Gamecocks lost their seventh-straight SEC game, and it doesn’t look any better moving forward. Well, this is only going to make things worse in Columbia for Beamer, who had spent a good chunk of money to keep a number of stars from hitting the portal, like Dylan Stewart. Is Kamario Taylor going to end up being the catalyst that brings Mississippi State back to college football relevance? Well, he already has, and looks darn good in the process. The 24th ranked Bulldogs defeated No. 19 Missouri, winning their first ranked game in over a decade, with Taylor passing for over 350 yards on the night. Look out, Alabama. The Bulldogs are waiting next week in Starkville. \ Karma finally comes calling for Michigan. LSU sends Texas A&M fans into panic mode Yes, you read that right. An Iowa Hawkeyes touchdown with only one second left on the clock left Michigan fans stunned, probably the same way Western Michigan fans felt during the week-one controversy that allowed the Wolverines to escape with a win. Three weeks later, it was Kirk Ferentz who delivered the karma like a Taylor Swift single, which had college football fans outside of the state chuckling I'd imagine. No, this looks nothing like a team that should be paying its quarterback Bryce Underwood over $3 million per season. In reality, this feels like a squad headed for a December bowl game, and nowhere near the Big Ten championship. At this point, maybe it would be wise for Michigan fans to start preparing for the Ohio State game to end the season, and not get their hopes up every weekend. That win against Oklahoma also looks even worse by the week. So, you thought Lane Kiffin would just go quiet into the night after losing to his former team last week in Oxford? Umm, no. Not only did LSU take out their frustration on Texas A&M, but they made it look easy in the 38-6 win. Sam Leavitt carved up the Aggies secondary, while Kiffin found himself running down the sidelines celebrating a fourth-down trick play that turned into a touchdown. Simply put, the Tigers made Mike Elko's squad look like a mediocre SEC team without much hope moving forward. We should probably go ahead and count the Aggies out of making the College Football Playoff, while LSU looks to have gotten the 'Lane Train' back on the tracks in Baton Rouge. What in the world moments on Saturday... Can someone explain to me how Louisville could lose at home to Wake Forest 30-27, with this squad battling for 'surprise' team of the season out of the ACC? Well, that went up in smoke inside their own stadium. Oh, and how could we not mention the job Luke Fickell did on Saturday, leading his Wisconsin Badgers into Happy Valley and leaving with the 24-20 win that left folks in State College shocked. People forget that Fickell didn’t just wake up and turn into a bad coach. He just hasn’t had the necessary resources in Madison. He still might not have everything he needs to rebuild the Wisconsin football team, but they darn sure made Penn State pay for potentially looking past the Badgers. Week four of the college football season delivered, which will setup a wild start to the month of October. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Expect anything less?

title: UK police arrest 'explosive' suspects near US airbase, key to Iran war
description: Multiple suspects were arrested under the Explosives Act near RAF Fairford, prompting evacuations as explosive ordnance disposal teams examined vehicles.
content: U.K. police say they arrested multiple suspects for offenses under the "Explosives Act" near a U.S. airbase in southwest England on Sunday. Gloucestershire Police say the arrests took place just two miles from RAF Fairford, which hosts U.S. Air Force assets. The U.S. has recently used the base in operations relating to the war in Iran. "A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act." ANDY BURNHAM TAKES OVER AS UK PRIME MINISTER, CALLS FOR 'NEW POLITICAL MODEL' "The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles," police added. President Donald Trump responded to news of the arrests while talking to the press later Sunday. "The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain. It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation," Trump said of the suspects. "They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great." A reporter then asked if the suspects were migrants, and Trump demurred. "It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know that we worked with a lot of them. We had them under review for a long time and we got them," Trump said. Authorities did not name the suspects or detail exactly how many were arrested. British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting wrote on X that the situation is "being dealt with." UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC Prime Minister Andy Burnham also released a statement on the arrests. "I know today's incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country. My thanks go to Gloucestershire Police, Counter Terrorism Policing, our Armed Forces and all those working to keep the public safe," he said. "The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe. The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts," he added. WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES The incident comes roughly a month after Iran-linked hackers were suspected of forcing a small British power generator offline for several days this summer. The British shutdown came weeks after hackers struck more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota, accessing technology used to remotely monitor and control pumps and other equipment. Minnesota officials have not publicly attributed the attacks. Several news outlets, citing U.S. officials and a leaked industry threat-sharing memo, reported that Iran was the likely culprit. title: Iran ‘miscalculating’ by betting on midterms after 3-hour talks, Trump officials warn
description: President Donald Trump says Iran is waiting on midterm elections to cut a deal, but Marco Rubio warns Tehran misreads U.S. presidential powers.
content: NEW YORK — Trump officials say Iran is miscalculating if it believes rising prices and the midterm elections will weaken President Donald Trump's hand in negotiations to end the nearly seven-month conflict. The administration is projecting confidence that mounting economic pressure will push Tehran toward a deal, even after three hours of talks this week ended without an announced breakthrough. "The president holds all of the cards here," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. Americans, meanwhile, are facing a mounting cost at home. The national average for regular gasoline reached $4.49 per gallon Friday, according to AAA, up from $3.16 a year ago. AAA said volatility in the Strait of Hormuz and high crude oil prices have driven the national average to its highest level ever recorded for this time of year. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged those costs Wednesday while arguing that allowing Iran to eventually obtain a nuclear weapon would carry a far greater price. THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES "It comes at a price and at a cost, there's no doubt about it," Rubio told reporters. "But the cost of not doing something about it is substantially higher, especially for future generations." Trump himself laid out the stakes in stark terms during his address to the U.N. General Assembly Tuesday, presenting Tehran with a choice between reaching a deal that would allow Iran to rebuild or facing potentially devastating further U.S. action. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said. "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" But Trump predicted Tehran would ultimately choose a deal, arguing that Iranian leaders are waiting to see whether the November midterm elections weaken his position. "They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," Trump said. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running." "I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran," Trump added. "It doesn't even enter my mind." A U.S. official told Fox News Digital Friday that discussions through mediators remained "positive and constructive," but said the administration was in no hurry to reach an agreement. "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush," the official said, adding that nearly 40 million barrels of oil had transited the strait over the previous 48 hours. The official predicted oil and gas prices would fall back to pre-conflict levels as the U.S. continues to maintain control of the strait. Trump said U.S. officials held a "very good" three-hour meeting with Iranian officials Tuesday as part of a renewed diplomatic push to end the conflict. But Rubio cautioned Wednesday against characterizing the talks as a "major breakthrough," saying they were largely a continuation of previous conversations. "I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation," Rubio said. Rubio also said the administration would make public any "good outcomes or things to announce jointly" stemming from its diplomatic engagements. No such announcement immediately followed the Iran meeting. Iran has since put forward a proposal of its own. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran presented U.S. mediators with a seven-day plan this week that would restore passage through the Strait of Hormuz at the end of the seven days if certain conditions are met, followed by renewed negotiations toward a broader agreement. The proposal draws from the memorandum of understanding Trump and Iran reached in June. A mediator told CBS News the latest discussions were positive but remained in their early stages. The stakes in Hormuz remain high. Commercial traffic through the critical oil chokepoint has been sharply disrupted during the conflict, although U.S. officials say the amount of oil moving through the strait is increasing. TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN "The diplomatic door is always open. The president is a deal maker," Pigott said. "But he's going to see the fundamental principle that they cannot have a nuclear weapon accomplished one way or another." Pigott pointed to growing oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the economic pressure Washington has imposed on Tehran as evidence that the balance remains in Trump's favor. "We are seeing oil move [through] the Strait of Hormuz, increasing every single day," Pigott said. "We're seeing the devastating effects on the Iranian regime from economic [actions]. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being denied to the regime through this blockade that we're seeing." Rubio offered a similar assessment Wednesday when asked about Trump's assertion that Iran may be waiting for the outcome of the midterm elections before making a deal. "I think the Iranians misread our system," Rubio said. "I think the Iranians are under this illusion that Democrats are going to win in November, and the president will no longer be able to do things against them." Rubio said Congress remains an important branch of government but argued Tehran misunderstands the limits of congressional power over sanctions and military action. "The president has extraordinary powers. Every president does," Rubio said. "He's the commander in chief, both constitutional and otherwise, to be able to carry out those functions." "So I think that the Iranians are fundamentally misreading our political system," Rubio continued. The administration is also confronting threats to energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have targeted Saudi Arabia as the conflict has expanded, adding another source of uncertainty for global energy markets. Rubio said Wednesday that the restart of a Saudi pipeline following attacks was "critical for their economy" and "critical for the global economy." He said energy infrastructure had been targeted by the Houthis as well as Shiite militias in Iraq that the U.S. says are backed by Iran. "Every time you guys ask me a question about the Middle East, it goes back to someone who's supported by Iran," Rubio said. Rubio said the U.S. would continue honoring its defense commitments to Saudi Arabia while declining to discuss what additional military options Trump could consider. We are living up to those commitments now."

title: Fake ChatGPT billing emails can steal your login
description: A phishing campaign impersonating OpenAI uses fake ChatGPT billing emails with a convincing login page to steal credentials and payment details.
content: If you pay for ChatGPT, an email saying there is a problem with your subscription could easily get your attention. Maybe your card expired. Maybe the payment failed. Either way, you probably want to fix it before anything happens to your account. Cybercriminals are counting on that reaction. Security researchers at Cofense uncovered a phishing campaign that impersonates OpenAI and ChatGPT. The fake email looks like a routine subscription notice. However, the button inside can lead to a convincing copy of the ChatGPT login page. Cofense says the campaign targets account credentials and payment information. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Get Better Healthcare With AI replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com SCAMMERS KNOW THE BEST TIME TO TEXT YOU How the fake ChatGPT billing email works The scam starts with an email that looks polished enough to make you pause. According to the Cofense Phishing Defense Center, it uses the real ChatGPT logo and claims your subscription payment needs attention. Then comes the pressure. The message prominently displays "Subscription Payment Required." It also warns that you have 48 hours to act. A large "Update Payment Information" button gives you an obvious way to supposedly fix the problem. Finally, the message signs off as "The OpenAI Team." If you are checking email between meetings or quickly scrolling on your phone, all of that can feel believable. Cofense says the attackers combine familiar images, bold wording and urgency to push people into acting quickly. One email address exposes the ChatGPT scam The sender's email address is one of the biggest red flags. Cofense found that the phishing message came from support@9527db6e1a[.]nxcli[.]io. That domain has nothing to do with OpenAI. OpenAI currently lists several domains that it uses for legitimate customer emails. They include @openai.com, @mail.openai.com and @email.openai.com, along with other official OpenAI domains used for specific communications. That makes the full sender address worth checking. Do not rely on the name that appears in your inbox. A scammer can make the display name look reassuring while using a completely unrelated address behind it. FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER The fake payment button adds another trick The button inside this phishing email adds another layer of deception. Cofense found that clicking "Update Payment Information" first sent users through a Google API redirect. The link then forwarded them to the attacker's malicious site. That can make a suspicious link look more convincing at first glance because Google appears along the way. We have seen criminals abuse trusted services in similar attacks before. CyberGuy previously covered how hackers used legitimate Google Cloud tools to send phishing messages that looked like authentic Google notifications. So, seeing Google somewhere in a link does not tell you where you will eventually land. On a computer, hovering over a button can sometimes reveal the destination before you click. Still, redirects can make that check less useful. The safer option is to skip the email link entirely. The fake ChatGPT login page looks convincing Once someone clicks through, the scam gets harder to spot. Cofense says the phishing page closely copies the ChatGPT login experience, complete with familiar logos, text and icons. However, the domain in the browser does not match the legitimate ChatGPT login domain identified by Cofense. If a victim enters login information, the fake site captures it and sends it to the attacker. The page then sends the victim to an error screen, which could easily look like a temporary login problem. By then, the attacker may already have the credentials. That is why it is worth checking the address bar before you enter a password. Scammers can copy the look of a login page. They cannot make an unrelated domain belong to OpenAI. We reached out to OpenAI for comment but did not hear back before our deadline. Tips to stay safe from fake ChatGPT billing emails 1) Check your ChatGPT billing directly If an email says there is a payment problem, skip the button. Go directly to ChatGPT.com or open the official app and sign in yourself. For web subscriptions, OpenAI says to check Settings → Billing . Some accounts may show Settings → Account → Payment → Manage instead. If you subscribed through Apple or Google Play, manage your subscription through that store. 2) Check the full sender address Expand the sender information and look at the actual email address. In this campaign, the sender used an nxcli.io domain. OpenAI publishes the domains it uses for legitimate communications, which gives you something concrete to compare against. 3) Look at the domain before signing in Check the browser address bar before entering a password or payment information. If the domain looks unfamiliar, close the page. Then open the service yourself through its official app or website. This same habit can protect you from fake banking sites. We recently covered criminals who bought sponsored search ads that sent victims to lookalike bank login pages. 4) Use a unique password and password manager Never reuse your ChatGPT password on other accounts. We recommend using a unique password and suggest a password manager to generate and store it. That way, one stolen password cannot easily unlock several of your accounts. 5) Turn on multi-factor authentication OpenAI supports two-factor authentication, or 2FA. You can enable it from the Security section of your ChatGPT settings. Depending on your account, available verification methods may include an authenticator app, push notification, text message or passkey. 2FA adds another hurdle if someone gets your password. However, enabling 2FA does not automatically end sessions that are already logged in. 6) Use strong antivirus protection Strong antivirus software can help warn you about malicious links and phishing websites. It can also block other threats that may arrive through scam emails. Keep that protection updated on every device where you check email or sign in to important accounts. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 7) Act fast if you entered your ChatGPT password Change your password immediately if you entered it on a suspicious site. Then open ChatGPT and go to Settings → Security → Active sessions . Review the listed devices and sessions. If you see something you do not recognize, log it out. OpenAI also lets you go to Settings → Security → Active sessions and choose Log out of all session s. The company says signing out across every device can take up to 30 minutes. If you use Google, Microsoft or Apple to sign in to ChatGPT, secure that account as well. 8) Contact your card issuer if you entered payment details If you gave a suspicious site your card information, call the number on the back of the card. Tell the issuer that your payment information may have been compromised. Then review recent transactions for anything you do not recognize. Your card issuer may recommend replacing the card. Follow its instructions rather than waiting for a fraudulent charge to appear. 9) Tell your workplace if a company account was involved Cofense says the phishing campaign targeted people using ChatGPT through personal and work accounts. If you entered work credentials or used a company-managed account, contact your IT or security team. They can review account activity and take additional steps if necessary. Kurt's key takeaways This scam works because the email looks like something you might actually expect to receive. A payment problem feels routine, and that can make people lower their guard. If you get a billing warning from ChatGPT, do not use the link in the message. Open ChatGPT yourself and check your account there. If you already entered your password on a suspicious page, change it right away and review your active sessions. If you shared payment information, contact your card issuer. Stop disrespecting the people that lived here for decades." Tye said he's received encouragement from residents around town. "I'm getting a lot of support," he said. PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH' "It all started when they bought the mosque, roughly six years ago," said Tye. SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT An old industrial machinery business is now a mosque, as is a former Baptist church. Regardless of where we stand on an issue, every resident deserves dignity and respect." title: Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington fires back at lone holdout juror's attorney after fiery interview
description: Kevin Reddington fires back at Edward Paltzik, calling the holdout juror's attorney a "histrionic individual" as Lindsay Clancy's defense fights on.
content: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington has fired back after the lawyer of the lone juror who wanted to convict her accused him of filing "Looney Tunes" motions that threaten the Constitution. "I think Ed ought to learn how to go into the courtroom and articulate his position rather than be a histrionic individual that's just mouthing off for the media," Reddington told Fox News Digital. Reddington's remarks came in response to social media posts and a recent interview from the juror's attorney, Edward Paltzik, who has argued that Reddington's push for an inquiry into the holdout is "a full-frontal attack on the U.S. Constitution" and a threat to the Sixth Amendment, which guarantees due process rights to criminal defendants. CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR TAPS FORMER TRUMP LAWYER TO FIGHT BACK AS HE’S ‘DRAGGED THROUGH THE MUD’: ATTORNEY "Every motion that has been filed is legitimate," Reddington said. "It's all based on sound, law, facts, jury questions, and I'm doing what I should do, representing Lindsay. And I'm pretty sure that Ed would have probably done the same thing, were it in Houston, and he was representing his client." In an interview with Ray Marcel, a YouTuber who streams under the pseudonym FugitiveTV, Paltzik also called for Clancy's execution, although she hasn't been convicted of any criminal charges and Massachusetts does not impose the death penalty. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR MAKES NEW PROMISE AS LAWYER WARNS OF PUBLIC ATTACKS "Ed, why don't you just shut up?" Reddington said. "Really, you foul individual." However, Reddington joked that he didn't get Paltzik's "Shooter McGavin" reference at first but agreed that it was a funny jab after having someone explain it to him. Paltzik fired back on Friday. "It’s really not complicated. I’m not backing down. I’m not backing off of it one inch. It should not be controversial at all that I called Lindsay Clancy a ‘demon.’ …She strangled her three innocent children," he told Fox News Digital. And as for the challenge from Reddington to see him in court, he said he's working to find local counsel and that filings would be coming. "Kevin Reddington was doing his job but the problem is it’s off the rails now," Paltzik continued. "I’m speaking as a criminal defense attorney for almost 20 years. I would never criticize a juror. And I would never file a post-trial motion to investigate the juror." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Reddington also took issue with the juror being described as the "lone holdout juror." LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS "He is the obstructionist juror," Reddington said. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS The juror, identified by his attorney as Michael Desronvil, has said that he believes Clancy was guilty of the murder charges against her in the strangling deaths of her three young children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. JUROR ON LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL SAYS 'WE LET DOWN LINDSAY' FOLLOWING MISTRIAL CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Eleven other jurors disagreed and wanted to find her not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect, in alignment with Reddington's defense argument that Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible for her actions. SEND US A TIP Due to the deadlock, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after a week of deliberations. Clancy is due back in court Tuesday for a hearing on several defense motions. Prosecutors may also announce plans to seek a second trial. "My real advice to Kevin — I think he should stop whining and go prepare for a retrial," Paltzik said. "Stop complaining. You only got 11, you needed 12." LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN Reddington, in a motion filed last week, called for a "limited inquiry" into the holdout, for information about his background and potential criminal history, phone records, courthouse surveillance video and more. He said it. And you can’t do that as an officer of the court. It’s an attack on the system. And this motion to investigate him? It’s because Michael disagreed with Kevin Reddington." That motion also centered on the holdout juror and allegations that he ignored the judge's instructions and the law. LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "The jury twice informed the Court that one of its members was refusing to apply the Court's instructions regarding the fundamental concept of reasonable doubt," Weinberg wrote. title: SCOTUS detention fight could unleash dangerous criminal migrants onto US streets, experts warns
description: A Supreme Court battle over bond hearings for detained noncitizens with criminal records could make it harder for ICE to keep detainees locked up.
content: A Supreme Court battle over whether certain noncitizens with criminal records are entitled to bond hearings during lengthy deportation proceedings could become a public safety concern by making it harder for the federal government to keep some detainees behind bars, legal experts warn. The Trump administration is asking the justices to take up Genalo v. D.C., a case involving a Dominican citizen with four criminal convictions who has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement while fighting removal. The dispute centers on a Second Circuit precedent requiring a bond hearing when mandatory immigration detention becomes "unreasonably prolonged." At that hearing, the government must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the detainee poses a flight risk or danger to the community. MACHETE-WIELDING MS-13 GANGSTER WANTED FOR MURDER WALKS FREE AFTER BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE RELEASES HIM: DHS Chad Mizelle, chair of litigation at the America First Policy Institute and a former acting associate attorney general and Justice Department chief of staff, told Fox News Digital the implications extend beyond immigration law. "We are talking about criminal aliens here," Mizelle said. "Those are individuals who have been accused of or convicted of an aggravated felony. Accused or convicted of murder. Accused or convicted of child rape. Accused or convicted of grievous harm upon another human being." "So these are the worst of the worst individuals," Mizelle continued. "Do we want those individuals walking the streets, re-committing, harming other individuals?" Mizelle argued Congress imposed mandatory detention on certain noncitizens with criminal records to keep them detained during removal proceedings, while the Second Circuit’s prolonged-detention rule could incentivize some detainees to drag out their cases long enough to seek bond. DOJ MOVES TO STRIP CITIZENSHIP FROM 17 PEOPLE ACCUSED OF HIDING DISTURBING CRIMES The man at the center of the administration’s latest petition, identified in court papers as D.C., is a 62-year-old Dominican citizen who illegally entered the United States and has four criminal convictions, according to court records. In 1997, D.C. was charged with multiple drug offenses, including selling and possessing a controlled substance. He failed to appear for trial, was convicted by a jury and sentenced in absentia to three to nine years in prison, but did not serve that sentence until 2024. In 2007, he was charged with possessing a forged instrument after presenting false identification to police and again failed to appear in court. In 2016, D.C. faced several charges stemming from a domestic dispute, including second-degree strangulation, third-degree assault and acting in a manner to injure a child under 17. He pleaded guilty to criminal obstruction of breathing or blood circulation and also resolved his earlier forged-instrument case with a guilty plea. Later that year, he pleaded guilty to criminal contempt. D.C. was finally arrested on the outstanding warrant from his 1998 drug conviction in April 2024. After completing his state sentence in September 2025, ICE immediately detained him while his removal proceedings continued. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT The district court subsequently ordered that D.C. receive a bond hearing under binding Second Circuit precedent but denied his separate request for immediate release. The government is now asking the Supreme Court to take the case before the Second Circuit itself rules — an unusual procedure known as certiorari before judgment. The administration turned to D.C.’s case after two other noncitizens at the center of the same legal fight saw their cases become moot. One, Carol Williams Black, had been detained for roughly seven months. His case became moot after he received a final order of removal and permanently left the United States. Black was convicted of sexually abusing a child in 2000. The Supreme Court therefore granted review in June only as to the second detainee, G.M. G.M., a lawful permanent resident from the Dominican Republic, pleaded guilty to second-degree assault in May 2015 after being accused of attacking and robbing a man during a 2012 incident in New York City. He was sentenced to two years in prison and was released early on parole in December 2016 after serving 19 months. ICE arrested G.M. at his home on Oct. 5, 2020, and detained him for 21 months without a bond hearing while removal proceedings continued. TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18TH-CENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH The Supreme Court was scheduled to hear his case Oct. 13. But in late August, New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul granted G.M. a full and unconditional pardon for the assault conviction that had formed the basis for his deportation proceedings and mandatory detention. Solicitor General John Sauer agreed the case was moot, and the Supreme Court dismissed it Sept. 11 without ruling on the merits. The administration then identified D.C. as its replacement vehicle and asked the justices to hear the same constitutional questions this term. FEDERAL JUDGE TIES ICE AGENTS' HANDS WITH RULING ON WARRANTLESS SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ARRESTS Carrie Severino, president of Judicial Crisis Network (JCN), said the dispute is likely to affect many similar immigration cases nationwide. "This is not a question that's only going to affect D.C., the criminal Dominican national at issue in this case," Severino told Fox News Digital. "This is an issue that's going to affect criminal aliens across the country." A victory by D.C. would impose new hurdles on the government, including additional hearings and use of resources, Severino said. "As we know, immigration cases, skipping out on showing up for court dates is incredibly common," she added. "This is not something that I think the court ought to be granting on a regular basis that they'd be letting people out on bond simply on their word that they're going to be coming back when they know that they are likely to be removed." The case also raises questions about who must prove whether continued detention is necessary. The Second Circuit ruled that the government must prove by clear and convincing evidence that a detainee should remain in custody. "And so, if the Supreme Court winds up affirming what the Second Circuit held, that means it's going to be harder for the government to be able to detain this particular population of criminal aliens or terrorism-linked aliens," Florida State University law professor Michael Morley told Fox News Digital. "There are going to be situations where the government is not able to show that a particular person is either likely to flee or poses a risk of danger and this dangerousness by a heightened or clear and convincing standard." "It means that these criminal aliens who are already subject to removal proceedings are more likely to be released into the community while those underlying removal proceedings continue to make their way slowly through the adjudicative process," Morley continued. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Supreme Court has not yet agreed to hear D.C.’s case.

title: Finland's Stubb credits Trump for pushing Ukraine peace talks while dismissing Russian invasion fears
description: Finnish President Alexander Stubb credits Trump with pushing for Russia-Ukraine war peace and says Finland is fully prepared for any Moscow threat.
content: UNITED NATIONS — As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Russia could take its war beyond Ukraine, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is striking a markedly calmer tone — saying Finland is prepared for Moscow and crediting President Donald Trump with pushing harder for a negotiated end to the war. "I think we're certainly in a better place than we were before President Trump started," Stubb told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "He's doubled down in the past year and a half to try to find a solution for peace with negotiators such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and many others." Stubb, who has been closely involved in the diplomatic effort, said he and Norway’s prime minister have worked largely "in the back office," relaying information among Ukraine, the United States and European governments. KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE "I think he's really working hard and hopefully we'll get a solution," Stubb said. The interview came during an intense diplomatic week in New York focused heavily on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in New York during UNGA week as Washington continued its effort to revive negotiations with Moscow. Zelenskyy said peace remained Ukraine's priority and thanked Trump for sending the two envoys to Kyiv after they had also held talks in Moscow. Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital after the meeting about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT "That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus," Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin, unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv. He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response. Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer. "Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said. But Stubb struck a notably calmer tone when asked about Zelenskyy’s warnings that Russia could eventually attack other European countries, including Finland, which shares the longest border with Russia. "As commander-in-chief in Finland, I sit on all the relevant information and I just don't see a factual basis for it," Stubb said. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT That does not mean, he stressed, that Moscow has stopped targeting Europe. Stubb distinguished between the "kinetic" war Russia is fighting in Ukraine and what he described as a broader "hybrid" campaign in Europe, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. "We have to see this as a campaign," he said. "Russia tries to intimidate Europe, scare us and get into our heads." His prescription was characteristically Finnish: "cool, calm and collected, take a sauna and a nice bath and deal with it." Stubb said Finland, a country with a population of 5.6 million, can afford that attitude precisely because it has spent decades preparing for a potential threat from its eastern neighbor. "We are calm because we are prepared," he said. He pointed to Finland’s mandatory military service, reserve force, artillery, long-range capabilities and extensive network of civilian shelters. The Finnish Defence Forces puts Finland’s wartime military strength at 280,000 personnel, with additional reservists available if needed. That deterrent received another boost just days before Stubb traveled to New York. Finland is acquiring 64 F-35A fighter jets to replace its F/A-18 Hornet fleet under a procurement decision announced by the Finnish government. The first two F-35s intended for operations inside Finland arrived at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, according to a Finnish Defence Forces press release. "We have obligatory military service. I did mine, my son did his. We have women who do it voluntarily. We have over 60 F-18s. We just bought 64 F-35s, the two first of which arrived. We have long-range missiles, air, land and sea. We have the capability to mobilize 280,000 troops within days in a conflictual situation. On top of that, we have land mines. And we have the biggest artillery in Europe together with Poland… On top of that, we have civilian shelters for over 4.4 million people out of 5.6." FINLAND'S PARLIAMENT VOTES TO LIFT DECADES-OLD BAN ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN HISTORIC NATO DEFENSE SHIFT "We don't have them because we're worried about Sweden," Stubb joked of Finland’s military capabilities. "We have them because we see a security threat coming from Russia." He said that level of preparedness, combined with Finland’s NATO membership, makes a direct Russian attack unlikely. Finland became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, after abandoning its longstanding military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We feel that we're very prepared, and that gives us a strong enough … deterrent that we don't believe that Russia is going to test a country like Finland," Stubb said. "And of course the icing on the cake is that we are now security providers in the Alliance NATO." Stubb also used his Sept. 22 address to the U.N. General Assembly to advocate for continued support for Kyiv, calling the "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine "particularly close to my heart." He said the coalition was working toward a "just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the U.N. Charter." Stubb made additional news on Ukraine during UNGA week, when he urged SpaceX owner Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage so Ukrainian forces could use the satellite network in areas containing Russian ballistic missile launchers, including inside Russia. He argued that doing so could help Ukraine target launchers firing missiles at Ukrainian cities. Yet Ukraine was only one piece of what Stubb described as an increasingly interconnected global security crisis. WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR? Asked about Trump’s call at the U.N. for countries to support efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, Stubb was unequivocal. "I agree, Iran should not obtain nuclear weapons," he told Fox News Digital, adding that Tehran should not use proxies or be able to produce missiles. Stubb also argued that the conflicts involving Russia and Iran can no longer be viewed in isolation, alleging that Moscow is providing intelligence to Tehran that Iran has used against U.S. military bases in the Gulf, while Iranian weapons have been supplied to Russia for use against Ukraine. "We're going in this merry-go-round where every bit of the conflict is linked to another," Stubb said. "The sooner we can end both, the better." Trump used his Sept. 22 U.N. General Assembly address to call for Iran's economic isolation and reiterate that Tehran should not obtain a nuclear weapon, while warning of further US military action if a peace agreement is not reached, according to Reuters. For Stubb, the proliferation of conflicts — from Ukraine and Iran to Gaza, Yemen and Sudan — is testing a diplomatic system already struggling to keep pace. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's not a zero-sum game," he said. "We have to deal with a multiplicity of conflicts right now, unfortunately." And for Trump, he added, that means "working around the clock."

title: From Gettysburg to Antarctica, military Bibles reveal prayers of families who sent loved ones to war
description: A new war exhibit at The Museum of the Bible features rare military Bibles from Gettysburg to Operation Deep Freeze, preserving handwritten prayers from families.
content: For generations of American service members heading into the unknown, one of the most important things tucked into a uniform pocket was a Bible. Some returned battered from war, while others read heartfelt prayers written by family members hoping their sons and husbands would come home. One type was encased in metal and carried over a soldier's heart. Another Bible traveled to the frozen reaches of Antarctica, sharing Scripture to the very ends of the world. RARE AMERICAN BIBLE AND FOUNDERS’ LETTERS TRACE FAITH’S ROLE IN BIRTH OF THE NATION Now, as the U.S. marks 250 years since the Declaration of Independence, the Museum of the Bible's "Bible in Times of War" exhibit is using those surviving artifacts to trace how American service members turned to God's Word for strength and hope through generations of conflict. Wesley Viner, an early modern curator at the Museum of the Bible and Marine veteran who curated the special display in Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital that some of the most powerful stories preserved in the collection belong not to famous generals or celebrated heroes, but to ordinary Americans whose names may have otherwise disappeared from history. Among the most recognizable artifacts are so-called "Heart Shield Bibles," small, pocket-sized Bibles with thin metal covers carried by some American service members during World War II and into the Korean War. THE DAY AFTER MEMORIAL DAY, AMERICA’S DEBT TO THE FALLEN STILL REMAINS The Bibles were frequently purchased by relatives for departing service members and designed to fit into a breast pocket over the heart, helping fuel stories that the metal-covered books could theoretically stop a bullet. Viner, however, said the truth is less cinematic. The thin metal covers were rather unlikely to stop World War II-era ammunition traveling at high speed, he said, though he would not rule out the possibility that one could have protected a service member from shrapnel or flying debris. "Many of the tales that surround the 'Heart Shield Bibles' are likely a bit exaggerated," Viner said. CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND But whether the books literally stopped bullets may obscure what they represented to the families who sent loved ones to war. "It was a source of protection. It was a source of strength. It would keep them safe," Viner said, describing the metal shield as largely symbolic. Some of the most affecting evidence of that hope survives in heartfelt handwriting inside the covers. Viner said small pocket Bibles were produced on a large scale during the first half of the 20th century, allowing families to purchase them for sons, brothers and husbands preparing to deploy. "To my dear boy, may God keep you safe," one note reads. Another simply says, "Praying for you at Christmas." ‘FREEDOMS ARE NEVER FREE’: A JEWISH AMERICAN SOLDIER BURIED WITH NAZIS FINALLY LAID TO REST WITH US TROOPS In many cases, Viner said, historians do not know who wrote the messages or who received them. He said the anonymity can make them even more powerful. "As I read those, I think about how profound and serious and meaningful that was for the family members who sent their kids, their loved ones off to war and gave them this as they left," Viner said. More than 80 years before the "Heart Shield Bibles," another now-tattered Bible traveled with a Union soldier whose life Viner was able to partially reconstruct because of the book he left behind. John Weissenheimer served in the 107th Ohio Volunteer Infantry, a largely German-speaking unit that endured bloody Civil War battles, including Gettysburg, according to Viner. Weissenheimer was already in his late 40s when he enlisted, older than what was typical for a soldier. Viner said enlistment records show Weissenheimer joined before many of the unit's major engagements. Years later, an inscription in his Bible places him at Lincoln Hospital in Washington, D.C., serving with the Invalid Corps, which was composed of injured, sick or otherwise disabled soldiers who could no longer perform regular front-line duty. The surviving evidence does not reveal exactly what happened to Weissenheimer, nor did he leave extensive notes explaining what the Bible meant to him. But the battered book establishes something perhaps even more interesting for historians in that Weissenheimer kept it. "If not for this Bible," Viner said, Weissenheimer would be "largely a forgotten name." "This Bible allows us to take this anonymous person from history, this person who no historical textbook is ever going to talk about, and surface them and tell their story," he said. Whatever Weissenheimer endured, Viner said, he ultimately reached a point where he could no longer serve in a regular unit, continued serving in the Invalid Corps and had his Bible with him. "For some reason, he found something in that Bible that meant a lot to him," Viner said. Not every Bible in the exhibit accompanied an American into battle, however. In the 1950s, Navy chaplain Peter Boal took part in Operation Deep Freeze, the umbrella term for U.S. military operations in Antarctica. During his time there, Boal gave a Bible to a man identified in its inscription only as "Bill." Viner said the museum cannot definitively establish Bill's identity, though he believes one possibility is Petty Officer William Stroop, who helped lead an expedition to establish a smaller Antarctic station. What Boal wrote to the recipient of that Bible, however, survives. "Best of luck on your journey," Viner recounted from the inscription. "We'll be praying for you. We hope the Lord brings you back safely." For Viner, the artifact shows the Bible serving a familiar purpose in a dramatically different setting. Instead of accompanying a serviceman through combat, it traveled with Americans venturing into an isolated and uncertain frontier. One of the oldest Bibles in the display reaches back to the nation's founding and comes with a story Viner said is probably more legend than fact. The German-language Bible was printed in Philadelphia in 1776 by Christoph Sauer and eventually became known as the "Gun-Wad Bible." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER One popular version of the story held that British soldiers seized copies from Sauer's printing operation, tore out the pages and used them as wadding for their muskets, hence the 'Wad.' Another version turned the story around, claiming American colonists confiscated the Bibles because the Sauer family held Loyalist sympathies. Viner said there is likely little truth to either tale, but conceded the competing stories are revealing in their own way. They suggest people understood that portraying an opponent as disrespecting the Bible could tarnish that side's reputation, reflecting the significance attached to Scripture at the time. The books also preserve more mundane, everyday records of what American service members actually did with the Bibles they carried. As smaller and more durable editions became increasingly available, Viner said surviving examples more commonly contain handwritten notes and other markings. Some service members used blank pages to record their movements. One World War I soldier effectively used his Bible as his own record of deployment, documenting his journey from his hometown to a recruiting depot, then to New York, England and France before eventually recording his return home. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Viner said the collection shows that service members facing the dangers and stresses of war responded to those circumstances in different ways, but many turned to Scripture for "strength, courage, relief" and "hope." Centuries later, some of the people who carried the books remain identifiable and others have been reduced to only a first name or precious few words written inside a battered cover. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the messages their families sent with them into battle remain familiar even in our modern eyes, like a prayer at Christmas, a hope for protection and a solemn plea that a loved one come back home. The Bibles in Times of War Exhibit is located on the second floor of the Museum of the Bible as part of the Bible in America section.

title: Massive ICE sweep fuels GOP push to lock Trump immigration crackdown into law
description: Hoosier Sen. Jim Banks says a five-day ICE operation netting 426 arrests in Indiana proves why Trump's mass deportation agenda must become law.
content: A massive five- day ICE operation that netted 426 arrests across Indiana is fueling Hoosier Sen. Jim Banks’ push for Congress to cement President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown into law before a future administration can reverse course. title: Florida man, 76, with suspended license allegedly admits to driving under the influence of rum, cocaine
description: Charles Ducking, 76, allegedly showed deputies his rum cup and admitted to doing cocaine minutes before a traffic stop in Polk County, Florida.
content: A 76-year-old Florida man with a suspended license allegedly admitted during a traffic stop that he had been drinking rum — later telling deputies he had also recently used cocaine — just four months after a separate DUI arrest, authorities said. Charles Ducking, 76, of Lake Wales, was pulled over after a sheriff's deputy allegedly observed him swerving while driving along U.S. Highway 27 in Waverly, according to the Polk County Sheriff's Office. The deputy detected the odor of alcohol and noticed that Ducking allegedly had slurred speech and watery eyes. When asked for his driver's license, Ducking allegedly told the deputy it had been suspended. FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED FOR DUI AFTER TROOPERS ALLEGEDLY FIND 34 OPEN ALCOHOL CONTAINERS IN VEHICLE "Well, I can't show you my driver's license cuz it's suspended cuz DUI. And I have been drinking a little bit right now," he said, according to the sheriff's office. Officials said Ducking then showed the deputy a silver thermal cup containing a brown liquid. "This here is my rum I'm drinking," he said, according to the sheriff's office. IOWA WOMAN WITH A PRIOR CONVICTION UNDER HER BELT ARRESTED FOR OWI ON LAWN MOWER A traffic deputy who responded to conduct a DUI investigation immediately recognized Ducking from a previous DUI arrest in May, the sheriff's office said. Officials said deputies also found a small orange container containing cocaine during a search of Ducking's vehicle, which allegedly prompted Ducking to tell law enforcement he had "done a line" 10 minutes before he was pulled over. During field sobriety tests, Ducking displayed several indicators of impairment, and breath tests registered blood alcohol concentration readings of .094 and .095, above Florida's .08 legal limit for drivers. "While we appreciate Charles Ducking's cooperation during the traffic stop, the fact of the matter is, he is lucky he hasn't yet killed someone or himself while driving drunk and high on drugs," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said in a statement. "He has tempted fate too many times, and he needs to make some serious changes in his life before it's too late," Judd continued. "I am proud of my deputies for their proactive patrolling to find impaired drivers and get them off the road." title: Israeli UN envoy's Starlink video reaches millions, with nearly 40% of Instagram viewers in Iran

content: A viral video of Israel’s U.N. ambassador offering an Iranian representative a Starlink device has reached around 9 million views across social media — and nearly 40% of its Instagram viewers are in Iran, according to analytics shared with Fox News Digital. A representative for Israeli Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon told Fox News Digital that the office was surprised by the video’s reach inside Iran, saying such an audience is unusual for Israeli diplomatic accounts. "We couldn't imagine to be the popular," the representative said, referring to the video's reach in Iran. Instagram audience analytics shared with Fox News Digital show 39.9% of viewers were located in Iran, the largest share from any country. title: Enes Freedom rips Cheryl Reeve for saying women's sports advocates 'don’t want transgender people to exist'
description: Enes Kanter Freedom called on Cheryl Reeve to step down after the Lynx coach said the transgender athletes debate targets trans people's existence.
content: Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom pushed back against Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve after she claimed the debate over transgender athletes is part of a broader effort by critics who "don’t want transgender people to exist." Freedom responded to Reeve in a social media post Saturday, rejecting her characterization of those advocating to keep biological males out of women’s sports. "Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve should step down immediately. You can’t lead women’s basketball while refusing to stand up for women’s sports. Can someone, for the love of God, please explain to her that: Protecting women’s sports is not an attack on anyone’s existence, nor does it erase a community. Coach, if you truly mean what you just said, then put your hypocrisy aside and prove it by drafting me in the 2027 WNBA Draft," Freedom wrote. LYNX COACH CHERYL REEVE VOICES SUPPORT FOR THE TRANS COMMUNITY AGAIN AFTER REGULAR SEASON FINALE VS FEVER Reeve made the remarks after the Lynx closed the regular season with an 86-66 victory over the Indiana Fever at Target Center Thursday. The game was accompanied by competing demonstrations outside the arena over transgender participation in women’s sports. "I think that’s probably one of the more meaningful things that would mark the season for me," Reeve said. "It’s that the transgender community is one that deserves our support, and what is happening in the name of some issues of transgender in sports — it’s really an attack on all transgender community. They don’t want transgender people to exist." Reeve said the reaction she received after wearing a "Trans Kids Belong" shirt during a nationally televised Aug. 2 game against Indiana made the gesture one of the most meaningful moments of her season. "The amount of communication of people who were affected by something as simple as wearing a T-shirt in support of them and helping them be seen — with the platform that we have in professional sports, it was a small gesture by me," Reeve said. "It’s something I believe in, obviously, wholeheartedly." "If I could have helped just one to feel differently about themselves, because for the transgender community this really is about life and death for them," she continued. "The number of parents of transgender kids that I heard from and how it helped them and their families, it helped their child think differently about themselves and that there is someone in our position, like we have as a leader. To know that there are people out there that believe in them, that they belong." The comments marked at least the fourth time Reeve addressed the transgender issue during a WNBA media availability this season. WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT SENDS TRANS INCLUSION MEMO AFTER ENES FREEDOM, ROYCE WHITE ANNOUNCEMENTS Reeve initially spoke about it following Supreme Court rulings that upheld state laws protecting women’s and girls’ sports. She later defended transgender participation before the Lynx’s first home game against the Fever, saying that "every kid has a right to sports" while acknowledging that eligibility becomes more complicated after puberty. The four-time WNBA champion coach also spoke privately with Fever guard Sophie Cunningham before their Aug. 2 matchup. Cunningham previously said she wanted to protect girls who should not have to compete against or share locker rooms with biological males, while emphasizing that she did not harbor hatred toward transgender people. "I think that I am here to extend love," Cunningham said. "But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men." Freedom inserted himself into the WNBA’s transgender debate in August by announcing that he intended to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft under the name "Enisa Freedom." He said the move was designed to test the league’s eligibility standards, which state that only women may play in the WNBA but do not publicly define eligibility through biological sex. ENES KANTER FREEDOM OPENS UP ON CONFRONTATION WITH NATASHA CLOUD THAT LED TO EJECTION, WNBA PURSUIT The former NBA center has repeatedly maintained that he is raising the issue seriously and is not attempting to demean transgender people. "I’m not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any group or anyone’s personal decisions," Freedom wrote in an earlier statement. "What I’m trying to do is bigger than clicks or attention." Freedom also publicly separated his campaign from the conduct of other former male basketball players who joined the WNBA draft effort, saying his goal had "never been publicity, political theater, cheap attention, or stunts." Former NBA player Royce White also responded to Reeve’s latest remarks, but took a distinctly different approach from Freedom. While Freedom offered a direct rebuttal to Reeve’s characterization of women’s-sports advocates, White issued an overtly satirical statement promoting his female alter ego, "Roysha." "I appreciate Coach Reeve’s sentiment toward Transgenders," White wrote. "In these increasingly polarized times, it appears a potential source of cultural common ground has emerged ... Kweeen Roysha! Pay is the perfect blend of MAGA and mainstream. I think there’s a real opportunity to create a bridge, because a lot of conservatives nationwide would like to see Roysha play in the WNBA. The Minnesota Lynx would be a perfect home as the new transgender capital of America."
