title: Pope Leo draws staggering 800,000 faithful to heart of Paris for massive outdoor Mass
description: Pope Leo XIV drew an estimated 800,000 to Place de la Concorde for a historic open-air Mass, urging French Catholics to share their faith openly.
content: Pope Leo XIV drew an estimated 800,000 people into the heart of Paris on Saturday for a massive open-air Mass, filling one of the French republic’s most storied public squares as he urged Catholics to openly share their faith in an "increasingly secularized society." Flag-waving crowds packed the Champs-Élysées and Place de la Concorde as the American pope traveled roughly 1.2 miles through central Paris in the popemobile before celebrating Mass. The Vatican estimated attendance at 800,000, roughly 200,000 more people than had registered in advance. People of faith gathered in the streets, with families lifting babies and young children toward the popemobile as Leo made his way through the French capital. POPE LEO XIV RECEIVES 'SYMBOLIC’ SPHERE IN CHARITY'S PUSH FOR AI TO 'PROTECT HUMAN DIGNITY' "Seeing you gathered here," Leo told worshippers, he was looking upon the "heirs of France’s long and beautiful history of faith," according to Vatican News. The pope called on French Catholics not to keep that rich inheritance to themselves. FROM DISNEY MAGIC TO ANCIENT FAITH: DAVID HENRIE ON WHY GEN Z IS FLOCKING TO CHURCH "Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied," Leo said. "From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France." The setting carried particular resonance in a country known for its strict tradition of secularism. AMERICAN BISHOP ROBERT BARRON CALLS OUT ST. PAUL'S CATHEDRAL IN UK OVER NIGHTCLUB PARTNERSHIP It is notable that the Place de la Concorde was an execution ground during the French Revolution, where devoutly Catholic King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette were guillotined. Today, the square is closely associated with the French republic and regularly hosts Bastille Day celebrations. The decision to celebrate a papal Mass there drew criticism from supporters of France’s strict separation of church and state, who argued another site would have been more appropriate. The images also offered a striking contrast with another massive Paris spectacle just two years earlier. The 2024 Summer Olympics opening ceremony drew worldwide controversy over a tableau featuring drag performers that Christian leaders and other critics said mocked Christianity. POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT' The French Bishops’ Conference said at the time that the ceremony "included scenes of mockery and derision of Christianity," adding that Christians around the world had been "hurt by the outrageousness and provocation of certain scenes." The tableau was widely interpreted by critics as a parody of Leonardo da Vinci’s "The Last Supper," though Olympics organizers disputed that interpretation. Leo’s visit comes as France experiences a notable increase in adult conversions even as the country continues a decades-long decline in overall Catholic participation. Annual adult baptisms in France have tripled since 2016, reaching 13,000 this year, according to The Associated Press. Overall baptisms, however, have fallen sharply over the longer term, from 513,000 in 1980 to 186,000 in 2024. YOUNG MEN ARE RETURNING TO CHURCH — AND IT COULD RESHAPE AMERICA’S FUTURE Leo thanked French families, young people, catechumens and new Christians for bearing witness to their faith in what he described as an "increasingly secularized society," according to Vatican News. The scale of the pope’s reception was already apparent the night before the Mass as some 80,000 young people packed France’s national stadium Friday for a vigil featuring fireworks and a theatrical retelling of the country’s Catholic history. "Thank you for your courage! Thank you for your presence," Leo told them in French. "Thank you for your faith. You are the saints of France!" At Saturday’s Mass, Leo invoked France’s Catholic heritage and drew on the biblical image of "living water," telling worshippers that Jesus Christ could satisfy humanity’s desire for "life, truth, unity, peace, communion, and happiness." He also invoked French Catholic saints including Irenaeus, Martin and Francis de Sales while praising those who continue to work for "life, the family, truth, peace, fraternity and justice." The sea of people rivaled some of the largest public celebrations to fill the Champs-Élysées in recent decades, including France’s World Cup victories in 1998 and 2018, according to the AP. Leo’s four-day trip to France began Friday with a visit to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral, the first by a pope since the devastating 2019 fire. content: Texas quarterback Arch Manning did a postgame interview with ESPN reporter Holly Rowe on Saturday, less than two weeks after apologizing for calling an AI-generated video that depicted her being slapped "hilarious." content: Comedian Bill Maher took aim at his own side of the aisle Friday night, mocking far-left critics who torched a struggling Massachusetts lesbian bar for daring to go mask-optional one night a week. MAHER SKEWERS WEALTHY CELEBS WHO PREACHED 'WE'RE ALL IN IT TOGETHER' DURING COVID AS AMERICANS STRUGGLED "But economically, it wasn't working," Maher said. title: Startups bring innovation to defense industrial base
description: Startups are helping modernize America’s defense industry with new technology and innovative ideas as the War Department diversifies its inventory.
content: New tools, longstanding partnerships and additional resources could be the keys to bolster the defense industrial base. The War Department is diversifying its inventory by working with startups and playing the long game through extended agreements with established contractors. "I do think these are unprecedented deals," Undersecretary of War for Acquisitions and Sustainment Michael Duffey said. "Nobody's been able to deliver the quality and the performance that Tomahawk and the Patriot provide for our war fight." The War Department has been announcing multi-year weapons production contracts. Some agreements extend as long as seven years, including a $22.9 billion deal with Raytheon for Tomahawk missiles, a $1 billion framework with Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin for THAAD components and a $58.62 billion contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot Missile Segment Enhancements. INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH "In the case of Patriots, it was a three-times production increase over what we were producing this past year," Duffey said. "We have a lot of new entrants that are bringing new great technology into the industry." The War Department is also investing more in new technology. The Department of War Innovation Unit works with commercial companies and startups to adopt new weapons and defense capabilities. Its budget has skyrocketed to nearly $1 billion in recent years. "I think the startups are going to be kind of the future. The primes have their purpose. They build the big weapon systems. They build aircraft carriers. But it takes a long time to move that ship in the right direction," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said. "The startups, just like we saw in Ukraine, have this ability of innovation to move at a faster speed and a more innovative technology, more creativity in the process, out-of-the-box thinking that we desperately need for our defense industrial base." Rocket Lab is one newer company that has increasingly been working with the War Department. Since the company was founded in 2006, it has received more than $2 billion in government contract awards. "I would say we've moving up the food chain, and now we are amongst the preeminent missile and missile defense test programs in the United States," Vice President of Global Launch Services at Rocket Lab Brian Rogers said. WAR DEPARTMENT OFFICIAL LAYS OUT PLAN TO REBUILD MUNITIONS STOCKPILE: 'AHEAD OF THIS PROBLEM' Rocket Lab has worked with the Department of War Innovation Unit to test its Haste Launch Vehicle, which the company says will help the U.S. accelerate future hypersonic capabilities. "We've already done a number of launches," Rogers said. "We got a lot more in the hopper, and it's all kinds of different technology applications." Defense technology company Castelion says one of its priorities is speeding up the manufacturing timeline. "We believe that it's much faster if you just go out and build the object you're trying to build into inner manufacturing, and then you find all of the problems in that process, and you correct them," Castelion Co-Founder and CEO Bryon Hargis said. "One of the things that we based the company on is really what worked in the Apollo era when we got to the moon as a country in under a decade. A lot of those practices have fallen out of favor. We're going back to what worked, and we're just implementing that again." The War Department is investing in that strategy with a multi-year agreement to eventually field Castelion’s Blackbeard Hypersonic Weapon. "It's just the agreement to have a future agreement," Hargis said. "If we meet those performance targets that we set out and said we could do, the department is saying they're gonna come in and buy a tremendous amount of munitions." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Castelion has secured $500 million in U.S. military contracts over the past 18 months and recently announced $1 billion in funding. "The future is very bright. We have a tremendous opportunity with this administration and what the department is doing to bring in new entrants," Hargis said. "The key thing that I think has been missing in the past decades is that we do not build enough, we do not go test enough, and they're correcting that. And that's going to lead to tremendous innovation in this space."

title: Vicious bear mauls couple until their French bulldog intervenes with tragic consequences
description: A black bear mauled a Northern California couple at their Trinity County home, and their French bulldog Cassie reportedly died trying to protect them from the attack.
content: A late-night encounter with a black bear turned tragic for a Northern California couple after the animal mauled the homeowners and fatally injured their French bulldog. The dog reportedly tried to protect them during the vicious attack, which left them hospitalized. In the early morning hours of Sept. 19, Jeff and Mallory Wilson's dog, Cassie, let out a single bark, prompting Jeff Wilson to go outside and check the backyard of their Trinity County home. BLACK BEARS INVADE LAKE TAHOE HOMES AS BREAK-INS SURGE AND LOCALS FORTIFY DEFENSES When he opened the door, a cinnamon-colored black bear emerged from behind their patio furniture, lunging at him and knocking him to the floor. The commotion woke his wife, who went outside and was also attacked by the bear, according to a GoFundMe organized by a longtime friend of the married couple. "I think the bear was startled by us just as much as we were startled by it," Wilson later told the news site Redheaded Blackbelt. During the attack, their dog Cassie threw herself between Wilson and the bear, which grabbed the dog in its mouth and started to run away with it, according to reports. The owners got the bear to drop their dog and finally scared it off. GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL Though badly wounded themselves, the couple rushed their dog to emergency care. The pet underwent surgery to treat multiple wounds, including along her spine but "tragically died two days" after the incident, according to the fundraising page. The page described the pet as "a deeply loved member of their family." The couple is facing continued medical treatment and recovery. Jeff Wilson, meanwhile, suffered two broken ribs and numerous bite and claw wounds, while Mallory Wilson sustained serious injuries to her head and face and other bite and puncture wounds. Each is facing continued medical treatment and recovery, the fundraising page says. SAVAGE BEAR ATTACK LEAVES WOUNDED MONTANA HUNTER WITH HORRIFYING OPTION The Wilsons own Radio Ranch, an off-the-grid "glamping" retreat in Trinity County, according to reports. The couple "[has] years of experience living and working alongside wildlife, and [takes] precautions to peacefully coexist with the animals that share their land," the GoFundMe notes. "We chose to live in rural Northern California because we treasure being surrounded by the natural world and the wildlife with whom we share it," the couple told KRON4. "This was an unprovoked and extraordinarily unusual encounter that none of us could have anticipated. "They are passionate animal lovers, which has made this extraordinarily rare encounter and the loss of Cassie heartbreaking on so many levels," the GoFundMe write-up noted. Jeff Wilson told local news outlets he believes the bear may have been startled after becoming cornered between a fence and gate at their home. As of Saturday afternoon, it raised over $16,000 of its $20,000 goal. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Fox News Digital reached out to the Wilsons and the GoFundMe organizer for comment. title: Someone could have opened an account in your name; check now
description: New account fraud victims jumped 31% in 2025, reaching 5.4 million. Criminals open accounts you may never see on your regular bank statements.
content: Most people think identity theft means someone gets into a bank account or starts charging things to a credit card you already use. But there is another kind of identity theft that can be much harder to spot. A criminal can use your name, Social Security number, birthdate or other personal information to open a brand-new account in your name. And this problem is growing fast. Javelin Strategy & Research found that the number of new account fraud victims jumped 31% in 2025, rising from 4.2 million to 5.4 million. That was the sharpest increase among the fraud types Javelin tracked. The fraudulent account could be a credit card sent to an address you have never lived at. It could be a phone or utility account with a company you have never used. Someone could even try to open a buy now, pay later account using your identity. That is what makes this kind of fraud so sneaky. The criminal may never touch an account you already monitor, so there may be no suspicious charge staring back at you from your bank statement. You may find out only when a strange bill arrives, a lender checks your credit, a debt collector calls or you spot an account that clearly does not belong to you. The good news is there are ways to look for those clues before the problem gets even bigger. 6 IN 10 IDENTITY CRIMES NOW BEGIN WITH A NEW ACCOUNT Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com How new account fraud usually works With fraud targeting an account you already use, you have a decent chance of spotting it quickly. A strange purchase shows up, your bank sends an alert or your card suddenly stops working. New account fraud can stay much quieter. A criminal applies for a new account using enough of your personal information to pose as you. If the application goes through, the account may be tied to an address, phone number or email account the criminal controls. As far as the lender or company knows, you opened it. The first clue could be a hard inquiry on your credit report, a new account you do not recognize or mail welcoming you to a service you never signed up for. But there is an important catch. Not every type of account appears on all three credit reports, and some phone, utility or buy now, pay later activity may not appear there. That is why checking your credit reports helps, but it should not be the only thing you watch. Why new account fraud keeps growing Criminals have more stolen personal information to work with than ever. Years of data breaches have exposed names, Social Security numbers, birthdates, addresses, email addresses and other details that can help someone impersonate you. A criminal may also combine information from multiple breaches, phishing attacks or data broker records to build a much fuller picture of your identity. At the same time, opening financial and other accounts online has become incredibly convenient. You can apply from your couch and sometimes get a decision within minutes. That convenience works in our favor when we are the ones applying. It can also give criminals more opportunities to try stolen identities without ever walking into a bank or store. The Federal Reserve has also warned that digital account openings create new opportunities for fraudsters, especially as stolen personal information and more sophisticated technology become easier for criminals to use. A closer look at how this can start A criminal may not get everything needed to steal your identity from one breach. Your name and email could come from one leak. An older breach might expose other personal information. A people search site may help fill in an address or phone number. Put enough pieces together and a criminal may have what is needed to start testing your identity against lenders, retailers, phone carriers and other companies. That also helps explain why identity theft can seem to come out of nowhere. The information used against you may have been floating around for months or even years before someone decided to use it. Where the evidence can show up New account fraud can leave clues in several places, and some of them are easy to miss if you do not know where to look. 5 steps to check right now You do not need to wait for a strange bill or collection call to find out something is wrong. A few quick checks can help you spot signs of new account fraud before it turns into a bigger problem. 1) Pull all three credit reports Go to AnnualCreditReport.com and review your Equifax, Experian and TransUnion reports. Free reports are currently available weekly, so you can check all three at once or stagger your reviews throughout the year. 2) Look for anything unfamiliar Pay close attention to accounts, hard inquiries, addresses and other information you do not recognize. If something looks strange, do not assume it is harmless. 3) Consider freezing your credit A credit freeze can make it much harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name because lenders generally cannot access your frozen credit report. Freezes are free to place and lift, they do not hurt your credit score and they stay in place until you remove them. You need to contact Equifax, Experian and TransUnion separately to freeze all three files. 4) Check your mail and email Look for messages about accounts you never opened, especially welcome notices, bills, password-reset messages and application updates. 5) Turn on monitoring and alerts Your bank and credit card companies may offer account alerts at no charge. Identity theft monitoring can go further by watching for certain credit inquiries, new accounts and other signs that someone may be using your information. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com. The faster you know something has changed, the faster you can investigate it. IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB? What to do if you find a fraudulent account If you spot an account you do not recognize, act quickly. These six steps can help you shut down the fraud, limit the damage and start cleaning up your records. 1) Contact the company where the account was opened Call the company's fraud department. Explain that you did not open the account and ask them to close or freeze it. Keep any confirmation they send you. 2) Report the identity theft Go to IdentityTheft.gov and create an FTC Identity Theft Report and recovery plan. That report can also help when you dispute fraudulent information. 3) Place a fraud alert or credit freeze A fraud alert tells businesses to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening new credit. An initial fraud alert is free, lasts one year and requires you to contact only one of the three major credit bureaus. That bureau must notify the other two. A credit freeze goes further by restricting access to your credit report. To freeze all three reports, contact each bureau separately. 4) Dispute fraudulent information Contact any credit bureau showing the fraudulent account and ask it to block the identity theft information from your report. To use the FTC's blocking process, send the bureau a copy of your FTC Identity Theft Report, proof of your identity and a letter identifying the fraudulent information. You can also dispute inaccurate information directly with the credit bureau. 5) Turn on monitoring and identity theft alerts Your bank and credit card companies may offer account alerts at no charge, so turn those on first. Identity theft monitoring can add another layer by watching for certain credit inquiries, newly opened accounts and other signs that someone may be using your personal information. That can be especially helpful with new account fraud because the criminal may never touch the accounts you already check. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com. 6) Keep a paper trail Write down who you contacted, when you contacted them and what they told you. Save letters, emails, case numbers and copies of anything you submit. Those records can save you a lot of frustration if you need to follow up later. 9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE Kurt's key takeaways New account fraud can be especially tough to spot because the criminal may never touch the bank accounts or credit cards you already watch. That is exactly why I want you to check all three of your credit reports instead of waiting for a strange bill or collection call to show up. You can pull your reports for free, look for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries and consider freezing your credit when you are not applying for anything new. Then add alerts or identity monitoring if you want another set of eyes watching for activity you might otherwise miss. The big takeaway here is speed. A fraudulent account that sits unnoticed for months can turn into damaged credit, collections and a much bigger cleanup job. Catch it early, and you have a far better chance of shutting it down before things snowball. When was the last time you checked all three of your credit reports for an account you never opened? title: Trump's home county hits pause on data centers over environment and electric bill concerns
description: Palm Beach County passed a one-year moratorium on data centers amid concerns over environmental impact, noise pollution and rising electric bills.
content: Palm Beach County — home to President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago — passed a one-year moratorium on the planning and construction of data centers as commissioners seek to conduct a thorough review of data centers’ impacts on the environment, noise pollution and electric bills. The moratorium, passed Thursday, comes just weeks after Trump said communities that reject data centers would "end up being backwards and poor." Among the wealthiest counties in the country, Palm Beach County includes the town of Palm Beach, home to 65 billionaires. "If you want to go through poverty, crime and squalor, I would say don’t approve of data centers," Trump said from the Oval Office Sept. 4. The Palm Beach County Commissioners’ 6-0 vote doesn’t put a permanent ban on data centers. Instead, it gives county leadership time to conduct environmental impact reviews before updating zoning rules for where data centers can be built. TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS' The moratorium applies to all new applications for data centers with an anticipated peak electrical load of at least 50 megawatts. "Many communities want the economic benefits a data center brings, but we all fear the higher power bills, the negative environmental impact, disruptive noise, the depletion of water resources," a Palm Beach County resident shared during Thursday’s meeting. Trump has made expanding data centers and accelerating artificial intelligence a cornerstone of his agenda, arguing the United States cannot afford to lose the AI race to China and warning that opposition to data centers only benefits Beijing. Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, housing thousands of powerful computers that store and process digital information while providing the computing power needed to train and run AI systems. In 2016, Palm Beach County approved the construction of "Project Tango," a proposed 202-acre AI data center, which is located 20 miles from Mar-a-Lago. The data center will also be built near an elementary school and homes. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI’S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS In July, commissioners voted 6-1 to reject a proposal to expand Project Tango by roughly 1.67 million square feet. But existing approvals for two 100,000-square-foot data center buildings remain in place. Residents at Thursday's meeting said Project Tango was the driving factor behind the push to hit pause on data center project approvals, with several residents advocating for no data centers to be built. "I think the best good neighbor data center is no data center," resident Sergei Kelly said. "We have the Everglades to our South and to our West. The coast to our East. I don’t think data centers, especially large data centers they want to build desperately, should be here at all." title: Cruz says winning AI race against China is 'single most important economic question' for America
description: Ted Cruz claims China and "effective altruism" backers are waging a deliberate influence campaign to shape AI policy and data center debates.
content: America's AI race against China, which has become a major point of debate as midterm elections approach, is a race filled with "coordinated" propaganda, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, warned. In recent months, data centers and AI policy have been debated in Congress and at the kitchen tables of American families. But Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee, told Fox News Digital much of the new opposition to data centers is being manipulated by a well-funded and coordinated campaign. "It's the same reason we saw Middle Eastern countries paying for anti-fracking movements," Cruz said. "Because if they can convince America, 'Don't develop your oil and gas, just buy it from us,' well, that's great for them and terrible for us. "The same is true on data centers. If they can convince Americans, 'You don't want data centers here, you want to just rely on the Chinese for AI,' that's great for China, and it's terrible for America." CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE Direct funding from the Chinese government into the U.S. on data center policies has not been revealed. However, in June, OpenAI announced it had banned ChatGPT accounts believed to have originated in China and said the accounts were generating social media comments and images alleging that data centers are raising electricity costs for Americans. OpenAI said in a statement that it shut down "two clusters of ChatGPT accounts likely originating from China that [OpenAI] banned after they used our models in support of apparent covert influence operations that promoted narratives in an attempt to manipulate a legitimate debate about American AI and wider tech policies." Cruz called the effort to craft policy to ensure the U.S. wins the AI race "the single most important economic question facing America today." INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE' "If China wins, AI will be focused on espionage and propaganda and control and surveillance because that's the Chinese Communist Party," Cruz said. "It will be their values. They will use AI to try to control you. If America wins, I want American values to be reflected in AI. I want free speech and individualism and free enterprise and privacy to be reflected in AI, not control and power." Cruz called opposition to AI advancement and data centers the "dominant position on the Democratic side." The third-term Republican said the Democrats' position is aligned with that of big industry players, including Anthropic, which he said wants an exemption from antitrust laws and to "get in bed with government" to control AI development. THE HIDDEN LEFT-WING NETWORK POWERING A ‘CONSERVATIVE’ REBELLION AGAINST A MAJOR TRUMP PRIORITY Cruz associated this position with leftist ideology and the emerging tech philosophy known as "effective altruism." "These folks from effective altruism are all hardcore leftists, and they want to use AI to push their leftist ideology," Cruz said. "Part of what we're seeing is a money grab, where there's an old concept in economics called rent-seeking, which is big companies typically go to government and say, 'Give me a benefit, entrench me.' We’re seeing the giant AI companies going to government saying, 'Hey, why don't you put us in charge of government, and let's set the rules so no one could compete with us.'" Parker Thayer, an investigative researcher at Capital Research Center in Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital last week that effective altruism is associated with what he called the "AI doomerism movement." Facebook co-founder and billionaire Democratic megadonor Dustin Moskovitz and his wife Cari Tuna have been leading financial backers of organizations associated with the effective altruism movement. Moskovitz left Facebook in 2008. The couple founded Coefficient Giving, formerly known as Open Philanthropy, and remain its "main funders," according to the organization. Tuna serves as its president. Coefficient Giving says its artificial intelligence work has expanded rapidly, with $168 million committed to AI safety, security and field-building in 2024 and $351 million in 2025. The organization says it is on track to commit more than $1 billion to similar work in 2026. In a 2021 grant application description, the organization said it seeks "to fund programs and events in a variety of areas of interest to Coefficient Giving, including effective altruism, global catastrophic risks, biosecurity, AI for epistemics, forecasting, and other areas." title: Sylvester Stallone shares harrowing new details about abusive childhood

content: Sylvester Stallone isn't looking for pity. The action star opened up about a childhood marked by abandonment, violence and an almost total absence of affection in a new interview, telling The New York Times he deliberately left some of the darkest stories out of his book because he didn't want readers to feel sorry for him. "I didn't put a lot of stuff in the book because I didn't want a pity party … but it was insane," he admitted. SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS WHAT HE SAID TO TRUMP AFTER SURPRISE HOLLYWOOD AMBASSADOR APPOINTMENT After his parent’s divorce, Stallone spent time living with his father in Maryland. One memory particularly stayed with Stallone. The Hollywood star said his father sent him to a store before church to buy bread. He returned with nut bread after running into friends. "And he kicked me in the stomach and hit me and like laid me out, got in the car, and went to church." Stallone said he was left lying in the street, saying, "Really, it's unbelievable. title: Legal expert details what travelers are entitled to after massive East Coast flight cancellations
description: Under U.S. law, travelers affected by the severed cable flight disruptions can claim a full cash refund, but rebooking first could void that right.
content: After a severed fiber optic cable disrupted thousands of flights to and from East Coast airports Monday, customers are entitled to a full refund under U.S. law, but they also have other options, Eric Napoli, chief legal officer at AirHelp, told Fox News Digital. "Under U.S. domestic law on flights, the rules are that you're entitled to a full cash refund," Napoli explained. "If you are flying to and from Europe and fall under European rules, if the cause of the delay is directly attributable to the airline, then you could be entitled to up to $700. In this case, this is completely outside of the airline's control. LAGUARDIA AIRPORT RUNWAY SHUT DOWN AFTER SINKHOLE DISCOVERED DURING ROUTINE MORNING INSPECTION "This is a tower-to-ground issue, so you don't get any compensation. But what you are entitled to is — if you decide not to take that flight, or whatever flight they give you next — a full cash refund," Napoli said. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed Amtrak for the cancellations, claiming a construction crew cut the cable. However, the company quickly pushed back. "This incident occurred on New Jersey Transit property and involved a New Jersey Transit contractor," Amtrak said in a statement. NJ Transit acknowledged working on the site where the cable was cut but claimed "the crew was digging approximately 10 feet away from the utility markings." Because the incident was not caused by any of the airlines, customers traveling to and from Europe are not entitled to a $700 cash payment that European law would entitle them to if the airport caused the delays, Napoli said. DELTA FLIGHT DIVERTED TWICE AFTER LAVATORY LEAK FLOODS CABIN, LEAVES PASSENGERS STRANDED FOR HOURS "In this scenario, European law wouldn't say that the airline has to pay compensation because the network connectivity issue was completely outside of the airline's control as it would be, for example, if a hurricane were flying in. If the aircraft had a technical issue, and they weren't able to fix it in time, that's part of the airline's business and operating model, so an airline would have to pay up to $700," he told Fox News Digital. Customers are entitled to a full cash refund under U.S. law. However, if they take an offer from the airlines to rebook their flights, they lose the option to get a refund, Napoli said. "Generally what happens is the airline will come to the passenger and say, 'Either we've canceled the flight or we've rescheduled the flight for the next day, and we've put you on another flight.' The passenger then has the option to say, 'Do I want to take the other flight, or do I not want to?' "Maybe now there's no reason to go see the game in Philadelphia, so you don't want to be rescheduled. In that case, you get your money back. If you decide to take the flight, then you wouldn't get your money back because you have consumed a service," he explained. He recommended customers take initiative in receiving their refunds rather than waiting for the airlines to reimburse them. "Generally, if you don't ask for it, you're not going to get it, so you have to be pretty proactive. Airlines have gotten really good now with offering rescheduled flights in their apps because a situation like this is also a headache for them. "The airlines have to suddenly find all of these people and rebook them. It's Tetris — along with the domino effect of delay after delay. The airlines will try to help, but for other things, like getting a food voucher, a taxi or a hotel, the traveler is going to have to be savvy and proactive," he continued. "That's where AirHelp comes in and helps. We have lots of information on our website and a 24/7 chat that keeps you updated. We also have an app that can let you know if your flight is delayed or if incoming flights are on time so you can look at sources like us. When it comes to things like compensation under European laws, airlines don't make it easy for you." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Napoli ultimately counseled travelers to remain savvy and calm. "Having information beforehand and knowing how to navigate is always best. Be prepared. Things can go wrong, and we get angry and upset. But getting angry at the people at the airport desk doesn't help the situation. It just makes you angrier. It's best to keep calm, talk to people civilly and, hopefully, things will work out," he told Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital contacted the Department of Transportation, Amtrak and New Jersey Transit for comment.

title: US, China strike deal to lower tariffs on $30B in goods after Trump-Xi Washington summit
description: The United States and China agreed to slash tariffs on $30 billion in goods after Trump and Xi Jinping's three-day Washington summit this week.
content: The United States and China agreed to lower tariffs on $30 billion in goods traded between the two countries after a three-day summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C. According to the White House, the $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions apply to "non-sensitive goods." U.S. exports, including agricultural products, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices will receive favorable tariff treatment in China. Meanwhile, U.S. imports of Chinese-made small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children's car seats will also receive preferential treatment. The agreement was reached through the U.S.-China Board of Trade, a body first proposed during Trump's visit to China in May and formally established during Xi's visit to Washington this week. XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE' U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC Friday that "a lot more details" about the new trade agreement will be released Monday. Greer said the tariff terms were hammered out after weeks of negotiations. Neither country has released the final tariff rates or all the products that will receive favored status going forward. This marks one of the most significant cooldowns in the trade war Trump launched against China in February 2025, when he levied a 10% tariff on all Chinese imports, citing Beijing's alleged role in the fentanyl crisis and illegal immigration. China hit back with levies on U.S. coal, liquefied natural gas, crude oil and cars. BESSENT REVEALS EXTENSION TO BUSAN AGREEMENT WITH CHINA UNTIL JANUARY At their peak, U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods reached a staggering 145% in April 2025, shortly after Trump unveiled his "Liberation Day" reciprocal tariffs. China responded with tariffs of up to 125% on U.S. goods. U.S. and Chinese negotiators met in Geneva in May 2025 and agreed to a 90-day truce that lowered U.S. tariffs to 30% and China's to 10%. The agreement was extended for another 90 days in August. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump and Xi reached another tentative agreement during talks in South Korea in October 2025. Under the deal, China agreed to crack down on fentanyl precursors, resume purchases of U.S. soybeans and ease restrictions on rare-earth exports, while the United States agreed to further ease tariffs. The two countries will now use the Board of Trade to negotiate additional tariff reductions and other trade disputes, leaving open the possibility of broader agreements in the months ahead.

title: Scientists reveal surprisingly easy exercise that may boost your mood in just 10 minutes
description: A University of Tsukuba study found that a slow 10-minute jog boosted attention, self-control and mood in young adults by activating the prefrontal cortex.
content: It might not take an all-out sprint or long trail run to lift your mood and sharpen focus, according to a new study. A new study from the University of Tsukuba in Japan looked at 24 healthy young adults who completed a slow, 10-minute run on a treadmill in one session and rested in another. After the easy jog, participants performed faster on a test of attention and self-control and reported feeling more alert and pleasant than they did after the resting phase, according to the small study published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience in August. 'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS Brain monitoring after the jog also showed more activity in parts of the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain responsible for focus and decision-making. The jog was purposely kept easy, with participants going at speeds from 1.9 to 3.7 mph on the treadmill. Their average heart rates clocked in at 105 to 107 beats per minute. "A single bout of running, even at very slow speed, elicits a pleasant mood and improved executive function," the researchers found. SIMPLE BODY MOVEMENT COULD HELP THE BRAIN 'CLEAN ITSELF,' RESEARCHERS FIND The finding "sheds light on the slow running benefits to brain health," they added. The benefits, they noted, stuck around even after participants' heart rates returned to baseline. JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS The greater the up-and-down head movement during the jog, the more positive the participants' mood was afterward, though that finding was exploratory and does not necessarily prove cause and effect. 5 COMMON WALKING MISTAKES THAT COULD HURT YOUR PROGRESS, ACCORDING TO AN EXPERT "Easy movement triggers the norepinephrine and dopamine pathways that wake up the part of the brain that is in charge of focus and self-control," said Dr. John La Puma, a California-based internist and author of "Indoor Epidemic," who was not involved in the study. Experts agree, however, that it does not mean one brief workout could be a cure-all. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "A brief jog should help someone get some energy in their system, which may make them feel better about themselves mentally and help them focus," said Dr. Scott Nass, a California-based family medicine physician at SwiftCareMD. But Nass, who also wasn't involved in the research, said the effect is likely temporary. For people living with depression or anxiety, a jog may briefly clear the mind but is "no substitute for medical care," he told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The study was also limited in that it included just 24 healthy, young adults and measured outcomes immediately after just one exercise session. The findings cannot be assumed to apply to older adults, novice runners or people with health conditions, and larger studies are necessary to confirm the results, Nass said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For a practical approach, La Puma suggested taking a 10-minute walk outside before the most mentally demanding part of the day. Add 30-second jogging intervals, keeping the pace easy enough to speak in full sentences without becoming breathless, he said. People with heart disease, high blood pressure, Type 1 diabetes, recent surgery or joint pain should check with a clinician before starting a new routine, La Puma advised. content: Oxford, Mississippi, Mayor Robyn Tannehill issued a stark warning Saturday about the dangers of kratom and other "gas station drugs" after packaged kratom was recovered during investigations into the deaths of two Ole Miss students. "To take kratom is really rolling the dice on death," Tannehill told "Fox & Friends Weekend." "So, our challenge right now is to make our young people understand the dangers of these drugs." TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS Tannehill said Oxford's city board passed a law prohibiting the sale of kratom at gas stations seven years ago and that local authorities have been aware of the substance's dangers for some time. "This is a substance that our police chief identified as dangerous in 2019, and we immediately took action," she said. "So, these investigations are ongoing. We are always trying to find the bad actors in our community that are choosing to sell these things to kids." The two students were found dead Sept. 21 in separate locations — one on campus and the other off campus. Although their causes of death remain undetermined, narcotics detectives are involved in both investigations. Authorities say if the reports find fentanyl, a special Mississippi law can be used to target the seller. "It's a place that takes care of each other. … The issues that we're dealing with right now are the issues that every college campus across the nation is dealing with. It's not unique to Oxford. title: Florida real estate sees surge from Washington high earners fleeing new millionaire income tax
description: Pacific Northwest millionaires are buying Florida real estate as Washington state's looming 9.9% income tax hike pushes high-net-worth individuals south.
content: Washington state millionaires are increasingly eyeing Florida real estate to escape a changing tax landscape in the Pacific Northwest, according to a luxury real estate expert. "I would say that the first thing is taxes. Income tax in Florida is 0%, and, in Washington state, it's 9.9% as of January 2028," Margit Brandt, a luxury property specialist, told Fox News Digital. "Capital gains in Florida is also 0%, and, in Washington state, it's 7%. I just think that they've created this really punitive tax environment that's unappealing to the high-net-worth individuals who are the high earners in Washington state, and that's been the biggest kind of feeder for our market here," she added. Washington's capital gains tax is tiered, with the first $1 million in taxable Washington capital gains subject to a 7% rate and amounts above $1 million subject to a 9.9% rate. Real estate is exempt from the tax. TRUCKING COMPANY OWNER SUING STATE OVER 'MILLIONAIRES TAX' SAYS POLICY HITS SMALL BUSINESSES The push comes after the Democratic-controlled Washington Legislature passed, and Gov. Bob Ferguson signed, a 9.9% levy on annual adjusted gross income above the law's $1 million threshold. Set to take effect Jan. 1, 2028 — with initial returns due in April 2029 — the legislation marks a major change for a state that has no individual income tax. The tax is already facing a court challenge over its constitutionality, while real estate insiders say the new law is influencing some wealthy residents' relocation decisions. SEATTLE MAYOR SHRUGS OFF MILLIONAIRE-TAX CONCERNS AS 44% OF BUSINESS LEADERS CONSIDER LEAVING "We've seen actual deals — big deals — happen with high earners from Washington state," Brandt said. "This is not hypothetical. These are closed transactions with people setting up a whole new life here in Florida." State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, the architect of the millionaire's tax bill, pushed back against Brandt's claims. "There are always people moving from state to state for a variety of reasons (weather, job changes, health, family members). I do not think we have any data to support the idea that substantial numbers of wealthy people are moving out of Washington," he told Fox News Digital, countering Brandt's remarks. While comprehensive data tracking millionaire migration due to the new tax are not yet available, a recent business survey found increased interest among respondents in relocating. A recent survey released by the Association of Washington Business (AWB), the state's chamber of commerce and manufacturers association, found that 24% of respondents said they were considering moving their businesses out of Washington. That figure is up from 17% in the previous quarter and nearly triple the rate recorded 16 months ago. Furthermore, 55% of surveyed business leaders said they are considering moving their personal residence to another state, a number that climbs to 67% in Spokane County, near the low-tax Idaho border. WHY STARBUCKS PICKED NASHVILLE OVER SEATTLE FOR EXPANSION, ACCORDING TO LOCAL BUSINESS REPORTER The shift is mirrored in high-profile individual departures. Jesse Proudman, founder and CTO of privacy-focused AI platform Venice.ai, told Fox News Digital in May he was leaving the Evergreen State, warning that a region once known as a "startup sanctuary" has grown increasingly hostile to business leaders. Similarly, coffee giant Starbucks announced in April it would invest $100 million to set up an additional support office in Nashville, Tennessee, a state with no individual income tax, where it expects to have 2,000 support jobs over the next five years. Starbucks said those jobs will include newly created positions, workers brought in-house and some teams moved from Seattle. Beyond balance sheets, Brandt said safety, culture and quality of life are primary drivers for wealthy transplants moving to Florida and other states, including Texas and the Carolinas. It's a whole new lifestyle," Brandt said, adding that Florida’s lack of a state estate tax and its proximity to the Caribbean appeal heavily to multi-generational wealth. "They want safety, security, good schools and to set up their financial future. Florida is just such an easy landing place, and I think we're going to see way more of it in the coming years." A spokesperson for Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash, told Fox News Digital: "This is an issue subject to initiative, currently on the ballot in our state. title: Record WNBA viewership proves the league's drama is driving fans to screens, not away from them | Matt Calkins
description: WNBA ratings hit a record 1.37 million viewers this season as drama involving Caitlin Clark and league controversies fuel unprecedented attention.
content: You're bored, and you want to convince your WNBA-loving friend that the league is a disaster. So you put together a list. You write down how the league's most popular player, Caitlin Clark, had her throat pushed in by Alyssa Thomas, but needed NBA Commissioner Adam Silver to step in and get Thomas suspended. You add how Caitlin is constantly left out of marketing campaigns, and was voted the 11th best guard in the WNBA by her peers. You throw in how the league's leaders still can't define what a woman is despite having a meeting on the subject. You jot down that teams regularly ban media (see: OutKick) they suspect will ask unflattering questions. You conclude with commissioner Cathy Engelbert once dismissing a fair question about her future by saying "I wonder whether you would ask that of a man," then note that she will retire after 2026. CAITLIN CLARK HELPS FEVER DELIVER WNBA'S LARGEST REGULAR-SEASON TV AUDIENCE IN 29 YEARS You give the list to your buddy. He just smiles. Check the TV ratings and attendance figures, he says. Shoot. He might just have you. Folks can complain about the WNBA being a circus all they want, but circuses tend to draw a lot of people into the tent. One could argue that the league has done a number on its reputation, but you can't argue with the number of eyeballs watching its teams. The WNBA averaged a record 1.37 million viewers across the ESPN networks during this regular season, which marked a 17% increase from last year. NBC and CBS also averaged at least one million viewers for their WNBA packages in 2026. And it's not just the broadcasts luring in fans. The league drew a record 3.79 million live attendees across 330 games, which is a 20.5% increase from last season. Yes, the two expansion teams inflated these numbers, but the average WNBA attendance of 11,474 was still a 5% increase from last regular season. How much of this is cash cow Caitlin Clark being healthy after missing most of last season? That certainly helps, but this goes beyond CC. Games not involving the Fever averaged 984,000 viewers this regular season — up 24% from last year. You can't tell me that isn't significant. You can't look at those numbers and say the WNBA is self-destructing. Perhaps one could argue that viewership and attendance would be even higher if smarter leadership kept the controversies at bay. But maybe, just maybe — the controversies are what's behind this boost. WILL THE WNBA’S UNSERIOUS, WEEKLY SITCOM DESTROY ONE OF THE GREATEST OPPORTUNITIES FOR WOMEN ATHLETES? As much as tradition and physical excellence drive sports viewership, drama is every bit as crucial. And whether it's the players' contempt for Clark, Sophie Cunningham's pointing meme, or the league's genuflection to trans activists —theater has the WNBA in the news every day. I once described it as half basketball, half WWE. My dad corrected me on that — it's half basketball, half Real Housewives of Hoop. When Clark barks at refs, or yells at White, or gets chewed out by Fever assistant coach Briann January — we don't turn away. Fans condemn players such as Thomas or Chennedy Carter or Mabrey for malicious fouls on Caitlin, but they don't skip the next game. Natasha Cloud losing her mind on Enes Kanter for wearing a shirt with the definition of a woman on it? Absurd. But it was a talker for a good week. Coach after coach giving pro trans answers when asked about the separation of biological men and women? Predictable, but incessantly newsworthy. The maligning of Fever supporters as racist middle Americans invading the league? Infuriating. But while fans roll their eyes one second, they glue them to the TV the next. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! I'll admit I'm as guilty as anyone. In addition to everything above, the WNBA's cowardice in banning media makes me want to stage a personal boycott. And yet, when the Fever start their playoff series against the Aces Sunday, I'll be as invested in that as any NFL game. There's a lot of talk about how the actions of players, coaches and leaders prevent the WNBA from being taken seriously. But part of me wonders if most of them even care about being taken seriously. title: Damaged fragment deemed 'unremarkable' turns out to be rare piece of Homer's 'Odyssey' history
description: A fragment of Homer's "Odyssey" Book 12 sat unnoticed for decades in Utrecht University's archives until a Radboud University professor recognized it.
content: An ancient fragment of Homer's "Odyssey" was hiding in plain sight for decades in a university library in the Netherlands — until a professor took a closer look. The discovery, announced by Utrecht University this month, was made in the university's special collections. Mark de Kreij, an assistant professor of Ancient Greek and Papyrology at Radboud University, came across the unidentified parchment while studying Greek manuscripts in the university's collection. EXPERTS STUNNED AFTER UNCOVERING HOMER'S 'ILIAD' ON EGYPTIAN MUMMY IN UNPRECEDENTED FIND De Kreij told Fox News Digital the fragment had originally been kept with Coptic Christian manuscripts, which he said was "probably why it was missed in the early research on the collection." By the time he examined it, however, the still-unidentified fragment had been moved to a box containing Greek manuscripts. Utrecht University said the fragment was first considered ordinary. "Hidden among these, first regarded as an unremarkable 7th-century fragment, was a damaged and discolored fragment with very small, neat letters," the university said. "De Kreij soon recognized a few words typical of the Homeric epics." ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CITY HIDDEN BENEATH EGYPT'S DESERT The fragment contains verses from Book 12 of the "Odyssey," including the pivotal moment when the sun god Helios discovers that Odysseus' crew killed and ate his sacred cattle. Helios then demands vengeance from Zeus, an episode recently depicted in the Christopher Nolan film adaptation. Researchers believe the manuscript was owned by a reader living in Egypt's Fayum Oasis, southwest of modern-day Cairo, around 300 A.D. The fragment has been dated to the third or fourth century A.D. And its age isn't the only thing that makes it a rarity. The university says only a few fragments like it exist across the world. ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS BATTLES COULD BE REWRITTEN BY LONG-LOST PAPAL LETTER "There are only around 30 fragments like it worldwide," the statement said. Though the university described the fragment as part of a "pocket edition" of the complete epic, one expert told Fox News Digital she was not convinced by that interpretation. "This is something that people held in their hand. This is something they carried with them." Anna Dolganov, a Roman historian and papyrologist at the Austrian Archaeological Institute of the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna, questioned whether the fragment came from a complete copy of Homer's epic. "The entire ‘Odyssey’ would require 480 pages," she said. ANCIENT BOOK OF REVELATION CITY GIVES UP STUNNING SECRET BURIED FOR 1,500 YEARS Dolganov noted that a parchment volume of that length would be extremely thick in such a small format, making it unlikely, in her view, that the codex contained the entire epic. The expert also pointed to the handwriting, which she described as more casual and cursive than what she would expect in a complete literary work. "What I think it's more likely to be is an anthology," she posited. "Or a private collection of excerpts from literary texts, possibly for use in schools, for education or a private anthology that would have been much, much smaller — not the entire 'Odyssey.'" De Kreij pointed to the text preserved on both sides of the parchment as evidence that it belonged to a complete copy of the epic. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Both sides contain passages from book 12 of the ‘Odyssey,’ which are nearly contiguous," he told Fox News Digital. De Kreij said an anthology is theoretically possible, but he knows of no similar examples from the period. Complete copies of works such as the "Iliad" and "Odyssey," by contrast, have numerous parallels, he said. Dolganov said the discovery also reflects Homer's widespread popularity in the ancient world, where his works played an important role in education. The ancient poet "was very popular indeed all over the Mediterranean world where Greek was learned," Dolganov said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Homer was used to teach Greek," she added, explaining that his works were widely used as school texts around the Eastern Mediterranean. Dolganov noted that dating ancient literary manuscripts can be difficult and imprecise, particularly in situations where scholars rely on handwriting as evidence. "It would be important not to overstate how certain we are that this is indeed as early as the third or fourth century," she said. "But it doesn't need to be to be a very interesting and exciting discovery." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ De Kreij said the dating is based on several features of the fragment, including its codex format, parchment material, the appearance of the ink and its handwriting. "The neat, small bookhand cannot be dated with absolute certainty, but there are good parallels from the late third and fourth century," he said. "All such dating has to be approximate, but in the scientific edition, I cite a number of dated parallels to back up my estimate." Dolganov also reflected on the human connection offered by the discovery. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This is something that people held in their hand," she said. "This is something they carried with them and read, and it's a text that's also accessible to us. "So it kind of connects us to the ancient reader because we are similarly excited by this timeless work of literature."

title: 'Primetime' Review: Robert Pattinson channels Chris Hansen in riveting dramatization of 'To Catch a Predator'
description: Fox News Digital reviews A24's new reality TV thriller "Primetime" starring Robert Pattison, Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. Directed by Lance Oppenheim.
content: "Have a seat." Those words were memorably said by Chris Hansen, the "Dateline NBC" correspondent who hosted the provocative reality series "To Catch a Predator" during the 2000s. Hansen, notably, had zero involvement in the making of A24's new film, "Primetime," which was adapted from a 2007 Esquire article titled "Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die." In fact, according to Hansen, the studio wanted him to sign a restrictive agreement before showing him the movie, which he refused to do. After watching "Primetime," you can see why A24 was hoping for a legal cover. Because unless you're Hansen or any other key people involved, it's difficult to know where the reality ends and where the fiction begins. ‘RESIDENT EVIL’ REVIEW: DIRECTOR ZACH CREGGER DELIVERS INFECTIOUS REBOOT TO GORY VIDEO GAME FRANCHISE Robert Pattinson steps into the role as Hansen, a self-aggrandizing and rather eccentric journalist looking to be taken seriously by his NBC colleagues — perhaps with the success of "To Catch a Predator." If you aren't familiar, "To Catch a Predator" exposed men who believed they were meeting minors after sexually explicit online conversations. Instead, they walked into sting operations that typically ended with Hansen emerging from another room to confront them before police made arrests. The show's producer, Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) is just as essential as its star. Her job is to keep the engine running and to make sure Hansen doesn't drift into a mental abyss. It isn't until she and Hansen are brought into the office of NBC chief Jeff Zucker (humorously played by Zucker himself), who informs them he's moving their show into primetime, giving them the daunting task of going up against ABC juggernaut "Lost" in the same time slot. 'THE DOG STARS' REVIEW: JACOB ELORDI FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN RIDLEY SCOTT'S DULL POST-APOCALYPTIC WESTERN In "Primetime," the predators are also the prey as Hansen and his team go to incredible lengths to nab a creep, but more importantly, to make great television. Some members of the team grapple with the ethics and morality of their line of work. Hansen, at least the film's version of him, views himself as a saint, carrying out a righteous mission despite his own shortcomings in his personal life. But it's far more nuanced for new hire Dan Plumb (Skyler Gisondo), a 23-year-old aspiring actor hired to play a 13-year-old decoy. You can tell how visibly shaken he is by the process, and he struggles with whether obtaining the coveted Screen Actors Guild membership card is worth ruining other people's lives. BOX OFFICE COMEBACK: HOW SUMMER 2026 OFFERS A GLIMMER OF HOPE FOR HOLLYWOOD IN THE POST-COVID ERA Pattinson has had an impressive year between "The Drama" and "The Odyssey" (not to mention "Dune: Part Three" in December), proving he's come a long way from his "Twilight" days. He gives a career-best performance as a self-obsessed, borderline unhinged NBC host. While he gets top billing, the emotional crutch of the entire movie rests on Gisondo's shoulders. Best known for his stint on HBO's "The Righteous Gemstones" and more recently playing Jimmy Olsen in the new "Superman" movie, Gisondo is able to show depth from Dan's charming naivety to utter demoralization. Wever also shines as the no-nonsense producer who has to put up with a lot of nonsense. Director Lance Oppenheim's background in documentaries shows in "Primetime" between the reliance on the hidden cameras that only fuels the intensity and the cutaways to various cultural references. The low-resolution style takes viewers back to a pre-4K era and the shadows provide a noir element. CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS The Verdict What can be viewed as an indictment of how sleazy the television industry can be, "Primetime" isn't exactly the feel-good movie of the year, but it's a riveting thriller that showcases outstanding performances from Pattinson, Gisondo and Wever. ★★★ ½ — SEE IT NOW "Primetime" is rated R for disturbing sexual material, graphic nudity, some violent content and language. title: Hidden California desert pet cemetery holds unexpected piece of White House history
description: Charley Stewart's Haven for Pets in Desert Hot Springs holds graves of Gerald Ford's dog Liberty and pets once owned by Liberace and Hollywood stars.
content: When members of the Secret Service swarmed Charley Stewart’s plot of land in the middle of California's Sonoran Desert, he wasn’t confused or worried. He knew what they had come for. "They have representatives, the Secret Service and the secretaries, and all those people come by," he told Fox News Digital. "It’s like a circus." Stewart owns and operates Haven for Pets, a pet cemetery in Desert Hot Springs. When one of the nation’s most famous dogs — former President Gerald Ford’s golden retriever, Liberty — was set to be buried there, Secret Service agents visited the cemetery to inspect the grounds ahead of the burial, Stewart said. DISCOVERIES THAT RESHAPED WHAT HISTORIANS KNEW ABOUT AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS "Before she got buried out there, the Secret Service had to go out and look for mines and walk around," the cemetery owner said. "I mean, Gerald Ford was the president of the United States." The female golden retriever arrived at the White House as a puppy and became the nation’s first dog, later giving birth to nine puppies in 1975 on the third floor of the White House. Liberty was the first dog to give birth in the White House. The frequently photographed canine enjoyed White House life. She posed on the North Lawn, lounged beside the commander in chief in the Oval Office, swam in the pool at Camp David and even received fan mail from Americans across the country. The Fords kept one of Liberty’s puppies, a female named Misty, who is buried alongside her mother at Haven for Pets. Their gravesites leave an unexpected piece of presidential history tucked away in Stewart’s pet cemetery. RONALD REAGAN'S GRANDDAUGHTER, KEVIN MCCARTHY HONOR LATE PRESIDENT'S LEGACY ON HIS 115TH BIRTHDAY Stewart’s Haven for Pets dates back to the 1960s. It opened as an extension of a full-service Palm Springs kennel called Dogtown USA, which was known for providing grooming services to celebrity pets. Dogtown was purchased by Stewart’s father, Charles Stewart, in 1959, and Stewart recalled the story of how the pet cemetery came to be. "My father told me a story one time. He went over to talk to some people, and their dog had died, and they threw it in a garbage can, and the head was hanging out," Stewart said. "From that horrible sight, my father said, ‘We’ve got to take care of these babies.’ And, so, he decided to do that. "It took a couple years to do the paperwork, but that’s what he did. … This was an input my father never got over." Haven for Pets’ celebrity canine clientele extends beyond the White House, all the way to Hollywood. STAGECOACH FESTIVALGOERS SPLIT ON WHETHER AMERICA IS HEADED IN THE RIGHT DIRECTION AHEAD OF ITS 250TH BIRTHDAY World-famous pianist Liberace has six of his dogs buried in the cemetery under headstones that list their owner as "Lee," his nickname. Actor Michael Landon and Academy Award-winning composer Jimmy Van Heusen also have their pets buried there. Stewart told Fox News Digital the VIP connections grew out of his family’s work caring for pets belonging to celebrities who lived in the Coachella Valley. "Going back to Leonard Firestone and the Marx Brothers down here in Thunderbird Country Club, my dad would take care of their dogs," he shared. "We’d groom them and we boarded them. … We did business with them." Roughly 1,000 pets are buried in the cemetery. In its early days decades ago, the burial rate was $35. These days it costs nearly $900. Stewart said that, at one point, the cemetery would handle five burials a week, but the figure has fallen to three or four a year because he wants to limit the frequency of burials and extend the life of the cemetery grounds. 1,000-YEAR-OLD CHURCH MYSTERY CRACKED BY STUDENTS FROM KING CHARLES' ALMA MATER Stewart told Fox News Digital the unadvertised cemetery is not easy to find, and he intends to keep it that way. "I don’t advertise the cemetery. It’s all word of mouth," he said. "I don’t want to speed up the process. The cemetery right now is set up in a way that it’s going to last way in excess of 200 years." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Stewart, who has been part of the cemetery for nearly his entire life, said he spends about two hours each day sitting in a lawn chair among the headstones, surrounded by the animals he believes "never die" and keeping watch over Liberty.

title: Dem House hopeful endorsed by activist who said 'evil Jews run the world'
description: Adina Flores, who endorsed Eric Jones for Congress, has posted content about Zionists, Freemasons and LGBTQ ideology on her social media pages.
content: Adina Flores, an activist and a self-proclaimed "civil rights" advocate with a colorful social media presence, is endorsing Eric Jones, the Democratic candidate for Congress in California's 4th Congressional District. The endorsement itself, which focuses on Jones’ promises to combat women’s sexual exploitation, is nothing out of the ordinary. But Flores’ Facebook, Instagram and Substack pages are full of eccentric content that frames political issues as a conflict between race, sexual orientation and secretive sources of influence. The endorsement raises questions for Jones, who has met with Flores multiple times about whether he agrees with Flores’ views, according to social media clips. In one video posted to Facebook, Flores stated she believed part of California, Sonoma County, was run by Jews. "But we’re literally run by the gay Jewish mafia — the Zionists in Sonoma County. The Jews still run the world. That’s where we’re at," Flores said. "All our money gets sent to Israel, but nobody wants to talk about that." JEWISH COMMUNITY IN DENVER ON HIGH ALERT OVER RISE OF DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MELAT KIROS "Evil Jews run the world through Masonic Lodges," Flores said in an August Instagram post. "Santa Rosa City Schools is always recruiting for little gay communists. Help save public school enrollment decline by sending your child off to liberal prison indoctrination centers," she said in another post earlier this year. When asked about Flores' online comments, Jones' campaign said he condemns prejudice toward the Jewish community. "I firmly condemn any and all hate toward our Jewish and LGBTQ+ communities. It has no place in our district. My wife is Jewish. We are raising our kids in a Jewish household. I'm a fierce advocate for our public schools and educators. And I have zero tolerance for hateful commentary toward my neighbors or my family," a campaign spokesperson said in a comment to Fox News Digital. Beyond her comment about Jews, Flores bashes what she sees as efforts to indoctrinate kids in LGBTQ+ ideology through control over institutions like schools and local government in much of her content. "I wasn’t doing any of the wokeness. I stood up for conservative parents. So, right now, look at this pride indoctrination. I’m not trying to be mean, but who made this logo? They got all the rainbow mafia colors, and it looks like a penis," Flores said, holding up a design made by a local school. The image depicts a tree on top of a hill, illustrated in rainbow colors. "Like, literally, that’s where we’re at. So, I’m sorry that’s f---ing cracked out. If your child is in public school, please remove them because they’re going to be gay and retarded. Thank you, Santa Rosa schools," Flores said. Flores' criticisms, usually couched in similar language, cut across both parties. "Every day my Instagram algorithm is filled with reels of Democrats and Republicans arguing back and forth deciding who is more gay and retarded even though they are two sides of the same bird [sic]," Flores said. LOS ANGELES SCHOOLS QUIETLY REMOVE COMPULSORY 'AFFIRM AND RESPECT' GENDER IDENTITY PLEDGE FROM LGBTQ TRAINING "The real puppet master, as always, the Freemasons. This is not a conspiracy. And that is who is pulling the narrative of both sides — red and blue." Flores recounted that she was once a government employee but was forced out of the role and is banned from serving in public roles again. "I got started in my activism because I am a former government employee. I’m a whistleblower who was forced out of the government." title: VAN HIPP: Why the Army should restore its grassroots link to America's communities
description: The Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army program was terminated in June 2025, severing a century-old link between the U.S. Army and Main Street.
content: I first wrote about the "Forgotten Americans" in early 2016 in an opinion piece for Fox News. The phrase was actually coined by Pat Buchanan when he served as a presidential speechwriter for President Nixon. Nixon used it in at least one speech but then started using the phrase "Silent Majority." In my piece, I talked about who the "Forgotten Americans" really are. They love their families and want a better life for their kids. They believe in American exceptionalism. They work hard, worship their God and go to church. They pay their taxes and obey the law. When America's security is threatened, the Forgotten Americans are always the first to volunteer to defend it. They want to see America's border secured, and they're concerned about "political correctness" being taught to their children in schools that they fund. A few months after my op-ed, the Trump campaign started using the phrase "Forgotten Americans," and it was a central part of President Trump's acceptance speech at the 2016 Republican National Convention. RENEWED PATRIOTISM AND CAREER OPPORTUNITIES FUEL ARMY'S BIGGEST RECRUITING SURGE IN YEARS For over 100 years, there's been no better link between the U.S. military and grassroots Americans than the Army's Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army (CASA) Program. Historically, the secretary of the Army has appointed at least one individual in each state to serve as a civilian aide to the secretary of the Army. That person has usually been a business or civic leader who serves in a purely voluntary capacity but has served as the link for telling the "Army story" and building support for the U.S. military in local communities. In fact, on the U.S. Army’s own website, it’s referred to as "The Army’s Link to the People." I believe we can have a laser focus on the technology America needs to protect our national security interests and keep the American people safe while still engaging with the grassroots and telling the Army story at the local level. Over the years, the CASAs have gone into schools in rural America to tell the Army story and instill patriotism among our nation's youth. They've also been a big asset in working with Army recruiters to address recruiting challenges at the local level. Fortunately, today, we have a secretary of war who has gotten personally involved to help ensure we meet our active-duty recruiting goals, but that hasn’t always been the case. Meeting a recruiting goal does not end the need to earn the trust of the next generation of soldiers and families. MCCHRYSTAL, BRIDGELAND: WANT TO STRENGTHEN AMERICA? REQUIRE A YEAR OF NATIONAL SERVICE CASAs have also offered tremendous support for our "Soldier for Life" program. The Soldier for Life program supports our soldiers as they transition out of uniform and into civilian life. CASAs have connected transitioning soldiers with local employers and guided them through other decisions they must make during the transition to civilian life. Over the years, I've been impressed, too, with the volunteer work of CASAs in helping military families facing a particular need. Unfortunately, in June 2025, the decision was made to terminate the entire Corps of Civilian Aides to the Secretary of the Army. In making the move, Army leadership said it wanted to focus more on technology than community engagement. I certainly understand the role of technology in today's modern battlefield. In fact, I had the honor last year of giving one of the keynote addresses at Taiwan's annual National Security Summit. In my remarks, I specifically focused on artificial intelligence, quantum and spectrum as the equalizers of the battlefield of the future. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION I believe we can have a laser focus on the technology America needs to protect our national security interests and keep the American people safe while still engaging with the grassroots and telling the Army story at the local level. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Army needs the innovation of Silicon Valley. It also needs the commitment of Main Street and the regular people who answer the call to serve — our Forgotten Americans. It’s time to restore the CASA program’s traditional, community-based role. Building the Army of the future should not mean losing its link to the people. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM VAN HIPP
