title: Trump revives rare budget maneuver to rescind $810M in congressionally approved funds
description: Trump used a pocket rescission to cancel $810 million in approved spending on refugee programs, diversity initiatives and migrant education.
content: The Trump administration announced Friday that it was canceling $810 million in congressionally approved spending for programs serving illegal immigrants, diversity initiatives and other efforts the administration argued do not benefit American citizens. To claw back the funds, President Donald Trump used a "pocket rescission," a budget maneuver the executive branch contends is within its authority but that Congress and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) say exceeds the president's authority. The vast majority of the cuts, some $567 million, were aimed at Health and Human Services programs that provided funding to non-government organizations supporting refugees, asylees and other noncitizens. The White House is also seeking to rescind $25 million for education programs for migrant students, claiming they supported things such as "an LGBT youth summit" and "Therapy for Latinx workshops." TRUMP ADMIN AXES TIES TO DOZENS OF PROGRESSIVE GROUPS IN 'DIRECT OPPOSITION' TO MISSION: 'DECISIVE ACTION' Programs the administration labeled "Woke International Education" were also selected for $70 million in cuts. The White House said the funding supports bringing foreign students and faculty to the United States and, in some cases, has funded doctoral dissertations on "queer and trans community building in foreign countries." Other programs receiving the axe included a Justice Department office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, Housing and Urban Development Department counseling services and a series of Health and Human Services grants the administration described as "outright harmful and blatantly ideological." The White House's announcement about the rescissions noted that several of the organizations are led by former officials in President Barack Obama's administration. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who faces a tough re-election campaign, condemned Trump's cuts and called it "the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse." WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD Under the most recent pocket rescission, the White House proposed canceling the funding near the end of the federal fiscal year on Sept. 30. Collins argued that this was intentional on the part of the Trump administration because if the money remains unspent until Sept. 30, it expires before Congress' 45-day review period can be completed. On top of that, the House of Representatives will be out of session through the November election, making it essentially impossible for Congress to respond. "The independent Government Accountability Office has concluded that pocket rescissions are unlawful and not permitted by the Impoundment Control Act," Collins said in a statement. "I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The OMB under Trump has argued that the Impoundment Control Act does not explicitly forbid the president from rescinding funds near the end of a fiscal year, according to a summary from the Congressional Research Service (CRS). OMB Director Russ Vought has repeatedly said the same. That same CRS summary said the GAO has likened pocket rescissions to a line-item veto, which would allow a president to strike portions of legislation without congressional approval, a power the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional. A year ago, Trump issued the first pocket rescission in nearly 50 years, seeking to cancel $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The Supreme Court declined to block the move, citing the president's authority over foreign affairs as it allowed litigation to continue. The last pocket rescission took place under former President Jimmy Carter, who proposed it well before the 45-day congressional review deadline.

title: KFC unveils radically different restaurant in major comeback push
description: KFC's new Open House restaurant in McKinney, Texas, blends art deco design, digital ordering and table service to test breakfast and late-night dining that could shape future locations.
content: A new KFC restaurant in McKinney, Texas, is about much more than debuting a new design. "This is the Kentucky Fried comeback made real in one restaurant," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie told Fox News Digital. The restaurant, dubbed Open House, serves as a testing ground for how the 75-year-old fast-food chain that Colonel Harland Sanders founded might modernize without abandoning the things that made it famous. WHY KFC'S FRIED CHICKEN TASTES DIFFERENT FROM THAT OF EVERY OTHER FAST-FOOD CHAIN KFC's challenge isn't necessarily getting Americans to remember the brand. It's getting them to think about it when deciding what to eat today. "There is a massive love for this American icon," Tan-Gillespie said. But in the U.S., she added, "we tend to be thought about in people's memories. We're not actually being considered in eating moments of today." That tension between nostalgia and relevance helped shape Open House. In developing the restaurant, KFC started with a question. "We sat back and said, you know, ‘If the Colonel were building a restaurant from scratch today, what would this look like?’" Tan-Gillespie said. AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY The answer incorporates Art Deco and mid-century modern influences alongside large glass windows, digital ordering and drive-thru technology. At the same time, the restaurant features lobby hosts, table service, booths and outdoor dining designed to encourage customers to gather. "For me, the philosophy is that we should be digital where it's helpful but human where it matters," Tan-Gillespie said. The menu follows a similar philosophy: Hold onto KFC's most recognizable products while experimenting with how customers want to eat chicken now, Tan-Gillespie said. Buckets and the chain's original recipe remain central, but Open House expands into tenders, wings, sandwiches, wraps and nuggets, along with new sauces, drinks, snacks, sweets and sides. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Breakfast is part of the experiment, too. Open House is scheduled to operate from 6 a.m. to midnight, giving KFC an opportunity to test breakfast and late-night occasions that traditionally haven't been a major part of its U.S. business. "We will see if those shoulder day parts work commercially for us and work for the guests, work for our team members," Tan-Gillespie said. "If they don't, we'll cut them back. And if they do, then we can look to scale them nationally." "I think the things that should change is making sure that we expand into the ways that customers want to eat fried chicken today." KFC also chose McKinney with scalability in mind. Tan-Gillespie described the Dallas-Fort Worth area as a fast-growing and competitive restaurant market, while McKinney provides a mix of existing KFC customers and consumers the chain hopes to attract. The suburban setting also gives KFC a test that could potentially translate to similar markets elsewhere. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS But even as KFC experiments with new formats, flavors, technology and day parts, Tan-Gillespie said some pieces of the brand aren't up for reinvention. "Buckets of original recipe fried chicken should not change," she said. "I think the things that should change is making sure that we expand into the ways that customers want to eat fried chicken today." title: BROADCAST BIAS: Media bash Sydney Sweeney but cover for leftist Macklemore

Sweeney is featured in mostly naked advertisements for a sports prediction market called Novig. She reported the four-time Olympic gold medalist swimmer Ariarne Titmus called the ad "a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft." title: PRESIDENT PAZ: Bolivia has rejected socialism and is open for business
description: Bolivia's leader outlines a shift from socialism to "capitalism for everyone," seeking United States investment in lithium, copper and natural gas.
content: Bolivia is beginning a new chapter. For nearly two decades, my country was governed by the Movement Toward Socialism. That period reshaped Bolivia’s economy, institutions and relationship with the United States. Today, my government is taking a different direction: rebuilding confidence, strengthening institutions, opening the economy to investment and creating more room for private enterprise and entrepreneurship. When I took office, Bolivia’s Central Bank had only $51 million in reserves. Ten months later, reserves had risen to close to $1.2 billion, and our objective is to continue rebuilding them. Inflation remains high, fuel shortages have tested our people and the work ahead is difficult. But the direction is clear: Bolivia is putting its economic house in order. TRUMP ADMIN BACKS BOLIVIA STATE OF EMERGENCY AS LEFTIST EX-LEADER'S LOYALISTS FRACTURE NATION During my campaign, I described our approach as "capitalism for everyone." By that I mean access to capital, the ability to invest, the freedom to build businesses and the opportunity to create jobs and prosperity. Ideology does not put food on the table. Employment does. Production does. Investment does. Economic growth does. This new economic direction is also creating the basis for a new relationship with the United States. My discussions in New York with Secretary of State Marco Rubio reflected an important change in the relationship between our countries. Bolivia seeks cooperation with the United States based on mutual respect, economic opportunity, security, investment and shared interests. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN The Trump administration has placed renewed attention on the Western Hemisphere, including economic strength, security and cooperation among the nations of the Americas. Bolivia intends to engage constructively in that conversation while pursuing its own national interests and rebuilding relationships that can contribute to growth and stability. Bolivia is open for business. But opening our economy does not mean selling our future. RESOURCE-RICH NATION PRAISES US TIES AMID WASHINGTON-BEIJING CRITICAL MINERALS RACE Our country possesses extraordinary natural wealth. We have natural gas, agricultural capacity, forests and strategic minerals including lithium, copper and tin that are increasingly important to the global economy. But we do not want to repeat the history of countries that exported their natural resources for decades while remaining poor. Bolivia cannot simply remove minerals from the ground, ship them abroad and watch other countries create the technology, manufacturing, jobs and value from them. We want long-term partnerships built around employment, training, technology, infrastructure, productivity and value added in Bolivia. AFRICAN GROWTH BOOM FOLLOWS TRUMP PUSH TO REPLACE AID WITH TRADE Our message to American and international investors is straightforward: Bolivia welcomes investment, capital, technology and expertise. We want companies that are prepared to build, produce, employ, train and grow alongside Bolivian workers and businesses. As I told the United Nations, Bolivia wants to be open to the world with dignity. US, SHIELD OF THE AMERICAS CONDEMN 'ONGOING EFFORTS' TO OVERTHROW BOLIVIA'S ELECTED PRESIDENT AMID UNREST That means economic growth must also serve the Bolivian people. A stronger private sector does not mean abandoning social responsibility. Our objective is to create better jobs, stronger institutions, better education, greater security and more opportunity. We must protect our forests and the Amazon, respect our Indigenous communities and ensure that development creates tangible benefits for the people who live here. The same principle applies to our young people. Bolivia’s future will depend on whether they can find purpose, work and opportunity at home. Investment should help create that future. TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT Bolivia’s economic direction is therefore based on a simple proposition: work with the United States, our neighbors, and the wider world; welcome productive investment; encourage entrepreneurship; expand private enterprise; and ensure that the wealth created in Bolivia also improves the lives of Bolivians. title: Wave of overlooked 'left-wing' lawsuits could come with an unexpected price tag for Americans
description: A report from Power The Future and the Heritage Foundation warns climate lawsuits could cost American households nearly $1,465 more per year.
content: FIRST ON FOX: American households could end up paying $1,465 more per year on average in energy costs if "anti-energy" climate lawsuits against oil and gas companies are successful, according to a new report first obtained by Fox News Digital. Americans will "pay a lot more" if the far-left "get their way," warned Heritage Foundation Chief Economist E.J. Antoni, who co-authored the report with Power The Future founder Daniel Turner. Hundreds of lawsuits and other state-level "climate Superfund" laws could increase the cost of gasoline, electricity and other everyday necessities Americans rely on, the report estimates. SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA The new analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear a closely-watched lawsuit next month out of Boulder, Colorado, that could drastically shape the future of climate litigation. "If those folks on the radical left wing who are anti-energy, if they get their way, your costs are going to go up," Antoni told Fox News Digital. "Your household is going to pay a lot more. The energy is going to get much more expensive. "You may think it's bad now, but it will get significantly worse." The report estimates energy companies could face an additional $194 billion in annual costs, which the authors argue would ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices rather than absorbed entirely by companies or their shareholders. Those costs could add roughly 41 cents to a gallon of gasoline and increase residential electricity rates by about 8.6%, according to the analysis. "Every single time a company is sued, yes, they pay some damages, but ultimately they will just charge people more for their product to recoup those losses," Turner told Fox News Digital. LAWSUITS COST EVERY AMERICAN HOUSEHOLD THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS; SUPREME COURT CAN HELP The report examined more than 300 pending lawsuits, three state "climate Superfund" laws, 12 state legislative proposals and one federal bill. Its estimate reflects a "full-success scenario" in which all of those measures prevail; it does not predict that they will. The analysis counted each lawsuit only once and excluded duplicate filings. In fact, Antoni said the estimate may be conservative because some lawsuits do not specify the damages they are seeking, leaving potential court awards open-ended. The legal efforts include New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act, which was blocked by a federal judge in August, and the Supreme Court’s pending Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County case. That case could determine whether state and local governments can pursue climate lawsuits against fossil fuel companies in state court. GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'HIDDEN CLIMATE TAX' HITTING AMERICANS NATIONWIDE, LAWMAKER WARNS Turner argued the lawsuits could also shift responsibility away from state and local leaders. "The concern about these Superfund lawsuits is that they absolve elected leaders from doing the bad, boring part of governing, which is infrastructure and mitigation strategies," he said. Despite the rise in climate lawsuits and state "Superfund" laws, Antoni said the issue has largely flown under the radar. title: Put down those textbooks and turn off the screens; here is a great way for kids to learn
description: Charlotte Mason's "living books" philosophy offers a powerful alternative to bland textbooks, transforming how children learn through great literature.
content: It’s late September. Kids are firmly back in school; routines are established and reading lists set. But what exactly is on the menu? The usual textbooks, which, if they’re in a government school, are often written by committee (with an agenda), range from uninspiring to outright woke. Or maybe most of your child’s school curriculum is delivered via lifeless and impersonal computer screens. But there is an alternative, a source whose advocacy first transformed the task of educating children over 100 years ago. Virtually unknown to public school parents, the British 19th-century reformer Charlotte Mason (1842-1923) has long been the hero of modern homeschooling in America and the movement’s best-kept secret weapon. WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO But her ideas and theories are not just applicable to the homeschooling community. Parents and educators can greatly benefit from Mason’s ideas about children and reading, which are even more relevant today. Creating a thirst for knowledge and lifelong love of learning was Mason’s goal. If children developed an early hunger for ideas, she reasoned, it would sustain them through their lives. Mason believed that, in addition to the proper vitamins and nutrients needed to thrive, children require ideas to chew on to properly grow. And the source of these ideas, she reasoned, was not typical textbooks. BEN CARSON, RILEY GAINES FIGHT SCRUBBING OF FAITH FROM KIDS' US HISTORY BOOKS FOR AMERICA'S 250TH That’s a perspective as true today as it was in Mason’s time. Most, if not all, textbooks children encounter in public schools are either bland by design, so as not to arouse controversy, or the opposite: brazenly geared to advance a woke agenda. Mason believed that the best resource for the ideas that will benefit children most came from a regular exposure to great art, great music and, above all, books of "literary quality" or great books. "For the best thought the world possesses is stored in books," she wrote in "Parents and Children." "Children must have books, living books ... the best is not too good for them; anything less than the best is not good enough." DOLLY PARTON'S BELOVED LITERACY MISSION SEES SURGE OF SUPPORT AFTER COUNTRY ICON'S DEATH Her idea of "living books" was about books written by a single author (not a committee), those that actively engage the mind, imagination and spirit, rather than simply presenting factual material. For example, a list of "living books" for early learners (grades 1-4) might include "The Trumpet of the Swan," "Black Beauty" and "A Little Princess." Titles for middle school students include "My Side of the Mountain," "Around the World in 80 Days," "To Kill a Mockingbird" and C.S. Lewis’ classic "Narnia" series. CLASSICAL EDUCATION AND AI COULD RESHAPE HOW AMERICA PREPARES ITS CHILDREN High school students can gain most from reading "Pride and Prejudice," "David Copperfield" and "Through Gates of Splendor," as well as the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. Living books like these can spark kids’ curiosity, thanks to their authors’ genuine passion for their subject. WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL Unlike textbooks, they use a compelling, even spellbinding style that draws the student into the plot and characters, triggering their imagination and emotions. Her idea of "living books" was about books written by a single author (not a committee), ones that actively engage the mind, imagination and spirit, rather than simply presenting factual material. Living books like "My Side of the Mountain" and "To Kill a Mockingbird" weave sometimes complex concepts and subjects into an approachable narrative in ways that allow children to more easily connect and identify with the material. Like those of us who grew up with favorite books, children are bound to remember details and themes, long after the work has been returned to the shelf. GEORGIA SCHOOL DISTRICT DEFENDS PULLING 'SEXUALLY EXPLICIT' BOOK DEPICTING CHILD RAPE AMID 'CENSORSHIP' CLAIMS Living books often feature unfamiliar words and language that challenge young readers to expand their vocabulary. Contrary to what lazy teachers may think, old-fashioned forms of communicating in English, like Charles Dickens’s novels or even the King James Bible, don’t turn off young minds. They broaden and deepen a reader’s grasp of the English language, which is crucial for their intellectual, even moral, growth. For instance, E. B. White, author of classics like "Charlotte’s Web," and "The Trumpet of the Swan," never hesitated to challenge his young readers with new words like "radiant" and "humble" because he believed, like Charlotte Mason, that children were smart, capable readers. AMERICAN SCHOOLS COST MORE THAN EVER BUT OUR STUDENTS STILL KEEP FAILING White once said, "Anyone who writes down to children is simply wasting his time. You have to write up, not down. Children are demanding. They are the most attentive, curious, eager, observant, sensitive, quick, and generally congenial readers on earth. … Children are game for anything. I throw them hard words, and they backhand them across the net." Finally, unlike typical textbooks, living books help students move from a passive learning mode to an active learning mode. Instead of simply memorizing what they need to know to pass a test, having students retell a story like "The Little Princess" in their own words, builds lasting communication and analytical skills. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Try some living books out on your children if you haven’t already. Books like Louisa May Alcott’s "Little Women" will teach them lessons about the importance of family, sacrifice, and generosity. Mark Twain’s "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" teaches about friendship, loyalty and moral courage. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Charlotte Mason used to say, "Education is an atmosphere, a discipline, a life." If our current educators have abandoned that hopeful vision, turning to living books can restore it, not just for children, but for all of us. title: Mistress may have handed prosecutors missing ‘why’ in ‘American Idol’ alum’s wife murder case: expert
description: The Caleb Flynn trial took a dramatic turn as mistress Alleigha Botner read explosive texts exchanged in the months before Ashley Flynn's fatal shooting.
content: The explosive testimony of Caleb Flynn's former mistress may have handed Ohio prosecutors a critical piece of their murder case against the former "American Idol" contestant — a potential answer to why he would allegedly kill his wife, a former prosecutor told Fox News Digital. "Motive. She provides a motive," Josh Ritter, a former prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor, said of Alleigha Botner's testimony. "She gives jurors a reason for why would this man murder his wife. "She seems like she was, by all accounts, a very nice woman," Ritter said about Ashley Flynn. "She's the mother of his children. Yes, he wanted out of the marriage. "Perhaps there was some financial gain in the idea of life insurance, but, you know, jurors oftentimes struggle with that question." He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges. Botner, who testified she carried on an affair with Flynn for roughly a year and a half, spent two days walking jurors through many of the 107,000-plus messages exchanged during their relationship. NEW JERSEY MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING WIFE WITH BARBELL ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED IN MESSAGES TO RELATIVES: REPORT Some contained explicit discussions about Ashley's death. And I've had this thought so often lately. How do we figure this out?" Botner also became emotional while reading one of her own messages to Flynn, expressing regrets that she wished she never wrote it. ALEX MURDAUGH LAWYERS ALLEGE ‘FABRICATED’ EVIDENCE WAS USED TO SECURE MURDER INDICTMENTS "I want to kill her, Caleb," she had written. "That makes two of us," Flynn allegedly responded. ALEX MURDAUGH MAKES 'EXPLOSIVE' BID TO BLOW UP MURDER CASE HINGING ON DNA, DIRTY MONEY AND LIES: EXPERT Ritter said it is the substance of those exchanges — rather than simply the existence of the affair or sheer volume of messages — that could prove significant for prosecutors. "It's the idea that he's even discussing her being dead," Ritter said. "He went as far as saying I literally would kill her. That's far beyond someone voicing their frustrations and venting to a lover that I wish my wife wasn't around, I wish she would leave, I wish we could get a divorce. "This is saying you want that person dead, that, in your view, that is your solution to the problem that you have." The messages grew particularly significant as prosecutors moved jurors closer to the night Ashley was killed. FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON FOUND GUILTY OF MURDERING ATTORNEY WHO VANISHED FROM BLOODY OFFICE Botner testified that Flynn told her in an August message he had stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail." Months later, Botner gave Flynn a Jan. 11 ultimatum to leave Ashley or she would end their relationship. When he failed to do so, Botner cut off communication until Feb. 14, just two days before Ashley's death. By the night of Feb. 15, the two were communicating again. Botner testified that Flynn discussed his plans for the following day, including telling family members about the divorce and obtaining a burner phone. Shortly after midnight, Flynn allegedly wrote to Botner, "It's happening." He then wrote, "February 16th – day I'll never forget." "You're about to be free," Botner responded. "I choose you," Flynn replied. Those were some of the final messages Flynn sent Botner before she learned Ashley had been killed, she testified. Ritter pointed to that timing as among the most significant evidence Botner brought to the prosecution's case. He noted that Flynn had spent months allegedly talking about wanting Ashley dead before the messages reached the eve of her killing. "The day before the murder takes place, he tells his mistress that tomorrow is going to be a big day, that he chooses her," Ritter explained. "He's made a decision, and that tomorrow, meaning Feb. 16, the date his wife was murdered, will be a day that he will never forget." But Ritter said the same enormous volume of messages prosecutors are using against Flynn also gives his attorneys an argument. The defense can contend prosecutors have cherry-picked the most damaging statements from more than 100,000 messages exchanged during an intense affair and stripped them of the broader context of two people using exaggerated and sometimes ugly language. title: Delivery drones could be waiting before you even order
description: Flytrex says its AI-powered Rooftop Dock system in Dallas-Fort Worth positions drones at restaurants before orders arrive, cutting delivery costs by 60%.
content: Your next food delivery could start moving before you even place the order. Flytrex is rolling out a system in Dallas-Fort Worth that sends drones to restaurant rooftops ahead of expected demand. AI predicts which locations are likely to get busy, then positions an aircraft nearby. If the prediction is right, the drone is already waiting when your food is ready. Flytrex says its new Rooftop Dock and predictive fleet positioning can cut its own delivery costs by 60%. The company also says customer delivery times can drop by half. The idea makes a lot of sense. Stop wasting time sending a drone to the restaurant after the food is ready. So, how does Flytrex know where to put a drone before anyone orders, and how could this expand beyond Texas? PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Get Better Healthcare With AI replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com AI tries to figure out where the next order will come from Flytrex uses machine-learning models to study past demand, location and the time of day. The software also looks at other activity across its delivery network. It then predicts which restaurants are most likely to receive upcoming orders. Instead of leaving every available drone at a central location, Flytrex can send aircraft closer to restaurants before customers order anything. That could make a big difference during busy meal periods. A pizza restaurant that usually sees a rush around dinner time could already have a drone waiting nearby. Once an order comes through and the kitchen finishes the food, the aircraft can get moving quickly. The current process can take longer. An operator may have to send a drone from another location after the restaurant has the order. The aircraft then flies to the restaurant before it can start the customer delivery. Flytrex wants to cut out that extra trip. The drone waits on the restaurant rooftop Once Flytrex decides where a drone should wait, the aircraft lands on its Rooftop Dock. The company says the system can go on an existing rooftop or another elevated area near the restaurant. According to Flytrex, the setup does not require additional real estate or structural changes. The company also says it can operate without placing a Flytrex employee at each restaurant. After the drone lands, it shuts down its motors and waits. When the food is ready, the aircraft lowers a hook into position. A restaurant employee clips the packaged order onto it without handling the drone. Then the aircraft takes off and heads directly toward the customer. That also removes the need for someone to carry the food to a separate drone launch site. Flytrex co-founder and CEO Amit Regev says those last few hundred feet between the restaurant kitchen and the aircraft have been one of the harder parts of drone delivery. "The truly challenging part has never been the flight; it's the last few hundred feet between the kitchen and the aircraft," Regev said. Why Flytrex thinks this could slash delivery costs Sending a drone to a restaurant before an order arrives could save more than time. Flytrex says its new setup cuts its cost per delivery by 60%. The company also says it can reduce customer delivery times by half. The drone no longer has to make a separate pickup flight from a central location. Meanwhile, restaurant workers can load the order without a dedicated Flytrex employee standing there. That could let each aircraft handle more deliveries over the course of a day. There is one big variable, though. The AI needs to put the drone in the right place. Customer demand can change quickly. Weather can shift ordering patterns. A local event could suddenly make one restaurant much busier than expected. If a drone ends up waiting at the wrong location, Flytrex may have to move it again. Dallas-Fort Worth is becoming a drone delivery testing ground Flytrex is launching the technology at active merchant locations across Dallas-Fort Worth. The company says it is also installing the system at more than 100 additional sites. That makes North Texas an important test for something Flytrex wants to expand much further. The company says it has completed more than 250,000 U.S. deliveries. It has also been building relationships with some of the biggest names in food delivery. In 2025, Uber invested in Flytrex through a partnership focused on Uber Eats orders. We covered that move when Uber Eats began preparing for drone deliveries. Flytrex also partnered with DoorDash in Dallas-Fort Worth. DoorDash has since expanded its own drone ambitions. We recently covered how DoorDash received FAA approval for its commercial drone delivery operation. CLEVELAND CLINIC LAUNCHES PRESCRIPTION DRONE DELIVERY FAA approval could help Flytrex reach many more cities Flytrex has another important piece in place as it looks beyond Texas. The company received Federal Aviation Administration approval for beyond visual line of sight operations, also known as BVLOS. That allows Flytrex to conduct approved flights without requiring a visual observer to keep each aircraft in direct sight throughout the trip. Instead, Flytrex can monitor multiple drones remotely from an operations center under the conditions of its authorization. Flytrex says the approval gives it a path toward expanding into the 37 largest U.S. metropolitan areas. That does not mean rooftop drone delivery will appear across all 37 markets at once. Flytrex still has to build out its network as it expands. The new rooftop system gives the company a setup it hopes to repeat from one market to the next. Flytrex has been building toward bigger food deliveries The rooftop system comes after several other moves from Flytrex. In April 2026, the company introduced its Sky2 delivery drone through a partnership with Little Caesars. The aircraft can carry up to 8.8 pounds, enough to handle two large pizzas. Flytrex also opened a manufacturing facility in Pilot Point, Texas. The company says the site can produce about 1,000 drones per year. Now Flytrex is tackling the next problem. Building more drones only gets you so far if those aircraft spend too much time traveling to pickup locations. Putting them closer to the restaurants before orders arrive could keep more of that fleet moving toward customers. What this means to you If Flytrex gets this right, you could spend less time staring at a delivery timer. The drone may already be waiting at the restaurant when your food is ready, so it can head toward your home almost immediately. That could also mean your meal spends less time sitting around before pickup. Then there is the cost. Flytrex says the system cuts its own delivery costs by 60%. The company has not said whether those savings will eventually lead to lower fees for customers, but a cheaper delivery model could make drone delivery easier to expand. Don't expect a drone hovering over your takeout spot tomorrow. Flytrex is starting in Dallas-Fort Worth, and expanding this kind of service will take time. The bigger takeaway is what happens before the drone ever takes off. If AI can put the aircraft where the next order is likely to happen, Flytrex could make the whole process faster without asking customers to do anything differently. CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS Kurt's key takeaways What gets my attention here is how simple the problem sounds once Flytrex points it out. The drone may be fast in the air, but that does not help much if it has to spend part of the delivery flying to the restaurant first. Moving drones ahead of demand could change that. The AI looks for where orders are likely to come from, while the rooftop dock gives the aircraft somewhere to wait. If Flytrex can get those predictions right consistently, it could cut a lot of wasted time out of each delivery. Dallas-Fort Worth should give us a good sense of whether this works beyond a handful of restaurants. Flytrex says more than 100 additional installations are underway, which should give the company plenty of chances to prove whether those big claims about speed and cost hold up. Would faster food delivery be worth having drones waiting on restaurant rooftops around your community, or would you rather keep all that buzzing out of your neighborhood? title: Crude oil prices slide after Iranian and US negotiators discuss opening Strait of Hormuz
description: Crude oil prices dipped Friday after reports that Iranian and U.S. negotiators engaged in side talks at the United Nations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile European and Middle Eastern allies rallied around Saudi Arabia amidst Houthi attacks.
content:
President Donald Trump has rejected Iran's proposed seven-day ceasefire and told aides he expects U.S. bombing of Iran to resume after the November midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing U.S. officials.

title: The frat omertà: Whistleblower warns of ‘code of silence’ after Ole Miss deaths, alleged Penn State coke ring
description: The Ole Miss student death and Penn State cocaine ring allegations echo a deeper crisis in Greek life, fraternity hazing survivor Andrew Lohse says.
content: "You need a code of omertà if you're trying to create an organization that's essentially like a criminal organization," Andrew Lohse said. Lohse, a 36-year-old fraternity hazing survivor and the author of "Confessions of an Ivy League Frat Boy," was talking about fraternities. As a Dartmouth student, the whistleblower exposed the stomach-turning indoctrination rituals he said he endured inside Sigma Alpha Epsilon. TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS When recent headlines came to light regarding the mysterious deaths of two students at Ole Miss — one of whom was in a fraternity — and the alleged frat cocaine distribution ring at Penn State, Lohse said he was immediately reminded of his time as a brother. "For years and years, [the last] 10 years, it's like whenever someone dies in a frat, like that's when my phone rings," Lohse told Fox News Digital. OLE MISS NAMES STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS OFFICIAL ADDRESSES POTENTIAL FOR FOUL PLAY One of the Ole Miss students who was found dead this past week, Ryan Strang, was a Phi Delta Theta fraternity brother. He was found at an off-campus home. Authorities found packages of kratom, a commercially available drug that has been derided as "gas station heroin," at the sites of both deaths. However, its role in either death was not immediately clear. Phi Delta Theta has not been accused of any wrongdoing. "The loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy," the fraternity said in a statement, in part. "Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them. "These losses reinforce the importance of a collective commitment to health, safety, and well-being on college campuses today. We encourage the Phi Delta Theta community to keep the Strang family, the Mississippi Alpha Chapter, and everyone affected by these tragic losses in their thoughts." Dangers like kratom did not exist when Lohse was in school, he said. "There was no kratom, no tranq, no smoking bath salts, no fentanyl. Back then, the cocaine was more or less just cocaine. It wasn't like every time somebody did cocaine they could die." OLE MISS TOXICOLOGY REPORTS EXPECTED SOON, AND RESULTS MAY TRIGGER ANTI-FENTANYL LAW, OFFICIAL SAYS At Penn State, prosecutors allege in court documents that pledges were coerced into cutting and packaging cocaine as part of an alleged organized drug ring led by former Sigma Chi member Agostino Abbatiello. "When I was reading that the pledges were in the background doing that, I thought that was sort of amazing, but in a bad way, but also extremely brazen," Lohse said. PENN STATE COCAINE BUST NETS 14 ARRESTS OVER ALLEGED PLEDGE COKE-CUTTING ‘INDOCTRINATION' RITUALS Fraternity culture made more news this past week in Madison, Wisconsin, where police said they found roughly 30 partially clothed young men packed inside a sweltering basement, covered in food, condiments and other liquids and several pledges showing signs of being physically assaulted. The Madison Police Department said officers were dispatched to the Alpha Epsilon Pi (AEPi) house Wednesday night and are investigating the hazing incident, with two people arrested. "AEPi Headquarters takes the allegations involving our Pi Chapter in Madison, Wisconsin, extremely seriously," Jonathan Pierce, the fraternity's chief communications officer, said in a statement. "We will cooperate fully with the authorities investigating this matter. "Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for. There is no place for it in AEPi," he added. "No exceptions. No excuses. We educate our members about their responsibility to ‘Be Your Brothers’ Keeper.’ This is not an optional value." ‘Sad moment’ "It's a sad moment, for society, civilization," Lohse said about some of the recent headlines involving fraternity behavior. "These organizations should be forces of good. Young men need it more than ever. Young men are more adrift than ever. There's no moral leadership. "There's a vacuum in the center of higher education and American society that used to be filled by God, by religion, by the church," he said, adding that it's "totally vacant now." During his time as a brother at Sigma Alpha Epsilon, he said, he was forced to "swim in a kiddie pool full of vomit while being urinated on," and "chug" vinegar or milk to the point that he and his fellow pledge brothers "would vomit" in a room covered with tarps. FORMER MICHIGAN HOCKEY PLAYERS ALLEGE COACHES IGNORED YEARS OF ABUSIVE HAZING RITUALS He also said he was forced into a small basement crawl space for a period of time. This was all in addition to constant coerced binge drinking, he said. "We're talking like 10, 15 plus drinks," he said. MIAMI SECRET SERVICE AGENT CHARGED IN NEAR-DEADLY FRATERNITY HAZING, OFFICIALS SAY He said the unwritten "code of silence" or "omertà" contributes to these repeated hazing or drug-related issues within frats. "The original 19th-century concept of the American fraternity is not what exists today," Lohse said. THREE COLLEGE FRATS IN CROSSHAIRS AS HAZING CLAIMS OF BOOZE, BURNS AND HOSPITAL TRIPS SPARK CRACKDOWN: SCHOOL "Essentially, you can look at a modern fraternity like a criminal organization. In most states, the unique behavioral attributes of a fraternity cross into criminal statutes, whether misdemeanor hazing or serious felony drug trafficking. You need a code of silence to protect that. "The organization forces the individual to compromise their own identity for the collective, taking something from its members to ensure the system perpetuates itself over time." GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL After hazing incidents during Lohse's time as a student, SAE was suspended from Dartmouth for the last 10 years and recognized again in August, The Darmouth student-run newspaper reported. When asked what advice he would offer students considering Greek life at major universities, Lohse stopped short of telling students flatly to avoid fraternities. Instead, Lohse urges young men to calculate the "opportunity cost" before pledging. "Consider that the upside benefit, while maybe not zero, pales in comparison to the downside risk," Lohse said, advising incoming students to reflect on what they truly want out of higher education. SEND US A TIP GOT A TIP? "Think about what you actually want out of college. Who do you really want to be around, and who is actually going to be there to help you? I think you'll find that a fraternity isn't going to provide that." Judson Horras, president and CEO of the North American Interfraternity Conference, told Fox News Digital that "student safety is our members' highest priority. The NIC has adopted enhanced health and safety guidelines and co-led advocacy to pass tougher anti-hazing laws in more than a dozen states, as well as the federal Stop Campus Hazing Act." Regarding the Ole Miss students' deaths, Horras said, "We are heartbroken by the loss of two University of Mississippi students, one of whom was a fraternity member. Our sympathies are with both families and the Ole Miss community. We will continue working with universities and families to keep every student safe." title: Mount Shasta climber recounts harrowing 500-foot slide, overnight crawl to safety: report
description: Zubayir Kazi lost all his supplies during a failed glissade down Mount Shasta's Avalanche Gulch and crawled through the night with grave injuries.
content: A California climber who survived a roughly 500-foot slide down Mount Shasta is recounting how he crawled through the night after losing his supplies and suffering serious injuries. Zubayir Kazi, 24, of San Jose, told NBC Bay Area he reached the summit Sept. 10, during his first icy summit attempt before things went wrong on his descent. "Everything I had with me just goes out of my hand and I find myself flying down the mountain," Kazi said. NOVICE CLIMBER SURVIVES 1,500-FOOT DROP ON CALIFORNIA'S MOUNT SHASTA AFTER HELICOPTER RESCUE DELAYED BY CLOUDS Kazi said he lost his food, water, cellphone and light, leaving him alone without a way to call for help. "My mentality became very one dimensional. I don’t know what’s the optimal thing to do, but I just know that I have to go lower because if I stay here and fall asleep, I’m going to die," he said. The U.S. Forest Service previously told Fox News Digital that Kazi lost control while attempting to glissade, or slide, down the snow and ice-covered Avalanche Gulch after reaching the summit. He suffered significant lacerations and injuries to his feet. NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING' Swelling forced Kazi to remove his boots, and he crawled through the night until reaching Horse Camp Cabin. His friends reported him missing after losing contact with him, prompting a multi-agency search. A hiker found Kazi inside the cabin the following day and provided him with food and water before rescuers arrived. "When the officers came in, it was the first time I really realized how badly I was injured. They said, 'You have no skin behind your leg'," Kazi said. HIKER, 61, BATTLES AGONIZING INJURY ON GRUELING CLIMB, RESETS DISLOCATED SHOULDER HIMSELF Kazi told NBC Bay Area he suffered significant skin and nerve damage and serious internal complications. He said doctors told him he could have died within hours. The Forest Service previously praised Kazi for knowing his route and telling friends about his climbing plans, while urging climbers to carry backup electronics, allow enough daylight and prepare to self-rescue. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kazi said the ordeal changed his approach to climbing. "It is very important to fully and properly account for all of the requirements and safety considerations necessary to complete a hike like this and not miss a single one, and I'd say to definitely not go alone," Kazi said. Fox News Digital could not locate contact information for Kazi to seek additional comment. Fox News Digital's Bonny Chu contributed to this report.

title: Trump’s Greenland deal shadows Xi visit after years of Beijing eyeing Arctic influence
description: Trump's Greenland security deal blocked China's Arctic ambitions days before Xi Jinping arrived for a state dinner with America's top AI executives.
content: President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington this week, one day after signing a Greenland security agreement that, once in force, would bar non-NATO states like China from establishing a military presence there, sharpening the Arctic security backdrop to their face-to-face talks. Xi’s three-day state visit unfolded against that backdrop, with Trump hosting a formal White House arrival ceremony, holding high-stakes talks, joining Xi for a tour of the National Archives and presiding over a state dinner attended by some of America’s most prominent technology executives. A senior U.S. official told Fox News Digital Trump and Xi discussed the economy, trade, "superintelligence" and cooperation on a range of shared priorities, though it remained unclear what concrete agreements emerged from behind closed doors. TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING Trump has so far stopped short of announcing a concrete agreement from Xi’s Washington visit, a contrast to his May trip to Beijing. Trump was already telling reporters before leaving China that the two countries had made "some fantastic trade deals," even though the White House did not release its full economic deal package until two days after the summit. Thursday’s state dinner drew 134 guests, including the two leaders and prominent technology figures such as Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Lisa Su of AMD, Tim Cook of Apple, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sundar Pichai of Google. Christine Balling, senior vice president for professional affiliations at The Institute of World Politics, told Fox News Digital that inviting America’s top AI tycoons to Thursday night’s state dinner was a strategic move to show Xi that the United States is the world’s top dog in the AI race. 'RED CARPET FOR A DESPOT': TRUMP'S LAVISH XI WELCOME COLLIDES WITH GOP ANTI-COMMUNISM MESSAGE "I think the significance of the timing of this meeting, whether it's intentional or not, shows that the Trump administration is taking the future of AI and the world very, very seriously," she said. "I think that is the most significant takeaway. But the bottom line is, I think the most important images were those of all of the AI techs who were invited to that state dinner." Greenland has emerged as a backdrop to Trump’s two meetings with Xi this year. Negotiations over an expanded U.S. security role there began months before Trump traveled to Beijing in May. Trump renewed his public pressure over Greenland during the summer as his administration continued negotiations aimed in part at limiting Russian and Chinese influence in the Arctic. Five days before Xi arrived in Washington, Trump announced a Greenland security agreement that was formally signed Sept. 22 and, once in force, would expand the U.S. military position while restricting Chinese military presence and certain sensitive investments in the territory. China has had its eye on Greenland for years, especially as it looks to expand its role in the Arctic. Beijing has shown interest in Greenland’s infrastructure and natural resources, including its valuable rare earth and critical mineral deposits. U.S. officials have also pointed to past Chinese efforts involving a former U.S. naval base and airport projects as signs of Beijing’s broader ambitions in the region. Balling is an expert in foreign policy, particularly in the Western hemisphere, and says Trump’s historic deal with Greenland struck a massive blow to China. title: Two powerful federal courts face push to break free from DC bubble as unlikely duo steps in
description: Senators Chris Coons and Ashley Moody introduced the Better Bench Act to drop the D.C. residency requirement for Court of Federal Claims judges.
content: A bipartisan team of senators is proposing legislation they say will broaden the pool of qualified judges available to serve on two powerful federal courts with nationwide jurisdiction. Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Ashley Moody, R-Fla., introduced a bill Tuesday that would remove the requirement that judges sitting on the Court of Federal Claims and the Federal Circuit live within 50 miles of Washington, D.C. Both courts have nationwide jurisdiction, though their specialized dockets differ. The Court of Federal Claims primarily handles claims against the federal government, while the Federal Circuit hears appeals involving patents, trademarks, government contracts and other areas. A decision from either court, for example, could affect Coons’ constituents in Delaware or Moody’s in Florida. The claims court hears arguments from entities seeking money or other relief from the federal government, whereas the circuit court, which is a feeder for Supreme Court justices, reviews decisions from lower courts and agencies in relation to the federal government. MIKE DAVIS: FEDERAL COURT SETS DANGEROUS PRECEDENT AGAINST 99-YEAR-OLD JUDGE "Americans deserve the best, most qualified judges, especially in areas like intellectual property law, where expertise is key to understanding complex cases and fairly deciding the future of many entrepreneurs’ businesses," Coons said of the legislation. "For too long, we have limited the pool of judges available to take on the toughest IP and federal contract cases to those willing to uproot their lives and move to Washington, D.C. No longer. This bipartisan bill ensures that courts of national jurisdiction can draw from a pool of national talent." Legal scholars who spoke with Fox News Digital saw merit in the senators' proposal. "It's often difficult to recruit top-level talent from across the country to relocate to the District of Columbia for these judgeships," Heritage Foundation senior legal fellow Zach Smith told Fox News Digital, noting that the Court of International Trade in New York City has a similarly broad geographic jurisdiction and lacks a residency requirement for judges. "Many other circuit courts of appeal cover multiple states, and often the judges on those courts sit throughout the states that that court covers, and then they often come together to meet and hear cases and hear oral arguments in a specific location. This type of geographic dispersal it's not an unusual arrangement." Thomas Berry, the director of the libertarian-aligned Cato Institute's Center for Constitutional Studies, largely agreed. ‘UNPRECEDENTED’: JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES "These courts have jurisdiction based on the issue involved, so, potentially, if this meant that the judges were able not just to live elsewhere, but even hear oral arguments elsewhere, that could potentially be more convenient for some types of cases if they're, say, involved parties on the opposite side of the country," Berry told Fox News Digital. Critics may argue that the proposed legislation could increase travel costs to taxpayers by requiring frequent travel for judges to and from D.C. Legal experts may also feel that the ability of judges to regularly meet face to face could lead to a loss of judicial collegiality. Berry noted that some studies show that, during the Coronavirus pandemic, court decisions had fewer dissents as judges spent less time in person with one another but qualified possible concerns by stating that "all of the other regional courts of appeals have been basically working under such a system for over 100 years, and clearly it hasn't gotten in the way from them doing the work that they're meant to do." SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES Neither expert felt that travel costs would be an issue in implementing this proposal. "For a court that covers the entire country, we should be considering nominating judges from everywhere in America based on merit — not their proximity to the D.C. bubble," Moody, herself a former Florida circuit judge and federal prosecutor, said of the legislation. "My Better Bench Act removes an outdated residency requirement to expand the pool of qualified Americans who can serve and allows our courts to be a better reflection of the nation as a whole." title: She grew up under Soviet rule; now the EU's top diplomat, she warns Europe against giving Russia what it wants
description: Kaja Kallas says Russia's sabotage and intimidation campaign aims to weaken European support for Ukraine, warning the strategy will escalate if it works.
content: NEW YORK — Russia is trying to scare Europe into backing off its defense in the region, European Union’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, claims, warning it will only lead to Moscow becoming more aggressive if it succeeds. "Their goal is to intimidate us from not supporting Ukraine, from refraining to support them and pressuring Russia," Kallas told Fox News Digital in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. "What is important for us is that we are not afraid," she continued. "Because, otherwise, this kind of intimidation actually pays off, and then we will see more of it across the world." For Kallas, Russia’s attempts to intimidate its European neighbors carry a history that reaches well beyond the war in Ukraine. FRONTLINE NATO ALLY SHARES SHOCKING TAKE ON RUSSIAN INVASION THREAT Her mother, Kristi, was just six months old in 1949 when Soviet authorities deported her — along with her mother and her grandmother — to Siberia during Stalin’s mass deportations from the Baltic States. Kallas’ maternal grandfather was separately sent to a Siberian prison camp. Kallas has recounted how her mother was transported east in a cattle car with fellow deportees drying the infant’s diapers against their own bodies during the freezing journey. The family spent roughly a decade in Siberia before being allowed to return to Soviet-occupied Estonia in 1959. Kallas was born in Tallinn in 1977 and spent the first 14 years of her life under Soviet rule. Estonia restored its independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union collapsed. Her family would go on to become deeply entwined with the new democratic Estonia. Her father, Siim Kallas, became the first president of the Bank of Estonia after gaining its independence, later serving as foreign minister and prime minister before moving to Brussels as a European commissioner. Kaja Kallas followed her own path from lawyer to member of Estonia’s parliament and then the European Parliament. In 2021, she became Estonia’s first female prime minister and three years later was chosen as the European Union’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy. It was a historic moment putting a politician who grew up under Soviet occupation at the center of Europe’s response to Russian aggression on the continent. That history has made Kallas one of Europe’s most prominent voices on Moscow even as officials in her native Estonia and elsewhere along NATO’s eastern flank now caution against interpreting Russia’s recent provocations as preparations for a conventional invasion. Russia invaded Ukraine more than 4½ years ago and shows no signs of backing off despite repeated promises that negotiations for an end to the war are ongoing. Asked whether she agreed with Estonian and other Baltic officials who say they do not see Russia preparing for such an attack, Kallas instead pointed to Moscow’s growing use of sabotage and the importance of deterrence. "We see that Russia is actually increasing their sabotage acts in Europe," Kallas said. "But, of course, how far they will go depends very much on us and whether we are investing enough in defense so that it acts as a deterrent." The debate comes as NATO countries confront a string of Russian aircraft and drone incursions, along with suspected sabotage and other hybrid activity across Europe. The incidents have fueled warnings in some European capitals that Moscow is probing the alliance for weaknesses, while officials closer to Russia have cautioned against equating those provocations with preparations for an invasion. US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Fox News Digital in a separate interview this week that his country's intelligence services see no indication Russia is preparing for a full-scale attack on NATO. "We have more and more this kind of panic in Europe that Russia will invade and will be full-scale aggressive against NATO and Europe and the Baltic States, Poland, but we don’t see it," Tsahkna said. "Our intelligence, we see very, very deep into Russia. We don’t see any change." Kallas, however, argued that Moscow's actions are designed to weaken Western support for Ukraine rather than simply test NATO's defenses. "Their goal is to intimidate us from not supporting Ukraine, from refraining to support them and pressuring Russia," she said. The pressure campaign comes as Washington continues its push for a negotiated end to the war. Kallas said Moscow has yet to demonstrate that it is serious about reaching one. "They should start with stopping bombing the civilians," she said, pointing to recent Russian attacks on Kyiv. "If they are serious about this, they should agree to a ceasefire, sit down at the negotiation table and talk to the Ukrainians." Kallas said Ukraine has already agreed to an unconditional ceasefire while "Russia is just playing games," arguing that coordinated pressure from Washington and its European allies could change Moscow's calculations. title: WATCH: Black bishop calls voter ID argument 'deeply insulting' after explosive noncitizen registration report
description: Earl Walker Jackson calls claims that Black Americans can't get voter ID "deeply insulting" and slams noncitizen voting as disenfranchisement.
content: EXCLUSIVE: Black bishop and author Earl Walker Jackson blasted Democrats and the left over what he called the "deeply insulting" and "deeply offensive" claim that minorities and African Americans cannot get IDs to vote. Debate erupted this week over voter ID requirements after Reuters reported that an investigation found 30,000 noncitizens were "erroneously" registered to vote in 11 states. Jackson, a nondenominational Christian leader and descendant of enslaved ancestors, said the findings underscored what he described as a growing problem of noncitizen voting that disenfranchises American citizens. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Jackson charged, "Why the Democrats are so committed to this can only be explained one way: They think it empowers people who shouldn't vote to vote, and they believe those people are going to vote for them. "This is nothing but a power grab," he posited, emphasizing that "every vote by a noncitizen does in fact cancel out the vote of an American citizen, or it amplifies it in a way that's illegal or inappropriate." BOMBSHELL VOTING SCANDAL ADDS TO PATTERN OF NONCITIZEN VOTERS AS TRUMP WARNS OF THREAT TO ‘HEART' OF DEMOCRACY Reuters reported Wednesday that more than 30,000 self-declared noncitizens were added to U.S. voter rolls since 2000. The outlet attributed the erroneous registrations to "software glitches and clerical errors" and said its review suggested "inadvertent bureaucratic failures, ‌rather than organized efforts to register immigrants illegally." Reuters said it was unable to determine how many noncitizens actually cast ballots. The errors occurred in California, Illinois, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, Utah and Virginia. Don Palmer, the senior legal fellow for election integrity with the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital that, due to legal loopholes and loose reporting requirements, he believes the 30,000 number "is actually quite low." "I think it's undercounting it. I think those are the identified noncitizens that have been accidentally or erroneously placed on the voter rolls through the mistake of the driver's license agency. I think it’s much more because we don't know in a lot of states, either they have not conducted the audits or they're not using tools to find noncitizens that may have accidentally been placed on the rolls," Palmer said. "The answer really is that there needs to be more care taken to developing a system of verifying citizenship, and you just don't see that in most states. BIDEN ADMINISTRATION GRANTED WOMAN GREEN CARD MONTHS BEFORE SHE ILLEGALLY VOTED IN 2024 ELECTION: DHS "If they're going to do voter registration, they need to make sure that there's a verification in place for identity and for citizenship, just as if you come into an agency, and you're getting a driver's license or identification card, you've got to show that ID. You've got to make sure that your identity is confirmed. "Similarly, if you're going to register someone to vote at the driver's license agency, there needs to be a verification process or a documentation process to ensure that you are a citizen." After hearing the 30,000 figure, Jackson told Fox News Digital "the sad reality is I'm not shocked." "I wonder if it's more," he said. "We've been told, particularly by Democrats, that that's not happening, that there's nothing to see here, and yet we hear again and again documentation that it is happening." With this in mind, he decried efforts to resist more stringent voter eligibility verification and identification. He took particular issue with those equating voter ID requirements as anti-Black and a new form of Jim Crow. "Forgive me for being personal about this for a moment, but I just find this deeply insulting and deeply offensive because the implication is that somehow if you are Black, no matter how wealthy, educated, well-to-do, somehow getting an ID is a problem for you," he said. "But, on the other hand, if you're White, no matter how poor, no matter how uneducated, no matter what your circumstances are, somehow you can get an ID. That's not a problem. I mean, it's preposterous." DESCENDANT OF SLAVES SHAMES SMITHSONIAN’S WOKE ‘INDOCTRINATION’ AGAINST THE ‘GREATEST NATION ON EARTH’ He pointed to the hotel where he was staying as an example. Should I say, ‘Wait a minute, oh, you're discriminating against me. You know, Black people can't get IDs; how dare you ask?’ he said. "I mean, it's ridiculous. But they don't have a right to vote in our elections, and they shouldn't be permitted to do so," he concluded. title: How a six-pack of beer and the Magna Carta could finally fix a problem plaguing Americans for decades
description: Kenneth Jouppi's $95,000 Cessna was seized over a misdemeanor beer conviction, and the Supreme Court will now weigh Eighth Amendment limits.
content: The Supreme Court will soon hear oral arguments in a case out of Alaska that centers around an airplane, a six-pack of beer and an amendment to the Constitution that traces its history back centuries as a legal expert lays out the potential impact of the ruling to Fox News Digital. "Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted," the Eighth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution states. That amendment is at the heart of a case that will be heard by the Supreme Court in December, and Cully Stimson, a senior legal fellow at Heritage Foundation, described it as "the case that libertarians and freedom-minded people have been hoping for years." SUPREME COURT REJECTS MICHIGAN FAMILY'S CLAIM THAT COUNTY COMMITTED 'HOME EQUITY THEFT' OVER $2,200 TAX DEBT Kenneth Jouppi, now 82, was operating a one-man air taxi service using his personally owned 1969 Cessna plane in 2012 when Alaska state troopers executed a search warrant on his plane and found alcohol on board, including one six-pack they said was plainly visible. At the time, Jouppi was on a runway in Fairbanks preparing to take a customer and her groceries to the remote village of Beaver near the center of the state. Having beer on board wasn’t illegal on its own, and Jouppi says he was not aware the woman had the beer with her. However, since Beaver had banned the possession or sale of alcohol within its limits, Jouppi was convicted of alcohol importation, a misdemeanor. The Alaska Supreme Court held that, under the alcohol importation ban, the state was required to confiscate Jouppi’s Cessna. Jouppi has since argued in court that the state’s seizure of his plane, valued at $95,000, runs afoul of the Eighth Amendment’s ban on excessive fines. Now, the Supreme Court will weigh in on whether he’s right. "Taking a guy's airplane, livelihood because he tried to take a six-pack of beer into a dry village, I mean, can there be a more outrageous abuse of the excessive fines clause?" Stimson said. "I don't think so. So, honestly, in a perfect world, it should be 9-0 for Mr. Jouppi." Stimson says the idea that governments should not be able to devastate citizens with fines dates back centuries to the Magna Carta, the 1215 English charter that limited the king’s power and established the principle that rulers are subject to the law. He explained in a recent Daily Signal article that prohibition on excessive fines is backed by "eight centuries of proportionality." THE FBI TOOK A WOMAN'S LIFE SAVINGS, BUT A NEW BILL WOULD END THE 'LAWLESS' SEIZURE OF AMERICANS' PROPERTY At the center of the case, Stimson explained, is whether Alaska’s forfeiture of Jouppi’s roughly $95,000 airplane was proportionate to his misdemeanor conviction for bringing a six-pack of beer into a dry village. Alaska argues the plane was worth less than 10 times the maximum possible fine of $10,000, while Jouppi’s attorneys point to the sentence he actually received: the minimum $1,500 fine and three days in jail. The Supreme Court will consider whether proportionality should be measured against the maximum penalty allowed by law or the specific punishment imposed in Jouppi’s case. "Alaska's brief spends a lot of ink on the purpose of these local rules that create dry cities," Stimson said. "They spend a lot of ink on alcoholism in Alaska and all the rest of it. All of that's irrelevant. If it was that important, they would have made it a felony, and they would have made it a really serious felony with a lot of jail time and a huge forfeiture. They made it a misdemeanor. He was convicted of a misdemeanor, and he got three days in jail." Stimson pointed to the trial judge in the case who refused to take Jouppi’s plane in the first place and said that was the correct decision. LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES "The state appealed that, it came back to the judge on remand from the Court of Appeals and the judge said, 'I find that the request by the state is a violation of the Eighth Amendment's excessive fines clause,'" Stimson said. "The state appealed again. It went to the Court of Appeals and then went to the Alaska Supreme Court," Stimson explained. "So, even the trial judge, when he had two bites of the apple, refused to take the plane. And I think you really have to give credit to that trial judge, who was in the courtroom, who understood that this was almost a 90-year-old man, who was an Air Force veteran, whose only job and means of income besides Social Security was flying this plane to villages as a taxi cab driver, essentially. "And, so, if the government can do that, the state or federal government can take your means of livelihood away from you for a misdemeanor, we're in deep, deep trouble as a country." When ruling on Jouppi’s case, the court will have the opportunity to rein in the ability of state and local governments to impose asset forfeiture, a longtime goal of civil libertarians, which has been an issue for decades in the United States as Americans have pushed back on excessive fines and seizures from government agencies. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Stimson told Fox News Digital the Supreme Court has only ruled on the excessive fines clause five times and has "never really laid out exactly what constitutes an excessive fine." He touted the significance this ruling could have and pointed to the amicus brief in the case filed by the Buckeye Institute in Ohio as something that "really stood out to me" "They talk about all the incentives built into the system that can be and are abused by law enforcement when they arrest you for this crime, and they take all of this of yours over here, or they arrest you for this little tiny crime and then they take this," Stimson said. "And, of course, when they take it, the proceeds of that benefit the law enforcement agency and pay for their extra weapons, their cars, their new buildings, their uniforms and the rest of it. So, the incentives are misaligned. And, so, I think the court hopefully will, No. 1, just for legal nerds like me, answer what the parameters are of evaluating excessive fines claims under the Eighth Amendment. "But two, write it in a way that disincentivizes law enforcement. From overreaching and abusing their authority that they currently enjoy." Fox News Digital’s Robert Schmad contributed to this report

title: Kamala Harris uses flower analogy to explain social media algorithms while discussing AI, midterms
description: Former Vice President Kamala Harris used an odd analogy involving pink and yellow flowers to explain how social media algorithms target users during a recent podcast appearance.
content: Former Vice President Kamala Harris used yellow and pink flowers to explain how social media algorithms can repeatedly feed users similar content, arguing that the technology can influence what people see online. Harris made the remarks during an appearance on "Off Air with Big Boy" after host Big Boy asked about AI, TikTok, Instagram and the role personalized algorithms could play in shaping how Americans consume information ahead of the midterm elections. "There is a part of this that is about understanding that, you know, if you keep seeing the same thing over and over again, know that you are being targeted," Harris said. "Because you looked at it the first time, they're just going to keep sending it to you, which means they're trying to dumb people down with the assumption that people don't have any interest beyond what they've already seen." CHRIS MURPHY CALLS FOR 'REGULATING THE INTERNET' SO PEOPLE WON'T FALL FOR A 'DEMAGOGUE LIKE DONALD TRUMP' Harris, who previously played a leading role in the Biden administration's work on artificial intelligence, continued with a colorful example. "The algorithm's suggesting I have no more interest. Because I'm looking at this yellow flower, I'm only interested in yellow flowers, as though my brain can't handle the fact that there may be a pink flower that I might be interested in looking at," Harris said. "Part of it is understanding how the algorithm is manipulating us and figuring out how we're going to psych it out a bit." Harris' explanation drew a mocking response from Fox News hosts, including Sean Hannity. "What was that?" Hannity said while reacting to the sound bite. HARRIS KEEPS 2028 DOOR OPEN AS SHE HITS MIDTERM CAMPAIGN TRAIL, WARNS ‘28 WON’T MATTER’ WITHOUT 2026 Hannity's guest, Fox News host Jimmy Failla, joked that Harris thinks "AI is Allen Iverson from the Philadelphia 76ers." Harris, the Democratic Party's 2024 presidential nominee, has not said whether she will seek the White House again in 2028. She has faced criticism in the past over her explanations of artificial intelligence, including remarks she made while serving as vice president in 2023. "AI is kind of a fancy thing," Harris said at the time. "First of all, it's two letters. It means artificial intelligence, but ultimately what it is is it's about machine learning." title: Reigning champion Indiana Hoosiers survive major scare from Northwestern in Big Ten opener
description: The National Champion Indiana Hoosiers barely survived Northwestern as penalties and Turbo Richard's injury nearly derailed their Big Ten opener.
content: The reigning National Champion Indiana Hoosiers haven't been tested much this season, and boy, did they ever get a test on Friday night. Despite being three-touchdown favorites, the Hoosiers found themselves battling the Northwestern Wildcats to the very end, eking out a 29-23 win at home. Coming into Friday night's game, the Hoosiers — despite getting off to a 3-0 start on the heels of a title — had dealt with one big criticism dogging them this season. Slow starts. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Head coach Curt Cignetti had to field questions about his team's play early in games against easier opponents. So, there was a lot of focus on whether or not that trend would continue as the Big Ten schedule got underway against the Wildcats. Well, the answer was... kind of? The Hoosiers opened the game with a 15-play, 67-yard drive that ate up around half of the opening quarter. However, the slow-start bug showed up again when a drive that should’ve ended with points on the board was instead capped by a huge defensive play from Northwestern. The Indiana defense managed to bail out the boys on the other side of the ball when Northwestern QB Aidan Chiles fumbled a snap before getting brought down in his own end zone for a safety. The Hoosiers battled through an unusual first half with an offense that looked a little disjointed at times and more penalties than you typically see out of them. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Worse, they suffered a big blow later in the half when running back Turbo Richard was hit late after going out of bounds and went straight to the locker room. There was no call on the play, which made a call against Indiana on a similar play moments later very unpopular with the folks at Memorial Stadium. Indiana tacked on a touchdown and extra point to take a 12-0 lead to the locker room at the half; of course, it didn't hurt that Northwestern rushed for -5 yards through thirty minutes. But just over halfway through the third quarter, Northwestern paid their first visit to the red zone and managed to get rid of that goose egg. Chiles wrapped up that drive, despite suffering what sure appeared to be a dislocated finger, and led the Wildcats to the first points Indiana had allowed since their season opener. And the Wildcats weren't done, with Chiles hitting Griffin Wilde in the back of the end zone at the start of the fourth quarter for an unbelievable touchdown. Northwestern head coach David Braun opted to go for two and try to tie it up, but the Hoosiers thwarted them on their first and then their second attempts after a penalty. Indiana answered back with a scoring drive of their own, with Lee Beebe Jr. — who handled most of the legwork after Richard's exit — putting the Hoosiers in the red zone with a 39-yard carry, before punching it in for a touchdown two plays later. Penalties were a story for Indiana, who averaged just three penalties per game so far this season, but wound up with nearly triple that. Some were costly too, including a holding penalty that set the Wildcats up on the Indiana 4-yardline, and a few plays later Chiles took matters into his own hands. Beebe threw down another huge play to put the Hoosiers back in scoring position. It looked like the Wildcats were on the cusp of another goal-line stand, but a costly defensive pass interference penalty gave Indiana a fresh set of downs, with QB Josh Hoover finding the end zone on a keeper that fooled just about everyone in the building. Northwestern tacked on a field goal on the ensuing drive, but Indiana managed to recover their attempt at an onside kick. That slow start habit is still going to be a talking point, as it let Northwestern stay in the game. And while the injury to Richard is a big concern, Beebe's play — he finished with 203 rushing yards — was a major bright spot.
