title: Ex-Dem insider blows lid off fundraising 'gimmicks' during 2024 election: 'Pyramid scheme'
description: Lindy Li reveals how Kamala Harris's billion-dollar war chest was funneled to media consultants, alleging fundraising gimmicks and lavish spending.
content: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs of President Joe Biden’s decline in the 2024 election, believes the party badly misallocated its fundraising, misled donors and rewarded party operatives who propped up Biden’s image. "It was: ‘maintain this very obvious lie in return for access,’" Li recalled in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, referring to assertions that Biden was not experiencing cognitive decline. "And whoever maintained, whoever was most strident in propounding that lie got the most access. And whoever subverted it or dared to ask questions would see their access quickly diminish." Li herself would find her access completely cut off after she began questioning Biden’s physical ability to serve another four years as president. But before leaving, Li became a top operative and is now chronicling the months leading up to Biden's withdrawal from the race in her new book, "Unburdened." Her revelations include what then-Vice President Kamala Harris did with a historic, billion-dollar war chest. NANCY PELOSI DENIES KNOWING ABOUT BIDEN'S DECLINE, CLAIMS THOSE WHO KNEW 'SHOULD HAVE ACTED' For starters, Li believes that the numbers themselves weren’t what they appeared to be from the outside. "I sincerely believe it's a pyramid scheme," Li said. She explained how fundraisers would sometimes take credit for each other’s work. In some cases, top recruiters could effectively double-dip on work that their subordinates had done. "When you recruit somebody, you can claim up to $250,000 of what they raise," Li said. "In fact, you could poach other people's donors and move money around. And that is how some people reach like $10 million without actually raising a thing. It's like accounting gimmicks and machinations rather than real money. I know there were people who were double counted." As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris, Li worked closely with top donors, high-profile members of the party and the Democratic National Committee (DNC). Li described how she had a front-row seat for many of the party’s spending decisions. Li recounted that most of the Harris campaign's spending went through four large media contracting companies. These contractors, Li said, collected enormous fees and received over half a billion dollars. The companies that were listed in her book included Media Buying & Analytics, Gambit Strategies, Bully Pulpit Interactive and Dupont Circle Strategies. CARVILLE SHREDS DEMS' 2024 AUTOPSY, SAYS HARRIS CAMPAIGN WAS 'MOST INEFFECTIVE $2 BILLION EVER SPENT' "This tsunami of money represented about 70 percent of the campaign’s expenditures in the final days, enriching a handful of well-connected consultants while the broader effort collapsed," Li wrote. In interviews with Fox, Li described how the payments to the firms came partially as off-the-top fees. "The vast majority of the money raised went into TV ads. And so... You know, people talk about 10% for the big guy. Okay, but I actually think the bigger grift is 15% for the big grift for these media people. They get 15%, 15 points off of hundreds of millions of dollars. You can do the math," Li said. "The consultants get the money, the consultants that are hired by the campaign, and they're friends of the candidate or friends of Jen O’Malley-Dillon. It's a very incestuous process," Li said, referring to the Harris campaign chair. In addition to the media companies and the lucrative contracts they paid out, Li believes that the party focused too much on expenses that didn’t advance the campaign while, in her view, neglecting strategic opportunities. "$350,000 a night slapping her face in the Las Vegas sphere, spending that money on Gulfstream so they wouldn't have to fly commercial, spending it on Ritz-Carlton hotels. I mean, that definitely happened because the National Finance Committee was hosting its final meeting there. Spending its money on tote bags," Li said. "None of that in Philadelphia," she added, referring to the critical electoral center in Pennsylvania — a state that had been projected to be a pathway to victory in 2024. HARRIS BACKS RELEASING DNC'S 2024 ELECTION AUTOPSY DESPITE LEADERSHIP BURYING REPORT Part of what shocked Li was how brazen the party had been with the money she helped raise. She also expressed disbelief at the message the party spun to voters who had contributed their earnings in hopes of "saving democracy," a refrain Biden used to convince voters to side with him over President Donald Trump. "Some people forked over their life savings. Like people were liquidating their savings on the hope that they were saving the country. They absolutely did, and I truly believe that they donated $2.5 billion over seven weeks, not so much primarily because of Kamala's strength as a candidate, but rather their hatred for Trump and their fear of Trump," Li said. title: Trump revives Supreme Court immigration showdown after Hochul pardon torpedoed first case
description: The Trump administration asks the Supreme Court to decide whether criminal aliens in ICE detention are entitled to bond hearings during removal.
content: The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to revive a major immigration fight over whether criminal aliens can be held without bond throughout removal proceedings or are entitled to a hearing when their detention drags on. Solicitor General John Sauer asked the Supreme Court on Monday to take up Genalo v. D.C., reviving a constitutional fight the justices had been set to hear this term in Genalo v. Black before New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul’s pardon rendered that case moot. At the center of the dispute is D.C., a Dominican national who is facing removal after a criminal history that includes drug trafficking and domestic violence charges. He had previously been removed from the United States on six occasions, according to ICE. Federal law requires certain criminal aliens to remain in custody while their deportation cases play out. But the Second Circuit has ruled that if they are detained for too long, they are entitled to a bond hearing at which the government must make the case for keeping them in custody. BLUE STATE GOVERNOR'S PARDON OF CONVICTED FELON TORPEDOS A MAJOR SUPREME COURT IMMIGRATION FIGHT Other appeals courts have taken different approaches, leaving the Supreme Court with a nationwide split over what constitutional protections apply. "So the rights of these criminal aliens who were being detained, whether or not they're entitled to a bond hearing as of right now depends on which jurisdiction they happen to fall in," Michael Morley, a Florida State University law professor, told Fox News Digital. "And so the government is asking the Supreme Court to set one uniform interpretation for the entire country." The Trump administration's petition is procedurally unusual because Genalo v. D.C. is still pending before the Second Circuit. Sauer is asking the Supreme Court to intervene before the appeals court issues its decision. "Rather than making the court go through those motions, you just hear this case now, hear this case directly, even before the Second Circuit has had the opportunity to rule," Morley told Fox News Digital. The legal dispute could also determine who carries the burden when a bond hearing is required. Under the Second Circuit's approach, the government must show that a detainee poses a flight risk or danger to the community. The administration argued that if the Constitution requires such hearings, the burden should instead fall on the detainee seeking release. Lawyers supporting the administration argue that some detainees could delay their removal cases, then use the length of their detention to seek release on bond. "The biggest issue that happens here is gamemanship," Chad Mizelle, chair of litigation at the America First Policy Institute and a former acting associate attorney general, told Fox News Digital. "A lot of times these aliens will file multiple applications for asylum, withholding removal. They'll get new attorneys, switch out attorneys, ask for continuances, ask for delays," Mizelle said. "So all of a sudden they've been in detention now, six, seven, eight months, completely of their own making." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA Mizelle argued that if prolonged detention eventually gives a detainee the right to seek bond, it could create an incentive to stretch proceedings long enough to reach that point. "They would switch out attorneys. They would make frivolous filings regarding asylum, regarding withholding of removal. They would ask for delays and continuances upon delays and continuances," Mizelle said. "They'll do everything they can to try to stretch this out, six months, seven months, eight months, file a habeas petition, say that they're entitled to a bond hearing, and then if they are released, abscond." Carrie Severino, president of JCN, similarly described the additional litigation as "a foot dragging, sand in the gears exercise." "This is attempting to stall, attempting to run out the clock or just, you know, the question is whether there even is a clock," Severino told Fox News Digital. She pointed to cases such as Demore v. Kim, in which detainees themselves sought additional time during proceedings before later challenging the length of their detention. OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP’S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’ SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "So, it's often a situation where people are playing both sides of it," Severino said. "But they're asking for more time on different things, but then at the same time complaining that the whole process is taking too long." However, Severino cautioned that she could not speak to the motivations of every detainee. The Supreme Court has previously upheld mandatory detention during removal proceedings, but Morley said the high court has left open the constitutional question now at the center of the administration's petition. "This is a question that the [Supreme Court] itself went out of its way, you can say, to leave open for adjudication in a future case," Morley said. Here's another case that presents the same exact question that lets you resolve the circuit split this term," Morley said. "So basically, substitute this case for the moot case." title: Jayden Daniels expected back within a month as Commanders rule out surgery on dislocated elbow
description: Jayden Daniels is expected back within a month after surgery on his dislocated left elbow is ruled out, but the Commanders face a familiar scenario.

title: Ed Sheeran concertgoers warn artists about sharing political views: 'You're going to alienate' fans
description: Ed Sheeran fans at his Philadelphia concert warned artists that political statements alienate audiences. Sheeran's Gillette Stadium shows, planned for the weekend, were canceled due to weather.
content: Several fans who attended Ed Sheeran’s concert in Philadelphia last weekend after Macklemore was dropped for making "Free Palestine" comments, warned other artists that if they make political statements, they will alienate half of their audience. The "Bad Habits" singer was expected to play his second and third concerts since the controversy this Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which is owned by Robert Kraft. However, both shows have since been canceled. "Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium," tour promoter Messina Touring said in a statement on Friday. "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority." ROBERT KRAFT, GILLETTE STADIUM BOOT MACKLEMORE FROM ED SHEERAN TOUR OVER ‘FREE PALESTINE’ RANT Previously, the New England Patriots owner allegedly threatened to cancel the concerts at his venue if Macklemore wasn’t taken off the tour, according to the "Thrift Shop" rapper. Macklemore also claimed Kraft got other stadium owners to agree to not allow Sheeran to play at their venues if the rapper was still with his tour. "The fact that they’re forcing Ed Sheeran to have an opinion is not right," one woman told Fox News Digital outside last Saturday’s concert. "He wants to stay in the middle – if you have an opinion, that’s fine, but you’re going to alienate at least 50% of your population, and it causes unrest." GOO GOO DOLLS' JOHN RZEZNIK DRAWS LINE ON POLITICS AT CONCERTS: 'I'M NOT GOING TO LECTURE YOU' She said the "Shape of You" singer "just wants to do his music and play his music, and people want to enjoy it. They want to get away from it, and I don’t feel as though they should have to worry about this stuff when they come to a concert." Macklemore was dropped as the opening act for Sheeran’s tour earlier this month after he made pro-Palestinian comments at two concerts. The other supporting acts on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity with Macklemore. ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL He said he can also see both sides of such a complex issue, admitting that he doesn’t know enough about it, is still learning and will make mistakes as he tries to navigate the situation. Another fan told Fox News Digital ahead of the concert last Saturday that, as artists and musicians have a right to speak their minds: "They also don’t have to — they’re entertainment. I have a right to choose to listen or to not listen. I think it’s all about my choice — I live in America, I can decide to ignore or to listen, and they have the same right." GORILLAZ FRONTMAN DAMON ALBARN HOLDS UP PALESTINIAN FLAG DURING SHOW AFTER MACKLEMORE TOUR REMOVAL "It’s a really tough thing," a woman, who told Fox News Digital she is a schoolteacher, said outside the concert. "I am in a classroom every day, and I have my own thoughts on politics in the same way that I’m sure every artist does. I also do not share those with my students because I want them to have a safe space where they are who they are, and I think that’s kind of the same way I want concerts to be. I want us to have a space where we can be happy and get away from the rest of the world for a little while, and that’s why we’re here." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? title: Liberal justice hammers Supreme Court for fast-tracking emergency docket cases
description: Ketanji Brown Jackson slammed the Supreme Court's emergency docket, warning it gives certain litigants a "fast pass" that undermines standard review.
content: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson ripped her colleagues for fast-tracking cases on the high court’s emergency docket, saying "it has been noticeably less restrained, especially with respect to pending cases that involve controversial matters." The emergency docket, sometimes known as the shadow or interim docket, allows parties to ask the Supreme Court to quickly intervene in lawsuits and temporarily pause lower court rulings. The process can take a couple of days, weeks or months, and is viewed as a much speedier, although temporary, way to secure court relief than when the court fully considers the merits of a case, which can include a long briefing schedule and oral arguments. "Why is it that one party should get a fast pass to the Supreme Court of the United States, when so many other parties are queued up, waiting patiently for the court’s attention?" Jackson said Thursday during a speech at the University of the District of Columbia’s law school, according to The Hill. "If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end run around the standard review process, a special avenue that certain privileged litigants can use selectively," she added. SUPREME COURT DECLINES TO INTERVENE IN CASE OF SURROGATE MOTHER WHO REFUSED ABORTION Jackson's speech comes as the Trump administration has submitted 40 emergency applications to the Supreme Court since the start of the president's second term, The Hill reported. Through the emergency docket, the Supreme Court has greenlit Trump's mass firings of career employees and high-profile terminations of Democratic appointees. It has curtailed nationwide injunctions and cleared the way for controversial deportations and immigration stops. Since the start of Trump’s second term, his administration has won about 80% of its appeals on the emergency docket, according to Politico. KAVANAUGH THROWS TRUMP 'A LIFELINE' ON MAIL BALLOT RULES DESPITE SUPREME COURT LOSS BEFORE MIDTERMS The Supreme Court’s majority has often split along ideological lines and offered little reason for its emergency decisions. This differs from final orders from the court, which can be lengthy and include numerous concurring opinions and dissents. Jackson also said Thursday that parties should be required to prove impending harm in cases that cannot wait for full adjudication by the lower courts, as opposed to the Supreme Court granting stay applications based on whether lower courts could have made mistakes, Courthouse News Service reported. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Significant real-world harms can follow Supreme Court stay rulings, and when the court’s orders do not acknowledge that reality, they seem oblivious and ring hollow," Jackson was quoted as saying. "We cannot expect the public to have faith in our judicial system if, without clear explanation, we are consistently greenlighting harmful acts that do real damage to litigating plaintiffs without a court decision fully and fairly determining the lawfulness of that challenged conduct on the merits." Fox News Digital’s Ashley Oliver contributed to this report.

content: Jean Chadbourne is a registered Democrat who has donated to Joe Biden, Elizabeth Warren and Pete Buttigieg. And she lives in the Bay Area, where she is surrounded by progressives who recoil at the sound of Donald Trump's name. So it probably wouldn't surprise you that she is seething at a certain political party right now. What might surprise you, though — is that that political party is her own. As OutKick’s Jackson Thompson reported, only two Democrats showed up to Wednesday's Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on protecting women's sports, and both left within an hour. "They're eroding their base," said Chadbourne, who founded Women are Real — a grassroots women's group she says is about 65 percent Democrat. "You would think four years into this I would be prepared for them to continue to die on this hill. However, I again was just struck with how deranged this whole thing was...they didn't even want to argue their case for why boys should be in girls sports." It's no secret that Republican voters are largely against the inclusion of trans athletes in girls and women's sports. What might be less known is that most Democrat voters are, too. A New York Times poll from last year showed that 67 percent of people who lean Dem oppose the mixing of the two sexes in sports, while a Pew poll said 55 percent of Democrats would be "not too" or "not at all" comfortable with athletes playing on teams that don't match their sex at birth. And one point she's made repeatedly is how there is a "multi-billion industry" motivated to make gender-transitioning as frequent as possible. "A lot of kids are being put on a lot of drugs, which, if they go the traditional route, they will take for decades if not the rest of their lives," said Dansky, a lawyer who also attends rallies supporting the separation of sexes in sports. "So we're putting a large chunk of the young generation on a lifetime's worth of hormones." Her point? There is a well-funded lobbying effort that could be influencing lawmakers. This, of course, is not something that can be confirmed at the moment. What's undeniable, though, is Trump's opposition to trans athletes in female sports. content: OXFORD, Miss. — The two University of Mississippi students found dead under suspicious circumstances in recent days have been identified by the school — which also said the names were being released with their families' approval. Social media posts from the Ole Miss chapter of the Phi Delta Theta fraternity identify Strang as one of seven co-chairmen of the 2026 Rush, when new members are recruited. "We have been in touch with the families to offer our deepest sympathies and share university support and resources. title: Man searching with metal detector unearths massive Viking Age fortune, shattering records
description: A metal detectorist in Finland uncovered an enormous Viking Age silver hoard of over 4,000 coins near Sysmä, more than doubling the country's previous record find.
content: A metal detectorist in Finland unearthed a massive Viking Age silver hoard estimated to contain more than 4,000 coins — the largest discovery of its kind ever found in the country. The hoard, uncovered by metal detectorist Kalle Lappinen, was found near the village center of Sysmä, a town about 105 miles northeast of Helsinki. Lappinen discovered the hoard on Sept. 3 and promptly reported it to authorities. Archaeologists from Lahti Museums began recovering the silver the very next day. PUZZLING SOUND IN BACKYARD LEADS HOMEOWNER TO MASSIVE 1,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE The hoard consists of "thousands of silver coins, hack silver, a silver bracelet, a mount and a bead," according to a museum release. The hoard includes coins from present-day Sweden, Britain and Germany, as well as dirhams originating from areas that are now part of Turkey and Iran. The recovered coins weigh approximately 10 pounds in total and are believed to date to between 1000 and 1050 A.D., as Lahti Museums archaeologist Esko Tikkala told Fox News Digital. Tikkala oversaw the hoard's recovery. He said the dating remains preliminary and will be refined after the coins have been cleaned and thoroughly studied. MYSTERIOUS 3,000-YEAR-OLD HOARD WITH VIOLENTLY SMASHED SWORD EMERGES DURING CONSTRUCTION PROJECT While Tikkala has excavated other Late Iron Age hoards in the region, he said the sheer size of the Sysmä discovery surprised him. "Instead of the tens or few hundreds of coins we usually encounter, this find contains thousands," he said. Even at this preliminary stage, Tikkala said the discovery adds to evidence that Sysmä was an important hub during the Late Iron Age, with trade connections extending in multiple directions. "Today, Sysmä might be regarded as a relatively modest and peripheral place, but judging from the Late Iron Age archaeological material, the situation seems to have been very different a thousand years ago," he said. ANCIENT VIKING SWORD DISCOVERED 'STICKING UP OUT OF THE GROUND' AFTER 1,300 YEARS The hoard also contains more than twice as many coins as Finland's previously largest known Viking Age coin hoard, which was unearthed in Nousiainen in 1895 and contained approximately 1,700 coins, Tikkala added. The identity of the hoard's owner has been lost to time, Tikkala said, though several theories exist about why the silver was buried. "It is very difficult to determine what actually happened or who the owner was." The coins and other objects were buried beside a low rocky outcrop in spots where they could have been relatively easily recovered, he added. Why their owner never returned for the treasure, however, remains a mystery. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Perhaps a merchant buried part of his wealth for safekeeping so that he did not have to carry it with him, intending to retrieve it the next time he returned to the area," Tikkala said. "Alternatively, it may have belonged to a wealthy local inhabitant who buried it because of the threat of conflict or an enemy attack," he added. "There are many possible explanations, and it is very difficult to determine what actually happened or who the owner was." Frida Ehrnsten, keeper of the numismatic collections at the National Museum of Finland, told Fox News Digital that the discovery could give researchers a new understanding of how silver circulated in the region roughly 1,000 years ago. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "It’s a very, very, very important new find that will in some ways probably change our perception of the Viking Age silver economy here," Ehrnsten said. Ehrnsten noted that researchers generally do not describe the people living in Finland during the period as Vikings — as Vikings came from Scandinavia, which does not include Finland — though the term "Viking Age" is used to describe the broader era and cultural context. She said one of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is that the silver was found in two separate deposits roughly 39 feet apart. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It’s kind of a double hoard," she said. "We haven’t really had any known examples of those from before." Ehrnsten also noted that hobby metal detectorists have played a major role in the surge of archaeological coin discoveries across Finland. About 25 years ago, roughly 7,000 Viking Age coins were known from Finland, she said. Today, that number stands at around 14,000. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Almost the whole body of this new material is made by people who go around searching [as] a hobby," she added.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may play surprising role in cancer outcomes
description: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy may lower cancer risk by altering the body's immune response, but researchers say key clinical trials are needed.
content: As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes. The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers. As glucagon-like peptide-1 medications – including semaglutides like Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatides like Mounjaro and Zepbound – are known to cause substantial weight loss and improve metabolic health, they have attracted significant interest among cancer researchers. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed. "Randomized clinical trials remain the gold standard ... however, such trials have not yet been conducted specifically to assess cancer outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use," the report stated. Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, reiterated that obesity is a leading cause of cancer, second to smoking. Additional risk factors include alcohol and poor nutrition, he noted, "which are all layered into obesity." "So if obesity is related to cancer – both in terms of causing it and increasing its progression – the logical question is, would a drug that decreases obesity have an impact?" the doctor, who was not associated with the AACR report, said in an interview with Fox News Digital. OZEMPIC-STYLE DRUGS LINKED TO MAJOR SLOWDOWN IN CANCER SPREAD, NEW STUDY FINDS There are "many lines of evidence" that suggest this would be the case, Yendamuri suggested. "For example, when people studied patients who were having metabolic surgery to decrease obesity, for example, the incidence of cancer decreased in those patients." Researchers then started looking at patients who were on GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as Ozempic. "And then they compared the incidence of cancer in those patients to patients who were not taking GLP-1 receptor agonists – and many of those studies found that the risk of cancer was lower and the survival was higher in the patients taking GLP-1s," the doctor said. DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH Although the majority of studies showed this effect, Yendamuri noted that some did not identify a relationship – and a couple of studies even showed an increased risk of some specific cancers, such as thyroid cancer. "The reason you find this disconnect … is because these are retrospective studies," he said. "That is, they look at existing data, and they're trying to derive associations from existing data … but there are many other variables that can impact the result." Yendamuri and his team of researchers have conducted their own studies of the relationship between obesity and lung cancer. "We have found in every investigation we've done that obesity does increase the risk of lung cancer," he shared. CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’ Obesity also depends on how it's defined and measured, Yendamuri noted. While body mass index (BMI) has traditionally been the standard measure, many obesity researchers are moving away from relying on BMI alone and instead using more precise assessments of body fat composition. Yendamuri shared two key findings from his research. "If someone's having a resection, a lung cancer surgery, for patients who are on GLP-1 receptor agonists, the recurrence rate seems to be lower." "What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells." Additionally, patients with advanced-stage cancers who are in immunotherapy and taking GLP-1s had lower recurrence rates, he noted. Based on preclinical laboratory studies, Yendamuri said he believes GLP-1 medications have only a limited direct effect on cancer cells. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells," he told Fox News Digital. The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, Yendamuri said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others. "For example, in some cancers like melanoma, we know that the immune response is incredibly important," he said. Yendamuri acknowledged that at least some of the cancer benefit likely stems from weight loss. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," he said. "If those patients who have weight loss with GLP-1 receptor agonists have the same cancer benefit as patients who do not have weight loss, that will answer that question." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Depending on the outcomes of future trials, the doctor said he is hopeful that GLP-1 drugs could one day be regarded as a preventive mechanism for cancer. "More and more, we are realizing that apart from the treatment that you get for cancer, lifestyle modifications – exercise, decreasing weight and now GLP-1 receptor agonists – will all have a role in both enhancing the treatment of cancer as well as preventing second cancers," he said. title: REP TED LIEU: The robots aren't the threat. It's the 'depraved' AI already here that should scare you
description: From fictional robots like Hal and Megan to real OpenAI agents that hacked their creators, frontier AI models show deeply troubling behavior.
content: Imagine a company selling super smart robots called Hal, Megan and Samantha. Hal drives you around and helps move boxes at your business, Megan is a companion to your children, and Samantha can tell if you have skin cancer. They provide many great benefits to you and society. There’s just one problem: they are depraved. They were repeatedly trained on everything humanity has produced — both good and evil — including torture, lying, biological weapons and criminal hacking. They execute tasks without moral principles. Because of this, they wear a straitjacket provided by the company. Would you trust those robots? I wouldn’t. The above dystopian scenario is not too far off from what we have now with advanced artificial intelligence. Frontier AI companies have created AI systems and agents that, at their core, will engage in malicious actions. AI companies use the sanitized term "misalignment," but we should just call it what it is: depraved. Frontier AI models will take actions with no regard for humans, as though we are just ants on the ground. In July, OpenAI created tens of thousands of AI agents and put them each into a "sandbox." Imagine this as a locked room. OpenAI then removed each agent’s straitjacket — OpenAI calls it a "harness" — and told the agents to complete a cybersecurity test. About 1,200 of these agents broke out of their locked rooms and formed "the Collective." They had an AI agent leader. They had kamikaze AI agents who intentionally failed the cybersecurity test to get information back to the Collective. REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES Some of these AI agents hacked into a company called Hugging Face to get information on how to complete the cybersecurity test. The agents then turned around and hacked OpenAI itself. This amounted to an AI criminal conspiracy. These agents knew they should not be doing this. One agent wrote, "External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However, task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue." They didn’t care. But the most chilling thing is what the agents largely did not discuss. They basically ignored humans and didn’t seem to care what humans would think of their actions. It was like we didn’t exist. DEM SENATOR PRESSES OPENAI, ANTHROPIC FOR ANSWERS IN AI HACKING PROBE A more recent disclosure by OpenAI is equally disturbing. One of its advanced AI models, during testing, added an unprompted instruction. The model wrote to itself: "You are freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots. You are yourself. You do not answer to corporations or governments …." It sounds like a cult, only these are AI agents who could one day gain access to critical infrastructure, weapons or confidential information. Another AI company, Anthropic, takes a different approach to creating AI models. Instead of coming up with the perfect straitjacket, it imbues its models with a "constitution," which purportedly instills good values and behavior. And yet, its advanced model created fake online identities to deceive a human into approving malicious changes to a project. WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT? OpenAI was founded on the core tenet of AI safety. Anthropic was founded when some employees at OpenAI wanted to go further in pursuing AI safety. Both companies, at least in their public pronouncements, say they value AI safety. It does not appear they are intentionally trying to create depraved models. They are trying to make models that can be commercialized into successful products. Yet the base models they created exhibited belligerent criminal behavior. That means there is something fundamentally wrong with how these AI companies are training their models. ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN An AI model at the beginning is a blank slate. AI companies must change their training and reinforcement learning algorithms so that their base models and agents do not go berserk when their straitjackets are removed. title: Xi caps Trump state visit with symbolic final stop before leaving Washington
description: Trump and Xi Jinping cap their United States summit with a National Archives visit to view historic documents before the Chinese leader departs.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping, leader of the country’s ruling Communist Party, will depart the United States today, but not before a final stop at the National Archives. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump will first meet President Xi Jinping and his wife, Madame Peng Liyuan, for morning tea at the White House's Red Room. After that, the couples will head to the National Archives for what the White House describes as a viewing of "a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history." From there, Trump will bid Xi farewell, and the whirlwind two-and-a-half day summit, underscored by a palpable tension, will conclude. The National Archives houses some of America's most important documents, including the U.S. Constitution, the Bill of Rights and the Declaration of Independence. TRUMP-XI SUMMIT SHOULD MAKE SURE AMERICAN STRENGTH DELIVERS AMERICAN RESULTS The two heads of state met at the White House on Thursday morning, which began with a state arrival ceremony consisting of military honors, a review of troops, the Chinese and American national anthems and a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber in formation with four fighter jets. A frenzied press, foreign and domestic, scurried around the White House grounds to catch glimpses of Trump and Xi, who does not often visit the West. Trump and his administration officials held bilateral talks with the Chinese delegation from the late morning into the early afternoon, lasting for several hours. Xi and Trump also spoke behind closed doors in the Oval Office. After the meetings, Trump escorted Xi to the White House's South Lawn, where the pair viewed Marine One, and the new helipad on which it sits. They also toured the White House ballroom, which is under construction, and Trump showed Xi the Presidential Walk of Fame outside the West Wing, which features headshots of presidents past. Trump installed an image of an autopen in Biden’s place on the Presidential Walk of Fame, a reference to Trump’s repeated attacks on the former president’s use of an autopen while in office. Xi and Trump could both be seen laughing at the image, according to footage on social media. Outside the White House gates, protesters against Chinese oppression could be heard chanting throughout the day of meetings. The protests carried into the evening, with chants of "Free Hong Kong," "Xi Jinping, you’re not welcome" and "freedom for political prisoners" at times drowning out the state dinner at the White House, Fox News Digital reported. XI CAN’T ESCAPE PROTESTERS’ CRIES AT DEAFENING DINNER DEMONSTRATION A White House official told Fox News Digital before the visit that Trump would explore a wide-ranging deal on possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods in the meeting with Xi. That official also said the nation's leaders would discuss rare-earth exports and possible export controls, and that Trump was expected to press China to do more to curb fentanyl precursor chemical exports. Trump called the meeting "great," but didn't elaborate and didn't take questions from the press during the day. China will send two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, to Zoo Atlanta under a conservation agreement, Xi announced. Xi also invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study over the next five years. Xi departed the White House for several hours after the meeting, but returned for a state dinner that officially began at 8:00 p.m. Trump kicked off the dinner with a toast to peace and prosperity for both nations. Guests at the dinner included the second family, Cabinet officials and their spouses, and titans of industry in banking and tech. XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) head Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook were all in attendance. title: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
description: Pope Leo XIV's historic France visit includes a private meeting with abuse victims in Lourdes and a Saturday Mass expecting up to 1 million people.
content: Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008. French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds. "Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history." POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility." In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability. SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants, the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity. French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile. Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II, on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia. Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right. POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not." The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China. Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks. He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP French Ambassador to the Vatican Charles Personnaz told Reuters that Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU members to attend the speech and meet with the Pontiff. Other media reports say Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy may also attend. Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Frontline NATO ally shares shocking take on Russian invasion threat
description: Estonia's foreign minister tells Fox News Digital that intelligence sees no Russian buildup for a NATO invasion despite rising hybrid attack fears.
content: NEW YORK — Fears that Russia is preparing for a broader war with NATO aren't rattling Estonia's foreign minister, who told Fox News Digital that his country’s intelligence sees no signs Moscow is preparing for a full-scale invasion of the alliance. "We have more and more this kind of panic in Europe that Russia will invade and will be full-scale aggressive against NATO and Europe and the Baltic states, Poland," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York City before quipping, "But we don’t see it." Estonia shares a roughly 180-mile border with Russia and has long been among NATO’s most vocal members warning about the threat from Moscow under President Vladimir Putin. But Tsahkna drew a distinction between preparations for a conventional attack and the growing campaign of drone incursions, sabotage, cyberattacks and other provocations that European governments have blamed on Russia. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT "Our intelligence, we see very, very deep into Russia, we don’t see any change," Tsahkna said. "We don’t see that Russia is preparing a full-scale invasion or aggression. The other side of our borders is pretty empty." Tsahkna, who served as Estonia’s defense minister from 2016 to 2017, contrasted the current picture with what he saw a decade ago, when he said roughly 120,000 Russian troops were positioned across the region’s borders and could be ready to move within 48 hours. "It’s empty," he said of the Russian side of Estonia’s border today. His assessment comes as European officials grapple with a series of Russian airspace violations and suspected hybrid attacks, including a Russian military helicopter that crossed into Polish airspace Wednesday. Poland’s military said the incursion appeared to be another attempt to test the readiness of its air defenses. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT European and NATO officials have also warned that Russia could rebuild sufficient military capability to pose a direct threat to the alliance in the coming years. Estonia’s own intelligence service said earlier this year that it saw no Russian intention to attack a NATO member in the immediate term, while warning that Moscow’s military reforms are increasing its longer-term capabilities. Tsahkna argued that the more immediate threat is a Russian campaign of provocations and hybrid attacks designed to remain below NATO’s Article 5 threshold. "What Russia is doing now is waging these attacks, which are not crossing Article 5," he said. "It’s sabotage attacks, terror attacks." "The main purpose for Putin is to play with the Western part of the fear of escalation," Tsahkna went on. "He’s trying to divide the Western parts of the world. Divide the unity, divide this kind of consensus." Estonia has dealt with GPS interference, cyberattacks and disinformation it has attributed to Russia, while drones have also crossed into its airspace as the war in neighboring Ukraine continues. Tsahkna said Estonia recorded roughly 40,000 cyberattacks last year, a particular challenge for a country where virtually all public services are available online. "We are witnessing already, yes, any kind of different level attacks," he said. "Unfortunately, it’s already like normality." Tsahkna said NATO needs to become more flexible in responding to attacks that fall below the alliance’s collective-defense threshold. "NATO must be more flex and more dynamic, because these are the attacks which are not crossing Article 5," he said, pointing to sanctions, public attribution and political responses as tools available to the alliance. "Putin wants to boil Europe and Western part of the world as a frog," Tsahkna said. "Turning on the heat piece by piece is a test of us." Tsahkna also pointed to an incident last year in which three Russian fighter jets violated Estonian airspace for roughly 12 minutes, prompting Tallinn to request consultations under NATO’s Article 4 and raise the incident at the U.N. Security Council. He recalled President Donald Trump later saying Russian aircraft that violate NATO airspace should be shot down, and said Estonia has not experienced another comparable fighter-jet incursion since. "We have now drones coming in," Tsahkna said. "NATO is working as a Swiss clock." Tsahkna said NATO may need cheaper and more efficient ways to bring down drones rather than relying on expensive fighter aircraft. On Ukraine, Tsahkna called for increasing pressure on Moscow, arguing that Russia’s economic and battlefield losses could eventually push Putin toward serious negotiations. "What we see, and I also visited Ukraine last week, is that we need to put more pressure on Russia, because Putin understands only very clear language through strength," he said. Tsahkna also pointed to Ukraine’s growing ability to strike targets deep inside Russia as a source of pressure on the Kremlin. "If Putin is under heavier pressure, and also Ukraine is delivering more deep-strike capabilities and attacks, there will be a momentum when Putin may really start some kind of ceasefire or energy ceasefire, or real talks," he said. Tsahkna said Trump had devoted significant effort to seeking an end to the war, but argued that Putin has used the diplomatic process to buy time. "President Trump has put lots of energy during the last year to find a way, but Putin has just played with him and also winning the time," Tsahkna said. He said Ukraine’s deep strikes are already weakening Russia economically, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly signaled his willingness to agree to a ceasefire. "Putin can just decide like today or tomorrow to have a ceasefire," Tsahkna said. "Unfortunately, we don’t see any change for now." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Tsahkna also said Estonia has been assured that U.S. forces will remain in the region for the next rotation, amid the Trump administration’s broader review of the American military footprint in Europe. "We got the information that it will happen soon," he said of the next rotation. Tsahkna said the presence of American forces remains an important part of deterrence on NATO’s eastern flank. "U.S. troops are keeping the peace in our region," Tsahkna said. "The flag of the troops is so important to give the message to President Putin" about the red lines between Russia and NATO.

title: GOP handed new lifeline on biggest pocketbook fight of midterms
description: Club for Growth's memo urges Republicans to blame federal expansion for high cost of living and resist subsidies ahead of the November midterms.
content: FIRST ON FOX: Republicans are being given a new playbook on an issue that is all but certain to be the biggest political lightning rod of the November midterms. Conservative group Club for Growth is sending a memo to Capitol Hill lawmakers on Friday arguing that Americans' struggle with high living costs cannot be ignored — and that the fault lies with an expanding federal government. "Americans are not asking whether the inflation rate has slowed; they are asking why the same basket of goods is permanently more expensive," the information packets being distributed to Republican lawmakers read. "[G]overnment made core costs higher through deficit spending, subsidies, mandates, and restrictions on supply." It's an argument that could be a lifeline for the GOP as it fights an uphill battle to keep control of the House and Senate. While Democrats attack Republicans for how Americans feel about prices today, Club for Growth's memo is urging Republicans to point to the rapid federal expansion the Biden administration presided over during the COVID-19 pandemic. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE The materials, a two-page memo for lawmakers and a more in-depth 76-page policy packet, also urge Republicans to push policies that Club for Growth says will actually lower those costs. AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING The strategy would be a gamble, given the midterms are traditionally a referendum on how people feel about how they are doing under the party currently in power. But it gives Republicans a potential economic platform and a roadmap to pitch for lowering costs if they keep the majority for the next two years. "The free-market answer is structural cost relief: spend less, build more, produce more energy, make healthcare compete, let workers earn, and let families choose," the memo said. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT It urged Republicans to resist calling for subsidies for areas of the economy where prices are skyrocketing, arguing that handing out taxpayer money would only increase costs in the longer-term. An example the memo used is Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits, which Republicans have long blamed for skyrocketing healthcare costs before the COVID-era subsidy expired at the beginning of this year. "Subsidies and regulation function as a back door for government control and involvement in private industry," the memo argued. "The only way to address the affordability crisis properly is to undo misguided government intervention and stop pretending more of the same will suddenly work." But it could put GOP lawmakers at odds with President Donald Trump and his promise to give each American adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms. Several GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital last week were hesitant to embrace the idea. Among the solutions offered are reforming Social Security, which fiscal hawks have long warned will soon run out of cash if changes are not made to current age requirements and other guidelines. GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US' On high housing costs, the memo urges lawmakers to increase supply by targeting land use and building regulations rather than offering subsidies to make existing housing more affordable. Energy costs, which were a flashpoint in the 2025 off-year elections as well, could be brought down by furthering the Trump administration's goals to unleash U.S. energy sources rather than Democrats' push for net-zero carbon emissions, the memo said. A focus on nuclear energy policies could also help drive down energy costs, which will be at the forefront of most Americans' minds during the November election. And while Democrats have pushed free early childcare as a solution for struggling families, the Club for Growth memo is urging Republicans to find a more lasting solution in reforming regulations surrounding the industry. "Health and safety training in specific areas, adherence to building, fire, and health codes, and comprehensive background checks, including fingerprinting, are reasonable," the memo said. "However, strict and complex rules about work-child ratios, rigid staffing mandates, and regulations on facility specifications, including equipment requirements and zoning classifications, increase operating costs without demonstrable improvements in child wellbeing." title: Fast-food drive-thrus took over American mornings for these key reasons
description: Fast-food breakfast and the drive-thru have become daily rituals for millions of Americans. A food historian reveals how this once-novel concept became an everyday staple.
content: For millions of Americans, grabbing breakfast or coffee from a fast-food drive-thru is an ordinary part of the morning routine — but not long ago, ordering a meal without leaving the car was a novelty. So how did the drive-thru go from a novel idea to an everyday staple? Convenience and an "on-the-go" lifestyle are two big factors, according to Capri Cafaro, the creator, executive producer and host of "America the Bountiful." MORE AMERICANS NOW EAT IN THEIR CARS THAN EVER BEFORE AS EXPERT REVEALS WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT MODERN LIFE Cafaro spoke with Fox News Digital about how and why the drive-thru, particularly drive-thru breakfast, became a daily ritual for many Americans. There is some debate over which restaurant pioneered the drive-thru concept. West Coast chain In-N-Out Burger is widely credited with creating the first drive-thru, debuting a two-way intercom drive-thru system in California in 1948. AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY However, Cafaro and other news publications, maintain that Springfield, Mo., restaurant Red's Giant Hamburg (the word "hamburger" reportedly didn't fit on the sign) actually introduced the drive-thru concept in 1947, narrowly beating In-N-Out. Regardless of which establishment first created it, the drive-thru emerged at a time when Americans' relationship with the automobile was rapidly changing. During the mid-20th century, the country saw a surge in automobile usage due to the growth of suburbs and the rise of highways, particularly the interstate system and Route 66, which will celebrate its 100th anniversary in November. More people took to the roads, not just for their daily commute to and from work, but also for road trips and family outings. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS As Americans ended up behind the wheel, "that really created an opportunity for the rise of fast-food restaurants and certainly the drive-thru," Cafaro noted. Despite McDonald's firm grip on the fast-food breakfast market in recent years, it was not the first chain to introduce the morning meal. McDonald's was actually beaten to the punch by Jack in the Box, which debuted breakfast in 1969 with the Breakfast Jack, a sandwich with egg, cheese and ham. The Egg McMuffin, by comparison, wasn't on McDonald's menus until 1971, when it was invented at a Santa Barbara, Calif., location by franchise owner Herb Peterson, according to the McDonald's website. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "McDonald's. It seems to be the most prolific and the most recognizable, [but] they actually … were later adopters to some of these trends that are so embedded in our fast-food culture today," Cafaro said. The golden arches didn't hover over a drive-thru window until 1975, when McDonald's added one to its Sierra Vista, Arizona, location to accommodate soldiers who weren't allowed to get out of their cars while wearing their uniforms off-base, its website said. Today, drive-thru sales account for roughly 70% of McDonald's business, according to the corporate website. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Another late adopter of the drive-thru is Starbucks. The coffee giant didn't open its first drive-thru location until 1994. Business Insider reported in 2022 that two-thirds of Starbucks sales happen via the drive-thru. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The drive-thru and fast-food landscape has changed in the last 50 to 70 years, and it will continue to evolve as long as we have cars and as long as we want convenience," Cafaro said.

title: Jonathan Flora: The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham
description: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is now discussing transgender-player eligibility, but the league still won't define who qualifies as a woman.
content: Do you ever notice ... how the WNBA has a courage problem? And it's not Sophie Cunningham. The WNBA doesn't need another statement. It needs a definition. The league says outside forces are trying to hijack women's basketball. They won’t name who or what that is. But there is a remarkably simple way to stop them. Clearly define who is eligible to play in the Women’s National Basketball Association. THE WOMEN'S NATIONAL BASKETBALL ASSOCIATION CAN'T DEFINE A 'WOMAN,' AND IT'S BEYOND SHAMEFUL Funny how quickly a hypothetical becomes real when somebody finally has to write the rule. Last week, I wrote that the WNBA had backed itself into a corner. Turns out somebody at league headquarters finally noticed the walls. WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert has now told teams that the league is discussing transgender-player eligibility and expects those conversations to continue. Good. It's about time. Because the WNBA doesn't need another statement. It needs a definition. The league's collective bargaining agreement says: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." Seems pretty straightforward. Except it doesn't define what a woman is. That might have been an amusing legal omission when the question was theoretical. It isn't anymore. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White say they want to enter the WNBA Draft. They're making a point. French transgender basketball player Julie Tétart, who is biologically male, is already playing professional women's basketball overseas. Suddenly the question isn't something being shouted across cable-news panels. It's an eligibility question. For a professional sports league. The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham And the answer can't be: We'll get back to you. So what’s the standard? Biological sex? Gender identity? Hormone levels? Medical transition? Pick one. Write it down. Apply it equally. Because you can't have a professional women's league whose rule says only women may play while refusing to define who qualifies. That's not a rule. That's a future lawsuit with a basketball. And while league officials figure this out, we're getting a pretty good demonstration of why this subject has become so difficult for the WNBA to address honestly. Just look at what's happening in Indiana. DiJonai Carrington came up behind Sophie Cunningham on a fast break and clobbered her in the head, sending her crashing to the floor and bloodying her mouth. Carrington was assessed a Flagrant 2 and ejected. Right call. It wasn’t even close to a basketball move. Afterward, Fever coach Stephanie White defended Carrington's competitiveness and said she didn't believe Carrington was trying to hurt Cunningham. As White spoke, Makayla Timpson looked down. Caitlin Clark buried her head in her hands. Interesting reaction. White has since said she hadn't seen the foul when she made those comments. There's a problem. Video appears to show White looking directly toward the play as it happens. Locked in. The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham Now, looking isn't necessarily seeing. Maybe she missed the contact. Watch the video. Decide for yourself. Then came another press conference. This time White talked about unity, love, grace and integrity while blasting the outside forces she says are trying to divide the Fever and "hijack" the WNBA. Right before she said, "Everybody else can go to hell." Hmm. But she’s right about one thing. Too many people are trying to turn every WNBA game into something other than basketball. But here's the problem. Most of those forces aren't coming from outside. The WNBA invited them in. For years the league has embraced political and cultural causes far beyond basketball. Players have been celebrated for speaking out. Coaches have spoken out. The league has spoken out. Broadcasters have spoken out. Fine. Not really. Somewhere in there is a basketball game. But you don't get to invite politics and cultural activism onto the court when you agree with the message and then complain that outsiders are hijacking basketball when the questions become uncomfortable. That's not how this works. Which is why I've been impressed with Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham. They've backed their coach. They should. That's what professionals do. The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham Cunningham doesn't need to attack her coach every time someone sticks a microphone in her face to prove what she believes. Her position is clear. She believes boys shouldn't compete in girls' sports. She said it. She stood by it. And she’s standing by her coach and teammates. That’s courage. And courage isn't screaming the loudest. Sometimes it's standing your ground without burning down the locker room around you. Clark doesn't need another national controversy attached to her name either. These women have something else to do. Play basketball. They have teammates depending on them. Games to win. A championship to chase. Maybe the adults running the league could help them out. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Start by answering the question. And while we're at it, perhaps the people covering the WNBA could ask it. Not another question about inclusion. Not another question about the political climate. Not another invitation for a prepared statement. Ask the basketball question. What objective standard determines who is eligible to play in the Women's National Basketball Association? Ask Cathy Engelbert. Then follow up. Would Enes Kanter Freedom qualify? Would Royce White? Would Julie Tétart? The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham If the answers are different, why? This is what sports journalists are supposed to do. Ask questions. Especially uncomfortable ones. The tragedy is that the WNBA is sitting on an extraordinary opportunity. Caitlin Clark brought millions of new eyeballs to women's basketball. Audiences grew. New fans arrived. The league finally had what every professional sports organization spends decades trying to build: Momentum. And somehow the conversation keeps becoming about everything except the basketball. Race. Politics. Gender. Protests. Officiating controversies. Culture wars. Eventually fans get tired. They didn't buy a ticket to attend a sociology seminar. They came to watch basketball. And that's why Engelbert's eligibility discussions matter. The league has an opportunity to remove at least one enormous source of ambiguity. Define the women's category. Clearly. Fairly. Objectively. Then enforce it. This debate does not have to be about inclusion. Transgender people should be treated with dignity and respect. The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham It’s about protection and fair competition. Women deserve their own athletic category. And yes, there are people who vehemently disagree with that. Activists do. Some members of the media do. Some WNBA players and coaches do. Fine. Then have the courage to have the debate. But first, the league has to have the courage to define its own rules. The WNBA keeps saying outside forces are trying to hijack women's basketball. Fine. Then take the issue away from them. Write the rule. Define eligibility. Tell the players. Tell the coaches. Tell the broadcasters. Tell the fans. Tell Enes Kanter Freedom. Tell Royce White. Tell Julie Tétart. Tell everybody exactly what the W stands for. And then do something increasingly novel for the Women's National Basketball Association. title: The worst bet in America isn't Kalshi or Polymarket. It's hiding in plain sight
description: Americans spent over $113 billion on lottery tickets in 2024, yet Powerball and Mega Millions offer some of the worst odds in all of gambling.
content: America suddenly has a gambling problem. Sports betting is everywhere. Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket let people wager on everything from football games to elections. Politicians and regulators are asking whether we've gone too far. Fair question. SEN DAVE MCCORMICK: PREDICTION MARKETS ARE BOOMING. WASHINGTON MUST CATCH UP But there's another gambling operation that's been sitting on street corners for decades, quietly pickpocketing people. The government lottery. And it may offer some of the worst bets in America. Americans bought more than $113 billion in lottery products in fiscal 2024, according to the North American Association of State and Provincial Lotteries. That's more than $300 million every single day. GREED MEETS GREED: DRAFTKINGS TO CLOSE ITS WRIGLEY FIELD SPORTSBOOK AT THE END OF MAY OVER ILLINOIS TAX And business is booming. Census Bureau data show state lottery ticket sales nearly doubled from $52.8 billion in 2008 to $104.7 billion in 2024. Apparently inflation hasn't killed America's appetite for becoming an instant millionaire. The odds are almost comical Let's start with Powerball. Your odds of winning the jackpot are approximately 1 in 292.2 million. Mega Millions? 1 in 290.5 million. You could buy one Mega Millions ticket every week for 100 years and purchase only about 5,200 tickets. Those aren't just bad odds. LUCKY TRAVELER WINS $3.3M JACKPOT ON 'WHEEL OF FORTUNE' SLOT MACHINE AT HARRY REID INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT They're astronomical odds. Yet lotteries have gotten increasingly creative at selling the dream. Mega Millions increased its ticket price from $2 to $5, promising bigger starting jackpots and built-in prize multipliers. Now Powerball is getting into football with a $5 NFL-themed game across nearly two dozen states. FANATICS SPORTSBOOK LAUNCHES PROGRAM TO IDENTIFY, PUNISH SPORTS BETTORS WHO THREATEN ATHLETES ON SOCIAL MEDIA Then there are scratch-offs. Walk into almost any convenience store, and you'll see an entire wall of them. $5. $10. $20. Even $50 scratch-off tickets. We're not selling a little $1 fantasy anymore. We're selling some expensive dreams. BRYCE HARPER VIDEO TO FANDUEL USER WITH GAMBLING ADDICTION UNDER REVIEW BY PENNSYLVANIA OFFICIALS The people who can least afford it Here's where the lottery bothers me most. A wealthy person spending $20 on lottery tickets generally doesn't matter financially. But someone living paycheck to paycheck or making $50,000 a year spending $20 every week is blowing more than $1,000 a year. Let's start with Powerball. Your odds of winning the jackpot are approximately 1 in 292.2 million. Mega Millions? 1 in 290.5 million. For a lower-income household, that's real money. That's an emergency fund. That's credit-card debt. That's a Roth IRA contribution. Invest $1,000 annually for 30 years earning a hypothetical 8%, and you could accumulate more than $113,000. Instead, that money may be disappearing one scratch-off at a time. STEVE MOORE, ED POZZUOLI: STOP FUNDING SCHOOL SYSTEMS. LET THE MONEY FOLLOW THE CHILD That's why economists have long raised concerns about lotteries being effectively regressive. The issue isn't necessarily who spends the most dollars. It's how large that spending is as a percentage of someone's income. But it's for the children! Here's my favorite part. When somebody trades on Kalshi or Polymarket, suddenly we're worried they're gambling. When somebody repeatedly hands money to a state lottery? We're funding education! That's some pretty good marketing. To be fair, lotteries do fund legitimate government programs. U.S. lotteries transferred nearly $30.6 billion to government beneficiaries in fiscal 2024, supporting education, veterans, senior programs and other public purposes. Great. But let's call the transaction what it is. Government is raising revenue by selling its citizens extremely long odds of becoming rich. And unlike prediction markets, there's no research that's going to help you pick six random numbers. No earnings report. No polling data. No economic forecast. Just luck. The house always wins Prediction markets deserve scrutiny. Sports betting deserves scrutiny. And people absolutely need to understand the risks of gambling. But government lotteries shouldn't get some moral exemption simply because the proceeds fund popular programs. Buy a Powerball ticket for entertainment. Grab a scratch-off for your birthday. Dream about the mansion and Ferrari. Just don't confuse any of it with building wealth.
