title: NHL sets its most confusing team history straight, and it's still pretty confusing
description: The NHL merged both Winnipeg Jets incarnations into one franchise history, creating quirks involving Teemu Selanne and Shane Doan's career records.
content: The NHL has officially worked out one of its most confusing team histories by consolidating the histories of both incarnations of the Winnipeg Jets. While it clears some things up, it kind of makes it all a little bit more confusing. The Jets and the league announced on Wednesday that the statistical histories of both incarnations of the team have been merged. That sounds nice and simple... but it isn't. What's confusing is that the original Jets, which started in the World Hockey Association in the 1970s, were a different franchise than the one that plays in Manitoba today. The original team was one of four that merged into the NHL, but split for Arizona in 1996. Meanwhile, the Atlanta Thrashers debuted in 1999 and relocated to Winnipeg to become the current Jets. So, the OG Jets history actually belonged to the Coyotes, while the new Jets were the zombified remains of the Thrashers. Things got even more confusing when the Coyotes hockey assets were sold to what became the Utah Mammoth. However, Utah was treated as a new franchise, with the Coyotes and Jets history staying behind. If you need to take a break to splash some water on your face, go ahead because now it gets worse... With the OG Jets history merging with the current Jets/Thrashers record books, that leaves the Coyotes as their own franchise. This leads to some weird quirks. One is that Teemu Selanne's legendary rookie campaign during the 1992–93 season is now, statistically at least, tied to the Thrashers' history in a way. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Meanwhile, Shane Doan was drafted by the Jets, played his rookie season in Winnipeg, and then played over 1,400 games for the Coyotes. Until now, in the record books, he only ever played for one franchise. Now, that fact is not totally accurate when you look through the record books. It also means that the late Dale Hawerchuk has become the current (and former) Jets' franchise leader in goals and points. Current Jet Mark Scheifele took those titles in 2025, and will need to do it again. However, he'll start the year seven goals and twenty-two points back from regaining the top spot. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There really is no way to make this situation completely confusion-free. But the new way seems to be the best option... even if it's pretty head-scratching in its own right.

title: California superintendent candidate ejected from sports league meeting for boisterous Title IX defense
description: Video shows Sonja Shaw confronting CIF Southern Section council members over transgender athletes in girls' sports before being removed from the meeting.
content: California state superintendent candidate Sonja Shaw was removed from a California Interscholastic Federation Southern Section Council meeting Thursday after delivering an unscheduled speech demanding officials address transgender athlete participation in girls’ sports. Shaw, the president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education, told OutKick she was forced to leave the meeting in Long Beach after officials deemed her to be trespassing. Police were called, according to Shaw, but she said the responding officers were "very nice" and did not have to intervene. Video provided to OutKick showed Shaw standing before the council and challenging its members over the issue. CALIFORNIA GIRLS’ SPORTS ADVOCATES VOW FIGHT AFTER JUDGE TOSSES TRANS ATHLETE CASE: 'FAR FROM OVER' "I’m here on the front lines to protect our girls and their sports," Shaw said, interrupting the meeting. "I’ve never been able to address you guys as a body." The meeting’s published agenda included a public hearing session allowing speakers three minutes each. Shaw said during the confrontation that she arrived at 9:07 a.m. and had repeatedly asked CIF officials to place the participation of transgender athletes on a meeting agenda. "If you think it’s okay for a boy to play against our girls in sports, which is happening, you’re Southern Section. You are the representatives to stand up and do something," Shaw said. "You can fight back and stop using the state law. Federal supersedes state law." An official then called for a brief recess, but Shaw continued speaking. "How about any of you that are okay with this sit down? Any of you that want to fight the good fight and protect our girls, stand up," she said. "Are any of you okay? You guys are all okay with this?" As officials approached Shaw and repeatedly told her that she had to leave, she called on police to escort her from the room. "Call the cops, Mike. Let them escort me out," Shaw said. "No, you know it’s not right to let me get three minutes." Shaw continued challenging council members as she was ushered toward the exit and asked those who supported her position to stand. "So we have one guy in the room that’s willing to fight for our girls," Shaw said after one attendee apparently rose. She also accused the organization of ignoring pleas from female athletes who have contacted her for help. "We begged you to put it on the agenda. Why don’t you tell them the truth? How many times I asked you to put it on the agenda? You have the emails," Shaw said. "You guys are [a] CIF organization. You refuse to put it on the agenda and talk about it. … We have girls right now reaching out to me asking for help, and you’re sitting here acting like I’m some crazy lunatic because I’m interrupting a meeting. "I’m recording because I want people to see that you’re the representatives doing nothing," Shaw said before leaving. "I don’t care about losing votes. I don’t care about a seat. The point is, none of you are willing to do anything." INSIDE THE TRANS ATHLETE PODIUM CONTROVERSY SENDING POLITICAL SHOCKWAVES IN CALIFORNIA AHEAD OF ELECTIONS The incident unfolded amid an ongoing clash between California and the federal government over the state’s transgender athlete policies. California law says students must be permitted to participate in sex-segregated school programs and activities, including athletic teams and competitions, consistent with their gender identity. CIF’s gender-identity participation policy follows that requirement. The Trump administration has argued that the policy violates Title IX’s protections against sex discrimination. The Justice Department sued the California Department of Education and CIF in July 2025, alleging their rules deny female athletes equal opportunities by allowing biological males to compete in girls’ sports. California officials have defended their policies as consistent with state law. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit against the California Department of Education and CIF on Aug. 31. The court did not decide whether allowing transgender girls to compete in girls’ sports violates Title IX, instead ruling that California lacked clear notice that excluding transgender athletes was a condition of receiving federal education funding. The Justice Department said following the decision that it was evaluating a potential appeal. The issue received national attention when transgender athlete AB Hernandez competed in the girls’ division at the CIF state track and field championships. CIF introduced a pilot process allowing an additional biological female athlete to advance and receive a medal in events involving a transgender competitor, but critics, including Shaw, argued the accommodation did not resolve the underlying fairness issue. Shaw has made parental rights and protections for female athletes central parts of her political platform. She advanced from California’s June primary and is facing San Diego Unified School District board member Richard Barrera in November’s election for state superintendent of public instruction. title: WATCH: Mass walkout before Netanyahu speech prompts fiery response from Israeli prime minister
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called departing delegates "moral cowards" after a mass walkout at the UN General Assembly in New York.
content: A mass walkout of delegates before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations General Assembly prompted a fiery response from the Israeli leader. As Netanyahu took the stage, dozens of delegates from across the globe could be seen streaming out of the chamber in New York City. Chants of protest could also be heard in the hall as the U.N. president called the assembly to order. After taking the stage, Netanyahu said, "Before I begin, just a quick announcement, if there are any other moral cowards who haven't yet left this hall, please do so now," as cheers erupted from the remaining delegates in the chamber. THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES The Israeli leader did not let up for the rest of his address. He began by laying out what he described as the stakes of the conflict in Iran. He proclaimed that "devastating Iran's nuclear facilities was hard, it was very hard to do, but for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make as prime minister. Because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead." "Now, you want to hear the ultimate irony?" he continued. "In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of the leaders even thanked us privately for taking out Iran's nukes." "It's hard to imagine more mind blowing hypocrisy, but that's exactly what it is," said Netanyahu. MELANIA TRUMP’S HOME-COUNTRY LEADER RIPS UN ‘DOUBLE STANDARDS’ AS TRUMP PROMISE IS REVEALED The protests came as conflict in the Middle East continued and Israel faced criticism over its actions in the region. Netanyahu's address drew protests from delegates inside the U.N. chamber and demonstrators outside the building, including Hollywood celebrities Elliot Page and Susan Sarandon. Despite the protests, the prime minister delivered a defiant message, telling critics, "You don't know what you're talking about." He cast Israel's fight as one for its own survival and the survival of all the world's nations against "barbarians." "For the past three years, our heroic soldiers have fought day in an day out in a seven front war. Do you know any other country the size of New Jersey capable of fighting a seven front war? And for three years, seven fronts Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran, militias in Iraq, militias in Syria, Palestinian terrorists in Judea, Samaria, they all ganged up on us to wipe us off the face of the earth, they failed. Because instead of collapsing, we delivered crippling blows to all of them, with our great American friends." "To the protesters outside, to the hypocritical delegates who left this hall. I ask, 'Where were you when the Iranian tyrants butchered and maimed tens of thousands of unarmed Iranian civilians? When they butchered and maimed thousands of their own people? Where were you? Did you organize mass rallies, hunger strikes? Did you protest outside the Iranian mission to the UN? Did you speak out for that matter, for Christians persecuted in Iran and throughout the Middle East?' No, no, you didn't, because you're phony human rights protesters," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He also thanked President Donald Trump for ordering U.S. action against Iran. "In this battle against the barbarians, we've had no greater partner than President Trump," said Netanyahu. "I thank him. I thank him for his bold leadership. He boldly confronted an enormous danger to America, Israel and the world." "He understood that if left unchallenged, the fanatic ayatollahs who chant, 'Death to America, death to Israel,' would eventually carry out their mad fantasies. So, Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilization," he said. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Netanyahu also criticized detractors in what he called "the eigth front in this war," which he said is "the war for truth." title: Rogan warns of youth support for communism as comic Yakov Smirnoff recalls escape from USSR
description: Joe Rogan slammed young Americans' growing push toward communism during a powerful conversation with Yakov Smirnoff about escaping the Soviet Union.
content: Podcaster Joe Rogan blasted what he described as a "push towards communism" among young Americans as he spoke to legendary comedian Yakov Smirnoff, who grew up in the USSR. Smirnoff, a Soviet-born comedian who became popular in the U.S. in the 1980s, described to Rogan how he and his father would secretly listen to Voice of America, a U.S. government-funded international news broadcaster, late at night, knowing that they would get in trouble if anybody knew. He also described how his mother was greatly concerned over what might happen if others found out that they were yearning for America. VANCE WARNS THERE WILL BE A 'SOCIALIST PRESIDENT IN THIS COUNTRY' IF GOP DOESN'T FIX ECONOMY FOR YOUNG PEOPLE Later in life, after working aboard cruise ships, he proposed that he and his family leave the USSR and apply for a visa to the U.S., and he recalled his mother warned that they might face repercussions if they did so, warning that it would be like "you're going to go through hell." "And my dad said, ‘Yeah, we will.’ And she said, ‘Well, if you're willing to do it, so am I,'" Smirnoff recalled. Smirnoff said the process of getting a visa to America was only possible because of a deal involving the Carter administration, Soviet emigration and U.S. grain. "[Carter] wanted to see some human rights in the Soviet Union. And the Soviet leadership was — they were starving. They didn't have food. So, they needed food from America. So, Jimmy Carter made a deal that we're going to give you grain, and you allow people to get out, and that's how we were kind of exchanged for some wheat, you know," he said. "That's how we got out." "Wow. Holy s---, man … you sometimes need to be reminded how fortunate you are," Rogan said of Americans like himself. "You know, Americans in particular, we're very, you know, it's not our fault. You know, people become accustomed to where they live. … And they think this is normal, which is one of the reasons why this push towards communism amongst young people is so infuriating to me." Rogan said he understood why some people might be drawn to socialism out of a sense of "empathy" and the contrast between "people that are so rich and people that are so poor." "But the solution is not to make the government decide who gets what because they never decide the right way," he warned. "They do what people do," Rogan warned of communist officials. "What people do when they have power is they enact total control over the population so that they can maintain power, and then they live in luxury. And then you wait in line for bread, and that's how it is all over the f---ing world. "And if you step out of line, they shoot you. That's where communism goes. So, what we need is, like, a more, a more moral and ethical version of capitalism." SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM Elizabeth Pipko, a former RNC national spokesperson and the daughter of immigrants from the Soviet Union, spoke to Fox News Digital about the exchange and her family having escaped from the USSR. "I’m especially moved by his story because it is so incredibly similar to my own family’s," she said. "My grandfather told me many times about the secret radio he kept hidden inside a pillowcase, where he and my young mother would listen to Voice of America. Living in the Soviet Union, they would listen and dream of a better life, never knowing that one day America would deliver on those dreams and more. "I hope people understand that stories like this are incredibly special, but they are not unique," Pipko continued. "For generations, America has been a beacon of freedom and hope to people around the world, including millions who suffered under the horrors of communism. America has defeated communism before — both in reality and in spirit — and will continue to do so until the bitter end." "We have a duty to protect what so many came here searching for and to keep our country free from the ideology that they escaped," Pipko added. "Not only for those who fought and died for this nation, but for the millions around the world who still look to America and know that, as long as she shines, anything is possible." And Rogan perfectly describes how socialism is bad for us because it is tyrannical and impoverishing. "What's most interesting to me, though, is that Rogan himself fell in the past for the allure of socialism that he criticizes by supporting Bernie Sanders in 2020, who himself praised and vacationed in the Soviet Union," he added. title: Breaking up Troy Aikman and Joe Buck would be a big mistake for ESPN | Bobby Burack
description: Troy Aikman and ESPN remain far apart in contract negotiations ahead of his Super Bowl broadcast, with no long-term offer on the table yet..
content: ESPN will broadcast its first Super Bowl this February, with Joe Buck and Troy Aikman on the call. It will mark the duo’s seventh Super Bowl broadcast together — and perhaps its last. Buck recently agreed to a new six-year, $108 million contract extension with ESPN. However, sources confirm to OutKick that Aikman and the network remain far apart in contract negotiations. Aikman’s current deal expires after the Super Bowl. Aikman, who turns 60 in November, has not received a long-term offer from ESPN. It remains unclear why the network is hesitant to make such a commitment. ESPN finally found an NFL analyst who meets the standard required for its most prominent broadcast booth. For years, the network cycled through analysts such as Jason Witten, Booger McFarland, Brian Griese and Louis Riddick. They each struggled. Meanwhile, Aikman is widely regarded as the best color commentator in sports. He has worked with Buck since 2002, when the two began calling games together at Fox. Unless Aikman is seeking Tom Brady money — reportedly $37.5 million annually — it would be difficult to view losing him as anything other than a mistake. title: Madison Beer gets new skin while Justin Herbert sinks to 0-2, Aaron Rodgers' ex lashes out & NFL or college?
description: Madison Beer's new Fortnite video game skin debuts as her fiancé Justin Herbert and the Chargers prepare to face the Buffalo Bills on Sunday.
content: 'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. The trailer dropped today, and folks — it's a humdinger. I thought it was fake. It was not. OK, grab you a controller and some pizza rolls, and settle in for a Thursday 'Cap! Yep. I woke up this morning to the absolute worst noise of all time ... silence. I went to take my morning pee, flushed, started to walk away, and then stopped. I didn't hear anything. No refilling. No noise from the back. No slow leak that's been annoying me for a year now. Just silence. I went to fill up the coffee maker ... and nothing came out. The worst feeling in the world. I went outside, checked on the water tanks, and the silence was equally deafening. The pump, which started to fade back in May, had finally breathed its last breathe. So, our house has been water-less all day. I've got a new one en route as we speak. Until then, if it's yellow, let it mellow! OK, let's use some virtual water and cleanse ourselves with Madison Beer becoming a new video game character while Justin Herbert tries to simply get a win: What are our thoughts on the new Madden movie? Just a tough scene here for Justin Herbert. The Chargers have been horrendous through two games this season, and that's coming from a miserable Dolphins fan. Herbert has been awful. Mike McDaniel's offense has been awful. And now, they get to go to Buffalo and face the best team in the NFL. Meanwhile, Herbert's new fiancee is out there modeling her tail off, and getting featured in a video game. Yes, for those who don't know (all of you, I assume), a Fortnite "skin" is basically just what your character can look like in the game. So, essentially, gamers can shoot people as a bikini-clad Madison Beer for the next few weeks ... if you're into that sort of thing. Different worlds. OK, let's keep this train rolling and check in on this new John Madden movie. The final trailer dropped today ahead of the release in a few weeks, and I've gotta say ... I think this one is in big trouble: Aaron's ex, reader mail & is the NFL serious here? It's just bad, right? This has nothing to do with Nicholas Cage, by the way. I love Nick. I think he's great. The two National Treasure movies are my childhood. PEAK cinema. But the Madden voice is horrible. Truly horrible. And what is Shane Gillis doing here? Why is he in this? Is it supposed to be a comedy? I was so confused. Maybe it'll be good. It won't be, but maybe! OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big night of football (and hopefully water!). First up? Remember earlier this month when Aaron Rodgers called out most of his exes, including Danica Patrick? Well, another former lover — Milwaukee Bucks Heiress Mallory Edens — has decided to clap back: "My ex is currently on a press tour talking about how he never loved anyone he dated after 2017. Unfortunately for him, I am also on a press tour, for a movie inspired by how down bad I was. Really exciting time for competing narratives!!" Get him, Mal! Rodgers and Eden dated, briefly, back in 2022. It never really evolved into anything serious, but apparently, it left enough of a mark for Mallory to clap back at Aaron four years later. For those who missed it, here's what Rodgers said earlier this month: "No one cares what they have to say until they say my name. I dated two women who nobody gives a f--- about unless they drop my name — and they like to say their version of the history of what actually happened." Rodgers never mentioned Mallory Edens, but he surely name-dropped Danica, calling her "depressed" and saying she had no interest in having sex. Seems like Mallory got off easy, if you ask me! Next? Let's empty the mailbox on the way out. On Monday, I asked a simple question: Which do you prefer? NFL or college? It all stemmed from last weekend's Saturday-Sunday slate, which I thought was clearly dominated by college football. From Jim A: "I speak from experience. College over NFL any day, any time. We had Browns season tickets from 1980-2024, and Buckeyes season tickets from 1987-2009. Over those years, I missed maybe six Ohio State home games and probably 20 Browns games. Both teams had ups and downs (mostly downs for the Browns) but Ohio State was always a much better, and much more fun atmosphere. I can say the same after having been to games at Ann Arbor, South Bend, and East Lansing. College offers more excitement, more pageantry, more history, more fun, and fewer bitter people (granted, Browns fans have every right to be bitter). I could easily sit on my couch starting at 9A for GameDay, and not leave the house until the west coast games were over after midnight. Sunday? I’d rather blow leaves or go to the grocery store." And, from Gary B: "College football is better then the NFL mainly because of the rabid fan base and loud stadiums. It doesn't matter if the game means nothing. Ohio State/ Michigan, Alabama/Auburn the stadium is packed and loud. There are states that don't have an NFL team but they all have college teams. It's football on a more personal level." Yeah, I think I have to agree with both Jim and Gary here. I don't imagine this weekend's slate of games is gonna change my mind much, either. Have you SEEN Saturday's slate of SEC football games? Lordy. What a wonderful time of year. OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Good class. I have a water pump to go install. title: Trump FDA pick repeatedly sidesteps Sanders' universal healthcare demands in heated clash

content: Sen. Dr. Heidi Overton, a physician who completed her residency at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore before joining the America First Policy Institute, faced off with the Vermont independent as she seeks to replace Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned earlier this year amid disagreement with the Trump administration over flavored vapes. "Do you happen to believe that healthcare is a human right that should be available to every man, woman and child in our country?" Sanders said Overton was not answering his question and tried again. "I live 50 miles away from the Canadian border," said Sanders, who hails from Burlington. "Somehow, everybody in that country can go to a doctor." Overton said she understands the importance of access to care and believes in getting patients the "best care possible." Sanders then moved on, saying he was running out of time. title: Backlash erupts over Hasan Piker’s upcoming speaking engagement at Cornell
description: Hasan Piker's Cornell University event drew sharp backlash from Hillel group on campus, which called his rhetoric "repulsive" and antisemitic ahead of his arrival.
content: Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has yet to take the podium at Cornell University, but he's already facing sharp backlash from critics who say his presence reflects deeper issues at the core of campus culture. The event, which is part of the "Students Not Bombs" campaign, is being hosted on Sept. 24 by the university's chapters of Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP), Young Democratic Socialists of America (YDSA) and Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP). Piker has a history of making controversial remarks, and famously said that America "deserved" 9/11, a statement that he later walked back and apologized for. He is also a vocal critic of Israel and U.S. foreign policy. WHO IS HASAN PIKER? MEET THE FAR-LEFT STREAMER WHO IS STIRRING UP CONTROVERSY AND DIVIDING DEMOCRATS Critics have already spoken out against the event, with the university's Hillel calling Piker's commentary "repulsive" in a statement posted to social media. "The university is a place to learn, to argue, to explore, and to debate. Mr. Piker's views, however, go against our values as Americans and Jews, and his hateful, antisemitic rhetoric is repulsive," Grinspoon Hillel at Cornell said in a statement. For William Jacobson, a clinical professor and director of the Securities Law Clinic at Cornell Law School, Piker's appearance on campus is not a one-off event, rather it represents what he calls a "campaign of intimidation." "It's not really surprising to me that the anti-Israel groups on campus have invited as incendiary a speaker as Hasan Piker. In fact, it's very much in keeping with the tactics of intimidation that they've been doing really as long as I've been at Cornell — which is approaching 19 years — but which has ramped up dramatically after October 7," Jacobson told Fox News Digital. JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS Jacobson cited past incidents in which conservative speakers faced disruptions, such as former U.S. senator from Pennsylvania and presidential candidate Rick Santorum, Tea Party movement co-founder Michael Johns and Ann Coulter, who is a Cornell alumna. In 2016, Santorum was heckled during an event at the university. He said that the protests at the Cornell event were demonstrating "liberal intolerance," The Cornell Daily Sun reported. The event with Johns in 2017 was made private on the advice of the Cornell University Police Department, according to The Cornell Daily Sun. Jacobson recalled that, despite the event being private, protesters found out where Johns was speaking and "banged on the doors." In 2022, Coulter was forced to end her event early after several attendees protested, eight of whom were removed from the room, the outlet also reported. The student newspaper noted that when Coulter returned to the university in 2024, she did not face the same amount of disruption, but one faculty member was arrested for disorderly behavior. Cornell University did not respond to inquiries addressing Jacobson's specific comments. But in a statement to Fox News Digital regarding the controversy surrounding Piker's event, a university spokesperson emphasized that student-hosted speakers do not carry the institution's official endorsement. "Guest speakers invited by student groups undergo a thorough review to ensure an event can be hosted safely. They are not subject to an approval process around content," the university spokesperson said. "The use of spaces by student groups does not represent an endorsement or approval of, or agreement with the theme of the event or the speech of its participants. As with any event, Cornell will respond appropriately to any reports of discrimination, incitement, or disruption." CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS While Cornell University maintains that all student groups have the ability to host speakers, Jacobson argues that even the coverage surrounding the events creates a distorted narrative on campus. Jacobson criticized The Cornell Daily Sun's framing of Piker's event, saying the student newspaper's characterization of the controversial Twitch streamer as a "left-wing political commentator" was overly generous. "'The Cornell Sun' has depicted Hasan Piker as just merely a left-wing activist, and we all know that that's not what he is. He's beyond left-wing. He's incendiary," Jacobson said. "To describe him in that superficial way like The Cornell Sun [sic] did, really, I think, does a disservice to its readers, because somebody just reading that wouldn't understand why is this even controversial. And unfortunately, that's something I've seen The Cornell Sun [sic] do repeatedly with regard to the anti-Israel movement on campus — they always tone it down." When reached for comment on Jacobson's characterization of their coverage, The Cornell Daily Sun told Fox News Digital, "We appreciate the concern, and we understand that this visit matters deeply to many people in our community. A headline can only say so much, which is why we hope readers will look to our full coverage." "Our initial article discusses the controversy surrounding Mr. Piker, including his statement that 'America deserved 9/11' and his recent comments regarding Israel and American Jews. We have since published a second article sharing statements from Jewish student organizations on campus, along with further remarks by Mr. Piker and reactions from students ahead of his visit," the statement read. The student newspaper said it would "continue to report on" Piker's event and the response on campus, adding, "We truly care about getting this story right, and about making sure the students most affected by it are heard in our coverage." HASAN PIKER ADMITS HE HAS 'DIALED DOWN' HIS OPINIONS AFTER PUBLIC AND DEMOCRATIC BACKLASH Jacobson emphasized that he was not calling for the event with Piker to be canceled, rather he was hoping it would start a dialogue about escalating political polarization on campus. "In some sense, I am glad they invited him, because maybe now we can have an honest conversation on campus about how poisonous the movement is that is bringing him to campus. That's the conversation we need to have, not 'should we kick them off, should we block them,'" Jacobson told Fox News Digital. title: Is everyone bricking their phone to stop doomscrolling?
description: The $59 Brick device promises to help curb phone addiction, but free iPhone and Android tools may already do the job. Here's what to try first.
content: There is a funny twist to the anti-FOMO craze. Now people are worried they may be missing out on the latest way to spend less time on their phones. You may have heard people talking about "bricking" their phones. Thankfully, they are not destroying them. A $59 product called Brick is getting attention because it lets you temporarily block distracting apps and websites, creating a physical barrier between you and whatever keeps sucking you back into your screen. I understand the appeal. If you have ever picked up your phone to check one text and resurfaced 40 minutes later wondering why you were watching a stranger remodel a bathroom, you know how quickly a quick check can turn into a scroll. Still, my first reaction is this: before you buy another piece of technology to keep you away from technology, use the controls already sitting inside the phone you paid for. Apple has expanded Screen Time in iOS 27. Android already has some useful Digital Wellbeing controls. A few simple changes can also make distracting apps a little harder to reach and help break that automatic urge to grab your phone. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com. Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward. CAN TECH REALLY GET YOU OFF YOUR PHONE AND INTO REAL LIFE? More than half of Americans think they spend too much time on their phones This trend is tapping into something much bigger than one gadget. Pew Research Center surveyed 9,750 U.S. adults from May 26 through June 1, 2026. It found 53% say they spend too much time on their smartphone. Among adults ages 18 to 29, that jumps to 70%. It stands at 64% among adults ages 30 to 49, then drops to 49% among people 50 to 64 and 25% among those 65 and older. Here is another number that grabbed me: 26% of U.S. adults say they use their smartphone almost constantly. Among adults under 30, that rises to 42%. A third of adults ages 30 to 49 say the same. Think about that phrase for a second. Almost constantly. Phones help us navigate, communicate and get an incredible amount done. I certainly would not want to give mine up. The problem begins when useful turns into automatic and you find yourself opening the same app without even remembering why you picked up the phone. Plenty of people are trying to cut back Awareness is already turning into action. Pew found 45% of U.S. adults tried to cut back on smartphone use during the previous 12 months. Among adults under 50, the figure reaches 58%. Yet among people who tried cutting back, only a quarter said they were extremely or very successful. That gap tells you a lot. Knowing you want to use your phone less and actually putting it down are two different things. The problem with willpower is that your phone is always right there, and the apps fighting for your attention are only a tap away. Teens are noticing the pull too. Pew found 45% of teens say they spend too much time on social media. Forty-four percent say they have cut back on social media use, and an identical share say they have cut back on smartphone use. Your phone may also be stealing sleep The effects can follow you right into bed. Pew found 62% of adults under 30 say their smartphone hurts the amount of sleep they get. Across U.S. adults overall, 41% say their phone hurts their sleep while only 5% say it helps. I suspect plenty of us know how that happens. The phone goes on the nightstand. You check one last thing, then another notification arrives. Before long, your bedtime has moved. That is why I think the bigger lesson in this trend is making distracting apps a little harder to reach. If opening an app takes more effort, you get a moment to decide whether you really want to go there. TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS Why people are 'bricking' their phones Brick takes that idea and turns it into something physical. First, you choose which apps or websites you want to block and create different modes inside the Brick app. To start a session, tap your phone against the physical Brick. Another option lets you begin remotely by pressing and holding the virtual Brick in the app for five seconds. Getting back into those blocked apps usually requires another tap against the physical Brick. That is the part I find interesting. Leave the Brick downstairs while you work upstairs, and your easy way back into those distracting apps is suddenly in another room. The device currently costs $59 and supports iPhones running iOS 17 or later and Android devices running Android 12 or later. Head to CyberGuy.com to get 10% off the Brick with our link. One Brick can also work with multiple phones. Meanwhile, Strict Mode makes common workarounds harder, including deleting the Brick app or changing certain settings during a session. If you lose the device or cannot reach it, you get five Emergency Unbricks. I like the thinking behind it. Sometimes a physical barrier can work better than another warning on the same screen you are trying to stop staring at. Still, I would try the free controls already built into your phone before spending $59. PHONE-FREE RESTAURANTS ARE TRENDING ACROSS THE US Use Screen Time to put limits on distracting apps Apple documents new Time Allowances and Screen Time Schedules in iOS 27. Apple also says all of your Apple devices need version 27 or later to use the latest Screen Time features across devices. If you do not see those newer options on your iPhone, App Limits and Downtime still give you useful ways to cut down on distracting apps. How to set an App Limit on iPhone Go to: Settings → Screen Time → App Limits → Add Limit Choose the app category you want to control. You can also tap a category to select a specific app instead. Tap Next, choose how much time you want to allow each day, then tap Done. For example, you could give yourself 30 minutes of Instagram or put a daily limit on your entire social networking category. It is a simple way to decide how much time you want to give an app before you are already deep into the scroll. Schedule time away from distracting apps If certain times of day are your weak spot, Downtime can help. Go to: Settings → Screen Time → Downtime → Scheduled Choose Every Day or Customize Days, then set when you want Downtime to start and end. During Downtime, most apps and notifications are restricted, while phone calls and apps you choose to allow remain available. You can also turn on Block at Downtime if you want the limit to be harder to ignore. OPINION: WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO You can decide which apps stay available by going to: Settings → Screen Time → Always Allowed That way, you can keep apps you genuinely need available without leaving every distracting app within easy reach. Look at your real screen-time numbers first Before setting any limits, spend a minute looking at where your time actually goes. Go to: Settings → Screen Time → Daily Average Tap Day or Week to see your usage. Scroll down to see Pickups and Notifications too. That pickup number may tell you even more than your total screen time. Maybe you spend only a few minutes at a time in an app but reach for your phone 80 times throughout the day. That tells me your challenge may be the habit of grabbing the device rather than one particular app. Start with whatever surprises you most. Use Focus to stop your iPhone from constantly pulling you back Notifications can undo all your good intentions, and you do not need Apple Intelligence to quiet them. Go to: Settings → Focus Choose a Focus such as Do Not Disturb, Personal, Sleep or Work. From there, you can decide which people and apps are allowed to interrupt you. You can also add a schedule, so Focus turns on automatically during the parts of your day when you want fewer distractions. This gets at something Screen Time alone cannot fix. Sometimes you did not decide to pick up the phone. The phone asked you to. Cutting down those invitations may be one of the easiest ways to stop checking it so often. Android has free anti-doomscrolling tools too Android phones include Digital Wellbeing tools that can show you how much time you spend in apps, how often you open them and how many notifications they send. Exact menu names can vary between Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones. On Google Pixel Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing Tap the chart to see your screen time, how often you open apps and how many notifications you receive. Set app timers Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers Next to the app you want to limit, tap Set timer , choose how much time you want to allow and tap OK . When your time runs out, the app closes and its icon dims. The timer resets at midnight. Use Focus mode Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Focus mode Choose the apps you want to pause. While Focus mode is on, you cannot use those apps and their notifications stop. Tap Turn on now to start it immediately or Set a schedule to have it turn on automatically. On Samsung Galaxy Set app timers Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers Tap Apps and app categories , then choose the apps or categories you want to control. Tap Add schedule , choose the days and amount of time you want to allow, then tap Save . Menu wording can vary slightly by Galaxy model and software version. Pixel can put a PIN behind your app limits On current Pixel phones, you can also protect app limits with a separate PIN. Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App limits → App limits PIN Turn on PIN for app time limits , unlock your phone, then create and confirm a four-digit PIN. This adds another step before you can change a limit on impulse. Make your Android phone less inviting before bed On Google Pixel Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Bedtime mode → Bedtime routine Choose when Bedtime mode should turn on. You can use a schedule or have it activate while your phone is charging during certain hours. You can also customize options including Grayscale, Keep the screen dark, Dim the wallpaper and Dark theme . On Samsung Galaxy Samsung handles this through Sleep mode . Go to: Settings → Modes and Routines → Sleep Tap When to start this mode, choose Sleep schedule , then set your usual sleep and wake times. Tap Save and then Done . You can also turn on options including Do not disturb, Grayscale and Dark mode while Sleep mode is active. 6 ways to win back attention from your phone You do not need to overhaul your habits overnight. Start with your biggest distractions and make them a little harder to reach. 1) Find the apps actually stealing your time Check Screen Time on iPhone or Digital Wellbeing on Android. Look for the apps taking the biggest bite out of your day and how often you pick up or unlock your phone. Do not try to fix everything at once. Start with the biggest problem. 2) Turn off notifications you rarely need Every alert is another invitation to look at your screen. Keep the notifications that deserve immediate attention. Silence the ones that are simply trying to bring you back into an app. 3) Set limits before you start scrolling Create your limits while you are thinking clearly instead of after you have already disappeared down a feed. Use App Limits and Downtime on iPhone or App timers and Focus mode on Android. 4) Make distracting apps harder to reach Move your worst offenders off the Home Screen. Log out when you finish. If you have to search for an app and sign back in, that gives you a little time to ask yourself whether you actually wanted to open it. You are creating your own speed bump. 5) Put physical distance between you and the phone Leave it somewhere else during dinner. Put it out of reach while you work. Charge it away from the bed. This may sound almost too simple, but sometimes distance works better than another setting buried inside a menu. 6) Make your limits harder to ignore Try the free tools first. If you continually override every limit, delete every timer or find yourself reaching for the same apps anyway, then consider something stricter. That might be a stronger software blocker or a physical device such as Brick. By then, you will know exactly what problem you are paying to solve. Kurt's key takeaways Here is what gets me about this whole trend. We have reached a point where people are buying a piece of technology whose job is to keep them away from another piece of technology. That says something. I love what my phone can do. I do not want a dumb phone, and I certainly do not want to throw my smartphone in a drawer. What I want is to be the one deciding when I use it instead of reacting every time an app decides it wants me back. That is why I would start with what you already have. iPhone gives you App Limits, Downtime and Focus. Android gives you app timers and Focus mode. Your phone can also tell you exactly where your time went. Use that information. If those free controls work, you saved yourself $59. If you blow through every limit you create, Brick or another stronger blocker suddenly has a purpose beyond joining a wellness craze. For me, the real test is pretty simple: when you pick up your phone, did you decide to do it or did your phone decide for you? If you could get back one hour of the time you spend on your phone every day, what would you do with it instead? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. title: Dems shamed as DHS brings ICE shooting receipts after politician called ICE officers ‘liars with masks’
description: The Department of Homeland Security accused Democrats and media of spreading lies about the ICE shooting in Austin as protests erupted citywide.
content: The Department of Homeland Security called out dozens of Democrats and members of the media for "spreading lies" about a recent ICE officer-involved shooting in Austin, while a former agency director suggested the political response may be by design. Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan national whom DHS says is an illegal immigrant in the U.S., was shot by an ICE agent during a chase Sunday. Perez was arrested and taken to a nearby hospital, where he was treated and listed in stable condition. The shooting has prompted protests in Austin and criticism from Democrats. On Tuesday, more than 100 Democratic members of Congress signed a letter demanding Perez’s release and saying he "is not receiving the care he needs in detention" and "still has the bullet lodged in his body." In a separate statement, Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said "despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center." Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, called ICE "liars with masks" and demanded the agency leave Austin. DEM REACTIONS WITHIN MOMENTS OF AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARK VIRAL OUTRAGE LOCALLY, ONLINE: 'DISQUALIFYING' In response, DHS posted on X that "sanctuary politicians and the media wasted no time in spreading lies" and that "no amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job to arrest illegal aliens from our communities." DHS called the claim that ICE refused to remove the bullet from Perez’s body "false." The agency said ICE "does not and would not advise, nor be the authority on, a medical procedure for an illegal alien at a hospital." Addressing reports that Perez was denied pain medication and made to sleep on the floor, DHS said Perez is "receiving medical care around the clock, including pain medication," and that after being released from the hospital, he slept on a bed a few hours after arriving at ICE’s detention facility. The agency also disputed statements from Perez’s lawyer that Perez entered the country legally and has a work permit. DHS said he "entered the country illegally under the Biden Administration" and "had no valid work permit, had no protective status, and had a final order of removal from a Department of Justice (DOJ) Immigration Judge." FEDERAL JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS DEPORTATION OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SHOT BY ICE OFFICER IN AUSTIN, ATTORNEY SAYS DHS said ICE "will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin." "DHS is tasked with enforcing the laws passed by Congress. We do not pick and choose which laws to enforce or where to enforce them. We will continue to enforce our nation’s laws," the agency said. Former acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey, who served toward the end of President Donald Trump’s first term, suggested some of the political pushback was by design. "The irony of it all is, with these ICE incidents, it's not just coincidental that the Democrats are against ICE performing their function of enforcing immigration laws… they don't want them actually doing their jobs," Fahey said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "They try to build these situations up to try to get negative attention toward ICE and more political pressure on them and advance their political agenda." Fahey suggested the Democratic Party’s "whole goal" is an open Mexican border and mass amnesty. He argued that Democrats’ response to the Austin incident shows they do not want what he considers responsible enforcement, but no enforcement. "They seem to have doubled down on [the 'mass amnesty' agenda] after the 2024 election, which in some respects is surprising," he said. "My opinion is their motive is… for the people here open the border because they think that will help them electorally currently and in the future – and all the other stuff is just noise to help achieve that." title: 4 GOP senators rebel against Trump on Iran war, vote with Dems to rein in authority
description: President Donald Trump dismissed midterm fears as Republicans defeated a Democratic war powers resolution despite surging gas and diesel prices.
content: Despite voter fury and rising fuel prices, most Republican senators stayed the course with President Donald Trump and his war on Iran in a vote Thursday. Though vulnerable Republicans on the campaign trail broke with Trump earlier this week, calling for an "immediate end" to the war, lawmakers on the Hill stuck with him and defeated another attempt by Democrats to rein in his war authorities as the conflict nears the eight-month mark. Still, there was a group of rebellious Republicans who had consistently voted with Democrats, including Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, Rand Paul, R-Ky. New blood was added this time with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C. REPUBLICANS BREAK WITH TRUMP TO REBUKE IRAN WAR — BUT IT WON'T CHANGE POLICY Tillis, who is retiring at the end of the year, argued his decision to vote for the latest war powers resolution came after the administration again blew past a 60-day deadline to involve Congress. "We know the resolution's not gonna pass, but it is important to start saying, ‘We deserve an update. You better start treating — Congress can be an assistance with this war effort, if you inform us,’" Tillis said. To Tillis’ point, the resolution that failed in the Senate, which passed in the House with seven Republican defectors, would have headed to the president’s desk, where it likely would have been vetoed. title: Foreign leader on Putin’s doorstep sounds alarm over Iran fueling Moscow’s war machine
description: Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs says Iran's drone tech helped Russia wage war in Ukraine as Latvia prepares to join a Strait of Hormuz coalition.
content: UNITED NATIONS — Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warned Wednesday that military cooperation between Russia and Iran poses a growing security concern, telling Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview that Iranian drone technology has helped Moscow wage war in Ukraine as Latvia prepares to contribute to a U.S.-led effort in the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, Rinkēvičs said Latvia, a country of approximately 1.84 million and still a core member of NATO's eastern flank, has already made the political decision to send military specialists to support international operations in the Middle East in response to President Donald Trump's request for European assistance. "Yes, I am concerned. Actually, we have already seen Iran helping Russia a lot, especially at the very beginning of Russia's aggression against Ukraine," Rinkēvičs said when asked about the growing cooperation between Moscow and Tehran. PUTIN AND IRAN 'NEED EACH OTHER DESPERATELY,' EXPERT SAYS, AS RUSSIA VOICES SUPPORT FOR REGIME "The first drones Iranian made, or Iranian-designed drones, were used by Russia. Now Russians are actually modernizing them, making completely new technologies. But, actually, the design is still Iranian." Earlier this week, Fox News Digital revealed documents obtained from the Russian Foreign Ministry detailing a roadmap between Russia and Iran for cooperation between 2024-2026 in multiple fields, including nuclear, finance and aviation, as well as infrastructure. Asked whether Europe should take a more active role in countering Iran's military activities and respond to Trump's call for support, Rinkēvičs confirmed that Latvia has already taken steps toward joining an international effort in the Strait of Hormuz. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT "From our side, we have already made a parliamentary decision. That our EOD (explosive ordnance disposal) diver specialists could be sent to the Strait of Hormuz or to the Middle East to help out the United States, the coalition that is being formed," he said. Rinkēvičs said Latvia hopes military activities will give way to a political solution and the restoration of global energy supplies, while expressing skepticism about the prospects for negotiations with Tehran and Moscow. "It's very, very difficult to have diplomacy with Iran. It's very difficult with Russia," he said. Turning to the security situation in Europe, Rinkēvičs said Latvia does not see evidence of an imminent Russian military invasion despite growing concerns about Moscow's intentions toward NATO's eastern flank. "If Russia were able to attack us ... that would have happened already," he said. "The Russian military is not the same as it used to be back in 2022. Remember they tried to take Kyiv in three days. They are still trying to take some certain small pieces of Ukrainian territory 4½ years after the full-fledged." IRAN’S DRONE HUNT ESCALATES AS TEHRAN TARGETS US SPY TECH TO EXPOSE BATTLEFIELD SECRETS Explaining the immediate threat to Latvia comes instead from sabotage, cyberattacks and information campaigns, which he described as intensifying, adding that European leaders face the difficult task of preparing their populations for potential threats without creating unnecessary panic. Rinkēvičs also warned that NATO must accelerate its adaptation to the rapidly changing nature of warfare, particularly the growing role of drones and missile technology. While traditional military equipment, including tanks and armored personnel carriers, remains essential, the president said the war in Ukraine has demonstrated how quickly new technologies are transforming the battlefield. The president welcomed increased NATO defense spending, crediting Trump's push for greater investment, but cautioned that additional funding alone would not resolve the alliance's military readiness challenges. "You have money, but not always you can buy the stuff immediately, or at least you can order things. And they are delivered soon enough," he said. We do have U.S. troops, not big numbers, but I think sufficient numbers are now stationed in our airbase in Lielvārde. "U.S. presence in the Baltics is very important, and we are working with our U.S. partners about further rotations."

title: Alaska has a voting system like no other state; Republicans worry it could cost them in November
description: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces Mary Peltola in Alaska's ranked choice voting Senate race, complicated by a "Decoy Dan" candidate on the ballot.
content: Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is in the middle of a competitive race as he seeks re-election this year in red-leaning Alaska in a midterm showdown that's one of roughly a dozen that will determine if the GOP keeps control of the Senate. Working against Sullivan as he runs for a third six-year term in the Senate is not only a rough political climate facing Republicans but also Alaska's unique electoral system, which includes four candidates from an open primary advancing to the general election and ranked-choice voting. Alaska is the only state in the nation to have a "top four" primary system in which candidates advance regardless of party affiliation. And it's one of only two states, along with Maine, to use ranked choice voting for statewide and federal races. Defenders of the system say it gives independent voters more choices, weakens party control and encourages candidates to appeal beyond their base. SEEING DOUBLE: THE SECOND DAN SULLIVAN ADVANCES IN ALASKA'S CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN Alaska GOP Chair Carmela Warfield has repeatedly referred to the state's electoral system as a "MESS" in social media posts. "It's hurting the Republican Party," veteran GOP strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital. Sullivan is battling former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The two candidates combined received over 90% of the primary vote. But Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher and registered Republican whom Marslender and supporters of the senator call "Decoy Dan" is also on the general election ballot. A conservative nonprofit group, Americans for Public Trust, claimed that the other Sullivan, who is not related to the senator, was working with Democrats to confuse voters. The Peltola campaign and Daniel J. Sullivan both denied the allegation. The Alaska Division of Elections disqualified him from the ballot, but the decision was overturned first by an Alaska Superior Court judge and later by the state Supreme Court. SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS There is also a third Republican on the Senate ballot: Gerald Heikes. He advanced to the general election when the fourth-place primary finisher, Democrat David Leslie, withdrew from the race. Marslender claimed that the current system has "become an easy way for the Democrats to game the system." Pointing to Daniel J. Sullivan's inclusion on the general election ballot, she said, "That never would have been allowed in the previous old system. … But because there's an open primary, he was allowed to be on the ballot. "Republican primary voters under the old system wouldn't have voted for him, and he wouldn't have been in there." With ranked-choice voting, voters rank candidates by preference, and if nobody receives a majority of first-choice votes, additional counting rounds occur until someone reaches a majority. Marslender said there's a perception that Republicans would unite around the incumbent senator in the general election. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB But, she said, in Alaska, which is the nation's largest and most remote state, "It's really hard to get a statewide message out" due to "the geographical challenges." Alaskans for Better Elections, which supports the system, has been holding events to help voters better understand how it works. "Alaska’s election system celebrates our independence, giving us the freedom to vote for the person who is best for the job," the group highlights on its website. The Senate race wasn't the only contest impacted by the current system. There were also eleventh-hour withdrawals that rocked the races for governor and the U.S. House, which also cast a shadow on the state's unique voting process. Alaska voters get to weigh in when they cast general election ballots to either keep or scrap the current system. Matt Schultz, a Democrat who suspended his congressional bid before the primary, supports keeping the system. But he told the AP, "We need to make things much more transparent and predictable and understandable by the general public so that we can truly have trust in our democracy again." Republican Lesil McGuire and Democrat Tom Begich, former state lawmakers who were both eliminated in the primary for governor, defended the system. Our election system was not designed to guarantee anyone a win. It was designed to solve a problem: elections in which a narrow, more partisan slice of voters decided the November ballot, resulting in hyperpartisanship that limited progress," they wrote in an opinion piece in The Anchorage Daily News. "We don’t support our current system because it was good for us as candidates; we support it because it’s good for us as Alaskans."

title: Hayden Panettiere's overdose shows fentanyl crisis 'doesn't discriminate,' Stanford psychiatrist says
description: Hayden Panettiere's fatal fentanyl overdose involved a lethal mix of opioids, benzodiazepines and quetiapine, a Stanford addiction expert says.
content: Hayden Panettiere's fatal overdose is a stark reminder that the fentanyl crisis has not gone away, even as the United States makes genuine progress in reducing overdose deaths since peaking in 2022. This week, the Greenville County Coroner's Office ruled that Panettiere died from the toxic effects of five drugs found in her system: fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol and Quetiapine. Dr. Anna Lembke, a Stanford psychiatrist and addiction medicine specialist, told Fox News Digital that while the circumstances surrounding the actress' death remain unclear, the combination of drugs in her system likely increased the risk of a fatal overdose. "We don't know if she sought out fentanyl. We don't know if she had a counterfeit pill that had fentanyl in it. She might have been prescribed fentanyl for pain," Lembke said. "She was also on a benzo. We know combining benzos and opioids increases the risk of overdose of each of those medications separately. It looks like she was also on Quetiapine, a mood stabilizer, but also highly sedating in the mix." HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEATH: DEA JOINS PROBE INTO WHAT HAPPENED TO LATE STAR Lembke continued: "We don't know where she sourced it, but it does look like it was a lethal polypharmacy, including fentanyl, which on its own is an incredibly lethal drug." The Cleveland Clinic defines polypharmacy as taking several medicines regularly, usually four or more. While Lembke cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about what exactly led up to Panettiere's death, she said the tragedy underscores a broader reality: fentanyl remains a deadly threat that can affect anyone. "This is still a very serious risk, and it's a risk that doesn't discriminate. Old and young, rich and poor, famous, not famous. Because of the increased access to these highly potent and potentially lethal drugs in the modern age, we're really all at risk for this problem," Lembke said. Fentanyl, a synthetic opioid up to 50 times more potent than heroin, has transformed the nation's illicit drug supply over the past decade. PRESLEY GERBER’S DEATH SPARKS QUESTIONS ABOUT OVERDOSE, WITHDRAWAL AND REHAB SAFETY Deaths involving synthetic opioids, primarily illicitly manufactured fentanyl, began climbing sharply in 2014 and reached a record 73,838 in 2022, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse. Fentanyl's potency is only part of what makes it so dangerous, Lembke said. Just as concerning is how trace amounts are concealed in counterfeit pills designed to look like legitimate prescription medications. Lembke said a "very real risk" for young people, even those who aren't struggling with addiction, is that they're given a pill at a party that looks just like Xanax or Oxycontin, when it is in fact a counterfeit pill that contains a small amount of fentanyl. "A single dose to an opioid-naive person could kill, which is why it's so important that we have data-informed discussions with young people in particular," she said. "The kind of experimentation with drugs in their youth that their parents might've engaged in relatively risk-free... it's not risk-free anymore" for young adults, she added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lembke encouraged parents to get ahead of the issue by talking openly about drugs before their children encounter inaccurate or misleading information on social media. If a parent or guardian recognizes their child has a substance-use disorder, Lembke said they should resist the impulse to brush it off as "normal teenage experimentation." "These drugs are far too accessible and far too lethal to just leave it to hoping that it will be a passing phase the kid will outgrow," she said. "We know that the earlier we intervene with addiction-related problems, the more likely we are to reroute that person on a new path of life." Lembke also offered a message to doctors, who she said should prescribe potentially addictive medications cautiously and closely monitor patients for signs of misuse. As a practicing psychiatrist, Lembke routinely prescribes stimulants for ADHD, opioids for pain and benzodiazepines for insomnia and anxiety. But she said physicians have a responsibility to prescribe them in the lowest effective amounts for the shortest possible duration.

title: Nikole Hannah-Jones' friend sends Black son to private school after NYT writer has education regrets
description: Jenisha Watts says her own childhood in struggling schools convinced her to choose private school for her son over the path Nikole Hannah-Jones took.
content: The Atlantic staff writer Jenisha Watts said Wednesday she plans to send her young Black son to private school, citing her own experience with struggling schools while choosing a different path from friend and 1619 Project creator Nikole Hannah-Jones, who recently confronted regrets about her daughter’s public school education. Watts said in her Atlantic essay that Hannah-Jones’ experience helped convince her she could not make the same decision for her son. "I could never make the choice she made," Watts said. "I know too well what can go wrong. I’m sending him to a private preschool, and I plan to apply for private kindergarten too." Hannah-Jones, who previously said that scrutiny of her decision should also focus on Black children whose families cannot afford better options, responded directly to Watts in a new statement to Fox News Digital. 'THE VIEW' HOST SUNNY HOSTIN CLAIMS HER CHILDREN EXPERIENCED RACISM AT PRIVATE SCHOOLS "I have a deep respect for Jenisha and all she has overcome," she said. "Our concerns and values as parents are always shaped, to some degree, by our own experiences as children. Unlike Jenisha, I got a parachute out of my segregated school, and that changed my life. And, as a result, I have always thought about the equal worth of children who didn't get that parachute and how that shaped their lives as well. "I still believe, as I always have, in public schools as necessary and common good, that education should be the great equalizer and that parents should not have to choose between doing what's right for their children and what's right for community." Hannah-Jones said the problems raised by both families ultimately required broader policy changes. "In the end, the inequality I write about and that Jenisha experienced is systemic and will only be fixed if we acquire the political will to make different policy choices that value the inherent worth of all of our children, even if those children happen to be born Black and poor," she said. MORE THAN 400,000 NEW YORK CITY CHILDREN ENROLLED IN FAILING PUBLIC SCHOOLS: REPORT School choice advocate Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, offered a sharply different assessment in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing Watts was right to prioritize her son rather than wait for improvements to the public school system. "Jenisha Watts is doing what a parent is supposed to do. She is putting her son first," he said. "Watts has options most families do not. The scandal is not that she is using them. The scandal is that politicians and teachers unions fight to keep those options out of reach for everyone else. School choice is the equalizer. Trapping kids in failure factories by zip code only makes inequality worse. "It is time to fund students, not systems, so all families can have a shot at the American dream. If Hannah-Jones and her friends actually want to help other children, they should fight for the funding to follow the student. You do not fix public schools by locking kids in them. You fix them by giving families a way out — and giving those schools a reason to change." GOV HOCHUL'S PLAN TO OPT NEW YORK INTO FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DRAWS UNION OPPOSITION Watts described Hannah-Jones as a "confidant and friend" and defended her against critics who accused her of sacrificing her daughter’s education for her ideals. But Watts said her own childhood in Lexington, Kentucky, where she described receiving an "abysmal education," shaped the choice she is now making for her son. Watts said those academic deficiencies followed her into adulthood. "I’m a staff writer for The Atlantic, and I’m writing a memoir, and I still can’t shake off my poor education," she wrote. KETANJI BROWN JACKSON AGREES WITH MICHELLE OBAMA’S CRITICISM OF ‘PLUCKING’ KIDS OF COLOR INTO ELITE SCHOOLS The debate followed Hannah-Jones’ recent New York Times Magazine essay revisiting a choice she first detailed in a 2016 Times Magazine cover story. Hannah-Jones said she eventually apologized to her daughter Najya after reviewing academic problems that followed her through elementary and middle school. Najya told her mother she wished her own education had received more consideration alongside Hannah-Jones’ concerns about educational inequality. "Sometimes I wish, instead of always thinking about other kids, you would have thought about me. I never really got the education I wanted," Najya said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE New York City Public Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels defended the public school system’s mission in a statement to Fox News Digital. "From day one, I have made it clear: Every student, regardless of background or ability, should feel affirmed, valued and held to high expectations," Samuels said. "At New York City Public Schools, we know that our students benefit from inclusive environments where every child has access to rigorous academics, student supports and diverse learning opportunities. "This is the crux of my vision of a truly integrated public school system, and I am committed to doing the work to make that a reality." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Watts said her decision was not meant as a condemnation of Hannah-Jones or parents who choose differently but reflected what she sees as a broader failure that forces families to weigh their children’s immediate interests against struggling schools. "America should not force parents to make that kind of choice," she said.

title: Canadian PM Carney says he was prepared for Trump ordering invasion
description: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he weighed the possibility of a U.S. invasion after Trump began calling Canada the 51st state amid tariffs.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the U.S. would invade Canada amid recent trade tensions. Carney made the statement in an interview with The New York Times published Wednesday, saying he weighed the possibility after President Donald Trump began referring to Canada as the 51st state. "I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk. That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case," Carney told the Times, arguing that "it would be irresponsible not to." CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT Trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada have continued to escalate over the past year, with Trump levying increased tariffs and Canada responding in kind. Carney admitted in a video statement earlier this month that Canada had come to overly rely on its economic relationship with the U.S. in recent decades. FORMER BIDEN AMBASSADOR BLAMES TRUMP FOR CANADA PLAYING 'FOOTSIE' WITH CHINA "The past 40 years has been a period of deeper economic integration with the United States. Truth is, it was easy business, but it meant we relied too much on one economic partner. It’s clear that time is over," Carney said. "This is why our plan, since I came into office, has been development and diversification, not denial, waiting to go back to some good old days and not continued dependence." FEARS OF A CANADIAN TRADE WAR ARE OVERBLOWN; SO FAR, IT’S MORE OF A SKIRMISH Trump last week dismissed reports that Canada may be joining the European Union as an associate member, saying the U.S. could impose heavy tariffs on Europe if he believed such a "laughable" move was made with "bad intention." "I think it's laughable," Trump responded. "If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things. title: Soros-linked prosecutor faces primary challenge as fellow Democrat targets his record
description: Fairfax County Commonwealth's Attorney Stephen Descano faces a Democratic primary challenge from a former federal prosecutor citing botched cases.
content: Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney Stephen Descano is facing a forceful rebuke from a former federal prosecutor who extensively criticized his record after announcing her bid to unseat him. Descano, a Democrat, has faced criticism over what opponents describe as lenient prosecutorial decisions, particularly in serious cases involving illegal immigrant suspects. Former federal prosecutor Brittany Dunn-Pirio said that if there weren’t systemic problems in his office, she would want to work there. "If this office were doing its job, I wouldn’t be running against it. I’d be applying to work for it. But it isn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her new campaign website after Washington, D.C.-area media reported her bid late Wednesday. VIRGINIA DEMS SPLIT ON DOJ PROBE OF SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF GIVING 'SWEETHEART DEALS' TO ILLEGAL ALIENS "I’m a Democrat. This race isn’t about whether reform was right. It’s about whether the office can tell the difference between a first-time nonviolent offender who deserves a second chance and a violent or sexual offender who doesn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her website. "It’s about whether deadlines are met, evidence is given to the defendant and victims are spoken to." VIRGINIA DEM DEFENDS SOROS-BACKED PROSECUTOR FROM DOJ PROBE AFTER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGING ALLEGATIONS Fox News Digital reached out to Descano and Dunn-Pirio for further comment. Descano campaign spokesman Nathan Kiker defended the incumbent's record, telling Fox News Digital that "Steve Descano has spent his tenure proving that you can reform the justice system and keep our community safe at the same time." "Today, Fairfax County is recognized as the safest large county in the nation because Steve focused on accountability and the root causes of crime rather than failed policies of the past. We are proud to put that record before the voters," Kiker said. Dunn-Pirio also pointed to "botched sexual assault cases" and prosecutors declining to meet with victims, along with her contention that the justice system too often favors the "well-connected." One case that has drawn the scrutiny of Descano’s office involves Abdul Jalloh, an illegal immigrant from Sierra Leone charged with murdering Stephanie Minter. Minter was stabbed and killed at a Hybla Valley bus stop in February after Jalloh had cycled through the criminal justice system following numerous previous arrests. Descano has pushed back on claims that his office simply allowed Jalloh to walk free, telling Congress his prosecutors obtained convictions against him "wherever possible." SOROS-BACKED DA'S LAX ILLEGAL IMMIGRATION POLICIES LED TO 'PREVENTABLE' BUS STOP STABBING MURDER: COMPLAINT Dunn-Pirio previously served as a prosecutor in Frederick County, Virginia, and as a federal prosecutor in the district covering Lexington, Kentucky. She said she resigned from the DOJ in 2025 after working on COVID-related fraud and similar cases. "I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," she said, according to a release obtained by FairfaxNow. She also said Descano’s office has spent too much time "failing the people I care about." A carousel on her new campaign website highlights cases that have drawn public scrutiny of Descano, including: REPEAT OFFENDER WITH DOZENS OF PRIOR CHARGES ARRESTED FOR BURGLARIZING CHURCH IN SOROS-BACKED DA'S COUNTY "We need a Commonwealth’s Attorney who can make this office work," Dunn-Pirio said. "Every person in Fairfax should feel safe, and every person in Fairfax should be able to trust the office that’s supposed to protect them." Descano’s campaign did not immediately respond to an additional request for comment on Dunn-Pirio’s criticism. Dunn-Pirio, most recently an associate at the civil litigation firm Harman, Claytor, Corrigan & Wellman, served as an assistant U.S. attorney in Kentucky for two years before resigning in November 2025. At the Justice Department, she specialized in COVID relief fraud and public corruption cases, according to her LinkedIn profile. "Most recently I was a federal prosecutor, and I resigned from the Justice Department because I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," Dunn-Pirio said. Before becoming a federal prosecutor in 2023, Dunn-Pirio served as an assistant commonwealth’s attorney in Frederick County, an assistant attorney general in the state criminal appeals courts and a law clerk to Judge Randy Bellows in Fairfax County Circuit Court. Dunn-Pirio emphasized that she is a "cradle Democrat," distinguishing her candidacy from a challenge to Descano from the political right.
