title: Missouri's redistricting mess created an election problem Supreme Court has days to untangle
description: The Eighth Circuit ruled Missouri must use its 2025 congressional map for the general election, but the Supreme Court could intervene before Sept. 28.
content: Missouri’s congressional map fight is hurtling toward another potential Supreme Court showdown, with courts at odds over which districts should govern the November election after more than 1.2 million Missourians voted in the August primary under a different map. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruled Monday that Missouri must use its 2025 congressional map in November, finding that switching to the state’s 2022 districts after the primary would violate the U.S. Constitution. But the appeals court paused its order until Sept. 28, 2026, opening a narrow window for another visit to the U.S. Supreme Court. Abhishek Kambli, a partner at Holtzman Vogel and former deputy associate attorney general at the Justice Department, told Fox News Digital the Supreme Court’s previous intervention does not necessarily signal how the justices will handle the latest ruling. "It’s unpredictable how they’ll rule, mostly because we didn’t get their reasoning in the last order," Kambli said. "So, we don’t know the precise reason why they decided to stay at that time." ELECTION CHAOS IN THIS RED STATE JUST GOT EVEN STRANGER FOR REPUBLICANS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING The Supreme Court previously stayed a federal district court's temporary restraining order requiring Missouri to use the 2025 map. The Eighth Circuit has now directed the lower court to enter a permanent injunction requiring the newer districts, putting the dispute in a different procedural posture. "So unless the Supreme Court steps in again, the state will be required to use the seven-one map for this election," Kambli said. Missouri held its Aug. 4, 2026, primary under the 2025 map. Roughly a month later, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that voters could challenge the map through a referendum, leaving the 2022 districts in place for the November election. Kambli said switching congressional maps between the primary and general election raises serious constitutional concerns. "You would have had a large number of Missourians who would have been disenfranchised because they voted for one set of candidates in the primary and will be voting for another set in the general," Kambli said. MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP "And what's even more concerning is sometimes those candidates are unopposed so that they miss their only chance to vote as a result of what the Missouri Supreme Court did here," Kambli continued. "So that's what's really at issue — is whether everyone gets an equal voice in a situation where the primary election is integral to the electoral system of the state." But Yale law professor Akhil Amar and University of California, Davis, law professor Vikram Amar have argued the opposite. After the Supreme Court’s earlier stay, Vikram wrote on SCOTUSblog that using the 2025 map in November would not protect anyone’s right to vote if those lines were never legally in effect. Akhil agreed with his analysis. "HB1’s district lines lack the force of law, full stop," Vikram wrote. "These lines cannot be used wrongly in November just because they were previously used wrongly in the primary. Two wrongs do not make (or vindicate) a right (to vote)." Meanwhile, Kambli placed much of the blame for the eleventh-hour legal scramble over which map to use on the Missouri Supreme Court, arguing the turmoil was "entirely preventable." VIRGINIA GOP, DEMS BATTLE IT OUT OVER REDISTRICTING BEFORE STATE SUPREME COURT Kambli argued that the Missouri Supreme Court could have resolved the map dispute earlier, noting that the issue remained unsettled even after the candidate filing deadline passed. Alicia Bannon, senior director of the Judiciary Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, pointed instead to delays by Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins as a key reason the dispute dragged on. Opponents of the 2025 map submitted more than 300,000 signatures in December 2025, but Hoskins did not formally reject the referendum petition until Aug. 4, the day of the primary. "Time passed. And passed further," Bannon wrote for State Court Report. "As early as December 2025, Hoskins asserted in separate federal litigation that a referendum on redistricting was not authorized by the state constitution. But he held off on issuing a certificate on that basis — which would have triggered judicial review — instead going through a lengthy process of verifying petition signatures." Bannon wrote that the Missouri Supreme Court’s criticism of Hoskins’ delays stood out, particularly the court’s rejection of his argument that it had waited too long to intervene. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The Missouri Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the referendum could proceed and faulted Hoskins for the delay, saying he had "created the confusion, expense, and practical difficulties of which he complains." Kambli argued the Purcell principle, under which federal courts generally avoid changing election rules close to Election Day because of the potential for disruption, weighs in favor of keeping the 2025 map because Missouri already used it for the primary. "The Eighth Circuit said that the Purcell principles support the injunction, not go against it," Kambli said. Bannon also warned that courts being too cautious can create its own problems. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It’s an approach that’s understandable in some circumstances but can also incentivize shenanigans to evade judicial review while harming voters’ rights," Bannon wrote. Bannon suggested earlier court action in Missouri could have helped avoid the last-minute dispute, including by moving the primary or setting a firm deadline for the referendum petition. But regardless of whether the Supreme Court decides to weigh in, the referendum will still be on the ballot. "If the Supreme Court does not stay the Eighth Circuit injunction, there's no doubt that the 7-1 map is what will be in effect for this election. There's still going to be a referendum on the ballot deciding that issue for future elections, but for this one, that's how it'll be decided," Kambli said.

title: Devils' new concession contraption lets you play hockey with a popcorn puck while watching actual hockey
description: The New Jersey Devils unveiled a branded popcorn bucket featuring a pinball hockey game on top, crafted by Levy Restaurants for stadium concessions.
content: Have you ever been at a hockey game and thought, "Man, I wish I could be playing some sort of hockey-like game right now with a piece of popcorn as a puck?" Me neither, but on the off chance that you have, the New Jersey Devils have gone into the lab and made your dream a reality. Behold! The official Devils-branded popcorn bucket with some kind of pinball hockey game on top! It's the work of the mad scientists at Levy Restaurants, and it could be the biggest salvo in the ongoing war for novelty stadium concession vessel supremacy. There's no denying that we live in the golden age of stadium food novelties. From beer sticks, skates, sabres, and horns to small-plastic Zamboni-brand ice resurfacers stuffed full of chicken tenders, it's one of those things that makes you proud to live in the present. NEW YORK ISLANDERS SET TO UNLEASH CULINARY 'DISASTERPIECE' ON UNSUSPECTING FANS THIS SEASON I'll take beer skates over rampant tuberculosis and no air conditioning any day. But this one troubles me a little. It's groundbreaking, but when the goal is to get people watching hockey, why would they need something to entertain them in the stands? I thought that was the game's job. Now, I don't have kids — just a dog and a little bit of disposable income — but I would be so annoyed if I bought my youngsters NHL tickets, popcorn at stadium prices in a souvenir bucket, and what do they do? Ignore the world-class athletes on the ice before them in favor of flippering a piece of Orville Redenbacher's Gourmet popping corn back and forth. It's like if you needed your kid to stop playing video games to power wash the deck, and when you went to unplug their PlayStation, you realized they were playing "PowerWash Simulator." Having said that, I feel pretty confident that I would be a very good popcorn hockey player. I just have shockingly quick reflexes and am good enough at geometry to track the bounces when the irregularly shaped popcorn piece hits the boards. title: US allies need to shoot down Russian aircraft testing NATO boundaries, Czech president warns
description: Czech President Petr Pavel warned NATO may need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones deliberately violating allied airspace to avoid weakness.
content: NEW YORK — Czech President Petr Pavel insists that NATO needs to outright demonstrate its willingness to respond to Russian aggression or else Moscow will continue to push the alliance and its European boundaries. "There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness," Pavel, a retired general and former chair of NATO's Military Committee, predicted in a conversation with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York City this week. Pavel said alliance members understandably want to avoid escalation, but risk sending the wrong signal as he warned Moscow views restraint as weakness and is testing allied defenses with its continued aggression. "What I am afraid of is that they see a lack of will on our side to take decisive action," Pavel said. "Within Russian perceptions it demonstrates weakness. And they respect power." The warning followed fresh incidents along NATO’s eastern flank, where a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crossed from Kaliningrad into Polish airspace Wednesday, prompting Poland to scramble fighter jets. Romania scrambled F-16s Thursday after another unidentified aerial target crossed its border from Ukraine. Denmark’s military intelligence service also warned Thursday that Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against NATO in the coming months and assessed a "low but growing" risk of a limited Russian military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia. ROMANIAN F-16 SHOOTS DOWN DRONE AFTER AIRSPACE BREACH, MARKING FIRST FOR NATO ALLY Pavel said in a speech before the U.N. General Assembly Wednesday that Russia's "aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security" and warned that the risk is growing. He told Fox News Digital that the pattern of recent escalation was familiar from his years at NATO, recalling Russian aircraft testing U.S. pilots over Syria and repeatedly violating Turkish airspace before Turkey shot down a Russian warplane in 2015. "They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be," Pavel detailed. NATO already has procedures for accidental airspace violations, Pavel said, including warning aircraft and attempting to establish contact. But he drew a distinction between mistakes and aircraft that deliberately enter allied airspace and refuse to respond. "If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on," the Czech president added. RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE The comments come amid recent drone incursions involving NATO members along the alliance’s eastern flank, including incidents in Poland, Romania and Lithuania. Pavel was similarly skeptical that President Vladimir Putin is serious about talks to end the war in Ukraine, saying he has seen no significant Russian effort to negotiate. He argued that while Moscow publicly expresses willingness to hold talks, the conditions it has attached would effectively strip Ukraine of sovereignty. He said a genuine negotiating process would require Russia to agree to a ceasefire first and then enter talks without preconditions. RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS The Czech president also warned that the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed another vulnerability across the NATO alliance: depleted weapons stockpiles and defense-production systems struggling to keep pace with demand. "With the amount of ammunition, especially intelligent ammunition, consumed over a short period of time, we all understand on both sides of the Atlantic how short we are when it comes to stocks of these kinds of equipment," Pavel said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He said the lesson for both Europe and the United States is to accelerate weapons production and overhaul procurement systems he described as "extremely long and rigid." Pavel’s warning underscores a broader challenge facing NATO as it weighs how forcefully to respond to Russian activity without triggering a wider confrontation, while simultaneously replenishing the military stockpiles needed to sustain deterrence over the longer term.

title: While Millennials cheer Toys R Us comeback, key piece of data reveals dystopian reason for its return
description: Toys R Us plans to open 120 new stores this holiday season, but surging adult toy sales among millennials are driving the iconic retailer's comeback.
content: If you came of age in the 80s or 90s, chances are you remember Toys R Us, the international toy retailer with the anthropomorphic giraffe for a mascot and the catchiest jingle in the business. "I don't wanna grow up, I wanna be a Toys R Us kid." Well, the truth of the matter is we did grow up, and about a decade ago, millennials aging out of the toy-buying demographic spelled doom for the once-titanic toy store, as Toys R Us filed for bankruptcy in 2017 and closed all of their stores the following year. 'TOY STORY 5' REVIEW: TOM HANKS, TIM ALLEN RETURN FOR TIMELY INSTALLMENT AS PIXAR GANG BATTLES RISE OF TECH But then, just recently, something unexpected happened. Toys R Us started to make a comeback, first as a part of larger retail stores like Macy's, and then, little by little, as standalone shops in malls and airports. THE NINTENDO 64 IS TURNING 30 YEARS OLD, HERE ARE SOME OF ITS MOST IMPACTFUL GAMES OF ALL TIME Now, Toys R Us is set to open 120 stores across the country this holiday season, bringing its total number of standalone U.S. stores to 160. Hang on just a second, though. Did you read the last part of that post? "As toy sales surge among adult shoppers," reads like there are a bunch of losers in their 30s and 40s pacing up and down the aisles of their local toy stores while shoving kids out of the way for the last Funko Pop. But surely that's not the case here, right? This is just a bunch of older Millennials with kids of their own passing on their love of toys and games to the next generation. Right? Yep, I knew it. It looks like the only reason Toys R Us is making a comeback is because a bunch of 90s kids who are now old enough to have kids of their own took that aforementioned jingle a little too literally. I know you "wanna be a Toys R Us kid," but you're 36 years old. It's time to let someone a little younger have a crack at the LEGO Star Wars set. I don't know what it is with my generation and having a serious case of arrested development, but they're almost allergic to acting their age. Listen, I'm not saying you're not allowed to have some of the same hobbies you had when you were 13. WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO Hell, I will still hop on the Xbox to blow off a little steam or watch movies and TV shows from my youth. But I also haven't been spending chunks of my salary on toys and video games for most of my adult life, and I donated all my Pokemon cards to kids at the summer camp I used to work at back in college. If I have bought a toy in the past two years, it was for my son, and that's the disheartening thing about these numbers. Instead of passing the "kid hobbies" torch, Millennials are just hoarding it to themselves. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Nostalgia is a powerful agent, one that I have been known to write about frequently, but there's a fine line between showing reverence for "the good old days" and outright refusing to live in the present. It's a ton of fun to see my son's eyes light up whenever he opens the package to a Spider-Man figure or a Bluey plushy, but I couldn't imagine someone with a beard and a car payment getting the same satisfaction from that. It all feels weird and a little dystopian. title: Ms Rachel defends her activism by pointing to Mister Rogers' political legacy on children's TV
description: Children's YouTube star Ms. Rachel cited Fred Rogers' civil rights pool scene and nuclear arms race episodes to defend her own political activism.
content: Children's YouTube personality Ms. Rachel hit back at critics of her political activism during an interview Tuesday, pointing to Mister Rogers, who she said was very political. Ms. Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, spoke to Kareem Rahma, host of "SubwayTakes," and broke down her hottest takes. "Mr. Rogers was political," she said. Mister Rogers, whose full name was Fred Rogers, is known for "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood," a children's program that ran from 1968-2001. MS RACHEL CLAIMS CELEBRITIES SILENT ON GAZA WOULD ‘PROBABLY’ SPEAK IF CHILDREN ‘WERE WHITE’ Ms. Rachel pointed to an example in the children's show in which Rogers invited Officer Clemmons, a Black character, to cool off in a small wading pool during the civil rights movement. The episode aired in 1969, at a time when some public pools still prohibited Black swimmers. Rahma called the episode "revolutionary." YOUTUBE STAR MS RACHEL DECLARES 'I AM POLITICAL' IN NEW MISSION TO SHUT DOWN ICE FACILITY "I've read that some people saw it and in their family it wasn't okay to share a pool, and they were like, 'Oh Mr. Rogers is doing it. It's okay for our family now.' And so it did make a difference and actually, people sometimes say to me or, you know, in the media, they'll be like, ‘Ms. Rachel should be like Mister Rogers and not be political.' And actually, he was political so much on the show. I think maybe they didn't watch it or maybe weren't paying attention because he did so many things," Ms. Rachel said. Ms. Rachel also pointed to a series of episodes from 1983, telling Rahma that Rogers was against the nuclear arms race. "He was against the nuclear arms race, and he had, in his neighborhood make-believe, he had King Friday building bombs because he thought the other neighborhood, Southwood, was building bombs, so he wanted to have 100 million and one bomb parts for his bombs and in the show. And then he was like, 'Now we don't have money for the music program because you spent it all on bombs. Queen Sarah, the wife, was like, ‘Why did you spend the tax money on bombs? We should have spent it on these other awesome things,’" Ms. Rachel said. She noted that Mister Rogers also testified before the Senate in support of funding for public broadcasting. "Nixon wanted to cut $10 million from the PBS budget, and he testified in front of the Senate, and he just shared from his heart how much care goes into his show and how he helps children manage, and feelings are manageable and mentionable, and it was huge and the very like-grrrrrr Senate guy was like, ‘You got your $20 million.’ And it was so touching. It's like the coolest video," Ms. Rachel said. She added, "And so he went to Senate and was like, 'No, government, don't cut funding to PBS.' Like, how political is that?" MS RACHEL CLAIMS 'NO ONE NEEDS A BILLION DOLLARS,' ENDORSES DEMOCRATIC PROGRESSIVES ABDUL EL-SAYED, CORI BUSH Author and psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Fred Rogers addressed serious social issues. His 1969 pool scene with Officer Clemmons was a powerful statement about racial equality. But there’s a difference between quietly modeling human dignity and turning your enormous platform with children and parents into a vehicle for your positions on today's political controversies." Alpert continued, "Rogers didn't need to tell his audience, 'Here is the correct political position.' He showed a Black neighbor that he was welcome in his pool. The lesson was contained in the act itself. Ms. Rachel is far more explicit about telling the public what she believes about Gaza, immigration and other politically charged issues. I think invoking Mister Rogers gives her a convenient defense: If Mister Rogers was political, then criticism of her activism can be dismissed as hypocrisy. But that's a false equivalence. You can admire what Rogers did in 1969 without concluding that every children's entertainer therefore has a mandate to become a political activist." YOUTUBE STAR MS RACHEL GIVES FUNDS TO DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED ROSIE O’DONNELL RANTS THAT TRUMP-ERA ICE FACILITIES ARE CONCENTRATION CAMPS WHERE INMATES ARE RAPED Alpert said Rogers was "influential precisely because he didn't beat people over the head with his politics." "He trusted the audience to understand the lesson. The pool scene didn't come with a lecture or a list of political demands. He showed people how to behave," Alpert said of Mister Rogers. Fred Rogers Productions did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Ms. Rachel's other takes included one about children in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody. "No child should be in immigration detention center ever," she said. "I've talked with some children, and the harm is so obvious." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "And we don't want to be people who abuse children. It's the medical neglect is abuse. So, they're actually abusing children. And some pediatricians I've talked to have even said torture. Some autistic children in there, like keeping the lights on 24 hours, just that they've been unable to go to the bathroom, to poop for nine days. And as parents, it's like, that's so wrong. Like you can't, and there was a girl they neglected that she had this respiratory stuff, and when they took her to the ICU, she had COVID, RSV. Her oxygen was like 52. So the medical neglect is abuse in there," Ms. Rachel said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP ICE did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Dem Senate hopeful rocked by explosive ex-aide claims as campaign cites ‘hardest period of her life’
description: Mary Peltola says her alleged outbursts came amid grief after losing her mother and husband months apart, pushing back on the New York Times report.
content: Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, is facing allegations from former aides that she erupted in anger, used offensive slurs, sent profane text messages and once shoved a staffer — claims her campaign disputes while denying that they reflect a broader pattern of abusive behavior. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that former Peltola aides alleged she was quick to anger, used anti-gay slurs and a slur targeting the mentally handicapped, sent edgy text messages and, in one case, shoved an employee. Though Peltola’s campaign disputed several of the allegations, her spokesman said some of her behavior came during a period of extreme grief after the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. "Mary suddenly and tragically lost both her mother and her husband in the span of a few months in 2023. At the time of their passing, Mary was parenting kids through their own grief, serving full-time in the U.S. House of Representatives thousands of miles from home, and running a competitive re-election campaign – all while shouldering the enormous burden of grief," a spokesman for her campaign told the media in response to the report. FETTERMAN LEANS ON UNLIKELY GOP ALLY AS DEMS SHARPEN THEIR KNIVES OVER EXPLOSIVE REPORT "Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief. But she treats her staff with respect and care, and she maintains close positive relationships with her staff spanning her nearly 30 years in public service," the spokesman continued. "Exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong." Peltola avoided reporters’ questions about the allegations after a Wednesday town hall, leaving without responding, Alaska News Source reported. While much of the behavior described in the New York Times article, such as Peltola’s alleged use of slurs and the shove, occurred during the aftermath of her personal tragedies, other incidents purportedly happened more recently. The atmosphere in Peltola’s congressional office allegedly drove aides to tears and prompted discussions about quitting, with some saying the stress caused them to lose weight or seek therapy, according to the New York Times. The outlet separately described anxiety and exhaustion among staff on her 2026 Senate campaign. BAD BOSSES ON CAPITOL HILL COULD FACE RECKONING UNDER NEW ANONYMOUS STAFFER REVIEW PLATFORM Some commentators from across the political spectrum defended Peltola or questioned the significance of some of the allegations. "I think most reasonably well-adjusted people would read this and feel pretty sympathetic toward Peltola rather than her annoying staffers," left-of-center pollster Nate Silver said of the reporting. A Democratic communications staffer noted that getting yelled at by your boss is relatively normal on the Hill. "Call me crazy, but I do not think it's very objectionable for Mary Peltola, who commutes from Alaska to Washington DC, to ask a staffer to feed her pet," Robby Soave, who writes for a libertarian magazine, said. Not everyone took the Senate hopeful’s side, however. "Mary Peltola has a problem with violence and aggression, and she doesn't deserve to be dog-catcher let alone a U.S. Senator. Mary should apologize for her unhinged behavior," Republican National Committee spokesman Nick Poche said of the reporting. "I thought Peltola was boring and useless until I read this," former Rep. Matt Gaetz wrote on X. "Was this leaked to help Peltola with Alaskan men?" Staffers complained to the New York Times about having to feed live crickets to Peltola's pet chameleon, Meatball. Some of the staffers who complained about the working conditions in Peltola’s congressional office returned to work for her Senate campaign. DEM SENATE HOPEFUL VOWS TO UNLEASH ALASKA OIL — BUT HER RECORD TELLS A DIFFERENT STORY Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the leading contenders in Alaska’s four-candidate general election for U.S. Senate, which will likely be one of the closest Senate elections of this cycle. Though traditionally a red state, shifting voter preferences combined with Peltola’s unique crossover appeal have put Alaska in play for the Democrats. title: Susan Collins defies blue-state headwinds in crucial Senate battle as new poll reveals striking split
description: Republican Sen. Susan Collins leads Democrat Troy Jackson 49%-46% in a new Maine Senate poll, but her edge falls within the margin of error.
content: A new poll indicates longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins is ahead of her Democratic challenger in a crucial Senate showdown in blue-leaning Maine. Collins, who is running for a sixth six-year term in the Senate, stands at 49% support among likely voters, with former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, at 46%, with 5% undecided in the New York Times/Siena poll. Collins' three-point edge is within the survey's margin of error. Democrats are heavily targeting Collins as they work to flip the seat, which is key to their efforts to win back the Senate majority from the Republicans in the midterm elections. The survey, which was conducted Sept. 15–22, is one of the first to indicate Collins ahead of Jackson since he replaced former Senate nominee Graham Platner in late July. SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Platner, a combat veteran and oyster farmer, won the June Democratic Senate primary in a landslide. But a month later he dropped out following an explosive report containing an allegation of rape from a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the report but stepped aside. Collins slightly trailed Platner in most polling at the time he ended his campaign. Jackson, who campaigned alongside Platner earlier this year as he unsuccessfully ran for governor, won a special nominating convention to fill the party's vacant Senate nomination. The poll release came as Collins pushed back against a report by ProPublica that the FBI sought to launch a pay-to-play investigation examining Collins and others. The investigation was later dropped and no one working for Collins was charged. Collins ripped the report as "offensive" and a "partisan hit job" orchestrated by Democrats. Jackson took to social media to claim that "Susan Collins is blatantly corrupt." Collins' advantage over Jackson in the new survey comes even as 55% of those questioned said they prefer Democrats to control the Senate next year, with 43% saying they'd like the GOP to retain the majority. COLLINS TEARS INTO NEW REPORT ALLEDGING PAY-TO PLAY SCHEME Likely boosting Collins are her favorable ratings, which are in positive territory, at 51%-48%. Meanwhile, Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and a one-time conservative Republican who became a Democrat over two decades ago and who is now running on a progressive platform, is underwater with 41% of those questioned viewing him favorably and 49% holding an unfavorable view. As he quickly became the frontrunner in the abbreviated race to replace Platner, Jackson faced a slew of media reports over his alleged temper and workplace conduct, as well as reported claims of mortgage improprieties and other potential liabilities, including his past strict anti-abortion stance. In August, a resurfaced 1988 police record which detailed accusations that Jackson assaulted a man and pushed his longtime partner during a late-night confrontation in Fort Kent, Maine, grabbed headlines. Jackson, in a statement, said, "I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now. But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman." WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLING Lana Pelletier, who, according to records, is Jackson's second cousin, shares two adult children with him. Collins, the only GOP senator seeking re-election in a state President Donald Trump lost in the 2024 election, is facing a rough political climate, amid Trump's underwater approval ratings, persistent inflation, soaring fuel prices and what polls indicate is an unpopular war with Iran. The senator, known as a moderate Republican who at times has voted against Trump, this summer received bipartisan praise after reaching a milestone by casting her 10,000th consecutive Senate vote. But Democrats are taking aim at Collins over her comments that she didn't regret her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, despite his crucial vote four years later to overturn the landmark Roe v. Wade abortion ruling. And following the fatal shooting in Maine this summer involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, Democrats heavily criticized the Senate Appropriations Committee chair for her support for ICE funding. But Collins has broken with Trump numerous times in recent months, criticizing his tariff war with neighboring Canada and voting against Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation. The senator has a history of surviving Democratic efforts to unseat her. Six years ago, she trailed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon, the then-Maine House speaker, but the senator ended up winning re-election by nearly nine points while former President Joe Biden carried the state by a similar margin. Fox News Digital reached out to both the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment on the new survey, but didn't receive a response at the time this story was published. In neighboring New Hampshire, the survey indicates Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas with a 50%-45% advantage over former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu, in the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Meanwhile, in Michigan, the poll indicates Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed ahead of former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers 49%-44% in the showdown to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. title: American businesses aren’t allowed to build. It’s time Congress helped them
description: Permitting delays average over two years and cost millions, crushing small manufacturers and defense startups before they can begin production.
content: America’s share of global manufacturing output has fallen from 25% in 1997 to 15% today. Absent intervention, it could reach 11% by 2030. Those numbers get thrown around a lot. What is said less is what they mean for Americans: The United States is losing its ability to produce the things it needs to defend itself, to power its economy and to care for its people. This failure is not because we lack talent, capital or technology. It is because we have made it nearly impossible to build anything here. This inability to build harms every American industry and every American job. Whether it is semiconductor fabricators, munitions or battery factories, rare earth production facilities, natural gas pipelines, oil refineries or medical manufacturing centers, all hit the same regulatory barrier: federal permitting law. INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE Among the various federal permitting barriers, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) stands as the most egregious. Unlike substantive environmental protections found in statutes like the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act, NEPA’s central function is procedural, requiring analysis and disclosure of environmental impacts before major federal actions. Over time, regulatory layering and aggressive legal interpretation transformed this reasonable "look before you leap" statute into a roadblock for projects with any sort of federal connection. SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES OVERHAUL TO CUT RED TAPE AND SPEED UP AMERICAN ENERGY PROJECTS This regulatory accretion has turned NEPA into a tool to stop nearly any meaningful project — across every state and political spectrum. It is not every day renewable energy advocates and oil and gas executives work together to reform a statute. Yet these and many other strange bedfellows have come together this year to fix a profoundly broken statute and allow America to build again. The numbers explain why. The median NEPA review in 2024 ran 26 months. The statute’s more demanding environmental impact statements averaged 3.8 years. Environmental assessments, the so-called fast track, routinely average a year or more. None of those timelines are legally required. They are what happens when bureaucratic caution and unlimited litigation combine in the absence of any countervailing pressure. TRUMP-APPROVED ENERGY PROJECTS AT RISK OF SUDDEN DEATH BY NEXT HOSTILE PRESIDENT And then there is the cost. DOE data showed mean environmental assessment preparation costs were over $300,000 while environmental impact statement costs averaged $6.6 million. Those figures exclude legal fees, staff time and the cost of litigation. These millions add to the bottom line of every potential domestic manufacturing project. For a major company, these delays and costs are annoying. For a small business seeking to open a factory or a startup raising its first manufacturing round, they are often a company-ending event. AMERICA FACES A CRISIS IN OUR MILITARY ARSENAL THAT TRUMP IS RACING TO FIX These are the types of businesses America most needs right now–the 50-person drone manufacturer, the battery startup and the defense tech company that won a Pentagon contract and needs to be in production before its runway expires are exactly the companies the current NEPA regime destroys. These are also the jobs Americans need. This regulatory Sisyphean task doesn’t improve outcomes, it materially delays or even kills meritorious projects. Investors cannot deploy capital if regulatory uncertainty clouds a project. SEN KEVIN CRAMER: CHINA BUILDS FOR WAR WHILE AMERICA WAITS ON PERMITS While the Supreme Court’s "Seven County" decision and recent executive actions have helped, only Congress can enact durable statutory reforms needed to restore NEPA to its intended procedural role. Here are some basic fixes. Over time, regulatory layering and aggressive legal interpretation transformed this reasonable "look before you leap" statute into a roadblock for projects with any sort of federal connection. Enforce the deadlines and limit endless litigation TRUMP ADMIN MOVES TO GUT BIDEN'S SIGNATURE ENVIRONMENTAL RULES Agencies need to enforce permitting deadlines. Aspirational goals do not motivate federal bureaucrats, but neither does the prospect of getting dragged into court. Both extremes perpetuate analysis paralysis. Get the permits done and when they’re complete, there should be finality, providing certainty for manufacturers, the capital backing them and the federal agency granting the permit. Revocations should be permitted only when there is an imminent, irreparable and specifically documented harm. Cut the red tape for companies which can least afford it THE MACHINES THAT KEEP AMERICA ALIVE ARE FAILING. WE FORGOT HOW TO REPLACE THEM Agencies which finance or permit manufacturing already have categorical exclusions, pre-cleared categories of routine actions normally not requiring a full Environmental Assessment or Environmental Impact Statement. Most have never shared those categories with each other, despite a 2023 law explicitly allowing them to do so. Congress should require agencies that finance or permit manufacturing to adopt a curated list of relevant categorical exclusions from other agencies. title: Riley Green thought he'd 'frame houses for the rest of my life' before becoming a country music star

content: Riley Green didn't leave school with the sole intent of trying to launch a music career. title: Female athletes, women's sports advocates speak on Capitol Hill as trans athlete issue hovers over midterms
description: Female athletes descended on Capitol Hill Wednesday to testify how biological males in women's sports threatened their safety and locker room privacy.
content: Female athletes and women’s sports advocates descended on Capitol Hill Wednesday to tell lawmakers how policies allowing biological males to compete in female athletics have affected their safety, privacy and athletic opportunities, while warning that the issue could follow candidates into the midterm elections. The Senate Judiciary Committee held a hearing titled, "Standing Up for Women in Sports: Ensuring Opportunity, Fairness and Safety for Female Athletes." The committee heard testimony from three witnesses: Independent Council on Women’s Sports (ICONS) co-founder Kim Jones; Carly Smolak, a former professional soccer player and Australian rules football player; and attorney William Bock III, who previously served as general counsel for the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency. Democrats did not invite a witness of their own. Ranking member Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., were the only Democrats who attended, and both left within the first hour. Durbin declined to question the witnesses. Jones, whose daughter competed against transgender swimmer Lia Thomas, told OutKick in an exclusive interview that the Democrats’ absence made the athletes and advocates feel dismissed. AMERICANS CLASH OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES AS DEBATE HEATS UP: ‘JUST GETTING OUTRAGEOUS' "It felt dismissive of women, of our concerns, of the right for young girls to expect to be treated fairly in the United States," Jones said. "For Democrats to say that we’re — I believe, you know, are my neighbors and friends — to actively say we’re not going to concern ourselves about what young girls and even all the way up through older women have been put through. "I mean, it’s misogynistic, and it is incredibly disappointing. I really hope that they change course and decide that the voices of women who have been hurt and shamed are important enough to listen to." Durbin used his opening remarks to argue that the hearing was ignoring other issues facing children and female athletes, including affordability, artificial intelligence, children’s cellphone use and declining trust in government. He also raised concerns that efforts to enforce sex-based sports categories could result in female athletes undergoing invasive inspections. Jones rejected both arguments. "It was incensing," she said of Durbin’s remarks. "One of the worst comments you can give to women who are trying to share the stories of what they’ve been put through by the denial of their sex and the denial of their rights is to suggest that this is not an important issue and that it’s dismissible. "It’s akin to saying, ‘I cannot care about brain cancer until you solve stomach cancer.’ It’s whataboutism in the most obvious form and telling women that we are not going to address the problems that you’re facing, including sexual abuse and harassment by the inclusion of male athletes in women’s sports and women’s locker rooms, until we solve every other problem in the world." OLYMPIC SWIMMER RÉKA GYÖRGY CALLS OUT VIRGINIA GOVERNOR SPANBERGER FOR WITHDRAWING FEMALE SPORTS REGULATION Jones said sex eligibility could be determined without invasive examinations, pointing to cheek-swab testing for the SRY gene. "There is no need for any kind of invasive inspections. There’s no need for any kind of traumatic experience," Jones said. Asked whether she expects the issue to influence the midterms, Jones said the protection of female sports should be "non-negotiable." "Of course," Jones said. "I think truth is always an important issue for anyone voting in the general public. I think that standing up for the rights and fair treatment of women in the United States is a ground-zero, non-negotiable issue. And this is a blatant public display of stripping that from women and girls." Smolak testified about discovering that a registered sex offender had joined an adult women’s Australian rules football team with which she remained closely connected after retiring. She said the individual was quietly removed after she raised the issue, but alleged that team members were not informed and the sport’s national governing body did not take sufficient action to prevent a similar situation. "So it felt like at every single level, the national level and largely the media level, it feels like nobody was doing anything about this issue," Smolak told OutKick exclusively. "And I didn’t want to see this happen again. If it happened once, it’ll happen again if we don’t put policies in place. And the obvious policy is that women’s sports are for biological females, are for women." SPANBERGER SPARKS OUTRAGE AFTER SNEAKILY ENDING YOUNGKIN-ERA WOMEN'S SPORTS PROTECTIONS Smolak said the response she encountered after raising concerns was "incredibly disheartening." "I’ve had people be more concerned about using his preferred pronouns than trying to prevent this from happening again or being even upset that it happened in the first place," she said. Smolak said she was not surprised Democratic senators did not remain to hear the full testimony. "I think they either know they have a losing issue or cannot make their argument based on the merits of their position," Smolak said. "And so they would rather distract about other issues that are unrelated or just not show up at all. But it’s infuriating." Following the hearing, additional female athletes spoke at a Capitol Hill press conference. Briley Lechner, a 17-year-old varsity volleyball and soccer player at Monroe High School in New York, said she and her teammates learned only after a volleyball match that a biological male had competed against them and entered their locker room. "All of us girls do our normal things. We get undressed, unconsciously trusting our friends next to us. We have girl conversations. We take girl pictures, videos and everything like that," Lechner said. "So to be told days after that there was a boy in the locker room where we get undressed, and there was a boy on the other side of the court, just is very hurtful. And it feels as if our protection was just stripped away from us and they don’t care." Lechner said the backlash she and her father received after speaking publicly would not silence her. "I’m not going to sit down until there is a change," she said. "And I’m going to continue to speak my word and share my story until us girls don’t have to feel uncomfortable and we don’t have to be fearful — not only in the locker room, but in the bathroom, on the court, on the field and any other sport." Former West Virginia State University soccer player Lainey Armistead discussed her involvement in litigation over West Virginia’s law restricting girls’ and women’s sports to biological females. The Supreme Court upheld West Virginia’s law earlier this year. "There are still girls in 23 other states, girls in New York, girls in California, who do not have the same opportunities that I did," Armistead said. "And we will not quit fighting for those girls. Women’s sports is not men’s for the taking." NCAA softball player Kendall Kotzmacher said her high school team lost in a state semifinal to a team with a transgender pitcher during her senior year. "Showing up to the field that day knowing that we were playing a man is a feeling that you can’t explain to another person," Kotzmacher said. "Showing up, seeing a male on the field for something you’ve worked your whole life for, and knowing there’s nothing you can do about it is unimaginable." Kotzmacher directly addressed Democrats who have minimized the prevalence of such cases. "To the Democrats that said this is a non-issue, they’re the reason that I’m going to keep speaking out and everyone else is going to keep speaking out," she said. "We have multiple women here that have suffered the same things that I have. And there are so many more that have stayed silent because people out there have told them not to speak up, who have scared them into not speaking up." U.S. Masters swimmer Angie Griffin said she lost a national title to a transgender competitor at the 2025 U.S. Masters Swimming Spring National Championship. Griffin said a grievance alleging unsportsmanlike conduct was filed against her after she and other swimmers protested the results, exposing her to a potential lifetime ban before she was cleared. "The process itself was the punishment," Griffin said. "The message to other women was clear: Speak up and you will pay a price." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "Women should not have to lose a championship, risk a ban, hire a lawyer or face public pressure simply to ask for a fair race," she added. "The path forward is clear: Prioritize women in women’s sports." Marshi Smith, a former NCAA champion swimmer and fellow ICONS co-founder, said the athletes’ accounts showed why adults in leadership positions needed to intervene. "It was a historic moment to see this issue come to such a huge platform, but it was also incredibly distressing to see that the Democrat senators were so dismissive of young women who are suffering across the country today," Smith said. "There are huge threats to women’s sports today, and adults really need to stand up in leadership positions and do something about it." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. title: David Charvet admits he walked away from Hollywood after 'Baywatch' to focus on fatherhood
description: David Charvet reveals why he left Hollywood over a decade ago and how "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test" let him prove something to his kids.
content: David Charvet is opening up about why he left Hollywood. In a new interview with Fox News Digital, the 54-year-old actor discussed his experience on Fox's hit series, "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test," and why he stepped away from Hollywood in 2013. "I left Hollywood because I wanted to be a good dad, and for me, today my children are my legacy," he said. "It's not the career you built or the money you have or all that. It's really what you leave behind. And what I'm leaving one day behind is really my children. And if I did it right in that way, then I think I've successfully done my job as a man on this planet. So, for me, there's no regrets." Having left Hollywood over a decade ago, Charvet expressed how "honored" he is "to be amongst all these people and just to be a part of it." ‘SPECIAL FORCES’ STARS JESSIE JAMES DECKER, HUSBAND ERIC SHARE KEY TO SUCCESSFUL 12-YEAR MARRIAGE The actor became famous playing lifeguard Matt Brody on "Baywatch," saying no one told him that he "was going to be a 'Baywatch' guy forever," but he doesn't mind. "That's where I got my start. The show was incredible, it reached everywhere around the world," he said. "I've had a lot of incredible opportunities from it. Incredible life lessons, incredible friendships and relationships, so for me, I'm just grateful, you know, I'm super happy with whatever the outcome has been." WATCH: David Charvet admits he left Hollywood in order to be a good dad to his two kids The original "Baywatch" helped launch not only Charvet's career, but also put Pamela Anderson, Carmen Electra and many of its other stars on the map. It was announced in September 2025 that a reboot of the series starring a whole new batch of lifeguards was in the works. In addition to seasoned actors, including Stephen Amel and Shay Mitchell, the show is also a launching pad for acting newcomers, Brooks Nader, Livvy Dunne and Noah Beck. "I got to say that what we created 25 years ago was very special. At the same time, there was only 14 channels at the time. So people got a chance to see that show more probably today than what people are going to see in the next season that's about to come," he said about the new series. "Our executive producers, which are, I believe, executive producers today, were real lifeguards, live the life as lifeguards, so there were real stories." WATCH: David Charvet calls the original 'Baywatch' 'special' 'BAYWATCH' STAR BROOKS NADER'S CONSERVATIVE PARENTS BANNED BIKINIS GROWING UP AS SHE SLIPS INTO RED SWIMSUIT Charvet is excited to see what the new generation brings to the show, but admits, "getting people to really watch something today is more of a challenge," and says the writers have to be "more creative" now than before, adding, "They got their work cut out for them." While he was considered a big star in his heyday, Charvet has "been out of the game" for over 20 years, and admits his "kids have never seen me on television or in movies or anything live." He explained to Fox News Digital that that was part of the reason he agreed to compete on the show, noting it "was really important for me to maybe show them that aspect of what I kind of gave up for them." He shares two children with his ex-wife, Brooke Burke; a daughter, Rain and a son, Shaya. "And also the idea of pushing myself to the limit," he said. "It's not every day that you get thrown out of a helicopter, or you jump out of 25 stories and things like that, and then also the mind games. Do I really have what it takes? To take on what we took on was a real thing that I wanted to see if I could do. So for me, it was a huge challenge, an incredible opportunity, and hopefully my kids will be proud." title: Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko's father killed in bear attack on remote Russia fishing trip
description: Andrei Kuzmenko's father, a longtime hockey coach, was fatally attacked by a bear while fishing in a restricted area of Russia's Republic of Tuva.
content: The father of Pittsburgh Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko has died after being attacked by a bear during a fishing trip in a remote region of Siberia, according to multiple Russian media reports. Alexander Kuzmenko, 62, was fishing with a group of people along the Bolshoy Yenisey River in Russia's Republic of Tuva when the bear attacked him, inflicting severe injuries to his head and face. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE According to Russian sports outlet Sport24, Kuzmenko was part of a seven-person group that traveled by boat up the river before establishing a camp along the shoreline in the remote Todzhinsky district, approximately 112 miles from the nearest village. The bear reportedly emerged from the forest and attacked Kuzmenko. His companions managed to drive the animal away and provide first aid before transporting him by boat to the village of Toora-Khem. From there, Kuzmenko was airlifted to a hospital in Kyzyl, the capital of Tuva, where he was admitted to intensive care. He later died from his injuries. Russian media reported his death on Thursday. Authorities say fishing group entered restricted area The attack occurred in an area where authorities had already restricted outdoor activities due to increased bear activity. ALASKA MOOSE HUNTER MIRACULOUSLY SURVIVES AMBUSH BROWN BEAR ATTACK, SAYS HE 'BLACKED OUT' According to Russian news outlet RBC, regional officials had prohibited fishing and campfires beginning Sept. 10, with additional restrictions introduced Sept. 17. The Republic of Tuva's State Committee for Hunting Supervision said the group entered the remote wilderness despite those restrictions. It is unclear whether Kuzmenko and his companions were aware of the warnings. Kuzmenko was a hockey coach who helped develop his son's career Alexander Kuzmenko was a longtime hockey coach who played an important role in his son's development as a professional player. According to Sport24, Andrei began his hockey career at the White Bears hockey school in Moscow, where his father coached. Alexander also coached several other professional hockey players, including Nikita Korostelev, Daniil Grigoryev and Alexander Pelevin. Andrei Kuzmenko made his NHL debut with the Vancouver Canucks during the 2022-23 season, recording 39 goals and 74 points in his rookie campaign. title: Biden-appointed judge hands Letitia James setback in latest Trump legal clash
description: New York Attorney General Letitia James and 18 states lost their legal challenge after a federal judge dismissed the DOGE Treasury lawsuit as moot.
content: New York Attorney General Letitia James’ legal battle against President Donald Trump over DOGE-linked access to sensitive Treasury systems ended Wednesday with a federal judge dismissing the lawsuit she spearheaded with 18 other states. The case stems from Trump’s January 2025 executive order establishing DOGE, which directed executive agencies to create DOGE teams and set July 4, 2026, as the termination date for the U.S. DOGE Service Temporary Organization. James led a coalition – which included New York and 18 other states – that sued the following month after Treasury gave DOGE-affiliated employees access to Bureau of the Fiscal Service systems, which process federal payments and contain sensitive financial information. JUDGE SAYS ISSUES IN TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ANTI-WEAPONIZATION CASE 'ALIVE AND KICKING' DESPITE DOJ PUSH Biden-appointed U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas ruled that the "plaintiffs’ claims related to access by DOGE-affiliated employees to sensitive Treasury information are dismissed as moot," according to Wednesday’s order. Vargas said the Treasury DOGE team had been disbanded, and no DOGE employees remained at Treasury, leaving no access practice for the court to enjoin. She separately dismissed the states’ claims over an automated payment-review system, finding they had not alleged that the process froze or canceled any specific federal payment due to them. The states argued the Trump administration unlawfully opened sensitive Treasury systems to DOGE, putting state financial information and federal payments at risk and exceeding the administration’s legal authority. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE THE SECRETIVE MINE DOGE HELPED DRAG OUT OF A DECADES-OLD BUREAUCRATIC BLACK HOLE In February 2025, Vargas granted the states a preliminary injunction barring Treasury’s DOGE team from the covered payment systems, then modified the order over the following months to permit access for personnel who complied with specified vetting, training, hiring, reporting and mitigation procedures. The Executive Order established DOGE and called for each department to assemble its own DOGE team to find fraud, waste and abuse before their termination date of July 4. TRUMP'S LAWYERS PUT DEM AG ON NOTICE FOR TARGETING HIS FAMILY IN NY FRAUD FIGHT: 'CANNOT STAND' James has been a longtime critic and legal adversary of Trump, launching a civil fraud lawsuit against him and the Trump Organization in 2022 after campaigning on investigating his business practices. The case initially resulted in more than $450 million in penalties, though an appeals court later upheld Trump’s liability while voiding the financial penalty. title: Falcons and Packers both searching for answers heading into 'Thursday Night Football' in NFL Week 3
description: Michael Penix Jr. takes over for Cooper Rush as the Falcons try to unlock Bijon Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts in a stalling offense.
content: Week 3 is here in the NFL, and I really hope it is nothing like Week 2. Let’s toss aside the sports betting aspect for a moment, but we saw three young quarterbacks- Caleb Williams, Jaxon Dart, and Jayden Daniels- get injured. Timetables are uncertain for some returns, but either way, football is better with primary quarterbacks available. We have two in tonight's game between the Falcons and Packers. The Atlanta Falcons are getting back a starting quarterback of their own. Well… kind of. They are getting Michael Penix Jr. back, but he is returning and taking over for Cooper Rush. The original starter was supposed to be Tua Tagovailoa, but he’s been unavailable all season. Penix Jr. will have his hands full trying to figure out what to do with this offense. They don’t lack playmakers - Bijan Robinson is solid, Drake London is a really good receiver, and Kyle Pitts (although drafted too high) is still a solid option. In the first two games, the Falcons were essentially outmatched. Is that because Rush was under center? In game one, they scored 13 points, but last week they could only get 3 points against a team that almost allowed 60 points in Week 1. The offense wasn’t terrible by some measures - they had 17 first downs, one fewer than the Panthers. However, they had three turnovers; if they shore those up, maybe it’s a more competitive game. MICHAEL PENIX JR. OFFICIALLY NAMED FALCONS STARTER FOR A SHORT-WEEK TRIAL BY FIRE AGAINST PACKERS On the other side of the field is a team with more than enough questions of their own. The Packers are 1-1, but it wasn’t easy to get that victory. They had to go into New Jersey to face the Jets, and they were forced into an overtime game with them. They came out on top 20-17. I don’t want to act like we should be impressed or pleased with that performance, but perhaps it is something to build on, and now they get their first home game. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! In Week 1 it wasn’t much better for the Packers. Green Bay was fine against the Vikings, at least for the first half of the game. They struggled to get much going against the Minnesota defense and gave up their lead in the second half. It wasn’t just that; they barely could score and couldn’t keep Carson Wentz from marching down the field. I do blame the front office. I’m not exactly sure that Jordan Love is an elite quarterback, but his receiving options certainly don’t help make him much better. Couple that with Josh Jacobs being out, and this offense should be expected to struggle. JETS COLLAPSE LATE AGAINST PACKERS, MISS CHANCE AT FIRST 2-0 START SINCE 2015 IN OVERTIME LOSS The Falcons haven’t done much on defense to give you reason to believe this, but there should be adjustments here. On a short week, facing 0-3, you’re trying everything out of desperation. I think they will put pressure on the Packers, and Love hasn’t looked all that comfortable yet this season. Maybe being at home will help, but I think that’s where we see a boost to their defense as well. Give me the under 45.5 for this "Thursday Night Football" game. title: Top public university’s ‘LGBTQ+ lab’ hit with race-bias complaint amid $700K in Trump-era federal funding
description: The University of Maryland's Lavender Lab faces a Title VI complaint alleging its advisory board and hiring practices discriminate based on race.
content: FIRST ON FOX: A University of Maryland research lab that received nearly $700,000 in additional federal funding from the Trump administration this year is facing a civil rights complaint alleging that it uses race and ethnicity to determine access to some research-related opportunities. The Equal Protection Project (EPP) filed the complaint with the Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights against UMD's Lavender Lab, a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded lab that studies suicide, substance use and other health outcomes among LGBTQ+ people and Black, Indigenous and People of Color. EPP is asking HHS to investigate whether the lab's LGBTQ+ Teens of Color Advisory Board and its research assistant selection practices give priority to non-White applicants. "Some people may ask what is wrong with prioritizing non-whites in a program which is designed to study non-whites," EPP founder William Jacobson told Fox News Digital. "When you receive federal funding, you cannot discriminate in the administration of your programs." JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY "You do not need to have an advisory board, you do not need to hire research assistants based on race to fulfill the purposes of this grant," Jacobson continued. The complaint comes as the Lavender Lab continues receiving millions of dollars through the NIH for research examining alcohol and drug use among "sexual minority adolescents of color." One of the lab's principal projects, titled "Long-Term and Daily Associations Among Intersectional Minority Stress, Structural Oppression, and Alcohol Use and Misuse Among Sexual Minority Adolescents of Color," began in May 2022 and is scheduled to run through April 2027. The complaint cites approximately $3.6 million in total federal obligations and roughly $2.2 million in outlays at the time of its filing. NIH records cited in the complaint show the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism provided another $695,192 for the project for fiscal year 2026. The complaint points first to the lab's LGBTQ+ Teens of Color Advisory Board, which said it was "specifically looking for teens in the US who identify as both LGBTQ+ and Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) to join our board" in an Instagram post. A NEW YORK UNIVERSITY FACES JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INVESTIGATION OVER 'BLACK MALE INITIATIVE' According to the complaint, board members are paid to help review research, provide feedback and participate in professional-development activities, with some also receiving leadership opportunities. EPP also targeted the Lavender Lab's research-assistant program, which offers positions to undergraduate and master's-level students. Although the positions are generally unpaid, the complaint stated that undergraduate research assistants may receive academic course credit, and some students may be able to participate through federal work-study. Research assistants generally commit to at least two semesters and a minimum of eight hours per week. The lab stated it "especially encourage[s] and invite[s] candidates from traditionally marginalized backgrounds" to apply and that applicants with experience conducting research involving "LGBTQ and BIPOC communities" through "cultural humility, intersectionality, and social justice approaches" will receive the "strongest consideration." "Discrimination based on race or ethnicity at institutions receiving federal funding is unlawful regardless of which group is targeted or benefits," Jacobson said. "Treating individuals as avatars of their demographic identity rather than as individuals with unique merits and circumstances undermines fairness, merit, social cohesion, and the rule of law." TRUMP ADMIN'S PUSH TO SCRAP DEI IN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKES LANDMARK STEP WITH NEW HIRING RULE EPP alleges that the language indicates race or ethnicity may play a role in the selection process. The complaint asks HHS to investigate whether the practices violate Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs, as well as the Affordable Care Act. "Because the Lavender Lab is operating under an HHS health care related grant, the non-discrimination provisions of the Affordable Care Act must be adhered to, and HHS has authority to enforce those provisions," Jacobson said. EPP's complaint also questions federal funding for research focused on intersectionality, which the Lavender Lab says guides its work. The lab studies how sexual-minority status, race, ethnicity and what it calls "structural oppression" affect health outcomes. "The conduct at the Lavender Lab calls into question whether HHS should be funding intersectionality-focused research at all," Jacobson said. "Intersectionality is a race- and ethnicity-focused group-identity approach. It is no surprise that where the focus is racial identity that programming could cross the line into civil rights violations." Jacobson said EPP has found federal dollars going to programs that use intersectionality and is calling for tighter rules on that funding. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "We have identified hundreds of millions of dollars of federal funding for programs that incorporate intersectionality," Jacobson said. "Given the civil rights danger from an 'intersectional' approach, we call on the administration to issue a new executive order and agency guidance closing the 'intersectionality loophole' by including intersectionality in the ban on unlawful discriminatory DEI practices in federal grantmaking." title: Reporter's Notebook: A guide to the college sports vote and Senate’s Ohio showdown
description: The Senate takes a test vote on a bill overhauling college sports NIL payments, transfer rules, and eligibility standards as midterms approach.
content: The Senate is poised to possibly pass by the end of this week a bill fundamentally altering money and eligibility rules in college sports. The Senate will take a test vote on the measure on Thursday. More than 70 senators support the bill that establishes a ceiling for how much money schools can allocate to pay students for their name, image and likeness. The legislation also limits transfers and sets eligibility standards. The Senate could pass the bill later on Thursday if there’s a time agreement. But does the Senate really want to make college sports the punctuation point before it leaves for the midterms? It’s possible that senators have no other choice. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., wants to do a bipartisan permitting reform bill. The legislation would deal with data centers, drilling and environmental concerns — but that bill is aspirational and not yet ready for a vote. Thune said last night that the odds favored the Senate staying in session next week, which they were scheduled to do anyway. What has emerged is a dispute over the Ratepayer Protection Act. That bill passed the House last week 417-3. It would defray the cost of utilities consumers must pay if they reside near data centers. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is one of the most vulnerable Republicans on the ballot this fall. He’s faced criticism back home for his support for data centers. So Husted asked the Senate last week to pass the House bill on the spot. FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE Reluctant to give Husted a win, Democrats blocked him. Now Republicans may want to stay in session and run all of the parliamentary traps to pass the Ratepayer Protection Act. For Republicans, that’s a better exclamation point before the recess. But look at this exchange yesterday between yours truly and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.: Pergram: Was this blocked in the Senate last week by Democrats as an effort to prevent Senator Husted from having a win in his competitive race? Schumer: Sen. Husted's bill is a fraud. It's voluntary. No company has to do it. The bill we have is mandatory. It is much stronger and is what is needed. WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE Republicans are sure to capitalize on the "fraud" part. You may even hear that in ads back in Ohio. Republicans will emphasize that Schumer is calling a bill which commanded 417 yeas in the House a "fraud." Therefore, Republicans want to get Democrats on the record about this bill. That could help lift the GOP before the midterms. And certainly Husted. title: The unlikely South American ally helping US troops with 'jail or hell' drug cartel crackdown
description: Ecuador's foreign minister says American forces work alongside Ecuadorian military and police in joint operations targeting drug cartels in Latin America.
content: NEW YORK — Ecuador has emerged as a key regional ally in President Donald Trump’s expanding crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working side by side to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country’s foreign minister told Fox News Digital. Foreign Minister Roberto Kury said the increasingly close cooperation with Washington has delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, pointing specifically to drug shipments uncovered through U.S. intelligence and joint work on the ground. "There is an intelligence (sic) and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly this week. "Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem," Kury noted of the stakes. U.S. and Ecuadorian forces on Wednesday "neutralized" what Defense Minister Gian Carlo Loffredo described as one of Ecuador's "highest value military targets" — immediate proof of the growing partnership in the two nations' war on narcoterrorism. "Alias ‘Charlie’ belonged to the Los Choneros group and the Oliver Sinisterra Front from Colombia, had ties to Mexico's Jalisco New Generation Cartel, and his main mission was to sow terror in our country. We promised it: "Jail or hell" and this one didn’t make it to jail," Loffredo wrote on X. War Secretary Pete Hegseth reposted and amplified that message, writing on X: "The Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C) in action." US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS For Ecuador, the stakes are enormous. Roughly 70% of the world’s cocaine passes through Ecuadorian ports, an FBI official told lawmakers earlier this year, according to the Congressional Research Service, as criminal groups battle for control of trafficking routes carrying cocaine produced in neighboring Colombia and Peru to markets abroad. For the U.S., Ecuador has become a proving ground for an early priority laid out in Trump’s foreign policy: using American military power against threats closer to home as Washington turns its attention back toward the Western Hemisphere. The explosion in the drug trade has transformed the small South American country. Once considered one of Latin America’s safer countries, Ecuador is now at the frontline of the region’s cartel fight, fueling a surge in violence that prompted President Daniel Noboa to declare an "internal armed conflict" against criminal groups and deploy the military against them. "We have found many drugs and shipments through this cooperation, so it’s very positive for Ecuador," Kury said of the partnership with the U.S. Asked whether U.S. forces were participating directly in operations against cartels rather than limiting their role to intelligence and training, Kury was unequivocal about the joint nature of the effort, noting, "They work together with our local authorities." But Kury stopped short of giving Washington carte blanche to use military force inside Ecuador when asked whether his government would permit the U.S. to strike a cartel target on Ecuadorian soil. WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES "Ecuador has our sovereignty, and they respect that sovereignty," Kury said, adding that Quito welcomes U.S. involvement "as long as we work together, aligned with our local military and our local police." Kury's comments come as Ecuador has emerged as a testing ground for the Trump administration's effort to take the fight against Latin American drug cartels beyond maritime interdictions and into partnered military operations on land. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has praised Ecuador as the U.S.’ most "aggressive" partner in its Western Hemisphere crackdown. He told reporters during a recent trip to Quito that U.S. and Ecuadorian "elite forces" from both countries "are working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organizations." The U.S. military is also shifting MQ-9 Reaper drones from Africa to Latin America ahead of anticipated operations against drug cartels, CNN reported Friday, the latest sign of Washington’s growing military footprint in the region. The drones are being reassigned from U.S. Africa Command to U.S. Southern Command as the administration expands a campaign that has already included strikes on suspected drug-smuggling vessels and closer operations with regional partners. Ecuador battles a cocaine trade that President Noboa has estimated at roughly $30 billion a year. The country is looking to Washington for additional help taking on the criminal organizations behind the explosion. Noboa said this week that his government asks the U.S. for help "every day" as Ecuador seeks to choke off a drug trade that has fueled years of violence and transformed the once relatively peaceful South American nation into a key front in the regional fight against organized crime. Kury said Ecuador and other countries in the region need more than funding from Washington as criminal groups increasingly operate across national borders. "Our countries in Latin America have the problem that we need support," Kury said. "We need not only monetary support but also intelligence, technical cooperation." "That’s why we have the Shield of the Americas," he added, pointing to the U.S.-led regional initiative against cartels. "I think that the whole Latin American continent should work together." The growing relationship extends beyond the cartel fight: Ecuador has also agreed to accept some third-country nationals deported from the U.S., part of the Trump administration’s effort to enlist regional partners in carrying out its immigration agenda. Kury told Fox News Digital there are limits and "explicit rules" governing the arrangement, describing Ecuador as a temporary stop rather than the final destination for those sent there. "The deported people come to Ecuador for a few hours, one day, two days, and they are then deported back to their country of origin," Kury said. "So it’s the way to cooperate, and that’s how we support each other, each country." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kury emphasized that Quito wants the expanding relationship with Washington to translate into greater U.S. investment and trade in Ecuador. "The United States is the main trade partner of Ecuador," he said, pointing to opportunities for American investment in mining, oil and gas, energy, tourism and agriculture. "We look not only [for] cooperation in the security side, but we also look to build more jobs in our country, to bring investment from the United States." The U.S. is Ecuador’s largest trading partner, with U.S. exports to the country totaling $7.7 billion in 2024 and accounting for 28% of Ecuador’s imports, according to the Commerce Department. Ecuador uses the U.S. dollar as its currency but does not have a free trade agreement with Washington.
