title: 'She-Hulk' star slams Tom Selleck, Michael Jordan as 'cowardly' for avoiding political talk
description: Actress Tatiana Maslany called Tom Selleck and Michael Jordan "cowardly" for not using their celebrity platforms to speak out on political issues today.
content: "She-Hulk" star Tatiana Maslany accused celebrities like Tom Selleck and Michael Jordan on Monday of behaving "cowardly" for not using their fame to push politics. Joining Mehdi Hasan on his podcast "We're Not Kidding with Mehdi & Friends," the Marvel TV actress was praised for her past support for the "Free Palestine" movement and accusing Israel of committing a "genocide" in Gaza. Maslany said that she believed it was her job as an artist to address political issues. "To me, artists are like mirrors to the world, to society," Maslany said. "We have to name things, whether it's emotional mirroring to people the human experience or it's speaking out or it's naming something. It's like such an important, intrinsic part of our job." MS RACHEL SAYS BACKLASH OVER HER GAZA POSTS 'DOESN'T FAZE' HER AS SHE CALLS OUT CELEBRITY SILENCE Hasan then asked what she thought about other celebrities staying silent on political issues, referencing a recent CNN interview with "Blue Bloods" and "Magnum P.I." actor Tom Selleck where he declined to discuss politics or NBA star Michael Jordan's famous "Republicans buy sneakers too" statement. "But all of it is political. Everything is political," Maslany responded. "All entertainment is political because it has a viewpoint and it has a perspective. It has visual representation of the world we live in or the kinds of things that are funny or acceptable or the ways that people relate to each other. It's all about inter-person, like there's no disconnect in my mind and to me, those are two very rich men who stand to lose a lot if they stand up for something." Hasan agreed with Maslany that celebrities were more concerned about "fewer opportunities to make money" by dabbling in political discussion, a sentiment Maslany called "bizarre" and "cowardly." DOLLY PARTON REFUSED TO PICK POLITICAL SIDES FOR DECADES: ‘I’M NOT IN POLITICS, I’M AN ENTERTAINER’ "Art should destabilize people, too. I'm not thinking, like Tom Selleck's going like ‘Magnum P.I. should really disturb people on a core level.' But like, art moves people, whether that's in like a shock way, a laughter way, all of it. It's a communication with the world ... It's such a bizarre mentality. It's so cowardly," Maslany said. title: ‘Rocky IV’ star Dolph Lundgren says he planned his own funeral during brutal cancer battle
description: Dolph Lundgren reveals in his new memoir "Fights Worth Fighting" that he planned his own funeral during his nearly decade-long cancer battle.
content: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255). Dolph Lundgren was preparing to die. The Swedish actor, who famously played Soviet boxer Ivan Drago in "Rocky IV," has written a new memoir, "Fights Worth Fighting: Finding Strength in Struggle." In it, the 68-year-old details his grueling journey with cancer. ‘ROCKY’ STAR DOLPH LUNDGREN SWEARS BY THIS SECRET FOR STRONG MARRIAGE Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links. The star was diagnosed in 2015 after doctors found a cancerous tumor in his kidney. Lundgren had surgery to remove the tumor and continued appearing in movies like "Creed II" and "Aquaman." After remaining cancer-free for five years, doctors discovered more tumors in 2020. He later learned the cancer had spread to his liver, both lungs, spine and in and around his left kidney. "I had a lot of difficult conversations with myself," Lundgren told Fox News Digital. "I definitely had a few tough ones. Of course, as most older men do, you do estate planning. You plan your will and who's going to get what. But in this case, it was around the corner. It was something I had to plan a little more in detail, like funerals and trying to figure out where I would be, what would be better for my family. Planning your own funeral is kind of a saying, but I literally was doing that. That was tough." WATCH: DOLPH LUNDGREN OPENS UP ABOUT CANCER BATTLE, BECOMING US CITIZEN IN ‘FIGHTS WORTH FIGHTING’ During that time, Lundgren said he considered ending his life. "At some point, which was even harder, I started thinking, 'Do I really want to be in bed weighing 60 pounds and having people come and see me like that? Or should I just end it myself?'" Lundgren said. "I started considering that. I spoke to my brother. We made a deal, and he would help me out if it came to that, if I made that decision. But it was a tough conversation." In the book, Lundgren wrote, "When I was deep into the cancer treatments and thinking about the possibility of killing myself, my brother, Johan, was going to help me, because I didn’t know what kind of condition I might be in once I made that decision. I could be in really bad shape by then and not capable of completing the suicide on my own." "There are countries in Europe, like Switzerland, that permit legal suicide for people who are terminally ill, but I still might have needed someone there to help me," he continued. "Johan and I talked about it, but once I met Dr. Drakaki and began feeling a little better, it never went any further than that." Lundgren’s longtime friend Johan Pramell also said in the memoir that the star "wanted to go out in glory like a Viking because he didn't want people to have to watch him suffer or fade away." Medical aid in dying is not synonymous with euthanasia, according to the Online Journal of Issues in Nursing. The journal states that laws allowing medical aid in dying permit eligible adults with terminal illnesses to self-administer medication when certain criteria are met. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Euthanasia, which is not legal in the United States, occurs when someone other than the patient administers medication with the intent of hastening the patient’s death, the journal states. According to Dignity in Dying, a U.K.-based advocacy organization, 10 countries in Europe have laws that allow people experiencing "unbearable suffering" to access assisted dying. But one thing was certain — Lundgren wasn't ready to die. "I have a certain discipline, a fighter's heart, since I was a kid," he told Fox News Digital. "I think that was helpful. I may have had these thoughts, but the other side of me wants to go another round to see what happens. Maybe the other guy will drop. You never know. I think that's a part of it." "But also, I believe being in good physical shape helped me, and continuing to work out through the whole thing," he said. "As much as I could, I would stay physically active. And then I was lucky to have my wife, who was very supportive, and my daughters." "They're the ones that kept me going by just their sheer presence," he added. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS At one point, a doctor in the U.K. told Lundgren he likely had two or three years left to live. Lundgren wrote in his memoir that he believed, based on the doctor's tone, his prognosis could have been closer to one or two years. After returning to Los Angeles, Lundgren sought a second opinion from Dr. Alexandra Drakaki, an oncologist at UCLA Health, whom he credited with saving his life. "At this point, I was depressed and had almost given up all hope," he wrote. According to the memoir, Drakaki determined that his cancer had been misdiagnosed, leading to a different treatment approach. "What she found was that my 'kidney cancer' cells had a mutation that is fairly common in lung cancer," he wrote. "That's why the medications I had been given for the past two years weren't working." After Lundgren went public with his cancer battle, one heavyweight stood in his corner: Sylvester Stallone. "Stallone and I have a long history, a good, long relationship together," he said. "We've known each other for 40 years. We've made six films together over that period. He went from being a mentor, a boss on set, director, producer. I was just a new kid on the block. And then slowly, we moved together and became more equals, I would say, two older guys who've been in the business a long time. And he has three daughters, I have two, and we share that as well." "When I got sick, he reached out to me," Lundgren said. "It was unexpected because he was the first one, actually, who reached out of everybody, even before some of my family, when it came out. And he was very emotional about it. It touched me. And that was another side of him that I'd never seen. Since then, we've been very close friends, even closer than before." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE In November 2024, Lundgren announced he was cancer-free. In his memoir, he reflects on whether performance-enhancing drugs may have played a role in his cancer battle. Lundgren wrote that he used anabolic steroids and other performance-enhancing drugs on and off from 1986 to 1996 while preparing for physically demanding movie roles. While he stressed that there is "no conclusive evidence" the drugs caused his cancer, he acknowledged they "might have helped cause" it, adding that he could not say for certain. "I wanted to be candid about my past and what I've been through," Lundgren explained. "And I think nobody knows what steroids and other performance-enhancing drugs do to us. The data is not conclusive. And I always thought it could not help me in my medical situation. I wanted to express a caution to people, to other young men, who may decide to try it, that it's not without risk." "I try to forgive and let go of everything from my past," he said. "That's very important to me. So, I don't blame myself. I was younger. I wasn't as smart as I am now. And I had pressures from the business. Is it really good for you? I doubt it. I really do." title: Americans lost over $20 billion to one type of crime. Here’s how we can fight it
description: Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet scams in 2025, with social media fraud costs eight times higher than 2020, FBI data reveals.
content: Almost all kinds of crime, from homicide to car theft, are down, according to the latest FBI data. That’s great news, but one type of less-reported crime is up — way up. Americans reported losing $20.9 billion to internet-enabled crime in 2025, 26% higher than the year before and the highest figure ever recorded by the FBI. Folks over 60 reported $7.7 billion of it, averaging $38,500 apiece. The real toll is even higher, since the Federal Trade Commission notes that most victims never make a report. It’s clear more needs to be done to protect Americans from these crimes. But many of the losses aren’t hacks where a firewall was breached or a password stolen. They’re scams where victims are persuaded to voluntarily send money to overseas bad actors. That’s an important distinction because a transfer that the customer has been convinced to make looks to every automated system in the chain like a legitimate one. CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY The fact that the money leaves the country should also inform government’s response. Treasury estimates Americans lost at least $10 billion in 2024 to scam operations in Southeast Asia, a 66% increase. These are sophisticated operations in Burma, Cambodia and Laos, many staffed by trafficked workers held in debt bondage or via violence. Social media has shifted these scams into overdrive. The FTC reports scams originating on social platforms cost Americans $2.1 billion last year, eight times the 2020 figure, and more than any other contact method. Sadly, artificial intelligence (AI) is being utilized by these thieves so that they no longer need to have English proficiency or a real photograph. AI VOICE SCAMS CAN CLONE YOUR FAMILY’S VOICE Washington’s reflex for years was to try to force domestic institutions to cover the costs. In December 2024, the outgoing Biden Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued the operator of the Zelle payment network and three of its largest participating banks over scam losses. The suit was dismissed with prejudice three months later, which was the right outcome. American banks are already the most active force in the fight against both fraud and scams. Those institutions run real-time risk scoring on outbound payments, warn customers mid-transaction when money is headed to a new recipient and block transfers that trip their models — often while a customer insists the nice man from "the fraud department" is legitimate. NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS Banks have, at great expense, already proven to be key partners with law enforcement. Juniper Research estimates financial institutions spent roughly $21 billion on fraud prevention in 2025. Because of banks’ coordinated efforts with law enforcement, the FBI’s Financial Fraud Kill Chain froze $679 million of $1.16 billion in attempted theft last year. Further crackdowns on thieves cannot come from banks alone. Scams today begin long before the money transfer. Sophisticated scammers engage via social media, calls, texts and emails to establish rapport and manipulate victims. These criminals trick consumers, sometimes for an extended time and while impersonating a loved one, then banks only see the last step. A defense that begins at the payment screen is insufficient. Meanwhile, reimbursement mandates would raise the cost of banking and payment services on which tens of millions of households depend while leaving foreign criminals with their stolen funds to carry out more illicit activities against Americans. The thieves only care if their online wallets are frozen and bosses are indicted, not if banks get stuck with the tab. Fortunately, the source-focused approach has shown progress. In October, the U.S. and U.K. jointly sanctioned 146 individuals and entities tied to Cambodia’s Prince Group, DOJ indicted its chairman, and prosecutors moved to seize 127,271 Bitcoin — billions of dollars’ worth, the largest forfeiture in Justice Department history. The Scam Center Strike Force has seized over $401 million for return to victims, and the FBI’s Operation Level Up has warned more than 8,000 Americans mid-scam. FBI SEIZES RECORD-SETTING $8 BILLION IN CRYPTOCURRENCY AMID INTERCONTINENTAL 'SCAM COMPOUND' CRACKDOWN But today’s temporary measures enacted by executive orders need to be made permanent via statute, and private-sector partnerships expanded. Collaboration requires intelligence sharing while protecting customer privacy. Juniper Research estimates financial institutions spent roughly $21 billion on fraud prevention in 2025. Because of banks’ coordinated efforts with law enforcement, the FBI’s Financial Fraud Kill Chain froze $679 million of $1.16 billion in attempted theft last year. Joint analytics between telecommunications, social media, technology and banking firms with Treasury and FBI data would provide a network map no institution can see alone. Additionally, safe harbor clarifications would mean flagging suspicious activity isn’t itself a legal risk. WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE Scam syndicates should also be designated as terrorist organizations where they qualify, exposing their financiers to material-support charges and any foreign bank touching the money to secondary sanctions. Meanwhile, the State Department should attach diplomatic costs to hosting scam compounds. On the home front, telecom, tech and social media firms have a civic responsibility to American citizens to work more with Treasury, FTC and FCC in stopping criminals from preying on consumers. A basic first step for these companies is taking down fraudulent ads, instead of earning revenue from them at the expense of innocent consumers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The best results will come from stopping criminals before they’re able to communicate with innocent Americans, alongside a source-focused strategy that attacks where the money goes. The thief is not in Charlotte or San Francisco but in a compound on another continent. Until that thief is punished, there’s no incentive for the scams to stop, and Americans will keep paying, one grandmother’s savings at a time. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM E.J. ANTONI

title: Texas triple murderer uses last words before execution to send message to death row inmates
description: Ker'Sean Ramey received lethal injection at Huntsville prison, one week after accomplice LeJames Norman was executed for the same triple killing.
content: A man convicted of murdering three people in their apartment while searching for drugs to steal was executed in Texas on Wednesday evening, a week after his accomplice was put to death for the same killings. Ker'Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville and was pronounced dead at 6:34 p.m. CDT, The Associated Press reported. In the execution chamber, a prison chaplain rested his hand on Ramey's shoulder before leading him in a brief prayer. The warden then asked Ramey if he had any last words, the AP reported. Ramey praised God and thanked his friends, family and fellow death row inmates, whom he called his brothers. ARIZONA EXECUTES MAN WHO KILLED VICTIM BY DOUSING HIM IN GASOLINE AND SETTING HIM ON FIRE IN 2002 ATTACK "To the brothers on Texas death row that grew up with me, that poured into me and showed what it means to be a man, because I came in young, and didn’t understand what manhood was... to you brothers... I greatly appreciate you," Ramey said moments before the injection was prepared. As the pentobarbital took effect, Ramey took a deep breath, sputtered and began snoring. After 10 loud snores and two that were barely audible, he went still. He was pronounced dead 14 minutes after the injection was first administered. Ramey became the sixth inmate executed in Texas this year, with the state set to carry out three more lethal injections over the next two months. In January 2007, Ramey was convicted and sentenced to death for the August 2005 shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, at a home they shared in Edna, a small rural city about 100 miles southwest of Houston. 74-YEAR-OLD BECOMES FLORIDA'S OLDEST INMATE EXECUTED AFTER 1982 KILLING OF TEEN LeJames Norman, Ramey's accomplice, lived across the street from the house and the two came to believe there was cocaine there, according to court records. On Aug. 24, 2005, the men walked over to the home while wearing masks and knocked on the door. After Lopez answered the door, they forced their way inside, records show. After finding no drugs, the two men fatally shot Lopez, then killed Peacock and Roberts when they arrived at the home. Before fleeing for good, Ramey returned and shot the victims again to ensure they were dead, according to court documents. Norman was executed on Sept. 16 at the Huntsville prison, where all executions are carried out in Texas. MANHATTAN PROSTITUTE PLEADS GUILTY TO KILLING 3 MEN WITH FENTANYL-LACED DRUGS IN ROBBERY SCHEME Hours before Ramey was put to death, the Supreme Court rejected his final appeal. Ramey's attorneys argued jurors never heard mitigating evidence about his upbringing, including that he endured physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty. State prosecutors urged the Supreme Court to reject the appeal, calling it "meritless" and arguing the record showed Ramey had exhibited an escalating pattern of criminal behavior. Norman was arrested about five months after the killings while attempting to re-enter the United States from Mexico, where he had fled. During Ramey's January 2007 trial, Norman testified that both men took part in the shootings, while Ramey's attorneys argued Norman was solely responsible. Norman pleaded guilty to capital murder and was sentenced to death in December 2008. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Lane Kiffin suggests Ole Miss broke rules with in-stadium music during LSU's loss to Rebels

title: Federal appeals court deals blow to Trump deportation agenda
description: The First Circuit formally struck down President Donald Trump's third-party country deportation policy after ICE attempted to remove a Peruvian migrant to Ghana this week.
content: A federal appeals court formally struck down the Trump administration's current format for deporting illegal immigrants to third-party countries on Tuesday. The Court of Appeals for the First Circuit issued a ruling last week that endorsed a lower court order that Immigration and Customs Enforcement must allow migrants a meaningful chance to claim they would be endangered if deported to a third-party country. This week, however, ICE officials attempted to move forward with deporting at least one migrant, who originally hails from Peru, to Ghana. LIBERIA AGREES TO ACCEPT 1,200 THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTEES FROM US WITHIN A YEAR The Trump administration has repeatedly used third-party countries for deportations to execute removal orders on migrants who claim they would be tortured if returned to their country of origin. ICE argued the Peruvian migrant, identified as John Doe, could still be removed because the First Circuit had not formally issued a mandate striking down the policy, according to The American Prospect. TRUMP PLANS TO DEPORT IRANIANS TO VIOLENCE-PLAGUED CENTRAL AFRICAN NATION IN NEW DEAL When asked for a clarification this week, the First Circuit formally issued that mandate, striking down a stay that had allowed third-party deportations to continue while the case was being litigated in higher courts. "Consistent with this court's September 18, 2026, Judgment, the March 16, 2026, stay pending appeal is dissolved," the appeals court wrote in a brief order on Wednesday. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT The First Circuit's ruling upheld a February 2026 decision from Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, who contended that the third-party deportations violated migrants' due process rights because it could send them to unfamiliar or dangerous countries without their knowledge. First Circuit Judge Seth Aframe, one of two Biden appointees on a three-judge panel that handed down last week's ruling, argued that Murphy was "sensible" to require DHS to allow migrants a "meaningful" chance to raise concerns about a country to which they could be deported. title: The secret list that tells scammers you're an easy target
description: Epsilon Data Management's "opportunity seeker" lists helped scammers target millions of older Americans, DOJ court filings reveal in detail.
content: Somewhere in a marketing database, something you did years ago could still be helping a company decide what you might respond to next. Maybe you entered a sweepstakes or signed up for a business seminar. That kind of response can become valuable data. Federal court records show just how far that can go. In a case involving data broker Epsilon Data Management, employees had a name for people targeted by certain solicitations: "opportunity seekers." Those opportunity seeker lists became especially valuable when they reached people running fraud schemes. And as you'll see, the idea of sorting people based on what they are likely to respond to has not disappeared. HOW SWEEPSTAKES ENTRY DATA CAN REACH SCAMMERS What opportunity seeker lists actually mean "Opportunity seeker" sounds like harmless marketing jargon. But in the Epsilon case, the Department of Justice (DOJ) showed how that label was being used inside a business unit that worked with fraudulent clients. According to Epsilon's deferred prosecution agreement, the company's clients included businesses sending deceptive solicitations involving sweepstakes, astrology, auto warranties, dietary supplements and government grants. Epsilon employees called the people targeted by those offers "opportunity seekers" and referred to the clients sending them as "opportunistic." The court filing also says those opportunity seekers frequently came from the same group: older and vulnerable Americans. Then there was the data behind the label. DOJ says Epsilon used transactional data and algorithms to identify "responsive buyers," or people most likely to respond to certain offers. Its database covered about 100 million U.S. households. Think about what that means. If you responded to one offer, that response could become a signal that you might respond to another. In the hands of a fraudster, that kind of information can make it much easier to decide who to target first. This went far beyond one company Epsilon eventually agreed to pay $150 million, including $22.5 million in criminal penalties and $127.5 million for victim compensation. Two former Epsilon employees, Robert Reger and David Lytle, were later convicted. A federal judge sentenced Reger to 10 years in prison and Lytle to four years. According to the DOJ, they sold nearly 100 lists of names and addresses to one fraudulent client. That client used the information in a scheme that defrauded more than 218,000 people out of more than $23.7 million. Even more alarming, DOJ says more than 12,000 people were defrauded by that single scheme more than 20 times each. Other cases followed. KBM Group entered a deferred prosecution agreement requiring a $33.5 million victim compensation payment and an $8.5 million criminal fine. DOJ says employees sold data tied to millions of Americans to more than a dozen clients they knew were engaged in fraudulent mass-mailing schemes. Macromark, a Connecticut direct-mail services company, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud. The company admitted that lists it provided to fraudulent clients resulted in at least $9.5 million in losses. Wiland Inc. later entered a non-prosecution agreement with DOJ that included $4.4 million in victim compensation over data sold to operators of fraudulent schemes. By June 2025, DOJ said its Consumer Data Victim Compensation Fund had returned more than $129 million to more than 100,000 victims across the country. A 2026 case shows this playbook is still alive It would be easy to look at the earlier cases and think this was an old direct-mail problem. It wasn't. In May 2026, a federal judge sentenced Troy Murray of North Carolina to 121 months in prison after he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. DOJ says Murray collected and sold lists containing names, phone numbers, home addresses and, in some cases, ages and email addresses of older Americans. His customers included people in Jamaica running lottery fraud schemes. And the scale was huge. From 2016 through 2023, DOJ says Murray sent scammers at least 22,000 lead lists containing information on more than 7 million older Americans. Those lists typically sold for $500 for 100 to 300 names. DOJ says Murray made more than $5.2 million while victims lost more than $9.5 million. That is what makes these lists so valuable to scammers. They do not have to spend time figuring out who might pick up the phone or respond to an offer. Someone has already handed them a list of people to try first. WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE The same kind of targeting is still sold as marketing These kinds of marketing lists are legal and can be used for legitimate advertising. Just because a list is for sale does not mean the company selling it or the company buying it is doing anything wrong. But the way some of these lists are described today sounds very familiar. As of September 2026, Geon Media advertises a list called "Prime Opportunity Seekers - Buyers Only!" It includes 397,532 names and focuses on people who purchased business opportunities after responding to marketing campaigns. Marketers can narrow that list even further using details such as age, income, net worth and location. Geon also requires buyers to provide a sample mail piece. NextMark advertises a list called "Sweeps Winners Only" made up of people who recently responded to sweepstakes offers. Its listing describes that audience as "highly impulsive" and promotes the list for sweepstakes, lotteries, credit cards and other offers. Exact Data also advertises categories with names including "Sweepstakes Opportunity Purchasers" and "Gambling, Lottery, and Sweepstakes Enthusiasts." Its listings were updated in September 2026. None of that proves fraud. What it does show is how valuable your past behavior can be. Respond to the right kind of offer, and that response can become a data point that helps someone decide what to put in front of you next. Why your response history can be so valuable For a scammer, finding someone willing to respond can be half the battle. Calling or emailing random people takes time. A list of people who have already responded to certain offers gives them a much better place to start. That is what made Epsilon's data so valuable. DOJ says the company's algorithms could predict which people were most likely to respond to certain mailings. If you had responded before, that behavior could become another clue about what might get your attention next. And there is a lot of money on the line. The FBI says people over 60 filed more than 201,000 complaints in 2025 and reported more than $7.7 billion in losses. The FBI does not say how many of those people were targeted through marketing or lead lists, so we cannot say those lists caused those losses. But the DOJ cases show something important: scammers have used targeted lists to help find people they believe are more likely to respond. That is why something as simple as entering a sweepstakes or responding to an offer can be more valuable than you might think. The response itself can become another piece of data about you. 6 steps to make yourself harder to target You probably cannot find every private marketing database that contains your name. However, you can reduce the information available about you and become much more selective about what you hand over going forward. 1) Search for yourself online Start with your full name. Then search your phone number and home address. Pay attention to people-search sites displaying your address, age, relatives, phone numbers or email addresses. If you find a profile, look for the site's opt-out or removal process. The FTC says you can request removal from people-search sites yourself for free, although you may need to repeat the process if your information appears again later. 2) Think twice before entering sweepstakes and promotions A legitimate contest can still collect information for marketing. Before entering, read the privacy policy and official rules. Look for language explaining whether your information can be shared with advertisers or marketing partners. The FTC specifically warns that contest promoters may sell information to advertisers, which can lead to more targeted advertising, promotional mail, calls and spam. 3) Skip optional information If an entry form asks for information that seems unrelated to the promotion, stop and ask why it needs it. Avoid handing over extra details simply because a box appears on a form. Also watch for prechecked boxes giving permission for additional marketing. Every unnecessary piece of information you share gives a company one more data point that can potentially be added to your profile. 4) Use a separate email address for promotions Consider creating an email address or alias used only for contests, loyalty programs and promotional offers. That keeps your primary email address out of some marketing databases and makes unexpected prize messages easier to spot. If someone contacts your main email account claiming you won a contest you entered with a different address, that alone should raise questions. 5) Never pay to collect a prize This one is simple. Real prizes are free. The FTC says anyone demanding taxes, processing fees, shipping charges or other payments before releasing a prize is running a scam. Also, never provide your bank account, credit card or Social Security number to claim a prize. If you are unsure whether an offer is real, find the company's official contact information yourself rather than calling a number in the letter, text or email. 6) Report fraud quickly if someone gets you If you sent money or personal information to a scammer, act quickly. Contact your bank or payment provider first if money changed hands. Report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov . If the scam came through the mail, you can also report it to the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. If someone used your personal information, IdentityTheft.gov can walk you through recovery steps. For anyone age 60 or older, the DOJ's National Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-FRAUD-11 (1-833-372-8311) offers free help Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern. DOJ says reporting certain financial losses quickly can improve the chances of recovering money, although recovery cannot be guaranteed. What a personal data scan can and cannot tell you There is no public search box that will show you every private marketing category attached to your name. A people-search or data-broker scan also cannot tell you whether your name appears on one of the specific "opportunity seeker" or criminal lead lists described above. And no data removal service can pull information back once criminals already have it. What a scan can do is show you where personal details such as your name, address or phone number appear across covered people-search and data-broker sites. From there, you can start reducing that exposure. If the scan finds your information, you have two options. You can contact sites yourself and submit opt-out requests, or you can use a service that handles much of that work for you. How a data removal service can help A data removal service can automatically send removal requests to hundreds of covered data brokers and people-search sites. Some plans also let you request removals from additional websites that fall outside the standard automated coverage. It is worth knowing the limits too. Some private data-broker databases cannot be scanned directly. Instead, removal requests are sent to brokers that may hold your information. These services also cannot remove certain government records, court records or information already circulating in criminal databases. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. Kurt's key takeaways For me, the biggest takeaway here is that scammers do not always have to figure out who might respond. Sometimes, someone else has already done that work for them. The Epsilon case showed how marketing data and algorithms could identify people likely to respond to certain offers. DOJ says those "opportunity seekers" frequently included older and vulnerable Americans. And this problem has not been confined to old direct-mail cases. In 2026, a federal judge sentenced a man who DOJ says sold more than 22,000 lead lists containing information on over 7 million older Americans to lottery scammers. At the same time, legitimate marketers still sell highly specific lists based on things like sweepstakes responses and interest in business opportunities. That does not make those lists fraudulent. It does show just how much our past behavior can say about what we may respond to next. You may never know every list that has your name on it. But you can stop handing out unnecessary information, remove exposed personal data where possible and slow down whenever an unexpected offer lands in front of you. Should companies be able to sell lists built around how likely someone is to respond to money-making or sweepstakes offers, especially when age and financial information can also be used for targeting? title: Caleb Williams' repost dismissed antisemitic incident involving Dave Portnoy – and almost no one cares
description: Caleb Williams reposted a comment on X that dismissed an antisemitic incident involving Dave Portnoy, raising questions about double standards in sports.
content: Most people — including Bears quarterback Caleb Williams — probably didn't think much of it. To them, it's just a repost on X that went after a common target for keyboard warriors. But what if it's more than that? Earlier in the week, Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy mocked Williams, calling him a "thespian" after he was carted off the field for what was revealed to be a hamstring strain. Portnoy said the emotion Williams displayed was akin to what you'd see for a season-ending injury such as an ACL tear, not a tweak that's put him on a week-to-week basis. CALEB WILLIAMS AVOIDS MAJOR HAMSTRING INJURY AS MRI REVEALS A STRAIN BUT NO TEAR AFTER VIKINGS GAME SCARE Williams didn't take too kindly to the call-out, and went after Dave on X — using not his own words but those of a poster named Daemar. ''The guy that had a kid arrested and expelled from school for throwing pennies at him is calling someone else soft LMFAOOOOOO," Daemar said of Portnoy. Williams reposted the comment — which garnered 1.3 million views and 35K likes — to little media or fan criticism. Except ... Daemar was running cover for a clear antisemite. Here's a more thorough explanation. In the fall of 2025, Mississippi State student Patrick McClintock was caught on camera yelling "F—k the Jews!" before tossing coins at Portnoy, who's Jewish. This wasn't a random gesture. The American Jewish Committee made note that such coin-tossing is an "age-old antisemitic trope about Jews and greed." Portnoy posted a video of the affair and condemned the act — calling the student a "loser" while decrying an uptick in his personal antisemitic experiences. As Outkick's Armando Salguero pointed out, McClintock was later arrested independently for disturbing the peace. In other words, Portnoy blasted an antisemite in a time when antisemitism is on the clear rise. Sorry, but that does not disqualify you from ridiculing a quarterback for being melodramatic. REPORTER FOR THE ATHLETIC FUMES OVER ARCH MANNING, SILENT ON JOSH JACOBS' ALLEGED VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMAN Portnoy has since responded to Williams' repost by accusing him of spreading misinformation about him. And though he seemed to make a peace offering by saying "I will not hold this against Caleb...I'm rooting for him and all of Chicago," one has to wonder what the response would have been like if the repost had been in a different context. For instance, if there had been a highly publicized anti-Black incident on a college campus, I doubt reposting an X user dismissing the affair would be treated so warmly by social media users. If there had been a homophobic or anti-woman gesture, there likely would have been a media uproar if a prominent athlete condoned it. Look what happened to Texas quarterback Arch Manning when he laughed at an AI meme involving ESPN's Holly Rowe getting slapped by Steve Sarkisian. Williams probably didn't know exactly what he was reposting, and giving this matter any extra attention doesn't help the team or the league. It's also predictable that much of the public seems to side with Williams on this issue. They probably don't know the full extent of what Portnoy — a highly polarizing figure — endured in Starkville that day. But it is noteworthy how different types of discrimination are treated. title: As expected, media mocks Jaxson Dart injury because he dared to introduce Trump on stage
description: Jaxson Dart's season-ending knee injury sparked calls to sign Colin Kaepernick and mockery tied to his appearance with Trump at a New York event.
content: When New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a season-ending knee injury this week, we knew there'd be two reactions from the overwhelmingly liberal sports media. First, they'd call for the Giants to sign Colin Kaepernick. They do it whenever an NFL team loses a quarterback, even though Kaepernick has not played professional football in a decade. Second, they'd mock Dart’s injury because he made headlines in May by introducing President Donald Trump at a New York City event. Both reactions materialized almost immediately. DAN LE BATARD DEMANDS THE MEDIA MAKE JAXSON DART 'UNCOMFORTABLE' FOR INTRODUCING TRUMP Sports blogger Mike Florio was the first to urge the Giants to sign Kaepernick. "The f—–g Trump curse strikes again," wrote Tara Setmayer, a former GOP communications director on Capitol Hill and CNN commentator, about Dart’s injury on X. Film and TV critic John Rocha shared a photo of Trump and Dart’s interaction, writing, "Everything he touches, y'all. Everything he touches..." Ron Filipkowski, the partisan editor of the anti-Trump outlet MeidasTouch, claimed he had predicted Dart’s injury after the quarterback appeared with Trump. "This was the moment I decided not to draft Dart in fantasy football. He had no chance this season after the Trump Curse," he wrote above a clip of Dart and Trump. The comment section resembles a fringe political message board, with readers celebrating the injury, asking whether Dart is "vaxxed" and claiming that he deserves this because he supported Trump. Interestingly, we do not know whether Dart is a Trump supporter. Yes, he introduced Trump at an event. But introducing the sitting president is not, on its face, a political statement. The event also took place in the city where Dart plays quarterback. For all we know, Dart would have accepted the same opportunity if a Democrat were in the White House. Despite what the legacy media tells you, some Americans would welcome the chance to associate with the president regardless of their political views. In fact, we suspect most Americans fall into that category. That said, we can probably deduce that Dart doesn't consider Trump a Nazi. And that is enough for some in the media to call him "MAGA" and poke fun at his injury. There's a trend. In 2020, then-ESPN commentator Mark Jones shared posts mocking 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa after Bosa suffered a serious knee injury. This type of behavior reflects how many Americans suffering from Trump Derangement Syndrome (TDS) react when something awful happens to a Trump voter or someone who does not express open disdain for the president. title: People are ditching their vapes only to pick up another surprising habit
description: E-cigarettes promised a clean off-ramp from smoking, but severe vape withdrawal is pushing former smokers back to traditional cigarettes, experts warn.
content: E-cigarettes have long been used as an alternative to traditional smoking, but public health data suggests some adults trying to quit vaping are turning back to cigarettes. Recent data from Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) shows that some smokers and dual users who stop vaping opt for traditional tobacco products instead, a shift that addiction specialists say may be driven by nicotine dependence and the challenges of withdrawal. Trent Carter, a board-certified nurse practitioner and CEO of Renew Health — a behavioral and mental health practice based in New Mexico — said that while the shift from vapes back to cigarettes might seem counterintuitive, there are behavioral reasons some users make the switch. SINGLE WORKOUT CUTS CRAVINGS, OFFERING NEW HOPE FOR SMOKERS TRYING TO QUIT "Vaping can become constant throughout the day, whereas a cigarette is more of a defined episode," Carter told Fox News Digital. "Subconsciously, you may not even realize that you’re constantly vaping throughout the day, whereas cigarettes you feel like you're more in control because you have to think about it. You [have] to go outside, you [have] to light it up." Unlike cigarettes, vaping can be done throughout the day and often indoors. That easy access can lead to more nicotine use and reinforce the hand-to-mouth habit, according to the expert. High potency, severe withdrawal E-cigarettes can be highly addictive because of the way they deliver nicotine. Many vaping devices use highly concentrated nicotine salts, allowing users to inhale large doses with each puff compared to traditional cigarettes. "If you're consuming a large amount with every single puff ... it's going to be harder to stop when compared to a lower dose," Carter said. SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA Nicotine dependence alters brain chemistry by stimulating neurotransmitters like dopamine that govern mood and pleasure, according to Cleveland Clinic. When someone abruptly cuts off high-volume intake, it can trigger rapid withdrawal symptoms, ranging from intense cravings and irritability to severe sleep disturbances and brain fog. Because high-potency vapes drive up physical tolerance, standard quitting aids — like over-the-counter patches or nicotine gum — can sometimes feel inadequate to a user seeking immediate relief. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "While a patch or gum could definitely help with the nicotine cravings, if you're not addressing the behavioral aspect of it, then you're really falling short," Carter said. "You're leaving a huge component of why they may be smoking — whether it's because of anxiety or even insomnia during the day." False sense of security When e-cigarettes first hit the market, early public messaging framed them as a healthier, doctor-approved alternative to smoking, which gave many consumers a false sense of security about how difficult it would be to drop the habit, according to Carter. "If you're being told something is safe or doctor-approved, we tend to feel we're making the right choice," Carter said. "While traditional cigarettes have toxins that e-cigarettes do not, if your daily consumption of nicotine becomes much higher, we find ourselves in a nasty cycle. You got rid of the toxins, but now you're consuming much more nicotine." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The elevated chemical intake carries a physical and mental toll, Carter cautioned. Heavy, uninterrupted nicotine ingestion can trigger blood pressure spikes, elevated heart rates, sleep disruption and heightened anxiety. Breaking the dependency loop For people trying to quit vaping, health providers warn that switching to cigarettes reintroduces harmful toxins, tar and carbon monoxide. Instead of switching between vaping and cigarettes, addiction specialists recommend medically supervised strategies that combine behavioral therapy with gradual nicotine reduction. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The goal shouldn't be to find another way to consume nicotine," Carter said. "The goal should be to treat the dependence itself." "It's not trading one for the other, but finding the underlying cause and addressing that head-on — that's how someone truly takes steps in the right direction." title: Mistress says she gave ‘American Idol’ contestant ultimatum before wife’s killing blew up affair

content: Former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn told his mistress he stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill" his wife and "not go to jail," one of a series of messages read to jurors Thursday in his Ohio murder trial. Alleigha Botner returned to the witness stand for a second day and walked jurors through months of messages in which Flynn allegedly talked repeatedly about wanting Ashley Flynn dead or gone. TEEN PLANNED MIDDLE SCHOOL MASSACRE BEFORE MAKING DEADLY ‘LAST-MINUTE CHOICE’ TO KILL MOM: OFFICIAL Botner later became emotional before reading one of her own messages aloud. "I want to kill her, Caleb," Botner wrote. Flynn allegedly responded: "That makes two of us." Flynn is accused of fatally shooting Ashley in the back of the head inside their home Feb. 16 before staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges. Botner had prefaced the message by telling jurors, "I just wish I didn't say this." In the same August exchange, Flynn allegedly went on to write that he had been "literally trying to find a way to get rid of her, to be rid of her." Botner responded that she was "not asking that you take her life, obviously," but said getting a divorce "would change everything." OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO Botner also testified Flynn once showed her a gun he kept in the center console of his truck, though she could not remember what it looked like. MICROSOFT EXEC'S GRIEVING WIDOW FACES MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING HIS MURDER AS SHE REVEALS EERIE FINAL CALL Asked when she advised Flynn how to delete data from his devices, Botner responded, "Multiple times." "One of them being the night before Ashley was murdered," she testified. Botner also testified that on the night before Ashley's killing, she used ChatGPT to research whether messages documenting the affair could be permanently deleted and sent Flynn screenshots of the results. She told jurors she feared the affair could surface during a divorce and cost her her job. Prosecutors established that Botner sent the screenshots about 5:47 p.m. Feb. 15, hours before Ashley was killed. title: Commanders push back on 'bulls—' viral narrative that they didn't care about Jayden Daniels' elbow injury
description: Dan Quinn says Commanders players were "gutted" after Jayden Daniels' elbow injury, pushing back on viral video showing teammates walking away.
content: You think you saw what happened after Jayden Daniels dislocated his elbow last Sunday, and it was troubling. The Washington Commanders quarterback was on the turf, writhing in pain, and his teammates seemed to simply ignore him. Most simply walked off the field. And it seemed to send the message that they didn't care. COMMANDERS FACE CRITICAL DECISION ON JAYDEN DANIELS' ELBOW AS SPECIALISTS REVIEW MRI RESULTS The Commanders have gotten crushed on social media for the video of players walking away – because it was jarring compared to New York Giants or Green Bay Packers players huddling around teammates when they went down. It suggested Daniels isn't beloved or even respected by teammates. "I'm glad you brought that up because it's just the opposite in fact," coach Dan Quinn said Wednesday. "These guys were absolutely gutted." Quinn said the timing of the injury happening on the final play of the first half and signaling the start of halftime played a major role in the walk-off. "When the half was over, the referees even came and said they can't delay the half and we can't stay on the field," Quinn said. "And they were like, ‘No, I'm staying.’ So it's just the opposite in fact. "They were gutted, they love this guy, and so halftime was hard. It was emotional in that space." The perception of the Washington walk-off may have come from television. The live broadcast went to a commercial at halftime. And ESPN's highlights showed Daniels collapsing to the ground as players walked by him, then cut to him leaving on the cart. But all that missed what happened in the stadium. Multiple players, led by backup quarterback Marcus Mariota, indeed came onto the field as trainers attended to Daniels and eventually called for the cart to take him away. Some of them even returned from the locker room to do it. "It’s bull—- what people are saying," left tackle Brandon Coleman told reporters. "Jay’s our guy and he’s been our guy. There’s no malice behind it." The narrative that the Commanders abandoned their quarterback is actually an excellent study on how social media wields the power to shape opinion, that opinion reaches legacy media, and then can reach into an NFL team's facility. Even when the narrative is basically fake news. JAXSON DART TORE HIS MCL AND MENISCUS REQUIRING SURGERY "We all care for our quarterback," offensive lineman Josh Conerly said. "You can’t go off a simple 10-second clip." Mariota takes over for Daniels at quarterback now while the starter and the team continue to figure out what to do about his injury, with options including season-ending surgery. There's nothing positive about the situation for the team. But Quinn made it clear ahead of time that Mariota is respected and he is confident in the new quarterback. "But with Marcus, he's one that's really in control, has good vision of it, what it is, where to go. You can hear that type of communication with him. title: Team USA golfers welcome Trump’s expected Presidents Cup visit, share pride in representing America
description: Wyndham Clark and Team USA players react to Trump's expected visit to Medinah for the Presidents Cup, sharing personal stories and patriotism.
content: Wyndham Clark is preparing to represent the United States at the 2026 Presidents Cup, with President Donald Trump expected to watch Sunday’s final round in person. "Being an American, having the President of the United States come and watch you play golf is something, as a kid, you don’t ever imagine or fathom happening," Clark told OutKick on Wednesday. "I just think it’s pretty amazing." The PGA Tour, which organizes the Presidents Cup, invited Trump to serve as honorary chairman, and he accepted. Sources familiar with the president’s plans told OutKick that Trump is expected to attend Sunday’s final round at Medinah Country Club. Like the Ryder Cup, the Presidents Cup is a team match-play competition. It pits 12 U.S. golfers against 12 players from countries outside the U.S. and Europe, while the Ryder Cup matches the Americans against Europe. CANADIANS NICK TAYLOR AND COREY CONNERS LAUGH OFF LAKE ONTARIO RENAMING AHEAD OF PRESIDENTS CUP The competition begins Thursday and runs through Sunday. OutKick spoke with several U.S. players Tuesday and Wednesday about representing their country and Trump’s expected visit. For Sam Burns, the conversation also provided an opportunity to talk about something he would like to see more of at home: Americans pulling for each other. "Being an American, I think it’s very important that we do support our president, regardless of your political views," Burns said. "I think if you look at our country now, it seems more divided than ever, and hopefully we can get back to the point where all Americans come together, and we’re all trying to kind of reach the same goal." Burns said he has played golf with Trump a few times, but emphasized that his respect for the presidency extends beyond whoever happens to hold the job. "Anyone who’s the president of this country, I respect that position, obviously," he said. SAM BURNS IS ONE OF AMERICA'S BEST GOLFERS, BUT FAITH, FAMILY AND THE USA MATTER MORE TO HIM THAN GOLF Chris Gotterup had a similar reaction when asked about the visit. "Whoever the president is, if they care enough to come watch us play golf, that’s pretty cool," Gotterup said. "I know we’re excited, and we’re going to go try to put on a good performance for everyone." Wyndham Clark recalls Trump’s 2023 US Open call For Clark, there is already a memorable Trump interaction to look back on. After winning the 2023 U.S. Open, Clark received a congratulatory call from Trump, who was out of office at the time. Clark described it Wednesday as "one of the coolest calls of my life." His first major victory came at Los Angeles Country Club, where he beat Rory McIlroy by one shot. Apparently, Trump had been paying close attention. "He was so complimentary, just saying how good I played. And honestly, it was amazing. He knew every shot," Clark said. "He was like, ‘This up-and-down on this hole, this up-and-down on this hole was amazing.’ And he really said a bunch of nice things." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Patrick Cantlay’s first meeting with Trump goes back even further. He said they met at the 2011 Walker Cup at Royal Aberdeen and have crossed paths several times since. This week, Cantlay hopes the president’s appearance gives the home crowd something else to get excited about. "I think it’d be great to have the president out, and hopefully it gets the crowd going," Cantlay said. "I’m expecting the crowd to be loud and behind us this week, and that’s what makes playing home team events so fun." Xander Schauffele found a slightly different angle. "I’m sure Secret Service wasn’t pumped that he made an early announcement on where he’s going to be, but they’ll do a nice job to keep him safe," Schauffele joked. "It’s awesome that our president loves golf and supports USA." What representing Team USA means to the players For Jacob Bridgeman, representing the United States at this level is something he has wanted for a long time. "This is the highest honor that you can get in all of golf," Bridgeman said. "Playing for the United States is the best thing that any of us can ever ask for, and it’s an honor." Bridgeman said he hoped to see multiple presidents attend and described the prospect of having them rooting for the Americans as making the experience feel "even more patriotic." US PRESIDENTS CUP PLAYERS EXPLAIN HOW CHRISTIAN FAITH BUILDS FRIENDSHIPS AND PUTS GOLF IN PERSPECTIVE Jackson Koivun, meanwhile, welcomed the chance to have teammates again. "I just love playing for Team USA," he said. "It’s always fun when you’re able to put on the red, white and blue and play on a team with guys who are fighting for the same cause." Love of country is even strong enough to get an Alabama guy and an Auburn guy working together. For a few days, anyway. Justin Thomas, who played college golf at Alabama, offered his practice rounds with former Auburn star Koivun as an example when OutKick asked about sports bringing people together. "I’ve been playing a lot of practice rounds with an Auburn kid this week," Thomas said. "I love him to death, but I hope he has a terrible Saturday," Thomas joked, clarifying that he meant the Saturday after Thanksgiving when Auburn and Alabama face each other in the 2026 Iron Bowl. For now, though, they’re wearing the same colors. "We have everybody here pulling for the USA," Thomas said. Schauffele made a similar point about the opportunity international competition gives Americans to cheer together. "If players and people can kind of gather under one flag in a sport, it is pretty awesome," he said. "Luckily, we’re able to do that in golf." These weeks can fly by during a career, he said, and he expects to appreciate them even more when he looks back. Right now, there is a tournament to win. "All of us guys that are on this squad, there’s nothing more we want to do than to go out and win and represent our country well," Burns said. "And that’s the plan this week."

title: Senators press President Trump to release home heating oil reserves amid soaring prices
description: Maine's U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King, Jr., called upon President Donald Trump to release home heating oil reserves to drive prices down.
content: Maine's two U.S. senators, Republican Sen. Susan Collins and independent Sen. title: America's beef supply shrinks as cattle farmer warns 'the numbers are just not here anymore'
description: U.S. beef production fell roughly 800 million pounds in early 2026 as cattle slaughter numbers declined, pushing farmers like Will Harris toward change.
content: Americans are seeing less beef produced domestically as cattle numbers decline, adding pressure to a market already facing high prices. U.S. commercial beef production totaled about 14.4 billion pounds from January through July 2026, down from roughly 15.2 billion pounds during the same period last year, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) data. The number of cattle commercially slaughtered also declined, falling from about 17.5 million during the first seven months of 2025 to 16.2 million during the same period this year, USDA data shows. NFL LEGEND REVEALS WHY EATING 'REAL FOOD' AFTER RETIREMENT LED HIM TO RAISE HIS OWN BEEF Will Harris, a fourth-generation cattle farmer and owner of White Oak Pastures in Bluffton, Georgia, told Fox News Digital that years of financial pressure have contributed to farmers reducing their herds. "Cattle farmers have for so long not made a profit that they have liquidated their herds, and the numbers are just not here anymore," Harris said. Harris said higher cattle prices have not yet led to the kind of expansion among producers that he has seen during previous cycles. "What's different is the higher prices the farmers are getting is not causing them to go back into business," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Starting or expanding a cattle operation can require significant investments in land, equipment and livestock, which Harris said can make it difficult for new producers to enter the industry. "There's so much money involved in owning land and equipment and livestock that it's just very hard for a person who is not producing to say, 'I think I'll start a farm,'" he said. Harris also expressed concern about the amount of beef the U.S. imports and what he sees as increasing dependence on foreign supplies. "What is happening is that the United States is becoming a larger and larger net importer of beef," Harris said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The U.S. both imports and exports beef, with trade patterns influenced by domestic production, consumer demand and global markets, according to USDA data. Harris has experienced a major shift in the way cattle are raised over his decades in the industry. After graduating from the University of Georgia with a degree in animal science in 1976, Harris returned to his family's farm and initially followed conventional farming practices, including the use of chemical fertilizers, antibiotics and growth-promoting technologies. Over time, he said, concerns about the long-term effects of those practices led him to change the way he operated the farm. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "They offered a performance boost in the short run," Harris said. "In the long run, they were literally damaging my land, my farm, my community." The farm now follows what Harris describes as regenerative agriculture, an approach he said is intended to work more closely with natural cycles rather than relying on conventional monoculture practices. For consumers trying to understand how their beef was raised, Harris said labels alone may not always provide all the information. "It's increasingly important that that consumer knows something about the farm that the food is raised on," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Harris encouraged consumers who are interested in how their food is produced to research farms and producers and, when possible, buy closer to home. "I wish that consumers would find a more local producer that they could do business with, they could support to help that guy stay in business," he said. title: Major pro-life group threatens to sue Trump FDA over abortion pill's alleged environmental risks
description: Students for Life of America threatens to sue the Food and Drug Administration, alleging it skipped Endangered Species Act reviews for mifepristone.
content: A leading pro-life organization has formally threatened to sue the Food and Drug Administration, accusing the agency of failing to conduct required environmental testing of the abortion drug mifepristone despite potential risks to the waterways and wildlife. Students for Life of America (SFLA), an anti-abortion advocacy group, filed a notice of intent to sue the FDA on Thursday, hours before Dr. Heidi Overton is scheduled to appear before the Senate for her confirmation hearing to lead the agency. The notice says that after the FDA approved mifepristone in 2000, it never consulted two wildlife protection agencies about the drug's possible harmful effects on federally protected species, which the group argues violated the Endangered Species Act. "We expect these environmental concerns to be taken seriously. I know Dr. Overton is aware of these concerns. Or we expect to see the Trump FDA in court. That's where this will end," SFLA President Kristan Hawkins told Fox News Digital in an interview on Wednesday. PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND Hawkins said the FDA now has 60 days to respond to SFLA's notice before a lawsuit is filed. Prior to the notice, the group had filed 11 citizen petitions to the agency urging action. In response to one of those petitions on Jan. 15, 2025 — five days before President Donald Trump began his second term — the FDA rejected SFLA's legal argument, saying it was not required to consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service before approving mifepristone. The SFLA notice cites six studies, four of which did not examine whether mifepristone was present in environmental water samples, to argue the drug may pose environmental risks warranting further federal review. Among the studies cited is a recent paper published in Issues in Law & Medicine, which reported anti-progesterone activity in water samples from three U.S. cities. HAWLEY URGES DOJ PROBE INTO ABORTION PILL MAKER OVER SAFETY CONCERNS Because mifepristone blocks progesterone receptors — preventing the hormone needed to sustain a pregnancy from doing its job — SFLA argues the findings show the drug has made it into the U.S. water supply. "Where do all the babies go in chemical abortions?" Hawkins said. "If we're talking 600,000 to 700,000 abortions a year being induced with chemical abortion pills, where are they happening? She doesn't go to a facility to complete the abortion. The abortion often takes weeks at home. She is told to go and sit on a toilet to flush." The study, however, did not directly detect mifepristone in the water. Instead, it looked for signs of substances that block progesterone, and the researchers said another compound could have produced the same result. Directly confirming the presence of mifepristone would generally require an analytical chemistry technique capable of identifying the substance itself. FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS Hawkins told Fox News Digital that the legal notice against the FDA is not reliant on one study but rather "rests on the failure of the FDA in 2000 to literally follow the law." "This should be something that unites all Americans, regardless of how you feel about the violence of abortion. I certainly am pro-life, I wanna see abortion ended. But we all want clean drinking water," she said. Hawkins said that message has resonated even with students who disagree with her organization's stance on abortion. SFLA has a strong presence on college campuses, with 1,575 active student groups across nearly half of America's traditional four-year universities. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With new leadership at the FDA on the horizon, Hawkins said her organization is reminding the agency of its responsibilities. "Today, Dr. Heidi Overton will be at the U.S. Senate," Hawkins said. "And we want to be very clear that when she gets to her desk, when she gets confirmed, and she sits down, the first thing she sees on her desk is our notice to intent to sue." "It is high time to hold the abortion industry accountable and to hold our government accountable for upholding our own laws that have been enacted to protect all of us as well as the animals within our country," she added.

title: Our son’s miracle is a testament to prayer and Fulton Sheen’s intercession
description: When Sheen is beatified on September 24, James, accompanied by my husband, me and our other seven children, will carry and present the first-class relic at the ceremony
content: Sixteen years ago, in the middle of the night, in the heart of Illinois, a miracle happened. It didn’t begin as a miracle, of course. The chain of events that would end with a miracle of biblical proportions started with me, laboring at home in the arms of my husband. Unbeknownst to us, our healthy baby boy had a knot in his umbilical cord. That knot tightened during his delivery, cutting off his oxygen supply. When the midwife caught him and placed him in my arms, he was stillborn. For the brief moments I held him, he didn’t cry. He didn’t breathe. He had no pulse. Our son, James Fulton, was taken from my arms and placed on the floor. My midwife and her assistant began CPR. My husband performed an emergency baptism, invoking the saints James was named after. Sitting on the floor, I felt like I was falling out of control. COLTON BURPO DESCRIBES MEETING JESUS AND HEARING ANGELS SING DURING NEAR-DEATH EXPERIENCE In my head, I repeated the name of my baby’s namesake, the late Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen — a Catholic televangelist who converted over 50,000 people during his lifetime and who boasted over 30 million weekly viewers for his Emmy-winning show, Life is Worth Living, which aired in the 1950s. In my moment of desperation, my heart and voice continuously called on Sheen to pray for me. I had no idea how profoundly this prayer would change my life — and the lives of millions of Catholics across America, if not the world. After 20 minutes, an ambulance arrived and took James and my husband to the hospital about 20 minutes away. My husband watched in shock as our tiny son — his cold, blue body hooked up to a heart monitor — lay lifeless and pulseless while every method to restart his heart failed. In a separate ambulance, headed to labor and delivery monitoring, I desperately prayed for the son I just wanted to love and hold. After 20 more minutes, the doctors and nurses finally stopped trying to resuscitate him and were seconds from calling the time of death. 'BLIND SIDE' STAR QUINTON AARON SAYS HE 'SAW JESUS' WHILE IN A COMA AFTER NEAR-FATAL STROKE At that moment, when all attempts had ended, James’ heart started to beat. He had been without a pulse for sixty-one minutes. Even then, everyone feared massive organ failure. The doctors stabilized James and transferred him to the NICU. We were warned that if James lived, his life would be filled with limitations and hardships. We prepared our hearts to love James no matter what. We also prayed for Sheen’s intercession for a miracle. During my pregnancy, we had decided to name James after Sheen and asked for his prayer over the life of our son. It was natural, therefore, to continue to call on him, to ask him to pray without ceasing for our sweet baby James. NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD It took years for the extent of James’ miracle to reveal itself. An MRI at three months showed zero brain damage. As he hit milestone after milestone, it was clear that God had truly restored our son. Independent medical professionals additionally confirmed that there was no medical explanation for James’ survival — let alone the fact that he doesn’t have any complications to this day. I knew in that moment that Sheen had interceded for me and my baby boy. I had no idea then, however, that our little miracle could help Sheen too. Years before, in 2002, Bishop Daniel Jenky opened the cause for canonization for Sheen in his hometown of Peoria. For those who don’t know, Catholic canonizations are multiyear processes the Church undergoes to determine whether an individual is officially a Catholic saint. It involves three stages, the data collection stage before someone is declared venerable, an investigation and miracle to declare someone blessed and a second miracle to declare them a saint. For the past 24 years, Catholics involved in Sheen’s canonization efforts have heavily scrutinized his life and works to ensure he merits the titles of "Venerable," "Blessed," and "Saint." In 2012, the Catholic Church declared Sheen "Venerable" after those responsible for investigating his life concluded that he had demonstrated "heroic virtue." LOST SERMONS FROM ONE OF CHRISTIANITY'S GREATEST SAINTS DISCOVERED AFTER 1,600 YEARS And in 2019, the Catholic Church declared that what happened to my son James was a miracle attributed to Sheen. My son’s first moments of life are the reason that Archbishop Fulton Sheen will be declared "Blessed" in Saint Louis on September 24. Today, James is a handsome teenager, if I do say so myself. He is funny, thoughtful and hardworking. He enjoys music, meteorology and working alongside his dad with the high school football team. He takes his faith seriously and has a personal devotion to Sheen. When Sheen is beatified on September 24, James, accompanied by my husband, me and our other seven children, will carry and present the first-class relic at the ceremony. This honor couldn’t be bestowed on a more grateful family. We hope that sharing James’ story and promoting Sheen’s cause for canonization will inspire more Americans to recognize the glory of God and the beauty of the Catholic faith. Sixteen years ago, in the Heart of Illinois, a miracle happened. People who do not know our family refer to that day as the anniversary of the miracle.
