title: Rand Paul: Politicians should stay out of college sports and let athletes compete freely
description: Sen. Rand Paul argues that politicians, not the NCAA, should decide college sports rules, athlete compensation, transfers and conference membership.
content: The people who oversee the Post Office now want to run college sports ... what could go wrong? The United States Congress has been called upon during the most important moments in American history to make difficult decisions about the future of our country. We have navigated wars, economic downturns and national disasters. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! These are the kinds of nationwide issues that a federal government should address. The Founders never intended for the federal government to usurp the authority of your local school board or your homeowners’ association. I don’t think it ever occurred to them that Congress would one day be charged with dictating the rules for college sports. And yet, with gas at over $4 a gallon, a persistent war with Iran and $40 trillion in debt, the Senate decided the most urgent thing it should do is dictate how college sports are run from Washington. It came to this decision, of course, after acknowledging that government caused the very problems this bill purports to fix. This is the exact scenario the great Harry Browne described when he said government "knows how to break your legs, then hand you a crutch and say, ‘See, if it weren’t for government, you wouldn’t be able to walk.’" I come to the floor today to offer an amendment that would avoid the federal takeover of college sports. Unlike the underlying bill, my amendment rejects the idea that politicians should run college sports. My amendment would put the trust in the schools, students, coaches and conferences to run their own sports. My amendment accomplishes this goal simply by granting an antitrust exemption so that college athletes and schools can make their own deals, without unelected judges or politicians micromanaging every detail of compensation and eligibility. Jason Russell, a journalist with Reason magazine perhaps summed up this bill’s federal takeover of college sports best when he wrote: "The backers of the bill believe politicians, not the NCAA, should decide how many transfers are allowed. They think politicians, not conferences, should set a compensation cap on how much schools can pay athletes. They think politicians, not athletes and businesses, should get to decide what is a legitimate private contract. They think politicians, not the colleges, should decide how many schools are in the Big Ten and SEC. They think politicians, not coaches, should decide when a coach is allowed to leave a job. "They think politicians, not athletes or agents, should get to decide what agent fees are. They think politicians should empower medical personnel, not athletes or coaches, to have "autonomous, unchallengeable" power to decide if an athlete plays or sits. "They even think politicians, not the NFL or broadcasters, should get to decide when professional football games are on TV. They think politicians should have a say in the length of the college football season." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE This bill is the culmination of a slow march towards federal control of college sports that began almost one-hundred and forty years ago in the courts. In 1890, Congress enacted the Sherman Act. The Sherman Act is a piece of antitrust legislation. But, quite quickly, antitrust became a weapon against businesses of all sizes. One of the most ridiculous examples of antitrust as a weapon of government control came in 1967. In Utah Pie Company v. Continental Baking Company, the courts determined that a bakery violated antitrust law by selling its pies too cheaply. Not long after, in 1969, the government sued IBM for dominating the computer market by innovating too quickly. That case ultimately ran on for thirteen years before the government finally dropped it, saying that it was "without merit." The logic of antitrust became so contorted that the Federal Trade commission accused cereal makers of maintaining a shared monopoly on the theory that the brands blocked competition by being so popular that they flooded store shelves with their products. After 10 years of litigation, the FTC dismissed the case, ruling that staff failed to prove the shared monopoly charges. Antitrust laws granted the courts the ability to intrude on private contracts and dictate how people should run their businesses. And courts have grown increasingly comfortable using that power, increasing the scope of antitrust law with each case. For over one-hundred years this country has left regulation of college sports where it belongs: with the institutions and individuals that participate in college athletics. Until 1984, college athletics were excluded from antitrust law because antitrust didn’t deal with noncommercial, amateur pursuits. But in 1984 the Supreme Court decided that the NCAA couldn’t impose television broadcasting restrictions on college football games. Rather than recognizing that there may have been an underlying reason for the restrictions, the courts threw out the restrictions and began the slippery path we are on today. That case established college athletics as a commercial enterprise, but it wasn’t until 2015 that the courts really sank their fangs into college athletics. In 2015, the courts finally decided that the NCAA could not require students to maintain their amateur status by refusing payment for use of their name, image and likeness. The court decided that eligibility rules for a private association are best decided by the government, not the members of the association. Since 2015, a flurry of cases has decided issues as parochial as how much individual athletes are paid out of broadcast revenues and how long student athletes are eligible to play. Government has shirked its real duties — deciding issues of national importance — to focus on something it knows nothing about. As important as college sports are to students and institutions, they aren’t something Congress should micromanage. Athletes and institutions should be free to make choices about who they want to work and play for, and what rules they should be subject to. This bill manages to interfere with college athletics at nearly every level. It limits the ability of certain employees to freely leave one school and accept a job at another. It decides how students may go about licensing their name, image, and likeness. It even decides when transfer students are eligible to play. The bill actually forbids a return to the historic model of amateur sports where athletes are not paid. The bill would also set up a Commission on the Future of College Athletics, a legislative commission that would recommend new rule changes to Congress in the future. It seems that we already have an institution dedicated to preserving the future of college sports: the NCAA. Congress should not mire itself in another endless cycle of solving problems it caused. It especially shouldn’t become the chief rulemaking body for something like collegiate athletics. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That is why I am offering an amendment that would actually solve the problems faced by college sports. My amendment would reverse previous interference and prevent future interference by exempting collegiate sports from antitrust laws. This would ensure conferences, colleges and athletes are free to negotiate and enter into agreements that benefit everyone, without the heavy hand of government dictating what parties can offer or accept. It would also prevent Congress from imposing rules governing such minutiae as eligibility for transfer students and the thresholds for reporting name, image and likeness income. I love college sports as much as anyone, which is why I think the best way we can protect college sports is to stop sticking our nose where it doesn’t belong.

title: Trump-Xi reunion comes with unfinished business — and a bigger battle looming
description: President Donald Trump hosts Xi Jinping to test whether China delivered on rare earths, AI and trade promises from their May breakthrough deal.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for a summit with President Donald Trump, four months after the two leaders reached a sweeping agreement that included Chinese commitments on rare earths, agricultural purchases, trade and investment. Trump hailed that agreement as a breakthrough for American farmers, manufacturers and workers. But the latest talks come amid uneven progress on commitments involving rare-earth minerals, agricultural and commercial purchases, trade and investment, while key disputes over tariffs, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, intellectual property and Taiwan remain unresolved. Under the May agreement, China committed to address U.S. concerns over rare-earth supplies and purchase at least $17 billion a year in U.S. agricultural products, while also approving an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft, restoring market access for American beef and resuming poultry imports. The two countries also chartered new boards on trade and investment. CHINA’S XI SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE Four months later, implementation has been uneven. Reuters reported that China is making progress toward finalizing its commitment to purchase 200 Boeing jets, while agricultural imports are projected to fall short of the agreed level and the new trade and investment boards are still being put into operation. AI is expected to be a major focus of the two-day summit, along with possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods and discussions over China’s rare-earth exports, according to a senior administration official. The May agreement, when Trump and Xi last met, also chartered new U.S.-China boards on trade and investment, though it did not resolve the broader economic and national security tensions between the two countries. REalloys CEO Lipi Sternheim told Fox News Digital China’s dominance of the rare-earth supply chain gives Beijing leverage over U.S. defense and technology industries, warning that the Trump-Xi meeting must preserve supplies while American production ramps up. "The fact that Trump and Xi are meeting and the main topic of the day is rare earths probably tells you and the American people all they need to know about the importance," said Sternheim. Sternheim said the immediate goal of the Trump-Xi meeting should be to keep rare earths flowing to U.S. defense manufacturers for the next two to three years, giving American companies time to build domestic mining, processing and magnet-making capacity and reduce their dependence on China. THE WEST STILL DOESN’T GRASP THE DANGER OF CHINA’S RARE EARTH ENDGAME He said that rare earth minerals are used to make the powerful magnets found in cellphones, electric vehicles, drones, robots and defense systems, including missiles, F-35 fighter jets, submarines and missile-defense systems. Heavy rare earths are especially important for high-temperature applications such as missiles and space systems, but China controls most of the mining, processing and magnet-making capacity. Sternheim cautioned that shifting production to the U.S. will not happen quickly. "You can’t build 40 years in two days," Sternheim said, adding that it will take years. Trump touted the U.S. lead over China in artificial intelligence during an address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, while declaring that U.S. government documents would begin referring to the technology as "superintelligence." AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD "Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," said Trump. "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. That's the group that wins. And we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else. And we're going to keep it that way." While Trump and Xi will be in meetings, first lady Melania Trump is expected to accompany Xi’s wife Peng to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art. The two will "explore works spanning centuries of artistic achievement and Sino-American cultural exchange." Thursday will begin with a prestigious State Arrival Ceremony, including 479 military personnel from all branches on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House. The day will end with a state dinner with high-profile guests, including many from the tech world. Those guests will include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former senior White House adviser Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP House Speaker Mike Johnson will also be in attendance, a source familiar told Fox News Digital.

title: Daughter of prisoner makes emotional plea to Trump during spotlight Xi summit
description: Ziba Murat hopes Trump will raise her mother Dr. Gulshan Abbas' case with Xi Jinping during the summit after eight years of imprisonment in China.
content: An American woman whose mother has been wrongfully imprisoned in China for eight years is hoping that President Donald Trump will ask Chinese leader Xi Jinping for clemency during the high-profile ongoing summit between the pair of world leaders Thursday. "We are doing everything we can to bring this in front of President Trump, and I know that if he knows about this case, he will care about this case," Ziba Murat told Fox News Digital in an emotional interview on her mother's continued imprisonment. "I hope we are pulling the right levers and President Trump can bring her home." Dr. Gulshan Abbas is Murat's mother. She was 56 when she disappeared from her home on Sept. 10, 2018. More than two years later in December 2020, Murat recalls Chinese government officials confirming in a press conference that Abbas was convicted on charges of taking part in organized terrorism, aiding terrorist activities and seriously disrupting social order — charges Murat describes as "made up" — and was sentenced to 20 years in prison. CHINA’S XI SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE "Her disappearance came six days after her sister, my aunt Rushan Abbas, spoke ... about what's happening to the Uyghur people back home, and then the Chinese government picked her up six days after," said Murat. "We didn't see it coming, honestly, because she is a retired doctor. She's not a political person. She's not an activist. She's just a grandma and, you know — it took us almost two years to find out what happened to her [and] where she's being held." Rushan Abbas runs Campaign for Uyghurs, a large nonprofit advocacy group for the Muslim minority population in China, which has been subject to brutal oppression at the hands of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). MOTHER RECOUNTS HORRORS OF BRUTAL CHINESE DETENTION CAMP WHERE INFANT SON DIED Abbas' case is a prominent one. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has used his position and official office to advocate on her behalf. Murat was the Republican leader's guest at the 2026 State of the Union speech. But progress in freeing her mother has been an uphill battle, considering the secretive nature of the Chinese government and tensions with the United States over issues like trade and intellectual property theft, among many others. Murat is hoping that some of that tension will abate after Thursday's bilateral summit, and that by the end of the day, she'll be one step closer to seeing her mother again. TRUMP-XI SUMMIT SHOULD MAKE SURE AMERICAN STRENGTH DELIVERS AMERICAN RESULTS Through tears, Murat described life without her mother, noting that she's missing out on precious memories with her family, 24 of whom are United States citizens. Murat's daughter was only 3 months old when Abbas disappeared. "It's been hard because, like I said, I was a new mom myself when all this started happening," she said. "And my sister had her second baby four weeks after ... my mom's disappearance." Her daughter, now 8, is starting to ask questions about her grandmother. "Just a couple of months ago, we were reading a book ... [the] encyclopedia for kids, and they have the pages of [the] family tree," Abbas said. "So we're going over, you know, talking about my husband's parents and then my parents, and she just sat there and looked at me. She's like, 'I saw aunt Rushan has grandma Gulshan's picture ... [and] it says my sister is gone.' Where is grandma?" Murat is trying hard to withhold the real answer to that question, and tells her daughter that Abbas is far away, and the family is hoping that she can come meet her soon. But with all the meetings Murat attends and the people with whom she discusses the case, her young daughter is starting to catch on. "Even without me telling her, she started to pick up things, and it just breaks my heart to see her, and I don't have answer to provide her on when her grandma will be home. So it's very frustrating." A senior White House official confirmed to Fox News on Wednesday that Trump is expected to ask Xi to release at least one prisoner, U.S. citizen Dr. Youlin Chen, who was arrested outside a Beijing airport by Chinese officials in 2024. "President Trump cares about religious freedom more than anyone and consistently brings up cases of persecution with President Xi," the White House told Fox News Digital. title: Melania Trump’s home-country leader rips UN ‘double standards’ as Trump promise is revealed
description: Janez Janša accused the United Nations of double standards on Gaza and Ukraine, and revealed Trump promised to visit Melania Trump's homeland.
content: UNITED NATIONS - Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša accused the United Nations of applying double standards to global conflicts, arguing that the international community's focus on Gaza has overshadowed Russia's war in Ukraine and other humanitarian crises, while revealing that President Donald Trump has promised to visit Slovenia, the homeland of first lady Melania Trump. Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Janša said the international body must give greater attention to conflicts beyond the Middle East rather than concentrating its diplomatic efforts on a single crisis. "We have to get rid of double standards," Janša said, calling for the U.N. to apply its available diplomatic and security tools equally instead of putting its attention, money and energy into one conflict while neglecting others. MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT The Slovenian leader said he was struck by how extensively Gaza dominated speeches during the opening of the General Assembly, while Ukraine, a war much closer to his country's borders, received comparatively less attention. For Slovenia and other European countries, he said, Russia's invasion represents an immediate security threat, with no clear indication that Moscow is prepared to negotiate an end to the fighting. Janša argued that the U.N. was established to prevent such conflicts and should not allow its attention to be consumed by one region. He also pointed to the persecution of Christians in Nigeria and other humanitarian crises, arguing that the international body must recognize that different countries face different security and humanitarian challenges. TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH Janša said he intends to raise the issue during his own address to the General Assembly, scheduled for Thursday. His criticism comes as Slovenia undergoes a significant shift in its foreign policy, particularly toward Israel. Under the previous government of Prime Minister Robert Golob, Slovenia recognized Palestinian statehood in June 2024 and imposed an arms embargo on Israel in July 2025. The government defended those measures as necessary to protect Palestinian civilians and uphold international law. Since returning to power, Janša has sought to strengthen Slovenia's relationship with Israel, marking a shift from the previous government's more critical approach toward the Jewish state. Earlier this month, Israel opened its first resident embassy in Slovenia, while Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar visited the country for talks aimed at expanding political and economic cooperation. The two governments also signed a cooperation program covering education, science, culture, youth and sports through 2030. Janša described his government's approach as a return to the traditionally good relations between the two countries rather than a dramatic diplomatic realignment. US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS He also criticized European governments that, in his view, have failed to recognize the broader strategic connections between Iran, Russia and the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. Janša said he has supported the Iranian opposition for decades and argued that lasting peace in the Middle East would remain elusive without political change in Tehran. He accused some European governments of applying inconsistent standards by supporting Ukraine while taking positions toward Iran that he believes fail to account for Tehran’s relationship with Moscow, citing Ireland and Spain as well as Slovenia under the previous government before this year’s change in leadership. Janša also suggested that some European leaders have used the Palestinian issue to divert public attention from domestic economic and political problems, particularly ahead of elections. The prime minister's visit to New York also provided an opportunity to strengthen Slovenia's relationship with Washington, a relationship that carries a personal dimension because of the country's most prominent American connection: First Lady Melania Trump. Born in Slovenia in 1970, Melania Trump grew up in the town of Sevnica before moving to the United States and becoming the nation's second foreign-born first lady. The prime minister praised Melania Trump’s work on initiatives for children, describing her role in the White House as a source of pride for many Slovenians. He said his wife met the first lady for the first time on Tuesday and that he also spoke briefly with President Trump. title: Bishop Barron warns communism ‘making a comeback’ in America ahead of Fulton Sheen beatification
description: Bishop Robert Barron warns communism is making a comeback in America ahead of Archbishop Fulton Sheen's beatification ceremony in St. Louis.
content: FIRST ON FOX: As tens of thousands are expected to gather in St. Louis on Thursday for Archbishop Fulton Sheen's beatification, one church leader is sounding the alarm on the rise of communism in America and urging Catholics to embrace the late archbishop's fierce opposition to the ideology. "Now, you don't need me to tell you that communism is making a comeback right now in our country," Barron said in front of the Gateway Arch on Tuesday. "And I think especially churchmen need, like Sheen, to raise their voices against it and, furthermore, as American churchmen, to speak out strongly on both American and Catholic principles against the re-emergence of this still very dangerous ideology." BISHOP BARRON SLAMS 'BORDERLINE COMMUNISTS' SANDERS, MAMDANI AHEAD OF TRUMP PRAYER EVENT: 'ECONOMY THAT KILLS' Sheen, an author and television personality who became one of the Catholic Church's most prominent voices in the 20th century, will be beatified at The Dome at America's Center. The Vatican approved Sheen's beatification in 2019 after recognizing a miracle involving the unexplained recovery of James Fulton Engstrom, a baby born without a pulse in 2010, according to The Associated Press. HOW THE 'LONG MARCH' THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONS LED TO SOCIALIST TAKEOVER OF DEM PARTY: 'NEED TO WAKE UP' According to Barron, Sheen believed communism could never coexist with religion, saying Sheen viewed it as "this hostility to religion." In his 1948 book, Communism and the Conscience of the West, Sheen described communism as a "complete philosophy of life" that attempts "to control man's inner life as well." "Communism has a theory and a practice; it wishes to be not only a state but a church, judging the consciences of men; it is a doctrine of salvation and as such claims the whole man, body and soul, and in this sense is totalitarian," Sheen wrote. In addition to serving as a Catholic bishop, Barron said Sheen was also "a very proud American." "Those two identities came together in a very powerful way, I'd say, and especially in the '40s and '50s, in Sheen's fierce anti-communism," he said. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: MY YEAR WITH DOJ'S RELIGIOUS LIBERTY COMMISSION: WHY I SAID YES Turning to the Declaration of Independence, Barron said Sheen argued communism, rooted in Karl Marx's teachings, also threatened the foundations of equality, freedom and individual rights. "Sheen knew if you take God out of the picture, you take equality, rights, freedom out of the picture," he said. "Our integrity as a democratic society is dependent ultimately on our belief in God." Barron urged church leaders to follow Sheen's lead and speak out against communism. title: Florida couple recounts 'miraculous' rescue after surviving harrowing lightning strike during evening stroll
description: Police bodycam video captured the frantic response after Aaron and Clare Walenga were struck on a popular trail in Winter Garden.
content: A Florida couple said they experienced nothing short of a miracle earlier this month when a bolt of lightning suddenly struck them during an evening stroll and sparked a frantic rescue by several good Samaritans whose heroism was caught on camera. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Aaron Walenga, 48, and his wife, Clare, 43, recounted the harrowing moment in Winter Garden that left Aaron disoriented and paralyzed on the ground, police bodycam video shows, as bystanders rushed in to perform lifesaving measures on his unconscious wife. "I couldn't move the way I wanted to," Aaron said. "I'm trying to get up. I am trying to get to Clare … I'm trying to talk, and I'm not really able to." Aaron and Clare said the incident happened Sept. 2, after the couple dropped off their three children at a weekly church youth group gathering. DASHCAM CAPTURES TERRIFYING MOMENT LIGHTNING NEARLY STRIKES UTAH TRUCK DRIVER "We dropped our kids off at church, and we use that as our date night, and we looked forward to it," he said. "So we went out and had dinner and then, we love to go for a walk." As they walked hand in hand along the popular West Orange Trail, a nearby storm quickly rolled in and a bolt of lightning struck the couple without warning. The next thing Aaron remembers was waking up in severe pain and confused. "My first thought was that we got hit by a car," he said. "I thought maybe a car just ran us over from behind because getting struck by lightning is nothing that would even enter our minds," Aaron said. MONTANA TEEN THROWS LASSO TO MAN IN YELLOWSTONE RIVER IN SPLIT-SECOND RESCUE While still disoriented, Aaron said he saw bystanders and first responders tending to his unresponsive wife. Four good Samaritans had apparently rushed to the scene, immediately calling 911 and performing CPR on Clare before responders arrived roughly 10 minutes later, the couple said. Witnesses told Clare that she had turned blue and stopped breathing for three to four minutes. "I like to talk about the amount of bravery that they showed… they could see the fence beside them that lit up," Aaron said. "It was a big moment to turn around and then go, 'Hey, I think we need to go that direction.' And they did." A hospital visit revealed that Aaron suffered fractured eye sockets, a broken nose, damaged teeth, facial cuts and burns on his hand and wrists, where he was holding an umbrella and wearing an Apple Watch. Despite undergoing a traumatic event, Aaron and Clare described their recovery as "miraculous," noting that they suffered serious conditions, including brain bleeds and heart damage, that they said completely healed within two days. "We're just seeing miracle after miracle and just too many divine things in this unfortunate circumstance to not be noted," Clare said. "We both had brain bleeds, and then I also suffered heart damage. And then when they followed up again two days later, it was healed. Neither of us had any brain bleed damage and my heart situation completely healed," she added. Clare, who suffered intermittent memory loss, regained her full memory roughly two days later. "God's not done with me yet," Clare said, adding that she feels immense gratitude to be alive. DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US' -- A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED Since the incident, the family said they have built a strong relationship with the good Samaritans who stepped in that day, adding that they are even planning to return to the trail in a few weeks. The couple said they are overwhelmed by the support they have received from their local church, neighborhood and school communities. Their pastor also helped bring their children safely home on the night of the lightning strike. "Our neighbors are taking care of our yard and our pool for us, so it's just so many things happening without us even asking," Aaron said. "It's very humbling to know that people out there really care for you, and to see the church the way it's supposed to be, where it's not just in a building. It's really the people that are around you, and it's been amazing to watch." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Throughout the ordeal, the couple said they never felt hopeless, crediting their faith for helping them through the shocking experience. "We've never asked ‘Why me?’" Aaron said. "We never got upset, we never felt hopeless. We really felt like even though it was a hard situation… God's been with us and there's a purpose behind it."

title: KAROL MARKOWICZ: 1619 Project founder Nikole Hannah-Jones learned the hard truth about schools
description: Nikole Hannah-Jones sent her daughter to failing New York City schools to live out her progressive values, but her decade-long experiment ended badly.
content: Nikole Hannah-Jones, founder of the 1619 Project and winner of the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for commentary, has written a blockbuster piece, "In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?" on the reality of sending her daughter Najya to failing schools in New York City. Hannah-Jones, a domestic correspondent for The New York Times Magazine covering racial injustice and civil rights, had tried to live out her progressive values and sent her child to the local, deficient public school. Writing in 2016 for the magazine, she noted that her neighbors in the quickly gentrifying neighborhood of Bedford-Stuyvesant were opting out of the local school. "I didn’t know any of our middle-class neighbors, Black or White, who sent their children to one of these schools," Hannah-Jones shared. Hannah-Jones did. Now, 10 years later, Hannah-Jones’ latest piece shows that her project had been a failure, at the cost of her child’s education. It’s a difficult read. Hannah-Jones wanted to live out her values, especially the belief that children should go to their local school and that school choice is unacceptable. But those ideas failed when they hit reality, and Hannah-Jones spent nearly a decade coming to accept that. 1619 PROJECT FOUNDER REGRETS SCHOOL CHOICE FOR HER DAUGHTER, ADMITS PUTTING IDEALS AHEAD OF HER EDUCATION The column illustrates the struggles her daughter had at her elementary school, where teachers were disinterested and bad behavior went unpunished, and then in middle school, where homework went unchecked and standards were low. Hannah-Jones believed that through her force of will, and her prominent position, which she mentions several times in the piece, she and her husband could improve these schools. What she’s missing is that it was her own misconceptions and bad ideas that got these schools into a bad position in the first place. STEVE MOORE, ED POZZUOLI: STOP FUNDING SCHOOL SYSTEMS. LET THE MONEY FOLLOW THE CHILD In 2018, Hannah-Jones gave a keynote address at the Color of Education event, an annual summit in North Carolina "dedicated to achieving racial equity and eliminating racial disparities in the education system." She spoke about how terrible it was that White kids in North Carolina were choosing charter schools instead of public schools in places "like Wake County that for years was a model of integration." So integration is good? But when a Black student in the audience asked Hannah-Jones for guidance on "navigating the predominantly White colleges and universities to which she has applied," Hannah-Jones was quick to respond that she should go to Howard University, a historically Black college or university (HBCU) because, well, integration is bad. Hannah-Jones ended that talk with this line: "The future of our children and the nation depends on progressives winning the fight to reclaim public schools." GOV HOCHUL'S PLAN TO OPT NEW YORK INTO FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DRAWS UNION OPPOSITION Well, progressives reclaimed public schools in New York City. There’s no way to look at New York City schools as anything but the testing ground for the exact policies Hannah-Jones would want. Progressive Mayor Bill de Blasio removed "screens" — competitive benchmarks such as attendance, grades and test scores for middle school admissions — during COVID-19, and the practice was maintained by the next mayor, Eric Adams. The schools are heavily influenced by teachers’ unions. Hannah-Jones opposes gifted and talented programs, and they have been severely reduced, no longer using entrance tests. New York City public schools also follow the practices that Hannah-Jones would want regarding kids with behavioral issues. And, with New York’s longtime cap on charter schools, most kids are trapped there with no other options. AMERICAN SCHOOLS COST MORE THAN EVER BUT OUR STUDENTS STILL KEEP FAILING But Hannah-Jones never accounts for her own bad ideas and how they fail in real life. When her daughter fails the state algebra test, it’s because standardized tests are unfair. She never once mentions teachers’ unions as the culprits behind why atrocious teachers and administrators remain at these schools, unable to be fired. When school choice is mentioned at all, it’s presented as the reason the middle school that was unsuccessful in teaching her very capable daughter was failing. When Hannah-Jones confronts her daughter’s middle school principal with the reality that her daughter didn’t get enough from her education, the principal, in tears, responded, "None of this surprises me. This is the reality of a segregated system, and it’s not just segregation by race and class, it’s by ability. This is the reality of school-choice systems." CHICAGO'S HALF-EMPTY SCHOOLS REVEAL A CRISIS CITY LEADERS REFUSE TO CONFRONT Yes, that’s the reality of school-choice systems, or it should be: Children who are capable and want to learn, and whose families make education a top priority, should be able to escape the kids who don’t want to be there and want to slow education down for everyone. In her article for the New York Times, Hannah-Jones spends a lot of time on demographics and household income, but there is an entire network of charter schools in New York, called Success Academy, that produces far better results than public schools while serving student bodies of similar means. At one point, Hannah-Jones visited her child’s elementary school lunchroom and found it to be pandemonium. She writes, "It was not the children that horrified me — kids of all incomes are rambunctious at lunchtime. It was the callous disregard of the adults. Students respond to the high or low expectations of institutions and the grown-ups who operate them, and it was clear that these children were getting the message." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But somehow these expectations are not acceptable to have in the classroom. Hannah-Jones described unruly kids being constantly "redirected" as "good educational practice. … Schools like hers tend to rely on a zero-tolerance disciplinary playbook and often simply remove misbehaving students from classrooms, depriving them of precious educational time they cannot afford to miss. But at Unison, teachers constantly worked to refocus students and mitigate conflict. This is good educational practice, but kids like Najya, who were just trying to do their work, saw this treatment as deeply unfair." It’s not just unfair; it is actually bad educational practice to let a misbehaving child distract the teacher again and again. It’s bad educational practice to allow one child to set an example that bad behavior will be met with no discipline. It’s bad educational practice to allow the good students to compete for the teacher’s attention with a student who shouldn’t be in the classroom. Most of all, ineffective or disinterested teachers have to be fired, something that the teachers’ unions, which ultimately run New York City schools with the support of people like Hannah-Jones, would never permit. But none of this is allowed to be said in Hannah-Jones’ far-left world. If the school is failing, it’s because of racism, not because its leaders have embraced bad educational practices and allowed them to continue indefinitely. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The question has become why Hannah-Jones would air these grievances about New York City public schools when she knew what the response might be. The answer, we have to imagine, is that her daughter ultimately attends one of the very few New York City schools that have "screens." Like progressive politicians such as Bill de Blasio or soon-to-be Congressman Brad Lander, Hannah-Jones had loudly opposed these kinds of schools, except for her own child. Therein lies the rub: When progressive policies meet reality, they are almost always failures, and those at the top of the progressive hierarchy always manage to get their kids out. If only the rest of us could escape those policies as deftly as those who push them. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM KAROL MARKOWICZ

title: MORNING GLORY: El-Sayed might have a problem with the Black vote in Michigan
description: Abdul El-Sayed's support among Black voters in Michigan is dropping fast, and even a Kamala Harris campaign appearance may not fix the problem.
content: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has a problem with a large slice of the state’s Black electorate. It doesn’t like him. That matters in a state where the voting population is 14% Black. (About 2% of Michigan voters are of Arab descent. 1.4% are Jewish.) BLACK VOTERS RIP DEMS OVER TAKING THEM FOR GRANTED IN EL-SAYED'S BACKYARD: ‘HUSH US UP’ In the most recent Washington Post–Schar School poll, Sept. 10–14, only 67% of likely Black Michigan voters supported El-Sayed. A Fox News poll from a month earlier, taken Aug. 6–10, found that 75% of Black Michigan voters said they would vote for El-Sayed. That is a trend in the wrong direction for El-Sayed. Two years ago, then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried the Black vote in Michigan with 87%. So, El-Sayed is significantly underperforming the most recent Democratic nominee for president. SOCIALIST POLITICIANS ARE 'MORE RACIST THAN THE KKK,' SAYS BLACK DEM OFFICIAL URGING VOTERS TO DITCH EL-SAYED The question is why is El-Sayed so weak with this particular demographic? El-Sayed has addressed this question very directly, including acknowledging that there is mistrust between parts of Detroit’s Black and Arab communities. El-Sayed may already have given up on Michigan’s significant Jewish vote coming around, but on Tuesday he campaigned with former Vice President Kamala Harris at an event aimed directly at Black women. It was an awkward "roundtable" that seemed to have been so narrowcasted at Black women as to have returned right out of peak Woke 1.0, which Congresswoman Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez assured us recently is an era behind us. Harris did not get that memo as her remarks Tuesday indicated. "The attack on DEI is an attack on maternal care," Harris opined as an uncomfortable-looking El-Sayed looked on, "including the need to protect Black women in connection with their pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care." The word salad chef of 2024 was back. HARRIS JOINS FORCES WITH RADICAL SENATE NOMINEE IN KEY SWING STATE AS 2028 WHISPERS SWIRL Whether or not the day’s appearance by the former VP helped El-Sayed at all with Black voters won’t be known for some time, but given the numbers in the public polling, El-Sayed had to try something to get Michigan’s crucial voting bloc at least start thinking about going to the polls in November even if that something was Harris, who has been notably absent from the critical Senate races until this week. There is little reason to believe that Harris is the answer to El-Sayed’s core problem. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES In an August 2026 interview with The Grio, El-Sayed was blunt about the Black-Arab-American divide in and around Detroit: "I think a lot of the mistrust among Black folk in Metro Detroit is well-founded, based on a kind of double standard that too often business owners, particularly in the Arab and, yes, Muslim communities have had when it comes to the way they do business in local communities," El-Sayed said. "You see money go in and then money leaves these communities rather than be reinvested in the community," El-Sayed continued. "It’s a conversation I’ve been having with the Arab and Muslim community for a very long time. We can’t sit here and talk about racism against Arabs and Muslims unless we’re willing to actually look inward and ask how is it that we’re engaging with the Black community in a way that is responsible?" So El-Sayed knows he has a problem with a key demographic. He has tried other approaches before bringing Harris into the state. El-Sayed declared he was open to "reparations" when he appeared with Fox News’ Jesse Watters, saying that an "incredible debt that was put upon Black folks as a function of slavery, that we have yet to pay." El-Sayed also told Watters the whole country should be discussing "how do we make people whole." The following month, El-Sayed was talking to leaders of the Black church, saying "unpaid debts" are owed to Black communities, debts that have "long since come due." BLACK CONSERVATIVE REVEALS HOW GOP CAN LOCK DOWN MINORITY VOTERS WITHOUT TRUMP ON BALLOT While the topic of "reparations" polls at 77% approval among Black Americans, only 18% of White voters support the concept. So the more El-Sayed pushes "reparations," the more likely he is to drive off the moderate independents already leery of his radical positions and friendship with Hasan Piker. Then there is the "Trump effect." President Trump collected 13% of the Black vote overall two years ago, and close to 20% of Black men. Does talk of DEI and maternal care at the El-Sayed-Harris roundtable Tuesday bring home votes among Black men? Does chatter about unspecified reparations even drive off the near quarter of the Black population that aren’t signed on to the concept? The long-standing tensions between the Black and Arab American communities in and around Detroit cannot be resolved in an election cycle that has focused on El-Sayed’s radical break with traditional Democratic campaign themes and profiles. El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, took more than two-thirds of Black voters in the primary. Republican nominee Mike Rogers knows this traditional Democratic stronghold is at least partially in play. We can’t see Team Rogers buy on "urban radio" or in other media serving the Black community, but we have seen Rogers making appearances throughout Wayne County and making many appearances with "Democrats for Rogers" groups featuring Black voters. Everyone knows that El-Sayed and his association with Hasan Piker has driven off the votes of a large number of Jewish Democrats. That the campaign is not connecting with Black voters as it must to give him a shot is the double nightmare for his campaign strategists. What can he do between now and November 3? It is hard to see a path to keep the moderate independent vote even as El-Sayed trots out traditional panders to the Black vote that don’t even resonate as credible or detailed. Even as El-Sayed struggles with basic messaging to core constituencies, Republican groups have poured more than $60 million into the Wolverine State. There are some polls showing El-Sayed with a lead over Rogers outside the margin of error. There were also lots of polls showing him winning the primary against Stevens by double digits, with one memorable miss putting him 18% up in a race he won by one point. The polling doesn’t add up given his problems with the Democratic base. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So stay focused on El-Sayed’s increasingly frenetic campaign and its sudden lurches here and there. There’s a reason radicals aren’t often nominated by major parties. Both Republican and Democratic Parties are built out of coalitions of interest groups. El-Sayed’s primary campaign fractured the traditional Democratic coalition. There is scant hard evidence that he has found a way to glue it back together again and then motivate it to vote between now and November 3.

title: Lawsuits cost every American household thousands of dollars. Supreme Court can help
description: Supreme Court's October docket tackles climate lawsuits, digital privacy and retirement plan claims as U.S. tort costs approach $1 trillion by 2030.
content: When the Supreme Court returns in October, several cases on its docket will offer a timely look at a growing problem in America’s legal system: the mounting cost of lawsuit abuse. The cases involve different industries and legal questions, but each reflects a broader fight over how far liability can extend and who ultimately bears the cost. Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, for example, could determine whether federal law precludes local climate lawsuits seeking relief for harms tied to interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions, opening or closing a path to potentially sweeping liability for energy producers. Other cases involving digital privacy and retirement-plan claims may affect the reach of statutory liability and large-scale business exposure. SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA Those questions matter well beyond the parties before the court. When liability expands, businesses must account for greater legal exposure through higher insurance premiums and compliance costs as well as reduced investment. Those expenses can ultimately become a "tort tax" that increases consumer prices and the cost of goods and services purchased by taxpayers. Recent evidence suggests that the burden is growing. A new Marathon Strategies report found nearly 200 "nuclear verdicts" of $10 million or more against corporate defendants in 2025, totaling more than $25.6 billion — a 40.7% increase from the year before. More broadly, U.S. tort costs reached $529 billion in 2022, or about 2.1% of GDP, and are projected to approach $1 trillion by 2030 if recent trends continue. Economic analyses go as high as $6,000 to the average household’s annual expenses. That makes lawsuit abuse an affordability issue as well as a legal one. And the cases already before the Supreme Court tell only part of the story. While they show where some of today’s biggest liability fights have ended up, cases moving through lower courts offer a preview of the new theories that trial lawyers are testing next and that the justices may eventually be asked to adjudicate themselves. Antitrust litigation against fire-truck manufacturers offers one example. Cities, counties and fire departments allege that major manufacturers conspired to restrict competition, driving up prices and stretching delivery times. Those are serious allegations, and proven collusion should carry consequences. But manufacturers point instead to pandemic-driven demand and disrupted supply chains as explanations for the price increases and delays. Fire trucks are also highly specialized vehicles requiring custom engineering, skilled labor and rigorous safety standards. Courts should demand strong evidence before allowing those market realities to be converted into sweeping antitrust liability, and localities should think twice before supporting such lawsuits. Even unsuccessful litigation imposes defense and insurance costs that the very municipalities suing for damages may ultimately have to absorb in future purchases — meaning a lawsuit intended to recover higher fire-truck costs could end up making the next truck more expensive. A similar dynamic is emerging in the grocery aisle. Lawsuits targeting ultra-processed foods are multiplying despite early setbacks, generally alleging that major food companies marketed addictive or unhealthy products without adequately warning consumers about associated health risks. Manufacturers of specialized formula for premature infants, meanwhile, face nearly 1,700 claims alleging their products cause a serious intestinal disease. JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIAL MEDIA ADDICTION WILL EASILY OUTLAST META'S MASSIVE MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR SETTLEMENT Both areas involve genuine health concerns, but both also show how mass litigation can gain momentum while causation remains contested. An early ultra-processed-food case was dismissed after a federal judge found correlation was not enough to establish causation, yet plaintiffs’ lawyers say they plan to appeal, continue filing similar cases and seek consolidation into multidistrict litigation. Recent evidence suggests that the burden is growing. A new Marathon Strategies report found nearly 200 "nuclear verdicts" of $10 million or more against corporate defendants in 2025, totaling more than $25.6 billion — a 40.7% increase from the year before. The formula litigation raises similar stakes. Juries have reached conflicting conclusions as the litigation has continued to expand, showing that fundamental questions about causation can remain unsettled even after a litigation campaign has grown to encompass hundreds or thousands of cases. FLORIDA SUES NETFLIX, ALLEGES STREAMER TRACKED CHILDREN AFTER PROMISING FAMILIES PRIVACY That is why these emerging legal fights deserve attention. Early setbacks do not necessarily end a new mass-tort theory. Claims can be revised and tested across jurisdictions until one gains enough traction to open broad discovery, encourage copycat filings and create pressure for industry-wide settlements. Legitimately injured consumers deserve recourse, but causation cannot become an afterthought simply because the potential pool of plaintiffs is large. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Taken together, the Supreme Court docket and these lower-court fights show the tort system at two different stages. The justices will confront liability questions that have already worked their way to the high court, while lower courts are testing theories that could become tomorrow’s major mass-tort battles. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That should strengthen the case for reform before those costs become more deeply embedded in the economy. Greater transparency around litigation funding and government contingency-fee arrangements, along with stronger screening of weak causation theories, can preserve legitimate claims while making abuse harder to sustain. Tort reform is not about protecting wrongdoers. It is about preventing an aggressive lawsuit economy from becoming another hidden cost American families are forced to absorb. title: Republicans face brutal midterm headwinds. Six forces could help them defy history.
description: With six weeks until Election Day, rising gas prices, Trump's 39% approval rating and redistricting wars will shape the 2026 midterm battle.
content: With six weeks to go until Election Day and early voting already underway in a handful of states, the conventional wisdom is that Republicans may be in for some setbacks in the midterms. As it defends its fragile House and Senate majorities, the GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the president's party lose congressional seats during the midterms. It's also battling high costs at the grocery stores and gas pumps tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, as well as President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings. But Democrats are saddled with their own issues, from an ideological civil war between the party's left wing and the establishment that has handed Republicans plenty of political ammunition, to a brand image that's nothing to brag about. Add to that the Democrats' major disadvantage as the GOP floods the airwaves with attack ads. Here are six forces that will likely determine whether Republicans can turn back a possible blue wave and hold power in Congress. WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLING 1. Inflation Six weeks until Election Day, and just as the voting begins, fuel prices keep rising, with the national average for gas nearly $4.50 per gallon and diesel topping $6.50 per gallon, according to AAA. Public opinion polls point to the economy, including the cost of living, as the top issue for voters in this year's midterms. That means that the issue that boosted Trump and Republicans to sweeping victories in 2024 is a major liability in 2026. And the rising prices in recent weeks, fueled by renewed fighting in the war with Iran and Ukraine and attacks on Russia's diesel industry, are doing the GOP no favors. "Gas prices were much higher under Biden than under ‘TRUMP.’ So were almost all other prices," the president argued Monday in a social media post, as he referred to former President Joe Biden. While Trump and Republican leaders point fingers at Biden, polls indicate voters increasingly place the blame for ongoing economic and inflation pressures on the current administration. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Democrats last week heavily criticized Trump and Republicans after the president argued that fuel costs were "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done," as he pointed to the attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities. Meanwhile, the latest Fox News poll indicated that by a wide margin, the Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation. But when asked about the overall economy, recent national surveys from Reuters/Ipsos and NBC News had the GOP and Democrats all knotted up on which party would better handle the issue. "My listeners are looking for prices to come down across the board," New Hampshire-based center-right talk radio host Jack Heath told Fox News Digital. "People elected President Trump to lower prices and improve their situation and people are looking for that improvement," Heath, host of "Good Morning NH," emphasized. "They're looking for Trump to deliver on his promises." 2. Trump's influence "I'm asking you to just pretend I'm on the ballot just one more time," the president said last week during a campaign stop in battleground North Carolina. It's a line Trump repeatedly used earlier this month, at the GOP's first-ever midterm convention. Facing what polls indicate is an enthusiasm gap with Democrats, the president and Republican leaders are hoping to energize the MAGA base, which doesn't always vote when Trump isn't on the ballot. While the president's approval rating in the Fox News poll stands at 39% among all voters, it remains at a sky-high 98% among self-described MAGA Republicans. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But some longtime Trump allies are starting to break with the president as they face challenging re-elections. GOP Rep. Maria Salazar won re-election two years ago by 20 points in South Florida's 27th Congressional District. But with Trump's negative poll numbers a potential anchor around her, Salazar last week released a TV ad criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement as having "gone too far," and that "Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today." Meanwhile, on Monday, two Trump allies who are in heated Senate battles — Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa and former Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan, broke with the president as they demanded a swift end to the war with Iran. Watch whether vulnerable Republicans create more distance from the president, or move toward Trump to juice Republican turnout. 3. Democrats' Leftward Lurch Republicans are aiming to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election, as they spotlight major Democratic primary victories this year by far-left and socialist candidates over more mainstream Democrats. "In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually, they’re communists," Trump charged at the midterm convention. The messaging is pronounced in Michigan's crucial Senate race, where GOP nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers, as he referred to Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, told FOX Business this week, "We don’t want this socialism nonsense in our state, and this guy is too extreme." 12 SENATE RACES THAT WILL DETERMINE WHO CONTROLS THE CHAMBER Polling gives a boost to the GOP's "commonsense vs. crazy" messaging. Fifty-five percent of registered voters surveyed in the latest Fox News national poll held an unfavorable view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), while only three in 10 saw the DSA in a positive light. The Fox News poll was the latest national survey to show that while the DSA has gained traction among Democrats, the group and the broader socialist movement in America face significant national skepticism. While the GOP full court press continues, in hopes of swaying undecided voters, Democrats are divided on its effectiveness. Ty Strong, founder and president of the Moderate PAC, warned that the GOP playbook "absolutely could be effective." But Shannon Jackson, a key consultant and advisor to progressive leader Rep. Ro Khanna of California, argued that Republicans are "reaching for things. I think the DSA issue is something they’re trying to make something, but it is not." Meanwhile, this year's primary surge by socialist and left-wing candidates isn't helping Democrats boost their brand. The party's favorable ratings hit historic lows in the months following the 2024 election, and the latest Fox News poll indicates Democrats are still well underwater, with 55% of voters viewing the party in an unfavorable light. 4. GOP's Money Bomb Republicans enjoy a formidable cash advantage over the Democrats, and they're using it in the final stretch leading up to Election Day. While Democratic candidates in many key races have outraised their GOP opponents, the Republican National Committee remains far ahead of the rival Democratic National Committee when it comes to cash-on-hand. And GOP-aligned outside groups, including the Trump-allied MAGA Inc., are opening the floodgates when it comes to ad spending, in order to try and level the playing field by overcoming the difficult political environment. Republican groups have outspent their Democratic counterparts by more than $83 million to run spots in ten crucial Senate races since the start of September, according to figures from AdImpact, a nationally known firm that tracks ad spending. While a financial advantage is not always decisive, strategists say it can often move the needle in a close contest. And in the 10 Senate races spotlighted by AdImpact, a onetime Democratic ad spending advantage over the summer turned into a major GOP deluge. While much of the ad dollars dished out by Republicans are to protect vulnerable seats, the money may help as the GOP works to flip open-Democrat-held Senate seats in Michigan and New Hampshire. 5. Redistricting Wars Thirteen months ago, Texas passed a new congressional redistricting map, giving Trump his first major victory in his push to give Republicans a big boost heading into the midterm elections by drawing more right-leaning districts. Fast-forward to present day, and as they fight to hold their razor-thin House majority, Republicans were the big winners, with partisan redistricting netting them potentially 10 additional right-leaning congressional seats in time for the midterms. But redrawing the maps and winning the seats are two different things, and some election analysts caution that the fierce headwinds facing the GOP could lead to Republicans falling far short of their original expectations heading into the redistricting wars. 6. House Field Narrows, Senate Map Broadens There are 435 seats in the House of Representatives, but the Cook Report suggests the battle for the chamber's majority could come down to just 21 districts it rates as a toss-up. The Fox News Power Rankings list 17 seats as true toss-ups. Decades of gerrymander, including this cycle's mid-decade redistricting, have made a major impact by narrowing the House battlefield, which may limit the number of pickups by the Democrats even if a blue wave forms. While the number of competitive House seats stays historically small, the Senate map is widening, which is a positive sign for Democrats. Democrats are feeling the heat in open-seat contests in Michigan and New Hampshire, two must-holds for them as they try to win back a Senate currently controlled 53-47 by the GOP. But Senate showdowns in red states, including Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa, are now considered very competitive. title: Parents accuse Oregon hospital of making them drive dead baby home to Seattle: lawsuit
description: A Seattle couple's $10 million lawsuit alleges Salem Health staff pressured them to transport their deceased baby's body home in their personal vehicle.
content: A Seattle couple is suing after hospital staff in Oregon told them to drive the body of their nearly 9-month-old son four hours home in their private car following his sudden death in an emergency room. Aleksandr and Nataliya Yeremeyev filed a $10 million lawsuit against Salem Health and Dr. Stefani Sorensen. The parents had allegedly sought respectful and dignified care and transportation of the remains of their son, Michael, but the lawsuit alleges staff insisted they bring the body back home with them. Michael was born with Down syndrome and spent the first six months of his life at Seattle Children's Hospital. "His parents had made sure that he had received really excellent care. So, I think it was a really, really sad and just very tragic way for his life to end and for it to be so undignified right there at the end," Anna Bruckenhoefer, the family's attorney, said in a statement, according to Fox 13. TWO FAMILIES SUE NORTH DAKOTA HOSPITAL ON ALLEGATIONS BABIES WERE SWITCHED AT BIRTH On September 22, 2024, the family was visiting Salem, Oregon, for a religious retreat when Michael developed rapid, shallow breathing late at night and was rushed to the emergency room at Salem Health Hospital, where he died, according to the complaint. When the parents asked how to arrange respectful transport to send Michael’s body back home to Seattle, hospital staff allegedly pushed back on the suggestion to contact a local funeral home because it would be "too expensive" and instead pressured the family to bring their son’s body with them in their own car, which they ended up doing due to feeling like they had no other option. "They have repeatedly asked the hospital for assistance in helping them with what are the next steps," Bruckenhoefer said. "This was all occurring overnight. They felt rushed that they had to make quick decisions and the hospital left them with no choice other than to take Michael's body with them and head back to Seattle." Aleksandr drove about four hours from Salem to Seattle with his son’s body laid across the backseat, while his wife and other children followed in a separate car. FAMILY OF TODDLER FOUND ALIVE IN MORGUE AFTER BEING DECLARED DEAD PLANS LEGAL ACTION He suffered severe emotional distress as he feared police stops, car crashes and the visible deterioration of his child's body, according to the lawsuit. When he arrived at a Seattle funeral home, the father had to clean bodily fluids that leaked onto the seat during the trip. "It is legal in the state of Oregon and in the state of Washington to transport a deceased with the proper permits. But that is not what our clients wanted to do here. They were looking for help. They were looking for guidance. They were looking for the hospital to tell them, "These are the next steps,'" Bruckenhoefer said. "This is a hospital. It's an emergency department. Unfortunately, death is something that they are accustomed to and that they deal with. They should have had procedures and protocols in place to assist the Yeremeyev’s while they were dealing with literally the worst moment of their lives. Instead, what they did is they just compounded their grief by essentially telling them that they were on their own in this." "No parents, no loved ones should ever be placed in the position that the Yeremeyev’s were placed in," Bruckenhoefer added. "Just completely surprised that something like this would happen in 2026." The lawsuit names Salem Health Hospitals & Clinics, Salem Health, Salem Emergency Physicians Service and Sorensen as defendants, alleging direct negligence, vicarious liability, and a breach of the heightened duty of care owed to bereaved parents for the respectful treatment and custody of a child's body. The family is seeking $10 million in non-economic damages for severe emotional distress and psychological trauma, although they plan to amend the complaint to include punitive damages. Salem Health Hospital said out of respect for privacy and because the matter is in litigation, it is unable to discuss the details of the child's care. "Salem Hospital responded in accordance with the family’s wishes and followed both hospital policy and Oregon state law in consultation with the appropriate local authorities, including the medical examiner," Salem Health told Fox 13 in a statement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Care with respect is a guiding principle of clinical practice at Salem Hospital and remains central to how we support patients and families during some of life's most difficult moments. We recognize the profound grief families experience following the loss of a loved one and treat every patient and family with empathy, dignity, and respect," the statement continued.

title: Federal judge orders Trump administration to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico
description: A federal judge ordered that President Donald Trump must restore White House press credentials for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, finding the outlets likely to prevail in court.
content: President Donald Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico suffered a setback Thursday after a federal judge ordered the administration to restore White House access to the outlets. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order Thursday blocking the ban and ordering White House officials to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" the outlets' hard-pass press credentials while their legal battle continues. The order will be in effect for 14 days. Kelly wrote that the outlets had shown they were likely to succeed on their claim that their White House "hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process." "This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it," Kelly wrote of the standard for obtaining a temporary restraining order. MAMDANI TELLS TRUMP BANNED WHITE HOUSE OUTLETS ARE WELCOME AT NYC MEETING Kelly also rejected, at least for now, the administration's national security justification, writing that "the record lacks factual support" for the contention that revoking the passes protected national security or that restoring them would endanger it. Trump announced the ban last week, writing on social media that the three outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES." Reporters from all three organizations were subsequently denied entry to the White House, with their press credentials deactivated or confiscated. The outlets and three individual reporters sued the administration, alleging the revocation of their White House press credentials violated their First Amendment free speech rights and Fifth Amendment due process rights. WHITE HOUSE TV POOL TO SUSPEND COVERAGE OF TRUMP EVENTS Lawyers for the Justice Department argued that White House press access is a privilege, not a right, and defended the president's authority to determine who receives access. Following Trump's ban, White House television pool members FOX News Media, ABC News, CBS News, CNN and NBC News announced Monday that they had agreed to suspend their pooled coverage of the president. title: Tennessee cops raided man's home after he criticized officer for speeding: lawsuit
description: A First Amendment lawsuit alleges Kingsport Police in Tennessee raided Joshua Gibbons' home after he filmed and criticized a cop speeding at night.
content: A Tennessee man who was arrested in a pre-dawn raid after he filmed and criticized a police officer sued the police department alleging it violated his First Amendment right to free expression. The civil lawsuit against the city of Kingsport, its police chief and its officers was filed by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) in 2023 on behalf of Joshua Gibbons, but he is only now making the complaint public after he was successful in having his conviction overturned and the remaining charge dismissed by the Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals. "They tried to intimidate me, but I’m not backing down," Gibbons said in a statement. "I can’t let this injustice stand, because my family doesn’t feel safe anymore. There’s no coming back from that raid on our home. They sent eight heavily armed officers to arrest me because I embarrassed them." In October 2022, Gibbons filmed a Kingsport Police Department SUV speeding at night without lights or sirens, which the lawsuit alleges violated department policy and state law. He followed the vehicle and approached the officer at a fast food drive-thru, where he filmed his brief criticism of the officer’s conduct. POLICE FATALLY SHOOT SWORD WIELDING MAN AFTER WOMAN FOUND TRAPPED IN CAR, OFFICIALS SAY "When he caught up with the officer, the officer did the right thing. He ignored Joshua Gibbons, didn't arrest him, didn't view it as a crime, and went and got his hamburger," FIRE senior attorney Adam Steinbaugh told Fox News Digital. Gibbons, who uploads videos of police on duty as a way to hold them accountable, later published a second video of an officer giving him the middle finger. A fellow citizen later complained to the department about the officer’s conduct, and the department responded by searching Gibbons’ YouTube channel for something to use against him, according to FIRE. The department found the video of their own officer speeding. But instead of disciplining the officer, officers were sent to arrest Gibbons. "The First Amendment protects the right not only to criticize and film police, but also to post it online. The police department didn't treat this as a crime until Joshua posted this online and embarrassed the department," Steinbaugh said. Steinbaugh also said the case was "as lawless as it was hypocritical" and that the department’s actions "were all to make an example out of a critic." According to the lawsuit, within two hours of being "made aware" of Gibbons’ video of the speeding officer, an arrest warrant for Gibbons was obtained for speeding, using a cell phone while driving and disorderly conduct. The warrant was obtained from a court clerk rather than a judge, according to FIRE. Just before dawn the following morning, eight armed officers were captured on security and cell phone footage raiding Gibbons’ house and arresting him in front of his elderly mother and his daughter, just nine days after he filmed and criticized the speeding officer. Gibbons then faced two trials over nearly four years before a Tennessee appellate court recently dismissed the charges. "That's a long process that can take a mental toll on someone. I think that Joshua wants to send a message to this department. I think he wants to see some reforms to this department, and we're happy to support him," Steinbaugh said. TENNESSEE OFFICIAL SAYS FLOCK CEO SHOULD BE HANGED 'PUBLICLY FOR TREASON' AS CONTROVERSIAL CAMERAS FACE REVOLT In the first trial, a judge acquitted him of the speeding and cell phone charges but found Gibbons guilty of disorderly conduct, saying he was "offended by the way" Gibbons was "talking to that officer." Gibbons appealed to the county circuit court, and a jury found him guilty of disorderly conduct. But in June, the Court of Criminal Appeals of Tennessee unanimously overturned the verdict and dismissed the disorderly conduct charge, finding there was "no evidence" that Gibbons’ criticism of the officer "prevented any person from doing any lawful activity." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The court said Gibbons "did not threaten anyone, did not engage in any violent behavior, and did not create a physically offensive or hazardous condition." The court noted that even "'profane and insulting' words alone will not rise to the level of a crime, particularly when uttered against the police, who 'are trained to exercise a higher degree of restraint than the average citizen.'" "If you are a law enforcement officer, you are required by your uniform and by the First Amendment to tolerate criticism. Some of that's going to be fair criticism, some of it's going to be unfair criticism. But you don't get to go and arrest people for it. That's the message we want to send to this department and to departments around the country," Steinbaugh said. Kingsport Police did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

title: Illegal alien allegedly grabs school police officer's gun, shoots him in femoral artery: DOJ

content: A Mexican national accused of grabbing a Dallas school police officer’s gun and shooting him after the officer stopped to help him has been indicted on a federal firearms charge, prosecutors announced Wednesday. Jose Santiago Pantoja-Morales, 27, allegedly shot the uniformed Dallas Independent School District (DISD) police officer during an Aug. 6 struggle after the officer encountered him near the Lyndon B. Johnson Freeway, according to a federal complaint. Pantoja-Morales, who prosecutors say was in the U.S. illegally, had allegedly jumped out of a co-worker’s car and into the freeway’s center median. The co-worker flagged down the DISD officer, who was on routine patrol and offered Pantoja-Morales a ride to a nearby safe location. ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF TRYING TO DISARM VIRGINIA POLICE OFFICER During the ride, prosecutors say Pantoja-Morales began rummaging through the officer’s bag in the back seat. The officer pulled over and tried to remove him from the car, but Pantoja-Morales allegedly resisted, leading to a physical struggle. During the fight, Pantoja-Morales allegedly grabbed the officer’s gun and fired once, striking the officer in the femoral artery of his right leg, according to the complaint.VIDEO SHOWS MOMENT CHICAGO MAN ALLEGEDLY USED SUV AS WEAPON AGAINST ICE AGENT, PROSECUTORS SAY Despite being wounded, the officer regained control of his gun. Pantoja-Morales ran from the scene and was quickly apprehended by law enforcement, prosecutors said. Another DISD officer provided medical treatment at the scene before the wounded officer was taken to Parkland Hospital for further treatment. A federal grand jury returned an indictment Sept. 16, charging Pantoja-Morales with possession of a firearm by an illegal alien, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas. NEVADA MAN FUNNELED 140 GUNS TO VIOLENT MEXICAN DRUG CARTELS, INCLUDING POWERFUL 'MILITARY-STYLE' RIFLES: DOJ "The illegal alien’s alleged actions in this case represent an attack on the rule of law and a direct threat to public safety," U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said in a news release.
