title: Why Trump zeroed in on Greenland, the world’s largest island, mostly covered in ice — in 3 charts
description: President Donald Trump says his Greenland deal gives the U.S. permanent control over the island's security while barring China and Russia from Arctic footholds.
content: President Donald Trump’s Greenland push has moved from threats to a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland that he says will give the United States "permanent control" over the island’s security and allow Washington to expand its military presence there. The agreement still requires approval from Danish and Greenlandic lawmakers. Its full terms have not been made public, but officials say it would leave Greenland under Danish sovereignty while barring China, Russia and other non-NATO adversaries from establishing military bases or making certain sensitive investments on the island. TRUMP THREATENS TARIFFS ON COUNTRIES OPPOSING GREENLAND TAKEOVER PLANS Greenland rarely draws global attention. But as Arctic ice melts and great powers compete for influence, the world’s largest island has become a strategic prize. A semi-autonomous territory of Denmark, Greenland is home to a key U.S. military base and sits near emerging shipping routes and critical mineral deposits. Greenland’s roughly 56,000 residents are spread across five municipalities, with most living in small coastal towns. About 80% of the island is covered by an ice sheet, leaving much of its vast interior uninhabited. Despite its small population, Greenland is nearly the size of Alaska and Texas combined. Its location off Canada’s northeastern coast places Greenland at the heart of Arctic defense planning. The U.S. has maintained a military outpost in northwestern Greenland since 1953 at Pituffik Space Base, now operated by the U.S. Space Force. Russia also maintains military installations in the region, while China has sought greater access since declaring itself a "near-Arctic state" in 2018. Retreating Arctic ice is opening shipping lanes around the island that could shorten trade routes between North America, Europe and Asia. The changing landscape has also drawn attention to Greenland’s rare earth elements and other critical minerals used in technology, renewable energy and military systems. CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS Rare earth elements are especially important in high-performance magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, generators and precision-guidance systems. They are also used in missile guidance, radar, sonar, satellites and advanced aircraft. China dominates the global rare-earth supply chain, accounting for roughly 60% of mining and more than 90% of processing capacity. As the U.S. and European Union seek to reduce their reliance on Beijing, Greenland has emerged as a potential counterweight. As competition over shipping routes, defense positioning and critical minerals intensifies, Greenland’s importance is likely to grow.

White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios said artificial intelligence companies concerned about the safety of their own technology should slow development themselves rather than wait for the federal government to force them to do so.
“If you do believe that you're developing a technology that is unsafe, or you don't want it out into the world, you can just stop it,” Kratsios said Sunday on “Fox News Sunday.” “You don't need someone to force you to do that.”
Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, was responding to concerns about increasingly powerful AI systems and calls for additional government action.
“There’s leaders of these companies that are going out and saying, we're gonna do all these measures, the government has to do all of these things, when in reality, they just need to slow down if they feel that they need to do so,” Kratsios said.
Kratsios argued that the federal government already has tools available to respond when AI systems pose specific risks, pointing to an incident this summer in which he said the government received credible evidence of cybersecurity issues involving a model.
“A letter was sent to them, and the model was pulled down until those cybersecurity issues were resolved,” he said.
The comments come amid a broader debate in Washington and Silicon Valley over how the government should respond to potential risks from increasingly capable AI.
Kratsios also rejected predictions that AI could spiral beyond human control, saying fears of “Terminator running on the streets” were the wrong message to send to Americans.
The Trump administration has generally pursued a policy of accelerating U.S. AI development while addressing risks through existing authorities and targeted safeguards. A June national security directive, for example, called for faster AI adoption while requiring systems used by the national security enterprise to be reliable, robust, steerable and controllable.

title: Obama criticizes Trump on approach to AI, escalates warning for stronger regulation
description: Barack Obama slammed Trump's AI stance at Colgate University, warning the administration is neither capable nor willing to build a regulatory framework.
content: Former President Barack Obama criticized President Donald Trump's approach to artificial intelligence on Friday, calling for stronger federal regulation as the technology rapidly advances and concerns grow over safety, jobs and human control. "The challenge we have is that, obviously, we have a president currently that has said that’s for losers," Obama said during an appearance at Colgate University in Hamilton, New York. "So we’ve got a gap of at least a couple of years, where things are moving really fast, and we have an administration that is not capable of or willing to — I would argue both — putting together a serious regulatory framework." Obama's remarks expanded on a warning he issued last week, when he privately urged Democrats to make AI a central political issue. DEMOCRATS EMBRACED AI’S GROWTH BEFORE TRUMP CAME ALONG — NOW THEY WANT TO SLOW IT DOWN RNC member and Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer told Fox News Digital last week that policymakers should recognize AI’s risks without handing greater control to Washington or the technology companies themselves. "You don't have to agree on politics to recognize reality: AI is moving incredibly fast, and policymakers need to understand both the opportunities and the very real risks that come with it," she said. "Where I likely disagree with President Obama is on what government should do about it. The answer isn't handing Washington bureaucrats more control, and it certainly isn't allowing Big Tech to write the rules that govern itself," she said. "We need guardrails that protect Americans while allowing American innovation to lead the world. That means protecting children, workers and our national security, while making sure China doesn't win the AI race," she continued. AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK The debate shifted again Saturday when Trump announced the creation of an "AI Force" and said he plans to appoint an AI czar, while reiterating that his administration would resist efforts to slow development as the United States competes with China. "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," Trump said in a lengthy Truth Social post. Obama, speaking during Colgate’s Family Weekend, argued that relying on companies’ financial incentives and potential liability was insufficient to manage the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems. "[The] government has to be regulating this!" Obama said. "I heard one of Donald Trump’s main advisors on this make the argument that, ‘The market will take care of it. These companies will solve the safety issues because they have every incentive to do so — if it turns out to be dangerous, people will just sue them, and they’re worried about financial liability.’ That’s not how we treat airlines! Or drug companies, or food companies." Kremer told Fox News Digital that she felt Obama was "directing his criticism at the wrong branch of government." "It is not the president's job to write laws. That responsibility belongs to Congress, and Congress needs to act," Kremer said."We need serious guardrails for artificial intelligence, but this should not become another partisan fight over Donald Trump or Barack Obama. AI is moving too quickly and the stakes are too high for that. Congress must do its job and establish clear, enforceable rules that protect our children, American workers, our national security, and our communities while allowing American innovation to continue," she added. Kremer also said that Republicans should lead the framework for AI. "Republicans should also recognize that if we fail to lead on this issue, we leave a political opening for the left to define the debate and write the rules. Conservatives should be leading with a framework that protects Americans, preserves innovation, respects states' rights and local control, and holds Big Tech accountable. We should not cede this issue to Democrats simply because some people believe any guardrail is anti-innovation," she said. TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS' "Voluntary commitments from the AI companies themselves are not sufficient. The companies developing the most powerful technology in the world cannot also be the only ones deciding whether that technology is safe," Kremer said. Obama's characterization of the administration came as the White House has pursued its own AI policy framework, though one focused heavily on encouraging development and limiting regulations it considers burdensome. The Trump administration unveiled a national legislative framework in March addressing child safety, free speech, workforce issues and energy costs while calling for a consistent national approach to AI policy. Trump also signed a national security directive in June ordering agencies to accelerate adoption of advanced AI while requiring systems used in national security settings to be "robust, steerable, controllable" and subject to clear lines of accountability. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The disagreement has intensified as executives inside the AI industry themselves call for additional safeguards. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged companies last week to slow the pace of improvements to frontier models, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk expressed support for greater caution. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment, but did not immediately hear back.

title: California animal rescue operator charged with felonies for alleged 'inhumane and unsanitary conditions'
description: Video shows the squalid conditions where 300 animals were found at Christine De Anda's unlicensed Los Angeles County kennel, leading to 35 charges.
content: A California animal rescue operator is facing up to 24 1/2 years in state prison after being charged with 35 felonies and misdemeanors for alleged cruelty to animals, as she is accused of leaving roughly 300 animals living in severe squalor. Christine De Anda, 57, operator of the "Rock ‘N’ Pawz" rescue, faces 12 felony counts of animal cruelty, two felony counts of grand theft of labor, and 21 misdemeanor charges ranging from failure to provide care to operating an unlicensed kennel, according to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office. Prosecutors requested that her bail be set at $914,500 ahead of her arraignment at the Antelope Valley Courthouse. FLORIDA MAIL CARRIER ACCUSED OF SNATCHING PETS ON ROUTE, TRAPPING 100-PLUS CATS AND DOGS IN ‘HOARDING’ HOUSE "For someone who calls herself an animal rescuer, there’s a fundamental responsibility to protect and care for the animals entrusted to her," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said. "Instead, purported rescuer Christine De Anda allegedly left these animals to suffer or die from starvation, dehydration, untreated injuries and painful urine and fecal burns in filthy conditions." "After repeated citations and warnings, Ms. De Anda continued taking in animals she could not care for, leaving hundreds to endure prolonged suffering," Hochman added. "These animal victims cannot speak for themselves and look to us to protect them. My office will hold their victimizer fully accountable for her inhumane actions." The charges stem from a March 20, 2026, search warrant executed by Los Angeles County Animal Care and Control (DACC). Investigators removed more than 300 animals — primarily dogs, but also cats, a pig, a rabbit, a goose and two goats — in what DACC Director Marcia Mayeda called the "largest companion animal search warrant and rescue operation ever conducted" in the department’s history. 117 DEAD DOGS FOUND AT ANIMAL RESCUE, MANY WITH GUNSHOT WOUNDS AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE FOR ANSWERS "More than 300 animals were removed from severely inhumane conditions," Mayeda said. "Animals were living in and saturated with their own excrement, had serious untreated illnesses and injuries, were emaciated, and were forced to live in small crates without adequate room to properly lie comfortably. Our teams have worked tirelessly to stabilize them, provide the medical care they needed, and help them recover." At least one cat was found dead from starvation and dehydration at the start of the investigation, authorities said. FLORIDA MAN ALLEGEDLY KILLS FAMILY'S KITTENS IN FRONT OF TEENAGE DAUGHTER AS FORM OF PUNISHMENT: OFFICIALS "Sadly, despite all efforts, we were unable to save every animal due to the extent of their illnesses and injuries," Mayeda added. "DACC is deeply grateful for the support of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Los Angeles, Pasadena Humane and Kern County Animal Services for assisting us with this rescue and the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office for its commitment to pursuing justice for these animals." The L.A. County DA's Office shared a video on YouTube of the animals at the shelter, showing the conditions that led to the charges. She is accused of violating multiple county codes, including operating an animal kennel without required land-use approval, maintaining unsanitary conditions and having structures with unpermitted construction, plumbing, electrical and grading work.

title: Trump says new arch will also deploy drones, position snipers and store ammo
description: Trump says his 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington Memorial Bridge will house drones, snipers and large quantities of ammunition storage.
content: President Donald Trump said Sunday that his planned triumphal arch near the Arlington Memorial Bridge will be converted into a military complex capable of housing drones, deploying snipers and storing ammunition. "At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch … into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch," Trump wrote on Truth Social. TRUMP REVEALS ARC DE TRIOMPHE-STYLE MONUMENT FOR AMERICA’S 250TH ANNIVERSARY Trump said the 250-foot structure would have the "rapid ability" to deploy large numbers of drones, as well as snipers positioned on the roof and plaza areas. He also said the complex would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition." "There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote. The monument, inspired by Paris’ Arc de Triomphe, is intended to welcome visitors crossing the Memorial Bridge from Arlington National Cemetery into the nation’s capital. The proposed structure would be clad in granite and topped with three golden statues. FROM THE GILDED OVAL OFFICE TO A NEW BALLROOM: A LOOK AT TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE PROJECTS The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers and veterans, who argue that it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Opponents have also questioned whether the project requires congressional approval under federal law. The National Capital Planning Commission has approved the site and preliminary plans, but the project still requires additional review. Construction was previously expected to begin this month. The arch is one of several major construction and renovation projects Trump has pursued in Washington. TRUMP GAVE THE OVAL OFFICE A GILDED MAKEOVER – AND COVERED THE COST HIMSELF The administration has also begun work on a 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom. The sprawling addition, announced last July, will accommodate approximately 650 seated guests and follow the White House’s classical design. The White House currently lacks a formal ballroom, and the new structure is expected to replace the East Wing. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the ballroom was estimated to cost $200 million and would be financed by Trump and private donors. Trump has introduced gold accents in the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, lined the "walk of fame" with portraits of former presidents, including a photo of the autopen representing former President Joe Biden’s time in office, added stone pavers to the Rose Garden lawn and installed two 88-foot flagpoles. The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for additional comment.

title: Waltz delivers blunt warning to nations defying Iran sanctions, touts Greenland deal
description: Ambassador Mike Waltz says President Trump will push Gulf leaders and allies to enforce Iran sanctions at the United Nations, warning of consequences for noncompliance.
content: UNITED NATIONS, NEW YORK: President Donald Trump will return to the United Nations this week seeking greater international cooperation in confronting Iran, even as his administration moves to reshape the global institution hosting world leaders, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview ahead of the gathering. US presses allies to enforce Iran sanctions ahead of the UN General Assembly With the U.S.-Iran war entering its seventh month, Trump is expected to address the General Assembly on Tuesday and meet Gulf leaders whose countries have been directly affected by the conflict. The gathering comes as Washington seeks to intensify economic pressure on Tehran, European allies confront Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, and the administration faces questions about whether its push to reduce the U.N.'s size and spending risks diminishing the organization's ability to respond to international crises. BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY Waltz outlined what Washington expects from its partners on Iran: full enforcement of sanctions against Tehran, with consequences for countries that fail to comply. "They will reinforce that message, but importantly, it's all of these countries actually enforcing the sanctions and what they're going to hear is there will be consequences for friend and foe," Waltz said. "The president is doing this for the future security of the world." European and Asian allies have largely resisted Trump's requests for assistance in the Iran conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes in February, Reuters reported on Sept. 18. The war has also disrupted energy markets, with Iran obstructing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and its Houthi allies tightening their grip on a critical Red Sea shipping corridor. Waltz said the administration intends to make sanctions enforcement a central part of its diplomatic push during UNGA. "The Iranian economy continues to crater," Waltz said, pointing to the country's currency, inflation and the U.S. naval blockade. "One way or another, the president has been crystal clear on our goals here that Iran cannot and will not have a nuclear weapon." His remarks follow a Sept. 17 U.N. Security Council vote in which Russia and China blocked an effort to continue independent monitoring of international sanctions on Iran. Trump is also expected to meet Gulf leaders to discuss the conflict and regional security. Waltz said the administration wants to hear directly from its Gulf partners about their concerns, describing the collective meeting as an important diplomatic opportunity. JEFF BARTOS SAYS UN REFORM IS NO LONGER AN 'OXYMORON' AFTER $570M IN CUTS A UN the Trump administration wants to change — but not abandon The Iran conflict is unfolding against a broader debate over the future of the United Nations, an institution Trump has repeatedly criticized and his administration has sought to substantially reform. On Sept. 16, the United States paid $725 million toward the U.N.'s regular budget and another $102 million for peacekeeping operations. The payments reduced Washington's outstanding debt and averted the immediate risk of losing its General Assembly voting rights in 2027. However, the U.S. still owed approximately $1.312 billion to the organization's regular budget, according to the U.N. Asked why American taxpayers should continue funding an organization the administration has repeatedly criticized for what it considers anti-American bias, Waltz pointed to efforts to reduce spending and redirect the institution toward its original mission. "The president is clear about getting the U.N. back to basics and helping it realize its potential," Waltz told Fox News Digital. He said the administration had secured more than $1 billion in budget reductions, with roughly 3,000 headquarters positions being cut and a reduction of approximately 25% in peacekeeping personnel. "We have the U.N. on a diet," Waltz said. But Waltz also made clear that the administration does not intend to abandon the United Nations. "There's got to be one place in the world where everyone can come together and put diplomacy first and can actually talk," he said. "We don't ever want to see a U.N. in Beijing or Moscow or Brussels." "If we just walked away, you'd have 192 countries talking without us," Waltz added. Gaza offers one example of how the administration intends to use the U.N. while limiting direct American military involvement. Waltz pointed to the U.N.-endorsed Board of Peace and the planned International Stabilization Force, which is intended to support security and a postwar transition in Gaza. The ambassador said he does not want American troops deployed there, arguing that international security operations should allow other countries to share the burden. The U.N. Security Council endorsed the Gaza peace plan and authorized the stabilization force in November 2025. The State Department said Sept. 18 that Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be in New York from Sept. 20–23 to meet foreign counterparts, advance U.S. security and economic priorities and continue the administration's campaign for U.N. reform. WALTZ CALLS OUT IRANIAN DIPLOMAT AT UN FOLLOWING DRONE STRIKES ON BAHRAIN AND KUWAIT Greenland agreement adds another dimension to allied diplomacy Trump arrives in New York days after announcing a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland aimed at expanding the American military presence in the Arctic while restricting adversaries from establishing bases or making sensitive investments on the island. The agreement falls short of Trump's earlier ambition to acquire Greenland, which remains an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Denmark and Greenland have stressed that the arrangement will not compromise the island's sovereignty or right to self-determination. Additional details of the agreement have yet to be made public. Waltz told Fox News Digital that the deal reflects the Arctic's growing strategic importance as melting ice opens new shipping routes and increases access to energy and mineral resources. "It's incredibly significant," Waltz said, pointing to Russia's Arctic military capabilities and the potential for new shipping routes to transform global trade. "It took some tough tweets, maybe some tough language," he said. "We now have an agreement with our ally Denmark." The agreement comes as European governments confront overlapping security challenges involving Russia's war in Ukraine, Arctic defense and uncertainty over transatlantic security arrangements, while Washington seeks greater allied cooperation in its campaign against Iran. TRUMP ARRIVES AT NATO SUMMIT AS IRAN RIFT LOOMS ABOVE ALLIANCE TALKS World leaders converge on New York The U.N. expects 73 heads of state and 45 heads of government, along with 49 ministers, 11 vice presidents and one crown prince, to attend High-Level Week, U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told reporters Friday. Member states have submitted approximately 1,000 requests for bilateral meetings, while about 168 events are scheduled alongside the official proceedings. The 81st General Assembly's General Debate begins Tuesday and runs through Sept. 28. Beyond Iran, world leaders are expected to address Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the future of Gaza, international security and the U.N.'s ability to respond to emerging global challenges. Waltz described the administration's approach with a slogan inspired by the president's political branding: "Make the U.N. great again." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the immediate diplomatic questions facing Washington are more concrete: whether allies will increase pressure on Iran, whether Gulf leaders can agree on a path toward ending the conflict and whether the administration's push for a leaner U.N. can coexist with its efforts to use the organization to address international security challenges.

title: Electric Mercedes motorhome targets 621-mile range
description: The Mercedes-Benz eActros 600 electric truck targets 621 miles per charge on a 28,000-mile round-the-world journey through over 30 countries.
content: If you think you've seen some wild RVs, this one may reset the scale. Professional truck driver and content creator Tobias Wagner, better known online as Elektrotrucker, is preparing to drive around the world in a specially converted Mercedes-Benz eActros 600. A full Bliss Mobil living module sits behind the cab, turning this electric truck into a rolling home. Wagner plans to make the entire journey on battery power. Mercedes-Benz Trucks says the route will cover about 28,000 miles through more than 30 countries over roughly one year, with a goal of no more than 80 charging stops. According to Mercedes, the trip would be the first known circumnavigation of the globe in a fully battery-electric truck. What really caught my attention is how far Wagner hopes to go between those stops. Here's how this massive electric motorhome works and why its 621-mile range target could be the toughest part of the trip. 100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com This electric Mercedes motorhome started as a long-haul truck Underneath the living quarters sits the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600, a battery-electric truck built for long-distance commercial freight. Its three lithium iron phosphate battery packs provide a combined installed capacity of 621 kWh. Mercedes normally designs the truck to travel about 310 miles under specific fully loaded long-haul test conditions. Wagner's expedition truck has a very different job. Instead of pulling a heavily loaded commercial trailer, it carries a custom living module. Mercedes also modified the truck with single rear tires and expedition equipment. Those changes help reduce weight and rolling resistance compared with a traditional freight configuration. The finished expedition vehicle reportedly has a maximum weight of about 34,170 pounds. Power comes from Mercedes' electric axle and four-speed transmission. The eActros 600 produces about 536 horsepower continuously, with peak output reaching roughly 805 horsepower. That's a lot of muscle for a vehicle carrying its own kitchen and bed. Could it really travel 621 miles on one charge? This is where the project gets especially interesting. Wagner and Mercedes believe the lighter expedition setup, combined with careful hypermiling, could potentially travel as far as 621 miles on a single charge. That would be roughly double the range Mercedes quotes for a fully loaded eActros 600. Mercedes says the lighter expedition vehicle should significantly exceed the eActros 600's normal long-haul range. How close he gets will depend on road conditions, temperature, speed and terrain. Why the 621-mile target could become important Wagner wants to travel about 28,000 miles while stopping to charge no more than 80 times. That works out to an average of roughly 350 miles of driving per charging stop, although the actual distances will vary considerably along the route. Some stretches could become much more challenging. The expedition will cross regions where high-powered truck charging remains difficult to find. The latest route includes Central and East Asia, Australia, the United States and several countries in Latin America. That's where stretching the truck well beyond its normal freight range could become useful. ROBOTAXI PIT STOPS COULD POP UP NEAR YOU Charging a 621-kWh battery takes serious power Eventually, even this giant battery has to plug in. The eActros 600 supports CCS2 fast charging at up to 400 kW. Mercedes says that level of charging can take the battery from 10% to 80% in about 70 minutes under its specified conditions. Mercedes has also demonstrated Megawatt Charging System technology at up to 1,000 kW, which can cut charging times dramatically on compatible equipment. Wagner's expedition setup has also been prepared for different charging systems around the world. It includes charging connections positioned on both sides of the truck. The project also has adapters designed for charging infrastructure in China and North America. That flexibility could prove essential once the truck leaves Europe. Mercedes revealed another important backup. Wagner has equipped the truck with his own Alpitronic DC charging station. That lets him charge from AC connections at up to 43 kW in special situations when conventional high-powered truck charging is not available. The back of the truck is a fully electric home Bliss Mobil added a roughly 13-foot expedition module behind the cab. Inside, Wagner gets a U-shaped dining area along with a kitchen. A bathroom sits toward the rear. There's also a drop-down bed that stores above the dining area when he wants more room during the day. The camper can sleep as many as four people. Wagner will have considerably more room because his primary travel companion is his dog, Krümelix. The living module also follows the electric theme. It uses a separate 400-Ah lithium battery supported by 1,000 watts of solar power. That system handles equipment such as the induction cooktop, refrigerator and air conditioning. It also powers other onboard systems without relying on diesel or propane. The motorhome reportedly carries about 106 gallons of fresh water. A multistage filtration system helps Wagner manage water during extended stretches away from traditional campgrounds. The camper can operate separately from the truck Bliss Mobil designed the expedition module as a largely self-contained unit. Its electrical and plumbing systems sit within the camper rather than depending on the truck itself. That approach allows Bliss Mobil modules to move between compatible truck chassis. Wagner's module does have a 24-volt connection to the eActros. That means the living area can draw energy from the truck's main battery when necessary. Still, the expedition has an obvious reason to conserve that electricity. Every bit of power used inside the camper could otherwise help move a nearly 17-ton vehicle farther down the road. There's an electric motorcycle riding on the back A giant expedition truck can handle plenty of roads, but there will always be places where its size becomes a problem. Wagner has another electric solution for that. A motorcycle carrier on the back holds a Honda WN7 electric motorcycle. When the road becomes too tight for the eActros, Wagner can leave the motorhome behind and continue on two wheels. The motorcycle uses a 9.3-kWh battery and produces about 67 horsepower. It's a useful backup for a trip designed to reach places far beyond normal highway rest stops. TOYOTA JOINS HYDROGEN TRUCK ALLIANCE PUSH Nearly $800,000 buys one very unusual motorhome None of this comes cheaply. A price sheet displayed with the vehicle broke down the cost of the eActros 600 truck, Bliss Mobil camper and additional equipment. The total is approximately $796,600 including tax based on the exchange rate used at the time. Call it nearly $800,000. The Honda electric motorcycle wasn't included in that figure. Of course, this also isn't a production RV you can configure at your local Mercedes dealership. Wagner's vehicle is a specialized one-off expedition build created around a commercial electric truck. We've seen other companies rethink how electric vehicles fit into camping. The CyberTrailer takes a different approach, using solar power and an onboard energy system to support off-grid travel. The around-the-world trip starts Sept. 20 Mercedes-Benz Trucks says Wagner will officially depart from IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, on Sunday, Sept. 20. From there, the trip is expected to last about a year. Mercedes says Wagner will travel through around 30 countries on five continents while putting battery-electric truck technology through real-world conditions well beyond familiar European freight routes. Mercedes says the planned route may still change as the trip progresses. The vehicle may be built for an extraordinary adventure, but the results could tell us something much bigger about electric transportation. What this means to you You probably won't be putting an $800,000 electric expedition truck in your driveway. Still, this trip could answer questions that eventually affect far more ordinary electric vehicles. Range is only part of the EV equation. Reliable charging becomes even more important when you leave major highways or travel through areas with limited infrastructure. Wagner will be testing both. If the eActros can consistently travel well beyond its standard commercial range, engineers will get another example of how vehicle weight and driving technique can change battery performance. The charging side may prove equally revealing. A vehicle can carry an enormous battery, but long-distance travel still depends on finding equipment powerful enough to recharge it. Wagner's onboard charging equipment gives him another option when high-powered public chargers are unavailable, but slower charging could add considerable time to the trip. We have already seen experiments that attack the charging problem from another direction. One electric road project is testing technology that can transfer power to vehicles while they drive. Wagner's trip takes the opposite approach. He is bringing a huge battery and finding out how far today's infrastructure can take it. Kurt's key takeaways I love a good road trip, but this one takes the idea to another level. What fascinates me most isn't simply whether Wagner can squeeze 621 miles out of this massive battery. I want to see what happens when he leaves the easy charging routes behind and has to make this technology work across more than 30 countries. That's where this trip could get really interesting. A giant battery and impressive range numbers are great, but you still need a working charger when you pull in. If Wagner can circle the globe with roughly 80 charging stops, that's a pretty strong demonstration of how far electric trucking has come. And if he gets stranded looking for power along the way, we'll learn something from that, too. content: A single gunshot during a post-tailgate fight near Notre Dame's South Bend, Indiana, campus struck a woman and a police officer Saturday night, authorities said. MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD Following the incident, police swiftly evacuated nearby businesses and parking garages. title: Lane Kiffin couldn't help himself, takes petty shot at Ole Miss fans after LSU loss in his return to Oxford
description: Lane Kiffin took a subtle jab at Ole Miss fans after his LSU Tigers fell 32-24, joking he had to leave to fill Vaught-Hemingway Stadium early.
content: Lane Kiffin has picked up his fair share of criticism over the years, but if there is one thing no one can argue about the man, it is that he isn't going to change his personality for the sake of the situation. One specific soundbite he delivered after his return to Ole Miss went the wrong way for him and his LSU Tigers perfectly encapsulates that. The Week 3 matchup between LSU and Ole Miss delivered in every way imaginable, which isn't often the case in such highly anticipated events. From the build-up of Kiffin stepping back on the field he coached on for six seasons, to the atmosphere inside the stadium, and to the game itself, it was the epitome of college football. The Rebels jumped out to a commanding 24-7 lead in the first half before the Tigers scored 17 unanswered points to knot things up and set the scene for a fourth quarter that could only be described as pure cinema. LANE KIFFIN WALKED BACK INTO OXFORD AS THE MAIN CHARACTER, BUT OLE MISS AND PETE GOLDING STOLE HIS SPOTLIGHT Ultimately, Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, the best player on the field, gave his team the lead back with just over six minutes remaining before LSU quarterback Sam Leavitt threw an interception in the end zone with a minute left to go to seal the deal for the Rebels, 32-24. Speaking with the media after his team's loss, Kiffin admitted it was emotional returning to Ole Miss both on game day itself and in the buildup to the top 10 showdown. Yet, despite the team he left on the eve of last season's College Football Playoff getting its revenge against his LSU Tigers, Kiffin couldn't help but take a subtle shot at Ole Miss fans. "You walk into a storm, ya know," Kiffin said, describing the atmosphere inside the stadium at Ole Miss. "That's what happens a lot of times in these games, you see it all the time. It's a buzzsaw. "You walk in, it's a buildup. The stadium is full an hour early; I guess I had to leave to get them to do that. So, you're welcome," Kiffin concluded with a smile. Saturday's contest, with Kiffin returning to Oxford, provided for one of the most unique setups in college football history, adding an infinite amount of juice to the game, but throwing a jab at the fans who supported you until the final minute of your six-year tenure was an interesting choice was an interesting choice by Kiffin. title: Beloved Mexican food disappearing from restaurant menus across America
description: Tamale entrees have dropped 7.8% on Mexican restaurant menus across the United States, and the grueling labor behind each masa batch is a key reason.
content: The tamale was once a familiar presence on Mexican restaurant menus in the United States, sharing space with tacos, burritos and enchiladas. Increasingly, though, diners looking for one may have to search. Tamale entrées have dropped 7.8% from menus over the past five years, according to Technomic's Ignite Menu data comparing the second quarters of 2021 and 2026. One reason may be a basic restaurant calculation: Tamales require considerable labor for something diners expect to be relatively inexpensive. POPULAR TEX-MEX CHAIN ABRUPTLY SHUTTERS REMAINING RESTAURANTS ACROSS AMERICA AMID INDUSTRY STRUGGLES Robert Mahon, director of operations for Mahon Hospitality Group, runs Amor Loco and Toro Loco in New York City, neither of which serves tamales. Mahon enjoys tamales himself and said his restaurants have discussed offering them, but the economics can be difficult. "Even though the ingredients might not be so costly, it's more the labor," Mahon told Fox News Digital. "It's so labor-intensive." That labor becomes apparent at Taquería Picoso in Alexandria, Virginia, where executive chef Elio Gomez keeps tamales on the menu. Gomez said his process takes about three days. His restaurant sources corn from Mexico, then cooks it through an overnight nixtamalization process. The corn is ground into masa, while fillings and banana leaves are prepared separately. The masa must then be mixed with fat, broth and salt and aerated to achieve the right consistency before the tamales can be assembled, carefully wrapped and cooked. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Training someone to do all that takes time, too. Gomez said he spent months working alongside the employee who now makes his tamales. Even with a recipe, Gomez said, a cook must learn how the masa should feel and how to wrap each tamale properly, so it doesn't dry out during cooking. All that work goes into an item that still doesn't generate taco-level demand. "No, definitely it's not the same demand as a taco, for example," Gomez said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Mahon said his customers aren't clamoring for tamales either. "They're not walking out of our restaurants if they don't have a tamale," Mahon said. "It's not expected as a staple anymore." Price presents another complication. Gomez charges $6 for a tamale, a price he considers inexpensive given the work involved. But some customers remember much cheaper versions. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Yet the tamale's declining presence on restaurant menus doesn't necessarily mean the food itself is disappearing. Gomez, who grew up in Mexico City, remembers tamales as an everyday breakfast food sold by street vendors in the morning. In the United States, he sees them being treated more as a special food associated with holidays and family gatherings. Asked what he would tell someone eating a tamale for the first time, Gomez described the masa as fluffy, the dish as rich and its appeal as deeply comforting. title: Aaron Rodgers’ famous exes from Shailene Woodley to the romance that sent him into a 'tailspin'
description: Aaron Rodgers says he regretted letting now-wife Brittani go years earlier, revealing the secret timeline from their 2017 meeting to their 2025 elopement.
content: Aaron Rodgers’ love life has taken him from Hollywood romances and a broken engagement to a secret wedding years in the making. Rodgers’ road to marriage was anything but a straight line. After high-profile romances with Olivia Munn, Danica Patrick and Shailene Woodley, the NFL star ultimately found his way back to the woman he says he regretted letting go years earlier. The now 42-year-old football star's dating life began drawing celebrity-media attention in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Actress Jessica Szohr was among his earliest well-documented Hollywood connections, but his relationships became substantially more public once he began dating Munn in 2014. AARON RODGERS MAKES BOMBSHELL CLAIMS ABOUT SHAILENE WOODLEY SPLIT Jessica Szohr The "Gossip Girl" star and Rodgers had an on-and-off relationship in the early 2010s. Szohr and the quarterback were first linked in 2011, after being spotted publicly together. The former couple initially ended things because of their busy schedules. The two reportedly rekindled their relationship in 2014 before calling it quits again. Their romance preceded Rodgers’ more heavily publicized relationships, and the pair appeared to remain on friendly terms afterward. While there aren't many public details about the couple's rumored relationship, People reported Szohr later attended Rodgers’ birthday party in 2017. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Olivia Munn Rodgers met Olivia Munn while presenting the Song of the Year award at the ACM Awards in 2014. Their relationship quickly became one of his most high-profile romances. While both had busy schedules, Munn explained how the two made it work. "There’s a lot of traveling, a lot of driving, and then you’re just really happy with the decisions that you make. And for me, it comes at a time in my life when I end up having to say no to some work because I gotta be somewhere else. It doesn’t make me sad or anything, because I want my life to be full and have all those experiences, so you kind of figure it out as you go," she told E! News in 2014. Engagement rumors between the two began to surface in 2016 and Munn even stepped out with a ruby on her ring finger. However, the two called it quits just a few months later. "When you are living out a relationship in the public eye, it’s definitely… it’s difficult. It has some extra constraints, because you have other opinions about your relationship, how it affects your work and, you know, just some inappropriate connections," Rodgers told ESPN shortly after the breakup. During their relationship, it became public that Rodgers was estranged from his family, and many of his fans blamed Munn for the rift. "There's this whole big narrative that stayed with me for so many years, but there was just this dynamic in the family that had nothing to do with me. It became this whole big thing, and people were like, 'I can't with her, she's keeping this family apart,'" Munn said during a 2025 appearance on the "Armchair Expert" podcast. In Ian O'Connor’s 2024 biography "Out of the Darkness: The Mystery of Aaron Rodgers," Rodgers shared that the cause of the schism was "deep-rooted." He also clarified that Munn "had nothing to do all the years" of prior estrangement. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Danica Patrick Rodgers traded Hollywood glamour for racing royalty when he began dating Danica Patrick. The former IndyCar and NASCAR star confirmed their romance in January 2018, years after the two had initially crossed paths at the ESPYs. The two had actually kept in touch via email before sparks flew. "We kept in touch a little bit, and there were some years we didn’t talk to each other, and then some every now and again, but it wasn’t until obviously recently that we actually had phone numbers. We referred to each other as Chicago and Green Bay – it was very cute," Patrick told Jenny McCarthy on her SiriusXM show. The relationship quickly became serious and highly visible, with the pair making public appearances and Rodgers openly discussing their life together. "We’re just two people who enjoy being around each other and love each other," he told Artful Living in 2018. "We’re really into each other… we’re really attracted to each other… we really enjoy traveling… She’s up for anything travel-wise, which is fun. She’s a good travel partner because she’s so laid-back and low-maintenance. And she’s a hell of a cook, so we love just staying in, too. She eats really healthy. She’s inspired me in that way." But there would be no trip down the aisle: after more than two years as a couple, Patrick's representative confirmed their split in July 2020. In a 2025 appearance on "The Sage Steele Show," Patrick spoke about her time with Rodgers, claiming that "the nature of the relationship was emotionally abusive." "He leaves a trail of blood," she said, later adding, "It gave me the greatest gift, the greatest gift, which is myself. It gave me the greatest gift of how much I needed to show up for myself and take care of myself." On a recent episode of "Not Just Football with Cam Heyward," Rodgers shared his side of the story, saying, "I dated Danica. She had just retired. She was depressed and not fun to be around. But I didn’t leave her because I was trying to be there and be a good partner. Then it was going a certain direction, obviously. There was no intimacy; there was nothing." "She tells a story that she was so blindsided… and that ‘he leaves a trail of blood around him.’ And I’m like, what are you talking about? That is not what happened, by any means." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Shailene Woodley If Rodgers’ previous romances generated headlines, his whirlwind relationship with Shailene Woodley took things to another level. Speculation the two were romantically linked first surfaced in 2020, but by February 2021, Rodgers stunned fans by revealing he was engaged while accepting his third NFL MVP award. Woodley soon confirmed she was the mystery fiancée. But the fairy-tale ending never arrived. Their engagement unraveled, and the pair ultimately separated in 2022 after attempts at reconciliation. The breakup has remained a subject of public discussion: Woodley has spoken about experiencing a deeply difficult period around that time, while Rodgers offered his own sharply different account of their relationship and split in September 2026. On Heyward's podcast, Rodgers explained that he didn't "ruin" the actress' life during their 2022 split. "I proposed to Shailene and she said yes. Now, she maybe felt like she was forced to make a decision. She could have said no," Rodgers began. "A couple days after that, she tells me, 'Before we get married, I gotta go f--- this guy,' and I’m like – because her story is that I ruined her life and gave her crazy depression because I left her. But in actuality, she told me that, and then she took off the ring by March – I proposed in December – and we had a couple of times where we tried to get reunited and nothing ever happened," he said. "There wasn’t even a relationship in 2022 to break off. She literally told me, 'I don’t want to be with you' after we tried some reconciliation in 2021. There’s just a lot of narrative out there that isn’t true," Rodgers clarified. Woodley has not responded to Rodgers' claims. WATCH: SHAILENE WOODLEY LAUGHS OFF QUESTION ABOUT EX AARON RODGERS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Brittani After years of very public romances, Rodgers ultimately married someone who has made a point of staying almost completely out of the spotlight. Rodgers revealed in June 2025 that he was a married man and later identified his wife only as Brittani. "In 2017, I met my wife, and at the time, she was leaving the States and going back to Europe," he told Heyward on the September podcast. "And my biggest regret is not begging her to stay or proposing right there, because that sent me right there into a tailspin of what can I be accused of as a partner in a relationship." The NFL star explained he met Brittani while she was living in Austin after attending the University of Texas. After the two didn't work out, she moved back to Europe before they reconnected years later. "She was engaged, then I got engaged, and luckily, for me, we came back together," he said. The couple quietly eloped in 2025, with Rodgers deliberately keeping his new wife away from the celebrity circus that surrounded his previous relationships. And the notoriously private quarterback is already looking toward their next chapter: Rodgers said in September 2026 that he hopes fatherhood is in his future after football.

title: Hamas allegedly built weapons depots across Europe, planned terror attacks as Oct 7 anniversary neared
description: Federal German prosecutors indicted seven suspects who allegedly stockpiled weapons for Hamas to target Jewish communities and Israeli diplomats.
content: The German federal prosecutor’s office recently announced that it indicted seven people for allegedly securing weapons for the Hamas terrorist organization, with the goal of launching terrorist attacks on the second remembrance date of the Oct. 7 massacre in Israel. The indictment has catapulted the danger of Hamas’ network in Europe to Israeli, American and European installations and citizens into the spotlight. According to the prosecutor’s office, "All of the accused belong to the foreign terrorist organization Hamas. Some time ago, the organization’s military wing (the so-called Qassam Brigades) began establishing weapons depots in Europe. No later than July 2025, Hamas planned a concrete assassination in Germany or Austria targeting representatives of Israel, people of Jewish faith, or persons with pro-Israel views." The seven suspects were arrested between October 2025 and May 2026. SUSPECTED HAMAS TERRORIST ARRESTED IN GREECE FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING ATTACK ON ISRAELI CRUISE SHIP The statement added, "The attack was to take place in close temporal proximity to the second anniversary of Hamas’s assault on Israel on 7 October 2023 — i.e., in early October 2025." The indictment listed the nationalities and first names and first letter of the last name of the suspects: German national Abed Al G., Danish national Yousif C., Lebanon-born Borhan El-K., Lebanon-born Wael F.M., German national Ahmad I., Lebanon-born Kamel M., Bulgarian national Mohammad S." German law shields the last names of criminal suspects for privacy reasons. The German prosecutors said the suspected Hamas terrorists "had already obtained a functional fully automatic rifle, 13 functional pistols and more than 700 rounds of ammunition. Mohammed A., who is being prosecuted separately, transported some of the weapons to Vienna and stored them there." According to the German paper Die Welt, "One of the accused was working as a confidential informant for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. The files show that the informant continued reporting to his intelligence handler while allegedly failing to disclose the full extent of his own involvement in obtaining ammunition for the group." EXCLUSIVE: ISRAEL SEIZES VAST IRAN TERROR AXIS ARSENAL WITH SURPRISING FOREIGN ORIGINS Sascha Adamek, a German journalist and the author of the 2026 book "Infiltration: Political Islam Continues Its Advance," told Fox News Digital, "Now the policy of previous federal governments is coming back to haunt them: until 2023 they allowed Hamas and its front organizations to use Germany as a ‘safe haven’ for fundraising and recruitment and also for the radicalization of young people. This dirty deal — that Hamas does not use violence in this country and is therefore left to operate freely — has long been obsolete." According to the most recent Federal German domestic intelligence report, Hamas could have had as many as 650 operatives in Germany during 2025, the last year of tracking. In 2024, 550 Hamas operatives were active and in 2023 the number totaled 450. The intelligence officials wrote in the report that "The figures refer to Germany and are partly estimated and rounded." According to the report, 1,250 Hezbollah operatives are active in Germany. UN AGENCY ACCUSED OF HAMAS TIES SEES ANOTHER EUROPEAN NATION CUT FUNDING When asked why Germany is allowing Hamas and Hezbollah operatives and members to conduct activities within its territory, the press office of the German Federal Ministry of the Interior told Fox News Digital in part, "Hamas, which has been banned from operating in Germany since 2023, has a network of supporters and followers; however, for many years they have tended to act with restraint in public and avoid any outward signs of connection to the organization." The Interior Ministry’s press office added, "Hezbollah, which is also subject to a ban on its activities in Germany, is not organized under any nationwide umbrella organization or similar supraregional structure. Rather, its supporters are spread across various associations throughout Germany. The focus of the activities of these associations — which are classified as affiliated with Hezbollah —lies in the religious and cultural spheres, as well as in educational programs for children, youth and adults that promote conservative Islam and a Shi’ite identity. In isolated cases, Hezbollah supporters in Germany have been known to engage in specific acts of support for the organization in Lebanon." When asked if the German government is lax, as critics argue, about eradicating Hamas and Hezbollah terrorism structures, the Interior Ministry said, "On November 2, 2023, the Federal Ministry of the Interior banned the activities of the terrorist organization Hamas in Germany, as these activities violate German criminal law and run counter to the principle of international understanding… Furthermore, its purpose or activities significantly harm the interests of the Federal Republic of Germany. In addition, the Federal Ministry of the Interior had already banned the activities of Hezbollah in Germany on April 30, 2020, as these activities also violate German criminal law and the organization is directed against the principle of international understanding." The interior ministry noted, "Federal and state security authorities consistently investigate leads regarding possible extremist activities as well as acts subject to criminal prosecution and continuously examine all countermeasures available under the rule of law." The statement also said, "The Hamas terrorist attack on the State of Israel on October 7, 2023, and the subsequent military operation by Israeli defense forces in the Gaza Strip continue to have an impact on the security situation in Germany and Europe. In addition to the heightened abstract threat level, there continue to be intense pro-Palestinian protests as well as corresponding agitation on social media. Various extremist actors in Germany are inciting hatred and violence against Jews or the State of Israel, or denying its right to exist." GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS The presence of indicted Lebanese men highlights the alliance between the two U.S-designated terrorist organizations, Hamas and the Lebanon-based Hezbollah. The Iranian regime-backed Hezbollah joined Hamas a day after the Gaza-based terrorist movement invaded Israel in 2023 and slaughtered over 1,200 people. Germany's Die Welt reported, "The prosecutors alleged the weapons operation was also coordinated from Lebanon, where a Hamas operative allegedly oversaw one of the procurement channels linking members of the network across Europe." Israel’s Foreign Ministry seized on the report about the planned Hamas terror attacks in Germany and Austria, posting on X: "Palestinian Hamas was planning terror on the streets of Europe. German prosecutors say Hamas plotted attacks in Berlin and Vienna targeting Jewish communities and Israeli diplomats – part of a network allegedly using Turkey as a base for terror operations against European targets. The goal: mark October 7 with more blood." Matthew Levitt, a leading scholar on Hezbollah and Hamas in Europe from the Washington Institute, told Fox News Digital, "I wrote the only long form, detailed expose on this a while back now in CTC Sentinel [Combating Terrorism Center}, based on court documents and extensive interviews." He added, "Hamas continues plotting in Europe, overseen by senior Qassam Brigades officials in Lebanon and with direct ties to senior Hamas leadership. One of the people arrested in Europe is the son of a senior Hamas leader, Basem Naim." Levitt published his article titled "Hamas Plots in Europe: A Shift Toward External Operations?" in the October 2025 issue of the West Point journal CTC. Levitt cited a 2024 German prosecution indictment of alleged Hezbollah terrorists planning possible attacks against an American military base and Israel's embassy. Levitt wrote, "The weapons, German officials concluded, ‘were intended to expand Hamas’ activities in Europe.‘ As the investigation progressed, German authorities determined — based on materials found on one of the defendants’ USB storage devices — that the Hamas operatives were considering specific targets in Germany, including the Israeli embassy in Berlin, the U.S. Ramstein Air Base in Rhineland-Palatinate and the area around Berlin’s Tempelhof airport." He told the German media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland (RND), "Germany has gone from being a retreat for Hamas to an active terrorist target." He stressed Hamas’ ideology and terrorism affects "all of us" and a coordinated response is required.

title: El-Sayed’s Senate bid raises new concerns over a powerful privilege that comes with the job
description: Abdul El-Sayed's ties to figures linked to Hamas and Hezbollah alarm conservatives as the Michigan Senate nominee could gain classified access.
content: Conservatives who spoke with Fox News Digital are raising concerns about what could happen if Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed wins his election and, by virtue of holding office, becomes eligible to receive certain classified information. Unlike congressional staffers and many executive-branch officials, senators are not required to obtain a formal executive-branch security clearance to be eligible for classified information related to their official duties. If El-Sayed wins in November, he would not have to go through the same formal security-clearance process as many other government officials because members of Congress are generally considered eligible for access to classified information by virtue of holding elected office. Those issues have raised concerns among some national security and policy experts. COUNTERTERRORISM EXPERT WARNS ABDUL EL-SAYED SENATE BID RAISES HOMELAND SECURITY CONCERNS "Anyone refusing to disavow America-hater Hasan Piker should never be elected to Congress. El-Sayed will use his perch in the Senate to undermine America and empower its enemies," Daniel Samet, a research fellow specializing in Middle East policy at the center-right American Enterprise Institute, told Fox News Digital. Samet argued that El-Sayed has associated with people who support the intifada and terrorist causes and that he has shown sympathy for radical Islamist ideology. Fox News Digital and other outlets have reported on El-Sayed’s appearances and political relationships with individuals who have expressed support for or made favorable statements about U.S.-designated terrorist organizations. In April, for instance, El-Sayed was introduced at a campaign rally by Amir Makled, a man who previously celebrated dead members of the terrorist organization Hezbollah as "martyr[s]." A few months later, at a mosque opening, El-Sayed shared a stage with Sheikh Fadhel al-Sahlani, a cleric who has previously praised Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack and made remarks minimizing the number of Jews killed in the Holocaust. EL-SAYED’S ISNA APPEARANCE DRAWS SCRUTINY OVER CONTROVERSIAL SPEAKERS He also accepted an endorsement from Osama Siblani, who has praised both Hamas and Hezbollah. Critics have also pointed to El-Sayed’s relationship with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who once said that America "deserved 9/11." El-Sayed has since called that statement "dumb," and distanced himself from Piker, though stopped short of totally disavowing him. "Abdul’s running to keep Americans safe and bring down costs for Michigan families. Mike Rogers spent his entire career selling out Michigan, and has directly profited off shady business dealings with foreign companies," campaign spokesperson Cole Wozniak told Fox News Digital. "Rogers made hundreds of thousands of dollars working for companies that partnered with Chinese firms posing ‘national security threats’ to the US, and worked for a Saudi-linked company that pushed for regulations that could have ‘enabled Saudi Arabia to develop nuclear weapons.’ Mike Rogers got rich selling out Michiganders and he can’t be trusted to keep us safe," the statement continued. On China, the El-Sayed spokesperson was apparently referencing Rogers’ work in the telecommunications industry at companies that had business dealings involving Huawei. While serving in the House, Rogers was a vocal critic of Huawei and his work in the telecommunications industry was related to improving national security. The Saudi Arabia jab was a reference to Rogers' work with a Saudi-linked company that drew criticism over its efforts to transfer nuclear energy technology to the Middle Eastern kingdom. "Mike Rogers spent his entire career fighting against national security threats like the terrorist organizations that fund Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign," campaign spokeswoma Alyssa Brouillet told Fox News Digital. "Mike has always and will continue to have America’s best national security interest." title: Sorority rush gets Ozempic makeover as some college women resort to weight-loss injections
description: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy are said to be quietly reshaping sorority rush culture, as college students chase an increasingly thin beauty ideal.
content: As GLP-1 medications continue to surge in popularity for weight loss and diabetes treatment, their use is rising among younger adults — with anecdotal reports suggesting the trend is making its way onto college campuses. Market research has shown that GLP-1s – including semaglutide (Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) – are growing fastest among adults under 40, particularly young women. A 2024 analysis published in JAMA found that 162,439 young adults ages 18 to 25 received at least one dispensed GLP-1 prescription in 2023. Women accounted for 76.4% of those patients, although the analysis included medications prescribed for both diabetes and weight management. PATIENTS TAKING WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS OFTEN MAKE 5 CRITICAL MISTAKES, DOCTOR WARNS Separately, the 2025 Monitoring the Future survey found that 2% of students in grades 8, 10 and 12 reported using a prescription GLP-1 medication, while another 2% said they had used one without a prescription. A recent feature in The Cut, "The Secret 'Ozempidemic' on Sorority Row," argues that GLP-1 weight-loss drugs have quietly become part of campus culture at some elite universities, particularly within the competitive sorority recruitment process. Three female students interviewed under pseudonyms said they were using compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide to improve their chances during rush and to meet an increasingly thin beauty ideal. The students described a pressure to look extremely thin, noting that social media and weight-loss competitions among friends have fueled increased GLP-1 use. POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER "For many young women who have just arrived on campus, thinness feels like the ticket into the best possible college experience," one student said. "I didn't realize that someone who was 19 and also not super-overweight could get on it. I was like, ‘I gotta hop on,’" another said. One former sorority recruiter said, "It's like, 'Well, there's no excuse for people to be fat because they could just get a GLP-1.'" ‘Cosmetic shortcut’ Jay Campbell, longevity and peptide expert and bestselling author, said that while these drugs were built to solve a metabolic crisis, they've been "hijacked as a cosmetic shortcut." "For someone who's metabolically dysregulated, they are a genuine medical intervention," he told Fox News Digital. "But to a 20-year-old sorority member with a normal BMI, they look like an aesthetic hack in a syringe." "Sororities are built on social visibility and constant comparison," Campbell said. "Everyone is looking at everyone's Instagram." "When one girl drops 15 pounds in six weeks, that news spreads through the sorority house faster than any diet fad in history, because the results are fast, dramatic, and don't require the discipline of nutrition or training." "When one girl drops 15 pounds in six weeks, that news spreads through the sorority house faster than any diet fad in history." College-aged women already tend to have "high body-image sensitivity," he noted, which is heightened in the age of "a full-scale social contagion." OZEMPIC USERS MAY BE MAKING A MAJOR WEIGHT-LOSS MISTAKE, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS "Many of these young women grew up already fighting disordered relationships with food and their physical bodies, and [now] you have a medication that can play on their insecurities." That’s not to say GLP-1s don’t benefit many patients. In clinical studies of people taking the medications for obesity, fat mass generally accounts for more of the lost weight than lean mass, Campbell pointed out. "The peptide isn't catabolic by itself – the real risk is that a healthy 20-year-old who isn't obese has far less metabolic and muscular reserve to lose from in the first place." When a young woman loses weight rapidly without consuming enough protein or doing resistance training, she may lose a greater proportion of lean mass, Campbell warned. Rapid weight loss can also contribute to the facial or body changes sometimes referred to as "Ozempic face" and "Ozempic body." 5 steps college students should take before starting a GLP-1 For college students considering a weight-loss medication, Campbell recommends taking the following five steps before beginning treatment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES No. 1: Know whether the medication is medically appropriate "If you're not obese or metabolically compromised, ask yourself honestly why you're taking a medication designed for a disease you don't have," Campbell suggested. No. 2: Protect muscle during weight loss While muscle loss is preventable, it requires work that most people using these drugs for cosmetic reasons aren't doing, Campbell said. "That means real protein intake, not a protein bar as an afterthought, and resistance training," he advised. "Skip both, and you will absolutely lose muscle tissue that you cannot easily get back at 20 years old." While adequate protein intake and resistance training may help reduce muscle loss, the amount of lean mass lost varies from person to person. No. 3: Understand fertility considerations "Fertility matters here in a way most college students never think about," Campbell said. GLP-1 medications should not be used for weight loss during pregnancy, experts agree. Semaglutide labeling advises stopping Wegovy at least two months before a planned pregnancy. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Tirzepatide has been shown to reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives during treatment initiation and dose increases, so the FDA advises using an alternate method for four weeks during those periods. No. 4: Discuss mental health and eating behaviors Mental health still deserves attention, particularly for young adults with depression, anxiety, eating disorders or a history of using food to cope emotionally. While the FDA has found no increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior from GLP-1 medications, patients should tell their prescriber about any new or worsening mood symptoms. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP No. 5: Recognize the limits of long-term data "Nobody knows what 10 or 20 years of GLP-1 use looks like in a woman who started at 20 with a normal body weight, because that population barely existed in the clinical trials," Campbell cautioned. "Consider this a reminder to stop treating a powerful metabolic medication like a lifestyle accessory." While GLP-1 medications can suppress appetite, Campbell added, "they will not fix a broken metabolic foundation or whatever underlying reason a 20-year-old feels she needs to lose weight in the first place." "We’ve built a pharmaceutical shortcut that used to require months of behavior change, and young women in high-visibility social environments are early adopters of anything that changes how they look, fast." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Campbell stressed that treatment should involve a qualified prescriber who evaluates the patient’s medical history and goals, provides appropriate monitoring, adjusts the dose as needed and helps manage potential side effects. title: TRACE GALLAGHER: Common sense isn't old-fashioned. It's exactly what America needs now
description: The Common Sense Department segment has become the most memorable 75 seconds on "Fox News @ Night," inspiring a new book and thousands of mugs.
content: Since October 2022, I have anchored a TV show called "Fox News @ Night." Monday to Friday, from 11 p.m. until midnight Eastern time, we cover the news that matters, interview compelling guests and debate the hottest issues. And we do it all in a lively, fast-paced hour of plain-talk television, sending viewers off to bed with a solid grasp of what’s happening in the world and a smile or two as their heads hit the pillow. It’s a modern show, and I don’t just mean the little @ sign in the name. I’m talking about our whole approach to the news. We boil it down and sort it out. We jump right in. And this last one is important: We call BS whenever it’s warranted. Which is often, given all the crap that’s floating around out there. And every night, we include a segment that has become the most memorable 75 seconds in our hour-long show. It’s called the Common Sense Department, and nothing I do on television brings me more joy. TRACE GALLAGHER: COMMON SENSE IS ALIVE IN AMERICA. WE JUST NEED TO LISTEN Every night, I pick something in the news, and I put it through my own filter of hard-earned common sense. You know how TV news works. Every time a major news story breaks—especially a political one—the spin machines start cranking at maximum volume. Suddenly, you’ve got a "panel of experts" flooding your screen, telling you that what you just saw with your own two eyes isn’t actually happening. They’ll look you in the face and insist everything is "deeply nuanced" or "incredibly complex." But let’s be real: Most of the time, it’s not complex at all. My job is simple, even if it’s harder than it looks. I react like a normal, intelligent person who’s been around the block a few times, seen the games people play, and isn’t buying the nonsense anymore. You see it, I see it, and we’re going to call it exactly like it is. That’s why we call it the Common Sense Department. And how do I do it? That’s easy. I rely on the commonsensical lessons I can pluck from my own life and the lives of the people around me. The wisdom I was raised with. What personal experience has taught me along the way. The values of family, faith, sports, community, history and patriotism. Insights drawn from stories exactly like the ones in this book. Just like life, it’s everything mushed together before it’s run through one person’s admittedly quirky brain. Mine. What a rare treat it is! Every night in the Common Sense Department, I really get to be me! And the viewers keep saying, "Give us more." I know this from the ratings. I know it from the social media comments and the emails. I know it from the people I run across when I’m out covering stories and just living my life. And I know it from the mugs. 'SHUT UP' AND LISTEN: TRACE GALLAGHER SHARES 'UNEXPECTED' WISDOM LEARNED FROM BEING A 'GIRL DAD' Yes, the mugs. At one point, we printed up some coffee mugs with the snarky slogan, "DID I OFFEND YOU WITH MY COMMON SENSE?" People couldn’t get enough of them. We keep needing to print more. Thousands and thousands and thousands more. The way things are going, our sarcastic call for common sense has really struck a nerve. As I mentioned, our Common Sense Department segments are 75 seconds long. Not two minutes, not one minute—always 75 seconds. And that’s no accident. One time, we tried doing the Common Sense Department in a minute. It felt like a wind sprint. Another time, we said, "Let’s do two minutes." It felt like a drive across Texas with kids in the car. "Are we THERE yet?" CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION "No, we’re NOT there yet—and we’re not stopping at Buc-ees!" That’s one of the great things about common sense. You can pack it into the TV equivalent of a carry-on bag. It isn’t too bulky or hard to handle. And whenever you happen to need it, it’ll be right there. I am not the first person to become a big fan of common sense. Thomas Paine beat me to it by almost 250 years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Of all the Founding Fathers, Paine is one of the most unlikely and least understood. If you’d known him back in England, you never would have thought he’d amount to much. He washed out as a schoolteacher. His tailor shop failed. He was fired from his job as a tax inspector for "claiming to have inspected goods he did not inspect." He had to sell his house to avoid debtors’ prison. He really, really hated taxes and wrote a pamphlet opposing them. When an American named Benjamin Franklin showed up in London in 1774 as a voice opposing British colonial rule, the two men struck up an instant friendship. It was Franklin who urged Paine to move to Philadelphia, where the American said revolution was in the air.
