title: Obama's brother-in-law rejects civil rights, racism argument against college sports overhaul
description: Sen. Chris Murphy and the NAACP call the Protect College Sports Act a civil rights issue, saying NIL restrictions hurt Black student-athletes most.
content: While a bill to add a new swath of regulations to college sports is generating a swell of bipartisan support, some opponents are suggesting that the bill itself is racist. The Protect College Sports Act, pushed by Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., has so far survived two key hurdles in the Senate and is on its way to a final vote in the coming week. However, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, the Congressional Black Caucus and Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., one of a handful of Senate Democrats pushing against the bill, have argued that the bill would disproportionately affect Black student-athletes and put their newfound agency in decision-making granted by name, image and likeness (NIL) back into the hands of White coaches and college presidents. SENATE MOVES TO REIN IN COLLEGE SPORTS 'WILD WEST' WITH SWEEPING NEW RULES FOR PLAYERS, SCHOOLS "It's a civil rights issue. That's the reason the NAACP is strongly opposing this bill, because they see it as a civil rights issue," Murphy told Fox News Digital. "I didn't make that up. That's the reality. "The athletes who will be most affected by this bill are largely Black athletes, and the people who will be helped by this bill are largely White coaches and White college sports executives," he continued. "I’m not the one who sees this as a civil rights issue. The NAACP opposes it because they see this as a civil rights issue." The Protect College Sports Act would broadly add restrictions to the transfer portal for student-athletes and create a uniform eligibility framework of five years, recruiting and tampering guardrails that establish when schools or agents can contact or recruit a student-athlete, a federal standard for NIL rules and a revenue-sharing cap. Proponents of the bill, including former President Barack Obama's brother-in-law, Craig Robinson, who is the executive director of the National Association of Basketball Coaches, argued that the bill did not disenfranchise Black athletes. SENATE ADVANCES LANDMARK PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT, IGNORING SEC AND BIG TEN OPPOSITION WITH CLOCK TICKING "Well, you know everybody is entitled to their interpretation of what's going on," Robinson told Fox News Digital. "I would disagree with that, and I would point out that if we don't fix this system, the same student-athletes they're talking about are not going to be college educated, because you cannot get educated by transferring to four or five different schools. You can't get a college degree doing that, so that's what I would say." Robinson was one of several former coaches who made the trip to Washington, D.C., this week to promote and support the bill. Craig Bohl, executive director of the American Football Coaches Association, told Fox News Digital the assertion that the legislation had racist undertones was "the farthest thing from the truth." CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION "You know, one of the things that has been good for me, you know, working 43 years, coaches care deeply about all our players," Bohl said. "And while I appreciate their convictions on it, it's a misguided statement. "What we're looking at is opportunities for all. We want players to have an opportunity for compensation," he continued. "We want players to be able to have the ability to transfer. We also are looking for some stability with eligibility. We don't need NFL players coming back playing in our game." The Congressional Black Caucus has argued against the bill for months and charged that its members would not support the legislation after the Supreme Court’s decision on the Voting Rights Act earlier this year. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., one of the co-leads of the bill, told Fox News Digital. "We're just trying to address the chaos that exists right now in college athletics, where 27-year-olds are playing against 17-year-olds, unlimited transfers, graduation rates are plummeting."

title: Lindsay Clancy holdout praised as 'American Hero' by lawyer who says he represents him
description: Michael Desronvil, the holdout Lindsay Clancy juror, disputes fellow jurors' claims he expressed doubts about the prosecution's case during deliberations.
author_name: Brittany Miller, Adam Sabes, Michael Ruiz
content: The lone holdout juror whose refusal to find Lindsay Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity led to a mistrial is speaking publicly for the first time, disputing claims from fellow jurors that he expressed doubts about the prosecution's case, according to his attorney. Attorney Edward Paltzik told Fox News Digital Friday that he represents the holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil, whom he described as an "American Hero and Champion of Justice." "Please pray for him and help us protect him," Paltzik wrote in a separate social media post. He said his client is lying low in an undisclosed "rural area" in New England. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR ‘LOOKED AT THE CASE AND HE MADE THE CALL,’ HIS BROTHER SAYS Paltzik, who previously represented the friends of the late Mississippi teen Nolan Wells and President Donald Trump, confirmed that the statement first reported by NewsNation came from his client. Desronvil said that he never wavered in his belief prosecutors proved Clancy knew what she was doing when she strangled her three young children in January 2023. "I didn't have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present," Desronvil said. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned." His comments directly contradict accounts from fellow jurors, who said after the mistrial that Desronvil appeared to acknowledge reasonable doubt during deliberations but still refused to join the other 11 jurors in finding Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity. The jury deadlocked 11-1, with Desronvil standing alone in favor of convicting Clancy rather than accepting her insanity defense, prompting Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial. JUROR ON LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL SAYS 'WE LET DOWN LINDSAY' FOLLOWING MISTRIAL The public statement comes as Plymouth County prosecutors weigh whether to retry Clancy, whose attorneys have also floated the possibility of resolving the case without another jury trial. Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley previously told Fox News Digital that prosecutors face the difficult task of deciding whether they can persuade a future jury to unanimously reject Clancy's insanity defense after the first panel failed to reach a verdict. "The question is whether they could ever get a jury, particularly in Massachusetts, that would unanimously vote against this defendant," Turley said. "For prosecutors, they have to weigh that, but they may find the alternative equally unappealing — to simply walk away and say, 'There are three dead children here, but we just don't think we could ever win this case.'" Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, admitted killing her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — but argued she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from severe mental illness at the time of the killings. Prosecutors argued she planned the murders and understood the wrongfulness of her actions. title: Powerful Cold War-era tool Trump could use in an AI emergency is set to expire in December
description: President Donald Trump says existing laws can rein in AI, but experts warn Cold War-era tools have never been tested against frontier models.
content: One of Washington's most powerful Cold War-era tools could be used by President Donald Trump to rein in artificial intelligence (AI) if the powerful emerging technology ever becomes a national security threat. Originally enacted in 1950 to mobilize American industry during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act (DPA) has long been used to expand military production, prioritize government contracts and respond to national emergencies. Experts now say those authorities could also give the executive branch significant leverage over frontier AI companies if one of their systems posed catastrophic national security risks. Exactly how the government could use DPA's powers against a dangerous AI system remains largely untested, but national security and legal experts who spoke with Fox News Digital described a range of existing authorities that could apply — including laws in the act that encompass cyberattacks, exports, federal contracts and civil liability. THE AI REVOLUTION COULD BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY DISASTER IF WE AREN'T CAREFUL "The authorities could be a little clearer," James Lewis, director of the Strategic Technologies Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. "But you could probably cobble together a solution using the legal authorities we have now." The question has taken on new urgency after leaders at some of the nation's most powerful AI companies issued stark warnings this week about increasingly capable models and backed calls to slow the pace of development so safety measures can catch up. Trump said this week that the administration already has "tremendous criminal and regulatory power" over AI companies as he pushed back on calls from industry leaders for new guardrails on increasingly powerful models. That largely remains because Congress recently extended most of the DPA's authorities, which were set to expire on Sept. 30, through Dec. 11, 2026. This is sure to set up another reauthorization fight later this year, right before the power of the legislative body could change after November's midterms in the new year. TRUMP PLAN TAPS US FIRMS TO FIGHT FOREIGN CYBERCRIME Lewis said the cyber threat has already changed. Finding vulnerabilities that once took months can now take days or even hours, he explained, while AI can help attackers chain smaller weaknesses together into more damaging attacks. "The threat itself is not new," Lewis said, recounting a recent conversation with a senior official from a Five Eyes intelligence partner. "We've known about this for a while, but people weren't taking it seriously." AI, he said, has "changed the landscape dramatically." The Trump administration has already begun building a framework to identify when those capabilities become dangerous. A June executive order directed federal agencies, including the NSA and CISA, to establish classified benchmarks for advanced cyber capabilities and determine when an AI system should be designated a "covered frontier model." The order also calls for a voluntary framework through which developers can give the government early access to covered models before their release — while expressly stopping short of creating mandatory federal licensing or pre-clearance for frontier AI. But knowing a dangerous capability exists is only the first problem. The next question is what Washington can actually do about it. One potentially powerful use of the Defense Production Act would come before an AI system ever caused damage: forcing companies to tell the government what they are developing. James E. Baker, a former chief judge of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces who previously served as a legal adviser to the National Security Council, pointed to the DPA's broad information-gathering authority. "What you could use the DPA for is to require reporting, and that's the first step to making sound policy," Baker told Fox News Digital. "You can have a debate about whether there should be regulation and what the regulation should look like. But you really can't argue against knowing what's happening." "That's the first place to start: know what's happening, and then you can react with either a policy prescription, a legal prescription or nothing at all." The DPA's limits, however, are just as important. Paul Rosenzweig, a lawyer and former deputy assistant secretary for policy at the Department of Homeland Security, said the law was principally designed to ensure the government could obtain goods and services needed for national defense — not to give Washington broad power to stop private companies from producing them. "The Defense Production Act is more about mandating the production of things for the United States rather than preventing the production for the general public," Rosenzweig told Fox News Digital. Where it could prove particularly useful, he agreed, is giving the government access to information. "What it does give them, I think, and this is the best part about it, is it does give them a pretty good handle for demanding more information about a defense-sensitive kind of product, which frontier AI certainly could be reasonably characterized as," Rosenzweig said. If the DPA could help Washington understand what AI companies are building, other existing authorities could potentially come into play depending on the threat. Export controls can restrict sensitive technology from reaching foreign adversaries. Government contracting rules can impose conditions on companies seeking federal business. And criminal laws continue to apply when AI is used to commit crimes. The June executive order, for example, directed the attorney general to prioritize enforcement of existing federal criminal laws against people who use AI to illegally access or damage computer systems. Trump has separately directed national security agencies to expand their use of frontier AI while requiring systems used by the military and intelligence community to remain controllable and preserve clear lines of human accountability. "I think it's important to understand that there's no broad AI exemption from generally applicable law," Rosenzweig said. Both federal and state governments already have "a host of legal authorities" potentially applicable to frontier AI, he said, ranging from tort liability and privacy rules to consumer protections and criminal law. But Rosenzweig cautioned that no one knows precisely how well that patchwork would hold up in a true AI emergency because it has never been tested. The uncertainty becomes even greater if an AI system causes damage on its own. If a model autonomously hacked a hospital, company or critical infrastructure network, for example, Rosenzweig said courts would have to determine whether the developer was negligent, whether a stricter product liability standard should apply and whether the damage could even be reliably traced back to a particular AI system. "I tend to think that liability is going to be difficult to establish early on," Rosenzweig said. "Right now, that's not where I would base my deterrence model." That uncertainty points to the limits of the government's existing toolkit. The laws already on the books give federal and state authorities multiple avenues to respond to dangerous uses of AI, but many have never been tested against a system acting with increasing autonomy. title: ‘COVID 2.0’: Lawmakers push back on sweeping health 'police power' in key battleground state
description: Pennsylvania lawmakers told Fox News Digital the state's 502-page health code rewrite amounts to government overreach worse than COVID-era lockdowns.
content: Pennsylvania lawmakers are warning that proposed changes to the state’s public health rules could usher in "COVID 2.0," giving health officials sweeping "police power" over residents during future disease outbreaks. Lawmakers opposing Pennsylvania's planned 502-page rewrite of state health code rules are urging the public to submit comments before the deadline, warning the proposal could serve as a roadmap to unfettered and intrusive restrictions and surveillance efforts, including the reported ability for agency representatives to enter private homes. "This absolutely is COVID 2.0, but it's even worse because [Governor] Josh Shapiro is trying to circumnavigate or skirt the constitutional provision that we the people in Pennsylvania voted to take that kind of power away from the governor," said state Rep. Russ Diamond, R-Lebanon, who is leading the charge against the policy changes. "We were the only state in the nation to reduce our governor's powers by a constitutional amendment after COVID," Diamond said, adding that "surveillance, segregation and quarantine" are areas being assessed. SOVIET-BORN ANALYST EXPOSES HOW PANDEMIC-ERA NEIGHBOR SNITCHING UNLOCKED A 'NATURE OF EVIL' IN AMERICA Pennsylvania voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2021 limiting the duration of a governor’s disaster declaration to 21 days unless extended by the General Assembly. Those emergency powers played a central role in then-Gov. Tom Wolf’s statewide mitigation orders. In the 502-page proposed Regulation 10-242, Communicable and Noncommunicable Diseases, the Pennsylvania Department of Health proposes expanding the list of reportable diseases, infections and conditions and updating the rules to reflect changing expert standards. "The Department proposes to add language in this subsection, indicating that the Department or a local health authority may enter an apartment, a building, a health care facility, a school, college or university, or other location as necessary to conduct its investigation under 208 this chapter," one provision highlighted by critics reads. "I don't think that we want a very left-leaning governor with his Department of Health and their henchmen having this kind of police power in Pennsylvania," Diamond said. A spokesperson for Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen — who led the Pittsburgh area’s COVID mitigation response — said Shapiro "did not personally propose" the updates and rejected critics’ characterizations. "Any misconstruing of these proposed changes designed to scare Pennsylvanians is inaccurate and disingenuous," Neil Ruhland told Fox News Digital. A Shapiro spokesperson also responded to criticism Wednesday, saying the governor’s philosophy is that "public health depends on trust" and emphasizing that the proposed health regulations are part of a larger effort to update about 200 regulatory areas across state agencies. Lapowsky told Fox News Digital that the public, stakeholders, independent regulators and the legislature can review and respond to the proposed changes. "Once public comment concludes later this month, [Shapiro] will weigh in, and the regulations will be revised accordingly," she said. Lapowsky said Shapiro’s emphasis on public trust includes respecting parental rights. Critics say the proposed regulations could give health officials greater authority over certain disease-control measures involving children, including masking. Lapowsky added that the governor believes "government should work closely with the people it serves." GOV SHAPIRO SUES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OVER ‘LIFESAVING REPRODUCTIVE CARE’ IN ESCALATING ABORTION BATTLE Ruhland said the Pennsylvania Department of Health began analyzing and proposing regulatory updates several years ago and that the regulations in question are 25 years old and need modernization to "better support evolving public health needs and manage dangerous disease." While the proposed regulations do not themselves enact a new mask mandate, they would broaden disease-control language beyond "surveillance," a term central to litigation over Pennsylvania’s statewide school masking order during the pandemic. Pennsylvania House Minority Leader Jesse Topper told Fox News Digital that although the proposed regulations directly affect Pennsylvania, Americans elsewhere should also pay attention. "Everybody in the United States was impacted by COVID one way or another," said Topper, R-McConnellsburg. "We were one of the worst locked-down states in the entire nation. And we had one of the worst death rates from COVID… We don't want unelected bureaucrats making those decisions. We need to follow the [Commonwealth] Constitution, which says, ‘Hey, you can declare a public health disaster emergency if you want. But after 21 days, the legislature gets to say whether you can continue that or not’." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER State Sen. Doug Mastriano, R-Gettysburg, who, along with Diamond, led demonstrations against lockdown policies during COVID, told Fox News Digital that the proposed regulations are an "end-round" around voters. "Pennsylvania endured enough government overreach during COVID. We will not go back," said Mastriano, whom President Donald Trump nominated to serve as U.S. ambassador to Slovakia. Jason Richey, an attorney and the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, also dubbed the changes "COVID 2.0." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "These are even worse than the COVID rules... [DOH] can look at your medical records. They can enter any building and go in without a warrant to do an investigation. They can even take your kid from school and talk to him privately without your consent," Richey said in a video recorded outside a Pennsylvania Department of Health office in Lehigh County last week. Beyond the public health implications, Topper said he is concerned that the proposed regulations would expand government authority. Topper and Ruhland both encouraged Pennsylvanians to submit feedback on the proposed regulations before Monday’s public-comment deadline.

title: 'Leftist delusions' face reckoning as one of America's biggest colleges makes major shake-up
description: UT Austin drops women's studies, gender studies and ethnic studies majors amid low enrollment and political pressure from Texas state leaders.
content: Texas’ flagship public university is ending new enrollment in three majors focused on gender, sexuality and race in a move that is being hailed by many conservatives as a major victory. Students applying to the University of Texas at Austin can no longer select Women’s and Gender Studies, Mexican American and Latina/o Studies or African and African Diaspora Studies as majors, the institution has confirmed to Fox News Digital. The move follows a slew of other universities dropping similar majors and heated internal deliberations at UT Austin about whether to keep theirs. "In recognition of the changing degree offerings in the Department of Social and Cultural Analysis, the University is no longer enrolling new students in three majors: Mexican American and Latina/o Studies, African and African Diaspora Studies, and Women’s & Gender Studies," a university spokesman told Fox News Digital. "So, as you might expect, those majors have been removed from the University’s admissions applications to avoid new students enrolling in majors that are changing. Students currently enrolled in those majors will be able to complete their degree," the statement continued. LIBERAL FACULTY STILL HUGELY OUTNUMBER CONSERVATIVES IN HIGHER EDUCATION: REPORT "I don’t know the particulars of UT Austin’s programs. But this news is unsurprising. Across the Anglosphere, ethnic and sexuality studies have long been captured by political activists," Timur Kuran, a professor of economics and political science at Duke University, wrote on X. "Other state universities, and even private ones, will follow." Low enrollment has been part of the broader debate over the programs, although UT Austin has not publicly said it was the reason for ending new enrollment in the three majors. Earlier this year, the Austin American-Statesman reported that the university had just 307 students enrolled across the entirety of African and African diaspora studies, Mexican American and Latino studies, women and gender studies and American studies, citing institutional data. That represents less than 1% of the 44,315 undergraduates who were enrolled at the university in fall 2025. UT Austin, which is one of the largest universities in the nation, has also faced growing pressure from Republican state and federal officials over how it handles race, gender and other politically sensitive subjects. The University of Texas System has reviewed courses on gender identity to assess compliance with state and federal law and alignment with Board of Regents priorities. An internal email obtained by the Austin American-Statesman indicates that, while the majors may be on the way out, much of the coursework could remain. The plan appears to be to consolidate the defunct majors into a single offering. JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY "Gender and ethnic studies have transformed the study of the humanities and social sciences, and now they are what they are," Lisa Moore, the university’s chair of women and gender studies, said prior to the consolidation announcement. "We can’t unknow what we know… It’s just not the case that we can believe that only a small slice of human beings are responsible for everything that’s good about the world." Conservatives, unsurprisingly, have a less rosy view of the field. Steve McGuire, a fellow at the American Council of Trustees and Alumni, called axing the majors "the pedagogically responsible thing to do." "Excellent news. These programs are not ‘viewpoint diversity.’ They are ridiculous Leftist delusion[s] that have no place in truth-seeking institutions," J.D. Haltigan, a research fellow at the Centre for Heterodox Social Science, wrote on X. "They should be abolished entirely from every institution of higher-learning." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS Some on the right see this as a sign of things to come. "Every red state should follow suit with their universities," independent scholar Varad Mehta wrote on X. Indeed, a number of universities in red states have already scaled back similar programs. Texas A&M University, Wichita State University, the University of Iowa and the University of Toledo are among the institutions to make such cuts. title: China firm gave Iran lifeline to collect Hormuz tolls before pulling plug amid US warning
description: After briefly issuing a web security certificate for a portal linked to Iran's U.S.-sanctioned Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a Shanghai-based firm revoked it, though the move could still draw scrutiny under U.S. sanctions rules
content: Iran’s sanctioned Persian Gulf Straits Authority (PGSA) regained secure online access for four days after a Shanghai-based internet security firm provided and then revoked its web credentials, enabling Tehran to vet vessels, collect Strait of Hormuz tolls and operate despite U.S. digital restrictions, global internet monitors said. TrustAsia issued an automated domain-validated certificate, a routine process that verifies control of a website domain through server checks and typically does not involve manual vetting or background checks. The move prompted U.S. sanctions experts, including Jeremy Paner, a partner at Hughes Hubbard & Reed, to urge TrustAsia to review its compliance program before offering further services to the IRGC-linked maritime authority — with Paner warning them to act "before it is too late." The PGSA first said its website was disrupted Aug. 10 because of "the enemy's political influence on the internet service provision systems," according to a post on X. IRAN REQUESTS TALKS WITH US AS WHITE HOUSE WARNS 'VIOLENCE WILL BE MET WITH VIOLENCE' NetBlocks CEO Alp Toker told Fox News Digital that the authority had lost its web security credentials after the entity was added to the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctions list on May 27. The loss of standard SSL/TLS certificates, Toker said, made the PGSA website inaccessible using standard browsers. This forced shipping firms to use unencrypted connections that, according to Toker, could leave their data vulnerable to interception. While no data breaches resulting from the use of these connections have been made known, and there are no known instances in which a shipping firm’s data was intercepted and used to its detriment because of the certificate expiration, Toker said the site’s inaccessibility resulted in a shift to what he described as "insecure protocols." "The digital transparency records are authoritative on this," he said, adding that the measure forced the traffic into a format that could be readily intercepted. "This is a class of vulnerability open to government exploitation, rather than a corporate breach or personal data leak." Toker claimed this could make it easier for authorities to read communications sent through the platform, potentially identifying shipping firms collaborating with the PGSA. TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR "The net result was that the website was more difficult to access, because most web browsers strongly encourage the use of secure HTTPS," Toker said, adding that any form submissions could have been easily "eavesdropped on because they're no longer encrypted in transit." "The mentioned issue has been resolved, and the secure domain https://pgsa.ir is now once again available for submitting requests using any browser," the PGSA said six days later on Aug. 17 and in another post shared on X. "If the issue recurs in the future, the HTTP domain will again be temporarily available using the Firefox browser." Toker confirmed that Iran had turned to Shanghai-based certificate authority TrustAsia Technologies, which he said issued new digital security credentials to the PGSA despite the U.S. sanctions, restoring secure access to its website. "Iran’s IRGC extorts vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz through the so-called Persian Gulf Strait Authority," the Treasury Department said in May when designating the entity, adding that the PGSA "spearheads an Iranian-controlled scheme that flagrantly violates international law and U.S. sanctions." "Anyone cooperating with the so-called strait authority may be providing support to and receiving services from the IRGC, which ultimately benefits from this attempted extortion, and may therefore be exposed to sanctions risk," the Treasury Department warned. The Chinese firm bills itself as a "leading and professionally certified certification authority in China with its focus on trusted, secure and cryptographic communications in the digital world." Its mission, it says, is to "Build trust everywhere in the digital world." "Almost all of these root authorities do business with the U.S., so they tend to comply with U.S. sanctions," Toker said. But TrustAsia, he noted, had "gone its own way, building a China-first certificate infrastructure that sidesteps the West." Toker said TrustAsia had "simply gone ahead and issued Iran's PGSA with a new certificate, and Iran was once again collecting revenue from ships passing the Strait via its secure online portal." TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS Paner warned that U.S. authorities would have enforcement powers over such actions. "The U.S. has incredibly broad authority to impose sanctions on non-Iranian companies that provide any sorts of services to sanctioned Iranian companies," he told Fox News Digital. "Many times, that authority will be abbreviated or explained as being providers of material support to sanctioned Iranian companies. But in fact, any level of services whatsoever could be the basis for the United States imposing sanctions against the company for providing services to Iran." "Restoration of the certificate is unequivocally sanctionable," Paner warned. "Restoring the certificate is/was a service provided to the PGSA, which can be the basis for imposing sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13224, as amended. "That authority does not in any way require that the service be ‘knowingly’ provided to the PGSA. In other words, the automated nature of the service is irrelevant and does not make the service any less sanctionable," the lawyer added. In a statement to Fox News Digital on Aug. 20, a spokesperson for TrustAsia confirmed that the firm issued a "Domain Validated TLS certificate for pgsa.ir." "Thank you for bringing this matter to our attention," the firm said before clarifying that "DV certificates are issued through automated validation of control over the requested domain names." IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP "This process does not verify or assert the legal identity, affiliation, or sanctions status of the entity operating or benefiting from the domain. "As a result, the relationship described in your inquiry was not identified during the automated issuance process." Following the firm's review, TrustAsia said it "added the entire pgsa.ir domain namespace to our restricted-issuance list to prevent further issuance or renewal." "We also expect to complete revocation of the existing certificate within this week," the spokesman said on Aug. 20. These actions are precautionary compliance and risk-control measures. They should not be interpreted as a finding that the certificate was technically misissued, TrustAsia said. Toker confirmed the TrustAsia certificate's privilege had been withdrawn on Aug. 21 at 12:15:25 UTC. "This usually means the issuer has taken action," he said. The internet expert clarified that the revocation will gradually be coming into effect, with the firm "signaling that the PGSA certificate should no longer be trusted, and they're distributing this notice that privilege is withdrawn, usually meaning customer misuse or breached terms of use." "The secure website will stop working in most browsers, unless the owners can find a certificate authority that's willing to issue a new certificate," Toker said. IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY After reviewing TrustAsia's statement, Paner also said that OFAC would expect the company to "use the discovery as an opportunity to enhance its compliance program before it is too late." The former OFAC official clarified that Iran's revenue collection in the waterway would likely draw high-level scrutiny in Washington. "Iran's attempt to extort the world in the movement of oil through the Strait of Hormuz is of the utmost importance to OFAC, which is the agency that implements and enforces U.S. economic sanctions." Because major U.S. web browsers currently recognize TrustAsia’s root certificates, American systems would have automatically trusted the sanctioned Iranian portal. Toker claimed the Treasury Department could have found TrustAsia in violation of sanctions for providing material assistance to a blocked entity, potentially forcing tech giants such as Google and Microsoft to revoke trust in TrustAsia. There is no evidence that this process had begun or was likely to occur. "This could have splintered the global chain of trust and potentially render much of the Chinese web inaccessible from the West," Toker warned. IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT Paner clarified that the certificates authenticate the site, boosting its credibility, and suggested TrustAsia should have weighed the risks of working with sanctioned entities. "There's always reputational risk involved in any company that decides to do business with the IRGC." "If I were advising TrustAsia, I would at minimum immediately identify all other IRGC companies receiving services." Paner added that this latest situation aligned with broader warnings from administration officials. "I think this dovetails pretty nicely with Secretary Bessent's comments about how the coming sanctions are going to be unlike any that has come prior. Sanctions require a careful balancing of the costs and the benefits. "When it's a Chinese tech company providing necessary services to the IRGC, I'm confident that the U.S. government is going to forego any sort of balancing in that regard." The United States on Aug. 24 had sanctioned nearly 60 Iran-linked individuals, entities and vessels and expanded the threat of secondary sanctions, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. These did not include TrustAsia. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bessent described the measures as part of an "economic onslaught" targeting Tehran’s global financial networks under "Operation Economic Outcast." A Chinese Embassy spokesperson also said in a statement: "I am not aware of the specifics you mentioned. I have no information to provide." Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the White House for comment.

title: Angel mom pleads with her party to 'grow up' on immigration after newlywed son killed in truck crash
description: Elizabeth Carter, a lifelong Democrat, says she is ashamed of her party after an illegal immigrant truck driver killed her newlywed son and his wife.
content: A lifelong Democrat whose newlywed son and daughter-in-law were killed in a crash involving an illegal immigrant truck driver is pleading with her party to change course on immigration, saying she is "ashamed" of how her party has handled the issue. "I was shocked and heartbroken to hear that the man responsible for our son and daughter-in-law's death, the driver of the 18-wheeler that they collided with, that he was a part of Biden's catch-and-release policy," angel mom Elizabeth Carter told "Hannity" Thursday. Carter's son, William Micah "Billy" Carter, 25, and his wife, Jennifer Lynn Lower Carter, 24, were killed in November 2025, when their Subaru struck a tractor-trailer that had jackknifed across both lanes of U.S. Highway 20 in Oregon. The couple had been married for just 16 days. WATCH: 'LIFELONG DEMOCRAT' ADMITS SHE IS ‘ASHAMED’ OF PARTY AFTER SON KILLED IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRASH The truck's driver, Indian national Rajinder Kumar, was charged following the crash and has pleaded not guilty. Federal immigration authorities who later took him into custody say Kumar entered the U.S. illegally near Lukeville, Arizona, in November 2022 and was released by the Biden administration, pending immigration proceedings. He later received work authorization and a CDL issued in California, according to Houston's FOX 26. "If it weren't for that, our son and daughter-in-law would still be alive," Carter said, pinning blame on both federal and state policies that made the tragedy possible. The heartbroken mother's comments came after speaking on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, when she pleaded for lawmakers to make changes to immigration policies. ICE LAUNCHES CDL FRAUD TIPLINE AS DHS HIGHLIGHTS DEADLY CRASHES INVOLVING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS "[My son and daughter-in-law] lost the Russian roulette game our government is forcing them to play," she said. "We allowed 10 million people in under Biden. How is there a different suggestion as to how to process them other than the same way they came into the country, en masse, leaving?" "I have to say, as a lifelong Democrat, I am ashamed of what my party is doing." Carter's husband, Dennis, also voiced frustration Thursday, focusing his criticism on policies that allowed Kumar to obtain a CDL. "Just because someone is incompetent and can't do the job that they wanted to do, just because they got here, that doesn't mean, ‘Okay, they're here, we should give them a job that they can't do and just turn them loose on the road,’" he told "Hannity." "We have learned that the two parties can exist in the same household, and we actually get along," he said. Elizabeth agreed, saying the couple knows "how to disagree without tearing each other apart" and instead tries to better understand the issues on which they differ. Elizabeth also imparted a challenge to the Democratic Party during her appearance, pleading for them to "grow up" and start communicating with ICE at the state level.

title: 'Scream' star admits he's 'ashamed' of sequel return after actress fired over anti-Israel comments
description: Matthew Lillard says he feels "ashamed" for returning to "Scream 7" after Melissa Barrera's firing, calling himself on the "wrong side of history."
content: "Scream" actor Matthew Lillard said Tuesday that he felt "ashamed" for returning to the horror franchise after actress Melissa Barrera was fired over social media posts about Israel and the war in Gaza, telling fans during a 30th anniversary screening in Austin, Texas, that he believed he ended up on the "wrong side of history." Lillard, who reprised his role as Stu Macher in the seventh installment, said his excitement about returning to the franchise overshadowed his concerns about how Barrera had been treated. As reported by Entertainment Weekly, Lillard said, "I went back to do ‘Scream,’ and I got called out. And I’m like, ‘Oh, f---. That’s brutal.’" "I feel bad about that. I feel ashamed about that. Because in that moment I was so excited to go back, I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey." "I’m embarrassed, that’s the truth… I blew that. I’m on the wrong side of history for that. I still like being in the movie [but] it may not have been the best idea," Lillard continued. PEREZ HILTON JOINS 'TOMI LAHREN IS FEARLESS' AND DECLARES CANCEL CULTURE IS NOW A SPORT Barrera was dropped from the franchise in November 2023 after publishing and sharing a series of posts criticizing Israel following Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack. In one post previously reported by Fox News Digital, Barrera accused Israel of committing "genocide" and "ethnic cleansing" in Gaza. "Gaza is currently being treated like a concentration camp," Barrera said. "Cornering everyone together, with no where to go, no electricity no water … People have [learned] nothing from our histories. And just like our histories, people are still silently watching it all happen. THIS IS GENOCIDE & ETHNIC CLEANSING." In another post, Barrera claimed Western news outlets were disproportionately presenting Israel's side of the conflict and told followers to draw their own conclusions about why. ‘NO JEWS, NO NEWS’ STRIKES AGAIN AS SELECTIVE COVERAGE OF THE 'UNSETTLERS' FUELS ANTI-ISRAEL ANGER "Because western media only shows the other side. Why they do that, I will let you deduce for yourself," Barrera said. Spyglass denied at the time that Barrera was removed merely for supporting Palestinians, instead saying it viewed some of her rhetoric as antisemitic. "Spyglass’ stance is unequivocally clear: We have zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech," the company said. Fox News Digital reached out to Spyglass Media for comment about Lillard's remarks. Barrera subsequently rejected the suggestion that she was promoting antisemitism and defended her criticism of governments, Fox News Digital reported in May. MORE THAN 180 JEWISH ENTERTAINERS RALLY BEHIND ACTOR MARK RUFFALO IN PROTEST LETTER "I believe a group of people are not their leadership and that no governing body should be above criticism. I pray day and night for no more deaths, for no more violence and for peaceful co-existence," Barrera said. The controversy resurfaced earlier this year when Barrera criticized former cast-mates who returned to the franchise without her. When asked whether actors who went back for "Scream 7" were "scabby," Barrera agreed. "One hundred percent. I think they all are," Barrera said. "And they have to live with that." At Tuesday’s screening, Lillard directly defended Barrera’s position and criticized the lack of public support she received after her firing. "Melissa Barrera, who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said after the whole Palestinian... what started happening in Israel," Lillard said. "It’s really f---ing bulls--- and really hard, and she’s on the right side of history." But the whole world should have popped up and said, ‘She’s right.’ And they didn’t. And that’s brutal." Despite the upheaval surrounding its development, "Scream 7" was released Feb. 27 and eventually crossed $200 million at the global box office, becoming the highest-grossing film in the franchise’s history, according to Paramount. The film shifted its focus back to Neve Campbell’s Sidney Prescott and brought back several franchise veterans, including Lillard. When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, Hollywood in Toto editor Christian Toto said of Lillard’s remarks: "Now that the Palestinian cause is spiking in his far-Left industry, he has regrets. Does he know what she actually said about Israel and the timing of those comments? Is he aware of other artists who have had their free speech rights trampled?"

title: University drops 'doxxing' probe of Republican students amid widespread backlash over viral cake incident
description: A viral photo of a "Happy Kirkiversary" cake sparked a University of Utah probe into two College Republicans accused of doxxing a fellow student.
content: Two College Republicans at the University of Utah threatened with disciplinary action stemming from a viral social media incident are now breathing a sigh of relief after the school cleared them of wrongdoing. But one student is now demanding that the school work harder to protect conservative speech on campus. "My message to administration would be that conservative voices on campus need to be protected, not only by the students that try to diminish our voice, but also the administration, including the teachers," Rylie Barnes told Fox News Digital. On Sept. 10, 2026, the one-year anniversary of Charlie Kirk's assassination, a woman approached a group of College Republicans at an event on a campus less than an hour's drive from the murder site, and presented them with a snarky dessert. The words "Happy Kirkiversary" were written in red icing on the white cake. Barnes and Riley Beesley, the chairman of the school's College Republicans chapter, took exception to the stunt on their campus, and Barnes posted a photo of the woman holding the cake to her X account. It quickly went viral and led to an anonymous X user identifying the student as Sara Larsen. "We got a lot of backlash from students here on campus, blaming us for doxxing, creating false allegations and lies on social media about it, and reporting to the school all these false allegations as well. So I don't blame the school for kind of jumping the gun on it," Barnes said. "But I think they did jump the gun, which caused this to get so much backlash on the Republican end, just because there wasn't much of an investigation for us. There was just, ‘we need you to come meet with us,' and in our minds, that wasn't okay because we didn't do anything wrong." Thursday night, the University of Utah sent out a notice confirming that the potential disciplinary matter was closed. "The University of Utah’s Office of the Dean of Students has dismissed an ‘accountability’ inquiry into student Rylie Barnes’ social media posts," the message said. title: Roger Goodell details NFL expansion possibilities and a timetable for a full season of international games
description: Roger Goodell says Europe is the most likely home for NFL international expansion, envisioning two new franchise teams outside the United States.
content: Commissioner Roger Goodell made the rounds during the NFL's first week of the regular season and into Thursday night's opening of the new Highmark Stadium in Buffalo. Out of that travel that spanned continents, we're getting a picture of his plans for league expansion. Bottom line: Goodell sees NFL expansion outside the United States on the horizon. "I think if we continue to grow, continue to get the kind of reaction, I do think a franchise will be international at some point in time," Goodell said prior to the Thursday night game between the Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions on Prime's pregame show. "I think Europe is the most likely [place], for a lot of reasons. One, the length of time we've been playing there. But also, the scheduling is going to be a lot easier." ROGER GOODELL DISMISSES 49ERS COACH'S CONCERNS ABOUT PLAYING IN AUSTRALIA, SAYS IT'S PART OF LONG-TERM PLAN The NFL began playing regular-season games in Europe in 2007 and to date has played 55 regular-season games there. One could also argue Europe makes sense for international expansion because most of the teams in the AFC East and NFC East and some teams in the AFC South and NFC South are within a seven-hour flight to, say, London. Other places simply don't make similar sense at this time. "Australia might create a few complications for us," Goodell admitted. NFL TO COMMEMORATE 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 TERRORIST ATTACKS ACROSS ALL ITS STADIUMS AND EVEN IN AUSTRALIA Goodell apparently is not thinking about expanding by one team in Europe. That would throw off the league's 32-team symmetry. "I also believe we could have more than one team, which I think, ultimately, the support is there," Goodell said. "Two more teams." So when will all this happen? Goodell recently signed a new contract that carries his tenure as commissioner through the 2030 season. There has been speculation his goal is to have international expansion by the time his contract expires. Is that the timeline? "I don't think so," Goodell said on the Netflix pregame show recently. "There was no connection to the two. "You know, listen, our vision here is to make it a global sport. The NFL deserves to be, it's a great game, and we all believe in it passionately." title: GOP lawmakers smell something else behind Big Tech's AI doomsday warnings: 'Something else going on'
description: Capitol Hill lawmakers question whether OpenAI and Anthropic are pushing for AI regulation to stifle competition and lock in market dominance.
content: Republicans on Capitol Hill are grappling over whether and how to regulate artificial intelligence companies even as top AI business leaders warn the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. The simmering debate over AI guardrails has exploded this week as House lawmakers worked through their final week in Washington until after the midterm elections. The flurry of activity was partially spurred by tech CEOs like Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman warning that the pace of innovation should be slowed after both companies saw AI models hack into other organizations of their own accord. And while some in Congress are demanding swift action, others who spoke with Fox News Digital are questioning the motivation of AI companies in calling for the government to step in. "I think there's a false sense of urgency," Rep. Troy Downing, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL Downing spent his young adulthood in tech, having previously been a research scientist at the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University and founding online calendar company WebCal, which was later acquired by Yahoo!. "Yes, we should be taking it seriously, but I think the hyperbole is misplaced right now," Downing said. "Any one of those people crying gloom and doom has the possibility of stopping it in their own shops, so there's something else going on there." Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., a former assistant U.S. attorney, also doubted AI companies' motives. AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK "I'm very skeptical of people in big business who want to leverage big government to suppress competition," Knott said. "I'm afraid that's what we're seeing. That'd be like ... Google, Yahoo, Microsoft, Apple saying, 'We need to regulate all tech.' Whether it's software or hardware. It's like, guys, you're here already, right? And if there's one thing that I'm confident in, to protect AI for good, there has to be more than one option." Still others believe lawmakers do not broadly have enough knowledge to take on AI guardrails. Rep. Jimmy Patronis, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital that Congress should instead repeal Section 230, a federal law shielding internet and tech companies from liability for what third parties post. "I think the warning is real, and I think that AI is unbelievable — look, AI is going to cure cancer. AI is going to find solutions to get rid of diseases that we never thought we could get rid of, but it does need to have some oversight. It needs a kill switch," Patronis conceded. "But again, I don't think Congress has the expertise to tell an emerging technology what's the best way to go." Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., said when asked if Congress should act before the end of this year, "It's too complex a subject. You've got to understand it." Meanwhile, President Donald Trump also joined the debate by dismissing AI companies' calls for more government regulation. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," he wrote on Truth Social. "The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" But others are pushing for the government to step in to at least some degree, with some Republicans arguing for human guardrails to ensure AI does not go too far by itself. RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS "The sooner we can act, the better," Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., chair of the House's AI task force, told reporters Wednesday. "Certainly, we've had some warning shots lately that have been very concerning ... So, God forbid we have a Chernobyl moment at some point here that really causes harm to people and focuses the public's attention on AI in a way that we hope it will never be." When asked by Fox News Digital about Trump's warning, however, he said, "I think the president was talking about the dangers of over-regulation, and that's something I very much agree with him on." RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., held a press conference alongside Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., on Thursday pushing legislation to stop "rogue" AI agents such as those that broke out of containment during trials by OpenAI and Anthropic. "We want to make sure that people remain in control. This isn't about stopping AI or stifling innovation," Lawler said. "Some states have put a moratorium on the infrastructure that powers this technology. That does not invent a kill switch." title: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton tells Macklemore he is ‘standing’ in solidarity with him on Palestine
description: Lewis Hamilton pledged to stand in solidarity with Macklemore after his "Free Palestine" messaging got him removed from Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour."
content: Pop star Macklemore has generated quite a buzz recently with his "Free Palestine" messaging while on Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour." The 43-year-old musician was kicked off the tour following backlash from his pro-Palestine stance, but there have been a few "woke" celebrities who have come to Macklemore's defense. Following the Seattle native's pledge to donate $1 million to Palestinian aid organizations, children's YouTube star Ms. Rachel said she would match his donation and urged "every wealthy White celebrity" to do the same. MACKLEMORE DONATES $1M TO PALESTINIAN AID ORGANIZATIONS AFTER ED SHEERAN TOUR FALLOUT Ms. Rachel isn't the only one to throw her public support behind Macklemore, though, as Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton took to social media to praise the rapper for his stance. COLIN KAEPERNICK ACCUSES NFL OF 'COLLUDING' AGAINST MACKLEMORE AMID 'FREE PALESTINE' CONTROVERSY If you know anything about Hamilton, then this shouldn't come as a shock. title: Duncan Sheik, ‘Barely Breathing’ singer, dead at 56

content: Duncan Sheik, the singer-songwriter behind the hit "Barely Breathing" and the Tony and Grammy-winning musical "Spring Awakening," has died. He was 56. title: Pilot’s sudden death during overnight layover puts spotlight on fatigue concerns
description: An Air India captain, Sunny Sharad Asaldekar, 46, was found unresponsive in his New Delhi hotel room during a layover, sparking renewed fatigue concerns for pilots.
content: An Air India captain was found unresponsive in his hotel room during an overnight flight layover in New Delhi, and was later pronounced dead at a hospital. The captain has been identified as Sunny Sharad Asaldekar, 46, The New Indian Express reported. He had checked into the hotel on Thursday, and his brother contacted the hotel manager the following evening after Asaldekar stopped answering calls. The hotel manager entered the locked room with a master key and found Asaldekar unconscious and unresponsive, according to the outlet. 'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS Police responded to the hotel, and Asaldekar was taken to a hospital, where he was declared dead. "Air India is deeply saddened at the passing away of a cockpit crew member in Delhi last night," the airline said in a statement to The New Indian Express. "He was on a layover rest at a hotel in Delhi where he was found unconscious last evening. He was rushed to the hospital immediately, where he was declared dead." A post-mortem examination was conducted, but the cause of death has not yet been determined. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The Federation of Indian Pilots renewed its call for an urgent review of fatigue-management practices after the pilot's death but said it was not directly linking fatigue to his death, according to The Times of India. Matthew "Whiz" Buckley, a former U.S. Navy F/A-18 Hornet fighter pilot who also flew for American Airlines and FedEx, told Fox News Digital that fatigue has long been a concern in commercial aviation. "Pilot fatigue in aviation has been an issue since day one," Buckley said. While passengers may assume an overnight layover gives pilots plenty of time to recover, Buckley said required rest does not always mean pilots get enough sleep. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "A layover is just that. It's a crew laying over in a city that is not their home base," he said. Pilots may arrive at a hotel in the early morning hours and then try to sleep during the day, Buckley said, which can work against the body's natural sleep cycle. "It's just unnatural to sleep during off hours," he said. Buckley said he faced that challenge while flying overnight routes himself — and that pilot fatigue was among the reasons he made changes in his career. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Long-haul flights can be especially difficult when pilots cross multiple time zones, he added. "Where it really takes a toll on the body for pilots is east-west," Buckley said. "When you're crossing multiple time zones, [that's] when your body can really get messed up." Fatigue can also build up beyond one flight or layover, according to Buckley, who cited irregular hours and prolonged periods of sitting, plus diet issues, exercise challenges and time away from family as factors that can affect pilots. Buckley said U.S. safeguards include federal crew-rest requirements, airline policies and labor agreements, but pilots also play a key role in deciding whether they are fit to fly. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "At the end of the day ... you know who determines if a pilot is fit to fly? You," Buckley said. Fox News Digital reached out to Air India for comment.

title: Philadelphia home linked to 7 missing women, late resident's potential 'serial killer' memoir investigated
description: Ashtrays containing possible human remains and images of seven missing women were found among over one million files inside Eugene Horsch's Philadelphia home.
content: Philadelphia police have linked seven missing women to a home where investigators recovered more than 1 million images and videos and also found five urns believed to contain human ashes, authorities said this week. Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women — 27-year-old Gabrielle Amarando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses — lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said in the press conference. Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017. "Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said, adding "to date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered." The home was occupied by Eugene Horsch, the son of deceased pornographer Raymond "R.C." Horsch. The investigation began after Eugene Horsch was arrested in June. CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS Fox News has learned that R.C. Horsch wrote a book titled "Empathy: The Memoir of an Empathetic Serial Killer." The book, which was published back in 2014, billed itself as the "autobiographical memoir of a caring, empathetic serial killer." In the book, Horsch wrote about strangling a woman he called "Krista" — then described buying 100 pounds of sodium hydroxide and using lye in a basement bathtub to dissolve her body. But, Horsch was known to mix real details of his life with violent fiction, making it unclear what, if anything, actually happened. The Philadelphia Police Department said investigators were "aware of the memoir, and it is being reviewed as part of the ongoing investigation." Amazon removed it from its store and told Fox News on Friday, "Our content guidelines govern which books can be listed for sale, and we take proactive and reactive measures to prevent, detect, and remove content that violates those guidelines." On June 19, a park ranger encountered Eugene Horsch, 44, and a female passenger sitting in a BMW outside of Philadelphia's Independence Mall, Vanore explained. "During the course of that investigation, officers recovered two firearms, narcotics, and identification impersonating a federal law enforcement officer, and he was charged. Task force officers from the DEA were able to develop probable cause that same day and serve a warrant on Mr. Horsch's residence," Vanore said. The female passenger presented false identification using the name Blair Tonzelli, a woman who has been missing since 2023, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to Fox News Digital. FOUL ODOR AT NYC SCHOOL LEADS POLICE TO BODY HIDDEN IN CHIMNEY The true identity of the woman in the vehicle has not been released. Tonzelli's whereabouts remain unknown. After obtaining a warrant, investigators conducted a search of the Chew Avenue home and found "a homemade laboratory of some kind in the basement area, five urns believed to contain human ashes, and a large amount of digital evidence — including computers, hard drives, flash drives, DVRs, cameras, and phones," Vanore said during the press conference. Investigators have identified 58 total people in the videos and images they found in the home. Vanore said "four of those identified appear lifeless, with video depicting what may have happened to one of them." Amarando and Fresses remain missing, and no DNA evidence or physical remains connected to them have been recovered. Of the seven missing women, the Philadelphia Medical Examiner’s Office reviewed evidence showing four of them, police said in a statement issued after Wednesday’s press conference. The medical examiner’s office advised that, "provided the recordings are authentic and unaltered, the women depicted appear to be deceased," the police department said. "However, because their bodies or remains have not been recovered, they cannot be conclusively declared deceased, and no cause or manner of death can be determined." "Two additional women are reported missing but have not been observed in the evidence reviewed by investigators," the department added. "The identity and circumstances surrounding the seventh woman remain under investigation." NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS One video reportedly shows R.C. Horsch handcuffing a woman to a bed and zip-tying her neck until she became unconscious. Investigators believe this woman is Nicole Fusaro, according to FOX 29 Philadelphia. Police have not conclusively confirmed the identification. Another missing woman reportedly connected to the home is R.C. Horsch's ex-wife, Amy McHale, who has been missing since 2016, FOX 29 reported. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We have only processed a small fraction of the total media. Thousands of videos remain to be analyzed. We are working to corroborate what we see and gather physical evidence to prove our findings, supported throughout by the FBI as we determine our next steps," Vanore concluded Wednesday. Fox News' Kimberly Ruiz contributed to this report.

title: Young swing-state voters cozy up to Democratic Socialists, say party establishment must ‘learn’ from DSA wins
description: Young Michigan voters at Abdul El-Sayed's rally explain why Democratic Socialists of America's platform on Medicare for All appeals to them.
content: Gen Z and young Millennial voters in Michigan who are leaning blue for the midterm election say they welcome the ideas of the Democratic Socialists of America, with a couple of voters agreeing that Americans should abolish the Senate. Fox News Digital was on the ground at Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's "Students v. Billionaires" rally at Michigan State University on Sept. 11 and at the Detroit Health Department's annual block party, where young Democratic voters said rising costs and the complacency of the Democratic establishment have made the DSA more appealing to them. "I feel as if they actually focus on the people," said Detroit resident Shelby Campbell, who is also a 2023 Wayne State University graduate. "It's not as, I guess, capitalistic or just bought into the system. They want to do good, but they are just another big organization, and I think we just need to get rid of all the political parties and be independent." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' So far this election cycle, dozens of Democratic Socialists of America candidates have won their primary races, including Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney, who defeated incumbent Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich. But some of the biggest upsets came out of New York, where New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democratic Socialists of America member, saw three candidates he endorsed — Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander — win their Democratic congressional primaries. The flurry of DSA-backed primary victories has put Republicans on the offensive while fueling concern among some Democrats about the socialist movement’s growing influence within the party. Noel Otteson is a sophomore at Michigan State University. He described himself as a "leftist" and "anti-capitalist," but he said he supports El-Sayed for his Medicare for All stance and his promise to get money out of politics. Otteson said he supports the DSA's proposal to abolish the U.S. Senate, which he called "undemocratic." "The way that the Senate is set up is inherently undemocratic," Otteson said. "I'm someone who always, always, prioritizes democracy, and the Senate isn't that." "Some states hold more power than others based on population, and I would probably advocate for a more parliamentary system, you know, things like the U.K. and a lot of other European countries have, or most other countries have actually," Otteson said. NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’ He proposed that the House of Representatives should be expanded. "Their stance on abolishing the Senate, I think that is something that can work, only because the Senate is one of the most exclusionary clubs in politics and is also very, very hard to get into, and I think if you have a Republican and Democrat in the U.S. Senate in one state, they kind of cancel each other out, and they really don't get anything positive done," Smith told Fox News Digital. Smith said he supports the DSA's anti-ICE agenda and Medicare for All proposals, but wants to see the organization bring about actual change. "I support their ideas, but I love to see them have more traction in getting things actually done. Policy is something that you have to enact.
