title: 'Gone too far:' GOP candidate runs to Trump’s left on signature issue in deep red district
description: María Elvira Salazar tells Trump his immigration enforcement has gone too far, warning that Hispanics who backed him in 2024 now feel betrayed.
content: Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Republican who represents a solidly red district in Miami, has broken with the president on immigration as the midterms cycle hits a fever pitch. "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar said in a newly released campaign advertisement. "Be careful what your advisors are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today. You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. "I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land." THE HISPANIC VOTE IS UP FOR GRABS IN 2026; CANDIDATES WHO IGNORE IT WILL LOSE A Fox News poll released Wednesday found President Donald Trump’s overall approval rating at 39%, with 61% of registered voters disapproving of his job performance. Voters disapprove of Trump generally by a margin of 61% to 39%, according to the poll. On immigration, however, only 56% of voters are unhappy with the president's performance, beating out his handling of the economy and foreign policy. VOTERS SAY REPUBLICANS OUTDO DEMOCRATS ON THESE KEY ISSUES: FOX NEWS POLL Salazar’s break with the president on immigration follows a legislative record that has combined tougher enforcement measures with support for legal status reforms. During her time in Congress, Salazar has supported tougher border enforcement while also backing legislation that would provide legal status to some long-term noncitizens, including through the bipartisan DIGNITY Act. She also voted for the 2023 Secure the Border Act and the 2025 Laken Riley Act, which expanded immigration enforcement and required the detention of certain undocumented immigrants accused of crimes. title: The New Yorker claims women can be 'kind of pregnant' in article questioning pregnancy tests
description: The New Yorker faced backlash for promoting an essay claiming a woman could be "kind of pregnant," sparking debate over pregnancy as a biological state.
content: The New Yorker drew criticism Thursday after promoting an essay that described the binary distinction between being pregnant and not pregnant as "misleading" and said a woman could be "kind of pregnant" or "a little bit pregnant." The essay, "The Unsettling Ambiguity of Early Pregnancy," by Apoorva Tadepalli, examined the uncertainty surrounding early pregnancy tests, miscarriage and viability through the writer's experience with multiple pregnancy losses and her current pregnancy. The magazine promoted the piece on X by saying at-home tests capture only a moment when an embryo has implanted and that someone could be "kind of pregnant, a little bit pregnant, or almost pregnant, or maybe pregnant" while still testing positive. MED SCHOOL DEANS COME UP EMPTY IN TENSE HEARING WHEN ASKED POINT BLANK IF MEN CAN HAVE BABIES: 'RIDICULOUS' Los Angeles County Republican Party Chair Roxanne Hoge, a mother of four, told Fox News Digital that uncertainty over whether a pregnancy will remain viable does not change whether a woman is pregnant. "As a mother of four and an actual biological woman, I must applaud the author for noticing that women do, in fact, make babies," she said. "While I sympathize with her on the very sad reality of carrying a pregnancy after a loss, this was a lot of words to try and pretend that a fetus is a clump of cells. You're either pregnant or you're not." Elizabeth Barcohana, America First Policy Institute California ambassador to the America First Women's initiative, said the distinction should be between the existence of a pregnancy and whether a woman knows that pregnancy is viable. "A woman cannot be ‘a little bit pregnant.’ Pregnancy is a physical, biological state that begins when a fertilized embryo implants in the uterus and triggers a chemical hormonal reaction," Barcohana said Thursday in a statement to Fox News Digital. "This article is not about being pregnant. It is about a woman’s experience about knowing whether she is carrying a viable healthy pregnancy." Tadepalli described testing positive during five pregnancies and spending periods of those pregnancies unsure whether she would miscarry. She said those experiences affected her ability to emotionally embrace her current pregnancy, with much of the essay examining what early testing can and cannot tell women about what will happen next. PRO-LIFE PUBLISHER FACING DEMANDS TO RETRACT CALLING ABORTION ‘KILLING’ FIRES BACK: ‘THE ANSWER IS NO’ Lisa Cusack, president of the Don’t L.A. My Burbank PAC, told Fox News Digital she viewed the article’s framing as an attempt to make pregnancy more subjective while arguing that uncertainty in early testing does not change whether a woman is pregnant. "This article just seems like a tortured attempt to make pregnancy into a subject experience in order to justify abortion," she said. "The fact that an at-home pregnancy isn’t sophisticated enough to pick up the beginning stages of every pregnancy doesn’t mean you’re ‘kind of pregnant,’ or that pregnancy itself, which literally begins with conception and ends with birth, is ‘nonlinear.’ "Women have always known that early pregnancies sometimes don’t take or show up on tests, but that doesn’t change the fact that you’re either pregnant or not, whether you know it or not or want it or not." WHAT MY SON'S ULTRASOUND TAUGHT ME ABOUT ABORTION — AND MASSACHUSETTS IGNORES Barcohana said that element of the essay was relatable to women who have experienced pregnancy loss and blamed The New Yorker’s presentation for shifting attention away from it. "The New Yorker’s editors betrayed the author with this provocative headline, because what she’s really talking about — in a vulnerable way that millions of women can empathize with — is the utility and impact on women of unreliable early testing," she said. "She tried to talk about something totally legitimate for women trying to start a family, and they [editors] hijacked it." Fox News Digital reached out to The New Yorker for comment but did not immediately receive a response. The distinction between detecting pregnancy and determining whether it is viable is also reflected in medical guidance. The Food and Drug Administration says at-home pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, a hormone produced after a fertilized egg is attached to the uterine wall. The agency notes that testing too early can produce inaccurate results and that a positive home test does not provide information about how a pregnancy will develop. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that pregnancy begins when a fertilized egg is implanted in the uterus, while pregnancy viability can require additional evaluation as development progresses.

title: Meyer Lansky’s grandson reflects on late mobster's crime empire, Las Vegas legacy and missing millions
description: Meyer Lansky II reveals personal letters and memories of his mob boss grandfather in a new book exploring the infamous organized crime figure's legacy.
content: To Prohibition-era gangsters, history buffs and true crime aficionados, he was Meyer Lansky, the financial mastermind who built an international gambling empire. To his namesake, he was simply "grandpa." Meyer Lansky II, the grandson of the late mob boss who helped establish organized crime across the nation, reflects on his grandfather through personal letters, photographs and firsthand memories in his new book with S. J. Peddie, "The Lansky Legacy: The Life and Letters of Meyer Lansky." "He never mentioned the names of anybody that he worked with. He was always cautious with that," Lansky told Fox News Digital. CHARLES MANSON'S GRANDDAUGHTER REVEALS MOMENT SHE DISCOVERED DARK FAMILY SECRET: 'IT WAS DEVASTATING' Growing up in Washington state, the younger Lansky initially saw his grandfather as a stern, serious figure who strictly compartmentalized his life. The elder Lansky never brought up his underworld dealings; instead, he focused on teaching his grandson how to present himself to the world, introducing him to fine details like tie pins and shoehorns. "Growing up in Washington state, I wasn't exposed to those kinds of things anywhere else," Lansky said. "He was always asking me about my grades, my studies and what books I was reading. "He’d give me basic advice: ‘Whatever you do, do a good job. Be honest with people, provide good service and people will come back to you.’" SAMMY 'THE BULL' REVEALS WHY HIS LOVE FOR JOHN GOTTI TURNED INTO PRISON HATE The elder Lansky, widely dubbed the "mob's accountant," rose to prominence in the early 20th century alongside childhood friends Benjamin "Bugsy" Siegel and Charles "Lucky" Luciano. Together, they revolutionized organized crime, building lucrative gambling operations from Havana to Las Vegas. "He was right alongside Luciano and Bugsy Siegel during the transformation of the syndicate into the modern American Mafia," Lansky said. That reputation carried real-world danger. The younger Lansky recalled a chilling incident from his childhood, when his grandfather's notoriety and perceived wealth nearly led to his kidnapping. As he grew older, the veil began to slip. EX-MOB CAPO ALLEGES FURIOUS RFK WEAPONIZED THE FBI AGAINST HIS FATHER OVER MARILYN MONROE "One day I was listening to the radio and heard that Treasury Secretary John Connally was going to Las Vegas to investigate Meyer Lansky," he said, referencing the decades-long, unsuccessful federal effort to convict his grandfather. "When my grandfather visited a week later, I told him, ‘Hey, I heard your name on the radio.’ He looked at me, smiled, and said, ‘You did?’ He didn't elaborate, but I knew at that point he realized I was going to figure out who he really was." title: Two regular dudes are about to fish for $1.25 million against the best bass anglers in the world
description: Eric Giessing and Kyle Carr will fish against 60 elite pros including Jacob Wheeler for a record $3.25 million purse on Old Hickory Lake this fall.
content: Eric Giessing and Kyle Carr are about to find out exactly how good they are at bass fishing. World Bass Enterprises (WBE) announced this week that Giessing, a 53-year-old amateur angler from Farmington, Mo., and Carr, a 39-year-old local tournament fisherman from Gatesville, Texas, have been selected as the two "Average Joes" who will compete in The Champions this fall. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS And WBE isn't sticking them in some separate amateur division. They're fishing the same tournament, for the same money, against 60 of the best professional bass anglers in the world. That includes a $3.25 million purse and $1.25 million for the winner. That’s the largest purse in bass fishing history. "Fans of every sport wonder how they'd fare competing against the pros," WBE founder and CEO Brian Bird said. "We thought it would be neat to give bass fishing fans the chance to actually answer that question. Eric and Kyle will now get to see how they stack up against the pros." Well, they're certainly going to get an answer. Here's what the 'Average Joes' are up against When Bird first told OutKick OutDoors about the Average Joes concept earlier this summer, the two spots were still up for grabs. Now we know the contestants, and WBE has since revealed the professional field they'll have to deal with. The Champions will pit its Stars and Stripes rosters against one another, bringing together elite anglers from the Bassmaster and Major League Fishing worlds. And there aren't many soft spots on either side. Start with Trey McKinney, whom OutKick OutDoors spoke with earlier this month after he wrapped up a historic Bassmaster Elite season. The 21-year-old became the youngest Bassmaster Angler of the Year in history and, at the St. Lawrence River finale, also broke the B.A.S.S. record for the heaviest one-day bag of smallmouth bass. Then there is Jordan Lee, a two-time Bassmaster Classic champion who won the sport's marquee event in consecutive years in 2017 and 2018. Hank Cherry is also a back-to-back Classic champion, while Jason Christie won the 2022 Classic. TREY MCKINNEY SAYS BASSMASTER VETERANS MADE HIM EARN THEIR RESPECT BEFORE HISTORY AOY SEASON And that's just one side of the field. The Stripes roster includes Jacob Wheeler, who has won four Bass Pro Tour Angler of the Year titles and captured REDCREST in 2026. Wheeler has racked up 12 Bass Pro Tour wins since the circuit began in 2019. There's also Dustin Connell, the only three-time REDCREST champion, and reigning 2026 Bass Pro Tour Angler of the Year Zack Birge. Oh, and Ott DeFoe, who won the 2019 Bassmaster Classic in Knoxville, is in there too. So, yeah. Good luck, fellas. The Two 'Average Joes' Aren't Exactly Beginners To be fair to Giessing and Carr, "Average Joe" doesn't mean either guy wandered into Bass Pro Shops last week and bought his first rod. Both have tournament experience. Giessing has been an amateur angler for five years and fishes primarily around Lake of the Ozarks. He started fishing as a kid with his late father and has competed in a variety of amateur events in recent years. And he's not shy about wanting to see how far he can take it. "My goal is to continue growing as a competitor, learning from every experience, and pushing myself to see how far I can take this passion," Giessing said. "I consider myself a power fisherman and enjoy the challenge of finding aggressive fish and figuring out what it takes to get them in the boat." Giessing said his ultimate goal would be reaching the professional ranks and competing at the highest level of tournament bass fishing. Well, this should be one hell of an audition. Carr also grew up fishing with his dad and now competes with Cen-Tex Bass Hunters in Belton, Texas, as well as the Tuesday Night Tight Lines 3x9 Series on Stillhouse Hollow Lake. "My dad taught me from an early age what it means to be a sportsman, respect the outdoors, and appreciate conservation," Carr said. "I've been hooked on bass fishing since I was a kid, and these days I enjoy putting that passion to work." He added: "At the end of the day, I just enjoy being on the water, chasing bass, and competing with good people who share the same passion for fishing." The jump from a Tuesday night tournament to lining up against Wheeler, McKinney, Connell and a pile of Bassmaster Classic champions is admittedly a pretty significant one. But that's also what makes this interesting. The Champions brings the two pro circuits together The inaugural Champions tournament will take place Oct. 28-Nov. 1 on Old Hickory Lake at Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tenn., just outside Nashville. The concept from the beginning has been to put top anglers from the sport's major professional circuits on the same water and settle things in one big-money event. Bird said Giessing and Carr won't be treated any differently just because they got into the field through a sweepstakes. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER "We're going to roll out the red carpet for them and treat them the same way we treat the pro anglers," Bird said. "Both 'Average Joes' have a chance to win the grand prize and the ultimate bragging rights, but no matter what, they'll be leaving Nashville with some prize money and a great story to tell." Well, fellas, you’ve got six weeks to practice. Good luck! Love all things fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

title: Fox News Poll: 71% think Trump administration lacks plan to end Iran war
description: A Fox News poll finds 70% of voters say Trump lacks a clear strategy for the Iran war, while 60% now call the military action the wrong decision.
content: Nearly seven months into the war with Iran, a new Fox News national survey finds views souring as voters feel the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the war, a growing number think the conflict will make the U.S. less safe and a majority believes the decision to take military action was wrong. Seven in 10 voters think the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the conflict, including 95% of Democrats, 83% of independents and 43% of Republicans. In addition, a growing 47% of voters say the conflict will make the U.S. less safe in the long run, up from 39% in April. By comparison, 32% think it will make the country safer, and 20% say there will be no difference. The rise in concern is largest among White voters, voters under 45 and independents. Sixty percent say U.S. military action against Iran was the wrong decision, while 37% say it was right, widening the margin to 23 points, up from 17 points in June (58% to 41%). Attitudes against the war have increased modestly across most demographic groups, with the largest shifts among Hispanic voters, voters under age 30, moderates and voters 65 and over. FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE "Typically, the public rallies around the president in response to a foreign policy crisis," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But two things are different here. First, President Trump hasn’t consistently and forcefully made the case for the war, and the U.S. doesn’t have boots on the ground. Both of those things matter for public opinion." FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Trump’s overall job performance stands at 39% approval and 61% disapproval. The president’s ratings on foreign policy are underwater by 24 points. His 37% approval is a second-term low and is just one point above his first-term low of 36% in September 2019. When asked to name the most important issue facing the country, in their own words, only 4% of voters say Iran and a miniscule 1% name foreign policy in general. By comparison, 34% mention the top issue of the cost of living. Meanwhile, by a 10-point margin, more voters say the Democrats are better equipped to handle foreign policy than the Republicans, a reversal from the previous midterm cycle when Republicans were more trusted by 6 points in September 2022. Israel and Ukraine A low of 48% say they side more with the Israelis than the Palestinians (38%) in the ongoing conflict in Gaza. That is down from 54% in June and a high of 68% at the conflict’s outset in October 2023. Since 2023, the sharpest decline in support for Israel — down at least 20 points — comes from women, Hispanic voters, voters under age 45, voters with a college degree and Democrats. Republican support has fallen 10 points during the same time. On Ukraine, voters favor the U.S. continuing to provide financial aid to fight Russia by 16 points (55% to 39%), roughly unchanged during the past two years. Democrats favor supporting Ukraine, while Republicans and independents are divided. One more thing… Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s upcoming visit to the U.S., more than twice as many voters say Trump is not tough enough on China (45%) as say he is too tough (20%). Three in 10 (30%) say his approach is about right. There is bipartisan agreement on this: the largest share of Democrats (44%), Republicans (47%), and independents (44%) say Trump is not tough enough on China. Republicans are more split, with 43% saying his approach is about right. title: Costco's unexpected new role in Americans' love lives: 'Secret sauce is the sampling'
description: From "Camp Costco" veterans meetups to food court date nights, the warehouse club is where Americans are building unexpected social connections.
content: As more of life moves online, people are finding an in-person connection somewhere unexpected: the aisles and food court of their local Costco. The membership warehouse club, known for its bulk grocery items and huge packs of home supplies, has joined the likes of bars, churches and parks as a public spot where people socialize, make friends and may spark or renew romance. Costco has become what sociologists call a "third place," a communal gathering spot where people build community outside their home and work environments, USA Today reported. GROCERY STORE SWITCH COULD SAVE AMERICANS MONEY WHILE SHAKING UP DINNER ROUTINES "Costco has turned shopping into an experience, not just an errand," Phil Lempert, a consumer and trend analyst known as the "SupermarketGuru," told Fox News Digital. "You go in for paper towels and walk out having sampled food, discovered something unexpected and maybe bumped into someone you know. Their secret sauce is the sampling." University of California, Davis students Sharon Hwang, Katrina Le and Steven Zhang organize a group of fellow students for a trip to their local Costco for a food court meal once or twice a quarter, USA Today reported. "If something small like a Costco trip can help someone meet new friends or feel a little bit connected, then I feel like we accomplished something," Hwang told the publication. Friends and social media influencers Analyse Talavera and Carmen Rene Smith have traded costly dinner catchups for Costco errand runs. "Especially in this economy, instead of going out and dropping $200 on dinner — which Analyse and I are good for — we go to Costco and stock up on meal prep for the week and then top it off with a $3 fro yo," Smith told USA Today. "Costco creates a kind of retail ritual: the treasure hunt, the samples, the food court, the great deal you want to tell somebody about." More than 25 years after two military veterans began meeting at their neighborhood Costco in Brentwood, Tennessee, for a Friday hot dog, the Middle Tennessee Veterans Support Group — "Camp Costco" — is still going strong, now supporting a couple of hundred service members across generations. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Nobody cares what rank you were or what service you were in," Marine veteran and group member Paul Napoli told USA Today. "Everybody mixes together." Some couples use their shopping trips as a substitute for date night, dubbing it "clubbing for married folks" or "the Kirkland Signature date night" after Costco's in-house brand. Still others use the store to find love, and some couples have chosen Costco as the venue for their nuptials, according to Reddit posts. It can also be a fun place to explore, Lempert said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Costco creates a kind of retail ritual: the treasure hunt, the samples, the food court, the great deal you want to tell somebody about," he said. "Consumers aren't just buying products. They're sharing an experience, and that's incredibly powerful in an increasingly digital and isolated shopping world." The appetite for that experience comes as in-person connection erodes elsewhere. Americans now spend about 35 minutes a day socializing, down from 45 minutes 20 years ago, and only 30% do any face-to-face socializing on a given day, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' American Time Use Survey. The surgeon general's 2023 advisory found roughly half of adults experience loneliness, and the Survey Center on American Life reports 44% have nowhere in their community to go regularly. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Costco shoppers, by contrast, are loyal, averaging 31 trips to the warehouse annually, according to consumer analytics firm Numerator. They also make the food court a regular habit, spending in line with what they spend at major regional fast-food chains, including In-N-Out. The membership model further creates a social aspect and sense of belonging, Lempert said. "You’re not simply a customer walking into a store; you're a member of a club. Costco has essentially made the membership card part of the consumer's identity."

title: Mamdani's new $4M NYC public bathrooms auto-open doors after 10 minutes
description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's $4 million public bathroom pilot installs Throne Labs units across NYC, but a strict 10-minute limit ends with the door opening.
content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani rolled out a $4 million public bathroom pilot Wednesday in Queens that will install 17 Throne Labs units across all five boroughs to address the city's restroom shortage. Company co-founder and COO Jessica Heinzelman explained that users get 10 minutes before escalating warnings culminate in the door automatically opening. Heinzelman detailed the final warning during a city news conference, saying users receive flashing lights and an audio notification before the door opens. SMART TOILET SEAT COULD DETECT AFIB IN 30 SECONDS "At 10 minutes, there are flashing lights. The audio comes on. And this is both in English and Spanish for all of these indicators," she said. "It says, ‘The door — your time is up, the door is opening.’ The door’s opening. That extends for about 30 seconds. So, if you are still pants down, we're not going to open the door on you. But then the door does open." Heinzelman told Fox News Digital Thursday that Throne Labs settled on the 10-minute restriction after reviewing typical public restroom limits and measuring how long people actually spend inside its units, saying most users leave well before the deadline. "The 10-min limit is a common standard for most timed public restrooms. We further validated measuring the average throne use time, with the vast majority of users across our markets leaving within 3½ minutes," she said. "Users are notified of the time limit prior to entering, and the throne provides multiple audio and visual warnings throughout the use. "At the tail-end of the use there is 30 seconds of audio and visual queues [sic] to leave. This has proven successful in other cities, balancing human needs and mitigating loitering." MAMDANI LAUNCHES FAST-TRACK HOUSING-COURT PUSH, SAYS LANDLORDS UNABLE TO COMPLY ‘SHOULD NOT BE A LANDLORD’ Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told Fox News Digital Thursday that the unusual feature should be weighed against New York City's longstanding shortage of public bathrooms and the high cost of building traditional facilities. "Anyone who’s walked the streets of New York knows the lack of basic public facilities is a real quality-of-life problem," he said. "Cities have managed to spend extraordinary sums building individual public toilets, so if this modular pilot can actually get clean, safe bathrooms on the street for a fraction of that, it’s a victory for municipal common sense. "After all, I’d much rather see the mayor doing the gritty, unglamorous work of solving an actual New York City problem than spending his time grandstanding about Middle East policy." AOC SLAMS ‘OPPRESSED’ TRUMP STATES WHILE TOUTING NYC SERVICES DESPITE $5B DEFICIT AND TRANSIT CRIME SPIKE The one-year pilot will place the ADA-accessible units at high-traffic locations in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island. According to the Mayor's Office, they will be free, operate daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. and can be opened through text message, QR code, the Throne app or physical tap cards distributed through community partners. Mamdani said the modular approach allows the city to avoid some of the infrastructure expenses associated with permanent bathrooms because the units do not require direct connections to water, sewer or power systems. During the news conference, he compared the price of the entire pilot with the historical cost of a single city restroom. "Seventeen costs about what one public restroom has historically cost in New York City. And that is part of why we have not built that many, because we've seen the cost of these restrooms just escalate year after year," Mamdani said. The 10-minute limit is designed partly to deter loitering and extended occupation. Throne Labs says users receive reminders at five and eight minutes, flashing lights and a more urgent message at 10 minutes and the door opens at 10 minutes and 30 seconds. The company said 81% of users across its network finish within five minutes and more than 95% at one downtown Los Angeles location finish within 10 minutes. NIGHTTIME BATHROOM TRIPS COULD REVEAL HIDDEN HEALTH ISSUES — HERE'S WHEN TO WORRY The same technology is already being used in California. Caltrain's current restroom pilot uses Throne units at Redwood City, Sunnyvale and Palo Alto stations and tells riders that after the 10-minute limit, "a visual and auditory warning will sound before the doors are opened." Long Beach also launched four Throne units in 2025 and subsequently extended its partnership after the initial pilot. The city's original announcement said the units contain 21 sensors that monitor cleanliness, usage and potential misuse while maintaining user privacy. The city's subsequent pilot feedback also showed at least one user raising concerns about the time restriction. In Long Beach's published community survey responses, one respondent said the city should increase the limit after nearly being caught inside when time expired. "Please make it more than ten minutes. I was almost embarrassed in front of strangers still using the restroom," the respondent said. Mamdani said New York City has roughly one public toilet for every 8,500 residents and characterized the 17 units as a first step toward a larger network. When asked about the restriction Wednesday, he offered a more succinct warning to New Yorkers accustomed to lingering in the bathroom. "This is not a place to scroll on your phone. title: High stakes, social media barbs remind college football fans that Auburn and Florida share history of hatred
description: Auburn and Florida renew their 84-game rivalry as new head coaches Alex Golesh and Jon Sumrall face off in their first SEC game Saturday night.
content: The center of the college football universe this coming weekend will undoubtedly be in Oxford, Mississippi, and it's easy to see why. Ole Miss and LSU are both top-ten teams with College Football Playoff and national title aspirations, but there's also the added bonus of former Rebels coach Lane Kiffin making his return to Vaught Hemingway Stadium for the first time as the new head coach of the Tigers. With all that in mind, there is a different game set to kick off around the same time in a different part of the SEC that will feature both extremely entertaining football and two fanbases with a ton at stake as well as plenty of hatred to go around. OLE MISS AND LSU WILL DELIVER CINEMA, BUT THE NEXT WEEK FOR EACH TEAM COULD BE THEIR MOST PIVOTAL TESTS In case you didn't know, Auburn and Florida are old rivals. I'm talking very old rivals. Before their annual matchups and bitter back-and-forth contests with LSU and Tennessee, the Gators considered the Tigers one of their biggest rivals, and the feeling was mutual on the other side. These two programs have met 84 times dating all the way back to 1912, and from 1945 until 2002, they played each other every year. Auburn holds the all-time series lead at 43-39-2, but the Gators have dominated the rivalry since 1990 when Steve Spurrier arrived in Gainesville, boasting a 12-6 record in that timeframe. That's not to say the Tigers haven't ruined plenty of Florida's best seasons in that stretch, and as a Gator fan coming of age during those years, I can speak to several personal experiences. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! I was a bit too young to remember 1994, when the Tigers marched into Ben Hill Griffin Stadium as 17.5-point underdogs and handed the top-ranked Gators their first and only regular season loss that year. I do, however, remember the 2006 Auburn team pouncing all over the second-ranked Gators to give that team their only loss en route to a national championship. The very next year, a reeling 2-2 Auburn squad upset top-five Florida in The Swamp, giving then-head coach Urban Meyer his first home loss as a Gator. That might explain part of why the rhetoric around this renewed rivalry is so toxic on social media this week, but it doesn't tell the whole story. History is only half of the equation here, as both the Tigers and Gators are breaking in new coaches who just as easily could have been on opposite sidelines. Saturday night will be the first SEC game for both Auburn head coach Alex Golesh and Florida head coach Jon Sumrall, so this contest will be a huge early test for two programs desperate to get off on the right foot in conference play. COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S CHAOS ERA IS HERE: TEXAS RALLIES, OREGON FALLS AND LANE KIFFIN EYES RETURN TO OLE MISS While the winner won't necessarily be out of the woods when it comes to proving they are ahead of schedule in year one, the loser will almost certainly be faced with some tough questions after failing to beat a team that is in a similar boat from a timeline perspective. There's also the added animosity Tigers fans likely feel towards Sumrall, who, by all accounts, was Auburn's top choice in their search for a new coach last November before he pivoted to the Gators. It's highly likely that both programs ended up with the best coach for them moving forward - I personally think Golesh will be great at Auburn and I'm obviously super high on Sumrall so far at Florida - but on Saturday night, Tiger fans will be eager to prove that the man who spurned them for a different shade of orange and blue made the wrong choice. Losing this game is going to suck for whichever coach, program, and fanbase fails to come out on top, and that's why it's so intriguing despite the fact neither team is ranked in the top-25. There are plenty of football-related aspects that make this matchup a must-watch, too, though. The chess match between Florida's offensive coordinator extraordinaire, Buster Faulkner, and Auburn's defensive coordinator DJ Durkin, who many consider one of the best in the conference, as well as the prospect of Gator running back Jadan Baugh going against the Tigers' stellar linebacker duo of Elijah Melendez and Xavier Atkins, will have football fans salivating. When you combine the off-field narratives with the on-field action, Auburn and Florida should provide one of the most entertaining matchups of the early season. title: Craig Counsell romanticizes Pete Crow-Armstrong's monster night against Braves on cusp of MVP honors
description: Pete Crow-Armstrong's two-homer night left Craig Counsell in awe, telling Alex Bregman at Wrigley Field that fans will tell grandkids about this season.
content: It may have taken until game 153 of the season, but the aura and abilities of Pete Crow-Armstrong finally got to Chicago Cubs manager Craig Counsell. The 24-year-old superstar has arguably been the most exciting player in Major League Baseball this season, having put together what feels like countless memorable performances, showing off his power at the plate, speed around the bases, and ability to cover a freakish amount of space roaming center field. During the Cubs' 8-4 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night, PCA registered his seventh multi-home-run game of the season, with three of the seven taking place over the last three weeks alone. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Something about Wednesday's two-home-run night, however, struck something within Counsell, so much so that he shared details about his emotions after his team's win over the Braves. "When he hit the second homer, Alex Bregman was standing next to me," Cubs manager Craig Counsell said, according to MLB.com. "I said, ‘Alex, we don’t get to see things like this.’ You spend your whole life in baseball, and you just don’t see this happen on a baseball field. You’re grateful to be a part of it." Crow-Armstrong's first home run of the contest came in the bottom of the third inning, and while it sent Wrigley Field into a frenzy, his second long ball of the night did, as Counsell alluded to, have a different feel about it. CUBS STAR PETE CROW-ARMSTRONG APPRECIATES THE WILD CONSPIRACY THEORY THAT BABE RUTH NEVER EXISTED As PCA stepped to the plate in the bottom of the seventh inning, the hometown crowd decided to shower him with "MVP" chants. Facing an 0-1 count, he got the low, slightly below-the-zone pitch he's enjoyed hitting all season, and responded to the chants with a home run to right-center field. "You’re grateful to see things like this," Counsell said. "And you’re grateful that the fans get to see a season like this, because they're going to talk about it. They're going to tell their kids about it. They're going to tell their grandkids about seasons like this." As the Cubs' manager, Counsell is always going to praise his players after special performances, but for him to go down the semi-emotional path and explain that people will talk a bout Crow-Armstrong's season to their grandchildren is taking things to a level not often seen, especially when it comes to regular season baseball. Crow-Armstrong's two homers give him 44 on the year, which officially moves him past Cubs legend and Hall of Famer Billy Williams for the most by a left-handed hitter in team history. PCA also connected for a triple during Chicago's win on Wednesday, giving him 81 extra-base hits on the year, another franchise single-season record. If, for whatever reason, a member of the Baseball Writers Association of America was still on the fence about giving the nod for National League MVP to Crow-Armstrong this season, Wednesday night's show may have persuaded them.

title: Dan Le Batard falsely claims that ESPN only hires and pays white people
description: Dan Le Batard accused ESPN of paying too many white people, but his argument omits Stephen A. Smith's $100 million deal and other key details.
content: Liberal sports host Dan Le Batard is complaining about white people again. This time, he is expressing his frustration with ESPN paying certain white people more money than he'd like. "Since George Floyd, the company of ESPN and the country of the United States were promising some sort of change over the last five years. But what has happened with the NFL Network and ESPN ... having put a whole bunch of white people in charge of how to select the next evolution of ESPN, this is what happened. I want to ask you guys if anyone is noticing this. Have you noticed that the people at ESPN who are getting the chances and big money ... are Joe Buck, Pat McAfee, Josh Pate, Rich Eisen, the Golics, Jason Kelce, Peter Schrager and the Mannings?" Le Batard said on his show. "As the money flows in to fund [ESPN], that is now sitting out the political discussion that it's a whole lot of white people hiring a whole lot of white people and giving the money to a whole lot of white people ... it's only those people getting that money. Has anyone noticed that?" he continued. DAN LE BATARD CLAIMS ESPN IS RUN BY MCAFEE AND 'WHITE PEOPLE' AFTER LAYOFFS, SLANDERS OUTKICK IN UNHINGED RANT To answer his question, no. Most people have not noticed that. For one, normal people don't count the number of white and black people on television. They don't care. More importantly, however, people haven't noticed what Le Batard is describing because his premise is false. Consider the names Le Batard cites. He lists Joe Buck and Pat McAfee among ESPN's highest-paid talents. They are. But between them is Stephen A. Smith, who is black. Last year, Smith signed a five-year, $100 million contract extension with the company. Because McAfee signed a licensing deal, Smith is ESPN's highest-paid full-time employee. ESPN did bring back Mike Golic and Mike Golic Jr. this year, as Le Batard mentions. But their inclusion in his argument is questionable because they returned on relatively minor deals to host a radio-only program. If Le Batard is going to mention them, he should also acknowledge that ESPN brought back Stan Verrett, a black commentator with a long history of toxic, embarrassing social media posts. The Mannings are also on a licensing deal, as are Charles Barkley and Shaquille O'Neal, who host "Inside the NBA" during the NBA Finals. The point isn't that ESPN has failed to pay star white talent—it has. The point is that Le Batard has selectively cherry-picked those deals to construct an argument about racial bias that doesn't withstand even modest scrutiny. In fact, there might not be another media network in the country, other than BET, that has prioritized excluding white people from its hiring practices as much as ESPN has over the past decade. The "change" Le Batard describes is that ESPN no longer entirely excludes white men from the hiring and promotion process, as it once did. After George Floyd died in 2020, talent agents recognized that ESPN would not promote any white male, regardless of his qualifications or fit for the role. The company gave nearly every new promotion to a black employee. Look at the commentators ESPN promoted during that period: Malika Andrews, Monica McNutt, Elle Duncan, Clinton Yates, Andraya Carter, Chiney Ogwumike, Ryan Clark, Marcus Spears, David Dennis Jr. and Christine Williamson. ESPN has since recognized that this overtly racist approach was not sustainable, particularly because most of its audience is white men. For the most part, the network now elevates and pays those whom management believes deserve it, regardless of their skin color. ESPN's most prominently promoted talent over the past year includes McAfee, Stephen A., Schrager, Jason McCourty, Josh Pate, Mina Kimes and Malika Andrews. There are some hits there, and some misses. However, because that group is about 50% white, Dan Le Batard has an issue — or pretends to. We don't find Le Batard's outrage genuine. If he were truly concerned about a media network hiring too many white people, he would run his own media company far differently. From what we can tell, Le Batard's Meadowlark Media has just one full-time black employee: a producer named Roy Bellamy. Everyone else at his company, which may have up to 40 total employees, is white, and mostly male. Why the hypocrisy? OutKick asked Le Batard that question on Thursday via text message: "Hi, Dan. I have two questions: By the way, happy to re-schedule that interview your rep scheduled with me any time." Le Batard did not respond as of publication. We will update this story if he does. But don't plan on a response. Le Batard tends to go silent when he exhibits hypocrisy, which seems to happen with frequency. Most notably, he has repeatedly declared zero tolerance for violence against women, despite once employing Howard Bryant, who was arrested for allegedly choking his wife in public. Le Batard was also the first host to interview Kamala Harris' husband, Doug Emhoff, after a Daily Mail report cited an alleged incident in which he slapped his ex-girlfriend. Despite the news and interest surrounding the scandal, Le Batard never asked Emhoff about the allegation. And yet, he criticizes other outlets for failing to ask subjects about allegations involving violence against women. At this point, you have to wonder why Le Batard is like this. How can he so calmly and falsely accuse others of doing exactly what he does? Is there something seriously wrong with him? Is he trying to overcompensate for his early, wild bachelor days? Is he still bitter that ESPN chose Pat McAfee over him? Is he simply a fraud? Unfortunately, despite his own publicist reaching out to set up an interview a few years ago, he ultimately declined to speak with OutKick. He has, however, mentioned both the site and me several times on his show. He has previously accused me of "wearing the [KKK] hood" and "trying to hold women in media back." title: WATCH: Gaffe-prone Seattle socialist mayor cuts off police chief in yet another awkward interview
description: Seattle Assistant Police Chief Nicole Powell's uncomfortable reaction when asked about Flock cameras alongside Mayor Katie Wilson went viral online.
content: Already known for awkward, gaffe-prone interviews and public appearances, Seattle socialist Mayor Katie Wilson is being mocked again for another uncomfortable on-camera moment. This time, Wilson, a Democrat and self-identified socialist, is being criticized for a strange interview about the city’s gun violence reduction plan alongside Seattle Police Assistant Chief Nicole Powell and Amy Barden, chief of Seattle’s Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) Department. At one point during the interview, Wilson interjected after a long pause when Powell was questioned by a reporter about the usefulness of new Flock-type surveillance cameras being installed in the city. KOMO News reporter Chris Daniels had asked Powell whether the new cameras could assist with Seattle’s slate of unsolved cases. The assistant police chief hesitated, looked down and began to speak twice before Wilson interjected. "Cameras are obviously a useful tool, right? We’ve seen in the 'Bite of Seattle' shooting there’s been camera footage from businesses around Seattle center, we have cameras at Seattle center, those cameras have been useful tools in solving crime, there’s no doubt about that," said Wilson. SEATTLE MAYOR GRILLED ON PUBLIC SAFETY CRISIS AS RESIDENTS DEMAND ANSWERS Visibly uncomfortable after Wilson interjected, the assistant police chief chuckled, motioned to the mayor and repeatedly looked off camera. The reporter continued pressing them, saying, "What’s going to be the metric of success?" Powell looked to Wilson, whose voice cracked slightly as she answered, "Ultimately, we want to see zero homicides, we want to see fewer homicides, and we want to see fewer guns shot." While Wilson spoke, Powell nodded along and looked to the side off camera again. The reporter persisted, asking, "Would either of you like to answer that question?" as he motioned to Powell and Barden. Barden jumped in quickly, steering the conversation away from Flock cameras. "From my side, in addition to shots fired and homicides, you want to look at referrals in the services and whether or not somebody is making meaningful improvement in their life," said Barden. BLUE-CITY POLICE CHIEF DRAWS SCRUTINY AFTER REFERRING TO KNOWN GUN VIOLENCE SUSPECTS AS ‘TRIGGER PULLERS’ After Barden finished speaking, the reporter turned the floor over to the assistant police chief, who laughed and finally answered, "Just to piggyback, taking a holistic approach, this strategy works." "It is proven in other cities like this, and it takes all of us," Powell added, as she looked back at Wilson and Barden. This comes as debate continues over the expansion of surveillance cameras in Seattle and other cities across the country. During her campaign last year, Wilson argued against expanding surveillance cameras in the city but has taken a different tone since becoming mayor. Last September, Wilson remarked that "turning on more cameras won’t magically make our neighborhoods safer. But it will certainly make our neighbors more vulnerable," reported The Urbanist. However, after becoming mayor, Wilson announced that she would pause expansion of Seattle’s surveillance-camera system pending a privacy and data-governance audit, while allowing the existing cameras to remain in operation. She said the city would use the audit’s findings to determine whether and how to proceed with further expansion. During the KOMO News interview this week, Wilson was pressed on when she would set a date for a decision. She answered, "I’m going to sound like a broken record on this, but we’ve been conducting this audit of our data security and storage and privacy practices, we’re expecting the results of that audit around the end of this month and so, at the end of this month, we’ll be making that information public, and then I’ll be making a decision about that expansion." SEATTLE MAYOR ADMITS BREAKING STARBUCKS BOYCOTT AFTER URGING RESIDENTS TO SHUN COFFEE GIANT The awkward on-camera moment was quickly called out by many online. Popular conservative account "End Wokeness" called it an "incredible moment." title: Ed Sheeran faces growing backlash as radio station bans songs, protest groups respond to Macklemore's removal
description: Classic Hits Radio announced it will stop playing Ed Sheeran's music after backlash over Macklemore's removal from the Loop Tour over Gaza protests.
content: Ed Sheeran continues to deal with the backlash surrounding Macklemore's removal from the singer’s U.S. tour. An Irish radio station announced Thursday that, in response to the controversy and feedback from listeners, it would no longer play music released by the 35-year-old "Shape of You" singer for the "foreseeable future." Dave Kelly, group program director at Bay Broadcasting, which runs Classic Hits Radio, told The Independent the decision "has been carefully considered" and "is not intended as a personal judgment on Ed Sheeran." "We acknowledge his own explanation of the circumstances surrounding recent events," Kelly said. "As an independent Irish-owned radio station, however, we believe it is important to listen to our audience and to stand alongside Irish artists who have made what is undoubtedly a significant professional decision based on their own convictions." ED SHEERAN SAYS HE TRIED TO ‘BUILD A BRIDGE’ OVER MACKLEMORE TOUR SPOT BEFORE VENUES SAID NO He added his company "believe(s) in peace, humanity and respect" as well as "the right of people and artists to express and act upon their sincerely held views." "In light of the strength of feeling expressed by our listeners and the decisions taken by Irish artists involved in the tour, we believe removing Ed Sheeran’s music from our playlist is the appropriate decision for Classic Hits Radio at this time," he concluded. The controversy began after Macklemore repeatedly called for a "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song, "Hind’s Hall," during his opening performance at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, Sept. 4 and 5. title: Lane Kiffin’s return to Ole Miss comes with betrayal, lawsuits and memories of him trying to burn it all down
description: Trinidad Chambliss stayed at Ole Miss despite Lane Kiffin's alleged efforts to lure him to LSU, and now the Rebels are ready to wreck his return.
content: OXFORD, Miss. - Just blocks away from a busy Ole Miss campus, residents of the small town of Oxford roamed 'The Square' on a Wednesday night that felt like a perceived calm before the storm that will have this city roaring over the next few days. An Ella Langley concert is scheduled for Thursday night, serving as an expensive kickoff party for a game that has drawn the attention of the entire college football world. Students strolled from campus to restaurants such as City Grocery, while visitors looking to stock up on Ole Miss gear stopped by Game Day Apparel for powder-blue hats featuring the phrase "Spot the Ball." MOUNTED POLICE, EXTRA PATROLS AND KIFFIN HATE: OXFORD PREPARES FOR OLE MISS-LSU GAME WITH EXTRA SECURITY Folks flocked to 'Off-Square Books' to hear my colleague John Talty discuss his new book on Lane Kiffin, which has already generated notably unfavorable reactions from those within Lane Kiffin's inner circle since its release. Inside Ajax Diner on Thursday afternoon, conversations shifted between the former head coach and the 2026 Ole Miss football team led by Pete Golding. SAM LEAVITT INJURY BOMBSHELL SENDS LSU-OLE MISS SHOWDOWN INTO CHAOTIC MODE, AS KIFFIN'S RETURN LOOMS But ... one talking point is persistent inside the landmark restaurant that opened in 1997. "We really need to win this game," one diner attendee said while clad in powder blue gear. "I can't imagine how that bastard will act if they [LSU] win." Maybe it'd be a different story if the outgoing coach didn’t try to burn it down There are plenty of people around Oxford who claim to know Lane Kiffin, whether through his six years in town or relationships built through late-night voice messages and text conversations. According to people who have spent time around him, the idea that Kiffin is a true "people person" remains debatable. "He didn’t really have use for you if there wasn’t something coming on the other end," Mike, from Oxford told OutKick. "Sure, he embraced the town, but he was spending more time in the yoga studios than the actual community. I'm not judging. He's a grown man, and he was single. "Obviously, you could tell he changed his life while here in Oxford. But, that doesn’t make him a good person, considering how he tried to burn this place to the ground on his way to LSU." OLE MISS FILES LAWSUITS AGAINST COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYERS WHO LEFT FOR LANE KIFFIN'S LSU About that burning to the ground. If Lane had just left for Baton Rouge without all of the chaos that came with him trying to pigeon-hole his way into coaching Ole Miss during their playoff run, maybe the feelings would be a tad bit different. But, that's not Lane, especially when he doesn’t get his way. From assistant coaches pulling double-duty, flying back-and-forth between Oxford and Baton Rouge, to Kiffin just waiting for the Rebels to lose in the Sugar Bowl so he could at least feel better about his decision to leave during the most chaotic time in Ole Miss history, nothing was cordial about his exit. LANE KIFFIN GOES OFF SCRIPT: HULK HOGAN, OLE MISS AND SOCIAL MEDIA DOMINATE SEC MEDIA DAYS It's one thing to get a divorce. It's another to take things out of spite or try to empty the bank account on the way out of a marriage. "He's calling players while they are in meetings in hopes of negotiating a deal with their agents to get them to transfer once the season ended," one Ole Miss donor told OutKick. "The man was doing everything in his power to create obstacles for the Rebels during their CFP run." SEC FILES BOMBSHELL LAWSUIT AGAINST LSU, LANE KIFFIN WHILE PRO PLAYERS FIGHT FOR COLLEGE ELIGIBILITY IN COURT That even included quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, who would return to Ole Miss for another season after being granted an injunction against the NCAA. Chambliss makes his return, through a court case. Those seem to follow Kiffin When the wheels were put into motion for Trinidad Chambliss to petition the NCAA for an additional year of eligibility, the thought process behind the move came from those within the Ole Miss athletic department. After alleging that a health issue during his time at Ferris State forced him into having to take a medical redshirt, the NCAA denied his waiver for an additional season. So, led by lawyer Tom Mars, after a call from Lane Kiffin, a lawsuit was filed against the NCAA in a small town court in Pittsboro, Mississippi. Inside A Louisiana Courtroom: SEC-LSU legal Circus Played Out Like A John Grisham Novel In Stunning Showdown We all know what happened from there, with Chambliss receiving his injunction by a local judge who shed a few tears while reading his order to the courtroom filled with supporters. The problem for Lane Kiffin was that he was thinking, before the case ended up in a courtroom, that Chambliss would follow him to Baton Rouge. Obviously, that part of the plan did not come to fruition, with Grove Collective founder Walker Jones putting together a deal for Chambliss that would keep him in Oxford, and away from the guy who tried his best to steal as much talent as possible from the Rebels roster. "This school was going to fight like heck to keep Trinidad and Kewan [Lacy]," another Ole Miss booster told OutKick. "We couldn’t lose those two guys, especially to Lane. This town has embraced those two, along with the entire team, like they are family. "Everywhere you go in Oxford, there are signs with their names or faces on it. When they decided to stay, we knew how much that bothered him [Kiffin]. I think in some different world, we would’ve paid them double, just to piss Lane off. He wasn’t going to get the entire family." LSU-OLE MISS SHOWDOWN INTENSIFIES AS TIGERS STAR SERVED WITH LAWSUIT PAPERS OUTSIDE FOOTBALL FACILITY And it seems as though court cases have just magically appeared around Kiffin, with the most recent battle taking place in Baton Rouge when Zxavian Harris and Dae'Quan Wright sued the NCAA for an additional season after exiting NFL preseason camps. As for Kiffin's interesting mind, even if LSU was not technically involved in the case, most of the football players involved in the Baton Rouge court were presumably headed to LSU. Well, there was maybe one player, Ethan Johnson, that supposedly went against the grain and ended up at South Carolina. "Somebody mentioned that when that one player [Johnson] decided to sign with the Gamecocks over LSU, ole Lane tried to get him taken out of that case in Louisiana," an Oxford local who had a relationship with Kiffin told OutKick. "Who knows, but it wouldn’t surprise me because that's how he operates. "It's his way or the highway. We learned that here. But, I'm not going to sit here and act as though we aren’t grateful for what he did for our program." All eyes on Oxford, as the college football world tunes in across the country Sure, some people simply want to watch the world burn. And this could be one of the wildest scenes college football fans have witnessed in quite some time. Ten months after Kiffin left Oxford on a private jet bound for Baton Rouge, he will return to Vaught-Hemingway Stadium as the head coach of the LSU Tigers. This will not be his first trip back to Oxford since leaving Ole Miss. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! There will be profanity. There will be middle fingers directed at Kiffin. But, there will also be a top-ten showdown that will have major ramifications for the season. title: Mackenzie Phillips makes new claims about father's alleged abuse
description: Mackenzie Phillips revealed a letter from a family friend corroborated her abuse claims against father John Phillips on Valerie Bertinelli's podcast.
content: For decades, Mackenzie Phillips said she lived with the pain of not being believed about her late father, John Phillips. Then an unexpected letter landed in her hands – and changed everything. Phillips opened up about a stunning letter from a longtime family friend that corroborated her claims of abuse by her late father during an episode of Valerie Bertinelli's podcast, "Get Naked." Phillips recalled receiving the letter while working at Breathe Life Healing Center. It's probably fan mail.' Because, you know, we get fan mail there," she told Bertinelli. "And I won't go into too much detail, but it was from one of the most credible sources you could ever know of a family friend saying that ... their husband observed something horrific when I was 9." "And I said, ‘Jeffrey’ – my brother, you know – 'I want to tell you.' He said, 'I don't want to know.' Nobody wants to know. Nobody wants to know, you know," Mackenzie said. "So I'm on my own again... I'm on my own in this nobody believes me." "Here's the thing is that I told the people – that said that I was lying – back then," she added. "They already knew. "And this woman said, 'I'm so sorry I didn't come forward to support you while you were on "Oprah." I was afraid. I didn't know what to do. But here's what happened.' And I'm sitting there. title: Best hikes in and around Oxford to get you ready for Ole Miss-LSU's week three showdown
description: From Sardis Lake's 13-mile Clear Creek Trail to the family-friendly Lamar Park walking loop, these Oxford hikes are perfect before Ole Miss vs. LSU.
content: The eyes of the college football world will be focused this weekend on Oxford, Mississippi, for the showdown between Ole Miss and LSU. Two top-ten teams in the SEC duking it out is already newsworthy, but with the added context of Tigers coach Lane Kiffin making his way back to Vaught Hemingway Stadium for the first time since his departure from the university, this one is sure to be a hot ticket. If you're lucky enough to be attending the game, you'll likely want to enjoy the great outdoors and take in all the natural beauty that the Magnolia State has to offer, and luckily for you, we here at OutKick OutDoors have you covered. BEST HIKES TO TRY AROUND LUBBOCK AHEAD OF TEXAS TECH'S WEEK ONE MATCHUP WITH ABILENE CHRISTIAN Here are four of the best hikes in and around Oxford to help you usher in the game on Saturday. South Campus Rail Trail For those of you wanting a real hike without ever leaving the friendly confines of Oxford, this one is an absolute slam dunk. The South Campus Rail Trail features a five-mile round trip trail that follows an old gravel railroad bed (hence the name), while the surrounding network contains more than 20 miles of single-track trails, according to the university website. It's right by campus so you don't have to travel too far, and it also features a quiet, wooded area to take your mind off the stresses of gameday. Whether you're looking for a straightforward walk or something a little more adventurous through the surrounding woods, South Campus Rail Trail is the move. Clear Creek Trail at Sardis Lake Serious hikers who actually came to work up a sweat will love Clear Creek Trail. It's a little further away - about 30 minutes from downtown Oxford - but the drive is well worth it. Clear Creek Trail offers a 13-mile loop around nearby Sardis Lake, and the trails are even split up for different levels of hikers. There's a three-mile beginner loop or an eight-mile beginner/intermediate combination, meaning there's something for everyone. The views of the lake are spectacular, especially during late summer and early fall, and the proximity to the water means hikers can make a full outdoors day that includes a little fishing if you've come prepared. 6 OF THE BEST FALL CAMPING DESTINATIONS IN AMERICA, PLUS GEAR BEGINNERS SHOULD PACK One thing to note is that this doubles as a mountain biking trail, so hikers should be aware of this and yield appropriately. The combo of the woods and the water make this a must-see. Holly Springs National Forest It's been called the antithesis of a college football Saturday, and although that sounds like a pejorative, I can assure you it's not. Holly Springs National Forest is probably the most secluded and serene spot on this list, so if you really just need to get away from it all before a stressful slate of SEC football, this is the place for you. 14 TAILGATING ESSENTIALS FOR GRILLING, WATCHING THE GAME AND STAYING WARM The area offers a remote destination for hikers who don't want to deal with the large crowds some of the more "touristy" destinations hold. The whole forest is home to 155,000 acres of federal land, and a special mention needs to be made for the recreation area at Chewalla Lake, which is great for hiking, fishing, canoeing, and more. With it being so secluded, you'll have to drive a bit to get here (Google Maps plots it as 65 minutes from Oxford), but that's the price you pay for being one with nature. If you're looking to broaden your horizons and really explore everything northern Mississippi has to offer, make the trek here. You won't regret it. Lamar Park So, you brought the whole family along for a little SEC football action? Great! If you're looking for a hike you and the kids can enjoy, Lamar Park is the place to be. It's a six-minute car ride from the stadium, so you won't have to worry about entertaining the rugrats on a long road trip, and once you arrive, you'll find a well manicured park and a low intensity walking loop for hikers trying to avoid a more strenuous workout. Anyone who is trying to get a little sunshine and some fresh air on the morning of the game without busting their butt should check this place out, as it's more of a scenic stroll than a heart-racing romp through the wilderness. title: Boston Red Sox send Sonny Gray to the mound against Texas Rangers in key MLB matchup tonight
description: Sonny Gray and the Boston Red Sox face the Texas Rangers in a crucial matchup with Wild Card and AL West division implications on the line.
content: Yesterday was a winning day on the diamond as both MLB plays that I put out came through for us and cashed. We only have about 10 games remaining for the teams. The playoffs are within reach for some teams, and others are looking at some options for the future. Tonight we have a game between one team that has already locked up their spot, the Red Sox, and another team still battling to try and get in, the Rangers. The Boston Red Sox are 12 games above .500, and they have been one of the best teams in baseball over the past couple of months. They've been very streaky, winning multiple games at a time and moving up the standings. The Red Sox are currently sitting in the second spot in the Wild Card, and they control their own destiny. Much of the early-season problem was how the team was playing in Boston. They are just one game over .500 at home, but they are 11 games above on the road. One guy who did excel in Fenway is tonight's starter, Sonny Gray. He has been good on the road as well and has put together one of the best seasons of his career. Gray is 17-5 with a 2.76 ERA and a 1.17 WHIP. This has been the most games he has ever won, and if it stands will be his second-lowest ERA ever. His road ERA is actually better than his home ERA, and his night games have been fantastic this season. He has thrown 13 innings this month and allowed just three earned runs. Gray faced the Rangers once this season, and he allowed just one earned run over six innings. The Texas Rangers have a much more difficult path to the postseason. The team is .500 for the year, and there are questions about whether anyone who wins the American League West will finish the season with a winning record. They have chosen a great time to get hot, though, as they've won their past four games and are now tied with the Astros for the division lead. They are also just one game behind the White Sox for the final Wild Card spot. This game would go a long way for the team in getting closer to one of those two options. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Coming into the season, I was expecting the Rangers to be one of the better teams in the division, mostly due to their rotation. Jacob deGrom, Nathan Eovaldi, and MacKenzie Gore were guys I expected to give them a good chance in the majority of games. Tonight, though, the Rangers won't rely on their starters. They are sending out Tyler Alexander to start the game. He brings a 3.38 ERA and a 1.28 WHIP to the table over 66.2 innings. The Rangers have a rough bullpen with a collective 4.27 ERA. title: US economy notches remarkable new record, sparking cheers: ‘Good job everyone’
description: Census Bureau data shows poverty hit an all-time low of 10.2%, yet 85% of Americans say their financial situation is worsening or unchanged.
content: Americans may not feel it in their wallets, but two major measures of economic well-being improved in 2025, as the nation's poverty rate fell to a historic low and inflation-adjusted median household income reached a record high, according to new Census Bureau data. In 2025, the poverty rate in the United States dropped to an all-time low of 10.2%, down roughly half a point from 2024, according to the Census Bureau. Even as the proportion of people living in undesirable conditions declines, however, the percentage of people who told Fox News pollsters that their personal financial situation was worsening or not changing held steady at around 85% for the duration of 2025. Many have attributed President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, which some conservatives fear could cost the GOP control of Congress in November, to his economic policies. Amid Republican unpopularity and consumer pessimism, even states that are usually reliably conservative, like Texas, Ohio and Alaska, could very well send Democrats to the Senate. FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS The Census Bureau defines poverty depending on the number of people in a given household and their income. A family with two adults and two children, for instance, would need to make less than $32,649 a year to be considered impoverished. The threshold for poverty increases as inflation lowers the value of the dollar. Median household income also reached an all-time high, growing by 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025. That gain, however, is erased by inflation as the dollar’s value declined by about 3% between 2024 and 2025. A number of factors could explain the gap between economic perception and improving macroeconomic indicators. "See a lot of mutuals on here in DC, New York, LA talking about high prices. Meanwhile folks I know in Alabama, Indiana, Georgia getting new jobs, raises, or expanding and growing," Andrew Beck, a partner at the consulting firm Beck and Stone, wrote on X. "Doesn’t help young folks in the blue states, but the South is booming." THE RED STATES CHARGING AHEAD WITH AMERICA'S WEALTH AS RIVALS WATCH BILLIONS SLIP AWAY Economic growth in Southern states has consistently outpaced the United States at large, spurred by internal migration and friendly business environments incentivizing large enterprises to move south. High gas prices, sparked by the president’s military operations in the Middle East, and price increases attributable to tariffs have also proven unpopular, hurting the president’s approval ratings even as poverty rates dip and incomes climb. Roughly two-thirds of voters in a recent Fox News poll said that they believe the Trump administration is making the economy worse. THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE Conservatives on social media have used the Census Bureau’s data to take a victory lap. "Poverty is bad. Every American should celebrate poverty rates are now the lowest on record. Good job everyone," Rep. Michael Baumgartner, R-Wash., wrote on X. "Keep it going." "Good news we can all celebrate," Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a critic of the president, posted. The number of people without health insurance also remained near historic lows, according to the Census Bureau. Some on the left, however, deny that poverty rates are actually declining. "Our elites terrorize the entire world while ordinary Americans continue to foot the bill. We spent trillions ‘fighting’ the terror we created to provide cover for our oil barons stealing 3rd World resources," Twitch streamer Hasan Piker wrote on X Thursday. "It only amounted to more death overseas, more poverty at home. All while the [military industrial complex] ballooned. No houses, no hospitals, no schools-just a growing crisis of homelessness, underemployment and diseases of despair in the wealthiest country on earth." With personal homeownership holding strong cultural importance to Americans, rising home costs fuel pessimism in ways that improvements in other areas can’t necessarily offset.

title: Pro-Trump group leads new coalition to undercut teachers unions
description: First on Fox: Linda McMahon backs the Let Teachers Teach Coalition to bypass bureaucracy and empower educators to drive change at local school boards.
content: FIRST ON FOX — A new national movement designed to bypass administrative bureaucracy and teachers unions is taking shape with the goal of improving the nation's education system. The initiative, the Let Teachers Teach Coalition, aims to empower local educators and return decision-making authority to classrooms and school districts nationwide. This coalition was launched by America First Policy Institute on Thursday, Constitution Day, to strengthen civics and history education and "put teachers, parents and students back at the center of America’s classrooms." POWERFUL TEACHERS' UNIONS SHARE STRIKING LINK WITH STATES STRUGGLING TO TEACH KIDS TO READ "Teachers dedicate their lives to the success and well-being of America’s children," U.S. Department of Education Secretary Linda McMahon told Fox News Digital. "Yet, too often, their ability to do that work is constrained by bureaucracy, political agendas and mandates that have little to do with helping students succeed," she continued. "The Let Teachers Teach Coalition is giving a voice to the educators who have spent too long navigating unnecessary regulations and restrictive systems," McMahon added. "When we give teachers the freedom to focus on teaching, we create an environment where students, families and communities can thrive and succeed." Spearheaded by the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), the coalition provides educators and parents with toolkits to navigate local school board politics and directly engage board members. The goal is to equip current, former and retired teachers, along with administrators and parents, to drive policy shifts at the grassroots level. "While some education policy is decided at the state and federal levels, many of the issues teachers face every day are determined by local school boards and districts," AFPI announced in a statement. "Let Teachers Teach will build a national network of educators and equip them to drive change from the classroom up — identifying problems, advocating for solutions and turning successful local policies into models that can be replicated across the country." MCMAHON TELLS HOUSE PANEL TRUMP ADMIN MOVING TO DISMANTLE ‘FAILED’ $3T EDUCATION BUREAUCRACY The coalition aligns directly with McMahon’s primary mandate from President Donald Trump of dismantling the traditional footprint of the federal Department of Education and returning governance to the states. Department officials recently pointed to national test scores showing that only three in 10 students are proficient in math and reading despite more than $3 trillion in federal taxpayer money spent since the department's creation in 1979. The movement coincides with McMahon’s ongoing 50-state Returning Education to the States tour and targeted local radio outreach, where she has been speaking directly with families about how K-12 schooling will look under the administration's decentralization plan. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TARGETS HEAD START BUREAUCRACY IN MOVE ADVOCATES SAY PUTS PARENTS IN THE DRIVER'S SEAT To facilitate the wind-down of federal oversight, the administration has rolled out interagency agreements, including shifting student loan collection and management operations to the Department of the Treasury. The administration is also championing the Education Freedom Tax Credit, set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, which will allow individuals to receive a tax credit up to $1,700 for contributions to approved scholarship-granting organizations. title: Erdogan's Turkey cracks down on LGBT community in name of preserving family values
description: Turkey reportedly arrested some 116 people and blocked 180 social media accounts in a sweeping crackdown on LGBT rights organizations across 15 provinces.
content: Turkish authorities launched an unprecedented crackdown on the country’s LGBT community on Sunday, raiding gay bars and shutting down activist organizations, in what the government said are efforts to protect Turkey’s family values. Since the nationwide crackdowns began, Turkish authorities have arrested and detained some 116 people across 15 provinces in actions against LGBT rights organizations and activists. The Turkish criminal justice system has also launched investigations of more than 160 people, according to Amnesty International. Amnesty International reported that 180 social media accounts belonging to LGBT organizations, activists, journalists and media outlets have been blocked or restricted. TURKEY’S NATO ROLE UNDER SCRUTINY AMID NEW REPORT ON HAMAS, MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES "This appalling escalation in Türkiye’s crackdown amounts to a full-scale assault on LGBTI rights and those who defend them. The relentless raids, arrests and demonization of LGBTI people under the spurious guise of ‘protecting the families’ demonstrates why defending LGBTI rights in Türkiye is more important than ever," Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe, said in a statement. In a statement posted on X, Turkey’s minister of justice, Akın Gürlek, said, "We are steadfastly continuing our efforts to protect the family, our children and our youth from all forms of exploitation, obscenity, crime and harmful content." Gürlek stated that the Ministry of Justice sent a comprehensive directive to the 175 chief public prosecutor's offices in all of Turkey’s 81 provinces to go after content and behavior that the government considers opposed to "public morality" and harmful to the country’s youth. "The best interests of our children are not open to debate for us. We will show no tolerance for any criminal organization targeting the institution of the family, the future of our youth, and the order of our society," Gürlek’s statement went on to say. WHO IS TURKEY'S RECEP TAYYIP ERDOĞAN? HOW NATO'S MOST UNPREDICTABLE LEADER KEEPS REINVENTING HIMSELF Turkey’s focus on family values and traditional norms is part of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Decade of Family and Population vision, a long-term strategy aimed at tracking population trends and promoting an increased fertility rate to spur population growth. Many see Erdoğan’s renewed emphasis on "family values," and his targeting of groups he portrays as threats to those values, as an effort to cement his legacy. An enduring question asked by analysts as Erdogan ages and approaches another election in 2028 is what kind of Turkey he leaves behind. "Erdoğan’s ‘family values’ agenda is about more than defending conservative values, it is about defining what kind of society Turkey should be and who belongs in it," Gonul Tol, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital. "The LGBT community is a particularly useful target because Erdoğan can portray it simultaneously as a threat to the traditional family, a Western import, and a symbol of the cultural values he says his movement is fighting against," Gonul added. With protests against the moves beginning to take shape, the crackdowns show no signs of letting up, even as international attention and condemnation begins to pour in. TRUMP BETS ON FORMER NATO TROUBLEMAKER AS TURKEY'S STRATEGIC VALUE SURGES Police used pepper spray against peaceful protesters in İzmir, along Turkey’s Aegean coast, and detained more than 95 people on Tuesday who had gathered outside İstanbul Courthouse in protest. Turkey, which officially became a candidate for the European Union in 1999, received strong pushback from the commission. A European Commission spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The Commission is concerned about the recent arrests and legal proceedings initiated against LGBTIQ+ activists, human rights associations, and businesses, as well as of the blockages of websites and social media accounts, accompanied with allegations concerning funding of civil society organizations. We are following developments closely."
