title: Michigan Republican lawmaker warns guaranteed income programs do not work, voices opposition to state policy
description: Michigan Republicans are demanding oversight of Rx Kids, a $300 million cash assistance program they say has become a guaranteed income experiment.
content: Guaranteed income programs do not work and amount to mere "redistributions of wealth," according to Michigan Republican state Rep. Jay DeBoyer, who joined other Republicans in the state Legislature in criticizing the programs, which have gained prominence in recent years. "Absolutely not. When does that stop?" Rep. DeBoyer, R-Clay Township, told Fox News Digital. "When you think about the role of government, the role of government is not to fund people's lives. The role of the government is to provide a conducive environment where you have opportunities for success." DeBoyer, who chairs the state House Oversight Committee, is leading a contingent of Michigan House Republicans demanding rigorous inspection of Rx Kids — a taxpayer-funded initiative billed as the nation's largest prenatal and infant cash assistance program. Lawmakers are raising alarms over how hundreds of millions of public dollars are being spent. DIRECTOR OF 'CASH GIVEAWAY' PROGRAM TAILORED TO NEW MOTHERS GRILLED ON HOW TAXPAYER FUNDING IS USED IN DEBATE The scrutiny boiled over during a June 2 House Oversight Committee hearing, where GOP lawmakers targeted the program’s lack of spending restrictions or income limits. Republican leaders argue the state-funded initiative has evolved into something far different than what was originally presented to the Legislature, accusing Democrats of using hundreds of millions of dollars in public funding to advance a broader guaranteed-income agenda. Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall told Fox News Digital that lawmakers were led to believe they were funding a targeted maternal and prenatal health initiative — not what he characterized as an open-ended social experiment. Under the current design, Rx Kids provides expectant mothers with a lump-sum payment of $1,500 during pregnancy, followed by $500 per month for six or 12 months after birth, depending on the participating community, regardless of household income. GOP lawmakers across the country have raised similar legal, budgetary, and ideological objections to guaranteed basic income (GBI) and direct cash transfer programs. In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Harris County over its Uplift Harris direct-cash pilot, prompting the Texas Supreme Court to block the payments in 2024. Harris County later terminated Uplift Harris and a successor program in June 2025 and moved to reallocate the funds. In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed Republican-backed legislation that would have prohibited local municipalities and counties from enacting GBI initiatives. Meanwhile, Iowa Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds signed House File 2319 into law on May 1, 2024, banning local guaranteed income programs statewide. CALIFORNIA GUARANTEED INCOME ADVOCACY GROUP RECOMMENDS PERMANENT POLICY FUNDED BY 'DEDICATED LOCAL TAXES' The director of Michigan's Rx Kids, Dr. Mona Hanna, told Fox News Digital that the initiative is neither a traditional guaranteed income program nor a universal basic income (UBI) model, pointing to its strict focus on the critical first year of a child's life. DeBoyer directly challenged that distinction, pointing to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) plan. The state document explicitly defines a "guaranteed income program" as a "cash payment provided on a regular basis to members of a community with no strings attached and no work requirement," citing Rx Kids as a primary example. "The truth is this is just about redistribution of wealth," DeBoyer said. "It's a distribution tactic that I would argue is not going to help moms and babies, when that's actually what we should be trying to do." Progressive advocates have pushed back against the Republican offensive. The Economic Security Project (ESP)— an advocacy group founded in 2016 to promote direct cash transfers — argued that direct assistance enjoys bipartisan support. "Cash is widely supported across ideological lines, and there’s long been growing momentum and political appetite for guaranteed income," Shafeka Hashas, the Director of Cash Initiatives, told Fox News Digital. "The majority of the Michigan Legislature supports this pilot," Hashas added. "Republican Senator John DaMoose wrote an op-ed in the Detroit Free Press about how Rx Kids is a pro-life policy and ‘fiscally responsible,’ and the program has been expanded in both urban and rural communities throughout Michigan by both Democrat and Republican leaders." GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE Hashas emphasized that economic pressures on young families necessitate immediate, flexible relief. "The bottom line is, people are struggling in our economy," Brown said. "It’s more expensive than ever to have a child. In acute moments of vulnerability, people need all the support they can get. It doesn’t make sense to malign cash assistance as a partisan idea when so many communities would benefit from the stability it offers." Meanwhile, the ESP has been pushing for guaranteed income long before affordability became a salient issue. Founded in 2016, ESP launched with more than "100 entrepreneurs, activists, researchers and philanthropists" advocating for direct cash payments. The ESP helped create over 100 guaranteed income pilots across the U.S. The broader campaign for direct payments includes Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, led by former Stockton, California, Mayor Michael Tubbs. Tubbs, who launched one of the nation's early municipal cash experiments, has long argued that federal tax dollars should fund income supplements to help lower-income Americans keep up with rising inflation, rent and groceries, claiming it's a viable policy to tackle affordability. As many guaranteed income advocates would like to make the policy permanent and even push it at the federal level, only Cook County, Illinois has approved such a measure so far. DeBoyer countered that established social safety nets already exist to support low-income families, but said those programs carry strict eligibility standards and oversight mechanisms that Rx Kids lacks. "We have a safety net. We spend literally billions of dollars on social welfare," DeBoyer said. "The difference is, in this particular spending, there are no parameters. There is no means test. Literally a millionaire qualifies for this program. An individual who's not an American citizen qualifies for this program." At the end of the day, we can say that this is about moms and babies, but that creates the potential for massive abuse."

title: Faint signal leads treasure hunters to massive discovery at legendary 400-year-old wreck
description: A 55-pound copper ingot worth up to $25,000 was pulled from the Atocha shipwreck site in the Florida Keys. The treasure-hunting crew says more great finds await.
content: A treasure-hunting crew searching a legendary 17th-century underwater shipwreck off the Florida Keys has recovered a massive 55-pound copper ingot — the latest find along a trail that its captain believes could lead to more treasure. The ingot was found by divers with Mel Fisher's Shipwreck Expeditions at the wreck site of the Nuestra Señora de Atocha, about 35 miles west of Key West. The Spanish treasure galleon was on its return voyage to Spain when it sank in a hurricane off the Florida Keys in 1622 — carrying silver, gold and emeralds. MYSTERY OF GOLD COIN SHIPWRECK FINALLY UNMASKED AFTER 30 YEARS: 'FANTASTIC CONCLUSION' Mel Fisher began searching for the Atocha in 1969. He spent years recovering artifacts from the wreck before his company prevailed in a lengthy legal battle over rights to its treasure in 1982. Fisher's team discovered the Atocha's famed "Mother Lode," or main cargo deposit, in 1985 — and the site still yields new finds decades later. Photos show the 55-pound copper ingot — or copper bar — heavily coated in marine encrustation after spending over four centuries underwater. In an August press release, Mel Fisher's Shipwreck Expeditions said the ingot has an estimated value of about $18,000 to $25,000. UNDERWATER ROBOTICS EXPERT REVEALS 'SHIPWRECK CITY' HIDING BENEATH MAJOR URBAN LAKE Captain Drake Nicholas was retracing an area from the salvage vessel DARE when his metal detector picked up a faint signal, he told Fox News Digital. The captain said he was following a "tight trail of coins" at the time. "I thought it was a cannon, but it ended up being a copper ingot, which was also very exciting." "Faint hits are always the most exciting because they lead to, you know, stuff very deep in the mud," said Nicholas. "And I got that very faint hit. I dug down like I always do ... and it got louder, and that's, you know, when the excitement really kicks in." DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS Nicholas said he initially mistook the ingot for a cannon due to its rounded shape, large size and bronze-copper coloring. "I was so excited," he said. "I thought it was a cannon, but it ended up being a copper ingot, which was also very exciting." Though the ingot may appear ordinary to the untrained eye, Nicholas said copper was a "very precious" resource in the 1600s — especially for making the bronze cannons that the Spanish Empire relied on. MAN FISHING WITH GRANDSON UNCOVERS MYSTERY WRECKAGE IN MUD FLATS, ARCHAEOLOGISTS INVESTIGATING "I believe that only certain people could actually own copper because it was making such strong cannons," he said. "It wasn't something [that] an everyday guy could have a stockpile of — it was more for the king and queen to make cannons." To make the ingots, metalworkers "would basically dig a hole in the sand and just pour copper into it," he said. "It would make this copper ingot or a copper bar," added Nicholas. "The size of what we've been finding lately is … leading us to what I believe is the rest of the treasure," Nicholas said. Part of that confidence comes from new technology that Nicholas said allows the crew to detect targets deeper beneath the dense mud covering the site. title: Colorado college TPUSA chapter enrollment stagnant amid fears of retaliation against conservatives
description: Rachel Cook says Fort Lewis College students face a "big fear" of joining the Turning Point USA chapter as conservatives report harassment.
content: A conservative student leader at Fort Lewis College in Durango, Colorado, says students face a "big fear" of joining the campus Turning Point USA (TPUSA) chapter because conservatives remain a small minority on campus. "In general, a lot of students are afraid of being ostracized by their peers or ... not being [accepted] — it's a very minority group," TPUSA Chapter President Rachel Cook told Fox News Digital. "Being a conservative on campus or even having conservative-leaning beliefs is not a popular idea here. We have seen a lot of disrespect and not a lot of people who are open to having civil discussion and discourse," Cook added. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION Cook took over leadership of the TPUSA chapter to promote ideological diversity on campus, arguing that Fort Lewis College needs more balanced dialogue representing different political viewpoints. "An officer has gotten spit at when we table, and we have had people be harassed," Cook said. "We work a lot with pro-life community members who come to campus and do their advocacy whenever we're not able to stand with them. Even in these past couple of weeks, people have come up to them, ripped their signs and attempted to hit them. A lot of people choose not to press charges." Cook noted that enrollment in the Fort Lewis College chapter has remained flat as students fear social and academic retaliation. The stagnation comes nearly a year after the student government's high-profile decision to recognize the chapter sparked intense opposition across campus — much of which was captured on video obtained by Fox News Digital. UC BERKELEY SUED FOR ALLEGEDLY STONEWALLING PROBE INTO VIOLENT AMBUSH AT TPUSA ROB SCHNEIDER EVENT David Peters, former chair of the La Plata County GOP and a retired Chevron executive, reflected on the incident and its lingering effect on the student group. "Their membership has been essentially flat. The issue is that a lot of students are reluctant to join the chapter for fear of retaliation," Peters said. Fort Lewis College officials maintained that campus security remains a top priority and said the college had received no reports of harassment involving TPUSA chapter members this academic year. "Fort Lewis College takes the safety of our students and visitors seriously. We continue to respond to all reports of safety concerns on campus," a college spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Fort Lewis College has not received any reports this academic year involving harassment of members of the college’s TPUSA chapter. Fort Lewis College has a system in place for students to report negative experiences." The ongoing tensions unfold amid a national surge in interest for TPUSA campus chapters following the Sept. 10, 2025, assassination of TPUSA co-founder Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University. In the aftermath, the national conservative organization reported receiving more than 120,000 inquiries from students seeking to establish local chapters. NEWLY LAUNCHED TPUSA CHAPTER CAUSES UPROAR AT MICHIGAN HIGH SCHOOL BEFORE FIRST MEETING At Fort Lewis College, then-senior Jonah Flynn initially led the effort to establish a chapter on campus. Although the Associated Students of Fort Lewis College (ASFLC) student government initially rejected Flynn’s proposal, the body ultimately reversed course and voted to approve the group during an emergency session. The approval vote prompted immediate pushback from anti-TPUSA demonstrators outside the meeting room. According to a Fort Lewis College campus police report, approximately 70 people attended the high-tension meeting, with verbal confrontations spilling out into the building lobby. Despite the friction, Cook remains optimistic about the chapter's upcoming initiatives. "We just finished up our vigil for Charlie Kirk, which was a beautiful memorial here at the college. We also have events planned for the Second Amendment — we are going shooting soon — and while a lot of things are still in planning, we're really excited for everything to come this semester."

title: Common kitchen staple may help relieve mild constipation, new research suggests
description: Researchers in Japan found that a daily vinegar drink with 750mg of acetic acid led to about 1.2 more bowel movements per week, according to a new study, even as experts urge caution.
content: People who suffer from mild constipation may find some relief with a simple daily vinegar drink, new research suggests, even as experts urge more study and share cautions. Constipation is a condition in which a person generally has fewer than three bowel movements a week, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Stools may also be hard, dry or lumpy and difficult or painful to pass. The NIH says adults should get 22 to 34 grams of fiber a day, depending on age and sex — though fewer than 10% of women and about 3% of men reach the recommended daily intake, according to federal dietary guidelines. THE 8 HEALTHIEST BEANS YOU SHOULD BE EATING MORE OFTEN, ACCORDING TO NUTRITION EXPERT Left untreated, chronic constipation can lead to hemorrhoids and anal fissures and, in severe cases, complications such as fecal impaction that may require emergency care. The NIH recommends changes to diet and lifestyle, such as increasing fiber intake with foods including legumes, whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds, as a first step in treating constipation — along with over-the-counter medicines if needed. Now, a new study has found that consuming vinegar in liquid form may also increase bowel movements. Published online in the journal Scientific Reports by Japanese researchers, the study reported that eating vinegar-based dishes more often was positively associated with better defecation status, though it remained unclear how much vinegar and its potentially active ingredient, acetic acid, were necessary to be effective. "Given that acetic acid may play a key role in the effects of vinegar and that its intake can be strictly controlled, we conducted a randomized controlled trial in which healthy adults with mild constipation (defecation frequency of 3–5 times per week) consumed a vinegar beverage instead of vinegar-based dishes to investigate the effects of vinegar on defecation," the researchers wrote. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The researchers randomly assigned a total of 44 participants — healthy Japanese adults between 20 and 69 years old — to consume either a beverage made with vinegar or a placebo drink at breakfast for four weeks. The participants reported to have an average of three to five bowel movements a week, which the researchers classified as mild constipation. The vinegar drink was made by mixing brewed vinegar with water, providing 750 milligrams of acetic acid in each 200-milliliter serving. The placebo used a small amount of citric acid instead of vinegar to give it a similar tart taste, so participants couldn't tell which drink they had. Both drinks were sweetened with sucralose and flavored with apple. "These findings … [support] a potential dietary approach for maintaining bowel health." During the first week, the vinegar group showed trends toward improvement in bowel-movement frequency, number of defecation days and stool volume compared with the placebo group. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ By week four, defecation frequency was "significantly higher" in the vinegar group than in the placebo group — about 1.2 more bowel movements a week — the study concluded. "These findings suggest that daily consumption of vinegar beverages may improve defecation status in healthy adults with mild constipation, supporting a potential dietary approach for maintaining bowel health," the researchers wrote. Both groups experienced gradual improvement over the course of the study — and the researchers suggested that some participants may have been habitually underhydrated, so the added daily drink may have played a part in relieving their constipation. "They did not study typical apple cider vinegar supplements or concentrated vinegar shots." They noted, however, that during the first week, participants in the vinegar group showed signs of greater improvement than those in the placebo group, implying that vinegar or acetic acid may have had an additional early benefit. Limitations of the study The study is intriguing and "a promising clue rather than proof that vinegar treats constipation," Florida-based registered dietitian Jamie Lee McIntyre, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "I wouldn’t leap from this study to recommending apple cider vinegar shots for constipation," she said. "The researchers used a standardized vinegar beverage containing a specific amount of acetic acid. They did not study typical apple cider vinegar supplements or concentrated vinegar shots." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Mizkan Holdings Co. Ltd., a Japanese food company that manufactures vinegar, funded the study; three of the researchers were employed by Mizkan. The scientists further noted that their findings "should be regarded as preliminary and require more confirmation in further studies." "For now, I'd stick with the constipation strategies we know have a stronger evidence base: adequate fiber and fluids, regular physical activity and a consistent bathroom routine," McIntyre said. "Vinegar can certainly be part of a meal, or serve as a wonderful base to a dressing or sauce, but I wouldn't consider it a constipation treatment based on this one small study." Dr. Eric Shah, a gastroenterologist and clinical associate professor at the University of Michigan, told Fox News Digital that there "is this misnomer that drinking more water helps constipation, when it just makes most people have to urinate more." "I wouldn't consider it a constipation treatment based on this one small study." The key to avoiding constipation is to stay adequately hydrated, take soluble fiber and consider pelvic floor physical therapy when needed, which is a growing field that is readily accessible from primary care, he said. "What generally comes out of those water trials is that mineral-rich water, particularly magnesium-rich, tends to help more with constipation in clinical trials. The mineral content is probably more important than the volume of intake for most people." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP McIntyre added that "more vinegar isn't necessarily better." "Because vinegar is highly acidic, drinking it regularly — particularly undiluted — can irritate the esophagus and contribute to dental enamel erosion," she said.

title: FIBA secretary general addresses why organization hasn't added 'men's' label to flagship World Cup event
description: FIBA's Andreas Zagklis linked the World Cup naming debate to ongoing transgender eligibility questions about who can compete in men's and women's events.
content: FIBA Secretary General Andreas Zagklis addressed the organization’s decision not to formally label its flagship global tournament the "Men’s Basketball World Cup," connecting the naming debate to broader questions about eligibility in men’s and women’s competitions. "The naming is of course a matter that the Central Board has discussed," Zagklis told reporters Sunday during a press conference ahead of the 2026 FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup. "The Central Board has for the moment maintained the current naming. We do not see that the aspect of men’s and women’s is something that devalues or values the other World Cup in such a way." FIBA officially calls its women’s tournament the "FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup." Its other senior five-on-five tournament remains the "FIBA Basketball World Cup," without "men’s" in the title. Zagklis added that the organization is also considering "broader concerns" over the separation of the men's and women's categories, and referenced studies over "who can compete" in each respective competition. FIBA SECRETARY GENERAL ANDREAS ZAGKLIS SPEAKS OUT ON CAITLIN CLARK'S IMPACT ON GROWTH OF WORLD CUP "We also need to be cognizant of the broader concerns about men and women, and the concerns as well as the studies we are making for our competition and who can compete in the women’s World Cup and who can compete in the other World Cup, which is not necessarily just the men’s World Cup," he said. Zagklis did not explicitly mention transgender athletes in his answer. However, FIBA has publicly confirmed that it is reviewing transgender eligibility and has established an interim approach while that process continues. Following the International Olympic Committee’s adoption of a policy protecting the female category, the FIBA Central Board confirmed in April that FIBA will follow the IOC standard for the Olympic and Youth Olympic Games. The federation said it is waiting for further guidance on the practical, legal and operational aspects of implementation. FIBA-run competitions, including its World Cups, remain subject to a separate review. In December 2024, the Central Board extended its process for adopting a formal transgender eligibility policy by two years. FIBA said it is collecting basketball-specific data and evidence related to transgender participation. A Gender Eligibility Committee composed of medical and legal experts is scheduled to give the Central Board its recommendations at the beginning of 2027. Until then, FIBA said it will not entertain transgender eligibility requests. The organization therefore has not announced a permanent policy for its own competitions, but transgender applicants cannot receive eligibility approval while the review remains underway. Zagklis' answers come amid ongoing controversy in the WNBA, which operates under a different set of rules. The WNBA’s collective bargaining agreement says only women may play in the league. However, it does not publicly define that term or provide specific eligibility standards for transgender or intersex players. Debate intensified after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham supported excluding transgender women and girls from female sports. Her comments prompted demonstrations supporting and opposing transgender participation outside WNBA games. WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT SENDS TRANS INCLUSION MEMO AFTER ENES FREEDOM, ROYCE WHITE ANNOUNCEMENTS THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White later declared themselves eligible for a future WNBA draft after publicly identifying themselves as women. Their announcements were widely viewed as attempts to challenge the wording of the league’s eligibility rule. A WNBA task force discussed the subject in August but did not adopt a new standard. The league said no immediate eligibility matter affected the WNBA and condemned "bad-faith" efforts to demean or marginalize others. Supporters of sex-based eligibility rules argue that clear boundaries protect fairness and opportunities in women’s sports. Supporters of transgender inclusion argue that blanket restrictions can discriminate against a small and frequently targeted population. Unlike the WNBA, FIBA has announced a formal review, created an expert committee and established a timeline for recommendations. But it has not disclosed the evidence collected so far or indicated what policy it may ultimately adopt. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Zagklis’ remarks did not announce a new rule. They showed that FIBA’s decision to leave "men’s" out of its World Cup name exists alongside a continuing discussion about how the organization will define eligibility for both competitions. When asked about the nature and purpose of the studies Zagklis was referring to and whether FIBA would anticipate biological males competing in the next FIBA Women's World Cup, FIBA pointed OutKick to the Central Board meeting back in April before the tournament began.

title: Champion athlete soils herself mid-race and keeps going, prompting fitness competition to change rules
description: HYROX Beijing 2026 winner Joanna Wietrzyk faced online backlash after an incontinence incident during the race, prompting new competition rule changes.
content: A popular global fitness competition is changing its rules after an explosive incident at a Sept. 12 competition. Australian professional athlete Joanna Wietrzyk won the race at HYROX Beijing — but the victory did not come without struggle. During the race, Wietrzyk experienced fecal incontinence but continued competing. Despite the incident, judges and officials did not instruct her to stop, prompting concerns about potential health and safety risks for other competitors. 'A WIN IS A WIN' SAYS ATHLETE WHO DIDN'T LET A LITTLE DIARRHEA KEEP HER FROM FINISHING IN FIRST PLACE The incident has sparked online debate — some people have supported Wietrzyk for her perseverance, while others suggested that her accident posed a potential biohazard. The athlete first addressed the incident in a since-deleted Instagram post, reportedly writing in the caption, "Go hard or go home … a win is a win. In all seriousness, thank you for all the support. I’ll be back soon x." The athlete has since faced criticism from those who argue that her decision posed a health risk to other competitors. In response, Wietrzyk released an official statement on Thursday, expressing her regret and announcing her retroactive withdrawal from the race. "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," she wrote in the statement posted on Instagram. COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY"I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track … I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused."Wietrzyk continued, "I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned." Wietrzyk’s coach, Chris Bayens, previously posted a statement on social media in her defense. "What happened was an extraordinary set of circumstances that were unforeseen, rapidly evolving and almost impossible to fully comprehend in real time," he wrote on Instagram. "Decisions were made under competition conditions by an athlete, judges and officials, all responding to a situation none of them could reasonably have prepared for." Bayens continued that these decisions can be reviewed and lessons can be learned, but "judging someone’s intent, character or morality through the clarity of hindsight is neither fair nor honest." FITNESS EXPERT VISITS GYMS NATIONWIDE, SHOUTS OUT 4 CLUBS FOR 'GETTING IT RIGHT' "Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human," he said. "Discussion is legitimate. The hatred and personal attacks that have followed are not." Moritz Furste, co-founder of HYROX, also released a statement following the incident. "I apologize to all that were directly or indirectly affected, as well as to everyone who felt like we did not handle the situation like we should have," he wrote. "HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end, it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not." FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS SIMPLE RULE TO GET IN SHAPE WITHOUT DREADING THE GYM: 'JUST MOVE' The statement continued, "Of course, we started improving event processes, plus making rulebook changes immediately. As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again. We learn and try to get better every day." What is HYROX? According to HYROX, the race combines cardio with weight training, involving a total of eight kilometers (about five miles) of running and eight functional workout stations. The structure of the competitions layers a one-kilometer run with one functional workout station, including SkiErg (a machine that simulates cross-country skiing), sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps, rowing, farmer's carry, sandbag lunges and wall balls. Launched in Germany in 2017, HYROX has grown rapidly worldwide, with recent reports putting participation at more than 1.4 million competitors globally. The organization describes the race as the world's fastest-growing fitness sport. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER More than 98% of HYROX competitors complete the race, with no time limit to finish and no qualification required to enter. "The structure of HYROX eliminates the generic fear of ‘coming last,’" the brand wrote on its website. Physical risks In an interview with Fox News Digital, California-based certified fitness trainer Ryan Read shared why the HYROX format can be so physically demanding. "Your body doesn't get much time to fully recover between efforts," he said. "You may go from running directly to sled pushes, lunges or rowing. That forces your heart, lungs and muscles to work hard for a long period." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ As the race progresses, maintaining proper form can become more difficult, according to Read, as the combination of intensity, duration and repetitive exercises can put a "significant amount of stress on the body." "Muscles become fatigued, and the body uses up stored energy and fluids," he said. "During hard exercise, more blood is directed toward working muscles and away from the digestive system. That can make digestion more difficult." "Real toughness also means knowing when your body is telling you to stop." Running in particular creates a repetitive movement that can upset the stomach. Combining this with dehydration, heat and eating too close to competition can worsen symptoms, Read cautioned. "This is why some athletes experience nausea, cramping, diarrhea or even vomiting during endurance events." There is a "big difference" between working through normal discomfort and ignoring a medical warning sign, according to the trainer. Elite athletes are often conditioned to push through pain, a mindset that can intensify during competition. Adrenaline can also make it harder to recognize when the body is in distress, Read said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Symptoms like vomiting, fainting, severe chest pain or extreme weakness "should not be treated as proof that someone is working hard enough." "Pushing through certain symptoms can turn a manageable problem into a medical emergency," he emphasized. "Real toughness also means knowing when your body is telling you to stop." Read suggested that fitness organizations should have "clear rules" for when an athlete needs to be evaluated or removed from a competition, and medical staff should be easily accessible throughout the event. "Equipment that becomes contaminated with vomit, blood or other bodily fluids should be taken out of use immediately," he said. "Simply wiping it quickly and sending the next competitor through may not be enough." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Bodily fluids can contain germs that may spread through contaminated surfaces or direct contact, Read said. "The exact risk depends on the fluid, organism and type of exposure. Competitor safety should come before keeping the event moving on schedule."

title: President John Quincy Adams knew one book people needed to read to become good citizens
description: John Quincy Adams wrote letters urging his son to read the Bible daily, believing Scripture was essential to raising citizens worthy of the Constitution.
content: Too few American students know enough about our Constitution. Still, fewer know there is such a thing as "Constitution Day." But this year, it might be worth taking up an assignment our sixth president gave to his son in a remarkable series of letters written while President John Quincy Adams served as minister to Russia. Adams did not focus on career advice for his son. He did not teach his son how to make money. Instead, Adams insisted upon this: Read the Bible. Every day. BILL BENNETT: WHAT I TOLD MY SONS ABOUT THEIR FAITH, FAMILY AND AMERICA Adams believed no education could be complete without it. He wrote to his son that when "duly read and meditated on," the Bible is "of all books in the world, that which contributes most to make men good, wise, and happy." And here’s where our Constitution comes in: Adams believed children formed by Scripture would become "useful citizens to their country" and "respectable members of society." GORSUCH HIGHLIGHTS STAGGERING DECLINE IN CIVIC LITERACY THAT PROMPTED HIM TO AUTHOR NEW BOOK There’s much ado today about civics education. And that’s a good thing. More educators and parents should ask: Should students memorize the Constitution? Learn about the three branches of government? Study the Federalist Papers? All extremely important. But John Quincy Adams understood something too many have largely forgotten. AMERICA’S NEXT 250 YEARS DEPEND ON PASSING FAITH AND FREEDOM TO OUR CHILDREN The Constitution details how we, a free people, govern ourselves. But it cannot teach rising generations how to become worthy of that freedom. That is why Adams spent letter after letter introducing his son to the New Testament and to the Hebrew Bible — to Genesis, Exodus, the Ten Commandments, and to the Law of Moses. He argued the Mosaic Law represented the greatest moral revolution of the ancient world because it united justice with humanity. TEN COMMANDMENTS BELONG IN TEXAS SCHOOLS AND THE SUPREME COURT CAN PROTECT THEM Unlike the legal systems of Greece and Rome, which largely emphasized civic order or individual virtue, Adams believed the Hebrew Scriptures taught something unprecedented: Duties toward other people were also duties toward God. The laws protecting the stranger, the widow, the orphan and even enemies reflect a moral vision unlike anything the secular world had produced. Adams admired the Hebrew Bible because it did something no human legislature could accomplish. THE BEDROCK OF AMERICAN LIBERTY WAS LAID IN JERUSALEM It recognized individual merit and responsibility. It legislated for human nature. The Constitution details how we, a free people, govern ourselves. But it cannot teach rising generations how to become worthy of that freedom. Governments can punish theft. They cannot eliminate envy. Governments can outlaw murder. They cannot command honor, gratitude, humility or self-control. John Quincy Adams’s letters were never simply about raising his own successful children. They were about transmitting civilization itself to all America’s children. Too many fathers today have outsourced the most important conversations about duty, morality and character to schools, to government institutions, to coaches or even to celebrities. Mothers play an indispensable role in raising virtuous children, but there is no substitute for the unique influence of an engaged father who teaches his son what it means to be an honorable man. DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE The consequences of absence are all around us. Young Americans increasingly struggle to distinguish rights from responsibilities. They know how to demand respect but not always how to earn it. They have been taught self-esteem more often than self-government. They build professional résumés but little aptitude for disappointment, mental resilience or for duty. ALEX BERENSON: GENTLE PARENTING CAN'T REPLACE THE STRENGTH OF A GOOD DAD This isn't merely an educational, civic or cultural problem. It's a fatherhood problem. For centuries, American fathers understood that one of their highest callings was to introduce their children to the moral inheritance that made liberty possible. Not because government required it. Because freedom required it. The Hebrew Bible teaches children that human beings are capable of both good and evil. Actions have consequences. Morality matters. And it importantly teaches every person bears the image of God. The Founders knew constitutions cannot preserve themselves. Republics depend upon citizens capable of governing themselves before they presume to govern others. John Quincy Adams understood this better than most. His letters to his son were, in many ways, one manual for raising a free citizen. Perhaps that is the lesson we most need today: If we want stronger schools, we need stronger families. If we want better citizens, we need fathers who teach virtues. John Quincy Adams’s letters were never simply about raising his own successful children. They were about transmitting civilization itself to all America’s children. If we want to renew American civics, we should certainly continue teaching the Constitution. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But we should also recover the book John Quincy Adams believed came first: The Bible. title: Homeowners in the heart of America’s AI boom are getting an unexpected payoff
description: Loudoun County homeowners save $5,800 a year in property taxes thanks to data centers, which generate 45% of all local tax revenue on just 3% of land.
content: Billions in build-outs of facilities to support the artificial intelligence (AI) boom have become a lightning rod in communities across America, but homeowners in the nation’s data center capital are seeing a surprising payoff — thousands of dollars in property tax relief. The massive projects have emerged as an issue in the 2026 midterm elections, as voters raise concerns about electricity costs, water use, land development and the strain on local infrastructure. Opposition has crossed party lines, forcing candidates to confront an industry that state and local governments spent years courting. Yet just outside Washington, D.C., the richest U.S. enclave of Loudoun County, Virginia, offers a striking case study of the industry's economic upside. Home to the sprawling tech corridor known as "Data Center Alley," Loudoun has the highest concentration of data centers in the world. Decades of development have transformed the county's landscape and dramatically expanded its tax base, offering a real-world look at the financial benefits proponents say the industry can bring to local communities. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS "Loudoun County has more data centers than anywhere else in the country. It's been sort of the capital of data center development for decades," Jared Walczak, vice president of state projects at the Tax Foundation, told Fox News Digital. "And because of that, Loudoun County property taxes are about half of what they would be without data centers. In fact, data centers provide about 45% of all local tax revenue to Loudoun County, not just property taxes, but all local tax revenue." Walczak said the impact translates into significant savings for individual homeowners. "The average homeowner would pay $5,800 more a year in property taxes if you didn't have data center development," he said, noting that data centers occupy only about 3% of the county's land. But the rapid expansion of data centers has also fueled concerns that their enormous electricity demands could leave residents footing a higher utility bill, potentially offsetting some of those savings. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS Walczak pushed back on that worry, arguing the industry's impact on homeowners' property taxes is clearer. "The property tax relief is real, measurable and significant," he said. "The energy costs are largely a solved problem." Walczak told Fox News Digital that the increased demand could require utilities to build new generation and transmission infrastructure, while adding more customers and electricity usage can also spread the grid's fixed costs across a larger base. The critical question, he said, is who pays for the additional infrastructure. "You pay for the additional generation and transmission capacity. The data center pays for that," Walczak said. "And then you actually see a slight reduction in energy costs for everyone." He pointed again to Northern Virginia, arguing that its experience challenges fears that a heavy concentration of data centers inevitably translates into higher electricity prices for residents. "If you look at the places with the largest data center development, you actually see declines in energy prices relative to the rest of the country," Walczak said. "You look at Northern Virginia, it has lower energy prices." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As communities across the country weigh the costs and benefits of the data center boom, Walczak said Loudoun County's experience offers a glimpse at what can happen when billions of dollars in new infrastructure become part of the local tax base.

title: Ridiculous USA Today column proves that the demand for misogyny in sports far exceeds the supply
description: A USA Today columnist cited Sydney Sweeney's sports ad, an Arch Manning joke and an arena rendering as proof sports don't want women around.
content: The demand for misogyny in American sports far exceeds the available supply. That's a problem for USA Today columnist Nancy Armour. Armour has built much of her professional brand around finding sexism and misogyny everywhere she looks in sports. So, what happens when women reach a better position in the sports world than ever before? Armour has to look harder. Much harder. In a column published Tuesday, Armour argued that American sports are happy to take women's money, but don't want women in their space or to treat them with "even the slightest shred of decency." Strong claim. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD What evidence did Armour use to support the idea that American sports, as a whole, don't want women around? A sports prediction market ad featuring a nearly nude Sydney Sweeney, Arch Manning laughing at a stupid AI video, and an architectural rendering that included almost no women. That's it. That's her entire case. The arena rendering barely warrants a response. An architectural rendering of Philadelphia’s future arena showed almost no women, the image was replaced within two days, and the building will be home to the city’s WNBA team. If that is evidence that women aren’t welcome in sports, the definition of evidence has lost all meaning. There's another problem, though. Armour has no trouble finding misogyny in an advertisement, a joke or a computer-generated crowd. But when males take opportunities in women's sports, she attacks the women who object. That's not an oversight. It's the clearest evidence that this isn't really about protecting women. Armour turns Sydney Sweeney ad into sweeping declaration about women Armour starts with perhaps the most absurd characterization of the three. "A betting company tells women their only place in sports is as a sexualized object," Armour wrote. Wait, when did Novig say that? It didn't. Novig produced one advertisement featuring one woman, Sydney Sweeney, using sex appeal to promote a sports prediction market. Somehow, Armour took that to mean the company declared that every woman's "only place in sports" is as a sexualized object. That's quite a leap. The ad didn't say anything about female athletes, female fans, female broadcasters or women's sports. Plus, Novig isn't selling "sports." Sports are the subject matter. The product is gambling. And the ad is clearly designed primarily to appeal to men, who make up the core audience for sports betting. So what? Not every product or advertisement has to appeal equally to men and women. Women’s clothing companies and cosmetics companies run ads aimed at women. Entire television networks and publishing genres cater primarily to women. No one treats that as evidence that those companies hate men. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! But when a sports prediction market company creates an ad tailored to its overwhelmingly male audience, Armour treats the existence of a male audience as the offense. In Armour's world, products aimed at women are called empowerment, while products aimed at men are called misogyny. Then there's Sweeney's role in all of this. According to Novig CEO Jacob Fortinsky, Sweeney approached the company, owns equity in it and drove much of the campaign's "visuals and messaging." In other words, an adult woman made a business decision to use her own image to promote a company in which she has a financial interest. Armour responded by calling the ad misogynistic, effectively condemning Sweeney for exercising that agency in a way that appeals to men. Apparently, women are free to make their own choices, provided Nancy Armour approves of them. NIKE-LINKED COACHINGHER PROGRAM FACES SCRUTINY OVER GENDER BIAS TRAINING AND DEFINITION OF GIRLS Armour later claimed that Novig "backpedaled" on its "misogyny." That's not even true. Fortinsky publicly defended the campaign, credited Sweeney with driving the concept and said the company was pleased with the response. Incredibly, Armour linked the word "backpedaled" to a story whose headline said the Novig CEO "defends" the ad. Armour anticipated that someone might point out that female athletes have posed nude for magazines, including ESPN’s famous "Body Issue." She insisted those examples are different because the athletes’ bodies were "the product of years of work and training" and should be appreciated for their accomplishments rather than "ogled over for sexual gratification." Huh. So Armour has appointed herself the arbiter of which women have bodies worthy of being displayed and which women are merely objects. Female athletes who pose nude receive her approval because their nudity serves an Armour-approved purpose. Sweeney voluntarily used her own sex appeal to promote a company she partly owns, and Armour branded her decision misogynistic because it was meant to appeal to men. Careful, Nancy. Deciding which women’s bodies are worthy of being seen and which aren’t sounds awfully misogynistic. Arch Manning gave an honest answer, so the media taught him a lesson Armour’s second example comes from a press conference after Texas’ comeback victory over Ohio State. Manning was asked whether he had seen any fan-edited clips from the game. He said he had seen an AI edit of Sarkisian’s postgame interview, then volunteered the specific clip. "Of him slapping Holly Rowe?" Manning said, laughing. "It’s hilarious." The AI video grew out of an awkward exchange after the game. Rowe attempted to interview Sarkisian moments after Texas completed a 20-point comeback and delivered one of the biggest victories of his career. Sarkisian shouted "Texas fight," flashed the Hook ’em sign and left to celebrate with his team. Rowe responded by throwing up her hands, rolling her eyes and walking off in a huff. Texas later said technical problems with ESPN’s equipment contributed to the failed interview. Similar problems had disrupted an attempted interview at halftime, but in that instance, ESPN’s Laura Rutledge explained that Sarkisian had waited patiently and said the network owed him an apology. So, what exactly did Manning do wrong? He laughed at a fake video making fun of this ridiculous scene. No woman was assaulted and Manning clearly wasn’t laughing at actual violence. He reacted honestly to an obviously fake parody of an awkward postgame exchange. Sports media members constantly complain that athletes are boring, guarded and coached to speak in clichés. Then an athlete offers one unfiltered reaction, and those same media members treat it as evidence of a deep moral failing. This is exactly why athletes never say anything interesting. Manning quickly learned the lesson. He issued the kind of carefully written, corporate apology that public figures release when honesty becomes more trouble than it’s worth. He apologized publicly, spoke privately with Rowe and received her forgiveness. Rowe could have ended the entire controversy by saying no apology was necessary. Instead, she publicly accepted Manning’s apology and referenced their private conversation. That allowed her to occupy both of the most powerful positions in this particular media ecosystem: the victim who had been wronged and the gracious authority willing to offer forgiveness. Victimhood is power in this world, and the more of it you can claim, the better. REPORTER FOR THE ATHLETIC FUMES OVER ARCH MANNING, SILENT ON JOSH JACOBS' ALLEGED VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMAN Plus, accountability only flows in one direction when someone is permanently cast as the victim. Everyone else must apologize to Rowe. Rowe never has to apologize for her own behavior, which included an incredibly petty on-camera reaction. But even after Rowe accepted Manning’s apology, that wasn’t enough for Armour. She wrote that Manning’s apology "doesn’t matter" because "the damage was done." Then what, exactly, would matter? Manning apologized publicly and privately. Armour still refused to let the incident end because resolution is useless to someone who needs permanent victims. The misogyny boat must stay afloat. Nancy Armour finds a professor who agrees with Nancy Armour To connect these three completely unrelated episodes, Armour turned to Purdue professor Cheryl Cooky. "It's about a reinscribing of those spaces and a reassertion of those sports as male-dominated and masculine-oriented institutions," Cooky told Armour. She added that when women gain power, society responds with a backlash. Well, there you have it. Two people subscribe to Armour's theory. Unfortunately, neither provided any evidence that these three incidents were part of a backlash against women gaining power. Did Manning laugh at a dumb AI video because he felt threatened by women gaining power? Did Sweeney create a sexually provocative gambling ad to punish female athletes for becoming more popular? Did whoever populated an architectural rendering with men do so as an act of resistance against the WNBA? Armour doesn't even attempt to prove any of that. The study Armour cited, co-authored by Cooky, examined the amount and quality of coverage women's sports received on selected television news and highlight programs during three sampling periods in 2024. Whatever someone thinks of that research, it doesn't establish the motives of Sweeney, Manning or the person who populated an architectural rendering. Cooky's contribution amounts to translating Armour's argument into academic jargon. "Male-dominated and masculine-oriented institutions" sounds more authoritative than "men don't want us here," but it doesn't make the claim true. Armour didn't find proof; she found a professor willing to repeat her conclusion so the same opinion could be presented as expertise. Nancy Armour sees misogyny everywhere, except when males enter women's sports The most revealing aspect of Armour's misogyny hustle isn't where she claims to find misogyny. It's the one place where she refuses to see it. In 2023, then-ESPN host Sam Ponder argued that women deserve fair, sex-based athletic competition. Armour responded with an 800-word attack and accused Ponder of using "fairness" to cloak her "bigotry toward transgender girls and women." "What ESPN's Sam Ponder calls 'fairness' is plain old bigotry," Armour's headline read. Got that? According to Armour, an architectural rendering, an advertisement starring Sydney Sweeney and an off-the-cuff remark by Arch Manning are major threats to women in sports. But a male athlete taking a roster spot, playing time, trophies or championships from girls and women isn't a threat. Worse than that, Armour attacks the women who object to those males. Careful, Nancy. You're starting to sound awfully misogynistic again. Look at the women Armour chooses to attack: Sydney Sweeney, Sam Ponder and Riley Gaines. They are strong, successful women exercising their own agency, and Armour turns on them the moment they make choices she doesn’t like. That's Nancy Armour's brand in a nutshell: men are responsible for everything wrong with women's sports, except the men who "identify" as women. Those men must be defended, even if doing so requires tearing down women like Ponder and Gaines. Armour can hold both positions because she isn’t applying a consistent principle about protecting women. She’s applying whatever progressive ideology demands at that particular moment. LEFT-WING SPORTS HOST SARAH SPAIN LAUNCHES DISGUSTING PERSONAL SMEAR OF SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM Sweeney voluntarily uses her own sex appeal to promote a company she partly owns? Complicit in misogyny. Ponder voluntarily defends women’s athletic opportunities? Bigot. Perfect. Women's sports are thriving, which creates a problem for the misogyny industry The strangest part of Armour's column is that she spends several paragraphs undermining her own argument. She acknowledges that women's sports have "never been more popular" and female athletes have "never had more visibility." She notes that WNBA TV ratings, franchise values and salaries are soaring. She points to signature Nike lines for Caitlin Clark and A'ja Wilson, women coaching in the NFL and NBA, merchandise designed specifically for female fans, women's sports bars and teams building their own stadiums. That sounds like incredible progress. Because it is. Women have more opportunities, influence, visibility and economic power in sports than at any point in American history. The evidence no longer supports declaring that American sports refuse to treat women with "the slightest shred of decency." So, Armour takes three minor and unrelated examples, assigns all of them the same sweeping motive and tells readers that the "male sports monopoly" is lashing out against powerful women. Essentially, the demand for misogyny now far exceeds the supply. And that's a major problem for people whose relevance depends on convincing women that they're still surrounded by it. Armour ended her column by declaring that there is room in sports for men and women. Duh. But Armour doesn't appear interested in making room. She needs a permanent crisis with permanent victims and permanent villains. title: Pope Leo XIV receives 'symbolic’ sphere in charity's push for AI to 'protect human dignity'
description: Photos show Pope Leo XIV receiving the "Sphere of Humanity" glass sculpture as 70 leaders prepare to draft the Codex Humanitatis on AI ethics.
content: A charity presented Pope Leo XIV with a unique piece of artwork in its push to "protect human dignity" and establish "what should stay human in the age of AI," an official told Fox News Digital. Photos released by Saint Peter for Humanity captured the pope receiving the "Sphere of Humanity" — a green, Murano glass sculpture that "incorporates handwritten passages from his first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, reflecting on human dignity, vulnerability, solidarity, conscience and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence" — during his General Audience in early September. The presentation came as Saint Peter for Humanity said it is gearing up next week to gather 70 leaders in New York City to "begin drafting the Codex Humanitatis, an independent initiative inspired by Pope Leo XIV’s call to safeguard human dignity as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly powerful and influential in people’s lives." "We recognize the benefits of AI. We just believe again that there is another force that should belong to that conversation; that other force is humanity," Olivier Francois, the organization’s president and chairman, told Fox News Digital. "So the Codex Humanitatis, which is our initiative, starts from that simple idea. AI should serve people, protect human dignity, expand human potential and advance common good." POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL "So what are we going to do in New York? We are going to gather 70 Nobel laureates, artists, thinkers, philanthropists, technology and AI experts, obviously that's important, and we will ask them maybe the hardest question of our times, you know, as artificial intelligence grows even more powerful, what must remain human?" Francois added. "So obviously, before we head over to machines, we should be clear about what we value most in ourselves. So we will try to define what being human means and what should stay human in the age of AI. So this is a little bit of the initiative we shared with Pope Leo while presenting the sphere and this symbolic gift." The sphere, based on an original design by Italian architect and designer Gae Aulenti, contains four handwritten passages from Pope Leo XIV’s Magnifica Humanitas, including, "In the era of artificial intelligence, when human dignity is threatened by new forms of dehumanization, ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human." The pope wrote in the encyclical released in May, "Each generation inherits the task of shaping its own era, of guiding history to become a place where the dignity of every person is safeguarded, justice is promoted and fraternity is made possible," yet "every era also runs the risk of creating an inhumane and more unjust world. OPINION: POPE LEO XIV’S AI WARNING SPEAKS DIRECTLY TO HOLLYWOOD’S MORAL CRISIS "For AI to respect human dignity and truly serve the common good, responsibility must be clearly defined at every stage: from those who design and develop these systems to those who use them and rely on them for concrete decisions," the pope wrote. "In many cases, however, the internal processes leading to a result remain opaque, making it harder to assign responsibility and correct errors. This is where accountability becomes crucial: the possibility of identifying who must ‘account’ for decisions, justify them, monitor them, and, when necessary, challenge them and remedy any harm caused. "Calling for prudence, rigorous evaluation and even, at times, a slower pace in adopting AI does not mean opposing progress; instead, it is an exercise of responsible care for the human family. This need is all the more urgent given the frequent imbalance between the speed of technological growth and the slower development of awareness, norms, safeguards and institutions capable of governing its effects," the pope also said. "It is not enough to invoke ethics in the abstract; robust legal frameworks, independent oversight, informed users and a political system that does not abdicate its responsibility are required. Otherwise, change will be governed only by technocratic thinking and presented as necessary and inevitable, ultimately imposing rules shaped by those who control data, infrastructure and computing power." Saint Peter for Humanity said in a statement about its New York gathering, "Working across ten groups, participants will develop a first draft of the Codex focused on issues including the future of work, accountability, information integrity, human oversight and the protection of children and families." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The draft will then enter a global consultation process before being refined into a final set of principles. Saint Peter for Humanity plans to engage governments, companies and institutions in translating those principles into practice, including through engagement at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos," the nonprofit added.

title: Harris joins forces with radical Senate nominee in key swing state as 2028 whispers swirl
description: Kamala Harris joins Abdul El-Sayed at a Michigan fundraiser on Black maternal health, raising questions about a potential 2028 presidential run.
content: Former Vice President Kamala Harris is set to join Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at an upcoming roundtable in Michigan, according to his campaign. The two will appear at a Black maternal health roundtable next Tuesday, raising questions about whether Harris might be trying to court the progressive wing of the party in preparation for a 2028 presidential run. "I’m just really looking forward to having her here, and she is somebody who so many folks in communities like Detroit look up to as an inspirational leader," El-Sayed told Politico in an interview on Wednesday. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN "I’m grateful that she’s coming in and having conversations about what it takes to get the turnout up, so that we can get on to working on some of these issues in the U.S. Senate," he continued. The scheduled roundtable comes after Harris endorsed El-Sayed last month, praising his stance on issues like affordability. "Dr. Abdul El-Sayed understands the power is with the people, and that the stakes couldn’t be higher in this election. While Michiganders struggle to afford everyday essentials — housing, gas, groceries, health care and child care — Trump and Republicans in Congress are giving away $1 trillion in tax breaks to the wealthy and powerful," Harris wrote. "Abdul knows that we need bold solutions to the crises facing America’s working families and he is ready to take on this fight," Harris continued. "I proudly stand with him to ensure we win a Democratic Senate majority in Nov." The news of Harris' upcoming visit to Michigan comes as The Detroit News, a prominent Michigan newspaper, endorsed El-Sayed's Republican rival, Mike Rogers, for Senate on Wednesday. "Mike Rogers is the prototype of a United States Senator," the paper said in its endorsement, referencing his 14 years in the House, Army career, and private sector experience dealing with cybersecurity. On the other hand, the paper skewered El-Sayed for his radical rhetoric, saying he "has worked so hard covering his tracks leading up to this Senate race that it's impossible to know who he really is or where he would stand in the Senate." "He has deleted social media posts that reportedly called into question his attitude about America in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. He's taken down roughly 100 YouTube videos that paint an unflattering picture of him and his cultural views," the paper concluded. "A candidate who feels the need to hide his past from voters is not someone who can be trusted to be the same person after Election Day as he was on the campaign trail." In addition to Harris' visit, El-Sayed is expected to have a busy final stretch of his campaign before the November election as he attends multiple fundraisers in California and New York. In late September, El-Sayed is scheduled to attend a Hollywood fundraiser at the home of George Soros' nephew, Jeffrey Soros, who is a movie producer. In addition to Soros and his wife, the host committee includes several Obama alums, including Crooked Media's "Pod Save America" hosts Tommy Vietor and Jon Favreau. Ben Rhodes, the failed architect of Obama's Iran deal, is also on the host committee. El-Sayed will also be visiting San Francisco during this West Coast swing. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK Next month, El-Sayed will also be going to New York City to attend a fundraiser hosted by several far-left activists, where the price to attend ranges from $250 to $57,800. Harris’ endorsement of El-Sayed marks just her second major progressive candidate endorsement in the 2026 midterms. She is also supporting Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine who is backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Before the midterms, Harris also supported New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was also DSA-endorsed, but only stated that she "supported the Democrat in the race." For his own part, El-Sayed has rejected terms like "progressive" and "moderate" and is not backed by the DSA. But like Mamdani, El-Sayed has made affordability — and the role of government — key pieces of his campaign. In addition to calling for lowering housing costs, he’s advocated for Medicare for All, opposes corporate tax carve-outs, and he supports tuition-free access to higher education. Notably, after now-former President Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 election, El-Sayed called on the party to rally behind Harris, citing her "potential" for leadership. "Considering all the dangers of the Republican nominee … it’s time for all of us to unite behind Kamala Harris to defeat Trump," El-Sayed wrote in a post in July 2024. title: Trump wants largest-ever Israeli heavy bomb transfer — but proposal has Congress preparing for $2.8B fight
description: The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 2,000-pound bombs for Israel, drawing fierce opposition from Bernie Sanders and Chris Van Hollen in Congress.
content: The Trump administration is preparing a $2.8 billion military aid package for Israel that would include 40,000 heavy bombs, according to multiple reports. It would be the largest proposed transfer of the powerful munitions to Israel in recent years, if it clears Congress. The proposed package includes 20,000 unguided bombs designed to destroy buildings and bunkers, known as MK-84 bombs, and 20,000 BLU-117 bombs, which are warhead versions fitted with precision-guidance kits — both bombs are 2,000 pounds per unit. Additionally, according to Reuters and The Washington Post, the proposal includes 20,000 much-tougher I-2000 penetrator warheads, which are designed to penetrate concrete or underground facilities before exploding. The package, which is not yet final, has been informally communicated to congressional committees that review major U.S. arms sales — and it's already drawing opposition from Democratic lawmakers. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is calling on Congress to reject the White House's proposal, and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., vowed that lawmakers will "work to stop it." HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL "The American people are sick and tired of funding Israel's genocide in Gaza," Sanders wrote on social media, accusing the Trump administration of "doubling down" by providing $2.8 billion in bombs to the Israeli government. "Not acceptable. Congress must reject these agreements." Van Hollen similarly criticized the proposed package and its use of U.S. taxpayer funds, writing, "How is this America First? We will work to stop it." The State Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Israel's Ministry of Defense declined to weigh in. "All foreign arms sales are moving through the appropriate process. We do not comment on pending sales," a senior administration official told Fox News Digital. Most of the package would be financed through Foreign Military Financing, which uses congressionally appropriated U.S. funds for eligible allies to purchase American-made defense equipment. If completed, the package would be the largest single sale of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in recent years. It would exceed a 2025 sale that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The Trump administration approved that nearly $3 billion sale after bypassing the normal congressional review process. It's unclear whether that bypass could or will be used again this time around. The weapons were at the center of a previous U.S. policy dispute, as well. During President Joe Biden's term, his administration paused a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in 2024 over concerns of the potential for mass casualties in densely populated Gaza. President Donald Trump lifted that hold after returning to office. TRUMP CONFIRMS ‘CRAZY’ NETANYAHU CLASH AS QUESTIONS MOUNT OVER PUSH TO HOLD FIRE ON HEZBOLLAH TERRORISTS The 2,000-pound bombs have multiple variants designed for different targets, including hardened and underground structures. Israel has used U.S.-made heavy munitions during its military operations in Gaza and Lebanon, while the United States has used similar weapons against hardened targets in previous conflicts. The proposed transfer comes as Israel remains engaged on multiple fronts. Israeli forces have continued strikes against Hamas in Gaza despite a fragile ceasefire, while tensions with Hezbollah persist following fighting in Lebanon. The United States and Israel also conducted military operations against Iran earlier this year. The package remains at an early stage of the U.S. arms sales process. Informal congressional notification allows relevant committees to review a proposed transfer before the administration proceeds to formal notification. title: Memphis mom says Trump brought peace to streets as Democratic DA battles task force oversight
description: A petition nearing 10,000 signatures demands DA Steve Mulroy drop his fight against Donald Trump's Memphis Safe Task Force accountability measures.
content: A Memphis mother says President Donald Trump’s federal crime crackdown silenced the gunfire that years of pleas to local leaders could not and finally allowed her children to play outside. "For once, I’m walking to my mailbox and it’s quiet," Dalisia Ballinger told Fox News Digital. "I’m hearing the birds chirp. I’m hearing the birds sing. I’m seeing children play in the middle of the street. I’m seeing fathers playing football." The striking turnaround turned Ballinger, a former journalist and violent-crime victim, into one of the most outspoken supporters of the Memphis Safe Task Force as the operation marks one year on the ground. It also put her at the center of a growing clash with Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy, a Democrat whose lawsuit against two new state oversight laws has sparked a petition demanding that he abandon the legal fight and disclose how his office handles cases generated by the task force. FORMER CHICAGO DETECTIVE SAYS ONE CITY'S MURDER PLUNGE OFFERS WINDY CITY CRIME BLUEPRINT "Public safety should not be up for debate," Ballinger said. "I don’t care if you are a Republican. I don’t care if you are a Democrat." Trump established the multi-agency operation through a presidential memorandum on Sept. 15, 2025, ordering federal, state and local authorities to coordinate against street and violent crime in Memphis. The task force is led by the U.S. Marshals Service and includes mobilized members of the Tennessee National Guard. The White House said Tuesday that the operation had produced 12,747 arrests as of Sept. 15, including 131 homicide arrests, 1,276 firearms arrests and 1,408 arrests of known gang members. The administration also credited the task force with taking 2,160 illegal guns off the streets and recovering 189 missing children. FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN Overall crime in Memphis fell nearly 36% compared with the previous year, while murders dropped 36%, robberies fell 42% and vehicle thefts plunged 57%, according to figures released by the White House. City data had already shown crime falling before the task force arrived, and the statistics do not establish how much of the decline resulted directly from the federal surge. "That era is over. President Trump rejected the excuses, restored law and order, and once again proved that decline is a choice," the White House said. FBI REPORTS LARGEST DROP IN VIOLENT CRIME AND MURDER SINCE 1937 AS HOMICIDES FALL MORE THAN 18% Ballinger said the change became personal when her children could play outdoors without the constant fear that had gripped her neighborhood. She recalled a shooting four houses away in which she said roughly 30 gunshots struck a home occupied by a grandmother and her grandchildren. The family never returned, she said, leaving the property overtaken by grass and weeds. TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN 'WORKING' AS CITY SEES HOMICIDES PLUMMET 43% SINCE 2025: SLAIN INTERN'S MOM "We’ve been begging for years for our local leaders for assistance and for help," Ballinger said. "My children deserve peace, and with the Memphis Safe Task Force being here, we’ve finally been able to get that peace." Now, she and other supporters argue the operation’s arrests mean little if prosecutors later reduce or dismiss cases without explaining why. PROSECUTOR OUSTED AFTER ALLEGED ROMANCE WITH ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SEX-CRIME SUSPECT: 'PATTERN OF MISCONDUCT' A Change.org petition titled "Stop Memphis DA From Protecting Criminals" had gathered nearly 10,000 verified signatures Wednesday. The petition calls on Mulroy to drop a May lawsuit challenging the Memphis Safe Task Force Accountability Act and a separate law that authorizes the Tennessee attorney general to audit his office’s decisions in task force cases. The accountability law requires Mulroy’s office to submit a report every 10 business days when it settles or dismisses a charge arising from the task force. The second law allows the state attorney general to review prosecutorial decisions in those cases and ask the Tennessee Supreme Court to appoint a temporary prosecutor. PRIMARY SHOWDOWN: CONSERVATIVE FIREBRAND MARSHA BLACKBURN EYES GOVERNOR'S OFFICE IN TENNESSEE Mulroy argues that both laws unconstitutionally single out Shelby County, intrude on the discretion of a locally elected prosecutor and burden his staff with duplicative reporting. His office said it already reports case outcomes under existing Tennessee law. "These bills target Shelby County unfairly and infringe on the rights of Shelby County voters," Mulroy said when the lawsuit was filed. He has characterized the dispute as a battle over whether Shelby County voters or state officials in Nashville control the district attorney’s office. Petition supporters see the lawsuit differently. "Thanks to President Trump, the Memphis Safe Task Force has delivered more for this city in one year than anyone thought possible," Ballinger, one of the petition's leading voices, said in a statement. "While federal, state, and local agents risk their lives taking criminals off our streets, DA Mulroy is fighting in court to hide how his office is undermining this task force." U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., and Tennessee state Sen. Brent Taylor previously pressed Mulroy for details after his office reported that 430 of 514 felony cases resolved in December 2025 ended without prison time and that 166 of the cases were categorized as violent. The lawmakers said the figures left unanswered how many defendants in violent cases received no prison sentence. Mulroy has accused his Republican critics of distorting crime data for political purposes. Ballinger rejected the claim that the petition is merely a partisan campaign against a Democratic prosecutor. "We have children. We have regular people that might not even be into politics," she said. "We deserve peace. Whether it’s on the East Coast, the West Coast or South, we all deserve peace." MISSISSIPPI DISTRICT ATTORNEY JODY OWENS RESIGNS AFTER PLEADING GUILTY IN FEDERAL BRIBERY CASE: REPORT The task force has also drawn fierce opposition. The ACLU of Tennessee and several Memphis residents have accused agents of aggressive policing and retaliation against people who record law enforcement. Four residents filed a federal lawsuit this year alleging harassment, unlawful arrests and physical mistreatment while exercising their First Amendment rights. The allegations have not been proven in court, while task force supporters point to thousands of arrests and sharply falling crime numbers as evidence the operation is working. Ballinger said legitimate complaints should be reviewed, but she does not believe they justify dismantling an operation she credits with making her neighborhood livable again. "I’m all for fairness, and I’m all for law and order," she said. "If we need to go back to the table [and] restructure so that people can feel safe, we can definitely put that on the board."
