title: Colbert wins Emmy after show's cancellation but avoids discussing Trump
description: Stephen Colbert dodged questions about Trump's role in canceling "The Late Show" after winning an Emmy, while the White House fired back sharply.
content: The White House on Tuesday denied President Donald Trump had any role in CBS' decision to cancel "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert," after the former late-night host dodged a question about Trump following his Emmy win in Los Angeles and defended the state of free speech. Colbert's former program won Outstanding Variety Series at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards Monday, months after "The Late Show" aired its final episode in May. When asked after the ceremony about free speech and the future of late-night television, Colbert said he remained optimistic about the medium. "If you can’t say something because you go to jail, that is a violation of free speech," Colbert said. "I think that late night is just as funny and just as vital as it ever has been, and I love watching Jimmy and Jimmy and John and John and Seth and everybody else. And I think I hope it goes on for a long time because you get to work with people like this, and that’s the greatest gift." STEPHEN COLBERT EMERGES FROM CANCELLATION TO URGE EMMY VOTERS TO SELECT JIMMY KIMMEL OVER OWN SHOW White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital the administration had nothing to do with the network’s decision. "Neither President Trump nor anyone else in the Administration had anything to do with this," Ingle said, in a Tuesday statement to Fox News Digital. "The reality is Stephen Colbert is a pathetic trainwreck with no talent, which is exactly why CBS canceled his show and is booting him off the airwaves." When CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister asked Colbert directly whether he believed his show had been canceled because of Trump, the comedian appeared to repeatedly deflect rather than answer the question. Variety reported that the exchange came during a post-Emmys interview with Wagmeister and Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh. COLBERT LASHES OUT AT CBS, SAYS CANCELLATION ‘REINFORCED A NARRATIVE’ OF ‘KNEE BENDING’ TO TRUMP "What... Gayle, that’s a beautiful dress," Colbert said. After the reporter repeated the question, Colbert continued the bit. "Oh, I’m sorry, I’m deaf on this ear. What did you... what did you say?" Colbert said. When they again attempted to ask whether Trump was responsible for the cancellation, Colbert deflected once more. "You wanted to know who the most important member of my staff was? It’s me," Colbert said. Media Research Center President David Bozell told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that Colbert’s refusal to address the Trump question stood in contrast to the speculation surrounding the cancellation and pointed to CBS’ financial rationale for ending the show. "Colbert suddenly does not want to talk about Trump? That’s rich. Obviously, Trump did not cancel his show," he said. "CBS looked at the audience, looked at the bill, and decided the joke had run long enough." JIMMY KIMMEL SAYS HE FELT 'DEFEATED' AFTER COLBERT SHOW WAS CANCELLED, SAYS CBS IS USING 'MADE-UP NUMBERS' CBS announced in July 2025 that it would end "The Late Show" franchise after Colbert's 25-26 season, calling the move "purely a financial decision against a challenging backdrop in late night." The network said the decision was unrelated to the show's performance, content or other matters involving then-parent company Paramount. The announcement came three days after Colbert attacked Paramount over its $16 million settlement with Trump involving a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Colbert characterized the agreement as a payoff connected to Paramount’s pending merger with Skydance Media. "I believe this kind of complicated financial sentiment with a sitting government official has a technical name in legal circles. It’s ‘big fat bribe,’ because it all comes as Paramount’s owners are trying to get the Trump administration to approve the sale of our network to a new owner, Skydance!" Colbert said at the time. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Fox News Digital reported that Colbert's manager, James Dixon, had been informed June 27 that CBS intended to end the show, before Paramount announced the Trump settlement and more than two weeks before Colbert publicly attacked the agreement. "The Late Show" had been losing roughly $40 million annually. The FCC approved Paramount's $8 billion merger with Skydance one week after CBS announced the cancellation. The transaction later closed in August 2025. Trump continued criticizing Colbert after the program’s May finale, calling the former CBS host talentless and celebrating his departure from late-night television. title: Florida State fans pining for Jimbo Fisher's return are living in the past, not in reality
description: Congratulations Seminoles fans on ousting AD Michael Alford, but Jimbo Fisher's age and Texas A&M struggles make his FSU return a tough sell.
content: Congratulations, Seminoles fans, part one of your master plan to return to the pantheon of college football has been completed. For those unaware, Florida State fired their embattled athletic director, Michael Alford, earlier this week. The reason that's so significant is multifaceted, but his main transgression and the thing that ultimately lost him his job was the recent skid of the once-proud FSU football team. And that all ties back to a decision Alford made back in 2024, when he gifted head coach Mike Norvell a massive contract extension with an almost absurd buyout. The monetary numbers were questionable, even at a time when Norvell and the Noles were trending in the right direction, but since then, the program has taken a sharp downturn, punctuated by an 8-18 record since their ACC Championship winning season in 2023. DID ALABAMA DOOM THEMSELVES TO MEDIOCRITY WITH KALEN DEBOER EXTENSION? So, now that Alford is sunk, the man he chose to anchor himself to has to be on the way out as well, right? In theory, yes, but there's still that pesky buyout number that keeps getting brought up. And then there's the other question that gets raised whenever schools even think about firing their current head coach: who can we hire? There are a ton of quality names out there that the Seminoles should absolutely consider as their next head coach, but one of the only names I keep seeing tossed around by fans on social media is former Florida State head coach Jimbo Fisher. KEEP AN EYE ON THESE UNDER-THE-RADAR NAMES DURING THIS SEASON'S COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHING CAROUSEL I get it. Things are brutal right now in Tallahassee, and Noles fans are just trying to cling onto something from the good old days, but I'm not so sure if Fisher is the answer. Let's start with his age. Fisher turns 61 in October, and while plenty of great coaches have had phenomenal seasons well into their 60s and 70s, the former FSU and Texas A&M head man hasn't donned a headset in three years, which might as well be dog years given how different the game of college football looks now. Speaking of Texas A&M, Fisher's last stop as a head coach with the Aggies left a lot to be desired. While in College Station, Fisher compiled a 45-25 record, which is fine, but definitely not what he was hired to do. His five and a half years as the Aggies' head coach was marred by inconsistent offenses and power struggles, as his inability to hand over the controls on offense before it was too late is partially what led to his demise. One of the reasons Fisher left the confines of Tallahassee - where he had won a national championship - for Texas A&M was (allegedly) the fact that Florida State would not meet his demands for more resourcing. The Aggies are one of the most well-resourced football programs in America, and the fact that he was never able to even make an SEC Championship Game shouldn't inspire confidence. I doubt the Seminoles are in a position, financially speaking, to give Fisher the funds he needs to compete on the national stage, and even if they do, would he be able to wind back the clocks and have FSU looking like the mid 2010s version of themselves? As I said earlier, I totally get it. As a Gator fan, when things were coming to a merciful end with Billy Napier, I started to talk myself into the idea of Urban Meyer coming home and coaching Florida again. But being realistic, that would have never worked. Meyer flamed out at his final stop in Jacksonville and he was nearly a decade removed from coaching in college football. Florida State needs to move forward, not backward. Find a hot, up-and-coming coach that will thrust the Seminoles into the modern era of college football. Just off the top of my head, a guy like Boise State's Spencer Danielson would be a home run hire to get the Noles back to where they want to be. But, of course, Florida State needs to find a new AD first. title: Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz's 'effective altruism' network tied to AI regulation push
description: Billionaire Democratic megadonor Dustin Moskovitz-backed "effective altruism" funder Coefficient Giving eyes $1B artificial intelligence push amid doomerism concerns.
content: Concerns about artificial intelligence spelling doom for the human race are being linked to a "cult-like" philanthropy movement known as "effective altruism" supported by billionaire Democratic megadonor and Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, according to a policy analyst. In response to former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation announcement on X, Parker Thayer, an investigative researcher at Capital Research Center in Washington D.C., went viral as he raised questions about whether the resignation was part of a broader network that aims to influence lawmakers and AI policy. "I resigned from Anthropic today," Coxon’s post read. "I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION Thayer quoted the post in a response that received interaction online with top lawmakers in Congress, including Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. "This post looks like the start of a VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion," Thayer posted. "The post is punchy, quotable, it almost seems professionally written. The first three accounts to quote tweet it all do so within 15 minutes of the initial posting." Thayer echoed claims made by White House AI advisor David Sacks that AI fears are overblown and potentially based on political motives. "I think this is becoming a panic," Sacks told CBS News correspondent Jo Ling Kent. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear. And I think this is a moment to really calm down a little bit and look at the issue rationally." SEN. BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE Coxon told Fox News’ Bret Baier last week that we are "on the doorstep of tremendous discoveries," but are running in too quickly. He emphasized the need for moderation. Baier asked Coxon if the issue could be figured out. "I think definitely. I think if we actually try instead of submitting to the inevitability of a doomed race or a hubristic gamble, then we can solve it," he said. "The problem is not unsolvable." TOP MEDIA OUTLETS FAIL TO DISCLOSE WHO IS BANKROLLING THEIR AI REPORTERS Coxon said he was acting alone when deciding to voice his concerns about the direction of AI, according to The Wall Street Journal. Fox News Digital sat down with Thayer to ask about his theories concerning the coordination behind Coxon's "sophisticated" resignation, which was in turn met with a slew of national television interviews and immediate notoriety. Almost overnight, Coxon's post became a major point of policy debate spanning across political parties and politicians, including President Donald Trump and socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Thayer did not offer a theory for which individuals or groups might have coordinated with Coxon, who has denied such claims. But Thayer said the "AI doomerism movement" is associated with "effective altruism," a philosophy he described as "cult-like." OPINION: REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES According to the Centre for Effective Altruism, the movement is defined as a "project that aims to find the best ways to help others and put them into practice." But Thayer noted that while the philanthropic movement may sound high-minded, Silicon Valley elites and members who donate and support "effective altruism" may have much more direct political goals in mind. Thayer did not have evidence that any individuals or groups connected to the effective altruism movement provided public relations or other support for Coxon’s post about his resignation. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION Moskovitz and his wife Cari Tuna have been leading financial backers of organizations associated with the "effective altruism" movement. The couple founded Coefficient Giving, formerly known as Open Philanthropy, and remain its "main funders," according to the organization. Tuna serves as its president. Coefficient Giving says its artificial intelligence work has expanded rapidly, with $168 million committed to AI safety, security and field-building in 2024 and $351 million in 2025 — a combined $519 million. The organization says it is on track to commit more than $1 billion to similar work in 2026. In a 2021 grant application description, the organization cited that it seeks "to fund programs and events in a variety of areas of interest to Coefficient Giving — including effective altruism, global catastrophic risks, biosecurity, AI for epistemics, forecasting, and other areas." Moskovitz, who Forbes estimates has a net worth of roughly $10 billion, contributed more than $50 million to support the Biden-Harris campaign from 2020 to 2024, including $46.89 million to the Future Forward PAC, which served as the main fundraising vessel for the failed presidential campaign. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ On Monday, the Department of War Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering posted to X: "Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!" As for the reasoning behind "effective altruism’s" commitment to the artificial intelligence policy space, Thayer said the fearmongering technique is comparable to the climate change narrative that has been traditionally peddled by the Democratic Party. "They basically just say kind of in the same vein as climate change activists like Al Gore used to, they kind of just make bombastic doomsday projections without citing really a whole lot of easily discernible evidence and just expect us to trust their expertise," Thayer explained. "First, they got you scared of the data centers based on a bunch of sketchy arguments about water pollution supposedly, and supposedly raising your electric prices, which don't seem to actually be true," he added. "And now they're getting you scared of the actual AI that the data centers are being used to launch." Thayer said that if AI critics were truly afraid of a potential doomsday scenario, they would be advocating for the extinction of artificial intelligence altogether. Instead, he says that it is a tactic to increase the government’s power over the industry while also acting in their own interest so "that they're the only ones who are allowed to build it." In an opinion piece published in Medium in 2024, Moskovitz noted that he was concerned about the potential risks AI poses, saying that a potential doomsday "situation may develop extremely quickly." "Contrary to the popular narrative about effective altruists working in AI, my interest in mitigating the potential risks isn’t rooted in specific predictions about the far future, but rather simple concern about the next few decades, when I and the people I care about are still alive to care about what happens," he wrote. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-LA, said a meeting at the White House to discuss AI policy could happen before the end of this week or the next. Trump also weighed in on the AI outlook in a post to Truth Social on Monday. "The people that say AI is going to destroy the World, and that Data Centers are bad for your neighborhood, are the same people that said, just a short time ago, that the World would be extinguished by "Climate Change." That HOAX never worked out for them, and now they’re on to the next one." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Moskovitz, Coefficient Giving and Coxon for comment.

title: Kamala Harris viciously mocked with resurfaced bumbling 'two words' explanation of AI after desperate call
description: Kamala Harris' rambling 2023 explanation of AI as "two letters" resurfaces after she posted a lengthy call to slow down AI development online.
content: Former Vice President and failed presidential candidate Kamala Harris is being mocked over a resurfaced clip of her "two letters" explanation of artificial intelligence after she posted a call to slow its development. Harris, who previously served as the Biden administration's AI czar, posted a lengthy statement on AI on Monday. In her post, Harris called for President Donald Trump to "do his job to protect America’s interests by pursuing a treaty with countries like China to stop dangerous uses of AI, limit the speed of its development, and adopt global standards for testing." In response, social media users recalled Harris’ attempt at explaining AI as vice president in 2023. "I think the first part of this issue that should be articulated is AI is kind of a fancy thing," Harris said. "First of all, it's two letters. It means artificial intelligence, but ultimately what it is is it's about machine learning." WATCH: KAMALA HARRIS TORCHED OVER ‘ZERO SENSE’ WNBA PEP TALK IN LATEST ‘WORD SALAD’ MOMENT She continued, saying, "And so, the machine is taught — and part of the issue here is what information is going into the machine that will then determine — and we can predict then, if we think about what information is going in, what then will be produced in terms of decisions and opinions that may be made through that process." "So," she went on even further, "to reduce it down to its most simple point, this is part of the issue that we have here is thinking about what is going into a decision, and then whether that decision is actually legitimate and reflective of the needs and the life experiences of all the people." After Harris' X post on Monday, conservative influencer "Western Lensman" reposted the 2023 video of Harris, writing, "Kamala Harris on AI when it's not a written statement crafted by a team of consultants." National security and global economics expert Kyle Bass reacted, "There’s not a chance in hell Kamala wrote this. Have you ever heard her say ‘frontier,’ ‘advancing,’ and ‘intelligence’ in the same sentence? Until now, her misfits had never produced anything this un-Kamala and then posted it on social media." Columnist S.L. Kanthan wrote, "One of the dumbest women now wants America to voluntarily slow down progress in AI." He posted another video of Harris explaining cloud storage. Harris said, "No longer are you necessarily keeping those private files in some file cabinet that’s locked in the basement of the house. It’s on your laptop, and it's then, therefore, up here in this cloud, that exists above us, right?" Author and national security expert Sarah Adams commented on Harris’ AI post, writing, "No one is looking for your thoughts on 'intelligence.'" Another user, influencer Andrew Aziz, and several others suggested that Harris’ post itself was AI-generated. KAMALA HARRIS DIVES INTO MIDTERM FIGHT ONLY TO GET ROASTED FOR NEVER HAVING 'AN ORIGINAL THOUGHT IN HER LIFE’ In her post, Harris wrote that AI is "advancing at an alarming speed," emphasizing what she characterized as industry leaders’ call to "responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development." She wrote that "a slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest," saying, "Pacing AI development does not mean giving up on this technology’s potential to produce life-saving benefits in fields like medicine — some of which we are already seeing. Rather, it is about setting up sensible guardrails so that AI does not completely escape human control and endanger our safety and collective future." Besides action from Trump, Harris called on Congress to "work at an urgent pace" to provide AI oversight, saying, "The United States must continue to lead the world in developing AI technology even as we seek to impose common-sense safety standards." Harris is not the only prominent Democrat to have called for increased AI regulation recently. Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats during a private fundraiser in New York City on Thursday to place artificial intelligence near the center of their political agenda ahead of the midterms and the 2028 presidential race while warning that the technology could become dangerous without greater oversight as voters increasingly raise concerns about jobs, privacy and data centers. "This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous," Obama said. "If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future." ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN Meanwhile, Trump on Monday rejected growing calls for safeguards and restrictions on AI, declaring that the technology needs a "STRONG AND SMART" president rather than additional restraints. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so." Fox News Digital's Lindsay Kornick and Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

content: Former Sen. Manchin framed the request as an urgent step to prevent companies developing advanced AI from facing additional pressure to race ahead before lawmakers establish rules governing the technology. "The president of the United States has the power to save humanity," Manchin said. "An IPO freeze is the kind of top-down mandate that conservatives have long opposed, and it would not even address the actual risk." "What the president should use his executive power for is to demand pre-deployment testing begin immediately. That is where the real safeguards belong, not in blocking companies from raising capital," she continued. PRESIDENTIAL FLIP? title: ‘Still waiting on the DOGE check’: Battleground state voters cast doubt on Trump’s new $5K promise
description: Detroit, Michigan, residents call gas prices, car insurance and rent "ridiculous" while dismissing Trump's $5,000 dividend as political "bribery."
content: Voters squeezed by rising costs are skeptical of President Donald Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend — with at least one resident pointing to a previous DOGE dividend proposal that never materialized. "I feel like that's a pitch to get more votes," Yolanda Lewis told Fox News Digital. "I'm still waiting on the DOGE check that he promised that we never received, so until he gives us a definite date saying when we're gonna get that and receive it, then I'll take that into consideration." Trump suggested in February 2025 that a portion of savings generated by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) could be returned to taxpayers, while Elon Musk entertained a proposal that envisioned payments of as much as $5,000. Trump later backed the idea of returning 20% of DOGE savings to Americans. DOGE reported $110.3 billion in savings from contracts, grants and leases, though a Government Accountability Office review later found that some of its estimates were inaccurate or lacked sufficient supporting evidence. Now, with affordability a top-of-mind issue for voters across the country, Trump has unveiled a new "Trump dividend" plan at the Midterm GOP Convention last Wednesday that would give $5,000 to American adults if Republicans maintain control of Congress. Several Detroit voters, interviewed by Fox News Digital at the Detroit Health Department’s annual Block Party on Sept. 12, rejected the proposal, with some calling it a "bribe" and others questioning whether the money would ever be paid out. TRUMP MAKES STUNNING FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND CASH PROMISE IN BID TO RALLY GOP VOTERS AT DALLAS MIDTERM CONVENTION "I think it's kind of irresponsible because what is the long-term impact of this money?" Jahdante Smith, the Green Party candidate for the state House of Representatives 9th district, told Fox News Digital. Smith, who supports Medicare for All, pointed to the nation's roughly $40 trillion debt in questioning how the proposal would be funded. "So where does that money come from? Where do you divert those funds from? Also, I think that it is sort of a bribe," Smith said. Michigan, which Trump won by 1.4% in 2024, has become a key battleground in the fight for Senate control as Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Saye and Republican Mike Rogers are both vying for Michigan's open Senate seat. El-Sayed called Trump's $5,000 proposal "unserious" during a rally in Lansing, Michigan. "Funny thing about it is like there's no world in which you can pay for it," El-Sayed said. "So how about you actually do some governing and like solve the Social Security problem. How about we guarantee people health care so they don't have to pay so much for that." Rogers' campaign did not directly comment on the former congressman's stance on Trump's $5,000 dividend plan. Instead, it pointed to El-Sayed's support for implementing a progressive tax plan. "You know what’s not serious? Challenging Mike to a 1:1 football scrimmage, taking money from Designated Terrorist Organizations and advocating to raise taxes for Michiganders while they’re already paying for Democrats’ mismanagement," said Alyssa Brouillet, communications director for the Rogers campaign. "Funny enough, those are things Abdul does." Prices are an acute concern in Detroit, where roughly a third of residents live below the federal poverty line. The city's median household income is below $40,000, according to U.S. census data. "Well, as a city Detroit retiree, affordability is very important, and I think the prices since Trump's been back in office have gone up on everything, especially gas, diesel, you know, affordabilities went out the window," William Davis told Fox News Digital. The current cost of gas in Detroit is $4.11 per gallon. Before the Iran war, gas prices hovered between $2.81 and $2.92 per gallon in January. TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME' Martesha Adams, a young mother and nurse living in Detroit, told Fox News Digital at the Detroit Health Department Block Party that she also viewed the $5,000 proposal as an attempt to win over struggling Americans. "The whole time I feel that he's been in the office, it's been a kind of game," Adams said. "America has been laughed at from everywhere. And the $5K for bribery, that's nothing. So I hope that people do not go for that bribe, and they really look into the politics." For Shelby Campbell, a 2023 graduate of Wayne State University, affordability has already forced significant changes. She said she sold her car because she could no longer afford Michigan's no-fault auto insurance and has struggled to find an affordable rental in Detroit. Campbell called Trump's $5,000 proposal "disgusting." "He shouldn't be able to offer people money if we have one party in office," Campbell said. "It's supposed to be about everybody and what we all want and need, so it's just bribery in my opinion." Campbell, who said she plans to vote for El-Sayed in the general election, argued that money already plays too large a role in politics. "I think he's genuinely a good guy, and he wants to get money out of politics, and I am all for that," Campbell said. "We seriously need that because big corporations buy our elections just like Donald Trump is trying to do." Other Detroit residents echoed Lewis' skepticism about whether Trump would actually deliver the proposed payments. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT Trump also proposed a separate $2,000 dividend last year funded by tariff revenue, though those payments never materialized. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I don't think it's realistic to think he's going to do that," Davis said of Trump's latest proposal. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Sunday on "Meet the Press" that the $5,000 payments would require congressional approval, while pledging to work toward Trump's proposal. "I never go out and give big commitments on the front end because I’ve got to work through it, and that’s what we do every single day," Johnson said. While Trump's proposal has garnered mixed reactions within the Republican Party, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, posted on X that he'd work to prepare a bill and get it passed before the election. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., rejected the idea that Trump was seeking to "bribe" voters. "The only thing that I knew of was that he has this concept of a dividend of all Americans being able to share in the success of America," Emmer told Politico. "Let the policy guys draft it. Let them debate it. Let them move it through committee," Emmer told Politico. "You get it to the whip’s office. We’ll pass it."

title: Nick Reiner won't face death penalty in Rob, Michele Reiner murder case

"After a careful and thorough review of all these factors, the District Attorney's office will not be seeking the death penalty in this case. That means that the maximum sentence that Mr. Reiner will be looking at is life without the possibility of parole." NICK REINER INDICTED IN MURDERS OF PARENTS ROB, MICHELE REINER AT BRENTWOOD HOME Reiner was charged with two counts of murder and included special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and lying in wait after a grand jury indictment. Prosecutors also alleged he used a knife. title: Trump blasts Supreme Court 'disaster' after justices rule against him on mail-in voting
description: Trump called Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas "legends" for dissenting and listed Supreme Court rulings that have gone against him.
content: President Donald Trump lashed out at the Supreme Court on Tuesday after justices ruled against his administration on a major mail-in voting initiative. "Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court, one that the Court System took forever to give, and then blamed it, in part, on no time left to implement a solution to our totally CORRUPT and out of control Mail-In voting 'disaster,' which is a laughing stock all over the World, and where we are the only country that has to endure such a Nation Destroying SCAM," Trump wrote. The president went on to praise Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, who dissented from Monday's order. Trump called the pair "legends." SUPREME COURT REJECTS TRUMP BID TO REVIVE STRICT MAIL-BALLOT RULES BEFORE MIDTERMS "It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left 'Dumocrats,' on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do – And now they have an open field to do so!" Trump wrote. Trump went on to list a series of cases where the Supreme Court has disappointed him, including its decision to strike down his tariff policies and void his executive order ending birthright citizenship. TRUMP CRITICIZES 2 SUPREME COURT JUSTICES BY NAME OVER TARIFF RULING "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court – it will likely cost me dearly for years to come – but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!" he wrote. The Monday order rejected the Trump administration's request for a stay in the implementation of a universal injunction against new mail-in ballot rules from the U.S. Postal Service. The rules would require federal ballot mail to be sent in envelopes bearing an election-mail logo, capable of being scanned by high-speed equipment and carrying a barcode unique to each voter. State and local election officials would also be required to submit envelope designs to the Postal Service for review and upload basic voter information to an online USPS portal. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE Under the USPS rule, mailings that failed to comply would not be accepted and would instead be returned to election officials to correct and resubmit. The court's Monday order went unsigned, but Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a concurring opinion that allowed room for a potential Trump victory down the line. He nevertheless argued that it is too close to Election Day to realistically implement the rules for the 2026 midterm elections. title: PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp reiterates it is not considering a returning member program for LIV golfers
description: Brian Rolapp declared the PGA Tour is not contemplating a returning member program for LIV Golf players, citing meritocracy and accountability.
content: The PGA Tour officially shared the details of what the new-look, two-tiered competitive model debuting in 2028 will entail on Tuesday, and CEO Brian Rolapp also made it clear that, as things stand now, LIV golfers will not be a part of it. The word "pathways" will be discussed ad nauseam leading into the 2028 PGA Tour season, with players looking to earn a spot on the upper-tiered Championship Series. It, however, will not be a term used for players on the once-backed Saudi breakaway circuit, as it was in January, when Brooks Koepka took advantage of the Returning Member Program window. "As I said a few weeks ago in Atlanta, there are really three things when it comes to anyone who wants to compete on the PGA TOUR. "One, the PGA TOUR is built on meritocracy. Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place. Two, we are a membership organization; we have rules, and those rules exist for lots of reasons, including fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter, and they must be enforced. "Which brings me to number three, accountability and discipline. These are essential elements for any sports league and are certainly for the integrity of the PGA TOUR and the sport. It's what holds the TOUR together. Those are guiding principles for us. In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member program like the one you saw in January." title: Iran's regime came for teenage twins. Their fate offers a glimpse of Tehran's widening death campaign
description: Iranian twins Taraneh and Romina Rahimi face execution and decades in prison after joining protests, as Iran's death penalty surge draws global alarm.
content: Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were 19, still in high school and living with their mother when masked men came for them in the middle of the night. According to their U.S.-based cousin, the twin sisters were dragged from their beds with bags placed over their heads about a month after they joined anti-regime protests in Isfahan. Their family was given no explanation and spent months searching courts, hospitals and government offices trying to determine where they had been taken. Four months later, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, was finally allowed to see them at Dowlatabad Prison. She barely recognized her daughters. ONE GLARING ISSUE GOES UNADDRESSED IN UN CHIEF'S HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH IRAN'S PRESIDENT Their cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, told The Guardian that the twins had badly swollen and bruised faces, injuries to their elbows, hands and feet, and significant hair loss that he said resulted from guards pulling them by their hair as they were moved between cells. He said their mother also learned that the sisters had been held in solitary confinement. Now 20, Taraneh Rahimi faces execution over her alleged role in the January protests, while her twin sister could spend decades in prison, in a case unfolding amid a sharp rise in Iran’s use of the death penalty. Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported that Taraneh was sentenced to death and an additional 11 years in prison, while Romina received a 36-year sentence. The sentences were issued by Branch 1 of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court and remain initial-stage verdicts. The twins are among 16 defendants prosecuted in what has become known as the "Isfahan Shohada Square" case. HRANA said 10 defendants received death sentences and the 16 defendants collectively received 256 years in prison. The sisters’ family says the abuse was intended to force confessions. IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY Nourmohammadi told The Guardian that Taraneh was threatened that prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless she signed a confession. The outlet reported that Taraneh later told the court that admissions attributed to her had been obtained through torture. Her mother was not permitted to attend the trial, according to the family. Radio Farda separately reported, citing Nourmohammadi, that the sisters suffered physical and psychological abuse and were forced to confess to accusations they deny. The Hana Human Rights Organization told Fox News Digital they have verified the torture allegations. Concerns about torture extend beyond the sisters. HRANA reported that another defendant in the same case, Ahmadreza Saeidi, told judges during the hearing that the investigating judge personally used an electric stun gun on his neck and genitals. Defense lawyers also reportedly complained that they had not been given access to substantial portions of the case file or adequate time to examine evidence before trial. The sentences come as rights organizations document a sharp rise in executions across Iran. COULD NARGES MOHAMMADI UNITE IRAN’S OPPOSITION? HUSBAND SAYS IMPRISONED NOBEL LAUREATE STILL FIGHTING The Washington-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran documented 901 executions during the first seven months of 2026, including 56 people executed on political or national-security charges. Behnam Ben Taleblu, Iran program senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the executions should be viewed as part of a broader campaign by Tehran to suppress dissent at home. "Despite the war in the region, despite the drone war, the missile war, the war over the Strait of Hormuz, the real war is the one that's happening on a day-to-day basis inside the Islamic Republic," Ben Taleblu said. title: Smithsonian move reignites 'woke,' 'Marxist' criticism as Latino museum avoids congressional approval
description: Mike Gonzalez's Heritage Foundation report alleges the National Museum of the American Latino promotes Marxist messaging and anti-Western ideology.
content: The Smithsonian designated its Arts and Industries Building as the permanent home of the controversial National Museum of the American Latino, a move critics say will allow the institution to move forward without another congressional fight over a museum they argue should not exist. The decision comes as the Smithsonian faces intensifying scrutiny over its historical exhibits. Mike Gonzalez, a former Bush State Department official and longtime critic of the Latino museum, argued its inaugural exhibition promoted a far-left worldview and said selecting the Arts and Industries Building was an effort to avoid a contentious Capitol Hill battle. "We need to fire the Smithsonian leadership," Gonzalez said. "We need to get rid of the Latino museum. It needs to be de-authorized. It should not exist." Gonzalez examined the Latino museum’s inaugural 2022 exhibition, "¡Presente!," in a Heritage Foundation report shared with Fox News Digital. He also testified alongside National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig during congressional hearings in July. The Smithsonian declined comment on Gonzalez’s report or his comments to Fox News Digital. Gonzalez argues the location decision matters because the Smithsonian already controls A&I, unlike the National Park Service sites previously under consideration. "They want to use this as kind of a ruse," Gonzalez said, arguing that the institution can avoid another congressional fight by placing the museum on property it already controls. TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED Gonzalez examined "¡Presente!," and argued that a series of panels reflected what he described as an anti-Western, anti-American worldview. He pointed to its use of the idea "we didn't cross the border, the border crossed us" as historically inaccurate and said it is a favorite mantra of those on the left who criticize immigration law enforcement. He said the language casts U.S. westward expansion primarily through the lens of displacement while obscuring the history of Mexicans who remained in territory acquired by the United States and later became American citizens. "I guess your guest today would count as one of them," he said of himself. "Even though I don't… run around calling myself a Hispanic. I'm a proud American of Cuban heritage." SMITHSONIAN PUSHED ‘REVOLTING’ SOCIAL ACTION TRAINING AFTER ‘WHITENESS’ CHART APOLOGY: EXPERT "They create[d] a hothouse, an incubator of grievances among these 70 million Americans of Hispanic descent," he said, adding that Sarria and another featured figure prove that point. That example involves Orlando Letelier, a foreign minister under former Marxist Chilean President Salvador Allende. A photograph from the exhibition shows a 1976 quote from Letelier discussing his imprisonment under the Pinochet dictatorship and his later "liberation" in the name of restoring human rights. "Orlando Letelier has nothing to do with America, other than the fact that he died in a car explosion in Washington D.C., in 1976, but I'm old enough to remember that he was a cause-celebre of the left [then]," he said. "This is not an American story. The only reason he's there is because the curators who worked in this exhibit betrayed who they are... They're Marxists." Gonzalez, who said his father was imprisoned by Cuba’s former "tin-pot dictator" Fulgencio Batista before the leader was overthrown by Fidel Castro in 1959, said the Latino museum also does a rank disservice to the true history of Marxist-Leninist rule in Havana. "Havana perhaps has not been at war since the British invasion of 1763 and yet it looks like it’s been carpet-bombed: It’s been carpet-bombed by socialism." The exhibit on Batista omits the oppressive reign of the Castro brothers and also features a cartoon mocking the U.S. for the Reagan-era Iran-Contra affair, the report said. title: Lindsay Clancy judge indefinitely impounds juror names, citing safety and 'divisive' attention
description: Judge William Sullivan sealed juror names in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial case, citing safety concerns and unauthorized identification of jurors.
content: The judge in the Lindsay Clancy case has indefinitely sealed the jurors' names, citing safety concerns and what he called "significant and divisive attention" on the trial. Judge William Sullivan issued the order on Monday and said while the court acknowledges that the jurors' names must be made available to the public, there is a "real and present" risk of harm to the jurors, stating he's impounding all names indefinitely until otherwise ordered. Sullivan noted that there have been "identifications of jurors and their personal information without their permission" in explaining his reasoning for shielding the jurors' names. "Some of the empaneled jurors have come forward and spoken to the media after the declaration of a mistrial on September 4, 2026. However, the majority of the jurors, deliberating and alternates, have maintained their anonymity, despite multiple requests to give statements," Sullivan wrote. "The Court concludes that there is a risk of immediate and irreparable injury should the list be made available to the public at this time." LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR DENIES BIAS ALLEGATIONS, WANTS 'CONVERSATION STARTED' ABOUT WOMEN'S MENTAL HEALTH In a separate filing on Monday, Sullivan ordered the impoundment of the clerk's list of potential jurors for the Plymouth County Courthouse for July 20 through July 24, during jury selection for the trial, "based upon threats and concerns over juror safety." "Immediate and irreparable injury and dangers to jurors and to the administration, is real and present," he wrote, sealing the names of the entire jury pool for people who were called to jury duty during that timeframe. That order is set to expire in 10 days. Clancy, 36, faced three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the slayings of her children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — who were discovered strangled at the family's home in January 2023. title: Army veteran paratrooper who deployed to Iraq, Afghanistan before helping rescue Fox News reporter dead at 50
description: Sean Michael Lee's cancer was linked to burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan, ending a life devoted to rescuing thousands from war zones and disasters.
content: Sean Michael Lee, an Army paratrooper who helped evacuate thousands from conflict zones after his service — including Fox News' Benjamin Hall — died Sunday after a battle with esophageal cancer. Lee was a 20-year veteran of the Army, having served multiple deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan as a member of the Army's storied 82nd Airborne Division, according to his obituary. "He was, to his core, a paratrooper. Long after he took off the uniform, the values forged there remained the organizing principles of his life: duty, loyalty, competence under pressure, and an unwavering commitment to the person beside him," his obituary reads. AMERICA’S PROMISE TO OUR AFGHAN ALLIES IS STILL UNFINISHED FIVE YEARS LATER Lee spent the years after his military service continuing to help people. In 2021, as Afghanistan's government was collapsing, Lee worked to help evacuate thousands during a chaotic withdrawal as a member of the nonprofit group Save Our Allies. Just a year later, Lee was in Poland helping deliver supplies to the frontline in Ukraine in the midst of Russia's invasion. It was there that Lee became a key part of extracting Fox News correspondent Benjamin Hall, who had been severely injured when Russian forces attacked his vehicle near Kyiv. Two members of Hall’s crew were killed in the attack. BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES "We got the call, we had just finished up a staff meeting with our folks back in the United States, and I can tell you that in about 90 minutes our guys were out the door and on the way," Lee explained to the Daily Caller during a 2022 interview. Lee also worked to help wounded veterans through The Independence Fund. In 2024, Lee helped deliver life-saving supplies to survivors of Hurricane Helene in North Carolina. He lived out of a tent in the Tar Heel state as he helped deliver aid to communities where support systems had collapsed, according to his obituary. LUKE COMBS AND ERIC CHURCH RAISE OVER $24.5 MILLION FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS AT STAR-STUDDED CONCERT FOR CAROLINA Most recently, Lee had been working under Secretary Doug Collins at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. "Sean spent his life running toward the crisis. After more than two decades in uniform and multiple combat deployments, he continued that service through The Independence Fund, Save Our Allies and ultimately the Department of Veterans Affairs," Sarah Verardo, a founder of The Independence Fund and close friend of Lee's, told Fox News Digital. "Whether evacuating Afghan combat interpreters and their families, helping establish field hospitals in Ukraine, or living out of his car to deliver aid in Western North Carolina, Sean went wherever he was needed most. His service knew no boundaries, and he never wanted fanfare or credit. He simply lived the ethos of ‘send me.'" Verardo said. She also explained how Lee and her husband, a fellow member of the 82nd Airborne who was wounded in combat, forged a close personal bond. "Sean walked alongside my husband for years following his catastrophic combat injuries and through his death, and for the better part of a decade, he was a constant presence in the lives of my three girls. He never missed a first day of school or a Halloween with us. Until his final breath, he remained that constant, living with us throughout his cancer battle and, even as his own world became smaller, still wanting to hear about dance recitals, science projects and all the ordinary details of their lives. He showed up for the defining moments and the ordinary ones because, to Sean, service was never a job or an assignment. It was simply who he was," she said. "Sean was the definition of a quiet warrior. Our family has lost one of our own, and our nation has lost a patriot whose service never stopped," Verardo concluded. He was part of the U.S. military's 2003 invasion of Iraq. He was also part of the storied Bravo Company in the 2-508 Parachute Infantry Regiment. Half of the company received Purple Hearts for an Afghanistan deployment that was documented in Ben Kesling’s book "Bravo Company: An Afghanistan Deployment and its Aftermath." Lee's two best friends — Sgt. Michael Verardo and Sgt. Allen Thomas — both of whom deployed with him to Afghanistan, passed away before him. Lee's cancer was the direct result of his exposure to the burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan. He died at age 50. VETERANS FACE SURPRISING THREAT AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS, STUDY REVEALS "I can’t even begin to explain what the world has just lost," former MMA fighter and Special Forces sniper Tim Kennedy wrote in a post on Instagram. "This country has lost one of the finest men ever to serve it," Kennedy's message continued. "Sean redefined the word service. He did not just volunteer to put on the uniform and join the 82nd Airborne. He dedicated his entire life to other people. He put his life on the line more times than anyone can count. Wherever people needed help, you found Sean. Whenever I needed help, I found Sean," Kennedy wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lee's life "cannot be measured simply in years, deployments, jobs, or missions. It is measured in people who made it home because he went toward danger," his obituary, shared by Heritage Funeral & Cremation Services, says. "In wounded men carried to safety. In Afghan families given a chance to begin again. In communities that received help when they believed they had been forgotten. In veterans whose lives were better because he continued serving them after his own time in uniform ended. And in the children who simply knew him as Uncle Sean: the constant, fiercely protective man who showed up."

title: China expert warns Beijing wants Americans — not the CCP — to spread its message
description: A China expert testifying before Congress says Beijing uses American organizations as "Trojan horses" to make its influence appear homegrown.
content: Congress will examine how foreign adversaries — particularly China — seek to influence American public opinion and policymaking at a hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. One of the expert witnesses told Fox News Digital ahead of the hearing that Beijing's greater advantage lies in shaping debate inside the United States through American organizations rather than direct Chinese propaganda. Matthew Johnson, a China expert and senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, said Beijing increasingly seeks to influence debates over national security and other strategic issues by working through American institutions and organizations, making its messages appear homegrown rather than directed by the Chinese government. HOUSE PANEL TO PROBE FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS "The idea is that it's not the Communist Party talking, it's actually institutions and individuals in the United States who are talking," Johnson told Fox News Digital. "That's actually the best outcome because then it looks organic... it looks like it's somehow being produced from within our society as opposed to by external actors." Johnson said one of Beijing's current priorities is slowing U.S. advances in artificial intelligence and data-center infrastructure—an area he said Chinese leaders view as central to strategic competition with the United States. He said China's influence strategy combines grassroots activism with efforts to shape thinking among academics, policy experts and other influential voices. His testimony comes as Congress continues examining the funding network linked to Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, whose nonprofits have become the subject of congressional investigations and a federal criminal probe. Fox News Digital previously reported that Singham directed at least $285 million into six pro-China, pro-communist nonprofit organizations beginning in 2017, including CodePink. Singham and the organizations have denied taking direction from the Chinese government, and neither Singham nor the organizations have been charged with wrongdoing. HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM Johnson is scheduled to testify Tuesday before the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, which will hold a hearing titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America." Lawmakers are expected to examine how foreign adversaries, including China, Cuba and Iran, may use nonprofits, activist networks and other organizations to shape U.S. public opinion and policy. "My goal is to raise the curtain to expose these operations and stop them from undermining our national security, capitalism and the American Dream," committee Chairman Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital. Johnson said the hearing focuses on what lawmakers describe as "malign foreign influence"—efforts by foreign governments to shape American public debate and policymaking by steering conversations toward their own strategic interests rather than those of the United States. "I try to break down influence in terms of looking at ways in which the framework of very sensitive strategic conversations is being steered in ways that seem to map onto China's strategic interests, not American strategic interests," Johnson said. He said the concept of a "Trojan horse" reflects Beijing's preference for influencing American debate through domestic institutions and individuals rather than direct government messaging. "From an American perspective, we want to be sure that it's Americans who are leading the debate on this issue, not Beijing," Johnson said. CHINA’S INFLUENCE MACHINE: FEDERAL RECORDS EXPOSE BEIJING’S PUSH TO SWAY AMERICA Among the organizations that have received funding from Singham's network is CodePink, the anti-war activist group co-founded by Medea Benjamin and Jodie Evans, Singham's wife. CodePink has spent years organizing disruptive protests inside Congress, campaigning against U.S. policy toward China, Cuba and Israel, and promoting its "China Is Not Our Enemy" campaign, which argues the United States should pursue cooperation with Beijing rather than confrontation. House Ways and Means Committee Republicans have accused the group of promoting narratives aligned with Chinese Communist Party interests, allegations CodePink denies. Asked why campaigns such as CodePink's "China Is Not Our Enemy" matter, Johnson said they promote an image of China that serves Beijing's strategic interests by downplaying the broader geopolitical competition between the two countries. "The idea that we don't want war with China, we want peace... these are all noble goals," Johnson said. "But... its strategic function is that it masks the fact that Beijing actually does seek a world order that is more shaped by Beijing in which the United States plays a lesser role." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Johnson said China does not have to convince Americans to support the Chinese Communist Party to advance its interests. Instead, he said, Beijing benefits when public debate shifts away from viewing China as a strategic competitor. "The real issue is whether there is actually a balance and whether we have enough transparency to allow us to assess whether there's a balance," Johnson said. Fox News' Asra Q. Nomani contributed to this report.

title: Mr T taught me a lesson every kid on Chicago's South Side needs to hear
description: From Robert Taylor Homes to Lake Forest, Mr. T's life proves that faith, hard work and self-respect can overcome even the toughest circumstances.
content: I recently watched the new Netflix documentary on Mr. T. I admit it was disappointing. It felt thin and rushed to me. The filmmakers clearly had no passion for the film since it failed to capture his nature, his complexities, his faith, his service, the hardships and the depth of the road that he traveled. A 48-minute documentary is not enough to do justice to such a life. After all, this is a man who traveled from the rough and violent housing projects known as the Robert Taylor Homes to the top of the world. Still, the documentary reminded me of why Mr. T has always been such an inspirational figure in my life, from my childhood even to now. I hold him up as a role model to my young kids at Project H.O.O.D. His life is one of hard work, doing the right thing and having a dream. Those are not clichés or empty slogans. They are the values that create opportunities in life. Laurence Tureaud was born May 21, 1952, the second-youngest of 12 children on Chicago’s South Side. His father, a minister, left when Laurence was five. His mother, Willie, earned a living cleaning houses in the Lake Forest area of Chicago, and her income to support all her children was supplemented by an $87 monthly welfare check. They were poor, but not in family or spirit. Mr. T talks of how they went to church, loved their mother and stayed away from the gangs. MR. T ON FAITH: 'I ANSWER ONLY TO GOD' One of my favorite Mr. T quotes is, "I was born and raised in the ghetto, but the ghetto was not born and raised in me." Like anyone in the Robert Taylor Homes, he saw violence and all the things that no child should ever see. He also saw racism. He saw white men call his father a "boy." Mr. T was a dreamer who had family around him and who never walked down the wrong path or went to jail because he could not bear to break his mother’s heart. That’s how love can save a child. In the documentary, he talks of how his brother went to fight in Vietnam as a Marine and came home only to be called a "boy." When Laurence was 18, he vowed that no one would ever call him a boy. He changed his name to Mr. T so that the first word out of anyone talking to him would be "Mister." What he was demanding was the respect and dignity that his family had been denied. He respected himself. WHO IS RAISING AMERICA'S CHILDREN? MENTOR WARNS KIDS ARE SEEKING ROLE MODELS ONLINE AS COMMUNITIES FADE At Dunbar Vocational High School, he became a football star and a city wrestling champion. He did not have a fancy gym to build his muscles. He worked out with his brothers on the concrete around the projects. They did push-ups. They did chin-ups from tree branches. They wrestled one another. They built those muscles the honest way. Mr. T won a scholarship to Prairie View A&M, but that did not work out. He moved to the Loop of Chicago because that is where the money was. For me, that is key because he put himself where the opportunity was. He wound up working three jobs at once, and one of them was as a bouncer at a club. It was there that he got the news that his mother had been robbed of her welfare money by thugs in the elevator of the projects. They told her to give them her money or they would cut her throat. Mr. T grabbed his shotgun and went into the projects, where he confronted gang members until he found the people who had made his mother fear for her life. After confronting those responsible, he decided to become a bodyguard. He would protect others the way he believed he had failed to protect his mother. THE WELFARE STATE BROKE BLACK FAMILIES. WORK CAN HELP RESTORE THE DREAM What I love about this story is that he turned what he believed to be a personal failure into a calling. I don’t think it was a personal failure at all, but what he was trying to do in his own way was make the world a better place. He would use his talents and smarts in that way. He didn’t fall into the gang life or anything like that. He created a new pathway in life instead. I don’t know where I read it, but I remember the story of when he was nine years old or so. He told his mother, "One of these days I’m going to be big and strong. I’m going to be a football player and a boxer. I’m going to buy you a beautiful house and pretty dresses." She didn’t laugh at him or mock him. She didn’t doubt him. She instead spoke to him of values and told him that the way to get there was to work hard, save his money and get after it. That’s what Mr. T did. It was those values, not the Hollywood fame, not the gold chains, not the "I pity the fool" line — it was those values that were the engine of his life. NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD That’s the part that I want my kids to hear. Not the mohawk or the tough scowl. I tell them that Mr. T was once just a child like them, born into a bad ZIP code. But he was a dreamer who had family around him and who never walked down the wrong path or went to jail because he could not bear to break his mother’s heart. That’s how love can save a child. And I tell them how Mr. T started at the bottom. He didn’t look for shortcuts or get-rich-quick schemes. He believed in himself, and he created his own opportunities. He used sports to discipline himself, he served his country, and he worked as a janitor, gym teacher and a doorman before anyone called him a "star." He stayed true to himself and made himself so unique that people just wanted to be around him. He was one of a kind and, most of all, he was real, and that’s why the world gravitated toward him. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION We spend far too much time telling the young kids on the South Side that the system or the Man is out to get them. We talk about systemic racism without going anywhere. There’s no hope in any of that. That’s why those conversations just peter out and die when we run out of doom and gloom. And what good does it do to poison a young child’s mind with all that negativity? That’s why I’d rather talk about South Side heroes like Mr. T. His life gives us the simple but brutally honest lesson: Your circumstances are real, and they may be unfair and stacked against you, but they are not your destiny. You are. Your faith, your work, your respect and the dream that you have for yourself — that is your destiny. You have to do the hardest thing in the world, which is to believe in yourself. If you do, you will reach heights you never knew were possible. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That is the simple truth I tell my kids every day. I even tell that to myself. I know I speak of opportunity all the time, but it is not a political talking point for me. It is the lifesaver. It is the boy who decides that he will buy his mother a house. It is the young man who decides that his circumstances will not define him. It is the man who decides his fate. I pity the fool who looks at Mr. T’s life and still tells our kids they cannot rise. And, yes, Mr. T did buy his mother a beautiful mansion, complete with an elevator, in the Lake Forest neighborhood where she used to clean houses. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM PASTOR COREY BROOKS

title: Oil squeeze tightens as Iran-backed attacks cripple Hormuz escape routes
description: A drone attack damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline as Houthi rebels seize strategic islands near Bab el-Mandeb, squeezing oil routes beyond Hormuz.
content: The U.S. is choking off Iran’s oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. But the routes meant to shield other Gulf producers from that disruption are now coming under pressure themselves. A drone attack last week badly damaged Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, a critical bypass that carries crude oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea. Repairs could leave it largely out of service for three to five weeks after it had been moving roughly 2.6 million to 4 million barrels per day in recent weeks. At the same time, Iran-backed Houthi rebels have seized additional territory and strategic islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean — adding pressure to another major shipping route already battered by years of attacks. And those repeated disruptions are already reaching American consumers. NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT U.S. diesel prices hit a record national average of $6.23 a gallon Monday, according to AAA, while regular gasoline averaged $4.32. Brent crude climbed as high as roughly $110 a barrel during the day. Washington has sharply curtailed Iran’s oil exports and trade, but the wider conflict is still disrupting energy supplies elsewhere in the region, especially as Iran-backed Houthi rebels strengthen their stance along the coastline in Yemen. THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE The question now is whether Iran is hurting enough to make the concessions Trump wants — and how much economic damage Tehran and its allies can still inflict while it holds out. The economic pressure on Tehran is mounting. Iran has gone weeks without sending meaningful new crude exports through Hormuz. Since the United States reinstated its naval blockade July 14, no Iranian crude cargoes have successfully crossed the strait to China, Tehran’s largest remaining oil customer, according to Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers.com. Iranian crude and condensate loadings fell to roughly 220,000 to 255,000 barrels per day in August, down from about 740,000 in July and roughly 2 million in March. Commercial shipping through Hormuz also remains deeply disrupted. Recent readings from Kpler, which tracks real-time data on global commodity flows and maritime shipping, have repeatedly put visible commodity-vessel transits in the single digits, even as the U.S. has worked to restore some movement through the waterway. Miad Maleki, a senior fellow with the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the pressure is increasingly reaching beyond Iran’s oil industry and into the broader economy. HORMUZ CRISIS HIDES A DEEPER OIL THREAT THAT COULD OUTLAST THE WAR "There are a series of indications" that the pressure is working, Maleki told Fox News Digital, citing the combined effect of sanctions, the naval blockade and growing diplomatic isolation. Iran depends heavily on trade through the United Arab Emirates and Turkey, Maleki said, and restrictions on those channels are making it harder to obtain foreign currency and essential imports. Gasoline could become an especially difficult pressure point. Iran remains one of the world’s major crude producers but lacks sufficient refining capacity to meet its own demand, leaving it dependent on imports that have become more difficult to secure. The regime can cushion some of the financial blow by continuing to print currency and pay salaries, Maleki said, allowing inflation to absorb part of the pressure rather than immediately cutting government payrolls. Physical shortages are harder to solve. But that does not necessarily mean Tehran has deliberately substituted the Bab el-Mandeb for Hormuz as a new source of leverage. Iran expert Arash Azizi said Tehran has already been forced to recognize that its ability to dominate the Strait of Hormuz is weaker than it once claimed. "Iran has realized that some of the leverage it has over the threat of Hormuz is gone," Azizi told Fox News Digital. "[Iran] is not able to close it effectively and is desperately trying to find a way to better its odds," he said. Azizi cautioned, however, against treating every Houthi move as part of a coordinated Iranian strategy to transfer pressure from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea. "Iran has limited control, and the Houthi-Saudi conflict has a dynamics of its own," he said. IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS Iran encourages and materially supports the Houthis, Azizi said, but does not exercise full operational control over the group. That distinction matters as the Houthis strengthen their position around Bab el-Mandeb. Their capture of Mayun Island, the port of Mokha and, most recently, the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands has expanded their reach around one of the world’s most important shipping corridors. Yet the group has continued to allow many vessels to pass rather than attempting a total closure of the strait. Azizi described the instability there as a "double-edged sword" for Tehran. Pressure on shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure can raise costs for Iran’s adversaries and increase anxiety in global oil markets. But a broader regional conflict can also make it harder for Tehran to achieve what Azizi described as its overriding objective: ending the war, preserving the Islamic Republic and beginning reconstruction. For Tehran, he said, the immediate goal is therefore less about opening a new front than improving the terms on which it can end the current one. Iran wants "some sort of a deal that puts an end to the war," preserves the Islamic Republic and allows it to begin postwar reconstruction, Azizi said. That shifts the central question back to Washington. The Trump administration has demonstrated that it can inflict severe economic pressure on Iran. What remains unclear is whether additional pressure produces the concessions Washington wants — and whether the costs Iran and its regional allies can still impose improve Tehran’s bargaining position or deepen its isolation. Azizi believes Tehran may already be prepared to move. "I think Iran is ready to make concessions," he said. "The question is, what concessions the United States would find acceptable?" He said Iran’s negotiating position has already softened from earlier in the conflict, when Tehran claimed sweeping authority over traffic through Hormuz. The regime’s principal red line now, he argued, is its own survival. Some Iranian officials may still believe continued pressure on energy markets and the U.S. economy could improve Tehran’s hand, particularly ahead of the midterm elections, Azizi said. But the imbalance in economic pain remains stark. "We are not hurting. Our daily life is not affected in a crazy manner by this war," he said of Americans. "Iran is hurting a lot more than the United States." "Iran is selling no oil," Azizi added. Azizi said the blockade, more than the administration’s latest sanctions package alone, has fundamentally worsened Iran’s outlook by restricting trade while leaving businesses with little idea when normal commercial activity might resume. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Maleki similarly said the regime can absorb inflation and financial losses for some time without immediately buckling. The more difficult test comes when financial pressure becomes physical scarcity. That makes the next phase of the U.S. campaign less about proving that Iran is hurting than determining whether Washington can turn that pain into an acceptable deal before Tehran or its regional allies find new ways to raise the cost of holding out. "They can keep printing rial," Maleki said. "But they can’t print gasoline."
